en: May the chest of the couch, possessing the luster of a cluster of *atasī* flowers through its beauty, pierce the vital spot of the eye of the mountain of collyrium.

For the sake of completing the work he intends to begin without obstacles and for the sake of its successful propagation, he seeks refuge in his own teacher, the Lord of Hastigiri—who is the very form of his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā)—known by the names Varadarāja and Praṇatārtihara; he does so because [the Lord] is the bestower of the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha), characterized by the attainment of the desired and the removal of the undesired, and is therefore a worthy refuge. By the term "Lord of the Elephant-Mountain" (dviradādrīśa), his accessibility (saulabhya) is expressed.
In ancient times, the eternal Viṣṇu was worshipped there by the Diṅnāgas; consequently, that great mountain became renowned by the name Hastigiri.

Thus, from the statement in the Purāṇa, it is understood that he was worthy of worship even by the elephants (diṅnāga) and other animals there. By the two words "Śrīnidhi" (Treasury of Fortune) and "Karuṇānidhi" (Treasury of Compassion), his power and compassion—qualities essential for being a refuge—are expressed. For one who is a treasury of fortune, there is no object among things to be given that is difficult to obtain; thus, there is no incapacity caused by a lack of material resources in the bestowing of desired objects.

"Indeed, that daughter of Janaka is immeasurable splendor"—by this, since the Lord of Fortune (Śrīnidhi) is a treasury of immeasurable splendor, even when removing what is undesirable, there can be no incapacity characterized by a lack of luster. By the word *hari*, the meaning "He who removes the misfortune of those who have taken refuge in Him" is established. Having thus prostrated before the Supreme Deity, he also prostrates before the deity named Sadarśana—who bestows upon him the qualities such as knowledge and power necessary for the composition of this work—with the words "outside."

"To him who had augmented the Vedas and explained the Vedas"—the meaning is that he pacified (*aśīśamat*) the agitation arising from the misinterpretation of the meaning, according to the maxim: "The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'This man will lead me astray. This form is derived from the root *śam* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), in the active voice (*kartari*), in the aorist (*luṅ*), with the reduplication (*caṅ*).

Just as a yogi dispels the fever of others through the power of his own capacity, so too it is indicated that he likewise pacified the internal fever of the Vedas and other scriptures through the power of his own capacity. "I take refuge in the one whose form is the *praṇava*"—the meaning is that he stands like the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable Om) and like the stage (*raṅga*). With the latter half [of the verse], he establishes the similarity between the commentary and both the stage and the *praṇava*, which was previously set forth by the word "parasya" (of the Supreme).

"The meaning of the letter *a* is Viṣṇu, the author of the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe; the meaning of the letter *m* is the individual soul (*jīva*), which is indeed subordinate to Him.

The letter *u* restricts the relationship between these two as being fit for nothing else. The *praṇava*, the essence of the three Vedas and consisting of three parts, has thus indicated this meaning."

According to the manner stated above, the *praṇava* reveals its status as a subordinate (*śeṣitva*). It is quite clear that the *bhāṣya* reveals its status as the supreme subordinate. Furthermore, Śrīraṅga also reveals its status as a subordinate by revealing its state of lying upon the Supreme Brahman as His couch. Although Śrīraṅga reveals a subordinate status characterized by lying upon the couch;

However, in the case of the *bhāṣya* and the *praṇava*, their status as the principal (*śeṣitva*)—characterized by ownership—is what they reveal; thus, there is no single common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*). Nevertheless, as in the example, "This city has now become like the orb of the moon, filled with all its notes," the attainment of a single common attribute occurs through *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) alone, specifically that form which is based on the identification of difference with non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*) upon the foundation of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).

Regarding the phrase "in the Vedāntas": although there is no difference in the connection with the Vedānta and so forth for both hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), the designation of the Vedānta as the primary means applies to hearing (*śravaṇa*) because it is the means of comprehension by way of being the expounder of the Vedānta; whereas the designation of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) applies to reflection (*manana*). As it is said: "One should hear from the Vedic statements and reflect through logical arguments. That which has been seen is that which has been made the object of clear meditation (*dhyāna*). However, in our own system, there is no distinction between meditation (*dhyāna*) and seeing (*darśana*).

They also say: "That which is the fruit of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*) within the theater (*raṅga-dhāman*) of the heart-lotus. Here, by comparing the lotus-heart-theater to the interior of the Vedas, the Bhāṣya is revealed as the locus for the manifestation of the Blessed Lord. [The text says] "the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). The means of knowledge is the Veda; the object of knowledge is the meaning propounded therein. Now, for the sake of what is intended to be accomplished, he expresses his hope for an understanding of the purport of the subject to be explained, saying: "unelaborated" (*avistṛtāḥ*)—referring to the words (*giraḥ*).

The general mention is for the purpose of including lamps and so forth; for this very reason, the commentary is explained with a single voice regarding everything pertaining to words, sentences, and compositions—firm, such that it cannot be set aside by fallacious reasoning.

Having thus performed the auspicious rites, he pledges his intention to compose [the work] with the words "In Śrīraṅga," etc. By the first epithet, his own excellence of intellect is shown, and by the second, his preeminence in goodness (*sattva*) for the sake of attaining [his goal]. "He urged" (*acūcudat*); the word "in the *Śrutaprakāśikā*" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Here, it is pledged that "the *Bhāṣya* shall be explained by me. In this regard, due to a specific arrangement [of the text], his engagement is motivated solely by the desire for service to the Lord (*bhagavat-kaiṅkarya*).

However, it is implied that this is not for the sake of displaying one's own scholarship. Now, even if the composition of the treatise were for the sake of pleasing him, it is meaningful solely for the purpose of communicating to others, according to the statement, "enlightening one another. Anticipating the objection, "The disciples already know [this] themselves; why do you exert yourself?", he says, "from the gurus. This serves as a rebuttal to the present objection, namely that [the work is] for the sake of ease.

Furthermore, if error were possible due to the absence of a continuous tradition (*saṃpradāya*), how could there be benefit for others? To this he says: "From the teachers" (*gurubhyaḥ*). Even so, since another interpretation might be possible in the composition of words, the possibility of error remains; therefore he says: "by those employed by him" (*tatprayuktaiḥ*). If that is so, for what purpose is their effort? To this he says: "having compiled" (*saṅkalayya*). The intention is that we have performed a compilation of exactly as much as was required from among the matters set forth by Varadaguru.

Furthermore, fearing that his own work might be considered unworthy of acceptance because it does not provide a complete exposition, he says "Who [is there]? (kaḥ). The meaning is that this objection applies equally to the *Nyāyasudarśana* and other such works. Moreover, he addresses the objection: "What is the use of these previously composed works? What is the point of your effort, which grasps only a few points? by saying "Of the portions heard" (*śrutāṃśa*). Even for those most proficient in the *Bhāṣya*, such as the authors of the *Sudarśanavivaraṇa* and others who understand the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*, this work, the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, must not be neglected.

However, it is to be accepted. For what purpose? For the sake of those portions of the meaning of the Bhāṣya—concerning the meanings heard by me from my teacher and expounded in the *Śrutaprakāśikā*—which were not mentioned in the *Sudarśana* and other such works.

For the sake of stability. Here is the illustration: "by the venerable ones" (*āḍhair*). In accordance with such authorities as, "In the Veda and in its deity," and "He who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and for the Guru as for the Lord," the comprehension of the meaning of the Commentary is obtainable through the grace of the Lord—the subject matter of that Commentary—as well as through the grace of the author of the Commentary or the one he propounds, who knows the entire meaning of the Commentary. Through a statement in the form of, "This is the meaning of this sentence," the meaning of the Commentary becomes easily understood.

Anticipating the objection that [the verb] might refer to the future, he says, "If he explained the commentary," and so forth. Now, one might object: since the rule "The *liṅ* is used for the cause and its effect" (*hetuhetumator liṅ*) restricts the *liṅ* to the future tense, let us grant that the *liṅ* does not apply here. But let us also grant that the *lṛṅ* does not apply either, because the rule "The *lṛṅ* is used when there is a reason for the *liṅ* and there is a failure of action" (*liṅnimitte lṛṅ kriyātipattau*) also refers to the future. Why then does the *lṛṅ* prescribed by the rule "The *lṛṅ* is used in the past tense when there is a reason for the *liṅ* and there is a failure of action" (*bhūte ca*) not occur? To this, they reply: [The answer is: It is because the word *vyavṛṇot* (he explained) is intended to express a present action (*vartamānakāla*). For the rule "The *lṛṅ* is used in the past tense... applies only when the action denoted by the verb is understood as having occurred in the past. However, in the present case, the action of explaining the commentary is understood as being in the present. Therefore, the *lṛṅ* does not occur. Furthermore, the *lṛṅ* is not applied because the condition for its application—the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*)—is absent; for the action of explaining the commentary did indeed take place. Thus, the *lṛṅ* is excluded both because the action is perceived as present and because the condition of "failure of action" is not met. Consequently, the *liṅ* alone remains applicable. And since the *liṅ* is used in the sense of the past tense according to the rule "The *liṅ* is used in the sense of the past tense when there is a reason for the *liṅ* and there is a failure of action," the form *vyavṛṇot* is established as expressing the past. Thus, the meaning is: "If he had explained the commentary, then the doubt would have arisen. Since he did not explain it, the doubt did not arise. This is the intended sense. Alternatively, the *liṅ* may be taken in the sense of the present tense, as in the examples "He should eat if he were to give" (*dadāti ced bhuñjīta*) or "He should go if he were to speak" (*bravīti ced gacchet*). In such cases, the *liṅ* expresses a present potentiality. Here too, the *liṅ* is used in the sense of the present, meaning: "If he were to explain the commentary, then the doubt would arise. Since he does not explain it, the doubt does not arise. This is the intended meaning. Or again, the *liṅ* may be used in the sense of the past tense, as in "He should have eaten if he had given" (*dadyāccedbhuñjīta*) or "He should have gone if he had spoken" (*brūyāccedgacchet*). In these cases, the *liṅ* expresses a past potentiality. Here too, the *liṅ* is used in the sense of the past, meaning: "If he had explained the commentary, then the doubt would have arisen. Since he did not explain it, the doubt did not arise. This is the intended sense. Thus, the *liṅ* is employed in all three tenses—present, past, and future—according to the specific requirements of the context. Therefore, there is no fault in the use of the *liṅ*. This is the conclusion. Thus ends the section on the *liṅ*. Now begins the section on the *lṛṅ*. As for the *lṛṅ*, it is used when there is a reason for the *liṅ* and there is a failure of action (*kriyātipatti*). What is meant by "failure of action"? It means the non-occurrence of the action. When there is a reason for the *liṅ* and the action fails to occur, the *lṛṅ* is used. For example: "If he had given, he would have eaten" (*dadyāccedbhuñjīta*). Here, the giving is the cause and the eating is the effect. If the giving had occurred, the eating would have followed. But since the giving did not occur, the eating failed to occur. Therefore, the *lṛṅ* is used. Similarly: "If he had spoken, he would have gone" (*brūyāccedgacchet*). Here, speaking is the cause and going is the effect. If speaking had occurred, going would have followed. But since speaking did not occur, going failed to occur. Therefore, the *lṛṅ* is used. Likewise: "If he had explained the commentary, then the doubt would have arisen" (*yadi vyākhyāsyaccet saṃśayo 'bhaviṣyat*). Here, the explanation of the commentary is the cause and the arising of the doubt is the effect. If the explanation had occurred, the doubt would have arisen. But since the explanation did not occur, the doubt did not arise. Therefore, the *lṛṅ* is used. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the *lṛṅ*. Now begins the section on the *luṅ*. As for the *luṅ*, it is used when there is a reason for the *liṅ* and there is a failure of action, and the action is understood as having occurred in the past. For example: "If he had given, he would have eaten" (*dadyāccedbhuñjīta*). Here, the giving is the cause and the eating is the effect. If the giving had occurred in the past, the eating would have followed. But since the giving did not occur, the eating failed to occur. Therefore, the *luṅ* is used. Similarly: "If he had spoken, he would have gone" (*brūyāccedgacchet*). Here, speaking is the cause and going is the effect. If speaking had occurred in the past, going would have followed. But since speaking did not occur, going failed to occur. Therefore, the *luṅ* is used. Likewise: "If he had explained the commentary, then the doubt would have arisen" (*yadi vyākhyāsyaccet saṃśayo 'bhaviṣyat*). Here, the explanation of the commentary is the cause and the arising of the doubt is the effect. If the explanation had occurred in the past, the doubt would have arisen. But since the explanation did not occur, the doubt did not arise. Therefore, the *luṅ* is used. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the *luṅ*. Now begins the section on the *lṛṭ*. As for the *lṛṭ*, it is used when there is a reason for the *liṅ* and there is a failure of action, and the action is understood as being in the future. For example: "If he were to give, he would eat" (*dadyāccedbhuñjīta*). Here, the giving is the cause and the eating is the effect. If the giving were to occur in the future, the eating would follow. But since the giving is not expected to occur, the eating is not expected to occur. Therefore, the *lṛṭ* is used. Similarly: "If he were to speak, he would go" (*brūyāccedgacchet*). Here, speaking is the cause and going is the effect. If speaking were to occur in the future, going would follow. But since speaking is not expected to occur, going is not expected to occur. Therefore, the *lṛṭ* is used. Likewise: "If he were to explain the commentary, then the doubt would arise" (*yadi vyākhyāsyaccet saṃśayo bhaviṣyati*). Here, the explanation of the commentary is the cause and the arising of the doubt is the effect. If the explanation were to occur in the future, the doubt would arise. But since the explanation is not expected to occur, the doubt is not expected to arise. Therefore, the *lṛṭ* is used. This is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the *lṛṭ*. Now begins the section on the *lṛṭ* with the suffix *tumun*. As for the *lṛṭ*

The conditional suffix *lṛṅ* does not occur either because the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*), though present, is not intended to be expressed, or because the causal relationship (*hetuhetumadbhāva*), though present, is not intended to be expressed. Instances where something existent is not intended to be expressed are observed, such as in the phrase "the girl is thin-waisted" (*anudarā kanyā*). Some, however, explain that in the statement "instability [arises] from profundity" (*gāmbhīryādanavasthitiḥ*), since the state of instability is described as having profundity as its cause, the act of describing it is not itself the cause.

Some raise the objection: "Since the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself has already explained the *Bhāṣya*, why do you exert yourself [in writing this commentary]? To ward off this objection, he restates the point, beginning with the words "bhāṣyañcet" (if it is the *Bhāṣya*). Here, the word "cet" does not mean "if," but rather expresses something that is certain as if it were doubtful, as in the expression "vedāścet" (if they are the Vedas). The meaning is: "If this is indeed the *Bhāṣya*, then he has certainly explained it himself; for the *Bhāṣya-bhāṣya* (the commentary on the *Bhāṣya*) is itself his own explanation."

For they define the characteristics of a *bhāṣya* thus: "Its own words are explained. [The author] refutes this with the word "vyākhyāna" (explanation). That being so, the particle "api" (even/also) must be supplied here. The meaning is that even so, because of the profundity of the words of the explanations contained within the *bhāṣya*, there is no finality—that is, it is impossible to attain a definitive conclusion regarding their intended meaning (*tātparya*). By what [is this like]? (Otherwise, as Kaiyaṭa suggests? the implication is that it would result in the non-commencement of the *vārttikas* and other such works. He establishes this lack of finality with the words beginning "mitamati" (one of limited intellect), and so forth.

"Is it not the case that, according to the logic of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed Lord himself in the form of an image (*arcārūpī*) is to be approached by those desiring full comprehension of the Commentary? What need is there for you? To this he says, "He is to be questioned. How is the Lord in the form of an image to be questioned? Why? To this he says, "For he... For that Lord, in the form of Nārāyaṇa and so forth, is not directly perceptible (*pratyakṣarūpa*) to us of the present day.

They explain that the meaning is: "Because [He] currently exists in the form of an image (arcā), He is not our instructor, unlike Nārada and others. Thus, beginning with the words "By the command of the Lord of Śrīraṅga," this is the formal declaration of the commencement of the *Śrutaprakāśikā*. Its subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the *Bhāṣya*; its purpose (*prayojana*) is to present the knowledge of its meaning by way of summary; and that purpose is neither established otherwise by previous commentaries nor tainted by defects such as error or negligence. Furthermore, those who seek that meaning are the qualified candidates (*adhikārin*). In this manner, the four preliminary conditions (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*) conducive to the engagement of discerning persons in his own work have been demonstrated.

He states the reason for the Blessed Commentator’s desire to explain the *Śārīraka-śāstra* among the eighteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) with the words beginning "of all," and so forth. He says "of those whose determination of objects of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition" because the Vedas would be disregarded by liberated beings who are capable of the direct realization of the Blessed One through their own nature alone, as they seek only the supramundane human goals. He says "desiring to acquire" because the Vedas would be disregarded by one who is deluded.

The meaning is: [the objects] that are desired or wished to be abandoned among worldly things, as well as the desirable and undesirable means for attaining them. He states the reason why the Veda differs from the scriptures of the Sāṃkhya and others—despite the lack of distinction in their capacity to convey supermundane human goals and their means—in the phrase "even there, not dependent on a person" (*tatrāpyapuruṣa*). With the words beginning with "and there" (*tatra ca*), he dispels the doubt as to why he would not wish to explain the first part [of the Veda]. The construction is: "having understood the first part, which is concerned with proximate fruits and their means. This means: having understood it without doubt.

"In the eastern part" means "unsubmerged. Here, by the qualification "modern," it is implied that just as there would be a loss of great fruit if the meaning propounded in the portion of the Vedānta were corrupted, so too [would it be] in that specific part.

It is also indicated that [the work] does not exist; the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that it was intended to be explained with the desire to revive it. The syntactical connection is that [the author] acted to remove thorns [from the path] and to fulfill the purpose of those tormented by the fear of worldly existence (*bhava*). Therefore, they say there is no tautology between "the desire to revive" (*ujjijīvayiṣā*) and "to fulfill the purpose" (*kṛtārthayitum*). However, some maintain that the "desire to revive" connects with the phrase "composed by former teachers skilled in discerning the real from the unreal," and thus they attribute the desire to revive to the former teachers themselves.

Others, however, state that there is a distinction between *ujjīvana* (reviving) and *kṛtārthīkaraṇa* (rendering purposeful) by way of the relationship between the means and the end (*dvāra-dvāribhāva*). Regarding the phrase "the practice of a wrong path" (*kupathapravṛtti*): a "wrong path" (*kupatha*) is a contemptible path (*kutsitaḥ pathaḥ*). The compound is formed with the word *patha*, not with the word *pathin*. Consequently, the form *kāpathya* does not occur here [as one might expect from *pathin*]. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa*: "The words *patha*, *panthā*, and *mārga* mean 'way'"; thus, there is an *akārānta* (ending in -a) form of the word *patha* which has the same meaning as *pathin*.

He states the reason for the disregard of the commentaries on the *Śārīraka* composed by Śaṅkara and others with the words "composed by the supreme seer" (*paramarṣipraṇītāni*). Because of the constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, the word "which" (*yāni*) is to be supplied here. The meaning is: if there exist commentaries upon those scriptures composed by the supreme seer that were themselves composed by great seers; the term "to be commented upon" (*vyākhyeyāni*) indicates that their meaning is profound. Regarding the phrase "disregarding those [original works], there are other things to be commented upon," the mention of "other things to be commented upon" is for the sake of providing an illustration.

The meaning is that just as other commentaries contradicting the *Śārīraka* [Brahmasūtra] lack authoritative status, so too do the commentaries composed by Śaṅkara and others, which contradict the commentary of Bodhāyana, lack authoritative status. Alternatively, in the phrase "and those composed by the great sages (*maharṣi*)," the word "and" (*ca*) is displaced; the sense is that if there exist both the texts to be commented upon, composed by the supreme sages (*paramarṣi*), and commentaries upon them composed by great sages, then those alone are the texts to be commented upon and those alone are the commentaries to be followed.

"Because there is no sublation [of the meaning]"—in the commentary on the sūtra *sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt*, the description of an alternative interpretation was provided in accordance with the views of others, as the author of the Vṛtti himself will immediately thereafter describe the meaning stated by him. Therefore, there is no contradiction between them. The point is that the matters of the earlier portion [of the Vedas] are to be studied, as in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa* and other such sections.
This concludes the consideration of the meaning of the verse beginning with *akhila*.

"Auspiciousness consisting of the worship of one's chosen deity" means that auspiciousness takes the form of a prayer for worship. For this very reason, he will later state: "The mention of the subject matter and the benediction beginning with 'may it be' have both been performed. Some, however, consider even the prayer for devotion to be a form of devotion itself. Alternatively, it should be understood that this was stated because, having perceived that worship is inherently favorable, it is possible for it to be performed by one who prays for it. [This concludes the section on] "those endowed with the practice of auspicious conduct."

Furthermore, this statement does not indicate that auspicious practices such as looking into a mirror are causes for the cessation of misfortune by virtue of being equivalent to recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), and so forth; nor is it an authority for the necessity of performing auspicious rites at the time of commencement. Therefore, one should not say that they rely solely on custom (*ācāra*) as the authority for the performance of auspicious rites. This is because the word "misfortune" (*vinipāta*) also includes obstacles (*vighna*) that hinder completion, and since the performance of auspicious rites is understood to ward off such obstacles, it is possible for [the aforementioned statement] to possess authoritative validity.

"According to the *Codanāsūtra*": this means that just as in the sūtra "Dharma is a matter characterized by injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*), when the nature of Dharma has been stated—that whatever is characterized by injunction is Dharma—it follows by implication that injunction alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus is the sense. Because the understanding of being bowed down is attained, prostration (*praṇati*) is also realized; the meaning is that prostration is thereby performed. But one might ask: how can it be determined that prostration has been performed merely by the mention of "being bowed" (*vinata*)?

If that were the case, one might object: "By the mere statement that 'the Blessed One bestows liberation upon lay devotees (upāsakas),' it would follow that all who utter those words have themselves performed the required worship, and thus liberation would accrue to them as well. If this is raised, we reply: there is no contradiction. For when the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakṛt), having understood that prostration—which is extremely easy to perform—is a means for achieving the desired goal in the form of protection and initiation (rakṣādīkṣā), teaches it to others, he may say that he too has performed it. This is because the verbal root *ṇamu* signifies "bowing down" (*prahvatve*). Thus, there is no inconsistency.

Now, having introduced the fact that the words *bhakti* and *vinata* convey the state of being bowed (*prahvībhāva*), it is inconsistent to introduce the word *namaḥ* as a means of conveying that same state without first providing a justification for the word *bhakti* itself conveying such a state. Nor can it be argued that no justification is provided for the word *bhakti* because its capacity to convey the state of being bowed is self-evident and independent of further proof.

If it is argued that, on the contrary, since the word *bhakti* itself is not well-known to mean "the state of being bowed" (*prahvībhāva*), its mention is more appropriate precisely because it requires a supporting justification—then this is not so; one must necessarily maintain the identity of meaning between the words *bhakti* and *vinata*. Otherwise, having proposed "bowing" (*vinati*) as the cause of protection, what connection would there be between that and a *bhakti* distinct from it when [the latter] is being requested?

Therefore, since the words *bhakti* (devotion) and *vinata* (bowed) have the same meaning, by explaining the sense of the word *vinata* occurring in the initial context—according to the traditional grammatical rule (*smṛti*) that "the root *ṇamu* [is used] in the sense of bowing" (*ṇamu prahvatve*)—the meaning of the word *bhākta* is also explained. For instance, in the passage from the *Śrīmadrāmāyaṇa*: "For he is known to be a knower of dharma and affectionate toward those who seek refuge; let there be friendship with him for you, if you wish to live," the fact that friendship consists in seeking refuge is established. With this in mind, it was stated that the verbal root is indeed "ṇamu prahvatve."

Nor should it be argued that if the root *nam* has the sense of "bowing down" (*prahvībhāva*), the word *vinata* could not refer to those established in the specific forms of knowledge called *nyāsa* and *upāsanā*; for, by virtue of the prefix (*upa*), it is possible for it to denote a bowing down characterized by a specific type of knowledge, and thus its capacity to signify a particular form of knowledge is possible.

Regarding the phrase "in the form of the object and the subject": the *viṣaya* (object) is Brahman; the *viṣayiṇī* (subject) pertains to the fruit of meditation. Nor should it be asked: "Even if meditation, which is expounded in the third chapter, is the subject, how can the fruit, which is expounded in the fourth chapter, be the subject? For there is no fault, since liberation, which constitutes the fruit, can be included as a subject because it consists of the experience of the Lord (*bhagavad-anubhava*). Regarding the term *bhuvana*: that which exists (*bhavati*) is a world (*bhuvana*).

Although the word *bhuvana* is derived in the Vedic language (*chandas*) by the rule “*bhū sū dhū bhṛs jibhyaśchandasi*” as ending in the suffix *kyun*, nevertheless, there is no fault because grammarians state that due to the traditional rule of “*bahulam*” (in various ways), it also has application in the common language (*bhāṣā*), as seen in the rule “*vā bhuvanam*. Thus, through its conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*), it excludes [the application to] potters and the like. Although the etymological derivation (*yoga*) would be over-extensive, the intention is that this is excluded by the conventional meaning.

Even if one accepts the conventional meaning [of the word *bhuvana*], the exclusion of potters and the like is established by the word *akhila* (entire) alone, because they lack the status of being the cause of all effects. Furthermore, the exclusion is also established by the word *līlā* (sport), since the activity of producing a jar—which is a form of effort—does not constitute the "sport" of a potter. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the statement was made with the intention of showing that even the word *bhuvana* alone, independent of the other words, establishes the exclusion of potters and others. [The phrase] "born from eggs" (*aṇḍajāni*)...

The meaning is that the worlds contained within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) are being observed; it does not mean "collections of eggs. This is because it is not well-known for the word *bhuvana* (world) to denote an egg. Furthermore, since the Brahman lacks even the scent of producing an egg, there would be the undesirable consequence that "completeness" (*sākalya*) need not even be intended in order to exclude that [Brahman]. Some, however, interpret it as "those born from eggs," meaning collections of eggs; for these too, being specific types of vast effects, can possibly be denoted by the word *bhuvana*.

Nor should it be said that the exclusion of Brahmā from [the category of creators] is established by his very nature as a non-producer of cosmic eggs (*aṇḍa*); for, in the absence of the word "akhila" (entire), since the quality of being the producer of some particular world—such as the earth-world and so forth—is possible even for the four-faced one (Brahmā), the word "akhila" possesses meaning insofar as it serves to exclude him. Thus, purity and impurity depend upon the nature of what is being negated.

Now, one might object: "If, in this case, the negation of the deficiency of the world is auspicious because that deficiency itself is inauspicious, then in the phrase 'the adversary of all that is to be abandoned' (*akhilaheyapratyanīka*), the word 'all' (*akhila*)—which occurs at the beginning of the statement regarding taking refuge in the Lord and expresses the negation of the deficiency of what is to be abandoned—would not be auspicious, since the deficiency being negated would itself be auspicious. To this we reply: No, for even there, in the phrase 'the adversary of all that is to be abandoned,' by the word 'adversary' (*pratyanīka*), which denotes that which causes cessation, [the deficiency is negated].

For it is the state of being an object of the operation of the activity of cessation that is negated when residing in the *heya* (that which is to be abandoned); and since the state of being an object of the operation of the activity of cessation residing in the *heya* is indeed inauspicious, its negation is itself auspicious. Thus, the distinction between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is also intended.

Since the word *akhila* is a synonym for the word *sarva*, and since the quality of being "all" (*sarvatva*) resides only in a plurality [of things], the distinction between the worlds is established by the principle that "there is a difference in ritual action due to number, because [the term] is applied to distinct entities. Furthermore, because plurality inherently contains differentiation, the distinction between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is also established, as the word *bhuvana* (world) denotes a vast and specific effect consisting of a combination of both consciousness and matter. Nor should it be argued that the word *sarva* does not depend upon plurality; [for it does].

Regarding the statement "The Viśvajit has all the *pṛṣṭhas*," it is not possible for the term *sarvapṛṣṭha* to be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the *pṛṣṭha* chants obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) from the Jyotiṣṭoma, because in the Jyotiṣṭoma there exist only two *pṛṣṭhas*, and thus the word *sarva* (all), which requires a plurality, cannot apply there. Rather, as established in the seventh [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras], it is an injunction of the six-day (*ṣāḍahika*) *pṛṣṭhas*: Bṛhat, Rathantara, Vairūpa, Vairāja, Śākvara, and Raivata. "Stability" (*sthemā*) means "firmness" (*sthiti*); that is to say, it does not mean "longevity."

The intention is as follows: although the suffix *iman* cannot be applied to the word *sthira*—because it is not included in the *pṛthv-ādi* group, and for this very reason it is stated in the commentary on the rule *priyasthira-* that "the suffix *iman* is not cited as an example for the word *sthira* because it is not read in the *pṛthv-ādi* list"—nevertheless, the *iman* suffix is to be understood as being added to the root *sthā* by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bahulavacanāt*), just as in the case of *animan*, *vemana*, and so forth. Furthermore, this word is well-established in the usage of the learned, as seen in such passages as "longer, compact, and possessing stability" (*drāghīyāṃsaḥ saṃhatāḥ sthemabhājaḥ*).

In the phrase "the arising, the manifestation, and the dissolution of the entire world," the word *vibhava* denotes persistence (*sthiti*). Now, it may be objected that the non-inclusion of liberation within the meanings of words such as "destruction" was indeed stated only by taking for granted its separate mention [in the verse].

That [interpretation] is not tenable, because a separate mention of it is not seen in this verse, and because the word *rakṣā* (protection) establishes the bestowal of fruits such as heaven; having raised this doubt, he demonstrates the impropriety of establishing the bestowal of fruits such as heaven as being [separately] signified by the word *rakṣā* with the words beginning with "vinatā" and ending with "iti. Regarding the two views of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*): it should be understood that the view of superimposition belongs to Śaṅkara, while the view of transformation belongs to Yādava and Bhāskara. Regarding the phrase "by its lack of being the primary meaning": [this refers to the fact that the word *rakṣā* does not primarily denote the fruit].

The meaning is as follows: since entry into the interior and so forth are not established if there is no distinction [between the Lord and the individual soul], it is possible for the natural force (*svārasya*) of the scriptural texts regarding entry into the interior and control to be maintained only within one's own system; therefore, in order to establish the distinctness of this system from the positions of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*), the possibility of entry into the interior and control must be stated separately. Regarding the phrase "of that which was explained at length":

the meaning is that this was already explained at length by the author himself elsewhere in the passage, "The play consisting of the creation, maintenance, destruction, entry into the interior, and control of the universe," and that the intention to state it here in brief is thus justified. For "play" (*līlā*) is indeed the activity of the efficient cause (*prayojaka*).

If it is objected: "How can this be so? For we do not observe that the instigation (*preṣaṇā*) consisting of the activity of a king who acts as an independent instigator is itself a play (*līlā*); nor do we observe that the request and so forth, which constitute the activity of a child's father acting as an instigator of the child's play, are themselves plays. On the contrary, we observe that the play belongs only to the child who is the one being prompted (*prayojya*). Therefore, how is this [your definition] possible? [The answer is: No; for the intended meaning is that "that activity is his play, but the activity of another is not."

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the activities of actors, rogues, jesters, and the like—such as their humorous performances—would not constitute "royal play" (*rājalīlā*); for such an objection is undesirable, since in those cases the term "play" (*līlā*) is used figuratively (*aupacārika*), being applied because they produce the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of play.

Nor should it be argued that, because the Blessed Commentator stated in the sūtra, "But as in the world, [His] mere sport (līlā) alone [is the cause]," that the purpose of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe is indeed sport—and thus by stating that creation and so forth have sport as their purpose, he indicated the absence of the nature of sport [in them]—therefore the word "sport" used here in reference to creation and so forth must be merely figurative. For the word "sport" is extensively used to denote a particular kind of activity performed by a person who is self-sufficient and has no other object of affection; and since this applies even to creation, maintenance, and so forth...

This is because the status of being a primary *līlā* (sportive play) is accepted by the final Siddhāntin; and because the commentary on the Sūtra, "But like the world, His *līlā* alone [is the cause]," will also be explained as having the intent that the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe constitute His *līlā*. Regarding the phrase "even though the destruction (*bhaṅga*) is logically a *līlā*": one should not object that since destruction is of the nature of annihilation (*nāśa*), and since annihilation—like creation, maintenance, and so forth—is equally a property residing in the object to be acted upon (*prayojya*), how can it be accepted as a *līlā* through this partial dismemberment? This is not to be said.

Because there is no usage such as "the jar breaks" (ghaṭo bhanakti) in the same way that one says "the jar perishes" (ghaṭo vinaśyati), the two are distinct. For this very reason, just as one says "the jar is born" (ghaṭo jāyate) or "the jar exists" (ghaṭastiṣṭhati), there is no such usage as "the jar breaks. Thus, the distinction is that birth and persistence are the operations whose agent is the jar, whereas destruction is not an operation of it. By stating that [Brahman] is *līlā* (sport), its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is established.

The sense is that by describing the creation and maintenance of the world as the *līlā* (sport) of the Supreme Self, and by stating that these are activities inherent (*samaveta*) in the Supreme Self, it follows that the Supreme Self alone is the material cause (*upādāna*), since He possesses the states that are to come into being.

Now, one might object: "If the word *bhūta* signifies those things whose existence has already been attained, then what kind of 'protection'—which is to be accomplished by the Supreme Self—can there be for those things that have already attained their own nature? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "and of those whose essential nature has been attained. Now, [one might further object]: "But..."

If it is asked: "Since for those who have already attained their true nature (*svarūpa*), the Lord's role consists in the non-deviation from that nature—just as He is the Lord for those who have not attained it—and since for those who have not attained their true nature, the Lord's role also consists in the protection that takes the form of attaining that nature, why is it stated separately that 'for those who have attained their true nature, His sole initiation is protection'? The answer is: because in the state of favorability (*ānukūlya-avasthā*), that protection is independent of any other cause; thus, its specific mention there is appropriate. Furthermore, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes mere relationship (*saṃbandha-mātra*).

Now, although the genitive case expresses a general relation, it nevertheless culminates in a specific relation for which there exists a manifestor. For example, the genitive used in the sense of non-distinction in "Devadattasya" (of Devadatta) culminates in specific relations—such as fatherhood, being a limb, or ownership—by virtue of its respective correlates, as in "son," "hand," or "blanket. Indeed, when it is said "the son of Devadatta," people do not understand a son who has someone else as his father and belongs to another master.

Furthermore, when the term *bhūtavrāta* (multitude of elements) is used, the relationship characterized as that between a whole and its parts (*samudāya-samudāyibhāva*) is understood to exist only between two multitudes of elements. Consequently, in the case of the phrase *bhūtābhūtavrāta*, the word *bhūtavrāta* would fail to apply due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*), according to the maxim that "that which is dependent [on another] is incapable [of forming a compound]," just as the word *āgneya* does not apply to the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice. Alternatively, one would have to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the analogy of the "parasol-bearer" (*chatrin*).

In cases such as *rājapariṣat* ("the king’s assembly") and so forth, however, words like *pariṣat* ("assembly") and *senā* ("army"), which denote a collection qualified by its specific members, do not invariably depend upon those members. Just as words like *vana* ("forest") and *ghaṭā* ("multitude")—which denote a collection of trees or elephants respectively—do not depend on their members because the members are already included within the meaning of the word itself; or just as in expressions like *putrīyati* ("he treats as a son") and *jīvatīti* ("he lives"), where the action of desiring or maintaining is already internalized, there is no further requirement for an external object.

Furthermore, in words such as *pariṣad* ("assembly"), there is merely a requirement for an owner, [expressed as] "whose is this assembly? Consequently, in the case of *rājapariṣad* ("the king's assembly"), the king is construed as the owner, meaning "an assembly whose owner is the king. Thus, even in that case, it is simply the ownership of those who are not kings that is excluded.

It should not be argued that this word *vrāta* is synonymous with the word *pariṣad* (assembly) and not with words such as *samūha* (collection), for if that were so, it would be necessary to state exactly that, rendering futile the demonstration that the genitive case signifies mere relation (*saṃbandha*). This is true; however, this word *vrāta* is indeed a synonym for the word *samūha*, as evidenced by the lexicographical entry: "a collection, a mass, a multitude" (*samūhanikaravrāta*). Nevertheless, since its [the genitive's] meaning would otherwise result in being purposeless, the intended specific distinction is established—this is the underlying intent.

Otherwise, since the intended meaning would already be established by the phrase *vinata-vividha-bhūta* alone, the word *vrāta* would yield no additional sense, resulting in the contingency of its redundancy. For this very reason, he will state later: "And thus the employment of the word (or term) *vrāta* would be purposeful. Furthermore, because all commentators have consistently employed the genitive case in the sense of a general relationship in the sūtra *brahma-jijñāsā*, it is established that even those things related to Brahman are objects of inquiry.

In this context, some maintain that the word *vrāta* denotes those who live by irregular occupations and subsist on physical exertion, in accordance with such authorities as "a beast, a human, or a bird. And it is stated in the *Kāśikāvṛtti* on the rule "vrātacphañorastriyām": "'Vrātāḥ' are those of irregular occupation who subsist on physical exertion (*utsedhajīvinaḥ*); 'those who subsist on physical exertion' means those who live by bodily labor."

Since the Smṛti passage beginning with "One may [even] sacrifice oneself" (kāmamātmānam) consists of the Lord's command and has as its object only the transmigrating conscious being, how can the fact that the Lord also intends to carry out the protection of those who have taken refuge be established by this Smṛti? To this, he says: "Such... (īdṛśī).

"And because [the Lord] is easily accessible, He is the cause for being sought as a refuge. Now, one might object: "Even if the status of being the cause of the universe—expounded in the first quarter of the verse beginning with *akhila*—culminates in His transcendence (*paratva*), how can the bestowing of liberation, expounded in the second quarter beginning with *vinata-vividha*, culminate in His accessibility (*saulabhya*)? For accessibility is not established merely by the fact of bestowing a human goal; if it were, then even the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) and the Golden Mountain (*kanakācala*) would result in being accessible. To this, we reply: "Not so."

This is because even the quality of being a giver culminates in accessibility (*saulabhya*). For it has been stated that accessibility is characterized by being approachable and by the granting of liberation (*mokṣa*). The author will state this later in the commentary on the sūtra "Because of the teaching of His attributes within" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.7), where he says: "Compassion, gentleness, affection, and magnanimity are employed for the sake of accessibility. Therefore, there is no inconsistency. The phrase "those who know Him become immortal" means that accessibility is characterized by the granting of liberation.

"He bows with his two arms," and so forth. By means of his "wings"—that is, his actions—the Supreme Self brings heaven and earth into being and bows down completely, becoming fully humble, toward those who have taken refuge in him. The meaning is based on such traditional texts (smṛti) as: "For the Supreme One becomes humble when beholding the humility of others."

Regarding the term *vidīpta* ("blazing"), since its natural sense is understood as excluding mere radiance (*dīptimātra*), and because the meaning "blazing" (*dīptam*)—qualified by the attribute of being "expounded in the first part"—is not naturally perceived [in that way], he says, "Alternatively, 'trifling pleasure,'" and so on. However, some, considering the lack of natural elegance in the second alternative due to the different objects of "radiance" (*dīpti*) and "blazing" (*vidīpti*), prefer the first alternative alone.

And they interpret that statement as follows: even in the earlier portion [of the Veda], Brahman is indeed the subject to be established in its form as fire and so forth, because it is known as such by the Upaniṣadic statement, "That indeed is fire, that is air"; however, in the Vedānta portion, it is "especially illuminated. "Especially" means without the mediation of [other] means. As for the "lack of excellence in the definition of etymological derivation," this refers to the demonstration of etymological derivation in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*).

The establishment of the excellence of the [divine] characteristics is treated in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa*. Regarding the phrase "by means of conventional power" (*ruḍhi-śaktayā*): the meaning is that since the word *Śrīnivāsa* is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) as referring to Nārāyaṇa, and since the statement "the Veda belongs to Śrīnivāsa" reveals that Nārāyaṇa alone possesses the Veda. Regarding the phrase "and the transcendence of the Veda by Him": this refers to the position of those who maintain the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vādin*). For he will state, introducing the word *Śrīnivāsa*: "By this very [statement], those who maintain the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference—who claim that the Veda transcends the Lord—are refuted."

By the term "in the supreme" (*parasmin*), he intends to indicate that through the suggestion of the meaning of the word *para* found in the scripture, "Through the knowledge of Brahman, one attains the Supreme," there occurs a recollection—by means of the recognition of the word *para*—of the exclusion of any other goal of attainment, which is the subject matter of the section beginning, "The [Brahman] is superior to this, on account of the designations of bridge, measure, connection, and distinction," as well as the subject matter of the section beginning, "Not even on account of place does the Supreme have [dual characteristics]," namely, its possession of both sets of characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*). With this intention, he says "in the supreme," and so forth.

It should be understood that, in reality, it is also possible for two meanings to be indicated. This is because it was stated without qualification that [wisdom] is of the nature of devotion (*bhakti*). Nor is the principle of *chāgo vā mantravarṇāt* intended here, as suggested by the preceding statement. Furthermore, since it was previously stated that wisdom is of the nature of devotion and thus knowledge in the form of devotion serves as the means, one might ask: "How is it now being established that constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) in the form of love (*prīti*) is the means? To this, he says: "of such a form" (*evaṃrūpā*).

One should not suspect a contradiction with the *Laghusiddhānta* text, which states: "The meaning is that this very constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*), culminating in the nature of the joy of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-prīti*), is what is denoted by the word 'devotion' (*bhakti*). This is because there is no fault here, as that is a different philosophical position (*matāntara*). Regarding the phrase "by those ending with *rakṣaikadīkṣe parasmin*," the word "iti" (thus) should be supplied after *rakṣaikadīkṣa*.

Therefore, it should be understood that the means (*upāya*) has been stated as being established in the passage ending with "in the other" (*parasmin*), which demonstrates that the "sole initiation of protection" (*rakṣaikadīkṣā*) is indeed the goal (*upeya*). Consequently, one should not raise the objection regarding the redundancy of employing the term "sole initiation of protection. [The phrase] "the Bhāṭṭas and Prābhākaras have been excluded" means that the creation of the world—since the word *bhuvana* denotes a vast and specific effect—is not accepted by those who assert, "the world was never otherwise than it is now.
(The consideration of the meaning of the verse beginning with "O Pārāśarya...")

Now, by the second verse, [the author indicates] the intermediate subject matter of his own work; the meaning is: "the collection of sūtras consisting of the words of Pārāśarya. Regarding the phrase "by means of such things as approaching the Teacher," the word "etcetera" (ādi) intends to include such passages as: "The glance of Viṣṇu, freedom from hatred, being oriented toward Him, and conversation with those of sattvic nature—these six are the causes for attaining the Teacher. This is because [the attainment of the Teacher] is understood to have the Lord’s glance as its cause.

The meaning is that, because the Lord is understood to be the primary benefactor by providing the teacher through His glances and other means of instruction, there is no room for the objection that verses such as "Know that from Him" (*tadviddhi*) do not indicate that [the attainment of the teacher] is caused by the Lord’s glance. As for the verse "He whose supreme devotion is toward the God," devotion (*bhakti*) is indeed a specific kind of affection produced by the sense of being a benefactor; in this context, by placing the devotion to the Lord on the side of the standard of comparison, its superiority is implied.

And that superiority depends upon the greater degree of assistance rendered. Therefore, the sense is that the Blessed One receives a greater degree of assistance than the Teacher (Ācārya). By the word *pārāśarya*, the excellence of his birth [is indicated]. Now, an objection is raised: since the suffix *yañ* is prescribed by the rule "from *Garga* and others, *yañ*" (*Gargādibhyo yañ*) within the section on lineages (*gotra*), how can the suffix *yañ* apply here to a descendant who is not a lineage-founder? It is said in reply: it is due to the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the status of being a lineage-founder, just as in the expression "Rāma, the son of Jamadagni" (*Jāmadagnyo Rāmaḥ*). Furthermore, it is well known that the author of the *Śārīraka-sūtras* is Bādarāyaṇa.
Anticipating the objection as to how that [work] can be said to belong to Pārāśarya, he says: "And it is intended to show that he himself is designated by the name Bādarāyaṇa."

The purport lies in the meaning of the word *vacaḥ* (speech). Although the nectar-nature of speech itself has been well-established, it is indeed easy to state that this applies to the word as well as to its meaning. For instance, the characteristic of being produced through the thorough investigation of the *Upaniṣads*—namely, the quality of being extracted from the midst of the ocean of the milk of the *Upaniṣads*—is equally applicable to the word as it is to the meaning. Furthermore, the quality of reviving the life-force of the self when it has been deprived by the kindling fire of *saṃsāra* is also easily predicated of the word; for just as the meaning is the object of such knowledge, the word is likewise the generator of the knowledge that brings about such revival.

The fact that the meaning has been well-guarded by the ancient masters can also be easily stated in the case of the word itself, by way of avoiding the affliction characterized by its being perceived otherwise. Furthermore, even in the case of a word, the states of having an unmanifested or manifested meaning are possible, respectively, due to its being situated at a distance or having been brought near.

The meaning is this: although the lack of consistency found in the concluding portion must be tolerated in accordance with the nectar-like words occurring in the opening, nevertheless, because [the qualities] such as being protected and brought [to the earth] pertain to the *meaning* (artha) and thus belong to the word (*śabda*) by way of that meaning, it is more reasonable—according to the maxim of "favoring the majority" (*bhūyonugraha-nyāya*)—that the single word "speech" (*vacas*) occurring in the opening should indicate the meaning, rather than accommodating the many inconsistencies in the concluding portion. This refers to the phrase "of the words 'Veda' and so forth."

Now, one might argue that in expressions such as “one who knows the Veda” (*vedavid*), it is equally easy to claim that the word *veda* lacks reference to its own form by relying on the fact that the word *vid* (to know) inherently refers to knowledge; just as in the passage “He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving” (*yaḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvavit*), the meaning is taken to be “he knows everything in every mode. For in that case, the word *sarva* does not function through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Similarly, when it is said “he knows the Veda,” from the verb *vetti*, one does not perceive a mere cognition of the Veda’s own form; rather, the understood meaning is that he knows it even in the manner of its specific contents—that is, by way of its capacity to convey various particular meanings.

If it is argued that for this very reason it is stated in the Mahābhāṣya on the sūtra *tad adhīte tad veda*—"He who merely recites the Sāman chants is not said to 'know the Veda,'" and "Only one who understands the meaning is said to 'know the Veda'"—this is not so; because in passages such as "O Blessed One, I am indeed a knower of the mantras, but not a knower of the Self," the word *vit* does not intend the comprehension of meaning, as the comprehension of meaning is not observed from the word *vit* in those instances.

Furthermore, if there is disagreement regarding such [examples] as "one who knows the Vedas," then, according to the maxim that "one should not rely on a disputed example," another undisputed example will serve, such as "this person has direct realization of the mantra"; thus there is no fault. For there is no disagreement here concerning the word "mantra" having the sense of the meaning of the mantra.

The statement that "speech is the seed of the [poetic] characteristics" establishes the relationship between the primary meaning of the word *vacas* (speech) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣyamāṇārtha*) of the sentence; for a sentence is indeed that which expresses a meaning. And it is said, "out of fear of the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *sudhā* (nectar). The sense is that one must admit a metaphorical indication in the sense of something resembling nectar. If it is objected that even in the case of the *rūpaka* (metaphor), a metaphorical indication of the word *vacas* in its meaning is equally necessary, we reply: true.

In your view, there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in the word *sudhā*; furthermore, in the compound *vacaḥ-sudhā* ("nectar of speech"), one must also admit *lakṣaṇā* of the word *vacaḥ* in the sense of the genitive case (*vacasaḥ sudhā*). However, in our view, the intention is that there is *lakṣaṇā* in the word *vacaḥ* alone. Now, an objection may be raised: even in the case of a metaphorical compound (*rūpaka-samāsa*) prescribed by the rules "upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ" and "mayūravyaṃsakādayaśca"—which you yourself favor—*lakṣaṇā* in the word *sudhā* remains indistinguishable [from your position], since the word *sudhā* refers to something similar to nectar.

If it is argued: "Since the rule 'the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified' (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*) would otherwise result in being non-mandatory, this present sūtra is commenced for the purpose of establishing a restriction regarding the relationship between qualifier and qualified; because the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the two words *vacaḥ* and *sudhā*, which have distinct meanings, is impossible without resorting to the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of similarity in the word *sudhā*; because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) 'with a word in apposition' (*samānādhikaraṇena*) is accepted as extending until the end of the chapter; and because it will be stated later that by the word *sudhā*, the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) is intended. [Response: This is not so. Even if the relationship of qualifier and qualified were established through the metaphorical indication of similarity, the compound would still be incorrect. Why? Because the word *sudhā* is a feminine noun ending in the vowel *ā*, and according to the rule *pumvat karmadhārayajātīyadeśīyeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.42), it ought to take the masculine form *sudhaḥ* when used in apposition with *vacaḥ*. Furthermore, even if the word *sudhā* were to take the masculine form *sudhaḥ*, the compound would remain incorrect because the gender and number of the first member would not agree with the second member. Therefore, the objection is refuted. Moreover, since the word *sudhā* is a feminine noun ending in *ā*, it cannot be construed as a qualifier for the neuter noun *vacaḥ*. Consequently, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is impossible here. Thus, the objection is rejected. Furthermore, the word *sudhā* is intended here to signify the quality of being a source of delight (*prītihetutva*), and not the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*). True; indeed, there is *lakṣaṇā* (figurative indication) even in our own position. Nevertheless, that [indication] is one taught by the rule: "That which is compared [is compounded] with *vyāghra* and so forth" (*Pāṇini 2.1.56*). However, in the case of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the indication of the word *sudhā* would not be sanctioned by the scriptures (*śāstrīyā*), but rather arbitrary (*aicchikī*). For this very reason, in the *bhakṣa-mantra* "of that drunk by Indra" (*indrapītasya*), although two types of indication exist in the *bahuvrīhi*, the position of the *bahuvrīhi*—which possesses two indications sanctioned by the scriptures—is adopted, while abandoning the *tatpuruṣa* which is joined with two arbitrary indications.

If one adopts the *tatpuruṣa* compound in the sense of "drunk by Indra," there is one figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the first member [of the compound], and likewise a figurative indication in the word *pīta* (drunk) as "that which has drunk" (*pītāvayat*). And the Teacher will state this in the section on "The Internal One, because of the teaching of its attributes" (*antastaddharmopadeśāt*), saying: "As for the usage 'the lotus of the heart,' it is used in its primary sense alone, because it is a compound formed according to the rule 'That which is compared with a tiger, etc. (*upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ*)."

However, some maintain that in the case of *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification), since only a superimposition (*āropa*) characterized by the delimiting property of the capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka-prakāraka*) and which is voluntary (*āhārya*) arises, it possesses primary status (*mukhyatva*) alone. For this very reason, they say that the word *ātman* has primary status in passages such as *annamaya-ātmā*, and that the author’s usage in passages like "If [it is argued] because of connection, it would be so because of the restriction" (*anvayād iti cet syād avadhāraṇāt*) is an instance of the repetition of an action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the rule 'upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ sāmānyāprayoge' (Pāṇini 2.1.56) prescribes composition only when the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) is not employed, and because the common attribute has been well-protected by the ancient masters [as being required], how can there be a compound when the common attribute is indeed employed? Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies that] just as in examples such as *puruṣavyāghro 'bhirūpaḥ* ("a man who is a tiger, handsome"), where there is a compound despite the non-employment of the common attribute in the form of bravery intended by the word *vyāghra*, even though the word *abhirūpa* is employed; so too here, due to the non-employment of the attribute in the form of enjoyability intended by the word *sudhā*.

Intending to show that the compound is logically justified, he says that by the word *sudhā* (nectar), the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) is intended. In the phrase "infinitude, etc.," the word "etc. refers to profundity and so forth. In the phrase "internal, etc.," the word "etc. includes the divine (*adhidaivika*) and the elemental (*ādhibhautika*).

Regarding the phrase "samiti kaivalyavyāvṛttiḥ" (the word *sam* excludes *kaivalya*): if it is argued that, upon examining this sentence, it appears that the Teacher's intention is that even *kaivalya* (isolation) falls within the category of liberation from *saṃsāra*, we say: not so. By stating "the word *sam* excludes *kaivalya*," those who speak thus indicate that *kaivalya* lacks the quality of being a complete cessation of *saṃsāra*, thereby admitting that [in *kaivalya*] there is still a persistence of *saṃsāra*.

Since the Teacher, having first established that the word *prāṇa* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), explains that the cause of *saṃsāra* lies in the non-attainment of the Supreme Self, it follows—given his acceptance of the absence of *saṃsāra* in the state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*)—that by the maxim "when the cause ceases, the effect also ceases," the attainment of the Supreme Self itself must necessarily be admitted as occurring in *kaivalya* due to the absence of *saṃsāra*.

In reality, however, when it is said that [Kaivalya] is "the reviver of those whose life-force has departed," the meaning understood is simply that it is the reviver—that is, the sustainer of the life-force—of those from whom the life-force has departed; for the word *jīvana* signifies the sustaining of life-force. Consequently, the resulting sense is that it is the one which recovers the very life-force that had departed. And thus, the quality of being the recoverer of the life-force in the form of the Supreme Self (paramātman), which had departed, is simply not applicable to Kaivalya.

If it is asked, "How then is the prefix *sam-* said to exclude *kaivalya* (isolation)?"—it is as follows: the word *prāṇa* refers to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), since the word *prāṇa* is used for the individual soul even in the *Bhūmavidyā*. Consequently, when it is said that [the teaching] is the "life-giver" (*jīvanī*) to those whose vital breath (*prāṇa*) has departed through the kindling of the fire of transmigratory existence—that is, those who are devoid of the experience of either the individual soul or the Supreme Self—the prefix *sam-* is employed to exclude *kaivalya*, because even *kaivalya* possesses the quality of providing the attainment of the *prāṇa* in the form of one or the other of those two souls.

Furthermore, the intention of the text should be understood as follows: that the state of being sustained by life, up to its very limit, is accomplished through the combination of the prefix *sam-* and the root *i-*.

Intending a *karmadhāraya* compound according to the principle of the section on the *niṣādasthapati*, he says, "many cognitions. With the intention that since a plurality of cognitions belonging to a single agent cannot possibly be mutually contradictory, a difference of agents must necessarily be asserted, he says, "or the cognitions of many. Regarding the phrase "by those who are constituent parts of the Gāyatrī," the sense is that the bringing of the nectar by the Gāyatrī is well-known from the section beginning, "Kadrū and Suparṇī," and from the mantra, "In the third heaven from here, Soma was."

Thinking that since the quality of being delicious (*rasyatā*) is naturally perceived through the word "let them drink" (*pibantu*), it is appropriate for "daily" (*anvaham*) to indicate its excellence, he says: "due to the excellence of its deliciousness. Alternatively, because demonstrating that the work brings satisfaction would yield little fruit, he says: "or due to its profundity."

"Also the word 'former teachers' (pūrvācārya)" means that the word "former teachers" occurring in the verse beginning with "well-guarded by the former teachers" is also intended here. The phrase "they condensed what was extensive" implies the following: one might raise the objection, "How can your commentary on the *Śārīraka* possess traditional authority (*sāṃpradāyikatva*)? For its source is not perceived. Nor should it be said that the commentaries of Ṭaṅka, Dramiḍa, and others are its source, because there is likewise no evidence for their own traditional authority. The sense is that this resolution of the doubt is also indicated implicitly.

With the intention that it would be inappropriate for the venerable Teacher—who has set out to provide an exposition of the *Bhāṣya*—to explain verses not contained within that *Bhāṣya*, [the opponent] raises an objection with the words, "But [this is] the meaning of the Sūtra," and so forth. "The performance of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalācaraṇam*) means the two verses beginning with "akhila-. "For the sake of the completion of the work without obstacles, etc."—by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), and qualified student (*adhikārī*) are indicated. "It must indeed be included therein"—the sense is that it is like the *Paspaśāhnika* in the *Mahābhāṣya*.

The objection is raised: "If it is argued that the state of being something to be commenced is expressed [by the word *atha*]. The intent of this doubt is as follows: just as in the statement, "I speak to you; here stands an assembly of the learned," the very use of the verb "I speak" leads one to conclude that the matter being spoken of is something to be taught, so too, by the meaning "is commenced," the word *atha* might be understood as expressing the fitness for commencement. [The response is: This is not the case, because [the word *atha*] does not have the purpose of making known the object of instruction.

Regarding the phrase "the state of being to be commenced" (*prastotavyatvam*), since it is impossible for the suffix *tavya* to have the sense of a command (*praiṣa*)—as prescribed by the rule "the kṛtya suffixes [denote] command and permission" (*praiṣātisarga*)—it must be stated that the suffix *tavya* here has the sense of fitness (*arha*), according to the rule "the kṛtya and *tṛc* suffixes [are used] in the sense of fitness" (*arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*). [Objection: "The fitness is not verbal. [Response: But having admitted that "the state of being to be commenced" is the expressed meaning (*vācyatva*), how can the verbal nature of "fitness" be denied? For, by the grammatical rule "the kṛtya and *tṛc* suffixes [are used] in the sense of fitness," the fitness for the *prastāva* (the introductory chant) is also the meaning of the word *prastotavya*.

If it is argued that it cannot be said that the "being the subject of the introductory praise" (*prastotavyatva*) is not admitted to be denotable (*vācyatva*), because the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even at that time" (*tadānīm api*) implies that this very point was admitted when proceeding [with the argument], we reply: no. By the word "also" in "even at that time," denotability is not admitted; rather, what is admitted regarding the "being the subject of the introductory praise" is merely its being the object of the cognition produced by that term.

And therefore, the point is this: just as when the sentence "There is smoke" is uttered with the intention that the listener, once smoke is cognized, will himself infer fire, the existence of fire is not verbal (śābda)—because there is no lack of compatibility with the primary meaning, and thus no metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) of fire in the word "smoke"—likewise, even though the fitness for commencement may somehow become an object of cognition induced by the word *atha*, it does not possess the status of being verbal.

But surely, in a sentence such as "there is smoke" which has fire as its intended meaning (*tātparya*), the existence of fire can indeed be considered verbal (*śābda*), since intention (*tātparya*) is also a basis for indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For instance, in cases such as "he eats water," since no purpose is achieved by conveying the literal meaning alone, one must admit that the mere eating [of water] is verbal. Similarly, when [the statement] "there are crocodiles in the river" is uttered to someone wishing to bathe in the river—

If it is argued that this is because the proponents of the Tantras accept that such a sentence [e.g., "Do not bathe there"] indicates the meaning of a sentence [such as "The water is dangerous"], we say no. This is because the fitness for commencement is a suggested (vyaṅgya) meaning; since it is not rooted in either denotation (śakti) or indication (lakṣaṇā), it lacks the status of being a verbal (śābda) meaning. Furthermore, when it is possible to convey the intended purpose through the well-known sense of "immediacy" (ānantarya), it is improper to assume the meaning of "commencement," which is obscure and serves a trivial purpose.

Alternatively, "non-verbal" (aśābdam) means "inexpressible" or "impossible. The sense is that although it might be possible to convey fitness (*yogyatva*) through some secondary mode of signification (*amukhyayā vṛttyā*), it cannot be conveyed through the primary mode (*mukhyatva*); and since the primary meaning can be grasped, it is improper to abandon it. This is the intended meaning when it is said, "thus, when 'unfit' (*ayogya*) is stated."

Even if one were to supply the phrase "atha ato brahmajijñāsā yogya" [then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman is fit], the meaning of "atha" would be "is undertaken" (adhikriyate); consequently, the meaning would be "the inquiry into Brahman is fit to be undertaken. And since fitness is understood from the context to mean precisely "being entitled" (adhikāra)—just as when it is said, "Let the fit Brahmins be brought," one understands that they are fit for being brought—[the meaning remains the same].

Furthermore, when it is said, "The inquiry into Brahman is commenced as something fit," the understanding that it is "fit for commencement" is established; nevertheless, the sense is that there would not be a verbal cognition (śābdapratīti) that "one is qualified [to begin]. For this very reason, he will state later: "'Qualified' is also a statement of the resultant meaning; it is not a literal expression. This is because particles such as *ca* are indicators (*dyotaka*). The sense is that the indicative nature (*dyotakatva*) of particles has been determined in the *Vākyapadīya*.

Anticipating the objection that this [difficulty] is the same even under the view that [the particle *tu*] signifies immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), he states "But here... and so forth, explaining that there is a difference due to the presence or absence of a purposeful function.

"Both [words] are auspicious (*māṅgalika*). The intention is that the suffix *ṭhak* is used here in the sense of "purpose. Although it is possible for the word *vā*—even when it does not present a correlate for a logical connection—to serve a purpose as an auspicious marker (as seen in the rule *bhūvādi*), nevertheless, since it is possible for it to be connected to the meaning of the sentence by presenting a correlate for that connection, it is improper to accept that it serves the sole purpose of being an auspicious marker in the absence of any other recourse; this is the underlying thought.

Regarding the phrase "then [the word] *atha* signifies a different subject from the one under discussion (*prakṛtāt*)," the ablative case in *prakṛtāt* is used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*. It does not mean "in the sense of 'other than'" according to the rule *anyārāditarartedikchabdāttasuc*, for that would depend upon something else being the primary subject. By the word *atha*, it is indicated that the alternative view (*kalpāntara*) about to be stated pertains to the very subject currently under discussion. For instance, when it is asked, "Is Brahman possessed of attributes (*saguṇa*) or without attributes (*nirguṇa*)?", it is understood that the alternative view characterized by being without attributes is presented specifically in relation to the Brahman under discussion.

It does not, however, depend upon a soul (*jīva*) or an insentient entity (*jaḍa*) distinct from that [Brahman]. Or, for example, as in the passage beginning, "Now, with reference to the self" (*athādhyātmam*). Therefore, the meaning of the word *atha* is dependence upon what has been previously introduced. For this very reason, he will state later on: "The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) does not arise because of inauspiciousness, lack of dependence on the subject under discussion, or incompleteness."

[Otherwise] the reason would be indistinguishable from the probandum. Now, even in the view that [the word *atha*] signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*), it cannot be maintained that the succession presented by the word *atha* can be made the reason [for the inquiry]. For it cannot be said that "the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken because of [mere] succession"; rather, it is the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*)—which is itself implied by the inquiry into Brahman—that is referred to as the reason by the word *ataḥ*. It must be stated that this very [inquiry into ritual action] also connects as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to the succession indicated by the word *atha*.

If it is argued that here too, in this context, it is the inquiry into ritual action (karma-vicāra) implied by the inquiry into Brahman that should be referred to as the cause by the word *ataḥ*, and not the "eligibility" (*adhikṛtatva*) presented by the word *atha*; we say no. For [the rule applies to] words such as "the latter half" (*uttarārdha*) and so forth, which denote a meaning that is dependent [on a prior referent].

According to the maxim, "The meaning is not determined prior to the connection with that which is to be expected," the word *atha* does not denote mere immediate succession (*ānantarya*). Rather, it denotes an immediate succession qualified by the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) as its antecedent. Consequently, since the inquiry into ritual action is also presented by the word *atha*, it is possible—under the view that [the word *ataḥ*] has the sense of immediate succession—for the inquiry into ritual action, presented by the word *atha*, to be referred to by the word *ataḥ* as the reason (*hetu*).
