The point is that under the view that [the word *atha*] serves the purpose of indicating a topic (*adhikāra*), this is not the case; thus there is a disparity. Now, one might object: since *maṅgala* (auspiciousness) is recited alongside [meanings such as] sequence (*ānantarya*) and so forth in the rule, "The words *atho* and *atha* [are used] in the senses of auspiciousness, sequence, commencement, inquiry, and totality," it must necessarily be a denotable meaning (*vācya*). Anticipating this objection due to a lack of conviction, he says: "Even if its status as a denotable meaning is admitted. This is because [the word *atha*] lacks any counter-argument against the reasoning of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The point is this: regarding the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position on the side of the "immediate" (ānantarya), the argument against the inquiry into action (karma-vicāra) being the cause [of the inquiry into Brahman] is countered by the impossibility of the qualification of the qualified person—namely, the cognition that actions yield small and unstable fruits, accompanied by the cognition that they yield immediate and unstable fruits. It is not the case that the prima facie position arises merely from [the opponent's] claims of inauspiciousness (amaṅgalatva), irrelevance to the subject at hand (prakṛtānapekṣatva), or incompleteness (akārtsnya). For even if the prima facie position is raised on grounds such as inauspiciousness, it is not possible for [the Vedāntin] to consider auspiciousness and so forth as the logical reasons (hetu) for refuting it.

This is because [qualities such as] being auspicious (*maṅgala*) and so forth are not accepted by those who hold the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣin*); for only that which is admitted by both parties may be employed as a logical reason (*hetu*). Nevertheless, the point is this: just as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), which is established by "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*), can serve as a reason in proving that the earth and other things have an agent when it has a member yet to be proven (*prasādhyāṅgaka*), so too can "being auspicious" and the like serve as reasons when they themselves have members yet to be proven.

Regarding the phrase "the question contained within the interrogative sentence": Now, since the question is presented by the word *atha*, it is fit to be referred to by the word *ataḥ*; why, then, is it not referred to by the word *ataḥ*? Nor should it be argued that it is not referred to as a reason because it is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For at the time of apprehending something as a cause, it is not required that the object to be apprehended as a cause be established at that very moment; this is because we observe such usage as "the fruit [comes] from the future rain," and because even in the interrogative sentence "Is the object known by the question?", the question itself is seen to function as a cause expressed by the instrumental case.

If it is argued that—in other cases—it is impossible to say that the word *praśna* (question), by virtue of referring to questionhood in general, refers to a question distinct from the one currently being posed, with that [distinct] question being indicated as the cause (*hetu*) by the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*), we reply: no. For even though a question is indicated as a property of the speaker in words such as *kiṃ* ("what?"), it lacks the status of being a constituent of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), just like dejection (*viṣāda*) in expressions such as "Alas! (*hā*) or "Oh, woe! (*hanta*). The intended meaning here is that a question does not possess the status of a denotable object (*vācyatva*) in the same way that it does in the case of words such as *praśna*.

"By the word *bhavati*. Some, however, say that the natural sense (*svārasya*) [of the word *atha*] is indicated by the phrase "the word *atha*" itself. Regarding the phrase "in other sūtras such as this": it should be understood that the designation "sūtra" in expressions such as "Now begins the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) is figurative. As for the phrase "for the word *atha* has its natural sense in the meaning of immediate succession": the point is that although the status of having that meaning in this particular usage is dependent [on something else], the mere natural sense itself is not dependent. For example:

In cases such as "Guru and Bhārgava," there is a cognition of the two planets [Jupiter and Venus] alone due to their mutual association, not of the teacher [Bṛhaspati] and Paraśurāma. And just as in the case of "Rāma and Kṛṣṇa," there is a cognition of Balarāma and Keśava alone, and not of Rāma (the son of Daśaratha) and Arjuna—so too here, although the determination of the meaning occurs through mutual association, another resolution should be seen in that there is no fault. These are "additional arguments" (*abhyuccaya-yukti*). These refer to the natural fitness of the words *atha* and *ataḥ*.
The phrase "intended by the word *atra*" means that it depends upon the antecedent matter implied by the term *brahmajijñāsā*. This is the sense.

(Now, the investigation into the function of the two words *atha* and *ataḥ*: Now, what is the intention behind the statement that "either one of the words *atha* and *ataḥ* is sufficient"? Does it mean that they produce a single uniform cognition, or rather, that they serve a single purpose—just as in the cases "there is a pot on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭaḥ*) and "the ground possesses a pot" (*ghaṭavad bhūtalam*)? Having thus posed this dilemma in his mind, [the author] considers the word *atha*, which generates a cognition having "inquiry" (*jijñāsā*) as its qualificandum and "subsequent duty" (*uttarakālakartavyatā*) as its qualifier, and the word *ataḥ*, which generates a cognition having "what has preceded" (*pūrvavṛtta*) as its qualificandum and "being the cause" (*hetutva*) as its qualifier.

He refutes the first position—that [the word] produces a cognition of a single form—with the words "now, since the word 'atha' brings about the immediate succession of time," and so forth. He refutes the second position—that [it functions] in the form of a proposition and a reason—with the words "the property to be proven is not merely the state of being something to be done."

The inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā) is to be undertaken by persons who have already investigated ritual action (karma), because it is possible for such persons—who have realized that the fruits of ritual actions are limited and transient—to realize the fruit of Brahman as being infinite and eternal. This demonstration is appropriate. Consequently, the word *atha* is required to indicate the qualification of the person as one who has investigated ritual action. The sense is that when this [qualification] is present, the stated meaning is obtained; for [the inquiry into Brahman] cannot be accomplished without having heard other scriptures (śāstra).

The phrase "of the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things, etc. is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the expression "implied by the word *atha*": the meaning is that it serves to dispel the doubt concerning the non-establishment of the specific cause implied by the fact that the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) is the cause [for the inquiry into Brahman] as suggested by the word *atha*.
(The subject matter of the commentary beginning with "having studied the Vedas with their auxiliary sciences"):

The meaning of the commentary passage "by having attained the knowledge of mere rituals which yield small and unstable fruits" is as follows: one who has attained—that is, reached—the knowledge of mere rituals which yield small and unstable fruits is "one who has attained the knowledge of mere rituals which yield small and unstable fruits"; the suffix *-tvena* denotes that state. Regarding the verse: "But he who, having initiated a disciple... [and so forth].

If it is objected: "Since the author himself will state later that this sentence, situated within that context, is intended to prescribe the title 'Ācārya' for one who initiates and teaches—just as there are prescriptions for the titles 'Śrotriya,' 'Upādhyāya,' and 'Guru'—how can this sentence be cited as an authority for the duty of studying the Veda together with its limbs (aṅgas) and its head (śiras)? We reply: not so.

The sense is that, according to the principle that "the body [is] the time and the designation [is] the definition," this sentence—by virtue of being syntactically unified with the injunctive sentence "one should become possessed of a teacher"—possesses authority as a part of that [injunction]. Consequently, the meaning of that sentence is indeed: "Having approached some teacher, one should receive from his presence the Veda together with its ritual manuals (kalpa) and its secret doctrines (rahasya). Alternatively, it should be understood according to the opinion of the Teacher (Guru).

For in the *Gurumatam*, since this statement serves as the source for the Vedic injunction—"One desiring the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) should teach the Veda along with the *kalpas* and the *rahasyas*"—it is established that the study of the *kalpas* and *rahasyas* is likewise accomplished, just like the study of the Veda prompted by the injunction to teach. Regarding the phrase "arising from scripture" (*āgamotthā*): that which arises from scripture is produced by a sentence assisted by inquiry (*vicāra*). That which is produced by discernment (*viveka*), liberation (*vimoka*), and so forth, however, consists of meditation (*dhyāna*) and the like. Since the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) has been stated as the cause [of the inquiry into Brahman], the word "established" (*siddhaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence immediately following.

Anticipating the question of how the manner of accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs, he states that accomplishment consists of both cause and effect through the passage beginning with "of the investigation of action" (*karmavicārasya*). Regarding the phrase "by means of the injunction for repetition and so forth": the sense is that if rites such as the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices were to yield inexhaustible results, then the injunction for their annual repetition would be rendered useless, as performing them again would be redundant.

Is it not the case that the injunction for repetition does not serve as a reason for understanding that the fruits of ritual actions are small and unstable? For, by establishing the necessity of repetition even for knowledge in the section [Brahmasūtra 4.1.1], "Repetition, because of the repeated instruction," and in the section [4.1.12], "Until death, for it is seen there as well," it would follow that liberation—the fruit of that knowledge—would also be non-eternal. If liberation is the fruit of knowledge characterized by daily repetition until death, then let it be the same here as well. Or, if [repetition is required] for the Soma sacrifice every spring;

If it were argued that, by accepting that the production of results is characterized by specific repetitions as prescribed—such as "for five years," "up to fifteen years," "every year," or "during the four-month periods"—then a gradation of results would follow from the gradation of those respective repetitions; then it would be equally applicable here, because the repetition of knowledge must also continue until death, and since the time of death is not fixed, a gradation of results would likewise arise from the gradation [of the duration] of that repetition.

Nor should it be argued that actions have impermanent fruits because, in the section of the eleventh chapter [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*], it is established—on the analogy of agriculture—that distinct fruits arise with each commencement of action; for that [sūtra] refers to actions other than those whose fruit-producing capacity depends on specific repetitions. This must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, there would be a difference in the fruit even in the case of the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice.

Nor [is this the case], because in the *Arthavādādhikaraṇa* sūtra—"On account of the accomplishment of the fruit from the action, there would be a distinction among them according to their magnitude, as in the world"—it is stated that there is a gradation of fruits in accordance with the relative heaviness or lightness of rites consisting of many or few auxiliary elements; and because, through such statements as "Those who give gold attain immortality," "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal," and "The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices is indeed inexhaustible," one understands that the giving of gold, the Soma sacrifice, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices—which are described as means to immortality—are not equal.

One might suspect that there would be a difference in the results—namely, that they would be meager or unstable. However, this is not to be feared; for in the section *Vikalpo’viśiṣṭaphalatvāt* (Sūtra 3.3.59), it will be stated that even though there is a distinction of weight between meditations on many qualities and those on few, as well as between them and *prapatti*, their resulting fruit—liberation—is of one and the same form. It is appropriate to apply this same principle to ritual action (*karman*) as well. Now, it may be argued: "It is true that the third [section] will state that meditations (*upāsanā*) possess the quality of being means to the fruit through repetition until death, and that meditations on many or few qualities and *prapatti* are means to the fruit by way of option (*vikalpa*). Even so, [the point remains].

If it is argued that during the deliberation on the Brahman (brahmavicāra), the fact that ritual actions yield small and unstable fruits is understood merely through the injunctions for repetition and so forth—because the logic to be explained later has not yet been grasped—we grant that this is indeed understood by that means. Nevertheless, because it would contradict what is to be explained later, the reasoning regarding the injunctions for repetition and so forth is merely fallacious; consequently, the cognition that the fruits of action are non-eternal, which is rooted in that reasoning, would also become fallacious.

Furthermore, even at the stage of the initial undertaking, since it is possible to understand the matters to be discussed from the scriptures already studied, there would be the undesirable consequence that those persons who possess an understanding of such aforementioned principles would lack the realization that ritual actions yield results that are meager and transient; consequently, they would not engage in the inquiry into Brahman.

Moreover, because inquiry—like the threshing of grain—has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) and must therefore be repeated until the result arises, it is possible to understand the principle set forth in the third chapter sūtra, "There is an option [between the two], because the result is indistinguishable," at the very stage of beginning the inquiry once again.

By this, the following objection is also refuted: that since the Soma sacrifice—enjoined for the sake of heaven by the rule "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with this Jyotiṣṭoma"—relies upon a fire-altar in the form of a mound (sthāṇḍila) as an alternative to the *uttaravedi*, and because the injunction of the quality of the falcon-shape for the sake of heaven in the passage "One desiring heaven should pile the Śyenacit" necessarily implies that the heaven produced by the Soma sacrifice when endowed with that quality must be inferior to the heaven produced by it alone, it follows that [the latter] has a small and impermanent fruit.

"Or for what other desire are other sacrificial rites performed? The Jyotiṣṭoma is [performed] for all [desires]. Thus, regarding the Soma sacrifice—which is enjoined as having all fruits as its purpose—and the Saubhara chant—which is enjoined as a means for three specific fruits by the rule, "He who desires rain, he who desires food, and he who desires heaven should praise with the Saubhara"—in the performance of these for their respective specific fruits, it is stated: "One should employ *hīṣ* as the *nidhana* for one desiring rain; *ūrk* for one desiring food; and *ū* for one desiring heaven."

Thus, just as there is a fixed arrangement of specific *nidhanas* [concluding chants], it is logical that there is a fixed arrangement of specific auxiliary qualities (*guṇa*) in the performance of the Soma sacrifice for the sake of heaven. Nor is there a rule that those things described in mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such as "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal" and "It is indeed imperishable," cannot be fruits; for we see that longevity and so forth mentioned in the *sūktavāka* mantra, as well as the "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) mentioned in the explanatory passage of the *Rātrisatra*, do indeed function as fruits.

Nor should it be argued that because the fruit of the Soma sacrifice is heard in the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*), the fruit mentioned in the mantra should not be accepted; for it is logical that the very heaven heard in the injunctive statement may be endowed with the specific qualification of eternality, just as the mantra—"Place this sacrifice and the sacrificer where the world of the seven seers of good deeds is"—presents it as being enjoyable in a particular world.

If it is argued that this is because the fruit obtainable by both the wife and the sacrificer is stated to be eternal in another mantra belonging specifically to the *iṣṭi* sacrifice—namely, "May they two grasp the undecaying light in heaven"—and because the sūtra of the *Panyadhikaraṇa*, "And [the scripture] shows its possession of fruit," specifically demonstrates that this mantra serves to bestow the fruit; [Response: This is not so. For even though the fruit is eternal, the performance of the action is not necessarily eternal. Moreover, since the fruit is obtained through the agency of the wife and the sacrificer, the fruit belongs to them both. Furthermore, the sūtra "And [the scripture] shows its possession of fruit" does not establish that this specific mantra alone bestows the fruit. Rather, it establishes that the fruit is obtained through the performance of the ritual act (*karma*) as a whole, which includes all the constituent parts such as the mantras. Therefore, the fruit is not established by this single mantra alone. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the *Panyadhikaraṇa*. Thus, the conclusion remains that the fruit belongs to the agent alone. As for the statement "May they two grasp the undecaying light in heaven," it merely expresses a wish (*āśīr-vāda*). It is not a scriptural injunction (*vidhi*) that establishes the fruit. Even if it were an injunction, it would be understood as referring to the fruit of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice itself, and not as establishing a separate fruit for the wife. Therefore, the wife does not possess the fruit. Furthermore, the word "grasp" (*ārabheta*) denotes the commencement of an action, not the attainment of a result. Hence, the fruit is not established by this mantra. Consequently, the fruit belongs to the agent alone. This concludes the section on the wife's lack of entitlement to the fruit. Now follows the section concerning the *dakṣiṇā*. The sūtra states: "The *dakṣiṇā* is for the priests, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the *dakṣiṇā* is for the priests or for the sacrificer. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is for the sacrificer, because he is the one who desires the fruit. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *dakṣiṇā* is for the priests, because the scripture explicitly states so. The scripture says: "He gives the *dakṣiṇā* to the priests. Since the verb "to give" (*dadāti*) implies the recipient, the *dakṣiṇā* must go to those to whom it is given, namely the priests. If it were for the sacrificer, the scripture would have used the verb "to take" (*gṛhṇāti*) rather than "to give. Therefore, the *dakṣiṇā* belongs to the priests. As for the argument that the sacrificer is the one who desires the fruit, that is not a valid reason. The desire for the fruit is merely a cause for performing the action; it does not determine the ownership of the *dakṣiṇā*. Ownership is determined solely by the scriptural statement. Therefore, the *dakṣiṇā* belongs to the priests. This concludes the section on the *dakṣiṇā*. Now follows the section concerning the *parikraya* (purchase). The sūtra states: "The purchase is for the sake of securing services, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the *parikraya* is for the sake of securing services or for the sake of the fruit. The prima facie view is that it is for the sake of the fruit. However, the established conclusion is that the *parikraya* is for the sake of securing services, because the scripture states: "He purchases the priests with the *dakṣiṇā*. The purpose of purchasing is to secure their services. If it were for the sake of the fruit, the scripture would not have used the term "purchase" (*parikraya*). Therefore, the *parikraya* is for the sake of securing services. This concludes the section on the *parikraya*. Now follows the section concerning the *svāmya* (ownership). The sūtra states: "But the ownership is for the sacrificer, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the ownership of the *dakṣiṇā* is for the sacrificer or for the priests. The prima facie view is that it is for the priests, as established previously. However, the established conclusion is that the ownership is for the sacrificer, because the scripture states: "He gives the *dakṣiṇā* to the priests. The verb "to give" implies that the giver retains ownership until the act of giving is completed. Once the act of giving is finished, the ownership passes to the recipients. But before that, the ownership remains with the sacrificer. Therefore, the ownership is for the sacrificer. This concludes the section on ownership. Now follows the section concerning the *anujñā* (permission). The sūtra states: "The permission is for the sacrificer, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the permission to perform the ritual is for the sacrificer or for the priests. The prima facie view is that it is for the priests. However, the established conclusion is that the permission is for the sacrificer, because the scripture states: "He asks permission from the priests. Since the sacrificer is the one who desires the fruit, he must seek permission to perform the action. Therefore, the permission is for the sacrificer. This concludes the section on permission. Now follows the section concerning the *praiṣa* (direction). The sūtra states: "The direction is for the priests, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the direction to perform the ritual is for the sacrificer or for the priests. The prima facie view is that it is for the sacrificer. However, the established conclusion is that the direction is for the priests, because the scripture states: "He directs the priests. Since the priests are the ones who perform the ritual acts, they require direction. Therefore, the direction is for the priests. This concludes the section on direction. Now follows the section concerning the *upadeśa* (instruction). The sūtra states: "The instruction is for the sacrificer, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the instruction regarding the ritual procedure is for the sacrificer or for the priests. The prima facie view is that it is for the priests. However, the established conclusion is that the instruction is for the sacrificer, because the scripture states: "He instructs the priests. Since the sacrificer is the one who oversees the ritual, he must provide instruction. Therefore, the instruction is for the sacrificer. This concludes the section on instruction. Now follows the section concerning the *pravara* (invocation). The sūtra states: "The *pravara* is for the sacrificer, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the invocation of the ancestral lineage is for the sacrificer or for the priests. The prima facie view is that it is for the priests. However, the established conclusion is that the *pravara* is for the sacrificer, because the scripture states: "He chooses the *pravara* for himself. Since the *pravara* is a personal attribute of the sacrificer, it must belong to him. Therefore, the *pravara* is for the sacrificer. This concludes the section on the *pravara*. Now follows the section concerning the *mantra*. The sūtra states: "The mantra is for the sacrificer, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the recitation of the mantra is for the sacrificer or for the priests. The prima facie view is that it is for the priests. However, the established conclusion is that the mantra is for the sacrificer, because the scripture states: "He recites the mantra for himself. Since the mantra is intended to express the sacrificer's intention, it must belong to him. Therefore, the mantra is for the sacrificer. This concludes the section on the mantra. Now follows the section concerning the *anumantraṇa* (subsequent recitation). The sūtra states: "The subsequent recitation is for the sacrificer, because of the scriptural statement. The question is whether the *anumantraṇa* is for the sacrificer or for the priests. The prima facie view is that it is for the priests. However, the established conclusion is that the *anumantraṇa* is for the sacrificer, because the scripture states: "He recites the *anumantraṇa* for himself. Since the *anumantraṇa* is intended to confirm the sacrificer's action, it must belong to him. Therefore, the *anumantraṇa* is for the sacrificer. This concludes the section on the *anumantraṇa*. Now follows the section

It is said in reply: as for what was stated—that there is scriptural mention of the repetition even of knowledge—that is not so, because knowledge is not the means [to liberation], whereas meditation alone is the means; and because that [meditation] is characterized by repetition. Even though the repetition of meditation is mentioned in the passage beginning with "until death" (*āprayāṇāt*), nevertheless, according to the text "one should meditate on the syllable Om until the end of life," it is only meditation performed up to the moment of death that serves as the means to liberation.

Regarding ritual action (*karman*), this is because we do not observe any scriptural statement establishing that ritual action characterized by such repetition is a means to liberation. This is because the passage, "He indeed, living thus for as long as life lasts," has meditation (*dhyāna*) as its subject matter. Furthermore, in the case of ritual actions, a difference in results necessarily follows from the varying degrees of repetition—such as five years or fifteen years—whereas in meditation and similar practices, no such variation in repetition exists, since they are effective only when repeated until the moment of death.

It is not appropriate to assume a deficiency in the fruit merely because the performance of the means for someone was not completed until the moment of death. For if that were the case, one might as well assume a deficiency in the fruit when a certain action is quickly accomplished by someone with strong limbs and a full complement of auxiliary factors. Indeed, we do not assume a disparity in the fruit based on the observation that for some, the sight of the Setu [Rāmeśvara] was accomplished without the affliction of disease, robbers, or similar obstacles.

Furthermore, the relative abundance or scarcity of qualities conducive to being drawn toward [the practice] cannot account for a disparity in results; for since there is no difference in the requirement to perform the practice continuously until death regardless of how it is done, ease or difficulty of performance is impossible. Therefore, because a gradation of results must necessarily be admitted based on the gradation of repetition, and because such gradation is absent in liberation (*mokṣa*), it must be stated that the fruit of ritual action is something other than liberation.

Furthermore, since devotion—which is characterized by tranquility and other such qualities and is produced by an internal organ purified through the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*) over many lifetimes—is superior to all else, liberation achieved through it cannot have ritual action as its means. Otherwise, there would follow the invalidation (unauthoritativeness) of the injunction for devotion, which is the most weighty of practices, and the injunction for surrender (*prapatti*), which is bound by a lack of confidence in the efficacy of the more arduous means; thus, rituals do not have liberation as their fruit achieved through devotion or surrender. This is the certainty regarding the non-eternality of the fruits of ritual action.

The intention of this text—expressed through such means as the injunction for repetition—is that [the inquiry into Brahman] is easily accessible for those who have already performed an inquiry into ritual action (*karma*).

"For the sake of abandoning ritual action by way of its fruit" means that abandonment by way of the fruit consists in the knowledge of the impermanence of that fruit; "to be known" means "to be investigated. The meaning is that it is explicitly stated that the inquiry into ritual action has as its result the knowledge of the impermanence of the fruits of ritual action. "For the sake of grasping its essential nature" means for the sake of thoroughly understanding the essential nature of ritual action, which is required for the inquiry to be undertaken in the third chapter.

Therefore, the argument that the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) is useful for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) by way of the knowledge of action being useful for rejection and acceptance is inconsistent. For there is no utility for rejection and acceptance in the inquiry itself, such that the inquiry into action could be useful for the inquiry into Brahman through them; this is because the obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karman*), which are to be accepted, are limbs of meditation (*dhyāna*) and not limbs of the inquiry.

Nor should it be said that even for one who has already begun inquiry, the performance of ritual action is required for the sake of purifying the mind, or that the renunciation of optional (*kāmya*) actions is required; for if that were so, the objection would arise that there could be no uninterrupted engagement in inquiry—since one would have to perform rituals for some time after the inquiry into action until the mind is purified. This doubt is refuted because the words "rejection" (*hāna*) and "acceptance" (*upādāna*) aim to make known what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted by way of [the realization of] impermanence and permanence, respectively.

For this very reason, he will state: "The cognition of [the Veda] as something to be accepted in its own nature is because it is included within the initial cognition of the infinite and stable fruit. Now, an objection may be raised: even though through the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) there exists a certainty that rituals yield small and unstable fruits, there is no certainty regarding their being *heya* (to be abandoned). This is because, in the latter portion [of the Vedas], there is an absence of certainty regarding the infinite and stable fruit; thus, for one who suspects that all [fruits] might be small and unstable, a certainty of their being *heya* cannot arise with respect to the rituals understood in the former portion. To this, we reply: No.

There is no fault, because the knowledge that [the fruits of action] are to be abandoned through the most intense degree of effort can arise; thus there is no contradiction with the text. This means that there is no contradiction between this [passage], which shows a single purpose consisting in the knowledge that the fruits of action are impermanent, and the text indicating two purposes: "knowledge of the nature of the required actions" and "knowledge that mere actions yield small and unstable fruits. Regarding the consequence that there would be no performers of action: [this refers to the objection that if the fruits were known to be impermanent, no one would perform actions].

The intention of the objection is as follows: for those who have not performed an inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), since there is an absence of certainty regarding the matters necessary for performance, performance itself would not be possible; and because performance pertains only to persons who have already performed an inquiry into ritual action, and because such persons would already have been occupied with extensive inquiry, it would follow that there would be no performers at all. This is expressed by the phrase: "even having heard [the Veda], those who desire heaven... and so forth.

If it is objected that this [following] answer does not apply to one who challenges the position by arguing that—since all those who have performed the preliminary rites (*kṛtaka*) are engaged in the inquiry into Brahman (*brāhmavicāra*), and since they have heard the section on detachment (*vairāgyapāda*)—there could be no desire for heaven at all, we reply: No; for the purpose of this [section] is to address those who are seen to still desire heaven even after having heard [the teachings]. Furthermore, it should be understood that even when the inquiry into Brahman has been performed, the performance of rituals aimed at heaven is possible due to the impurity of the mind caused by defects in unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
(The Inquiry into the Meaning of the Genitive Case)

Regarding the phrase "in specific relations such as objecthood (*karmatva*), instrumentality (*karaṇatva*), and so forth": Now, upon careful consideration of this sentence, it appears that objecthood, instrumentality, and the like are understood to be specific sub-varieties of the general relation that constitutes the meaning of the genitive case. However, it is not tenable to say this;

for by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* ("the genitive is used in the sense of the 'remainder'"), the genitive is taught to apply to cases other than those of objecthood and so forth—that is, to meanings distinct from the primary nominal stem-meaning (*prātipadikārtha*). This is because there is no relationship of general-to-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-bhāva*) between the meaning of the accusative and the meaning of the genitive, just as there is no such relationship between the meanings of the accusative and the instrumental.

If it is argued that—on the basis of what was stated by Bhartṛhari: "Relation is distinct from the *kārakas*; it is preceded by the relation between action and *kāraka*, and it is expressed whether the action is explicitly mentioned or not"—there exists in examples such as "he hears the actor," "one should eat beans," and "he imitates the Blessed Nārāyaṇa" a relation characterized by the status of the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*), which is distinct from [the standard] objecthood (*karmatva*) and others, and is preceded by the relation between action and *kāraka*—we say: no.

In cases such as "one should eat māṣas," there is no evidence for postulating anything other than [the relation of] objecthood (*karmatva*). This is because it is accepted that the second case endings (*dvitīyā*) and others are prescribed as exceptions (*apavāda*) to the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), and thus the restriction based on the relationship between the general and the particular is logically established. As for the statement "the other case endings are prescribed": although the sixth case is also prescribed by the rule "the sixth case is used for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*), nevertheless, the other case endings are prescribed specifically for those particular relations such as the object and so forth.

The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), however, is prescribed for the general sense of relation; yet, one must supply the word *eva* (only) and the particle *api* (even/also) and construe it as follows: "of the *pariṇā*s, even those connected with the *brāhmaṇas*. But surely [some] read: "in the acceptance of the general sense of relation" (*saṃbandhasāmānyaparigrahe*). In that case, there would be a grasping only of those *pariṇā*s situated within the general relation and their very own adjuncts (*tadanubandhinām*), but not of the adjuncts of the *brāhmaṇas*.

For he does not read "brāhṛparigrahe," by which the suffixes connected with the *brāhmaṇa* might be understood. For this very reason, it is stated later, "the genitive is accepted" (*ṣaṣṭhī kṛhrate*), but not "the suffix *pari*" (*parī*) as well. Even if it were said, "the genitive is accepted in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī parigṛhrate*), the inclusion of those [suffixes] connected with the *brāhmaṇa* would still not be established.

If it is argued that [the prohibition applies] only to those [compounds] connected with the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), [the response is] no; for even in the case of those connected with the nominative (*prathamā*), it is possible in some way for them to be connected with the general category of connection through a mediated relationship—this is the intended meaning. "Because of the connection with the principal [member]" means: just as when it is said, "The king has gone out," the going out of his retinue is understood, so it is here—the sense is this. "The prohibition of the compound (*samāsa*) has its scope" means: [it applies where there is a specific condition].

The meaning is that this is an opportunity not barred by the counter-exception (pratiprasava) stating, "A genitive case ending characterized by connection with a *kṛt* suffix is compounded. Now, one might ask: why does the prohibition of compounding by the rule "and [in the case of a word] denoting the object" (*karmaṇi ca*) not apply? It does not, because that [prohibition] pertains specifically to the genitive case prescribed by the rule "when both [agent and object] are applicable, [the genitive is used] for the object" (*ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*). For example: "The milking of cows is wonderful, [performed] by an untrained cowherd. With this in mind, the venerable author of the Bhāṣya stated: "[The genitive is used] for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows."

Although the word *jñāna* is formed with a *kṛt* suffix, the sense is that there is no occasion [for the genitive] because it is barred by the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). This is because [the phrase] "they know ghee" (*sarpiso jānīte*) is capable of being construed with a verb ending in a *tiṅ* suffix. The meaning is that this genitive, like [the one] in connection with a *tiṅ*-ending word, is a genitive characterized as a "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Nor should one suspect the rule "of the root *jñā*, when not meaning 'to know'" (*jño 'vidarthasya*) to be redundant if it were merely a "remainder" genitive; for the restatement is for the purpose of prohibiting compounding, so that the genitive is indeed heard and not elided. And elision occurs only in a compound. And it has been said by Bhartṛhari:
"And when the action is heard again in that which has been designated as the instrument (sādhana), the genitive case is prescribed for every word to prevent compounding. Thus [it is said].

This is because the application of both the nominal stem (*dhātu*) and the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is for the purpose of expressing that [instrumentality]. Consequently, since *sarpiṣaḥ* lacks the status of being either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*), the genitive case is not one characterized by connection with a *kṛt*-suffix; such is the intended meaning. Although, according to the rule "the genitive is used for the instrument of a verb meaning 'to know' when it does not mean 'to perceive'," the genitive is a residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) and thus its meaning is not instrumentality, nevertheless, the point here is that since the instrument—intended as a residual element—is indeed the expressed meaning, yet it lacks the status of being either agent or object, there is no possibility of the genitive being one characterized by connection with a *kṛt*-suffix.

If it is objected that stating that the verbal root (*dhātu*) has "activity" (*pravṛtti*) as its meaning is irrelevant, we say no; for while the root *jñā* (to know) has knowledge as its meaning, it is transitive and thus there is the possibility of an object (*karman*), whereas if it had activity as its meaning, even that possibility would not exist—it is for the purpose of demonstrating this distinction.

[Objection: But surely this is not a genitive case? [Response: Indeed, even though it was not employed by the author of the Sūtras, because it was employed by himself, and because the definition of a Bhāṣya consists in explaining what one has oneself employed, there is no fault in its explanation. This is well known to all people: even in other works, when explaining words for the sake of another's understanding, authors are seen to employ synonyms for terms they themselves have used, such as "capacity (śakti), efficacy (sāmarthya), and causality (kāraṇatva)—that is to say, they are synonymous. Thus, they explain even their own employed terms up to the point of conveying the meaning to others.

If it is argued that, therefore, for the sake of explaining the compound, since there is no lexicon or similar work regarding the case endings when the meaning of the genitive used in the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) employed by oneself is ambiguous, it is proper to provide the explanation through grammar alone—this is not so. For there is no rule that the explanation of a compound word must be performed solely by means of an analytical sentence; thus, [it may be explained as: "The desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is the desire to know whose object is Brahman (*brahmakarmikā jijñāsā*); it ought to be undertaken."

The intended meaning is this: let it be explained simply that the word *brāhma* refers to the action of a Brahmin (*brāhma-karma*); why resort to presenting a compound analysis (*vigraha-vākya*) that depends on an explanation of an ambiguous meaning? For a compound (*samāsa*) is indeed the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the case-meaning by means of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). However, this [definition] should be understood as referring specifically to Tatpuruṣas with elided case-endings (other than Karmadhārayas) and to specific types of Avyayībhāvas. "For the sake of determining the specific indicated meaning" means for the purpose of demonstrating: "this is the meaning of this case-ending, which is indicated by this nominal stem."

Now, how does this doubt—"not by means of grammatical instruction" (nānuśāsanena)—arise? Since it is established that the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is what must be explained, and since lexicons and the like are indifferent regarding its specific meaning, it is appropriate to provide an explanation through grammatical instruction. Thus, once the determination has been made that "this is the meaning of this case-ending," the meaning in the form of the object (*karmatva*) is indicated by virtue of semantic fitness; therefore, it is entirely proper to state the meaning of the case-endings for the sake of such a determination. For this very reason, even the subsequent statement, "There is no hamlet on the Ganges" (*na gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), would not be tenable [if the meaning were already fixed independently].

For here, an instruction regarding the denotative word (*lakṣaka-pada*) with respect to its indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) is not being presented; rather, an instruction is presented for the purpose of stating that the objecthood (*karmatva*), which is to be indicated by implication (*lakṣaṇīya*) through the force of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and other factors, is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

For this very reason, even the passage in the *Parihāra* (the refutation) stating, "But that restriction applies only when there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the meaning of another nominal stem by means of one nominal stem," is not tenable; for here too, the consideration of compatibility (*yogyatā*) and so forth must be required in order to indicate only "objecthood" (*karmatva*) from among the objecthood, agenthood, and other properties of the Brāhmaṇa. If you say this, [we reply: you are ignorant of the meaning of the sentence. For it is not being objected here that the explanation of the genitive case by the force of the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), "The sixth case-affix is used after a word denoting the agent or the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*), is inappropriate.

[Objection: Why is this explanation provided—which would otherwise result in a censure—by means of the rule “*kṛdyogalakṣaṇā ṣaṣṭhī samasyate*” (a genitive case ending characterized by connection with a *kṛt*-suffix is compounded), which aims to justify the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of a word ending in a genitive suffix characterized by connection with a *kṛt*-suffix through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when that case-ending has been elided? For there is no need for a grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) regarding the fact that the use of the word *gaṅgā* in the sense of the bank through metaphorical indication possesses grammatical correctness. [Response: This objection is not a fault, because it is possible to offer a rebuttal: while the grammatical correctness of using a word through metaphorical indication in a particular sense depends upon a grammatical rule, [in the present case] such a dependence does not apply. Thus, there is no defect.

Now, if the primary meaning of a word with an elided case-ending were the meaning of the elided case-suffix itself, there would be a contradiction with the *Niṣādasthapati* section [of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtras], because a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound would not involve metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Out of dissatisfaction with this, he says: "Or, what harm is there to us if it is not the primary meaning?"

One might object: "If the meaning of a case-ending prescribed by its connection with another word is actually present, then in the expression 'he pays homage to the gods' (*namaskaroti devān*), the accusative in the sense of the object would not have greater force than the dative caused by the connection with the word *namaḥ*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the case-ending denoting a kāraka," for [the condition of] being prescribed by connection with another word certainly exists here as well.

Now, one might object: even though the genitive prescribed by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) is occasioned by its connection with a word ending in a *kṛt*-suffix, there is no loss of its status as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) expressive of a *kāraka*, for grammarians conventionally refer to it as the "genitive of the *kāraka*" (*kāraka-ṣaṣṭhī*). For this very reason, the accentuation of the *kāraka* applies in the rule *gatikārakopapadāt kṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.139); otherwise, that [accentuation] would not apply. This is true; it certainly possesses the status of a *kāraka*-case-ending. Furthermore, because it is occasioned by its connection with an *upapada*, it also possesses the status of an *upapada*-case-ending.

Moreover, its relative weakness—compared to case endings that denote *kārakas* independently of the connection with a governing word (*upapada*)—is established by experience. This is because, as in the case of "he makes a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is not immediately perceived in the expression "the making of a jar" (*ghaṭasya kṛtiḥ*). Nor should it be argued that, since the genitive in the rule "the sixth case ending is used for the agent and the object when a verbal noun (*kṛt*) follows" (*kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ kṛti*) is a case ending based on a governing word (*upapada-vibhakti*), the accusative would take precedence and subvert the genitive; for this very rule is introduced specifically as an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general application].

But this is not the case; for in examples such as *kanyāyā alaṃkartā* ("the one who decorates the girl"), even the genitive used in connection with a *kṛt*-suffix would be indistinguishable from a case-ending based on a governing word (*upapada-vibhakti*), and thus it could not be sublated by the dative prescribed on account of connection with *alaṃ*. It should not be argued that [the dative] cannot sublate it because [the genitive] is stronger; for sublation is possible due to its higher status (*paratva*). Furthermore, since the genitive in the sense of the object (*karman*) is also accepted as a "case-ending based on a grammatical factor" (*kāraka-vibhakti*) because it is prescribed specifically for a particular factor, it can be sublated by the case-ending caused by connection with the word *alaṃ*, which is merely a "case-ending based on a governing word" (*kevalopapada-vibhakti*).

"By virtue of its dependence on the reference to another word. And it has been stated in the third [book], under the sūtra "And in the case of the *sūktavāka*, there is an injunction of time, because it serves another purpose": regarding the statement "He casts the *prastara* [grass-bundle] with the *sūktavāka*," the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) argues that the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in "with the *sūktavāka*" must be used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*). To this, [the Siddhāntin replies]: "In all cases, because the relationship between action and factor (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) is more intrinsic, it is proper to state that the *sūktavāka* is connected to the act of casting the *prastara* precisely as a factor (*kāraka*)."

If, however, one were to rely on the sense of "specifying a particular state" (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*), the connection [of the word *sūktavākena*] as a factor of action (*kāraka*) would not be established. Furthermore, its syntactic connection as an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of specification (*lakṣaṇakriyā*) is not tenable; for in the phrase "the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) specified by the *sūktavāk*," there is an absence of a word expressing the act of specification itself, and thus it would require another word to express that act. Therefore, the instrumental case here is not used in the sense of specifying a particular state, but rather the instrumental is indeed used in the sense of an instrument. This is because, according to the stated principle, a derivative case ending (*upapadavibhakti*) is weaker than a case ending based on a factor of action (*kārakavibhakti*).
"But the non-primacy [of the secondary meaning] has been refuted" means that it has been refuted by the words "What loss is there for us?
(The investigation of the meaning of the word *brāhma*).

Regarding the claim that the word *puruṣottama* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*): although a conventional meaning characterized by the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) is accepted when the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) is over-extensive, nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated by accepting a common ground for application (*samānapravṛttinimitta*), because the word *puruṣottama* is recited as a synonym for Nārāyaṇa—just as conventional status is not to be accepted in cases such as *śacīpati*, *vākpati* (or *pārvatīpati*), *śrīvatsavakṣas*, and so forth, nor in words like *prodgātṛ*, *ahīna*, or *dhārya*.

It has been stated that there is a distinction in terms of volition (*cetanā*). Even though the word *uttama*—derived from the prefix *ud*, which signifies "rising up," combined with the verbal root *tam* meaning "to accomplish," and the suffix *tamap*—does not have "distinction" as its primary meaning; and even according to the view that words are not etymologically derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), "distinction" is not its meaning, because the word *uttama* is never employed in the sense of mere distinction alone.

For this very reason, even the statement, "Even grass and the like possess differentiation from what is other than themselves," is not tenable. Nevertheless, since one must resort either to a *pañcamī-samāsa* (genitive compound) in accordance with the authority of the scripture, "And [He] who is higher even than the Imperishable," or to a *saptamī-samāsa* (locative compound) by means of a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) based on the rule "after a locative,"—and because differentiation (*nirdhāraṇa*) must necessarily be expressed by the fifth and seventh cases according to the two sūtras "That from which there is a selection" and "The fifth case in the sense of distinction"—differentiation (*vailakṣaṇya*), being synonymous with separation (*pṛthakkaraṇa*), is the actual meaning.

It should be understood that this was stated with this very intention. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of establishing [the meaning]": the meaning is that it is for the purpose of establishing that the ground for the application [of the term *Brahman*]—namely, its nature as unsurpassed greatness—is possible because Puruṣottama is the locus of the assumption of faultlessness and the mine of all auspicious qualities. However, it is not [meant] as the actual ground for the application [of the term].

The point is this: one should not be deluded into thinking that for the word *brāhmya*, "being free from defects by its very nature" is another ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) distinct from "vastness" (*bṛhattva*). He states the force of the meaning [of the term] as "for the seeker of liberation, [the bliss] which is free from all defects. By its being beyond the reach of speech and mind, it is said to be "limitless" (*anavadhika*). [Objection]: Since the qualities of Brahman surpass all others, and since a "surpassing" (*atiśaya*) must have a limit (*avadhi*)—as the surpassing of the bliss of Indra and others is indeed limited by the bliss of humans—how can it be limitless?

If it is argued that the excellence of Brahman-bliss is indeed the limit (avadhi) for all blisses from humans up to Prajāpati, and therefore, because it is the limit for all, it is superior to all—thus [the term] "limit" (*avadhi*) is used in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) to signify a boundary—[we reply: no, because the word *avadhi* here signifies "measure" (*iyattā*). Consequently, the meaning is that the excellence of Brahman-bliss is unlimited (*aparicchinna*). Alternatively, "being without a limit" (*anavadhikatva*) means simply being devoid of a limit of inferiority (*apakarṣa-avadhi*) that resides in the same locus as itself. By the word "itself" (*sva*), excellence (*utkarṣa*) is referred to.

The distinction lies in this: the excellence residing in the bliss of Indra and others, when compared to the bliss of gods and so forth, possesses a limit for its own co-located inferiority because it is co-located with an inferiority that has Bṛhaspati’s bliss as its terminus; however, the excellence residing in the qualities of the Lord lacks such a limit, owing to the absence of any co-located inferiority. Alternatively, the excellence of others is "limited" (sāvadhika) because it is defined in dependence upon limits such as gods and humans.

Regarding the subject of Īśvara (the Lord), however, because we observe the use of the suffix *atiśāyana* (expressing excellence) as being independent of any qualifying word (*upapada*), the excellence inherent in Him is understood without depending on the cognition of a limit; thus, He is "limitless" (*niravadhika*). For this very reason, while the lordship of others is designated by specifying a boundary—as in "Lord of Ayodhyā" (*Ayodhyeśvara*) or "Lord of Mithilā" (*Mithileśvara*)—with respect to Īśvara, there is only the cognition and usage of the term "Īśvara" itself, without the introduction of any such limitation.

For this very reason, in the passage "He is known from the word alone" (ŚBh 1.3.24), it is established that the status of being *śruti* (direct Vedic testimony) belongs to the word *īśāna* itself when it is independent, and not when it is dependent on a correlative term; as the learned have stated: "Those who know the true meaning of words, the knowers of the Vedas, declare that a word denotes its primary [meaning] without qualification, whereas for others [secondary meanings], it does so through qualification."

The word "group" (*gaṇa*) is intended to signify inclusion. Only when each individual attribute—such as the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*) and so forth—constitutes a group of qualities does its "innumerability," which will be described later as a qualifier of that [Brahman], become logically consistent. Otherwise, there would be only one single group comprising all the qualities, and thus the qualification of "innumerability" would be incoherent.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this was stated taking for granted the fact—established through the objection and its resolution in the passage beginning with "Now, if the term 'limitless excellence' were a qualifier of the collection [of qualities]"—that both "limitless excellence" (*anavadhikātiśayatva*) and "innumerability" (*asaṃkhyeyatva*) are qualifiers of the collection of auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇagaṇa*). [Otherwise,] the *bahuvrīhi* compound would not be possible due to the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The sense [of the objection] is that in the analytical exposition (*vigraha*)—"one whose collection consists of infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities"—a *bahuvrīhi* compound would not be possible because of the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the members being compounded, according to the rule: "A *bahuvrīhi* is desired for items that are coreferential. [The phrase] "only those included therein" refers to this: here, the distinction between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) is that in the example, learning, conduct, and so forth, are taken collectively.

In the case of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), however, the absence of any further excellence is understood through both scripture and reasoning as applying to both [the group and its members]. Regarding the phrase "of those who have emerged from that": this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). One should also observe that if the collection of learning, conduct, and so forth were to belong [only] to the aggregate, then it would follow that the individual members contained within that aggregate would lack learning and the rest. Regarding the phrase "because it would follow that there is an absence of learning and so forth": the meaning is that the cognition of the connection with learning and the rest would not occur. "Because they possess excellence in comparison to the qualities of the Blessed One" means:

The meaning is: "because of being inferior in comparison to the qualities of the Blessed One. Regarding the phrase "the matter proposed through the power of the word": the intention is to demonstrate that the word *brāhma*—which is derived from the verbal root *bṛh*—has its primary application (*mukhyavṛttatva*) only where there is a fullness of the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely, the connection with the quality of greatness (*bṛhattva*); whereas in other cases, it has a secondary application (*amukhyavṛttatva*). He states another interpretation: "In that regard, among other meanings," meaning "among all the objects within the scope of the usage of the word *brāhma*."

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "in those other than Puruṣottama. The meaning is that there is a connection with the quality of greatness (*bṛhattva*). Therefore, the full sense of the sentence extends only to this point: "Hence, in that case [the term 'Brahman'] is secondary (*gauṇa*). For this very reason, the introductory objection—"Why should there not be a secondary sense for Puruṣottama and a primary sense elsewhere?"—is consistent.

Otherwise, since the statement "for everywhere [the word *brāhmaṇa* applies] by connection with the quality of greatness" would already result in establishing that the primary sense resides in Puruṣottama and the secondary sense elsewhere, the introductory objection—"Is there not a lack of consistency in the objection that [the term] is secondary in Puruṣottama?"—would be inappropriate, and the subsequent text would have to begin simply with "What follows from this? In this view, the commentary passage "for everywhere the word *brāhmaṇa* [applies] by connection with the quality of greatness" is a supplement to the preceding text.

In the former view, [the subsequent passage] serves as a supplement to the preceding text. For this very reason, the word "etcetera" (ādi) was employed in the phrase "by the words 'everywhere,' etc. Alternatively, the introductory transition is simply "what follows from that? Indeed, the intended meaning of the question "What follows from that? is: "How, by that much alone, is your thesis established—that Puruṣottama alone is denoted in the primary sense? Why might the opposite not be the case?"

There is no fault in stating that this very same meaning is expressed by the passage beginning with "gauṇatvam" (the state of being secondary) regarding Puruṣottama; nor should it be seen as necessitating recourse to two separate explanations. Regarding the phrase "also in the case of the quality of greatness (*brāhṛguṇa*) and so forth": [an objection is raised]—"But surely, since both [qualities] are accepted as the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in accordance with the authority of the scriptural statement, 'Because of its greatness (*bṛhat*) and because of its nourishing (*bṛṃhaṇa')', there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the quality of greatness and the like. And one must necessarily accept it thus; otherwise, the over-extension to the quality of greatness and so forth would remain as it was, because the ground for application would still exist [there]."

If it is argued: "It is not the case that only the *japā* flower and the like—which are red by means of a coloring substance such as lac and which themselves are the substratum of redness—are denoted by the word 'red' because they do not contract [their nature]; rather, it is not so for the *japā* flower alone. Nor is it the case that only a mountain which has a mountain as its substratum is denoted by the word 'mountain', and not a mountain that does not have another mountain as its substratum, even though the latter is by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) a substratum of mountain-ness, since it is not a substratum of mountain-ness in terms of its attributes (*dharmataḥ*). [Response: This is not so.

Why is it called *brāhman*? According to the authoritative evidence, "the qualities (*guṇas*) in this are great (*bṛhantaḥ*)," the very state of possessing great qualities (*bṛhadguṇakatva*) is the basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Although the greatness of its own nature (*svarūpabṛhattva*) and its expansiveness (*bṛṃhaṇatva*) are also included therein, the intended meaning lies precisely in this. Alternatively, the phrase "greatness by way of qualities" does not mean a greatness residing in the qualities themselves; rather, it refers to a specific majesty (*māhātmyaviśeṣa*) inherent in the essential nature (*svarūpaniṣṭha*), consisting of preeminence (*jyāyastva*) caused by the possession of great qualities.

Therefore, "being greater than all" (*sarvato jyāyastvam*) is "greatness" (*bṛhattvam*). The sense is that this alone is the ground for the application of the word *brāhman*. Regarding the phrase "of the non-restriction of the word's power": if it is objected that by accepting both [greatness and being greater than all] as grounds for application, there is indeed a restriction of the word *brāhman*'s power—since greatness based on qualities would exclude [the application of the word] to things like the *brāhman-qualities*—we say: no. For here, the phrase "of the word's power" does not mean "of the word *brāhman*'s power."

Rather, the meaning is that [the word *brāhma*] functions by virtue of the power of the word "quality" (*guṇa*) occurring in the sentence that establishes the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *brāhma*, namely: "The qualities in this [Brahman] are great. Alternatively, the meaning is that since even the ground for application—just as in the case of the word *brāhma*—is itself the denotable object (*śakya*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of restriction (*saṃkoca*) if one were to say that only the specific quality of greatness (*bṛhattva*) is the denotable object.

Nor does the fact that both are denotable objects entail a restriction of the individual instances (*vyakti*) denoted; for since the restriction of instances is already established prior to this on the grounds of the absence of usage, it cannot be dependent upon this [alleged denotation].

"Therefore, [it is] *brāhmaṇa*. Now, it might be argued that the meaning of "therefore" (*tasmāt*) should be stated as "from the Lord of All" (*sarveśvarāt*), because in the preceding sentence—"the word *brāhmaṇa* has its primary application (*mukhyavṛtta*) in that very [Lord]"—the term "in that very" (*tatraiva*) refers specifically to the Lord of All. For if one were to refer here to the *brāhmaṇa* [in the sense of the caste], there would result the fallacy of negating something that was never even suggested (*aprasaktapratiṣedha*).

If it is argued that the primary application of the word *brāhma* to one who is not a *brāhmaṇa* is not possible—such that its negation would be purposeful—it is replied: the phrase "from him" (*tasmāt*) is not an explanatory statement of the meaning of *brāhmaṇa*, but rather a completion of the elliptical sense. The intention is this: the status of being *brāhma* is established for the Lord of All, who possesses infinite excellence both by nature and by qualities. Beyond this, if one were to accept that there is yet another primary referent of the word *brāhma* even than Him, there would result the fault of multiple meanings (*anekārthatva*).

Some, however, say that the term *brāhmaṇaḥ* means those who possess infinite greatness (*niravadhika-bṛhattva*). In the preceding sentence, in the phrase "in that very [state]" (*tatraiva*), the word *tat* (that) also refers specifically to one who possesses unsurpassed greatness, and not to the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*). Likewise, they maintain that in the subsequent passage, "due to the connection with a mere fraction of His qualities" (*tad-guṇa-leśa-yogāt*), the meaning is simply "due to the connection with a mere fraction of the quality of greatness. According to this view, the portion stating, "And He is indeed the Lord of All; therefore, the word *brāhmaṇa* is used in its primary sense only in reference to Him," would be redundant.

Now, one might object: "If the usage in other cases is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), why would that usage not be universal? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "But the figurative [usage]," because a figurative usage cannot be subject to further questioning and thus is not universal. One might further object: "A word which is observed even in a single instance to be based on a genus (*jāti*) does not, by not abandoning that [genus], come to depend upon another cause."

Thus, by the principle of the section concerning *barhis* and *ājya*, since "bigness" (*bṛhattva*) alone is the basis for the application [of the term] without deviation, there is no fault such as the assumption of multiple powers or the status of being figurative. This is because the non-usage of the word *brāhmaṇa* with respect to triads (*tryaṇuka*) and so forth is intelligible—just like the non-usage of the word *bṛhat*—and the non-usage of words such as *barhis* by the Āryas with respect to unrefined grasses and the like is likewise intelligible.

In passages such as "But Jaimini [thinks so] because of its primary sense" and "And it may belong to one [thing], like the word *brāhma*," the usage of the word *brāhma* for the Supreme Self is justified by the principle: "A word applies to the primary [meaning] without qualification, while it applies to others only with qualification. This is because the cognition of greatness residing in the Brahman does not depend on the perception of a limit (i.e., a comparative standard), and thus, compared to other forms of greatness whose cognition depends on the perception of a limit, it resides more rapidly in the mind. Therefore, the usage is established according to the aforementioned rule.

If it is argued that one cannot claim that "unrestrained lordship" (*niraṅkuśeśvaratvam*) alone is the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word [Īśvara], setting aside "lordship" (*svāmitvam*) as the basis—on the grounds that the word *nareśvara* is not applied to the master of one's own wife, sons, and so forth, nor is the word *īśvara* applied to a mere lord of the earth and the like—it is not so. For if that were the case, even the word *go* (cow) would have "the state of being a goer" (*gantṛtvam*) as its basis for application, since it is etymologically derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍo*, according to the rule "from *gam*, *ḍo*."

However, since its non-application elsewhere is established—as in the case of words such as *barhis* (sacrificial grass) or *ājya* (clarified butter)—one need not assume that it possesses a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) for a specific type of goer. Furthermore, if one were to assume a specific conventional meaning for that which possesses a dewlap and so forth based on its necessary non-application elsewhere, and thereby conclude that the other [type of goer] is not denotable, that would apply equally to the present case; such is the direction of the argument.

However, some, while accepting that "bṛhattva" (greatness) is the basis for the application [of the term], argue that since it is the perfection (*pauṣkalya*) of that very greatness which is established in the Blessed Lord, "bṛhattva" alone is the basis for the application. For the perfection of the basis for application is not itself the basis for application. Consequently, they maintain that the Siddhāntin does not accept a conventional meaning (*rūḍha-artha*) distinct from the etymological meaning (*avayava-artha*).

"Regarding those who are fit for the metaphorical application of the word 'Bhagavān'. [Objection: But since Vasiṣṭha and others have been described as "fit to be addressed as Bhagavān," how can you say they are merely fit for the metaphorical application of the word "Bhagavān"? [Response: Not so; according to your own view, the meaning is "those who are fit for the metaphorical application of the word 'Bhagavān'. [Objection: Is it not your own conclusion that there is no universal application of the word "Bhagavān" to Khāṇḍikya and others? Because of this unease, he says: "Furthermore, it is based on direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."

Regarding the phrase "by means of an understanding rooted in scripture": one might object, "But since the scripture stating 'origination and dissolution' (*utpattiṃ pralayaṃ ca*) is indeed authoritative, why should Vasiṣṭha and others not also possess primacy through an understanding based on that? Furthermore, in the verse beginning with "knowledge, power, strength, and sovereignty" (*jñānaśaktibalaiśvarya*), the phrase "without exception" (*aśeṣataḥ*) indicates that these qualities serve as the grounds for the application [of the term "Lord"] for all [beings] individually; they do not refer to them collectively. For if that were the case, the plural form "the denotables" (*vācyāni*) would not be used.

If it is argued that, since the six grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) beginning with knowledge have been mentioned, one might consider this to be "too little" and thus conclude—by the phrase "without the qualities and so forth to be abandoned"—that all auspicious qualities distinct from knowledge and the rest, yet distinct from those to be abandoned, are grounds for application (just as in the verse: "Whatever being possesses majesty, splendor, or power..."), we say: No, for [the text states] "This word 'Bhagavān' and likewise the word 'Puruṣa'... [and so on].

The sense is that this is in accordance with such corroborative texts as, "And they both abide in the eternal Vāsudeva," and because the word *bhagavat* alone is never used for anything else. For this very reason, it was stated that he is called *puruṣottama*. Although in the sentence "Knowing him thus," following the previous passage, "I know this Puruṣa," it is the Great Puruṣa (*mahān puruṣa*) who is introduced and not the *puruṣottama*; nevertheless, it should be understood that the statement was made with the intention that the two terms ultimately converge on the same referent.

"Therefore, the Lord of All alone is the object of inquiry (*jijñāsā-karma-bhūta*). Since there is no evidence for assuming a restriction of the word *ataḥ* occurring in this sentence to its mere capacity to signify the state of being an object of inquiry for one afflicted by the three-fold suffering, he says: "Or rather, 'therefore' (*yadvā ataḥ*). The word to be explained is *ataḥ*. Whether unlearned or learned, [the word] is primary (*mukhya*) with respect to the Blessed Lord; that is to say, it has grasped the conventional relationship [of meaning], which means it denotes the Blessed Lord through its primary function (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*). [The phrase] "intentional" (*buddhipūrvikā*)...

"Acquisition through intelligence" (*buddhipūrvikā vyutpattiḥ*) refers to cases where acquisition is grasped by means of the pointing with fingers by mothers, fathers, and others toward [objects such as] mother, father, maternal uncle, and so forth. "Arbitrary acquisition" (*yādṛcchikavyutpattiḥ*), however, should be understood as referring to cases where acquisition is grasped after observing the activity of the person being prompted upon hearing a sentence such as, "Bring the jar. This will become clear in the determination of the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*). In the expression "the sacrificial post and the Āhavanīya fire," the word "potsherd" (*kapāla*) has entered [the compound] by way of incidental mention (*saṃpāta*);
this is because it is a worldly term.
(Investigation of the meaning of the word *jijñāsā*)

And the performance of the action is subordinate to the ritual act (*karman*). Now, one might object: if the primary element were the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*), then in cases such as "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), it would follow that the rice-grains themselves are the objects to be enjoined; moreover, since being primary is invariably associated with being a restatement (*anuvāda*), it is contradictory for that which is primary to be the object of an injunction; and furthermore, in instances such as "One should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*) or "One buys [the Soma] with a red cow" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*), it is observed that it is precisely the accessory (*guṇa*) that is enjoined. How then can this be? It is said in reply: because desire is dependent upon the beauty of its object.

This is because, although [the knowledge] is not something to be accomplished by an effort dependent on human will, it can nonetheless be prescribed as a duty since the knowledge being sought is dependent on human will by virtue of being achievable through an effort governed by desire; such is the meaning of that [text].

However, some argue that although the maxim—"of the meanings of the base and the suffix, the meaning of the suffix alone is predominant"—is generally observed in cases such as *aupagava*, this is not so in instances like *aśvena jigamiṣati* ("he wishes to go by horse") or *asinā jighāṃsati* ("he wishes to strike with a sword"). In these cases, we observe that the meaning of the base itself possesses verbal predominance—characterized by its independent presentation—and enters into a syntactic relation (*anvaya*) with other co-occurring word-meanings, in comparison to the desire expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*). This is likewise the case in the expression *brahma-jijñāsā*.

They explain the intention of the Bhāṣya as follows: it is only for the knowledge of the meaning of the *prakṛti* (the verbal root) that there is the possibility of its connection with the word "to be performed" (*kartavya*), which is supplied from the context. "Knowledge in the form of apprehension" (*pratītirūpaṃ jñānam*): here, the word "with reference to" (*uddiśya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, the syntactical connection here is as follows: "With reference to knowledge in the form of valid cognition (*pramiti*), the implied knowledge in the form of reasoning (*tarka*), which consists of a specific mental operation, is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*). This is what has been stated by others. Alternatively, the meaning is that the thing to be enjoined is verbal (*śābda*); for it will be stated later that "knowledge in the form of reasoning is inferential (*ārtha*)."

And in the consideration of the implied meaning (*ārthika-vicāra*), there is the connection with the duty that is to be undertaken (*adhyāhṛta-kartavyatvānvaya*). For it is stated in the *Kalpataru*: "But the scriptural [meaning]—that the desire for knowledge of Brahman ought to arise immediately after the desire for liberation—is precisely this. Thus, the previously mentioned position is more sound. The sense is that, compared to the status of being the object of injunction (*vidheya*) for that which is implied by the meanings of the root and the suffix, it is more appropriate for the meaning of the root itself to be the object of injunction.
(This concludes the refutation of Yādavaprakāśa’s interpretation of the Sūtra.)

"Because it is independent of the refutation of *pradhāna* and so forth. This means: because it is independent of the refutation of the status of *pradhāna* and so forth as objects of inquiry (*jijñāsya*) by way of refuting *pradhāna* and so forth. Consequently, the point is that the refutation of the status of *pradhāna* and so forth as objects of inquiry—by way of refuting *pradhāna* and so forth—is fruitless, as it is not required for the inquiry [into Brahman].
(The description according to the Vṛttikāra)

"Immediately after the knowledge of action derived from the *bhāṣya* and the *vṛtti*. It should be understood that the ablative case is employed by accepting the word *anantara* as a directional term (*dik-śabda*) synonymous with the word *paścāt* (after). "The treatise concerning that [Self] is called the *Śārīraka*. It is called *Śārīraka* because it describes the embodied Self (*śārīra*). [The root] *ke* means "to sound. The form is derived from the rule "the suffix *ka* follows a verbal root ending in *a*, provided no upasarga precedes it. Regarding the fact that the *Mīmāṃsā* constitutes a single unified work:
