If this were so, then since grammar, astronomy, and the like would have a single purpose—namely, the capacity to assist the Veda—and thus possess a unity of object, there would follow the undesirable consequence that they too would constitute a single auxiliary limb (*aṅga*), because mutual expectancy exists when their respective purposes are being accomplished. Nor should it be argued that their unity as auxiliaries is not desired; for if that were the case, here too there would be unity by virtue of being "Mīmāṃsā," but not unity of scripture (*śāstra*). To this we say: no, for if that were true, such a counter-argument would lead to the consequence that even the distinction between the first and second hexads (*ṣaṭka*) would result in a lack of scriptural division.

Nor should it be argued that there is unity [of the inquiry] because the subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), and qualified person (*adhikārin*) are identical here as well—just as in the case of the common introductory statement, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*)—since here too the subject matter in the form of the meaning of the Veda, the purpose in the form of knowledge thereof, and the qualified person desiring that [knowledge] are one and the same; and because a common introductory statement that underlies both inquiries will be established later. [Objection: But is it not improper to claim that "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) is a common introductory statement?

If that were the case, the word *atha* would not have the meaning of "immediacy following the inquiry into ritual action" (*karmavicārānantarya*), which would result in the fallacy expressed by the maxim: "He who desires the growth [of the branches] incurs the loss of the root. For immediacy following the inquiry into ritual action is not possible for the twenty-chapter Mīmāṃsā as a whole, but only for the four-chapter [Pūrva-mīmāṃsā]; it is with this underlying intention that he says, "Or rather," and explains: "It follows both [types of] dharma, being common to each."

The meaning is that the "balancing of the counter-argument" (*pratidharmasama*) fallacy occurs when a counter-proposition is established by following either the same class (*sajātīya*) or the opposite class (*vijātīya*) based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). The balancing of the counter-argument is of two kinds: that based on similarity (*sādharmyasama*) and that based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyasama*).

In this regard, in the sūtra enumerating the divisions of *jātis* (futile rejoinders), the specific types have been enumerated as follows: "Similarity (*sādharmya*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), superiority (*utkarṣa*), inferiority (*apakarṣa*), verbal similarity (*vākchala*), non-verbal similarity (*sarvachala*), [the fallacies of] alternative (*vikalpa*), the goal (*sādhya*), attainment (*prāpti*), non-attainment (*aprāpti*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*), the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), non-arising (*anutpatti*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), the topic under discussion (*prakaraṇa*), the reason (*hetu*), implication (*arthāpatti*), non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), occurrence (*upapatti*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), permanence (*nitya*), impermanence (*anitya*), and the [fallacies of] exhaustion (*kāryasama*). Immediately following that, it says: "When a conclusion is drawn through similarity or dissimilarity, the two [futile rejoinders] based on similarity and dissimilarity arise because of the application of the opposite of those properties. Thus, the enumeration of the specific types has been made.

The meaning is that the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* pertains only to the two specific [cases]. Now, one might object: "An inquiry into the meaning of the Veda should not be undertaken immediately after its study, because its meaning is not intended to be expressed. To refute this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) which applies to the entire Vedic corpus, the sūtra "Then, therefore, the desire to know the meaning of the Veda" (*athāto vedārthajijñāsā*) ought to have been composed; thus, a specific proposition with such a limited purpose is improper.

In the case of the *jāti* known as *sādharmya-vaidharmya-sama*, however, since the general proposition (*pratijñā*) serves merely to focus the student’s intellect and there is no prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) to be refuted, there is no fault even if it is [merely] implied; for this reason, with a sense of dissatisfaction, he says: "Or rather, [the definition is] simply 'Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma'. [He explains: "The means to supermundane welfare" means that which has the status of being a means to welfare cognizable solely through the Veda. But, one might object, in this way, would it not follow that even the *śyena* sacrifice and others would be considered Dharma?

Nor should it be argued that its exclusion [from being *adharma*] is due to its distinction from that [i.e., *adharma*] by virtue of not producing a powerful undesirable result; for if that were the case, it would follow that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is *adharma*, since He is the cause of all things. If this is said, it is not so. For if that were the case, the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others would not be *dharma*, because—as in the statement "The *jyotiṣṭoma* [is prescribed] for all [desires]"—it is a means for attaining all fruits, and thus, by way of being a means for the destruction of enemies, it would produce a powerful undesirable result. It is indeed accepted that when performed with the destruction of enemies as its fruit, it lacks the status of *dharma*.

If it is argued that only the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice—which is not delimited by a performance resulting in fruits such as the ruin of enemies—is a *dharma*, then in that case, since the Brāhmaṇa [caste] is not a category of things to be performed, it is possible even for a Brāhmaṇa to possess the status of being a means to a non-worldly good (*alaukika-śreyaḥ-sādhana*) while being undelimited by a performance associated with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavad-an-iṣṭānubandhi*). Therefore, the intention is that the general proposition is simply "the inquiry into *dharma*" (*dharmajijñāsā*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "How can those things which are accessible to the senses possess the nature of *dharma*? Anticipating this, he says: "Even though they are perceptible by the senses" (*teṣām aindriyakatve 'pi*). The phrase "by that very form" (*tādrūpyeṇa*) means "in the form of being perceptible by the senses. But, one might object: "By asserting that the word *dharma* is common to both [types of *dharma*] and thus proposing an investigation into two kinds of *dharma*, you cannot claim that only one of them is present in the mind."

Therefore, since the statement of the definition of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the *Codanāsūtra* does not serve as a restrictive rule for this [definition], he says "by virtue of being apprehended in the prior portion" out of dissatisfaction with that view. Intending to show that even a specific proposition (*viśeṣapratijñā*) is necessary, he says "either by way of the treatise (*tantra*) or by implication (*arthataḥ*). The phrase "with the desire to ward off the suspicion that it is merely verbal" means that the intention is to justify the established linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). [He says] "because its nature as worship of the Supreme Self is not understood."

Nor should it be argued that, just as there is no contradiction with the primacy of the verbal expression even when the servant-hood of the king’s man (rājapuruṣa) is understood from the term "king’s man" because the person is perceived as the substantive, so too there is no contradiction with the primacy of the verbal expression when the nature of the action as being the propitiation of the Supreme Self is understood, because the action appears as the substantive; for here, "primacy of the verbal expression" means not being perceived as subordinate to anything else.

Nor should it be suspected that this [qualification] does not apply to the term *rājapuruṣa* (king’s man), because in reality, when the *puruṣa* is understood from the word *puruṣa* [as part of the compound], its application is justified. Some, however, say: "He states another argument: 'because there is no comprehension of it being of the nature of propitiation of the Supreme Self.'"

Is it not the case that, just as in the usage of the word *dharma* in passages such as "the eternal *dharma* which is Kṛṣṇa," there is—similar to the superimposition of grace (*prasāda*) characterized by a distinction from well-known grace consisting of a physical form upon the king who bows down, namely, "this grace has taken on a physical form"—and similar to the superimposition of *dharma*-ness characterized by a distinction from well-known *dharma* consisting of a physical body upon Rāma, namely, "Rāma is *dharma* incarnate"?

There is no lack of restriction regarding the power of words [to denote a specific meaning] in the case of a statement belonging to the Purāṇas—such as "He whom they call Indra, whom they call Varuṇa," which is consistent with its intended purpose of superimposing the nature of Dharma characterized by its distinction from the well-known Dharma whose form is eternality; for such a statement is like the aphorism "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*), whose sole purpose is to determine the meaning of the word "Dharma" under investigation.

Or, let it be granted that the *Brahmasūtras* are common [to both systems]; nevertheless, since Jaimini has proposed an inquiry into both types of dharma, the *Brahmasūtras* ought to have been composed by him as well. Indeed, one cannot even imagine an obstacle for such a great sage. As for the hypothesis that he desisted upon seeing his own teacher, Bādarāyaṇa, desiring to compose the *Brahmasūtras*, that is not tenable due to a lack of evidence and because no such popular tradition is observed. For these reasons, the author says "even though" (*yadyapi*), expressing a sense of dissatisfaction with the previous view. This refers to those who have not heard the Vedānta.

The point is this: if one performs ritual action for the sake of pleasing deities such as Vāyu, since those deities are perishable, they might perish even before they can bestow the fruit upon one who has been pleased by the rites; thus, those who have not heard the Vedānta might develop a lack of faith in ritual action due to the thought that it is fruitless. However, for those who have heard the Vedānta, there is no such doubt, because the inner controller (antaryāmī) of each respective deity—who is the one to be propitiated by each specific rite and who bestows fruits according to the action—is eternal, persisting through all kalpas.

Or rather, [it refers] to those who have not heard the Vedānta; the word "even" (api) is to be supplied. The meaning is that even for those who are not dispassionate, there would be a lack of faith in ritual action. For this very reason, he will say later: "for those other than those free from passion, regarding the Agnihotra and so forth," and so on.

Now, one might object: "If [Bādarāyaṇa] was refuting the corporeal form of the deities and so forth with such great effort while lacking any intent regarding them, then why would the principle of 'not-censuring what is not intended' (*na-hi-nindā-nyāya*) not apply even to Bādarāyaṇa when he establishes the corporeal form of the deities? Anticipating this unease, [the author] says: "Alternatively, [it is because of his] excessive intent toward the authority of the Veda and the necessity of performing ritual actions. For if the corporeal form of the deities existed, the lack of authority of the Veda would follow, according to the method stated in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (Cūḍānikā) beginning with the sūtra, "If it be argued that there is a contradiction regarding ritual action" (*virodhaḥ karmaṇīti cet*).

Furthermore, since the ritual action (*karman*) is subordinate to the deity because it is intended for the deity’s gratification, and since the action lacks the capacity to produce the fruit [independently], what essentiality of the action would even be lost? Therefore, the sense is this: if Jaimini, out of an extreme devotion to the authority of the Veda and the necessity of ritual action, cast but a slight glance toward the refutation of the deity’s embodied form (*vigraha*), what harm is there? This is as stated in the *Rātrisatra* [Adhikaraṇa].

In the fourth [book of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā], it is established that when the *rātrisatra* sacrifice—produced by the injunction "Light, a cow, long life"—is in need of a fruit, it is more appropriate to simply assume that "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*), which is provided by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "Those who perform these nights indeed become established," serves as its fruit through a modification of meaning; however, one should not, according to the logic of the *viśvajit* sacrifice, assume the nature of heaven itself and then assume that as its fruit.

And thus, by that very same principle, the sense is that there is also intentional meaning (*tātparya*) regarding the corporeal forms of deities and so forth mentioned in the *arthavāda* passages. Therefore, it is established that "the property belonging to that [original] should be extended (*atideṣṭavya*) to this [modified case]. This refers to the second section of the eighth chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], namely: "That which has its mark [is the deity], because of its connection with the purpose, like the name. It does not apply here to the substance and the deity.

Is it not the case that there exists the sūtra: "In the event of a conflict, [the procedure] shall be determined by the offering material (*havis*), because the ritual action is designated by that"? When this sūtra is present, [it means]: "Wherever there is a conflict between the similarity of the material and the deity—for instance, in the case of the *aindra-puroḍāśa*, where there is similarity of deity [with the *sānnāyya*], the procedure of the *sānnāyya* would apply, and there is similarity of material [with the *puroḍāśa*], the procedure of the *puroḍāśa* would apply—it is precisely by relying on the similarity of the material that the restrictive rule (*niyama*) proceeds."

Why? Because the sacrificial offering (*havis*) is perceived in the ritual action. Since the ritual action known as sacrifice—which consists of the act of relinquishment—is perceived in the sacrificial offering, and because the sacrificial offering is seen as that which is being relinquished, such similarity [of the new rite] with the model rite is required by virtue of the substance being an internal factor. For when searching for a similarity based on the injunctions regarding the word and its meaning, it is precisely the internal similarity that is required; thus, it is established that in the case of the *aindra-puroḍāśa*, only the procedural details (*vidhyanta*) of the *āgneya* sacrifice apply, and not the procedural details of the *aindra-sānnāyya*.

If it is argued that [the distinction] is not based on the perceptibility or imperceptibility of the substance and the deity, let it be so; for even that point is to be accepted because it does not contradict the meaning already stated. "For the purpose of refuting the contrary position" means for the purpose of refuting [claims such as] the lack of authority of the Vedas.
(This concludes the section determining the sequence between the Mīmāṃsā of Ritual Action and the Mīmāṃsā of Brahman.)

Why should there not be an investigation of the *brāhmaṇas* prior to the second chapter? Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that, just as the validity [of the Vedas] established in the first chapter (*prathama-lakṣaṇa*) is a prerequisite (*upajīvya*), so too are the means of differentiation such as 'difference in words' (*śabdāntara*) and others, as well as 'direct statement' (*śruti*) and 'indicative mark' (*liṅga*) mentioned in the chapters on difference (*bheda-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, equally prerequisites? How then can this objection be raised? If it is argued: "In this treatise, for the purpose of establishing the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all Vedāntas with Brahman, only the introductory indicators (*upakrama*, etc. need to be known, not the direct statements, indicative marks, and so forth," [we reply: No, because direct statements, indicative marks, and the rest must be relied upon for the purpose of unfolding the meaning of those introductory indicators.

Indeed, it is not possible to determine that "the opening statement concerns Brahman" without perceiving such things as the direct mention of Brahman (*brāhma-abhidhāna-śruti*) and so forth. Nor can it be said on this basis alone that only direct mention, indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth are useful for the harmonious interpretation (*samanvaya*), while the opening statement and other factors are not; for even among direct mention and the rest, the knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) depends upon the context (*prakaraṇa*) and the indicative marks of intention such as the opening statement. For context is indeed the statement of the principal subject matter together with its expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*); and the determination of what constitutes the principal subject matter is to be ascertained through the indicative marks of intention.

Furthermore, in those passages where there is a conflict between *brāhma* (direct scriptural statement) and *liṅga* (indicative mark), the superiority of the *brāhma* must be determined by the *liṅgas* of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), such as the opening context (*upakrama*) and so forth; thus, both the *śruti-liṅga* group and the *upakrama-ādi* group are required. Nor is there a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*) between the *upakrama-ādi* and the *śruti-liṅga-ādi*. There is no fault in this mutual dependence because their spheres of application differ: the *śruti-liṅga-ādi* are required for the establishment of the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the *upakrama-ādi*, while the *upakrama-ādi* are required for determining their relative strength (*balābala*).

Therefore, since direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth must indeed be relied upon, and because those [means] exist even prior to the third chapter for that purpose, there is no reason at all for the doubt that [the discussion of these means] should occur before the second chapter, nor for its refutation.

Now, even if the Vedas and other means of knowledge are dependent [on the Mīmāṃsā] in the manner described, there is no need for the *Pūrvatantra* (the prior system) for the sake of understanding them; for here itself—in the sūtras such as "The abode of heaven, earth, etc., [is Brahman] because of its own word," "Ether [is Brahman] because of its characteristic mark," "And likewise because of the connection within a single sentence," and "Because of the context"—there is the possibility of comprehending the nature of the Vedas and so forth, and in the sūtra "And there is no sublation because of the greater strength of the Vedas and so forth," there is the comprehension of the relative strength of the Vedas and other means of knowledge.

For in that regard, no definition of *śruti* and the other means of proof has been stated. In some places, a definition for mere syntactical unity (*vākyaikya*) alone has been stated: "A single sentence consists of a single purpose, provided that if it were divided, there would be mutual expectancy. However, those definitions which have been stated by the commentators on that [topic] are not useful. To explain:

It has been stated that the definition of *śruti* (verbal testimony) is "an independent utterance. However, this is unestablished in all cases, because [words] depend upon the recollection of their expressive power (*śakti*) and so forth. If it is argued that what is intended is independence from the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of other words, we say no; for even though the word "he" (*saḥ*), when employed on a smoky mountain, depends upon the intervention of inference, it would follow as an absurd consequence that any word—even one that provides a logical mark (*liṅga*)—would be *śruti* with respect to the object possessing that mark (*liṅgin*), simply by virtue of its independence from the co-utterance of other words.

Furthermore, in the section beginning with "He is known from the word alone" (*śabdādeva pramitaḥ*), regarding the subject sentence "The Person is the size of a thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣaḥ*), there would be the undesirable consequence that this is not a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) because it would depend on the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the term "thumb-sized" to convey that the Supreme Self is measured by a thumb, [rather than being conveyed by the word "Lord" (*īśāna*) itself].

If you argue that the word *īśāna*, which denotes the Supreme Self, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *aṅguṣṭhamātra* (thumb-sized), ultimately results in the cognition of the substrate (*dharmin*) as being measured by the size of a thumb, and thus possesses independence in making that substrate known—just as in the case of "He sprinkles the rice grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), where the accusative case ending denoting the most desired object of the action, through its coreferentiality with the word *prokṣati*, results in the cognition of the mere action as being characterized by sprinkling—then [we reply]: [Consider] "Space [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark" (*ākāśastalliṅgāt*).

Thus, regarding the scriptural passage under discussion, in the statement "Space (*ākāśa*) is indeed greater than these," the word *jyāyas* (greater), through its co-occurrence with the word *ākāśa*, results in a reference to the entity that is actually space; since there is no requirement for it to indicate anything beyond the mere subject (*dharmin*), it follows that if this very space were to be proven to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it would result in [the objection that] it would constitute a direct scriptural authority (*śruti*).

Likewise, even the definition of a mark (*liṅga*) as the capacity of a thing (*vastusāmarthya*) is not applicable; for the marks consisting of the unique attributes of Brahman—such as unsurpassed bliss and so forth—which are described in the passage "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition" (*ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt*), lack the nature of being a mark in the sense of the capacity of a thing. Furthermore, it is quite clear that the *prakaraṇa* (context) defined in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā as "the expectancy for a procedure" (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) is not useful for the inquiry into Brahman, because Brahman, being an established entity (*siddharūpa*), is devoid of any expectancy for a procedure.

However, no single, inclusive definition of the characteristic of *sthāna*—consisting of proximity (*saṃnidhi*) and numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) as stated in the *Pūrvatantra*—is observed here. Furthermore, the claim that "designation (*samākhyā*) is an etymological name" is not tenable; for while names such as the *hotṛ-camasa* exist in the *Pūrvatantra*, and names such as the *brāhmī-vidyā* (mentioned in this scripture in passages like "He [attained] the Brāhmī-vidyā, the foundation of all knowledge"), might possibly qualify as designations, names such as *ādhvaryava* and *audgātra* do not.

If it is argued that because the form of a word accepted [by the opponent] consists of a collection of base and suffix, it cannot possibly possess the status of *samākhyā* (name/designation) as a single unitary word, and therefore, since the *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth found therein are not required here, nothing beyond the definition of the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) is required—then [we reply]: [This is not so. For even if a word is composed of a collection of base and suffix, its status as a single word is established by convention (*saṃketa*), just as the status of a single substance is established for a jar or the like. Furthermore, the status of a single word is not denied to a compound (*samāsa*) consisting of multiple words, such as "Devadatta" or "Pācaka," which are well-known in the world as single words. Moreover, the status of a single word is not denied to a sentence (*vākya*) consisting of multiple words, such as "Bring the cow," which is well-known in the world as a single sentence. Therefore, since the status of a single word is established through convention, there is no contradiction in the fact that the *samākhyā* is a single word. Consequently, the *samākhyā* is indeed a distinct means of proof from the others. Thus, the conclusion is that the *samākhyā* is a separate means of proof. This concludes the section on *samākhyā*. Now begins the section on the relative strength and weakness of the means of proof. Among these, the relative strength and weakness of the six means of proof—*śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, *prakaraṇa*, *sthāna*, and *samākhyā*—will be explained. First, regarding *śruti*: *Śruti* is the direct denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) of a word. It is of three kinds: *vidhi-śruti*, *niyama-śruti*, and *parisaṃkhyā-śruti*. Among these, *vidhi-śruti* is the direct denotative power of a word that enjoins what has not been previously established. *Niyama-śruti* is the direct denotative power of a word that restricts to a specific instance what is otherwise optional. *Parisaṃkhyā-śruti* is the direct denotative power of a word that excludes one alternative when two or more are possible. An example of *vidhi-śruti* is: "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. An example of *niyama-śruti* is: "One should perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). An example of *parisaṃkhyā-śruti* is: "One should eat only five fruits. Here, although the eating of other fruits is already implied, the mention of "only five fruits" serves to exclude the eating of other fruits. Now, among these, *vidhi-śruti* is stronger than *niyama-śruti* and *parisaṃkhyā-śruti*. Why? Because *niyama* and *parisaṃkhyā* involve the assumption of many unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*). Specifically, in the case of *niyama*, one must assume both the production of an unseen result from the restriction and the non-production of an unseen result from the non-restriction. In the case of *parisaṃkhyā*, one must assume both the production of an unseen result from the exclusion and the non-production of an unseen result from the non-exclusion. However, in the case of *vidhi*, only the production of an unseen result from the performance of the enjoined act needs to be assumed. Therefore, *vidhi-śruti* is stronger than *niyama-śruti* and *parisaṃkhyā-śruti*. Furthermore, *niyama-śruti* is stronger than *parisaṃkhyā-śruti*. Why? Because in *parisaṃkhyā*, one must assume the aforementioned fourfold unseen results, whereas in *niyama*, only the two-fold unseen results need to be assumed. Therefore, *niyama-śruti* is stronger than *parisaṃkhyā-śruti*. Now, regarding *liṅga*: *Liṅga* is the indicative power (*sāmarthya*) of a word. It is of two kinds: *sāmānya-liṅga* and *viśeṣa-liṅga*. Among these, *sāmānya-liṅga* is the indicative power of a word that indicates a general connection. *Viśeṣa-liṅga* is the indicative power of a word that indicates a specific connection. An example of *sāmānya-liṅga* is the word "juhvati" in the passage: "He offers oblations with the *juhū* ladle. Here, the word "juhvati" indicates the general connection between the *juhū* and the offering of oblations. An example of *viśeṣa-liṅga* is the word "pṛṣadājyena" in the passage: "He sprinkles with speckled butter. Here, the word "pṛṣadājyena" indicates the specific connection between the speckled butter and the sprinkling. Now, *viśeṣa-liṅga* is stronger than *sāmānya-liṅga*. Why? Because *sāmānya-liṅga* requires the assumption of a further word to establish the specific connection, whereas *viśeṣa-liṅga* establishes the specific connection directly. Therefore, *viśeṣa-liṅga* is stronger than *sāmānya-liṅga*. Now, regarding *vākya*: *Vākya* is the syntactic unity (*ekārthībhāva*) of words. It is of two kinds: *sāmānya-vākya* and *viśeṣa-vākya*. Among these, *sāmānya-vākya* is the syntactic unity of words that expresses a general meaning. *Viśeṣa-vākya* is the syntactic unity of words that expresses a specific meaning. An example of *sāmānya-vākya* is the passage: "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; one should offer the *āghāra* libations. Here, the syntactic unity of the two sentences expresses the general connection between the *āghāra* libations and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. An example of *viśeṣa-vākya* is the passage: "One should sprinkle with speckled butter at the *upāṃśuyāja*. Here, the syntactic unity of the two words expresses the specific connection between the speckled butter and the *upāṃśuyāja*. Now, *viśeṣa-vākya* is stronger than *sāmānya-vākya*. Why? Because *sāmānya-vākya* requires the assumption of a further word to establish the specific connection, whereas *viśeṣa-vākya* establishes the specific connection directly. Therefore, *viśeṣa-vākya* is stronger than *sāmānya-vākya*. Now, regarding *prakaraṇa*: *Prakaraṇa* is the context (*prakriyā*) of a ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*). It is of two kinds: *mahāprakaraṇa* and *avāntaraprakaraṇa*. Among these, *mahāprakaraṇa* is the context of the primary ritual (*pradhāna*). *Avāntaraprakaraṇa* is the context of a subordinate ritual (*aṅga*). An example of *mahāprakaraṇa* is the context of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. An example of *avāntaraprakaraṇa* is the context of the *prayāja* offerings. Now, *avāntaraprakaraṇa* is stronger than *mahāprakaraṇa*. Why? Because *mahāprakaraṇa* requires the assumption of a further word to establish the connection with the subordinate ritual, whereas *avāntaraprakaraṇa* establishes that connection directly. Therefore, *avāntaraprakaraṇa* is stronger than *mahāprakaraṇa*. Now

In that case, [the author] establishes the authority of the Veda with the sūtra, "And for this very reason, its eternity"; the authority of the mantras and arthavādas—which proves the existence of the capacity required as a cause for eligibility for knowledge by establishing the corporeal nature of the deities through mantras and arthavādas—with the sūtra, "Bādarāyaṇa [holds that there is] even beyond that [the world of Brahman], because it is possible"; and the authority of the Smṛtis and so forth—with the sūtra, "If it be said that [the world] is from the Word, we say no, because of its origination [from Brahman], as is known from perception and inference."

Furthermore, since the validity of the *Smṛtis* and other such texts is established by one who employs the term "inference" (*anumāna*) with the sense of "that which leads to the inference of [the meaning of] the *Śruti*" as its basis for application, even the definition of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) would not need to be relied upon. If it is argued: "In the *Pūrvatantra*, the establishment of the validity of the Vedas and so forth is clearly presented through the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), whereas here there is no such clear understanding," we reply: because a specific understanding can be attained through the [author's] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).

If it is argued that it has been stated, "The specific meaning is understood from the explanation; for a rule is not invalid due to doubt," and this is true, [the response is as follows]: Even though there is a disparity among the *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth mentioned therein, as well as among the respective [means of proof], there is no disparity regarding their authority (*prāmāṇya*). Thus, even while relying on the authority established there explicitly (*kaṇṭharaveṇa*), the objection arises: why should the consideration of the *brāhmaṇa* passages not occur prior to the second [section] (*dvitīya*) given the disparity among *śruti* and the rest? Therefore, there is no inconsistency; this is the intended meaning. (The Definition of the Injunction to Study).

Regarding the statement that the knowledge of the Self has grain and the like as its means: if it is argued that it would be more appropriate to say that the knowledge of the Self becomes subsidiary (śeṣa) by way of the Self only when the Self itself is subsidiary to ritual action—and not conversely, that the Self becomes subsidiary when the knowledge of the Self is subsidiary by way of the Self—the answer is no. In the phrase "in the state of being subsidiary to ritual action" (*karmaśeṣatve*), the locative case denotes a causal condition (*nimitta-saptamī*), as in the expression "one kills the leopard for its skin. The word *sati* here carries the sense of "being fittingly so" (*sāmīcīnya*).

If the self were appropriately a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) by way of being an instrument (*dvāra*), then the self’s status as a subordinate element would be properly established. "Appropriateness" (*sāmīcīnya*) regarding the state of being a subordinate element means being an integral constituent (*saṃnipātitva*). Therefore, the sense is that if the knowledge of the self were a subordinate element of ritual action, its appropriate subordinacy—characterized by being an integral constituent—would be established by way of the self, just as the sprinkling of rice is [established] by way of the rice grains. "Since it is possible for the self to function as an instrument" means that its possibility of functioning as an instrument exists by virtue of its being something to be refined (*saṃskāryatayā*).

If it is argued that "let there be subsidiarity (śeṣatva) on account of the bestowing of the fruit," one should not say: "In this way, because the deity, like the ritual act, would be a bestower of the fruit, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of equal status and equal primacy. For it is logically consistent [that the deity is subordinate], just as acts such as shaving the beard—which exist for the purpose of the enjoyer—do not possess equal status with the sacrifice and are thus subsidiary to it.

Even if one adopts the reading, "let there be the status of being the remainder (śeṣitva) by virtue of bestowing the fruit," it should be understood that just as acts such as shaving the beard—which serve the purpose of the enjoyer who is the remainder of the sacrifice—are consistent with being auxiliary to the sacrifice, so too are those [acts] which serve the Supreme Self who is the remainder of the sacrifice consistent with being auxiliary to the sacrifice; however, this does not apply to activities such as looking at books. The Bhaṭṭas have stated that there is a rule of study (adhyayana-niyama) for the sake of knowing the meaning; but that has been rejected by the Guru (Prabhākara) through the refutation of the desire for knowledge of the meaning.

The sense is that, according to our own view, regarding the rule for Vedic study (*adhyayana*) for the purpose of grasping the syllables (*akṣara-grahaṇa*), since there is the possibility of a desire to grasp the syllables—characterized by the capacity for independent pronunciation—and since there is no other [eligible] subject to be excluded (*vyāvartya*) due to the existence of other means, the status of this as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) must be set aside. This is said "provided that it is subsidiary to study through the medium of initiation (*upanayana*)."

Nor should it be argued that the eighth year, intended by the word "first," does not serve as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) toward study even by way of being its substratum (*ādhāra*). For [the rule]—"Having performed the *upākarma* on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months"—prescribes [study] at a specific time devoid of the restriction of being within the eighth year; whereas [the rule], "One should observe the student-life (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years regarding one Veda... prescribes it within that [specific period].

Since it is impossible for the study—which is to be accomplished over many years—as stated in the rule "or every twelve [years] for all," to have the eighth year as its constituent part (*aṅga*), it is established that it must be the initiation (*upanayana*) itself that has the eighth year as its constituent part. Consequently, by indicating the time that is a constituent part of the initiation as if it were a constituent part of the study through figurative usage (*upacāra*), the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*) makes known that there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate between initiation and study; for the time is subordinate to the study by way of the initiation.

The sense is that the priority of study—which has initiation (*upanayana*) as its constituent part—established at the eighth year is thereby proven. And because it is prescribed by a sūtra concerning what is not intended for the agent; the word "of the ātmanepada" is to be supplied. The sūtra concerning what is not intended for the agent is the sūtra beginning with "honoring" (*saṃmānana*). [This refers to] the injunction regarding the constituent parts of study.

[Objection: Since the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has a visible purpose, it is improper to assume an invisible one; therefore, study consists merely in repeating what the teacher utters and is not independent. Thus, the fact that study must be preceded by a teacher is established by implication. Consequently, since the requirement of being preceded by a teacher is already established, it need not be enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of study by this sentence; so how can this be an injunction regarding a subordinate element of study? [Reply: This is not so. [For it is said: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa boy at eight years of age..."

In the injunction "one should teach him," since teaching is prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), if the injunction were to enjoin study itself—just as the injunction "one should sacrifice" enjoins the act of sacrificing—then initiation (*upanayana*) would be established as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that [study] due to its being mentioned in syntactic proximity (*samabhivyāhāra*) with it. In the absence of that [proximity], however, because one would not understand that initiation is enjoined as a subordinate element of study by the statement "one should initiate [the boy]," it would follow that initiation is enjoined for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Consequently, study would also result in being independent.

And thus, the sense is that the word "should teach" (*adhyāpayet*) is required [as a complement]. Alternatively, the sense is that just as the injunction "One should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*) possesses the status of an injunction because it prescribes a sacrifice obtainable through the implication of the sentence "He draws the cup for Indra and Vāyu" (*aindravāyavaṃ gṛhṇāti*), so too the phrase "should teach" possesses the status of an injunction because it prescribes the necessity of being preceded by a teacher, which is obtainable through the implication of the injunction regarding initiation (*upanayana*).

Although the form "adhyāpayīta" is indeed written in the Mīmāṃsā texts, here the Vedic form "adhyāpayet" is written; nevertheless, this very reading is more appropriate as it accords with the rule *budhayudhanaśajaneṅ*. Regarding the phrase "by the mention of the suffix -ktavatu [in the word] 'upanayana'": the sense is that, just as in the case of "having performed the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," the mention of the suffix -ktavatu indicates the identity of the agent, and from that, the identity of the performance is understood, whereby the relationship of subsidiary (*aṅga*) and principal (*aṅgin*) is established.

The sense is that its status as an internal factor (*antaraṅgatva*) is established by direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*). Since the fact that the *upanayana* sacrament pertains to the student (*māṇavaka*) is established by the direct second-case ending [in the word "māṇavakam"], and since study is fixed upon him, it follows that its status as an internal factor—consisting in being fixed upon that sacrament—is established by direct revelation. Therefore, it is not logical for it to be a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of teaching.

The point is that if [the action] were subordinate to the act of teaching (*adhyāpana*), the fruit of the action would reside in the agent; consequently, the *ātmanepada* ending would be established by the rule "svaritañitaḥ" alone, and thus this [present rule] would be redundant. "For the purpose of prohibiting the restriction thereof" means: since the *ātmanepada* would not apply when the fruit does not go to the agent due to the restrictive rule "only when [the fruit] goes to the agent," the present rule effects its removal. The meaning is that the *ātmanepada* is thereby obtained.

Regarding the statement, "one should choose the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*)," someone has argued that the form *vṛṇīte* must derive only from the root *vṛṅ* (meaning "to choose"), and not from any other, because there is no mention of the *ñi*-class [root *vṛñ*] in the list of roots for the *śnā*-affix. Consequently, they claim that the rule *svarita* does not apply here, and thus the desired result is not established. That is incorrect.

(Regarding the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing," because it is also listed with the *śnā*-affix): Although the verbal root "vṛñ varaṇe" (to choose) is not listed in the *dhātuvṛtti* under the *kyṛ*-class (*divādi*), it is nevertheless listed in the *Kalpadruma* as "vṛ gna vṛñ vṛtau. It is this very root that is intended here. This is because the form occurs precisely from that root, as "vṛñ varaṇe" is listed in the *kyṛ*-class (specifically the *svādi* sub-class) with a long vowel (*vṝñ*), and the formation of that particular form is possible only from that source. Now, one might object that the root "vṛṅ saṃbhaktau" (to desire, to seek) is more appropriate here; for "saṃbhakti" indeed means "prayer" or "requesting."

For this very reason, in examples such as *avadyapaṇyavaryāḥ*, *etistuśāsvṛ*, and *īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ*, the authors of the Vṛtti and others have cited only the root *vṛṅ* (in the sense of "to choose") regarding the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, if you argue that the application of the rule *svaritañitaḥ* is not applicable here, and that its application would result in exactly what is desired, that may be true; however, it is possible to demonstrate the undesirable consequence of the absence of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in common usage when the word is employed with the intention of "choosing" (*varaṇa*) rather than "choosing for the sake of service" (*saṃbhakti*). Consequently, even in the case of officiating priests, by virtue of being chosen...

The intended meaning is that [the *ātmanepada* suffix] occurs because there is the possibility of a result consisting of the form of the fire’s consecration (*agni-saṃskāra*). Regarding the phrase "intervened by the consecration of the fire": the meaning is that if the consecration of the fire were not intervened [by another action], the *ātmanepada* would not occur, because [in that case] the agent would not be connected with the result. "The connection with the result is not intervened for the agent of the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) rite. Consequently, the application of the rule beginning with "svarita" (Pāṇini 1.3.72) occurs only when the non-intervened result belongs to the agent. Here, the non-intervened result—consisting of the fire characterized by the consecration—belongs precisely to the agent of the *ādhāna*; thus, the *ātmanepada* is justified by the rule beginning with "svarita. This is the intended meaning.

"Because the object is connected with a fruit that is not common [to others]. The meaning is this: if the fruit of an action is primary and accrues to the agent—that is, if the fruit for which the action is undertaken belongs to the agent who is expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), then the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) occurs. For this very reason, it does not occur in cases such as "the priests sacrifice" (*yajanti yājakāḥ*) or "the cooks cook" (*pacanti pācakāḥ*). Although in these instances the fruit of the agent exists in the form of sacrificial fees and wages, there is no fault, because the undertaking of the action is not for the sake of those fruits.

The meaning is that this is established exactly as such in the section of the eleventh chapter [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*], which states: "Because actions are subordinate to a purpose, their completion through direct perception [of the result] constitutes their finality," as in the case of the injunction "one threshes the rice."

"The *saktu-homa* (grain-offering) is like the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person. The sense is this: just as roasted grains (*saktu*), being devoid of utility for either a past or future purpose, cannot be the object of the *saṃskāra* of the *homa*, and thus—due to the absence of the *saktu-homa* being a subordinate action (*guṇakarma*)—it is a principal action (*pradhānakarma*); so it is here. It should be understood that the statement regarding the "refinement of the person" is made with this intention. For while the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is understood to be the object of the action, the person is not. Although the view held by the Prābhākaras—that the act of study is an "action for the sake of another" (*arthakarma*)—is precisely what must be refuted; [nevertheless, the present argument proceeds on the basis of their position].

But it does not have the nature of a *puruṣasaṃskāra* (a refinement of the person), because that has not been stated by others. Nor should it be argued that if study lacks the nature of a *svādhyāyasaṃskāra* (a refinement of the Veda), it would necessarily follow that it is a *puruṣasaṃskāra*, since there is no possible form that is excluded from both categories; for even in the case of optional rites such as the *prayāja*s—which are devoid of the status of *guṇakarma* (subordinate acts)—there is an absence of the status of *puruṣasaṃskāra*. Thus, the intent is merely to exclude the status of *pradhānakarma* (principal act). Furthermore, it is incorrect to conclude that [study] results in mere attainment (*prāpyatva*).

And this is not the case with Vedic injunctions; for even in the instance "he milks the milk," there is no undesirable consequence of the milk being a subordinate object of purification (*saṃskārya*), because in that case too, the status of being a *saṃskārya* is accepted since the invisible merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by the restrictive rule of filling [the vessel] is admitted.

Therefore, the sense is that the acquisition of the Vedas through study—which, when there is a desire to recite one's own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*), consists in grasping the collection of syllables that produces firm impressions regarding the objects of knowledge—namely the strings of letters, words, and sentences characterized by an uninterrupted flow of memory and accompanied by mastery over the places of articulation such as the palate and the head for unerring pronunciation—is the acceptance of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the *svādhyāya* produced by the rules governing that study. This is illustrated in the case of the injunction, "Gold should be worn."

The sense is that in the third [chapter], it was established that wearing golden ornaments serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Regarding the phrase "acceptance by the opponent," the meaning is "acceptance by the adversary. As for the statement "even though it is understood from the natural force of the suffix in such cases as *saktūn juhoti* (he offers groats)," one might object: "In the case of *maitrāvaruṇāya daṇḍaṃ prayacchati* (he gives a staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa), just as in the case of the undesired (*anīpsita*) according to the rule *tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam*, the accusative case will apply to the object; why then resort to a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*)? To this, we reply: No.

For in that case, the consecration (*saṃskāra*) belongs to the staff by means of the act of giving, and not to the giving by means of the staff as its instrument. Here, however, there is a new transcendental result (*apūrva*) produced by the oblation (*homa*) which has groats (*saktu*) as its instrument, and not by the groats themselves acting as the objects of the oblation; thus there is a disparity. [Objection: Even under the view that the purpose of study is the knowledge of meaning, there is no abandonment of its status as an object (*karman*); for the fact that study is to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*) is established by the sense of the text, and its being restated with the accusative case—as in "he places the sacrificial pap" (*carum upadadhāti*)—is logically consistent.

In the section concerning the fire-altar (*agniprakaraṇa*), by the injunction "he places the sacrificial pap (*caru*)", when the placing of the *caru* is being enjoined as an auxiliary to the altar-mound (*sthaṇḍila*), it is established by the very fact of the matter that the *caru*'s status as the object of the purificatory rite (*saṃskārya*) of placing is reiterated by the accusative case-ending; for since the *caru* cannot directly effect the altar-mound, and since its manifestation of that [mound] is seen through the *caru* being placed upon it, the fact that the placing is an auxiliary to the altar-mound is mediated by the purification of the *caru*. Thus, the *caru*'s being the object of the purificatory rite of placing is indeed already established by the sense of the passage.

If it is argued that here too, since study cannot be the direct cause of the knowledge of meaning—which occurs at a later time, following the commencement of Mīmāṃsā inquiry immediately after its completion—it is established by the facts that the knowledge of meaning is seen to arise through the medium of the Veda (svādhyāya) grasped during study and subsequently ascended into memory at a later time; therefore, the fact that the Veda is the object of the purificatory act (*saṃskārya*) of study is already established by the nature of things and is merely restated by the suffix *-tavya*—this is not correct.

The point is this: although there is no fault in the Bhaṭṭa school’s position—wherein one maintains that "one should cultivate the knowledge of the meaning by means of the Vedic recitation (svādhyāya) acquired through study"—by relying on the meaning [of the injunction], in the Guru’s school, which does not accept that study is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the Veda, one must abandon the meaning of the suffix *tavya* by relying on the sense: "one should cultivate the knowledge of the meaning by means of the study whose instrument is the Veda. To demonstrate that the comprehension of the meaning possesses a purposeful utility, he says: "useful for performance" (*anuṣṭhānaupayika*).

"By the word *ca* (and), [the second option] is conjoined. Although this is common to both positions, nevertheless, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it indicates contradiction; whereas in the second position, it is intended to conjoin the essential nature of the recitation (*japa*) and so forth—this is the distinction. Anticipating the question, "What is the basis for the separate mention of the mantras included within the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*? he says: "The separate mention is 'like the mantras'."

Since the application of the suffix *vat* (denoting "possessing the quality of")—which serves to establish that [the Veda] possesses mantras that are beneficial—is entirely inappropriate in the present context, he says "or else, as in the case of a child," relying instead on the suffix *vati*. Regarding the phrase "recitation with restrictive rules": although the restriction is obtained from another sentence that prescribes the auxiliary details (*aṅga*) and does not fall within the very body of the study itself, the intended meaning is that the knowledge of the meaning does not fall within the body of that study; rather, it refers exclusively to one's own branch (*sva-śākhā*).

The word *adhyāya* refers to the Veda, and the word *sva* (one's own) denotes that which has come down through the lineage of one's father and grandfather. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating, "of the mass of syllables called the Veda, denoted by the word *svādhyāya*"; for that [commentary] also intends to mean "of the mass of syllables called one's own Veda."

Nor should it be argued that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is the objective of the injunction to study, the qualification inherent in the objective—just like the singularity of the "cup" (*graha*)—is not intended to be significant; and therefore, the injunction would result in the study being applicable to both one's own and others' Vedas alike. This is because, given the infinity of the Vedas, it is impossible to study them all, and thus a restriction is required. Under such circumstances, it is logical that the qualification of "one's own," which is part of the objective, is indeed intended to be significant. Regarding the term *mātra*: An objection is raised that in expressions such as "drink milk only" (*kṣīramātraṃ piba*), the word *mātra* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) whose status as such is restricted to its position as a subsequent member of a compound (*uttarapada*).

If it is argued that the suffix *mātrac*—prescribed by the rule "the suffixes *dva*, *saC*, *ghna*, and *mātrac* [are used] after words denoting measure" (*pramāṇe dva-saC-ghaÑ-mātracaḥ*)—is intended solely for the purpose of expressing measure, and therefore does not apply here, we say no. This is because even in cases such as *ūrumātraṃ* ("as high as the thigh"), the suffix *mātrac* conveys the meaning of measure through the cognition of the exclusion of other things; furthermore, there is no evidence for assuming that the word following the suffix is necessarily a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) distinct from the suffix *mātrac*. The intended meaning is that this is just like the sentence "one should establish the sacred fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*).

And this point was established in the third section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] by the rule: "That [act] is for the sake of its own material cause, just as other unattached injunctions (*anārabhyavāda*s). For there, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that the injunction for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) extends up to the sacrificial rites (*kratu*), like the purchase of Soma and so forth—was refuted; rather, since only the non-worldly fires such as the *āhavanīya* are capable of satisfying the requirement for a fruit, the injunction for the establishment of the fires rests solely upon that [act itself].

It has been established that [the injunction] does not culminate in the sacrifice (*kratu*). "Referring merely to the *ādhāna*" means it refers merely to the *ādhāna* performed for the purpose of establishing the sacred fires (*agni*). Regarding the phrase "of that which is not employed as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to the learning (*grahaṇa*)," one might object: "In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is not employed as a subordinate element to the learning, because the Vedic study is understood to be the principal (*śeṣin*). This is not so. The word-division is: "of that which is not employed as a subordinate element to the learning. Furthermore, the word "learning" (*grahaṇa*) here refers to the act of taking up (*adhyayana*).

The meaning is that there is no evidence for the *svādhyāya* (Vedic recitation) being directed toward the Supreme Self (*ātmaparatva*), since it is not enjoined as subservient to the knowledge of the meaning. This is the underlying idea: in common worldly usage, one understands the intention (*tātparya*) of sentences by uttering words with the aim of comprehending their meaning; then, for the sake of fulfilling that purpose, when the primary sense is impossible, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth are postulated—but not by mere utterance alone. For this very reason, figurative indication is not postulated through the mere utterance of the words "cow," "horse," "man," or "elephant."

When it is understood that their utterance is intended for the comprehension of specific meanings—that is, when the *tātparya* (purport) is grasped—it is precisely then that, for the sake of fulfilling that purpose, the elision (*adhyāhāra*), indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and so forth of words such as "cow" are postulated, as in the cases: "This cow is a bull," "The horse is swift," "The man is of restrained activity," and "The elephant is of great strength."

And thus, since there would be no intention (*tātparya*) for the utterance of Vedic sentences if it were not aimed at the comprehension of their meaning, there would follow the undesirable consequence of abolishing the employment of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), secondary usage (*gauṇavṛtti*), syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*), ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), and the determination of distinctions (*vyavadhāraṇakalpanā*) for the sake of establishing that [intention]. Therefore, one must necessarily maintain that even in the Veda, utterance is directed toward the comprehension of meaning. Furthermore, as in the world, since in the Veda there is no utterance prompted by personal desire (*rāga*) directed toward that [comprehension], it must be accepted as being prompted solely by an injunction (*vidhi*). And since no injunction other than the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is observed, [it follows that the Veda is for the purpose of understanding its meaning].

Therefore, even one who does not wish to do so must admit that study—in the form of repeating after the utterance from the mouth of the teacher—is enjoined with the aim of understanding the meaning. And thus, although the understanding of the meaning is a perceptible result (*dṛṣṭaphala*), the injunction exists for the sake of establishing the intended meaning (*tātparya*), which would otherwise not be established through other means. (This concludes the justification for engaging in inquiry out of natural inclination.)

The meaning is that this is due to the inherent nature of words as possessing the power to convey meaning. Although the general principle that words are directed toward their meanings—established through worldly linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*)—may occasionally be set aside in certain worldly sentences due to defects in the speaker, such a defect is absent in the case of the non-human (Vedic) word; furthermore, because there is no possibility of subversion, the utterance of a word intended for the purpose of generating knowledge of its meaning is inherently capable and independent of an injunction (*vidhi*). Now, it might be argued that the mere fact that words are directed toward their meanings is established by linguistic usage.

Nor can it be argued that a sentence such as the *agnihotra* injunction is intended solely for its specific respective meaning, and that since such a sentence requires to be uttered with a view toward that specific meaning, the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) must therefore have that [specific meaning] as its purpose. This is not so; for even by means of the injunction to study, that [specific purpose] is not obtained. Indeed, the injunction to study does not operate by aiming at the knowledge of each specific meaning for every individual sentence in order to bring about the utterance of that particular sentence.

If it is argued that, given the injunction "one should cultivate by means of this [study] whatever can be cultivated through the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya)," and since only the knowledge of the specific meanings of those respective passages obtainable through reasoning can be cultivated by the study of the *agnihotra* and other such sentences, the intended meaning (tātparya) regarding those specific meanings is established as a matter of fact—then let it simply be that the sentences concerning the *agnihotra* and so forth possess an inherent orientation toward their meaning, which, upon the application of reasoning, culminates in having that specific meaning as their intended purpose.

What is the use of the rule regarding pronunciation? Moreover, if one were to respect the pronunciation in the Veda merely because it is observed in common worldly usage for the purpose of understanding meaning, then [one would find that] even when listeners perform the pronunciation of a sentence intended by an independent speaker for the sake of conveying a meaning other than the one he intended, no such intentionality (tātparya) toward that [other] meaning is observed in that sentence.

However, since it is observed that the intention (*tātparya*) of an independent author lies precisely in that which he aims at when uttering a statement for the sake of its comprehension, one might assume that the Veda’s status as a human composition (*pauruṣeyatva*) must also be postulated in order to establish its intention. But in reality, even in the world, intention is not dependent upon utterance; for instance, when a silent person writes something down and gives it to another, or when one sees what has been written by another and mentally recollects a verse or the like, there is an absence of utterance [yet an intention exists].

However, the thought "let there be a comprehension of this meaning from this sentence" is dependent upon the speaker’s intention (*vaktr-vivakṣā*). Therefore, there is no room whatsoever for the assumption that the injunction to study has the comprehension of meaning as its fruit, for the sake of establishing the *tātparya* (purport). In the world, the fact that a word is directed toward meaning—established through linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*)—culminates in the specific detail intended by the speaker; in the Veda, however, it culminates in the specific detail obtained through reasoning (*nyāya*). And it must be accepted that the assumption of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth follows accordingly.

For this very reason, even by one who considers the establishment of the Veda’s possession of a purport (tātparya) to be the fruit of the injunction to study, it is determined through reasoning that the injunction to study takes the comprehension of meaning as its fruit; having thus ascertained the purport, the natural force of the suffix *tavya*—which would otherwise indicate that the mere acquisition of the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text) is the fruit—is overridden.

The determination that the injunction for Vedic study has the aforementioned meaning as its purport is not dependent on an injunction for recitation aimed at the comprehension of meaning, because no such other injunction exists; for if this very injunction were required [for its own establishment], it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Rather, it must be said that [the determination of purport] depends solely on pure reasoning (*nyāya*). Therefore, the idea that the injunction for Vedic study must be assumed to have the comprehension of meaning as its fruit for the sake of establishing the purport is, first of all, untenable. This is the intended sense.

"But there is application elsewhere" means that the application of the study [of the Veda] is to the recitation of the sacred text (*svādhyāya*) itself, rather than to the knowledge of its meaning. This is because of the statement "of that which has been grasped through study," referring merely to what has been memorized.

If it is asked: "How can the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* passage 'of that which has been acquired through study' (*adhyayanagṛhītasya*) be merely 'that which has been acquired through study,' such that it would justify the phrase 'from that which is merely acquired' (*gṛhītamātrāt*)?"—we reply as follows: In the preceding *Bhāṣya*, "because it is observed that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) acquired through study possesses the capacity for the comprehension of meaning," the nature of [the Veda] as a producer of valid cognition (*pramiti*) has been established. Since the capacity to produce a mere superficial understanding (*āpātapratīti*) is contradictory to that very [nature], the previous statement [is intended to show this contradiction].

The meaning is that [the text] refers to those who have mastered the *mīmāṃsā* auxiliaries; therefore, in order not to contradict that, this statement is understood as referring only to those who have not yet grasped it. Some, however, say that since the phrase "one who has mastered the *mīmāṃsā* auxiliaries" is not explicitly stated, it is established by the maxim "every sentence implies a restriction. They explain the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) as "having seen those things perceived at first glance. Others, however, also construe it as "having seen those perceived objects which possess a purpose. [This is established] precisely through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for their status as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*).

Nor should it be argued: "Since the status of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) as objects is understood through the direct hearing of the accusative case in the phrase 'and all the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas' (*vaidāṅgāni ca sarvāṇi*), why should the auxiliary sciences not be something to be attained, just like the Veda itself? For if that were the case, the study of the auxiliaries would terminate merely in the grasping of the syllables; consequently, since the auxiliaries would fail to assist the Veda, their status as auxiliaries (*aṅgatva*) would be undermined. Therefore, in accordance with the primary nominal stem (*prātipadika*), just as in the case of "he offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), the accusative status must be abandoned by changing the case-ending.

This is because the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) must be accepted; furthermore, since the interpretation "one should effect the knowledge of the meaning by means of the limbs (*aṅga*) which have recitation as their object" is also possible, there is no fault even if one restates the status of recitation as the object already established. The sense is that this is just as in the case of "he places the *caru*," where the status of the *caru* as the object of placing, already established by the statement "one should prepare the sacrificial mound with the placed *caru*," is restated by the accusative case ending.
(Resolution of the contradiction with the Smṛti on the Return Home.)

With what intention was this stated? The meaning is: with what intention was the relationship of sublation and that which is to be sublated (*bādhyabādhakatva*) between the *Śruti* and the *Smṛti* stated? Now, one might object: in such passages as "Having studied, one should bathe" (*adhītya snāyāt*), the meaning is "having completed the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) whose object is study," and not "that whose instrument is study and whose object is the knowledge of the meaning."

This is because, as in the cases of "Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," "They proceed loudly with the Pravargya," and "They proceed with the Avabhṛtha in the waters," there is no mention of the instrumental case; consequently, there is no recognition of a productive operation (*bhāvanā*) having that [act] as its instrument. Now, one might object: in the passage "One who has performed the fire-piling (*agni-cit*) should not run when it rains," it is precisely the completed productive operation having the piling (*cayana*) as its instrument that serves as the occasion (*nimitta*), and not merely the completed state of the root-meaning itself.

And thus, it is established in the fifth [book of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] that the duties of the fire-piler (*agnicit*) proceed only at the conclusion of the sacrifice. If it is asked, "Why should it not be the same here?", we reply: no. For in that case, by the rule "after the root *ci*, when *agni* is the object," the suffix *kvip* is prescribed for the root *ci*; consequently, the basis (*nimitta*) is the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) which has already come into being, having the fire as its object and the act of piling as its instrument. Here, however, in the rule "having studied the Veda, one should bathe," the suffix *ktvā* conveys the state of being prior in time belonging to the efficient force which has already come into being, having the Veda as its object.

But this does not apply to [the injunction] whose function is the fruit of knowledge of the meaning. Therefore, since there would indeed be a contradiction in the case where the injunction for study has the knowledge of the meaning as its fruit, the author says—out of dissatisfaction with that view—"Moreover, even if there were a contradiction," and so forth. "By the remainder of the teacher's duties" means by the time not occupied by service to the teacher; or alternatively, "by the remainder" means "without remainder" (i.e., completely). "When the *niveśa* has occurred, the obligatory [rites]"—*niveśa* here means marriage.

Now, one might object: since the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" applies without distinction to anyone merely desiring heaven, and since a Śūdra is no different in his desire for heaven, the consequence that he too would perform the rite is unavoidable; for prohibitory Smṛti texts such as "One should not give instruction to a Śūdra" can reasonably be understood as referring only to those Śūdras who are devoid of the desire to learn. Anticipating this dissatisfaction, the author says: "Furthermore, by the sacrificer... [and] "...because it is obtainable through study."

The sense is that the Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), which has been refined through study and yet remains expectant of a purpose, finds its application in all ritual acts accomplished by means of that recitation. Regarding the phrase, "He who, indeed, without knowing the seer..."—the well-known reading of the Śruti is: "He who, indeed, without knowing the seer, the meter, the deity, and the Brāhmaṇa [application] of a mantra, performs a sacrifice or teaches it, strikes against a pillar or falls into a pit. The meaning of this is as follows: *ārṣeya* refers to the seer (*ṛṣi*); *gāyatryādi* refers to the meter; and *daivata* refers to the deity, such as Agni and so forth.

The *brāhmaṇa* passage is an injunctive statement (*viniyojaka-vākya*). A priest or teacher who is ignorant of the lineage of the seers (*ārṣeya*) and so forth becomes a stationary object, falls into a pit, or dies; his Vedic hymns (*chandas*) become devoid of power. For one who knows them, however, the opposite occurs. Therefore, one should know these [details] for every mantra. One should not argue that this contradicts the subsequent text because it is impossible to enjoin what is already prompted by natural inclination (*rāga-prāpta*), such as accepting gifts, sexual intercourse during the fertile period (*ṛtu-saṃveśana*), and so forth. This is because [the knowledge of the seers and other details] is not something that could be undertaken merely out of spontaneous desire.

This passage has the following purport: since there is observed a state of being subject to injunction (*vidheyatva*) among those who possess [the desire] even when that desire is only partially fulfilled, there is no absolute contradiction between being prompted by desire (*rāgaprāptatva*) and being subject to injunction. The subsequent passage, however, concerns the object of what is eternally obtained through desire; thus, no contradiction arises. Now, upon careful consideration of this section, it appears as if there is an inquiry into whether the knowledge of meaning is subject to the injunction of study (*adhyayanavidhi*) or is prompted by desire. And yet, this is not tenable.

This is because even the Mīmāṃsakas do not accept that the knowledge of meaning is something to be enjoined by the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*). Indeed, they maintain that the knowledge of meaning is merely the fruit (*phala*) of the injunction for study, and not something to be enjoined itself, since a fruit cannot be an object of injunction. This is established in the fourth book (*caturtha-adhyāya*) in the *Lipsā-sūtra*, in the second section (*dvitīyika-adhikaraṇa*) under the rule "And the fruit [is understood] when not in proximity to an action," and also in the eighth book (*aṣṭama-adhikaraṇa*) under the rule "But because the action has not been commenced."

If it is argued that this is because the non-prescriptibility of the fruit was established in the first chapter of the *Ekādaśa* [of the *Tantravārttika*], we say no; for here, by the term "knowledge of the meaning" (*arthajñāna*), it is specifically *vicāra* (critical inquiry) that is intended. Since the Mīmāṃsakas themselves accept that *vicāra* is prescriptive, it is logical that it should be rejected on the grounds that it would otherwise be obtained through mere worldly inclination (*rāga*). Furthermore, by this very statement—namely, "He who, indeed, without knowing the lineage of the seers... and so forth—the attainment of *vicāra* is already implied by the knowledge of the meaning prescribed by those scriptural passages; therefore, it is not tenable that *vicāra* should be prompted by the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*).

The meaning is as follows: just as sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Darśapūrṇamāsa, which are prescribed by their respective injunctions, do not require further performance for the sake of achieving their own success through the Āhavanīya and other fires established by the injunction for setting up the sacred fires (ādhāna), so it is here.

Now, regarding the statement "for actions there is the fruit of being small and unstable, and the fruit of being infinite and stable," one should observe that the connection of the words "in this regard" (*ity atra*) with the preceding and succeeding positions (*pūrvapakṣa* and *siddhānta*) occurs in reverse order.

When it is said, "once the essential nature [of action] has been determined," since this would require the mental supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the sense that "even though the essential nature alone has been determined, one has learned through the injunctions for repetition and so forth that the fruits of actions are meager and unstable," its comprehension would be delayed; therefore, he explains it otherwise: "or rather, the essential nature of the injunctions regarding action has been determined."

Regarding this position, the introduction to this commentary is as follows: Now, one might raise the objection: "In rites for the propitiation of the Supreme Self—such as [the verse] 'By his own duty, having worshipped Him, a human being attains perfection,' which are understood to yield infinite and stable fruits—how can there be an understanding that they yield small and unstable fruits? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The nature of the injunctions regarding ritual action has been determined."

Even in this view, one should understand that there is an underlying unease: although the phrase "in the nature of the injunction for ritual action" (*karmavidhisvarūpe*) refers to the mere nature [of the action] devoid of its being an adoration of the Supreme Self, the realization that it consists in the adoration of the Supreme Self—which would prevent the realization of its limited and unstable results—is absent; thus, the delayed realization of the meaning "having understood its limited and unstable results" remains the same [as in the other view]. Some explain it thus: "In that regard, it has been described in the nature of the injunction for ritual action."

The compound *vidhisvarūpam* means "the injunction and its nature. The meaning is that [this] has been explained both in the context of the injunction regarding the ritual action and in the context of the nature of the ritual action itself. Furthermore, when the injunction for the repetition of the Cāturmāsya and other rites every year has been explained, the certainty arises that the fruits of the Cāturmāsyas are exhaustible; for if the fruits of the Cāturmāsyas were inexhaustible, then one would realize—by the very fact of their spontaneous arising—that performing them again would result in futility.

Thus, while defining the nature of the Cāturmāsya and other sacrifices, as well as the nature of the Viśvasṛjāmayana and others which are accomplished over a year including the rainy season, the underlying intention is this: since the impermanent nature of the fruits of the Cāturmāsya and similar rites is easily understood by a person whose mind has attained purity through the grace of the Supreme Person worshipped via obligatory and occasional duties—such a person being aided by a mind that reflects upon the maxim, "Since the fruit arises from action, there would be a difference [in its duration] due to its transformation, as is seen in the world"—even though these rites require little expenditure of wealth or effort.

The meaning of "by which" (*yena*) is an indication intended for consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consequently, since the feminine gender in "by which" (*yayā*) should not be applied—because the word "which" (*yat*) must refer back to the very same Brāhma-vidyā that is being pointed out in the phrase "he declared that Brāhma-vidyā in its true nature"—the sense is as follows: therefore, [it means] "having investigated and accomplished those [means]. Now, one might object: in the passage "one should be endowed with tranquility, self-control, and so forth," it is not the essential nature of tranquility and the rest that is being defined, but rather their status as auxiliary factors to meditation (*upāsanā*).

If it is argued that this [requirement] is not something to be relied upon (*upajīvya*) regarding the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to hearing for one who has attained the strength of scripture through hearing—that is not so; for the meaning of "tranquility" (*śama*) as the cessation of activity toward objects not prescribed by scripture is to be established in that very section (the *Śamadamādyadhikaraṇa*). This is the intended sense. Alternatively, he says, "or rather, [he attains] the infinite and stable [Brahman] through knowledge," because the statement "through Brahman-knowledge one attains [Brahman]" could be taken as having its authority extending up to the attainment of Brahman—which is an infinite and stable fruit—and thus it would be improper to restrict it merely to the teaching of the quality of having an infinite and stable fruit. It is out of this underlying unease (*asvarasa*) that he states this alternative.

"Because the object has been shown"—this means the essential nature of Brahman (*brāhṛsvarūpa*). And thus, the sense is that the term "the seer" (*paśyaḥ*) ultimately results in nothing other than the vision of Brahman.
