Regarding the phrase "a conjunction is appropriate": here some [object] that "this collection of particles *nanu* and *ca* has only the meaning of *nanu*, since no meaning beyond that is perceived; for while the word *nanu* indicates doubt and so forth which are attributes of the speaker, the expression *nanu ca* does not have a meaning equivalent to the word 'doubt' (*śaṅkā ca*)."

Therefore, they maintain that one need not be overly insistent on establishing here that the word "ca" has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). [Objection: To establish the independence from the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), it should be stated that the knowledge of the perishable nature of the fruits of rituals—produced by the Vedic sentences—is what is required, and not the knowledge of the imperishable nature of the fruits of the meditation on Brahman (*brāhmapāsanā*). To this, he says in the passage beginning with "of the meditation on Brahman," etc. (The Shorter Section on the Prima Facie View).

The first *evakāra* (the particle *eva*) is for the purpose of excluding [anything] other than that which is intended to be stated. That which is intended to be stated is the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*); "other than that" refers to the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*). Regarding this, some maintain that the *evakāra* connected with the word *yat* serves merely as an embellishment of the sentence, like words such as *tāvat* or *khalu*. For there is no comprehension of any meaning additional to what is already expressed by the sentence—even when accompanied by the *evakāra*—to the effect that "only that which the inquiry into Brahman necessarily requires must be declared as having preceded."

They argue that this statement is intended solely to exclude the necessity of the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) having preceded [the inquiry into Brahman], and not to exclude the fact that the inquiry into ritual action is necessarily required. However, this is merely a manifestation of ignorance regarding the meaning of the particle *eva*. For when the particle *eva* is attached to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), its purpose is to exclude the connection of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) with anything other than that [qualificand].

When it is said, "Pārtha alone is the archer," the particle *eva* (alone) indeed excludes the attribute of being an archer from anyone other than Pārtha. The meaning of the sentence "Pārtha alone is the archer" is: "There is no archer other than Pārtha. For this very reason, it has been determined in the *Pūrvatantra* that in the injunction, "One should recite [the mantra] 'twenty-six' alone," the *ṣaḍviṃśati* mantra itself is not being enjoined; rather, the use of any other mantra is being prohibited because of the connection with the particle *eva*.

Consequently, the meaning of the sentence "whatever it necessarily requires" is as follows: "Whatever is not necessarily required as something distinct [from the cause] is not a prior condition (pūrvavṛtta). Thus, the first *evakāra* (the particle 'only') serves to exclude the possibility that the property of being necessarily required applies to anything other than the referent of the word *yat*; the second, however, excludes the status of being a prior condition for anything other than the referent of the word *tat* as indicated by the word *yat*. This much, however, is the distinction: the first *evakāra* is merely reiterative (*anuvādī*).

But the second [interpretation] is that which was stated previously. Since the study of the Vedāntas alone is not sanctioned by the scriptures, he says, "Or rather, even for one who has studied the entire Veda. This does not mean that it excludes connection with anything else; rather, the meaning is that it does not exclude the study of the earlier portion (the Karmakāṇḍa). Now, one might raise the objection that in the injunction "one should praise with the Sāman," only the Sāman as a whole is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of the ritual through the medium of the praise, and not the *udgītha* and so forth. Dispelling this doubt by revealing the nature of the *udgītha* and other such parts, he states what is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the passage beginning with "of a single Sāman," and so on.
Now, how can the *sāman* consist of five parts? For it is observed to have seven forms: the *hiṅkāra*, the *prastāva*, the *ādi*, the *udgītha*, the *pratihāra*, the *upadrava*, and the *nidhana*.

For this very reason, having raised the objection that the injunction "one should meditate upon the Sāman as sevenfold" would be untenable because the *hiṃkāra* is included within the *prastāva* and the syllable *oṃ*, denoted by the word "etcetera," is included within the *udgītha*, [the author] says, intending to show that there is no inconsistency in its being fivefold: "The *prastāva* is sung preceded by the *hiṃkāra*. Thus, the meditation on each part is enjoined. "Indeed, all these beings enter into breath alone and emerge from breath alone."

The phrase "this very deity is connected with the *prastāva*" and "this very deity is connected with the *udgītha*"—the word "in such passages" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In some places, meditation on the *praṇava* and other components that constitute parts [of the chant] is enjoined; the reading "one should meditate upon this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*" is the correct one. Some read in the middle: "there, meditation on the *praṇava*, which has become a part of the *udgītha*, is enjoined. We do not see its correctness.

The fact that the sentence, "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha," is intended to enjoin meditation on the *praṇava*—which is a constituent part of the Udgītha—will become clear under the sūtra, "And because of pervasiveness, [the meditation] is appropriate" (*Vyāpteśca samañjasam*). However, some say that the meaning of the commentary's phrase "based on a constituent of ritual action" (*karmāṅgāśraya*) is as follows: the *praṇava* is the beginning of the Udgītha, being the first part of the Udgītha which itself is a constituent of ritual action; the meditation is upon that. It is for this very intention that they state: "In that context, meditation on the *praṇava* as a constituent part of the Udgītha is enjoined."

Anticipating the objection—"Since the employment of words is within one's own control, according to the maxim *svāyatte śabdaprayoge*, why was the formulation in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) adopted as 'the meditations based on the *udgītha* and other parts of the ritual' (*karmāṅgāśrayāṇy udgīthādyupāsanāni*), instead of saying 'the meditations concerning the *udgītha* and other parts of the ritual' (*karmāṅgodgīthādiviṣayāṇy upāsanāni*)?"—he replies: "It is said that the meditations have the *udgītha* and other parts of the ritual as their basis. This is done so that it may be understood that what is being considered as the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkāra*) is meditation in general.

[Objection: Surely, because the reason is formulated as "having as its substratum a constituent part of ritual action" (*karmāṅgāśrayatva*), there will be a grasping of exactly that much [of the subject] upon which the reason comes to rest; thus, just as in the case of "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," there is a grasping of the smoky mountain, so it shall be here. [Reply: True. However, in a state where there is no recollection of such a logical principle (*nyāya*), the cognition would arise taking mere meditation (*upāsana*) as the subject. For this very reason, the word "would be perceived" (*pratīyeta*) was employed to indicate mere cognition (*pratītimātra*).

"You are unacquainted with the specialized knowledge (*vijñāna*) of the *Śārīraka* treatise. Here, "knowledge of the treatise" (*śāstravijñāna*) refers to the knowledge that is the subject matter propounded by the treatise; it is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyamapadalopa*). This very point is explained by the phrase beginning with "that which is propounded as the primary subject in the treatise," and so forth. The word "propounded" (*pratipādya*) here has the sense of "produced" (*utpādya*). This is because, in accordance with the usage of others—such as in the expression "for the sake of the attainment (*pratipatti*) of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self"—the word "attainment" (*pratipatti*) is used interchangeably with "production" (*utpatti*).

And he will say: "They are capable of establishing [the truth] and bringing it about. Therefore, it should be understood that the figurative usage here is not a fault. Regarding the term *mithyājñāna* (false knowledge), the meaning is that it is a *madhyamapadalopa* (elision of the middle term) compound, signifying "knowledge whose object is false" (*mithyāviṣayaṃ jñānam*). Alternatively, intending to show that the purpose is precisely the cessation of root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), he says: "or, false ignorance" (*mithyābhūtam ajñānam*). The two occurrences of the word *tu* serve to exclude two possible doubts.

One doubt is that meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth is required for the knowledge of Brahman (*brāhmavidyā*), because such meditations are studied in the *Upaniṣads* and are established in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*. The second doubt, intended by the phrase "What follows from that?", is the suspicion of a lack of connection [between these meditations and the knowledge of Brahman]. The meaning is that [the text] is intended to successively remove these two doubts. Here, the followers of Bhāskara raise an objection; the reason for this will become clear later. [The phrase] "not intended as a complete conjunction" [is used].

In his view, the meaning is that in the passage "This very [Self] they seek to know through the study of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacanena*), the instrumental case ending—according to the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* ("when joined with 'with,' that which is subordinate")—acknowledges that the study of the Vedas and so forth are subordinate in relation to the "desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*) mentioned in the text. Since he accepts that ritual actions (*karma*) are merely auxiliary factors (*phalopakāry-aṅga*) to knowledge (*vidyā*), he does not accept their equal combination (*samasamuccaya*). This is the sense; the phrase "as in the word *samuccitya*" in the expression "because of the instruction by way of combination" (*samuccityopadeśāt*) is used as an illustration.

For this statement, "antara upapatteḥ," pertains to the subject matter of the knowledge of Agni and the knowledge of the Self (ātma-vidyā) as found in the commentary on that section (*adhikaraṇa*). The sense is that the combination (*samuccaya*) of these two is not admitted. It is described by way of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*). Nor should it be argued that the word "combination" does not tolerate such a disparity; for we observe the use of the word "combination" even in the case of the combination of subordinate and principal parts (*aṅga-aṅgi-samuccaya*). The sense is that an equal combination (*samasamuccaya*) is not heard here. The particle *ca* expresses a combination of the conveyors (*pratipādaka-samuccaya*).

The meaning is that there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of the two means of knowledge, namely Śruti and Sūtra. As for the question of how the knowledge of that [Sūtra] can be prior, the meaning is that it is prior to the inquiry into the Brāhmaṇas. This was stated with the intention of what will be demonstrated later; the point is that in passages such as "And also because it is seen in the intermediate state" (*antarā cāpi tu taddṛṣṭeḥ*) and "And there is need for all, on account of the scriptural statement of sacrifice and so forth, as in the case of the horse" (*sarvāpekṣā ca yajñādiśruteraśvavat*), the combination of the knowledge of Brahman (*brāhmī vidyā*) with specific ritual acts, or the absence thereof, will be established for specific types of qualified aspirants (*adhikāriviśeṣe*).

Since the *brāhma-vidyā* residing in a specific qualified person has not been specified here, it is appropriate that the question of its combination with other rites or its non-combination applies generally to all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*). With this in mind, he says: "Or rather, [the combination] of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*)," and so on. The word "of knowledge" (*vidyāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. The meaning is that there is a combination with the obligatory and occasional rites, but not with those performed for a desired result (*kāmya*) or those that are prohibited (*niṣiddha*). This is because [knowledge] is preceded by the understanding of the nature of the ritual elements (*padārtha*).

Although there is no need for Mīmāṃsā to understand the meaning of sacrificial items and other such things—since proficiency in their meaning can be achieved through grammar, lexicons, and the statements of authoritative persons—and furthermore, since Mīmāṃsā itself does not have the understanding of word-meanings as its purpose because it deals with meanings already well-known in the world, nevertheless, the distinction between what constitutes a valid object of knowledge and what does not depends upon Mīmāṃsā; this is the intended sense.

Alternatively, it should also be observed that even in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā*, since there are such observations as "the injunction to sacrifice [prescribes] a collection of substance, deity, and action," and since there is the observation of the determination of meanings such as "spoiled" (*vyāpanna*) and so forth, it is possible for it to also determine the meaning of individual words. Not understanding this intention, the opponent objects: "But [how can one know] from the sentence 'Bring the cow'? [The reply is: "Having first understood the meaning of the sentence..."

Having observed the activity of the prompted elder in bringing the cow immediately after hearing the words of the prompting elder, and having ascertained that this activity toward bringing the cow is produced by the cognition of the cow's being the object to be accomplished (kāryatā) because it is an activity toward bringing the cow—just like any other accepted activity toward bringing the cow—one concludes: "And that cognition, since it did not exist prior to the sentence and arises immediately after the sentence, must be produced by the sentence."

Therefore, the meaning is that one should understand that "the bringing of the cow is the sentence-meaning. Consequently, the knowledge that "this is the meaning of this sentence" occurs only preceded by the knowledge of the sentence-meaning; it does not mean that the knowledge that "this is the meaning of this sentence" arises preceded by the knowledge of the word-meaning, namely, "this is the meaning of this word."

He reveals his own intention by stating: "It is said: from a word for one who has acquired proficiency. He clarifies that what constitutes the state of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning being preceded by the knowledge of the word-meanings is simply this: that the presence of the word-meanings, produced by the words through their *vṛtti* (function), is the cause of that which is delimited by the nature of verbal cognition (*śābdajñānatva*). It is not, however, that the knowledge of the status of being a sentence-meaning is preceded by the knowledge of the status of being a word-meaning, such that there would be occasion for this objection. Thus he says: "Even in the case of proficiency, it is not [the case] regarding the cognition of the sentence-meaning."

Although the purpose at hand is established merely by stating that the recollection of word-meanings produced by words is the cause of verbal cognition (śābdajñāna) as delimited by the nature of such cognition—and thus the explanation of the prior existence of the cognition of sentence-meaning at the stage of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) is not useful for the present topic—it should nevertheless be understood that it is presented here for the sake of refuting the misconceptions of others. Regarding the phrase "in accordance with the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* mantras": the intention is that the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* mantras dedicated to the deity Sarasvatī were recited previously.

It has been determined that the performance [of the subsidiaries] follows that very same order. When it was argued that there is no fixed rule because there is an absence of any restrictive factor such as the sequence of the Vedic text or the order of recitation, it was established in the fifth book—under the sūtra "Or rather, by the order of the principal [acts], because the subsidiaries are for its sake"—that, in order to achieve proximity to the principal act, the duties such as the *nirvāpa* (offering of the oblation) obtained through the *codaka* (extended injunction) must first be performed for the sacrifice dedicated to a female deity according to the order of the principal acts. Thus, it is simply a matter of the difference in the causes that determine (or establish) the sequence.

The sense is that there is a disparity between the two cases (hetuvaiṣamya): in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the sequence of the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses is the regulator of the sequence of the subordinate elements (*śeṣi*); however, in the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*), it is the relationship of cause and effect. This is because meditation (*upāsana*) itself is the subordinate element (*śeṣin*) with respect to its own inquiry. Since meditation is the subordinate element only with respect to its own inquiry, the sequence resulting from the sequence of the subordinate elements would apply only to the subject matter of the inquiry into ritual action (*karman*) in the third chapter of the *Śārīraka*; it would not apply to the entire subject matter of the *Karma-mīmāṃsā* within the *Śārīraka*. [This is stated] "because of its dependence on that."

The meaning is: "because it is required for meditation" (*upāsanāpekṣitatvena*). Immediately after the phrase "of the entire Brahman-mīmāṃsā," the word "as a supplement to meditation" (*upāsanaśeṣatvena*) must be supplied. And "having relied upon Yādava’s position" means that both his intended views—namely, equal conjunction (*samasamuccaya*) and the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*)—are perceived [in the text]. "He raises an objection from the side" (*pārśvasthaś codayati*).

The sense is that [the opponent's view] is presented as being preceded by a consideration of the actions desired by the Yādavas; furthermore, if it were a text of the Siddhāntin (the proponent), there would follow the inconsistency of a refutation-text that negates the duality of means and end. The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the objects of exposition. The sense is that the word "ca" is construed with the word "aṅgabhāva" (auxiliary status), which is supplied [in the text] in the accusative case.

One might object: "If the passage beginning with 'bāḍham' (certainly) is intended to address an objection from either Bhāskara or the Siddhāntin, then the Bhāṣya passage refuting the duality of the probandum and the probans would be a negation of something that was never raised. To reject this doubt, he says: "When [he says] 'bāḍham', etc. He explains: "The specificities consist of exclusion and inclusion," which means they take the form of existence and non-existence.

Regarding the phrase "opposed to all particularities" (*sakalaviśeṣapratyanīka*), if the word "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) were taken to include even its own inherent attributes (*svagatadharma*), then the exclusion of both "knowership" (*jñātṛtva*) and "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) would already be established by that alone. Consequently, the explicit mention of the exclusion of knowership and knowability by means of the suffix *-mātra* would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Or rather, by the term 'opposed to all particularities'... The meaning is that it is included within the cessation of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*). The intention is as follows:

in the root text, the phrase "cessation of the perception of all distinctions" (*sakalabhedadarśananivṛtti*) describes the cessation of the perception of difference as being the very nature of the cessation of nescience (*avidyānivṛtti*), based on the metaphorical identification of cause and effect.

"From one [sentence], many sentences"—the meaning is that the sentence "Knowledge and ignorance" (*vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca*) constitutes a single unit. "From those of unclear meaning, [to those] of clear meaning"—the phrase "intended predominance" (*prābalyaṃ vivakṣitam*) is to be supplied. Now, one might object: "If the finitude of action is heard in scripture, how can the finitude of its fruit be stated? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "By this sentence," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: it has been stated that [the finitude] is by way of the fruit, because action itself is finite and thus need not be taught [as such], and because, on the authority of scriptural passages such as "Just as... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6), it is the fruit alone that is finite, as established by statements such as "that becomes finite for him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1). This is in accordance with other scriptural texts regarding the statement concerning the combination [of knowledge and action].

Although in the passage beginning with "And as for what was said," the conjunction (*samuccaya*) is perceived only within the act of stating—namely, "just as there is a duality of the probandum and the probans, so too has the requirement of an object (*karma*) been stated"—and not within the act of establishing (*nirvāha*), nevertheless, this should be understood as a statement of the resulting meaning (*phalitārtha*).

Regarding the statement, "And as for what was said, that knowledge depends upon rituals such as sacrifice," since the phrase "that which was said—that knowledge depends upon rituals such as sacrifice" naturally suggests that the very fact of its dependence is what is indicated by the word *yat* (that), one might suspect that it would be inappropriate to explain in the subsequent sentence that this dependence serves the purpose of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). Anticipating this objection, [the author] explains that by the phrasing "knowledge depends upon rituals such as sacrifice," it is implied by the sense (*arthāt*) that [rituals] are required by knowledge.

Since it is said that "whatever action has been mentioned," and because the word *yat* (whatever) refers specifically to action, there is no contradiction in establishing its utility for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). With this intention, he says: "by this mode of expression. This means that while there is a natural consistency in the manner of the reference (*nirdeśa*), there is no such natural consistency in the word *phala* (fruit). Thus, the first explanation serves to refute the view of Yādava. In this [second] position, however, there is natural consistency in the word *phala*.

The statement "knowledge requires rituals such as sacrifice," which serves to remind one of the sūtra concerning the relationship between the primary and its subsidiaries (*aṅga-aṅgibhāva*), lacks natural consistency. In the second explanation, which refutes the view of the Siddhāntin, there is natural consistency in the statement "knowledge requires rituals such as sacrifice," but there is no natural consistency in the word "result" (*phala*). Therefore, in order to establish the natural consistency of both words, he explains it—refuting the position of Bhāskara—with the words "or rather, 'sacrifice and so forth,'" and "like the *prayāja* offerings."

If it be objected: "Even if Bhāskara accepts that sentences concerning sacrifices and the like serve merely as *phalopakāry-aṅga* (auxiliaries contributing to the result) with respect to knowledge, he does not accept that they have the attainment of the result [of liberation] as their purpose; therefore, in the refutation of their being intended to establish liberation, there would be the fallacy of 'prohibiting what was never proposed' (*aprasaktapratiṣedha*)," we reply: this is not an absolute prohibition of something unproposed. This should be understood because the intention is that since the *prayāja* offerings and so forth—which assist the instrument—can reach as far as the final result by way of assisting that instrument, [the objection does not apply]. As for the phrase, "He wishes to kill with a sword": [this is used as an analogy].

The status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is understood with respect to the act of killing, not with respect to the desire to kill (*jighāṃsā*). Similarly, the sense is that by the sentence "they desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*), the *brahmayajña* (Vedic recitation), *yajña*, *dāna*, and *tapas* in the form of fasting from desires—which are denoted by the term "Vedic recitation"—are understood to be the causes for knowledge. Regarding the phrase "by two sentences": one sentence is "when the desire to know has arisen," and the other is "thus, through hundreds of previous births. It is clear that [these practices] possess an internal or intimate character (*antaraṅgatva*).

The sense is that [these means] are heard to be conjoined with knowledge (*vidyā*). And it has been stated in the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* on the *Sarvāpekṣā* section: "Because they are conjoined with knowledge, tranquility (*śama*) and the other [internal means] are proximate to the means of knowledge; because they are conjoined with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), sacrifices (*yajña*) and the other [external means] are more remote. For it is prior to the desire to know that action finds its application. As it is said: "Having brought about an inclination toward the Inner Self through purification, actions—having accomplished their purpose—set like clouds at the end of the rainy season."

Thus it is said. Just as sprouts and the like are produced through both plowing and non-plowing—where there is plowing before the sowing of seeds and no plowing thereafter—so too it is said: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for that same person once he has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means."

The sense is that, according to such statements, the performance of ritual action (*karma*) continues until the purification of the mind reaches the point of direct inclination toward inquiry (*vividiṣā*), after which renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) occurs; thus, since it is accepted that knowledge (*vidyā*) is perfected through both action and its renunciation, [the text says] "for the sake of performance even now. Regarding this, some maintain that since the performance of action is desired for a person who has not yet produced the desire to know (*avividiṣu*) until the arising of that desire—even in this very life—the word "in another birth" (*janmāntara*) does not serve to exclude this doubt.

Moreover, they say that this is precisely to demonstrate that the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*) is to be accomplished through the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites over the course of many births. Regarding the phrase "perfected through many births" (*aneka-janma-saṃsiddha*): by the natural force of the word "other births" (*janmāntara*), one might think it refers only to the immediately preceding birth; however, since it is impossible for that single birth to constitute "many births," the intention is that this [current] birth must also be included. Regarding the term "purificatory statement" (*śodhaka-vākya*): it means a statement that eliminates the suspicion of defects regarding [the soul's] causality.

"‘Not action’ means this: sacrifices and the like are not the instrument [of liberation]. ‘Capable of producing’ means: having the supreme goal of the oneness of the Self. Regarding the statement in the Commentary, ‘the grasping of the meaning as established by reasoning’: the meaning is that one grasps the sense consisting of the purport—that all Vedānta passages have the oneness of the Self as their purport—preceded by an investigation into the logical principles (nyāya) such as the introductory context (upakrama) which determine that purport. It does not, however, mean the grasping of the literal sentence-meaning, because in his system, that is the result of hearing (śravaṇa)."

The intention of the particle *eva* ("only") is that [the subject] comes from that which was previously mentioned. Although what was introduced earlier has the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karman*), and not the nature of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth—due to the difference in their manifestations—nevertheless, it should be understood that the particle *eva* is employed by relying on their identity in terms of having the nature of "objects" (*artha*).

Having explained the subsequent passage, “*arthasvabhāvādeva*,” as establishing the impossibility of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), he now explains the passage beginning with “*yadvā anena vinā jijñāsānupapatteḥ*” as being intended to refute the objection that “let action (*karman*) be the prerequisite. He states the essential meaning of the portion “*anena vinā jijñāsānupapatteḥ*” as follows: “the meaning is that [the desire to know arises] from the very nature of the objects such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth. This refers to the sense of the first particle *eva*.

The meaning is that [the text] rejects causality as something distinct from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the object. It is said that "the intrinsic nature of the object, such as tranquility (*śama*), has been stated. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); the meaning is that the intrinsic nature of both of those [knowledge and action] has also been stated. In this context, the statement regarding what is intended is made with the intention that the two intrinsic natures of knowledge and action are not at all relevant to the subject matter; it is not, however, because the term "intrinsic nature of the object" was not explicitly mentioned.

Therefore, it should be understood that the exclusion of other possibilities (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of what has occurred previously (*pūrvavṛtta-ayoga*), which will be stated as the reasons for the fourfold means (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*)—designated here as the very nature of the object (*artha-svabhāva*) and independent of anything else—are logically consistent. For the word "this" (*idaṃ*) refers to the fact that the fourfold means have occurred previously; the phrase "for the word 'this'" (*hi... idaṃśabdaḥ*) means "for [the statement] 'this alone has occurred previously. The term "therefore" (*tasmāt*) means "because of the nature of the object, namely tranquility (*śama*) and so forth. In the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), the phrase "rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*) which veils the true nature of Brahman" is used.

Furthermore, this is not a *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of "that which is a concealer" (*ācchādikā*) and "ignorance" (*avidyā*), for if it were, then by the rule of masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*), it would have to be "concealing ignorance" (*ācchādakāvidyā*). Rather, the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of an abstract state according to the rule "ṇvul after a verbal root," as in the words *kārikā* (a verse) or *śāyikā* (sleeping). Thus, *ācchādikā* means "that which acts as a concealer. Following that, there is a compound with a dative [of purpose] (*tādathryacaturthī*). The meaning is therefore "ignorance that performs the act of concealing. One should also consider another interpretation: namely, that it refers simply to the perception of difference (*bhedadarśana*) as being non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*).

The intention is that the perception of the distinction between bondage and its root is indeed not ultimate (*apāramārthika*). Following such authorities as, "This subtle Self is to be known by the mind," and "But it is seen by the intellect with its tip [of focus]," and in accordance with the statement of Vācaspati—"the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), aided by the ripening of the cultivation of the meaning of the [great] sentence, manifests the immediacy (*aparokṣatā*) of the referent of 'That' within the referent of 'Thou'"—he says "the cognition that brings about cessation" (*nivartako bodhaḥ*), favoring even one who considers the mind alone to be the cause of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman.

"Arising from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇajanya*)" means up to that point. "Qualified by distinctions of being situated far or near" means that there is no redundancy, as in the case of [the recognition] "This is that Devadatta. By the word "intending" (*abhipretya*), the removal of doubt is indicated; this means the removal of doubts not explicitly stated. Intending such authorities as "By means of dharma one removes sin" and "Actions are for the ripening of the impurities," he says, "usefulness through a traditional succession" (*paraṃparayopayogam*).
(The Section on the Shorter Conclusion) He replies by accepting those points among the positions of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that are not contradictory.

"An answer (uttara) may be of four kinds: by way of a false admission (mithyā-saṃpratipatti), or by way of a counter-attack (pratyavaskandana), or by way of a plea of prior judgment (prāṅnyāya-vidhi-siddhi).

The sense is that even what is called *saṃpratipatti*—that is, an admission (*abhyupagama*)—can function as an answer. He says "cessation of the obstacle" because it is improper to admit the cessation of an ignorance (*avidyā*) that is held by others to be either existent, non-existent, or inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*). The phrase "said to be accomplished through action" implies the addition: "by one who maintains a duality of things to be accomplished. [The phrase] "leveling the path and leading [the disciple] to it" [is explained as follows].

The sense is that since a stone does not reach a specific destination merely by the leveling [of the path] characterized by the removal of obstacles on the way, a separate effort is required there for the sake of reaching it. Now, one might object: "The removal of obstacles alone is what is to be accomplished through knowledge;"

The objection that "the attainment of Brahman occurs by itself alone" is incorrect; for it is understood from the statement, "The knower of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* attains the Supreme," that even the attainment of the essential nature of Brahman is accomplished through knowledge (*jñāna*). Anticipating this, [the author] refutes it by resorting to the identity between the removal of obstacles and the attainment of Brahman, stating: "Or else, of another state... This is said while restating both the opponent's view and his own. Now, one might object: it is not the opponent's view that the knowledge produced by the sentences of the Vedāntas is intended (*vidhitsita*) by those texts for the purpose of removing ignorance (*avidyā*).

Since it is established in common experience that knowledge functions as the remover of ignorance, there is no need for an injunction; furthermore, because knowledge is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is not dependent on the person, it is accepted that the statement “it is to be seen” (*draṣṭavyaḥ*) is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). For this very reason, the passage from the *Bhāṣya* stating, “because its establishment occurs from the sentence itself even without an injunction,” would be improper, since it is incorrect to treat something as already established when an injunction has not been admitted. This is true.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated with the intention that, because of the hearing of injunctive suffixes such as "is to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*) and "one should see the Self" (*ātmānaṃ paśyet*), even in that [Advaita] view, the status of being an object of injunction must necessarily be accepted. Now, one might object: "Even if the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence cannot be an object of injunction because it is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the activity consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) which is conducive to it will be an object of injunction. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the hearing of that, for the person... [and] "The injunction to study alone... and so forth.

According to the view of Vācaspati, since the injunction for study is accepted as extending up to the comprehension of the meaning, and since the attainment of the comprehension of the meaning through the Veda already studied is impossible without inquiry, inquiry necessarily follows. And it has been said by the Mīmāṃsakas: "When Dharma is being cognized by means of the Veda acting as the instrument, Mīmāṃsā shall fulfill the role of the procedure (itikartavyatā)."

Thus, just as the investigation of the first part [of the Veda] is established by the force of the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), so too the investigation of the second part is established for that very reason. Although the injunction to study has as its fruit merely the acquisition of the mass of syllables, nevertheless, because it possesses the same character as the investigation of the first part, the investigation of the second part is likewise established; such is the sense of the argument regarding the lack of purpose (*vaiyarthya*) of the injunction. Nor is the fact that the knowledge of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) is a means to the highest good (*śreyas-sādhanatva*) something non-worldly (*alaukika*).

The point is that even though gambling and such acts are prompted by passion (*rāga*), they are enjoined for the sake of the transcendental merit (*apūrva*) of the sacrifice, as in the injunction, "He plays with dice. "Until I am released, then I shall attain [the Self]"—for the Śruti says: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall attain [the Self]. This refers to one who knows the Brahman. "Only so long" means the delay is of just that duration. "Until I am released" means until he is released from the *prārabdha* karma that initiated the present body.

"Then I shall attain [perfection]"—the meaning is "then I will attain. The change of person (*puruṣavyatyaya*) is a Vedic usage. Alternatively, by supplying the word "of that" (*tasya*) and "to me" (*me*), there is no change of person; otherwise, the [Vedic] passage would result in meaninglessness, because it is the knowledge produced by the sentence itself, being independent, that effects the cessation of ignorance. This is the meaning.

Without mentioning specific injunctional statements (*vidhivākya*), he states the purpose of the general teaching—"because [the result] is established even without an injunction"—in order to demonstrate the contradiction with numerous scriptural passages (*śruti*). "Contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*) means a negation by that which possesses greater force. For the prefix *vi-* denotes distinction (*viśiṣṭa*); thus, a "contradiction" is a qualified negation (*viśiṣṭapratiṣedha*). And its being "qualified" consists in its being defined by superior strength.

Although it has been clarified by both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa that in the rule "vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam," the word *vipratiṣedha* has the well-known worldly meaning of "mutual contradiction," nevertheless, the point here is that if one were to rely on that established meaning of mutual contradiction for the word *vipratiṣedha* in the present context, the use of the instrumental case in the word *śāstraiḥ* would be untenable.

[Objection: But surely, what occasion is there for the cessation of ignorance for every person? To this he says: "Because ignorance is one. This means that its non-removal does not constitute a defect; the word "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. [Objection: Is it not the case that ignorance is indeed one, such that upon the liberation of one, there would be the liberation of all? Furthermore, even though knowledge has arisen in someone, and yet the manifestation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) continues for every person at present according to the analogy of a burnt cloth—this has certainly not been accepted by anyone. [Reply: True.

Regarding the phrase "of every person" (*sarvasya puṃsaḥ*), there is no fault because the word "every" (*sarva*) intends to refer to the distinction between locations characterized by various internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which are associated with a single *jīva* whose limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is a single ignorance (*avidyā*) in the context of the manifold body (*kāyavyūha*). However, some explain that the term "of every" does not refer to all persons, but rather refers only to those persons who have produced knowledge. [The phrase] "because its root, known as ignorance, has been severed" means...

Nor should it be asked how the persistence of the effect can occur upon the cessation of the root cause; for its persistence is logically established even from the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*). Nor should it be said that such persistence belongs only to action and knowledge; for we observe the persistence of the fragrance of a flower in a flower-casket even after the flower has been removed. Since destruction in general—distinct from the destruction of the latent impression—is pervaded by the presence of a latent impression, and since the destruction of ignorance is likewise pervaded by a latent impression, a latent impression necessarily persists even in the case of the destruction of ignorance, and by virtue of that [impression], [the effect continues].

The meaning is: "because the appearance of difference is logically possible. For others have described three modes regarding liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*): first, ignorance has been destroyed in its entirety, yet its latent impression (*vāsanā*) persists in the form of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), and the appearance of the body and so forth, rooted in that [impression], continues like a potter's wheel. This is the first view.

Another view holds that a portion of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) belonging to the root ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which possesses both the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and the power of projection, continues to persist as the cause for the persistence of the present body and so forth by means of *prārabdha-karma*; this [persistence] is of the nature of a fragment of ignorance (*avidyā-leśa*), and this appearance has that as its basis. Another view holds that, according to the analogy of a burnt cloth, the root ignorance itself persists, and this appearance has that as its basis. All of this is intended [by the author] in the *Bhāṣya* by the phrase "by having its root severed" (*chinnamūlatvena*) and in the *Ṭīkā* by the phrase "by having its root, known as ignorance, severed" (*chinnāvidyākhyamūlatvena*).

He states examples for "instruction from a reliable person" (*āptopadeśa*) and so forth in sequence, beginning with the words "in a certain place, [hearing] the sentence 'there is water,' etc. The term *bhramita* is derived from the causative root (*ṇyanta*) with the suffix *kta* in the sense of the object (*karman*). Nor should it be asked how a sentence can be the cause of a delusion that persists for a very long time; the point is that such persistence is possible because a continuous succession of recollections of the sentence's meaning can occur over a long period.

In this context, because a perceptual error is removed by the perception of a specific [contrary] object and not by the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta*), it is said that [the person] was "long deluded by the sentence 'it is a snake'. Furthermore, [if you argue that] another means of removal [could suffice] because there is no difference in their being cognitions, that is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*); for your position accepts that even latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are removed only by the repeated direct realization of the Self. This is the intended meaning [of the phrase]: "if one intends that [the cognition] brings about its own destruction by itself."

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), by means of the particle *eva*, only the subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) itself is to be excluded; here, however, everything other than itself is to be excluded—this is the distinction. Regarding the "contradiction" (*vyāghāta*): if the latent impression (*vāsanā*) were independent of anything other than its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there would be a contradiction with its stability; for if it were the independent cause of its own destruction, then, due to the absence of any other requirement, it would necessarily be momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

However, some say that the meaning [of the objection] is that there is a contradiction between the object and the agent (*karmakartṛ-vyāghāta*) if one accepts that a thing is both its own destroyer and its own destroyer. Regarding the phrase "destroyed by the penultimate": the *apūrva* and so forth are destroyed by the result; sound is destroyed by the penultimate [moment], because it is accepted that "the destruction of the final and penultimate [moments] occurs according to the logic of Sundopasunda. In cases where the destruction of color and so forth is produced by the destruction of the substrate (*āśraya-nāśa*), it should be understood that they are destroyed by the destruction of their cause. Furthermore, the delusion regarding the object of destruction persists.

The sense is that [the world] is pervaded by the cognition of falsity (*mithyātva*). Regarding the phrase "its root called latent impression (*vāsanā*) has been severed": although the commentary (*bhāṣya*) states—on the grounds that "that which has its root severed does not lead to bondage"—that the meaning is "by virtue of having ignorance (*avidyā*) as its severed root," that [explanation] would have been more appropriate to refute here; nevertheless, since it is stated that [the world] consists of latent impressions, it must be understood that the statement was made thus because latent impressions alone are to be designated as the root. Furthermore, this must be accepted even by the opponent from the perspective of conventional reality (*vyāvahārika*).

Although this state of being empirical (vyāvahārikatva) indeed exists even in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), such as latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, the intended meaning here is that—just as the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self sublates the entire universe—the knowledge of the oneness of the moon does not remove the defect of cataracts and the like, because it does not penetrate the true nature of the substratum of those defects. Intending to show that the cognition of a double moon, which produces wonder and the like, does not produce fear and the like, he says: "with respect to a person possessing the delusion of a rope-snake and so forth."

It should also be understood that there is no fault even if the double moon, being an extraordinary phenomenon (*autpātika*), serves as a cause for fear. For if authoritative instruction were to produce a certainty regarding the unreality of an object perceived directly, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "in a conflict between scripture and perception, perception is more powerful" would be undermined. Anticipating this objection, he says, "or rather, the true nature of the object as it is. One who doubts based on authoritative instruction proceeds to observe with careful attention; the point is that in such a case, the removal of error occurs through observation alone.

"For the removal of difference occurs through a visible means. The meaning is that if [the means] were to operate through an invisible means (*adṛṣṭadvāratva*), it would not be possible for even a brief practice of *nididhyāsana* to eliminate vast latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Consequently, the objection—that the statement "this is not a snake" functions as a direct remover [of fear] and thus does not operate through a visible means—is refuted; for by the phrase "through a visible means," what is intended is precisely the absence of operation through an invisible means.

Now, if [ignorance] is to be sublated by means of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), is it being argued that there is an absence of sublation during the state of empirical transaction (vyavahāra), or at all times? Not the first, because that would lead to an undesired consequence (iṣṭāpatti). Nor the second, because no corroborating example (dṛṣṭānta) is agreed upon.
[As it is said: "Merely through the birth of the perfect knowledge arising from sentences such as 'That thou art,' ignorance, along with its effects, has not been, is not, and will not be."

He raises an objection according to the stated method: "But [the snake] through the medium of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)," arguing that even for a snake whose cessation has been brought about by meditation, there is sublation by the final cognition. [The response is: "Its status as something to be sublated is never established. For the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is this: that which is to be removed by a cognition of a certain object through the medium of the unseen is not sublatable by that cognition. Consequently, although the snake—which is removable by the cognition of Garuḍa through the medium of direct perception—is removed by the final cognition produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), it does not follow that it is sublatable by the cognition of Garuḍa.

For sublation (*bādha*) is indeed cessation together with the ignorance that constitutes the root; it is not the case that the knowledge of the snake's root is ceased by the knowledge of Garuḍa, such that there would be sublation. Consequently, if the latent impression of difference were to be removed by the knowledge of Brahman in the form of meditation through the medium of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), then it could not be something sublatable by the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*) which is the knowledge of Brahman. Yet, you maintain that it is sublatable by that knowledge—this is the intended sense.

Alternatively, does [the opponent mean that] because the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman in the form of meditation through the medium of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), it merely attains reality; or rather, is it the absence of falsity, characterized by being sublatable by a knowledge that does not operate through unseen merit? It is not the first, because that is acceptable [to us]. Nor is it the second, for even though the latent impression of difference has ceased, since it is sublatable by the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*) without the medium of unseen merit, its falsity is possible—just like a snake [perceived in a rope] that is sublated by meditation. Thus he raises the objection: "But [if it is] through the medium of unseen merit... and so on.

It is incorrect to claim that the final mental modification (*caramavṛtti*) is what removes the snake that had previously ceased to exist through the medium of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), because it is impossible for that which has already perished to be destroyed again; furthermore, since the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) cannot be removed by a final modification acting without the medium of *adṛṣṭa*, its falsity (*mithyātva*) would not be established. Nor should it be argued that using the example of a snake [removed] solely by meditation is inappropriate—given that even a jar destroyed by a blow from a mallet and the like would result in being real—because such an example is indeed acceptable.

And then, intending to show that [the world] would possess reality like a jar that can be overturned by a mallet or the like, or like a snake that can be overturned by meditation, he refutes this with "no. He says, "like the sentence regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma. The sense is that otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the sentence regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma—when conjoined with the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—would produce direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the dharmas such as the Jyotiṣṭoma itself. [From] *Bhāvaprakāśikā* (on the means of devotion):

The meaning is that the verbal root is *cāyṛ* in the sense of “seeing,” because it is recited [in the Dhātupāṭha] as “*cāyṛ* in the senses of worship and perceiving. The intention is that another sentence expressing a specific knowledge devoid of doubt is intended; the meaning is that the sentence beginning with “One should meditate on the Self as *Om*” is what is intended. [The phrase “by the principle of the recognition of all branches” means: But surely, how can there be identity among the Agnihotra, Jyotiṣṭoma, and other rites recited in various branches, given that they possess distinct connections (*saṃyoga*), forms (*rūpa*), injunctions (*codanā*), and names (*ākhyā*)?

If it is asked: "Since there is no identity of injunction (*codanā*) here and no identity of name (*ākhyā*), how can this principle (*nyāya*) apply? Otherwise, why should there not be identity of meaning with the [injunction] 'He is to be heard'?"—the answer is: No. For the root argument for the principle of "cognition across all recensions" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*) is indeed the existence of a means of recognition (*pratyabhijñāpaka*). And here too, there exists both the similarity of connection with the same fruit in the form of liberation and the similarity of form characterized by having Brahman as their object.

Likewise, there is a correspondence of position between the terms *nididhyāsana* and *prajñā* in the passages, "It should be reflected upon (*mantavyaḥ*), it should be meditated upon (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*)," and "Having known [it], one should exercise wisdom (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*). Therefore, that very same thing is recognized. For this very reason, in the section concerning the "seeing" (*īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*), it was explained that the Brahman denoted by the word *sat* in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*)," is indeed Brahman, because of the uniformity of approach (*gati-sāmānya*)—that is, because of the commonality of understanding found in all Vedānta texts such as, "In the beginning, this was the Self alone (*ātmāvā idamagra āsīt*)" and "In the beginning, this was Brahman alone (*brāhma vā idamagra āsīt*)."

That very commonality of destination is the principle of the "corroboration by all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*). Furthermore, if the general knowledge denoted by the word *prajñā* were the means for attaining the great [Brahman], it would follow that meditation (*dhyāna*)—characterized as the worship of the Guru—would be rendered useless. Therefore, one must state that its final culminating point lies elsewhere; such is the sense in which a single unified meaning is possible. For this [result] has the acceptance of what was unspoken and required as its fruit, but not the abandonment of what was already spoken.

And thus, in the case of the injunction "it should be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), if it were an injunction for mere knowledge (*jñāna*) alone, the aforementioned abandonment [of the object] would be established. Therefore, the point is that even by means of a word expressing knowledge in general, it is a specific [form of knowledge] that must be enjoined.

One might object that if a word denoting a universal were to denote a particular, there would be *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication). Anticipating this, [the author] states, "In that regard, it is the goat because of the wording of the mantra," intending to convey that since a universal is exhausted in each individual instance, the denotation of a particular by means of a universal is not a fault; this was determined in the discussion on *chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*. In the case of "It is the goat because of the wording of the mantra," the subject matter is merely the fact that the general terms found in the injunctive sentence are restricted to the particular [animal] as established by the wording of the mantra.

Therefore, having raised the doubt as to how general words situated in an injunctive sentence can be restricted to a specific [meaning] situated within that same injunctive sentence, he says, "In the same way, even in the Smṛtis," in order to demonstrate that this principle does not concern only injunctions and mantras, but rather has universal application to all general terms, showing that the restriction of general words to a specific meaning is observed even in the Smṛtis.

"Because writing, reciting, and so forth are not prohibited"—this means because they are not forbidden; that is to say, because they are excluded by the rule understood from this very statement. Alternatively, "because they are not prohibited" means because they are permitted. Here, the mention of writing is for the sake of providing an illustration. Anticipating the objection that "the injunction for hearing (śravaṇa) must serve to exclude inquiry that is not dependent on the mouth of a guru," he says: "in the case of approaching a guru."

[Objection: Even if the word *śravaṇa* does not itself mean "approaching the teacher," since hearing (*śravaṇa*) has approaching the teacher as its constituent part (*aṅga*), the exclusion of inquiry that does not depend on the teacher’s mouth is established by the force of the injunction for hearing accompanied by the injunction for its constituent parts. [Response: Out of dissatisfaction with this, he says: "And even though that [approaching] is not enjoined here... Nor should it be asked how there can be an injunction for approaching based on a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that [hearing] in the absence of an injunction for the principal act (*aṅgin*); the sense is that this is possible, just as in the case of "Having bathed, one should eat," where bathing is enjoined based on a restatement of eating already prompted by natural desire (*rāga*).

Regarding the phrase "the injunction of another auxiliary," [the author] raises the objection that there might be an injunction for "learning" (*pāṇḍitya*) and "silence" (*mauna*)—which are intended to be enjoined in that context—by means of the two [injunctions] "it is to be heard" (*śrotavyaḥ*) and "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavyaḥ*); he then refutes this with the words beginning "supported by reasoning" (*nyāyopeta*), stating that when another alternative is available, it is improper to resort to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*). Now, one might object: the mutual qualification of hearing and reflection, which take the forms of learning and silence, is not established; therefore, how could there be a qualified injunction?

For if the syntactical form were "having heard, one must reflect," then there would indeed be a suspicion of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). Otherwise, even in cases such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper," "Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in a whisper," and "Agni and Soma are to be sacrificed to in a whisper," it would be possible to enjoin a third sacrifice qualified by the two [previous] sacrifices; consequently, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) based on the non-differentiation of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would be untenable.

If it is argued that in cases such as "He offers the *samidh* oblations," one might likewise conclude that there is an injunction for the final *prayāja* qualified by the four [oblations] beginning with *samidh*, some reply: "Just as in the case of 'He chooses the *ārṣeya*,' and 'He chooses three,' where despite the presence of distinct verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*), there is an injunction for the choosing of the *ārṣeya* qualified by the number three, so too here, a suspicion may arise that there is an injunction for reflection (*manana*) qualified by hearing (*śravaṇa*) in the passage 'It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon. This is the resolution stated by Yādavamiśra.

The meaning is that the resolution [of the objection] is that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are enjoined because their purpose is not already perceived (*adṛṣṭārthatayā*). That, however, will become clear under the sūtra, "Because of the difference of words and so forth" (*nānāśabdādibhedāt*). Regarding the phrase "it will be explained": the point is that there is no fault in its not being explained in the Bhāṣya at this time. Regarding the form *draṣṭavya*: although the form is established even by the suffix *-tavya*, nevertheless the suffix *-tavyat* was employed by the Teachers with a view toward a specific accent (*svaraviśeṣa*).

However, some maintain that in the passage from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the suffix -tavya is not intended to convey the sense of obligation (*vidhi*), because when either of the two suffixes *-tavya* or *-anīya* is to be employed, the former is adopted since it is taught first.

The word *asakṛt* (repeatedly) in the Sūtra is intended to exclude two or three repetitions. Although the word *asakṛt* refers merely to multiplicity, and multiplicity is common to two, three, and so on, it should be understood that it is stated thus because the term is most commonly used in reference to a greater number. Here, [the author] takes up the Sūtra: "Repetition... [He explains: "The word *asakṛt* in the Sūtra is for the purpose of excluding two or three repetitions."

The reading "Since the word 'meditation' (upāsana) is not heard [in the context], the Sūtra’s intent toward that [meditation] is not clear; therefore, he states its meaning: 'This very... is the correct one. Some, however, say, "He says 'two or three repetitions' by way of the 'lion's glance' (siṃhāvalokita)," citing the phrase "one should approach the nights" (rātrīrupeyāt). Although this sentence does not actually exist [in the source text], for the Rātrisatra, the originative injunction is simply "Light, Cow, Life-span" (jyotir gaur āyuḥ). Furthermore, even in that case, regarding the subject of a Satra sacrifice, the singular verb "one should approach" (upeyāt) is not possible.

Since the sentence must be construed with the plural ending as "upeyuḥ," nevertheless, according to the maxim that "an example need not be strictly adhered to," the two sentences—"One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara" and "In which [year] one offers this sacrifice"—should be cited as the illustrative examples.

"Because it is preceded by this statement": "Now, he who worships another deity [thinking], 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; for he is incomplete. One should worship [the Self] as the Self alone"—thus says the Śruti. By the method of the lion’s glance (*siṃhāvalokita*), he explains the portion of the Chāndogya passage that has not yet been commented upon, beginning with the words "he who knows that," and so forth.

"Just as all the lower throws (ayāḥ) go to one who has won with the *kṛtāya* throw, even so everything that people do well goes to him who knows this—this is what was said by me. This is indeed a scriptural statement (*śruti-vākya*). And this [passage] is the reply of another swan to a swan who had asked, "Who indeed is Raikva with the cart? regarding the true nature of Raikva. "Just as to one who has won with the *kṛtāya* throw"—the *kṛta* is a well-known throw in the game of dice.

When that [four] wins, then the others—the three, two, and one—are defeated; they come together and merge into it. The meaning is that when the four is made the winner, the three, two, and one are contained within it, because those values already exist therein.

In this way, everything that all creatures in the world perform as good and auspicious action—that is, whatever kind of dharma they practice—converges upon and unites with this Raikva, who stands in the place of the *kṛtāya* throw. The meaning is that all of that dharma is included within his own dharma; the fruit of every living being is included within his own fruit. Regarding the passage beginning "He who knows that," the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is: "That which he knows."

Whatever is to be known that Raikva knows, if anyone else were to know that same thing to be known, he too would attain, just like Raikva, the fruit consisting of the entire collection of all auspicious dharmas; this is the ellipsis. This was said by me.

The meaning is that Raikva said, "This has been stated by me in this manner. With the intention that by describing the greatness of the knower of the *brāhmaṇa* known to Raikva, the greatness of both Raikva and the *brāhmaṇa* becomes declared, the Teacher [Śaṅkara] stated: "The meaning is that both Raikva and the *brāhmaṇa* which he knows have been spoken of by me. However, it should not be understood as if [Raikva meant], "When this was spoken by me, [you should see it] as the literal meaning of the words."

This is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that [the practice] might be interrupted because it occurs repeatedly. The sense is that, according to the maxim "he studies twice a month," that which is performed by breaking it up through the recollection of memory does not constitute *dhyāna*. Because passion (*rāga*) and the rest are attributes of the living self (*jīva*) and are not attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he states—due to this lack of conviction—"Or rather, it is like 'the platforms are crying,'" referring to the passage: "This very self is in the heart; its etymological derivation is this: 'it is in the heart' (*hradi ayam*); therefore it is called the heart (*hṛdayam*). He says "it causes the heart to arise" with this intention.

Intending a *karmadhāraya* compound in the term *hṛdayagranthi*, he says: "characterized by the word *hṛdaya*. Now, one might object: how can the phrase "when that which is higher and lower has been seen" (*tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare*) indicate that knowledge takes the form of direct perception (*darśana*) during the stage of the means? For the word "seeing" (*darśana*) used therein could also be understood as referring to knowledge in general, as in the expression "one who sees the meaning of the scriptures" (*śāstrārthadaśī*). To this he replies: "even though the word 'seeing' may possibly refer to knowledge in general," because hearing and the other [means] have been mentioned separately.

The implication is that, consequently, there would be the contingency of the word expressing the universal (sāmānya) becoming redundant. Nor does this entail the same separation for *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) and *darśana* (vision), according to the principle "nor [are] air and action [the same], because of the separate teaching" (*na vāyukriye pṛthagupadeśāt*); for the Supreme Self is not an object fit for vision, and since the word *darśana* has its primary meaning only in the sense of visual perception, one must resort to a secondary (figurative) sense here. The word *dṛṣṭa* (seen) likewise signifies an object equivalent to that [visual perception].

In the phrase "when He, the higher and the lower, is seen" (*tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare*), the word *dṛṣṭa* has the same meaning as *tattulya*; that is, it signifies direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), because of its recognition [as such]. Nor should it be argued that there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*) in determining the meaning of these two phrases—"when He is seen" and "He is to be seen"—on the grounds that they are mutually dependent; for the phrase "when He is seen" does not require dependence on words such as "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) in order to show that the word *dṛṣṭa* here does not refer to knowledge in general, whereas the word "to be seen" and so forth does depend on [the context] to show that it functions in the sense of being a means (*upāya*).

The dependence on the statement "when that is seen" is not a fault of mutual dependence due to the difference in the means [of realization]. This is because the fruit is specified in both the preceding and following passages. The meaning is that since the fruit of immortality alone is specified in the passages preceding and following the statement "The Self, verily, should be seen," direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) itself is not the fruit. The phrase "it is vitiated by eight defects" refers to the alternative (*vikalpa*).

Since it is possible for a single performer to undertake both *vrīhi* and *yava* through different ritual applications (*prayoga*), it is appropriate that [the option] be afflicted by the eight defects; however, since it is impossible for one person to undertake two knowledges (*vidyā*), how can there be affliction by the eight defects here? Anticipating this objection, he says: "In this case as well, the occurrence of defects arises according to possibility. The meaning is that because there is the occurrence of two defects in each [knowledge] due to the difference in performers, a set of four [defects] is possible. [This refers to] "the operation which serves as the means for perception."

Although the objection that a combination (*samuccaya*) of vision and meditation is possible—since it is possible for vision alone to be the object of an injunction—is indeed appropriate, vision is not fit to be enjoined; for, as in the case of "the clarified butter is to be looked at" (*paśyatyavekṣitamājyam*), the injunction of knowledge is accepted [elsewhere]. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the objection regarding the enjoinability of an activity was raised by following the perspective of others. Therefore, the relationship of means and end between the two is not established by any other means of knowledge.

The intended meaning here is that if another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) were to exist, the relationship between the probandum and the probans would be understood from that very source; therefore, this [scriptural injunction] would be redundant as it would depend upon that other means. "If [it is argued]: 'Together with meditation, [there is another cognition]' regarding direct realization"—the term "direct realization" is used as an illustration. The meaning is: if it were argued that, for the sake of either direct realization or liberation, another cognition—identical in form to perception—is to be enjoined by the word "is to be seen" (*dṛṣṭavya*), in conjunction with meditation through the method of combination (*samuccaya*).

And because that meditation and [the knowledge] do not stand in a relationship of means and end (*dvāra-dvāribhāva*), it is possible for them to have a connection through some mutual contribution toward a single goal; thus, their combination is possible. Nor should it be argued: "How can a connection through mutual contribution toward a single goal be established, since the knowledge whose form is identical to the vision (*darśana*) is something to be accomplished by meditation, and thus they do stand in a relationship of means and end?"—for this doubt belongs to one who harbors the misconception that such a thing does not exist. This is what they mean by saying "because it is possible. Furthermore, it is because one may assume an intended meaning (*tātparya*) even in the four supplementary verses (*catuṣśeṣa*).

The meaning is: [meditation] in the forms of the commencement of the realization of the meaning through instruction, repeated practice, vision, and that which has the same form as vision. Now, one might object: if, by the injunction "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*), meditation that has the same form as vision is prescribed, why could it not be the case that by "it is to be reflected upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), reflection (*manana*) that has the same form as profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*) is also prescribed? This would be like [the statement] "Upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is the loosening of all knots," since liberation is taught to follow immediately after reflection in the passage, "Having reflected, the wise man does not grieve."

If it is argued that because the words *manana* and *nididhyāsana* have distinct meanings, there is no evidence for the secondary sense of either, and therefore the secondary sense of the word *nididhyāsana* should not be resorted to—then [the same applies here]. To accord with such scriptural passages as "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death," "Having seen Him, the yogi is liberated," "When He, the higher and the lower, is seen," and "But then, meditating, he beholds Him who is partless," even the direct realization produced by a purified mind [must be accepted as the primary meaning].

Because the possibility of being an injunction exists; for, according to the principle "But there is an injunction regarding the wearing [of the sacred thread], because it is something not previously known" (*vidhistu dhāraṇe 'pūrvatvāt*), an injunction must be accepted. And because, in the present context, a clear injunction is heard. If it is argued that even so, the use of the root *dṛś* (to see), which denotes visual knowledge, would be figurative with respect to mental direct perception (*mānasasākṣātkāra*), we reply: this is no different. Furthermore, since mental direct perception—which resembles the direct perception at the time of liberation—is of the nature of a fruit (*phala*), it cannot be an object of injunction. Therefore, the intended meaning is that meditation (*dhyāna*) is enjoined as having a form identical to that of direct perception.

If it is understood that [the meditation] has the cause of the world as its object and consists of *nididhyāsana* (profound contemplation) whose form is identical to [direct] vision (*darśana*), one might ask: "How is this meaning apprehended by this statement? For the meaning apprehended by this is simply that all [cognition], such as reflection (*manana*) and hearing (*śravaṇa*) regarding the Self, has the entire [world] as its object, because of the non-difference between the material cause and its effect; it does not mean that everything having the cause of the world as its object is identical in form to direct vision. To this we reply: No. When the Self—whose object is the meditation whose form is identical to direct vision—is seen and known, then indeed everything [is known].

The statement is justified because the sense that "it becomes known," "omniscience occurs," and "liberation occurs" is clearly perceived therein. Precisely because of this lack of satisfaction [with the previous argument], he says: "Furthermore, regarding various types of ignorance... and "...because capacity is stronger than context."

For this very reason, [the author] will state in the adhikaraṇas beginning with "Ānandādayaḥ pradhānasya" and "Akṣaradhiyāṃ tvavarodhaḥ sāmānyatadbhāvābhyām" that qualities such as truthfulness (satyatva) and knowledge (jñānatva)—though mentioned in the specific contexts of particular meditations (vidyā)—are common to all meditations. [The phrase] "by means of the figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the words 'Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa'" and so forth is used because we observe that the words 'Darśa' and 'Pūrṇamāsa', which denote specific times, indicate the ritual acts themselves.

Likewise, in passages such as "One seeking to perform malevolent magic should sacrifice with the Śyena," the word *śyena* is accepted as being used figuratively for the ritual action based on its connection with the quality of swooping down and seizing, as indicated by the supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*): "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey]. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is because the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the middle region has been admitted.

Regarding the point of doubt as to whether, in the passage "He fixes half within the altar and half outside the altar," the phrase "within the altar" prescribes a specific portion of the altar as an accessory (*aṅga*) of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), or whether it indicates the location for measuring the post by means of a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in conjunction with "outside the altar"—the conclusion is that a specific portion of the altar is prescribed as an accessory of the post, because resorting to secondary signification is improper.

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the statement "half outside the altar" (*ardhaṃ bahirvedi*) is merely a restatement of what is already established by the sense of the matter, [the author argues]: if one half of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is measured within the altar according to the rule "half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*), there would be no scriptural authority regarding whether the other half is measured within the altar or outside the altar; consequently, the other half might at times also fall within the altar due to human whim. This is not an acceptable conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would result in the statement "half outside the altar" being a merely optional restatement (*pākṣikānuvāda*). Furthermore, if both [rules] were to be enjoined as independent injunctions, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Therefore, one should measure [the sacrificial post] in such a place where, when measured, half is within the altar (*antarvedi*) and half is outside the altar (*bahirvedi*). For the verbal root *mī* (from *ḍumiñ prakṣepaṇe*, "to cast") has the meaning "one should cast"; thus, the sense is that this is a definition of a specific location, as established in the *Pūrvatantra* under the section on secondary characteristics (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*). This is what is meant by "by means of the four sentences."

The following four statements should be considered: "Meditation (*upāsana*) must be [repeated] cognition, because it is heard in that context"; "One should perform the cognition once, since the purpose of the word has been fulfilled, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings"; "But it is established [that meditation is repeated] from the word 'meditation'"; and "It must be meditation, which is constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*), because of the scriptural indication and the etymological derivation. The meaning is that this is not only in the *Chāndogya*. Thus, "constant recollection" is heard in the *Chāndogya*, in the *Bhūmavidyā*: "Upon obtaining recollection, there is the loosening of all knots."

In the Saṃvarga-vidyā, it is heard in the scripture: "The deity whom you worship. Therefore, the meaning is that one should not think that [the deity] is only that [which is already present]. It is simply the acceptance of what has presented itself spontaneously. For if something is not dear, even if it presents itself spontaneously, it is rejected; if it is dear, it is accepted when it presents itself spontaneously. But if it is most dear, the sense is that there is the state of being chosen, which consists in its being prayed for.

An objection is raised: "Since leaves, flowers, and the like are seen to be objects of affection and objects of choice by the Blessed Lord even though they lack affection for Him, how can the commentary beginning with 'of whom' (*yasya*) be justified? Anticipating this, he says: "Being chosen by the Blessed Lord [occurs] when there is sentience.
