This means that being most dear to the Blessed Lord occurs when there is sentience; for it is precisely that [sentience] which is under discussion in that passage. Alternatively, the meaning is that being chosen is preceded by being most dear.

The sense is that being beloved in itself belongs only to one who possesses love for oneself; and for whom there is being beloved in itself, for that very person there is being chosen in itself. Regarding the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent. When, by the rule *gatyarthākarmaka...*, the suffix *kta* is prescribed with the intention of expressing an intransitive meaning, this rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* indicates that it occurs in the sense of the future within an expression of hope (*āśaṃsā*). Now, an objection: the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* is observed only in cases where the speaker’s hope is directed toward another.

If it is argued that this is just as in the cases, "If it rains, the rice will flourish," or "If the teacher has arrived, the grammar has been studied"—and as in the rule "The *liṅ* and *loṭ* [moods] are used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*)", where *liṅ* and *loṭ* are employed precisely within the scope of the speaker's desire—[we reply: no; for we do not observe the authors of the treatises using them solely in the sense of the speaker's desire, and because it is impossible to determine that they are restricted to that scope merely by showing such examples.

The point is that, regarding the domain of the optative (*liṅ*) and the imperative (*loṭ*), since usage occurs only when there is a desire on the part of the speaker, it is appropriate for it to be so [i.e., a desire]. This is as in the expression "an experience being experienced" (*anubhūyamāno 'nubhavaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "the word *priya* has as its meaning only the state of being an object of affection": this is common to both the first and third positions. The distinction is as follows: in the first position, the determination that the state of being an object of affection resides in affection itself is figurative (*aupacārika*); in the third, because even a cognition whose nature is future affection can possibly be an object of another affection, it is primary (*mukhya*).

In the second alternative, however, the meaning of *priya* is simply "favorable," and not merely "the object of affection"; this is the distinction. Although the word *priya*—by the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*—is formed with the suffix *ka* in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), since it is prescribed by the rule *kartari kṛt*, it should nevertheless be understood that, like the expression "the sweetmeat is pleasing to Devadatta" (*devadattāya rocate modakaḥ*), its meaning ultimately culminates in being an object; thus, there is no inconsistency in its having the sense of "object."

However, this remains to be considered: since it is precisely the nature of being *prīti* (joy/affection) that must be established, according to the maxim "when the use of a word is within one's own control," one should have specified "she herself is of the nature of *prīti*" (*svayam api prītirūpā*). Thus, the designation "*priyā*" (the beloved) in the Bhāṣya appears inappropriate. Therefore, it seems the second position alone is correct—that the meaning of the designation "*priyā*" is simply its state of being extremely favorable (*anukūlatva*). Alternatively, [one may interpret]: "The constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is itself extremely favorable"; here, "*prītirūpā*" (of the nature of joy) is the understood ellipsis.

And therefore, it is appropriate that she [the constant remembrance] is what is sought after by the verse beginning with "For that very joy... (*tataśca ata eva hi yā prītiḥ*). If the word "consisting of joy" (*prītirūpā*) were omitted, then while it would be stated that "she is sought after," one might understand that the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*) itself is what is sought after. However, this is not correct; for it should be observed that in the verse "That joy which... (*yā prītiḥ*), it is joy alone that is shown to be what is sought after, whereas the constant remembrance is not shown to be what is sought after.

If it is objected that in the verse beginning "That joy which... (*yā prītiḥ*), the primacy of the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) that has taken the form of joy is not perceived, we reply: no. Because of the co-occurrence with the term "recollection" in the phrase "that [joy] of mine who remembers You," it is possible to derive the sense that the recollection in the form of joy is what is being sought as the goal. Thus, it refers to the constant recollection in the form of joy.

Nor should one raise the objection: "In the passage 'svayamatyarthapriyā' (she is herself exceedingly dear), if the word *priyā* found in the commentary is taken to mean 'the object of love,' then the state of being love itself (*prītirūpatva*) is not obtained in the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*). How, then, can it be said that 'constant recollection is of the nature of love'? There is no contradiction in stating that it is of the nature of love, because even the demonstration that it is the object of love has the purpose of demonstrating that it is of the nature of love. [Objection: But surely, according to the lexicographers (*naighaṇṭuka*), only synonymy would be understood.

But it is not merely the fact that they terminate in the same object; regarding this, he says: "and functioning with respect to the same object. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of *eva* (only/exclusive); thus, only the functioning with respect to the same object is understood, and not synonymy (*paryāyatva*) as well. For if that were the case, since *sevā* (service) would also be a synonym for *bhakti*, it would contradict the usage of the learned authorities who state: "Abundant service is what is denoted by the word *bhakti*. [The phrase] "contradicted by the force of the scriptural statement" refers to: "O high-minded one, I am to be attained through unswerving *bhakti* or through *prapatti*, and not otherwise..."

This has been refuted by the force of the statement, "By the power of the word," and by the force of the statement, "The meaning of the scripture is indeed [to be realized] all at once. The sense is that the distinction is established based on the difference between those who are capable and those who are incapable. Now, however, it is said "by way of the single purpose of Śruti and Smṛti"; the meaning is that this is for the sake of establishing the non-contradiction between the Śruti and Smṛti passages that prohibit other means. And this will become clear later in the passage beginning with "of the supplement and the thing to be supplemented. This is stated in order to demonstrate the single purpose of the *Puruṣasūkta*.

The meaning is that this is intended to demonstrate that the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* has as its ultimate purport the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), based upon the fact that it shares the same subject matter as the *Puruṣasūkta*. Regarding the statement "I am not [attained] by the Vedas," two verses are cited: "Not by the Vedas" (*nāhaṃ vedaiḥ*) and "By you alone, with undivided devotion" (*bhavatyā tvananyayā*). With the intention of showing their identical meaning, the verse "That Supreme Person" (*puruṣaḥ sa paraḥ*) is also cited:
"Not by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be known in such a manner as You have seen Me."
"O scorcher of foes, by you alone—who are undivided from Me—can I, being of such a nature, be known in truth, seen, and entered.

These three verses, beginning with "That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable through undivided devotion; within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded," [are cited]. [The opponent argues that these are unnecessary] because of the risk of redundancy with the phrase "thereafter" (tadanantaram).

In the verse, "By devotion he comes to know Me in truth, both who I am and what I am; then, having known Me in truth, he enters [Me] immediately thereafter," the meaning is that if the word "then" (*tataḥ*) were used to refer back to knowledge (*jñāna*), there would be a redundancy with the phrase "immediately thereafter" (*tadanantaram*). Now, one might object: in the phrase "immediately thereafter," the pronoun *tat* refers to knowledge; whereas in the word "then," the pronoun *tat* refers to devotion (*bhakti*), which is the cause of knowledge.

If it is argued that there is no tautology in the statement, "Then, having known Me in essence through devotion, after that knowledge he enters Me," the answer is no; for since the fact that devotion is the cause of knowledge is already established by the phrase "Through devotion one comes to know Me," there would be the contingency of redundancy. The intended meaning is that what must be stated is something else entirely, namely, "then he enters. Nor should it be asked: "Since the devotion previously specified in 'Through devotion I am known' lacks the status of being a cause for attainment, how can that devotion be referred to by the word 'then' (tataḥ)? [This is not a fault, as the sequence of stages is implied.]
Since it is impossible for the word "tataḥ" (then/from that) to refer to that very same individual, it refers instead to an individual of that same class; thus, there is no fault.

"Or there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*). The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), because if mutual dependence were established, self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) would also necessarily follow. "By the power of unknown merit" (*ajñātasukṛtavaśāt*): protecting cows and so forth, performed by a hunter for his own livelihood through the killing of a tiger, is called "unknown merit. The meaning of the sentence "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*) is being considered here; the intention is that it is not the meaning of a sentence enjoining a rite that can be accomplished with little effort. Thus, the defects such as self-dependence would certainly arise.

Now, it may be argued that for one who has reached a state of emaciation due to an aversion to food, even when there exists a desire characterized by an orientation toward food in order to avoid that condition, an appetite culminating in actual engagement with it does not arise because of the defect of an imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātu-vaiṣamya) caused by severe indigestion and the like; therefore, [the Self] is like a medicine that causes relish. Thus, [it is said]: "The Supreme Bliss is vast..."

Regarding the point that "knowledge is the means for attaining That," even when a person—who possesses faith born from the greatness of mental serenity produced by the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites whose fruits were not sought after throughout hundreds of prior births—has developed a desire characterized by an orientation toward the attainment of Brahman and the knowledge thereof, there arises no inclination extending to actual engagement in the means of knowledge, such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), due to the obstruction caused by the accumulation of many defects of past sins gathered since beginningless existence, which produce an addiction to sense objects.

If it is argued that the engagement in ritual actions is indeed justified for the sake of achieving such a desire (ruci) preceded by the removal of obstacles—on the grounds that otherwise one would find no way to understand passages such as "The pleasure of those lacking discrimination" (*yā prītir avivekānām*)—we reply: this might be the case if an authority were found that establishes the means to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) as something not otherwise established; then some kind of reconciliation could be made. But such an authority does not exist.

The sense is that, while there is a general rule stating that "between the meaning of the base and the meaning of the suffix, the meaning of the suffix is predominant," the specific rule—"that which is expressed by the suffix *san* (desire) is predominant over the object of the verbal root"—is more powerful, as seen in examples such as *aśvena jigamiṣati* ("he wishes to go by horse"). Intending to show that the mere act of denotation is irrelevant because it has already been accomplished previously, he says: "the meaning is 'we shall establish [this]'" (*upapādayiṣyāmaḥ*). Thus, the word *tat* refers to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

Nor should it be suspected that the performance of rituals is redundant because the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is already established prior to the commencement of meditation; for the point is that rituals are required so that the desire to know—which serves as the cause for meditation—may persist daily through their daily performance. This also applies to the requirement of ritual until the end of one's life; the meaning is that rituals are required either directly or indirectly for that [desire to know].

(And thus, even in the view that [the stages of life] are for the purpose of the desire to know, since there exists a mere state of being required: he states the purpose of presenting the Sūtra—setting aside the Vedic statements which ought to be shown when there is an inquiry into the means of valid knowledge—with the words "by the presentation of the Sūtra. [The phrase] "even though they are subsidiary to the stages of life" means "they are also limbs of knowledge"; that is to say, they are required by knowledge. Therefore, the sense is that even in the view that they are for the purpose of the desire to know, there is no inconsistency, because the mere state of being required exists. (The sevenfold means.)

Regarding the phrase “the indication of the cause of the sentence”: because an *itaretara-dvandva* (mutual conjunction) conveys a collective sense (*sāhitya*) characterized by aggregation (*samuccaya*). For this very reason, in the first section of the eleventh book (*PMS 11.1.1*), it was established that the six sacrifices collectively serve as the means for achieving the result, so that the collectivity understood through the *dvandva* compound in the expression “by means of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa” would not be sublated. This is the intended meaning. As for the statement “aggregation (*samuccaya*) is a distinct category of meaning”: although there are four meanings of the particle *ca*—namely, aggregation (*samuccaya*), option (*anvācaya*), mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), and collective whole (*samāhāra*)—all four are indeed forms of aggregation (*samuccaya*) that stand in opposition to option (*vikalpa*), which is the meaning of the particle *vā*.

For indeed, in the case of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) such as "Bring the cow and the horse," or in the case of an incidental mention (*anvācaya*) such as "Go for alms and bring the cow," or in the case of mutual association (*itaretarayoga*) such as "Devadatta and Yajñadatta do [the work]," or in the case of a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*) such as "Bring the umbrella and the sandals," there is no cognition of an option (*vikalpa*), which is the meaning of the word *vā*. Nevertheless, the point is that—just like the word *vā*—the word *samuccaya* (conjunction) applies both to the specific sub-types of conjunction mentioned [above] and to the general category of conjunction that stands in opposition to option.

Regarding the phrase "the basis of birth" (*jātyāśraya*), one might ask how there can be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the expression "purity of the body is discernment" (*kāyaśuddhir vivekaḥ*). Anticipating this doubt, he explains—starting with the words "concerning the subject of food"—that in the sentence "from food that is not defiled by being [inherently] unfit for consumption" (*jātyāśravanimittāduṣṭād annāt*), since it is understood that the purity of the body is the goal to be accomplished through food that is distinguished from what is defiled, the word "discernment" (*viveka*), which denotes the cause, indicates by implication (*lakṣyate*) the resulting purity. As for "those defiled by birth," these are the *kalañja*, the *gṛñjana*, and so forth. It is said: "One should know that garlic, the *gṛñjana*, onions, mushrooms, eggplants, lotus stalks, and bottle gourds are defiled by their very nature.
(*laśunaṃ gṛñjanaṃ caiva palāṇḍuṃ kavakāni ca / vārtākanālikālābūn jānīyājjātidūṣitān //*).

The foregoing should be understood in this manner. Since metaphorical usage is improper when the primary sense is possible, he says "or else. Let "discrimination" (*viveka*) mean the discernment from the body; as to how there can be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he says "from the impure," and so on, up to "remember Me.
[As it is said: "Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that thought."
"Therefore, at all times, remember Me and fight"—such is the sequence of the verses. Regarding "truth" and "the welfare of beings":
"Truth is said to be the welfare of beings; straightforwardness is equanimity of mind; compassion is the desire for the welfare of beings; and forbearance is the endurance of dualities."
Such authoritative evidence is to be observed. The collection of statements establishing straightforwardness (*ārjava*) and other virtues is thus encompassed:
"Giving, sacrifice, honoring the virtuous, the preservation of the Vedas, and straightforwardness—this is to be known as the supreme dharma, which bears fruit both in this world and after death."

The sense is that this constitutes a collection of statements. Intending to show that non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed a distinct state of being (*bhāvāntara*), he says, "the lack of luminosity" (*abhāsvaratvam*). Regarding the explanation of the word "dejection" (*dainya*): adopting the view that the absence of luminosity is distinct from dejection, he says, "contrary to luminosity. The word "and" (*ca*) is displaced in order; the meaning is that the phrase "and born from that" (*tajjaṃ ca*) is displaced. The meaning is: dejection arises from the deficiency of place and time, as well as from the recollection of objects of grief, and [the other] is born from that.

It should be understood that if the word *dainya* (dejection) were not used before the word *tajja* (born of that), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the pronoun *tat* could not refer back to dejection. Alternatively, [the phrase] "by way of being separate sentences" (*bhinnavākyatayā*) means that in this view, there is a division of the sentence "dejection born of that" (*tajjaṃ dainyam*), and its placement later [in the sequence] results in the fault of supplying (*adhyāhāra*) the word *tat* in the phrase "and that dejection born of that" (*tacca tajjaṃ dainyam*). Such internal inconsistency (*asvarasa*) is to be understood.
(The meaning of the Vedic text is "and [one should seek] knowledge").

"Taking the meaning of this statement as the basis" means taking the meaning of the statement, "Karmas are for the ripening of the afflictions" (*kaṣāyapaktiḥ karmāṇi*). "In order to exclude that" means [it is said] so that it might exclude both [possibilities]. That is, since it is observed that [knowledge] excludes both, the meaning is that this is to exclude the doubt that karma, like its own prior karma, might likewise exclude its own subsequent [karma]. However, some hold that the word "prior" (*prācīnam*) does not refer to what is prior in relation to karma.

The collection of karmas performed over many hundreds of births, whose constituent parts have not yet manifested, is referred to by the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*). In this context, if the word *prācīna* (ancient) were a reference to that [collection], then it would be established that when such karma is destroyed, there is no destruction of those karmas that follow immediately after it—which is not what is intended. Nor can it be said that the word *avidyā* refers only to the final karma, for that would contradict such passages as "when the dross has been cooked away by karmas."

The statement that "by those various actions there is the destruction of those very things that preceded them" is not intended as a final conclusion; for if that were the case, it would follow that the destruction of all preceding factors occurs by the very first action alone. Furthermore, once it is stated "having crossed over," there would be no room for even the suspicion of non-adherence to subsequent actions, and thus that suspicion would not need to be dispelled. Moreover, it would follow that knowledge arises at the very moment immediately following that [destruction].

Therefore, they consider that in the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase "all karma prior to knowledge" (*jñānaprācīnaṃ karma*)—even including that accumulated over many births—is intended solely to indicate completeness (*sākalya*). It is not, however, intended to mean that for some [beings] those things denoted by the word "death" (*mṛtyu*), being "karma prior to [knowledge]," are to be warded off; for that would be irrelevant. They hold that its construction is "having reached and remaining," for in their view, the root *tṛ* signifies reaching (*prāpti*). Alternatively, this may be the construction favored by Śaṅkara. The suffix *-liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

The meaning is "in the sense of being possible" (*saṃbhavārthika*). Consequently, the interpretation offered by others—that he who knows *vidyā* as the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) and *avidyā* as its cause, together with their respective causes and effects, crosses over death—which is *avidyā* since it has *avidyā* as its material cause—by means of that modification of the internal organ which consists of [that *avidyā*], and through *vidyā*, which is characterized by knowledge constituting his true nature (*svarūpabhūta-jñāna*), attains immortality (*amṛtatva*)—is indicated here as being unworthy of even mention.

Since the knowability of the limbs (*aṅga*) is established even when the knowability of the primary [subject] (*aṅgin*) is stated—because it is already proven by what was not explicitly mentioned—there is little purpose in conjoining them; therefore, he explains otherwise: "Or rather, 'in the case of dharma' (*yadvā dharme ca*). Because the two things to be conjoined are contradictory, they can only be understood through a dictionary definition; thus, he explains with the intent of conjoining the stated meanings: "Or rather, 'they are indicators of each word' (*yadvā pratipadadyotakau*)."

Regarding the verse beginning with “In both dharma and artha,” it should be understood that since commentators have explained the word *ca* (and) as signifying both a conjunction of opposites (*virodhi-samuccaya*) and a conjunction of what has already been stated (*ukta-samuccaya*), its inclusion as an illustrative example is appropriate in both cases. [This applies to the phrase] “both merit and sin.”

In accordance with the introduction to the *Bhāṣya*, which states, "And action, consisting of merit and demerit, is an obstacle to knowledge," and considering that the subsequent *Bhāṣya*—namely, "by way of being an obstacle to the arising of Vedic knowledge"—is preceded by an introductory remark stating, "To the question 'What follows from that? he says," [the author] maintains that the word *pāpman* (evil/demerit) does not refer solely to other types of sin.

The sense is this: although in the passage "all evils" (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*), the word *pāpman* (evil) could possibly refer to all sins not explicitly mentioned by the word *duṣkṛta* (misdeed), the word *pāpa* (sin) cannot possibly have that restricted scope; furthermore, because the immediately following sentence, "He is indeed free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā hy eṣaḥ*), which corresponds to the cessation of all things to be discarded, must necessarily include the subject of good deeds (*sukṛta*) as well, our desired objective is established by that much alone.

However, some explain that in the phrase "all evils" (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*), the word *pāpman* does not refer to other sins not mentioned by the word *duṣkṛta*; this is because of the natural force of the term itself. Nor should it be argued: "If this is so, how can the word *pāpman* in the immediately following sentence serve as a reason for the word *pāpman* in the preceding sentence to have the sense of 'all'? For, in the absence of a subverting factor, it is improper for two words occurring within the same context to possess different meanings. This is how they describe it.

One might object: "Could it not be that even in the sentence 'This [Self] is free from evil' (*apahatapāpmā hy eṣaḥ*), the word 'free from evil' means the cessation of only a few unspecified evils? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For [it would be improper] if there were a mention of the cessation of only a few unspecified evils. This refers to the fact that, although the word 'evil' (*pāpman*) is used figuratively in relation to grief and so forth.

In the statement, "He is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, and free from sorrow," although it is possible for the word *pāpman* (evil) to be used figuratively with respect to sorrow and the rest—since they are mentioned separately from the word *pāpman* and since there is no common ground for its application (*anugata-pravṛtti-nimitta*) to them—it cannot be used figuratively with respect to merit (*sukṛta*), because a common ground for its application does exist in that case.

Nor should it be argued that because the metaphorical sense (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted according to the "umbrella-logic" (*chatrinyāya*), there is a contradiction between two modes of operation (*vṛtti*) such that neither could be primary; for even so, since a metaphorical sense based on predominance (*bhūman*) is possible—as in the case of "he lays down the *sṛṣṭi*-bricks"—one must not resort to a figurative sense (*gauṇī vṛtti*) based merely on the presence of a characteristic (*liṅgasamavāya*), as is done in passages such as "he lays down the *prāṇabhṛt*-bricks. This is the intended meaning. Some, however, maintain that this was stated with the view that the contradiction between two modes of operation is not a defect.

Others, however, following the statement of the author of the *Vākya*—namely, "Time, old age, death, grief, and so forth are enumerated"—maintain that the term "evil" (*pāpa*) is used in its primary sense even with respect to grief and the like. They argue that even if it were not used in its primary sense, there would be no deficiency; for although the commonality of being an object of the word "evil" might not serve as a logical reason, there is a commonality of the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and thus in the phrase "by means of dharma [one removes] evil," it is indeed used in its primary sense. (The meaning of the sentence concerning the desire to lead upward.)

Regarding the phrase "the two occurrences of *yat*": the meaning is that there are two instances of the word *yat*, namely in the phrases "whom he wishes to lead upward" (*yam unninīṣati*) and "whom he wishes to lead downward" (*yam adho ninīṣati*). It is understood as referring to the state of being a causal agent (*kārayitṛtva*) by means of bestowing knowledge. The meaning is that from this statement we perceive that the two intentions expressed by the two occurrences of *yat*—namely, the actions known as merit and demerit which are the causes of heaven and hell—are the causes for the desire to lead upward and the desire to lead downward, which in turn function as the motivators for making one perform those actions.

The meaning is that, consequently, it is established that the capacity of actions to motivate further action is mediated by knowledge. Now, one might object: "Even if it is established by this much that what is termed 'sin'—namely, the performance of improper action—is a cause for the undertaking of actions that lead to hell through the mediation of the knowledge of what ought to be done, it is not yet established that it acts as an obstacle to the arising of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). To this we reply: if there were no obstruction to right knowledge—characterized by the recognition that a prohibited action produces a powerful undesirable result—then it would follow that no inclination toward such an action could ever arise; therefore, [an obstacle must necessarily exist].

Since it must be stated that [sin] is an obstacle to right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), it is established that it is also an obstacle to the knowledge of Brahman. Otherwise, the very engagement in sinful actions would be impossible. Regarding the phrase "it relates to all actions and deities in general": because the verse "they join him with the intellect" (*buddhyā saṃyojayanti tam*) does not specify any particular action as the object of the intellect, it would only establish that [sin] is an obstacle to knowledge concerning everything in general, and not an obstacle to the knowledge of the Lord which is the cause of liberation.

Likewise, because of the mention of deities in general in the phrase "The gods do not take up a staff," the intended agency of the Blessed Lord himself—as expressed in the words "He indeed [is the cause]"—is not obtained; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "because of not being excluded from the generality of perfect knowledge," this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa); it should also be understood that the Blessed Lord is likewise not excluded from the generality of deities.
(This refers to the meaning of the passage beginning with "By dharma [one destroys] evil").

The meaning is that since [the means] has already been taught previously, there is no fault in not mentioning it now. Regarding the phrase "because it is heard here": this means because it is heard in such passages as "He removes evil through dharma," within the context of "Therefore they say sacrifice is supreme" and "Therefore they say truth is supreme. [Otherwise,] the sense would have to be "removing [evil]."

If it is objected that, by adopting as the meaning of the word "sin" (pāpa) the quality of being a means to an undesirable result at that particular time, there would follow the consequence that even those actions performed for the sake of heaven—which are means to undesirable results such as sons or cattle for a certain person at a specific time—would be destroyed [by the mere knowledge of Brahman], we reply: no. This is because, according to the logic stated in the *Yogasiddhyadhikaraṇa*, it is impossible for an action performed for the sake of another result to destroy, within that very same performance, the sin that is a means to undesirable cattle and so forth.

And in the present context, since sacrifices and other rites enjoined by the passage beginning with "by sacrifice" require a specific means [for their fruit], the statement "by dharma he removes evil" serves to provide that specific means; thus, it is logical that the removal of evil occurs even through those rites performed for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, this is because they are included within that which is denoted by the word "evil."

If it is argued that since sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma are well-known as *dharma*, they would become *adharma* for a seeker of liberation because they are means to what is undesirable for him; and that this would lead to the consequence that whatever is undesirable for a person at a particular time would then be *adharma* for that person at that time, thereby rendering the distinction between *dharma* and *adharma* unstable—this is not so. For we accept this very consequence. The conventional usage of *dharma* and *adharma* is indeed relative to a specific person. Intending that the word "tat" (that) carries the sense of "tasmāt" (therefore), he explains [the verse] with the words "śrutismṛti... (scripture and tradition...).

The word *evam* (thus) is to be explained as follows. The phrase *upāyatrati-bandhaka-nirāsārtham* (for the purpose of removing obstacles to the means) is the grammatical split (*cheda*). Therefore, because the knowledge of Brahman depends upon the performance of rituals performed without desire for their fruits (*phalābhisandhi*). If it is objected: "Granted that the meditation on Brahman—which is accomplished through ritual action—depends upon the inquiry into that [action], it does not follow that the inquiry into Brahman itself depends upon it," we reply: No. This is because the intention is that, since the two primary elements (*śeṣin*)—ritual action and meditation—are to be performed in a specific order, the two inquiries (*vicāra*) which are subordinate (*śeṣa*) to them must also follow that same order.

He says "Knowledge indeed... and so forth, stating that [the inquiry into Brahman] also possesses the capacity to produce the knowledge of the instability of the fruits of karma, which serves as a qualification for the specific candidate required by the inquiry into Brahman.
(Refutation of the view that the fourfold means of qualification must precede [the inquiry into Brahman])

"And the sevenfold means" (sādhanasaptakam) refers to discernment, liberation, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "beginning with": "The eternal and the non-eternal are present [in all things], thus they are 'eternal-non-eternal entities' (nityānityavastūni); their properties are likewise so called. Discernment between these two substrates—the eternal and the non-eternal—and between their respective properties, is 'discernment of eternal and non-eternal entities' (nityānityavastuvivekaḥ). What is meant is this: let there not be a discernment directed toward specific substrates such that one thinks, 'This is the Truth and Eternal; this is the Untruth and Non-eternal. Rather, one simply determines the discernment between the two substrates, the eternal and the non-eternal, in their general form, as well as between their properties."

Eternality is truth; that which possesses this is eternal and true, and thus it is the object of reliance (*āsthā*). Likewise, non-eternality is untruth; that which possesses this is non-eternal and false, and thus it is the object of non-reliance (*anāsthā*). Therefore, among these objects and subjects currently being experienced—which are the spheres of the notions of "you" and "I"—that which is established as real, eternal, true, and blissful shall become the object of reliance.

"But that which is impermanent and unreal will be abandoned as it is encompassed by the threefold suffering"—this is the "discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities," which arises for one whose internal nature (*sattva*) has been purified through actions either from a previous birth or from this life, by means of both experience and logical reasoning; such is the remainder of the passage [from the *Vivaraṇa*].

The meaning is as follows: even in the absence of a specific determination such as "this is eternal" or "this is non-eternal," there must nonetheless exist the properties of eternality and non-eternality in relation to their respective substrata (dharmin); this general determination is precisely what is meant by the term *nityānityavastuviveka*. In the manuscript collections, the reading "the eternality of an eternal substratum is its reality (*satyatva*)" is observed; in that context, the word "of the eternal" (*nityasya*) is intended merely as a statement of the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

The final meaning is as follows: that subject (*dharmin*) which possesses permanence and reality is to be accepted (*upādeya*); that subject which possesses impermanence and unreality is to be abandoned (*heya*). This is the distinction. The reading "of that subject" (*yasya dharmiṇaḥ*) is indeed easy to understand. As for the phrase "if [one thinks] that which defines [the object] is to be abandoned," the word "impermanent" (*anityam*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the expression "at the beginning and at the end": this means in the two states of performing the practice and experiencing its fruit.

"And because of its independence, there is no possibility of it having occurred previously. This means that because that other scripture (the *Āgama*) brings about the state of being free from expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*) regarding the investigation of the *Brāhmaṇa*. For this very reason, he will likewise state in the conclusion: "Because other scriptures bring about the state of being free from expectancy regarding the investigation of the *Brāhmaṇa*. "Because of its utility for its own purpose" means because of its utility for the commencement [of the inquiry]. "Dependent on the principles therein" means dependent on the injunctions for repetition and so forth. Furthermore, "starting from the very first sūtra... [and so on].

Although, even if the Sūtra were intended to establish the subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), and qualified candidate (*adhikārin*), such a circularity could easily be asserted—resulting in the undesirable consequence of the destruction of the very Sūtra that describes the utility of commencing the treatise—nevertheless, the intention here is that the first Sūtra has not been explained by others as being intended to establish the invalidity of other scriptures and so forth.

Therefore, it should be understood that by introducing another refutation with the words, "Furthermore, [it has] impermanent results," one is merely raising the question of the impermanence of results such as heaven based on other scriptures and one's own speculative reasoning; it is not, however, raising a question regarding the opening sūtra of this very scripture. This refers either to the weakness of other scriptures or the strength of one's own scripture. The meaning is: either the weakness of other scriptures devoid of the strength of one's own scripture, or the strength of one's own scripture devoid of the weakness of other scriptures.

"Or both combined. This means the weakness of other treatises (*śāstra*) and the strength of one's own treatise. Regarding "the weakness of one's own treatise," the meaning is that in the absence of the strength of one's own treatise, it would share the same fate as other treatises.

For this very reason, [it is said] "of the knowledge of the affliction by the threefold suffering. Nor should one suspect that this contradicts the statement: "He alone is to be investigated for the sake of immortality by those afflicted by the three torments"; for that statement also intends to convey the understanding that the fruits of ritual action (*karman*), produced by the inquiry into such rites, are inferior and unstable, and thus there is no fault.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the realization—born from the inquiry into ritual action—that rituals yield only small and unstable fruits, along with the desire for infinite and stable fruits, can indeed constitute the fourfold qualification (sādhana-catuṣṭaya) as accepted by others, we grant that there is no contradiction; nevertheless, the Commentator’s [Śaṅkara’s] emphasis lies in the fact that it is logical for the inquiry of each preceding chapter to be a prerequisite for the subsequent one, just as in the case of the aphorism, "Now, therefore, follows the definition of the subsidiary" (*athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*).

The fixed order of sequence was stated on the basis of the nature of the subject matter to be explained (*vyākhyeya*). Now, its establishment is being stated on the basis of the nature of the explanation (*vyākhyāna*) itself. Since the two subjects to be explained—namely, ritual action (*karman*) and meditative worship (*upāsanā*)—which are the primary matters (*śeṣin*) revealed by the Vedas, stand in a relationship of cause and effect and thus possess a temporal sequence of priority and posteriority, the sequence of the two investigations (*vicāra*) that are subordinate to them is likewise stated. The meaning is that the sequence of this present treatise is now being stated because it depends upon the principles set forth in the *Karmakāṇḍa*. This was stated for the sake of illustration.

The intention is as follows: upon examining the Bhāṣya statement, "And their status as means is to be determined through application (*viniyoga*)," it is understood that the fourfold set of means possesses a status as a means that is to be established by the *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth, which are expounded in the third chapter [of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtras]; therefore, it appears that [the inquiry into Dharma] must precede them. However, this is not tenable.

One should not suspect that there is room for the talkative claim that because the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) has as its cause the apprehension of logic (*tarka*) and so forth—which constitute the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*) and its procedures as expounded in the science of logic (*tarkaśāstra*)—it follows that the science of logic must also precede it; for the purport of the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) here is that [the inquiry into ritual] depends upon that [logic] only insofar as many of the matters to be expounded therein generally require a determination by it.
(Summary of the Meaning of Pūrvamīmāṃsā)

"The definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been set forth" means that the nature of the means of valid cognition—consisting of injunction (*vidhi*), explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), mantra, name (*nāmadheya*), tradition (*smṛti*), custom (*ācāra*), supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*), and capacity (*sāmarthya*)—has been explained. "Or the distinction between the scriptures" is to be understood according to the view of the Guru (Prabhākara). Regarding "the causes of distinction": in injunctions such as "he sacrifices," "he offers oblations," and "he gives," there is a distinction between sacrifice, giving, and offering, based on the difference in words consisting of the distinct verbal roots *yajati*, *juhoti*, and *dadāti*.

In injunctions such as "He offers the *samidh* oblation" and "He offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation," the distinction between the *prayāja* offerings arises from the repetition of the word "offers" (*yajati*) five times in the form of a non-specific restatement (*aviśeṣapunaḥśruti*). In the passage "He immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," the distinction between the sacrifices—deducible from that [immolation]—is established by the number seventeen, which differentiates them from their respective deities. In sentences such as "Now this is the *Jyotis* [sacrifice]," the sacrifices bearing those names are distinguished from the previously mentioned *Jyotiṣṭoma* by means of their designations, *Jyotis* and so forth.

The meaning is that difference is established through "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) and other criteria as follows: when curds are added to heated milk, that becomes the *āmikṣā* (coagulated milk) dedicated to the Viśvedevas. Then, regarding the statement "the whey (*vājina*) for the Vājins," since the sacrifice is already occupied by another accessory in the form of the *āmikṣā*, the accessory of the whey finds no place therein; thus, the sacrifice of the whey is distinct from the sacrifice of the *āmikṣā*. Similarly, the monthly *agnihotra* is distinct from the obligatory *agnihotra* due to the "difference of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*). In this manner, difference is demonstrated by means of "difference of words" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "direct statement (śruti) and indicative mark (liṅga)": Direct statement is a word that is independent [of other means of proof]. It is threefold: enjoining (vidhātrī), denotative (abhidhātrī), and applicatory (viniyoktrī). Among these, the enjoining direct statement consists of words such as *liṅ* (the optative suffix); the denotative consists of words such as *indra*; and the applicatory is threefold: consisting of a single case-ending (*ekapratyaya*), consisting of a single word (*ekapada*), and consisting of a case-suffix (*vibhakti*). In this regard, the first type is the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the sentence "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*). For that [suffix] conveys the subordinate status (*śeṣatva*) of the number "oneness" (which is expressed by itself) toward the factor of instrumentality (the *karaṇakāraka*) which is expressed by itself.

The second [type of case] is the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), as in the word *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"). By this, the status of the sacrifice expressed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is established as being subordinate (*śeṣatā*) with respect to each of the actions denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*). The third [type of case], which conveys the status of being the primary object (*śeṣitva*), is twofold: that which conveys the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) and that which conveys the status of being the primary object (*śeṣitva*). In instances such as *vrīhīn prokṣati* ("he sprinkles the rice-grains"), the accusative case conveys the status of being the primary object—characterized as the state of being most desired (*īpsitatamatva*)—with respect to the action of sprinkling and so forth, in the case of the rice-grains and other such items.

In the statement, "When the Soma has been purchased, he hands over the staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa," the direct hearing of the dative case (*caturthī-śruti*) indicates that the Maitrāvaruṇa possesses the status of a *śeṣin* (the primary beneficiary), characterized by being intended as the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) of the act of giving.

In the statement "he purchases [the Soma] with a ruddy [cow]," the instrumental case (*aruṇayā*) indicates that the quality of redness (*aruṇya*) is subordinate (*śeṣa*) to the efficient force of the purchase (*kraya-bhāvanā*). In "he brings earth from the pit" (*cātvālānmṛdamāharati*), the ablative case (*cātvālāt*) indicates that the pit is subordinate to the action of bringing the earth. In "he places the oblations on the altar" (*vedyāṃ havīṃṣyāsādayati*), the locative case (*vedyām*) indicates that the altar is subordinate to the action of placing the oblations. Thus, the third, fifth, and seventh cases indicate subordination (*śeṣatva*). However, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) sometimes indicates predominance (*śeṣitva*), as in "one desiring sensory power should sacrifice with curds" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*), and sometimes it indicates subordination, as in "the *yājyā* verse belongs to the sacrificer" (*yajamānasya yājyā*).

Since a genitive case-ending, which merely teaches a relationship, can result in either [of two possible meanings] depending on suitability (*yogyatā*) and other factors, the *liṅga* (indicative power) is the capacity of the thing itself. That is twofold: the capacity of the word (*śabda-sāmarthya*) and the capacity of the meaning (*artha-sāmarthya*). In this regard, the mantra "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*) has the status of being subordinate to the act of cutting (*lavana-śeṣatā*) due to the *liṅga* consisting in its capacity to manifest that act of cutting.

Regarding the injunctions "he cuts with the *svadhiti*," "he cuts with the *sruc*," and "he cuts with the hand," although the *svadhiti* and other implements are heard in scripture as general means for the act of cutting (*avadāna*), their specific application to the cutting of meat, liquid substances, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and so forth, is determined by the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting of their respective capacities. A sentence (*vākya*) is the juxtaposition of words devoid of any [direct] scriptural statement (*śruti*) that would indicate either the status of being subordinate (*śeṣatva*) or the status of being principal (*śeṣitva*). For example: "One desiring heaven should perform the *Agnihotra* sacrifice."

Or, for example: "The Maitrāvaruṇa priest gives the command and recites the invitatory verse. For there is no second-case (accusative) scriptural mention indicating that heaven is the primary object (*śeṣin*) to be produced in relation to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) of the oblation, nor is there any third-case (instrumental) scriptural mention indicating that the Maitrāvaruṇa is a subordinate factor (*śeṣa*) as an agent in relation to the commanding and reciting. The nominative case, however, is taught merely with respect to the meaning of the nominal stem itself. Therefore, the understanding of the relationship between the subordinate and the primary arises through the sentence (*vākya*), which consists in the co-occurrence of words (*padasamabhivyāhāra*).

*Prakaraṇa* (context) is the expectancy for the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*) regarding that which is understood as something to be done through an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*), but whose specific mode of execution is not yet known—namely, "In what manner should it be performed? This is of two kinds: *mahāprakaraṇa* (primary context) and *avāntaraprakaraṇa* (subordinate context). Among these, by the first, the subsidiary status (*śeṣatā*) of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth with respect to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and others is established; by the second, the subsidiary status of the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) and other such acts—which are recited in proximity to those [subsidiaries] like the *prayāja*—with respect to the *prayāja* and others is established.

Position (*sthāna*) is twofold: according to numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) and proximity (*saṃnidhi*). Among these, by the former, the mantra "O ladle, may you be undecaying; may I become undecaying," which is recited between the two mantras dedicated to Agni and Agni-Soma, is established as a subsidiary to the *upāṃśuyāja* sacrifice to be performed between the two sacrifices to Agni and Agni-Soma. Proximity (*saṃnidhi*), however, is twofold: proximity of textual recitation (*āmnāna-saṃnidhi*) and proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-saṃnidhi*).

By the first [criterion], the mantra "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods" is subordinate to the sprinkling of the *sāṃnāyya* vessels, as it lacks both the major context (*mahāprakaraṇa*) and the intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*). By the second [criterion], the characteristics of the animal sacrifice are subordinate to the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice. *Samākhyā* (name/designation) is an etymological term; it is of two kinds: worldly and Vedic.

The meaning is that the relationship between the subordinate (śeṣa) and the principal (śeṣin), along with its exceptions, has been elaborated upon in the third chapter: namely, that the Hotṛ priest’s status as a subordinate with respect to the drinking from the *camasa* cup is established by the Vedic designation (*vaidika-samākhyā*) "the Hotṛ's cup" (*hotṛcamasa*), and the Adhvaryu’s status as a subordinate with respect to the threshing and other such acts is established by the worldly designation well-known among ritualists (*laukika-samākhyā*) "pertaining to the Adhvaryu" (*ādhvaryava*).

"By means of those things for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), [there is the application] of those things for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). This means: by means of sacrifices that serve the purpose of the person, there is the application of those things that serve the purpose of the sacrifice. In other words, it is the *śeṣin* (the principal) that effects the application of the *śeṣas* (the subsidiaries). The *śeṣin* alone impels the performance [of the subsidiary] for the sake of its own accomplishment, and not even that which is produced subsequently. Nor does the *śeṣa* impel the *śeṣin*.

Even when many subsidiaries exist, where the application of something already impelled elsewhere occurs [in another context], there it is precisely that which impelled it elsewhere that impels the subsidiary, and not some other thing, even though it may be the *śeṣin*.

And thus, in the sentence "one pours curds into heated milk," when there is an expectancy for another object (*karman*) for the act of pouring curds—which is being enjoined and takes two objects—the co-occurring "milk" (*payaḥ*) is construed as that other object; because it is designated by the locative case as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it results in being the primary object (*pradhānakarman*). Consequently, since it is designated in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *tat* (which refers back to the milk mentioned in the context as the primary element), it is understood to be of the nature of milk; and precisely because it is the *āmikṣā*, it is the subordinate element (*śeṣitva*).

The bringing of curd (*dadhyānayana*) enforces its own performance as something that is a subordinate element (*śeṣabhūta*); however, the whey (*vājina*), which is produced as a byproduct of that same process, does not. Therefore, the application of the bringing of curd occurs only upon the failure of the *āmikṣā*, and not upon the failure of the whey. Similarly, although the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇā*) is connected to two actions—scratching and throwing—according to the texts "He scratches with the black antelope horn" and "He throws the black antelope horn into the *cātvāla* pit," the horn is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) toward the act of scratching because of the instrumental case ending used for it in that context.

Regarding the throwing away (*prāsana*), however, because the horn is the subordinate element (*śeṣin*) [indicated] by the accusative case, once its purpose—namely scratching—has ceased, there is no further application (*prayukti*) for the procurement of another black antelope horn if that specific one is lost prior to the throwing away, for the sake of the throwing away itself. The meaning is that the capacity for performance (*anuṣṭhāna-śakti*), which constitutes the nature of application, has been defined as being subject to exceptions (*sāpavādā*). This is illustrated by the rule: "He scatters the husks with the cake-pan" (*puroḍāśakapālena tuṣān upavapati*). Here, since the pan is employed for the scattering of husks only as a subordinate element belonging to that which was already employed for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), there is no requirement to procure a pan for the scattering of husks in a case where no cake exists. Thus, the capacity for performance is established as being contingent upon such conditions.

Regarding the phrase *śrutyartha* (based on direct scriptural statement and purpose): in passages such as "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates the Brāhmaṇa," the sequence of the two initiations is determined by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the suffix *-ktvā*. In the cases of "He offers the Agnihotra" and "He cooks the gruel," the sequence between the oblation and the cooking is determined by the purpose (*artha*). In passages such as "He sacrifices to the Samidhs" and "He sacrifices to Tanūnapāt," the sequence is determined by the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*).

In the case of the acts such as *upākaraṇa* (dedication) and *niyojana* (binding), which are subsidiary to the Prājāpatya sacrifices enjoined by the rule, "He sacrifices seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," the sequence of the subsequent acts like *niyojana* follows the very order of the *upākaraṇa* that was first performed among the animals. In the *Sādyaska* sacrifice, regarding the animals to be sacrificed together according to the rule, "He sacrifices the animals together" at the place of the *savanīya*, among the *agnīṣomīya*, *savanīya*, and *ānubandhya* animals being sacrificed together, the *savanīya* takes precedence due to its position in the original model sacrifice.

The meaning is that this has been established in the section defining the order [of ritual performance] (*kramalakṣaṇa*), such as when it is ordained: "There are two *sārasvata* oblations"; since these two rites—having male and female deities respectively—are determined by the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses to have the rite dedicated to the female deity first, the order of their constituent parts (*aṅga*) must likewise follow the order of the primary acts (*pradhāna*). Thus it is explained.

Regarding the "determination of the qualified person" (*adhikārinirūpaṇam*): *adhikāra* is the ownership of the fruit [of the ritual]. Regarding "general extension" (*sāmānyātideśa*): extension (*atideśa*) is the principle that "this should be performed in the same manner as that. It is of three kinds: (1) extension by means of a direct scriptural statement, such as "The rest is the same as the Śyena," whereby the specific auxiliary parts of the Śyena sacrifice are extended to the one-day (*ekāha*) rite named *iṣu*; (2) extension by means of name (*nāman*), as in the case of the *Agnihotra* within the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana*, where the properties of the regular (*naiyamika*) *Agnihotra* are extended by the injunction, "He performs the *Agnihotra* for a month."

The meaning is that in the seventh [book], the general extension (*atideśa*)—expressed by the inferential statement, "In the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), such as those dedicated to Sūrya, the auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) must be performed as in the archetype (*prakṛti*)"—has been established. Regarding "specific extension" (*viśeṣātideśa*): the meaning is that in the eighth [book], the specific consideration of the relationship between the archetype and the modification—namely, "this ritual has that ritual as its archetype"—has been carried out. Regarding "adaptation" (*ūha*): [the meaning is that this is treated in the ninth book].

The meaning is that in the ninth [book], *ūha* (modification) is considered as the alteration of mantras, *sāmans*, and purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) resulting from their connection with modified items that have taken on the function of original items. Regarding *bādha* (sublation): it is the cessation of original auxiliary elements (*prākṛtāṅga`) that have reached a modification by way of its function, due to the loss of the purpose (*dvāralopa*), substitution (*pratyāmnāna*), prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), or exclusion (*paryudāsa*). For example, in the case of *kṛṣṇala* beans, there is the cessation of threshing (*avaghāta*) because of the loss of its purpose, which consists in the removal of the husk; and in the case of *śara* grass, there is the cessation [of *kuśa* grass] due to its substitution.

The meaning is that sublation (*bādha*) has been defined in the tenth book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*] as follows: by the prohibition, "One does not perform those two [Ājyabhāga offerings] in the animal sacrifice," there is the cessation of the two Ājyabhāgas in the animal sacrifice; and by the exclusion (*paryudāsa*), "In the Mahāpitṛyajña, one does not choose a lineage-ancestor (*ārṣeya*)," there is the cessation of the choice of a lineage-ancestor. Regarding "tantra" and "prasaṅga": *tantra* is the performance of ritual subsidiaries (*aṅga*) once for all with reference to multiple primary rites (*pradhāna*).

The meaning is as follows: when subsidiaries (aṅgas) are performed with reference to two groups of three—such as the mirror and so forth—and because there is identity of place, time, agent, and other factors, the subsidiaries are performed by way of *tantra* (simultaneous performance), since no distinction is perceived among them. *Prasaṅga* (incidental benefit) is the accomplishment of the benefit for one thing through that which was performed for the sake of another; for example, the accomplishment of the benefit for the *puroḍāśa* (sacrificial cake) that falls within the procedure (*tantra*) of the animal sacrifice (*paśu*) by means of the subsidiaries performed for the sake of the animal. In this manner, *tantra* and *prasaṅga* have been examined in the eleventh and twelfth chapters respectively.

"And the dependence on *saṃkarṣa* (the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa*). The sense is that in the passage, "That is improper, just like the *pradhāna*," the dependence on the principle [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], namely "Or rather [the rites are] distinct because the deities are distinct" (*nānā vā devatāpṛthaktvāt*), will be revealed.

It is called "the argument of cumulative addition" (*abhyuccayayukti*). This is because, even though the subject matter [of the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā*] is not the primary topic, it is required for the sake of direct connection; thus, if one were to rely on the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) as having preceded this *Śārīraka-śāstra*, then since the refutation of other systems that contradict the doctrine of Brahman as the cause—which will be carried out in that very section (the first pāda)—would also be useful, it would follow that the entire inquiry into the meaning of the *Mīmāṃsā-śāstra* must have preceded it. Therefore, it is termed the "argument of cumulative addition."

One should understand this to be the statement of the author of the Vākya: "Its purpose is for the sake of the accomplishment of karma, because of its etymological derivation. The meaning is that, since it consists of the vision of Brahman, it depends upon the knowledge of Brahman.

Although not all meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth take the form of the vision of Brahman—since that is absent in passages such as "One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in the worlds" and "One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman in rain"—nevertheless, because specific meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth that do take the form of the vision of Brahman are of the nature of the vision of Brahman, they require the knowledge of Brahman; this is the meaning. Even if these specific meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth were of the nature of the vision of Brahman and dependent upon the knowledge of Brahman...

By this much, there is no dependence upon the knowledge of the *brāhmaṇa* for the investigation—conducted under such rules as "the restriction of that [is not fixed] because it is seen in that" (*JS* 3.3.39) and "in the case of the auxiliary parts, according to the nature of their substratum" (*JS* 3.3.40)—into whether meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) or the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Rather, that was merely an incidental determination. However, the intention is that there is indeed a dependence upon the knowledge of the *brāhmaṇa* in those investigations of meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth which proceed by taking the perspective of the *brāhmaṇa*, such as "the view of the *brāhmaṇa* [prevails] because of its excellence" (*JS* 3.3.51).

If it be objected: "Is it not the case that the inquiry 'The meditation on the *brahman* [is appropriate] because of its excellence' (B.S. 4.1.5) would result in the prior occurrence of Sāṃkhya and other scriptures which purify the nature of the mind and so forth? For since the scriptural text 'One should meditate on the mind as *brahman*' applies equally to the mind and other faculties, those scriptures would also necessarily be relied upon. We reply: No; for such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is no fault, as this argument is merely a corroborative reason (*abhyuccaya-yukti*). The meaning is that these [Sāṃkhya and other systems] bring about the knowledge of *brahman* quickly.

Nor should it be argued that it is contradictory for these [meditations] to produce the knowledge of Brahman while being dependent upon that very knowledge of Brahman; for there is no contradiction in the meditation on the *udgītha*—which arises from scriptural tradition (*āgama*) and depends on the knowledge of Brahman—serving as an auxiliary to the meditations produced by discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth. Therefore, the meaning is that this contemplation is also appropriately included here, just like the reflection on tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and other qualities which produce the knowledge of Brahman. This applies whether there is dependence on one or dependence on both.

The meaning is as follows: In the aphorism "Desire to know Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*), it is proposed that everything connected with Brahman is to be investigated. Therefore, since the investigation of its meditations (*upāsanā*), their fruits, and all their ancillaries has been proposed, there is a direct connection (*sākṣāt-saṅgati*). Furthermore, because they are required by meditation, they possess the status of being ancillary to meditation; and because they consist of the vision of Brahman, they also possess the status of being ancillary to Brahman. Consequently, they hold a position of greater importance even compared to tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities that are ancillary to meditation alone.

The reason for the connection with the investigation of the prior section is that [the subject matter] has karma as its constituent part and its locus. Ultimately, the intention is that even this [subject matter] is common [to both], because it is common to both pure knowledge (*vidyā*) and the karma that is a constituent of knowledge. This is because those two are characterized by the specific connections mentioned previously.

If it is asked: "At the stage of investigating the sequence between the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*) and the inquiry into Brahman, how can one speak as if that [sequence] were already established, saying: 'For an inquiry into Brahman is not possible prior to an inquiry into ritual action, because the two are characterized by a specific relationship of connection'? The answer is: No; for the very unity of the scripture (*śāstraikya*)—consisting in having a single purpose through non-contradictory intermediate sentence-meanings characterized by a specific relationship of connection that determines a particular sequence—is the primary argument for the inquiry into ritual action being a prerequisite. Any other [reasoning] is merely a secondary supporting argument (*abhyuccayayukti*).

There is no fault in speaking [of something] as if it were already established. Regarding the phrase "qualified by the three differences": although there is equality in the requirement for both [the study of ritual and the study of the Upaniṣads], because it is impossible to perform the inquiry into ritual action [simultaneously] and because it is enjoined in the portion of the Upaniṣads, it is appropriate here in this treatise to state that the inquiry has been conducted by the author of the Sūtras as having the inquiry into the Brāhmaṇa-mīmāṃsā as its result; however, it is not appropriate to use even the fact of being investigated in the Brāhmaṇa-mīmāṃsā as a logical reason (hetu). To this, some reply: "No, because the intention applies only to the two differences."

Others, however, state that because the authors of the Sūtras follow their own independent inclinations, the fact that [a topic] was not treated by Jaimini but was treated by Bādarāyaṇa is also a demonstration of another logical reason; namely, that it is a primary reason consisting in its being invariably required.

Now, one might object: since a sacrifice consists essentially in the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity, should not the investigation of the deity itself precede all other investigations? Furthermore, it must necessarily be accepted that the word *atha* (then) refers to the immediate succession of the investigation of the deity, and not to the succession of the investigation of ritual action (*karma*) which is separated by an interval. To this it is replied: even the *Saṃkarṣakāṇḍa* has as its subject matter specifically those rituals whose details have not yet been investigated.

For it is well known that Jaimini, having composed the *Dvādaśalakṣaṇī* (the twelve-chapter work), observed that certain portions therein had not been investigated, and thus composed again the *Caturlakṣaṇī* (the four-chapter work). It is for this very reason that the commentary (*Vṛtti*) passage—"This *Śārīraka* (the *Brahmasūtra*) is joined with the *Jaiminīya* consisting of sixteen chapters"—is also consistent.

For this very reason, that which is cited as a corroborative authority in the *Bhāṣya* under the section beginning with "just like the offering" (*pradānavat*)—namely, "the deities are indeed manifold because of their distinctness"—is seen only in the work of Jaimini, and not in the *Devatākāṇḍa* of Kāśakṛtsna. From this also, it follows that the *Saṃkarṣa* deals exclusively with ritual action (*karma*). It is for this reason that some maintain the practice of referring to it as the *Devatākāṇḍa*. Thus, it is universally accepted as such in the *Bhāṣya*.

"Agreed upon by all" (*sarvasaṃmatā*) is a compound formed with the sixth case [genitive] in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣalakṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*), according to the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*; however, it should be understood that the sixth case is not used here because of the prohibition in the rule *ktena ca pūjāyām*. The phrase "included within the force of the matter to be stated" means that the resolution of this [objection] is itself the resolution of that [previous one]; such is the intended meaning.

Regarding the phrase *apinopapādayiṣyamāṇasya*: the sense is that because the particle *api*—according to the rule “*apiḥ padārthasaṃbhāvanānvavasargagarhāsamuccayeṣu*” (Pāṇini 1.4.96)—functions here as a term of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and not as a term of secondary mention (*anvācaya*), it signifies predominance (*prādhānya*). Alternatively, since particles have multiple meanings, the sense is that it indicates predominance. Regarding the phrase *vakṣyamāṇajñātrādayaḥ*: the sense is that these [terms] constitute the detailed explanation of the specific words [mentioned previously].

Since the statement beginning with “Being alone” (*sadeva*), which aims at the exclusion of heterogeneous things and so forth, will be cited as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the proposition (*pratijñā*) [of the Upanishads], it is appropriate that the term “particular” (*viśeṣa*) refers precisely to heterogeneous things and the like; with this intention, he says: “or [particulars] belonging to the heterogeneous, the homogeneous, or its own [nature]. [He further states: “and they are of the nature of both positive concomitance (*anvayin*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). This means they are both of the nature of existence (*bhāvarūpa*) and of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvarūpa*). Anticipating the objection—“How can Brahman, which tolerates particularity, be the opposite of that [non-duality]?”—he says: “It is the remover [of duality] through its own knowledge.”

[The opponent argues that] there would be emptiness (*tucchatā* / *śūnyatā*) [of all things], because the sense is that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have only specific objects as their domain. Since even the property of being knowable (*jñeyatva*) is included by the word "entire" (*aśeṣa*), its exclusion by the suffix *-mātra* would be redundant; therefore, he explains it otherwise, saying "or, as an adversary" (*yadvā pratyanīka*). The sense is that, because of the mention of "adversary" (*pratyanīka*), there might be the suspicion that the property of being an adversary is what persists, and thus that suspicion must be dispelled.

This [point] is also established by the force of the entire word; therefore, he explains it otherwise: "Or rather, by the suffix *mātrac*, it is 'entirely' in reality. Nor should one suspect tautology with the phrase "opposed to all particularities," because the meaning of "opposed to all particularities" here is that it is the object of a cognition that excludes all particularities, whereas in this context, its being eternally devoid of them is stated; thus there is a distinction. By the particle *eva* (only), there is the exclusion of Brahman as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*).

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Since it is stated that Brahman alone, devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), is the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*), the meaning is that the ultimate reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—consisting of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahman*) and so forth, which are distinct from that—is thereby excluded. This should be understood because it is explained in that very manner later on by the passage beginning with "distinct from that" (*tadatirekī*) and so forth. Thus, it has been shown that the multiplicity of things to be negated is established.

The sense is that, although the word *nānā* can function to exclude things other than the *brāhmaṇa*, it does not require a reference to the *brāhmaṇa* itself [as something to be excluded]. (In the Bhāṣya: "The distinction between the knower, the object of knowledge, and the knowledge produced by them. Here, "knower and object of knowledge and the knowledge produced by them" (*jñātṛ-jñeya-tatkṛta-jñānāni*) refers to those three; "distinctions" (*bhedāḥ*) is connected with each of these individually. For this very reason, he will later state that there are "subordinate distinctions within each category."

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the subsequent passage which demonstrates that the word "difference" (bheda) is concomitant with knowledge alone; for it should be understood that such a designation is justified because even by that [subsequent passage] the concomitance is possible. By the phrase "by this, [knowledge] manifested through a mental modification" (*vṛttisphurita*), the meaning is: "by this qualification, namely *autatkṛta*. In its absence, by the word "knowledge," only consciousness manifested through a mental modification would be grasped, which is the meaning of the scripture cited from the position of the proponents of falsehood (the Mādhyamikas).

The term *sadeva* (Being alone) excludes difference from the dissimilar (*vijātīyabheda*); *ekam eva* (only one) excludes difference from the similar (*sajātīyabheda*); and *advitīyam* (without a second) excludes internal difference (*svagatabheda*). Although it has been explained that in the sentence "one only, without a second," the word "one" serves to negate internal difference, the particle "only" (*eva*) to exclude difference from the similar, and the term "without a second" to exclude difference from the dissimilar, it has also been said: "A tree's internal difference consists of its leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth; its difference from another tree is similarity; and its difference from the dissimilar is from stones and such."

By means of the three— namely, the determination of identity, the restriction [to that], and the negation of duality— the three possibilities regarding both existent and non-existent entities are successively excluded.

Thus, this particular interpretation has been presented because it has been explained in various places by that [author]. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* and the *Kalpataru*: "By the words 'Being alone,' name, form, and so forth are excluded prior to creation; by 'one only,' it is denied that there exists anything such as the Mahat and its effects which have fallen into the category of its own products; by 'without a second,' any other instrumental cause is denied"—and nothing more than this.

[Objection: One might argue that in the statement, "The tree has an internal difference consisting of leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth," since there is a cognition of the internal difference as having leaves, flowers, etc., as its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), it is not perceived that the difference is *defined by* (or *consisting of*) the leaves, flowers, and so on; rather, what is perceived is simply the difference *having* those as its counter-correlates. In this treatise, however, difference is described as being of the nature of the similar (*sajātīya*) and the nature of the dissimilar (*vijātīya*).

One should not raise the objection as to how these two [passages] have the same meaning (*raikāthrya*). Nevertheless, it should be understood that there is no fault because they are seen to be used by others in such a way. This is because it is an elaboration of that very [point], meaning that by the passage beginning with "As a spider... and so forth, the state of being the source of all beings (*bhūtayonitva*) is indeed elaborated. Regarding the word "of whom" (*yasya*): for one whose resolve is "the Brahman is my thought," for him that Brahman is "thought"—that is, correctly known; but he for whom the Brahman is merely an object of thought does not know the Brahman.
"Unknown" means not known as an object by those who do not know [it] as it truly is; the meaning is that it is known as an object by those who know [it] as it truly is.

Regarding the phrase "intended to negate the state of being a knower": although the statement "not [the seer] of seeing" means that you should not see the Seer—the one pervaded by the consciousness that constitutes its own nature, which is the illuminator even of that [seeing]—by means of the mental modification produced by the eye (cakṣurjanya-antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) which is itself illuminated by that [Seer].

Others have stated that the meaning [of the passage] is simply that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is not an object of that [vision], and thus its status as an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) is denied. Nevertheless, with the intention that by denying its status as an object of knowledge the denial of its being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is also established, he said that the sentence is intended to deny its being a knower. Some, however, have explained it in that way following certain proponents of false doctrines (*mṛṣāvādin*); it was said here in accordance with that. But they consider that there is no fault in not elaborating upon that, because later, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), he will clarify it by means of the alternative—"Is the word 'dṛṣṭeḥ' in the ablative or the genitive?"—and thus it need not be explained at this point.

The word *sāmānādhikaraṇyena* is to be split [as a compound]. For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is seen to serve the purpose of sublation (*bādhārtha*). Indeed, coreferentiality is fourfold: coreferentiality in superimposition (*adhyāsa*), coreferentiality in negation (*apavāda*), coreferentiality in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), and coreferentiality in identity (*aikya*). Coreferentiality in superimposition occurs in such passages as "One should meditate on Name as Brahman."

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the sense of sublation (*apavāda*) is as in the statement, "That which appeared as silver was mother-of-pearl"; for this co-referentiality serves the purpose of sublatting the previously arisen cognition of silver. Indeed, this alone is called "co-referentiality for the sake of sublation. Co-referentiality in the sense of the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is found in cases such as "the blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*). Co-referentiality in the sense of identity (*aikya*) is found in cases such as "the cuckoo is *pika*" (*kokilaḥ pikaḥ*).

"Modification is the configuration of a jar and so forth, and it is a mere name.
