Here, the particle *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only); the suffix *-dheya* is used in its own primary sense (*svārthe*); and the meaning is that "mere name" (*nāmadheya*) signifies nothing more than a name alone. For thus says the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* of Śaṅkara: "Modification is a verbal handle and a mere name. By speech alone is modification commenced as existing—such as 'jar,' 'bowl,' or 'water-pot'—but in reality, no such thing as modification exists at all. This is merely a name and is unreal."

"‘Earth alone is the truth’"—therefore, this passage also must be interpreted as being consistent with that [preceding statement], since it is a restatement of it. Now, one might object: "It would have been more appropriate for the sentence ‘Then fear comes to him’ to follow immediately after the sentence ‘He goes from death to death,’ because they both equally establish what is harmful. To this, he says: "Because [the objection] is to be refuted by the same reasoning starting from ‘When indeed... [and so on]. This is because they are to be resolved by a single logical principle.

The meaning is that [the objection] must be refuted because its purpose is to negate the manifoldness inherent in *abrahman*. Regarding the reading "both-liṅgatva" (*ubhayaliṅgatva*), it refers to having both form (*sākāratva*) and being formless (*nirākāratva*). It should be understood that in the section beginning with "Not even on account of place" (*na sthānato 'pi*), the prima facie view—which maintains a conjunction of the two characteristics consisting of having attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) and being without attributes (*nirviśeṣatva*) based on the force of scripture—has already been rejected. Some, however, interpret the connection as follows: "both-liṅgatva" means having both form and being formless, and then separately "having form" (*sākāratva*).

In that context, it has been stated thus because, even if one resorts to either of the two characteristics—namely, having form (*sākāra*) or being formless (*nirākāra*)—within the nature of possessing both characteristics, the position of being exclusively with form (or the position of being both with and without form) is rejected; however, they say this is not because it is the literal meaning of the word "possessing both characteristics. The meaning is that its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is difficult to define, and that it is sublated (*bādhitatva*). This means it is characterized by a locus, time, and cause that are themselves sublated.

The meaning is that falsity arises because space, time, and causal conditions cannot be established, since they are sublated; for it is impossible for there to be a suitable place or time for mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth—which are seen by a person sleeping in his own house—to reside in a single corner, nor is there a suitable cause for the production or cognition of events such as marriage, the birth of a son, and the nurturing of that child, which are experienced by a person who has slept for only a moment. Thus, due to the impossibility of determining their space, time, and causes, they are false.

Anticipating the objection that the citation of the sūtra demonstrating the falsity of dream-objects is irrelevant at the stage of establishing the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca), he says: "The falsity of dream-objects," etc. This is the meaning of the Purāṇa according to the view of others.

The verse beginning with “*pratyastamitabhedaṃ*” is the speech of Keśidhvaja found in the seventh chapter of the sixth section (*ṣaṣṭhāṃśa*) within the *Yogaprakaraṇa*. The verse beginning with “*jñānasvarūpaṃ*,” however, is the verse of salutation (*namaskāraśloka*) in the second chapter of the first section (*prathamāṃśa*). This group of four verses beginning with “*paramārthastvamevaikaḥ*” appears in the fourth chapter of the first section during the hymn of praise by the sages dwelling within the pores of the skin (*romāntarasthānām munīnām*) to Ādivarāha.

The verse beginning with "tasyātmaparadeheṣu" and the verse beginning with "veṇurandhravibhedena" are the two opening verses of Ādibharata in the fourteenth chapter of the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*). The verse beginning with "yadyanyo'sti" is the opening verse of Ādibharata in the thirteenth chapter of that same part. The verse beginning with "so'haṃ sa ca tvam" is the verse at the conclusion of the instruction of Ādibharata in the sixteenth chapter of that same part.

The verse beginning with "vibhedajanake" is a statement by Keśidhvaja within the section on yoga in the seventh chapter of the sixth part [of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa]. The verse beginning with "jñānasvarūpaḥ" is recited in the twelfth chapter of the second part.
[This is] the definition of falsity (*mithyātva*).

"Capable of being removed by the knowledge consisting of the volition of the Almighty Lord and others. This means: that which is to be removed by the knowledge in the form of the volition (*saṃkalpa*) of the Lord who possesses power (*śaktimān*). In other words, it means "capable of being removed by knowledge assisted by power. This is because what is intended to be expressed is the state of being removable by knowledge alone. For this very reason, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to sins and the like, which are removed by the sight of a bridge when accompanied by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) of being devoid of an umbrella, sandals, and so forth. "Capable of being removed by a powerful erroneous cognition. For cessation (*nivṛtti*) is indeed one's own absence (*svābhāva*).

And that [non-existence] is common to both the imagined (*kalpita*) and the non-imagined (*akalpita*). Consequently, through a powerful erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*), the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) that "the real silver does not exist" indeed occurs; thus, the imagined non-existence is produced by that [cognition], and it is logically consistent for the real silver to be sublated (*nivartyatva*) by it. Alternatively, the meaning is that "sublation" (*nivṛtti*) is simply the state of being cognized as "not existing," and this is possible even for real silver. It is not, however, the state of having already ceased to exist (*nivṛttatva*).

Although it might be argued that if one simply says "the state of having ceased," there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding false objects that are yet to cease, nevertheless, the intended meaning here is that [the definition] was not stated as "being the counter-positive of a cessation produced by knowledge. By means of the two sections—[the first] on "being perceived" and [the second] on "being removable by knowledge"—which culminate in the establishment of *khyāti* (illusory appearance) and *bādha* (sublation), that which is to be proven is indicated: being distinct from the non-existent while being distinct from the existent. Therefore, he reveals his own established doctrine with the words, "By this definition, the distinction between existence and non-existence is established," and so forth.

How can there be superimposition upon Brahman, which is perceived as possessing qualities such as omniscience? One might object: "Surely, for an omniscient being, there is only a contradiction in its being the *draṣṭṛ* (perceiver) of superimposition, but not in its being the *adhiṣṭhāna* (substratum) of superimposition; nor can it be said that being perceived as possessing qualities such as omniscience is incompatible with being the substratum for the superimposition of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*), because at the stage of superimposition, it is not perceived in that way."

If it is asked: "In that case, how can this objection be raised, or how can the rebuttal be made by means of the non-connection with the quality of omniscience?"—the answer is no; for there is the possibility of the intended meaning of the objection being: "Since the possession of qualities such as omniscience is merely imagined, how can [Brahman] serve as the substratum for superimposition?
This concludes the examination of the defect in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*).

"The two states of one and the same [entity]" means two parts; the intention here is not plurality, such that their multiplicity would be authoritative—this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "Aditi [release] the bonds": in the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, the mantra containing the word *pāśān* (bonds) in the plural is heard: "May Aditi release the bonds."

In this doubt—whether it is displaced to groups of animals (*paśugaṇa*) or remains fixed in the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is displaced to groups of animals possessing multiple nooses, because the use of the plural number for a single noose is improper. However, since the noose intended by the word's primary meaning and the object denoted by the case-ending are both possible only in the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice, and since displacement is impossible due to the requirement of the number which has not yet been offered, the number of nooses is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the plural number is used merely for the sake of specification; this was established in the ninth [chapter] by the rule: "In the case of conflicting injunctions, there would be an option because they are equal; but regarding a subordinate quality, an improper assumption applies because it pertains to only one part. Regarding the doubt that "prakṛti" is being mentioned [here], the intention is that it is due to the recognition of the Sāṃkhya doctrine. As for the phrase "one should know Māyā as prakṛti," the meaning is that one should know Māyā—which is ignorance (avidyā) characterized as distinct from both being and non-being—as the *prakṛti*, that is, the material cause (*upādāna*).

It should be understood that this is because the word *prakṛti* is seen to have the sense of "material cause" (*upādāna*) in passages such as "And [Brahman is] the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples," and because others have also explained it in that way. However, some describe the relationship between the subject and the predicate as follows: "One should know *prakṛti* to be *māyā*, which is illusory. Regarding the phrase "of those intent on demonstrating defects":

The sense is that for those who have set out to claim that even the Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions, serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) due to the influence of defects, it is not possible for passages such as "Indra [acts] through *māyās*" to have as their purport the establishment of difference. "Internal diversity mentioned in the same context": the sense is that if this were the case, there would be no inclusion of things that are either of the same class (*sajātīya*) or of a different class (*vijātīya*). "Because there is no excess in the object to be established": the meaning is that although there may be differences in the modes of establishing the falsity consisting in the perception of the world, there is no difference in the specific portion of the matter to be established (*upapādanīyāṃśa*).

The state of ignorance being removable by the knowledge of oneness is for the sake of both [fearlessness and fear]. Now, if there is the absence of both, the compound is "avyayam" (an indeclinable). From that, the form arises through the substitution of "am" in the fourth case according to the rule "nāvyayībhāvāt. Regarding the phrase "for according to the meditation": although in the doctrine of the proponents of falsehood (Mṛṣāvādin) the knowledge of Brahman is not of the nature of meditation (*upāsanā*), nevertheless, because the same principle applies, it should be understood that this statement is intended to show that the fruit corresponds to the knowledge. "Ignorance which is the cause of that" means that it is of the nature of impurity, characterized by the non-apprehension of things as they truly are, which serves as the cause of delusion.

"In order to make known the state of having unity as its object" means in order to demonstrate the state of having ultimate unity as its object. Consequently, the intention is that the non-duality indicated by the injunctive sentence for meditation, "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone," is ultimately real because it is established by the statements whose purpose is to teach the true nature [of the Self]. In accordance with this teaching, the meditator addresses the deity.

The point is that because the Chāndogya statement "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is solely intent upon establishing identity, the Jābāla statement "O venerable deity, you indeed am I" (*tvam vā aham asmi*) and the Aitareya statement "He who is I, he is that one" (*tad yo 'ham so 'sau*) are also seen to be in accordance with it. However, one should not consider the latter to be a response to the deity following the instruction "That thou art," for both belong to different contexts. [The text continues: "One should meditate on [the Self] as the Self. (*ātmety upāsīta*)...

The meaning is that one should realize [the Self] as "I am. For this very reason, it is stated in Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Sūtra, "It is to be realized as 'I am'," because that Sūtra is intent upon establishing the reality of the Self according to the doctrine of non-falsity (mṛṣāvādimate), and not because it is intent upon establishing meditation on [the Self] as the Self in the sense of "one should meditate on it as the Self" (ātmetyupāsīta). However, some [hold] that the meaning is: "In reality, one should meditate on the Self itself as the Self."

Furthermore, by means of establishing that [the Self] is the real Self, the exclusion of the meditation on the Self from being a meditation on a mere symbol (pratīkopāsana) is also established; for they say that this Sūtra aims at excluding it from being a meditation on a symbol by means of establishing its status as the real Self.
[Objection: In the case of a contradiction with perception, the scripture possesses greater authority.

"But surely, the cessation of all distinctions is contradicted by perception"—this is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*. [The objection is: "The absence of all distinctions is contradicted by perception; how can it be made an object by knowledge produced by the scripture (*śāstra*)? How, then, could it be that which is propounded by the scripture? This should be understood in the same way for what follows as well. [This refers to] the doubt that "the production from a defective cause and its absence are the determining factors in the relationship between the sublated and the sublator."

The meaning is this: in some cases it is the state of being rooted in a source; in some cases, it is being beyond perception (*parokṣatva*) and so forth; and in some cases, it is the presence or absence of being produced by a defective cause, while there is equality characterized by the absence of any cause for the opposite—namely, strength or weakness. This is because all such [alleged] grounds will be refuted later on.

Having raised the objection that, since the presence or absence of a defective cause is suspected to be the determinant of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator when equality exists, it would be improper to refute the role of equality as a determinant, he explains [the text] beginning with "tulyatve sati duṣṭakāraṇa... [and so on]. He states, "the word *tulya* is employed," meaning that the word *tulyatva* (equality) is employed. He further clarifies that by the word *tulya*, a part [of the term *tulyatva*] is being taken up.

The meaning is that since there is the possibility of "similarity" (*tulyatva*) itself being a logical reason (*hetu*), it is appropriate to include the qualifying portion by means of the word "similarity" in order to exclude that [possibility]. The phrase "when there is similarity" is explained as "when there is an absence of the causes for superiority or inferiority that have been previously established. Because it would be cumbersome to understand a qualified entity through the word "similarity" alone—which merely denotes a qualifier—he says, "or rather, by way of being non-conclusive" (*aprayojakatvena*). Thus, "similarity" is restated by way of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The meaning is "similarity to the *kevala* (the pure). One might object: "In that case, since there is similarity with that which was primarily suspected [of being the cause], and since the probans consisting of the absence of being produced by a defective cause (*duṣṭakāraṇajanyatvābhāva*) has not been stated here, its lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*) would not have been established. Anticipating this objection, he says, "provided there is no other dissimilarity," thereby including that [probans] by means of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). As for the phrase "various conceptual constructions" (*vividhavikalpa*), it is either a qualifier of the "manifest world" (*prapañca*) or a qualifier of "difference" (*bheda*). In the interpretation as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), it is a qualifier of the "manifest world."

The point is that in a *karmadhāraya* compound, however, there is a distinction regarding the qualifier. Regarding the phrase "ignorance of effects" (*kāryāvidyā*), Vācaspati stated in the first chapter: "Of [the Self] which has as its companions two kinds of indeterminable ignorance. And in his commentary on that, he says: "One is beginningless and of the nature of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa), as will be explained in the section concerning the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*); the other is the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of successive prior delusions. And in Śaṅkara’s *Bhāṣya*: "Thus, the superimposition of the non-self upon the inner self is not contradictory."

"In this way, the learned consider such superimposition (*adhyāsa*), characterized as above, to be ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, the fact that the perception of difference is ignorance has been revealed. "It is intended for another purpose" refers to the opponent's intention; the meaning is that because it is intended for another purpose, it does not sublate direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[This concludes the section on] the superior strength of the scriptural texts concerning non-difference.

One might object: "The objection that [the cognition] which apprehends difference would necessarily be sublated is not tenable, because it results in the acceptance of what is already desired. Anticipating this, he states, "That which was said to be faultless," in order to present an undesirable consequence: if that [cognition] were also sublatable, then its cause would likewise have to be a defective one, which is the very point being made. [The opponent replies: "But sublatibility must be asserted; however, being produced by a defective instrument is not possible [in this case]."

When it is asked, "How then is consistency maintained?", the response "It is true" indeed accepts the sublation [of the opponent's view]; furthermore, what was stated—that there is no production from defective causes—is also accepted. However, one must simply say that what was asked—"How is consistency maintained?"—is not accepted. If it is asked, "Why is there a statement of non-acceptance regarding production from defective causes?", [the answer is: No.

There is no fault here, because it has already been established that the question "How is [the cognition] maintained? culminates in the point that it would also be produced by a defective cause (*duṣṭakāraṇa*). In reality, however, the intended meaning is that in sentences such as those concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice, there exists either the defect consisting of the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) or the defect consisting of the human error of mistaking the intended meaning (*tātparyabhrama*), and thus they are indeed produced by defective causes. This is because, if invalid cognition (*apramā*) were to arise even in the absence of defects, it would follow that invalidity is intrinsic (*svatastva*). This is how it should be understood.

However, some explain the introduction to the commentary beginning with "But [it may be objected] (*nanu ca*") as follows: they argue that if the perception of difference is sublated because it is produced by the defect consisting in the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference, then the cognition of difference produced by sentences such as those concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice would likewise be sublatable, since it too is produced by the defect consisting in the latent impression of difference. This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because you yourself have established that [the Veda] is faultless due to its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*). With this intention, they raise the objection. In this view, [the passage continues]: "The reliance on difference... (*bhedāvalambana...*)

There is the natural consistency (*svārasya*) of the Bhāṣya beginning with the words "the younger brother" (*mbinaḥ*). It should be observed that if the text were intended to mean that either one [of the two rules] is sublated without being determined which, it would contradict that [Bhāṣya]. Regarding the phrase "due to the sequence of the arising of cognitions" (*pramityutpattikramāt*): the sense is that since this is a manual for performance (*prayogaśāstra*), it conveys its meaning only by repeating itself at each individual performance; therefore, it is easy for others to state the reversal [of the order] based on the sequence of the cognitions resulting from the different performances. "When there is a simultaneous occurrence of two disconnections (*apaccheda*) in a single performance" means:

When the simultaneous disqualification (*apaccheda*) of both the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartṛ* occurs, there arises the doubt: should an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) be performed or not? In this regard, the disqualification being incurred by both cannot be designated by one alone. Therefore, since the causal condition (*nimitta*) for the rite is destroyed by simultaneity, the conclusion reached in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the expiation should not be performed.
To this, [the Siddhāntin replies]: "This would indeed be so, if the agency of both were dependent upon one another;
however, it is known that each one acts independently and individually."
"Because of that disjunction, agency belongs to each of the two [performers] individually.

(Śāstradīpikā). Time alone is one; therefore, expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed. This was established in the sixth book [of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtras]: "Because of the scriptural mention of division, there is no expiation when [the acts] occur simultaneously"—this is the sense. Now, since the conclusion was reached that "there shall be an option because of the contradiction," there is a conflict; out of dissatisfaction with this, he says: "or performance by way of option."

The question is: why should the preceding rule not be an obstacle to the arising of the subsequent one? The meaning is that, according to the principle of the section on "commencement" (*upakramādhikaraṇa*), the preceding rule possesses greater force because its counteragent has not yet arisen. As for the phrase "because the occasion has occurred": for when the occasion (the cause) exists, the rule conditioned by it must necessarily proceed, since that very occasion constitutes its complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

In this regard, when a contradictory cognition has arisen, the subsequent cognition that necessarily arises as its opposite emerges precisely by way of subverting the preceding one; this is established by the very nature of things. Therefore, by the nature of reality, a subsequent scripture causes the cognition of its own meaning only through the subversion of the cognition residing in the prior [text]. However, the preceding cognition, as it arises, is not produced as either something to be sublated or as a sublater with respect to anything else; rather, it arises merely in its own form.

The meaning is this: in that case, within a single application (*prayoga*), since it is impossible for two scriptural meanings to coexist, whichever is sublated must be the sublated, while that which performs the sublation must logically be the non-sublated. To one who might believe that it is impossible for a previously established meaning to be altered by a subsequent scripture, he states the counter-argument based on a conditional rule (*naimittika-śāstra*): "Furthermore, as has been stated," etc. This is because it falls under the category of the section concerning the alteration of a previously established meaning. *Prakaraṇa* here means *prakriyā* (methodological treatment).

The meaning is "of such a kind. The intention is that [the later rule] possesses a character equal to a prior rule that is eternally established, not subject to application, and not otherwise-effecting, as well as to a rule based on a specific cause (*naimittika*). The sense is: if the later rule were not to sublate the earlier rule, then even a rule based on a specific cause would not sublate an eternally established rule (*nitya*). Since the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is clear and thus need not be further justified, he justifies the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) by stating "as having the three aims (*trivarga*) as its fruit. For it is for one whose ultimate goal is reality (*tattva*) that there is the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*).

The meaning is that there is a sequential order [of the Vedāntas] based on the sequence of their causes (*nimitta*), just as there is a sequence of weapons [based on the sequence of their targets], or based on the sequence of those qualified [to receive them]. The intended purport here is that the Vedāntic statements are directed toward the purpose of subverting all knowledge of duality produced by the beginningless *karmakāṇḍa* and other [scriptures], through a knowledge generated by the investigation of Vedāntic passages that occurs immediately after the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*).

Therefore, one should understand that the objection—that in the view of falsehood (mṛṣāvāda), since there is no rule for the prior engagement of the inquiry into karma, there would be no sublation of its distinctions—is unfounded. Now, for one who says that the principle of "severance" (apacchedanyāya) does not apply, the statement "because its fruit is observed" is irrelevant; for the observation of the realization of attributelessness (nirguṇatva), which is the fruit thereof, is not admitted by the opponent. To this he replies: "Eating, playing, enjoying," and so forth. For one who investigates [the Self] is qualified for the knowledge of the supreme Brahman devoid of attributes.
Those who are dull-witted and unable to directly realize the supreme Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions,
are instructed by means of descriptions involving distinctions.

The sense is that when their minds have been brought under control through the practice of the *saguṇa-brahman*, that very [Brahman] manifests directly, free from the conceptualization of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is the meaning of the statement. Alternatively, it refers to such scriptural passages as "He who is omniscient," and so forth. In this interpretation, however, there is an awkwardness in the distinct mention of two groups: "those devoted to the meditation on the *saguṇa-brahman*" and "those devoted to the exposition of the nature of Brahman. Furthermore, it should be observed that the assumption of the intention behind the phrase "devoted to meditation" (namely, that all are devoted to meditation) is an overly strained interpretation.

The meaning of the sentence "truth, knowledge," and so forth, is that they share a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*); otherwise, one would have to say "in two or more" (*dvayeṣu*). The intention is that [this definition] applies because it produces multiplicity in what is otherwise one. Anticipating the objection that the definition is not correct—since in the phrase "subsistence in a single object" (*ekasminnarthe vṛttiḥ*), the word *eka* could mean the number one, or "otherness," and so on—the author states the meaning of the two words *samāna* and *adhikaraṇa* with the intention that the intended sense can be obtained by explaining *samāna* as "one" (*eka*) through its commentary: "a common (*samānam*) substratum (*adhikaraṇam*) is one (*ekam*)."

Furthermore, at the time of explaining the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the passage beginning with "of those [words] having different grounds for application," the following doubt was set aside: that when the portion "in a single object" (*ekasminnarthe*) is to be explained, the explanation of the term *samānādhikaraṇa* itself is not relevant. This is because, by the force of the word *samāna*, the word *eka* refers to what is common (*sādhāraṇa*). Nor should it be argued that this results in circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*).

The point is that the mutual association [of words] is observed to convey a specific meaning, as in the case of "the teacher and Śukra" (*gurubhārgavau*). Nor should it be argued: "What inconsistency is there in a single word having the number one as its referent? For it is possible for the two words 'blue' (*nīla*) and 'lotus' (*utpala*) to have as their denotation an object that is the locus of the number one. This is because [in the phrase] "many lotuses," the two words do not have as their denotation an object that is the locus of the number one.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "existence" (*sambhava*). For this very reason, even in the rule "for two actions having the same agent, [the suffix -ktvā is used] for the earlier time," the oneness that constitutes the meaning of the word *samāna* (same) must be understood as commonality alone, and not as a specific number; for in examples such as "having cooked, he eats" (*paktvā bhukte*), the agent does not possess the number one. This should be understood as a manner of resolving an objection, which will be clarified in the discussion of "blue lotuses" (*nīlāny utpalāni*). Thus, the previously stated position is the more sound one.

The meaning is that this is for the purpose of establishing the verbal status (*śābdatva*) of the specific intended objects. "Residing in that" means having the same case-ending (*samānavibhakti*) when intent upon the identity of the qualificand. Now, an objection: if the case-ending of the qualifier thus signifies identity, there would be a contradiction with the *Niṣādhasthapati-ādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the "forester-chief"); for, just as in a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound one must accept a secondary denotation (*lakṣaṇā*) of the nominal stem in the sense of the elided case-ending, so too here one would have to accept a secondary denotation of the word *nipāda* in the sense of identity conveyed by the qualifier’s case-ending. Therefore, the case-ending of the qualifier serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvārthakatva*).

If it is argued that [the compound] does not have oneness as its meaning, we say no; for even if oneness were the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), there is no evidence for the primary nominal stem (*prātipadika*) to indicate it through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, there is no rule of necessity that the analytical statement (*vigraha*) and the compound (*samāsa*) must have identical meanings.

The intention is that, since it is established by experience that in a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound the relation appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the verbal cognition, even if one resorts to secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for that purpose, there is no such signification in the case of the identity between the object and the agent, because it is established by experience that this identity appears precisely through the force of the relational context (*saṃsargamaryādayā*). Some, however, hold that the meaning of "subsisting in a single referent" (*ekasminnarthe vṛttiḥ*) is "the state of possessing two case-endings that subsist in a single referent."

Furthermore, because the case-ending of the qualifier is identical in meaning with the case-ending of the qualified, it serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*), acting as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the meaning of the qualified’s case-ending. The statement that “the indication of identity of case-endings is what is intended by the term *vṛtti* (compound)” also has its purport in this very point. For this reason alone, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as “the nature (*svarūpa*) of the jar,” since in those instances the two case-endings have different meanings.

If it is objected that, in this case, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the nominal suffix and the verbal suffix in the expression "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), because the verbal suffix expresses a meaning distinct from its own base form, we reply: no; for they maintain that in such instances, the usage of the term "coreferentiality" is not primary (*amukhya*).

Forgetting that the word *eka* (one) has been stated to have a common referent (*sādhāraṇārthatva*), [the opponent] objects: "But [in the case of] 'blue lotuses' (*nīlāny utpalāni*)... [The author replies: "By another co-occurring word" (*samabhivyāhṛtapadāntareti*). The meaning is this: "subsisting in a single referent" (*ekārthavṛttitva*) consists precisely in subsisting in a substratum that possesses a different form presented by another co-occurring word; it does not mean "not subsisting in two individuals. [The opponent says: "Lotus-ness exists in things that are not loci of blueness," which means that lotus-ness exists only in those things that are not loci of blueness.

Regarding the position that there is a simultaneous syntactic connection (anvaya) of those [words] presented all at once according to the maxim of the pigeons on a threshing floor, he says: "Even though the qualifiers are possible... This means that because there is no difference in the grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is lost. On this point, some say: "The phrase 'because there is no difference in the grounds for their application' is a reason for synonymy and for the redundancy of other words; therefore, by the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*), it should be construed with what precedes as well as with what follows."

Nor should it be argued that these terms cannot be synonyms because there exists a difference among their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), such as "truth" (*satyatva*) and "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*). For truth and the other qualities do not exist anywhere other than in the Pure [Brahman]; thus, since sentences such as "the True" (*satya*) and so forth refer—by way of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*)—to the essential nature alone, they do not establish those qualities even in the Pure [Brahman]. Consequently, due to the absence of a difference in the grounds for application, they maintain that these terms are synonyms. Others, however, define synonymy as having neither less nor more meaning; that is, having no meaning in excess of the qualifier or the qualified.

In this regard, they state that the mere absence of a difference in the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is not the reason [for synonymy]; for even though there is no difference in the grounds for application between the words "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and "pot" (*kumbha*) when used with the intention of different substrates (*viśeṣya*), they do not possess the aforementioned synonymy. Therefore, they say that the reason is the absence of the loss of the characteristic of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

"Therefore, regarding 'the state of being the cause of the world'": since the words "truth," "knowledge," and so forth, bring to mind a nature that is the opposite of the unreal, the insentient, and the limited, for this very reason, the delusions of unreality, insentience, and so on—which might otherwise be suspected of belonging to the cause—are dispelled by the terms "truth," "knowledge," and so forth; this is the meaning. [The phrase] "just as there is no synonymy due to the difference in their respective scopes" means as follows.

The meaning is that because blackness, redness, and so forth are distinct, there is a difference between the exclusions delimited by each of them—which serve as the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—and thus they possess non-synonymy and semantic meaningfulness. Nor is it the case that, having accepted a difference in order to establish the non-synonymy of the exclusions of the unreal (*anṛta*), the inert (*jaḍa*), and the limited (*paricchinna*), one could then ask how they can have a single referent (*ekārthatva*).

Nor should it be argued that if difference (*bheda*) is admitted for the sake of establishing that the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) of the false, the insentient, and the limited are not synonymous, how could they then have a single referent (*ekārthatva*); for although the exclusions appear at the stage of the presentation of the word-meanings (*padārtha*), at the stage of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), there is no contradiction in their having a single referent, since only the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as qualified by those respective exclusions is what is cognized.

Nor should it be argued that even at the time of the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the qualification by exclusion (*vyāvṛttivaiśiṣṭya*) must appear; for when there is a desire to know only the whiteness of the post itself, the answer "it is excluded from blackness, etc. has already been provided, and thus it is impossible for this sentence to convey a meaning distinct from its own form. For this very reason, sentences such as "Being, Consciousness, etc."—being answers to a question regarding the mere nature of Brahman—do not convey a qualification by exclusion.

The point is that for this very reason, it is logical that the definition of *akhaṇḍārthatva* (the state of having an indivisible referent) as "being the generator of a valid cognition whose object is not a relation" holds true. Some, however, maintain that in sentences such as "Being is True-Knowledge-Bliss," there indeed shines forth a qualified nature consisting in the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the false, the insentient, and the finite. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the definition of *akhaṇḍārthatva* as "generating a valid cognition whose object is not a relation" would be compromised; for there is no contradiction even if the form of *akhaṇḍārthatva*—defined as having a meaning where the qualifier and the qualified are non-different—has as its object a qualified nature (*vaiśiṣṭya*).

This is because the qualifiers and the qualified—which are the objects of the cognition produced by the word "satya" (truth)—are in reality devoid of difference and consist of the very nature of Brahman as exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); likewise, they serve as the objects of the qualified and the qualifier in the cognition produced by the word "jñāna" (knowledge). This is because, if the exclusion from falsehood (*anṛta-vyāvṛtti*), which is the nature of Brahman, is identical to the exclusion from insentience (*jaḍa-vyāvṛtti*), there is no difference between the two exclusions that function as qualifiers.

Nor should it be argued that there would be synonymy because they possess a single ground for application (*ekapravṛttinimittakatva*); for they maintain that synonymy consists precisely in having neither less nor more meaning, and since distinct counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*)—which serve as qualifiers in the form of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*)—appear [in the cognition], the possibility of synonymy does not arise.

[Objection: Since it is necessary that what is presented by a word through its primary power (śakti) must have the delimitor of the denotable capacity (śakyatāvacchedaka) as its qualifier, there arises the undesirable consequence that even the presentation of the very nature of Brahman—which is produced by words through their primary power—would necessarily have qualifiers such as "truth" (*satyatva*) which serve as the delimiters of the denotable capacity. Consequently, this would result in the collapse of the doctrine that [the Mahāvākya] has an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*). Therefore, one must admit that even the presentation of the nature of Brahman as excluded from the false, the insentient, and the limited occurs only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Anticipating this dissatisfaction, he says: "Even if secondary indication is admitted... [and] "The determination of the purport toward identity based on the force of the identical case-ending. This is as follows:

This is an illustration. It should also be observed that this is because it is a defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) and because it provides an answer to a question concerning the mere nature of Brahman. The claim that "metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for all words is not a defect" means "for all nominal stems (*prātipadika*)," since a case-ending (*vibhakti*) cannot indicate a single referent. Alternatively, if the singularity denoted by the case-ending were understood as a relational property (*saṃsarga*), the status of the sentence as having an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) would be compromised, as that [relational meaning] shares the same character as truth and so forth.

And it should not be argued that there is a contradiction with the preceding text on the grounds that the determination of the purport of identity [of Brahman] arises from the force of the identical case-ending; for they explain that the intention is that, since the question and answer concern the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, the purport is understood to be merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman. When the objection was raised that "truth, knowledge, and so forth are perceived as attributes," the author, fearing the fault of denying what is actually perceived in saying "it is said 'no'," states: "The intention of one who says 'it is said "no"' is as follows."

"All words terminate in a single denotation" (*ekābhidheyaparyavasānam*). "The denotation of a single word" (*ekasya padasyābhidheyam*) refers to that which is to be expressed; "terminating therein" (*tatra paryavasānam*) means having its final rest solely in the meaning of a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*). It does not mean the meaning of a sentence. However, the point is not that the indivisibility of meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) of words consists merely in their terminating in the meaning of a single sentence; for if that were so, every sentence would be indivisible in meaning. Rather, it is the words themselves that terminate in a single meaning.

The particle *eka* is displaced [in the compound]. The meaning is that the state of having an undivided referent (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) consists precisely in the fact that the words terminate in the single referent of a single nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and not merely in their terminating in a single principal referent. Consequently, the doubt—that if words terminate in a single referent, the sentence likewise terminates in that same one, and if the sentence terminates in a single referent, the words likewise do so, because a sentence does not exist apart from its constituent words—is refuted. [This is stated] by the phrase "by the entire sentence."

The meaning is that the point of refutation lies in the portion stating, "there is a difference in meaning due to the difference in qualifiers," which implies that [the word] refers to the qualifier alone. The phrase "by the difference in qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇabhedena*) is the term to be explained. This expresses the refutation in the view that [the words] denote [their meanings] simultaneously. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood that in the second alternative—the view that they denote sequentially—the refutation stated is that there would be a mutual inherence (*anyonyasamavāya*) in the connection with other qualifiers. The meaning is that the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not established.

The meaning is that there is a failure to establish the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as consisting in having reference to a single object alone. The intention is that two objections are intended here. In this regard, some raise the doubt that if [the words] have reference to a single object alone, the futility of other words and synonymy necessarily follow; yet, they argue that even when there is reference to a single object alone, it is possible for there to be non-synonymy and no futility of other words. Thus, they maintain that the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the two defects—namely, the futility of other words and synonymy—is avoided.

The intent lies solely in the refutation of the two [objections] regarding the possibility of avoidance. Consequently, if [the text] were restricted to a single object alone, there would be synonymy and the redundancy of other words. Even if that [objection] were somehow avoided, there would be the undesirable consequence of destroying the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consisting in the fact that [the words] reside in a single object. Thus, they say that the commentary (*ṭīkā*) passage should also be construed with this very purpose. As for "exclusion" (*vyudāsa*), it is the resulting implication.

The meaning is this: although nothing other than the sacrificial post (yūpa) presented by the word *satya* (real) is expressed by another word, nevertheless, the exclusion of falsehood (*anṛta*) and error is accomplished by the word *satya* alone; the exclusion of insentience (*jaḍa*) and error by the word *jñāna* (knowledge) alone; and the exclusion of limitation (*paricchinna*) and error by the word *ananta* (infinite) alone; for the presentation of the exclusion of falsehood, insentience, and limitation is dependent upon those respective words.

Because the presentation of the true nature [of the object], preceded by the exclusion of this or that [superimposed attribute], alone effects the removal of the false, the insentient, the limited, and error. Just as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), even though there is no difference in the object itself—since it is the very same nature already known through two acts of cognition (*abhijñā*)—a distinction is observed in recognition characterized by its power to remove the delusion of difference caused by the two cognitions; this distinction arises from causes such as the synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of two points in time. In the same way...

The meaning is as follows: the apprehension (*upasthiti*) produced by the word "truth" (*satya*) removes the error of unreality (*anṛta*) only when it is preceded by the recollection (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of unreality; likewise, the apprehension produced by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) removes the error of insentience (*jaḍa*) only when it is preceded by the recollection of insentience. Thus, the exclusion of the unreal (*anṛta*), the insentient (*jaḍa*), and the limited (*paricchinna*) is established as the result. The phrase "by way of the causal form" means by way of the aspect of unreality and so forth, which subsumes multiple word-meanings.

(Regarding the phrase "because it is intended to define [the nature] by restating its causality"): the meaning is that it is intended to enjoin a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). "It is called an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the moon" means as follows: the state of being the cause, which resides in the Brahman-with-attributes (*saguṇabrahman*) variegated by *māyā*, serves as an incidental indicator of the undivided consciousness (*akhaṇḍacaitanya*)—which is what is sought to be defined—by way of being an external characteristic (*taṭastha*), just as the tip of a branch is an external indicator of the moon. Its essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), consisting of reality, knowledge, and bliss, is like the "supreme luminosity" of that [moon].

Nor is the extrinsic definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) consisting in being the cause of the world redundant, since the exclusion of others is not necessarily established by the intrinsic definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa) alone—namely, the nature of truth, knowledge, and bliss.

However, in the case of the moon and so forth, although its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is understood by the phrase "the most excellent light" alone, if one who desires to see it were to wander their eyes everywhere in search of the moon, there would be distress; to prevent this, it may be said that the *taṭastha-lakṣaṇa* (incidental definition) is useful for the purpose of restricting the gaze to a specific location. Yet, this cannot be asserted here, because the meaning of the word *brahman*—which denotes unsurpassed greatness that opposes the threefold limitation (*pariccheda*) through the presence of contextual factors (*prakaraṇa*), qualifying words (*upapada*), and the like—is such that no such restriction is possible.

The intention of the proponents of illusion (mṛṣāvādins) is as follows: since Brahman, which is devoid of phenomenal proliferation (niṣprapañca), is what one desires to define, its state of being devoid of proliferation is established through the method of superimposition and negation (adhyāropāpavāda)—just as [one says] "that which appeared as silver was mother-of-pearl"—by stating that Brahman is the material cause of the world's illusory manifestation (vivarta). Thus, because the status of being the material cause of the universe must be predicated of Brahman, the extrinsic definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) is effective. Furthermore, the intrinsic definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa) is also necessary for the purpose of realizing the specific nature of its own essence. This is the view of the proponents of illusion.

"It will be explained later that [the word] has its primary meaning"—the remainder of the sentence is "in the Ānandamayādhikaraṇa. And it is this metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*) that is intended here. However, this should be understood according to the view that "it is obtained through *tātparya*," because it is impossible for *tātparya* itself—the seed of metaphorical indication—to be the very nature of metaphorical indication. The meaning is that this is also agreed upon by others.

The intention is that, because of the prohibition of a genitive compound by the rule *ktena ca pūjāyām*, [the word] is joined with a past passive participle (*ktānta*) via a third-case compound according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. Regarding the phrase "not contrary to the intended meaning" (*tātparyāviruddha*): the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*) are to be supplied as the remainder. The point is that there is no insistence that simply because the primary meaning is accepted in instances not contrary to the intended meaning, the primary meaning must also be accepted in instances where it is contrary to the intended meaning. The acceptance [of the primary meaning] follows as a consequence because the grounds for such acceptance exist; for even if in reality there were no such acceptance, one would still have to accept it against one's will.
The sense is that [the suffix] must be understood as such.
Regarding the view that all [suffixes] are figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), the example from the Prābhākara school cited in the *Bhāṣya* is as follows:

since the primary function of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others applies exclusively to the unprecedented effect (*apūrva-kārya*), the action-effect (*kriyā-kārya*) is conveyed by the optative suffix and other such terms through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For in passages such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), the action cannot be made known as an effect to the person to be impelled (*niyojya*), who is one desiring heaven, by means of the word "optative" (*liṅ*) [if taken in its primary sense]. This is because one who desires something understands only that which is not different from what is desired—that is, the immediate means to the desired end—as being the effect, and not a mediated means.

However, because the action (*kriyā*)—as a means (*sādhana*)—is non-durable, it lacks the quality of being an immediate means for what is desired, and thus it is not fit for connection with the person impelled by desire (*kāmin*). Therefore, once it is established that the *liṅ* suffix must denote the *apūrva* (the unseen potentiality) which is durable until the attainment of the fruit, the Prābhākaras maintain that the *liṅ* used in common worldly usage to denote an action as something to be done is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇikī*), since it is improper for a word to have multiple primary meanings. This is the intended sense of the phrase "of those [words] denoting [the *apūrva*] as connected with that."

The meaning is: [this refers] to those words which express a sense through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) while being endowed with the word-meaning *nimīlana*. "When there is indication for the words that convey its effect" means: when indication applies to them, by that same cause, indication follows for other words as well; however, one should not be deluded into thinking this is a case of a causal relationship (*hetumat-bhāva*), because such a relationship is not applicable here. For the indication of one word is not the cause for the indication of another word; rather, it is simply the impossibility of the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*).

The point is this: since a primary meaning in the form of an effect distinct from action is impossible, there must necessarily be *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) for the optative suffix (*liṅ*)—which expresses an effect distinct from action—in expressing an action as the effect; and likewise, since a primary meaning in the form of an entity connected to an effect distinct from action is impossible for the other words as well, there is a necessary *lakṣaṇā* for those words that express such meanings in expressing meanings connected to action. For this very reason, he will later state: "the abandonment of the status of referring to a single part of the effect which is the qualified enduring [entity]," and so forth.

Could it be that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth denote merely "that which is to be done" (*kāryamātra*)? Now, in common usage, since the nature of the action (*kriyāsvarūpa*), which is the locus of "being to be done," is already conveyed by the verbal root (*prakṛti*), the power (*śakti*) of the optative suffix and the like must reside in "being to be done" alone; just as the singular number and so forth [denoted by] the singular ending and the like express only the number "one-ness" and not its locus, because that locus is already conveyed by the verbal root. Therefore, the meaning of the optative suffix and the like is simply "being to be done."

Furthermore, it is the rule of worldly sentences that there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the action denoted by the verbal root and the state of being an effect denoted by the suffix, through the relation of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*). In the Veda, however, since it is impossible for the *apūrva*—the substratum of the state of being an effect—to be obtained from any other source, it must be asserted that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth denote the very nature of the effect as qualified by the state of being an effect. Consequently, if the optative suffix and so forth denote the qualified [entity], then they would denote the *apūrva* alone, and not the action.

If, on the other hand, it denotes a qualifier, then it would denote only that which pertains to the action, not that which pertains to the *apūrva*. Therefore, since a single meaning common to both worldly and Vedic usage cannot be found, and because it is cumbersome to postulate a separate denotative power for each case, and because it is improper for a Vedic word to have a non-primary meaning when following a worldly word, the "task" (*kārya*) alone is the primary meaning.

In the world, however, corporeality (*kāyatva*) is conveyed through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, while metaphorical indication is necessary for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, there is no reason for other worldly words to undergo such indication. For there is no distinct mode of understanding (*vyutpatti*) regarding the other Vedic words—contrary to the worldly understanding of the optative suffix and so on—as there is in the case of the Vedic optative suffix, where one must postulate a different mode of understanding that contradicts the worldly understanding of the optative suffix.

Since the property of denoting what is connected with an action (*kāryānvitābhidhāyitva*) is no different in Vedic words other than the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth than it is in worldly words other than those optative suffixes, there is this much distinction: in the world, the action to be performed (*kārya*) takes the form of an activity (*kriyā*); in the Veda, however, it is something distinct from that. Nevertheless, the property of denoting what is connected with an action is common to all.

If you argue that a separate linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) must be postulated for every distinct individual instance, then in cases such as “Bring the cow” (*gām ānaya*) and “Tie up the cow” (*gāṃ badhāna*), one would likewise have to postulate a second acquisition distinct from the initial one; this is true. However, let it be that in all instances this word *liṅ* and so forth denotes only an action to be performed (*kārya*). When it refers to the action itself, since the nature of that action is already established by the verbal root (*prakṛti*), the suffix then functions to denote its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).

For example, in the statement "The staff-bearer recites the directions," although the word "staff-bearer" denotes a qualified entity, it refers primarily to the qualification [the staff]; nor is there figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here. Consequently, when a word denoting an action is employed in reference to an act, it attains the status of referring primarily to the qualification—namely, the nature of being an action—while remaining within the primary mode of expression (*śrutivṛtta*). It does not become figurative on this account; thus, in both cases, there is indeed primacy.

As for the one who objects: "If this is so, then since [the word] expresses the general nature of the task (*kārya*), even in the case of a desire-injunction (*kāma-adhikāra*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—being presented by the same word—would have to be what is expressed as the task; thus, the theory of the expression of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) would collapse. Therefore, at the very moment it is understood that the word expresses the *apūrva* due to its connection with the person desiring the result (*kāmin*), one must simultaneously determine that the verbal root is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to denote the action in order to avoid that [consequence]"—that person should be instructed as follows: "Alas! Have you not heard: 'For him who eats stones, the *mudga*-bean cakes are easy to digest'?"

For if the connection with the person to be enjoined (niyojya) causes one to set aside even the word *liṅ*—which is understood to express "task-ness" (*kāryatva*)—and lead it toward the *apūrva*, how could that same [connection] not be capable of leading [the word] toward the *apūrva* when it expresses "task-ness" in general? Therefore, although it expresses "task-ness" in general, where there is the status of being the person to be enjoined for one who desires a fruit, it denotes the *apūrva* by the force of that [connection]; elsewhere, however, due to its inclusion within the same word, it denotes the action (*kriyā*).

Therefore, since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) denotes the general sense of "action" and is thus common to both the unseen potency (*apūrva*) and the action, one would not have to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) anywhere at all. Even so, the intention of those who propound that all words are figurative—those who speak falsely—is this: if you accept figurative indication for the optative suffix and so forth in ordinary worldly sentences, why do you not likewise accept figurative indication for the other words?

"By the scriptural statements accompanied by the arguments already stated. Therefore, some say that the word *ataḥ* (therefore) functions as a conclusion meaning "from the reasons already stated. Otherwise, the syntactical connection—namely, "the Vedāntas, demonstrating this very collection of topics through statements accompanied by arguments"—would become strained, and it would result in a distinction between the [individual] statements and the Vedāntas [as a whole].
[This refers to] the fact that perception has pure Being (*sanmātra*) as its object.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to recount a distant event while bypassing the immediately preceding one, he says, "Because of the contradiction with scripture and direct perception. This mention of the distant event is for the purpose of demonstrating the connection (*saṃgati*).

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). The sense is: "even if contradiction were admitted. Nor should it be argued that if the word *ca* has the sense of *api*, there is a contradiction with its previously stated sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*); for since *api* can also have the sense of conjunction, there is no contradiction. One might object: "It is incorrect to say 'no contradiction is seen at all,' because the perception of contradiction is difficult to deny and because the reason [given] would be futile. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "He asserts non-contradiction."

He states the reason [in the commentary] to dispel the suspicion that the phrase “because it apprehends only undifferentiated Being” (nirviśeṣasanmātragrāhitvāt) is not a valid reason due to its being in a different grammatical case (vyadhikaraṇa). The meaning is that the intention of the Bhāṣya is that perception is not contradicted by scripture because it apprehends only undifferentiated Being. [The phrase] “because there is the possibility of the perceived being of the nature of an error” means: because in the perception that apprehends only Being, there is the perception of the object as having distinct characteristics (vilakṣaṇaviṣayaviṣayakatva); it does not mean because of the perception of difference (bhedapratīti).

For if that were so, it would result in a contradiction with the doctrine that perception grasps only the existent (sanmātra); furthermore, the doubt regarding that [doctrine] would not be removed by the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "of a different character" (*vilakṣaṇa*), because even an error can be a cause for a distinct empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). The meaning of the Bhāṣya passage—"Because those two have cognitions occurring at different times as their results, whereas perceptual cognition exists within a single moment"—is as follows: Does perceptual cognition produce both types of empirical usage simultaneously, or sequentially? It says "those two" (*tayoḥ*) to show that it is not the first case.

The meaning is that it is because [the cognition] which occurs at a different time—consisting of the recollection of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and so forth—is its result. The meaning is that it is impossible for two types of linguistic usage (vyavahāra)—one dependent on the cognition of the counter-correlate and one independent of it—to arise simultaneously at a single moment. He refutes the second [position] with the words "And of perceptual cognition... The point is that one should not argue that the linguistic usage of difference can be established by another subsequent perceptual cognition; for there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the subsequent [cognition] being a perception.

"What does 'grasping both simultaneously' mean? It means that which produces two simultaneous linguistic usages (*vyavahāra*); this should be understood in accordance with the *Bhāṣya* and in conformity with the subsequent passage: "The root [cause] may exist either simultaneously or sequentially. Furthermore, the phrase "when the cognition of a jar as distinct from a cloth is required" is to be supplied even in the case of an uncommon usage (*asādhāraṇa-vyavahāra*). [The opponent asks: "If perception has only the thing-in-itself (*svarūpa-mātra*) as its object, how is the possibility of a linguistic usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) established?"

The meaning is: if the object were merely its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the essential nature of the jar and so forth were not the object, how could the linguistic usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) regarding the form of the jar and so forth be possible?

Now, as for the refutation of difference: if it is argued that since the apprehension of the mere essential nature of the jar and so forth does not depend on the knowledge of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), what inconsistency is there in the essential nature of the jar being an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*)? It is said in reply: the jar and so forth, perceived immediately after the operation of the sense organs, are perceived as indeed distinct from everything else; for in that regard, no doubt or error is observed concerning their difference from "that which is other than them" (*taditara*).

Furthermore, since difference (*bheda*) is necessarily perceived along with its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*), it cannot be apprehended by perception; for even those things that are not in contact [with the senses] may serve as counter-correlates due to spatial or temporal separation. Therefore, the appearance of a counter-correlate that is unfit for perception is of the nature of an error (*bhrānti*). Thus, according to the intention of the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādins*), because difference—which is known only through the same cognition as that which it qualifies—and the jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth, which are known only through the same cognition as their difference, are both objects of error, perception grasps only undifferentiated pure Being (*sanmātra*);
it does not grasp the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of jars and the like.

One might object: "For a proponent of difference as intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), the consequence that the linguistic usage of difference would apply to everything is not undesirable; for once the intrinsic nature has been perceived and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is remembered, such usage is indeed intended. Anticipating this, he explains [the verse] with the words: "because of the consequence of a linguistic usage of difference independent of a counter-correlate. He further clarifies: "of the perception of the intrinsic nature [of the thing] in the context of the acquisition of word-meaning (*śabda-vyutpatti*). This means that even in the view that difference is an additional entity (*atirikta-bheda*), it refers to the perception of the intrinsic nature of difference itself. Likewise, he notes that there must also be the perception (or recollection) of the counter-correlate.

The phrase "even in the view that difference is non-distinct from the essential nature" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The point is this: in the position of the Naiyāyikas and others who maintain that difference is distinct [from the object], the recollection of a word whose meaning is well-established and so forth is the cause for the *vyavahāra* (linguistic usage) of difference, but not for the cognition of difference itself; likewise, in our own view, even the apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and so forth pertains only to the *vyavahāra* of difference. Thus, it is said: "another difference which constitutes the essential nature."

Nor should it be suspected that there is a contradiction between being of the same nature (*svarūpabhūtatva*) and being a distinct entity (*bhedāntaratva*), for the point is that the relationship of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is possible by resorting to an imagined distinction (*kalpanika-bheda*). Now, one might object: "Since no further individual instances (*vyakti*) are admitted, there is no infinite regress. Anticipating this lack of conviction, he says: "Furthermore, it has been stated that 'the property [is expressed] by another word. If the relationship of property and property-bearer were established by resorting to an imagined distinction, then it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a jar could have a jar as its own substratum.

The meaning is this: by asserting that the relationship between property (*dharma*) and property-possessor (*dharmin*) is established by resorting to an imagined difference, one would be abandoning the position of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and instead adopting the position of a [separate] property (*dharma*). Regarding the phrase "the conventional usage of difference is made for the jar": since there is no recurring property called "difference," the word "difference" would only be applied to that particular individual with which its connection was previously grasped, and not to others; thus, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of uniform conventional usage. If it is argued that it is a property, then the aforementioned fault remains.

The meaning is that if [the universal] were a distinct property (*vyāvṛttadharma*), there would be an elimination of inclusive linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*). The intention is that "only pure existence" (*sanmātra*) would have to be accepted, because that alone possesses an inclusive nature (*anuvṛttasvarūpa*). Regarding the position that it is a property, the phrase "as before" applies. Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of "knowability" (*prameyatva*), there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because the property in the form of an inclusive distinction (*anuvṛttabhedārūpadharma*) functions as its own and others' establisher (*svaparaprakāśaka*); for the reason is that such a thing is not admitted by either party. And the same would apply to the fragment of that [property] as well.

The sense is that even for that which has become twofold, there would be a further state of being twofold. In the Bhāṣya, the phrase "tasyāpi bhedaḥ, tad-dharmaḥ, tasyāpi" [is used]; the ellipsis is "bhedaḥ tad-dharmaḥ. Consequently, for that too there is a distinction, and that distinction is its property; for that too there is a distinction, and that distinction is its property—thus the meaning is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

In the commentary on the phrase *bhede ca tasyāpi bhedastaddharmaḥ*, since it is possible to understand the pronoun *tasya* (in the genitive case) as referring to the second difference—which was mentioned immediately prior in the words *bhede ca*, which resides in the property that is difference itself, and which has its own nature as its counter-correlative—it would be improper to understand it as referring to the first difference which is separated [from it]. For if that were the case, the statement *tasya bhedaḥ* ("the difference of that") would be inappropriate, as the statement *bhedastaddharmaḥ* ("difference is its property") alone would have been more suitable.

And because [the previous argument] is purposeless, out of dissatisfaction [with that], he says: "Or rather, the difference of a property from its own nature, etc. In the first position, by the phrase "its difference is also a property of that," there is merely the establishment of another difference whose locus is that [first] difference; in the second position, by the phrase "its difference is also a property of that," there is merely the establishment of another difference whose locus is that [first] difference.

Regarding the second position, the distinction is that even in the case of a difference whose locus is difference itself, the establishment of difference occurs by means of the statement, "its difference is also a property of that. He explains, with the words "And that is threefold," etc., that in the commentary on the phrase "when there is the apprehension of an object qualified by properties such as genus (jāti)," the word "etc. includes the properties of being a locus (dharmitva), being a counter-correlative (pratiyogitva), and being a substratum (dharmitva). For indeed, in the cognition of the difference of a jar from a cloth, there are three causes: the jar...

The first is the cognition of the cloth as the substratum (dharmin) and the color-form as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin); the second is the cognition of the difference and its substratum, namely the color-form and the cloth; and since the cognition of the qualifier and the qualified is the cause of the cognition of the qualified entity, the third is the cognition of the jar's exclusion from the cloth and its being the locus of the property of "jar-ness"—this is the final meaning.

Nor can it be argued that even if the cognition of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is a cause for the cognition of absence, there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) because the cognition of the locus and counter-correlate as qualified by the properties of "being a locus" (*dharmitva*) and "being a counter-correlate" (*pratiyogitva*) is not required; for one might claim that the cognition of difference (*bhedajñāna*) is required only for the cognition of the locus and counter-correlate as qualified by "being a locus" and "being a counter-correlate," but not for the mere cognition of the locus and counter-correlate. This cannot be maintained, because prior to the cognition of difference, in the absence of a cognition having as its qualifier the counter-correlate as qualified by "counter-correlateness-ness" (*pratiyogitvatva*), there would be no cognition of difference having the counter-correlate as qualified by "counter-correlateness" as its qualifier.

This is because a cognition having counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) as its qualifier (*prakāra*) is the cause [of the absence-cognition]. For this very reason, since there would otherwise follow the erroneous perception of a reversed relationship between property and locus (*dharmadharmibhāva*), a cognition of the locus in its specific form is required; this is the intended meaning regarding the fact that even for the knowledge of a property and its locus, there must be a cognition of them as property and locus respectively.

The meaning is as follows: the phrase "and moreover" (*kiṃ ca*) indicates that he is now presenting a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*); it signifies that there is not merely an absence of evidence for [the opponent's position], but that there is also a subverting proof. Nor should it be said that a subverting proof—such as "Is difference the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or a property (*dharma*)?"—has already been presented earlier; for the intended sense is that such arguments lack the status of a formal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because they are merely forms of reasoning (*tarka*). Furthermore, the phrase "due to the existence of a contrary condition" (*viparītopādhisadbhāvāt*) means that the opposite of the probandum—in this case, "truth"—is established by the presence of its causal factor, namely, being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*).

Is it the result of correspondence (*saṃvāda*), or rather the result of sublation (*bādha*)? A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the existence of a cloth is correspondence; a means of valid cognition that apprehends its non-existence is sublation. A means of valid cognition that apprehends an entity (*bhāva*) is correspondence; a means of valid cognition that apprehends a non-entity (*abhāva*) is sublation. And being a "result" (*phala*) is simply being an object (*viṣaya*).

The meaning is as follows: "You yourselves must reflect on whether the exclusion of a cloth perceived in a jar and so forth results in a corroboration (*saṃvāda*)—which is the nature of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apprehending the existence of a cloth—or whether it results in a sublation (*bādha*), characterized by the cognition of the non-existence of a cloth. For if the exclusion of a cloth were of the nature of the cloth's existence, there might even be a suspicion that it is a result of corroboration; however, if it is of the nature of non-existence, its status as a sublation is established even against one's will. This is the intended sense.

Now, one might object: "How is it established that cloth and other things are sublated merely by the establishment of the absence of cloth in the statement 'the pot exists'? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says, "The absence of earth-clods and so forth," with the intention that since sublation cannot exist apart from the non-existence that constitutes the fruit of sublation, that very non-existence which is the fruit of sublation is what constitutes being sublated. [This establishes] the identity of existence and consciousness.

The word "also" (*api*) conjoins the fact that difference (*bheda*) is established through illusion (*bhrānti*). For its meaning has been described as "that which is established through illusion does not follow the path of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the intended sense is that the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) and difference are both established through illusion. Although the intended meaning is established by the fact that difference is conjoined with [the preceding] by means of "also," one should understand that it was stated thus by taking the final result into account. [This is expressed in the *Bhāṣya*: "Therefore, existence is indeed consciousness" (*tasmāt sadanubhūtireva*).]

If it is argued that even a jar or the like must be non-different from existence and consciousness because difference is difficult to define, we say no; for this argument is merely an overstatement, and thus such an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) is not a fault.
[This concludes the discussion on] the self-luminosity of consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "and furthermore, [the refutation] of the counter-inference": if by the word "furthermore" (kiṃca) the refutation of the counter-inference is being conjoined, then by the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and there is dependence on experience," another inference is being conjoined. And if by the word "furthermore" another inference is being conjoined, then by this word "and" the refutation of the counter-inference is being conjoined; such is the meaning.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the question "Who is the regulator [of this]?", he says [the word] "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
