This word is intended as a conclusion of what was previously stated, serving to dispel the doubt as to why knowledge should be included among the category of illuminators by virtue of its existence. Furthermore, it is because the fallacy of the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*) has been removed from the two reasons we have stated—namely, that "knowledge is illuminated by another because it is an entity (*vastutva*)" or "because it is manifest (*bhāsamānatva*). The sense is that the limiting condition raised by the opponent—the absence of being manifest by its own existence—has been refuted. [This is established] because it is manifest by its very nature (*svarūpeṇa*).
The meaning is that, by the pervasion (vyāpti) that whatever is known by a person is produced by their own cognition, one's own cognition alone is inferred, and not that of another.

The rejection of uniqueness has borne fruit; that is to say, the uniqueness [of the property] belonging to a particular person. This meaning is clear from the subsequent text: "The property of the object is distinct from cognition. As for those who do not accept duality and so forth—

The meaning is that in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is no possibility of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) based on the claim that "the perception of a specific object which serves as the basis for such a conceptual cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)—from which duality and so forth arise—is itself what generates the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'duality' and so on; there is no such thing as a 'duality' existing as a distinct form. [Otherwise] there would be an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga*). This refers to a specific, momentary conjunction of the self and the mind. Furthermore, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*).

The sense is that pleasure, pain, and so forth are internal because they possess the nature of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*). Regarding the statement, "that which is apprehended without being sought to be known is seen": this means that it is apprehended even when there is a contrary desire such as, "I would not wish to know this. Since it is apprehended without being sought to be known, it would follow that it is cognizable through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). The meaning is that, because that [mental perception] is also cognizable by mental perception and is thus apprehended without being sought to be known, it necessarily becomes the object of yet another mental cognition.

"When there is knowledge, there is desire" means that when knowledge exists, there arises a desire to know (*bubhutsā*). The sense is that such a desire arises precisely when something is known in a general way but remains unknown in its specific details. Regarding the position that what is not desired to be known cannot be grasped, it was previously stated that this would lead to an infinite regress of successive reflective cognitions (*anuvyavasāya*). Now, even under the position that what is desired to be known is grasped, he describes a succession of cognitions mediated by desire: "Furthermore, if it were so... That is to say: if it is argued that while a cognition is grasped when it is desired to be known, pleasure (*sukha*) and the like are not.

Furthermore, although there is the possibility of a pervasion between pleasure and the like with [their own] cognition (*pratīti*), cognition itself does not possess the property of being pervaded by cognition; for when there is no desire to know (*bubhutsā*), that cognition does not arise. Nor should it be argued that desire to know cannot be a cause because it is afflicted by mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); the point is that its status as a cause is observed in cases such as hearing the sound of a lute amidst a confusion of various sounds. "When it is grasped by perception" means that the qualification of the reason (*hetuviśeṣaṇa*) is the state of not being graspable by perception. [The phrase] "the subject (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*)" [is used].
It would have to be stated that knowledge is apprehended by the mind because it is a momentary specific quality of the self while being apprehended by perception;
however, this has not been so stated. Therefore, the implication is that this intended position is not accepted.
This concludes the instruction on the formal argument for self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*).

"Because it is the cause of that conventional usage (*tad-vyavahāra-hetutvāt*). This refers to "that which is both *tat* (the object) and *vyavahāra* (conventional usage)," not "the conventional usage of that (*tasya vyavahāraḥ*). For if it were the latter, there would be no distinction [between the two reasons], since the entirety [of the definition] would be included within the second reason.

Nor should it be argued that because the term *dharmavyavahārau* (dharma and conventional usage) is used, and these two together constitute *taddharmavyavahārau*, there is no inclusion of the entirety in the second reason; for the word *tat* itself occupies the position of the word *dharma*. [The phrase is] "distinct from the causal complex of experience (*anubhūti-sāmagrī-vyatirikta*)."

Nor should it be argued that the property of being an experience (*anubhūtitva*) would be dependent on something else because it depends upon a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) distinct from the experience itself; for since the property of being an experience arises through the very same causal complex that produces the experience, the property of being an experience is not dependent on anything other than the experience. If, even while the experience exists, the property of being an experience were absent in the absence of something else, then the property of being an experience would be dependent on that other thing. However, since the property of being an experience is established by the mere causal complex of the experience itself, it lacks dependence on anything else.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) because it is produced solely by the causal complex of cognition itself. Alternatively, the phrase "distinct from the causal complex of experience" means that it does not depend on another instance of the same class.

In this regard, the inference should be formulated as follows: "Cognition (*anubhūti*) is necessarily devoid of a requirement for a similar instance (*sajātīya*) in order to produce its own inevitable manifestation (*prākaṭya*), because it is the cause of manifestation in another object through its own connection; whatever is the cause of a certain property in another object through its own connection is necessarily devoid of a requirement for a similar instance in producing that same property within itself. The second inference is likewise.

Just as that house at that time was devoid of a friend, because it was not perceived as possessing a friend at that time; for whatever is not perceived as possessing something at a certain time, it is then devoid of that thing—this is the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*). Now, one might object: "If a property produced by itself were to belong to another, how could experience possess that property? For there is an absence in experience of any property belonging to another that is produced by itself. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The meaning is 'absolutely similar to the property to be established by itself'."

He demonstrates the proof for the word *dharma* referring to another [property] in the sense of a property produced by itself in the statement: "Because it is the cause of that property in another object," since this is stated as a reason (*hetu*). Since the term "in another object" is seen in the context of the reason, it must also be stated in the context of the probandum (*sādhya*) as "in another. When it is said "because it is the cause of that property," only a property whose cause is experience (*anubhūti*) is to be understood. Consequently, that very property which was specified in the reason is what is to be understood by the term "probandum-property" (*sādhyadharma*).

The sense is that since that very property (*dharma*) is impossible here [in the case of the object], the probandum (*sādhya*) is the possession of a property belonging to the same class as it. Regarding the phrase "it must necessarily exist in itself": one might object, "But for those who maintain that manifestation (*prākaṭya*) is revealed by another, its necessity is not admitted with respect to the experience (*anubhūti*); for if it were so admitted, then out of fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), one would be forced to admit self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) itself. To this we say: no.

When knowledge has arisen, since no doubt or the like is observed, its manifestation (*prākaṭya*) is necessarily present; thus, the application of inference for such a case is established. Alternatively, because the cognition of another person is seen to be inferable, there would be the consequence of sublation (*bādhaprasaṅga*). The sense is this: even if manifestation occurs independently of anything else, there would be sublation because—in all other cases where there are properties of the same class produced by that [cognition]—there is an absence of dependence on anything else.

One might object: "In the view of those who maintain such an inference, since it is not admitted that cognition is an object of inference (*anumeya*), how can one raise the charge of sublation (*bādha*) by taking its non-inferentiality as the ground? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For [non-inferentiality] does not consist in being beyond the scope of another cognition. He explains: "The reason is 'experience' (*anubhūti*) which is independent of its own kind. The point is this: if it were stated that "experience is a verbal designation (*vyavahāra*) not dependent on anything else," then because experience possesses a verbal designation not dependent on anything else—by way of a relationship characterized as that of cause and effect (i.e., the relation between the experience and its subsequent linguistic usage)—the argument would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*).

The meaning is as follows: since the absence of the word "that" (*tat*) in the reason (*hetu*) fails to establish even in the probandum (*sādhya*) the sense that a property of the same class as what is produced by itself is independent of anything else, there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is because the property of color (*rūpa*), which is the logical reason (*hetu*) for visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*), depends upon something entirely of its own class—namely, taste (*rasa*)—in producing its own necessarily concomitant qualities such as duality (*dvitva*) and so forth.

Is it not the case that one's own relation (*svasaṃbandha*) is a relation determined by oneself (*svanirūpita*)? Consequently, that which is the relation with fire is not determined by itself. Even though the relation is one and the same, according to common usage we speak of "the relation determined by fire in the jar" and "the relation determined by the jar in the fire"; thus, because a relation does not reside in itself by way of having itself as its counter-correlative (*svapratiyogikatva*), they indeed say: "For a thing is not conjoined with itself."

Furthermore, even if the production of another form depends upon fire, there is no deviation [in the argument] because it does not depend on a pot of its own kind; expressing dissatisfaction with this, he says: "Moreover, the word 'another object' (arthāntara)... It means "referring to that which is of a different genus from the specified genus. The word "necessary" is to be supplied as the remainder. For a pot [does not arise] from itself or from what is conjoined with it, and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that there is again a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) because a jar, while bringing about its conjunction with a cloth or similar object, requires another jar for its own state of being conjoined with a jar; for this is precluded by the very phrase "necessarily occurring" (svāvaśyaṃbhāvi). Indeed, it is not necessarily the case that every member of the class of jars must be conjoined with another jar.

Now, an objection may be raised: since we observe that a conscious being who, through its own connection, imparts the state of being conjoined with consciousness to an insentient object, must itself necessarily be conjoined with consciousness, the same dilemma regarding dependence on a member of its own class remains. Furthermore, for a conscious being who imparts the state of being governed by a conscious agent to an insentient object, there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because such a being would require another conscious agent to govern itself. Nor should it be argued that this is avoided by the very term "necessarily occurring" (*avaśyaṃbhāvi*); for even the Supreme Self is governed by His devotees.

Likewise, [if it is argued that] one brings about the status of being a disciple (*śiṣyatva*) in a Kṣatriya through one's own connection, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the status of being a disciple in oneself as a Brāhmaṇa, because that depends upon another Brāhmaṇa. Nor should it be said that the status of being a disciple for Brāhmaṇas is not necessarily present, since death is possible even before the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*); for in that case, one could equally say that visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) is not necessarily present even in the example of color and so forth. Furthermore, one could likewise say that the manifestation (*prākaṭya*) of even a cognition (*anubhūti*) is not necessarily present. Therefore, if it is argued that this inference is unestablished (*apratiṣṭhita*), [we reply: [The argument continues: It is not so. For even if the status of being a disciple in a Brāhmaṇa is not necessarily present, the status of being a disciple in a Kṣatriya is necessarily brought about by the connection with a specific Brāhmaṇa. Moreover, the status of being a disciple in a Brāhmaṇa is indeed necessarily present, because after the initiation ceremony, death is impossible until the completion of the study of the Veda. As for the claim that visibility is not necessarily present in color and so forth, that is not correct; for visibility is necessarily present in color and other such objects, because they are produced as possessing the nature of being visible. Similarly, it cannot be said that the manifestation of a cognition is not necessarily present, because it is established that the manifestation of a cognition follows immediately upon its production. Therefore, this [opponent’s] objection does not invalidate our inference.

Regarding this, some say that the conclusion of the argument is as follows: whatever is the cause for the application of a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) toward everything other than itself, that [cause] does not depend on anything else for the application of that same convention toward itself.

Consequently, they claim that those who hold the conceit that experience (*anubhūti*)—which serves as the cause for the application of conventions such as "it is experienced" or "it is manifested" with respect to everything other than experience—is, like existence (*sattā*), independent of anything else for the application of such conventions toward itself, offer the following inference: experience is one, because it is the locus of existence (*sattā-sthānīya*).

"In the son, who is the cause for the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'son-ness' (*putratva*). Nor should it be argued that this is already excluded by the term "distinct entity" (*arthāntara-pada*) itself because the son also possesses fatherhood; the point is that even a eunuch son is possible, as he does not possess fatherhood. "Simultaneous with its own relation": the similarity to its own relation consists in not occurring at a time other than that which does not exclude its own relation. Consequently, it should be understood that this [similarity] exists even in the manifestation (*prākaṭya*) produced immediately after the relation with cognition. "For [there is no such thing] as the exile or death of a father and so forth."

[Objection: But surely, even in the cases of exile and death, the relationship of cause and effect certainly exists, since the status of being a father and a son does not cease even when [the son] has departed. While there is no longer a physical conjunction when he has gone abroad or died, such an absence of conjunction exists even when [a person] has merely gone to another village; therefore, the mention of exile and death is entirely redundant. [Reply: This is not so.

The relationship between the father and the son—consisting of the final element (the semen) and so forth—in the manner described in the *Pañcāgnividyā*, is that which produces the status of being a son. However, the relationship mentioned in the sūtra, "Then the union of the semen and blood," does not endure for very long. Therefore, the intended meaning is as stated in the *Nayaviveka*: "The father’s act of procreation establishes the relationship with the one to be produced at the very moment of birth, and not at any other time."

To summarize the point already stated, he shows it by saying: "This is what is meant. [The definition is: "Experience, when possessing a quality that is absolutely similar to another quality produced by itself in another, is devoid of any necessity for dependence on something absolutely similar to itself. If it were merely said that "experience is devoid of dependence," there would be a contradiction because its own nature (*svarūpa*) depends upon instruments; to avoid that, it is specified as "possessing a quality. Even so, if the example were the color-form (*rūpa*), which depends on the eyes and other factors to become visible, it would lack the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*).

To avoid that [objection], it was stated that [the cognition] is "devoid of dependence on a homogeneous [cognition]. Nevertheless, since the eyes and other sense organs are homogeneous with respect to the universal *sattā* (existence), the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) remains as before; therefore, it was stated that it is "absolutely homogeneous. Even so, because the cognition of another might be conducive to a usage dependent on yet another cognition, there would be sublation (*bādha*) in part; hence, it was stated that it is "devoid of a restriction of dependence."

Even so, since the state of being an experience (*anubhūtitva*) does not depend on another experience, it would follow that the probandum is already established by that [experience itself]. To avoid this, the term "residing in another" (*paragata*) is used. Since a property residing in another does not reside in the experience itself, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*); therefore, the term "of the same class as the property residing in another" (*paragatadharmasajātīya*) is used. Even if it possesses a property of the same class as one residing in another, it would still follow that the probandum is already established because it does not depend on something absolutely similar [to itself]; to avoid this, the qualification "produced by itself" (*svajanya*) is added.

"Because it is the cause of a property that is of the same class as its own necessarily future property, belonging to itself, and existing at the same time. If one were to say merely "because it is the cause of a property," there would be an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntya*) with respect to jars and the like, since they are causes of their own qualities produced by baking (*pākaja-rūpa*). Even if one specifies "another's" (*parasya*), there would still be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a substance that produces conjunction with another substance, for in that case, the substance's own state of being conjoined depends upon another substance. Therefore, it is specified as "of a different class from itself" (*svavijātīya*).

Nevertheless, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since the nature of being a body (*śarīratva*) is attributed to a body of a different class (*vijātīya*), there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the conscious self (*cetana*), which, while being its own body, depends upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) which is of the same class as itself. To avoid this, the term "inseparable from itself" (*svāśrayāvinābhāvī*) is used. By this, the intended meaning is that [the quality] pervades all things of its own class.

Nevertheless, there would be a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a father who is the cause of his son’s status as a son, yet whose own status as a son depends on another father, or in the case of an axe which is the cause of a piece of wood’s splitting, yet whose own splitting depends on another axe; therefore, the qualifications “having a relationship with itself” (*svasaṃbandha*) and “simultaneous in time” (*tulyakāla*) are added. The purpose of these terms should be understood in the same way in other inferences as well.

The passage "the meaning is that [it is] the conventional usage ‘experience’" should be understood as resulting from a scribe’s error; for in the subsequent context, while the conventional usage "it shines forth" (*prakāśate*) is something to be produced, the conventional usage "it is experience" (*anubhūtiḥ*) is not something to be produced. Regarding the term "conditioned" (*sopādhika*): the meaning is that the specific relation itself is the condition (*upādhi*). Regarding the phrase "for [it would be] a remover": for the self-luminosity of a lamp must either consist in its being a remover of its own darkness, or it must consist in its producing knowledge of its own object.

The self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of knowledge consists precisely in its being the producer of the practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) regarding its own object. The sense here is that we perceive no contradiction whatsoever in this. For if it were the case that the very same thing were both the effect and the agent, then indeed there would be a contradiction. But what contradiction is there in stating that something is itself the agent while producing—whether it be the practical transaction regarding its own object, the cognition of its own object, or the removal of darkness associated with itself? In this regard, the phrase "if [it were] by way of another form" (*cākārāntareṇa cet*) refers to that.

If there is another aspect (ākāra) even in that case, there is no contradiction at all. The point is that, as seen in passages such as "He made Himself by Himself" (*tad ātmānaṃ svayam akuruta*), the status of being the object (*karmatva*) exists in the form qualified by gross sentient and insentient matter, while the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) exists in the form qualified by subtle sentient and insentient matter. Regarding the phrase "of knowledge itself when unknown": this means "of that which is not yet manifest. This should be understood in accordance with the concluding passage: "Therefore, [it is] precisely of that which is manifest."

"If it follows that there is an absence of being preceded by [an object as] the object of knowledge (*jñānakarmatāpūrvakatva*),"—the sense is that the non-subversion of the rule that [action] must be preceded by its status as the objective factor (*karmakārakatva*) with respect to knowledge is what is intended. Nor should it be argued that the rule "linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is necessarily preceded by a cognition having that as its object" is indispensable, lest it follow that one thing could be the object of linguistic usage based on a cognition of something else; for the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is simply that "linguistic usage is preceded by cognition."

The sense is that, in order to avoid over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding insentient objects, another restrictive rule is postulated—that the cognition of an object is the cause of its empirical usage—yet this is not the case even in the instance of cognition itself.

Regarding the phrase "this very experience is self-luminous" (*seyaṃ svayaṃprakāśānubhūtiḥ*), he explains that by the word "that" (*tat*) in the expression "that very being" (*saiva satī*), the identity with existence (*sadaikya*) is referred to; and by the word "this" (*idam*), the fact that it is not the object of any other means of knowledge—established by the refutation of the inference based on manifestness—is referred to. Alternatively, since the reference to the identity with existence would be useless for what is to be stated later, he offers another explanation: "or, [the meaning is] 'in its self-luminosity'. He states that the second alternative is rejected because there is no subject to be grasped (*grāhya*).

The meaning is that in inference and other such cognitions, because the object to be grasped is not an obstruction, it is impossible to refute [the cognition] by its absence. Therefore, it is said: "a modification in the form of a positive entity" (*bhāvarūpa-vikāra*). The point is that destruction (*nāśa*) is not a modification in the form of a positive entity, because it is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*). An objection is raised: "If the probandum is the absence of modifications in the form of positive entities, then the absence of destruction in *anubhūti* (immediate experience) is not established. Due to this unease, he says: "Or rather, 'a modification of a positive entity' (*bhāvasya vikāraḥ*). The resulting implication is that being unproduced while possessing the nature of a positive entity is the reason for the absence of any other modification.

Although it has been stated that there are no modifications of an entity because of its lack of origination—which implies the qualification of being "unoriginated"—even by that much, it is impossible to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Since antecedent non-existence is of the nature of an absence, it lacks modifications related to an entity; nevertheless, this was said with the intention that another inference—namely, "because it is unoriginated while being an entity"—is necessary to ensure that the qualified absence of modification in an entity results in the absence of the property of being modified in the entity itself. This concludes the demonstration of the eternity of consciousness (*anubhūti*).

"By the cessation of the pervading [cause], birth ceases"—the sense is that the cessation of birth has already been stated as being due precisely to the cessation of plurality (*nānātva*). Furthermore, one should observe that the absence of a locus for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) constitutes an additional refutation here. Alternatively, he demonstrates the establishment of pervasion through the force of the final conclusion even within the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) as it stands, using the words "Or rather, just as... [and so on]. [The text states: "Experience does not possess a property consisting of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)."

These two inferences should be understood as indicative of the two subsequent inferences concerning the absence of attributes such as eternality and so forth. Intending to show that the status of consciousness as the Self (*saṃvidātmatva*) is naturally understood through the argument for the existence of a knower (*jñātṛsadbhāva*) in the verse beginning with "yato nirdhūtanikhila...", the author explains [it] by saying "by the negation of all distinctions. Alternatively, intending to show the possibility of a non-mediated reason for the Self's nature as that which has shaken off all distinctions, he explains [it] by saying "or rather, by the Vedāntas of the Self..."

Anticipating the objection that there is tautology between the terms “substratum” (āśraya) and “knower” (jñātṛ), he states—intending to show that there is no tautology because the latter serves as an explanation of the former—that “the substratum is indeed distinct from its own nature. Then, in response to the doubt as to what the reason for the absence of a knower might be, he demonstrates that the phrase “distinct from its own nature” provides the reason for that absence by stating: “precisely because it is distinct from the nature of consciousness.”

In the first commentary on the *Bhāṣya* passage, "This very Self is of the nature of self-luminosity," [the author] removes the redundancy of the *Bhāṣya* statement "and because of its non-inertness" by stating: "He says that self-luminosity is both the nature [of the Self] and its independent proof."

The meaning is as follows: since the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) of consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the Self (*ātman*) has already been established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and since that which is self-luminous is unarisen due to the absence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and other such states, and since that which is unarisen cannot possess multiplicity (*nānātva*), it was stated that self-luminosity proves the identity of consciousness and the Self by way of proving the absence of multiplicity between them. Now, however, its proof of the identity of consciousness and the Self is being stated by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*). [This refers to the rule] "the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent" (*kartari ktaḥ*).

Because the root *āp* has the sense of "going," or because there is an intention to express its intransitivity—as in the rule "for roots meaning 'to go' or being intransitive, the suffix *kta* denotes the agent"—this is the intended meaning.
Now, as for the demonstration that the Self lacks the status of a knower:

one might object that although the knowerhood of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) is established by perception in the form "I know," the knowerhood of the Self is not so established. Anticipating this, [the author] says: "because the fact that the Self is the object of the notion of 'I' is established by the perception of one's own experience. Alternatively, it means "while knowerhood is being perceived. The intention is that this point is recalled by the word *śakala*, which denotes a "part."

With the intention that the Bhāṣya statement "For [the Self] is a knower" (jñātṛtvaṃ hi) is aimed at removing the doubt regarding the non-establishment of the previously stated reason, he demonstrates the impossibility of agency by saying "For [the Self] is a knower."

In this [previous] explanation, because there is a lack of intrinsic consistency with the word *svātman* (the self), and because it would be improper to state the reason—the impossibility of agency—which requires further justification, and because it would be inappropriate to fail to resolve the doubt "what follows from that" before providing such justification, he explains it otherwise, beginning with the words: "Or else, what is called 'knowership'... Having raised the objection, "If one intends to express that [the self] is the substratum of knowledge which constitutes its very nature (*svarūpa*), how can the word 'agency' (*kartṛtva*) be applicable? he says: "Agency is being the substratum."

Although there is no need for further proof regarding the impossibility of agency within one's own self, the commentary beginning with "Therefore, 'I am a human being'" is explained as referring to another reason—namely, that agency belongs to a deluded person—because it would otherwise be inappropriate to resolve the doubt [raised by the opponent] with the question, "What follows from that? In this view, it should be noted that the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), which refers back to what was previously stated, lacks its natural force. This is because [the opponent's position] shares the commonality of being insentient and consisting of transformation.

The meaning is: "due to the similarity [of the Self] with insentience (*jaḍatva*) and changelessness (*avikāritva*). This is because it is seen in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) that [the terms] are used as "the changing substance, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)," "the unchanging," and "the witness (*sākṣin*). Otherwise, one would have to say "the changing substance, the ego-sense" and "in the unchanging witness. Nor should it be argued how the knower-ship (*jñātṛtva*), being of the nature of a modification (*vikāra*), can itself be a modification; for there is no contradiction between being a modification and being subject to modification.

Although equality in the relationship between substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) is not a determining factor—since such a relation does not exist between substance, quality, genus, and individual, and so forth—nevertheless, the sense is that the insentient is always seen to rest upon the sentient, and that which undergoes modification is always seen to rest upon that which is modified. However, some maintain that upon examining the *Bhāṣya* passage, "In the changeless Witness situated within the knot of the ego, which is a substance subject to modification," it is understood that the existence of a modification within that which is devoid of modification is simply impossible.

They do not maintain that the relationship of substratum and superstratum exists only between two things that are equal. This is because there is a scriptural passage concerning deep sleep which states: "Indeed, this one does not know himself at this time, thinking 'I am this'; nor indeed these beings. The meaning is that this person in deep sleep does not know himself in the form "I am this."

"It is refuted by the counter-argument of the body" means that even if the body were the agent, the Self is still observed to be the enjoyer; this is the sense. In reality, however, the Self does not possess even the status of being an enjoyer. If it is objected: "In that case, there would arise the contingency of bondage and liberation having different loci (vaiyadhikaraṇya), since liberation resides in pure consciousness (cinmātra) while bondage—in the form of agency and so forth—resides in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)," we reply: no.

There is no fault, because it is accepted that transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) resides solely in pure consciousness (cinmātra), by virtue of its being the locus for the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth. Not satisfied with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating "because [the body] is the object of the notion of 'I'," which—given the extreme weakness of the doubt regarding the non-selfhood of the body in the illustrative example—proceeds to say: "Or rather, because it is not an object of the notion of 'I' according to authoritative means of knowledge. In this view, the word "only" (*eva*) found in the *bhāṣya* passage "it is well-known only to those who accept authoritative means of knowledge" carries the sense of the word "just as" (*yathā*).

Alternatively, by the force of the word *tathā*, the word *yathā* must be supplied. In this view, it should be understood that the term *pratyaya* in the commentary’s phrase "from the object of the notion of 'I'" (*ahaṃpratyayagocarāt*) has the meaning of "error" (*bhrānti*). However, some observe the word *yadvā* in manuscripts immediately after the passage, "Because the knower also is established by means of valid cognition as being distinct [from the body], it must be accepted as such. We do not, however, see its correctness.

This is because it is more appropriate for the phrase "the object of the non-authoritative *ahaṃpratyaya*" to serve as an introduction to the word "from the *ahamartha*" found in the Bhāṣya; consequently, taking "from the object of the *ahaṃpratyaya*" as the pratīka (citation) is also incorrect. It is proper to take "from the *ahamartha*" alone as the pratīka. Nor is this a citation of the preceding phrase "from the object of the *ahaṃpratyaya*."

This is appropriate; for in that passage which is intent on establishing the self's transcendence of the body, they state—anticipating an objection by taking its transcendence of the gods for granted—that "if one were to [regard] the knower as the Self despite it being sublated by valid means of knowledge. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "even though [the knower] is the object of the authoritative cognition 'I'."

Since it was previously stated in the passage beginning with "in the changeless witness" (*avikriye sākṣiṇi*) that the status of being a knower is impossible in the Self, and since it will be explained later that this delusion of "I know" is produced by that [ignorance]—thus making the delusion of being a knower in the Self logically consistent—it is in accordance with what precedes and follows that the commentary beginning with "Thus, for one whose very nature is changeless experience" (*evam avikriyānubhavasvarūpasyaiva*) is explained as being intent on establishing the appearance of being a knower in the Self. Alternatively, in order to follow the natural sense of its own words, he explains it otherwise: "Or rather, the status of being a knower... (*yadvā jñātṛtvam iti*).

Thus, the non-ultimate nature of the state of being a knower has been stated. The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* passage, "because 'I know,'" is that the sense of "I" (*ahamartha*) alone is the knower; therefore, the state of being a knower does not belong to the Self as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as its ultimate attribute. This is the intended sense. By stating that [the word] refers to the substantive (*viśeṣya*), there is no tautology; the meaning is that it refers to the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*). How can there be the expression "it manifests through delusion" (*bhrāntyā vivartate*)? For the meaning of the term *vivarta* is indeed "it is perceived through delusion."

Furthermore, anticipating the objection that this would result in redundancy, he says: "The designation is like that of a young elephant (*karikalabha*). The sense is that it is similar to the expression: "On Jānakī’s cheek, which steals the luster of the tusk of a young elephant.
This is the Great Established Conclusion (*mahāsiddhānta*).

"He promises this as such" means he is eager to speak it. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur here because of the prohibition in the rule *saṃpratibhyāmanādhyāne*, where *ādhyāna* (longing) is excluded. *Ādhyāna* means longing, and in this context, the root *jñā* preceded by *prati* is intended to convey the sense of longing. Thus, the reading *pratijānīte* is indeed straightforward. However, some maintain that in the passage beginning with "The goal is indicated by the term 'Supreme Person'," the reading *pratijānāti* (active voice) is more appropriate, as it better suits the meaning.

In that context, it is appropriate to use terms such as "Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣa*) for mere recollection; however, here it is more appropriate to say "he declares. They maintain that this [usage] has been transposed due to the error of a scribe. Regarding the phrase "the specific relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge": the specific means of knowledge is the *Upaniṣad*, and the specific object of knowledge is the Supreme Person; the relationship between these two is that of the signified and the signifier, which is made explicit by the very Vedic text: "That person who is known through the *Upaniṣads*" (*taṃ tvaupaniṣadaṃ puruṣam*). This is the meaning.

Regarding this, the phrase "he has attained a state of purity through devotion" (*bhaktyā śuddhabhāvaṃ gataḥ*) is intended. It should not be argued that the grammatical connection should instead be "one should know from the scripture through devotion" (*bhaktyā śāstrād viddhi*), rather than "he has attained a state of purity through devotion," on the grounds that devotion serves as the cause for the purification of one's disposition (*bhāva*). This is because the requirement for a reason is already satisfied by the word "from the scripture" (*śāstrāt*) alone; thus, devotion cannot be construed as the cause in that context. Furthermore, since the purification of disposition requires a cause, the intended meaning is that the connection is indeed "he has attained a state of purity through devotion."

Having explained the preceding qualifiers—such as "clothed in beginningless sin" and "pertaining to the Upanishads"—as being the causes [of the subsequent description], he now explains them as effects, saying: "Or rather, by means of perfect knowledge," and so forth. Regarding the term *dunirrāsatvam*: it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which is difficult to remove. The reading *dunirasatvam* is likewise easy to understand. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "accepted by various disputants": the sense is this: "all accepted means of valid cognition" (*sakalapramāṇam*) refers to whatever is accepted by whichever [disputant]; that is to say, everything that is accepted by each respective person.

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya will state: "Even in disputes regarding the number of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this alone is the object of all those means of valid cognition that are universally accepted. One should not mistakenly think that *pratyakṣādi* and *sakalapramāṇa* form a *dvandva* compound; for if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to include presumption (*arthāpatti*) and the rest, since the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) was previously stated to mean inference (*anumāna*). Alternatively, the word "all" (*sakala*) is intended to include other means of valid cognition such as presumption without restriction by means of the word "etcetera. Thus, the means of valid cognition possess specific objects.

"The word 'this' (idam) is for the purpose of excluding that [other possibility]. The sense is that it is impossible to point to something universally agreed upon by indicating it as "this is the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) through a finger-pointing method (*ṛṅgagrāhikayā*). Alternatively, following the singular number [of the word], he explains it otherwise: "or rather, not any at all. On this point, some consider the phrase "or rather" (*yadvā*) to be the result of a scribe's error, maintaining that the natural elegance of the text exists precisely in its absence. [He says: "The scent is experienced."

The meaning is that because experience appears as a qualifier, every object is indeed qualified by the qualifier that is its nature as experience; thus, there is no state of being devoid of qualifiers (*nirviśeṣatva*). Now, one might object: "In the phrase 'But as for one's own experience which is presented as a means of valid cognition' (*yastu svānubhavaḥ pramāṇatvenopanyastaḥ*), since the particle *tu* is intended to indicate a specific means of valid cognition characterized as one's own experience, it is inconsistent to use the particle *tu* to indicate a specific convention (*samaya*). Anticipating this objection, [the author] shows that even the demonstration of a difference in conventions...

He says that there is no fault because [the statement] culminates in demonstrating the disparity between the characteristic of one's own fundamental experience and [other] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), thereby qualifying "convention" (*samaya*) with the word "but" (*tu*). Now, if the qualified object is itself [the subject], how can there be a *bahuvrīhi* designation such as "that which has a qualified object"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This designation is like [the expression] 'the body of a stone-son' (*śilāputraka*)," because it has the same meaning as "established by one's own experience."

The meaning is that, because the subsequent passage is intended to exclude other types of experience, it is more appropriate to speak of [the term "experience"] in a figurative sense. Now, one might object: since the word *svānubhava* (one's own experience) could possibly refer to another cognition in the form of a *anuvyavasāya* (reflective awareness), how can there be certainty that it refers to the stated meaning by virtue of being synonymous with that [other term]? To this, he replies with the words beginning, "And the word *anubhava* does not refer to *anuvyavasāya*," and so forth. [He explains: "By way of having a past object."

The meaning is that, because present cognition is self-luminous, it is impossible for an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) to have a present object; rather, it is necessarily restricted to past objects, and thus it is untenable for that which has a past object to be a perception (*pratyakṣa*). "With a forgotten latent impression" (*pramuṣitasaṃskāram*) means with an unawakened latent impression (*anudbuddhasaṃskāra*). "Other" (*anyat*) means with an awakened latent impression (*udbuddhasaṃskāra*).

Nor should it be said that, due to the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of a jar, the jar alone is the object of memory and not the cognition of the jar; for since that [cognition] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it is logically consistent that the very memory generated by it is itself a memory of the experience. If it is argued: "But the causal complex for inference (*anumiti-sāmagrī*) is stronger than the causal complex for memory; moreover, when there is a desire to infer (*anumitsā*), it is even stronger still. Consequently, it is indeed possible for a cognition—even one whose impression has not been lost—to become the object of an inference," we say: no.

The intention is that even so, the convention of that circle [of scholars]—namely, that [the object] is established by the direct perception of one's own experience—is not maintained. Indirectness (*parokṣatva*) occurs by way of the object; for even in the case of cognitions such as inference, it resides in the cognition itself.

The sense is that because everything present is directly perceived (*aparokṣa*). "The reason would be non-different from the subject" means that the reason would be identical with the subject; the implication is that the reason would thus be *svarūpāsiddha* (unestablished in its own nature). "For the reason must pervade the subject" means that the reason must reside in the subject. "Furthermore, of another" means that, due to its own relation, it is precisely the cause for the conventional usage of that [term] in another object, because it consists in the exclusion of itself (*svavyāvṛtti*); the sense is that it would be *vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*, which means *svarūpāsiddha*.

And thus, by the phrase “by its own specific [attributes],” it is established that there is pervasion (vyāpyatva) while residing in itself (svavṛttitve sati). Consequently, the intended meaning is that being distinct from existence (sattātirekitva) is what serves the purpose of being specific to itself. Therefore, one should not suspect the redundancy of the phrase “by those distinct from existence. The meaning is that when the nature of being cognition (dhītva) is established, self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) is thereby established. Thus, the sense is that once cognition-ness is proven, self-luminosity follows as a consequence.

But surely, since the nature of being a cognition (*dhītva*) and self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*) are perceived through the fact that the knower has the nature of illuminating an object, it appears from the *Bhāṣya* that the perception [of the knower] as having the nature of illuminating its own object is the direct proof for both being a cognition and self-luminosity. Because there is dissatisfaction with the interpretation that this [perception] proves being a cognition and that being a cognition proves self-luminosity—arguing that such an interpretation lacks the natural force (*svārasya*) of the *Bhāṣya*—he explains it otherwise: "Or rather, being a cognition is merely the essential nature of cognition (*dhīsvarūpamātra*)."

The meaning of the Bhāṣya is stated as follows: the nature of consciousness (*dhīsvarūpa*) and its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) are established because it is perceived as having the essential character of illuminating objects. Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of the Self" (*ātmasphuraṇam*), the meaning is "the manifestation of the essential nature of the Self. As for the expression in the Bhāṣya, "by those who know it [the Self] as non-different from their own intended [nature]," the sense is that the opponent establishes [the plurality of selves] by arguing: "Because it is unproduced, it is eternal; and because the Self is eternal, it cannot tolerate multiplicity."

The meaning is that previously, the state of having qualifiers (*saviśeṣatva*) was stated by means of reasons refuting the absence of qualifiers; this is according to the commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating, "therefore, [it is the cognition] of that which is qualified by certain qualifiers. Then, regarding the phrase "by some": the meaning is according to the commentary stating, "because it is perceived as having the nature of illuminating objects for the knower. However, some explain it as being according to the commentary stating, "by its own intended distinctions of that kind," provided that [the context] exists. Thus, both verbal testimony and perception have as their object that which possesses qualifiers.

Regarding the phrase "having determined the self-luminous function (*svaprakāśavṛtti*)," the distinction is as follows: in the first position, the self-luminous function does not enter into the scope of all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which have specific attributes (*saviśeṣa*); however, in the second position, even that [self-luminous function] is included therein. Regarding the phrase "that which is agreed upon by both disputants due to its being internal," in the first position, the superiority asserted by the opponent is not accepted by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*); likewise, the excellence of the proponent's view in making known the reality with specific attributes is not accepted by the opponent.

In this view, the distinction is that the form [of the object] being internal (*antaraṅga*) is agreed upon by both parties. Now, regarding the phrase "by the word *nirviśeṣa*": the meaning is "by the word *nirviśeṣa*" in the statement "there is no entity devoid of attributes" (*nirviśeṣaṃ vastu nāsti*). "The negation is untenable" means that [the opponent] maintains that every cognition whatsoever is of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*). The sense is that there is a fault in negating the object of valid knowledge (*pramiti*), but not in negating the object of an erroneous cognition (*bhrānti*), because of the distinction between error and valid knowledge. Regarding the phrase "generated by the word *nirviśeṣa*": [this refers to the cognition produced by that term].

The meaning is that the error, which would otherwise entail the non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is sublated by the means of valid cognition [stating] "that which is without distinction does not exist. I state the reason for its being an error: "having as its object things incapable of mutual connection. The point is that being an error consists precisely in having as its object a connection between things that are mutually unconnected.

Some, however, explain the text differently regarding the word *nirviśeṣa*, [interpreting it as]: "The word *nirviśeṣa* in the Bhāṣya sentence—namely, 'the word is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to a featureless reality (*nirviśeṣavastu*)'—is what is meant. On this view, the text "the prohibition of the featureless reality being conveyed by a word is untenable" would be its natural sense. To this, [the author] replies: "Not so, because of the distinction between erroneous and valid cognition."

The meaning of the statement, "An error regarding an object that is unfit for mutual connection, produced by words denoting the indeterminate (nirviśeṣa), is sublated by words that produce valid cognition," is as follows: the error consisting in the verbal cognition of the indeterminate—which has as its object a property and a property-possessor unfit for mutual connection, being produced by words denoting the indeterminate—is sublated by those words that produce the valid cognition of the absence of verbal means of knowledge (*śabdapramāṇakatva*)—namely, by the words "the indeterminate is not [known] through verbal testimony"—and is thus recognized as an error. For the awareness of being an error is indeed what constitutes sublation (*bādha*). [This applies to the phrase] "the locus and its specific... and so forth.

The meaning is: [it is established] by way of the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*), by way of the property that is the counter-correlate (*pratipakṣa*) of the negandum which is unique to that locus, and by way of its nature (*dharma*). Since the opponent also accepts Brahman—the referent of the term "without distinctions" (*nirviśeṣa*)—as the locus characterized by the absence of distinctions, the word "locus" (*adhikaraṇa*) here has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary sense. The property that is the counter-correlate of the negandum and is unique to that [Brahman] is the "property that is the counter-correlate of the negandum unique to it. Otherwise, due to the definition of a locus, there would be no syntactic connection at all for the negating word.

The meaning is that, in the absence of a ground for the application of the word "nirviśeṣa" (devoid of distinctions)—namely, the state of being the locus of the non-existence of distinctions—the word "nirviśeṣa" would be entirely meaningless. He states another objection: "na hi nirvibhaktikaḥ" (for it is not without case-endings). The implication is that there would consequently be an application of number, which is the meaning of a case-ending. Regarding the phrase "padāntarānanvitaḥ" (not connected with other words): the implication is that if one says, "There exists a reality devoid of distinctions," there would necessarily be a connection with "reality-ness" (vastutva) and "existence" (astitva). [He then mentions] "abhidhānam anyapadārthasya" (the denotation of the meaning of another word).

The sense is that, according to the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) "anekam anyapadārthe," the denotation of a meaning distinct from the individual forms [of the constituent words] is unavoidable. This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); for since a *bahuvrīhi* compound is prescribed in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), it should also be understood that the denotation of a specific relation consisting of possession is unavoidable. And regarding the employment of a *tatpuruṣa* compound: the sense is that by the compound "nirgato viśeṣāt" (excluded from the particular), because of the rule "nir-ādayaḥ krāntādyarthe pañcamyā" (prefixes such as *nir-* form compounds with a word in the fifth case in the sense of 'gone beyond' etc.), the state of being the locus of the action of exiting (*nirgamana*) must necessarily be cognized.
[End of] the examination of non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*) [cognition].

Regarding the phrase "of the object experienced by non-conceptual [cognition]": the meaning is that because non-conceptual cognition must be defined as the cause for the synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of the object being experienced by conceptual cognition, and because it is thus to be accomplished by conceptual cognition, conceptual cognition was defined first. It should also be understood that the presence of conceptual cognition—which was mentioned later—in the mind is conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*). The phrase "the nature of conceptual cognition has been shown" implies that although it was mentioned later, it is treated as if it were earlier.

Immediately after the passage "tri-kona-iti," there is the reading "yadvā anupapannam vyudasyati tri-kona-iti," which is easy to understand. The connection with the ablative case [in *anupapannāt*] is with the phrase "because it is impossible to grasp [the meaning] through the sentence that raises the doubt [by means of] superimposition (*adhyāhṛta-śaṅkā-vākyena*)."

Thus [the meaning is as follows]: the sense is that this [statement] serves to reject the doubt expressed in the sentence "the apprehension of that which is devoid of all particulars must be postulated. Since it is impossible to apprehend any object whatsoever, the apprehension of something devoid of all particulars cannot be postulated; this is the intended meaning, with the word *kalpyam* (to be postulated) connected to the ellipsized *na* (not). He demonstrates that very connection with the words "the observed pervasion," etc. The phrase "of the first and second individuals" means "of the two apprehensions of the first and second individuals."

Regarding the phrase "in the perception or non-perception of the persistence of cowness": even when the earth is perceived by the eye, its odor is not perceived, because odor is not an object suitable for the eye; however, that is not the case here—this is the intended meaning. He refutes [the objection] by stating that it does not exist because it is not established as separate [from the configuration]. The meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) passage, "because there is no cognition of the possessor of the configuration without the configuration," is simply that the possessor of the configuration does not exist without the configuration. The intention is that the mention of the absence of cognition is for the purpose of establishing that [non-existence].

The meaning intended by the term *saṃsthānarūpa* (the form of configuration) is as follows: the sense is that inseparable existence (*apṛthaksiddhatva*) itself is what is intended by the word *saṃsthāna*. Alternatively, the construction is: "it is explained by the word 'thus' (*ittham*)," because the apprehension [of the two] is possible through the relationship of the mode (*prakāra*) and the bearer of the mode (*prakārī*). The phrase "of the mere universal and the individual" (*jātivyaktimātrayoḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding the statement "the universal and so forth, as well as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*)," there is one position that here only the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is grasped, not the qualified object. [However, the correct view is that] just like the qualifier, the qualified object is indeed grasped as well.

Another [opponent] says that it is merely the specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) that is not apprehended. But surely, this is because the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) possesses a counter-correlate (*sapratiyogika*). When a person qualified by a staff is known, the status of being a qualifier with respect to the person has its counter-correlate in the staff, appearing in the staff; and the status of being the qualified with respect to the staff has its counter-correlate in the person, appearing in the person. Therefore, since the relation of qualifier and qualified—which constitutes the object of the cognition of the qualified—possesses a counter-correlate, the cognition of that [relation] must be required beforehand. This is the sense.

Nor should it be argued that the proponent of non-conceptual perception (nirvikalpaka-vādin) intends for the cognition of the qualifier alone to be the cause, and not the cognition of the qualified object; for this is not a fault, as it represents a different position. The meaning is that even for that [proponent], the nature [of the universal] is its own qualified object; thus, the specific character of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth as being qualified by the definition of being a qualifier is not apprehended at first, such that one would have to admit a primary cognition of the qualified object.

The meaning is that "the state of being a qualifier does not [occur] first" refers to the absence of the qualification by the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva-vaiśiṣṭya*). If it is argued that "it is merely the essential nature (*svarūpa-mātra*)," the sense is that the individual (*vyakti*), the universal (*jāti*), and their respective states of being qualifiers are apprehended as mutually unqualified. The implication is that even with that much, a reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualified is possible. Regarding the phrase "of the qualifier and its own nature": a reversal would follow at the stage of the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭa-pratīti*) for the qualifier and its own nature which were previously apprehended as not being mutually connected.

Therefore, the implication is that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) here even for that [second property], because it too would require another property to manifest itself. If [it is argued] that this is to avoid the consequence of the cognition of the qualified (*vaiśiṣṭya-pratīti*) occurring first due to the inversion [of the qualifier and the qualified]: since the very nature of the universal (*jāti*) and so forth constitutes their status as qualifiers, by the very nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*), no possibility of inversion arises. Because there is no other property [to serve as a further qualifier], the possibility of a cognition of the qualified does not arise first, nor is there an infinite regress; such is the meaning. [The opponent suggests] that it might occur both as a qualifier and as a qualified.

Nor should it be argued that even though the nature of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*)—which is identical to its own essential form (*svarūpa*)—is apprehended beforehand, there is no contingency of it being cognized as a qualifier because the "qualifiedness of being a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatā-vaiśiṣṭya*) does not appear [in indeterminate perception]. This is because the point here is that since that qualifiedness is also of the nature of the essential form, its manifestation is necessarily required. [Furthermore,] the condition (*upādhi*) would be "having as its object a thing cognizable by a distinct causal complex. Now, in the view of those who maintain the existence of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), the causal complex for a determinate cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) consists of the cognition of the qualifier.

"But in the case of the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), it is not so," [the opponent argues], because the limiting condition (*upādhi*)—namely, "being cognizable by a distinct causal complex" (*bhinnasāmagrīvedyatva*)—has been refuted; this is based on such an assumption. Regarding the phrase "because of the establishment of being excluded from the subject" (*pakṣavyavacchedyatvasiddheḥ*): that by which there is the establishment of being excluded from the subject is "the establishment of being excluded from the subject"; the meaning is "of that which excludes the subject alone. Alternatively, the meaning is "because of the establishment of the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) from the subject. The intention is that, as in the case of "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) when raised by a sublation (*bādhonnīta*), a limiting condition can only exist when there is a favorable logical reasoning (*anukūlatarka*).

Regarding the acceptance of [the property] as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) on the strength of reasoning, he provides two examples beginning with "just as in the case of non-existence through destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). This is the sense: just as in the case of the limiting adjunct consisting of contact with wet fuel—which is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) and possesses the quality of having a beginning (*ādimattva*), and which pervades the probandum as delimited by the probans—both specific qualifiers, namely "being a positive entity" (*bhāvatva*) and "having a beginning" (*āditva*), are included within the category of limiting adjuncts due to the force of favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*), even though they are not required for the pervasion of the probandum; so too it is in the case of "being cognizable by a different set of causal conditions" (*bhinnasāmagrīvedyatva*).

It should also be observed that the term "distinct" (*bhinnā*) can function as a qualifier of the *upādhi*, even if it is not useful for establishing its pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*). "In all cases where there is fire" means: even in a place devoid of wet fuel.

If it is argued: "Since the property of being a qualified cognition produced [by causes] (janyaviśiṣṭajñānatva) is an *avacchedaka* of effectness (*kāryatā*)—because it resides in all effects in the absence of a subverting argument—it must be stated that there is a uniform causal efficiency toward that which is delimited by it; thus, once the causality of the cognition of the qualifier is established, the cognition of the qualifier that serves as the cause for non-conceptual cognitions such as those at the onset of waking will itself be established as being non-conceptual"—we say: no. For the property of being a qualified cognition is simply the property of being a cognition whose object is the relation between the qualifier and the qualificand.

And this [appearance] is accounted for by the very causal complex that brings about the manifestation of the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation; it is not, however, a delimited effect (kāryatāvacchedaka), because it arises through the force of the objects themselves, like the case of "blue jar-ness. Objection: One must necessarily admit that in the cognition of a qualified object, the cognition of the qualifier is a cause; otherwise, since the sense-organ contact with both the universal and the individual is identical, the established order—well-known to all—that sometimes a cognition arises having the universal as the qualifier and the individual as the qualified, and sometimes the reverse, would be undermined.

If it is argued that once the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is accepted as a cause, the rule—that a qualified cognition arises having that [qualifier] as its qualifier—is easily stated, we say no. For in a case where there is an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) whose object is both [the qualifier and the qualified], since there is no distinction between the two in terms of being previously cognized, and because there is nothing whatsoever to determine the status of qualifier and qualified, the resulting lack of determination would remain exactly as it was before. And if it is claimed that in that case an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) serves as the determinant—

Let that alone be the determinant in all cases; what is the use of accepting the causality of the cognition of the qualifier? Is it not established that the cognition produced by the proximity of "cowness" (gotva) has "cowness" as its qualifier (prakāra), and not the individual (vyakti) as its qualifier?

If it is argued that if the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) were not the cause of the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), then a cognition produced by the "universal as a means of proximity" (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) might sometimes have a particular qualifier that was not previously apprehended—since there would be no rule that the qualifier must be one already previously apprehended—[we reply]: No; for there is simply no such thing as a cognition produced by the universal as a means of proximity that has all individuals as its object. Therefore, since the cognition of the qualified is accounted for solely by the causal complex consisting of the manifestation of the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*), the state of being a cognition of a qualifier cannot be the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).

[Response: Water. For if the two forms of cognition—non-conceptual and conceptual—were as epistemically valid as the pair consisting of inference and non-inference, then, since a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) would arise from the general causal complex (*sāmānyasāmagrī*) alone, one might fear that every cognition would become a qualified cognition. To avoid this, one would have to postulate a specific causal complex (*viśeṣasāmagrī*). But that is not the case, because the non-conceptual is not established even at the outset; for every cognition is indeed conceptual. Indeed, every act of awareness is of the form "this is thus."

Otherwise, cognition would be objectless, just like a cognition devoid of any specific mode (niṣprakāraka); likewise, even desire would be objectless and beyond the senses, and the same would apply to aversion and so forth—enough of this excessive deliberation. Having all this in mind, he concludes: "Therefore, non-conceptual [cognition] is precisely that which has the nature described above, while conceptual [cognition] occurs during the apprehension of an individual object (*piṇḍagrahaṇa*) as being a second instance and so on."

The intended meaning is this: it is impossible to establish that initial and subsequent cognitions—which lack the apprehension of persistence—are devoid of conceptual construction (savikalpaka), because the very apprehension of something as "initial" or "subsequent" necessarily involves the apprehension of persistence.
This concludes the refutation of the doctrine of both difference and non-difference (bhedābheda-vāda).

In this context, it is argued that the two cognitions—the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) and the cognition of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—are the proofs for both difference and non-difference. Now, one might object: since co-referentiality is not observed in cases of absolute difference or absolute identity, let co-referentiality be the proof for difference-and-non-difference; however, how can the rule of simultaneous apprehension be a proof for difference-and-non-difference? For the rule of simultaneous apprehension does not consist in being the object of a single cognition, since that is observed even in the case of identity.

Nor can there be the status of being the object of two simultaneous cognitions, because that is absent in the case of a universal and an individual; nor is there a rule regarding the simultaneity of two sets of causal conditions for cognition, since the set of conditions is also one due to the unity of the cognition itself.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of a collective cognition (samūhālambana) of a jar and a cloth, although there is unity of apprehension, a duality of causal complexes (sāmagrī) is observed; for in that case, a distinction between causal complexes can indeed be established—namely, that the contact of the sense organ with the jar is the causal complex for the cognition of the jar, while the contact of the sense organ with the cloth is the causal complex for the cognition of the cloth—but here such a distinction does not exist. Furthermore, the contact of the sense organ with the universal (jāti) is not the causal complex for the cognition of the universal.

It cannot be argued that there is a distinction between the causal complex for the cognition of an individual and the contact between the sense organ and the individual; for neither difference nor non-difference is established by direct perception (*adhyakṣasiddhi*). Furthermore, if difference were established, the rule of simultaneous apprehension—which depends upon that difference—could not serve as a proof for difference, but rather would only prove non-difference.

Furthermore, even if a cognition permeated by a single word—such as "this is one like that before"—establishes the identity between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), how can the non-apprehension of difference in the first individual establish non-difference? For it is not the case that everything unapprehended at first is non-existent; nor is there any logical principle that things are non-existent simply because they are not perceived during a state of non-perception of particulars. To this, it is replied: the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) is precisely the fact of being an object of a single apprehension, and that indeed establishes identity.

By means of that [non-difference], it establishes both difference and non-difference, because many subsequent statements consistent with that are found later on. Now, an objection might be raised: "In this way, since the apprehension of the first individual (*piṇḍa*) permeated by a single word and the apprehension of non-difference could also establish both difference and non-difference through the medium of non-difference, it would be improper to state separately that those two establish non-difference; for it would be more logical to unify all three. To this we reply: True, regarding the aspect of establishing both difference and non-difference through the medium of non-difference...

These three also constitute a single group. However, since those two [reasons] possess the nature of being combined with a corroborative argument (*abhyuccaya-yukti*), they are placed together in one group. For this very reason, there is no opportunity for a refutation regarding their object, because they are merely corroborative. "Terminating in itself" (*svaparyavasita*) means "resting in itself" (*svaniṣṭha*); that is to say, it is devoid of the nature of dependence on another.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is not an 'uncommon' (*asādhāraṇa*) reason for proving both difference and non-difference? For, since there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) possessing both difference and non-difference, the status of being uncommon—which consists in its exclusion from such instances—does not apply. Precisely for this reason, [the author] states, "Furthermore, it is indeed contradictory," out of dissatisfaction with the argument that there is no un-commonality because there is no similar instance possessing the thirteen differences from water and so forth when proving the difference of earth from others. He then says: "The rule of simultaneous apprehension is a prover of duality."

The meaning is that there is a rule (*niyama*) regarding simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*), which establishes duality. Regarding the *Bhāṣya* statement, "In both cases, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) is the same," [the author] explains it as being intended to dispel a specific doubt, fearing that it might appear to have little purpose since there is no disagreement regarding the relationship of qualifier and qualified in both instances. He does so with the passage beginning, "If this were so, [then] genus (*jāti*), earrings (*kuṇḍala*), etc. He explains the word "same" (*samāna*) found in the *Bhāṣya* as meaning "because of agreement between both parties" (*ubhaya-sampratipatteḥ*).

Thus, because the description of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) was cumbersome, he explains it otherwise: "Or rather, [it refers to] those things existing in separate spatial arrangements. This is for the sake of establishing the rule that "the necessity of simultaneous perception does not apply elsewhere. The meaning is that there is a rule of non-separability (*apṛthaksiddhatva*) which is the cause of simultaneous perception. Therefore, one should not raise the objection: "Since non-separability has already been established as the basis for the determination of simultaneous perception, how can this doubt arise?"

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*); having accepted this, [the author] explains it as being intended to exclude other possibilities, saying "these alone. Since the restrictive sense of the word "but" is not its primary meaning, he explains it otherwise, saying "or rather, because there is the possibility of a relationship between qualifier and qualified. "The absence of a cloth in a jar": the remainder [of the sentence] is "by way of the relation of identity" (*tādātmya-sambandhena*). Or else, the meaning is that "the absence of a cloth" is the "absence of cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*). "Difference" (*bheda*): the meaning is "difference from a cloth.
This is the refutation of the claim that inference and other means of knowledge have only the indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*) as their object.

It appears that in the *Bhāṣya*, by stating "that very object is without distinctions through the specific natures of the things contained within it," one is asserting that when an object—which is the domain of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and possesses distinctions—is extracted as being without distinctions by means of its specific natures, there results both a failure to establish its lack of distinction and a contradiction with one's own words. However, this is incorrect, because it constitutes a criticism of what was not stated [by the opponent].

Fearing that others might claim the extraction [of the essence] has been stated regarding the object of their own experience, he says "the means of valid cognition," etc., to show that by this very statement a refutation of the extraction of the object of one's own experience is being expressed. "They are sublated by reasoning" (tarka-parāhata). Therefore, the remainder of the sense is: "the non-differentiated [reality] is established by one's own experience free from contradiction. Anticipating the objection that mere recollection serves little purpose, he explains it otherwise: "or rather, previously established by one's own experience. This concludes the refutation of the perception that grasps only pure existence (*sanmātra*) and the dismissal of the arguments against difference (*bheda*).

It is not only the case that [the objection] is "with qualification" (*saviśeṣa*). Although, when it is said, "Even what was stated has been refuted," it would be more appropriate to state a conjunction with a different point already previously refuted by the opponent, rather than a conjunction between the demonstration that [the opponent's view] has a qualified object and the impossibility of demonstrating that [our own view] has an unqualified object; nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated in such a way because it is seen in other contexts, such as "What is desired is established, and what is undesired is refuted. This refers to the phrase "and the impossibility of demonstrating that [it] has an unqualified object."

Since perception that grasps only pure existence has been cast far aside, the impossibility of establishing that [perception] has an object devoid of qualifiers is established; thus, there is a conjunction based on this established impossibility. This is why he says: "Not only has the difference in objects been established. [This applies] even when there is a delay caused by the recollection of the counter-positive.
