Regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that a positive perception (*sadgrāhipratyakṣa*), which lasts for only a single moment, lacks the capacity for the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) that delineates difference (*bhedollekha*) while depending on the recollection of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogismaraṇa*): even under the view that difference is an entity distinct [from its substratum], since difference is difficult to deny, one must abandon the rule that perception lasts for only a single moment; rather, for the sake of delineating difference, its persistence over multiple moments must be postulated through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*).

The intention is as follows: if the status of being a "differentiator" (bhedatva) for genus (*jāti*) and so forth were easily established even without such a postulation of a defiled [entity], then what need is there to say that the reasoning put forward by the opponent has been refuted? Regarding the first *ca* (and): one might argue that since the quality of self-establishment (svaparanirvāhakatva)—which is referred to by the word *ataḥ*—serves as an independent cause in avoiding infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and other faults, there is no other item to be conjoined (*samuccetavya*) to be conveyed by the *ca* associated with the word *ataḥ*; therefore, like in the phrase "na ca," the *ca* is merely a rhetorical ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*). To this we reply: no.

By relying on the word "and" (*ca*) as having a displaced position [in the sentence], there is no fault because it is accepted that there is neither infinite regress (*anavasthā*) nor mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*), which are other defects. Regarding the phrase "when the avoidance of infinite regress is established": although this doubt does not arise for one who asserts that self-establishment and establishment of others are proven out of fear of infinite regress—just as in the case of consciousness and form (*rūpa*) and so forth—it should nevertheless be understood that this [objection] proceeds by disregarding such a view. [The opponent claims: "It deserves to be rejected when its cause is examined."

The sense is that the effect, which has been apprehended even if not clearly, does not deserve to be denied for fear that it would lead to the undesirable consequence of having to investigate its cause. "The cognition of the sublated nature of the phenomenal world" means the cognition whose object is the distinction consisting in the state of being sublated. He rejects the fifth position with the words, "nor [is there] the state of having a sublated object. "That being so" means that if every distinction were sublated, then since the distinction consisting in the world's state of being sublated would itself be sublated, the reality of the world would necessarily follow.

"In the determination of one's own scripture, [the distinction] is true" means: if the scriptural meaning characterized by the distinction consisting of sublation were true, then because the reasoning regarding the difficulty of defining distinction would not apply, other distinctions that are authoritative would likewise have to be true by virtue of the same logic. Alternatively, if the falsity of the distinction—which is the subject matter of one's own scripture—were untrue, it would follow that its opposite, truth, would emerge. Some, however, hold that only when the determination of the subject matter of one's own scripture is true will the conclusions reached in the world be true.

They say that if this [worldly consensus] were false, why would the truth of the world's determination not be [false]? [The opponent replies: "Because it depends on the very nature of words, it does not constitute a refutation of the [ultimate] meaning."

Just as a single object, though independent when expressed by its own word, becomes dependent when expressed by words such as "cookedness" or "lightness," or just as in your own view—where you maintain that the non-difference of knowledge, bliss, and so forth constitutes the nature of Brahman—the very nature of Brahman, though independent when expressed by the word "Brahman," becomes dependent when expressed by the word "non-difference," so too here let it be that the jar, though independent when expressed by the word "jar," becomes dependent when expressed by the word "difference."

The sense is that for a single act of going, there is the observation of the verbal expressions "goes" (*gacchati*) and "moves" (*calati*), and for effort, there is the observation of the verbal expressions "does" (*karoti*) and "exerts effort" (*prayatate*). This is because it is seen that the dependence or independence upon an object (*karman*) is determined by the very nature of the words themselves. "The entity such as a buffalo which delimits that" means the delimiter of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

The meaning is that the word "cow" (*go*) indicates the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) by means of the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), which is the cause of the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) having buffaloes and other such things as its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*). "The distinction due to an incidental attribute" (*taṭasthopādhibheda*) means the distinction due to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the pot. "The optional use or non-use" (*vaicchyau prayogāprayogau*) means that even when cowness is known by way of other objects such as buffaloes, the use or non-use [of the word "cow"] remains optional.

However, it should not be thought that [the cognition of difference arises] from the mere cognition of "cowness" (gotva), for it must be understood that such [mere cognition] cannot account for the linguistic usage of difference. Regarding the phrase "exclusion resulting from the connection with that": the meaning is that it is because there is a cognition of exclusion which is brought about by the connection with another property whose nature is difference. Regarding the phrase "equally applicable even in the case of non-difference": [it refers to the following verse: "The terrifying specter of difference—whether it be the essential nature (svarūpa) or a property (dharma)—is but a specter of difference arising from the mere attachment to the letter 'a' (i.e., the negative particle)."

The intended meaning is that this is because of such a statement. Furthermore, there would be synonymy between the words "brahman," "advitīya" (without a second), and so forth. The underlying sense is that since the word "second" (*dvitīya*) refers to difference (*bheda*), the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) has the meaning of non-difference (*abheda*).

The meaning is that the consequence of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) arises precisely through the state of being known (*jñātatā*). Nor can it be argued that because a mere cognition grasps only pure existence (*sanmātra*), reflective awareness is possible even through the state of being unknown (*ajñātatā*); furthermore, it should not be said that while the production of the state of being known is indeed desired regarding the aspect of pure existence, it is impossible regarding other aspects because they lack the state of being known—this is because the intent is directed toward the previously mentioned refutation. The word *samaveta* (inherent) refers to that which has the nature of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); the sense is that in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and illusion (*māyā*) are not accepted.

"By way of possessing such-and-such a configuration" means by way of possessing a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*). "By way of being qualified by time" implies that time is perceptible by all the sense organs. However, in the case of determinate perception (*savikalpaka*), there is the qualification of many factors such as place and so forth. Although, according to the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), even in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) place and the rest do indeed function as qualifiers, the intent here is that they do not appear in indeterminate perception because they lack the quality of persistence (*anuvṛttatva*). Some also maintain that this was stated with the intention that, in the case of smell, there is initially no apprehension of place.

The demonstration that *jāti* (universal) consists of configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is explained in two ways, based on the conclusion reached in the *Bhāṣya*—which negates anything other than configuration that is cognized by a single uniform cognition—as follows: either because configuration itself is what is cognized by a single uniform cognition, or because anything other than that which is cognized by a single uniform cognition lacks any basis in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). With this in mind, he explains it in both ways starting with the words "this [cow] possessing dewlaps, etc. The phrase "by another name" refers even to the proponents of the theory of transcendence (*atirekavāda*).

The sense is that the intention [of the Bhāṣya] is that it is not logical for there to be an identity of genus admitted by one of two parties when the configuration is admitted by both. However, some explain that even in the theory of "excess" (*atireka-vāda*), since the matter can be established by what is admitted by both parties, nothing additional should be postulated; this is clearly perceived as the natural meaning of the Bhāṣya. Others maintain that configuration (*saṃsthāna*) has been accepted by opponents as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) of the whole (*avayavin*). Although this [argument] concerns only a specific type of substance;

The sense is that even if [the universal] were not omnipresent, by that same method, its denial could be established elsewhere as well; thus, there would be the total abolition of universals (*jāti*) alone. The meaning is that such abolition would not occur, because even in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), a universal in the form of a configuration (*ākṛti*) is admitted in certain cases. "Common to both universal and non-universal" means common to specific conjunctions of parts, whiteness, and so forth.

Regarding the question, “Why [is it asked] ‘what is the word *sva*’ in the phrase ‘its own unique [property]’? and so forth: although the word *sva* here denotes that which is under discussion, such that whatever is a unique property (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*) of something is its configuration (*saṃsthāna*), as in the rule “the unique property is the definition” (*asādhāraṇa-dharmo lakṣaṇam*), where the word *saṃsthāna* is indeed synonymous with the word *lakṣaṇa* according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), and thus there is no room for doubt; nevertheless, this elaboration should be understood as intended to clarify the understanding of the student.

"Because there is an absence of a single ground for the application of the word [‘cow’]"—this is the point. Nor should it be argued: "Why might there not be some word that denotes a fragmentary cow (*khaṇḍa-yau*), just as there are words such as *gṛṣṭi*, *dhenu*, *vaśā*, and *avaṣkayaṇī*? The sense is that this is not the case, because such a word is not perceived. Then what [is the relationship] between the universal (*jāti*), the form (*rūpa*), and the configuration (*saṃsthāna*)?

How is there a distinction between specific configurations (saṃsthāna) consisting of particular conjunctions of parts and configurations such as whiteness and the like? Since both are indistinguishable in their nature as configurations (*saṃsthānatva*), the word *utpala*, which denotes a genus (*jāti*), possesses primacy, whereas the word *nīla* and others, which denote qualities (*guṇa*), possess the status of a quality. Consequently, words such as *nīla* function solely as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). For this very reason, according to the rule "a qualifier is frequently compounded with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam*), the compound is formed as *nīlotpalam*.

The intention of the objection is: "But how could there be a determination such as 'the blue lotus'? [This is asked] assuming that what is intended here is the definition of a genus (*jāti*), form (*rūpa*), and configuration (*saṃsthāna*).

Now, one might object: "Since the general definition of configuration (*saṃsthāna*) has been established by the principle that 'whatever is the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of a thing is its configuration,' and since this constitutes a universal (*jāti*), then the fact of being a unique property will itself be the definition of configuration in the form of a universal; so what is the point of this further inquiry? Furthermore, even regarding configurations such as whiteness and the like, it is necessary to intend that all instances are highly similar to the specific form under discussion, because even whiteness and so forth [are defined] by their specific form.

For it must necessarily be stated that the property of having a commonality consists in the individuals being highly similar. Genuses such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) in the form of configuration (saṃsthāna) are distinct in each individual; likewise, qualities such as whiteness (śauklya) in the form of configuration are also distinct in each individual. If it is asked, "What is the distinction [between this and] unification through extreme similarity (sausādṛśya), which is common to both genus and non-genus?"—it is due to a lack of understanding.

The meaning is this: having abandoned the previously stated position—that the commentary's statement, "configuration (saṃsthāna) is a form (rūpa) unique to itself," is intended to define the nature of configuration as common to both genus (jāti) and non-genus (ajāti)—it is now explained that the definition being given pertains exclusively to configuration in the form of a genus.

If it is asked, "In this interpretation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), what is the seed of dissatisfaction? it is said in reply: In the *Bhāṣya* passage, "Perception is indeed qualified by distinctions characterized by genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which consist of the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of things," if one intends the word *saṃsthāna* to mean configuration as an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), then for the Naiyāyikas and others as well, the fact that genus is an uncommon property is already established. Consequently, the attempt to prove that "genus is nothing but configuration" would be redundant, because configuration is already accepted by both parties.

Furthermore, it is not tenable [to claim] that the uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is admitted by both parties in the Bhāṣya. Therefore, it is established that the previously mentioned words "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) refer to a specific kind of conjunction of parts. Consequently, for the sake of consistency with those, it is appropriate to state this [current term] in the same way; thus, the meaning is that the interpretation of the Bhāṣya—"What is called configuration?"—is intended to refer solely to configuration as the form of the class-character (*ākṛti*). Hence, one should understand that there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the view that configuration is a specific property consisting of the form of the class-character.

"It is not possible [to establish sequence] either spatially or temporally. The meaning is that the sequence (*ānupūrvya*) of the phoneme *au*—characterized either by being in a location immediately following the location of the phoneme *ga*, or by occurring at a time immediately subsequent to the time of the phoneme *ga*—is not possible, because phonemes are eternal and all-pervading (*vibhu*). "Because it is based on articulation" means that the sequence of the phoneme *au* consists precisely in its being the object of an articulation that occurs immediately after the articulation of the phoneme *ga*. [The phrase] "the difficulty regarding the alternatives concerning the substratum (*vṛtti-vikalpa*), etc. refers to the aforementioned problems.

If similarity were to exist by way of a single part, then because it would lack the status of being the locus where similarity is fully resident (*paryāptyadhikaraṇa*), the term "similar" (*sādṛśaḥ*) could not be applied to that which is not the locus where similarity is fully resident—just as the word "two" is not applied to a single thing that is not the locus where duality is fully resident. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the entity] having parts. If, on the other hand, it were to exist in its entirety, then similarity would not reside in both [the object and the standard of comparison]. Thus, the meaning is that there is no room for these objections; rather, the usage would simply be "similar to a cow" (*gavā susadṛśaḥ*).

The particle *eva* has the sense of "and" (*ca*). Thus, the meaning is that there would be the usage "and so forth. Regarding "the word 'cow'": the meaning is that the usage "the word 'cow'" itself would not occur. Alternatively, since the convention for the word "cow" is grasped only with respect to a specific individual, the meaning is that there would be the usage "something similar to that. And this was stated with the intention that, at the stage of learning [the language], there is no apprehension such as, "That which has such a form is a cow."

Anticipating the objection that "in the absence of a recurring property (*anugata-dharma*), the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) between fire and smoke would not occur by way of a general property (*sāmānya-dharma*)," he says: "And the apprehension of pervasion... The sense is that it is possible to include all [individuals] within a single conceptualization through their extreme similarity, characterized by their common configuration (*saṃsthāna*). [This refers to] "only the group of forms that are opposed to the configuration already perceived."

The point is this: although silver-ness is indeed contradictory to the whiteness perceived in the mother-of-pearl, nevertheless, because that contradiction does not manifest itself, there occurs an error (bhrama). For whiteness is the unique property (*asādhāraṇa*) of what is white. Consequently, from the perception of whiteness—which consists in the exclusion of non-whiteness—only the superimposition of non-whiteness is removed; however, the superimposition of silver-ness is not removed, because the silver-ness, which is the exclusion of non-silver, has not been grasped. This is the sense. [This concludes] the justification of the fact that the establishment [of the object] consists in its differentiation.

"Previously, with reference to the counter-correlate (*pratiyogyapekṣayā*). The sense is that this is based on the passage from the *Bhāṣya*: "It is precisely of the universal (*jāti*) and so forth that there is dependence upon a counter-correlate. Although it was not explicitly stated in the passage "It is precisely of the universal and so forth that there is dependence upon a counter-correlate" that the linguistic usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) requires the recollection of a counter-correlate, rather than merely stating that the universal and so forth possess their own and others' differences; nevertheless, the intention is that this meaning is also intended there. [The questioner asks: "In that case, what is meant by 'linguistic usage of difference'?"

Although it was previously stated that "the linguistic usage of difference depends upon a counter-correlate," nevertheless, since difference would be untenable if universals such as *gotva* (cowness) were themselves devoid of counter-correlates, this very point will be challenged by the following passage from the Bhāṣya; such is the intention of the sentence.

One might object: “How can it be said that [the definition applies] to ‘the cognition and linguistic usage of all things, both those of its own class and others’? For since other animals such as buffaloes cannot possibly belong to the same class [as cows], the expression ‘others who are of the same class’ is impossible. Anticipating this doubt, he says: “Immediately following the specified universal” (*nirdiṣṭasāmānyānantara*). The specified universal is the universal of cowness (*gotva*); the universal immediately following it is a higher universal that directly pervades it, such as animality (*paśutva*) and so forth. In the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*), the mention of “those of the same class” (*sajātīya*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of those of a different class (*vijātīya*) and the like.

It should be understood that the term "homogeneous" (*sajātīya*) was included with the intention of showing that, once the capacity to remove confusion regarding homogeneous objects has been stated, the capacity to remove confusion regarding heterogeneous objects (*vijātīya*) is established by implication (*arthāt*). Regarding the phrase "absence of being self-sufficient" (*paranirvāhakatvābhāva*): although the *Bhāṣya* states, "Indeed, 'cowness' and so forth are themselves the exclusion from everything else," and thus intends merely to establish that the exclusion of jars and other things resides within cowness and the like; [the present argument goes further].

However, it is not the case that the capacity to sustain another (*paranirvāhakatva*) follows from the capacity to sustain itself (*svanirvāhakatva*), because the capacity to sustain itself is impossible in the absence of the capacity to sustain another; this is the extent of the argument. Furthermore, in accordance with the inference that "it is a different object due to its own relation," one should have demonstrated that the capacity to sustain another is impossible in the absence of the capacity to sustain itself. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the statement was made in that manner with the intention of expressing that very extent [of the argument]. Therefore, [the text says] "of the properties" (*dharmāṇām*).

But surely even a property such as color (*rūpa*) does not oppose error in every respect, since we observe there too errors such as the non-difference of the quality from the qualified substrate; for even today we see the persistence of different views based upon that [color], and because it has been stated by yourself that "there is an error regarding the non-distinction of the cloth-substance from its color," and because a substratum also excludes itself from other properties, and because even a jar excludes itself from its own locus such as the ground, and because even consciousness excludes itself from cognitions of other objects—how then can this [distinction]...?

If it is argued that there is a fixed rule (vyavasthā), we say no; for even though other distinguishing properties exist among dharmas such as color and so forth, there is no undesirable consequence [in our position], and if they are established by valid means of knowledge, there is no fault in accepting an infinite number of entities. Therefore, it should be understood that what was stated was simply the possibility of difference (*bhedatva-sambhava*), and not that "only that [specific thing] possesses the possibility of being a difference."

"Of the very nature of the properties (*dharma*)," etc. The meaning is this: the very nature of a property is itself the difference (*bheda*) of its own substratum—the jar—with respect to another substratum that possesses a different property contradictory to it. Thus, with respect to a qualifier, the very nature of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is itself the difference.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the earlier text which states: "The difference belonging to the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*), which is opposed to error with respect to its own inherent properties, is the connection with another property. For the phrase "the nature of the qualificand" means "the unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of the qualificand," and thus it results in the meaning that the difference from a qualifier such as color (*rūpa*) is simply another qualifier such as touch (*sparśa*). To the question, "Of what, or what indeed, is the unique term? he says: "And that term is established through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*)."

The meaning is that it is established by worldly convention (*loka-vyutpatti*) that "this specific word denotes this particular object. Alternatively, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is that which is opposed to the cognition of identity with any other object intended as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). In this latter view, one should note the underlying unease (*asvarasa*): since the essential nature of the reality (Brahman) is not opposed [to anything], it would fail to possess such an essential nature.
[This concludes] the refutation of the inference for falsity (*mithyātva-anumāna-bhaṅga*).

"Because another entity serves as a limiting adjunct (upādhi)" means that since other places and times exist as limiting adjuncts, there is sublation (*bādhitatva*) even in those cases with respect to the perceived adjunct; this is the intended meaning. In the phrase "in errors where subverting cognition has not arisen," the two locative case endings are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning is: "in errors produced in persons for whom subverting cognition has not arisen. Therefore, the term *anutpanna* is not used [instead of *anuditabādhaka*]. "By the cognition of the person who challenges" means: by the cognition of that person who is the challenger.

The intended meaning is that the cognition of error itself constitutes the nature of sublation (*bādha*). Regarding the phrase "the establishment of the qualifier and the qualified": the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the condition (*upādhi*) as it has been apprehended; the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is the state of being sublated. Regarding the phrase "by way of introducing a succession of unestablished properties": this refers to cases such as the argument that if there were an origination of origination, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), whereas if there were no origination, origination would be eternal—because in those cases, one introduces the concept of the "origination of origination," which is absolutely impossible. However, in the present case, the "falsity of falsity" (*mithyātvamithyātva*) is not at all unestablished.

The meaning is that this is because the *brāhmaṇa* has accepted the falsity of falsity (*mithyātva-mithyātva*). This is an illustration [of the fallacy]: "Since it is impossible to conceive of a property (*dharma*) as being either identical to or different from its substrate (*dharmin*), the negation of the substrate's being qualified by that [property] constitutes the *nityasama* (the 'equivalence to the eternal')."

Such is its definition. Furthermore, it is not here stated that if falsity (*mithyātva*) were real, there would be a destruction of the substrate’s (*dharmin*) possession of that falsity; rather, what is asserted is the loss of non-duality (*advaita-hāni*). On the contrary, because your own statement—asking whether difference resides in something different or non-different—serves only to negate anything characterized by "different" and so forth, it constitutes a *jāti* (a futile rejoinder) due to self-contradiction.

For it has been said: "Relying on this very [notion of] birth, the throat-rumbling clamor of the Buddhists, Cārvākas, and Vedāntins—who argue with dry logic—is the cause of delusion for the ignorant. Regarding the phrase "even when the mallet has perished": one should not say that even a perished mallet possesses ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva) like a jar; for if ultimate reality were absent, that [jar] would not serve as an example.

Just as when the destroyer is destroyed, that which was to be destroyed does not re-emerge, so too, even when the reason proving the falsity of the sublater of the reality of phenomenal appearance (*prapañca*) is itself sublated, there is no re-emergence of that which was sublated; it is on account of this similarity that it serves as an illustration. "Even though the sublating cognition is false" means: even though the reason—such as "being an object of perception"—which is the object of the sublating cognition, is sublated. This should be understood because the present inquiry concerns precisely whether the means of proof (*sādhana*) is ultimate or non-ultimate. "Because of the difference between the producer (*kāraka*) and the indicator (*jñāpaka*)."

[Objection: "But surely, if the destroyer is also sublated, then the destruction itself must be unreal. For the reality of the destruction does not follow from the unreality of the mallet. Therefore, the two cases are indeed equal. [Response: No; for the meaning of my statement—that when the sublater is sublated, the reality of the sublated would follow—is that it is observed that when the destruction of the cause of destruction occurs, there is no destruction of the effect, namely the destruction itself. Thus, your argument is utterly inconsistent. This is the intended sense [of the verse]: "even in the case of the sublation of the error regarding the bee on the stalk."

The meaning is as follows: a certain female bee, having developed the delusion that a *palāśa* flower was a male bee, was dissuaded from it by the thought that it was merely a *palāśa* stalk; and in such a case of delusion—where the delusion regarding the male bee in the stalk was removed by the perception of specific details—it is said: "Because it is seen to be sublated by the reality of the stalk. As he will state: "The female bee, through her delusion of a male bee, embraced the *palāśa* stalk, which she mistook for a male bee. This is because [the delusion] is shown to be sublatable by the ultimate reality of the stalk.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that [the reason] "because it is sublated by the palāśa-flower" applies as well. Therefore, regarding "in your view": the sublation of the delusion concerning the ultimate reality of the bee consists precisely in its being characterized by the prevention of the arising of another cognition that contradicts it. And likewise, in the case of the world (*prapañca*), the sublation of the delusion concerning the ultimate reality of the probandum and the probans—namely, "visibility" and "falsity"—must be stated as being characterized by the prevention of the arising of another cognition that [affirms] the reality of the world.

Furthermore, since even that delusion would require another means of cessation—namely, knowledge of the ultimate reality of some property—there would merely be a succession of delusions; the result would be that there could be no cessation of ignorance in its entirety. This is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "In this case, as in instances such as the delusion regarding a forest fire, it is quite sufficient to say that if the delusion regarding the *prakṛti* were to remove the delusion [of the Self], there would be no cessation of ignorance in its entirety; why such great effort? This is true, but there is no fault, as it is for the purpose of instructing on the true nature of each respective category.

"Successive [moments] are of the nature of error"—the sense is that this is because the properties of the means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*) are not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*). Regarding "destruction by itself": if it is argued that even if destruction occurs through another cognition (*jñānāntara*), its status as conceptual (*kālpakatva*) is established—just as in the case of the destruction of a jar or other objects—and thus the fault remains that there would be no cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) without remainder, some reply that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Others, however, maintain that since a resolution has been somehow provided by relying on the view that the cessation of ignorance produced by knowledge is the very nature of Brahman (the *brahmasvarūpa*)—that is, a fifth category—and since others accept that destruction produced apart from knowledge consists in its dissolution back into its own cause, it follows that the ignorance which serves as the cause must indeed persist; such is their intention. Nevertheless, [the author says] "of pure Being" (*sanmātrasya*).

This is an illustrative instance (*upalakṣaṇa*); for it is possible to perceive even the sky through the eye by prioritizing the superimposed blueness, and since its possession of color is possible through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), its visibility is established, and thus its being known by a single means of knowledge is proven. This is the intended meaning. [Thus,] the logical reason consisting of the rule of perceptibility (*dṛśyatva-niyama*) is refuted.

"Is it not the case that here there is a rule regarding being an object of perception?"—the meaning is that "being an object of perception" is defined as the necessity of depending upon a consciousness distinct from itself for its own empirical usage. "Because of the absence of difference between existence and experience"—the meaning is that since [existence] is non-different from self-luminous experience, its self-luminosity must be asserted. "Because the rule of being an object of perception is not established by way of self-luminosity."

If the falsity of difference is established by the very reason of "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*), then the validity of the reason of "being an object of perception" depends upon the falsity of the difference between existence (*sat*) and consciousness (*anubhūti*), because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Brahman, which is of the nature of existence; and if that validity exists, then the falsity of difference follows—this is the meaning of the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). "By another means of cognition" means by such [reasons] as "insentience" (*jaḍatva*) or "limitedness" (*paricchinnatva*). "In that case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established" refers to the reason of "being an object of perception. "The nature of being solely an object of perception" [is the intended meaning].

The meaning is that it is devoid of self-luminosity. Regarding the phrase "and being ultimate realities": the intention is that if permanence and so forth were not ultimate realities, then impermanence and so forth would necessarily follow as a consequence.
This concludes the refutation of the reason based on their exclusion [from the locus].

This is because it is accepted as being excluded from falsehood and the like. Now, one might object: "Even if you accept that exclusion from falsehood consists in being distinct from falsehood, you have still not accepted that there is an 'exclusion' (vyāvartamānatva) which is the opposite of 'persistence' (anuvartamānatva). We reply: No; for when there is exclusion in the form of being distinct (*vilakṣaṇatva*), its counterpart—exclusion in the form of non-persistence (*ananuvṛttatva*)—is also established. Therefore, it performs its own function.

The meaning is that it is an obstacle to inference by way of producing the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). "Like the property of being an experience" (*anubhūtitvavat*): the point is that the property of being an experience, which is not distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*), serves as the prover for the probandum, which is self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). "And the word 'non-ultimate' (*aparamārtha*)": here some maintain that the word *aparamārtha* refers to the word *brāhma* by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Consequently, they argue that in the statement, "The exclusion of insentience (*jaḍavyāvṛttatva*) from Brahman is not ultimately real," the word "Brahman" is redundant, because the mere fact of being excluded [from insentience] is itself not ultimately real. For this very reason, they say that the natural sense of the subsequent passage, "even in the case of a jar and so forth," is also preserved.

Others, however, explain the underlying point as follows: by stating "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthatas*), no solution is provided at all; for since the other [instance of] exclusion is also of that same nature, it is impossible to employ "exclusion in the ultimate sense" as a logical reason (*hetu*), because the distinction [between them] is unestablished. Thus, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). [Objection: But surely the reason is not unestablished, since it is "exclusion belonging to that which is not ultimately real" (*aparamārthabhūta-vyāvartamānatva*) that has been made the reason. The establishment of "exclusion belonging to that which is not ultimately real" occurs precisely when "mere exclusion" (*vyāvartamānatvamātra*) is absent therein.

If it is argued that otherwise there would simply be the exclusion from the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), we say no; for if that were the case, being excluded from the non-ultimate would mean being devoid of exclusion (*vyāvṛttiśūnyatva*). Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) would be the very state of being devoid of exclusion, rather than exclusion itself—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "only of that which is sublated in the locus where it is apprehended": here the construction is that the exclusion of only that which is sublated in the locus where it is apprehended (*pratipannopādhau bādhitasyaiva*) establishes falsity (*mithyātva*), in accordance with the subsequent text: "but not merely the state of not being grasped."

He states another alternative here: "the specific exclusion (vyāvṛtiviśeṣa) denoted by the word 'exclusion' [is what is meant]. The sense is that the construction should be understood as follows: "only for that which has been sublated is a specific exclusion possible, which establishes its falsity. Regarding the phrase "cognition of negation" (niṣedhadhībodha): sublation (bādha) is the cognition of the erroneous nature of the prior cognition, produced by the cognition of negation. "The nature of being a negation is the state of being a sublater": this means that a cognition which apprehends the absence of the object of the prior cognition is the sublater. Regarding the phrase "by not following all similar instances" (sarvasapakṣānanuyāyitvena): [this refers to the reason being a unique property].

Nor should it be argued that, because the nature of falsity defined as being the counter-correlate of negation (*pratiyogitva*) is absent in the locus of the qualification (*upādhi*), these [examples] cannot be considered "similar instances" (*sapakṣa*). This is because they do possess "falsity" in the sense of being removable by knowledge; thus, it is possible to maintain that they are similar instances. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the identity between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the qualification (*upādhi*). The phrase "the delimiting factor of the qualification" means the substratum (*āśraya*); the intention is that one should not mistakenly think it refers to the definition of a qualification as "pervading the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpaka*) and so forth. Regarding the statement "in the case of an error concerning space and time, another object is the qualification": this refers to an error concerning space.

If it is argued that there is no mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) because time and so forth are superimposed upon another object for the sake of worldly transaction—just as illusory silver is superimposed upon a piece of mother-of-pearl—and that the superimposition of silver on the piece of mother-of-pearl does not depend on a prior superimposition of the piece of mother-of-pearl elsewhere, and thus no suspicion of mutual dependence arises; nor is the rebuttal regarding "the difference between individual instances of error" tenable, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence of infinite regress and the obstruction of the production [of cognition]—then we say: not so.

The phrase "due to the difference between the manifestations of error" means that because there is a distinction between the manifestation as an appearance (*prātibhāsika*) and the manifestation as empirical reality (*vyāvahārika*), the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the appearance upon the empirical reality is possible; this is because, according to his intention, there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*) or infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Regarding the expression "delimited by that which serves as its delimitor": one should not argue that it is sufficient to say that the falsity (*mithyātva*) of an object is established simply by its non-existence at the place where it was perceived. This is because the qualification "delimited by a particular space and time" is necessary to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases such as non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*).

"Of that which is delimited by another action. This is the meaning: here there is no superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of time itself, such that there might be a doubt regarding the presence or absence of another limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Rather, it is the superimposition of the connection with the solar activity characterized as "evening-ness" upon time. Nor is that which is perceived as evening-ness incapable of being the substrate for the error of evening-ness, because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Nor should it be argued that [the evening time] is not perceived as being "daytime" because of their contradiction; for when a time is perceived as being connected with an action such as milking cows (*godohana*), which is distinct from both [daytime and nighttime], the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of "evening-ness" upon it is possible. Thus, a restriction (*niyama*) is established. The meaning is that a restriction is made when both existence and non-existence are applicable. The connection with another attribute in the form of "existence," as apprehended by the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), is what is sublated;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of conceptual oscillation (*vikalpa*) even in cases such as "the jar is blue" or "the cloth is white. This concludes the refutation of the argument based on persistence (*anuvartamānatva*).

Regarding the first [position], it was stated that the defect is *siddhasādhanatva* (proving what is already established). Here, some [in the prima facie argument] have proposed that "pure being (*sanmātra*), which is observed persisting through all cognitions, is the ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*)," thereby suggesting that the ultimate reality consists in the persistence of the universal of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) denoted by the term "pure being. In that case, establishing the ultimate reality of the universal of existence on the grounds of its persistence is nothing but *siddhasādhanatva*.

The clear meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is understood to be that establishing the non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthya*) of qualifiers by means of their being excluded [from the ultimate] is undesirable. It is not appropriate to introduce the text there by way of an alternative view (*vikalpa*). For if that were the case, even according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the word "Being" (*sat*) would be accepted as denoting only that entity which is fit for connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the objection and its resolution—"Is it not the author's intention that this 'Being' alone is the ultimate reality?"—are explained according to the intended meaning.

The state of persisting (*anuvartamānatva*) establishes ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*); the state of receding (*vyāvartamānatva*) establishes the non-ultimate nature of others. Since it has been stated that by these two reasons, ultimate reality belongs only to the universal whose form is existence (*sattā*), denoted as "pure being" (*sanmātra*), and not to others, [the following applies]: first, because the ultimate reality of existence (*sattā*) as intended by the opponent is established even in our own system through the reason of persisting, there is either the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) or the objection based on its being already established; or else, there is the resolution of this by means of an alternative position (*vikalpamukhena*).

They think [the objection] is "because it does not apply," but this is without substance. For the doubt might arise that even that which is designated by the word *sat* (Being), which is accepted by the opponent as persisting as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is also established by the Siddhāntin to be ultimately real; therefore, the text must be introduced precisely by means of an alternative analysis (*vikalpa*) in order to dispel such a suspicion. Nor should it be argued that there is no consistency with the subsequent commentary, which states, "Therefore, the entity is not merely Being alone" (*na sanmātrameva vastu*), because in the phrase "not merely Being alone," the ellipsis "capable of being proven" (*sādhanārham*) must be supplied.

This is because the intention is that since the ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*) of an object capable of being related to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is already established, it cannot be further proven. As for the claim that the objection and its resolution—"Now, the author's intention is indeed that only the existent (*sat*) is the ultimate reality"—are displayed out of place, that is not so; for in the statement "the author's intention is indeed that only the existent is the ultimate reality," the word "described" (*varṇita*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Furthermore, if it were argued that existence (*sattā*) is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) because it persists, then there would be the suspicion of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For it is only this much—that "the existent alone is the ultimate reality because it persists"—that is to be proven; thus, since the objection that this is not a case of proving the already established is possible, [the opponent argues: "it is unestablished due to a difference in locus" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*). The meaning is that if one says, "everything other than experience is not the ultimate reality because experience persists," the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished because it does not reside in the subject (*pakṣa*).

"In the third part, [it is stated that] there is the proof of what is already established": the meaning is that it has been stated that the ultimate (paramārtha) and the non-ultimate (aparamārtha) are distinct from the reality that is of the nature of experience (anubhūti), because they are recurring (anuvartamāna).

He establishes the very non-establishment of the substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*) with the words: "of that which is denoted by the word 'existent'. Regarding the phrase "it is established like the word 'excluded'": otherwise, because of the uniform usage [in expressions] such as "the jar is excluded" and "the cloth is excluded," one would have to admit a distinct, recurring entity denoted by the word "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), which serves as the substratum for all superimpositions. Similarly, due to the uniform usage [in expressions] such as "a sky-flower is non-existent" and "a man's horn is non-existent," one would have to postulate a recurring "non-existence" (*asat*) upon which the excluded man's horn and so forth depend. This is the intended meaning.

"In the absence of that, it is the inference stated by the opponent"—the meaning is that what is stated by the opponent is the proof for the impossibility of being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*). "Because of the impossibility of grasping the relationship between word and meaning"—the sense is that, having inferred the elder's cognition of the task to be accomplished through his activity of bringing the cow, one grasps the word's power (*śakti*) with respect to that [cognition]. "For the purpose of excluding past experience"—the meaning is for the purpose of removing the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of that definition to past experience.

The meaning is that this is for the purpose of excluding that [objection]: since in the past state the manifestation (*prakāśa*) is not present, the presentness of manifestation denoted by the suffix *-śānac* is absent; consequently, it would follow that manifestation through mere existence (*sattā*) is impossible there. As for the phrase "even though [there is] past experience": the sense is that in the case of past experience, because its own existence (*svasattā*) is indeed absent, the quality of having an existence that is non-deviant from manifestation (*prakāśāvyabhicāri-svasattākatva*) certainly exists.

Since, in the past state, there is simply an absence of that very nature characterized by a particular condition, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the definition. Nevertheless, it was stated "in the present state" for the purpose of explaining a specific meaning. Here is the logical connection (*anvaya*): because manifestation is impossible without another cognition, the absence of the definition in the experience of the past—which has already been established—is effectively excluded by the word "by its existence" (*sattayā*) itself; therefore, the phrase "in the present state" is redundant.

The phrase "not so" (*neti*) means that [the author] demonstrates that [the property of] being non-opposed to ignorance—which pervades the probandum characterized as "non-experience"—is not a valid *upādhi* (limiting condition), by showing its pervasion of the probans through the contingency of its presence in the subject (*pakṣa*). The phrase "of the non-experience-ness [which would result] if experience were an object of experience" means: of the non-experience-ness that is being contingently attributed (*āpādya*) to experience if it were an object of experience. Regarding the word "samīpasthaiḥ": the sense is that the meaning "by those standing nearby" is obtained due to the influence of the prefix *upa*.
This concludes the refutation of [the arguments concerning] the non-arising of consciousness (*saṃvit*) and so forth.

"At that time" is a qualification of the absence (*abhāva*). The meaning is: "the absence at that [specific] time. This is because there is no contradiction in apprehending an absence belonging to a different time; for if one were to say, "Experience [perceives] only that which exists at its own time," the subsequent commentary would result in the negation of something that was never even raised as a possibility. The sense is that the proposition "no" must be supplied; that is, the proposition should be formulated in accordance with the aforementioned alternative views.

The meaning is this: the thesis is either that the restriction of experience to grasping what exists at its own time is not caused by the nature of the object to be grasped (*grāhya*), or that it is not caused by the very nature of the experience itself as a grasper (*grāhin*). He raises an objection in order to refute the position that it depends on the specific nature of the object to be grasped, beginning with "Now, if it is thought... This is an elliptical indication; it should be understood that the second position—that it is due to the nature of the absence of the object to be grasped and the experience—must also be considered. [The opponent argues: "It must necessarily be preceded by perception. For one such as you would not speak in this manner if there were no perception.

Therefore, the meaning is that by saying "you speak only after having seen," he takes "seeing" as an established fact and then challenges [the opponent] as to where that seeing occurred. He states that "by the word *pratyakṣa* (perception), perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*) is meant," because the word *pratyakṣa* is common to both the object and the cognition. Furthermore, this is obtainable through its association with the phrase "born of the sense organs. Alternatively, it is stated that "perceptual cognition is meant" in order to exclude the objects of perception characterized by the activities of the organs of action, such as walking and so forth.

"How is there a difference between valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa-jñāna*)? This is the point: even if one does not accept the rule that all cognitions apprehend only what exists at their own time, one must nevertheless accept the rule that valid cognitions apprehend only what exists at their own time; otherwise, the distinction between the valid and the non-valid would not be possible. For the distinction between the valid and the non-valid is established by the presence or absence of the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the object of cognition (*prameya*).

If a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were to arise even in the absence of an object of cognition (*prameya*), how could there be an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between them? Therefore, one must accept the rule that [the cognition] exists at the same time as [its object]. Consequently, it should be understood that [valid cognition] must be defined as grasping an object that exists at the same time as itself. The phrase "of mere cognition" (*jñānamātrasya*) means "of mere valid cognitive cognition" (*pramāṇajñānamātrasya*); this is because the restriction is suspected only in that case. The phrase "because they do not grasp objects existing at a different time due to the non-attainment of a present object" is to be understood accordingly.

In this context, there is a compound with the negative particle (*nañ*) in the word "grāhi" (grasping) which refers to that which exists at the same time [as the cognition]. Since an object existing at the present moment cannot be grasped, it is impossible to grasp an object existing at the same time; furthermore, you yourself have admitted that what does not exist at the same time lacks the status of being an object. Therefore, the meaning is: since these [cognitions] are devoid of objects, and because the object of knowledge (*prameya*) itself is absent, how could there be an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the object of knowledge? This is stated in response to the inquiry, "How is that established?"

The meaning is this: even if there is a perception occurring at a different time, how could the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of these [perceptions] existing at another time with an object of cognition (*prameya*) existing at a different time be established? The phrase "the connection of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the object" implies a grammatical coordination (*anvaya*). The coordination is that the invariable concomitance is not a connection with an object existing at the same time as itself. Thus, falsity becomes the opposite of the means of valid cognition.

The meaning is that the very state of being the opposite of the falsity of the object of cognition (*prameya-mithyātva-pratyanīkatva*), as residing in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-gata*), is the relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the object of cognition. Since the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) refers to the previously mentioned absence of a rule regarding simultaneous existence for things separated [in time], it would be more logical to refer—as the reason—to the observation of the grasping of things existing at different times among those things accepted as means of valid cognition, which was just mentioned; however, because of the lack of such a natural flow [of interpretation], he says, "Or rather, the meaning is thus."

In the former position (*pakṣa*), the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with its object (*prameya*) is the subverter of the apprehension of the whole; in our position, however, there is the refutation of its being a prover—this is the distinction. Some hold that from the means of knowledge known as analogy (*upamāna*), which consists in the similarity of a cow to a *gavaya*, there arises analogical cognition (*upamiti*) in the form of the realization of the similarity between the cow and the *gavaya*. Others maintain that from the cognition of the individual object qualified by similarity to the cow, there arises analogical cognition in the form of the valid knowledge of the relationship between a name and the named, expressed as: "This individual object is denotable by the word 'gavaya'. He restates both these views with the words beginning "The [object] cognized by analogy," and so forth.

Fearing that there is a redundancy because the words *cet* and *yadi* have the same meaning, he says: "The word *yadi*... [and] "the word *ca* has the sense of *yadi*. This means that the word *cet* has the sense of *ced*. For this very reason, he will later say, "If it were so" (*tathā cet*). Intending to supply the word *tathā*, he says: "The meaning is 'if it were so' (*tathā cet*). [He then states: "The perception of another state consisting of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*)."

Just as the non-existence of a jar is another state in the form of a positive entity, such as the state of being a lump of clay (*piṇḍatva*), so too the non-apprehension of the cognition of a jar consists in the abandonment of the state of apprehending the cognition of a jar, and is thus itself the apprehension of another positive entity, such as a cloth. In some cases, there is even a contraction [of consciousness]. For this very reason, he will later state: "The contraction of cognition, or its transition to another state. Consequently, that which is a positive state consisting in the apprehension of another state is the apprehension of another object.

The meaning is that this very [non-perception] is the non-perception of the cognition of the jar and so forth. On this point, some say: "The non-perception of a cognition that is [otherwise] perceptible consists in the perception of another state of being of a positive nature; for indeed, the perception of its [material] mass and so forth is precisely the non-perception of the jar as a perceptible object."

Upon examining the text—specifically the passages, "In that way, later on, the absence of knowledge delimited by past time is either a contraction of knowledge or the knowledge of another object," and "The absence of the knowledge of an elephant delimited by past time is either a contraction of knowledge or the knowledge of another object," as well as the passage, "The non-apprehension of the two [the elephant and its knowledge] delimited by past time"—it follows that the apprehension of the absence of a jar is itself the non-apprehension of the jar.

They object: "The non-apprehension of the cognition of an elephant is understood as the very apprehension of the absence of the cognition of an elephant; yet this is not tenable, because the apprehension of the absence of a jar and the non-existence of the apprehension of a jar are distinct. Furthermore, if the apprehension of the absence of a jar were itself the non-existence of the apprehension of a jar, then the statement that 'the absence of a jar is inferred by means of the mark (liṅga) which is the non-apprehension of the jar' would be contradicted. For it cannot be said that an absence is inferred by the apprehension of an absence. This [objection] is not valid.

Since, according to the stated method, the apprehension of non-existence does not consist in the non-apprehension of that [object], the intent [of the text] is precisely this: "Non-apprehension is either a contraction of cognition or another state.

Anticipating the objection that the word "furthermore" (*kiṃca*) is inappropriate because there is no single subject matter—given that the preceding passage is devoted to establishing prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) while the subsequent passage is devoted to establishing impermanence (*anityatva*)—[the author] proceeds with the subsequent passage...

Intending that even the preceding text has as its purport the impermanence [of cognition], he says: "Of cognition, in its self-manifestation... Then, [he says]: "...by way of defining the manifestation of the object. This means: by way of defining the occasional nature of the manifestation of the object. Therefore, there is no lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*). The intended meaning is this: in the sentence, "And its non-apprehension is due to the apprehension of consciousness as limited by time," the non-apprehension of consciousness is understood as the probandum (*sādhya*).

The fact that cognition is delimited by time is perceived as the reason [for its non-existence]; because it is delimited by time, it does not exist at another time, and thus "non-cognition" means the absence of cognition. The meaning is that this results in a lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśeṣa*). Furthermore, this is also an illustration of the lack of logical connection (*ananvaya*) in the argument that "there is no cognition of that [object] for the cognition [itself]. Nor should it be said that the word "of the cognition" (*saṃvedanasya*) connects with the phrase "by being delimited by time," because the phrase "by being delimited by time," having already connected with the word "of cognition" (*pratīteḥ*), is already syntactically complete and lacks further expectancy.

Therefore, the meaning is that the non-apprehension of this cognition—that is, its lack of conformity with the linguistic usage regarding the existence of jars and so forth—is due to the fact that [the object of] apprehension is delimited by time; such is the intended sense. However, some explain that in the phrase "due to the apprehension being delimited by time," the word "apprehension" (*pratīteḥ*) is not intended [to refer to the object]; rather, the meaning is simply "because the cognition itself is delimited by time. They further argue that in this way, there is no identity between the reason and the probandum (*sādhyāviśeṣa*), since it would not follow that "there is no non-apprehension of that [object]. Thus he states another *arthāpatti* (presumption).

Is it not established that perceptual cognition has the nature of making its own object known as existing at the same time as the cognition itself? For in the perception of a jar, no doubt is observed at that time as to whether "the jar exists now" or "it does not."

Furthermore, if perception itself were to appear as existing at all times, it would necessarily cause its own object to appear as existing at all times as well. However, since there is no appearance of eternality—defined as being unconditioned by time—in its object, such as a jar, there is likewise no cognition of knowledge itself as being eternal, defined by its lack of temporal limitation. On the contrary, knowledge is cognized precisely as non-eternal, characterized by its being conditioned by time.

And it should not be argued that "if there were indeed the manifestation of eternality in cognition, then by the same principle, the same would follow for the object as well; for perception is possible simply through an indifference toward whether [the object] is eternal or non-eternal," because this can be connected as part of a single coherent argument by stating: "in self-luminous cognition, since the property of eternality is absent, the manifestation of the property in the form of eternality must necessarily occur. This is true, yet the reasoning [proposed] is not sound.

When it is argued that if knowledge were eternal, its object would likewise be so, [we reply] that this is not the case with the direct perception of God; therefore, what remains to be stated is merely that [knowledge] possesses an occasional suitability for its own empirical usage. For this very reason, he will say later: "The two [limits] are mentioned as being auxiliary. Precisely because it is not self-luminous due to having two limits—prior and posterior—the non-manifestation of its impermanence makes it equally easy to state the non-manifestation of its permanence, which consists in the absence of those two limits.

Even in the view that eternity is characterized by being unconditioned by time (*kālāparicchinnatva*), since the limitation by time is not self-luminous (*asvayaṃprakāśa*), the manifestation of eternity—defined as the absence of such limitation—is not possible. Due to this underlying difficulty, he says: "Or else, there would be the consequence of [eternity] applying to jars and so forth. This means that the definition of eternity must be something common [to all things]. The point is that the definition of eternity as "being connected with all times" cannot apply to time itself. [The phrase] "because inference and so forth are objects of perceptual knowledge" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The cognition "this is now past" takes as its object the state of being past—defined as being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in the time that serves as its own locus—in the case of a past entity. Even in the instance of the verbal usage "this is now past," it is precisely this state of being past, defined as being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in the time that serves as the locus for the use of the word "now," that appears. Consequently, if cognition were eternal, every moment of time would be a locus-time for that cognition; thus, the distinction between the past and the future would be untenable.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be the impossibility of the manifestation of pastness and so forth in the knowledge of God; for it should be observed that even in that case, the manifestation of pastness is to be justified by taking into account the difference in cognitions based on the difference in objects. In fact, however, they say that the point of the objection is that if inference and the like were eternal, they would be nothing but perception because they would be unproduced cognitions; and consequently, their objects as well would have to be eternal.
[The non-manifestation of consciousness devoid of an object.]

The meaning is that non-experience and lack of practice are well known as causes for mere non-recollection; that is, they are well known as the causes for the rule of non-recollection. By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "non-experience and lack of practice," death, the torments of hell, and so forth are included. The meaning is that these are what are grasped by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the expression "the departure of the body and so forth, which cause the suppression of all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). [The verse continues: "Cognition directed toward something else, the absence of sharpness in the intellect, intense suffering and the like, insanity, lack of practice, and long duration [of time]."
And in the case of those obstacles to the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), one must postulate an unseen deficiency (*adṛṣṭavaiguṇya*).
Since death does not occur when these [obstacles] are absent, the absence of knowledge is inferred.

Thus, [the following] is established: therefore, it is the word "restriction" (*niyama*). Since it has been stated that there is an absence of the departure of the body and so forth—which serve as the causes for the restriction of non-recollection—it would be more appropriate to say "due to the restriction of non-recollection" (*asmaraṇa-niyamāt*) and not simply "due to non-recollection" (*asmaraṇāt*). If, however, one were to state the absence of distractions and so forth which serve as the causes for the restriction of non-recollection, then it would be proper to say "due to non-recollection. The meaning is that because of the mention of the absence of the departure of the body and so forth—which serve as the causes for the restriction of non-recollection—it is more appropriate to say "due to the restriction of non-recollection."

Alternatively, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "non-repetition of experience and so forth," distraction toward other objects is expressed. Consequently, these [factors] are merely causes for non-remembrance. Therefore, even in the absence of the disappearance of the cause, the birth of a god, or the afflictions of hell—which are the causes for the rule of non-remembrance—non-remembrance of what was experienced is possible due to the force of causes such as distraction toward other objects. Thus, the word "rule" (*niyama*) is used for the purpose of excluding that [possibility]. This refers to the phrase "in the absence of the stated obstructors."

Where there is an experience free from the obstacles consisting of the forms that cause verbal denial, there is recollection; thus, recollection is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of unobstructed experience. Consequently, when the absence of unobstructed experience is to be proven by the absence of its pervader—namely, recollection—the absence of the qualified [experience] is established within that which possesses the qualifier, since the qualifier itself (the absence of obstacles such as the departure of the body) is already established.

The sense is that [the argument] culminates by taking the absence of the experience of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) as its basis. However, one should not be deluded into thinking that the aforementioned non-experience is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the recollection mentioned; for such a pervasion is impossible. Regarding the term "conjunction" (*anuṣaṅga*): the meaning is that the word *anubhavābhāva*, which originally appears in the nominative case, is transformed into the genitive case and conjoined [with the preceding phrase], so that it is not merely from the rule of non-recollection that the absence of experience is established.

He dispels the misconception that the word *ahaṃkāra* refers to the *ahaṃkāra-tattva* produced from the *mahat-tattva* by stating, "the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃpratyaya*). That which has the notion of "I" is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). For this very reason, he will later state: "Even for the knower and the known, their being the cause of memory must be accepted, even against one's will. It should be understood that this does not refer to the knower as the object of a cognition or to the known object itself. To the objection that if the referent of "I" persists, there would be the consequence of its being manifest [even when not perceived], he says: "it shines forth" (*prakāśate*).

And here the word "ca" (and) must be supplied; [the phrase] "it persists and it shines" follows. Therefore, the meaning is that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). However, "it shines" is not an explanation of "it does not persist," because there is no inconsistency with the literal sense [of the original statement].

"Taking that as the object with the intention of refuting it"—the meaning is that he objects by taking the mere word "experience" (*anubhava*) as his point of reference. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "consciousness alone is the experience of the self," the interpretation of *ātmanubhave* as a locative case (meaning "in the experience of the self") in a non-co-referential construction is strained; therefore, he explains it otherwise, stating that the meaning of the passage beginning with "consciousness alone" is as follows: "that consciousness which consists in the manifestation of the substratum (*dharmin*)."

If it is objected that, since manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*), this contradicts the subsequent passage which establishes that manifestation is an attribute of consciousness in the form of being conducive to empirical usage (*vyavahārānuguṇya*), we reply: no. It should be understood here that the application of the word "consciousness" to "manifestation" is possible through the metaphorical treatment of the attribute and the substrate as non-different. Regarding the phrase "conducive to empirical usage": the implication is that, consequently, its having a substratum (*sāśrayatva*) is established.

If it is objected that, for one who maintains that consciousness is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*), it is improper to prove its qualified nature by means of the manifestation of a property of consciousness—namely, "appearing-ness," which is synonymous with "conformity to empirical usage"—we reply: no. For when one asserts that consciousness, in the form of our own manifestation (*sphuraṇa*), is without distinction, they must first admit that the manifestation distinct from the consciousness that is the very nature of the Self is itself without distinction; only then can such a statement be logically established, since the non-difference between the manifesting manifestation and the manifesting Self would otherwise be impossible.

For it has not been stated that consciousness is non-distinct from the nature of the Self by another [means]; rather, it has been stated that it consists precisely in the manifestation of the Self. Therefore, it should be understood that it is appropriate to establish that the manifestation of the Self is a specific state of consciousness (*saṃviśeṣa*). Regarding the phrase "by the mark of the non-remembrance of what ought to be remembered": this expresses the state of being an object of exceptional attention (*ādārātiśaya-viṣayatva*). By this, there is an exclusion of things such as grass. The words "and by that which is arising" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Consequently, the meaning is that at that time, one's own absence is also apprehended through the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form of the experience "I was conscious of nothing," which is produced by the mark of the non-remembrance of what ought to be remembered.

"That is indeed a refutation of the formulation" means the following: since the opponent has asserted that [consciousness] is eternal because it is unproduced (*anutpanna*) in its state of being experienced, to abandon that and instead prove [eternality] by means of "being unproduced while qualified by existence" (*bhāvatva-viśiṣṭānutpannatva*) constitutes the fallacy of "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*), which occurs when one adopts a different reason (*hetvantara*). Such a refutation is a "refutation of the formulation" (*uktidūṣaṇa*). However, a case of "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*) is a "refutation of the matter" (*arthadūṣaṇa*). Therefore, the sense is that only the latter is worthy of being pointed out as a demonstration of skill in logic (*tarkakuśalatā*). This is because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) for this qualification.

By speaking in this way, it is effectively stated that what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is the state of being an ultimate transformation. Consequently, because there is no locus for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—given the absence of an ultimate transformation as the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the absence of origination as the nature of the probans (*sādhana*)—the property to be pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) is unestablished; such is the meaning. This will be made clear later.
[This concludes] the refutation of the non-differentiation from experience.

"Because of the uselessness of the qualification regarding its ultimate unreality. This means that in the phrase "ultimately devoid of differentiation because of being unproduced," the qualification "ultimately" (paramārtha) serves, according to the previously stated method, to establish the non-establishment of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). However, one should not think this refers to the qualification "illusory" (*mithyābhūta*), for that is not a qualification [in this context]. The meaning is that by the same logic, the difference in philosophical systems (*darśanabheda*) is also established.

If it is argued: "Surely, by establishing the difference in the objects seen, the difference in the acts of seeing is also established—just as the difference in cutting follows from the difference in what is to be cut. Since it is perceived that a difference in the object (*karman*) is the cause for a difference in the action (*kriyā*), why abandon that and provide an explanation based on 'equal logic'? This is true; however, because even when there is a difference in the objects seen within a single collective cognition (*samūhālambana*), there is no difference in the act of seeing, that [former argument] lacks logical consistency. As for the example "just as the difference in cutting follows from the difference in what is to be cut," [it is not applicable here].

It should be understood that this interpretation was provided in order to avoid other doubts and because it possesses the nature of being a logical argument (*yukti*). The phrase "even conjunction and so forth" means "merely by virtue of having a distinction manifested by the related term (*saṃbandhin*). For the related term is twofold; the meaning is "the related term that manifests the distinction," since it is that which is under discussion. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being irrelevant to the subject at hand.

The object (*vastu*) whose distinctions are manifested through relation is also twofold: that whose existence and sequence depend on the related term, and that which is not so. The sense is that in the former case there is indeed an intrinsic distinction, whereas in the latter it is adventitious (*aupādhika*).

The meaning is that even when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent, there is merely the lack of necessity characterized by the non-exclusion of the probans (*sādhana*); this is simply the lack of necessity characterized by the presence [of the probans] where the probandum is absent. It does not, however, have the characteristic of occurring in all three positions [the subject, the similar instance, and the dissimilar instance]. Since there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) in negative inference (*vyatirekī-anumāna*), it is appropriate to explain "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*) as "unrestricted" (*aniyata*). This is not, however, according to the acceptance of others. Now, [one might object]: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and eternity—these are the attributes."

If it is argued that because these [attributes] appear as distinct even though they are not separate [from Brahman], the opponent has thereby accepted that eternality and other such qualities—which are positive in nature—are indeed the very essence of Brahman; we say no. The point is that in that case, eternality and so forth can be understood as having the nature of being unconditioned by time and the like. He states the meaning of the term *prakāśa* (manifestation) as it applies to both [cases]: "in both cases" means in the case of consciousness (*cit*) and the non-conscious (*acit*). The point is that because of the similarity in usage—as in "knowledge manifests" (*jñānaṃ prakāśate*) and "the jar manifests" (*ghaṭaḥ prakāśate*)—the term is common to both.

"Being possessed of a cognition included within the causal complex for its own empirical usage (*svavyavahāra-sāmagrī*). This means "being the object of a cognition conducive to its own empirical usage. Nor is there a lack of uniformity (*anugama*) in this view; for uniformity is possible through the criterion of being either non-cognizable by cognition or other than that [non-cognizable]. It is precisely because of this lack of elegance that he says, "Or rather, they say thus.
