In all cases, the word "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) has as its uniform meaning simply the state of being the counter-correlative (*prati-sambandhin*) to empirical usage. That [counter-correlativity] is twofold: in some cases, due to being the object of cognition, and in others, due to identity with it—this is the sense. Here, the term "entity" (*padārtha*) refers to both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*).

The *Bhāṣya* states that "conformity to empirical usage (*vyavahārānuguṇyam*) is common [to both]. Having explained this as conformity to its own empirical usage residing in all categories of reality, both conscious and unconscious, [the author] explains—by the words "or else, the light residing in knowledge"—that the conformity to empirical usage regarding all objects, conscious and unconscious, resides only in consciousness, since it is the meaning of the term "light" (*prakāśa*). [He further explains] that it consists in being the cause of empirical usage; that is to say, it consists in being the cause of empirical usage. Being the object of empirical usage (*vyavahartavyatva*) is common to both.

The sense is that being the cause of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is unique to cognition. Regarding the phrase "being the selfhood and favorability": the meaning is with respect to one's own linguistic usage as qualified by selfhood, favorability, and unity.

And it is well known that eternity consists in being without a cause while existing; the meaning is "being without a cause provided that it exists. It should be understood that the qualification "provided that it exists" is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which does not exist [in the sense of being eternal]. If it were [merely] "it exists," there would be a partiality toward the subject (*pakṣapāta*); the meaning is that from this [definition], partiality toward the subject would arise. If it is a cognition (*pratīti*), it must be stated to belong to someone and to have an object; such is the meaning.

If it is argued: "Is there not some underlying intention when one says, 'If [the action of] accomplishment (*siddhi*) is in accordance with the *Bhāṣya*, then it must be said that 'accomplishment is with respect to someone' (*kasyacit prati*), rather than saying 'if it is cognition' (*pratītiśced')"? To this, it is replied: Because accomplishment is inherently transitive (*sakarmaka*), the statement "if it is accomplishment, it would be with respect to someone" is untenable. Furthermore, if it were said, "If it is accomplishment, it is with respect to someone," then one would have to say, "The accomplishment of the jar is with respect to Devadatta. Indeed, it is appropriate to say, "The jar will be accomplished with respect to Devadatta."

But Devadatta is not established *in relation to* the jar. Consequently, there would arise a contradiction with the subsequent commentary which states: "Because for some person, some collection of objects exists in the form of being established. Therefore, it should be understood that the term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is employed here as a synonym for mere cognition (*pratīti*), and thus the word "cognition" is used with an object (*sakarmaka*) in order to demonstrate this point.

If it is objected: "Since it is easy to state in the Bhāṣya that consciousness (*saṃvit*) belongs to someone with respect to something, the phrase *sidhyati cet* (if it is established) serves as a means (*praṇāḍī*) to support the status of cognition as an establishment; we see no reason for [the author] to offer a refutation by prioritizing this," we reply: No, because there is no fault, as it is merely a difference in phrasing. The objection raises a challenge regarding the rejection of the dependence on a knower mentioned by the words "to someone" (*kasyacit*). The meaning is that it raises a challenge regarding the rejection of the dependence on the counter-correlative of the "establishment" (*siddhi*) specified by the word "whose" (*kasya*).

In accordance with the subsequent text, he says "with reference to the self" (*ātmānaṃ prati*) with the intention of using the dative case *ātmane*. Although, when the expectation arises as to whose establishment [is meant]—and when one says "of the self"—the meaning "the counter-correlative of the self's establishment" is obtained, it need not be explained as "with reference to the self" for that purpose. Furthermore, the answer to "whose? ought to be in the genitive case alone, not in the accusative; nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated thus for the sake of clarity.

The word *ātman* denotes itself. If the word *ātman* were intended to refer to the established correlate characterized by being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), then the answer "the established correlate" to the question "What is the established correlate? would be incoherent. Therefore, the intention is that it refers to another opposite (*pratidvandvin*).

Nor should it be asked how that which is established with respect to a class of objects can also be established with respect to itself; for one must understand that while the former is characterized as the object denoted by the word *prati* in the sense of a correlative (*pratisambandhitayā*), the latter is characterized as the object (*viṣayatayā*). Thus, the expressions "with respect to itself" (*ātmānaṃ prati*) and "with respect to a class of objects" (*arthajātaṃ prati*) are perfectly intelligible. But who is this self that is the correlative of establishment?

Since the word "self" (*ātman*) has been explained as referring to itself, it is impossible to deny that part [of its meaning]; therefore, the sense is: how can that which is indicated by the word "self"—namely, the self—be related to itself as its own correlate? The implication is that there is a contradiction in a thing being its own correlate. However, it should be understood that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) itself is not included among the things to be denied. This concludes the refutation of consciousness as the self.

Regarding the phrase "of the nature of consciousness" (*saṃvidātmabhāvasya*): it should be understood that the word *ātman* refers to the counter-correlative of "establishment" (*siddhi*), and not to "self" (*sva*) or "other" (*para*); for the status of being a counter-correlative of "otherness" does not depend on further justification. Regarding the phrase "the relation of attribute and substrate" (*dharmadharmibhāva*): the implication is that, therefore, there is no room for knowledge devoid of qualifiers (*niṣprakāraka-jñāna*). Regarding the question "for what purpose here?": the meaning is whether [the term] expresses origination (*utpatti*) or cognition (*jñapti*). [The phrase] "because the agent (*kartṛ*) is also an object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)"...

Now, one might object: even if through recognition—expressed as "This is that very same thing I previously experienced"—the non-difference between the previously experienced object and the present object is established, how can this establish the non-difference of the experiencer? For at that time, the experiencer was the "I" (mad-artha), and now the experiencer is also the "I"; since this cognition could possibly occur even if there were a difference between them, provided it does not have their non-difference as its object.

Nor should it be argued that identity is established because the recollection by one person of what was experienced by another is impossible; for while identity might indeed be established by that reasoning, it is not so established by the perception of recognition (*pratyabhijñā-pratyakṣa*). If you object: "If our concern lies solely with that [reasoning], then since it is possible to accept the reasoning regarding the eternity of recognition—which will be stated later—as the proof, it is improper to take the status of being the object of recognition as the proof," we say: no.

The point here is that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) can be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), based on the thought: "That very same object which was previously experienced by me is now being experienced by me. Regarding the phrase "origination and persistence are established": the meaning is that from the cognition "I know," which involves the perception of an agentive effort (*kṛti*) conducive to the act of knowing, there arises the perception of origination; and from the perception of the present tense (*laṭ*) applied to the root-meaning, there arises the perception of persistence. An objection is raised: "In expressions such as 'I know,' only the status of being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) of the root-meaning is perceived."

But it is not the possession of an effort conducive to that [cognition]. For this very reason, if there is dissatisfaction with the claim that even the Supreme Self—the substratum of eternal cognition—is perceived as the substratum of cognition in the statement, "I know all things past," then the perception, "Cognition has arisen in me," should be taken as the authority regarding its arising. The point is that the expression "in me" refers precisely to the cognizer; for since the suffix *tṛc* denotes agency, there is the perception of having arisen at the immediately preceding moment. As for "cessation," it refers to the cognition of a cloth.

Although it might be easy to say that destruction consists in being endowed with the final moment—just as origination consists in being endowed with the first moment—it should nevertheless be understood that the destruction of each preceding state is simply its connection with each succeeding state.

"The self, indeed, reconnects"—the implication being that it is not the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that does so. The sense is: if experience itself were the self, how could there be a reconnection of the identity of the experiencer within that experience? "Consciousness alone is accepted by both [parties]"—in the *Bhāṣya*, it is understood that the knower is not accepted by both; since even those who maintain false doctrines accept that [consciousness], it is improper to claim that this [statement] is intended to refute their specific doubts.

He refutes, as an incidental discussion, the view of certain Buddhist sectarians who do not accept the existence of a knowing subject (*jñātṛ*). He says: "By certain Buddhist sectarians... [The meaning is: because it is contradicted by perception (*upalabdhi*), the identity of consciousness with the Self (*saṃvidātmatva*) is untenable. That is to say, the meaning of the claim that consciousness alone is the Self and that there is no Self distinct from it is that this [claim] is contradicted by the perception of something distinct from it. Therefore, let there be the perception of the knower as well; the identity of consciousness with the Self is not thereby contradicted by perception.

It should be understood that the objection—that there is no apprehension whatsoever of consciousness (saṃvit) as being non-self—is refuted. To avoid the consequence of resorting to such a strained interpretation, he explains [the passage] with the aim of refuting the suspicion that it might be a false statement: "Or rather, by [stating] that consciousness is the ultimate reality... The establishment of the "I-sense" (ahamartha) as the self is based on its being accepted by others as the object of the "we-cognition" (asmatpratyaya). Even for a proponent of falsity, since it is admitted that both the conscious and unconscious portions appear within the "we-cognition" in the form of the notion "I," it should be seen that there is no fault even according to the literal reading. [He mentions] "the three-fold positive concomitance" (anvayitraya).

Although it would be perfectly consistent to present each subsequent reason as a proof for each preceding one—just as in the case of negative arguments (vyatireki) such as: "Experience is the Self because it is inward," "Experience is inward because it is self-luminous," and "Experience is self-luminous because it is experience"—as well as: "The referent of 'I' is not the Self because it is outward," "The referent of 'I' is outward because its manifestation depends on knowledge," and "The referent of 'I' has a manifestation dependent on knowledge because it is distinct from consciousness"; nevertheless...

It should be understood that this was stated in order to demonstrate the variety of means of proof (*sādhana*). In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the phrase "nothing other than pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is the referent of 'you' (*yuṣmadartha*)" means that the referent of 'you' is precisely the non-self (*anātman*); this should be understood because [the statement] "That is the Self" (*sa ātmā*) serves as a counter-indication (*pratinirdeśa*). Regarding the phrase "the other four inferences":

The meaning is that he states the refutation of two pairs of inferences: first, setting aside the two inferences—"Because experience (*anubhūti*) is consciousness (*citti*), it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*)" and "Because the referent of 'I' (*ahamartha*) is consciousness, it is not self-luminous"—he states the refutation of the other two inferences: "Because experience is self-luminous, it is the inner subject (*pratyak*)," and "Because it is the inner subject, it is the Self (*ātman*"); and [the refutation] of the further two inferences: "Because the referent of 'I' is not self-luminous, it is external (*parāk*)," and "Consequently, it is not the Self."

Now, one might object: "In the cognition 'I know,' how can there be the manifestation of subjectivity (*pratyaktva*), characterized as being the substratum of knowledge? To this, he replies: "Precisely because it manifests as the substrate. If it is argued that this is not a valid answer for one who maintains that even the aspect of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) shines forth in "I," because both aspects are perceived as not being the locus of the mental modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*), we say no. For in the cognition "I," two distinct aspects are not perceived. Furthermore, if they were indeed perceived, then the statement that consciousness (*cit*) is not the self (*anātmatva*)—on the grounds that it is the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*)—would be contradicted. This is the intended meaning.

He says that "self-nature" (*pratyaktva*) establishes the opposite [of what is intended]. This means it establishes the selfhood (*ātmatva*) of the referent "I. Furthermore, regarding the reason of "self-luminosity," he intends to show that it possesses a "counter-balanced" (*satpratipakṣa*) status. This is because the intention here is that the meaning is sublated due to the absence of equal strength [between the two opposing arguments]. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the preceding text, which states that the reason of "self-nature" results in a strengthening of its non-establishment (*asiddhi*). Alternatively, it should be understood that the mention of "counter-balanced" status is made with the intention of pointing out a specific distinction.

"Both the non-establishment and the establishment of the reason consisting in the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of consciousness as its own nature are established. Previously, the non-establishment was stated by means of the reason that [the Self] is distinct from the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*); now, the distinction is that it is stated by means of the reason that [it] is not the object of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). Alternatively, the meaning is that the non-establishment of the reason—self-luminosity—which proves the self-nature of consciousness, is established. Therefore, one should see that there is no risk of tautology. "[The cognition of suffering] by virtue of its connection with which... [is the phrase].

The remainder of the sentence is "it becomes a cause for agitation. For the scripture is not independent of hearing and so forth. Although the word indeed conveys its meaning for one who has completed the study of the scripture together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*), nevertheless, the scripture’s capacity to generate a cognition that culminates in practical application (*anuṣṭhāna*) is dependent upon hearing and other such means. Furthermore, hearing is dependent upon the desire to know (*bubhutsā*), and that [desire] is dependent upon [the scripture’s] culminating in a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "of that which is to be known": the meaning is "of that which is to be known by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*)."

This also includes the statement regarding the permanence of the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*). Although the permanence of the referent of "I" was not established in the sūtra *na ātmā śruteḥ* (2.3.18), but rather that of the Self (*ātman*), it should be understood that the aforementioned statement was made on the assumption that its identity as the Self had been established.
[Regarding] its being of the nature of knowledge and possessing knowledge as its quality...

The phrase "the meaning of 'I' is distinct from that [body]" refers to the *Bhāṣya* passage: "And this knower, the meaning of 'I'... Here, the term "knower" (*jñātā*) is a qualifying attribute containing a reason. As he will state later: "For it is not the case that a lamp or the like lacks luminosity simply because it is illuminated by the power of its own radiance. Therefore, having raised the objection—"How can the knower possess the quality of being self-luminous (*ananya-prakāśatva*) if it is itself illuminated by the power of the radiance of its own attribute, which is knowledge?"—he speaks with the intention of showing the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason proving non-selfhood (*anātmatva*), namely, "being illuminated by another" (*anyādhīna-prakāśatva*). This is the meaning.

Regarding the question "And how is that so?", he says: the intention of the objection is, "How can that which has light as its substrate possess the nature of light—consisting of knowledge that is both objective (sakarmaka) and subjective (sakartṛka)—as denoted by terms such as 'experience' (anubhūti)? [The reply is: "Consciousness (caitanya) is the state of being knowledge (jñānatva). This means it is the state of being conducive to empirical usage (vyavahārānuguṇatva).

Because the intention here is that the ocean of knowledge is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) within the Self, and because it has been stated that the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) when applied to the Self is conventionally established (*ruḍha*) as referring to that which is self-luminous, it is precisely this self-luminosity characterized by compatibility with empirical usage that is intended here by the word "knowledge. The sense is that this is appropriate for that which is not denotable by words such as "element," "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), and so forth, and which is neither an object (*karman*) nor an agent (*kartṛ*). This refers to the fact that the referent of the "I" (*ahamartha*) has consciousness as its very nature.

Intending to demonstrate the scriptural authority for the fact that the Self has consciousness as its very nature—characterized by a luminosity that does not depend on anything else—through such passages as "This person is unknowable, he is self-luminous," [the author] raises the objection: "How can that which possesses the quality of luminosity have a luminosity independent of anything else, given the absence of the capacity characterized by the observation of a similar kind? He then demonstrates this capacity by showing that the possession of the quality of luminosity is observed in lamps and the like, which possess the nature of luminosity. This is the meaning.

However, it should not be thought that [the self] has the nature of consciousness characterized by self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). By this, upon examining the passage stating, "I shall state the scriptural authority for the fact that the referent of 'I' (*ahamartha*) has the nature of consciousness," it is understood that having the nature of consciousness is precisely what constitutes being luminous independently of anything else (*ananyādhīnaprakāśatva*).

Since it is logical that the reasoning—"that which has luminosity as its intrinsic nature is not dependent on another for its manifestation"—serves to support the scriptural texts establishing non-dependence on another for manifestation, there must necessarily be an identity between having consciousness as one's intrinsic nature and being non-dependent on another for manifestation. Consequently, the self (the *aham-artha*) is non-dependent on another for its manifestation, because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatvāt*).

The objection that there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans—since both consist in having consciousness as their intrinsic nature—is refuted, because having consciousness as one's intrinsic nature does not possess a single uniform form. Some, however, explain that this demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the previously stated inference: "The referent of 'I' has a manifestation independent of anything else, because it is self-luminous. Nor should one suspect a discrepancy in formulation by arguing, "In that case, 'self-luminosity' was the reason, whereas here 'having manifestation as its intrinsic nature' is stated," for the two are identical.

The phrase "because it shines while [the object] sleeps" also has the meaning "because its very nature is luminosity. Even under that interpretation, there is no fault. Regarding the term *ātmadīpa* (self-lamp): here it is a *dvandva* compound containing a collective sense (*samāhāra-garbha*). Therefore, it should be understood that in all four cases, there is no inconsistency in the use of the dual number. The phrase "of such a kind" means being conducive to empirical usage through directness or indirectness, regardless of indifference. Alternatively, it means "of the lamp of the self and the light of knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūta-jñāna*). The phrase "of such a kind" refers to this.

The meaning is that there is a flickering between the lamp and its light, or between the self and the knowledge that constitutes its nature. Regarding the phrase "without fear of the fallacy of the probandum being deficient" (*sādhyavaikalyanāśaṅkayā*): this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), and it should also be understood to include the fallacy of the probans being deficient (*sādhanavaikalya*). Regarding the phrase "the object inherent in that which is qualified by form" (*rūpitatsamavetārtha*): one should not argue that the exclusion [of the probandum] is not achieved because the "object inherent in that which is qualified by form" is a different property (*dharmyantara*) from "form" itself; for it will be made clear in the subsequent text that the term *dharmyantara* signifies a substance other than its own substratum.

"The commentary beginning with 'caitanyasvābhāvatā' (the nature of consciousness) and so forth" means: although the nature of [this work] as *tarka* (reasoning) was previously introduced starting from the passage "yaḥ prakāśasvabhāvaḥ" (that which has the nature of light), nevertheless, it should be understood that it is stated thus—beginning with "caitanyasvābhāvatā"—because there is no contradiction even in its being of the nature of *tarka*. "Because of the statement regarding its having knowledge as its attribute and its being the very essence of knowledge" means: the intention is that this demonstrates both the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*).

Is it not the case that "of camphor and so forth, whose fragrance is perceived from a distance" (*dūropalabdha-gandhānām*) is a qualification containing a logical reason? The meaning is: "because camphor and so forth have a fragrance perceived from a distance. Therefore, the claim made by some—that "this phrase 'whose fragrance is perceived from a distance' is interpolated, for if it were so, it would result in the absurdity of the text 'such as a casket or a box' being a negation of something irrelevant"—is refuted.

In this context, because there exists a difference in meaning between the "box" (*samudga*) and the "casket" (*saṃpuṭa*) in terms of their general and specific forms, there is no suspicion of tautology. [The phrase] "only those very parts acknowledged by both parties" means that for these very components which serve as the substratum for the perceived fragrance, their mere remaining in a state of immobility is what is meant by "lightness."

However, there is no assumption for them [the atoms] such as: that their specific conjunction constitutes a substrate (upaniṣāda); that another property (dharmyantara) arises caused by that; that they disintegrate in the subsequent moment; that the substratum perishes dependent upon that; or that in the subsequent moment thereafter, another substratum arises through the state of being a mass (puñjībhāva), and so forth. Therefore, the sense is that there is no excessive complexity (gaurava). "Akṛti" means inactive, i.e., motionless. "Due to connection with air, fire, and so forth."

It should be understood that the very connection with light (*tejas*) is the cause of possessing rays. Regarding the phrase "of the rays belonging to the class of *gatva*": even for those that have entered the water after shattering the pot-sherd, there would only be an emergence back upward from there shortly thereafter; the point is that they do not come to rest there. As for the statement "the perception of heat occurs precisely through the transfer of particles of fire": the meaning is that the perception of heat occurs solely through the transfer of particles of fire associated with fire, even without [the fire itself] disintegrating.

"Even when heated by the sun, there is no transfer of parts due to the scattering of rays," according to the subsequent text. Some, however, maintain that the transfer of scattered parts occurs when [the gem] is heated by fire. Anticipating the objection—"For this very reason our desired conclusion is established, since it is understood that those very scattered parts constitute the light"—this is refuted by the subsequent text: "transferring into water and so forth. They explain that it is perceived as the effect of the parts of fire taken up by the pearl.

In this regard, some might ask: if the sun’s rays cause heat by means of the constituent parts of fire, why could it not be that the fire causes heat through the entry of the constituent parts of the sun’s rays? For the mutual interpenetration of both is established by authoritative scripture. Therefore, since there is no distinction between the two in terms of their heat, one must simply state that both are causes of heat; it is not the case that one acts through the medium of the other.

For when it is said, "The wind rains dust and dries [it]," no further means is required for the act of drying; nor is there any such requirement because fire is observed to be a cause of heat even during the day.

In that case, since there would be no entry of the components of the sun’s rays, it could be said that fire itself is the cause of the heat; for by the principle stated in the Sūtra, "following the rays," it is established that the sun's rays are the cause of intense heat at night. Thus, due to the absence of entry by fire at that time, there would be no cause for such heat—this being the point of comparison. Furthermore, it should be observed that if the components of fire and so forth were to enter, there would be no defect even if the solar rays were to enter as well (so they say).

Regarding the phrase "nanu ploṣaṇadravībhūteti," some maintain that this passage is an introduction to the commentary on the verse beginning with "ūrdhvam udgacchet," which demonstrates the contradiction between the natures of upward movement and lateral movement; it is not, however, an introduction to the commentary on the verse beginning with "viśaraṇapiṇḍībhāvasvabhāvavirodha," because the commentary on the verse beginning with "na hi viśaraṇasvabhāva" was already introduced prior to that. Therefore, they argue that it is appropriate to take "ūrdhvam udgacchet" as the specific point of reference (pratīka).

The meaning is that it is precisely the straightness [of the light] that is perceived through its connection with the shadow. If there were no rule regarding the straight-line propagation of light, then in a place where darkness is separated from the lamp's light by an intervening pillar, the light would have to travel via a curved path—just like dust particles driven by the wind—and consequently, even the darkness therein would not possess straightness. Now, one might object: there is no rule that the connection with the shadow occurs only at a straight location relative to the obscuring object.

For if that were the case, when an intervening object is in close proximity to a lamp, a shadow with a broad tip and a fine root would not be perceived; to this he says, "the expansion of the shadow. The meaning is that the broadness of the shadow's tip is caused by the broad tips and fine roots of the rays being described. This is the intended sense: to whatever extent the rays, possessing tips inclined toward spreading, are obstructed, to that same extent the shadow extends. [This occurs] "by means of the causal complexes for production and destruction."

The sequence of inference here is as follows: "The third conjunction of fire with the wick-parts produces the lamp, because it is a conjunction of fire with the wick-parts, like the first conjunction of fire with the wick-parts. "The destruction of the first wick-part is the cause of the destruction of the lamp, because it is the destruction of a wick-part, like the destruction of the final wick-part. In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that the determination of perception, such as the excess of heat and so forth, must be explained.

This is an illustration; it should be understood that while the abundance of substratum is not a property of light (*prabhā*), it is equally well-stated that it is a property of those particles of fire (*tejas*) which possess manifest touch and accompany it. By this [is meant] the scriptural statement that will be cited. Now, as for the designation of knowledge and so forth as being self-luminous...

If it is argued that the establishment [of self-luminosity] is achieved by taking its nature as consciousness (*caitanya-svabhāvatva*), since it has been demonstrated that being of the nature of consciousness is indeed self-luminosity—and therefore there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—we reply: no. This is because it was previously stated that in the phrase "nature of consciousness," what is intended is merely the state of being a cognition characterized by consciousness (*caitanyalakṣaṇajñānatva*) insofar as it is conducive to empirical usage (*vyavahārānuguṇatvamātra*); it does not intend to mean being the ground for the application of terms such as "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), "experience" (*anubhūti*), or "realization" (*avagati*). Thus, there is no fault.

The term "exclusion" (*vyatireka*) is used here to signify "without remainder. The sense is that, in contrast to the expression "the internal, entire lump of salt," the phrase "the external, excluded [from the] entire lump of salt"—when "entire lump of salt" is stated—necessarily brings about the cognition of all its internal parts in their uncontracted state; this is established by experience.

"Apprehended as related to itself": the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that if its relation to itself were not apprehended, it would not be apprehended as being related to itself. "It would be cognizable by another cognition": the sense is that a cognition whose object is the relation between the knower and the act of knowing must necessarily have as its object the knower and the act of knowing, which constitute the relata.

If it is argued that one might likewise ask: "In this case, how could the qualification by 'cognition-ness' appear in the self, as well as the qualifications by 'immediacy,' 'conformity,' and 'oneness,' since it is impossible for a thing itself to be its own object—that which is the locus of a relation?"—this objection is also acceptable, because the knower's relation [to cognition] is indeed included along with the cognition whose object is that relation.

The meaning is that because the relationship between the knower and the determination (*vyavasāya*) is also an object of cognition, a "cognition of the cognition" (*anuvyavasāyānuvyavasāya*) must be admitted along with the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) which has as its objects the knower, the determination, and their relationship. For the referent "I" (*ahamartha*), whose very nature is to be a qualificand (*viśeṣya*), presents itself [to consciousness]. Nor should it be argued: "Since the self lacks the capacity to grasp its own attributes—such as being a cognizer, being favorable [to cognition], unity, and distinctness—how can its status as a qualificand be grasped? This is because the status of being a qualificand is not something additional to its own nature, and thus its apprehension is possible.

Nor should it be argued that even when the natures of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are apprehended, how can there be the linguistic usage of a "qualified object" (*viśiṣṭa*) if their being defined in relation to one another is not apprehended? This is because the very non-apprehension of the non-relation (*asaṃsarga*) between them produces the same effect as the apprehension of a relation (*saṃsarga*), or else because such an apprehension is possible since that [non-relation] is also of the nature of those two [entities]. Now, it must be admitted that the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by the word *pratyak* has the self (*ātman*) as its object; for in that case, two distinct manifestations (*prakāśa*) must be accepted.

If it is argued that this objection need not be raised because we do not accept self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) characterized by being non-objective (*avedyatva*), and thus there is no fault even if two manifestations exist, that is true; however, the cognition "I know the jar" is produced by the visual sense-organ (*cakṣurindriya*), and not, as in the Nyāya school, a form of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) produced by the mind (*manas*). For it is impossible for the self to be the object of a cognition produced by the eye. Therefore, it is the substratum (*dharmin*) alone that shines forth as "I."

The intended sense is that it is more appropriate to say that the aspect of the cognition of a jar appears by virtue of its own self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*). For in that case, [the appearance] is caused by insentience (*jaḍatva*); the meaning is that in the case of insentient objects, simultaneous manifestation alone is the determinant for being apprehended by a single cognition.

"Let it be the etymological cause (*vyutpatti-nimitta*). This means that just as in the case of the statement, "Devadatta is denoted by the word 'Vāsasvī' (clothed)," clothing is merely the etymological cause for one who understands the word "Devadatta," and is not included within the scope of its primary denotation (*śakya*), so it is here. [Objection: But even in our view, since there is the etymology "that by which something is known" (*jñāyate 'nena*), the term is applicable to the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*)—that is, to *vṛtti-jñāna*—and thus it remains applicable to the related object (*saṃbandhi-śabda*). [Response: [This is true].

The meaning is that it is inconsistent to ascribe the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*) to an insentient modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), and because the conventional usage of being a "possessor" (*saṃbandhitva*) applies only to that which is denoted by the word *jñāna* ending in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

Or [is it] self-luminosity for itself? Here, some argue that since the third alternative—that consciousness is manifest to itself—has been refuted on the grounds of its non-establishment, a fourth alternative—that consciousness is self-manifesting to itself—cannot possibly arise; therefore, it is not appropriate to treat the *Bhāṣya* passage, "Therefore, the 'I'-principle, which is non-inert, is the Self because it is established toward its own self by its very existence," as a refutation of the fourth alternative.

Therefore, it is strained to explain the *bhāṣya* beginning with "tasmāt" as being primarily intent on rejecting another alternative, when its natural sense lies in the conclusion of the refutation of the previously introduced options. Likewise, it is also strained to describe that very *bhāṣya* as being intent on refuting two alternatives of the fifth option—namely, that [the object] possesses suitability for empirical usage without being an object of knowledge, and that it possesses luminosity independent of another cognition.

Indeed, the Bhāṣya passage—"Therefore, the 'I'-entity (*ahamartha*), which is non-insentient and established for its own self by its very existence, is the Self"—cannot serve as a refutation of the fifth alternative, which holds that [the Self] is merely being fit for empirical usage without being the object of cognition. For in that case, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) must be raised against the 'I'-entity itself, not against the claim that the 'I'-entity is the Self.

Since, even in the case of consciousness (*saṃvit*), there exists suitability for empirical usage (*vyavahārānuguṇatva*) independently of being an object of knowledge—just as it does in the case of the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*)—it would be more appropriate to say that the referent of "I" is the Self (*ātman*). Therefore, the intended fourfold alternative is: (1) having luminosity conditioned by its own existence; (2) having an existence whose luminosity is never absent; (3) appearing to itself while possessing that [nature]; or (4) having luminosity independent of connection with anything else. They maintain that this is understood in exactly the same way in the *Bhāṣya* as well.

"Contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) is a defect common to all [positions]. The meaning is that since the very thing appearing as "I" is the Self, and since that [Self] is perceived as the substratum of knowledge, it is perceived precisely through the distinction of [its own] knowledge. Alternatively, the meaning is that there is a contradiction by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which grasps [the fact] that "I know" is a property of the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*). "By either of the two: inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) or contradiction (*virodha*). In one's own system, inconclusiveness consists in the [reason] occurring in all three positions [of the subject, the similar instance, and the dissimilar instance].

The meaning is that, according to the opponent's view, there is a contradiction consisting in the property of occurring only in the similar and dissimilar instances [of the subject]. Regarding the phrase "that whose existence does not deviate from manifestation," some say that the reading "that whose existence does not deviate from manifestation" (*na vyabhicarati prakāśaṃ yasya sattā*) is correct, because that alone is the appropriate sense; for what is intended is that existence itself is pervaded by manifestation, and because the word *avyabhicarita* in the Bhāṣya ends in the *kta* suffix used in the passive sense (*karman*), and thus cannot end in the *kta* suffix used in the active sense (*kartṛ*).

This explains how [the self] appears for another. The point is this: in the cognition "I am happy," since the meaning of "I" appears as being subordinate to the happiness, and since happiness itself is of the nature of manifestation, the state of being the fruit of manifestation—characterized by being subordinate to the manifestation of happiness—also appears in the cognition "I am happy."

Now, regarding the claim that the "I-sense" (ahamartha) is established through error: one should not say that the *Bhāṣya* states "it does not appear as the knower," because it is understood from that very statement that it is the knower who is established through error, not the "I-sense. For this reason alone, the *Bhāṣya* on the refutation states: "The 'I-sense' is perceived as the experiencer; [the text] says 'experience is the I'. Furthermore, in the *Bhāṣya*: "Experience is, in the ultimate sense, without object and without substrate (*nirāśrayā*),"—here the words "substrate" (*āśraya*) and "object" (*viṣaya*) are used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*).

The meaning is that [consciousness] is devoid of being the locus of knowledge and being the object of knowledge. This is in accordance with the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) commentary: "That state of being a knower is established through illusion, just as the nature of silver is [superimposed] upon a fragment of mother-of-pearl, because agency is impossible for experience (*anubhūti*) in relation to itself. For this very reason, the objection—that it is unnecessary to establish that [consciousness] is devoid of objects and loci in ultimate reality once it has been demonstrated that the state of being a knower is established through illusion—is also refuted.

In this context, it should be understood that the demonstration of the non-emptiness of being an object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣayatva*) is intended as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and not because of its utility for the subject at hand. Alternatively, the meaning is that [the self] is empty of a cognizer (*jñātṛ*) that is superimposed through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) while lacking a substratum. For this very reason, one should observe the natural sense of the text: "the referent 'I' (*ahamartha*) would be perceived in coreferentiality with experience. In that case, there is no superimposition based on a mere relation.

The intention is that by means of this, the cognition [of the self] as being in a different locus from the object of the word "I" (ahamartha) would be established, just as in the expression "the face in the mirror. For light indeed appears in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the gem. If it is asked: "Why is it not possible for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the object 'I'—which is the locus of experience—to occur upon the experience itself, just as the superimposition of the gem, which is the locus of light, occurs upon the light? We reply: No. In that case, there could be a superimposition of non-difference between the locus of light and something other than the substrate (the gem) and the light itself. However, such is not the case here.

The meaning is that it is not possible [for the two to be identical] because duality does not exist in a single entity (*anu*). Regarding the phrase "of the two grounds for the application of the two words": one might object, "How can *mālinyatva* (the state of being a garlanded woman), which is the ground for the application of the word 'mālinī', and *rāgatva* (the state of being passionate), which is the ground for the application of the word 'rāgā', reside in the directions and the sky? Or how is there the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of direction-ness and the state of being a beloved woman when there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the beloved woman upon all directions, as in the verse 'She alone is my [direction] in all directions'? To this we say: no.

In such a case, because an error is possible through the superimposition of a relation (*saṃsargāropa*) characterized by a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), one might argue: "Let there be a superimposition of a relation here as well. However, this should not be said; for if that were so, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cognition "I am in experience" (*anubhūtāv aham*), just as there are the cognitions "the beloved in the quarters" (*dikṣu kāminī*) and "turbidity in the quarters" (*dikṣu mālinyam*). This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "because of the arising of superimposition upon that substratum": by stating that the non-manifestation of the nature of experience (*anubhūtitvāsphuraṇa*) is the cause of error, it would effectively be stated that the non-manifestation of experience is the cause of superimposition.

The sense is this: consequently, because the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) would lack the status of being a cause, there would follow the undesirable consequence that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) could not arise. He raises an objection by stating that "the non-arising of superimposition is difficult to maintain," meaning that superimposition arises precisely because of the non-manifestation of that [substrate]. This means that superimposition arises because the manifestation of that [substrate] is not a cause. [He replies: "Because that which is not apprehended cannot function as a substrate. This means [it refers to] that which is not apprehended at the time of superimposition.

He states another objection: "of that which is devoid of object and locus. Some, however, say it means "of that which is not apprehended," i.e., "not apprehended in any way whatsoever"; they claim this is the statement intended to establish that [point].
This is the refutation of the view that the property of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is a quality of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

"From the scriptural statement concerning the nature of the knower" means from such statements as "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, higher than the high" and "The seer sees everything," and so forth. "Situated within the knot of such egoism" means situated within the insentient substance that is subject to modification; however, one should not think it means situated within an insentient substance whose nature is change itself, because of the preceding text's reference to the "unchanging" (*avikriya*), and because it conforms to the *Bhāṣya* which speaks of the "locus of modification. "Because it is an object of sight" is the meaning.

The meaning is that "because it is visible" is the remainder [of the argument]. Regarding "the distinction between the body and the self": the meaning is the absence of the status of being a knower in the body. Regarding "in some cases, of that which is the cause for the absence of the status of being a knower": [an objection] might be raised that, if this were so, the status of being a knower would be necessarily conditioned by sentience (*cittva*). And this is not a desired consequence, because it would entail the absurdity of the status of being a knower belonging to *dharmabhūtajñāna* (knowledge as an attribute).

It should not be argued that "consciousness" (*cittva*) is not "selfhood" (*ātmatva*), and therefore the absence of the former does not entail the absence of the latter—namely, the absence of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*)—because the relationship of "that which is to be entailed" (*prayojya*) and "that which entails" (*prayojaka*) between selfhood and being a knower has never been perceived. [Response: This is not so; for even if the relationship of "that which is to be entailed" and "that which entails" between selfhood and being a knower is not perceived, it is observed that the absence of selfhood is the cause of the absence of being a knower. This is the intended meaning. In fact, however, in the expression "due to insentience, etc. (*acetanatvādīti*), it should be understood that "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*) and so forth are indicated by means of a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (possessive) *bahuvrīhi* compound.

"In order to establish the previously stated pervasion (*vyāpti*)" means: "In order to establish the pervasion previously stated [in the verse], 'And because the property of being a knower is a characteristic not common to insentient things. The phrase "for we do not [prove] the body's being a seer, etc. means: since the body is insentient (*jaḍa*), it does not possess the quality of being a seer; therefore, it is not the Self (*anātman*). We are not proving the distinction between the body and the Self to the Cārvāka (who does not accept such a distinction). Rather, the meaning is that we prove only that the body is not the Self because the Self has the nature of pure consciousness (*dṛśisvarūpa*), whereas the body does not.

Regarding the statement "the absence of being a seer is caused by insentience and so forth": in the phrase "insentience and so forth" (*acetanatvādi*), because "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*) is included by virtue of it being an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* (non-applicative) *bahuvrīhi* compound, even though there is an absence of being a seer, "insentience and so forth" refers precisely to visibility. This is intended in the subsequent passage as well. [The term] "uncommon to the proponent of falsehood" (*mṛṣāvādyasādhāraṇa*).

If the object of perception (*dṛśya*) possesses the nature of being a perceiver (*draṣṭṛtva*), then why should it not also possess the nature of being perceived (*dṛśitva*)? And if it is argued that it is impossible for an action (*karman*) to be an act (*kriyātva*), then it is likewise impossible for an action to be an agent (*kartṛtva*); the point is that the states of being an object, an agent, and an act are mutually contradictory. Although, according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), even the act of seeing (*dṛśi*) is admitted to be an object of sight, this should be understood as stated here merely in accordance with the opponent's view. [The phrase "merely by being the object of the cognition of silver" (*rajatapratyayagocaratvamātreṇa*) refers to this.]

Just as the cognition of silver has silver as its object, so too the "I"-cognition (*ahaṃpratyaya*) has the Self (*ātman*) as its object, because it is established that "I-ness" (*ahantva*) is itself "Self-hood" (*ātmatva*). Therefore, being the object of the "I"-cognition does not contradict Self-hood; on the contrary, the point is that it is precisely what establishes Self-hood. [The opponent objects: "But then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-Self-hood and so forth in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*."

The meaning is as follows: if one were to argue that "if the Supreme Self were the agent, it would follow that it is not the Self," and thus conclude in the opposite case that "therefore, it is not the agent," there would be the consequence of contradicting scriptural texts concerning agency and so forth; in the second case, [the reason] would be unestablished (*asiddhi*) with respect to the Supreme Self. This refers to the situation where, while accepting that the Supreme Self is the locus of action in the form of vibration (*spanda*) and is the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*).

The meaning is that [the object] is established as being admitted [by the opponent]; and consequently, such an admission is unproven—this is the sense, because in a *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum), only that which is already accepted by the opponent can serve as the *āpādaka* (the condition leading to the undesirable consequence).

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), regarding the statement "the designations 'rising' and 'setting' depend upon the *prasara*," the word *prasara* is understood in the sense of "spreading forth" (*prasaraṇa*). Thus, the meaning perceived is that the conventional usage of "rising" and "setting" for the whole (*aṃśin*) consists in its association with, and its absence from, such spreading forth (*prasaraṇa*).

Since the word *prasara* ends in the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*), it is understood as denoting the agent of the act of spreading; thus, with reference to the spreading aspect alone during the state of contraction, the designations "arising" (*udaya*) and "setting" (*astamaya*) are applied. However, the meaning that these [terms] do not apply to the whole (*aṃśin*) is also understood. Therefore, he explains them as having two referents: "the presence and absence of the spreading. He says, "also by way of another perspective."

The meaning is that since that [nature] is not an inherent form (*svābhāvika-rūpa*), the word "and" (*ca*) in the commentary—used in the phrase "and it is not inherent"—is intended to be displaced in its syntactic order. Regarding the question "What is the inherent form?", he says [the following]. On this point, some offer one interpretation: that the scriptural texts concerning immutability (*nirvikāratva*) are prohibitions against inherent modification. Others offer another interpretation: that they are prohibitions against mere modification in the liberated essential nature (*svarūpa*) which is inherently free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

In that regard, concerning the previous explanation, the word "that" (*tat*) in the Bhāṣya—referring to the statement "and that [agency] is not inherent, but rather produced by karma"—denotes agency. Consequently, the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the substratum of agency, is not inherent but is adventitious (*aupādhika*). Its inherent form, however, is indeed changeless. Thus, the meaning is that the scriptural passages negating modification refer to the inherent nature.

With this second explanation in mind, the text proceeds by asking, "How is its natural form? They say that there are two distinct explanations for the following reasons: in the first explanation, the objection—"How is its natural form?"—would remain unresolved; or else, the subsequent text—which speaks of immutability—would be inconsistent unless it were intended to refer to the natural form as free from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, they maintain that these are indeed two separate explanations. [The phrase] "never of the inert ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)" [is used].

Because it is taught as the opposite of insentience (*jaḍatva*) and because of the natural force of the word *svarūpa* [referring to the essence], he explains it otherwise, saying: "Alternatively, the word *svarūpa* refers to the substratum (*dharmin*).
This is the refutation of the defense of the knowerhood (*jñātṛtva*) asserted by others.

The case-ending is included within the compound. *Chāyāpatti* means reflection. Consequently, just as when it is said, "Because of the proximity of the sword to the mirror, there is a reflection of the sword [in the mirror]," one understands both that the mirror is reflected in the sword and that the sword is reflected in the mirror; likewise, when it is said, "the reflection in consciousness" (*cit-pratiphalanam*), both meanings are indeed possible: either the reflection is in consciousness, or consciousness itself is the reflection.

By this, the doubt is removed: "Just as when it is said, 'Devadatta’s acquisition of Yajñadatta’s wealth,' the meaning 'Yajñadatta’s acquisition of Devadatta’s wealth' is not obtained, so too, when it is said, 'Consciousness is permeated by the reflection of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra),' how could the meaning 'the reflection of consciousness in the ego-sense' be obtained? For [in our view], the word *chāyāpatti* does not denote a mere reflection; and since a reflection requires a locus just as a genitive case requires a referent, there is not even a scent of inconsistency.

Regarding this, some hold that the reading in the Bhāṣya, "What is this 'falling under its shadow' (tacchāyāpattiḥ)? is appropriate, since it was previously stated as "by falling under its shadow" (tacchāyāpattyā). Consequently, the following alternative is justified: does the word *tat* refer to the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), or does it refer to consciousness (*saṃvit*)? Even with the reading "falling under the shadow of consciousness" (*cicchāyāpattiḥ*), it should not be explained as "falling under the shadow of the state of being a knower" (*jñātṛtva*), because such an interpretation is not found in the Bhāṣya; furthermore, the position that it is "falling under the shadow of the state of being a knower" has not been raised by opponents.
For this very reason, there is no room for the objection: "Why are contact and conjunction not excluded from that which is endowed with the reflection of consciousness?

[The answer is: "Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the unconscious *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were conscious; and likewise, while the qualities (*guṇas*) are the agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] appears as if he were the agent."

In accordance with the manner stated above, the Bhāṣya raises the objection that the status of being a knower—characterized by being the substratum of activity co-located with consciousness—is possible through the mutual reflection resulting from the proximity of the conscious and the unconscious, as expressed in the words "of that which is insentient by nature."

Even though he has merely demonstrated the general possibility of being a knower, since he has not specified the particular substratum—whether it be the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or consciousness (*caitanya*)—and considering that in the phrase "by the falling of the reflection of consciousness" (*cicchāyāpattyā*) two types of compounds are possible (either a genitive-tatpuruṣa or a locative-tatpuruṣa), and having determined that the phrase "the possibility of that" (*tatsaṃbhavaḥ*) refers to the arising of the state of being a knower, he asks, "What is this 'falling of the reflection of consciousness'? [in order to determine] by whose falling of a reflection that [state of being a knower] arises, and where knowledge arises.

Is it that consciousness (saṃvit) undergoes the reflection of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)? And thus, by virtue of that reflection, it follows as a matter of fact that the state of being a knower (jñātṛtva) resides in consciousness itself. This is the meaning of the commentary regarding the impossibility of being a knower in both cases [the self and the intellect] mentioned hereafter: for being a knower consists in agency (kartṛtva) that is co-located with consciousness (caitanya).

The sense is that where there is consciousness, there is no agency, and where there is agency, there is no consciousness; thus, in neither case is the production of real knowership established through the falling of a reflection. For this very reason, they say that the subsequent commentary, "nor is there unreal knowership in either," is consistent with its own natural meaning (*svarasa*).

"And contact [occurs] in accordance with the nature of perception. This means that because validity (*prāmāṇya*) is the default state (*autsargikatva*), it must be accepted as being like the saltiness of *rumā* wood; it is not, however, like the heat of an iron ball. This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "of the staff and Devadatta": the sense is that such is observed in the case of an iron ball and fire, and so forth. Furthermore, contact between two things that do not exist separately is untenable.

If it is argued that contact is observed between fire and smoke—or between the body and the self—as they exist inseparably, we say: not so. The point is this: since knowledge and the ego-sense are perceived as attributes (dharma), if they were established as non-separate (apṛthaksiddha) in accordance with that perception, why could the state of being a knower (jñātṛtva) not also be real?

Regarding the phrase "of that which has not arisen": through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because manifestation is the cause of arising, "arising" itself becomes designated by the term "manifestation. The sense is that, based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "that from which it is manifested" (*abhivyajyate asyāḥ*)—using the suffix *ktin* in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*)—the word "manifestation" can possibly have "arising" as its referent. Because of dissatisfaction with this [first] view, he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*). [He states: "Manifestation consists in the arising of illumination. If it is objected: "But then there would be no difference from the second position, namely 'its illumination' (*tat-prakāśanam*)," we reply: No.

In the second alternative, the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) involves duality; however, it should be understood that this is not the case here. With this intention, he will state that "manifestation" (*prakāśana*) is the arising of the manifestation of the object of experience. Regarding the word *svataḥ-siddha* (self-established), it means being unilluminable by anything else and not dependent on another.

Because both [possibilities] are possible in the form of being something to be established (*utpādyatva*), he explains both by means of the passage beginning with "for by its own nature" (*svataḥ siddhatayā hi*). "Previously" means by the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "from that very [source]" (*tata eva*). "Assisting" (*anugrāhaka*): assisting means the means of assistance (*anugrahasādhana*). "Because it is not included within either of the two categories" (*koṭidvaye 'py anantarbhāvāt*): the meaning is that every instance of assistance is not included within either of the two categories. "Recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is assistance": the experience of pervasion and so forth, which serves as the cause for that [recollection], is the assistant to inference (*anumāna-anugrāhaka*).

Nor should it be argued that "assistance" (anugraha) is something entirely different from the awakening of a latent capacity through the readiness for the production of a result; for how could recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth alone constitute the nature of assistance? This is because there is no evidence for the existence of an "assistance" apart from the means of proof (*sādhana*). The statement that "inference is assisted by the recollection of pervasion" is justifiable in the same way as saying "it is experienced by experience"—this is the intended meaning. As for the phrase "by being the cause of the connection with the sense organ," this is actually an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for inference and other such means as well.

It should be understood that this is because the negation is equal [in both cases], namely, "neither the sense organs nor inference. Regarding the phrase "by way of connection" (*anupaṅgeṇa*): the meaning is "by way of connection with the subsequent commentary. He states, "But this is the intention of the commentary," and so forth, to show that although both teachers have mentioned that alternative view, it is intended by the commentary as a point of deliberation (*vikalpa*). Regarding the statement "the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāra*) is an incorporeal substance": the meaning is "a non-solid substance. Since it is logical to refute other positions immediately after refuting the two primary positions, the refutation of that [third position] by the words "not, first of all" (*na tāvat*) would be inappropriate; therefore, he explains it otherwise: "Or rather, [regarding] the ego-principle... and so forth.

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that ignorance, which has consciousness as its locus, could never be destroyed by anything at all. If it is objected: "But since [ignorance] is something to be removed by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), how can it be argued that it cannot be destroyed for another person?"—the answer is no. This is because the position that [ignorance] is removed by the ego-sense has already been discarded like a miscarriage; rather, it must be accepted as a proven fact that [ignorance] is removable by knowledge alone. It should be understood that this objection is raised in the context of that [accepted principle].

For this very reason, even when the acceptability of experience being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*) is admitted, the objection that the statement in the text—“in mere cognition devoid of the state of being an object”—which proceeds by assuming such objectifiability, contradicts what was said previously regarding the absence of object-status (*viṣayatvābhāva*), is also refuted; and it should be understood that this is because the commentary beginning with “nor is there the state of being the locus of consciousness” (*na ca saṃvidāśrayatvam*) is merely incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). Thus, the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) has been shown.

The point is this: in the inference that "because there is an absence of being an object of knowledge, there is no state of being known by ignorance," there is a negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) because the two properties—the state of being an object of knowledge and the absence of the state of being an object of ignorance—do not occur elsewhere than in the subject (*pakṣa*). The term *jñānanivartyājñānatva* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose nature is ignorance which is to be removed by knowledge. Regarding the phrase "conformity with cognition and linguistic usage" (*pratīti-vyavahārānuguṇya*): if the word *pratīti* were taken to mean "knowledge" (*jñāna*), then since conformity with knowledge cannot exist within knowledge itself, the statement "because knowledge and its means possess a nature conforming to cognition" would be inconsistent; such is the intended meaning.

What is the meaning of the claim that both validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) are extrinsic (*paratastva*)? Is it that, just as coldness and heat in earth are extrinsic while its lack of both heat and cold is intrinsic (*svatastva*), so too is the case here? Or is it that [validity] is produced by a causal complex distinct from the general causal complex for cognition, yet is apprehended by whatever causal complex apprehends that [cognition]? Having thus formulated the alternatives, he refutes the first on the grounds that it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [cognition] being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and so forth.

The meaning is that if both validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) were absent, then every object would likewise lack both the possession of those qualities and their absence, and thus everything would be a mere nothingness (*tucchatva*). He states another objection: "validity and invalidity... [and so on]. [He says] that through connection with those [qualities], the cognition itself possesses such a nature.

The meaning is that, just as salinity appears in wood due to its connection with *rumā* salt, or just as the appearance of heat and so forth occurs in earth—which is neither hot nor cold—due to contact with fire and water which are respectively hot and cold, so too is the appearance of validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) possible. [Objection: But this is untenable if [validity] were extrinsic (*parataḥ*). [Response: Then validity and invalidity would both be mere non-entities (*tucchatva*), because they would be absent elsewhere and would also be non-existent here. However, since heat and coldness can exist elsewhere, they are not non-entities.

He refutes the second [position] with the words "the desire to know validity" (*prāmāṇyabubhutsā*). The meaning is that since the apprehension of validity itself must take the form of a certainty, if there were a requirement to apprehend validity even in that [apprehension], it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Alternatively, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "because of the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature, etc.," the infinite regress is included. He explains both [points] with the passage beginning "validity and [the validity of] validity," and so forth.

"In some cases, it is accepted that manifestation occurs by virtue of being situated within the self" means that the demonstration of the lack of pervasion (*anaikāntya*) in the case of lamps and the like is intended to indicate such an acceptance; this is the sense. Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "by the reflection of ocular light," "reflection" (*pratiphalana*) means "rebound" (*pratihati*). As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "in reality, there is no cause here, whether by way of a positive entity (*vastu*) or by way of a defect (*doṣa*)," the meaning is that nothing—neither in the form of a real object nor in the form of a defect—serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in this case.

For in the case of perceptual valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramā*), the object denoted by the term "entity" (*vastu*) is the cause; therefore, it should be understood that the causality of the entity is logically established. Regarding the phrase "by way of the relation between property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*)": since the suffix *tasi* functions as a substitute for all case endings, the meaning is "by means of the entity through the relation of property and property-possessor. Regarding the phrase "the state of being a corporeal, transparent, and gross substance": the meaning is that the reflection of ocular light—which is occasioned by the state of being a corporeal, transparent, and gross substance—is the cause in the form of a defect (*doṣa*) for the perception [of the object] by virtue of its presence therein.

In reality, because of the absence of a cause, there is no state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). The meaning is that since the cause consisting of the nature of a substance—which is characterized by the relationship between attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*)—is absent, the state of being a knower is not perceived. Therefore, regarding the phrase "even self-nature" (*pratyaktvam api*), the particle *api* (also/even) is displaced in the sequence; the construction is "even the establishment of self-nature does not exist," implying that for consciousness (*jñapti*) as well, the establishment of self-nature is not achieved.

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "It must be said that experience also manifests in that very same way," the author introduces it by explaining the meaning of the phrase "in that very same way" (*tathaiva*) as "by way of clear manifestation" (*viśadāvabhāsatvena*), stating: "because there is an absence of manifestation [otherwise]. Now, one might object: "Let the meaning of the word 'thus' (*tathā*) simply be 'as the sense of 'I-ness' (*ahaṃtvena*). In this case, let even the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with 'For one who has awakened from sleep' (*na hi suptotthitaḥ*) serve as a supplement to that, acting as its justification. This is true; however, such an interpretation is appropriate for the purpose of revealing another supporting argument. [The phrase refers to] "only in the waking state."

The meaning is: even if one were to admit an indistinct manifestation during a state that is unfit for such an indistinct manifestation, what harm would there be to us who admit it during a state suitable for it? Regarding the phrase "for the sake of establishing the nature of self-luminosity" (*pratyaktvasiddhyartham*): the sense is that this would contradict the statement "therefore, [the self] is devoid of the notion of 'I'" (*ahaṃbhāvaviyuktā*). "This is a specific kind of recognition" (*pratyabhijñāviśeṣaḥ*): in the portion "I am happy," it is of the nature of memory; in the portion concerning sleep and the portion concerning time—namely, "I slept"—it is of the nature of an inference produced by the reconnection of two cognitions based on the mark (*liṅga*) of non-apprehension of what is otherwise fit for recognition. This is the summary.

The meaning is: a specific kind of causal cognition. Now, [one might object]: from the memory of smoke on the mountain and the cognition that it possesses smoke pervaded by fire, there arises the inference "the mountain has fire"; thus, even with respect to the portion consisting of the mountain, this is of the nature of an inference.

It is not of the nature of memory. Thus, when the self—which is of the nature of pleasure—is the object of memory, the inference of its connection during the period of sleep is itself of the nature of an inference regarding the self-aspect; it is not of the nature of a *parāmarśa* (inferential consideration). This is because it is impossible for the property of being an inference (*anumititva*) to be non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*). Or, let it be granted that being an inference is non-pervasive. Even so, why should the cognition "I am happy" not have as its object the "I" (*ahamartha*) which is currently of the nature of pleasure? For there is no mention of that [past] state in that aspect, by virtue of which its status as memory could be determined.

Since the experience latent during sleep is beyond the scope of space, time, and other such categories, and since there is no distinguishing feature whatsoever within the self existing at the time of sleep, it is impossible to take that self as the subject (*pakṣa*) of an inference; how, then, could the connection with sleep be understood through inference regarding such a self? Therefore, as long as it is not admitted that some other attribute remains manifest in the self during the state of sleep, it is not easy to maintain that the cognition "I am happy" consists of a recollection of happiness belonging to the time of sleep.

If it is argued that therefore this entire section is not sound, they reply: It is established that in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), a favorableness (*ānukūlya*) distinct from the waking state (*jāgrat*) appears; and that [favorableness] does not consist of knowledge that is part of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). If it were so, that favorableness would appear even during the waking state.

Therefore, just as the unique favorability manifesting in the state of liberation (*kaivalya*) is not something made manifest by the knowledge that constitutes its own nature (*svarūpa-bhūta-jñāna*), so too the favorability manifesting in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is manifested by that very same knowledge which has become an attribute (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*). However, in the waking state, due to the obstruction caused by karma that yields waking experiences, that favorability is not an object of the attribute-knowledge; yet in the state of deep sleep, it is indeed an object.

Consequently, because such an object is apprehended, that cognition possesses self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* statement, "Thus, happiness and the state of being a knower are known," is perfectly consistent. While there is a dependence on the senses when there is an outward expansion toward external objects, for this same reason, the *Bhāṣya* statement, "It is established by means of the senses," is likewise consistent. Furthermore, through knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), a recollection distinct from the waking state and others becomes possible, characterized by a specific degree of favorability.

Therefore, since experience can produce mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), recollection is also possible; for at that time, time itself can be made an object by knowledge as its attribute (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*), because time is cognizable solely through knowledge. Furthermore, when the self is recollected at that time as possessing a specific state of favorability, it is possible for the absence of knowledge—which constitutes sleep—to be apprehended by the mark (*liṅga*) of the non-apprehension of what is otherwise capable of being recollected. There is no contradiction even in the experience of the portion consisting of sleep, provided that the subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) pertains to all aspects [of that experience].

"And because it is established by its own nature (*svarasasiddhatvāt*). In reality, however, even if the distinguishing form does not manifest through the attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), there is no inconsistency. This is because, in the case of the Self—which is distinct from the waking state and is the object of a memory whose content has been wiped away—an extraordinary excellence of bliss is experienced. At that time, either the absence of knowledge in the form of sleep is inferred by the mark (*liṅga*) of the non-recollection of objects, or else, since that sleep is currently non-existent, the pastness of the sleep is inferred by that mark; thus, there is no logical flaw. This concludes the demonstration that the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) is the Self.

Furthermore, the claim that "this [consciousness] is established through the door of the senses" contradicts the natural sense of the Bhāṣya. The meaning is that it contradicts the Bhāṣya which states: "In the state of the *kṣetrajña*, its nature is contracted by karma and exists according to the varying degrees of intensity of those respective karmas; this is established through the door of the senses. This is because [the Bhāṣya] speaks of its persistence as the witness of ignorance in the statement, "you did not know anything at all."

The meaning is: by that witnessing-consciousness of ignorance which exists during deep sleep—postulated because the recollection of the form "I was not aware of anything" upon waking from sleep would otherwise be inexplicable—and which takes the form "I do not know. Consequently, one should not raise the objection: "Even if the experience of ignorance in the form 'I did not know' were possible during the state of deep sleep, how can there be an experience of ignorance in the form 'I was not aware of anything'? [This is because] the "I-sense" (ahamartha) is the substratum of ignorance.

The meaning is that one must also admit that the referent of the word "I" (*ahamartha*) is the locus of ignorance, and one must likewise admit that it is manifested [in that state]. This should be understood as follows: for example, when there is the recollection of a courtyard previously experienced as qualified by the absence of an elephant, such as in the statement, "There was no elephant in the courtyard this morning. In the view of the opponent (the Naiyāyika), the cognition "I did not know anything at all" is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) regarding every aspect [of the experience]; therefore, the illustrative example must be stated in accordance with that position.

However, in the final Siddhānta [view], because the aspect of the locus (*dharmin*) alone constitutes the form of the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection), the inference of the absence of an elephant—based on the mark of non-perception of a perceptible object (*yogyānupalabdhi*) and expressed as "there is no elephant in the square"—which will be explained in accordance with our own system, consists of the aspect of the square alone as its *parāmarśa*. Therefore, it should be understood that only such a case where the square alone was previously perceived will be cited later, for the sake of consistency with our own position.

He raises an objection: “By the reflective awareness ‘I slept happily,’ [it would follow that] even in your view, there would be reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) regarding every aspect [of the experience], just as in the view of the opponent. [The opponent replies: “If there is such a subsequent synthesis (*anusandhāna*), then it could not be a state of deep sleep at all.
