[The author counters: “But surely, even in the absence of a memory-knowledge produced by the external or internal organs, the experience of ignorance—which is designated as ‘sleep’—is possible through the Witness (*sākṣin*) alone; thus there is no contradiction with the state of deep sleep. [The author replies: “No; for there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) that ignorance is manifested by the Witness. This is the intended meaning.

"Paroktānyathāsiddhim" means the "establishment-by-other-means" (anyathāsiddhi) asserted by the Naiyāyikas and others who do not accept the experience of bliss during deep sleep (*suṣupti*). It should not, however, be thought to refer to the "proponents of falsehood" (*mṛṣāvādins*), for even they accept the experience of bliss. Nor should it be argued that the proponents of falsehood also accept the absence of the experience of bliss because the *Pañcapādikā* states, "The recollection of bliss is caused by the absence of suffering"; for the commentator on that work, Prakāśātman, reveals that this statement is merely an exposition of the opponent's view.

In reality, however, since this is a section investigating the existence or non-existence of the referent "I" (ahamartha), the Bhāṣya statement "just as there is happiness now" should be explained as having the meaning: "just as 'I' exists now, so may it exist for me. It should be understood that even in the case of the proponents of falsehood (mṛṣāvādins), such a statement is possible; therefore, there is no inconsistency even in that view. [The phrase] "instability" means the absence of experience.

The point is this: at that time, even in the absence of the object "I" and its experience, the mode of experience such as "as [I am] happy now" results from the necessity of accounting for the recognition of the happiness of the "I-object. This refers to the experience of the "I-object," even though the "I-object" itself is the object of negation. As stated in the Bhāṣya: "of the knower [in the thought] 'I knew,'" and "I did not know."

The sense is that the portion consisting of the "I" (the subject) takes the form of the recollection of an object experienced during deep sleep, and since validity is possible for a recollection only with respect to the nature of the object being recollected, one should not suspect—as the Naiyāyikas and others do—that this portion also possesses the status of direct experience (*anubhava*), because the nature of recollection (*smṛtitva*) is established by experience itself.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "In cases such as 'I did not see Rāma,' even though the referent of 'I' (ahamartha) is absent at that time, there is no inconsistency in the negation of the connection with past cognition in the case of 'I did not know [it],' because the 'I' is present; how then can this be so? "Objects of the manifestation of the cognized" means they are not objects of the manifestation of the knower. "The cessation of the referent of 'I'" means the absence of the cognition of the referent of 'I'. "The cessation in the square" means the cessation of the cognition of the square.

This should be understood as follows, based on the introduction: "He raises an objection regarding the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that proves the absence of the experience of the referent 'I' (*ahamartha*). Alternatively, it should be understood that even the absence of the experience of the referent 'I' ultimately results in the absence of the referent 'I' itself; thus, there is no contradiction.

The commentary beginning with “I did not know,” etc., explains—following the two previous interpretations—that [the passage] aims to demonstrate a contradiction through aversion. Regarding the phrase “of injunction and prohibition”: the meaning is that because the word “I” takes the form of a reference to the *ahamartha* (the self as subject) experienced in deep sleep, it constitutes an injunction (*vidhi*) by virtue of being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding that *ahamartha*; whereas the statement “I do not know myself” takes the form of a negation of the *ahamartha* by way of negating cognition (*jñāna*).

In the Bhāṣya, "being a witness" (*sākṣitvam*) is defined as "directly knowing" (*sākṣāj-jñātṛtvam*). The meaning is "primary agency of knowledge. This primacy of the agency of knowledge culminates in the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*). Therefore, it should be understood that there is no room for the objection: "How can the verbal root *jñā* (to know) be construed with the word 'directly' (*sākṣāt*), given that the designation *gati* is prescribed only for words in composition with a *kṛt* suffix? Now, one might object: since the suffix *śatṛ* in the word *ajānataḥ* is a substitute for the present tense marker (*laṭ*), it would imply a desire to express the ongoing nature of the act of knowing.

Furthermore, anticipating the objection that even the cessation of knowledge in the form of direct realization would mean there could be no designation [of the witness] as existing, he says: "the meaning is 'one who does not know'" (*ajñātuḥ*). The sense is this: since suffixes such as *-tṛ* (agentive) are common to all three times, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the inclusion of the present time in these suffixes is for the sake of indicating the current state of one who is studying the Veda (*vedādhyāyārtham*). However, the author of the *Vārttika* established the final position (*siddhānta*), stating: "Or rather, it is not so, because others are seen [to use them] in reference to mere time. (Note: The text contains a repetition of the phrase "the prima facie view regarding the inclusion of the present time in the suffixes -tṛ etc."; this has been streamlined in the translation.)

In the Bhāṣya, it says "in the sense of the direct seer" (*sākṣāddraṣṭari*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that from the word *sākṣāt*, when the "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) is the meaning to be expressed, one recalls the word *sākṣin*. By this, the Sūtra is explained. For such is the meaning of the Sūtra: when the "seer" is the meaning to be expressed, the suffix *-in* occurs after the word *sākṣāt* to form a name (*saṃjñāyām*). "The waking self is the example" (*sapakṣa*): the inference (*anumāna*) has the following form: the Self appears as "I," because it manifests for itself, like the waking self.

Nor should it be argued that the manifestation of the waking self as "I" is unestablished; for those [philosophers] admit that the cognition "I" has as its object a synthesis of consciousness and the non-conscious, and because the status of the self as the supreme locus of valid knowledge has been established by the force of the intuition "May I exist," it must be understood that the manifestation of the waking self as "I" is indeed established, and thus its being a similar instance (sapakṣa) is entirely appropriate. This concludes the demonstration of the persistence of the referent of "I" in liberation.

Furthermore, regarding the commentary’s phrase “he who [is so] from the perspective of ultimate reality” (*paramārthataḥ*), the construction is as follows: he who, due to internal and other sufferings, conceives himself as suffering—thinking “I am suffering”—or who, through delusion (*bhrāntyā*), conceives himself [as such], thinking “I am one possessed of delusion,” he alone [is the one meant]. Intending that the instrumental case in “through delusion” (*bhrāntyā*) is used in the sense of a state of being (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe tṛtīyā*), he says: “he who conceives his own self as being possessed of error,” and so forth. He alone is the means for the cessation of delusion.

For one who asserts that the state of being a sufferer (*duḥkhitva*) is established through delusion (*bhrānti*), it is not appropriate or fitting to engage in activity for the sake of removing that state of suffering, because the state of suffering would have ceased by its very nature. Consequently, one must say that, having reflected, "The delusion of my being a sufferer persists; may it cease," one engages in the means for achieving the cessation of that delusion. Yet even that is impossible according to your view, because there is an absence of both the possession of delusion and the capacity for reflective awareness (*pratisaṃdhātṛtva*) in the self-luminous experience (*anubhūti*).

Therefore, it must be stated that the activity [of the means of knowledge] is for the sake of removing one's own delusion regarding the *ahamartha* (the referent of "I") alone, and not for its own destruction—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "he states an inference," the words "in being manifested as 'I' in liberation" are to be supplied. Furthermore, the meaning is that "there is also an inference. It should be understood that because there is no other way to construe the word "and" (*ca*), the connection has been shown in this manner. The term to be explained is "by way of appearing thus"; its explanation is "by way of appearing for itself."

The ellipsis to be supplied is "and by way of appearing as 'I'. This should be understood because both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) must be demonstrated. Regarding the phrase "not identical with the probandum": the meaning of "it shines forth as 'I'" is its fitness for the linguistic usage "I"; and since this is already admitted—because the capacity [for such usage] exists at all times due to being habitually used as "I" during the state of transmigratory existence—it should not be said that this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). [Otherwise, there would be] identity with the probandum.

The meaning of "non-distinction from the probans" (*sādhyasya-sādhanena-aviśiṣṭatvam*) is "being already established" (*siddhatvam*). By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "it manifests as 'I' alone," what is intended is that manifestation is always conducive to linguistic usage (*vyavahārānuguṇya*). Since this [conduciveness] is not accepted by the opponent, there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*). Consequently, since there is no possibility of suspecting an identity between the "manifestation for oneself" (*svasmai bhāsamānatvam*)—which is commonly agreed upon as consisting in appearing as something subordinate to another—and the "manifestation as 'I'" (*aham iti bhāsamānatvam*)—which is disputed in the state of liberation (*mukti*)—how can the suspicion regarding non-distinction from the probandum be dismissed?

Regarding the phrase "by proving a qualification contrary to the probandum (*sādhyaviparītaviśeṣasādhakatayā*"): the meaning is that he raises the suspicion that [the reason] is contradictory to a specific qualification intended to prove [the probandum]. This is because transmigratoriness (*saṃsāritva*) is the opposite of that which is to be proven—namely, the state of appearing as "I" residing in liberation, which is obtained through the force of the property of being a subject-attribute (*pakṣadharmatā*). He states that [the reason] possesses a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*) because sublation (*bādha*) is consistent with the application of a reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*), and thus he offers another refutation. The sense is that the reason, such as transmigratoriness or sentience, is associated with ignorance in the form of karma (*karmarūpāvidyā*), and that [association] does not exist here [in the case of the Self].

Regarding the phrase "when there is a unity of attributes" (*dhamryaikye sati*): the meaning is that the superimposition of a relation (*saṃsargāropa*) is produced by *rajas*, while the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyāropa*) is produced by *tamas*. Some, however, say that the mere superimposition of something upon what is different from it is due to *rajas*; the superimposition of something upon its opposite is due to *tamas*; for example, the cognition of "attribute-ness" or "darkness-ness" in respect to an attribute or light, respectively. Regarding the phrase "because it is not a cause of ignorance, etc. (*ajñatvādyahetutvāt*), the difficulty lies in its implying that [the qualities] possess the nature of the substrate (upādhi) which is nescience (*avidyā*). Therefore, he states another alternative: "Or rather... (*athavā*).

"How then?"—with these words, he introduces the commentary [of Śaṅkara] with the passage beginning, "The great elements and the ego (ahaṃkāra) are included within the field," and so forth. The word *uttaratra* (later on) is to be construed with *parihārāt* (because of the refutation). "Ego-state" (*ahaṃbhāva*) means the cognition "I am. If it is asked: "Since the word 'instrument' (*karaṇa*) can possibly refer to the intellect (*buddhi*), why not accept that 'the instrument of the ego-state' means the perception of the ego-state, that is, the perception of 'I-ness' (*ahaṃtva*)?"—True, there is indeed such natural consistency [in that interpretation].

Nevertheless, since this very thing is the cause for the contempt of superior persons, in the subsequent commentary the word "this" (*ayam*)—referring to the meaning of the instrumental term—is unfit for reference because it is not neuter. Therefore, it must be stated that the meaning of the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is what is being referred to. Furthermore, in this context, if the word *ahaṃbhāva* were to mean "the state of being 'I'" (*ahaṃtva*), there would be an inconsistency because it would be impossible for that to be designated by the word "cow" (*go*). Consequently, the intention is that by the word *ahaṃbhāva*, it is precisely the notion of "I" (*ahaṃbuddhi*) that is being referred to.

The intention is that by the word "this" (*ayam*), the state of egoity (*ahaṃbhāva*)—which is not the subject under discussion—is intended. The meaning of the commentary, "But this very thing is *ahaṃkāra*," is as follows: that *ahaṃkāra*, which is another name for pride (*garva*) and is the cause of insulting superior persons, is taught in the scriptures as something to be abandoned; the construction is that "this very thing" is that [egoity]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the word "this" referring back to the *ahaṃkāra* that is the effect of the *mahat-tattva* (the Great Principle), which is the subject at hand. This is because the *ahaṃkāra* characterized as the state of egoity (*ahaṃbhāva*) has not been previously established [in the context].

Furthermore, because it is impossible to designate [the self] as "this very thing is the *ahaṃkāra*" as if it were an established fact, it is logical that the root *kṛ* refers to the intellect (*buddhi*). This is because, in the expression "he makes the sound like a frog" (*śabdadarduraṃ karoti*), the root *kṛ* is stated to have the meaning of "knowing. For this very reason, one should understand that the expressions "he makes a sound" (*śabdaṃ karoti*) and "a grammarian" (*śābdikaḥ*) are thus justified. In many lexicons, the reading "these two words, *ahaṃbhāva* and *ahaṃkāra*, contain within them the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃbuddhi*)" is observed; however, in that context, the word *ahaṃbhāva* is the result of a scribe's error.

Regarding the phrase "the sense of 'I' (ahaṃbhāva) in the non-self body," the word *ahaṃbhāva* here is like the word *ahaṃmati* in the rule "avidyā'haṃmatiḥ striyām" (avidyā and ahaṃmati are feminine). This is because [the former] lacks the suffix *-cvī*. Here, the etymology is in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), whereas in the previous case, the etymology was in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*); this is because the subsequent sentence provides the etymology specifically for the word *ahaṃkāra*. "Here, the etymology is in the sense of an abstract state" means: in the delusion consisting of the notion of self in what is not the self. "In the previous case" refers to...

The meaning is: in that which is called *ahaṃkāra*, the effect of the principle of *mahat*. Regarding the phrase "by being within the scope of what is to be adopted": the intention is that this is because the necessity of performing the cognition of "I" (*ahaṃbuddhi*) is stated in the passage, "Now, therefore, the instruction on *ahaṃkāra*. As for the statement "that word *ahaṃkāra*," the distinction here is as follows: the word *ahaṃkāra* is of two kinds—derived from a form ending in the suffix *cvipratyaya* and not so derived. That which is derived is further twofold: an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) and an agentive noun (*kartṛsādhana*). The one derived from a form ending in *cvipratyaya* is an abstract noun denoting pride (*garva*).

The word *ahaṃkāra*, derived from a suffix ending in *cvipratyaya* and denoting an instrument (*karaṇa*), refers to the *ahaṃkāra-tattva* (the principle of ego). However, the word derived from a suffix ending in *ac* and functioning as a noun (*bhāvasādhana*) denotes the *ahaṃ-pratyaya* (the notion of "I") which is the object to be acquired (*upādeya*). To the objection—"In the verse beginning with 'And hear now of ignorance,' it is stated that the notion of self in what is not-self is the supreme cause [of bondage], but not the notion of 'I' in what is not-self; therefore, how can this verse serve as proof for the meaning you have stated?"—he replies with the words "In this very Purāṇa," and so forth.

"The connection with the aforementioned error" means the connection with the error consisting in the cognition of a self in what is not-self. With the possibility of the word-break "the non-connection of ignorance" (*avidyāyā ayoga*) in mind, he explains that very same meaning by way of its opposite: "because the referent of 'I' (*ahamartha*) is not the self. "The non-connection with error" means the non-connection with the state of being an error regarding the self.
[This concludes] the refutation of the superior authority of scripture in the face of perceptual contradiction.

"If it is argued that by this [example], the fact that other perceptions are rooted in defects is inferred"—this means that since some perceptions are seen to be rooted in defects such as cataracts (*kāca*), one might infer that other perceptions are likewise rooted in cataracts and similar defects. Thus, in all subsequent instances, the word "defect" (*doṣa*) should be understood as referring to defects such as cataracts. Consequently, the doubt—namely, how this statement could be self-contradictory for a primary proponent of falsehood when addressed to his own partial adherent—is dispelled.

He demonstrates the method for connecting the phrase "What is this defect? with the words "that which was stated" in the Bhāṣya. The meaning is as follows: by means of this specific formulation of the sentence, "What is this defect?", he asks what that "defect"—the very root that was mentioned as the basis for the possibility of alternative explanations (anyathāsiddhi)—is, such that all perception of difference would be sublated by scripture.

Regarding what was stated—namely, "what is the fault in [the word] being neuter? and because it is extremely difficult to establish grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the masculine [term]—he explains it otherwise: "Or rather, by the force of the word *yat*. This means: "because pervasion (*vyāpti*) as a reason is not observed," the remainder of the sense being "of the nature of the latent impression of difference" (*bhedavāsanātvasya*). That is to say, because the latent impression of difference is pervaded by being the cause of erroneous cognition (*viparītajñāna*), the meaning is that there is a necessary connection (*saṃbandha*) due to its predominance.

"In the commentary, [it is said] 'that which sublates all distinctions heard through hearing'—the meaning is that reflection (*manana*) and so forth consist in the repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) of the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, which was understood at the time of hearing (*śravaṇa*) by way of having sublated all distinctions."

Nor should it be doubted: "Even if reflection (*manana*) consists in the practice of the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, why should the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self not also consist in the practice of the sublation of all differences? For the purpose of establishing the oneness of Brahman and the Self, it is necessary to ascertain that the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self involves the sublation of difference, in order to establish the falsity of everything other than it; furthermore, this consideration regarding whether [the realization] consists in reflection will be carried out in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*.

First, it is agreed that [the appearance of duality] has its root in the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of differentiation; the sense is that this is because it is rooted in the latent impressions of the distinction between base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth. And that [impression] is a defect (*doṣa*).

If it is objected: "Since a defect (*doṣa*) is the cause of error, how can the knowledge produced by the Vedānta—which has pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as its object—be considered a valid cognition (*pramā*), given that it would then necessarily be produced by a defect? The answer is: No. For even the knowledge consisting of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is false (*mithyā*) because it is distinct from Brahman; therefore, its being produced by a defect is necessary. Furthermore, since it is produced by an error regarding its own objective fitness (*yogyatābhrama*), the knowledge produced by the scripture must also be admitted to be an error. This is the intended meaning. And the realization of falsity follows from the realization that [the world] is sublatable by knowledge.

Now, it may be argued: at the time of hearing [the scriptures], since the falsity of everything other than Brahman is already understood through the scriptural text itself, namely, "There is no diversity here," and since the realization of falsity must have a defect as its root, it follows that the defect lies precisely in the persistence of the notion of difference. If this is so, why resort to this circuitous path when a direct one exists? To this, some reply: indeed, at the time of hearing... [text fragment]

The fact that [the perception of difference] is produced by a defect (*doṣajanyatva*) was not understood during the stage of hearing (*śravaṇa*), because it is only in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* itself that the falsity (*mithyātva*) of that which is distinct from Brahman and the fact that the cognition of difference is produced by a defect are being investigated; furthermore, since the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* belongs to the second chapter, which consists of reflection (*manana*), there might be the apprehension that, due to the lack of knowledge regarding its being produced by a defect at the time of hearing, the knowledge generated by the scripture (*śāstra*)—being posterior—would act as a sublater. It is for the purpose of dispelling this doubt that the commentary states, "understood during the stage of hearing," and so forth.

Furthermore, since reflection (*manana*) serves to consolidate the meaning understood through hearing (*śravaṇa*), at the very time of hearing there must necessarily be a cognition of the falsity of difference; consequently, there must also necessarily be a cognition that such a cognition is produced by a defect (*doṣa*). Otherwise, even if the understanding arising from the scriptures during the time of hearing were subsequent [to the prior cognition], it would not have the power to sublate [it], because its object would still be the falsity of difference—this is the sense they express.

"Exclusion of the mass of words" (śabdarāśivyāvṛttiḥ) means the exclusion of the mass of words that do not constitute the scripture (aśāstrabhūta-śabdārāśivyāvṛttiḥ). The word "by you" (tvayā) is to be explained [as the agent]. "The state of being devoid of all particularities due to self-established nature" (svataḥsiddhatvena nirdhūtanikhilaviśeṣatvam): the sense is that because it is self-established, there is an absence of origination due to the non-existence of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), and as was stated previously, "other modifications, which are dependent upon origination, do not exist."

In order to refute the opponent’s position—which is the very head of the conceptual construction regarding the ultimate reality—he refutes the view that [the world] is not the ultimate reality by stating, "If it were the proof... (*sādhakaṃ cet*). Although the refutation of its conventional status (*vyāvahārikatva*) will be addressed later in the Bhāṣya starting with the words, "Who is this so-called 'conventional' person? (*ko'yaṃ vyāpahāriko nāma*?), it should be understood that this was stated here as well, intending to show that these same refutations are applicable even in this context. The term *yauktikabādha* means "sublation by reasoning" (*yukti*), according to the rule *tena dīvyati* (Pāṇini 4.1.2), which prescribes the suffix *uñ* in the sense of "one who plays/diverts himself with that. Thus is the sense.

Regarding the phrase "produced by the scribe's own timira": here, some [commentators] hold that because it was previously established that the cognition of unreality occurs solely on the basis of being a cognition produced by a defect—even when not sublated by perceptual or other cognitions apprehending the absence of that [unreality]—it is this very point that is intended to be demonstrated here as well. Thus, for a person with *timira* who already knows [the truth], even though no subverting valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has arisen regarding the non-existence of the double moon, the double moon [appears] merely through the recollection of one's own defect.

This is because [the opponent's argument] aims at the point that Brahman is known as false simply by being the object of a cognition produced by defects (*doṣajanya-jñāna*), since such false cognitions are observed even among those who perceive Brahman; furthermore, even if no person—whether through a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that is indirect (*parokṣa*) or direct (*aparokṣa*)—engages with a cognition grasping the non-existence of Brahman despite its being devoid of distinctions, Brahman’s falsity will still be understood precisely as being the object of a cognition produced by defects. This is also supported by the statement regarding Brahman being "beyond the reach of other persons," which intends to demonstrate the non-arising of any means of knowledge—such as scripture (*upadeśa*), etc.—that could grasp an absence in the form of a direct perception.

Furthermore, because [the cognition] is successful, there is no need for those suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) to seek out authoritative testimony (*āptavākya*) and the like when their vision is impaired by cataracts; thus, there is an absence of even such hardship. For this very reason, the subsequent passage stating that "the determination of falsity occurs through the cognition of another person" is also untenable. If the determination of falsity were to result from the arising of a sublation (*bādha*) through the cognition of another person, then it would follow that falsity is determined solely by that subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*). How, then, could the notion of falsity be established in a case devoid of such a subverting cognition?

If the cognition of falsity—whose sole refuge is the state of being an object of knowledge produced by defects—is established through an alternative method even in the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) for other persons, then it would be possible for those very people afflicted with ophthalmia (*taimirika*), once their own [illusory] cognitions are known, to cognize falsity simply because those objects are objects of knowledge produced by defects; thus, the recourse to other persons would be useless. Therefore, they prefer the reading "of one whose own ophthalmia is known. [Objection: But [the text says] "it is false together with its own object, Brahman."

The commentary is not improper; for one might object that falsity (mithyātva) ought to be attributed only to a cognition produced by a defect (*doṣa*), since the nature of the cognition itself is not false. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It was stated [in the commentary] by way of accepting the opponent's view. The sense is that because it is accepted that the person who perceives two moons possesses falsity along with the error (*viparyaya*), here too falsity is attributed to both the cognition and its object.

[Objection: But surely, according to the opponent's view (*paramata*), even the cognition of the oneness of the moon is merely false; why then is the falsity of the cognition of two moons specifically stated to be due to its being produced by a defect (*doṣa*)? Nor should it be said that the cognition of the oneness of the moon is "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*) while the cognition of duality is not, because both are of the same nature insofar as they are not sublated by any valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Response: No.

It should be understood that by accepting the view that ignorance (avidyā) residing in the consciousness delimited by this "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) manifests in the form of a semblance of the cognition of silver, the illusory nature of the cognition of silver is demonstrated; furthermore, because it is of a phenomenal nature, the cognition of two moons is distinct from the cognition of the moon's oneness, and because it is produced by adventitious defects.

Since the term "application" (*prayoga*) is appropriate only for inference (*anumāna*), one might ask: "How can the term 'application' be used for reasoning (*tarka*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because it is a statement that demonstrates pervasion (*vyāpti*). Regarding the phrase "unestablished in either [of the two parties]": in my view, this means "not established. Consequently, the objection that the unestablished nature of the *āpādaka* (the subsumer) is a defect should be understood as being devoid of merit. Some, however, forgetting its status as reasoning, raise the objection of unestablishedness; for this very reason, they say it will be refuted precisely by resorting to its status as reasoning.
This concludes the refutation of the notion that truth can be apprehended through what is unreal.

Regarding the phrase in the *Bhāṣya*, "even though it is not real (*asatya*)": it should be understood that the phrase "because it is a cause of fear" from the preceding passage is to be supplied here. Regarding the *Bhāṣya* statement, "it is indeed real (*vastubhūta*) in the case of a net and so forth": "real" (*vastubhūta*) is a qualification of the specific appearance (*pratibhāsa-viśeṣa*) of the face and so on; it is not a qualification of the net and such. The meaning is that being an object (*viṣayatva*) consists precisely in being manifest (*pratibhāsamānatva*). The sense is that the intention of the *Bhāṣya* is that being manifest is all that is required for the conventional usage of "objective support" (*ālambana*). Therefore, [the text says] "unreal in that form."

The meaning is that [the object] is not [required] even in the form of being manifest. Likewise, "manifesting directly" means being perceived as existing. Therefore, the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) based on the case of knowledge of another's mind is refuted. "It is not required as a cause for cognition" means that while it lacks causality, it possesses the status of an object (*viṣayatva*). In the case of something existing, however, both [causality and object-status] are present; this is the meaning of the sentence. In reality, it is simply the state of existing.

The meaning is that even though a thing exists in the form of mere appearance, it does not exist in reality. This is the point: some properties depend upon the existence of the substratum (dharmin), while others do not. Among these, properties such as being manifest, non-existence, pastness, and futureness are independent of the substratum; whereas properties such as causality and having a form are dependent upon it.

In that regard, existence in reality (*vastuto vidyamānatvam*) consists precisely in the subsistence of a thing as qualified by properties that depend upon the substratum (*dharmin*). And "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) is [effected] by its own objective support (*ālambana*). It should not be argued that if exclusion is produced [by the objective support], then because the objective support is unreal, it would follow that truth is established from the untrue. The point is this: the state of being an excluder (*vyāvartakatva*)—which consists either in being known by the cognition that produces the notion of exclusion, or in having a specific nature that determines its belongingness—is possible even for that which is non-existent at that time. Otherwise, even in the view that [exclusion] is non-different [from the object], the same fault would apply.

If it is argued that "it is indeed possible for non-existent things alone to function as objects (*ālambana*) due to the influence of defects, and from that very fact they can also serve as differentiators (*vyāvartaka*), since being a differentiator does not necessarily consist in being a cause; thus, since the desired conclusion is established by this justification alone, what is the point of this further investigation?"—this is true. However, it should be understood that even the status of being an object (*ālambanatva*) is not possible for that which is absolutely non-existent, and this [investigation] is undertaken incidentally (*prāsaṅgika*) to demonstrate that. In some cases, its comprehension occurs through implication (*arthāt*).

"From an object with which the rays of the eye, reflected by a mirror, have come into contact"—this is the meaning. "Because of appearing in some cases"—the intention is that this refers to the state of dreaming.

Avoiding the redundancy between the terms *asataḥ* (of the non-existent) and *nirupākhyasya* (of the indefinable), he explains [the passage] as being intended to refute two alternative positions, beginning with: "The meaning is 'of that which is non-existent,' i.e., distinct from the existent," and so forth. In the Bhāṣya, the phrase "of the means and the goal," etc., [is explained].

Although Vācaspati Miśra, while commenting on Śaṅkara’s *Bhāṣya* on the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*—which states: "The comprehension of the real letters such as 'A' is seen to result from the comprehension of the unreal lines"—says: "Even though the nature of the lines is real, nevertheless, they are unreal according to convention (*yathāsaṃketam asatya*). For those who establish the convention do not say, 'This letter is to be understood by means of such a distinction of lines,' but rather, 'Such a distinction of lines is itself the letter A.'"

Furthermore, because it is stated that "from an incorrect convention, there arises the comprehension of correct phonemes," and thus the comprehension of true syllables is caused by the comprehension of false syllables, there is no identity between the probandum and the probans. Nevertheless, the intent remains focused on the previous refutation. Regarding the phrase "by the lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokena*): [one might object] that the refutation was already stated under the third position—that the letter *repha* is perceived as having the nature of a phoneme—within the context of the position that it is the cause of a portion of cognition.

If it is asked why there is this "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*) when it is logical that the refutation is stated regarding the aspect of being composed of phonemes (*varṇātmatā*), some say that the mention of the lion’s glance is appropriate because they intend for the aspect of being composed of phonemes to have entered into the first position. Others, however, hold that this is an alternative explanation for those who do not accept that the treatise proceeds by way of tenfold alternatives (*daśavikalpa*) through the "lion’s glance"; therefore, they believe the word "or" (*vā*) must be supplied.

Regarding the phrase "by means of that which has the nature of non-existent phonemes" (*avidyamānavarṇātmanā*), the state of being non-existent (*avidyamānatva*) is a qualification of the nature of the phonemes (*varṇātmatva*). Intending to show that even though the phoneme exists, its nature as a phoneme is non-existent, he explains it as a qualification by saying "by means of having the nature of non-existent phonemes. The meaning of the commentary's statement "even from a line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavayād api*) is as follows: one should not accept the view that the cognition of a real gavaya arises from an unreal gavaya superimposed upon a line; for there is no evidence for the superimposition of a gavaya upon a mere line.

Rather, by showing a line resembling that of a gavaya, they inform [the person] that "a gavaya is similar to this," and they understand it exactly in that way. And that similarity is indeed real. This concludes the refutation of the theory of *sphoṭa*.

Regarding the phrase "the distinction of *katva*, *khatva*, and so forth": here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), qualities such as acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), high-pitched (*tāra*), low-pitched (*mandra*), and long (*dīrgha*) are included. Regarding the statement "sound is superimposed" (*śabda āropita*): the meaning is that it is superimposed upon the sound whose nature is *sphoṭa*. According to the system of the proponents of *sphoṭa* (*sphoṭavādin*), everything—such as *khatva* and the like, as well as acute accent and so on—belongs exclusively to the *nāda* (articulated sound); for they maintain that apart from both *sphoṭa* and *nāda*, there are no phonemes (*varṇa*) at all that could serve as the substrata for *katva* and the rest. However, for those who maintain the eternity of phonemes (*varṇanityatvavādin*), the phonemes that serve as the substrata for *katva* and the rest are eternal.

The distinction is that qualities such as high pitch (*tāra*) and length (*dīrgha*) belong to the sound (*nāda*), not to the phoneme itself. [The opponent claims] that the "particularity of manifestation" (*abhivyaktiviśeṣa*) is real; here, "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) means cognition (*jñāna*). For this very reason, he will later state: "in a form qualified by the manifestation which has *katva* (the property of being *k*) and so forth as its objective support. Now, as to why the drum-sound (*dundubhi*) and the like are not excluded, he says: "but that [sound] is unmanifested. The meaning is that since even that [drum-sound] is not distinct from the letter *ga* and so forth insofar as it possesses the nature of *ga*, there is no exclusion by the word "only" (*eva*).

"Because it lacks the quality of being a cause for the cognition of a different object already experienced. This is the underlying point: does the assistance (*sācivya*) of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) occur directly in the cognition of the meaning from the word, or through the mediation of the memory of its own constituent phonemes (*varṇa*)? In neither case is the causality of the latent impression possible. Since the experience of the word-meaning and the cognition of the word-meaning are not produced by the latent impressions of the phonemes, they cannot provide assistance in that cognition. Nor can there be assistance through the mediation of the memory of its own phonemes; [for that memory would itself require a cause].

Because mental impressions (*saṃskāras*) only cause the recollection of their own respective objects, a collective recollection (*samūhālambana-smṛti*) is impossible. For this very reason, he will state later on that "acting simultaneously is logical. By abandoning the definition of a word (*pada*) as a collection of phonemes delimited by a single meaning, and instead adopting the view that a word is a collection of multiple phonemes ending in a single case-suffix, the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) is refuted; thus he says, "And not because of the unity of meaning," [meaning] that the unity of meaning follows from the unity of the word.

The sense is that the conceptualization of an object as having a form that serves as the basis for the application [of a word] is dependent upon following the usage of a single term. And it has been said: "Because blue lotuses have a single basis for the application of one word, they possess a single configuration; however, the 'cowness' of a broken [potsherd] is not like that, because there is no single word [applying to them]. Alternatively, since individual pots are manifold and thus lack unity in themselves, the unity of the denoted object is based solely on the unity of the expressive word; this is the sense. Thus, there would be no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

If being merely *subandha* (bound by a suffix) or being merely *tiṅanta* (ending in a verbal suffix) were the criteria for being a *pada*, there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*). However, if both are unified by means of their commonality as *vibhakti* (inflectional endings), such a fault does not arise; this is the intended meaning. Some, however, argue that in the rule *ekavibhaktau*, the word *eka* is redundant, because the mere fact of ending in an inflectional suffix (*vibhaktyantatva*) is itself non-overextended (*anatiprasakta*). This is because a collection of words such as *nīlo ghaṭaḥ* lacks the status of ending in an inflectional suffix according to the *pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā* (the technical rule regarding the mention of suffixes).

For a case ending (*vibhakti*) does not arise from a composite whole (*samudāya*); otherwise, it would follow that even [the individual words within a compound] would possess the status of a *pada* according to the rule "that which has a *sup* or *tiṅ* suffix is a *pada*. They argue that there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) because the designation *pada* is possible even for the constituent words of a compound by relying on the internal case endings. However, in the case of words such as *saindhava*, which denote multiple meanings, those meanings already employed [in a specific context] would not have the status of a *pada*. Therefore, he says: "established through a single derivation" (*ekavyutpattisiddha*).

The point here is that the capacity to convey a single meaning [belongs to words] according to the distinction of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Consequently, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the definition to a sentence] is avoided, because even a sentence conveys a single meaning characterized by a relation (*saṃsarga-lakṣaṇa-viśiṣṭa-rūpa*). It should be understood that while a sentence’s capacity to convey a qualified meaning is obtained through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of words possessing mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, it is not obtained through linguistic convention. Just as there is no dependence on the eye in the cognition of "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*).

The meaning is that, just as the cognition of "audibility"—defined as being the object of a cognition produced by the eye—is not itself produced by the eye, so too the cognition of "soundness"—defined as being graspable by the ear—is not produced by the ear.

[This refers to] the cognition of visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*), audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*), and so forth. Now, one might object: even if audibility is designated as occupying the position of visibility, sound-ness (*śabdatva*) is not designated as occupying the position of visibility, but rather as occupying the position of color-form-ness (*rūpatva*). Consequently, just as color-form-ness differs from visibility, so too sound-ness ought to differ from being grasped by the ear (*śrotragrāhyatva*); otherwise, there would be a tautology in saying "sound" and "audible. To this we reply: no.

If being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*) were the very nature of being color (*rūpatva*), then it would follow that even a jar (*ghaṭa*) and other such objects would possess the nature of color; therefore, although being color is distinct from being visible, there is no subverting argument against [the claim that] being sound (*śabdatva*) is the nature of being perceivable by the ear (*śrotragrāhyatva*). Nor should it be argued that being perceivable by the ear is over-extended (*atiprasakta*) to qualities such as *katva* (the property of being *ka*), for there is no subverting argument against the view that being sound is the nature of being a quality perceivable by the ear. Some, however, describe even being color as simply the nature of being a quality perceivable by the eye.

"Preceded by the recollection of the word as something already understood" means that for a person who has grasped the pervasion of the definition of "word-ness"—namely, that qualities such as *katva* and *khatva* are perceivable by the auditory organ—the inference of "word-ness" occurs precisely without the prior recollection of that pervasion.
This is the refutation of the doubt regarding the truth of the treatise (*śāstra*).

"In the case of the causes for the realization of truth" (*satyapratipattihetuṣu*): the phrase "in the view of those who maintain the reality of phenomenal proliferation" (*prapañcasatyatvavādimata*) is to be supplied. It should be understood that this is not according to our own view; for in our own view, there is nothing other than the Vedānta that serves as a cause for the realization of truth. Regarding the commentary's statement, "of the knowledge produced by a scripture that is false": the meaning is that since the scripture does not exist, the cognition arising from the delusion "the scripture exists" must necessarily be a delusion.

This is because, in the preceding section of the text, the erroneous nature of the cognition "the scripture exists" has already been established. Otherwise, due to the absence of a relationship between the preceding and succeeding sections as that of the proven and the proof, the preceding section would be rendered entirely purposeless; this should be understood from the fact that the purpose is fulfilled by the statement beginning with "of the ignorance which is the cause of the false scripture. Furthermore, the claim that the identity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun is not being propounded because the passage is intended as a mere praise (*stuti*) would constitute a departure from established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*). Now, an objection may be raised: "A scriptural text whose purport is praise is more authoritative than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."

The passage beginning with “The sun is the sacrificial post” (ādityo yūpaḥ) does not have its purport in the identity of the sacrificial post and the sun; for even in that case, if it were intended as a statement of praise, there would be the consequence of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, because it is not intended [to convey such an identity], the statement “The sun is the sacrificial post” and so forth does not sublate perception. Nor should it be suspected that, by this logic, the corporeal form of deities and the like would also not be established—since they too would lack a [primary] purport; for when there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge, validity regarding the perceived object is established even in the absence of a [primary] purport.

If it is argued: "In cases such as the corporeal form (*vigraha*) of a deity, since there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), even if that form is established, it is not so in the case of the identity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun, because that [identity] contradicts other means of knowledge and lacks *tātparya* (intended meaning). Furthermore, in the case of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*), since the six marks of *tātparya* are present, there is no fear of contradiction with perception; this is indeed our established conclusion"—we say: No. For even if an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for praise has an internal *tātparya* directed toward the object serving as the means for that praise, there is no resulting split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even the corporeal form of deities and so forth would remain unestablished; furthermore, since all followers of the Veda accept that the authority of the Vedas resides solely in their intended meaning (*tātparya*), it is altogether improper to claim that the passage does not establish the identity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun because its purpose is mere praise (*stuti*). Rather, the ultimate conclusion is simply that there is no identity between the sacrificial post and the sun, because such an identity is impossible as an intended meaning due to its contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*).

The point is this: even though the world of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca*) is false, it is established that the [Vedic] texts do not have that as their intended meaning (*tātparya*) because they would contradict other means of valid cognition. This is the meaning of the verse beginning with *asaṃnikṛṣṭa*: regarding the definition of scripture (*śāstra*) as “scripture is [a source of knowledge] regarding an object not in contact [with the senses] through the instrument of words,” the phrase *asaṃnikṛṣṭa* is intended to exclude two things. What are those two? Determination by way of identity (*tādrūpyeṇa paricchittiḥ*), and determination by way of its opposite (*tadviparyayataḥ paricchittiḥ*). In other words, the absence of both a proving and a subverting means of valid cognition (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

"Characterized by not being the object of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)" means "not being sublated by other means of valid cognition. Intending to show that the word "thus" (*iti*) in the Bhāṣya phrase "thus, [the view] is poorly established" appropriately refers to the refutation of the superiority of the [opposing] scripture (*śāstra*), he says: "the refutation of the superiority of the scripture. Intending to highlight the natural sense of the word "fallacious reasoning" (*kutarka*), he says: "as for that which is perception" (*yattu pratyakṣam*). This is the section on the Śruti.

"In that case too" means "even in the example. "Modification" (*vikāra*) refers to a state such as being a jar (*ghaṭatva*). Now, one might object: since in the previous instance there was a reference by the word *mṛnmaya*—which ends in the suffix *-maya* denoting a modification—it would be appropriate here as well to refer to it by the word "modification" (*vikāra*). Consequently, since in the previous instance the substrate of the state was referred to by the word *mṛnmaya*, it would be more appropriate here to refer to the substratum itself by the word "modification."

If it is argued that this does not refer to the state (*avasthā*), that is true; for in the previous case, the word "made of clay" (*mṛnmaya*) referred to the possessor of the state. However, in this instance, such a reference is not appropriate. For if that were the case, the non-difference between cause and effect would not be established. Indeed, the mere fact that a jar is touched by a lump of clay for the sake of a specific effect does not prove the non-difference between the toucher and the touched. Therefore, one must admit that the words "clay" (*mṛd*) and "modification made of clay" (*mṛnmayavikāra*) have distinct meanings.

For this very reason, the intended meaning is that in the passage "Only 'clay' is real," there is no reference to the state indicated by the immediately preceding word for the modification (*vikāra*). [The phrase] "by means of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) 'This is clay, this is a pot'" is used. On this point, some hold that because of the force of the particle *iti*, or because the cognition or the word itself must be what is referred back, the meaning of the Śruti is that the cognition "it is clay" alone is real.

The subsequent passage should be understood as stating the resultant meaning: that if that cognition is true, then the non-sublated nature of the clay-substance (*mṛd-dravyatva*) is established. Nor should it be argued: "What is the fault in adopting the following meaning: 'That which consists of clay—namely, 'clay' alone—is true, authoritative, and is so perceived by an authority'? For the word *iti* must be construed with either the authority (*pramāṇa*) or the perception (*pratīti*), such that one would have to say either "it is perceived by an authority as 'clay'" or "it is perceived by that authority which has the form 'clay'."

It must be said: for when the instruction is given that "it is cognized through a means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇataḥ pratīyate*), such a cognition of the logical concomitance (*anvaya*) becomes possible. They argue that because the word "truth" (*satya*) brings about cognition, it functions as an indicator (*gamaka*) in that way. Others, however, maintain that just as in the case of the expression "cognized through a means of valid knowledge as being made of clay" (*mṛttiketyeva pramāṇataḥ pratīyate*), since the understanding of "truth" in the same manner is established by experience and thus cannot be denied, there is no fault in stating that "that which is true is cognized through a means of valid knowledge as being made of clay" (*mṛnmayaṃ mṛdviketyeva satyaṃ pramāṇapratipannam*).

For this very reason, there is no room for objection even regarding the *Ṭīkā* statement that "the meaning is that it is authoritative precisely as a substance consisting of clay"; for they argue that even that sentence serves as a means of comprehension (*gamaka*). Now, one might object: when the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is to be refuted by way of demonstrating the non-difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*), why is it necessary to establish that a modification (*vikāra*) is obtained?

If it is asked, "For what purpose is it demonstrated that even the name is non-different [from the material], since it possesses a specific utility?"—this is true. It must be understood that unless it is established that even names such as "pot" belong to the lump of clay itself, the non-difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) will not be firmly established; therefore, that too must be demonstrated. Now, one might object: "Since even the Naiyāyikas and others accept the existence of the nature of clay within clay-made objects like pots and bowls, how does this result in the refutation of the theory of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*)? We reply: No.

The intention of the scripture, "Only 'it is clay' is true," is not merely to establish that [the pot] is simply clay; rather, its purpose is to establish the non-difference from the material cause—the clay substance—through the recognition of non-difference expressed as, "This very same clay-substance is this [pot]. Regarding the phrase "when the knowledge of all is established": the meaning is that this question was asked when [Yājñavalkya] was asked, "What is that thing by the knowledge of which everything becomes known? O Venerable Sir, please tell me that."

The deluded one suspects that although "the non-existent" (asat) is of a different nature from "the existent" (sat), this is not by way of its being of a dissimilar class (*vijātīyatva*). This is the intended meaning: by the single word "this" (*idam*) in the phrase "this is indeed existent," one must exclude from the world designated by the word "this"—prior to its creation—its being of a different nature from the existent, its being other than it, or its being opposed to it; however, there is no negation of the distinction of dissimilar classes within this entire world.

For example, when it is said, "The jar exists in the forenoon," the particle *eva* excludes from the jar either its being of a different genus than existence (*sad-vijātīyatva*), or its being other than existence (*sad-anyatva*), or its being opposed to existence (*sad-virodhitva*); it does not, however, exclude all distinctions consisting of difference from things such as cloth throughout the entire world. Now, an objection may be raised: if by the phrase "existence alone" (*sadeva*) the existence belonging to the period prior to creation is understood, then the fact that Brahman is the cause would remain unestablished.

Fearing that if the term *sat* were used to denote Brahman, the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) would not be refuted—since the existence characterized by fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition (*māna-sambandha-yogyatva-lakṣaṇa-sattā*) is not conveyed by the word *sat* alone—he says: "For the word *sat* [denotes] fitness for connection with a means of valid cognition. The sense is that this ground for the application of the term (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) is fully present in Brahman alone. Now, one might object: since the world possesses the nature of Being (*sad-ātmatva*) even now, the word "in the beginning" (*agre*) is redundant.

Furthermore, since the exclusion of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*) is already established by the phrase "there was only one," the statement "there was Being alone" (*sadevāsīt*) would be redundant. Moreover, if the word "this" (*idam*) refers to the world, it is incorrect to say "there was Being," because the world cannot be identical with Brahman. Nor is it correct for the phrase to refer to Brahman as having that [world] as its body, because it is impossible for the word "this" to convey a meaning as extensive as Brahman to Śvetaketu, who has not yet studied the Vedānta. [Reply: This is not so; for the word "this" refers to this world prior to its creation.

The meaning is that in the beginning, Being alone existed—that is, the Brahman alone existed as Being, one, with name and form undivided. The word "in the beginning" (agra) is indeed meaningful because the world no longer possesses such a nature of Being [now]. Even when it is said, "there was only one Being," although there is the understanding that name and form were undivided, the word "Being" (sat) remains meaningful because it is intended to establish that [the world] has that very Brahman as its essence.

If it be objected: "But since this has been explained in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* and the *Śrutaprakāśikā* as 'this entire world was indeed one and existent prior to creation,' how can it be so?"—it is not so; for while "existent" (*sat*) serves as a qualifier of the subject (*uddeśya*) which is already established, it is not included within the category of the predicate (*vidheya*) because it is unestablished [in that specific context], and thus its intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies precisely here [in the present argument].

Although Śvetaketu, who had not studied the Vedānta, did not understand this at the very moment the statement was made, nevertheless—with the thought that he would understand that Brahman has the universe as its body through the word "this" immediately after the teaching on the identity of the body and the Self—it was taught by the Teacher [Uddālaka] that "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. Thus, there is no contradiction when it is so stated. Now, one might object: just as in the forenoon a jar and the like were merely clay, and afterwards they came into being in the form of a jar and so forth; [so too must the world have been previously non-existent].

If it is asked, "Why should there not be a designation such as 'the jar, the bowl, and so forth, consist of clay alone'?"—we reply: no. For one who has heard the scriptural passage beginning with "having entered by means of this living self," there is no possibility of suspecting that [the world] is a transformation of Brahman in its own essential nature; rather, there arises only the perception of the body-self relationship. Consequently, even by the word "this," there can only be the perception of Brahman whose body is the universe.

"Of the specific qualities of the dependent nature (*paratantra-rūpa*)," means of time, unseen destiny (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth. He demonstrates the connection with the subsequent sentence starting with "only one," etc. "By the existence of Brahman at all times" means that because the non-difference of Brahman—which is the substratum for the fullness that is the ground for the application of the word 'Being' (*sat*)—is taught in the passage "This was Being alone," any suspicion that the effect might ever be non-existent is removed. "Aiming at the refutation of the Vaiśeṣika doctrine" [means as follows].

And it should not be argued that, such being the case, the restatement, "In the beginning, indeed, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," would be untenable because they do not accept it as such; for the same fault applies even in the refutation of the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda). Indeed, nothing "one and without a second" is accepted by the proponent of emptiness, since he accepts only the perpetual emptiness of all things.

The sense is that if that sentence does not intend to convey oneness and non-duality, then the same would apply to the Vaiśeṣika as well. This is because [the Upaniṣadic teaching] depends upon the refutation of the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others. If it is argued: "But was that not already refuted in the passage 'Clay alone is real'? Otherwise, having accepted that everything is possible through the knowledge of one thing, the request for instruction—'May the Blessed One indeed tell me that'—would be untenable," we say: No.

The point here is that [the opponent's view] has been refuted with supporting arguments following a restatement of their position. As for the example, "just as that which is produced from clay has clay as its essence," one should not object by asking how such a consequence can be drawn since it is not admitted that the world is produced from the Existent (*sat*). For it is said: "In the beginning, the world was non-existent (*asat*)."

Now, when it is said that "the existent was [previously] non-existent," it would imply that the existent has a non-existent as its material cause (*upādāna*). One should understand that this objection is raised based on the certainty that, just as when it is said, "Previously the jar, bowl, and so forth were clay, and later the jar and so forth came into being," the relationship between material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) is thereby established. The meaning is: how could there be the possibility of a state without a substratum?

The meaning is this: just as the great principle (*mahat*) and the rest, which have *prakṛti* as their material cause, do not lack manifestness, so too for an existent thing that has the non-existent as its material cause, there is no attainment of non-existence; for since the attainment of the state of existence is impossible, how could a state without a substratum be obtained? "By being of that very nature" means: in the preceding sentence, "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*), "having that as its self" (*aitadātmyam*) means "having that as its essence" (*etadātmakam*); the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own primary sense.

And therefore, the sense is that even in the subsequent statement, "That is the Truth," the reality of the world—characterized by the previously mentioned form and consisting of that very [Brahman] as its supreme substrate—is established. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the relationship of body and embodied between the world and Brahman has already been stated by the phrase 'This is its self,' the further specification 'That is the Self' is redundant. To dispel this doubt, he says: "as in the case of 'Rāma is Lakṣmaṇa’s elder brother. Alternatively, it may be read as: "That is your Self."

In this context, the avoidance of redundancy between the two statements, "That is the Self" (*sa ātmā*) and "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), must somehow be considered. The phrase "ending with that" means that the meaning of "That thou art" extends up to those [preceding stages]. This refers to the fact that the words *tat*, *tvam*, and so forth, culminate in that [realization], which is the essential, resultant meaning of the entire section beginning with "That thou art"; however, it should not be understood as referring to the meaning of the sentence "That thou art" alone, for that sentence by itself does not possess such a comprehensive meaning.

"By the apavāda-sūtra *igupadhāt kaḥ*. This means by the apavāda-sūtra *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. If it is argued: "The suffix *ka* characterized by the condition *igupadha* does not sublate the suffix *ac* prescribed for the *pacādi* group; for if that were the case, forms such as *devama* would result in failure [to be established], since the recourse to the *pacādi* list is intended precisely to sublate the suffix *ka*," we say: no, because of a lack of understanding of the matter.

It should be understood that in the rule *nandigrahipacādibhyaḥ*, there is no fault in stating that the suffix *ka*—characterized by having a vowel with the marker *i* as its penultimate (*igupadha*)—sublates the suffix *ac*, because the latter is suspected of being an optional (*aupasaṃkhyānika*) suffix added by the statement "the suffix *ac* should be prescribed after all verbal roots. This is because the term "beginning with *pra*" (*pracādi*) is seen used for even such optional *ac* suffixes in various treatises.

"The meaning of the root [√śās] is 'instruction' (śāsana). Regarding this, some raise an objection: as for the claim that "the meaning of the root is instruction because of its common usage," that is indeed true. Since the author of the *Dhātuvṛtti* has explained it as "instruction is the making known after having analyzed," it ultimately culminates in "teaching" (*upadeśa*). This is because in sūtras such as "In the *upadeśa*, a nasalized vowel [is called *it*]" and "A substitute is like the original, except in rules concerning *al*," the *Mahābhāṣya* states that "the root √diś denotes the act of utterance."

In passages such as "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the *ahaṃkāra*," the term *ādeśa* means "instruction" (*upadeśa*). The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* statement "The teacher instructs this" is "he teaches this. In passages such as "That is not to be taught" (*tadaśiṣyam*), it has been explained as "not to be spoken. Consequently, *ādeśanam*, *śāsanam*, and *upadeśanam* are synonymous.

Furthermore, that [the root] *kṛ* has that [teaching] as its object is established by the Brāhmaṇa passage, "O Blessed One, teach me this deity," because there is no contradiction between the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*), and it is therefore improper to follow the unidiomatic sense of the suffix. Nor should it be argued that even if it is the object of *anuśāsana* (instruction), it is not the object of *śāsana* (command); for according to the rule "the root *śās* is used in the sense of instruction" (*śāsu anuśiṣṭau*), *śāsana* itself is of the nature of *anuśāsana*. Consequently, the attempt to justify the *ghañ* suffix by superimposing the status of being the object of *kṛ* is also inappropriate, since such a superimposition is unjustified.

If it is argued that there is no superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) [upon the agent], because that too exists [in reality], we say: no; for if that were so, it would be improper to accept a lack of naturalness (*asvārasya*) in the grammatical suffix (*pratyaya*) according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*). For this very reason, in cases such as *asāc chinnati* ("he cuts with ease"), although there is a superimposition of agency upon the instrument by way of the maxim *brāhmaṇadarśyutkarṣāt* (the excellence of the one who shows the Brāhmaṇas) due to the intention to express an excess of facility, there is no possibility of superimposing instrumentality upon the agent. Were that the case, it would lead to disaster, just like the superimposition of being a servant upon a king.

For this very reason, in the sūtra "the most effective means is the instrument" (*sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*), having justified the usage "he cooks with a pot" (*sthālyā pacati*) by intending to express the status of being the most effective means on the part of the cooking-pot (*adhikaraṇasthālī*) due to its thin-walled nature, it is further established that there is no possibility of intending to express the agency as an instrument, because they belong to different categories. Indeed, the agent is the one who employs all the instruments; for one possessing a hundred coins cannot compete with one possessing a single coin. Thus, the absence of an intention to express the agency as an instrument is demonstrated.

Furthermore, when the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is intended to be expressed, the suffix *ghañ* does not apply because it is superseded by the subsequent suffix *lyuṭ* according to the rule "karaṇādhikaraṇayośca. Nor does the suffix *ghañ* apply by virtue of the rule "halaśca," because in that case as well, the term "in a technical name" (*saṃjñāyām*) is understood to carry over.

Nor should it be argued that, even in your own view, the suffix *ghañ* could not occur in relation to an action (*karman*), because *ghañ* is prescribed only when there is a technical name (*saṃjñā*) by the rule "also when [denoting] a factor other than the agent, provided it is a name" (*akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*). For this has been established in the *Padamañjarī* and other works by taking the particle *ca* ("and") in the phrase "also when [denoting] a factor other than the agent" (*akartari ca*) to have a separate syntactical connection (*bhinnakamatva*), such that [the suffix occurs] even when it is not a name. Furthermore, the author of the *Vārttika* stated: "The mention of 'name' (*saṃjñā*) is purposeless, because *ghañ* is seen everywhere."

Furthermore, if the suffix *ghañ* were to signify the instrument (*karaṇa*), it would contradict what was stated previously—that by the word "instruction" (*ādeśa*) the Governor (*praśāsitṛ*) is denoted—because only the instrument of governing would have been denoted, while the agent of governing would remain undenoted. As for the claim that "the quality of being a governor is unique [to Brahman]," that too is not correct; for even if the word "instruction" denotes merely the instrument of governing, it does not denote the state of being a governor.

Even when that [Brahman] is denoted, since the status of being the primary object of knowledge belongs exclusively to Brahman—just as the quality of being the unconditioned ruler does—it follows that in the aphorism *brahmajijñāsā*, by accepting the genitive case in *brahmaṇaḥ* as denoting the object (*karman*), it is stated that Brahman alone is the object of the verbal desire to know (*abhidhānikajijñāsā*), whereas its worship and so forth are merely implied (*ākṣepya*).

Furthermore, having raised the objection that the word "ruler" (*ādeśa*) alone would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), it must necessarily be admitted that the word "him" (*tam*) functions as a qualifier of the ruler, because of the provision of this specific qualification. For if the meaning of the word "ruler" itself were "sovereign lordship" (*praśāsitṛtva*) without any further attributes, then, since that [sovereignty] belongs exclusively to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the word "him" would not serve as a qualifier.

As for the claim that by stating [the Self] is "to be questioned," its being "to be taught" is established, that is incorrect; for since such a statement is unnecessary, the intended meaning is simply that it is "to be known through instruction. This is because the statement that it is "to be taught" is precisely what is required to dispel the notion that one might think, "Even if I did not ask previously, I shall now know it on my own. For this very reason, in passages such as "I ask you about that which is based on the Upaniṣads," the fact that the object of inquiry is "based on the Upaniṣads" (aupaniṣada) is stated as a defining characteristic of its being "to be taught."

As for the claim that "the status of being the efficient cause (nimittatva) is required for the sake of establishing the proposition that all is known," that is not correct. For, by the force of the proposition that "all is known through one knowledge," it is possible to obtain the status of being the efficient cause as well—just like the status of being the material cause (upādānatva)—since that [status] cannot otherwise be accounted for; thus, it need not be stated separately. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that such [separate status] is untenable.

In reality, however, the statement that "knowing all through knowing one" is untenable when other causal factors exist is also inconsistent. For even if eternal glory (nityavibhūti) remains unknown, "knowing all through knowing one" is established because the entire category of effects is known; since the word "all" refers only to the creation preceded by the resolve for manifold existence within the scope of the "this-ness" (idam-kāra), why would the promise of "knowing all through knowing one" not be consistent even when such other causal factors exist?

To this it is replied: Since these two have been taught separately as "this is the instruction," there must necessarily be a difference between the teaching and the object of the teaching, according to the principle that "the vital air and its function are not identical because they are taught separately"—just as in the case of an invitation and an entreaty, or like the words "tree" and "forest-plant," and like the words "affection" and "devotion. For even when used in reference to the same object, the difference in experience [implied by such distinct terms] is difficult to deny.

For when it is said, "he commands" (*ādiśati*), there is understood a state of being a commander, an ordainer, or an issuer of orders—one who employs such words so that a punishment follows upon the transgression of the sentence. The linguistic usage of "he commands" (*ādiśati*) pertains exclusively to a master (*prabhu*). For this very reason, the author of the *Nyāsa* described the distinction between *ādeśa* (command) and *upadeśa* (instruction), stating: "The root *diś* preceded by the prefix *ā-* [denotes] one who enjoins..."

[The word *īśvara*] expresses the sense of "one who causes [something] to be done" (*prayojanavacana*), because it is understood in that very way in such passages as "He is the inner entered ruler, the knower" (*antaḥ praviṣṭaḥ śāstā jānan*). Consequently, since the meaning in the form of "commanding"—which is synonymous with "governing"—is understood through the natural force of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), the suffix *ghañ*, which in your view denotes any case-role (*kāraka*) other than the agent, is taken by us to indicate the agent characterized as the prompter of all case-roles, by virtue of its semantic fitness, just as in your own system the *ghañ* suffix denotes the object.

Because the primary meaning of the word to be enjoined possesses such a nature, one must resort to a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that favors the primary sense of the root-meaning, which has not yet encountered a contradiction. For instance, in passages such as "fifty-five threefold years," since the words *trivṛt* and so forth naturally favor their primary sense of "days," one accepts a non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) for the secondary word "years"—which, being common to many meanings such as solar or lunar months, is incapable of being determined otherwise.

Likewise, in such cases as "He sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," the instrumental case-ending is accepted as having a secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) denoting the accusative, in accordance with the nominal stem *prayāja-śeṣa*. Similarly, in passages such as "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed the seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*)," the plural number heard in the text is understood to have a figurative meaning (*gauṇārtha*) following the word *ṛṣi*, because this was established in the passage "On account of the impossibility of the figurative [sense], and because of its prior mention" (*gauṇyasaṃbhavāt tatprākśruteśca*).

Now, although the term *ādeśa* lacks extensive conventional usage in the sense of "instruction" (*upadeśa*)—its synonym being "commanding" (*praśāsana*)—nevertheless, since its primary meaning is not entirely abandoned when it signifies "instruction," while in your view the suffix would abandon its primary meaning through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the agent; therefore, according to the maxim of the "one who eats from a bronze vessel" (*kāṃsyabhojī-nyāya*), just as the use of fresh grass is adopted for the single-potsherd offerings to Heaven and Earth in accordance with the *jaghanādyā* [text], so too in the case of "He offers to the Brāhmaṇas all at once" (*ekadhā brāhmaṇebhya upaharati*).

Just as the word *ekadhā*—which commonly signifies both "once" (*sakṛt*) and "together" (*saha*)—is accepted in the sense of "together" when favoring the weaker injunction that establishes a different act of eating; and just as in the case of the statement "seventeen [animals] dedicated to Prajāpati," although the plural number is capable of being construed with the genus *prajā*, one accepts a qualified construction in accordance with the weaker injunction that establishes the eleven cuttings (*avadāna*) produced from a single animal, thereby accepting a distinction between sacrifices implied by the connection between the substance and the deity.

In accordance with the rule for the suffix *ghañ* in its minimal sense, it is more appropriate that the root *śās* (to command) has the meaning of "instruction" (*upadeśa*) as its primary sense; this is because there is no abandonment of the root's primary meaning. What remains is merely the abandonment of its most commonly established meaning, and that does not constitute a fault.

If it is argued that for this very reason—in passages such as "the wives sing along" (*patnaya upagāyanti*)—even though the word *gīti* is commonly used for vocal singing (*śārīra-gāna*), its primary meaning is established by its application to non-vocal singing on instruments and the like, and thus it has been concluded in the tenth book (*daśama-adhyāya*) that the wives, by augmenting the nearby drumming (*dundubhi*) and other sounds with reed-flutes (*kāṇḍavīṇā*) and so forth, do not exclude the *ṛtvij*s [from their duties], we say: not so.

Since the word *gāna* denotes the chant (*gīti*) or the mantra according to the principle of the *barhirājya-adhikaraṇa*, it is appropriate that it refers here to the chanting of the drums and other instruments present therein. However, in this case, because the word *ādeśa* is never used in such a sense—as in the lack of usage in expressions like "the disciple gave instructions (*ādideśa*) to the teacher"—and because it lacks the meaning of general utterance or the like, the words *upadeśa* and *ādeśa* (just as the words *upadeśa* and *atideśa*) have distinct meanings.
