Therefore, if the word *ādeśa* were to mean "instruction" (*upadeśa*), one would inevitably have to abandon its primary sense; thus, it is secondary (*jaghanya*).

This is because the secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) is appropriate only as a last resort. In reality, however, regarding the sūtra *upadeśe 'janunāsika it*, one might raise the objection that the suffix *ghan*—which would otherwise be precluded by the suffix *lyuṭ* according to the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayośca*—cannot apply under the rule *akartari ca kārake*. Anticipating this, the author of the Bhāṣya justified the use of *ghan* by citing the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. By that same principle, since *ghan* can be established even in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) by that very sūtra, there is no occasion for a secondary sense; therefore, we consider it correct that the word indeed signifies the status of being a controller (*praśāsitṛ*).

"Only so long is his delay"—that is, for one who is established in the knowledge of the True (Sat), the delay is only that long, until he is released from the body produced by past karma (*prārabdha*). Then, immediately thereafter, he attains union with Brahman; this is the meaning. And thus the Atharvaṇa has been obtained.

The meaning is that in the section [of the *Brahmasūtra*] beginning with "pāriplavārthāḥ," it was established that the narrative tales (ākhyāyikās) such as "Śvetaketu, the son of Aruṇi, was..."—which are recited in proximity to [injunctions regarding] knowledge—are subordinate to those [injunctions] as their explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). Although this explanatory passage is not exclusively devoted to the existence of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*), nevertheless, once the intention toward the existence of attributes is determined by another indicative mark (*liṅga*), it follows that even the explanatory passage is exclusively devoted to that [same conclusion].
This is stated in the second part [of the *Brahmasūtra*], in the seventh [section], as the speech of Yama to his own messenger.
Just as gold is held to be one and undivided, despite the distinctions of bracelets,
crowns, earrings, and so forth, so too is Hari proclaimed to be one, despite all the conceptual constructions of gods, animals, humans, and the like.

"Just as the atoms of the surface of the earth return once again to oneness with the earth at the end of the wind, so too do gods, animals, humans, and others [return] at the end to that eternal one who is free from the impurities of the guṇas. This is because it has that single goal; the meaning is that it proceeds toward that ultimate purpose.

Having raised the objection as to how the *Bhāṣya* can describe the imperishability (*avyayatva*)—which consists in the absence of defects—as a "wholesome quality" (*kalyāṇaguṇa*) given that higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) has as its object that which possesses distinctions, [the author] replies: "It is with the intention that the state of being opposed to defects is itself a quality. "The meaning is as before" means the exclusion of Brahman as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*).

"Because of the multiplicity of the excluded counterparts (*vyāvṛtti-pratiyogin*). This means: because of the multiplicity of the excluded counterparts—namely, the unreal (*anṛta*), the insentient (*jaḍa*), and the finite (*paricchinna*). "Because of the consequence that the words would be synonyms. Here too, the phrase from the subsequent sentence—"due to the absence of a difference in the basis for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*)"—is connected by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣi-nyāya*). Now, one might object: "The higher genus (*para-jāti*) 'Being' (*sattā*), which is common to jars and other things, is the basis for the application of the word 'sat' (being)."

If it is argued that there is no synonymy [between the terms], because the *Kalpataru* states: "The generic properties (*jāti*) of knowledge and bliss—consisting of consciousness and bliss which have acquired differentiation through the limiting adjunct (*upadhāna*) of the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*)—are distinct; and thus, although the intended referents (*lakṣyārtha*) of the words 'Being,' 'Knowledge,' and 'Bliss' are non-different, they do not constitute synonyms because they denote these aforementioned generic properties"—this is not so. For if the existence (*sattā*) inherent in jars and other objects were the denotation of the word 'Being' (*satya*), then "Being-ness" (*satyatva*), being over-pervasive (*atiprasakta*), would result in its failing to be the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman.

Furthermore, you yourself accept that truth (*satyatva*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman; for a universal (*sāmānya*) common to both real and unreal objects is impossible, and because such a universal would be shared by the unreal, it could not successfully exclude the unreal. Moreover, this would contradict your own established doctrine that the absolute reality (*paramārthikasattva*)—defined as being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time—is the scriptural definition of Brahman. Finally, without a distinction coextensive with the substratum (*dharmin*), it is impossible for "knowing-ness" (*jñānatva*) and "bliss-ness" (*ānandatva*) to constitute universals (*jāti*), merely through a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*), just as the case of "ether-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and the like.

Furthermore, because [qualities] such as "knowability" (jñānatva) would fail to qualify as defining characteristics of the Pure [Brahman] if they resided in the conditioned consciousness (upahita-caitanya) which possesses a difference co-extensive with its own substrate (dharmisamasattāka-bheda). By this, the following view is also refuted: that words such as "Real" (satya), which denote the variegated Brahman (śabala-brahman) qualified by reality and so forth, possess only a secondary, figurative sense (lakṣaṇā) when applied to the Pure Brahman, and thus are not synonyms. This is because properties such as reality cannot logically belong to the variegated [Brahman], which is of the nature of the unreal, non-luminous, and limited.

Or rather, in that case, there would be the exclusion of untruth, non-luminosity, and limitation only for that [qualified Brahman], but not for the pure [Brahman] which does not possess attributes such as truthfulness. Therefore, since truthfulness and the other qualities cannot exist elsewhere than in the pure [Brahman], and since the sentences beginning with "Truth" (*satya*) have an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*) only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), those qualities are not established even in the pure [Brahman]. Consequently, because truthfulness and the rest are absolutely non-existent [in the pure Brahman], it is impossible to resolve the objection of synonymy by resorting to their mutual difference; thus, the meaning is that synonymy is established.

"Whether as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) or as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This means: do the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) merely constitute objects of cognition that are useful for the cognition of the word-meanings which, in turn, serve as the basis for the cognition of Brahman—which has become the meaning of the sentence—or is it the case that they also constitute objects of the cognition of the sentence-meaning itself? This is precisely the meaning of the phrase "being external to that which is characterized. Furthermore, the state of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is not something distinct from being either a qualifier or a secondary characteristic.

Regarding the statement, "The auditory organ is space delimited by the ear-canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*)," it should not be argued that the ear-canal cannot be a qualifier because, if it were, it would follow that the ear-canal itself is the auditory organ—since there is a rule that whatever qualifies the qualificand must also qualify [the definition]—nor can it be an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), for if space merely indicated by the ear-canal were the auditory organ at some time, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is incorrect, because even in that case, the ear-canal can be included within the very category of the incidental indicator; since the conjunction with the existing ear-canal functions as an incidental indicator, no fault arises.

"External to the secondary indicator (*upalakṣya*). This is the intended meaning: Is the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) for the purpose of conveying the essential nature (*svarūpa*), or for the purpose of conveying the property of being knowledge (*jñānatva*) and so forth? It cannot be the first, because that has already been cognized previously. Nor can it be the second, because it would contradict its status as a secondary indicator. "At the time of denoting the sentence-meaning by all the words. The grammatical connection is: "by all the words at the time of denoting the sentence-meaning. Alternatively, "by all the words" means "by the production of a single cognition," that is, through the generation of one unified cognition.

Therefore, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Now, one might object: "If [the meanings] were denoted simultaneously, the determination of the relative strength and weakness among *śruti*, *vākya*, and so forth would be entirely untenable; for the rule that the *śruti* of a word is stronger than the *vākya*, and the *śruti* of a suffix is stronger than the *śruti* of a word, would be like pouring water on a cast-off handful. Anticipating this objection, the author says: "Even in the case of sequential denotation. This means: the position of one who does not accept sequential denotation—that is, the view of those who deny sequential denotation.

Even when [the two] are presented simultaneously, [the distinction] does not disappear. For, in the case of the relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*), the knownness or unknownness of that sentence is irrelevant. Rather, what was already understood through another means of knowledge (*māna*) prior to the operation of that sentence is restated (*anūdyate*); for the distinction is precisely this: that which is not yet established is enjoined (*vidhīyate*). This is the intended meaning. Anticipating the objection—"If priority and posteriority do not constitute the definition of subject and predicate, how can there be a cognition of the division between subject and predicate?"—he says: "By a single sentence. For [this distinction] is indeed possible at the stage of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

If it is argued that the knowledge of the distinction between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted—characterized by the states of being known and unknown—is not useful for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha), such that its apprehension would have to be established prior to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning during the stage of reflection (*parāmarśa*), we say: no.

The meaning is this: in such cases as "one should wipe the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), since there is no determination of the specific mode of expression—such as whether it means "one should wipe the cup," "one should wipe one [cup]," or "that which one wipes should be one"—the comprehension of the sentence-meaning without doubt does not arise; therefore, the mode of expression established by logical reasoning subsequently brings about the understanding of the sentence-meaning. Regarding the phrase "because the same case-ending has the purpose of signifying the oneness of the substantive alone": the intention is as follows. As for what was stated—that there is no presentation of the oneness of the qualified entity—that is indeed accepted.

This is because we do not accept the demonstration of identity between the qualifiers. Nor should it be argued that the mere demonstration of identity between the qualificands is desired even by the opponent; for there is no abandonment of the connection with the qualifiers as understood from the nominal stem itself. This is because, in a single qualificand, one does not abandon the two qualifiers—identity and oneness—which are obtained through the maxim of "one thing having two [attributes]. Furthermore, the derivation [of word-meaning] is rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*); the meaning is that it is not rooted in scripture (*śruti*), as is the case with the derivation of words such as "heaven" (*svarga*).

Furthermore, perception itself makes known the identity of the qualified substratum (*viśeṣya*). In cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) or "the one with earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*), one perceives through the linguistic usage of elders that the case-ending of the qualifier refers to a single qualified substratum even when there are multiple qualifiers; this is because the acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) occurs precisely in that manner. Otherwise, one would have to abandon the view that the case-ending of a qualifier signifies non-difference (*abheda*).

The point is that there is no cause other than the linguistic proficiency derived from the usage of preceding elders for the fact that a case-ending expressing a qualifier does not intend identity. If it is argued that "the distinction of the qualified [object] is set aside there by perception," the meaning is that in the case of Brahman, which is beyond the scope of perception, a distinction of the qualified resulting from a distinction of qualifiers would be unavoidable. This is because identity is cognized due to the oneness of the word denoting the substratum and the employment of a common case-ending.

This is an illustration: the general rule (*utsarga*) is that when there is a difference in qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is a difference in the qualified (*viśeṣya*), as seen in examples such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young. However, in cases like "Khaṇḍa is bald" (*muṇḍa*), the distinction arises because of mutual contradiction (*viruddhatva*); what is not contradictory does not effect a distinction at all. Since qualifiers effect distinctions, let it be so in relation to the substratum of those qualifiers themselves, but not even in relation to the substrata of other qualifiers. For one should observe that in cases such as "the blue lotus," blueness does not exclude [the object] from being long as well.

As for what was said regarding "having the same case-ending" (*samānavibhakti*): one should not argue that since identity is understood through having the same case-ending, this objection cannot possibly arise for the opponent, as it would entail the collapse of their doctrine of *akhaṇḍārthatva* (the state of having an indivisible meaning). This is because, according to the definition—"*Akhaṇḍārthatva* is the state of being restricted solely to the meaning of a single nominal stem" (*prātipadika*)—it is precisely the connection with another nominal stem that is excluded, and not the connection with a case-ending as well. Thus, the objection is possible for one who holds such a view; this is how it should be understood.

"In the case where [the meaning] is not additional, there is a failure of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*). This means that there is a failure of the reason in the form of identity as understood through a common grammatical case-ending; this should be understood because it is concluded later [in the text] as "the failure of the reason consisting in the contradiction to the cognition of identity. Alternatively, *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is either the presentation of an object of relation that is impossible or dissimilar, or it is a relation with that which is possible.

Intending to show that [the reason] is not possible in the case of what is capable [of being otherwise established], he says: "even though it is non-characteristic (*alakṣaṇikatve’pi*). This refers to the argument: "The subject under discussion, the sentence, has as its ultimate object an indivisible reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*), because it is a defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), or because it is an answer to a question concerning that alone, like the sentence 'The moon is the most excellent light'. By this, the following inference is refuted as a means of valid knowledge: "The sentence beginning with 'Truth' (*satyādivākya*) is grounded in an indivisible reality, because it is a defining statement, or because it is an answer to a question concerning that alone, like the sentence 'The moon is the most excellent light'"; for the over-extension [of the reason] is avoided by noting that co-referential sentences such as "a blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) lack the status of being defining statements.

It should also be observed that the property of being a sentence whose characteristic is an uncommon form (*asādhāraṇarūpalakṣaṇavākyatva*) is pervaded by having a determinate meaning (*sakhaṇḍārthatva*) alone; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*)—being an answer to a question concerning that [uncommon form] alone—would possess an indeterminate meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*). Furthermore, in the case of the example "The moon is the most excellent light," the example is unestablished because it is an answer to a question regarding a differentiator (*vyāvartaka*) and an uncommon form. Moreover, if the proposition is that [the Veda] is incapable of propounding a determinate meaning consisting of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

The point is this: although the sentence of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*) possesses the capacity to convey the qualification of being "non-fragmentary" (i.e., having a non-limited meaning) in the sense of the absence of a fragmentary meaning, it lacks the capacity to convey a positive fragmentary meaning; therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the phrase "by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone [is] the connection with the qualifier": the meaning is that because the two qualified entities, as recalled by the nominal stem, are presented as mere identity by means of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), one should not think that the connection of blueness with the lotus occurs through the nominal stem "blue" (*nīla*).

For if that were the case, since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of blueness in the lotus would already be established by the nominal stem *nīla* alone, it would follow that the cognition of identity conveyed by the case-ending would be rendered purposeless; this is how it should be understood.

By this, it is intended that two doubts are dispelled. The doubt raised directly by the opponent is refuted by the phrase *sisṛkṣoḥ* ("desiring to create"), which establishes the Supreme Lord as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). The doubt raised by a bystander—that the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) has not been established—is refuted by the portion of the commentary stating that material causality was indeed established by the text, "In the beginning, this was Being alone, one only. The meaning is that the term *advitīya* ("without a second") is intended to negate any independent entity [other than Brahman]. For this very reason, it is stated in Śaṅkara’s *Upaniṣad-bhāṣya*: "Regarding the word *advitīya*..."

Just as, apart from clay, a potter or the like is seen to be the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) that transforms the clay into another form such as a jar, so too, apart from Being (*sat*), a second distinct entity would have to be admitted as its auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); however, this is denied by the term "without a second" (*advitīya*). It is explained precisely with the intent of negating any other instrumental cause, in the sense that "there exists no second distinct entity for this [Being]," thus it is "without a second."

Furthermore, it should be observed that since the statement, "In the beginning, before creation, there was Being alone, without a second," has been explained by the opponents themselves as referring to the period prior to creation, how can the mere fact of being non-dual at the time prior to creation entail its falsity?
[This concludes] the resolution of the contradiction with the texts concerning the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman.

In the alternative [put forward by the opponent], is it being asserted that knowledge does not have knowledge as its substratum because it is itself knowledge, or because it is impossible for two substances of the same genus to stand in a fixed relationship of attribute and substrate? Regarding the first option, the commentary states: "Because the knower is indeed of the nature of knowledge. Its meaning is that it is possible for the knower also to be of the nature of knowledge. Regarding the second option, however, the commentary states: "Of that which is of the very nature of knowledge," and so forth.

The first interpretation holds that the *bhāṣya* passage, "For all the Śrutis declare nothing but the state of being a knower," serves as a supporting argument for the refutation of the first alternative (*vikalpa*) and is supplementary to it. In this interpretation, one must rely on the fact that the *bhāṣya* sentence "For all the Śrutis declare nothing but the state of being a knower" supports the more distant *bhāṣya* statement, "Because the knower alone has the nature of knowledge"; furthermore, the forced interpretation of the particle *eva* (only) as having the sense of *api* (also) should be seen as an underlying unease with this reading.

In the second explanation, however, the engagement by way of an alternative (vikalpa) is the same as before. Therein, the meaning of the commentary beginning with "of the knower alone" (*jñātu-reva*) is as follows: the word *jñātṛ* (knower) is a noun denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*) ending in the ablative case. Furthermore, the particle *eva* (alone/only) is intended to clarify that the very quality of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), which you have presented as contradictory to the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*), is in fact the very means of establishing that nature of knowledge. This is because, since the absence of the nature of being a knower is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades [the absence of] the nature of knowledge, the quality of being a knower is not contradictory to it.

In this interpretation, the commentary—stating that "all the Śrutis indeed speak of the state of being a knower" (*jñātṛtva*)—is intended to strengthen that [state] by demonstrating its scriptural authority (*śrautatva*). Furthermore, in this explanation, one should note the underlying dissatisfaction that the recourse to a construction emphasizing the abstract quality (*bhāvapradhāna*) is strained. In the third explanation, however, the meaning of the commentary beginning with "of the knower alone" (*jñātureva*) is that there is no contradiction between the knower's very existence and his having the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpatva*).

And this commentary does not intend to refute either of the two alternatives of the dilemma; rather, it is solely intent upon asserting non-contradiction. One should discern the distinction as follows: having raised the dilemma—whether the knower’s lack of being a substrate for cognitions is stated because of the absence of the relationship of property and property-bearer (*dharma-dharmin*) between two things of the same class, or whether it is because of [the knower's] being cognition that he is not a substrate for cognitions—the first alternative is answered with the words "of the very nature of cognition itself," and the second is answered with the words "for [he possesses] the state of being a knower indeed. Thus, the intended meaning is as before.

The meaning is: "Is this stated by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), or by way of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*)? and so forth. This refers to how the status of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) becomes established, as in the scriptural passage beginning with "Of the lords... (*tam īśvarāṇām*). Furthermore, the manner in which it becomes established will be clarified later on.

Regarding the statement "knowledge has all things as its object": in the passage "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," the fact that knowledge has all things as its object is shown; in "It thought," its role in the collective whole (samaṣṭi) is shown; in "This deity thought," its role in the individual (vyaṣṭi) is shown; and by the use of the first person in "Let me create," its relation to the Self is shown—this is the meaning. And regarding "the granting of desires": the sense is that without knowledge of the desired object, the granting of it would be impossible. "Deity-hood" means being worthy of worship through ritual action.

*Ārādhāna* is an action that serves as the cause for the affection of one worthy of worship. From this, it is established that [the Self] possesses knowledge corresponding to its form; that is, it possesses the nature of being a *pati* (Lord) and a *śeṣin* (Principal). By "being a *śeṣin*," the meaning is "having consciousness as the principal. This is because the designation of *pati* is not applied to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, which are themselves the principals (*śeṣins*) of subordinate rites such as the *prayāja*. Therefore, the sense is that the status of being a knower is established. Thus, it is indicated that [the definition] culminates in the second specific attribute.

And thus, the intention is that even the portion beginning with "He has neither effect nor instrument" is relevant to the present subject. This consists of both a specific affirmation and a specific negation. By the passage beginning with "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*), there is a specific affirmation; this is the meaning. If a restriction is made in order to avoid redundancy, it follows the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). In this case, the phrase "concerning a subject other than the specific attributes mentioned" is to be supplied. That is, the restriction applies to the subject matter of the specific attributes already mentioned. Nor is this merely the maxim of "the goat and the animal" (*chāgapaśunyāya*); [for that would imply a total exclusion of others].

Indeed, the principle of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) is itself the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*). This must be stated precisely because it is so observed in common usage. For just as the term "principle of the general and the particular" is applied to the principle of the general rule and its exception by taking the general term to have a scope distinct from the particular, there is no fault in applying the term "principle of the general and the particular" to the "goat-sacrifice" principle (*chāgapaśunyāya*) as well, by taking the word denoting the general to terminate in the particular. It should be understood that the mention here of the "cow-and-bull" principle (*gobalīvardanyāya*) was made incidentally for the benefit of the students.

One might object: "How can it be said that the prescription of qualities and general attributes is not seen in the Śrutis? Anticipating this by noting that such [qualities] are indeed seen in passages such as, "He who is the time of time, the possessor of qualities (guṇin), the knower of all," the author says: "associated with defects. This means "associated with the absence of defects."

The point here is that since the word "guṇa" (quality), which is mentioned in conjunction with "not being subject to time"—a state characterized by the fault of being subject to time—must refer to a specific quality rather than establishing a general rule regarding qualities, one must resort to this as a mere *abhyupagamavāda* (a concessionary argument). It was stated, "of the sentences concerning [Brahman] as possessing qualities," with the intention of referring to the statements of the *Smṛti*. Furthermore, the word "or" (*vā*) should be supplied here; the meaning is: "or it was stated, 'of the sentences concerning [Brahman] as possessing qualities,' with the intention of referring to the [Smṛti] statements."

Alternatively, raising the objection, "How can there be an acceptance of the prescription of qualities and commonalities that are absolutely unperceivable?", he says, "By tens of thousands of years," and so forth. "With the intention of the Smṛti statements" means: by means of these Smṛtis, through the inference of a Śruti that prescribes qualities and commonalities similar to these, [the author] has stated [the validity] of the passages concerning the possession of qualities (saguṇavākya). "In the statement of the counteragent to defects."

Regarding the phrase "guṇadoṣau" (in the very context of "guṇadoṣau"): the meaning is that, just as in the case of "guṇadoṣau," this refers to qualities (*guṇa*) in general as the opposites of defects (*doṣa*), and thus refers to what is generally to be accepted (*upādeya*). This is according to the maxim of the goat and the animal (*chāga-paśu-nyāya*) due to the force of the context. Consequently, since even the general statements found in the *Smṛtis* require a conclusion in a specific sense, the statement in the *Bhāṣya*—"because there is no contradiction between the passages concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*)"—is concluded as being intended to include these [general statements].

Another statement follows: "It is also not tenable to resort to the falsity of the object for either one. Here, the phrase "in the case of admitting contradiction" (*virodhābhyupagame*) is to be supplied as a complement. Furthermore, the word *api* ("also") is to be construed out of its normal position. Thus, the meaning is: even if contradiction is admitted, it is not tenable to resort to the falsity of the object for either one. This is the intended sense. Consequently, the subsequent passage beginning with "therefore, previously [it was] resolved that there is no contradiction" is also consistent.

Otherwise, if there were a single unified statement (*ekavākyatva*), the previously stated [view] would be impossible. Alternatively, the word "also" (*api*) should be supplied [to read]: "Or rather, this is the intended meaning here. Both words "previously" and "now" are not intended to be emphasized (*avivakṣita*). The point is that, in accordance with the actual state of things, there is no contradiction; even if a contradiction did exist, it would cause us no harm. The sense is that there is no rule of necessity regarding the simultaneous occurrence of both [simultaneous] disconnections (*apaccheda*), because the disconnection of either one alone is possible. Thus, the contradiction is limited to the context of Prayāga.

Because two ritual applications (prayoga) occasioned by two simultaneous disconnections (apaccheda) cannot be performed at once, there is a contradiction between the two scriptural injunctions; therefore, the sense is that such a conflict is occasional. It has been stated regarding this subject of indefinite contradiction and sequence:
"Sequence, contradiction, and the invalidity of the earlier [injunction] do not exist simultaneously due to a restrictive rule; in that case, the principle of *apaccheda* would apply."

Thus it is said. Now, one might object: "The inference based on scripture that contradicts perception does not proceed; this is the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*). That principle does not apply here. If, on the grounds of the commonality of being 'swift' and 'slow' in their operation—just as in the case of perception and inference—the two types of scriptural statements regarding the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman were to have the same referent, then the statement concerning the unqualified would simply lack authority, like a mere Smṛti."

If non-authoritativeness is indeed intended, then why does the *apaccheda-nyāya* (the principle of the subsequent annulment) not apply? For it is said that the *apaccheda-nyāya* does not apply because of the fear that its application—being restricted to cases of fixed sequence—would result in the total invalidation [of the preceding]. Therefore, since the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*) does not apply to the subject matter of the Vedic revelation, [the author], due to this lack of satisfaction, says: "Or rather, let it not be so; it is precisely the principle of the section on the beginning (*upakramādhikaraṇa*). [As in: "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa."

He approached his own deity; he was torn asunder. He saw this four-potherd offering to Varuṇa; he offered it—beginning thus, the conclusion is heard: "As many horses as one might receive as a gift, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should one offer. In that regard, in the introductory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the sacrifice to Varuṇa is understood as belonging to Prajāpati, the giver of the horse; yet in the conclusion, it belongs to the receiver. Since there is a contradiction between these two, [the principle is applied]:
"Because it is a subordinate element and because it is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*), the *arthavāda* involves figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)."

"In the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view that even though the injunctive statement (vidhyuddeśa) is subordinate, it does not suffer a loss of its own meaning—[the following is established]: Since the arthavāda, though subordinate, is stronger because its contradiction has not yet arisen, and since the injunctive statement, despite being primary, has not yet attained its own form [independently], the primary injunctive statement, being itself unestablished, is incapable of subverting the arthavāda which is already present and established; therefore, the injunctive statement itself adopts conformity with it. Thus, by internalizing the sense of the causative suffix (ṇic)—that 'one should receive' means 'one should cause to receive'—it follows that the benefit belongs to the giver alone."

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Consequently, since either the statement regarding the possession of qualities (*saguṇavākya*) or the perception grasping difference (*bhedagrāhipratyakṣa*) has already functioned previously, the logic of the section on the introductory statement (*upakramādhikaraṇanyāya*) alone applies; thus, this is the method of the introductory statement (*upakramanaya*). [Regarding the phrase] “by way of existence (*sattayā*) or by way of being manifested (*māyamānatayā*)”: Now, an objection is raised: because the cognition “this is silver” is beset by a doubt regarding its invalidity (*aprāmāṇyaśaṅkā*), and since only a cognition not so beset can act as an obstacle to a contrary cognition, there is no contradiction in the arising of the cognition “this is not silver.”

If it is argued that this elaborate discussion is redundant because even the doubt regarding invalidity (aprāmāṇya-śaṅkā) results in a doubt about the object itself, and thus its non-arising should not be suspected—since the mere fact that the causal complex for the doubt of invalidity is postulated as being stimulating by the force of the result (phala-bala) suffices as a refutation—the answer is that such elaboration is justified for the purpose of instructing the student.

Nor should it be argued that if the cognition of the qualified nature [of Brahman] were to prevent the arising of the cognition of its opposite—the unqualified nature—by the logic of the *Upakrama-adhikaraṇa*, then there would follow the undesirable consequence that the cognition of non-grasping does not arise when there is a cognition of the grasping of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup; and likewise, in the case of the "simultaneous disconnections" (*apaccheda*), there would be the consequence that a cognition contrary to the prior one does not arise. This is because the logic of the *Upakrama-adhikaraṇa* applies only to cases where there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) within a single passage, whereas such unity is absent in cases like the grasping or non-grasping of the *ṣoḍaśin*. Nor should it be argued that there is no syntactic unity even between the passages concerning the qualified and the unqualified [Brahman].
"The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings,
the supervisor of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious, absolute, and devoid of qualities."

The point is that since a single unified meaning (*ekavākyatva*) is perceived in such passages, and because other passages concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇavākya*) are similar to them, they too cannot produce a cognition of a meaning contrary to those [passages]. As for the phrase "because it depends on the reflective awareness 'this is silver'": the objection raised is how a cognition contrary to that [prior one] could arise by contradicting what it depends upon (*upajīvya*), given that the cognition "this is not silver" presupposes the cognition "this is silver. [The response is: "The subsequent valid cognition has the nature of mother-of-pearl as its object."

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*): even though the cognition "this is silver" has as its object the absence of silver-ness (*rajatatvābhāva*), although there is dependence (*upajīvyatva*) regarding the mere aspect of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) being the object, there is no defect in its apprehending that absence because there is no dependence regarding the aspect of the silver being the object in the thing present before one (*purovartin*). In the reading *udīyamānam*, it should be understood as a form of the root *iṇ* in the sense of "going. [The phrase] "because of the abundance of indicative marks (*tātparyaliṅga*) such as 'Bliss is Brahman'" [is the reason].

The sense is that even with respect to the *brāhma* [bliss], since the scripture makes known that only the experience of bliss—which is subordinate to that [knowledge]—is the fruit, one understands that the purport (*tātparya*) of the Śruti lies in the bliss of Brahman.

Regarding the phrase "the conclusion that the Ānandavallī has as its object the qualified [Brahman] is appropriate," the meaning is that such a conclusion is logical. Although the reading "paryavasituṃ yuktam" is seen in some places, there the derivation must somehow be explained by taking the root *as* in the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepaṇe*), preceded by the prefix *ava*, and applying the rule "vaṣṭi bhāgurirallopam avāpyor upasargayoḥ" (Bhāguri desires the elision of the *a* of the prefixes *ava* and *api*), followed by the suffix *tumun*. Thus, the form *paryavasitum* is obtained.

From the root *antakarmaṇi* (meaning "to finish"), when the suffix *tumun* is applied, because that suffix is not *kit*, the substitution of *i* for the penultimate vowel by the rule *dyatisyatimāsthām* does not occur. For this very reason, the Teacher will say in the *Anandamaya-Adhikarana*: "Those who have reached their conclusion, having set out to reach a final conclusion. The phrase "ever-new" (*nityanavam*) means "in such a way that it becomes ever-new. The compound *yuvādhyāyakaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya* meaning "one who is both young and a student. The sense is that the youthfulness of the student culminates through the act of studying.

*Āśutarakriyaḥ*: from the word *āśu*, meaning "possessing swift action," the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added; the form results from the elision of the *ṭi* (the *u*) after the suffix. Alternatively, the form may be understood as resulting from the elision of the *matup* suffix according to the rule "vinmatorluk" applied to the word *āśumat*. *Aśanakṣamaḥ*: eating is *āśa*; from that word ending in *matup*, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added. Regarding *āśiṣṭha*: from the word *āśis* (blessing) occurring in the sense of a benediction, or from the word *āśimat* (possessing a blessing), the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added, resulting in the form *āśiṣṭha*. In all these cases, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied, and by the rule "vinmatorluk," there is the elision of the *matup* suffix.

Regarding the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārtha-*: the sense is that since the word *suhita* means "satiated," and since "filling" (*pūraṇa*) is also of the nature of being satiated. However, the word *pūraṇa* in this context [of the present discussion] is not to be understood as the word *pūraṇa* [from the aforementioned rule], because that refers to the suffixes used for ordinal numbers (*pūraṇapratyaya*). Regarding the phrase *ṣaṣṭhyanujñānāt*: the meaning is "because of the permission of the genitive case" by this sūtra, which is intended to prohibit genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Regarding *aniṣṭanivartyatvena*: the meaning is "by virtue of its being the remover of what is undesirable."

The intention is that there is a superiority of bliss in the four-faced [Brahmā]. In the passage "those who are a hundred," the word "hundred" refers to a greater number; thus, the sense is that there is no limitation. Since the sentences in this context are intended to convey specific numbers, it is appropriate that even in the phrase "those who are a hundred of Prajāpati," they are intended to convey a specific number. Therefore, he offers an alternative interpretation to avoid this [objection]: "Or rather, [it refers] to 'those who are a hundred, he is one.'"

The intended meaning is that when the state of being the bliss of Prajāpati existing throughout the three periods of time is stated, its unlimited nature (*aparicchinnatva*) is established. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of possessing the manifestation of the three quarters" (*tripādvibhūtimattayā*): if it is asked, "How can the statement regarding the infinity of bliss through the possession of the manifestation of the three quarters be applicable to one who asserts that the bliss of the Lord is already unlimited?"—on this point, some maintain that the reading should be: "If it is asked, 'How is there unlimitedness? [the response follows].

And this is its meaning: "How can 'limitlessness' (aparicchinnatva) be understood by the statement 'those who [attain] a hundred'? On the contrary, limitation alone is perceived. Therefore, they describe the objection as extending up to the point that 'limitlessness is not established. Consequently, in order to refute that, it must be demonstrated by this scriptural statement that even limitation is not established; they say that the limitlessness of bliss is likewise established."

Others, however, raise the following objection from the perspective of an impartial observer: "Why is the meaning explained by taking the word 'hundred' (*śata*) to refer merely to the bliss of Prajāpati existing throughout the three periods of time, or as referring merely to a number exceeding one hundred, thereby contradicting the natural sense of the Śruti text, 'A hundredfold is the bliss of Prajāpati'? The literal meaning of the text itself should be accepted. To dispel this doubt, they say: "It is like the atom [in relation] to Mount Meru.
This refers to the meaning of the Śruti passage beginning with "He enjoys" (*so 'śnute*).

But surely, since the Brāhmaṇa passage—"By the Brāhmaṇa he attains the Supreme"—establishes that the Brāhmaṇa alone is the object to be attained, and since the Brāhmaṇa passage—"This is his supreme bliss"—declares that the Brāhmaṇa alone is the bliss of the knowers, and because desires are perceived as non-different from it, and because the Brāhmaṇa, being an exposition of the mantra, is more authoritative, the meaning of the mantra "together with the Brāhmaṇa" must be described in accordance with the Brāhmaṇa alone.

Anticipating the objection that the meaning of the mantra "dvā suparṇā" is described in accordance with the *Brāhmaṇa* in the *Paingi-rahasya*, [the author] states: "Because it is observed that mantras take the form of explanations provided by the *Brāhmaṇas*. The sense is that since it is observed that mantras themselves also take the form of explanations [of their own meaning], the ground for superiority—namely, the nature of being an explanation—is common to both without distinction. Regarding the phrase "being the cause of clear comprehension": generally, *Brāhmaṇas* possess the quality of being causes for clear understanding.

The meaning is that since mantras are indeed profound, the statement regarding the superior authority of the Brāhmaṇas is entirely acceptable. If it is objected: "But in the Ānandamayādhikaraṇa, some maintain the superiority of mantras; thus, by citing the very superiority of mantras as being stated by others, there is a contradiction"—we reply: no, for that too should be understood as a different opinion, and thus there is no contradiction.

Because the state of being *vipaścit* (all-knowing) is not mentioned [separately] from that [Brahman], and because it is consistent with [Brahman’s] being the enjoyer, [the author] dispels the doubt that Brahman might be associated with a separate enjoyer by stating that "the state of being *vipaścit* is also spoken of as a quality of the object of enjoyment. Nor should it be suspected that its separate mention is redundant since it too is indicated by the word "desires" (*kāma*); the point is that a separate mention is justified by the intention to express its preeminence, according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Regarding the phrase "because of the non-mention of a distinction": [it refers to the fact that in the passage] "desires together with Brahman," they are not presented as distinct.

The meaning is "because of the specific instruction. And because of the natural force of the immediate context of the application. The point is that if it were "he enjoys all desires together with the Brahman," then there might even be a suspicion that the agent of enjoyment—the one referred to by the word "he"—is the locus of the conjunction. "For the sake of avoiding that" means for the sake of avoiding that by way of accepting [the alternative] as desired. It is like the statement, "that which is within Him is what must be sought."

And this was stated with the intention that, having accepted that the word "in that" (*tasmin*) refers to the small ether (*daharākāśa*), the quality alone is what must be sought; however, in reality, since it will be shown later that in the phrase "that which is within that" (*tasmin yad antaḥ*), the pronoun *tat* refers to two things—the lotus-shaped ether and the object [Brahman]—it follows that both Brahman and its qualities are objects of meditation. Thus, one should understand that equal primacy is established for both, rather than primacy belonging to the qualities alone.

Alternatively, the sense is that since the word *saha* indicates subordination (*aprādhānya*), it is inappropriate to speak of the subordinate status of the Brahman; furthermore, in accordance with the passage on the Dahara-vidyā, its purport lies precisely in their equality. By the phrase "in order to state the predominance of the quality," it is established that the coexistence of objects of enjoyment (*bhogya-sāhitya*) alone is intended by the Commentator regarding the word *saha* found in the scripture. Otherwise, there would be a loss of the predominance of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-prādhānya*).

The sense is that, if the intent were to emphasize the association with the enjoyer, it would follow that the individual soul (*jīva*), as the enjoyer, would be established as primary in relation to the *Brahman* that is the object of enjoyment.
This explains the underlying intention behind the passage beginning with "of whom the unknown... (*yasyāmataṃ* etc.).

"Only those things possessing qualities (saguṇa) are observed to be objects of knowledge (jñeya)"—here, the particle *eva* (only) is displaced in its order. The meaning results in: "Only the knowability of things possessing qualities is observed; their unknowability is not observed. Consequently, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of knowability is established. And thus, it should be understood that by the absence of that [knowability], the absence of the state of possessing qualities can be logically inferred. [This is stated] in the Bhāṣya as: "by the presence or absence of the cognition of Brahman."

If it is argued: "Does not the statement 'He becomes non-existent indeed' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1) declare that only a cognition characterized by non-existence (*asattva*) is the cause for the destruction of the Self, and not the ignorance of that [Self]?"—[we reply: In the passage "If he knows the Brahman as non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), the syntactical connection is "if [he] knows the Brahman [and finds it] non-existent"; the meaning is "if he does not know the Brahman. Likewise, in the passage "If he knows the Brahman as existent," the meaning is "if [he] knows the Brahman [and finds it] existent. This is according to the intention of the venerable Commentator (Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda).

Alternatively, the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) should be described in accordance with the sacred scriptures (*śruti*). Therefore, in the phrase "in some sentences" (*keṣucid vākyeṣu*), the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) must be explained [as referring to the scriptures], as well as the phrase "all the scriptures" (*sarvāḥ śrutayaḥ*). Now, one might object: the principle of the "cognition of all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*) has as its result the acceptance of unmentioned portions that are not included within the essential nature of the primary subject. However, in this case, knowledge—which is the means to liberation—enjoined in another scriptural passage is not being restated (*anūdya*) to have Brahman as its object by being enjoined as a subordinate quality (*guṇatayā*); rather, it is the knowledge of Brahman itself that is being enjoined.

Because the [previous] argument—that "by which that [negation] proceeds"—is unsatisfactory, he says: "Or rather, in some cases, it has as its object Brahman. Since others have stated that being an object of mere knowledge alone implies the absence of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), this text’s intent—being merely to refute the alternatives such as being an object of meditation—is inappropriate; therefore, out of dissatisfaction, he says: "Or rather, knowledge consists of meditation. [The phrase] "sublated by the injunction of qualities" means "even though it is sublated. Consequently, the meaning is that there is no lack of proof for the reason consisting in the absence of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*).

[The opponent argues: "Having set aside unknowability, it implies knowability. Let there be no further search for a means of knowledge regarding knowability; the meaning is that this very possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*) is sufficient as the proof for knowability. If it is objected: "Once the possession of qualities—which must be established in every respect—is proven, the proof of knowability by means of that possession of qualities is redundant, according to the maxim: 'When the latter is established, what is the use of the former?'"—to this some reply: "Even though the possession of qualities itself is the ultimate probandum..."

In that very context, such is the purport of the commentary; nevertheless, the following doubt arises there: "How could it establish the possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*) even for that which is consistent with scripture, given the absence of knowability (*jñeyatva*), which pervades that [quality]? Its resolution is stated by the words beginning with "having set aside 'non-knowable' (*ajñeya*)," and so forth.

Just as, when it is objected how a sacrifice—which is momentary and devoid of activity until the point of its fruit—can be the means to attain heaven, it is said that by the very force of establishing its status as the means to heaven, the existence of an activity persisting until that point is also inferred; so they say. In this context, the word "tatraiva" (in that very [context]) is to be explained.
This is the meaning of the scriptural passage beginning with "na dṛṣṭeḥ."

"Because it is adventitious and because it is a quality," and "by virtue of its association with the adventitious quality of consciousness. In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the words "adventitious" (*āgantuka*) and "quality" (*guṇa*) have the abstract state as their primary meaning; the word "consciousness" (*caitanya*) brings forward the substratum (*dharmin*). Consequently, the intended sense results in: "by virtue of consciousness's association with adventitiousness and the state of being a quality. This is the underlying point.

In the Bhāṣya, by the statement that the knower possesses adventitious consciousness as a quality, it is understood by the natural force of the words that the self, as the knower, is the subject (*pakṣa*), that insentience—characterized by having ignorance as its nature—is the probandum (*sādhya*), and that adventitious consciousness, which will be presented in the sūtra *jño'ta eva* as a proof for the insentience maintained by the followers of Kaṇāda, serves as the logical reason (*sādhana*).

Setting aside that [view], since it is contrary to the style of the sentence to claim that the two reasons—being adventitious (*āgantukatva*) and being a quality (*guṇatva*), which establish non-selfhood (*anātmatva*)—are intended to prove the side of knowledge (*jñānapakṣaka*), he says out of dissatisfaction: "Or rather, what is called consciousness (*caitanya*) is the illumination of objects. The sense is that for that which is by nature intrinsically conscious (*svataś-caitanyasvabhāva*), it is impossible for consciousness to be adventitious.

Having raised the objection that the suffix *-ktvā* is untenable because there is no identity of agent—since the act of negation "having rejected the individual self" (*jīvātmānaṃ pratiṣidhya*) is performed by the Scripture (the Śruti), whereas the act of meditation (*upāsana*) is performed by the individual self—the commentary explains this by supplying a word denoting an act of speaking whose agent is the Scripture, namely: "of seeing, hearing, thinking, and meditating" (*dṛṣṭi-śruti-mati-nididhyāsanānām*).

In this view, it is more appropriate that the meaning expressed is "meditate upon [this]"; for the reading "the word of the sentence is inappropriate" is unsatisfactory, [the author] says: "Or rather, the word 'abhidadhāti' (he declares) is to be supplied. Thus, when the meaning of the sentence is established, there is another sentence: "He declares, 'Meditate upon [this]'—this is the meaning of the sentence. Here, the sense is that in the phrase "He declares, 'Meditate upon [this]'—this is the meaning of the sentence," the word *iti* does not refer back to the immediately preceding meaning "he declares," but rather to the portion "Meditate upon [this].

Because it is not observed for the word *iti* to refer to something remote, [the author], being dissatisfied, says: "Or rather, having negated and abandoned [it]. This is the meaning of the scriptural passage concerning bliss (*ānanda*).

"In the Commentary, it is stated that knowledge alone which is favorable is called bliss (*ānanda*). Here, by the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, the status of being bliss is excluded for unfavorable knowledge, but not for the object [of knowledge] as well. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no contradiction with the doctrine that the manifestation (*vibhūti*) is bliss. Regarding the phrase "for of the bliss that has become a property (*dharma*)," the meaning is "but not of bliss in its mere essence. This is the meaning of the scriptural texts that negate duality.

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that in the Bhāṣya, the passage beginning with 'yatra hi' was first cited under the statement 'nanu yadidamuktam'? However, at the time of presenting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the entire sentence was cited after the sentence 'mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti'. What is the reason for adopting a different order of citation, abandoning the manner in which they were cited during the *pūrvapakṣa*? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer: "By means of the two passages beginning with 'yatra hi'. Previously, the [second] passage was cited later because its purpose was to demonstrate the cessation of difference.

However, it should be understood that the present inclusion [of the verse] together with the portion of the text negating difference—namely, "neha nānāsti" (here there is no diversity)—is because it is joined with the word *iva* and is intent on demonstrating the negation of difference. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of the repetition of the act of negation": this means "repeatedly," that is, in many places. This is because the suffix *śas* is prescribed for a *kāraka* when expressing "much" or "few" according to the rule "bahvalpārthācchaskārakādanyatarasyām"; and since the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is also a *kāraka*, the sense of repetition is thereby established, which is what is being stated as the implied meaning.

It should be understood that this is not for the sake of a causal condition (*pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "having the form of the delusion of becoming many": if omniscience were already established beforehand, a subsequent delusion would be untenable. For omniscience does not exist prior to the delusion of becoming many in Brahman, because the delusion of becoming many itself constitutes omniscience, and since that [delusion] is dependent upon ignorance (*avidyā*), it cannot be opposed to ignorance. Therefore, a contradiction must be admitted.

And therefore, the meaning is: how could [the scripture] establish the negation of difference—such as "not here, not there, not manifold"—which contradicts the meaning established by other scriptural passages supported by reasoning?

One might object: "Even though the scriptural texts denying difference are set aside by other contradictory scriptural texts supported by reasoning, there is no fault here because there is no such contradiction in the cited scripture which establishes that the knowledge of difference leads to what is harmful—namely, 'He goes from death to death'—which is augmented by the statement 'Those who see duality are the seers of evil. To this, he says: 'And here contradiction is understood. The construction is: the state of being the cause of transmigratory existence is heard [in scripture]; even there, contradiction is understood."

Furthermore, since the presentation of meanings contrary to the sacred word (*śruti*) is equal in all cases, one must accept only that meaning which is supported by reason (*nyāya*). The sense is this: the scriptural statement of difference (*bheda-śruti*) is supported by reason, whereas the scriptural statement of non-difference (*abheda-śruti*) is its opposite; therefore, it is impossible for the statement of non-difference to convey a meaning that contradicts the statement of difference supported by reason.

By this, the objection that the mere demonstration of mutual contradiction between two statements is irrelevant to the present context is refuted, because it is relevant to the subject matter according to the manner explained above. Regarding the phrase "in the state of liberation, which is the fruit of meditation": here, the status of being the fruit of meditation should be understood as occurring through a mediated succession (*paraṃparayā*). Here, by the force of the context, the word "world" (*jagataḥ*) is to be supplied [as the object of the verb]. Consequently, the intended meaning is that the word "world," when supplied, does not extend its denotation to include the substantive (*viśeṣya*) [to which it might otherwise be subordinate].

How is it that its being the inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*) is established by its being the food of that [world]? If it is argued: "Even if it is not established by the phrase 'the food of that,' it would be established by another scriptural passage such as 'He has entered within as the teacher of people,'" we say no; for since this very passage possesses the capacity to convey that meaning, the investigation of that passage's meaning is appropriate for the purpose of instructing the disciple. The doubt regarding the three reasons is as follows: its being an effect of that [world] establishes its being the inner ruler of that world, and its being the self of that [world] establishes their identity.

The sense is that being the inner controller (*antaryāmikatva*) of that [Brahman] is not, however, a direct means of establishing identity. Although it was stated that "because the world is the effect of Brahman and because it has Brahman as its inner controller, there is identity due to having that as its self (*tadātmakatva*)," the mention of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is [seemingly] contradicted by the contingency of suspecting that being the effect and being the inner controller are themselves what establish the state of having that as one's self. Thus, regarding *kāryatva*:

Anticipating the objection as to how immutability—which consists in the absence of defects—can be designated in the Bhāṣya as a "wholesome quality" (kalyāṇaguṇa), he says: "Being the opposite of defects is called a quality. The phrase "as before" means that this serves to exclude Brahman as possessed of qualities (saguṇabrahman).

"By way of the multiplicity of the excluded" means by way of the multiplicity of the counter-correlates of exclusion, namely, the unreal (*anṛta*), the insentient (*jaḍa*), and the limited (*paricchinna*). "Because of the consequence of the words being synonyms" refers here as well—by the maxim of the crow’s eye—to the phrase in the subsequent sentence, "due to the absence of a difference in the grounds for application" (*pravṛttinimitta-bheda*). Now, one might object: is it not the case that the universal *sattā* (Being), which inheres in jars and so forth, is the ground for the application of the word "real" (*satya*), while the universals *jñānatva* (cognition-ness) and *ānandatva* (bliss-ness)—which inhere in consciousness and bliss that have acquired differentiation through the limiting adjunct (*upadhāna*) of the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*)—are [the grounds for the application of the words] "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*)?

If it is argued that, even though the referents indicated by words such as "truth" (satya), "knowledge" (jñāna), and "bliss" (ānanda) are non-different, these words are not synonyms because they denote the aforementioned universals (jāti) and thus do not have identical denotative meanings—as stated in the *Kalpataru*—we say no; for if existence (sattā) as it inheres in jars and other things were the denotation of the word "truth," then "truth-ness" (satyatva), being over-extended, would fail to be the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of Brahman.

Furthermore, you yourself accept that truthfulness (*satyatva*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman; yet, since this [truthfulness] would be common to both real and unreal objects due to its connection with the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) that inheres in them, it fails to exclude the unreal. Moreover, there would be the consequence of contradicting your own established doctrine, which holds that the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikasattva*)—defined as being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time—is the scriptural definition of Brahman. Finally, without a difference (*bheda*) possessing the same level of reality (*samasattāka*) as the substrate (*dharmin*), it is impossible for "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*) and "bliss-ness" (*ānandatva*) to function as universals (*jāti*) based merely on a difference conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*), just as the case of "ether-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and the like.

Furthermore, because properties such as "knowability" (jñānatva) reside in the conditioned consciousness (upahita-caitanya)—which possesses a difference co-extensive with the substrate (dharmin)—they cannot be considered defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of the pure [Brahman]. By this, the following view is refuted: that words such as "Real" (satya), which denote the variegated Brahman (śabala-brahman) qualified by reality and other attributes, possess "indication" (lakṣaṇā) toward the pure Brahman, and thus they are not synonyms. This is because reality and other such qualities cannot belong to the variegated [Brahman], which is unreal, non-luminous, and limited. Even if they did belong to it, the exclusion of unreality, non-luminosity, and limitation would apply only to that [variegated entity] itself, and not to the pure [Brahman] which is the substratum of reality and the rest.

Therefore, since properties such as reality (satyatva) cannot exist elsewhere than in the Pure [Brahman], and since the sentence expressing reality and so forth has an indivisible meaning (akhaṇḍārtha) only through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), that [indivisible meaning] would likewise not be established even in the Pure [Brahman]. Consequently, because reality and the other attributes are absolutely non-existent [in the Pure Brahman], it is impossible to maintain that the words are not synonyms by taking their mutual difference into account; thus, the synonymy of these terms is established—this is the meaning.

The meaning of the alternative is as follows: whether by way of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) or a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), do the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) merely constitute objects of cognition for the word-meanings that are utilized in producing the cognition of Brahman—which has become the sentence-meaning—or is it the case that they also constitute objects of the cognition of the sentence-meaning itself? This same meaning also applies to the phrase "external to that which is indicated" (*upalakṣyād bahirbhūta*).

Furthermore, the state of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is not something distinct from being either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) or a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇatva*). For if the ear-cavity were not a qualifier in the expression "the auditory organ is space delimited by the ear-cavity," it would follow that the ear-cavity itself is the auditory organ, since there is a rule that whatever is connected with the qualifier must necessarily be connected with the qualificand.

Nor should it be argued that [the term "space"] functions as a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), because this would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that space—even when merely indicated by the ear-cavity—would occasionally constitute the auditory organ (*śrotra*). This is not a valid objection, because even in that case, it can be included within the very category of the secondary indicators; since the conjunction with an existing ear serves as a secondary indicator, there is no fault. Regarding the phrase "distinct from the indicated object," the intended meaning (*bhāva*) is as follows: Is the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) used for the purpose of apprehending the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of the self], or for the purpose of apprehending the property of being cognition (*jñānatva*) and so forth? It cannot be the first, because that has already been previously apprehended.

Not the second [alternative], because it would contradict its status as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). The construction is: "by all words at the time of denoting the sentence-meaning" (*sarvaiḥ padair vākyārthābhidhānadaśāyām*). Alternatively, "by all" means "by producing a single cognition," that is, by generating one unified cognition; therefore, one should understand that there is no logical inconsistency in the connection.

[Objection: But surely, if there were simultaneous denotation, the determination of the relative strength and weakness among *śruti*, *vākya*, and so forth, would be entirely inconsistent; for the established rule—that word-*śruti* is stronger than sentence (*vākya*), and suffix-*śruti* is stronger than word-*śruti*—would be rendered null and void. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "Even in the case of sequential denotation. This means: "The position of one who does not accept sequential denotation"—that is, the view of the proponent who rejects the theory of sequential denotation.

The point is this: even if they are presented simultaneously, the distinction does not disappear; for when there is a relationship between the subject (uddeśya) and the predicate (upādeya), the mere fact of being known or unknown by the cognition of that sentence is irrelevant. Rather, what was already understood through another means of knowledge (*māna*) prior to the operation of that sentence is restated (*anūdyate*), whereas what has not been so established is enjoined (*vidhīyate*). This is the essential distinction. Anticipating the objection—how can one discern the division between subject and predicate if the characteristics of being subject and predicate do not exist due to their temporal sequence—he says: "by a single sentence. [This] is indeed possible at the stage of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

If it is argued that the knowledge of the distinction between the object to be designated (*uddeśya*) and the object to be acquired (*upādeya*), characterized by being known and unknown respectively, is not required for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—such that its apprehension would need to be established during the stage of reflection prior to that comprehension—we say no. For in cases such as "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), if there were no determination of the specific modes of expression (e.g., "He should cleanse the cup," "He should cleanse one [cup]," or "That which he cleanses, that is one"), the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would not arise free from doubt.

The sense is that [the sentence] conveys the meaning of the sentence only after the syntactical structure (*vacanavyakti*) has been established through logical reasoning (*nyāya*). Regarding the phrase "because the case endings are identical due to the oneness of the substantive alone" (*viśeṣyamātraikyaparatvāt samānavibhakteḥ*), the intended meaning is as follows: it is indeed accepted that the sentence establishes the identity of the qualified entities (*viśiṣṭaikyapratipādana*); for we do not admit the establishment of the identity of the qualified entities. Nor should it be argued that even the opponent accepts the mere establishment of the identity of the substantives alone; for the connection with the qualifiers, which is understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), is not abandoned.

This is because, according to the maxim "one [attribute] in one qualificand is two," there is no abandonment of the two qualifiers—singularity and being a qualifier—which have been obtained; furthermore, the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*), meaning it is not rooted in convention (*śakti*) like the etymological derivation of words such as "heaven" (*svarga*).

Furthermore, perception itself makes known the identity of the qualified substratum (*viśeṣya*). Thus, in cases such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) or "the man with earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*), one perceives through the linguistic usage of elders that the case-ending of the qualifier refers to a single qualified substratum even when there are multiple qualifiers; this is because linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) is acquired precisely in that manner. Otherwise, even the view that the case-ending of a qualifier expresses non-difference (*abheda*) would have to be abandoned, for there is no [scriptural] basis for the claim that the case-ending of a qualifier is intended to express identity.

The sense is that there is no other cause [for the cognition of difference] than an understanding dependent upon the linguistic usage of elders, handed down from one to another. If it is argued that "the distinction of the qualified [substratum] is set aside in that case by perception," the intention is that in the case of Brahman, which is not within the scope of perception, the distinction of the qualified based on the distinction of qualifiers is unavoidable. This is because a cognition of identity arises from the unity of the words denoting the subject (*dharmin*) and from the use of the same grammatical case-ending. This is [an objection].

The general rule is that when there is a difference in qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is a difference in the qualified (*viśeṣya*). This is because [such a distinction] is not observed in cases such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young," and because in cases such as "the broken one" and "the shaven one," the qualifiers are contradictory. However, the capacity to differentiate is non-contradictory and thus does not actually differentiate; the claim that qualifiers possess the power of differentiation is made with respect to the substratum of those qualifiers themselves, and not even with respect to the substrata of other qualifiers. Indeed, it should be understood that in cases such as "a blue lotus," the quality of blueness does not exclude [the object] from being long as well.

As for what was said regarding "identical case-endings" (*samānavibhakti*), it should not be argued: "Since the apprehension of identity through identical case-endings would entail the collapse of the opponent's [Advaitin's] doctrine of partless meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*), how can this doubt of the opponent even arise? This is because one must consider that the doubt is possible for someone who thinks that "partless meaning" consists merely in being restricted to the single referent of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus only a connection with another referent of the nominal stem is excluded, whereas a connection with a case-ending is not. Thus, the doubt is conceivable.

"In the view that [the word] does not denote anything additional, there is a failure of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*); this means there is a failure of the reason consisting in the contradiction with the cognition of identity apprehended through the use of identical case-endings. This should be understood because the conclusion later on states, 'there is a failure of the reason consisting in the contradiction with the cognition of identity. Alternatively, intending to show that indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—whether as the presentation of an impossible or dissimilar correlate for connection, or as a relation with what is possible—is not possible in the case of what is incapable [of primary denotation], he says: 'even though it is not indicative (*alakṣaṇikatvepi*)."

The following argument has been refuted: "The disputed sentence has an undivided (non-dual) meaning, etc.; the inference that 'the sentence consisting of "satya" and so forth is established in an undivided meaning, because it is a defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*), or because it is an answer to a question regarding that alone, like the sentence "The moon is the most excellent light," is the proof; and since sentences of co-referential apposition such as "a blue lotus" lack the status of a defining statement, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)."

It should also be observed that the property of being a sentence whose characteristic is an uncommon form is pervaded by having a determinate (sakhaṇḍa) meaning; otherwise, since the Karma-kāṇḍa would also be an answer to a question concerning that alone, it would follow that it too possesses an indeterminate (akhaṇḍa) meaning. Furthermore, in the example "the moon is the most excellent light," the illustrative instance is unestablished because it is an answer to a question regarding a differentiator and an uncommon attribute.

And if the proposition is that [the sentence] is incapable of conveying a *khaṇḍārtha* (particularized meaning) consisting of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), then the sense is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*); for although the propositional statement possesses the capacity to convey the qualification of being a *khaṇḍārtha* consisting of the absence of a positive entity, it lacks the capacity to convey a *khaṇḍārtha* consisting of a positive entity. Regarding the phrase "by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone [is there] the connection with the qualifier": the meaning is that the nominal stem merely brings to mind the two qualified entities, and the case-ending conveys only their identity.

However, it should not be thought that the blue-ness (nīlatva) is construed with the lotus by means of the nominal stem *nīla*; for if that were the case, since the construing of blue-ness with the lotus would already be established by the nominal stem *nīla* alone, it would follow that the expression of identity by the case-ending is rendered purposeless—this is how it should be understood.

The sense is as follows: by the phrase *sisṛkṣoḥ* ("of the one desiring to create"), which establishes the Supreme Lord as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), the objection raised directly by the opponent is refuted. Furthermore, by the portion of the commentary stating that the status of being the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) is established by the text, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only," the objection raised by a bystander is refuted. Thus, the meaning of the term *advitīya* ("without a second") is that it is intended to negate any other independent entity.

For this very reason, in Śaṅkara’s commentary on the Upaniṣads as well, the term *advitīyam* (without a second) is explained specifically for the purpose of negating another instrumental cause. Just as in the case of clay, something other than the clay—such as a potter—is observed to be the instrumental cause that transforms it into the form of a jar and so forth, so too, in the case of Being (*sat*), a second thing would follow as a cooperative cause distinct from Being; this is what is prohibited. Thus, "without a second" (*advitīyam*) is interpreted as meaning that no second, separate entity exists for it, thereby focusing solely on the negation of any other instrumental cause.

Furthermore, it should be observed that since others have already explained the passage "In the beginning, there was only Being, one without a second" as referring to the period prior to creation, how could the mere fact of being without a second at the time prior to creation entail the conclusion that [the world] is false?

In the alternative analysis—whether the status of being the locus of knowledge is asserted because [the Self] is of the nature of knowledge (in order to avoid contradicting statements that it is devoid of qualities), or because the relationship of subject and attribute is impossible between two substances of the same genus—the commentary provides the refutation of the first position as: "Because the knower itself is of the nature of knowledge"; the meaning of this is that it is possible for the knower also to be of the nature of knowledge. As for the refutation of the second position, the commentary states: "Of that which is of the very nature of knowledge," and so forth.

The commentary, however, "For all the Śrutis declare that [the Self] is indeed the knower," serves as the justification for refuting the first alternative. This constitutes the first interpretation, which is supplementary to that [refutation].
