In this interpretation, one must resort to the fact that the commentary passage "For all the Śrutis declare that [the Self] is indeed the knower" justifies the more distant commentary passage "Because the knower is of the very nature of knowledge. Furthermore, the forced interpretation of the particle *eva* (indeed) as having the sense of *api* (also) should be regarded as a point of discordance.

In the second explanation, however, the engagement by way of an alternative (vikalpa) is the same as before; therein, the meaning of the commentary beginning with "of the knower alone" (*jñātureva*) is as follows: the word *jñātṛ* is primarily expressive of the state [of being a knower] (*bhāvapradhāna*), and the particle *eva* is intended to clarify that the very quality of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) which you have presented as being contradictory to the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*) is, in fact, the very proof for that nature of knowledge.

In this view—that the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is not contradictory [to the absence of knowledge] because it is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of the nature of knowledge—the commentary stating that "all the Śrutis indeed speak of the state of being a knower" is intended to strengthen that point by demonstrating the scriptural authority (*śrautatva*) of the state of being a knower. Furthermore, in this interpretation, one should note the underlying unease regarding the reliance on a construction where the reference is made with the abstract state (*bhāva*) as the primary factor, which is somewhat strained.

In the third explanation, however, the meaning of the commentary passage beginning with "of the knower alone" (jñātureva) is that there is no contradiction in the fact that the knower, being [itself] the knower, has the nature of knowledge. Furthermore, this commentary does not intend to reject either alternative of the dichotomy; rather, it is solely for the purpose of asserting non-contradiction. Having raised the dilemma—whether the knower's lack of being a substratum for knowledge is asserted because of the absence of the relation of attribute and substrate between two things of the same class, or whether it is due to its being knowledge itself—it first addresses the first alternative.

The phrase "of that which is of the very nature of knowledge" answers the second [objection]. The distinction is to be understood as "for it is indeed the state of being a knower," with the intended meaning being as explained previously. Does this mean it is stated by way of logical pervasion (*vyāpti*), or by scripture (*śruti*), and so forth? The meaning is: how does the state of being a knower become established? The answer is: "in such scriptural passages as 'Him, the Lord of lords... The manner in which it is established will be clarified later.

The meaning is that the omniscience of knowledge—expressed in the passages "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (*sarvajñaḥ sarvavit*)—is shown by the phrase "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*) as being applicable to the collective whole (*samaṣṭi*); by the phrase "This deity thought" (*seyaṃ devatā aikṣata*), its applicability to the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) is shown; and by the use of the first person "Let me create" (*sṛjai*), its connection to the Self is demonstrated. Furthermore, there is the quality of granting desires; the point is that without knowledge of the object desired, it would be impossible to grant it. And "deity-hood" (*devatātva*) means being one who is propitiated through ritual action (*karma*).

Action is that which serves as the cause for the pleasure of one worthy of propitiation. Consequently, it is established that [the Self] possesses knowledge whose form is pleasure. "Lordship" (patitva) means "being the enjoyer" (śeṣitva), which in turn means "being a conscious enjoyer" (śeṣicetanatva). This is because the designation of "lordship" is not applied to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the like, which are merely subordinate elements (śeṣa) such as the Prayāja offerings; therefore, the meaning is that the status of being a knower is established. [This concludes the discussion on] the second specific distinction...

The state of being a dweller [in the heart] has been indicated; therefore, the sense is that even such passages as "He has neither effect nor instrument" are relevant to the present topic. This refers to specific injunctions and specific prohibitions: by "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*) and so forth, there is a specific prohibition; by "whose desires are true" (*satyakāma*) and so forth, there is a specific injunction. If a restriction is made to avoid redundancy, it follows the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). In this context, the phrase "referring to objects other than those specifically mentioned" is to be supplied.

Its restriction is to a specific object that has been grasped. Nor is this merely the "goat-sacrifice" maxim (*chāgapaśunyāya*); rather, the "general-particular" maxim (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*) is indeed the "general-exception" maxim (*utsargāpavādanyāya*). For it must be stated that it is precisely because of such observation in linguistic usage that the term "general-particular maxim" applies to the "goat-sacrifice maxim" as well—just as the term "general-particular maxim" applies to the "general-exception maxim" by taking the general term to have a scope distinct from the particular. This is done by taking the word denoting the general to terminate its application in the particular.

Because of the absence of defects; in this regard, the mention of the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*) should be understood as having been made incidentally for the sake of favoring the disciples. Now, one might object: "How can it be said that the general injunction of qualities is not seen in the Śrutis? Anticipating this doubt—given that such [qualities] are indeed seen in passages such as "He who is the time of time, the possessor of qualities, the all-knowing"—the author says: "associated with the mention of defects. The meaning is: "associated with the mention of the state of being free from defects."

The sense is this: since the word "quality" (*guṇa*), which is mentioned alongside the absence of defects characterized by being subject to time (*kālakālya*), must refer to a specific quality rather than establishing a general injunction of qualities, one can only resort to the position of a hypothetical concession (*abhyupagamavāda*). It was stated, "of the sentences concerning qualities," with the intention of referring to the statements of the *Smṛti*. And here, the word "or" (*vā*) is to be supplied; the meaning is that it was stated, "of the sentences concerning qualities, or [it was stated] with the intention of referring to the statements [of the *Smṛti*]."

Alternatively, raising the objection, "How can there be an acceptance of the prescription of qualities and common characteristics (*guṇasāmānya*) for that which is absolutely unperceivable? he says, "By tens of thousands of years," and so forth. The meaning is: with reference to the statements of the *Smṛtis*, by means of the inference of a *Śruti* text prescribing qualities and common characteristics equal to those [stated] in these *Smṛtis*, it was said, "[this applies] to the passages concerning the possession of qualities (*saguṇavākya*). Regarding the phrase "the statement of the counteragent to defects":

The meaning is that, as in the phrase "merits and defects," this refers to the general category of merits that counteract defects—that is, it refers to the general category of things to be adopted—by virtue of the context, according to the maxim of the goat and the animal. Consequently, since even the general statements found in the *Smṛtis* must be understood as culminating in specific applications, the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "of the passages concerning the qualified [Brahman]," is justified for the purpose of including these; such is the intention. Here, the intended meaning is as follows: the sentence in the *Bhāṣya* ending with "because there is no contradiction between the passages concerning the qualified and the unqualified" is complete.

The phrase "even resorting to the falsity of the object of one [of the two] is not tenable" constitutes another statement. Here, the ellipsis "the acceptance of contradiction" (*virodhābhyupagama*) must be supplied; furthermore, the word *api* ("even") is to be construed out of its natural order. Thus, the intended meaning established is: "Even if one accepts the contradiction, it is not tenable to resort to the falsity of the object of either one. Consequently, the subsequent passage—which begins by stating that "previously, there was no contradiction"—is also logically consistent.

Otherwise, if they were a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), the statement "previously" would be impossible. Alternatively, the word "also" (*api*) should be supplied [to read "the intention here is also this"]: both the two words "previously" and "now" are not intended to be emphasized; rather, it is stated that there is no contradiction when one conforms to the actual state of things. The meaning is that even if a contradiction exists, it does not cause us any harm. The point is that there is no rule of necessity regarding the simultaneous occurrence of both [simultaneous] excisions (*apaccheda*), because the excision of only one of them is also possible. [The phrase] "contradiction limited to the time of performance" means...

The meaning is that because the two applications—the cause (the *nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittika*)—triggered by the two separate cases of disconnection (*apaccheda*) cannot be performed simultaneously, there is a contradiction between the two scriptural injunctions; therefore, [the application] occurs only occasionally. It has been stated regarding this subject of indefinite contradiction and sequence: "Sequence, contradiction, and the invalidity of the preceding [injunction] due to a rule do not exist there; in such a case, the principle of *apaccheda* applies."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "The inference of scripture that contradicts perception does not proceed; this is the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*). That principle does not apply here. If, based on the commonality of being faster or slower in their operation like perception and inference, the two types of statements—those concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman—were to have the same objective domain, then the statement regarding the unqualified would simply lack authority, just like the Smṛti."

If non-authoritativeness is indeed intended, then why does the *apaccheda-nyāya* (the principle of the later superseding the earlier) not apply? For it is said that the *apaccheda-nyāya* does not apply out of fear that its application to a matter of fixed sequence would result in the total invalidation [of the preceding]. Therefore, because of this lack of consensus—that the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*) does not apply to the subject of the Vedic revelation—it is said: "Or rather, let it not be so; it is precisely the principle of the section on the introductory statement (*upakramādhikaraṇa*). As it is said: "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa."

He [Prajāpati] approached his own deity; he was rent asunder. He saw this four-potherd offering to Varuṇa; "He offered it"—beginning thus, it is heard in the conclusion: "As many horses as one might receive as a gift, so many four-potherd offerings to Varuṇa should one offer. In that regard, in the introductory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the sacrifice to Varuṇa is understood as belonging to Prajāpati, the giver of the horse; whereas in the conclusion, it belongs to the receiver. When there is a conflict between these two, because the explanatory passage is subordinate and a restatement (*anuvāda*), it must be taken figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*).

"Even though the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) is subordinate, it does not suffer the loss of its own meaning. When this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been reached, [the siddhāntin replies]: because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), though subordinate, is stronger due to its lack of contradiction at the time of its arising, and because the injunctive statement—despite being primary—has not yet attained its full realization, the primary injunctive statement, being itself unrealized, is unable to sublate the explanatory passage situated within its own context which has already attained its realization; rather, the injunctive statement itself conforms to the requirements of that passage. Thus, by incorporating the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) into the word "pratigṛhṇīyāt" (he should accept), it means "he should cause [another] to accept," and therefore the desired result belongs to the giver alone.

This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Consequently, since the statement regarding the possession of attributes (*saguṇavākya*) or the perception apprehending difference (*bhedagrāhipratyakṣa*) has already occurred previously, the logic of the section on the introductory statement (*upakramādhikaraṇanyāya*) alone applies; thus, this is the method of the introductory statement (*upakramanaya*). [Regarding the phrase] "by way of existence or by way of being known": now, one might object that because the cognition "this is silver" is beset by a doubt as to its validity, and only a cognition unbeset by such doubt can act as an obstacle to a contrary cognition, there is no contradiction in the arising of the cognition "this is not silver."

Nor should it be suspected that even the doubt regarding invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-śaṅkā*) does not arise, since such a doubt would ultimately result in a doubt about the object itself; for this objection can be refuted simply by postulating, on the strength of the observed result (*phala-balāt*), that the causal complex for the doubt of invalidity acts as an "excitant" (*uttejaka*). If it is argued that this elaborate explanation (*prapañca*) is therefore superfluous, we reply that its elaboration is justified for the purpose of instructing the student. Furthermore, it is not the case that if the knowledge of the qualified nature [of Brahman] arises, the knowledge of its opposite—the qualityless nature—cannot arise because of the principle of the section on the "commencement" (*upakramādhikaraṇa-nyāya*), leading to the undesirable consequence that the perception of non-grasping (*agrahaṇa*) would not arise when there is the perception of the taking up of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup.

Likewise, it should not be argued that even in the case of a subsequent passage (*apacchada*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of a cognition contrary to what preceded; for the principle of the section on the "Commencement" (*upakramādhikaraṇa*) applies only to cases where there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), whereas in cases such as the acceptance or rejection [of a rule], that unity is absent. Nor should it be said that there is no syntactic unity even between the passages concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa* [Brahman]), as in:
"The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
the overseer of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious, alone, and devoid of qualities."

The sense is that since a single unified meaning (*ekavākyatva*) is perceived in such passages, and because other texts concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇavākya*) are similar to them, they too cannot produce a cognition of a meaning contrary to those [passages]. Regarding the phrase "because it depends on the recollection ‘this is silver’": the objection here is how a cognition contrary to that [prior one] can arise, given the contradiction with what is depended upon (*upajīvya*), since the cognition "this is silver" is dependent upon the cognition "this is not silver. [The response is: "The subsequent valid cognition has the nature of beingness (*śuktitva*) as its object."

This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication). Even though the cognition "this is silver" has as its object the absence of silverness (*rajatatvābhāva*), although the aspect consisting merely in the objecthood of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*) is dependent (*upajīvya*), there is no fault in its apprehending that absence because the aspect consisting in the objecthood of silver with respect to the thing present before one (*purovartin*) is not dependent. In the reading "udīyamānam," it should be understood as a form of the root *iṇ* in the sense of "motion. [The phrase] "because of the abundance of indicators of purport such as 'Bliss is Brahman'" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇaḥ*) and so forth.

The meaning is that, even with respect to the *brāhma* [bliss], since it is taught that only the experience of bliss which is subordinate to that [knowledge] possesses fruitfulness, one understands that the scriptural statement regarding *brāhmānanda* has that as its intended purport.
(The Ānandavallī concerns the qualified [Brahman]).

The reading is *paryavasitam yuktaṃ*. The meaning is that its conclusion (*paryavasāna*) is appropriate. In some places, the reading *paryavasituṃ yuktaṃ* is observed. In that case, one should somehow justify it by deriving it from the root *as* (meaning "to throw") preceded by *ava*, with the elision of the final vowel of the prefix *ava* according to the rule "Bhāguri effects the elision of the [final] *a* of the prefixes *ava* and *api*," followed by the suffix *tumun*.

Because the suffix *tumun* is applied to the root *antakarmaṇi*, there is no *kit* quality [for the suffix], and consequently, the substitution of *i* (as prescribed by the rule *dyatisyatimāsthām*) does not occur. For this very reason, the Teacher will say in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*: "those who have reached their conclusion, having set out to reach a conclusion. The phrase "so that it may be eternally new" means "in such a way that it becomes eternally fresh. The compound *yuvā cāsāvadhyāyakaśca* ("he is both young and a student") is a *karmadhāraya*. The meaning is that the youthfulness of the student culminates through the act of studying.

*Āśutarakriyaḥ*: This form arises from the word *āśu*, meaning "possessing swift action," when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is added and the *ṭi*-portion (*u*) is elided. Alternatively, it may be understood as derived from the word *āśumat* ("swift") with the suffix *matup* dropped according to the rule "the elision of *vin* and *matup*" (*vinmatorluk*). *Aśanakṣamaḥ*: Here, *āśaḥ* means "eating" (*aśanam*). From this, the suffix *matup* is added, and then the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied. *Āśiṣṭhaḥ*: This form is derived from the word *āśis* (meaning "blessing"), which refers to the domain of benediction, by adding the suffix *iṣṭhan* either directly or from the stem *āśimat* (possessing a blessing). In all these cases, the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied and the suffix *matup* is elided according to the rule "the elision of *vin* and *matup*" (*vinmatorluk*).

Regarding the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārtha-*: the sense is that because the word *suhita* means "satisfied," and fulfillment (*pūraṇa*) is also of the nature of satisfaction. However, the word *pūraṇa* in this context [of the present discussion] is not to be understood as the word *pūraṇa* [from the aforementioned rule], because that [word in the rule] refers to the suffixes of ordinal numbers (*pūraṇapratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "because of the permission of the genitive": the meaning is that by this sūtra, which is intended to prohibit genitive compounds, there is an implied permission for the genitive. Regarding the phrase "by way of averting the undesirable": the meaning is "by way of preventing what is unwanted. Regarding the phrase "the intention being the superiority of the bliss of the Four-Faced One": [this is the intended meaning].

In the phrase "those who are a hundred," the word "hundred" refers to a number exceeding that; thus, the sense is that there is no limitation. Since the sentences in this context are intended to convey a specific number, it would be more appropriate for the phrase "those who are a hundred of Prajāpati" also to convey a specific number; therefore, he offers an alternative interpretation: "Or rather, [it refers] to 'those who are a hundred, that is one. The sense is that once it is stated that the bliss of Prajāpati exists throughout the three periods of time, its unlimited nature is established.

"And by virtue of possessing the manifestation of the three quarters. Now, one might ask: "If the unlimited nature of the Lord's bliss has been ascertained, how can the limited nature set forth by the statement 'those who are a hundred [of those]' be consistent? And for one who asks this, how would the statement regarding the infinity of bliss by virtue of possessing the manifestation of the three quarters be applicable? To this, some say that the reading should be: "If it be asked, 'How is there unlimitedness? [instead of "How can the limited nature..."].

And this is its meaning: "By the sentence 'those who are a hundred,' how can indefiniteness be understood? On the contrary, definiteness alone is perceived. Therefore, they describe the objection up to the point that indefiniteness would not be established. Consequently, in order to refute that [objection], it must be demonstrated by this scriptural statement that definiteness is not established.

Intending to demonstrate the sequence of the unlimited nature of bliss (*ānanda*), they say that by this statement, having established the non-establishment of limitation, the unlimited nature is also established by means of another proof (*pramāṇa*).

Others, however, raise the objection of a bystander: "Why is this explained—either by restricting the meaning of the word 'hundred' to the bliss of Prajāpati alone existing in the three periods of time, or by taking the word 'hundred' to mean merely a large number—in contradiction to the natural sense of the Śruti, 'A hundredfold is the bliss of Prajāpati'? The literal meaning as heard in the text should simply be accepted. To dispel this doubt, they say: "[The bliss of the individual] is like an atom compared to Mount Meru" (this refers to the meaning of the Śruti passage beginning with "He enjoys," etc.).

Now, one might object: since the Brāhmaṇa passage, "Through the Brāhmaṇa [he] attains the Supreme," establishes that the Brāhmaṇa alone is the object to be attained; and since the Brāhmaṇa itself, in the statement "This is his supreme bliss," declares that the Brāhmaṇa is the bliss of the knowers, and because desires are perceived as non-different from it—and furthermore, because the Brāhmaṇa is more authoritative as being the explanatory commentary (*vivaraṇa*) upon the mantra—the meaning of the mantra "together with the Brāhmaṇa" (*saha brāhmaṇā*) must be described in strict accordance with the Brāhmaṇa.

Anticipating the objection that the meaning of the mantra "dvā suparṇā" is described in accordance with the *Brāhmaṇa* in the *Paingirahasya*, [the author] states: "Because it is observed that mantras take the form of explanations of the *Brāhmaṇas*. The sense is that since it is also observed that mantras take the form of explanations of the *Brāhmaṇas*, the reason for their authority—namely, the fact of being an explanatory form—is common to both [the mantra and the *Brāhmaṇa*].

Regarding the phrase "because they are the cause of clear comprehension": generally, the Brāhmaṇas possess the quality of being causes for clear understanding, whereas the Mantras are profound; it is on this basis alone that the statement regarding the superiority of the Brāhmaṇas is entirely acceptable—this is the meaning. If it is objected: "In the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*, some maintain the superiority of the Mantras, and since you have cited the very superiority of the Mantras as the view of others, there is a contradiction"—we reply: no; for that too must be seen as a different opinion, and thus there is no contradiction.

Because the state of being *vipaścit* (the all-seeing) is mentioned, and because that [state] is consistent with being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the suspicion that the Brahman might be associated with an enjoyer is set aside; for it is stated that even the state of being *vipaścit* is a quality of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Nor should it be suspected that its separate mention is redundant since it is already indicated by the word "desires" (*kāma*); the point is that the separate mention is appropriate according to the maxim of "cattle and bulls" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), intended to express its preeminence. [This concludes the section on] "because of the mention of distinction."

The meaning is that this is because they are designated as distinct by the phrase "desires together with the Brahman. And it is also because of the natural force of their immediate juxtaposition. The point is that if the text were "he enjoys all desires together with the Brahman," then there might indeed be a suspicion that the enjoyer—referred to by the word "he" (saḥ)—is the locus of that conjunction. "In order to avoid that" means: in order to avoid that [suspicion] by accepting the desired conclusion. It is like the statement, "That which is within Him is what must be sought."

This was stated with the intention of accepting that the phrase "in that" (*tasmin*) refers to the small ether (*daharākāśa*), and thus asserting that the qualities themselves are what must be sought. However, in reality, since it will be explained later that the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "what is within that" (*tasmin yad antaḥ*) refers to two things—the small ether and the Brahman—it should be understood that both Brahman and its qualities are objects of meditation, and thus their equal primacy is established, rather than the primacy of the qualities alone.

Alternatively, the sense is that since the word *saha* indicates subordination (*aprādhānya*), it is improper to speak of the subordinate status of the Brahman; furthermore, in accordance with the passage on the "small ether" (*daharavidyā*), its purport lies precisely in equality. By the phrase "to express the predominance of the quality," the meaning is as follows: through this statement, "to express the predominance of the quality," it is established that the Bhāṣyakāra intends by the word *saha* occurring in the Śruti merely the accompaniment of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Otherwise, there would be the predominance of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).

The sense is that, if the intent were to emphasize the association with the enjoyer, it would follow that the individual soul (*jīva*), as the enjoyer, would be established as primary in relation to the *brāhmaṇa* who is the enjoyer.
(This is the description of the underlying intention of the passage beginning with "To whom it is unknown," etc.)

"Only those possessing qualities (*saguṇa*) are observed to be objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). Here, the particle *eva* (only) is to be construed out of its natural order. The meaning results in: "Only the knowability of things possessing qualities is observed; their unknowability is not observed. Consequently, the pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) of knowability is established. From this, it should be understood that by the absence of that [knowability], the absence of possessing qualities can be logically inferred. In the *Bhāṣya*, it says: "by the presence or absence of the cognition of Brahman."

If it is argued: "Does not the statement 'He becomes non-existent indeed' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.1) declare that only a cognition characterized by non-existence (*asattva*) is the cause for the destruction of the Self, and not the ignorance of that [Self]?"—[we reply: according to the intention of the venerable commentator [Śaṅkara], the syntactical connection of the passage "If he knows the Brahman as non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1) is: "If he knows the Brahman [and yet finds it] non-existent. The meaning is: "If he does not know the Brahman. Similarly, in the passage "If he knows the Brahman as existent," the meaning is: "If the [phrase] 'he knows the Brahman' exists [therein], i.e., if he knows the Brahman. This is the purport of the Blessed Commentator.

Alternatively, the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) should be described in accordance with the sacred scriptures (*śruti*). Therefore, in the phrase "in certain sentences" (*keṣucid vākyeṣu*), the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be explained as referring to [the fact that] "all the scriptures" (*sarvāḥ śrutayaḥ*) [teach this]. Now, one might object: the principle of the "recognition of all recensions" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*) results in the acceptance of unmentioned parts that do not fall within the essential nature of the primary subject. However, in this case, knowledge—which is the means to liberation—enjoined by another sentence is not being restated (*anūdya*) merely to have its status as an attribute of Brahman enjoined in some instances; rather, it is the knowledge of Brahman itself that is being enjoined.

Because there is a lack of consensus as to how that [negation] proceeds logically, he says: "Or rather, in some cases, it concerns the subject matter of the Brāhmaṇas. Since others have stated that being the object of mere knowledge alone implies the absence of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), this text’s intent—being merely to refute the alternative views such as its being the object of meditation—is inappropriate; therefore, out of dissatisfaction with that, he says: "Or rather, knowledge consists of meditation. Regarding the phrase "sublated by the injunction of qualities": the meaning is "even though it is sublated. Consequently, the point is not merely that the reason—the absence of being an object of knowledge—is unestablished (*asiddha*).

It implies knowability by subverting unknowability. The meaning is: let there be no search for another means of knowledge regarding knowability; this very quality of possessing attributes (*saguṇatva*) is sufficient to establish knowability. If it is objected that once the possession of attributes—which must be established in every respect—is proven, establishing knowability through the possession of attributes is redundant, according to the maxim "what is the use of the prior when the subsequent is already established?", some reply that although the possession of attributes itself is the ultimate probandum (*paramasādhya*);

In that very context, such is the purport of the commentary; nevertheless, the following doubt arises there: "How can it establish the possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*) even for that which is consistent with scripture, given the absence of knowability (*jñeyatva*), which pervades it? Its resolution is stated by the words beginning with "having set aside unknowability" (*ajñeyatvaṃ bādhitvā*).

Just as, when it is objected how a sacrifice—which is momentary and devoid of activity until the point of its fruit—can be the means for attaining heaven, it is said that by the very force of establishing its status as the means to heaven, the existence of an activity persisting until that point is also inferred; so too [they] say. In this context, the word "tatraiva" (right there) is to be explained.
(This is the meaning of the scriptural passage beginning with "na dṛṣṭeḥ").

"Because of being adventitious and because of being a quality. And [this means] "by virtue of being endowed with the adventitious quality of consciousness (*caitanya*). In the *Bhāṣya*, the words "adventitious" (*āgantuka*) and "quality" (*guṇa*) have the abstract state (*bhāva*) as their primary sense; the word "consciousness" (*caitanya*) serves to present the substratum (*dharmin*). Consequently, the intended meaning results in: "by virtue of consciousness possessing the states of being adventitious and being a quality"—this is the underlying point.

In the *Bhāṣya*, by the phrase "the state of being of the nature of ignorance for the knower due to its association with the adventitious quality of consciousness," it is understood from the natural flow of the argument that the self as the knower is the subject (*pakṣa*), that insentience—characterized by the nature of ignorance—is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), and that adventitious consciousness is the probans (*sādhana*) intended to establish the insentience favored by the followers of Kaṇāda, as will be presented under the sūtra, "Therefore, [the self] is indeed a knower" (*jño'ta eva*).

Setting aside that [interpretation], he says—"Or rather, consciousness (caitanya) is the illumination of objects"—because it would contradict the style of the passage to claim that the two reasons, namely *āgantukatva* (adventitiousness) and *guṇatva* (quality-ness), which establish non-selfhood (*anātmatva*), are intended here. The underlying sense is that for that which is by nature intrinsically conscious, adventitious consciousness is impossible.

In the commentary [on the passage], "Having negated the individual self (jīvātman), one should meditate only upon the Supreme Self (paramātman), the Self of all beings," it is stated that "the individual self is negated. Since the action of negation has the Śruti as its agent, whereas meditation has the individual self as its agent, there is an absence of a common agent; therefore, the suffix *ktvā* [cannot be applied].

Anticipating the objection regarding the impossibility [of this construction], he explains it by supplying words that express the agent of the hearing, the speaker, and the action—namely, "of seeing, hearing, thinking, and meditating. In this view, it is more appropriate to say that the meaning expressed is "meditate upon" (*upāssva*); however, because the word *vākya* (sentence) is not properly joined [in that context], he offers an alternative: "or rather, the word 'abhidadhāti' (denotes) is to be supplied," thus forming the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) as a distinct sentence.

In the phrase, "the meaning of the sentence is 'one should meditate,' [and] 'it denotes,'" the word *iti* refers not to the proximate meaning "it denotes," but rather to the portion "one should meditate"—this is the intended sense. Because it is not observed that the word *iti* can refer to something remote, and because this would be unsatisfactory, he says: "Or rather, having negated and abandoned [the former].
(The meaning of the *Ānanda* Śruti.)

In the commentary, it is stated that "knowledge alone which is favorable is called bliss. Here, by the use of the particle *eva* ("alone"), the status of being bliss is excluded for knowledge that is unfavorable, but not for the object [of that knowledge] as well. Therefore, it should be understood that there is no contradiction with the doctrine that the manifestation (*vibhūti*) is bliss. Regarding the phrase "for of the bliss that has become a property" (*dharmabhūtānandasya*), the meaning is "but not of bliss in general" (*ānandamātrasya*).
(The meaning of the scriptural texts denying duality.)

Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that in the Bhāṣya, the passage beginning with 'yatra hi' was first cited under the statement 'nanu yadidamuktam'? Yet, at the time of presenting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the entire sentence was cited after the sentence 'mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyumāpnoti'. What is the reason for adopting it in a different manner, setting aside the manner in which it was cited during the prima facie view? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer: "By means of the two passages beginning with 'yatra hi'. Previously, it was cited later [in the *siddhānta*] because its purpose was to demonstrate the cessation of difference.

However, it should be understood that the inclusion [of this phrase] together with the portion of the text negating difference—"neha nānāsti" (here there is no diversity)—is because it is joined with the word *iva* and is intended to demonstrate the negation of difference. The meaning is "the repetition of the act of negation. The term "repeatedly" (*bahuśaḥ*) means "in many places," since the suffix *śas* is prescribed for a *kāraka* when expressing much or little according to the rule "bahvalpārthācchaskārakādanyatarasyām," and because the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is also a *kāraka*. Thus, this is a statement of the resultant meaning, as the repetition has been established as the consequence.

It should be understood that this is not by way of being an object of cognition (*pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "the form of the delusion of becoming manifold": if omniscience were already established beforehand, a subsequent delusion would be untenable. For Brahman does not possess omniscience prior to the delusion of becoming manifold; rather, the delusion of becoming manifold itself constitutes omniscience, and since that [delusion] is dependent upon ignorance (*avidyā*), it cannot be in opposition to ignorance. This is the intended meaning. Therefore, a contradiction must be admitted.

Therefore, the meaning is: how could [the scripture] establish the negation of difference in passages such as "There is no diversity here," which contradicts the meaning established by other scriptural passages supported by reasoning?

One might object: "Even though there exist other contradictory scriptural passages supported by reasoning, there is no fault here because there is no such contradiction with the cited scripture which establishes that the knowledge of difference is useless—namely, 'He goes from death to death'—which is reinforced by the Smṛti passage, 'Those who hold to duality see what is unreal. Anticipating this doubt, he says: 'And here a contradiction is perceived. The construction is as follows: it is heard [in scripture] that [difference] is the cause of transmigratory existence; even there, a contradiction is perceived."

Furthermore, since the presentation of mutually contradictory meanings is equal everywhere, one must accept only that meaning which is supported by logic (*nyāya*). The sense is this: the scriptural testimony of difference (*bheda-śruti*) is supported by logic, whereas the scriptural testimony of non-difference (*abheda-śruti*) is contrary to it; therefore, it is impossible for the scriptural testimony of non-difference to convey a meaning that contradicts the scriptural testimony of difference supported by logic.

By this, the objection that the mere demonstration of mutual contradiction between two statements is irrelevant to the present context has been refuted, because, according to the method stated, it is indeed relevant to the subject at hand. The phrase "in the state of liberation, which is the fruit of meditation" (upāstiphalabhūtamuktidaśāyām) should be understood here as referring to the state of liberation being the fruit of meditation through a mediated sequence (*paraṃparayā*). Here, by the force of the context, the word "of the world" (*jagataḥ*) is to be supplied; thus, the intention is that the word "world," when supplied, does not extend its scope to include the substantive [to which it might otherwise refer].

How is the status of being its inner ruler established by the fact of being its food? If it is argued that even if this is not established by the phrase "its food," it is nonetheless established by another scriptural passage such as "He has entered within, the ruler of people," we say no; for it is appropriate to investigate the meaning of that very passage in order to instruct the disciple, since that specific passage possesses the capacity to convey that very meaning. Thus, there might arise a doubt regarding the three reasons.

The meaning is this: its being an effect is to be established by its having that as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*), and its being of the same nature as that is what establishes their identity; however, its having that as its inner controller is not itself a direct establisher of identity.

Although it might be argued that the statement, "Because the world is one with Brahman due to its being an effect of Brahman and because of its having Brahman as its inner ruler," is contradictory—since the status of being an effect and the status of having [Brahman] as an inner ruler could lead to the suspicion that they are themselves the grounds for [the world] being identical to That—it should nevertheless be understood that there is no fault. This is because the intent is merely to demonstrate a way of reconciling what already exists, and because such an application will also be explained later and is thus intended.

The meaning is that there would be a difference in the referents of the word *aikya* (oneness). The intention is that it is not possible for a word used only once to have two distinct meanings without resorting to a secondary figurative sense (*vṛtti*). Consequently, regarding the phrase "by the world being of the nature of That": since a word used only once must rely on a single meaning, and because it is improper to accept a non-primary oneness of the substrates (*prakāryaikya*), when one must instead rely on the meaning in the form of non-difference (*abheda*), it is entirely improper to say "because of the oneness of the world through its being of the nature of That. The underlying point is that the non-difference between the world and Brahman is sublated by perception.

Furthermore, how can it be said that it is improper to state "because of the identity [of Brahman] with the world by virtue of having that as its nature"? Why is it not stated instead that "it is improper to state [the identity] because of being identical with its body"? The doubt that this is so due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamakābhāva*) has been refuted, because it was stated that [Brahman] is the Supreme Brahman qualified by the world. The sense is that the connection of identity is not accepted with the meaning of the word *jagat* (world) when it is understood as an abstracting term (*niṣkarṣaka*). And there is no difference in meaning for the word *eka* (one/identical).

Although this doubt is already refuted by the statement that [the Lord] is qualified by the universe (*jagad-viśiṣṭa-brahma-para*), and thus the elaboration of their identity (*aikya*) might seem superfluous, it should nevertheless be understood that he analyzes and demonstrates the nature of this identity for the sake of instructing the disciple. "The identity of the entity qualified by the conscious and unconscious [principles] as they undergo two states" means the identity of the entity qualified by the conscious and unconscious [principles] when they have entered the two states characterized by grossness and subtlety. "Just as [in the case of] form, touch, and so forth."

Just as a mass characterized by specific color and touch, having reached the state of being a "lump" (*piṇḍatva*), attains identity with a jar characterized by specific color and touch that has reached the state of being a "jar" (*ghaṭatva*)—wherein consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) occupy the place of the color, touch, and so forth residing in the jar, while the two states [of lumpness and jar-ness] occupy the place of lumpness, jar-ness, and so on—it has been stated thus. However, this much is the distinction: in the case of Brahman, there is the possession of states through the medium of the conscious and the unconscious; whereas in the case of the jar and so forth, [it is not so].

It should be understood that this refers to the entity as characterized by states mediated through [the senses of] form, touch, and so forth. In this context, the appropriate illustration is the identity of the entity as qualified by a body that has undergone two states—namely, childhood and youth. For this very reason, he will say: "This very same person has become young. Alternatively, it should be seen that "having undergone two states" is a qualification of both consciousness and the non-conscious; for the inherent sense of the forthcoming text is that there is identity of the substratum (dharmin) which serves as the locus for qualifications consisting of states occurring at different times. Thus, there is no loss of the identity of the entity.

The meaning is that there would be a loss of the identity between the qualified entity [Brahman] and the world. Now, in this interpretation, the word *jagat* (world), which denotes the world in its abstracted form, must be supplied; and it must be stated that the word *brāhṛ* refers to the Supreme as qualified by the subtle sentient and insentient [matter], when proving their non-difference based on the reasons of "being born from that" (*tajjatva*) and "having that as its cause" (*tallatva*). This is because one must adopt the sense that "all this [universe] with its gross body is the *brāhṛ* with its subtle body, by virtue of being born from that and having that as its cause. However, if the reason is simply "not being other than that" (*tadananyatva*), then the word *brāhṛ* refers to that which is qualified by the state of being the *brāhṛ*.

Because [Brahman] is qualified as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), there is a difference in the nature of the word *brahma* here. In the phrase *tajjalān*, the single word *tat* refers to that which is qualified by the subtle sentient and insentient [principles] in relation to both origin and dissolution; however, in this [present case], it refers merely to that which is qualified by the state of being Brahman.

Having first proposed the non-difference of the world from Brahman in the statement, "All this, indeed, is Brahman," and then having set forth the reasons for that—namely, being of its nature (*tadātmatva*) and being its inner ruler (*tadantaryāmitva*)—with respect to the world which serves as the qualifier, there arises a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the reason and the subject. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is naturally understood that both being an effect of Brahman and being its inner ruler serve to establish that the world is identical with Brahman. Keeping all this in mind, [the author] says: "Or rather, of the entire world... and so forth.

"Sound is the extract. Now, in this position, does the *Bhāṣya* intend to express merely its being an effect (*kāryatva*)? Or rather, its being derived from that (*tadupādeyatva*)? Not the first, because mere effectness is not a necessary condition for identity with that in the sense of non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhatva*). Otherwise, it would follow that a jar is identical with its staff, since the jar is non-separately existent from the staff. Furthermore, the world cannot have Brahman as its material cause (*upādāna*), because it is distinct from Him; for there must necessarily be non-difference between a material cause and its product.

Furthermore, what is it that is observed in the world to be the primary means of establishing identity? It is the state of being the material cause (*upādeyatva*). On the other hand, the state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmikatva*) establishes only a non-primary identity. Therefore, if it is asked how both can function as means for establishing identity within a single entity through their conjunction, it is replied: it is precisely the state of being the material cause that establishes the nature of being identical with that [cause] in the form of non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhatva*).

Nor should it be argued that because the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) are non-different, the status of being an effect cannot establish non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhatva*); for even though clay and a jar are non-different, their non-separate existence is possible, since the mere absence of separate existence is not incompatible with non-difference.

Nor should it be asked how the world, being distinct from Brahman, can be the effect (*upādeya*); for it is accepted that that which possesses a future state is the effect, while that which possesses a prior state is the material cause (*upādāna*). And since the world possesses a future state, it is an effect; by that same fact, Brahman also possesses a future state. Therefore, both are effects with respect to Brahman as qualified by the subtle world, which possesses the prior state.

If it is argued that, since the world also possesses its prior state according to the aforementioned reasoning, Brahman would likewise incur the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of being its material cause (*upādāna*), we reply: no, because there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) for Brahman’s status as its material cause. Nor should it be said: "How can there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), given that there is no other nature of being a material cause than possessing a prior state? For the definition of a material cause consists in a specific property distinct from that [mere possession of a prior state]. This is because the definition is possible in the form: "Material causality is simply being the object of the technical usage (*vyavahāra*) of the term 'material cause' by the learned."

If it is argued that in this view, the statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman" entails a figurative application (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "Brahman" to that which is non-distinct from Brahman—since it must be accepted that everything in the world is non-distinct from Brahman because it is an effect (*upādāna*) of Brahman and because Brahman is its inner controller (*antaryāmin*)—the sense is that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). The meaning is that identity consists precisely in being included within the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). Consequently, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) passage "because of identity through having that as its nature," the instrumental case-meaning (*tṛtīyārtha*) is not intended.

The sense is that the intention of the Bhāṣya is this: since there is no other kind of unity produced by having that [Brahman] as one's essence, the very fact of having that as one's essence is itself unity. On this point, some explain the meaning of the Bhāṣya as follows: just as all individual souls (jīvas) are one because their essential nature consists of the form of cognition, so too there is a unity between the conscious and unconscious entities and Brahman, in the sense of being included within a single qualified whole; for the meaning is explained later in the passage, "It should be viewed as one alone. This, they say, is the meaning of the Bhāṣya.

It is heard in this context [of the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*]: "There is no diversity here. Furthermore, in the *Kaṭhavallī*, the statement "What is here, that is there; what is there, that is here" should be understood as being supplementary to the injunction of unity, because the sentence "There is no diversity here" is explicitly stated in certain passages. The meaning is: because the prohibition of anything equal or superior is explicitly stated by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) in certain passages, and because the "logic of the goat and the animal" (*chāgapaśunyāya*) is explicitly stated in the Commentary in certain passages.

Since it is intended here to demonstrate that the sentences cited as negating difference actually negate only the difference in modes (*prakāra*), it is appropriate to cite a sentence that prescribes a difference in modes as a means of establishing that point, and thereby to show how that relates to the sentence which sets forth a difference in effects (*kārya*).

However, since it is not appropriate to cite a sentence prescribing a difference in the effect and then demonstrate by means of that a sentence prescribing a difference in the mode, [the author], out of dissatisfaction with this, shows that the cited sentence itself intends to enjoin both kinds of difference, beginning with the words "Or rather, in the Chāndogya," etc. "This scriptural passage" (*iyaṃ śrutiḥ*): here, the word to be explained is "this" (*iyam*). "The seer is established in himself" (*svaniṣṭho draṣṭā*).

The meaning is that the seer, conceiving [the object] as residing in himself (*svaniṣṭhatvena*), perceives the object—which he likewise conceives as residing in himself—by means of an instrument which he also conceives as residing in himself. The final sense is that an error regarding the self-residence (*svaniṣṭhatva*) occurs in respect to the agent, the instrument, and the object. He states another reason: "because of the statement 'of this'. Since it is impossible to say that "selfhood" belongs to a specific person, the intention is direct perception; such is the meaning of the word "became" (*abhūt*). The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever that resides in itself. The meaning is that there is no error regarding self-residence anywhere.

"According to the principle of 'Aditiḥ pāśān'": in the passage "May Aditi release the bonds," although plurality is expressed by the plural number, it is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Similarly, the meaning is that even the gender—either masculine or neuter—indicated by the case-ending modification in "asmin" (or "etasmin") is not intended to be significant. Nevertheless, some degree of lack of natural aptness (*asvārasya*) remains unavoidable.

For this very reason, in the tenth [book of the Mīmāṃsāsūtra], regarding the passage "He takes the Bārhaspatya cup," it is stated that when the deity is enjoined by way of a reference (*anuvāda*) to the archetypal cups, the singular number is improper because they are many; thus, even if the number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*) because it resides in the object of reference (*uddeśya*), the contradiction of the expression (*abhidhānabādha*) is unavoidable. Furthermore, the mantra "O Agni, bring him forward" applies only to the Sārasvata sacrifice.

The sense is that [the word] does not apply because it would contradict the gender inherent in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as established in the ninth book [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*]. "Even so, there is a lack of natural consistency" (*asvārasya*)—this means that [the meaning] is not conveyed by the word co-occurring in the same sentence (*samabhivyāhṛta*). "Because it is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the cause of fearlessness"—the sense is that it is appropriate to demonstrate that which is the very opposite of what was presented in the preceding sentence as the cause of fearlessness, namely, the cause of fear. "Established as one with the previous" (*pūrvasiddhaikya*).

This is because this form is possible from the root *vidlṛ* ‘to obtain’ itself, which is listed with the *śap* suffix; whereas the form is impossible from the root *vida* ‘to know’, which has the meaning of comprehension (*avagati*), as it is listed with a lost suffix (*luptavikaraṇa*) and is conjugated in the *parasmaipada*. Nor should one raise the doubt that identity could be said to be obtained now even if the meaning were ‘obtaining’, for the sense is that identity was already established previously. [The phrase] “as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and the limit (*avadhi*)” [is used].

The intention is that when there is a desire to express co-referentiality (*sāhitya-pratiyogitva*), the instrumental case is used, as in "difference with a jar" (*ghaṭena saha bhedaḥ*); when there is a desire to express the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*), the ablative case is used, as in "difference from a jar" (*ghaṭād bhedaḥ*); and when there is a desire to express a relationship (*saṃbandha*), the genitive case is used, as in "the difference of a jar" (*ghaṭasya bhedaḥ*).
(This concludes the section on the ancient jar.
The phrase "for the purpose of demonstrating [this]" connects with what precedes it.
"He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—he, undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins.
This verse is in the tenth chapter. Starting with "All beings abide in Me," this half-verse is in the ninth chapter. "I am the source of the entire world"—this half-verse is in the seventh chapter.
"Or rather, what is the use of much speaking? Know this, O Arjuna:
pervading this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I stand as the world.
Thus says the verse in the tenth chapter.
"There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings; the one who stands at the peak (Kūṭastha) is called the imperishable."
But there is another, the Supreme Person, who is declared to be the Supreme Self;
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
O Bhārata, he who knows me as the Supreme Person without delusion, being all-knowing, worships me with his entire being.
"Thus, O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by me.

By understanding this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has fulfilled his purpose"—so it is said in the fifteenth chapter. Regarding the phrase "not subject to karma": this state of not being subject to karma and the state of supremacy (paramatva) apply through the liberated soul to the Blessed Lord who possesses a liberated body and is designated by the word *akṣara* (the Imperishable); for we observe that in passages such as "great and noble," the attributes of greatness and nobility apply [to the Supreme Being] through their presence in the individual soul.

Nor should it be argued that since a direct connection with the Blessed Lord is possible for "supremacy" (*pāramya*) and "self-sovereignty" (*svārājya*), an indirect connection is improper; for, just as in the case of "brahminhood" and so forth, an indirect connection must be asserted here as well due to the principle of *prāyapāṭha* (contextual sequence), and because it is more appropriate that liberation—referred to by the proximate word "immortal" (*akṣara*)—serves as the mediating link. This is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, in this context, words such as *brāhman* and so forth do not extend to the Supreme Self; rather, the word *Bhagavat* itself, through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), refers to that which has Him as its body. Consequently, the meaning is: "The Supreme, the Self-ruling, the Imperishable, the Liberated One—he alone is that which constitutes His body. Regarding the phrase "in the intention of excluding another master": when the Lord's status as the master of the universe is stated, one might suspect He too has another master; thus, by the term "the Self of the Lord" (*ātmeśvara*), any other master is negated.

Therefore, the intention is that the words *pati* and *īśvara* have the same meaning. Furthermore, one should not suspect the grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutva*) of the compound; for if one intended a coordinate relationship (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the sense of "the highest person" (*uttamaścāsau puruṣaśca*), the form would result in *uttamapuruṣa* according to the rule "san-mahat-parama-uttama-utkṛṣṭāḥ [are compounded] with those being honored. Thus, the compound is established as correct.

The sense is that there is a doubt regarding grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) because, under the three alternative rules—"the ablative in a selection" (*yataśca nirdhāraṇam*), "the sixth case in a distinct meaning" (*ṣaṣṭhī vibhakte*), and "the locative" (*saptamī*)—in the cases of the ablative, sixth, and locative, the compound with the word *uttama* would not apply. This is because in examples such as "the ablative with *bhaya*" (*pañcamī bhayena*), the word *uttama* is absent; because the sixth-case compound is prohibited by the rule "not in a selection" (*na nirdhāraṇe*); and because there is no specific grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) for a locative compound. [The author replies: "And because of being most authoritative" (*āptatamatvāt*). The sense is that the compound will be formed through the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "the locative" (*saptamī*).

"Only when there is the intention to express grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). For, according to the rule *sanmahatparamottama* (Pāṇini 2.1.61), in the case of a compound, the word *uttama* [is placed first] by the rules governing compounds.

Because it is designated by the nominative case, the technical term *upasarjana* (subordinate member) would apply according to the rule "that which is designated by the nominative in a compound is an *upasarjana*. Consequently, by the rule "the *upasarjana* is placed first," the word *uttama* would necessarily undergo *pūrvanipāta* (prior placement). The point is that if one resorts to a compound based on the analysis of the rules "the fifth case" (*pañcamī*) or "the seventh case" (*saptamī*), then the word *puruṣa*, being in the fifth or seventh case, would indeed be designated by the nominative [in the original rule], and thus, as an *upasarjana*, its prior placement would be inevitable.

The five verses beginning with "sa sarvabhūtaprakṛtim" are recited at the conclusion of the fifth chapter of the sixth part. The seven verses beginning with "śuddhe mahāvibhūtyākhye" are recited in that same chapter prior to the verse "sa sarvabhūtaprakṛtim. The three verses beginning with "samastāḥ śaktayaḥ" constitute Khāṇḍikya’s speech to Keśidhvaja in the seventh chapter of the sixth part. The verse beginning with "evaṃprakāram" occurs at the conclusion of the first part.

The five verses beginning with "paraḥ parāṇām" are recited at the beginning of the Purāṇa; the two verses beginning with "prakṛtiryā mayākhyātā" are found in the fourth chapter of the sixth part (ṣaṣṭhāṃśa) in the section on reabsorption (pratisaṃcaraṇa); the two and a half verses beginning with "dve rūpe" are at the conclusion of the first part (prathamāṃśa); and the three verses beginning with "viṣṇuśaktiḥ parā proktā" are the words of Khāṇḍikya in the seventh chapter of the sixth part.

The passage beginning with "Pradhānaṃ ca pumāṃścaiva" and ending with "puruṣātmanaḥ" is found in the seventh chapter of the second part (dvitīyāṃśa). The phrase "tadetadakṣayaṃ nityam" occurs at the conclusion of the first part (prathamāṃśa).

Intending a *karmadhāraya* compound in the term "all-obscuration" (*sarvāvaraṇa*), he explains it as: "that by which all that [is past] is transcended. Because the word "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) is dependent upon an object, he explains it as a genitive compound: "or, the obscuration of the knowledge of all objects. He explains it as "from the power of knowledge" because a restriction to mere [empirical] knowledge is not appropriate. [He explains the phrase] "whose nature is the quality of possessing all auspiciousness" as: "that whose nature is the quality of being entirely auspicious."

Regarding this, they say that even if one does not rely on a *bahuvrīhi* within another *bahuvrīhi*, the meaning is still established by adopting the analysis: "that whose nature (*ātman*) or essence (*svabhāva*) is the quality of being auspicious (*kalyāṇatva*), which is the 'auspicious quality' (*kalyāṇaguṇa*). "By a specific intention" means by the intention that the divine form is more highly cherished than even the [other] qualities. "Worthiness of being cherished" means suitability. "The suffix *-niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of the agent" refers to the fact that the term *bahulam* (in various ways) is included in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.

Regarding the phrase "the unsuitability of that which is intended" (*abhimatasyānanurūpatvam*): here, the word *abhimata* has the sense of "that which is grasped by desire," since it was already stated previously that the meaning of the word *abhimata* is "suitability. Some, however, describe that the meaning of the compound *icchāgṛhīta* is "suitability," and that only in that case does the natural elegance (*svārasya*) of the text prevail. But that is not quite correct; for rather than resorting to the view that the word *icchāgṛhīta* means "suitability," it is more appropriate to resort to the view that the word *abhimatyarha* (meaning "worthy of being intended") means "suitability."

Regarding the phrase "of eternal will": the sense is that, consequently, it is established that even the eternal form is assumed by eternal will. Now, one might ask: when "knowledge, power, and sovereignty" (*jñāna-bala-aiśvarya*) ought to have been specified, why is there the specification "splendor, power, and sovereignty" (*tejas-bala-aiśvarya*)? To this he replies: "There is no intention here to express a sequence. Regarding the phrase "common to all qualities": one might object that in passages such as "possessing great intellect" and "possessing great heroism," since each is qualified by "greatness," let there be greatness in every case.

If it is argued that even so, the commonality of all qualities (*sarvaguṇasādhāraṇya*) is not established by this statement—because it is impossible to apply the quality of "greatness" (*mahattva*) to splendor (*tejas*), power (*bala*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), which were mentioned prior to the word "great" (*mahat*)—we say no; for the intent here is that their establishment occurs through the same logical principle (*nyāyasāmya*). Regarding "ignorance and egoism" (*avidyāsmitā*): *asmitā* is the state of being "I" (*asmitva*), that is, the sense of "I-ness" (*ahantva*). It means, in short, the cognition of "I-ness" with respect to what is not the self (*anātman*).

He explains the meaning of the two words *rūpa* and *svarūpa* mentioned in the verse: *rūpa* means the body (*śarīra*), and *svarūpa* means that which is unique to itself (*svāsādhāraṇa*). Alternatively, [the term *sarvajña*] may mean "one who finds everything" (*sarvaṃ vindati*) or "one who knows everything" (*sarvavettā*). Here, although the root *vid* (in the sense of "to obtain") is marked with the augment *iṭ*, one should understand that the absence of *iṭ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). This serves to distinguish [the Lord] from the knowledge of multiple forms belonging to those who are eternally liberated (*nityamukta*). That is to say, it excludes the knowledge whose objects are the various eternally liberated beings. Or else, ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*).

It should not be asked, "If it is not other knowledge, how can there be an absence of knowledge? For in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is no contradiction in a positive entity (*bhāva*) having the nature of an absence (*abhāva*). Alternatively, if [the term] qualifies "knowledge," there are two statements. However, in the view where it qualifies "Brahman," there is indeed a single statement: "That very knowledge by which the reality qualified by the absence of defects and so forth is known, perceived, or understood—that alone is knowledge; anything else is ignorance."

However, under the view that [the word "that"] functions as a qualifier of knowledge (*jñāna-viśeṣaṇatva-pakṣa*), there would be two distinct sentences: "That knowledge by which the Supreme Self is known, seen, or reached is qualified by the absence of defects and so forth," and "That [Self] is indeed knowledge. This is because otherwise, the two occurrences of the word *tat* (that) would result in redundancy. Nor should it be argued that this is like the passage, "That indeed is the bright, that is the Brahman, that is called the immortal," for even there, one must admit a division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*) due to having no other recourse. This refers to the previous verse beginning with "of that which is beyond the scope of words" (*aśabda-gocarasya*).

The meaning of the verse is: "O twice-born one, although that Brahman is beyond the range of words, the word 'Bhagavat' is applied to its worship by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Thus it is said to be figurative (*aupacārika*). Now, [an objection]:
That which is declared by the Vedic texts as the Brahman, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu—
that alone is the essential nature of the Supreme Self, denoted by the term "Bhagavat."

If it be objected: "Since the word *bhagavat* denotes that first [principle] which is of an imperishable nature—as established in the preceding verse—and since the Supreme Self alone was introduced there, how can the pronoun *tat* (in the phrase *aśabdagocarasyāpi*) refer to the liberated soul?"—this is true;
however, [the term *bhagavat*] is employed there in accordance with the conventional usage for designating an object worthy of worship.

The sense is this: since the word *bhagavat* cannot be applied figuratively (*aupacārika*) to the Supreme Self—as indicated by the statement, "This word [is used] not figuratively, for elsewhere it is used figuratively"—and because there would be a contradiction with the preceding and following sentences which establish that the word *bhagavat* has its primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) as the Supreme Self, one must conclude that the pronoun *tat* (in *tacchabda*) refers to the liberated soul (*mukta*), even though that was not the immediate subject. Regarding the phrase "the root *bharati*, when joined with a specific suffix, is conventional (*rūḍha*) in the sense of 'master'": this means "when joined with the specific suffix *tṛc*. In the expression "the root *bharati* is conventional in the sense of 'master'," the term *bharati* is used as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The phrase "or even *bibharti*" should also be understood here. Regarding the expression "of the verbal root alone": although the capacity to denote the owner (*svāmin*) belongs only to that which is joined with the suffix *ḍa* and not to the root devoid of the suffix, nevertheless, the intended meaning is that this applies even to that which lacks the suffix *tṛc*. Alternatively, the suffix *ḍa* serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*). For this very reason, it should be understood that it has been stated: "the letter *bha* is endowed with two meanings" and "the letter *ga* is the meaning. Thus, the grounds for the application [of the terms] are stated by extracting them [from the compound].

The meaning here is as follows: in this case, both "being a sustainer" (*saṃbhartṛtva*) and "being a supporter" (*bhartṛtva*) are the bases that fully qualify (*paryāptyadhikaraṇa*) as the grounds for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *bha*; therefore, it is said to be "endowed with two meanings. However, in the case of the letter *ga*, qualities such as "leading" (*netṛtva*) do not each individually serve as a basis of full qualification; rather, they do so only when combined, just as the meanings of an injunction (*vidhi*) consist of the combination of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), and not producing a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭājanakatva*). For this very reason, there is the use of the singular form in the expression "the meaning of the letter *ga*" (*gakārārthaḥ*).

However, some say that in the case of [the word] *saṃbhartṛ*, the basis of the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is extracted from its substratum by means of the particle *iti*. Since these two [grounds] are considered distinct, it is stated that [the word] is connected with two meanings. In the case of the letter *ga*, because there is no use of the particle *iti*, there is no extraction of the ground for application from its substratum; thus, since only the substratum of the ground for application is grasped, and because that is singular, the expression "the meaning of the letter *ga*" (*gakārārthaḥ*) is used—this is their intention. [The phrase] "because of being inherent in the verbal root" (*dhātulīnatvāt*)... [is used].

If it were the case that only verbs accompanied by prefixes (*upasarga*) possess the capacity to express action, then—since such prefixed forms are not listed among the *bhū* and other roots—the designation "root" (*dhātu*) would not apply to them. Furthermore, since the meaning of the root is understood even in some instances without a prefix, the root alone must be the signifier of multiple meanings. Prefixes such as *pra* and others, however, are merely indicators (*dyotaka*) that serve as causes for the recollection of specific nuances, much like context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth. And this dependence on an indicator occurs only in certain cases due to the inherent nature of the word's power (*śabdaśakti*). The point is that, for example, the word *hari* depends on context and other factors only when it refers to a frog or similar objects.

"Udgamayitā," "gamayitā," and "saṃgamayitā"—it should be understood that these are presented according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and not according to the sequence of the verse beginning with "netā. By the word "netā," the meaning of the term "gamayitṛ" (the one who causes to go) is expressed; the sense is that the quality of being a protector is stated, because in passages such as "adhibhūrnāyako netā," it is precisely the quality of protection that is perceived.

He demonstrates how the term *gamayitā* (the one who causes to go) reveals the meaning of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) even without the prefix *sam*: "or, [he leads] the causal state. Some, however, hold that the meaning of *straṣṭā* (the creator) is "creatorship," and the meaning of *gamayitā* is "protectorship" in the form of "causing to go"; there is no dispute between them. But because the verb *nī* (to lead) takes two objects, the phrase "leading his own self, which has become the cause, into the category of effects" expresses his nature as the withdrawer (*saṃhartṛ*).
Alternatively, they maintain that this verse also serves to demonstrate the meaning of the word *netṛ* (leader). This refers to the verse beginning with "The origin and dissolution... as follows:
"He who knows the origin and dissolution, the coming and going of beings, as well as knowledge and ignorance—he, indeed, is to be called the Blessed One (*bhagavān*)."
This is the meaning of the verse.

To the question, "How is it possible to contemplate [Her]? he replies. If it is asked, "How does this verse provide a solution to the objection raised by the verse beginning with 'forms consisting of all powers' (*samasta-śakti-rūpāṇi*)?", some maintain that the intention of the verse is that contemplation is possible because the supreme form, which is the substratum of all powers, is of the same nature as the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others belonging to the same class as gods and so forth. Others, however, believe that it is specifically the incarnations (avatāras) such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa that are to be contemplated by one engaged in yoga, and that for one engaged in yoga, the supreme form itself may be contemplated.

However, some maintain that this introductory passage (*avatārikā*) should be considered, because since it is intent upon demonstrating that the Supreme Lord possesses all powers and is the cause of all forms, it does not serve to resolve this doubt. Anticipating the objection—"Since *līlā* (sport) occurs subsequent [to creation], how can it be the cause?"—he says: "The intention for that (*tad-abhisandhi*) is the cause. The meaning is that the word *līlā* indicates the intention for that [creation]. He then states what the purpose is.

The sense is that since it would follow the logic of Asamañja if mere play were the purpose, mere play cannot be the purpose; this is the intention. [He states] the verse which extends [this principle] to the Supreme Self.

If it is argued that just as Devadatta is devoid of qualities, so too is Yajñadatta, one observes that when this is said, no specific quality of Yajñadatta—such as being a giver of food—which is known through other means of knowledge (*māna*), is thereby established for Devadatta. What proof, then, is there for attributing to the liberated self (*muktātman*) another attribute established by other means of knowledge regarding the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the specific, modified attributes (*vaikṛta-vaiśeṣika-dharma*) of the effect would apply to the primordial cause (*prakṛti*).

Furthermore, if it is argued that—since it is possible to cite the very words of the context, such as "having attained the state of being that [Self]" (*tadbhāvabhāvamāpannaḥ*), which explicitly establish the similarity of the liberated self with the Supreme Self—it would follow the logic of "covering the head while pinching the nose" to instead cite a statement that implies equality with the Supreme Self by merely attributing the qualities of the liberated self to the Supreme Self; we say: no.

The point is that, in the absence of any sublation, this too is logical; for after saying, "Like Devadatta, Yajñadatta has sons," when it is stated that "Yajñadatta has four sons," the understanding that Devadatta also has that many sons is established by experience. However, some hold that in the Bhāṣya, the citation of the verse beginning with "of such a kind" (*evamprakāram*) was made solely with the intention of presenting the evidence for being devoid of all things to be abandoned.

Likewise, in the commentary on the summary of the meaning of the cited statements, he will say, "The supreme Brahman is by its very nature devoid of even a trace of all defects," and so forth; but this is not for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the phrase "in which all distinctions have vanished."

They say that this is because the section of the Bhāṣya beginning with "He who [knows] me as unborn and beginningless" and ending with "is known to be indeed the ultimate reality" is undertaken solely for the purpose of determining specific points of meaning propounded in the Smṛtis and Purāṇas in general, and thus it is not undertaken merely for the purpose of determining the meaning of the specific verse "In whom all distinctions have subsided"; furthermore, they maintain that the refutation of those statements in their particular sense will be carried out later on through a detailed examination of the preceding and following passages.

The point is that this verse is shown to have a qualified (saviśeṣa) purport because it establishes [the Lord's] eternality, omnipresence, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because the conclusion is present in the mind": since verses such as "All these powers... occur within the context of the summary of Yoga, they share the same nature as a conclusion; thus, the meaning is that that [qualified reality] alone is present in the mind. This is indicated by the passage beginning with "devoid of activity, inexpressible... which states: "Devoid of activity, inexpressible, mere pervasion, incomparable..."
It is the object of self-awakening, mere existence, and devoid of defining characteristics.
The state of Viṣṇu, who consists of knowledge, is described as having a tranquil mind, being pure, difficult to conceive, and firmly established; that is said to be his supreme state of knowledge.
In that regard, O twice-born one, those yogins who attain dissolution through the cessation of cognition go to a state of seedlessness, having uprooted the cycle of worldly existence.

"Such is the supreme state called Viṣṇu—stainless, eternal, all-pervading, imperishable, and devoid of everything to be abandoned. This is the sequence of the verse.
