Thus, the transfer of the qualities of the liberated to the Blessed One has been established. Now, one might object: "Could not even the passage beginning with 'devoid of activity' refer solely to the nature of the Supreme Self? Furthermore, the phrase 'of such a kind' need not be a transfer [of attributes], but may rather be a summary of what has already been stated."

Nor should it be argued that a difference must necessarily be asserted because of the perception of distinction in the earlier passage, "the supreme abode of Viṣṇu," and because of the teaching in the verse beginning with "of such a kind" that "the supreme abode is named Viṣṇu. This is because in the expression "the supreme abode of Viṣṇu," the word *pada* refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), as is appropriate in the case of "the nature of a jar. Otherwise, [it would contradict] the following: "That subtle supreme abode of Viṣṇu, declared by the words of the Śruti, is itself the essential nature of the Supreme Self, which is denoted by the term 'Bhagavat'."

This is because [the meaning] is understood from such passages as: "The wise always behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Nor should it be argued that if the preceding verse also referred to Brahman, the mention of its pervasiveness and other attributes in the words "thus pure, eternal, pervasive, and undecaying" would be redundant; for this is not so, since the pervasiveness and other qualities have already been stated in such passages as "its mere pervasion is incomparable. This objection is to be resolved by both sides alike. For this very reason, the phrase "in which all distinctions have vanished" (*pratyastamitabheda*) does not refer to the liberated soul either.

For in that context, the status of the embodied one—knowable through the Vedānta and possessing the luster of the sun—as the auspicious object of focus (śubhāśraya) is stated. And therein, by asserting that the auspicious object of focus is indeed the embodied one, it is first the divine nature of the Self as the objective support (ālambana) that must be rejected, not the nature of the individual soul (jīva). Once the Supreme Self is established as the object of meditation, the consideration of the Supreme Self’s perfectly pure nature as the object of meditation follows.

If it be argued that, consequently, without refuting that [position], one would be abandoning what is required and accepting what is not required in the refutation of the pure nature of the *jīva* as the object of meditation—[we reply: no, because this objection culminates in non-dualism (*advaita*) and thus cannot be refuted separately; and since the matter of non-dualism has already been rejected by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācāryas*), we desist now, as there is no portion remaining to be refuted.

For the commencement [of a section] being dependent on the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) is primary, whereas being dependent on the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is not; thus, out of dissatisfaction [with that view], he says, "or rather, the commencement of the first part. [He states this because] there is a contradiction with the natural sense of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*). The point is that in the sūtra "The vital breath [is Brahman], because of the subsequent connection" (*prāṇastathānugamāt*), it is demonstrated that a commencement contrary to the great sentence is weak. [Therefore,] the purpose of the qualities of the subtle [Brahman], which constitute the remainder of that [great sentence], must be described.

The meaning is that even for the primary *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice, there is no compliance with the time of the lunar festival (*parvakāla*) because it conflicts with the principal Soma sacrifice; this is because it has been determined in the section concerning "Conflict between the quality of a subsidiary and its purpose" (*Aṅgaguṇavirodhe ca tādārthyāt*). The meaning is that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), though being a supplement to an injunction, possesses greater force when it occurs at the beginning [of a section], as established in the section on "The Beginning" (*Upakramādhikaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "the question, the answer, and the obtaining of a boon":
"O knower of dharma, O highly fortunate one, I desire to hear from you how the world came into being, how it continues to exist, and how it will come to be again."
"You shall understand, exactly as it is, the ultimate nature of the deities;
and your intellect shall become stainless regarding both active and withdrawn action."

Because [if the text were taken as referring to a featureless entity], there would arise the inconsistency of the granting of boons and so forth, which is concordant with the composition of the section containing questions and answers regarding the creation of the world, its sequence, its methods, and so on. The sense is that if the subject matter were a featureless entity, the question "What is the substrate? would have the answer "The substrate is the featureless" itself. Furthermore, if one resorts to a third-case tatpuruṣa compound, it is strained to assume that the word *ātman* has the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*). Likewise, it is strained to assume for the word *saṃsthita* the meaning of "being qualified."
And because of the difficulty of comprehending the specific forms of all objects, he says, as an alternative, "or rather, by way of being established as the Self.

Here, in the phrase "established in the Self" (*ātmasaṃsthita*), there is a locative *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "established in the Self. It should be understood that the portion "by way of being established as the Self, because He has all bodies as His body" serves to justify that meaning. The word division is "the ultimate ground of all, established in Himself. Thus, the section on the non-limitation of the object (*vastvapariccheda*) concludes; this refers to the remainder of the two positions mentioned in the text.

For the non-limitation of an entity (*vastvapariccheda*) is indeed twofold: its fitness for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all entities, and its lack of equals or superiors in respect to its qualities. With this in mind, [the author] says, from "fitness for coreferentiality with all entities" up to "due to the impossibility of equality or superiority. Since the non-limitations of space and time are established by the two [scriptural passages], "The highest of the high" and "The Supreme Self," he specifies "by qualities other than eternity and omnipresence. [He then states: "endowed with the five conceptualizations."

The meaning is that [an object] is endowed with the five types of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), namely: name (*saṃjñā*), genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and characteristic (*vayava-lakṣaṇa*). These very things denoted by words are the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). "Specification by color and so forth" (*rūpavarṇādinirdeśa*) is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*). The intention is that the qualifier which is the object of such specification is "specification-qualifier" (*nirdeśaviśeṣaṇa*), according to a *madhyamapadalopa-samāsa* (compound with the middle term elided).

In this view, the qualifying term in the description is redundant, since its meaning is understood even without it; therefore, due to this lack of elegance (*asvarasa*), he speaks with the intention of referring to a *dvandva* compound: "or rather, by means of the forms of words that express color, form, and so forth. Because impermanent things such as color and form do not possess color and form themselves, possessing color and form (*rūpādimattva*) is not a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of impermanence; thus, due to this lack of elegance, he says: "or rather, [it is] pervaded by impermanence (*anityatvavyāpya*). [The phrase] "the two states of 'is born' and 'exists'" refers to these two stages.

On this point, some say that while other entities are designated by six terms—such as "exists," "is born," and so forth—the Brahman is always designated by the term "exists" alone and not by the other five. Since this statement is appropriate, they argue there is no fault even if two states are not included. Regarding the phrase "of the *auṇādika* suffix": the meaning is that it is because of the inclusion of the word "variously" (*bahulam*) in the rule "the *aṇ* and others occur variously. Regarding the phrase "he determined it to be infinite": the meaning is that the Śruti says "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma*).

Because the term *paramātman* is observed to be used occasionally even for the individual soul (*jīva*). This is because the term *paramātman* is seen to be used occasionally even for the individual soul in such passages as: "Of the air that pervades [all] without distinction, so too is this of the Supreme Self."

By the very introduction of the verse beginning with "The primordial nature (prakṛti) which has been described by Me," there arises the possibility that the individual soul (jīva) might also be included in the statement of the preceding verse, "The Supreme Self (paramātman), the support of all, the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). Therefore, intending to establish that the status of being the support of dissolution belongs specifically to the Supreme Self—the Supreme Lord—who is directly designated by names such as Viṣṇu, the state of being the support of dissolution was described in the preceding verse: "The primordial nature which has been described by Me."

Furthermore, the meaning is that, through the syntactic unity of these two verses, the Supreme Self—in whom both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* dissolve—is the support of all, the Supreme Lord named Viṣṇu, as established by the Vedānta. By this, the doubt as to how the individual soul (*jīva*) is excluded by the word "dissolve" (*līyete*) is dispelled, just as in the expression "he who possesses hardness supports [the earth]."

Regarding the passage, “Salutation to Him who possesses hardness and sustains [the world], whose nature is that of the earth,” the meaning is that He possesses hardness by way of the earth within His own nature as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). The sense is that the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of fitness (*arha*), according to the rule of the frequentative inclusion (*bahulagrahaṇa*). Out of dissatisfaction with this [interpretation], he says: “Or rather, ‘of the bound one (*baddha*) by way of his own form. This means “of that which belongs to the class of the bound. Thus, it is stated that [His] essential nature is unmixed (*asaṃkīrṇa*).

The sense is that, by the force of the example of fire and moonlight—which possess mutually unmixed natures—it is established as such even in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). Regarding the statement "the world is said to consist of consciousness and the unconscious": although the word *jagat*—derived from the etymology "it goes" (*gacchati*) and "it perishes" (*naśyati*)—refers only to perishable things and thus cannot refer to the liberated soul (*mukta*), it is established that the liberated soul is also included by virtue of the same underlying principle (*tulyanyāyatayā*). This refers to words denoting Brahman that occur in a single context.

The meaning is that because such passages as "Two forms of that Brahman" and "The power of the supreme Brahman, as well as this entire world," refer to Brahman, and because the word *brahman*—which is used in grammatical apposition with the word *para* (supreme) in the phrase "That supreme imperishable is Brahman"—is utterly inappropriate when applied to the individual soul (*jīva*).

Now, one might object: "If by the two terms *kṣara* (the perishable) and *akṣara* (the imperishable), there is a reference to Brahman in its states as effect and cause, then there would be a lack of correspondence with the example of fire and its light—which are distinct from one another and do not stand in a relationship of cause and effect. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "And that the world has the status of being like the light," and "And that [it]. The meaning is that there would be a violation of the natural force of the negative formulation (*vyatireka-nirdeśa*). Now, one might suggest: "Let the word *rūpa* refer to the essential nature (*svarūpa*)."

One might ask: why could it not be that the two forms of Brahman are the "formed" (*mūrta*) and the "formless" (*amūrta*)? In that case, one need not intend to emphasize the abstract state (*bhāva-pradhānatva*), nor would there be any lack of propriety regarding the genitive case. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the absence of intending to emphasize the abstract state. Since the terms "essential nature" (*svarūpa*) and "form" (*rūpa*) are presented as distinct entities among the categories of essential nature, form, qualities, manifestations, and so forth, it would follow that the term "essential nature" (*svarūpa*) would lose its propriety; consequently, because it is impossible for the word "form" (*rūpa*) to encompass the essential nature itself, one must necessarily intend to emphasize the abstract state.

Therefore, the sense is that the terms *mūrta* (the formed) and *amūrta* (the formless) lack internal consistency [in this context]. If it were argued: "The Brahman has two forms"—that is, having proposed that the Brahman has two forms and then stating "the Brahman is both formed and formless," the sense would be that the two forms resulting therefrom are precisely "formedness" and "formlessness. [The phrase] "ending with the substratum, the perishable and the imperishable" means that there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the perishable and the imperishable as the essential natures and the formed and the formless [as their attributes]. [The phrase] "by the word *jagat* (world), which denotes that which possesses states" [is used].

The meaning is that in the passage, “That Brahman is the Imperishable (akṣara), while this entire world is the Perishable (kṣara),” the co-referential application (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the terms *akṣara* and *kṣara* with the words *Brahman* and *jagat*—which denote the possessor of states—is impossible. Furthermore, the meaning is that it is impossible for the word *śakti* to denote the effect, because it is impossible for it to denote Brahman in its state as an effect. To the objection that even if the word *śakti* does not denote the effect, it might refer to the effect through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), he replies: “even by way of metaphor.”

The primary meaning of the word *śakti* (power) is a specific substance (*dravyaviśeṣa*) that is non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*) and conducive to an effect. However, in figurative usage, the sole basis is the mere state of being a qualifying attribute conducive to an effect; this is the sense [of the text]. Some, however, explain it here as follows: the word "qualifying attribute" (*viśeṣaṇa*) refers to a non-separately established qualifier (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), and the word "or" (*vā*) must be supplied. Consequently, they interpret it to mean: "that which is either conducive to an effect or a non-separately established qualifier is fit to be designated by the term *śakti*. They maintain that primacy belongs to our own view.

The meaning is that it possesses the status of being the primary method (*mukhyakalpatva*). For this very reason, it was stated by Vedāntācārya in the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*, in the section defining *śakti*: "The designation of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), the nesciences (*avidyā*), and the world as the power of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahma-śakti*) is also [to be understood] through metaphorical usage (*gauṇī*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*)," because of the statement regarding the connection with the three types of contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
"The [power] called *brāhmī* is known as *karman* (action), and likewise consists of both [aspects].
Sanandana and the others are *brāhmī*, endowed with the contemplation of Brahman (*brāhmabhāvanā*)."
"By the cultivation of karma, others— ranging from the gods down to the immobile beings—
and those among Hiraṇyagarbha and the rest, consist of the nature of Brahma-karma in two ways."

In the manner thus stated, there is a triad of meditations (*bhāvanā*) consisting of the meditation on action (*karma-bhāvanā*), the meditation on the Veda (*brahma-bhāvanā*), and the meditation on both. It should be understood that *bhāvanā* means latent impression (*vāsanā*) or mental formation (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the semantic diversity of the word *brahma*: in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, it is said, "By austerity, the *brahma* is built up" (*tapasā cīyate brahma*); and in the passage, "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from Him this [world] is born, called *brahma*, as well as name, form, and food," the word *brahma* is employed in the sense of primordial matter (*pradhāna*).

In that very same context, in the passage "By austerity, the *brāhman* is built up," the word *brāhman* is employed to denote the Supreme Self. This is clear from such [Sūtras] as "That which has the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is Brahman], because its attributes are mentioned" and "And there may be [the use of a singular term for many], as in the case of the word *brāhman*. Anticipating the objection that since residing in all bodies is impossible for a single individual soul (*jīva*), and that if the term referred merely to souls in general, the plural number would result due to the multiplicity of souls, he states: "The singular is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*).
This should be understood as being like [the usage in expressions such as] "A human being travels to all countries. And [he mentions] "their gradation" (*tattāratamyam*).
Among inanimate things it is very slight; it is greater among stationary beings;
it is greater still among reptiles, and even greater among birds.
Wild animals are superior to birds; by their capacity, domestic animals are superior to them;
human beings are superior even to domestic animals; and men endowed with power are superior [to others] by their capacity.
O King, even higher than those are the deities such as the Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas;
Śakra is superior to all the gods, and Prajāpati is superior even to him.

The meaning of the passage beginning with “and from that [Puruṣa] Hiraṇyagarbha, characterized by Śakti,” is as follows. “For the purpose of excluding that” means for the purpose of excluding the nature [of being a genus] which is based on generic class (jāti). Now, one might raise the objection: why could the phrase “by Viṣṇu-śakti” not mean “by the Śakti whose form is Viṣṇu”? Anticipating this, he says: “Otherwise, that too would be a Śakti. He explains the meaning of the word “here” (atra) as “because of the cause, etc. “A drop of water” (jalakaṇikā) implies that water is the cause and the drops are the effects.

Having explained the simile according to the first interpretation, he explains it according to the second interpretation with the words, “or [the power] of conjoining and disjoining. In this view, the meaning is that it bears both the attached and the unattached, having conjoined and having disjoined them. Regarding the phrase “of the self of Pradhāna and Puruṣa,” this genitive form *pradhānapuruṣātmanaḥ* should be understood as an adjective qualifying the word *Viṣṇoḥ*. To avoid the fault of textual interpolation (*adhyāhāra*), he says, “or rather, after the word *pradhāna*.”

"In the phrase 'all this indeed is that' (*tad eva sarvam etad*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word 'that' (*tat*). Although it would have been more appropriate to explain the commentary on the coreferentiality with the word 'that' only after explaining the commentary beginning with "the nature of having a body" (*śarīrarūpatanvaṃśatva*) in accordance with the sequence of the *bhāṣya* to be explained, nevertheless, the coreferentiality with the word 'that' has been explained here in accordance with the sequence of the cited Purāṇic statement.

It should be understood, however, that the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), because there are clear proofs establishing the status of being a body for words such as "body" (śarīra) and "subtle body" (tanu), has provided his explanation by bypassing the sequence of the Purāṇic citations previously mentioned.
(The meaning of the Purāṇic citation cited by the opponent:

The bodies of gods and others are perceived as limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Their status as adjuncts consists in their causing the attribution of properties such as difference (bheda) residing in the Self, just like a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) [colors a crystal]. [Objection: But surely, liberated beings (*mukta*) cannot be objects of worship?

One might raise the following objection: since there is no possibility of the liberated inner self being unattainable, its status as a "beautiful support" (*śubhāśraya*) or as an object of focus for a mind engaged in yoga cannot be denied; furthermore, because the nature of the worshiper—being the locus of bondage such as agency—is itself unattainable, there is no possibility of it being considered a beautiful support, and thus denying it would result in the fallacy of denying what was never a subject of doubt (*aprasaktapratiṣedha*). Therefore, why could this verse not be a denial that the nature of the Supreme Self alone is the object of focus for a mind engaged in yoga? Anticipating this doubt:

The meaning is that this instruction is given to prevent the practice of meditating upon that very nature which is to be manifested at liberation, since there is the possibility of it being mistakenly regarded as an object to be attained and thus meditated upon. The expression "instruction for non-contemplation" (*ananusandhānopadeśa*) should be understood as a *karmadhāraya* compound, similar to the phrase "smoke from mosquitoes. Alternatively, the reading may be "for the sake of non-contemplation" (*tathā-ananusandhānāya*). Some, however, say: "for the sake of contemplation in such a manner" (*tathā-anusandhānāya*), meaning "for the sake of contemplating [it] as not being an object of meditation. The word "in this context" (*asmin prakaraṇe*) is the term to be explained.

"How can [the deity] be a single part of Viṣṇu’s body?"—the meaning is that since Viṣṇu is the one who sustains [the deity] by being its body, it is impossible for [the deity] to be the sustainer of that [body]. This statement—that [the deity] resides in a single part of the body—is made with the intention that when the triad of powers is present, it is impossible for each individual power alone to have the entire body as its locus. Alternatively, the meaning is that this "single part" which constitutes the body is limited, and [the deity] resides therein.

Now, [the author] dispels the doubt that even if such a body as the substratum of Viṣṇu’s three powers is impossible, such a body might still be possible for Brahman, by stating: "the body which is its substratum. Regarding the phrase "having as its object the form known as the Supreme": because in passages such as "And that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu," the supreme form is indicated as distinct [from Viṣṇu] through a correlative (vyatireka) reference, [it follows that it is not Viṣṇu himself].

The meaning is that because the supreme form itself is designated by the term "supreme power" (*paraśakti*) based on its verbal root, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is indeed appropriate in the expression "the power of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuśakti*). Regarding the phrase "a distinct designation has been made": "distinct designation" (*vibhajyanirdeśaḥ*) means the designation of that which is to be divided; the sense is that it is a designation of what is to be analyzed. The word *vibhāga* ends in the accusative case and is derived from the verbal root with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The meaning is as follows: although in the preceding sentence, in the phrase "by means of the division of the formed and the formless" (*mūrtāmūrtavibhāgena*), the word *vibhāga* does not denote the object of the action, nevertheless, since the act of dividing was introduced by the word *vibhāga* in that preceding sentence, there is no inconsistency in referring to that object here by means of the word *vibhāga* ending in the accusative case. Some, however, raise this objection: "But why not indicate the object being divided by the words 'the formed and the formless' themselves?"

Anticipating the objection, "What is the purpose of the word 'division' (vibhāga)? they say: "Because it was stated [in the previous verse] as 'by the division of the formed and the formless'. However, [the term] intends the sense of "possibility. This is because the *kṛtya* suffixes are prescribed in the sense of possibility by the rules "kṛtyāśca" and "śaki liṅ ca," and because it is established [elsewhere] that "it cannot be accomplished even by one joined with yoga. The phrase "for the sake of including many individuals" means for the sake of including all individuals.

Regarding the phrase "having the form of the supreme power" (*paraśaktirūpam*), because there might be a delay in the cognition of the Supreme Self due to its being a correlate to "form," he says "or consisting of the supreme power" (*paraśaktyātmakaṃ vā*). As for the phrase "in the embodied form of the Blessed One":
"The embodied form of the Blessed One is free from desire for any support;
this indeed is declared to be *dhāraṇā*, wherein the mind is fixed."

This means that such is the meaning of the statement. "The declaration elsewhere of his unfitness" means that in another verse there is a declaration of his unfitness. He establishes the very conclusion of the context with the words beginning "others, however, [regarding] the tiger among men," etc. Anticipating the objection that the absence of purity is being propounded only for those who are bound, and not for those who are liberated, he says "others, however," referring to the text, by way of a "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokita). "Because of the mention alongside a pillar," etc.

If it is argued that this statement—that [the limit] is due to the co-utterance with "pillar" (stamba)—is incorrect because (1) it would result in the redundancy of the word *paryanta*, (2) it would entail the forms "stambaparyantāḥ" or "stambaparyantam," whereas the form "stambaparyantāḥ" is not established, and (3) since it is more appropriate for the prefix *āṅ* to have the meaning of either a sentence or a recollection (*smaraṇa*), the rule "āṅ in the sense of inclusive limit" (*āṅabhividhau*) is improper; therefore, the claim is untenable—then it is replied: Since the possibility of *āṅ* having the sense of an inclusive limit exists, [the alternative] which must be postulated in the absence of any other recourse...

Since it is improper for the word *āṅ* to have the sense of "recollection" (*smaraṇa*) within the sentence, it is compounded with the word *brāhma*. The term *stambaparyantāḥ* is a separate word. Consequently, because the word *stambaparyanta*, which is mentioned in proximity, is seen to express an inclusive limit (*abhividhi*) regarding the "stump," the intention is that the *āṅ* in the word *ābrāhma* also expresses an inclusive limit.

The meaning is that because identity is perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "The world is Brahman," as shown by such passages as "The luminaries are Viṣṇu. This means that no coreferentiality is observed between a piece of mother-of-pearl and [the notion of] silver; that is to say, one never observes an instruction such as "All silver is mother-of-pearl" in the same way as the instruction "The entire world is Brahman. If that were the case, then even the statement of negation would be [inapplicable].

The meaning is this: if an affirmative statement were to convey a non-ultimate difference as if it were ultimately real, then why would a negative statement not likewise convey what is in fact ultimately real as being non-ultimately real? It is not merely a matter of two forms [of cognition].

For you state that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) depends upon sublation (*bādha*), whereas I do not merely deny that coreferentiality depends on sublation; rather, I assert that it is even opposed to sublation. The sense is that if there were opposition with anything else, it would entail the collapse of coreferentiality.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: once it has been established in the Bhāṣya that Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, the meaning—that this [established doctrine] must be reinforced by means of Itihāsas and Purāṇas—is known from the statement, "One should fully reinforce the Veda with Itihāsas and Purāṇas. The meaning is that the necessity of performing this reinforcement after hearing [the Vedic teaching] is understood from the verse beginning with "Itihāsas and Purāṇas."

Nor should it be argued that the sequence of *upabṛṃhaṇa* (elaboration) immediately following *śravaṇa* (hearing) is not understood from this statement, because we do not hear the words "having heard, one should elaborate," but rather hear only "one should elaborate. This objection is refuted because, since *upabṛṃhaṇa* consists in clarifying the meaning of what was heard, the sequence of *upabṛṃhaṇa* immediately following *śravaṇa* is thereby obtained. Consequently, the doubt—namely, "How can it be said that 'upon the completion [of hearing] from this sentence, elaboration is to be performed,' when the understanding of the meaning could possibly occur even before hearing from this sentence?"—is set aside.

However, some maintain that even though the understanding of the meaning may arise from the preceding sentence, for one who has not heard the Vedānta, the knowledge of the necessity of performing the supplementary elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) conducive to engagement does not arise; therefore, the meaning is that the cognition of the duty to perform the supplementary elaboration conducive to engagement arises only immediately after the hearing [of the Vedānta]. [The phrase] "for the sake of hearing specific compositions such as the Mahābhārata" is used. If it is asked: "But if this statement merely restates what is established by logic (*nyāya*), how can it incite one to hear specific compositions such as the Mahābhārata?"—the answer is: no.

There is no fault here, because even this explanatory statement (anuvādaka) serves as a means to turn one away from the objects of natural inclination, thereby facilitating engagement [with the injunction], just like the statement, "Do not play with dice; practice agriculture. The objection, "But if that is so," intends to suggest that it is untenable to claim a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatva) on the grounds that [the agent] thinks, "He will deceive me. Consequently, one should not think that there is a contradiction in [the statement] rejecting both types of purposes—visible and invisible.

The meaning of the passage beginning with “What do your cows do among the Kīkaṭas? is as follows: O Maghavan, what do your cows do in the lands of the Kīkaṭas? The sense is that they provide no benefit whatsoever. He explains this very point: they do not milk for the *āśira* (the mixture used for the *pravargya* rite), nor do they heat for the *gharma* (the clarified butter used for the *pravargya*), nor do they provide the milk required for the *dharma* (heating vessel), because those residing in that region are atheists (*nāstika*).

"Bring and subdue the wealth of King Pramaganda, the lord of Kīkaṭa—the wealth located at Naicāśākha, in the city of Nīcāśakhi; increase it! This meaning is immediately understood. However, since this would entail the loss of authority for the eternal Veda by having it convey a non-eternal historical fact (the account of a king named Pramaganda), the word "Pramaganda" is instead interpreted as referring to a usurer, based on the etymological derivation: "one toward whom excellent wealth (pra-maganda) will come."

The term *naicāśākha* does not denote wealth belonging to a *ṣaṇḍa* (a eunuch or a specific class). This being the case, since usury and similar activities are constant by way of their continuous flow (*pravāha*), there is no contradiction with the connection to non-eternal objects. Likewise, in the expression "the lover (*jāra*) of Ahalyā," the meaning is simply that Ahalyā is the night—so called because she dissolves (*līyate*) during the day—and her "lover" is the Sun, the cause of her fading away; thus, there is no contradiction with the connection to non-eternal objects. And so, even if the story of Pramaganda, Ahalyā, and others should flash forth due to the similarity of words, the established position of the Mīmāṃsakas is that such [associations] are simply not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*).

The meaning of this section is as follows: in the very same way, regarding those specific deities and other entities established by terms such as *Nārāyaṇa* and *Parabrahman* within the portions of the Vedānta, an elaboration (*upavṛṃhaṇa*) must be performed in order to dispel any suspicion that their meaning is not intended to be expressed.
"He recites the word 'parāsa' (poison), yet he too is a youth fond of elegant poetry;
though bitten by Time, he has gone to his own home."
Chāyā heard the name of Parāśara; he too was a youth, refined by the study of elegant poetry.
"Alas! Such is the course of time; we too have been sent to our own husband."

Thus it is recited. This is the speech of a certain woman who was astonished, having remembered that her husband—who was devoted to the recitation of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* at specific times—had now become intent on improper poetic discourse, and having remembered her own cessation from wandering at will. Therefore, it should be understood that this [text] is directed toward another purpose. Now, one might object: "But the word 'Parāśara' indeed occurs in the *Parāśarapurāṇa* as well, and therein the supremacy of Śiva alone is shown from beginning to end. To this we say: No.

The sense is that, since the term "Parāśara" is not well-known as a designation for [the author of] the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*— unlike [the case of] the *Parāśara-smṛti*— the word "Parāśara" occurring in the verse intends to refer specifically to the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
(Regarding the excellence of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*) "Of Agni and Śiva," etc.
"Mixed, as well as those characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and likewise *tamas*—these fourfold types of *kalpas* are declared to be the days of Brahmā.

Since this passage describes the division of the *kalpas* themselves into *sāttvika* and so forth, and because of the observation in the phrase "now, among the *sāttvika* *kalpas*," the terms "among the *tāmasa*" and "among the *rājasa*" are all qualifiers of the *kalpas*. Consequently, the meaning is that they know the greatness of Agni and Śiva proclaimed in the *tāmasa* *kalpas*, and the greatness of Brahmā proclaimed in the *rājasa* *kalpas*.

The meaning of the phrase "in which kalpa" (*yasmin kalpe tu*) is as follows: because of the hearing of the words "of that and that" (*tasya tasya*) in the second half [of the verse], for whichever Purāṇa has been proclaimed as establishing the majesty (*māhātmya*) of a particular deity such as Viṣṇu, that [Purāṇa] is the one that establishes its majesty. The word "that" (*tat*) must be supplied [as the subject], since the phrase "which was proclaimed" (*yatproktam*) is heard in the preceding part. That Purāṇa, which establishes the majesty of each respective [deity], has as its very nature the nature of that specific kalpa.

For the essential nature of a *kalpa* consists in its being characterized by *sattva* and so forth; the realized meaning is that it is described by a *brāhmaṇa* who abounds in the quality of *sattva*. Consequently, it should be understood that the realized meaning is as follows: the majesty of Agni and Śiva is described by a *brāhmaṇa* abounding in *tamas*, the majesty of Brahmā by one abounding in *rajas*, and the majesty of Viṣṇu by one abounding in *sattva*.

Some, however, say that regarding the phrase "in whichever eon whatever was proclaimed," the meaning is that the majesty of whichever deity the Purāṇa was composed concerning is described according to that deity's own nature (*svarūpa*). Others, however, take *tad* as a separate word in the phrase "according to its nature" (*tatsvarūpeṇa*). They propose the following construction: "In whichever eon whichever Purāṇa was proclaimed, its majesty is described according to the nature of that [Purāṇa]. For in this way, the two genitive endings in the expression "of that and that" (*tasya tasya*) become meaningful.

And its essential nature is the unique form consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* itself; therefore, they say the meaning is that [the Lord] is described by means of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Now, an objection:
"In that regard, those who are the causal selves were born directly from Maheśvara:
Brahmā for creation, Hari for protection, and Rudra for dissolution."
Nevertheless, out of mutual envy and desiring to surpass one another,
they propitiated their father, the Supreme Lord, through ascetic penance.
In another kalpa, Brahmā, who is identical with the universe, created Viṣṇu and Rudra;
likewise, in another kalpa, Viṣṇu created Brahmā and Rudra, and similarly, Hara [created the others].
"Neither by this [number] is there any increase or decrease in them in any way;
those various [Purāṇas] were composed by the great sages with reference to the specific events of their respective Kalpas. A wise person is not confused by that."

One might argue: "Could this statement not be intended to establish the authority of all the Purāṇas by means of demonstrating the ultimate historical accounts occurring in their respective Kalpas, in accordance with the Purāṇic dictum? For in the phrase 'the majesty of each [Purāṇa],' since it is appropriate to refer back to the previously mentioned Kalpa with the words 'in which Kalpa,' one can maintain that it is precisely the majesty associated with that Kalpa—which is described both in its own essential nature and in the form of the Purāṇa active in that Kalpa—that is being extolled. To this, we reply: No.

Because the verse beginning with “*trayaste kāraṇātmanaḥ*” has not been cited by earlier authorities, its authority cannot be ascertained; furthermore, if the intended meaning were that “the greatness of whichever *kalpa* a particular *purāṇa* was proclaimed in is described by that *purāṇa*,” then it would be incorrect to say it is described “by its own nature. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated [above].

"Otherwise-cognition" (*anyathājñāna*) and "contrary-cognition" (*viparītajñāna*). "Otherwise-cognition" is the cognition of a property as being otherwise than it actually is; "contrary-cognition" is the cognition of one thing as another thing. However, some say that these two take the form of superimposition through association (*saṃsargāropa*) and superimposition through identity (*tādātmyāropa*), because there is no error regarding the substratum (*dharmin*) itself. Regarding the statement, "Sattva is light and illuminating," in the phrase "Tamas is indeed heavy and enveloping," the word "indeed" (*eva*) is connected everywhere: Sattva is accepted by the Sāṅkhya teachers as being light and illuminating.

The cause of upward movement is buoyancy (*lāghava*), which is indeed a quality opposed to heaviness (*gaurava*); for it is from buoyancy that fire rises upward, and from it that air moves horizontally. And that buoyancy is the cause for the engagement of the instruments—the eyes and so forth—with their respective objects. Therefore, it is illuminating. For that *sattva*, being itself inactive, tends toward exhaustion regarding its own effects; and it is supported by *rajas* and set into motion. Thus, because it impels, *rajas* is the supporter.

In this context, the cause is its mobility (*latva*). Since it is itself mobile by nature, it is the impeller that sets dust in motion while remaining itself unmoving. And such dust is set in motion only in certain instances by *tamas*, which is heavy and enveloping, acting as an obstacle to movement here and there; thus it is said, "*Tamas* is indeed heavy and enveloping. "Enveloping" means it is the cause of restriction.

The sense is that because *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* have the respective functions of illumination, activity, and restraint, it is established that *sattva* possesses the quality of luminosity (*prakāśakatva*), and *tamas* possesses heaviness as well as being the cause of the dullness of the instruments (*karaṇa*). Therefore, there is no fault in this statement [of ours]. In reality, however, since this statement is found in the *Sāttvika* *Garuḍa Purāṇa*, one should observe that even if the authority of this statement from the *Tāmasa* *Matsya Purāṇa* is not established, there is no harm. By means of this statement, [it is shown that] the [Purāṇas] are rooted in *sattva* and the other qualities.

If it be argued that, even though there is no contradiction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) grasping duality and non-duality, since it is possible to determine that all dualistic cognition is rooted in defect (*doṣa*) in accordance with such scriptural authorities as "by people whose self-certainty is fixed by their own karma" and "from that [Self] indeed arise the distinctions of mountains, oceans, earth, and so forth," then perceptual experience (*pratyakṣa*) grasping duality would not be an adversary to the Śruti teaching non-duality—[we reply: No; for it remains unestablished even now that those statements demonstrate that the perception of difference and the like are rooted in defect.

"'Not this, not this; there is nothing else beyond this. This is its meaning: 'Now, therefore, the instruction is "not this, not this"; thus, there is nothing else superior to this Brahman indicated by the words 'not this, not this. The sense is that this possesses the same logical status as statements such as 'When there was darkness, neither day nor night existed, neither being nor non-being—Śiva alone was,' and 'Śiva is the one to be meditated upon,' because they share the same force as the statement 'They arise from space alone.'"

Regarding the phrase "measured at ten thousand": the contradiction with the statement establishing [the number] as six thousand may be resolved through differences in meter (*vṛtta*) and so forth, or by taking it to mean merely an excess, or by the fact that the specific number is not intended to be emphasized (*avivakṣitatva*). Regarding the phrase "having resorted to" and "out of compassion": she herself had resorted [to him]; therefore, the sense is that Sītā’s words indicate Rāma’s own lack of cruelty (*ānṛśaṃsya*) toward her. Furthermore, regarding the two words "from which" (*yataḥ*) and "how" (*yathā*): [they are to be understood as follows].

The meaning is that just as [the question] "from whence and how it was" [is asked], so too [the question] "from whence and how it will be" is asked. Regarding the phrase "by the intervention of another question": this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa); it should be understood that this applies to the word "and" (ca) and others as well in the passage, "And from whence this moving and unmoving world [proceeds]. For pervasion occurs by way of being the Self (ātmatayā).

Although, by the force of the meaning of the suffix *mayaṭ* in the word “*yanmayam*,” only pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) might be established and not selfhood (*ātmatva*), nevertheless, because of the co-occurrence with creation and dissolution, it is the pervasive cause of persistence that must be inquired about; thus, the sense is that selfhood is established. Now, one might object: since it is established that whatever is the place of origin for something is likewise its place of dissolution, the questions regarding the place of dissolution and its manner are inappropriate. To this, he says: “the question regarding the place of dissolution. This refers to [the distinction] between being mediated and not being mediated.

The distinction should be understood as follows: according to the Siddhānta, [liberation] is mediated by a means (*sadvārakatva*); according to the views of Yādava and Bhāskara, it is unmediated (*advārakatva*); and according to the view of Śaṅkara, it consists in the cessation of the delusion regarding the effect (*kāryabhramanivṛttirūpatva*). Furthermore, this [distinction] is based on the suspicion of a difference between the agent and the instrument, because in the world one observes a difference between the producer and the instrument. Regarding the reason for not explicitly citing the two verses of inquiry beginning with "Those elements which are the means of knowledge" (*yatpramāṇāni bhūtāni*) in the commentary, he states: "the two verses of inquiry concerning the essential nature" (*svarūpapraśnaślokadvayam*).

Anticipating the objection that the expression “the object of the acts of maintenance and dissolution” would be inconsistent because maintenance and dissolution are intransitive, he states: “By the words ‘maintenance’ and ‘dissolution,’ protection and withdrawal are intended. He explains the word “this” as meaning “that which is understood through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). Regarding this, some maintain that in the commentary [of Śaṅkara] stating “and this is identity,” it is appropriate for the word “this” to refer to coreferentiality.

Furthermore, it is appropriate to explain the word *tādātmya* as referring solely to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that expresses identity. Coreferentiality expressing identity between the inner controller of the world—the referent of the word "world"—and the Supreme Self—the referent of the pronoun "That"—is based on their oneness; it is not, however, based on the oneness of the world and Brahman as the pervaded and the pervader.

Because it is a response to the question "What am I?", the coordination expressed in the phrase "And the world is He" is naturally understood as a grammatical construction of apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, if the word "identity" (*tādātmya*) were intended merely to refer to the oneness apprehended through such apposition, then the commentary’s statement—"But this is not caused by the oneness of substance between the pervaded and the pervader"—would be inconsistent with its own intent; for there can be no suspicion that an identity characterized by such oneness could itself be based upon further oneness.

Therefore, the word *tādātmya* (identity) itself must be construed as having the sense of *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality). They say that the intent of the *Ṭīkā* is also precisely on this point. [The objection] that identity is not seen through mere pervasion (*vyāpti*) means that grammatical coreferentiality is not observed in such cases as "the movement is the pot. However, one should not be deluded into thinking this refers to numerical oneness (*aikya*), for even in the case of the body and the self, there is an absence of oneness characterized by identity; this is the intended meaning. The sense is that oneness is impossible between two things upon which contradictory properties—namely, being the pervaded and being the pervader—are superposed. [This is established] because it is proven by scripture (*śruti*). *Brāhma...* [text fragment].

"This is the view of the proponents of knowledge (*jñānavādins*). Although the sense of "modification" (*vikāra*) is also accepted [by them], the point is that since this is already established by the word *yataḥ*, this alone is what they intend. Now, one might object: even in your own system, since the suffix *mayaṭ* merely implies "abundance" (*prācurya*), the meaning extending up to "Self-ness" (*ātmatva*) is not obtained; and even if one were to assume such a meaning, it would involve a conceptual burden (*pratipatti-gaurava*). Thus, the suffix *mayaṭ* would be equally meaningless [in both views]. To this, he replies: "By accepting the literal meaning of the scripture. He states this as a unique refutation.

The sense is that it is improper to resort to meaninglessness when meaningfulness is possible, as this principle applies equally to both proponents of difference (*bhedavādin*) and non-difference (*abhedavādin*). Now, an objection is raised: the commentary stating, "the answer would have been 'Viṣṇu alone,'" is incorrect. Does this imply that the word *jagat* (world) should not have been used here? Or does it mean that the particle *eva* (alone) should have been used? It cannot be the first alternative; for when the question "What is the world? is asked—where the world is the subject—the answer must likewise appropriately concern the world as its subject.

Nor is there the employment of the restrictive particle *eva*, because its function is already established by the maxim that "every sentence is restrictive. Furthermore, the answer "the world is Viṣṇu alone" would be incoherent; for an answer such as "shell is indeed silver" is never observed anywhere. Anticipating this objection—that the answer should have been "it is merely false," rather than through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of two contradictory forms—the author, keeping the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya in mind, says "in the view that [the suffix] has its own meaning as its primary sense," and so forth. [The phrase] "that which presents one of the two forms" refers to this.

The meaning is that [the word] presents one of the two forms, namely truth or falsity; thus, "Viṣṇu" is a word that presents one of these two forms. In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) stating "Viṣṇu alone," the intention of the word *viṣṇu* is not toward the state of being Viṣṇu, but rather toward one of the two forms: truth or falsity. The meaning of "abundant" (*prabhūta*) is "plentiful" (*pracura*). Although in the *Kāśikā* it is explained as "that which is presented or introduced by way of abundance."

The commentator Hāradatta has also stated: "Although the word *prakṛta* denotes merely that which is under discussion, nevertheless, by the inclusion of the term *vacana* (speech), this specific qualification is obtained here. For the inclusion of *vacana* is for the purpose that [the designation] should apply to that which is commonly used in the world as a synonym for *mayaṭ* when referring to what is under discussion. Nevertheless, since this [definition] is even more excellent than that, it should be understood as superior. He raises an objection regarding the phrase *yanmayam*.

This is because it is impossible for a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that presents two distinct forms to constitute a subsequent [qualification]. Although it is possible for the coreferentiality that presents the two forms "the world is false" to be subsequent, the intended meaning here is that it is not possible for the coreferentiality "the world is indeed Viṣṇu" to be subsequent; it does not mean that such coreferentiality is impossible because it is based on the relationship between body and self (*śarīrātma-bhāva*). The phrase "the status of being a suffix denoting its own meaning (*svārthika*) is rejected" connects with what precedes.

The possibility that [the suffix *mayaṭ*] has its own primary meaning (*svārthika*) is not set aside on the grounds that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) cannot be based on the relationship between a body and a self; for if that were the case, there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*), since the fact that coreferentiality is based on the body-self relationship remains unestablished even now. "Contradiction of the meaning" means a contradiction in the identity of the insentient and the sentient. Furthermore, it is because it would be illogical for it to serve as the answer to the question "composed of what? (*yanmaya*); the point is that, in order for the suffix *mayaṭ* to have a meaningful function, it would be more appropriate to ask about either a modification (*vikāra*) or an abundance (*prācurya*).

One might object: "Is the suffix -maya not redundant, since the question regarding its modification as 'consisting of that' could arise? Anticipating this, he says: "Because the material cause (*upādāna*) was what was asked by the word 'yataḥ'. He avoids the redundancy between the two statements—"the state of being the opposite of all that is to be discarded would be sublated" and "the Brahman would become the locus of all that is inauspicious"—by means of the passage beginning with "satya-saṃkalpa" (of true resolve).

Because it is possible to state the occurrence of both faults with a single word without any contraction [of meaning], he avoids the charge of tautology by saying, "or else there would be the loss of the dual gender," and so forth. Now, one might ask: how can the form *sthāpyate* ("is established") be grammatically correct when the intended meaning is "will be established" (*sthāpayiṣyate*)? To this he replies: "because it occurs immediately thereafter. The sense is that this is according to the grammatical rule: *vartamānasāmīpye vartamānavadvā* ("when there is proximity to the present time, the present tense may optionally be used"). Regarding the phrase "the seven verses have as their object the salutation": [it refers to the verse beginning] "To Viṣṇu, the unconchanging, the pure, the eternal Supreme Self, whose form is always of one kind, the all-conquering."
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, to Hari, and to Śaṅkara;
to Vāsudeva, the Savior, whose activity consists of creation, preservation, and dissolution.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the cause of liberation, who possesses the nature of both the one and the many, whose essence is both gross and subtle, and whose form is both unmanifest and manifest.
Salutations to that Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, who is the source of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, and who is himself composed of the world.
Having prostrated before the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is the support of the universe, subtler than the subtlest, and who dwells within all beings, and is infinite;
That which is, in ultimate reality, the nature of consciousness and absolutely stainless,
appears through erroneous perception as having the nature of an external object.
Having prostrated before Viṣṇu, the great lord who devours the universe during its dissolution and sustains it during its creation— the unborn, imperishable, and immutable sovereign of the worlds.

Thus ends the *Saptaślokī*. The meaning is that its nature as an extensive exposition is established. The intention is that the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) connects with the immediately preceding phrase, "in order to speak at length what was stated in brief. It should be understood that the statement, "the meaning is that its nature as an extensive exposition is established," expresses the sense resulting from that syntactical connection (*anvaya*). And regarding the question concerning the maintenance of the arms: the meaning is "and the question concerning the maintenance performed by the mother, father, and others. Regarding the phrase "of the matter explicitly stated": [it refers to the fact that the meaning has already been directly expressed].

The meaning is "of selfhood" (*ātmatvasya*). Regarding the phrase "of that which will be described at great length": since expansion (*prathana*) here occurs by means of words, the suffix *ghañ* is prohibited in the context of verbal roots when the object is a word—according to the rule *prathane vāvaśabde*; therefore, the term used is "vistara" (extensive). Regarding "Īkṣati" and "Ānandamaya": the first half [of the verse] expresses the distinction between Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), which constitutes the subject matter of the *Īkṣati* and *Ānandamaya* sections of the Brahma-sūtras. The intention is that the phrase "to Him whose form is eternally uniform" expresses the meaning of the *Antarāditya-vidyā*. Regarding the phrase "the exclusion of [the analogies of] the king and the sky."

The meaning is that by the word *viṣṇu*, there is the exclusion of the king (*nṛpa*), and by the word *sarvajiṣṇu*, there is the exclusion of the sky (*nabhas*). Since the term *sarvajiṣṇu* lacks inherent applicability (*svārasya*) to the Controller (*niyantṛ*), and since the act of controlling is established as a matter of course through the very force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), he explains that the word *jiṣṇu* refers to being untouched by the defects residing in the object of pervasion (*vyāpya*). Alternatively, [it is said] "by the word *viṣṇu* alone. [An objection is raised: "How can Viṣṇu be the cause?"

Although the state of being the cause of the world is not explicitly stated in the verse beginning with “to the changeless one” (*avikārāya*), it should nevertheless be understood that this was mentioned because the state of being the cause was declared in the preceding verse: “all has emerged from Viṣṇu. [The phrase] “by means of the incarnate form named Viṣṇu” means by means of a particular form (*vigraha*). [The expression] “like the designations of words such as ‘god’ or ‘human’” is used.

The point is this: just as in the case of Rāma and others, even though they lack human nature—which is a specific transformation of the qualities such as *sattva*—they are nonetheless designated as "Rāma is a human" because they possess a form similar to that of humans; likewise, it is logically consistent to apply the term "power" (*śakti*) figuratively to the individual souls who are the power of the Lord, on account of their being of the same genus [as the Lord] by virtue of being His self.

However, some, not accepting that the word *śakti* is used figuratively, explain the intention as follows: just as [the Lord] is denoted by words such as "Deva" because He has the bodies of Devas and so forth, the designation of the word *śakti* is primary when applied to Him who has the world—existing as His power—as His body. Anticipating the objection that it would be improper to say "salutation to the one whose nature is both single and manifold, whose self is both subtle and gross," instead of saying "salutation to the one whose self is gross and subtle," they state: "residing in the intellect. The sense is that the word "manifold" (aneka) is in immediate proximity [to the word "single"].

"Of the creation and so forth contained within the egg"—the meaning is that this is because it was stated [in the previous verse], "for the purpose of the acts of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. "'Existing outside the egg'—the meaning is that this is because it will be stated [in a later verse], 'Viṣṇu, the great Lord, who devours the universe during its maintenance and creation. Now, one might object: "Could the subsequent verse, 'The support of the universe,' not also refer to Time? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The subsequent verse refers to the collective individual soul (samaṣṭijīva). [This is] by way of being a delimiting factor (avacchedakatayā) and by way of being delimited (avacchedyatayā).

The sense is that because the world is delimited by time, time possesses the quality of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*); yet, because [time] itself is delimited by moments (*nimeṣa*) and so forth, it also possesses the quality of being delimited (*avacchedyatva*). Regarding the term *bhūta*, it means "that which has come into being" (*bhavatīti bhūtam*). The intended meaning here is that the suffix *-kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) because the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), and not that it refers to the present tense; this should be understood. Regarding the phrase "qualified by the individual *kṣetrajña*s": the meaning of the verse beginning with "whose nature is knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpam*) is as follows: "whose nature is knowledge" means having the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is of the nature of knowledge—as its body (*śarīraka*).

Furthermore, qualities such as absolute purity are qualifiers by way of the individual soul (*jīva*). This is just as in expressions like "highly noble" or "of great wisdom," where "greatness" is connected through the medium of nobility and knowledge respectively. It should not be argued that the connection should be direct; for while absolute purity is directly established in the Supreme Self by such scriptural statements as "to the changeless, to the pure," the presence of error within that omniscient Being cannot possibly be direct. Therefore, it must be stated that [the connection] is mediated by an intermediary.

Alternatively, [the author] explains [the passage] as follows: having considered that the word *śāstra* in the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—which intends to establish that the scripture is devoted to demonstrating the error based on Brahman, whose nature is non-differentiated knowledge, with reference only to the single verse beginning with "jñānasvarūpam"—the commentary beginning with "yadi" (if) was interpreted as being intended to demonstrate the contradiction with the conclusion should the aforementioned meaning [of the scripture] be accepted; yet, considering it improper for the word *śāstra* to refer to only a single verse, he explains it as being intended to show the impossibility of the question and answer that are about to follow.

"It is useful for the commencement of the treatise. The word division is "svayaṃ nirguṇaḥ" (himself devoid of qualities). He avoids the objection that "subjection to karma" and "fitness for connection with karma" are synonymous by stating, "Even for the liberated one there is subjection to karma," and so forth. Anticipating the objection that—since Brahman alone is the ultimate reality—one should have designated them as "the powers of Brahman" rather than "the powers of the state of being Brahman" (*brāhṛṇo bhāvaśaktayaḥ*)—he says: "The designation [is justified] because of identity with Brahman, just like the designation [of the Self as 'I']."

The meaning is that although one should have said *brāhṛātmakam*, there is no inconsistency in using the word *tādātmya*—since the term *tādātmya* signifies non-difference—in the expression *brāhṛtādātmyam*, which functions like the repeated reference by the pronoun *tat* to that which was previously indicated by the word *brāhṛ*. However, if it is argued that in the present context, when it is said "*brāhṛṇo bhāvaśaktayaḥ*," the meaning "the powers of the being of the *brāhṛ*" is not obtained—just as when it is said "the nature of a jar" (*ghaṭasya bhāvarūpam*), the meaning "the nature of the jar" is not obtained—that is true; [for] it is a part of a compound...

It is not a qualifier of something else; nevertheless, just as saying "the devotee of Śiva" implies that Śiva possesses the nature of the Blessed One (Bhagavattva), so too, when it is said "the powers of being belonging to Brahman," it follows by implication that Brahman alone is of the nature of being—this is the intended meaning. Precisely because of this lack of elegance, he says: "Or rather, 'the powers of being belonging to Brahman'."

The meaning is that anything other than that [Self] is false. You alone are established in yourself (*svaniṣṭha*); the meaning is that there is nothing other than you that is established in itself. Consequently, the word *paramārtha* refers to that which is established in itself. *Paramārtha* means the supreme (*parama*) or most excellent (*utkṛṣṭa*) object; that is to say, it is independent (*svatantra*). As for the phrase "for [the definition] is accompanied by being pervaded" (*vyāpyatvasahacaritam hi*), the meaning is that it is qualified by being pervaded. Regarding the phrase "indicating the definition of a body," the meaning is that it indicates the definition of a body as stated in the words "of whichever sentient being... (*yasya cetanasya*).

"Jagaccharīraka" is a vocative address meaning "O You whose body is the universe. "Atatparyantasya" means "of that which does not have that [universe] as its body. Since it is inappropriate for the word *paramārtha*—which can denote the supreme goal—to refer to a thing established in itself (svaniṣṭha), he says, out of this sense of unease: "Alternatively, the word 'one' (*eka*) refers to preeminence (*prādhānya*). As for the phrase "for that which is excluded by the word 'without companion' (*asahāya*)," one might object: since the word *eka* denotes what is common to other things, to that which is primary, and to number, there could also be another meaning for it that is distinct from what is excluded by the word "without companion."

If it is asked, "But since [the word *eka*] does not mean 'primacy' alone, how can this word *asahāya* (without companion) indicate that *eka* has the meaning of 'primacy'?"—it is not so. This is because the qualifier "in the sense of 'without companion'" merely indicates the possibility of other meanings. As stated in the Mahābhāṣya on the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ*: "This word *eka* has many meanings. It signifies 'without companion,' as in *ekāgnayaḥ* (those who maintain a single fire) and *ekahalaḥ* (one who owns a single plough). It signifies 'number,' as in *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ* (one, two, many)."

The meaning is that [the word *eka*] functions in other senses as well, based on the statement, “One protects the subjects, another [protects] strength,” and because of the *Nighaṇṭu* definition: “*Eka* means principal, other, and alone. Regarding the commentary (*bhāṣya*), one might raise the objection: “It is incorrect to say ‘all this is indeed identical with you (*tvadātmaka*) and there is nothing else apart from you (*tvadanya*)’, for the world, being identical with Him, cannot be something other than Him. Anticipating this, he explains by supplying the missing words: “Other than you (*tvadanya*) means not having you as its essence (*atvadātmaka*). That is to say, it would mean existing independently (*svaniṣṭha*).

One might object that the introductory phrase, “It is said that a portion of a half-verse establishes the meaning already stated,” is inappropriate, because the commentary beginning with “Therefore this is said” does not state that the word *mahiman* alone—which was intended by the phrase “a portion of a half-verse”—establishes [the point], since it also presents the pervasion of all (*sarvavyāpti*) as an establishing factor. Anticipating this objection, I say: “Because pervasion is the nature of greatness (*mahiman*). It is not the intention of the commentary that the pervasion of all is untenable if everything is illusory; rather, let there be the pervasion of all.

The sense is this: whether there be some pervasion (*vyāpti*) or something else, it is not appropriate to establish its greatness; this is precisely the intent of the exertion (*saṃrambha*) of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*). Anticipating the objection that stating a lack of intention regarding the word employed is unnatural, he says: "Or rather, pervasion serves to justify the stated meaning.

The word "therein" (*tatra*) must be supplied after the phrase "the world is in reality of the nature of You" in the Commentary. Consequently, the meaning is: "therein [in that which is] the world which is in reality of the nature of You."

By this, the objection that—since it is impossible for the portion "the world is in reality of the nature of You" to indicate the form of a mistaken perception—it would be more appropriate to express it with either a genitive or locative case ending as "in the world which is in reality of the nature of You" or "of the world which is in reality of the nature of You," and not otherwise, has been refuted. The word division here is: *mām ebhyaḥ param avyayam iti atra*.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If it is admitted that the immediate delusion of identifying the body with the self is sublated by the mediate knowledge produced by the scriptures, why should the perception that grasps duality not likewise be sublated by the knowledge produced by the scriptures? Furthermore, one might ask: "In the absence of causes for error such as similarity, how can there be a delusion of identifying the body with the self? Dispelling these two doubts, he explains the delusion of identifying the body with the self, stating: "And the delusion of identifying the body with the self is caused by [false] association."

The meaning is as follows: just as the perception that "water is hot" is suspected of being erroneous due to contact with a fiery substance and the presence of a defect, and is consequently sublated by the authoritative scripture (*śāstra*) which apprehends water's inherent nature of coldness—this is the intended sense (*bhāva*).

Nor should it be argued that, because Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) are likewise related as material cause and effect and are thus mutually interconnected, why should the perception of existence residing in Brahman not also apply to the phenomenal world? For if the mere contact with Brahman were the defect, then even the non-dualistic scripture (*advaita-śāstra*)—which is itself unreal, invalid, and merely conventional—would be apprehended as real, valid, and conventional; thus, being suspected of this very defect, that scripture too would fail to be a sublater [of the world].

Furthermore, since mental proliferation (*prapañca*) lacks existence, even its association with Brahman is impossible; thus, it cannot be a defect—this is explained in detail elsewhere. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "fit for the yoga that is the means to direct experience" (*anubhavasādhanayogayogyā*): those whose minds are purified and thus fit for the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*), which is the means to direct experience, are so described. Purity is the cause of fitness, and the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) is the cause of purity; explaining it with this intent, a *tatpuruṣa* compound with the instrumental case (*yogena yogyā*) is intended here.

The word *yoga* here refers to *karmayoga*. Since there is no difference between fitness (*yogyatā*) and purification (*pariśuddhi*), their relationship as cause and effect—as in the previous case—is not intended to be expressed. Furthermore, the designation *yogya-pariśuddhi* (fitness-purification) is justified, just as one might say "a firm staff capable of producing a jar. Intending this, he says: "the meaning is either 'by yoga' [meaning] fitness or purification. By the term *akhilajagat* (the entire world), the non-conscious (*acid-rūpa*) world is intended.

Regarding this, some say that there is no fault even if, as in the previous verse, the intention is to refer to the world as having the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). This is because there is no defect even if one says, "they see the world, which has the nature of consciousness, as being of the essence of knowledge. Alternatively, they maintain that even in the previous verse, the word *jagat* refers only to the non-conscious (*acit*). Consequently, the meaning would be: "seeing the world—which consists of the forms of gods, humans, and so forth—as having the nature of knowledge and the nature of the Self," and thus they possess the delusion of identifying the body with the Self. Therefore, they argue that there is no inconsistency between the two uses of the word *jagat*.

"Summarized in the first verse," and so forth. This is the meaning: he states [the faults] "in detail" (*vistareṇa*)—that is, as common to all verses—along with the repetitions, contradictions of meaning, and contradictions with the intent of the scripture that were not mentioned in the first verse, which was stated merely with reference to that specific verse alone. The phrase "common to all verses" is an explanation of the word "in detail. However, the words "summary" (*saṃkṣepa*) and "detail" (*vistara*) do not refer to a summary or detail regarding the nature of the faults themselves.

Indeed, the nature of the refutation was explained in detail in the first verse as the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the words "you" (*tvam*) and so forth, and as being in contradiction with the context of the praise of Mahāvarāha; however, in the subsequent [verses], it is stated concisely as the metaphorical indication of the words and the contradiction with the context. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. Regarding the phrase "contradiction with the intermediate context" (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*): it means contradiction with the beginning, conclusion, and other elements of the intermediate context.
(The distinction between the non-duality of the mode and the non-duality of the modus.)

"Of the verse to be cited" means: because of the nature of the words *anya* (other) and *para* (supreme) in the verse beginning with "If there is any other supreme [being]... It means that it is of this very same kind; that is to say, it possesses the same single mode of operation. "Like the injunction for the *puroḍāśa*" means: like the sacrifice which has the *aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa* as its substance and Agni as its deity. This should be understood in light of the fact that, in the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, the injunction regarding the *āgneya-aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa* was rejected [as a primary injunction]. "When the obstructing factor is absent" means...

The meaning is that even when there is an absence of the conditions that would obstruct the reconnection with pleasure and so forth, the non-occurrence of such reconnection is established as the state [of liberation]. Regarding the suffix *mayaṭ*, it is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). The meaning of the verse beginning with "In his own body and in the bodies of others" (*tasyātmaparadeheṣu*) is as follows: "Even though existing" (*sato 'pi*)—here the genitive case is used in the sense of disregard (*anādara*), according to the rule "the sixth [genitive] is used in the sense of disregard. Thus, disregarding the existence [of the self] within one's own body and in the bodies of others, the ultimate reality is simply the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), which is characterized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), uniform (*eka-mayam*), identical (*samānam*), and of a single form (*ekarūpam*). This is the meaning.

The venerable Viṣṇucittārya, however, has explained this word *jñāna* as referring to *dharmabhūtajñāna* (knowledge as an attribute) on the grounds that the emphasis of the negative formulation (*vyatirekanirdeśa*) in the phrase "even though it exists, there is knowledge" suggests this. Alternatively, because the view that the suffix *-mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*) is not the primary intention, he states: "Or rather, the word *eka* has existence (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning. Thus, "the state of having a single object" (*aikārthyam*) is shown;

the meaning is that the lack of contradiction between the two statements is demonstrated. Furthermore, the manner in which this lack of contradiction is demonstrated should be seen in the commentary composed by the author of the work (*granthakṛt*) upon his explanation of the verse beginning with "in which all distinctions have subsided" (*pratyastamitabheda*).

"The singular number is not appropriate"—this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that even in the phrase "one who is existent is also one," the singular number would be inappropriate. Furthermore, the singular number would likewise apply to the word "body" (*deha*); consequently, the plural number in the phrase "in his own body and in the bodies of others" (*tasyātmaparadeheṣu*) would be inappropriate—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the "three positions": "another, distinct [from me]" is the first; "this is I" is the second; and "this other [person] is another" is the third. Now, one might argue that a distinction can indeed be stated on the basis of "I-ness" (*ahantva*) and "otherness" (*tadanyatva*).

Nor should it be said that "I-ness" (ahantva) also resides in the Supreme Self; for if that were so, there would be no possibility of even suspecting that such statements as "I am Brahman"—which convey the non-difference between the referent of "I" and Brahman—could indicate a difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, and thus no effort would need to be made to refute such a suspicion.

Since the word *aham* (I) is a synonym for the word *ātman* (self), and since the universal property of selfhood (*ātmatva-jāti*) is common to all individual souls (*jīva*) as well as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the properties such as "I-ness" (*ahantva*) and so forth have as their sole ground for application the mere nature of being the self. Consequently, there is no possibility of contradiction between this view and statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) or "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), which establish that Brahman is the substratum of the universal property of selfhood; thus, any effort to refute [the opponent's position] would be futile. Anticipating this objection, the author says: "Previously, among gods and others... and "it was stated that the form is different."

The point is this: when one ought to specify that "this has such-and-such a form" and "this has another form," by saying instead "it has a different form," the implication is that even regarding the form, there is merely a state of extreme similarity, not actual identity.

"In every respect, if equality is admitted" means that equality is admitted even on the basis of having a single substratum. Regarding the reading "the difference is designated as *ṣaḍja* and so forth," even though this is the case, when it is said that there is a "difference of designations," one should not think that—just as a single jar has different designations such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) or "pot" (*kalaśa*)—there is merely a difference in the designations *ṣaḍja* and so forth, while no difference exists in the things designated. This is because the difference in the things designated depends upon the difference in their designations.

The point is that, according to the maxim *tadadhīnatvāttācchabdyam* ("it is so called because it depends on that"), the term "difference in designations" (*saṃjñābheda*) used in the Bhāṣya is applied metaphorically to the difference in the designated objects (*saṃjñin*) themselves. If it is objected: "One must admit that the apprehension of the connection with designations such as *ṣaḍja* occurs only in a substratum (*dharmin*) already grasped through some form that excludes others; therefore, since a differentiating form must be accepted even in the absence of a difference in designation, how can there be 'identity with that single [form]'?"—this is true.

The intention here is that the connection with a name is generally the cause for the cognition of difference; it is exactly the same in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). The meaning is: since difference is established in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), let it be the same in the case of the subject of the illustration as well.
