As for the statement "where there is the example of space": just as a single space possesses different forms according to the difference in time, so too a single Self possesses the distinctions of gods and others according to the difference in time—this much alone is the point to be stated here.

Therefore, one should observe that it is not necessary to be occupied with such investigations as: "Which individual instance is prior?", "Which individual instance is posterior?", "In which instance is there an original teaching (upadeśa)?", or "In which instance is there an extended application (atideśa)? This refers to the doctrine of the partlessness of space held by the Vedāntins. Here, the term *niravayavatvavāda* means the doctrine (*vāda*) regarding partlessness (*niravayavatva*). And the object of that doctrine is space (*nabhas*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency regarding the instrumental case (tṛtīyā), because by the rule "when both [agent and object] are applicable," the instrumental cannot occur in the sense of the agent. As for the phrase "with the intention of referring to a distinction of spatial parts": one should not argue that, in this way, individual souls (jīvas) would likewise be merely distinctions of space like the ether (ākāśa)—a view even acceptable to those who maintain the monism of the Self—for the intended meaning is that difference is established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) apprehending a difference that cannot otherwise be accounted for, such as the distinct distribution of pleasure and pain.

This is because, in that very context, an illustration based on similarity (*sāmya*) is stated. Nor should it be argued that, since in the passage "Just as fire cast into fire would attain equality" (*samānatva*), similarity alone is already established even prior [to the casting], the term "equality" (*samānatva*) must be understood as meaning identity (*aikya*) itself; for, since identity is sublated [in this case], the term refers specifically to a particular kind of similarity consisting in the relinquishing of the specific forms that differentiate [the two fires].

"Stated in the four chapters" means stated in the four chapters beginning from the thirteenth chapter of the second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the immediately preceding statement regarding its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). "Otherwise" means [if one were to take it as] referring merely to the form of knowledge. "That delusion of difference" means the delusion of difference caused by the forms of gods and so forth.

One might object: since the phrase "the nature of the Self" (*ātmasvarūpa*) alone serves as the term denoting the object to be characterized, for what purpose is the word "all" (*sarva*) included in the commentary in the statement, "All this is the nature of the Self"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of all three words—'I', 'you', and 'all'," and so forth. It is observed that the word "nature of the Self" (*ātmasvarūpa*) stands in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "all" (*sarva*) alone in the verse; therefore, one might ask how the words "I" and "you" can stand in coordination with the word "nature of the Self. To address this doubt, he says: "The meanings of 'I' and 'you' are of the same class [as the meaning of 'Self']" (*ahaṃtvamarthasajātīya*).

The intention is that the word *sarva* (all) is also employed together [with the other terms] in the Bhāṣya—namely, in the statement "All this is indeed the nature of the Self"—in order to demonstrate that since the word *sarva*, which denotes objects of the same class as the object denoted by *ahantva* (I-ness), is seen to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ātmasvarūpa* (the nature of the Self), it follows that the words *ahaṃ* (I) and *tvam* (you) are also in coreferentiality with it.

In this context, although the word *sarva* (all) has the capacity to denote the referents of both *ahaṃtva* (I-ness) and *tvantva* (you-ness), one should understand that the statement regarding its denoting what is of the same class as the referent of *ahaṃtva* and *tvantva* is made with the intention of applying the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). Furthermore, this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); for even in the opponent's view, in the passage "So am I, and he is you," the opponent accepts that the word "he" (*saḥ*) refers to the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), thereby admitting a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the indicated object. [The objection continues: "But [if it is argued] 'by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā'), however... etc.

The intention is that words such as "I" (*aham*) and "you" (*tvam*), which denote the Self as qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), have a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) directed toward the essential nature of the substantive alone—just as in the expression, "The space within the jar is indeed the great space. Alternatively, he explains it differently: rather than regarding the word "by this" (*anenā*)—which stands at the beginning—as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the word denoting the substantive, it is more appropriate to take the phrase "by what is called 'the essential nature of the Self'" (*ātmasvarūpamityanena*) from the conclusion as referring to the meaning expressed by the term "the essential nature of the Self" (*ātmasvarūpa*). Thus, the word "by this" (*anenā*) is a qualifier of the substantive.

The intended meaning is that [the word *sarva*] is not a qualifier of the term denoting the object of perception (*upalakṣya*). Now, one might raise this objection: "In this interpretation, since the statement 'all this is the very nature of the Self' is exhausted merely by indicating the locus [of the Self], the co-referentiality with the word *sarva* is not mentioned as a reason for its co-referentiality with the words 'I' and 'you'. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In this interpretation... Even though the co-referentiality with the word *sarva* was indeed demonstrated in the previous interpretation...

This is indeed already established; nevertheless, if the focus were on the word [itself], the statement "all this is the very nature of the Self" would be intended merely to demonstrate the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "all. In the second interpretation, however, it serves only to indicate the locus for pointing out that which is to be characterized (*upalakṣya*); such is the difference between the two.

Regarding the second interpretation, in the phrase “of words such as ‘I’ and ‘you’,” one should understand that the term refers to the meanings by the etymological analysis (*vyutpatti*) “those things for which ‘I,’ ‘you,’ and so forth are the words,” because it is impossible for a word to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with itself. One might object: even if they are merely indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), coreferentiality can still be observed through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in examples such as “the pot-space is the great space” or “the tip of the branch is the moon. Anticipating this objection, he says: “If [you mean] the words ‘I,’ ‘you,’ and so forth.”

Nevertheless, the meaning is that since the coreferentiality [of the Self] is already established by the phrase "that which is the very nature of the Self" (*ātmasvarūpam*) alone, the coreferentiality with "I-ness" (*ahantva*) and so forth is redundant. Regarding the purpose of words such as "I" (*ahaṃ*) according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), he says: "The word 'I' is relative," and so on.

One might raise the objection that if "directness" (*pratyaktva*) alone were the ground for the application of the term, then since all selves are direct with respect to themselves, the word "I" would erroneously apply even to the Supreme Self. Anticipating this, the author states "relative" (*āpekṣika*), intending to show that while directness is indeed the ground for its application, the capacity to utter the word independently is the qualifying condition (*upādhi*). He says "in the present context" (*prakṛta*); the meaning is that it has been introduced starting from the thirteenth chapter of the second part.

This is the meaning of this verse: "I too am that Self, whose sole form is knowledge; you also are such; all this, which is the very nature of the Self, has knowledge as its sole form. Therefore, abandon the delusion of difference among Selves caused by forms such as gods and so forth."

First, [the question is] whether [the verse] refers to identity with the nature of the Self. The intention of the word "first" is that identity with the liberated supreme [Self] will be refuted later. Regarding the verse *dvā suparṇā*: they are called "two birds" (*suparṇau*) because of their similarity to birds. "Sayujau" means always existing together. The word "sattvam" is to be split as "sattvam" = the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇam*). The third case ending in "yena" is used in the sense of manner (*itthambhāve*). The meaning is that, by the force of the reasoning already stated, even a weak case-ending used as an upapada must be tolerated. Thus, both are specific agents.

The meaning is that the designation of "agent" (*kartṛ*) is prescribed for both by the rules "the independent one is the agent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*) and "the prompter of that [agent] is also the cause" (*tatprayojako hetuśca*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that this is what is stated; such is the sense here in the phrase "and likewise scripture" (*tathāca śrutiḥ*). And that is very clear in that [scriptural passage]. Furthermore, it is because the context of the treatise is intent upon refuting [the view that there is] multiplicity even in liberation (*muktau*).
If wealth is indeed for the sake of Dharma, why then is the ultimate goal abandoned? For expenditure is made specifically for the purpose of attaining sensual desires.
O Lord of Men, if a son were the ultimate reality, he too would belong to another;
for that father who exists for the sake of another is indeed the ultimate reality for him.
Thus, O King, there is no ultimate reality (paramārtha) here in this world;
for the ultimate reality consists of the effects of causes without exception.
If the attainment of sovereignty and so forth mentioned here were [considered] from the perspective of ultimate reality,
then since things either exist or do not exist in ultimate reality, they would [simply] cease to be.
In your view, sacrificial rites are considered to be accomplished through the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
even in that regard, hear from me as I speak how they exist for the sake of another.
Whatever effect is produced by clay as its material cause, O King, that arises as something made of clay because it follows the nature of its cause.
In this way, whatever action is accomplished by means of perishable substances such as fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and kuśa grass,
that action itself must be perishable.
The wise accept that the ultimate reality is indeed imperishable;
however, that [world] is perishable, without a doubt, as it is produced from perishable substances.

Therefore, that very action which yields no fruit is considered by you to be the ultimate reality (paramārtha), because it serves as the means for liberation; yet the ultimate reality itself is not a means.

Meditation, O King, is not the self; that which is designated by the word "ultimate reality" (paramārtha) is the true goal. It creates distinctions from others, yet ultimate reality itself is without distinction.
The union of the supreme self and the individual self is held to be the ultimate reality;
for this [union] is not false, since one substance does not become the nature of another substance.
Therefore, O King, all these are undoubtedly superior;
however, O protector of the earth, hear from me in brief the ultimate truth.

"Single, all-pervading, equal, pure, devoid of qualities, and beyond primordial nature"—this is the meaning of the section [of the text]. Regarding the phrase "by way of summary and detail": "Thus have I spoken to you, O Khāṇḍikya, who questioned me."

"What else could be done for you beyond this brief and detailed exposition?"—this is the verse. The meaning of this is correct; the sense is that it accords with the Smṛti text: "Just as gold [is purified] through contact with fire. Regarding the phrase "he leads him to his own state" (*ātmabhāvaṃ nayatyenam*), there are two interpretations: in the first, the word *ātman* refers to the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) or to the attractor (*ākarṣaka*); in the second, the word *ātman* refers to the meditator (*dhyātṛ*). In both these positions, the word "attractor" (*ākarṣaka*) refers to fire through its etymological derivation (*yogika-vyutpatti*). In the three subsequent positions, it refers to the magnet (*ayaskānta*).

The third interpretation is that the word *ātman* refers solely to the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), while the word *bhāva* refers to activity (*iṣṭā*). The fourth [interpretation] is that the word *ātman* refers to the essential nature (*niṣkṛṣṭasvarūpa*) of both the iron and the magnet in the analogy and the thing illustrated. The fifth [interpretation] is that the word *ātman* refers to that which attracts the object of meditation, and the word *bhāva* signifies attainment (*prāpti*); this is the summary to be understood. Furthermore, by the phrase "moving along" (*anusaṃcaran*), difference (*bheda*) is shown.

The sense is that by the word *anu*, it is stated that the movement of the liberated soul follows after the movement of the Supreme Self. Furthermore, the word *samāna* is also employed in the sense of identity. If it be objected: "The use of the word *go*—which is a synonym for *vāk*—in the sense of 'ray' does not prove that the word *vāk* has the meaning of 'ray,' because that would be an unestablished reason (*aprayojakatva*). Therefore, the investigation into the term *sāmānādhikaraṇya* in the section on the refutation is also improper," we reply: No.

This is because the intended meaning of the word *sama* (equal) as "common" (*samāna*) remains unestablished even today; thus, such a statement is justified. The phrase "even if the primary sense is accepted" implies that this is like the case of the word *hari* [meaning both "lion" and "monkey"] being applied to frogs and other animals. The phrase "but that [word] serves the purpose of commonality" means that commonality is understood through the secondary function (*lakṣaṇā*) of a word expressing similarity. He explains how that is established by secondary function with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). Because commonality is defined in relation to multiple things, it is described as "having multiple correlates" (*aneka-pratiyogika*).

Because a mother has no commonality with her son regarding her son, nor does a daughter-in-law have commonality with her father-in-law regarding her father-in-law, it is said that [the relationship] is "of one form" (*ekarūpa*) toward both the son and the father-in-law respectively. Thus, the wealth is related to those two. Consequently, since the property held in common possesses a similarity of relationship—which constitutes the meaning of the word *sama*—the application of *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) is justified, because there exists a basis for it in its connection to the primary meaning from which the metaphorical sense arises. This is the intended sense.

The conclusion is that because similarity depends upon common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*), a word expressing similarity refers to the common attribute which establishes that similarity. In this way, he teaches this same principle even in cases such as "co-referential" (*samānādhikaraṇa*) or "simultaneous" (*samakāla*) within the context of an example, stating: "likewise, [the words] 'blueness' and 'lotus-ness'... [and] "...by both through being conjoined. The meaning is: "by those two of which simultaneity is predicated. [He also notes: "In the case of substances, time, and so forth, there are words such as 'equal' (*sama*) and 'identical' (*samāna*)."

Although, according to the example "existing at the same time" (*samakālavartin*), it would be more appropriate to say that the words *sama* and *samāna* apply respectively to time and substance—thus resulting in the terms *samāna-sama* for substances, time, and so forth—nevertheless, there is no inconsistency because the word with fewer syllables (*alpāctara*) [is listed first] or because the sequence was not intended to be significant. It is called *yug* because it is joined (*yujyate*).

In this regard, some maintain that since the form *yujyate* cannot belong to the root *yujir* (meaning "to join") belonging to the *raudhādika* class when used in the passive (*karmaṇi*), and although such a form could belong to the root *yuj* (meaning "to meditate") in the passive, that meaning would not be relevant to the present context, one must state that this very form belongs to the passive of *yujir* (meaning "to join") itself.

And in that context, since the suffix *kvip* is prescribed by the rule *ṛtvigdadhṛk* etc., or the suffix *kin* by the rule *satsūdviṣā* etc., or the suffix *kip* by the rule *kiṣ ca*, they cannot apply to the object (*karman*); therefore, *kvin* applies only to the agent (*kartṛ*), as in the case of *pācaka* (one who cooks) from *pacyate anena* (that by which one is cooked). This forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *saha*, which signifies "similar" (*sadṛśa*). Indeed, the word *saha* is a synonym for *sadṛśa*, as in the example *sasakhī* (accompanied by a friend), meaning "one who is similar to a friend. This *bahuvrīhi* has an analysis (*vigraha*) that does not contain its own constituent members (*asvapada-vigraha*).

The meaning is that its collection of qualities (*guṇajāta*) is identical. And in that regard, by the rule "of the subordinate member" (*upasarjanasya*), there is the substitution of *sa* for *saha*. Regarding the phrase "because of the abandonment of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of fire-ness": the meaning is that if fire-ness were abandoned even while [the fire] is not separate [from it], it would follow that the deity Fire itself does not exist. [Objection: But when two contradictory sequences are perceived through two sentences, how can there be no contradiction? To address this unease, he says: "Furthermore, these belong to the fire... The answer has already been given; the meaning is that it was stated that "the limiting adjunct consists of the body, the internal organ, and so forth."

Regarding the phrase "because that which is to be attained possesses qualities": one should not argue that the sūtra, "The option [of different meditations] exists because the fruit is not distinct," might have as its scope only those meditations other than the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā)—such that, since the object to be attained by all meditations is of a single nature, it would follow that it must possess qualities (saguṇatva) everywhere. The point is that there is no evidence for such a restriction. Furthermore, the discussion regarding the option between different meditations should be consulted in that very same context.

The meaning is that one should understand that even the option (*vikalpa*) is effectively stated in that passage, because by stating that what is to be attained is of a single nature—namely, that it must be endowed with qualities—it is revealed that the fruit is not differentiated. Regarding the commentary's statement, "Even though [he is] possessed of a mind," etc., the meaning is that it has been explained: "Even though he does not mentally pursue the deity as being devoid of qualities or as possessing qualities, nevertheless he worships the deity as indeed possessing qualities; in that case too, the deity is attained as one endowed with qualities."

And this is the meaning of it: one whose mind is fixed on the Truth (*saccita*) does not mentally pursue a host of qualities that are devoid of the Deity. Even if, like one established in the *dahara-vidyā*, he does not remember the Deity as distinct from [the qualities] such as "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*), nevertheless he resorts to the Deity as possessing those very internal qualities. In that case as well, the Deity is attained precisely as being endowed with qualities (*saguṇā*).

Because the multitude of auspicious qualities is intrinsically connected to the very nature of the deity, even when a deity is meditated upon by someone through attributes unique to the Supreme Deity—such as being the cause of the entire universe—the deity is nevertheless meditated upon as qualified by all auspicious qualities that are inherent to its own essential nature. Therefore, the meaning is that in the *Sadvidyā* and the *Daharavidyā*, Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa*) alone is the object to be attained; thus, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between these two forms of knowledge. Regarding the phrase "this is that cow," he says [in response] to one who is in disagreement: "this is rice," etc., which is an illustrative example (*upalakṣaṇa*).

"Even though it is primary, it lacks internal consistency (*asvārasya*). This means that while it is primary with respect to the aspect of the universal (*jāti*), it is non-primary with respect to the aspect of the individual (*vyakti*). The meaning is that it is not entirely non-primary. "The lack of internal consistency arises from the abandonment of the aspect of the individual" means that whereas there is a high degree of similarity (*sausādṛśya*) between one universal and [another] universal, there is no such high degree of similarity between one individual and another individual, because a distinct form (*bhedakākāra*) is perceived [between them]. He provides the reason for explaining the term "primary" as "not being entirely non-primary" by stating: "For it is not the case for the liberated... and so forth.
The meaning is that this was stated previously: "That which possesses unsurpassed excellence both in its essential nature and in its qualities is its primary object.

In the verse, he shows the word relevant to the present context with the phrase "tathaiva" (in the same way) in this verse. This is for the purpose of making known that they belong to a single section [of the work]. [As it is said:
"O King, knowledge is the means of attainment regarding the supreme Brahman, which is the goal to be attained."
In the same way, the Self, in which all mental formations have been completely exhausted, is that which is to be attained.
O twice-born one, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has knowledge as its instrument;
having accomplished the task of liberation, it indeed ceases once its purpose is fulfilled.
Having attained the state of being that very essence, he thus becomes non-different from the Supreme Self;
and any difference that exists for him would be produced by ignorance.
"When the ignorance that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction,
who will create the unreal distinction of the Self from Brahman?"

Such indeed is the sequence of the verse. Regarding the phrase *tadbhāva* in the verse, it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) with an object of comparison. [The analysis is: that whose nature (*bhāva*) is like its [the original's] nature is "of that nature" (*tadbhāva*), meaning it possesses a similar intrinsic character (*svabhāva*). The intention is that in the explanation as *tadbhāvabhāva*, the second word *bhāva* serves a more significant purpose. Since the word *tadbhāva* found in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) would be a determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*) and thus inconsistent with the verse, he says: "For when the compound is intended to be explained... (*samāse vyācikhyāsite sati hi...*) to show that it is not improper [to treat it as such].

In order to avoid the discrepancy between the verse (*śloka*) and the commentary (*bhāṣya*), he says: "Or rather, the word *tadbhāva* occurring in the *bhāṣya* [is to be understood as follows]. Now, one might object: if the word *tadbhāva* in the *bhāṣya* were a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then the *bhāṣya* statement, "The state of that is the state of the Brāhmaṇa," would be incorrect. Anticipating this doubt, he explains it by supplying several words: regarding the term *tadbhāva*, it means "that which is perceived as being related to the Brāhmaṇa denoted by the word *tat*. The second occurrence of the word *bhāva* signifies "existence" (*sattā*).

Although in this view there is a redundancy of the second word "existence" (bhāva) as in the opponent's position, the intended meaning here is that the sense favored by the opponent is impossible because non-difference is sublated. Since its success is possible by way of precluding the cognition of another meaning, the mere analysis of its own form would be useless; with this in mind, he says: "Or rather, it becomes devoid of difference. [The phrase] "what was just mentioned is not tenable" refers to this.

The sense is that because difference (*bheda*) is imagined, its being produced is impossible. Regarding the conclusion: "And its difference would be caused by ignorance. The difference between [the states of] a god and so forth, which is superimposed upon the Self, would for that liberated one be caused by ignorance; the meaning is that it would be known as being caused by karma. Alternatively, there is an elision of the vowel *a* in the word "abhavet" (it would not be), as in the expression "apacasi tvaṃ jālma" ("you cook poorly, you fool"), following the rule "the *n* of the negative particle is dropped before a verbal suffix in a reproachful sense. This is how it should be understood.

The analysis is: "A distinction of a single nature has arisen pre-eminently. This is because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of its being natural, which would lead to the possibility of it being subject to abandonment (*heyatva*). Regarding the view that the word "of Brahman" (*brāhmaṇaḥ*) ends in the genitive case, since the distinctions such as gods and so forth, as well as the defects rooted in them—namely karma and ignorance (*avidyā*)—must be admitted as residing in Brahman itself, [one must ask]: if ignorance, which is the veil over Brahman, were to be removed by knowledge, then who would be the master capable of removing that [ignorance], given that [the text says] "The supreme Brahman is of the nature of knowledge; that which is to be removed is false in nature.
If ignorance were to conceal [Brahman], who is the lord to remove it? (quoted from *Vedāntasiddhāntamuktāvalī*).

The meaning is that, according to this logic, since there is no other cause for its cessation, it follows that [the self] must be innate (*svābhāvika*). The sense of the verse is that it perishes when the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are removed. The intention behind the phrase "who will do it? is that "who will sustain it? Regarding the word "non-existent" (*asanta*), since its use here as a synonym for "impermanent" is weak, he says "due to the absence of limiting adjuncts. In this interpretation, it should also be noted that the root *kṛ* (to do) in the phrase "he will do" has its natural force in the sense of "producing."

[The opponent argues: "It is fruitless because there is nothing to be excluded. [The author replies: "But this is not presented as something that performs exclusion; rather, it is stated as the cause for the non-arising of further difference once the ignorance that constitutes the conceptualizer has perished, such that the existence in the form of being conceptually constructed no longer persists. [The author answers: No, because the very same fault mentioned previously remains the intended point.

The phrase "situated in the heart-region" (hṛddeśastha) means "within oneself. The intention is that it is necessary for [the Lord] to enter into the interior of that [heart] in order to cause its rotation, based on such scriptural authorities as, "He has entered within as the ruler of those who know, the Self of all," and "He who rules from within. However, some maintain that since the word "all beings" (sarvabhūta) itself extends up to sentient beings, the word "heart-region" is intended to refer specifically to the internal space of individual living beings (jīvas).

Nor is it incorrect for the *Bhāṣya*—which states, "nor [the identity] of consciousness, matter, and God"—to intend the negation of the unity favored by the proponents of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādins*), because those [proponents] do not themselves accept the identity of matter and God. With this in mind, [the author] explains [the passage] as intending the negation of the unity favored by Bhāskara and others, using the words "of the world and Brahman. Then, fearing that it would be improper to negate the views of other schools at the conclusion of the refutation of the *mṛṣāvādin* position, he introduces the following section as being intended to refute that very [other] view, saying: "Or rather, [it refutes] the *mṛṣāvādin* alone. (Thus ends the Purāṇic methodology. Now, the sevenfold inconsistency;
first, the inconsistency regarding the locus.)

"How can delusion arise?"—this might be the doubt that [delusion] could arise even in the indeterminate (nirviśeṣa) [Brahman], as expressed by the word "parikalpita" (imagined). Therefore, the sense is that the term "defect" (doṣa) is used [to address this]. "For they are veiled by untruth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2); the meaning is that they have been led away, brought to a state of inversion.

"Just as those who do not know the location might pass over a hidden treasure of gold again and again without finding it, even so all these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman (brahmaloka) and do not find it, for they are held back by untruth"—thus says the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. In the Commentary, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), such scriptural passages as "Non-being was not" (*nāsad āsīt*) are intended. In the Commentary, [the phrase] "due to the impossibility of the identity of the individual soul" (*jīvaikyānupapattyā*) [is used].

The meaning is this: since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*) is impossible given that they are superimposed with contradictory attributes, it must be admitted that those attributes are merely imagined (*kalpita*); therefore, one must accept the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*) which effects such imagination. Furthermore, even if the Self were real, we observe that it serves as the locus for both error and its sublation; thus, the distinctness of the Self from the real is not established by means of error and sublation. Moreover, the logical reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddhi*), because error and sublation do not reside in that [Self]. To address this, he says: "being the object of error and being the object of sublation."

In the passage from the *Bhāṣya* stating "because of the impossibility of error and sublation," the words "of the silver in mother-of-pearl" (*śuktirūpyasya*) must be supplied as the ellipsis. This is because later, in the *Bhāṣya* explaining that point, it introduces the argument: "It should not be accepted as such even on the grounds of perception, error, and sublation," and then shows: "because of the perception of silver and so forth in mother-of-pearl and the like. Furthermore, this is because others also present [this example] regarding the silver in mother-of-pearl due to the impossibility of [their own theories of] manifestation and sublation.

Nor should it be argued that it is inconsistent to first assert that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world and is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, and then to establish the perception, error, and sublation (*bādha*) regarding the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell as being caused by that [ignorance]. This is because such a statement is justified by the intention that the material cause and its effect are non-different (*abheda*).

Since those who define the material cause as "that which produces an effect non-different from itself"—thereby stating the definition of the material cause for both illusory transformation (*vivarta*) and real modification (*pariṇāma*)—accept the non-difference between the material cause and its effect, the establishment of the perception and sublation regarding the silver in the shell results in the establishment of them within the material cause itself.

One might object: since it is stated in the *Bhāmatī* under the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, "For we do not assert non-difference, but rather we negate difference," it must be said that there is no non-difference at all between the material cause and its effect; however, this is not so, because that statement is intended merely to reject a non-difference that possesses the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as Brahman.

Alternatively, since the falsity of the silver in the mother-of-pearl shell is established through the impossibility of its being contradicted by experience, one must seek an illusory material cause for that which is illusory; thus, with the intention of showing that ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise established as being distinct from both the real and the unreal, such a statement is justified. However, some maintain: "Because the cognition of ignorance in the form 'I am ignorant' is seen to be sublated by the scriptural text 'Not here, not there' (*neha nānā*), and precisely because of this, it is an error, the objects of these cognitions, delusions, and sublations are exclusively ignorance itself, and not the silver in the mother-of-pearl shell."

They maintain that the subsequent demonstration of falsity (*mithyātva*) regarding shell-silver and the like—by means of cognition, error, and sublation—is indeed a separate argument and is not a mere elaboration of this [present] one. Furthermore, they say that even the statement from the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, "Therein, he refutes at length the reason stated by the opponent regarding indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*)," must be interpreted in some way as a commentary on what was mentioned there [briefly].

The phrase "because of the impossibility of manifestation and sublation" (*khyātibādhayoścāyogāt*) clarifies this meaning by stating "due to the impossibility of manifestation, error, and sublation otherwise" (*pratītibhrāntibādhānyathānupapattyā*). One should discern that manifestation establishes [the object] as distinct from the non-existent (*asat*), error establishes it as distinct from the existent (*sat*), and sublation is common to both. Nor is it improper to present error as a reason against the proponent of non-existence (*asadvādin*), for in his view, the status of being an "error" is not even admitted.

It should not be argued that, for the purpose of sublation (*bādha*) and the establishment of erroneousness (*bhrāntitva*), sublation itself should be the reason; for what is the use of this establishment of being an error? The point is that since the state of being an error is established by the experience, "I was mistaken in thinking [this] to be silver," and since its existence cannot be denied even by a proponent of reality (*sadvādin*), it is possible for it to serve as a logical reason (*hetu*). "Existence is thus" refers to the example provided for the absence of the opponent's position. He refutes the position that Brahman is the substratum (*āśraya*):
if Brahman, being pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), were the substratum, then the previously mentioned defects regarding other substrata would not apply.

The sense is as stated in the verse: "Pure consciousness alone, which partakes of the nature of both substrate (*āśraya*) and object (*viṣaya*), is without distinction (or division); for that which is posterior cannot be the substrate nor the object of that which is already established. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, even if [consciousness] possesses the quality of being knowledge (*jñānatva*), since it would be insentient (*jaḍa*) according to the system of the Naiyāyikas and others, it would be impossible for it to be opposed to its own true nature; therefore, he states that "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*) is what is intended. Some say that self-luminosity is intended because it lacks the nature of knowledge characterized by being a subject (*viṣayitva*).

Now, is the common characteristic of the nature of Brahman and the cognition having that as its object—namely, "self-luminosity"—the state of being a manifestation non-different from its own nature, or is it the state of being a manifestation whose object is its own nature? It cannot be the first, because that [non-difference] is absent in the case of valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*).

The second [alternative] is not tenable; for if there is no difference [between the cognition and its object], the relation of subject and object (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) cannot exist, and thus it would fail to pervade its own nature. Anticipating this objection, he intends to show that what is intended here is "having that as its object" (*tadviṣayakatva*), defined as being conducive to the conventional usage regarding that object. Thus he says: "the meaning is 'being a cognition whose object is its own nature'"; and "the meaning is 'due to the absence of a disparity between the object'. Because there is no disparity between the objects, there is no lack of distinction.

The meaning is "because of going," which is the intended sense. However, it should be understood that the meaning of "due to the non-apprehension of a distinction" is not the absence of a difference in the object; for if that were the case, the objection, "How can there be a non-apprehension of a distinction? would not arise. "This is one Devadatta": the meaning of "one" is non-difference (*abheda*), but this is for the sake of clarity.

Just as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—such as "This is that Devadatta"—the object of the cognition "This is Devadatta" is the non-difference of Devadatta from the one present before us, no less than in the case of identification (*abhijñā*) such as "This is Devadatta. For there is no twofold nature in non-difference by which a disparity in their objects could arise. Nevertheless, it should be understood that it is recognition alone, and not identification, that serves to remove the delusion of difference.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that the relation of a single object to two points in time is the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) but not of the two acts of direct perception (*abhijñā*); for the identity [of the object] and its relation to the two times are established by the two acts of direct perception themselves. The point is that, since [recognition] would not have as its object something unknown by the two acts of direct perception, it could not serve to sublate the delusion of difference, which is not sublated by the two acts of direct perception. "Delusion of duality" means the delusion of difference.

The correct reading is: "If [qualities] such as truthfulness (*satyatva*) and consciousness (*jñānatva*) exist, the word 'intrinsic nature' (*svabhāva*) is used to show that they are not distinct from the essential form (*svarūpa*). Here, in the phrase "if there exists the intrinsic nature of truthfulness and consciousness," the word *svabhāva* refers to a property (*dharma*). The meaning is that if properties such as truthfulness and consciousness exist, the word *svabhāva* is employed to demonstrate that they are non-different from the essential form. Identity (*aikya*), moreover, consists in the relation with two times and two places.

Nor should it be argued that this [recognition] is also established by the two supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), as has already been stated; for even when the two supernormal powers exist, there is no experience such as "I have known the connection with two times. Moreover, since such an experience is observed when recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) occurs, experience itself is the witness here. The point is that if one were to deny experience, it would follow that [the world] must be disregarded. The term "error of duality" (*dvitvabhrama*) is used everywhere to refer to the error of difference (*bhedabhrama*).

One might object: "Is it not the case that being a valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) is not the cause of removal, but rather the opposition to error (*bhramavirodhitva*)? And since that [opposition to error] is possible even in the case of the nature of Brahman (*brahmasvarūpa*), [the ignorance] should be removed. To dispel this doubt, he says: "Because it is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhānatvāt*), like the conch-shell and so forth. Alternatively, he states another reason for its not being a remover: "Because it is the substrate."

If it is accepted that the status of being an underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is opposed to error only by depending on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because such is observed in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like, then—by way of a counter-argument—he refutes this by stating: "the status of being an underlying substrate would be an object of another cognition. [The phrase] "the cessation of the status of being an underlying substrate" means that the cessation of the status of being an underlying substrate would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*).

If it is argued that even in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like, the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is non-opposed to error, then, for the same reason, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it must be cognizable by another cognition in order to serve as the substrate of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). And if, in that case, being cognizable by another cognition were due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), then non-opposition to error would likewise be due to insentience; thus, Brahman would not be non-opposed to error—this is the meaning of the section. Therefore, the first position has been refuted.

If the cognition of the true nature [of the Self] were not the remover of ignorance, then ignorance would necessarily follow even in the case of pleasure and other objects known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). Furthermore, since the *Vivaraṇa* states, "The term 'knowledge' is used metaphorically with respect to a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*"), that which contradicts such metaphorical knowledge cannot logically be a non-means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Nor should it be argued that, just as there is no contradiction with the solar light, so too—due to its being a mere mental construction—ignorance does not contradict the cognition of the true nature [of the Self].

Just as there is no internal darkness possessing the same ontological status as sunlight that is opposed to it, so too, since there is no other ignorance possessing the same ontological status as the light of consciousness that is opposed to it, one must state that only *atāttvika* (non-ultimate) ignorance is opposed to knowledge; thus, [the existence of] ignorance [in the ultimate sense] is impossible.

Furthermore, if one were to accept that only the *vṛtti-jñāna* (cognitive modification), which is an attribute of the *aham-artha* (the ego-sense), possesses the capacity for opposition, then one would have to assert that knowledge and ignorance share the same locus (*samānāśrayatva*). Consequently, following the experience "I am ignorant," one would have to accept the position that ignorance resides in the *jīva*, and not the position that it resides in the pure Consciousness denoted by the term *Brahman*; this is how it should be understood.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase "the contradiction of ignorance consisting in the reality of the phenomenal world" (*prapañcasatyatvarūpājñānavirodhitva*) should be understood to mean "the contradiction of ignorance consisting in the reality of the phenomenal world and its appearance," because it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: "The reality of the phenomenal world and its appearance constitute ignorance in the form of projection (*vikṣepa*). For ignorance is indeed that which obstructs knowledge.

Nor should it be asked how ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is to be removed by knowledge (*jñāna*), can be an obstacle to knowledge; for it should be understood that those [Vedāntins] admit that the ignorance to be removed by the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*) is an obstacle to the manifestation of the Self, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*). This was stated in this manner precisely because of the opponent's own admission. For this very reason, Vācaspati said at the beginning of his treatise: "Of Him who is the source [of the world], accompanied by the pair of indeterminable ignorances (*anirvācyāvidyādvitaya*)."

In this context, one form of *hrekā*—beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpā*)—is that discussed in the section concerning the Deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*). Another is demonstrated in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* itself, where, having introduced the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the non-self upon the Self, it states: "The wise consider this very superimposition, characterized in this way, to be ignorance. He provides the reason for explaining it thus [as a positive entity] with the words, "for not by its existence" (*na hi sattayā*). Since existence itself is absent, it is impossible for the nature of ignorance to consist in being accompanied by existence (*sadvitīyatva*); rather, the meaning is that ignorance is simply the cognition of being accompanied by existence.

Regarding the phrase "the cognition whose object is Brahman as qualified by having a second": the meaning is that the cognition of Brahman, which consists in the knowledge of [Brahman] having a second, has ceased. Some introduce the commentary on the words "but its own nature is established by its own experience" (*svarūpaṃ tu svānubhavasiddham*) as follows: If the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) were what is propounded by the scripture, then since that alone would be the subject taught by the scripture, Brahman itself would not be established through the scripture and would consequently lack any means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇikatva*). To this, he says: "But its own nature is established by its own experience. (The impossibility of concealment).

Regarding their concealment (*tirodhi*): although the rule *upasarge dhoḥ kiḥ* does not apply here, it must be justified by the frequent usage of such forms, based on the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Regarding the phrase "of knowledge, which has the Self as its unique cause": this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood to include "immediacy" (*pratyakṣatva*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because its uniqueness is not manifest": [an objection] might be raised that being a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharmitva*) is simply the exclusion of common properties (*sādhāraṇadharmavyāvṛtti*).

And that [exclusion] is non-different from the very nature of perceptibility and so forth, just as the exclusion of whiteness is non-different from the nature of blueness. Therefore, if it is argued that while the nature of perceptibility and so forth is manifest, the claim that the exclusion of common properties—which is non-different from it—is not manifest merely results in the "concealment" (tirodhāna) asserted by the opponent, we say: no; because we observe the delusion of non-difference from common properties regarding perceptibility and so forth, there is no evidence that the exclusion of common properties residing in perceptibility and so forth is of the nature of its own essential form (svarūpa-rūpa).

However, in the case of blackness and so forth, since there is never any delusion of non-difference from whiteness, the exclusion of that [blackness] consists of its very nature (*svarūpa*). It should be understood that even in that case, if there were a delusion of non-difference from whiteness, the exclusion of that [blackness] would be accepted as something distinct from the essential nature. "Residing in our state" means residing in the state of the expansion of the self-luminous, attribute-like knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) as conceived by us; that is to say, it is always self-luminous. The meaning is that concealment (*tirodhāna*) would amount to the very destruction of the essential nature.

[Objection: Let concealment (*tirodhāna*) be simply the absence of manifestation. Nor is there a contradiction between manifestation and non-manifestation, because non-manifestation is merely superimposed and thus not contradictory; furthermore, in cases such as "I do not know the meaning you have stated," the state of being unknown is experienced even with respect to an object that has already been heard. [Reply: This is not so. For when the true nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is manifest, even the conceptualization of non-manifestation cannot arise.

This is because the non-firehood superimposed upon fire does not obstruct the effects of fire, and because the non-luminosity superimposed upon light does not obstruct the effects of light. Furthermore, in cases such as "I do not know the meaning you have stated," there is no proof for a contradiction between manifestation and non-manifestation, since the object is simply the absence of a cognition that consists in the ascertainment of existence. Otherwise, one would face the absurdity of the experience: "The jar manifests and yet does not manifest."

By this, the view that "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*) is simply the fitness for erroneous linguistic usage—expressed as "it does not exist" or "it does not manifest"—is refuted; for even the postulation of obscuration characterized by such erroneous usage is impossible with respect to the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is itself manifest. Furthermore, since the nature of bliss (*ānanda-svarūpa*) is manifest, it is impossible to speak of obscuration regarding that aspect. Nor should it be argued that obscuration exists because the unlimited bliss does not manifest; for since there is no differentiation within bliss, it is impossible to speak of its non-manifestation.

Nor should it be argued that even while bliss (*ānanda*) manifests during the state of *saṃsāra*, its unconditioned aspect (*anavaccheda*) does not manifest; for if the manifestation of the bliss belonging to the time of liberation were established, the unconditioned portion would fail to be a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), which according to that school's view would lead to the undesirable consequence of there being no distinction between *saṃsāra* and liberation. Nor can it be argued that the distinction between *saṃsāra* and liberation is due to the non-manifestation or manifestation of unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*); for in the Advaita system, since there is no sensory pleasure (*vaiṣayikānanda*) distinct from the bliss of Brahman (*brāhmananda*), gradations of excellence or deficiency are impossible.

If it is argued that if Ānanda shines forth, it is that very same Ānanda belonging to the state of liberation, and thus there is no disparity in the experience of bliss between saṃsāra and mokṣa—this is easily stated in the Mṛṣāvāda (Illusionist) doctrine. Nor should it be said: "Just as in your own view, although the bliss of the jīva's essential nature and the bliss experienced in the state of kaivalya are non-different because both are of the nature of the essential self, you nevertheless admit that this bliss was previously veiled and is now experienced as having excellence, since its non-existence was previously a matter of conventional usage; so too might it be here. For in that case, even though the bliss is one and the same, [the difference lies in the removal of the veil].

In that bliss (*ānanda*), there exists a distinction such as intensity (*tīvratva*) or mildness (*mandatva*). Consequently, during the state of *saṃsāra*, the mild favorability within bliss appears through the knowledge that constitutes its essential nature (*svarūpa-rūpa-jñāna*); however, the intense favorability residing therein appears through the attribute-knowledge (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*) in the state of liberation (*kaivalya*). This is our established doctrine (*prakriyā*). We do not, however, accept that even intense favorability is of the nature of the essential self (*svarūpa-rūpa*) and self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), which would lead to a logical flaw. Therefore, the sense is that concealment (*tirodhāna*) is untenable with respect to the essential nature as it is being manifested. (The incongruity regarding the essential nature.)

"Because [the status of] being a knower and so forth [is unreal] from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthatas)" means that if experience were without a substratum, then since the knower would simply not exist, the state of being a knower and so forth would likewise be non-ultimate. Now, one might object: the statement "without an object and without a substratum" is merely a restatement of the opponent's position. An opponent does not provide a qualification out of a desire to give an opening for the refutation of his own view; rather, he provides it precisely because it serves the purpose of his own stated argument.

And in the present context, since it is conducive to the false nature (mithyātva) intended by [the author] himself, it is proper to state that this qualification is indeed purposeful; it is not for the sake of refuting others. Because of this underlying intention (*asvarasa*), he says: "Or rather, because of the difference between the object (*viṣaya*) and the substratum (*āśraya*)," and "the mention of non-existence (*asattva*) and appearance (*pratibhāsa*). It should be understood that "without object and without substratum" is the mention of non-existence, while "experience" (*anubhūti*) is the mention of its appearance. "Distinct from its own nature" means distinct from the nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is Brahman.

"Because two unconditioned consciousnesses (*dṛśi*) are not admitted. This means that, in relation to the nature of consciousness which serves as the unconditioned substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), no additional, defective, and unreal unconditioned consciousness is admitted. "The same applies even in the case of the unconditioned position" means that since the dilemma of whether consciousness is conditioned or unconditioned falls under the category of the unreal, there is no distinction in the necessity of postulating another cause for everything that is unreal.

The phrase "by way of its being non-ultimate" (aparamārthatvena) means that he dispels the misconception that a conceptualized word has conceptualization as its purpose. "Because experience itself is the defect" means because it is the defect that produces ignorance (avidyā). "It is resolved by its beginninglessness through a continuous flow" refers to the intention [of the author], namely, that Vācaspati, in the Sūtra *tadadhīnatvādarthavat*, introduced the analogy of the seed and the sprout. This, moreover, is also an indication of its beginninglessness in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Just as a pot, though situated at a distance from space—which is partless—delimits a portion of it and thereby becomes connected with that portion, so too ignorance, though standing apart from pure consciousness (cinmātra), delimits it and produces the individual soul (jīva) as a partial manifestation, and thus remains connected with it. In this way, ignorance stands apart from pure consciousness, delimits it, produces the individual soul as a partial manifestation, and abides therein; therefore, there is no mutual dependence. As it is said: "Just as a pot or the like exists in space within a region created by itself, so do those skilled in knowledge consider ignorance to have the individual soul as its locus."

It should be understood that Vācaspati, the proponent of ignorance residing in the individual soul (*jīva*), has also accepted the beginninglessness of its essential nature (*svarūpa-anāditva*), because he maintains that when both the soul and ignorance are beginningless, mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) is not a fault, as there is no impediment to their origination or manifestation. [The phrase] "by the defect's capacity to establish itself and others" [is used].

If it is argued that, since there are four ways of resolving [the objection], the opponents' threefold resolution of the infinite regress (*anavasthā*) contradicts what was stated previously, some reply: "Because the proponent of the ignorance of the individual soul (*jīvājñānavādin*) has only mentioned the difficulty of establishing beginninglessness through a continuous stream (*pravāhānāditva*), its self-sustaining nature (*svaparanirvāhakatva*), and its self-explanatory nature (*svarūpānāditva*), but has not mentioned essential beginninglessness (*svarūpānāditva*); and because the proponent of the ignorance of Brahman (*brahmājñānavādin*) likewise has not mentioned beginninglessness through a continuous stream, there are indeed only three ways. [The phrase] "conditioned by being the ultimate reality" (*paramārthatvaprayuktā*) refers to that which exists in the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-vastu*).

"Dependence on proof" means that its proof is contingent upon its being ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*). "Proof contingent upon its not being ultimate reality" means that even a defect (*doṣa*) has entered into the category of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of non-ultimate things. Even though a non-ultimate thing is independent of the causal complex of ultimate things, it certainly remains dependent upon the causal complex of non-ultimate things.

The sense is this: although the swallowing of a vast palace by a small mouth does not depend on a cause for swallowing that is ultimately real (*paramārthika*), it is nevertheless observed to depend on a collection of factors such as magical spells and herbs which serve as the cause for swallowing something that is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*). Regarding the consequence of the identity between the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the superimposed (*adhyasta*): under the view that [the superimposition] establishes itself and others, it follows that the very same thing is both the substrate and the superimposed within that very substrate.

Furthermore, since there is no mutual contradiction between the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and that which is superimposed (*adhyasta*), it could be asserted that everything is merely imagined within its own essential nature; thus, the sense is that no other locus distinct from the superimposed object would need to be required.
(The impossibility of indefinability)

"If it is argued that this is because of a contradiction with pervasion (*vyāptivirodha*)," the meaning is that existence (*sattva*) is pervaded by the absence of non-existence (*asattvābhāva*). "It is observed to have the nature of both being and non-being" means that since it is apprehended as having the nature of both being and non-being through error (*bhrānti*) and sublation (*bādha*), it is appropriate to accept that very [nature]. "In the case of the actual state of things, it must be either existence or non-existence" means that when the actual state of things is investigated, it must be one or the other of existence or non-existence. "If it is argued that it is observed to be distinct from both being and non-being," [the response follows].

The sense is that even if [the object] were of the nature of pure existence (*sanmātra*), there would still be an absence of the form of both [existence and non-existence]. Regarding the phrase "by means of *anyathākhyāti* and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), *akhyāti* and *yathārthakhyāti* are intended. Regarding the phrase "provided that it exists" (*sattve sati*): the meaning is "only provided that it exists. As for the claim that "the sublation of the manifestation (*khyāti*) is established through the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*)," one should not ask: "Even if the non-apprehension of difference serves to establish the manifestation, how can it serve to establish sublation? For this is logically consistent, just as one says, "The famine was caused by the rain."

Alternatively, the phrase "by the non-apprehension of difference" (*bhedāgraha*) is an elliptical expression; the meaning is that both the apprehension of difference (*bhedagraha*) and the non-apprehension of difference give rise to appearance (*khyāti*) and sublation (*bādha*). He establishes this point with the words "of that which exists," etc. They maintain that *khyāti* is the presentation of something already present as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a difference whose non-connection (*asaṃsarga*) was not previously grasped. In that case, the cognition of that object as having a difference already grasped constitutes *bādha*. (This is the failure of the means of valid cognition.)

He establishes that very nature [of the statement] as being an exposition of that [ignorance]: "I am ignorant" (*aham ajñaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "the mention of the nature of ignorance": the meaning is that in the statement "I am ignorant," there is a mention of the nature of ignorance itself, which is devoid of its effect consisting of the veiling of objects (*viṣayāvaraṇa*); whereas in the statement "I and another," there is a mention of ignorance specifically characterized by its effect, which is the veiling of objects. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tattvadīpana*, the commentary on the *Vivaraṇa*: "In the [statement] 'I am ignorant,' the fact that ignorance has a substratum (*sāśrayatva*) is perceived; in [the statement] 'I do not know myself and another,' the fact that it has an object (*saviṣayatva*) is perceived."

The sense is this: since the very cognition "I am ignorant" apprehends the nature of ignorance as being qualified by an additional attribute in the form of its objectivity (*saviṣayatva*), it is of the nature of a clarification (*vivaraṇa*) of that [ignorance]. Regarding the phrase "exclusion of ignorance in the form of an effect": in passages such as, "Listen also to the true nature of avidyā, O son of Kuru: it is the notion of the Self in what is not the Self," even the notion of the Self in what is not the Self is the referent of words such as "avidyā" and "ajñāna"; therefore, the meaning is the exclusion of that [notion].

And he will state that even the notion of a self with respect to what is not the self is denotable by the term "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "the ignorance persisting in deep sleep": the meaning is that it is the ignorance which continues through the state of deep sleep. Since the knowledge that is an effect—consisting of the notion of "I"—does not persist in deep sleep, the purpose [of this specification] is to exclude that.

One might object: "The experience, 'I do not know myself or anything else,' cannot be taken as proof for the persistence of ignorance during deep sleep, because in deep sleep there is no possibility of mentioning either the referent 'I' or any other object. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the waking state... The meaning is that in the waking state, there is an experience of ignorance delimited by objects in the form of the referent 'I' and things other than it, through the witness (*sākṣin*) which is of the nature of determinate perception (*savikalpa-pratyakṣa*); whereas in deep sleep, there is the experience of that very same ignorance as being devoid of objects.

Furthermore, it should not be thought that, according to the view of Tattvaśuddhikāra, there is a total non-apprehension of the ignorance of the cause during the waking state; for it is impossible for ignorance, which is manifested by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), to be unknown. Nor should it be argued that a state of objectless ignorance is impossible, or that the experience of ignorance as being objectless is impossible; for there is no defect in the manifestation of ignorance during deep sleep (suṣupti) as having the mere inner self (pratyagātman) as its object.

Now, one might object: "In the waking state, the witness (*sākṣin*) possesses an objective reference (*viṣayollekhitva*), as in the thought 'I do not know the jar'; what fault is there in its possessing such an objective reference even in deep sleep? For it is not the case that the presence or absence of an objective reference by the witness is what determines waking or non-waking; therefore, it has been stated in the *Vivaraṇa* that 'every object is always an object of the witness-consciousness, either through being known or through being unknown'? To this we reply: True.

In the waking state, one perceives specific objects distinctly, as in "I know the jar," or "I know the cloth"; however, since no such distinct perception of objects is observed in the state of deep sleep, some underlying cause must be postulated in accordance with that fact. This has been stated not only by modern authors such as the author of the *Tattvaśuddhi*, but is likewise established in the traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*). Thus he says: "Only in the waking state... [and] "This is the experience of ignorance: 'I am ignorant'; etc.

The meaning is that this experience of ignorance is expressed as, "I do not know myself or another. Now, one might object: "In the statement 'I do not know,' only ignorance itself is experienced, not its status as a cause. Therefore, how can it be said that perception has ignorance as its cause? Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "By way of being an obscuration in the phrase 'I do not know. The underlying sense is that the ignorance which is the effect does not possess the quality of being an obscuration.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "Perception, first of all, has as its object the ignorance that is the cause [of the world]": the construction is that the immediate manifestation—"I am ignorant; I do not know myself and another"—is perception whose object is the ignorance that is the cause. Consequently, one should understand that there is no tautology between the two terms "perception" and "immediate manifestation. Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "For that [ignorance] is within the scope of the sixth means of knowledge": the meaning is that it is within the scope of the sixth means of knowledge *only*. By the word "only," its being within the scope of perception is negated; the sense is that it is not within the scope of perception. For this very reason, it will be stated later: "The non-existence [is known] through perception..."
It has been stated: "Even if one accepts that [non-existence] is not an object [of perception].

Let this [non-existence] also be the object of a sixth means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding this, they raise an objection: In the *Bhāṣya* on the passage, "But this [non-existence], like 'I am happy,' is immediate (*aparokṣa*)," the word "this" (*ayam*) refers to the cognition (*anubhava*), not to the object; for the direct perceptual experience, as indicated by the particle "iti" in the phrase "like 'I am happy,'" is used as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Indeed, it was not said, "like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. Furthermore, non-existence is unfit for perception, whereas this cognition is of the nature of perception.

Therefore, since it is more appropriate to establish the very point that a subject-object relationship between these two is impossible, it is proper to refer to the cognition itself by saying "this" (*ayam*), and not to refer to the object. Consequently, one might argue that the introduction should simply be: "Let this experience also be produced by a sixth means of valid cognition. This, however, is not the case, because one means of cognition does not invalidate another. [The statement] "prior non-existence is the object of a non-perceptual means of cognition" means that its object is exclusively non-perceptual.

Consequently, there is no room for the objection that this [definition] is untenable because we observe that fire and other such objects, which are the domain of indirect means of knowledge (*parokṣapramāṇa*), can also be directly perceived (*aparokṣatva*). The phrase "by a means of knowledge that apprehends an existent" (*bhāvagrāhakapramāṇena*) means as follows: since perception (*pratyakṣa*)—by virtue of grasping only an object with which it is in contact—can only occur in relation to existents (*bhāva*) through the fivefold types of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, the sense is that even if one were to admit that perception, whose nature is solely to grasp existents, could apprehend non-existence (*abhāva*) by postulating another type of contact characterized by "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇatā*), [the definition remains valid].

Furthermore, in the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the phrase "even if perceptibility is admitted," while the meaning is clearly understood as "even if the apprehensibility of non-existence by a means of valid cognition that apprehends existence is admitted," there is no inconsistency in this introductory statement (*avatārikā*). Moreover, there is no room for the objection that [this would be so] because it is universally established that verbal testimony, inference, and other means which apprehend positive entities also apprehend non-existence.

The meaning is that because there is no apprehender (*grāhaka*), there is no cognition of its absence. That is to say, due to the absence of the knowledge of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), which serve as the causes for apprehension, the cognition of absence cannot arise; it does not mean that there is no cognition of the absence of the apprehender itself, for such an interpretation is seen in the subsequent commentary (*bhāṣya*) where it says, "This is what is meant."

Nor should it be argued that if the word "grāhaka" (apprehender) refers to a cognition whose locus is the counter-positive that produces the apprehension, then no such immediate objection could arise because the cognition whose object is an absence would itself be an apprehender; for such an objection is possible from one who is ignorant of the intended meaning. Some, however, [interpret the reason] as "because of the absence of an apprehender," meaning because there is no cognition that apprehends the absence.

"It is not the cognition of its absence" means that there is no mental representation (*ullekha*) of its absence. They argue that this is because the phrase "this is what is meant" can be justified even as a mere partial justification. Regarding the statement "the prior absence of cognition is the object of apprehension": here, the word "prior" (*prāk*) is not intended to be significant; the meaning is simply that "the absence of cognition is the object of apprehension."

Otherwise, since antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) cannot have all cognitions as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it must be stated that it has only specific individuals as its counter-correlates; in that case, there is no contradiction [with the cognition of the self]. It should be understood that "the self exists as the substratum (*dharmin*) of non-existence" means that the cognition of that [non-existence] exists because the self is its substratum; however, one should not mistakenly think that it is a cognition [of the self] in the form of being a substratum, for cognition in that specific form is not the cause of that [cognition of non-existence].

The meaning of the Bhāṣya—namely, whether there is a cognition [of the object] as a subject (*dharmin*) or as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—is precisely this. Regarding the phrase "in this view": it means the acceptance of the position that [the object] is not within the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Consequently, the doubt that "how can there be a contradiction with immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) merely because it is inferable (*anumeya*), given that both [immediacy and mediacy] are observed in the case of fire and the like" should be understood as refuted.

The meaning is as follows: the ignorance that veils the jar is not contradicted by the knowledge of the jar. That is to say, when there is knowledge of the jar, the ignorance veiling the jar is indeed not contradicted; nor is it contradicted by the knowledge of the object (the jar) or the knowledge of the substrate (the self), because they do not possess the nature of existence and non-existence respectively; rather, the meaning is that both are of the nature of positive entities (*bhāva*).

This very meaning is established by the natural sense of the *Bhāṣya* and in accordance with the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa*, which states in its preceding discussion: "In the theory that ignorance is perceived as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa-ajñāna*), it cannot be maintained that there is no possibility of another positive entity—even when the knowledge of the locus and the counter-positive exists—just as there is none for the absence of knowledge. For if one were to take the literal meaning [of the opponent's objection], it would follow that the very cognition whose object is the jar would itself become the object of the cognition "I do not know the jar," which would lead to the undesirable consequence of the non-establishment of knowledge.

The meaning is that although both are positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*), their opposition is established—just like that between light and darkness—because [ignorance] is to be removed by the knowledge of the true nature of things (*vastuyāthātmyajñāna*).

In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that "the consciousness of the witness (*sākṣicaitanya*) does not have the true nature of the object as its domain. This means that the consciousness of the witness is not a valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) whose object is the true nature of the thing, because only valid cognition has the power to remove ignorance (*ajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*), although it is possible for it to refer to the proximate object—namely, ignorance—it would be improper for it to indicate the non-acceptance of the remote true nature of the thing as its domain. For this reason, [the author] states, "or in the absence of being the object of ignorance. [He explains: "For it is not by the cognition of silver... The meaning is that it is impossible for that which establishes [an appearance] to simultaneously sublate it.

"But is it not stated in the Commentary that this ignorance is indeed positive in nature (*bhāvarūpa*)? On this point, they raise an objection: "How can the object that distinguishes ignorance be manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), given that the establishment of an object depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? It is replied: Every entity is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness, whether in its state of being known (*jñātatā*) or in its state of being unknown (*ajñātatā*).

In this regard, it must be stated that this is a restatement of the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa* text: "Therein, an object [as a particular] requires the mediation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of being known; however, another [object, namely the Self], is always manifest as the negator of ignorance, either in its general form or its particular form. And the meaning of that [text] is as follows: "How [is it that one says], 'I do not know myself or another'?"

If one were to say, "I do not know the object you have mentioned, nor its numerical measure, nor the meaning of the scripture," would this ignorance delimited by an object be manifest to the Witness (sākṣin)? No, because it is impossible for the Witness to manifest the object that delimits the ignorance; for the Witness lacks independence regarding external objects, just as the mind lacks it in the Nyāya system. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rendering other means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas) useless. Therefore, the existence of the jar and so forth—which delimit the ignorance—must be admitted to be established solely through the means of valid knowledge.

Furthermore, valid cognition is the opposite of ignorance; it does not, like a witness, establish ignorance such that it would fail to contradict it. Consequently, the experience of ignorance is impossible.

This is the intended sense of the doubt: even though an atom lacks the quality of being graspable by the mind (*manas*) in itself, just as an atom is cognized by the mind through the state of being known—as in the cognition "the atom is known"—so too, even an object that is inherently incapable of being grasped by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) alone when unconditioned by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) bearing its specific form, is nevertheless always manifested by that witness in the form of either "known" or "unknown. This occurs because the atom is made known by the witness through the state of being known, even when it is not conditioned by a modification corresponding to its particular form.

However, there is this distinction: when an object appears as "known," there is a requirement for the intervention of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because being known is produced by a means of valid cognition. But since non-cognition (*ajñātatā*) is self-established, an appearance as non-cognized does not require the intervention of a means of valid cognition. Consequently, every object indeed appears as non-cognized at the stage when a means of valid cognition has not yet operated; thus, there is no dependence on a means of valid cognition for the appearance of the object, which would otherwise result in a contradiction with non-cognition.

The intended meaning of the refutation is that the cognition of objects such as a jar, which is of the nature of a witness (*sākṣirūpa*), is not opposed to ignorance, because—as was stated previously—it lacks the capacity to sublate it, since it merely serves as its instrument of proof. Indeed, this very passage has been explained in exactly this way by the author of the *Tattvadīpana*. Why, then, is it here restated in a different manner, setting aside that [explanation]?

In this regard, the following is the resolution: It is true that the *Vivaraṇa* author explained the explanatory passage (*vivaraṇavākya*) in that manner. Nevertheless, since the *Vivaraṇa* author does not accept that an insentient object (*jaḍa*) can be the objective domain of ignorance (*ajñāna*), one must state that in his view ignorance is delimited solely by the inner self (*pratyagartha*), and not by objects such as jars. Therefore, intending that the doubt and its resolution must both concern the inner self alone, and intending that the sections on the doubt and its resolution should be construed accordingly by the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya*, it should be understood that he has restated [the matter] in that way.
