The meaning of the Bhāṣya is also exactly thus: that the duality of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender produced by that [duality] is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). However, some say: "Because of the effort there to establish the ultimate reality of the duality of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and the duality of the apprehension, and because of the effort to support the duality of the forms of the apprehended by means of the duality of the apprehension, it is simply the non-apprehension of the non-connection between the duality residing in the apprehension and the moon, and not the duality residing in space. That is not correct.

Because it would entail the consequence of entering into the Prābhākara school’s doctrine, and because it would result in a contradiction with the subsequent commentary (*uttara-ṭīkā*) which demonstrates the differences from the Prābhākara view, that [position] is to be disregarded. Regarding the phrase "the function of the eye has become twofold": one might object, "In the verse, only duality—in the form of 'the moon and [its] duality'—is perceived. On what basis is it determined that this is the duality residing in the cognition (*vitti*)? For it is impossible for the function of the eye to apprehend the duality of cognition, as it lacks the capacity to grasp cognition. To this we reply: No.

"But since the two functions are being expanded," because the duality residing in the functions is the subject under discussion and because it is self-luminous, it is appropriate to understand that very duality [as the referent].
(The meaning of the scriptural passage intended to refer to ignorance:)

[This refers to] that which is the absence of reality (*ṛtābhāva*) and that which is opposed to reality. Nor should it be argued: "Since a pot is the locus of the absence of a pot, what fault is there in reality being the locus of the absence of reality? For just as it is impossible for existence and non-existence to have a common locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is likewise impossible for them to stand in the relation of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). Nor should it be argued: "In this way, if the absence of the absence of a pot exists in a pot, it would follow that the pot itself exists. This is because, just as both the pot and its absence are absent in the absence of a pot, it is logically consistent that both the pot and its absence are absent in the pot.

For this very reason, others maintain that since Brahman—which is of the nature of the absence of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*)—is unfit to be the locus of the phenomenal world, the world’s falsity consists in its having as its locus something unfit to be its own locus, namely, Brahman. For this same reason, the objection that "the property of being color (*rūpatva*), which is opposed to color, must reside in color" is also refuted; for here, what is intended by "opposition" is the relation between the destroyed and the destroyer. And in their view, the meaning is that Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, is the destroyer of ignorance (*ajñāna*). He raises an objection: "For even merit... and so on.

It should be considered as a counter-objection (*pratibandī*): if, on the strength of the scriptural text, "Neither non-existence existed nor did existence exist," the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) denoted by the word *tamas* is [concluded to be] indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), then, by the force of the authority of the text, "The beginningless Brahman, which is superior to Me, is said to be neither being nor non-being," it would follow that Brahman as well is distinct from both being and non-being. This is the meaning. In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), it is stated: "That which is called *tamas* is the collective aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) of non-consciousness (*acit*)."

If it is asked, "How can there be a dissolution of the individual manifestations of consciousness and matter—designated by the terms 'existent' and 'non-existent'—into the aggregate of matter? we reply: no. For, by virtue of their fitness, there is no fault in the term "satya" (real) signifying the dissolution of the subtle forms of consciousness and matter into the *hari-raja* (the causal matter). As stated in the Commentary: "It is true that [it is] by the word *tamas*."

[Objection: But surely, since the proponent has stated that what is denoted by the word "tamas" is the aggregate of non-consciousness (acitsamaṣṭi), how can it be restated [here] with the words "It is true," etc., as being the subtle state of *prakṛti*, which is itself the aggregate of non-consciousness? For in the preceding passage, only *tamas* was said to be the aggregate of non-consciousness; neither was it stated that *prakṛti* is the aggregate of non-consciousness, nor that *tamas* is its subtle state. [Reply: No, because there is no contradiction between the two, and thus such a restatement is appropriate. This is intended as a sequential presentation of the material cause (*upādāna*).

The meaning is that this refers to the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), who, at the stage of presenting the prima facie position, employs the statement "But [one should know] Māyā as Prakṛti" immediately after the sentence "Darkness existed. The point is that the sentence "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti" is employed right after that very passage in order to dispel the doubt that the word "darkness" (tamas) might refer to the primordial matter (prakṛti) favored by the Sāṃkhya school.

Objection: Is it not the case that, by restating the *māyā* established in the passage, "The Illusionist creates this universe, and another is bound within it by *māyā*," the subsequent sentence, "But one should know *māyā* as *prakṛti*," enjoins *prakṛti*—denoted by the word *prakṛti*—as the material cause (*upādānatva*)? For in passages such as "And *prakṛti* [is Brahman], because of the non-contradiction of the initial proposition and the illustrative examples," the word *prakṛti* is well-known to signify the material cause; and because other commentators have also explained it in that way.

If it is argued that since the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the material cause (*upādāna*) is established from that very [text], it is more easily stated by the opponent that the status of being the *prakṛti* (material cause) is enjoined by way of restating *māyā*, we say: no. This is because, although the word *prakṛti* can mean "material cause," its conventional usage is so prevalent as to primarily bring to mind the *prakṛti* consisting of the aggregate of non-intelligent matter (*acit-samaṣṭi*). Therefore, even in his own system, it is more appropriate to enjoin the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*)—in the form of being *māyā*—of that very [aggregate]. Thus, the phrase "not by the *māyāmātra* Sūtra" is used.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction between this commentary—which establishes [the Lord's] capacity to create a manifold variety of objects—and the commentary on the sūtra beginning with *māyāmātraṃ tu kārtsnyena*, which explains that the word *māyā* signifies "wonder. The phrase "it is understood from the plural number" implies that the *avidyā* favored by you is singular. The phrase "the appearance, however, has as its object duality and so forth" means that it has as its object the non-existent duality of the moon and so forth.
(This concludes the meaning of the ancient text concerning *avidyā*.)

Intending to show that the prefix *vi-* can have two possible meanings—namely, "diversity" (*vaividhya*) and "contrariety" (*vaiparītya*)—he states: "The etymological derivation [of *vijñāna*] is in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), as in 'that by which one knows diversely,' or 'that by which one knows contrarily. The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to the rule *karaṇādhikaraṇayoś ca*. He provides the authoritative proof for the statement "ignorance is non-cognition" (*vijñānam avidyā*) with the passage beginning "But when it is pure," etc. For its "negation" (*vyatireka*) will be explained later. If the word *vijñāna* were intended to mean knowledge of the nature of Brahman—as in the verse "Cognition is one, its own, and without division"—then [the following objection would apply]: regarding the negation of that [Brahman], there would be a contradiction of the negation of the world-appearance (*prapañca*).

The intended meaning is that [the other interpretation] would result in the inconsistency of the verse beginning with "yadā tu śuddham. One might object: "Since it is possible to state that the meanings [of the words] are manifested or imagined within consciousness (*vijñāna*), and since Śrīdhara has explained it in that way, how can it be determined that the word *vijñāna* here signifies ignorance (*avidyā*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "‘...within consciousness’ (*vijñāne vijṛmbhitānīti*). The reason is "due to lack of naturalness" (*asvārasyāt*). The sense is that the compound ending in the locative case is forced, because one must resort to a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) to justify the locative construction.

The reading is *napuṃsakapadasya*. If the reading were *napuṃsakāntapadasya*, it would mean "of a word ending in a neuter [case-]suffix," which serves to indicate its neuter gender. [The phrase] "because of the impossibility of being a qualifier for the masculine noun *bhedaśabda*" [is used].

Since the root *jṛbh* in the sense of "bending the limbs" is intransitive, if one were to rely on the word *vijṛmbhita* as ending in the suffix *kta* with the agent (*kartṛ*) according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka*, or as ending in *kta* with the object (*karman*) from the causative (*ṇyanta*), there would be the undesirable consequence of its being dependent on the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*). Furthermore, since the neuter gender is appropriate only for the alternative where the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*, the word *vijṛmbhita* must indeed end in a suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*).

Nor should it be asked how differences (*bheda*) can have the nature of the meaning of the verbal root *vijṛmbh* (to expand); for such usage is justified through metaphorical application (*upacāra*). Consequently, once it is established that [the term] ends in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), since the expectation for an agent of the state (*bhāva*) consisting of expansion is more intense than the expectation for a locus, the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) alone is appropriate—this is the sense. "There is no intention regarding the plural number" means that it merely restates the plurality already established by perception and other means of knowledge; this is the sense. "Characterized by the insentient" (*jaḍopalakṣita*).

The meaning is: in the single reality that is the Self (*ātman*), which is perceived as distinct from the body, internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and so forth; that is to say, distinctions belonging to the insentient (*jaḍa*) do not exist. This means that distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the internal organs do not exist. Intending a *karmadhāraya* compound for the words "reality" (*vastu*) and "distinction" (*bheda*), he says: "Alternatively, one instance of the word 'reality' refers to form (*ākāra*). The intention is that the first occurrence of the word "reality" refers to the insentient.

In this view, since it must be stated what is perceived as true by those whose self-certainty is unimpeded, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of having to supply (*adhyāhāra*) the phrase "as true" (*satyatvena*). Furthermore, because the second half-verse would then lack syntactic unity with the first half-verse, he explains [the verse] by supplying only the word *api* (even/also), saying: "Or rather, not merely... [and] "that which occurs subsequently. By this, the intention is that the *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "that ignorance for which the perception of difference is the cause"—is intended in the commentary (*bhāṣya*).

In this view, ignorance regarding the task consists of the sense of "mine," attachment, aversion, and so forth; the meaning is that even for that, prior karma alone is the cause. Nor should it be argued that since the perception of difference is the cause of the ignorance triggered by the perception of difference, how can karma be the cause? For the intended meaning is that karma alone is the root cause. In this view, the phrase "assumed in many ways by minds divided by the differences of their own karma" means: by those whose minds are divided by the differences of their own karma—that is, by those who perceive the differences among members of their own kind.

The word *citta* refers here to *buddhi*. [The opponent argues that] it is accepted in many ways as being endowed with the cognition of effects. Regarding this position, because the phrase "accepted in many ways" (*bahudhābhyupetam*) is excessively strained, he states another alternative: "or, [it is so called] due to the difference of bodies such as those of gods, etc. This is a restatement of the absence of difference between like and unlike things (*sajātīya-vijātīya-bheda-viraha*). With the half-verse beginning "consciousness is one," there is a restatement of the absence of difference between like and unlike things.

The meaning is that this is a restatement of the negation [of duality], because the difference consisting of a distinct self of the same class (*sajātīyātmabheda*) is negated by the half-verse beginning with "Consciousness is one," and the difference consisting of a non-self of a different class (*anātmabhūtavijātīyabheda*) is negated by the half-verse beginning with "Therefore, consciousness is not [the Self]. Thus, the absence of internal difference (*svagatabhedarāhitya*) is being stated; the meaning is that what was understood from the first half-verse is being restated in the same manner. Regarding the second position, he states its conformity with the *Bhāṣya*: "For with this intention... [He says] "In the *Daśaślokī*": in the twelfth chapter of the second part of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, [it says]:
"Thus is this configuration of the earth and likewise of the luminaries..."
The [extent] of the continents, the oceans, and the mountains has been proclaimed.
And those who indeed dwell within the rain-clouds and the rivers.
"Having introduced the subject with the words, 'Their essential nature has been declared; hear now their summary once more':
'O Brahmin, from that body of Viṣṇu [which was] water, the earth [arose]...'"
It has arisen in the form of a lotus, joined with mountains, oceans, and so forth.
The luminaries are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu, the colors are Viṣṇu, the mountains and the quarters are Viṣṇu;
the rivers and the oceans—all that exists and all that does not exist is He alone, O best of brahmins.
Since the Blessed One is of the nature of consciousness and possesses an infinite form rather than being a material entity,
know that the distinctions such as mountains, oceans, and so forth are merely the manifestations of consciousness.
But when knowledge is pure, possessing its own innate form, free from defects, and all karma has been exhausted,
then indeed the fruits of the tree of conceptualization no longer arise as distinctions between objects within things.
Does there exist anywhere anything that is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and which is eternally of one single form?
O twice-born one, since whatever undergoes change never remains as it was, how can there be any reality in that?
The earth becomes a jar; from the jar, shards; from the shards, powdered dust; and from that, atoms.
Perceived by people whose certainty regarding the self is stilled by their own karma—tell me, what is the real substance here?
Therefore, O twice-born one, there is no collection of objects whatsoever, anywhere or at any time, that exists apart from consciousness;
consciousness alone is conceived as manifold by minds divided by the differences of their own respective karmas.
Knowledge is pure, stainless, free from sorrow, and devoid of all attachment such as greed;
it is one, eternally one, the supreme, the highest Lord—He is Vāsudeva, than whom nothing else exists.
Thus have I described the true nature of existence according to its reality; knowledge is that which is true, while anything else is untrue.
Furthermore, regarding that which pertains to conventional worldly usage, I have also explained to you how it rests upon the world.

"The sacrifice, the animal, the fire, the entire assembly of priests, the Soma, the gods, and desire consisting of heaven—these and other such things are seen as the paths based on ritual action; and the enjoyments of the worlds, beginning with the earth, are their respective fruits."

Thus the *Daśaślokī* has been recited. (The reading found in the root text is: "And that which is situated in this world... There is no disagreement here. Although one might argue that since the words "exists" (*asti*) and "does not exist" (*nāsti*) in the verse "O best of Brahmins, that which exists and that which does not exist... can be construed as referring to entities in the form of existence and non-existence, there could be disagreement regarding the word "exists" being used to refer to the Self; nevertheless, the intended meaning is that there is no dispute regarding the words "non-existent" (*nāsti*) and "unreal" (*asatya*) referring to the insentient, and moreover, they refer exclusively to karma.

The meaning is that it is solely intent upon investigating the manifold nature of the root of karma, since this will be stated later on. "Dissociated subtle form" means that the subtle form of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, which is dissociated from their mutual relationship as instrument and object of experience, is what is being referred to. Regarding the phrase "contained within the *Bharata*," the sense is that because it was introduced in the first chapter with the words, "O Maitreya, I shall relate his life story to you again," it is now said to be "contained within."

Now, one might object: since it is possible for the word *saṃkṣepa* (abridgment) to mean an abridgment of the entire meaning of the scripture, it would be a strained interpretation to assume that the life of the original Bharata is present in the mind [of the listener] by virtue of the promise made in the first chapter, and then to imagine this [present work] to be its abridgment. Furthermore, if its nature as an abridgment were already promised, then the detailed narration would follow naturally; in that case, Maitreya’s question, "O Blessed One, everything has been told," regarding the life of the original Bharata would be inappropriate. To this we reply: No.

The intention here is that since the nature of the summary as a whole is being discussed, the nature of the specific summaries that are about to be described is also possible [within it]. Regarding the phrase "mere existence, beyond the reach of the senses": although these sentences do not belong to this particular section, they should be understood as having been stated with the intent of explaining that those passages belonging to this section—such as "Since the Blessed Lord is of the nature of knowledge"—must be shown to have the same meaning. The word *iti* (thus) indicates the conclusion.

Since the word *ātman* in the sentence “Viṣṇu is the Self” can be construed with the word “the relationship of body and self,” even though it is separated by other words, the insertion (*adhyāhāra*) of the word “intending” (*abhipretya*) is inappropriate; with this in mind, he says: “or the meaning is ‘the relationship of body and self’. Regarding the phrase “of that which consists in the corroboration of the teachings of identity found in all the Śrutis,” the word “all” (*sakala*) refers to those branches of the Veda not studied [by one]. And its “corroboration” (*upavṛṃhaṇa*) is the clarification of their meaning. Alternatively, the word “all” refers to the branches of the Veda that have been studied.

Intending that there are two possible ways for the meaning to arise—namely, the refutation of that [objection] and the demonstration of the existence of statements with meanings contrary to it—he explains [the passage] as "even in those branches not studied. Regarding the phrase "there is an instruction of identity," the word "who" (*yaḥ*) is to be supplied as the subject, because later on the word "of him" (*tasya*) is heard in the statement, "this is precisely its meaning. This refers to the three occurrences of the word *iti*.

Thus, the sequence of the argument here is as follows: intending that the very basis for the teaching of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—which takes the form of an elaboration (*upavṛṃhaṇa*) of the identity found in all the Vedas, such as the verse "That which is water is indeed the body of Viṣṇu," and which will be explained starting from the verse "The luminaries are Viṣṇu"—is precisely the relationship of body and self, [the author] states that even the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), being a transformation of water, is the body of Viṣṇu, since water is an effect of Viṣṇu.

Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the preceding text, which states, "intending 'Viṣṇu is the Self,'" for that [statement] is not a fault as it constitutes a different interpretation. Some, however, interpret the verse by saying that its purport is to state that, according to his intention that "Viṣṇu is the Self," the very basis for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the relationship between body and self (*śarīrātmabhāva*). [The phrase] "since Viśvarūpa is imperishable" means: "For that world, called the Person (*puruṣa*), consists of all the sense organs and the internal organ."

Having indicated [the identity] through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "that very one," the meaning is that—when the question arises as to how there can be such coreferentiality between two distinct things—the relationship of body and self is explicitly stated as the cause by means of the ablative case in the word "yataḥ" (from whom), in the passage: "The imperishable one, whose form is the universe, is the Self of all beings. And this has been clearly explained by the Author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*.

"The meaning of the three quarters is stated" means that because the meaning of the fourth quarter—"O best of Brahmins, that which exists and that which does not exist"—will be clarified by way of restatement through the commentary passage beginning with "In this regard, there is that which consists of existence and that which consists of non-existence," it is said that "the meaning of the three quarters is stated. However, some maintain that the meaning of all four quarters is stated without restriction, since there is no disagreement regarding the fact that the essence of the verse is devoted to teaching the identity [of the Self] dependent upon the relationship between the body and the Self.

However, they say that this is the distinction: because the meanings of the terms *jyotis* (light) and so forth occurring in the first three quarters have already been determined, there is no further inquiry (*jijñāsā*) regarding them. Since the meanings of the words "is" (*asti*) and "is not" (*nāsti*) occurring in the fourth quarter have not yet been determined, it is appropriate to restate only the subject matter of that quarter through such an inquiry. They say this is "by way of restating the specific meaning of the sentence. This means it is appropriate by way of restating the final, established meaning of the sentence. By way of restating the specific meaning of the sentence; that is to say, by way of restating the final, established meaning of the sentence.

It was stated that [the opponent] says, "This is not the reason for its being of the nature of existence. This means, however, that he does not say, "This is the reason for its being of the nature of existence.

By the phrase, "Since the Blessed Lord is of the nature of knowledge," because there is no presentation of the idea that "this is of the nature of existence, this is not of the nature of existence, and this is the reason for its not being of the nature of existence," the word *āha* (he says) is taken as a representative particle (*pratīka*). Now, one might ask: how is it obtained from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) that [the Lord] "abides as the Self of all fields and knowers" (*kṣetra-jña*), since the "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*) has not been previously mentioned?

Nor should it be argued that the term *asti* (exists) in the phrase "O best of Brahmins, that which exists and that which does not exist" serves to present the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field); for, since Maitreya was unaware of the distinction between "this is of the nature of existence" and "this is of the nature of non-existence," the word *asti* lacks the capacity to present the *kṣetrajña*. Thus, there is no evidence that the Blessed One—who abides as the self of the *kṣetrajña*—is presented by the expression "all that exists. Anticipating this objection, [the author notes that] even if he is not presented by the words *asti* and *nāsti*,...

Since words such as "light" (*jyotis*) and others denote composite entities, it is possible for both the sentient and the insentient to be presented [by them]; however, because it would be impossible to teach that the one whose body is the insentient possesses knowledge as its very nature, or to deny that He has the bodies of gods and so forth by saying "He is not a real entity," the term "one whose form is everything" (*aśeṣamūrti*) refers, by virtue of appropriateness, only to Him whose body is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).

Consequently, the Blessed Lord, who is of the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpa*), becomes one whose body is knowledge (*jñānaśarīraka*) when residing within the body of the Knower (*kṣetrajña*). (The word *svarūpa* here refers to *śarīra*, or "body. This results in the conclusion that He does not possess a body consisting of entities such as gods and so forth. Furthermore, this also results in the discernment between the body and the Self. Intending to convey this—just as when it is said, "He possesses a ring; he possesses silver, but not gold," it follows that "the ring is of the form of silver, not of the form of gold"—he says, "by the word 'entire,' even the insentient [is included]."

The objection that "the negation of the reality of the object is untenable" is addressed as follows: the intention is that for the Blessed Lord, whose body is consciousness (*cit*), the negation—"but it is not a real entity"—of His having gods, humans, mountains, oceans, the earth, and so forth as His body, results ultimately in the negation of the states of being a god, human, and so on, with respect to the non-conscious (*acit*) portion that constitutes the body. Regarding the phrase "a qualification of the specific ritual action performed by the priests": this is like the redness of the turban, which is a qualification of the specific performance [of the rite] through a traditional lineage.

The intention is that in the usage of the word *paramparayā* (by way of succession), there is the qualification of the *ṛg-vij* priests; therein [is the qualification] of the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), and therein [is the qualification] of the redness (*lohitya*). In the passage, "Salutation to Him who, by virtue of His hardness, sustains [the world], whose nature is the Earth," the sense is that hardness exists in the essential nature [of the Lord] through the medium of the Earth. In the commentary, the phrase "from this very [cause]" means "for this very reason."

Now, one might object: even if the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) lacks the form of a god or other such beings because his essential nature is pure consciousness, it is not necessary that the distinction between gods and others be a manifestation of that consciousness. This is because the mere fact of being non-different from the Knower of the Field does not necessitate being a manifestation of His consciousness; otherwise, it would follow that the Supreme Self, His eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*), and so forth, would likewise be manifestations of that consciousness.

Nor should it be argued that for gods and others—who are established as impermanent and distinct from the individual soul (jīva)—it is necessary that they be mere manifestations of that [supreme] consciousness; for even today, the impermanence of the distinctions such as gods and so forth is not certain. Or, if it were certain, then since their impermanence would be established as being fit to be designated as "unreal" (asatya), the statement—"Therefore, know that the distinctions of mountains, oceans, earth, and so forth, are manifestations of consciousness"—which was intended to demonstrate impermanence by way of being a transformation of karma, would result in being redundant.

Furthermore, if it is argued that since the field (*kṣetra*)—abiding as the self—is not of the nature of gods and so forth, the very form of gods and others is a manifestation of consciousness (*vijñāna-vijṛmbhita*); and since that which abides as the self of gods and others is not of the nature of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who is pure consciousness, it would follow that the Knower of the Field too is a manifestation of consciousness—[we reply: no.

However, since the view that the nature of the gods and others is the natural form of the Supreme Self abiding as the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) has been rejected by the statement "but not a real entity," there arises the expectation, "In what form [do they exist]? In response to this, the statement "they are the manifestations of consciousness" expresses that their form is adventitious; thus, there is no fault. For this very reason, the word "natural" (*svābhāvika*) is employed in the Commentary to indicate that knowledge alone is the natural form. Therefore, the status of being the cause of the distinctions among gods and others is mediated [by consciousness].

The meaning is that the distinctions among gods and other beings arise through the investigation of the diversity of preceding [lives] and through karma. Since karma and ignorance can function as mutual causes—like a seed and its sprout—one should not entertain doubts regarding a reversal of the relationship between cause and effect. This is established by the statement: "They are the manifestations of consciousness, whose nature is knowledge."

By the phrase "having the nature of knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpaḥ*), since that which has the nature of knowledge is stated, its reality is understood through the realization of its freedom from transformation; whereas by the phrase "the manifestations of consciousness" (*vijñānavijṛmbhitāni*), its state of being subject to transformation is established. Therefore, the intent is that the commentary says, "by virtue of having the single form of self-established knowledge" (*nijasiddhajñānaikarūpatvena*).

One might object: since the passage beginning with "But when [the mind is] pure" (*yadā tu śuddham*) serves as an exposition of what was previously stated, how can the author of the *Bhāṣya* accept that he is merely expounding upon that very same position held by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*)? Anticipating this doubt, he states, "In the formulation of the prima facie view," to show that there is no fault in relying on that [previous argument] regarding the non-contradictory portions. Regarding the phrase "the analysis of the meaning of the words 'nirdoṣam' and so forth": although one should have said "of the words 'apāstadoṣam' and so forth," it should be understood that the word *nirdoṣa* is employed for the sake of brevity.

Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is *yadvā nirdoṣam ityādi* (or rather, "faultless," etc.). The phrase "of the words" means "of the words contained in the verse. Regarding the expression "rooted in the conceptualization of a self as the fruit of karma": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that whose root is the conceptualization of a self. This is because there is no fault [in such a view] according to the logic of the seed and the sprout, due to the distinction between individual instances (*vyaktibheda*). [This applies] both to the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and to the word "volition" (*saṃkalpa*).

Since it is possible for the term *vijñāna* (consciousness), which signifies the investigation of diversity, and the term *saṃkalpa* (volition), which signifies the unification [of that diversity], to function as cause and effect, there is no contradiction in the statements: "They are the manifestations of consciousness" and "They are the fruits of the tree of volition."

The meaning is that when one of two things has been stated, the other is established by implication. Thus, the meaning of the word *bhogya* (enjoyable) becomes clarified. This is because, in the subsequent sentence, those very distinct entities (*vastubheda*) which were previously introduced as being "for the sake of enjoyment" (*bhogārtha*) are referred to as being "that which is enjoyed" (*bhogyabhūta*). [The suffix -ya] signifies precisely the state of having the accomplishment of enjoyment as its purpose. In this sense—namely, "the cause of that [enjoyment] is conjunction and production"—the suffix *yat* is applied to the word *bhoga* according to the rule *godvayacaḥ*.

However, it is not a word ending in the suffix *ṇyat* according to the rule "ṛhaloṇryat," because if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including places of enjoyment (*bhogasthāna*) and so forth under the term "the object of enjoyment" (*bhogya*). This is the intended meaning. The phrase "for the purpose of explaining the words to be explained" means that since the word "in objects" (*vastuṣu*) and so forth has not yet been explained, [this is] for that purpose. "He cites the word to be explained" means he cites the word "the object of enjoyment" (*bhogya*) found in the Śruti passage "the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment. "The reason has not been stated" means that although the reason for being denoted by the word "exists" (*asti*) has indeed been stated by the phrase "whose nature is knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpaḥ*), it was nevertheless not explicitly stated in the Bhāṣya.

Therefore, in the commentary on the preceding verse, it was stated that "the other is denoted by the word 'is'," but the reason for this was not set forth; such is the sense. Regarding "instruction on the prompter": the meaning is instruction on the grounds for the application of the words "is" and "is not. Regarding "here, the denotable object": the meaning is that in this verse, the referent of the word "is" is precisely that which is denoted by the word "is."

In the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the statement "the insentient object, which has become one's own object of enjoyment, is observed to be changing at every moment," two interpretations are provided—both being possible due to the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*)—with the intention that the meaning can be understood in two ways: either "an object that changes at every moment is observed as an object of enjoyment" or "the insentient object of enjoyment is observed to be changing at every moment. This is expressed by the words beginning with "asthira" (unstable), etc., because the usage [of the term] is more frequent in the context of visual cognition (*cākṣuṣajñāna*).

Although there would be no fault even if it were stated that "it is perceived by the eye through direct perception," nevertheless, it should be understood that the term "is experienced" (*anubhūyate*) was explained [in this way] in order to include means of valid cognition other than visual knowledge (*cākṣuṣajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "the completion of the commentary on the verse," the words "in this interpretation" (*asyām yojanāyām*) are to be supplied as the remainder.

The intended meaning (*bhāva*) is as follows: in the former construction, where [the word *ālakṣyate*] is understood to mean "is perceived," "is experienced," or "is enjoyed"—or alternatively, "is perceived as an object of enjoyment"—the utility of the phrase "this is the meaning" (*ityarthaḥ*) would be possible, as it serves to demonstrate such an uncommon sense. However, in this [present] construction, since the term *ālakṣyate* is already well-known in the sense of "is experienced" (*anubhūyate*), the phrase "this is the meaning" (*ityarthaḥ*) is redundant; therefore, it functions solely as an indicator of completion (*samāpti*).

And in this very view, the subsequent commentary beginning with "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*) is intended to state the purport of the two verses. Having this very point in mind, [the author] will say later: "Or rather, he states the purport of the two verses. However, in the previous interpretation, since the phrase "this is the meaning" (*ity arthaḥ*) does not indicate the conclusion, the subsequent commentary beginning with "this being so" is intended to explain the meaning of the words "bring the fuel" (*brūhi*) and so forth. Having this very point in mind, the passage beginning with "he states the meaning of 'bring the fuel' and so forth" was written.

Therefore, one should not object that the statement beginning with "brūhi" (speak) at the conclusion of the commentary on the verse is contradictory; for the qualification beginning with "the meaning of the word 'asti'" (asti-śabdārtham) is established by implication (*sāmarthyasiddhatayā*), and not as something denoted by the word itself in the phrase "vastvasti kim" (is there any reality?), because in that context the word *asti* has the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*). Thus, the suspicion that it is identical to the word *vastu* (reality) should not be entertained; this refers to the word *vastu* in the phrase "vastvasti kim."

"By this [phrase], 'that which is denoted by the word *asti*'"—in the previous interpretation, there was the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of "worthy of the word *asti*" (*asti-śabdārham*). In this present view, however, the distinction is that there is the ellipsis of the word *asti* in the sense of the verb "to exist" (*bhavati*). Regarding the phrase "in the formulation of the prima facie position" (*pūrvapakṣa-yojanāyām*): the intention is that, for this reason, the fact that the meaning of the two verses was not stated separately in the prima facie position does not constitute a fault. Regarding the phrase "and being denotable by the word *asti* as delimited": the meaning is "being denotable by the word *asti* when accompanied by other words, such as 'it exists at that time' (*tadānīmastīti*)" or "it exists now" (*idānīmastīti*)."

It must be clarified that the point in question concerns the identity of the mode (*ākāra*). Since the suffix *dhā* is prescribed by the rule "after a numeral, *dhā* is used in the sense of 'dividing'" (*saṃkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā*) to denote a manner that constitutes a division, the meaning of *bahudhā* must be described as "in many ways. Consequently, the word *eka*, which is its correlative, must also have "identity of mode" as its sole meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the suffix *dhā* (forming *vidhā*) should be applied here according to the rule "adhikaraṇavicāle ca" (Pāṇini 5.3.43), as in the example "Make one heap into five. For "alteration of the locus" (*adhikaraṇavicālana*) means making a single thing manifold; that is to say, it means the production of a different number. However, the production of a different number for consciousness is not its natural state. Therefore, the suffix *dhā* must be taken in the sense of "dividing" (*vidhā*). Consequently, the intended meaning is that the word "one" (*eka*) must be understood as referring solely to the unity of its mode (*prakāra*).

Now, one might object: since the suffix *dhā* is heard in the word *bahudhā* in the sense of a distributive repetition (*vidhārtha*), as in the case of *pañcadhā bhukte* ("he eats five times"), it must be stated that a multiplicity of modes belonging to the action is perceived, and not a multiplicity belonging to the cognition, because the meaning of the suffix *dhā* is the multiplicity of the action. Consequently, in the phrase *bahudhābhyupetam* ("accepted in many ways"), the result would be a multiplicity of modes belonging to the act of acceptance (*abhyupagama-kriyā*), and not a multiplicity of modes of cognition.

Furthermore, in the statement "consciousness is one," how could the identity of the modes of consciousness be established? [One might argue] that this is because there is no means of cognizing it, since oneness and plurality have different objects. This is not so; for the intention is that the plurality of the act of acceptance results in the plurality of the accepted consciousnesses, and thus oneness and plurality share the same object. The meaning is that [the difference] is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*).

Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of contemplating [the world] as consisting of gods and so forth, if this is merely a conditioned state? By the two verses beginning with “That body of Viṣṇu is indeed water,” it has been established that the world—composed of both consciousness and the non-conscious—is the body of the Lord in its state of union and in its state of separation.

By the two verses beginning with “Since the Lord is of the nature of knowledge,” the distinction between consciousness and the non-conscious has been established; furthermore, it has been shown through positive and negative concomitance that consciousness is denoted by the word ‘real’ (satya), while the non-conscious, being a transformation of karma, is denoted by the word ‘unreal’ (asatya).

Having already established through the two verses beginning with "Is there any reality? (*vastvasti kim*) that the non-conscious (*acit*) is denoted by the word "unreal" (*asat*) even according to the manner in which the world is perceived, and having concluded in the half-verse "Therefore, not consciousness" (*tasmānna vijñānam*) that the word "real" (*sat*) denotes consciousness alone and not the non-conscious, one might object: "Since there is no other point to be supported, nothing is seen here that could serve as the subject of the disciple’s inquiry—which is the cause for introducing the half-verse 'Consciousness is one' (*vijñānamekam*). This is true.

This is meaningful because it serves as a conclusion establishing that the substance in question (acid) possesses the quality of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), which is the basis for the application of the term "unreal" (*asatya*).

"Of the word immediately following the word expressing the destruction of karma": the word expressing the destruction of karma is the word "viśuddhi" (purity); the word immediately following that is the word "vimala" (stainless). "By virtue of its supreme nature, which is devoid of connection with a body": the meaning is that the phrase "devoid of contact with *prakṛti*" and the phrase "devoid of connection with a body" have the same significance. "Common to both the conscious and the unconscious": the meaning is that it is intended to distinguish between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). "In other words as well": this means in words such as "existent" (*sat*), "non-existent" (*asat*), and so forth.

One might object: "Why could the phrase 'and desire consisting of heaven' not simply mean that heaven is the object of desire? Having raised this doubt, and having further raised the doubt regarding the phrase 'and desire for the enjoyments of the earth and so forth'—[the author replies] that since the fruit will be stated later in the words 'and the enjoyments of the earth and so forth are their fruits,' it is more appropriate that [the former phrase] refers specifically to the desire for heaven; thus he says, "because the fruit will be stated later."

One might object: "How can the verse beginning with 'The sacrifice is the animal' (Yajñaḥ paśuḥ) have as its primary purpose the exposition of the nature of action (*karma*)? For even if animals and the like enter into the sacrifice as its constituent parts, the deities designated by the word 'fire' and the enjoyments of the worlds such as the earth—which are the results and thus not subordinate to the action—cannot possibly be considered action. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of the deity and of the result," and so on. "In every case, it indeed goes" means that it certainly goes. "Subject to karma" means that it is indeed subject to karma. "Fixed, immovable, and eternally uniform" [is the meaning].
"Whatever I have told you regarding this world, one who is subject to karma indeed wanders everywhere therein;
having known this [Self] as certain, immovable, and eternally uniform, one should act so that one enters Vāsudeva."

The meaning is that by the words “fixed,” “immovable,” and “always of one form” found in the verse, the state of being uniform is stated respectively in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*), attributes (*guṇa*), and form (*rūpa*). Regarding the phrase “always of one form,” he intends to show that uniformity is appropriate in terms of form; alternatively, [the phrase] means “in terms of essential nature, attributes, and form. This connects with the preceding [text], meaning it connects with the proposition-statement at the beginning of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) which says, “It is not so.”

The meaning is that [the terms] do not refer to something distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. Just as the words "existent" (*sat*) and "unreal" (*asatya*) when employed in the context of Brahman do not refer to something distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, so too the words "non-existent" (*na asti*) and "unreal" (*asatya*) when employed in the context of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) do not refer to a state of being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. Regarding the phrase "contradiction by way of the object": although being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent is also contradictory to existence, the word "non-existent" would denote merely the absence of existence, and nothing more than that—this is the intended sense.

Regarding the phrase "in response to the doubt that falsity (*mithyātva*) consists precisely in perishability": this means "in response to the doubt of an outsider" (*taṭastha-śaṅkāyām*), because such a doubt does not arise for one who asserts the doctrine of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādin*); for if it did, the dispute would reach its conclusion [on that very point]. The commentary states: "It clarifies the nature of perishability. This introductory remark was composed with the following intention: having considered that the nature of perishability consists in being perceived otherwise through a specific transformation at another time—since what was experienced in one form at one time is later apprehended differently due to a particular modification—it is said that "the text clarifies the nature of perishability" by establishing non-existence through such an alternative perception via specific transformation.

However, some introduce the commentary beginning with "by one aspect" (*ekenākāreṇa*) as follows: "But was it not stated that in the passage 'Does the entity exist? Is the earth the pot-ness?', only perishability (*nāśitva*) was established, and not the lack of a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇakatva*) or sublation by cognition (*jñānabādhyatva*)?"

Anticipating the objection that "we do not see any decisive factor here," [the author] states in the two verses beginning with "Is there any real thing? (*vastvasti kim*) that since it is impossible for non-existence—which is established by the fact that what was perceived otherwise at one time is perceived otherwise at another time—to terminate in either (1) a state of insignificance (*tucchatva*) characterized by the unfitness for relation with any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or (2) the nature of falsity (*mithyātva*) characterized by being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a negation within the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of the specific place and time [of perception], it must terminate in perishability (*vināśitva*) alone.

Intending to show that [the term] "paryavasāna" (conclusion) is appropriate, he says: "by means of a single aspect at one time. Regarding this position, they state that there is no need for the labor of resorting to the assumption of an objection from an outsider (*taṭastha-śaṅkā*)—namely, the doubt that "being perishable (*vināśitva*)" itself constitutes falsity (*mithyātva*), or the doubt as to how perishability is excluded from the falsity of being non-existent (*tucchatva*). The meaning is that the ground for the application of the word "non-existent" (*nāsti*) consists in its implication of perishability.

The meaning is as follows: since perishability (*naśvaratva*) is the ground for the application of the word "non-existent" (*nāsti*), perishability is the referent of "non-existence. Consequently, the intent of the *Bhāṣya*—which states that "the non-conscious [object] always contains the sense of non-existence"—is that it always contains the sense of destruction (*nāśa*). Regarding the phrase "being the object of a cognition associated with natural existence": the meaning is that natural existence is not ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*). The point is that because even insentient things (*acidvastu*) are associated with a natural existence that is not ultimately real, they themselves are also not ultimately real.

Nor should it be argued: "Since ultimate, intrinsic reality (*paramārthasvābhāvikasatyatva*) is absent in that which is non-conscious (*acidrūpa*), how can there be the conventional usage of 'non-ultimate' (*aparamārtha*) for the non-conscious through connection with that [reality]? For, based on the cognition "the non-conscious possesses unreal reality," some relation—which constitutes the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound—must be stated. This is because it is endowed with the sense of the suffix *-asti* (existence) as qualified by "non-ultimacy. The meaning is: "because it is endowed with an unreal, intrinsic reality" (*aparamārthasvābhāvikasatyatvopetatvāt*). (The impossibility of a sublater).

"Therefore, it has as its object the Self with its adjuncts. By this, the meaning is "by means of the attributeless reality" (*nirviśeṣavastu*); or rather, the meaning is "by virtue of having the attributeless reality as its object. For in that context, the citation of the representative symbol was made in the words: "'Born from the waters, Hiraṇyagarbha,' [and so on] for eight [verses]."

Consequently, the meaning is that one must state the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the verse "From the lightning, all moments of time were born from the Person" (*sarve nimeṣā jajñire vidyutaḥ puruṣād adhi*), which occurs in the subsequent section beginning with "Born from the waters" (*adbhyaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ*), and the verse "I know this great Person, sun-colored" (*vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam, ādityavarṇam*) found within the section "In the boundless water" (*ambhasy apāre*).
(The Meaning of *Tattvamasi*)

"For sameness of locus (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is fourfold according to others. In the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* on the sūtra "And because of pervasion, [the word 'Brahman'] is appropriate," four positions regarding sameness of locus are presented: superimposition (adhyāsa), sublation (apavāda), identity (ekatva), and qualification (viśeṣaṇa). Among these, "superimposition" means that when the cognition of one of two things has not yet been set aside, the cognition of the other is superimposed upon it.

It occurs as follows: just as when the cognition of "Brāhmaṇahood" is superimposed upon a name, the cognition of the name persists even while the cognition of Brāhmaṇahood is present, and it is not removed by that cognition of Brāhmaṇahood; or as the superimposition (adhyāsa) consists in the cognition of Viṣṇu and others upon images and the like. Sublation (apavāda), however, is when a subsequent cognition of the true nature of an object arises and becomes the remover of a previously established, certain cognition of its falsity regarding some thing.

Just as the notion of a self with respect to the aggregate of the body and the senses is removed by the subsequent, true cognition "That thou art" directed toward the Self itself; and just as the error regarding direction is removed by the cognition of the true nature of direction; and unity consists in two words being placed in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) while functioning to denote a non-distinct object—such as "elephant is *sindhura*" or "cuckoo is *pika*"; and the relation of qualifier and qualified is exemplified by "the blue lotus."

It should be understood that this is also an illustration of that [case]. This refers to passages such as, "All this is indeed Brahman. Now, an objection may be raised: since the passage is intent upon the injunction for tranquility (*śama*), and unlike passages such as "The name is Brahman," it lacks the intent to enjoin the viewing of everything as Brahman, others do not maintain that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) exists in superimposition (*adhyāsa*). If one asks, "How then can this be stated?", we reply: if they do not so maintain, then, according to the maxim "one need not rely on an example [if there is another]," another example accepted by both parties must be sought.

"Devoid of qualifiers such as 'abiding' (*sthiti*), etc."—the sense is that the action of abiding is impossible at the time of bringing [an object]. "By means of a qualifier such as abiding, etc."—the sense is that the nature of being a qualifier consists precisely in this: when something is known as possessing an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) to be conveyed, there arises a cognition of the connection with other qualifiers distinct from the intended referent (*tātparya-viṣaya*); it does not consist in being connected with the predicate (*vidheya*). "In a manner suitable for connection"—the meaning is: in a manner suitable for connection either by being simultaneous with the predicate or by having a different time from the predicate.

For this very reason, the sense is that even place, time, and so forth function as qualifiers in such cases as "This is that Devadatta. Regarding the phrase "the abandonment of even one": for this same reason, in the section [of the *Brahmasūtra*] beginning with "In other cases also, it is thus on account of the connection" (*sambandhād evam anyatrāpi*), concerning the *Vyāhṛti-vidyā*, in the passages "Its secret name (upaniṣad) is 'ahar' with respect to the deities" (*tasyopaniṣadahar ity adhidaivatam*) and "Its secret name is 'aham' with respect to the self" (*tasyopaniṣadaham ity adhyātmam*), because the word "its" (*tasya*) denotes the specific location previously mentioned as qualified by its respective context, there is a fixed determination of those respective names, and not otherwise.

The sense is that it has been established that [the word] lacks fixedness because it denotes only the substantive (viśeṣya). Thus, its being the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatva*) is cast far away. Therefore, even by opponents, it is accepted that the cognition of the "devoid of attributes" (*nirviśeṣa*) occurs through the word *tat* only by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). "Because it is unfit for recollection" means: because it is unfit for the recollection produced by the word *tat*. "Gold is recollected" [is the example].

Nor should it be argued: "How can this objection be raised, given that even when there is a perceptual synthesis (*pratyakṣika-pratisaṃdhāna*) characterized by being permeated by that word, the fact that [the object] is the referent of a synthesis produced by that word has not been established"? This is because the intention is that it is possible for something that is unfit to be the referent of a synthesis permeated by that word to also be unfit to be the referent of a synthesis produced by that word. This applies even to the case of verbal [cognition].

In reality, however, even in a case where, through perception, that gold is recognized as such by setting aside its status as a ring, there is no fault even if it is stated that the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) pertains specifically to the object qualified by the state of being a ring due to the assistance of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). This is said with the intention of providing a general characterization of the causal factor (*prayojaka*). Consequently, the meaning is that even the factor of orientation consisting of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva*) and so forth is included by the phrase "qualified by the insentient" (*acid-viśiṣṭa*). Otherwise, [the term would fail to include] the past and the future.

If one accepts the simultaneity of objects on the basis of the simultaneity of cognitions, then a rule would have to be accepted that the object of cognition must exist at the same time as its cognition. Consequently, even in the case of past and future objects, in order to maintain the simultaneity of the object and the subject, it would follow that either the subject must be past or the object must be present—this is the intended sense.

"From the aforementioned example" means from the example: "The mother-of-pearl is itself the silver. "Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the indicated [object]" means because it has been established that [the statement] is intended to convey the identity of the indicated objects by way of positive concomitance (anvaya); this is the meaning of "because of the grammatical coreferentiality with the indicated object. "The reading should be examined" implies that the word *āśraya* is invariably masculine. "The word *āśraya* refers to the object" means it refers to the act of making something an object [of cognition].

He states his own established position: "Alternatively, the meaning is that the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is that which serves as the locus for the form being superimposed. It is called *bhrama* because one errs (*bhramyate*). The form being superimposed (*āropyākāra*) is precisely the silver and so forth. Its "locus" (*āśraya*) is that which is resorted to (*āśrīyate*), meaning it is the support; the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule "in the sense of an object [other than the agent]" (*akartari ca kārake*) under the governing heading "and after a prefix" (*paraśca*). Nor does it follow that it must be masculine by the rule "those ending in *añ*, *ya*, and *ap* are masculine," because here the suffix is *ac*.
For it is said: "The suffixes *kta* and *lyuṭ* are used in the neuter for the abstract state (*bhāva*); the suffixes *ktin* and others are used in the feminine;
therefore, suffixes such as *ghañ* and others are used only in the masculine, as in *pākaḥ*, *cayaḥ*, and *lavaḥ*."
This must be said, because that [suffix] has as its domain *ghañ* and other suffixes used in the sense of an action (*bhāva*). As it has been stated:

"The *ghañ* and other suffixes occur in the sense of an action; they are exclusively masculine when denoting a factor of action other than the agent (*kartṛ*), and they occur only in the masculine and neuter, never in the feminine."

Thus, it should be understood that since the agent and other factors (*kāraka*) such as the object possess both masculine and neuter genders, the neuter gender is stated here because the substantive (*viśeṣya*) itself is neuter. For example, in the phrase "with regard to the *palāśa* flower": although in the verse, once the bee’s delusion regarding the stalk—mistaking it for a bee—is removed, only the mere contact with the *palāśa* flower is perceived; [nevertheless, the neuter form is used].

Since the phrase "through the delusion of a bee" (*bhramarabhrameṇa*) is construed only with "first [there was] no delusion" (*ādāvabhramam*) and not with "she embraced" (*āśliṣat*), and since that much alone is relevant to the subject at hand, one should nevertheless understand that the capacity of the embrace of the *palāśa* flower to dispel the delusion of the bee is also introduced for the purpose of clarifying the erroneous nature of the cognition of the bee. Regarding the phrase "of the cessation of the object of the delusion": "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) means removal (*apahāra*), that is to say, non-existence (*asattva*).

The *Bhāṣya* states: "If one does not admit the concealment of the ultimate reality of dharmas, then error (*bhrānti*) and sublation (*bādha*) are difficult to establish. In this context, sublation (*bādha*) consists in the removal of the object—that is, the non-existence of the object. Consequently, whether another error is removed or not, sublation is the non-existence of the object whose nature was that of a forest fire (*dāva*).

The meaning is that the non-existence of a property contradictory [to another] depends upon the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of that contradictory property; for example, the bark of the *palāśa* flower is ultimately real. Intending that "sublation by error" (*bhrāntibādha*) means simply the destruction of an error, he raises an objection: "If it is argued that the cessation of the delusion of being a forest fire occurs through the delusion of it being a bee. This refers to another error having the unreal as its object of truth (*asatye satyatvaviṣayabhrama*).

Now, one might argue that even the cessation of that [error] occurs through another error, and the cessation of that too through yet another error; thus, by resorting to such a succession of errors, the complete cessation of all ignorance would be impossible. It is thought that the intended meaning is established by this much alone, and therefore we do not see much purpose in the subsequent passage beginning with, "Then what? The cessation of the cognition of 'forest-ness'."

Furthermore, if it is argued that since the status of being an error can be established simply by taking the non-bee as the object of the notion of "bee-ness," there is no need to establish it as far as its being the object of "true-ness," we say: no; for this passage is justified as an instruction that a cognition which apprehends a contradictory form as true possesses greater strength and thus functions as a sublater. [Otherwise] the complete cessation of all ignorance would be untenable.

The sense is that even if one observes merely the cessation of an error through another error, one who desires the complete cessation of ignorance in liberation must, even after going very far, accept an ultimately real (pāramārthika) property. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "after the cessation of the bee's error": the sense is that once the cognition of the tree-stalk (*vṛntatva*) has led to the certain determination of the absence of "bee-ness," there arises an unavoidable cognition of the ultimate reality of the cognition of "tree-stick-ness" (*dāvatva*), because the cognition of "bee-ness"—which served as the sublater—has been determined to be unreal.

"It has ceased precisely by the apprehension of the ultimate reality of the palāśa flower. Although the cessation of the delusion that [the insect] is a wasp on the stalk is possible even through the mere delusion regarding the ultimate reality of the bee—wherein no subverting cognition arises—it should nevertheless be understood that this was stated with the intention of referring to those cases where that delusion ceases only through the knowledge that the bee is actually a palāśa flower. "If it were not so" (*na syāt*) means "if it were to perish" (*naśyet*).

Is it not the case that both falsity and truth would then follow for that very [subsequent cognition]? For the relationship of sublation—characterized by the status of the destroyed and the destroyer—is independent of falsity and truth; this is because we observe the relationship of the sublated and the sublator, characterized by the destroyed and the destroyer, only between two cognitions that possess equal ontological status (*tulyasattāka*), as previously stated.

Nor should it be argued that the falsity of the object of the sublated cognition and the truth of the object of the sublating cognition must be mutually dependent, such that the falsity or truth of the object of the final cognition would follow; for that [final cognition] remains unestablished even now. With this underlying unease, he says: "Furthermore, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) also... Even when there is self-destruction, destruction is merely a change of state.

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of destruction by another cause, it is easy to say that destruction is merely a change of state; for the intended meaning is that in cases where cessation occurs through knowledge, it is the very root-ignorance (*avidyā*) itself that ceases, and thus destruction does not consist in the attainment of another state. For this very reason, where a jar is destroyed by the blow of a hammer, there is merely a dissolution into its own material cause; it is not, however, the absolute cessation of the jar.

The sense is this: where the cessation of silver occurs through the cognition of mother-of-pearl, there is a total cessation along with its own material cause (*upādāna*), and not a dissolution into its own [immediate] cause; such is the position of the opponent. This is called the "analogy of the prince" (*rājakumārasamādhi*). It will be clarified in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samanvaya* section by the passage beginning, "A certain prince... And it has been stated by others as well: "Just as the state of being a tiger ceases for a prince upon the recovery of his memory, so too does the ignorance of the Self cease through sentences such as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*)."

Because the state of possessing qualities such as omniscience is not within the scope of perception and other means of knowledge. Although it is possible for that which was previously understood from the preceding context—namely, the one possessing qualities such as omniscience—to be the subject (*uddeśya*), nevertheless, the objection must be seen that in that case the use of the second-person pronoun "thou" (*asi*) would be untenable. Furthermore, because the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) is not within the scope of perception, if the Inner Controller were already established [prior to this teaching], then the instruction would be rendered purposeless; this is how it should be understood.

Now, one might object: although the relationship of body and embodied has been established by the phrase "this is its self" (*aitadātmyam*), the meaning conveyed by the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)—namely, that the word *tvam*, its referent, and the cognition thereof, culminate in the Supreme Self—has not yet been established; therefore, the status of the subject and the predicate remains unproven. Anticipating this objection, [the author] demonstrates that even this has been established within this very context.

It should be understood that this was stated on the assumption that the meaning of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is that the words beginning with "this" (*idam*) culminate in the Supreme Self. [The opponent argues: "But surely, in cases such as 'Fire is the remedy for cold,' even though there is an absence of being a restatement (*anuvādya*) or being an injunction (*vidheya*) based on whether something is already established or not, there is no fault in having a distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*) consisting of independence and dependence within the expression itself."

Nor can it be said that being the subject of restatement (*anuvādyatva*) and being the object of prescription (*vidheyatva*) are identical to being the thing designated (*uddeśyatva*) and being the thing to be undertaken (*upādeyatva*), because in such cases as "one should sacrifice on the full moon day," time—which is not something to be undertaken—is seen to be prescribed; this is the sense. Some, however, maintain that the terms "designated" (*uddeśya*) and "to be undertaken" (*upādeya*) refer respectively to being the subject of restatement and being the object of prescription, while the term "designated" refers to that which is expressed by the word occurring in the enjoining sentence (*prāpakavākya*).

Although there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamaka*)—since the word *tvam* (you) also possesses the sense of being the object of an injunction, as it extends to the Supreme Self denoted by the term *aitadātmya* (this-ness), which is the predicate in the enjoining sentence "This world has that as its self"—nevertheless, since both [the first and second persons] are equally eligible for use when no such criterion exists, the intention is that the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) is employed. Thus, the use of the second person is made in accordance with that [intention].

Even though the referent of the word *tvam* is established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), when there is a desire to express its status as the base (*prakṛti*) for the referent of the word *tat*, the second person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) is employed because the base itself is the agent of the action of being. For this very reason, it is explained in the rule *yuṣmadyupapade* that in the mantra, "O Agni, may I be thou, or mayest thou be I," the person is based on the base, such that [the form] becomes "may I be thou" (*ahaṃ tvaṃ syām*) or "mayest thou be I" (*tvaṃ vā ahaṃ syāḥ*).

Consequently, the meaning results in this: that the creator of the world possesses qualities such as omniscience and is indeed identical with you (the Self), because the application of words follows the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), and the presence or absence of other means of knowledge (*māna*) is irrelevant here. For this very reason, the Teachers themselves will state this in the section [Brahmasūtra 4.1.3] beginning with "But they approach [Brahman] as the Self" (*ātmeti tūpagacchanti*). Nevertheless, it should be understood that another method has been presented here; by the phrase "having the Existent as their support" (*sadāyatanāḥ*), the relationship between the substratum and the supported is expressed.

In the passage "sanmūlāḥ satpratiṣṭhāḥ," the word *sat* refers to the qualified [Brahman]. The word *prajā* (creatures) also refers to Brahman in its state as an effect, because it is impossible for Brahman alone to be the material cause. However, in the passage "sadāyatanāḥ," the word *sat* refers merely to the essential nature of the substantive, and the word *prajā* does not extend to Brahman either.

Alternatively, [the term *prajā*] may refer only to the individual soul (*jīva*) as qualified [by Brahman]. Even such a discrepancy in meaning must be accepted because it is supported by authoritative scripture. Or else, the word *prajā* everywhere refers only to the qualifying attribute. In this view as well, the justification has already been shown: namely, on account of the syntactic unity with the passage beginning "having Being as their root" (*sanmūlāḥ*). In the sentence "All this indeed," the status of being a reason is clear through the use of the particle *iti*; however, the fact that the word *an* signifies the relationship between the body and the embodied is not explicit. In the phrase "having Being as their abode" (*sadāyatanāḥ*), the relationship between the body and the embodied is explicit.

The state of being a cause is not clearly defined. Therefore, the meaning is that, according to the maxim of the "lost horse and burnt chariot," both [the body and the self] determine each other because they stand in mutual expectancy.

"The relationship of body and self is established" means that by the demonstration of the selfhood [of one], the bodyhood [of the other] is also established as a consequence. "It would be common to both" means that, consequently, it would terminate in either one alone. "This designation" refers to the designation beginning with "whose self is the body. "The locus and the subject" [refers to the relationship between the substratum and that which resides within it].

The sense is that by the phrase "He who dwells in the self," the relationship between the locus and the occupant is stated; by "the inner one of the self," the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader is stated; by "whom the self does not know," the relationship of the ignorant and the wise is stated; and by "He who from within rules the self," the relationship of the governed and the ruler is stated. Regarding the expression "of earth, water, etc.": it should be understood that the absence of the suffix *ap* (as in *pṛthivyādi*) is due to the fact that the rule for the final member of a compound (*samāsānta-vidhi*) is not universally obligatory.

Since its purpose is fulfilled by the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa alone, [the author] states the purpose for citing the Subāla passage—"He who moves within the earth"—with the words beginning, "Even in the state as cause," and so forth. Regarding the statement, "Because of the hearing [in scripture] that 'by means of this living self (jīva),' etc.," he replies with, "Having entered into that," and so forth. If it is objected: "Even though such other passages exist in another Śruti, why should the non-difference between the individual self (jīva) and Brahman not be established for Śvetaketu—who has not heard other Vedānta texts—by this very sentence, 'By this living self (ātman)'? The answer is: No.

In this context as well, by the statement, "O dear one, all these creatures have Being as their root," there is an explanation that the referent of the word "creatures"—the conscious principle conjoined with the non-conscious—possesses Being as its body and so forth; and by the designation of difference in such passages as, "O dear one, then he becomes merged in Being," the removal of the delusion of non-difference is established. [The phrase] "by name and form" indicates the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense of the means (*ity-arthabhāve*).

Although it is possible for name and form to function as instruments (*karaṇa*) in the act of differentiation—since the unified entity is differentiated, that is, made known, by means of these two instruments—nevertheless, while the status of being an instrumental case (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is possible, the status of being a dependent case (*upapada-vibhakti*) would be improper. However, one should understand that this is not a fault, because the intent is to demonstrate an alternative means [of understanding]. "One who brings about the relationship between the name and the named" means: in the case of the father or others who establish the convention (*saṃketa*).

This is because, in comparison with words such as *gaṅgā* or *agni*, the status of being a "name" (*nāmatva*) is not well-established [for them]. Nor should it be argued that even for the jar (*kalaśa*), which is denoted by the word *ghaṭa*, the status of being a name does not exist at all, on the grounds that the word *ghaṭa* lacks the character of a proper name (*saṃjñāśabda*). The point here is that the word *nāman* in this context signifies merely the capacity to denote objects like jars and so forth in general, and thus it is not a synonym for the term *saṃjñāśabda*. It refers precisely to the derivation of words that denote those various forms currently being produced.

The meaning is simply this: the accomplishment of being denotable by words that express those respective forms. Now, one might object: let it be granted that *nirukta* (etymology) is the accomplishment of being denotable by words; nevertheless, it is only the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) that are established as being denotable by names.

"It is not Brahman, because there is no evidence for its culminating in Brahman; even in the passage 'In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated,' the word 'this' (idam) refers to the world and does not denote Brahman"—having raised this objection, [the author] establishes that the denotation of names culminates in Brahman by means of the passage beginning with "There, by the words 'May I become many,'" etc. In this context, the meaning is: provided that the differentiation of names consists in the production of the state of being denotable by names. This serves as a rebuttal to the objection regarding the absence of worldly linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*).

The meaning is as follows: just as the doubt—"How is it that there is no learning of what is unprecedented (*apūrva*) among worldly people?"—is resolved by the fact that the unprecedented is not within the scope of worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too [is the present case]. This refers to the conclusion being drawn through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) regarding that which was previously proposed through grammatical non-coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

That is to say, the relationship of the body and the self—which was indicated through non-coordination by the *bahuvrīhi* compound "having this as its self" (*etadātmyam*) and by the general term "all this" (*idaṃ sarvam*)—is concluded specifically through grammatical coordination in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). However, this does not apply to the sentences of formal conclusion (*nigamana*).

If it is argued: "Just as in the case of the statement 'All that possesses smoke also possesses fire,' where—despite the fact that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of fire-possessingness by smoke-possessingness has already been demonstrated through the commonality of the mountain—the sentence 'The mountain possesses fire,' which indicates fire as delimited by the specific nature of *this* mountain, still functions according to the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*); why should this not be the case here as well? We reply: No. For even in that instance, in a situation where there is a certainty based on the commonality of the mountains present before one—such as "These mountains possess fire"—the absence of a distinction between subject and predicate is accepted. This is the underlying point.

"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of avoiding contradiction between the scripture on difference and the scripture on identity': the meaning is that it is for the sake of ensuring that both [scriptures] do not contradict their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Regarding the statement 'it is stated by way of a single method' (*tantra*): Bhāskara’s view is that while difference and non-difference are both inherent (*svābhāvika*) in the case of the non-conscious (matter) and Brahman, in the case of the conscious (individual soul) and Brahman, non-difference is inherent whereas difference is adventitious (*aupādhika*), because of the scriptural declarations of non-difference in the state of liberation."

One should observe the distinction that this is the view of Yādavaprakāśa, who maintains that both difference and non-difference are inherent even between consciousness (*cit*) and Brahman, because difference is specified even in the state of liberation.
