This is established by his own statement, "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth; by the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), the contextual passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" are also included. The meaning is that the abandonment [of the literal sense] results [from the context]; thus, the abandonment of the word-meanings follows directly from the abandonment of the natural sense.

The sense is that for the Veda, there is no abandonment greater than the abandonment of its true meaning. Since it is established by scripture that the defects of the individual soul (*jīva*) are removed through the knowledge of Brahman, the notion that Brahman is inherently endowed with eternal defects is contradicted; anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "Or rather, it is the fitness for connection with those respective defects. Just as the individual soul’s fitness for connection with defects is inherent, so too would it be for Brahman, which is non-different from it—this is the meaning. [Objection: But surely, there can be no contradiction with the scriptural teaching of identity with the faultless Brahman.

In his view, only Īśvara is faultless (*nirdoṣa*); the substance of Brahman, which consists of the aggregate of the conscious (*cit*), the unconscious (*acit*), and Īśvara, is not faultless. Anticipating the objection that this would contradict the teaching of the identity of the soul with the faultless Brahman, he says: "Of the words *sat*, *brahman*, *ātman*, etc. The result is a contradiction with the scripture stating that [Brahman] is faultless. The final meaning is that if the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman were to be established, it would contradict the scriptural statement regarding the faultlessness of Brahman. [The phrase] "the removal of what is to be discarded" (*heyāpaha*).

Just as in the case of *stragiyam* (meaning "this [garland] which takes away life"), this form is derived either by adding the suffix *ḍa* according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*, or by adding the suffix *kvip* according to the rule *kviṣ ca*. Regarding the *kvip* alternative, one should note that it is stated in the *Dhātuvṛtti* that because of its inclusion in the *bahv-ādi* group, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply; and since the rule *ṝnnebhyaḥ* [prescribes *ṅīp*] does not apply here either, the form is established. Consequently, one should not raise the objection: "How can this form be valid, given that the rule *ape kleśatamasoḥ* prescribes the suffix *ḍa* only when *kleśa* and *tamas* are the accompanying words (*upapada*)? This is because the suffix *ḍa* is seen elsewhere as well.

He says this in order to exclude [the application of the definition] to sticks and the like. By the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the phrase "in the state of being the body," the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*'s statement "being a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇatva*) is understood as "being a qualifier by way of non-separate existence" (*apṛthaksiddhatayā*), and not merely being a qualifier in general; such is the sense. This is because, in various instances of usage, one observes a recurring form [of expression].

Now, one might argue that although a common property—namely, being a non-separately established qualifier (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*)—exists among genus, quality, and substance, and serves as the basis for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) independent of possessive suffixes (*matvarthapratyaya*), there is nevertheless no single basis for the application of words such as "deity" (*deva*) that is common to the body, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), similar to how the word "Ganges" applies to the current, the bank, and so on. Consequently, the body—which is the locus of the genus "deity-ness" (*devatva*) and the like that serves as the basis for the application of those words—is primary; whereas the self, which is not the locus of that [genus], is secondary.

If it is asked, "What is the solution stated for the objection that there should be only secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) due to the connection with that [body]?", it is replied as follows: Divinity and so forth alone are the grounds for the application (pravṛttinimitta) of words such as "god" in common to both the body and the self. This is because, based on uncontradicted usage such as "the man is fat, he is a god," one accepts the body as the locus of divinity and so forth; and likewise, based on uncontradicted usage such as "I, who am a god, know," one must also accept that the self is the locus of divinity.

Nor should it be argued that this application [of the term] is based on the discrimination between the body and the self; for even one who possesses the discrimination between the body and the self—realizing "I am not the body"—does not have the realization "I am not a god or a human. Furthermore, although the self is the substratum of the basis for the application [of the term] "god" by way of the body, it is not denoted by that word because it is not the direct substratum of the basis for the application.

Otherwise, it would follow that even the ground, which is the substratum of potness by way of the pot, would be denotable by the word "pot. This need not be asserted; for although the ground lacks denotability by the word "pot" because there is no uncontradicted means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) grasping the ground as the substratum of potness—such as the cognition "there is potness on the ground" or "the ground is a pot"—nevertheless, in the case of the uncontradicted cognition "I, who am a god, know," the ground [of the self] possesses the status of being the substratum of the basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely "godhood," in its true nature.

This is because it is also necessary that [the self] be denotable by that word [‘deva’]. Just as a sacrifice and the like, though mediated by the *apūrva*, possess the status of being a means to heaven, and just as a bedstead and the like, though mediated by a mattress, possess the status of being the substratum for a reclining Devadatta, so too it is not contradictory for the self, though mediated by the body, to be the locus of divinity and other such attributes. However, there is a distinction: the ground possesses only the status of being the substratum for a pot, but not the status of being the substratum for "pot-ness," because it is not perceived as such.

In cases such as "hot water," however, because there is an absence of uncontradicted cognition and linguistic usage [to that effect], the words "hot" and so forth do not denote [the water]. For this very reason, there is no room for the objections raised by the Śrutis, such as: "If words denoting inseparable attributes were to denote the substratum itself, then words denoting light—which is inseparably established with lamps and the like—would also follow as denoting the lamps themselves. This is because the lamp and so forth do not possess the status of being the locus of the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) consisting in the nature of light.

Now, an objection might be raised: "In the *Bhāṣya*, the statement that 'the bodies of humans and so forth' possess the nature of being modes (*prakāra*)—defined as being non-separately established qualifiers (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*)—is over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), as it would apply to things like staffs and the like. Anticipating this, [the author] says: "conjoined with either one" (*anyatarānvitam*). But then, it may be argued that it is incorrect to define "being a mode" as "non-separately established qualification conjoined with either of the two: having the Self as its sole substratum or having that [Self] as its sole purpose," because the qualifier is redundant. Furthermore, if that were the case, one should simply say: "it is prompted by either having the Self as its sole substratum or having that [Self] as its sole purpose."

Regarding the phrase "Why [is there] the state of having the Self as the sole substratum and the state of having that as the sole purpose?"—because this definition is unsatisfactory, he explains it as referring to the three grounds for non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhi*), or alternatively, by means of the term "being a mode" (*prakāratva*). As for the statement "And because they are perceived only as qualifiers of the Self," since this portion of the commentary can possibly be intended to present the proof for being a mode, its nature as an exposition of being a mode is unestablished.

Therefore, one should not ask: "Why could it not mean that being a mode (*prakāratva*) consists in having as one's sole nature the state of being a mode? For if that were the case, since the body would also be understood to have as its sole nature the state of being a mode by virtue of having that [Self] as its sole substratum, its sole purpose, and its qualification (*viśeṣaṇatva*), the *Bhāṣya*—which indicates a distinction between the state of being a qualification and the state of having as one's sole nature the state of being a mode by treating them as the probans (*upapādaka*) and the probandum (*upapadya*) respectively—would be contradicted.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that being a qualifier consists precisely in being perceived as a qualifier. Regarding the phrase "in the bodies of servants and so forth": it should not be argued that there is no possibility of over-extension (ativyāpti) because even though a servant’s body serves the master’s purpose, it also accomplishes the servant’s own purposes; for if that were the case, [the definition] would fail to apply to a body that serves as a means for the enjoyment of a wife, son, and so on. This is the sense.

Now, one might object: since it has been explained that being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) is indeed cognition as a qualifier, then if one says that "being cognized as a qualifier" is the same as "being cognized as a limiting attribute (*viśeṣaṇatayā*)," there is no distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśeṣa*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The mention of the fifth case [ending] is figurative. Regarding the phrase "this triad": it should be understood that the statement of "triad" is intended according to the second explanation of the commentary on the passage beginning with "the bodies of humans and so forth. Regarding the term "own-nature" (*svarūpa*): the sense is that here the word *sva-* denotes "one's own" (*ātmīya*).

The meaning is as follows: since there is no other cause [for their non-separation], being cognizable by a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*) is stated to be the cause. Being cognizable by a single causal complex is the cause for being an inseparable qualifier (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*); therefore, due to the absence of that [complex], it is said that there is no inseparable qualifier-status. It should be understood that only when this is the case does the introductory passage of the *Bhāṣya*, “of that which is capable of being perceived separately,” achieve consistency. This is for the purpose of excluding the nature of being cognizable by a single causal complex.

Regarding this, some [object]: "In the case of the phrase 'the nature of having a single mode (*prakāra*)', it is more reasonable that the word *eka* here also serves to exclude the possibility of not being a mode, just as it does in that other instance; and since that [exclusion] is precisely what is stated here, that alone is correct. It is not, however, intended to exclude the nature of being cognizable by a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*), because while [the word *eka*] indicates inseparable qualification (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) in cases such as 'having a single substratum' (*tadekāśrayatva*), it does not indicate the absence of being cognizable by a single causal complex."

For this very reason, even the introduction to the subsequent passage—"If [the fact that] having a single substratum and so forth is the sole determinant for being an inseparably established qualifier"—is not tenable; because, as shown by the aforementioned method, the absence of being cognizable by the same causal complex has not been established previously, it is impossible to restate [the opponent's position] as "only having a single substratum and so forth. Furthermore, the question "How then is there the rule of simultaneous perception? is also improper. For its intended meaning is this: if being cognizable by the same causal complex is not the determinant for being an inseparably established qualifier, then [what is]? Inseparability...

Furthermore, since there is no necessity that qualifiers such as universals (*jāti*) and individuals (*vyakti*) be cognized by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) based upon that would also not exist. For one who objects in this manner, the rebuttal—"The rule of simultaneous apprehension is indeed based on being cognized by the same causal complex"—is improper; for the objection was already formulated precisely by accepting that [basis]. Moreover, the need to supply the words "the rule of simultaneous apprehension exists" with respect to the universal and so forth is also a strained interpretation.

Furthermore, regarding the Bhāṣya statement, "It is difficult to maintain that this [object] has as its sole nature the mode [of cognition] when it is perceived separately," the meaning naturally understood is precisely that it is difficult for that which lacks the necessity of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) to have as its sole nature the mode [of cognition]; therefore, that alone is the appropriate meaning.

Does the intention [of the opponent] be that "that [inherence] does not exist" because there is no proof for its having a single nature as a mode (*prakāra*)? Or is the intention that, since being a mode is its very nature, when an object is perceived as qualified by a certain nature, that object must be perceived as necessarily endowed with that nature; and thus, if inseparable existence (*apṛthaksiddhatva*) were its nature, it would have to be perceived as qualified by that [inherence]? Having raised these alternatives, the first is refuted in the Bhāṣya with the words "like genus and so forth" (*jātyādivat*). The second is refuted in the Bhāṣya with the words "but the rule of simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambhaniyamastu*).

The rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyamaḥ*) means the rule of apprehending [the object] together with its mode of appearance (*prakāratayā*). This is in accordance with the subsequent commentary which states, "it presents [them] together with their mode of appearance. He demonstrates the subverting argument against the accepted rule—that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which grasps an entity must grasp it as qualified by its respective intrinsic nature—by saying, "just as the eye... and so forth.

They say that the point is this: just as the earth's natural connection with smell, taste, and so forth is not perceived [in certain states], it is likewise possible for its being a mode (*prakāra*) of the self residing in the body and its being of the nature of a mode to remain unperceived; therefore, one cannot deny the fact that its sole nature is to be a mode, as established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Regarding "in the second head of the first alternative": the meaning is that the second alternative [is proposed] because being cognizable by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*) is also a contributing factor due to its being a concomitant (*anuyāyin*). Regarding "due to the existence of a concomitant contributing factor": the meaning is due to the existence of a concomitant contributing factor in the form of having the same substratum (*tadekāśrayatva*), and so forth. Regarding "in the case of odor and so forth in the second head": [this refers to the example].

Although it might be argued that—since the state of being an inseparable qualifier (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) has been established in the case of bodies and so forth, which are perceived by distinct causal complexes (*bhinnasāmagrīvedya*), and since no suspicion arises regarding its being the determinant for an inseparable universal (*apṛthaksiddhasāmānya*)—and furthermore, even if "being perceivable by the same causal complex" (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*) were accepted as the determinant for the specific kind of inseparability residing in universals such as *jāti*, that [determinant] could not be rejected; nevertheless, its rejection is irrelevant to the present context.

It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of refuting the misconceptions of others. The word "eka" (one) is intended to exclude [the possibility of being] cognized by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*). The particle "eva" (only/alone) is for the purpose of excluding the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*). Regarding this, some say that it is more appropriate to hold that the word "eka" is intended to exclude the state of not being an objective qualifier (*aprakāratva*), while the particle "eva" is intended to exclude the rule of simultaneous apprehension and being cognized by the same causal complex.

"In the commentary, for the purpose of demonstrating the discrimination of categories (padārtha-viveka)": the sense is that by means of words such as "deity" (*deva*) and so forth, the body and the self cannot be made known through discrimination; however, by means of words such as "body" (*śarīra*) and so forth, they can be made known through discrimination. "They are intended to be restrictive (*vaivakṣika-niṣkarṣaka*)," meaning that they are restrictive when there is an intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). [The suffix] *ṭhañ* is applied because it occurs in the sense of "belonging to an intention," according to the rule *adhyātmādi-tvāt*. "Because there is no difference in their denoting attributes inseparably established [with the substrate], like words denoting a genus (*jāti*)."

If it is argued that, since words such as *nīla* (blue) are similar to words such as *go* (cow), just as words like *go* do not apply to the universal (*jāti*) alone, words like *nīla* should likewise not apply to the quality (*guṇa*) alone—since we do indeed employ expressions such as "the whiteness of the cloth"—this is not so. For although the universal *gotva* (cowness), being the ground for the application of the word *go*, is not the object of the word *go* because it does not reside in itself, the blue color is properly denoted by that word (*nīla*) because it is the substratum of *nīlatva* (blueness), which is the ground for the application of the word *nīla*.

The phrase "for the sake of the grammatical correctness of the word by way of its having three genders" means that if [the suffix] were a secondary derivative (*pratyaya*), then words such as *śukla* would be established as having three genders—just as in the case of *daṇḍavān*, *daṇḍavatī*, and *daṇḍavat*. And it was stated by the venerable Kātyāyana: "The elision of the suffix *matup* should be prescribed after words expressing qualities; and thus the establishment of gender and number is achieved, and it also serves to produce a specific accent. The meaning is that in the case of words such as *nīla*, if one resorts to their being formed with the suffix *aṇ* (as in *aśarādyañ*), the distinction of accent is also established.

"The mention of the elision of the *matup* suffix [in the rule] is for the sake of indicating gender and accent. This means that the mention of the elision of *matup* and so forth is for the purpose of [indicating] gender and accent. Therefore, the objection—that it is improper to state that the elision of *matup* is for the sake of [indicating] accent—is refuted. For this very reason, [it is said]: "of the word *rāga*. In the rule "there is elision (*luk*) of *matup* after words expressing qualities," since the elision of *matup* is prescribed only after words expressing the possessor of a quality by way of the quality itself, there is no elision of *matup* in the case of the word *rāga*, because it is not of such a nature.

In reality, however, since it would follow that words such as *nīla* (blue) would lose their status as denoting a possessor of a quality (*guṇin*)—whether by resorting to the elision of the possessive suffix (*matup*), or by treating the word as ending in the *arśas-* suffix (*ac*), or by metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), or by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—the elision of the *matup* suffix and so forth are certainly not accepted in the final system (*siddhānta*). It should be understood that the three genders are thus justified by the principle: "Gender is not to be taught [by grammar], for it depends on common usage. Furthermore, it is only in relation to earth and the other elements that words such as *gandha* (smell) function as restricted qualifiers (*niyata-niṣkarṣaka*).

Although in usages such as "smell is earth" or "taste is water," it is observed that the words *gandha* (smell) and *rasa* (taste) extend to denote the earth and water themselves, and although one might argue that in those cases they are used metaphorically—making it easy to claim that in passages like "I am the taste in the waters" the Supreme Self is being spoken of metaphorically, since a metaphorical identification with taste would be logical—[the following applies].

In passages such as "I am the taste in the waters," although the word *rasa* refers to that which possesses taste (the quality-bearer), the expression "taste in the waters" would otherwise be improper; nevertheless, the sense is that when many words such as *rasa*, *gandha*, and so forth are applied to the Supreme Self, it is improper to resort to a figurative interpretation when a primary sense is possible.

Because individual instances are infinite, it is impossible to apprehend the expressive power (*śakti*) in all of them; furthermore, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), individuals are not the meaning of words, since a relation is defined by its regularity (*niyama*), and such regularity is impossible when there is no restriction. Moreover, if one were to admit that the expressive power resides in the individual, it would follow that the powers themselves are infinite. Therefore, the universal (*jāti*) alone is the meaning of a word.

Alternatively, as stated by the Bhāṭṭas, the manifestation of the individual (vyakti) will occur either through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or through implication (*ākṣepa*). This is because when a universal (*jāti*) appears as qualified by its very nature—characterized by its dependence on [an individual]—it is impossible for that universal, whose form is essentially defined by the individual, to convey its own nature without taking the individual into account. Therefore, the very causal complex that brings about the manifestation of the universal causes it to be known by including the individual as well. For there is a rule that whatever does not appear without something else must necessarily be conveyed by the conveyor of that other thing.
Nor should it be argued: "If both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are to be conveyed, why should there not be a denotative power (*śakti*) for the individual as well?

For although the cognition whose objects are both the universal and the individual is indistinguishable in being produced by the word, the denotative power is postulated only for the aspect of the universal; this is because only that which cannot be obtained through any other means is a denotatum (*śakya*). As for the aspect of the individual, its apprehension is possible as a necessary consequence (*nāntarīyakatayā*).

Therefore, anticipating the objection that "the cognition of the individual need not be accepted as resulting from implication (ākṣepa) or indication (lakṣaṇā), since the presence of the individual can be accounted for according to the method stated by the Prābhākaras; thus, one need not postulate a denotative power (śakti) for the individual," he refutes this with the section beginning with "Even though words denote the body" (*yadyapi śarīravāciśabdāḥ*). [The meaning is: because being a word that denotes an inseparable qualifier (*ayutasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) acts as an obstacle to indicating the qualified (*viśeṣya*); that is to say, it is impossible for that which is the substratum of the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), such as blueness, to be indicated by that word.

If it is argued: "In the view that [words] denote the universal (jāti), for words such as 'cow' (go), the universal 'cowness' (gotva) is not the ground for application (pravṛttinimitta); rather, that very universal is the word-meaning. Thus, when there is an indication (lakṣaṇā) of the locus by a word denoting the superstratum, what inconsistency is there? We reply: No. It is observed that the indication of the word 'Ganges' (gaṅgā) occurs only with respect to the bank and so forth, which are presented under a form other than its own primary meaning, namely as 'bankness' (tīratva) and the like. However, in this case, the individual (vyakti) is not presented under any other form apart from the universal that constitutes its own primary meaning.

Furthermore, in cases such as "Look at the cow" (*gāṃ paśya*) or "The cow stands here" (*gaur atra tiṣṭhati*), although the universal (*jāti*) is indeed capable of syntactic connection, there is no indication of its incompatibility; therefore, since the cognition of the individual qualified by the universal arises without any consideration of such incompatibility, there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in those instances. On the contrary, in cases such as "The cow is eternal" (*gauḥ nityā*) or "The cow is the universal" (*gauḥ jātiḥ*), the cognition of the universal arises precisely because of the incompatibility of the syntactic connection; thus, it is more appropriate to hold that secondary signification applies to the universal itself. Moreover, it is inconsistent to abandon the individual—which is fit for practical activity such as bringing [the animal]—and accept as the word-meaning the universal, which is unfit for such activity, while the very factors that establish the primary power (*śakti*) of the word pertain to the individual.

Likewise, it would be inconsistent to abandon the power [of words] directed toward individuals—the domain of abundant usage and cognition in expressions such as "the cow is non-eternal," "the cow is white," "the cow possesses a dewlap and so forth," "bind me," "the cow goes," and "bring the cow"—because the intended meaning (tātparya) lies in the forthcoming refutations, such as the fact that suffixes like *tva* and *tal* would become redundant if words like "cow" were to refer exclusively to the genus (*jāti*). This is because the same difficulty regarding the impossibility of establishing a relationship applies equally to words denoting the genus and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that even for words such as "universal" (*jāti*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted at the stage when one perceives the impossibility of a [direct] relation; the point is that figurative indication has never been observed in the case of words denoting universals and the like. [Objection: This is the same even in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Since words denoting universals and so forth are also words denoting qualifiers that are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇa*), why should they not denote the individual (*vyakti*)? Furthermore, the distinction [of those words] from [the word "individual"] by virtue of being "extractive" (*niṣkarṣaka-śabda*) and so on can easily be stated. Nevertheless, the intention here is the refutation previously mentioned.

He refutes the Prābhākara position by stating that the form (*ākṛti*) alone is the object of the word’s power. [The opponent objects: "If it is intended that the dependence characterized by being a qualifier of a substance, unity, and existence is what is meant by the cognition of dependence through a genus-word (*jātiśabda*), then since the denotation of the individual (*vyakti*) is already established, the mention of dependence—whether defined as the incapacity for connection with other qualifiers or defined as the incapacity for the state of being a grammatical factor (*kāraka*)—is redundant."

If it is argued that the sole cause for the designation or non-designation of dependence—characterized by having as its single nature the state of being either perceived or not perceived as a substance—is simply the perception or non-perception of the individual [substance], this is true; however, it should be understood that such a doubt might arise in the mind of some dull-witted person. But [the point remains] that there is a connection with other qualifiers.

Now, one might object: just as in the case of the statement "perceive the genus (jāti) as pervasive," where the genus denoted by the word *jāti* is connected both with another qualifier—namely, its quality of being pervasive—and with the action of seeing as its object (*karman*), so too, in examples such as "the white cow stands," although it has never been observed that the genus understood from the word *go* (cow) is connected with another qualifier or with the action as a grammatical factor (*kāraka*), nevertheless, such dependence is not expressed by the word itself.

If it is argued that the phrase *garvādiśabda* (the word "pride" and so forth) does not convey either the incapacity for connection with other qualifiers or the incapacity for the status of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant)—for when "cow" (*gauḥ*) is uttered, the fact that "cowness" is incapable of being a *kāraka* is not conveyed by the word itself—the answer is: true; however, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) here is that a specific kind of dependence (*pāratantrya*), which is the cause of such incapacity for the status of a *kāraka* and so forth, is indeed conveyed by words such as "cow. Regarding the expression *mukhyārthaguṇasaṃbandhī*: it is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *mukhyārtha* (the primary referent) and *tadguṇa* (its qualities).

The indicated meaning (*lakṣya*) is that which is connected with the primary meaning; the secondary meaning (*gauṇa*) is that which is connected with the qualities residing in that [primary meaning]. The rebuttal—that "the absence of frequent usage" does not hold because of the absence of frequent usage—is untenable. Nor is it the case that the phrase "because of the absence of frequent usage regarding the genus (*jāti*), since words such as 'cow' have a conventional indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) directed toward the individual (*vyakti*)" means that there is frequent usage regarding the individual but an absence of frequent usage regarding the genus; rather, it simply means "there is an absence of frequent usage."

Therefore, it should not be said that this is an "unspoken censure" (anuktopālambha). Since the statement "because of frequent usage in reference to the individual" (vyaktau pracuraprayogāt) results in the meaning "because of the absence of frequent usage in reference to the genus" (jātau pracuraprayogābhāvāt), there is no such thing as an unspoken censure. Regarding the phrase "because of the observation of independence from an abstract suffix" (bhāvapratyayānapekṣatvadarśanāt), the meaning is: "because of the observation in some cases of even independence from an abstract suffix. Consequently, it should be understood that the observation in some instances—such as in "the whiteness of the cloth" (paṭasya śauklyam)—of dependence upon an abstract suffix does not constitute a fault.

In the case of genus (*jāti*), however, nowhere is independence from abstract suffixes observed; the point is that usages such as "the cow of Khaṇḍa" or "the cow of Muṇḍa," which have genus as their object, are never seen [to occur without such suffixes]. He establishes the acceptance of conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) with the words "for words such as 'white'... and so on. If it is argued that "conventional usage" (*nirūḍhi*) means being followed in all applications...

The meaning is: if it is argued that what is called *nirūḍhalakṣaṇā* (established secondary signification) is that which follows from all applications (*sarvaprayoga*), and not merely that which follows from frequent application (*pracuraprayoga*). [The opponent says: "The usage of the word 'cow' (*gavyavahāra*) is continuous. However, this should be viewed as merely superficial; for here we observe usage that does not depend on an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), and this would contradict the previous text which states, "And the independence from an abstract suffix is difficult to maintain. [The author replies: "In your view, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*)."

The meaning is: for those who maintain that both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are the denotata of a word. [The opponent argues: "The substance (*dravya*), which serves as the counter-correlate (*pratisambandhin*), must be perceived as subordinate (*upasarjanatayā*). [The proponent replies: "The universal must have the individual as its substratum, because it is a universal; thus, the individual, being implied, appears as subordinate, just like fire in the statement 'the mountain possesses fire' (*parvato vahnimān*). [The opponent gives another example: "It is like [the relationship between] a son and a father."

The meaning is that, just as there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word "father" (which implies the father by the word "son") and the word "son," so too coreferentiality cannot occur between words denoting a genus and an individual—such as "cow" and "Khaṇḍa"—when they function as the implied and the implied-upon respectively. Regarding the term *vivakṣita* ("intended"): it means "the object of the speaker's intention" (*tātparyaviṣaya*). He explains the phrase *viśeṣyatvena* ("as the qualificand") by the term *pradhānatayā* ("as the primary element"). The phrase *tadavacchedārthatvāt tasya* ("because it serves to delimit that") means that the father is mentioned for the purpose of excluding [others] from the son.

Alternatively, the syntactical connection is: "because it has that [the object] as its purpose by way of being primary. Its delimitation is its relation [to the object] by virtue of its being primary; [the word denotes the agent] because it has that [delimitation] as its purpose.

This means "because of making [the primary object] predominant. Regarding the phrase "by way of being related to the intended meaning," he states the example "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) as the thing to be excluded by the word "intended" (*vivakṣita*). In reality, it is the bank itself that is related to the Gaṅgā, and it appears precisely as a bank; it does not appear as being related to the Gaṅgā. Nevertheless, if both the current were understood through primary denotation (*śakti*) and the bank through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), there would be the consequence of a contradiction between two modes of operation (*vṛtti*). Therefore, the current is not intended [as the primary object].

The sense is that the universal (*jāti*), however, possesses the status of being the object (*viṣayatva*) in the cognition of the word. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); for since the bank (*tīra*) is presented through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it appears as the primary [meaning], whereas the individual (*vyakti*)—which is merely implied and not presented by the word's own function—cannot possibly appear as the primary [meaning]. This is the intended meaning here.

The intended sequence of the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: if the individual cow were not denoted by the word "cow," while appearing as related to the object intended by the word's primary purport, then it would not be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by the word "cow. Regarding the phrase "conjoined with a word-qualifier" (*śabda-viśeṣaṇa-upaśliṣṭa*): the meaning is that a thing presented by a word can only function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) toward another thing presented by a word, and not toward something merely implied (*ākṣipta*).

This refers to the identity of the qualifiers (*prakāra*) and the identity of the cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇa*). The meaning is that both the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* have the nature of consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*), and there is an identity between those two. As for the objection that "a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) should be suspected": although there is no occasion for a split in the sentence because it has been established that "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is of the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*), nevertheless, this [objection] should be understood as being stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position].
(A summary of the inconsistency of grammatical coreferentiality [*sāmānādhikaraṇya*] according to the opponent’s view.)

Regarding the phrase "if one accepts [the properties] as qualifiers, [then Brahman would be] primary": the meaning is that, in order to avoid the redundancy of other words, if one accepts the exclusions (vyāvṛtti) indicated by the words "real" (satya) and so forth as qualifiers, then let the primary qualities of reality and so forth themselves be the qualifiers, since there is no distinction between them. This is as I intend.

Although the opponents have not presented as a formal proof the argument that the cognition "I desire" would be untenable if the word "I" did not denote desire and so forth as qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—since the absence of the word "I" denoting desire qualified by the internal organ is established by the very lack of evidence for its denoting pots and the like qualified by the internal organ—nevertheless, this [argument] has been formulated with the intention that the untenability of desire being a qualifier in the cognition "I desire" can also be made into a proof.

This must be observed: it is not the case that cognition (*jñapti*) alone qualifies the cognizer (*jña*). The point is that if cognition were the very nature of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*), then the status of being the substratum of cognition—as experienced in the thought "I know"—would not belong to the "I-sense. Regarding the phrase "with the intention of explaining its meaning": since, in the state of delusion, there is no cognition at all of the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is no such usage with the intention of explaining its meaning; and even though the cognition of the substrate is possible in the state of awakening, there is still no such usage with the intention of explaining its meaning. This is the sense.

"The root [of the usage] is that it denotes Yajñadatta. One should not say, "Even this is indeed desired by you," for if that were so, it would follow that the distinction between what is denotable and what is non-denotable would be destroyed; such is the sense. Regarding the phrase "even when the word 'serpent' is applied to a rope": the meaning of the expression "the rope is a serpent" occurring at the time of waking is this: "For all this time, due to the cognition of the rope as being a real serpent, the rope was the object of the application of the word 'serpent'. Regarding the phrase "having a superimposed object": [this refers to the state where the word applies to something that has been mentally projected].

The meaning is that the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the locus upon which an object is superimposed. Regarding the second [interpretation], it refers to the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. The point is that by the word "thou" (*tvaṃ*), only the essential nature of the substratum in its state as the individual soul is intended to be expressed, while the state of being the individual soul itself is not intended to be expressed. Thus, the phrase "that whose qualifying attribute is unintended" means that the state of being the individual soul is the qualifying attribute that is not intended to be expressed.

If, by the mere cognition of the identity of the pure consciousness (cinmātra) related to the individual soul (jīva)—which is the primary referent of the word "thou" (tvaṃ)—the identity of the individual soul with Brahman (which is the primary referent of the word "that," tat), the falsity of bondage such as agency and so forth related to that primary referent, and the ultimate reality of that [bondage] as being merely its substrate are established, then likewise, upon the cognition of the identity of the person (jana) who is the secondary indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) of the word "janapada" (country) with the Brahmin (brahmaṣṭa), there would also follow the identity of the primary referent of the word "janapada" and the falsity of properties such as "being a country" (janapadatva) which belong to that primary referent.

And he establishes that its ultimate reality consists merely in its being the locus of those properties, stating: "For [it is not the case that] 'the country has abandoned the Brahmin,'" and "there is the prescription of its being that. This means: there is the prescription of its being the referent of the word "that" (tat). Regarding the phrase "by way of a difference in locus with respect to cognition," the meaning is: by way of a difference in locus between the word "you" (tvam) and the verbal root "to know" (jñā), as in the expression "you know."

Even though there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a portion of the expressed meaning (*vācya*), since the non-difference between the primary meanings is not established, and since the falsity of the properties of the primary meanings—which would be based on that [non-difference]—is likewise not established, he provides an example: "For [in the case of] 'the mountain is burning,' etc. In the sentence "The mountain is burning," the word "mountain" indicates a portion of the mountain included within its expressed meaning, and the word "burning" indicates its substratum. Consequently, there would be identity only between the two indicated [meanings].

However, it does not follow that the primary meanings of the two terms—the mountain and the fire—nor the attributes of the mountain such as its ridges and trees, nor the attributes of the fire which is the primary meaning of the word "blazing," such as its nature as fire (*vahnitva*) and its power to burn (*dagdhṛtva*), are established as being unreal. Likewise, in this context, the identity of the primary meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* would not be established, nor would the falsity of their respective attributes, such as limited knowledge (*kiṃcijjñatva*) and omniscience (*sarvajñatva*), be established; such is the intended sense.

Although it is not the view of others that the identity of the individual soul (*mukhya*) and the Supreme (*artha*) is what is understood, nevertheless, this should be seen as stated by relying on the established doctrine of that school [the Bhedābheda-vādins] that the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman (*brāhṛa*) is understood. For according to the Yādava school, there exists a whole (*aṃśin*) called Brahman distinct from the conscious (*cit*), the unconscious (*acit*), and the Lord (*īśvara*). However, in the Bhāskara school, one should note the distinction that there is no substance (*dravya*) called Brahman which serves as a whole distinct from the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord. As for the phrase "identity in some form": [this refers to the specific mode of unity].

The meaning is that although there is no non-difference between a jar and a cloth due to their common property of being substances (*dravyatva*), a distinction characterized by the presence or absence of the grounds for applying the terms "jar" and "cloth" is perceived; yet, one does not observe that non-difference is expressed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Regarding the phrase "in the form of cause and effect": the meaning is that there is difference in the form of effects such as jars and bowls, whereas there is non-difference in the form of the causal clay. Regarding the phrase "just as there is difference, so too is there non-difference": the meaning is even when both difference and non-difference are admitted. Regarding the phrase "the difference of parts of the cloth": the word "of those employed" (*prayuktānām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Because there is not even a partial non-difference from the substantive denoted by the words *paṭa* (cloth) and *abda* (year). Now, one might argue: "Since the terms *vyakta* (the manifest), *avyakta* (the unmanifest), *puruṣa* (the person), and *kāla* (time) bring to mind the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller respectively—as in the statement, 'The manifest is Viṣṇu, as well as the unmanifest, the person, and time'—and since it is possible for the word *brahman* to function with a meaning that does not exceed those [entities], grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established; thus, there is no inconsistency. To this we say: No.

The intent of the critique is that although the nature of being Brahman (*brāhmatva*) may be common [to all], in statements such as "the manifest is Viṣṇu," the Lordship (*īśvaratva*) denoted by the word "Viṣṇu" is absent from both the conscious and unconscious portions; therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Viṣṇu—as in "the manifest is Viṣṇu, and likewise the unmanifest"—is impossible. This is because, while the usage "the jar is clay, the bowl is clay" is possible, the usage "the jar is the bowl" is not.

One might inquire: by the word "hand, etc.," is the sense organ (indriya) such as the hand or foot intended, or rather its physical substrate (golaka)? Having thus raised this dilemma, he refutes the first alternative with the words, "even in the case of cutting, etc. This is an elliptical expression; it should be understood that because the sense organs—which endure until the end of the kalpa—do not perish even when the body is destroyed, they cannot be non-separately established attributes (apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇa). He refutes the second alternative with the words, "of each respective physical substrate."

Even in the view that there is both difference and non-difference by way of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikabhedābheda*), from the passage beginning with "even in the case of... up to the end of "...co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) indeed," since co-referentiality brings about the cognition of identity, it brings about the cognition of the identity of the entity as qualified by those attributes; however, it does not bring about the cognition of the identity of distinct entities. If it were otherwise, there would be the fault of the meaning being contradicted (*bādhitārthatva*).

The sense is that this follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Regarding the phrase "because the intended oneness is not established": if what is intended is identity with another existent (*sadantara*), that is unestablished; and if what is intended is non-difference from mere existent-substance (*saddravyamātra*), then since that is already established by perception, the instruction would be redundant—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "if it is a unique form belonging to a specific part": the meaning is "the state of being the Lord" (*īśvaratva*). Regarding the phrase "co-referentiality with a word denoting a part other than that": the sense is that it would be like saying "the pot is the bowl" (*ghaṭaḥ śarāvaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "another unique form": the meaning is "such as Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇatva*) and so forth. (This concludes the presentation of the summary of the established doctrine.)

Regarding the statement "from the root *pā* in the sense of protection": this means that [the word *pati*] ends in the suffix *ḍati* according to the rule *pāterḍatiḥ*. Regarding the phrase "and because of the usage of the word *pati*": this means because of its usage in the form *gṛhapati* ("householder"). The word *pati* is established by convention (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the one who possesses the remainder (*śeṣin*). For this very reason, in the rule *antarvat-pativator nuk*, since it is stated that the augment *nuk* applies specifically in the sense of "husband" (*bhartṛ*), the Mahābhāṣya provides a counter-example—taking for granted that the sense of "owner" (*svāmin*) is indeed the sense of the possessor (*śeṣin*)—in the form: *tvayā patimatī pṛthivī* ("by you, the earth is possessed of a lord").

Regarding the phrase "patnī yajñasaṃyoge," the venerable Patañjali stated: "This word *pati* denotes sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Pāṇini also made this meaning of sovereignty explicit in the rule "patyāvaiśvarye. Furthermore, Jaimini, in the ninth book, conducted an inquiry into the modification (*ūha*) and non-modification (*anūha*) of mantras, taking for granted that the term *meghapati* signifies the master (*svāmin*), as in the rule: "The status of being a *meghapati* belongs to both the master and the deity due to their conjunction. Therefore, there is no disagreement regarding its denotation of the master.

For this very reason, when it is stated that he is the "Lord of the universe" (*viśvasya patim*), the subsequent negation of any other master in the phrase "the Lord of himself" (*ātmeśvaram*) is appropriate for the purpose of excluding the possibility of another superior lord even over him. Furthermore, the word *pati*—which, although synonymous with "husband," also signifies a "master" or "supporter" as in the list "husband, beloved, lord, supporter" (*dhavaḥ priyaḥ patirbhartā*)—is distinct [from the ordinary sense].

In the case of the expression *meghapatibhyāṃ megham*, since it is used even for a deity, and because Jaimini has demonstrated that the terms for "lord" (*svāmin*) and "deity" (*devatā*) share a common application in the statement, "The state of being the lord of the cloud arises from the inherence [of ownership] in both the owner and the deity," one should observe that whether or not there is a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in that sense is optional; however, no disagreement can be maintained regarding its meaning as the "principal" (*śeṣin*), which is a synonym for "owner" (*svāmin*) and "ruler" (*īśvara*). Furthermore, the *Nighaṇṭu* states: "A wealthy man, one who is affluent, a rich man, an owner, a leader, a husband, and a ruler."

"By the force of the second-case [accusative] ending, as in the case of *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) and so forth. This means that just as the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*)—characterized by being a desired end—is established for rice-grains (*vrīhi*), which possess the state of being an object to be accomplished as taught by the second-case ending, through their connection with the *bhāvanā* (efficient force) that requires a desired end by virtue of the power of the scriptural statement; likewise, even in the absence of words such as "lord" (*pati*), the relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) is established for the universe, whose status as a body is understood from scripture, by the implication of its being a body. [The Sūtra states: "Because it is for the sake of another, being a composite, and because of the reversal of the three attributes (*guṇa*) and so forth, and because of superintendence... [Sāṃkhya Kārikā 17].

"The Spirit exists because there must be an enjoyer, and because there is activity for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*). This is a verse from the *Sāṃkhya*. Since every composite entity necessarily exists for the sake of another—just like a bed, a seat, and so forth—it follows that the body, being a composite, is established as existing for the sake of another; this is the meaning. By the phrase "the other is unborn" (*ajo 'nyaḥ*) from the scripture, he intends to demonstrate the distinctness [of the Spirit] from Nature (*prakṛti*) when one is liberated upon casting off Nature; thus he says, "he states the difference in liberation," beginning with "the unborn. This is because it follows immediately after the discussion concerning the Pradhāna.

The point is that although the preceding statement, “separately [from Me] the Self,” does not involve a reference to the *pradhāna*, nevertheless, because the subsequent statement does involve a reference to the *pradhāna*, there is a logical connection with it. Regarding the phrase “by the word ‘mine’”: the meaning is that it is by means of the genitive case, which indicates distinction (*vyatireka*). Regarding the phrase “non-confusion of intrinsic natures” (*svabhāvāsaṃkara*): the meaning is the non-confusion of intrinsic natures such as being the presiding overseer (*adhyakṣatva*) and so forth.

Since the context concerns dissolution (*laya*), it is stated that even *tamas* undergoes dissolution itself; thus, one might raise the objection that the theory of the transformation of Brahman (*brāhmapariṇāmavāda*) would thereby be accepted. To ward off this doubt, it is said: "It is merely the unification of *tamas*. This means that the portion of *tamas* transformed into the forms of the imperishable (*akṣara*), the manifest (*vyakta*), the Great Principle (*mahat*), and so forth, and the portion of *tamas* remaining untransformed, attain unity. This too is a definition of a body (*śarīra*).

The meaning is that being governed by entering within—possessing the three characteristics previously stated, such as "the substance belonging to which conscious being"—is also a definition of the body intended by the author of the Bhāṣya.

"Even in the absence of hearing [the word] 'entry' (anupraveśa)"—this is the sense in the passage, "It was differentiated by name and form. For the maxim of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*) consists in the fact that a general term finds its final application in a specific term that has been brought to mind. However, since the state of being preceded by entry does not fall within the essential nature of the differentiation of name and form, it cannot be conveyed by a specific term; therefore, because this [case] cannot be the subject of the maxim of the general and the particular, he says, out of dissatisfaction: "Or rather, 'all the Śākhās'..."

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "by means of the apprehension of the grāhaka": the *grāhaka* is the *apūrva* that possesses an office (*sādhikāra*), meaning the *paramāpūrva* which possesses a fruit. The *apūrva* understood from the sentence, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," is the *paramāpūrva*.

The "apprehension by the grāhaka" refers precisely to the denotation of its own meanings—such as the *prayāja* offerings and the threshing of rice—which are characterized as effects (tasks) associated with the *paramāpūrva*, by those sentences recited in proximity to it, such as "He offers the *samidhs*" and "He threshes the rice," which have the inherent nature of denoting meanings already connected to a task (*kārya*).

By such a grasping by the "grasper" (*grāhaka*), in all instances—whether they be substances, qualities, or actions, or entities existing as the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*)—where the subservience to the grasper is understood like a pigeon in a threshing floor, the status of the sacrifice as a subordinate without an intermediary (*advāraka-śeṣatva*) is determined through its being the instrument (*karaṇa*). The meaning is that the subsidiarity of the rice (*vrīhi*) is determined through the sacrifice, and the subsidiarity of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites is determined through the rice, by means of the grasper-evidences such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) regarding the subservience to the instrument and the subservience to the intermediary. This is expressed by the phrase, "by the grasping by the grasper [with the thought] 'May I become manifold'."

The Supreme Self stands in the place of the grasper, and its grasping is volition (*saṃkalpa*). Regarding this, it has been explained somewhat; the meaning is that it was previously explained in detail.

"In both ways, there is fitness for the designation 'knowledge'. Although the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in the phrase "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) does not have this specific meaning [of being characterized by the quality of knowledge], it should nevertheless be understood as a statement of the resulting implication. The meaning is that both [interpretations] are tenable. In this regard, it should be observed that because the term "knowledge" signifies "having knowledge as its quality" according to the principle "because that is its essential attribute" (*tadguṇāsāratvāt*), it is actually quite consistent [with the former interpretation].

In the commentary beginning with "by the power of Brahman alone through its own volition," the term *brāhṛ* (of Brahman) is explained as "possessing bodies of the nature of the stable and the moving" (*sthiratrasaśarīratayā*), in accordance with the natural sense of the word *brāhṛ* as referring to the extracted Supreme Self (*niṣkṛṣṭaparamātmaparatva*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "not having Brahman as its self" (*abrāhṛātmaka*), the word *brāhṛ* is explained as referring solely to the Supreme Self, stating that it denotes the absence of being presided over by Brahman as the inner controller (*brāhṛantaryāmikatvarahitatva*).

Intending that the word "Brahman" refers to the reality qualified by the sentient and the non-sentient in accordance with the natural force of the phrase "by way of having the form of the stable and the moving," he explains it as follows: "Or else, [it is explained] by way of having the form of the stable and the moving. This is because the scriptural texts concerning unity have as their purport unity in terms of mode (*prakāra*). However, this should be understood as a supplementary point to the first position, following the analogy of a lion’s backward glance (*siṃhāvalokita*). Regarding the Bhāṣya passage, "Everything would cast him away": "Everything," acting as the agent, would "cast him away," meaning it would exclude him.
"Exhaled" means produced without effort, that is to say, manifested by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Regarding the phrase "aindrāgnaśca" (and the offering to Indra and Agni), the reading "aindrau dvau āgneyaśca" (two offerings to Indra and one to Agni) is correct; it constitutes six offerings. However, some have offered this interpretation regarding the reading "aindrāgnaśca": the offering to Agni (āgneya) should be performed on both the full moon and the new moon days as a single act, just like the Agnihotra oblation which is performed in the evening and morning. This is because no other word or linguistic element is perceived that would establish a distinction between separate ritual acts (*karmabheda*).

For this very reason, in the eighth [book], regarding the sūtra: "There is an option in a single action because there is no division, since the injunction is one," it is stated that because the single Āgneya sacrifice bears both the name *paurṇamāsī* and the name *amāvāsyā*, when it is performed at the time of the full moon, it bears the name *amāvāsyā*. Consequently, by virtue of the scriptural injunction, "One should touch the *amāvāsyā* with the Pañcahotṛ mantra," why should the application of the Pañcahotṛ mantra not also occur at the full moon? If it is argued that there is no deficiency (*avaiguṇya*) in the Āgneya, that is true; there is indeed no deficiency in the Āgneya.

Because that [day] possesses both designations, if one were to touch the oblations—such as the Agniṣomīya and others—which are to be performed at that time together with it, there would be a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) due to the absence of the designation "Amāvāsyā. Therefore, it has been determined that for the sake of favoring those [oblations] as well, the touching performed must indeed be accomplished by means of the *caturhotṛ* formula.

Nor can it be doubted that, because one touches the *āgneya* with the *pañcahotṛ* formula, why could one not touch the *agnīṣomīya* and other offerings with the *caturhotṛ* formula? For it is prescribed for only one [offering] that "one touches the oblations placed nearby. Here, by examining the texts such as the *Duṣṭīkā*, which state that "the distinction is made solely on the basis of favoring different oblations," it follows that there is only a single rite called *āgneya* included within both the Full Moon and New Moon triads; there is no division of the *āgneya* rite itself.

If there were a difference [between the two acts], then since the application of the Pañcahotṛ-mantra would not even arise in the case of the touching of the Āgneya cake at the time of the Full Moon sacrifice within the archetype (prakṛti), the doubt regarding the lack of fixed rule and its subsequent resolution would be irrelevant. Consequently, it is logical that there is only one single ritual act connected with two times, just as the ritual act called Agnihotra is connected with the two times of evening and morning. Therefore, the completion of the number six must be effected by means of the offering to Indra-Agni prescribed for one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice.

In this context, "by originative injunctions" refers to such statements as: "The cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni is constant at the new moon and the full moon. An "originative injunction" (utpattivākya) is a statement that produces the initial cognition [of a ritual act]. The reading "separately originated but not separately explained" is more appropriate than the sequence of the manuscript. The meaning is that, having unified them by way of their being means to heaven, the text enjoins them as things to be performed.

Having unified and combined those two groups, [the Vedic injunction] prescribes them as something to be performed by one who desires [heaven], in the form of being a means to attain heaven. The meaning is that it prescribes them as a means, in the sense that "one should so employ them that all six sacrifices together become the means to attain heaven. Alternatively, the construction is: "having unified, that which stands [as such]. The meaning is that the action exists as a single composite whole.

The Supreme Self alone is both in the state of cause and in the state of effect. This is the sequence of the logical connection (*anvaya*) here: statements such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "All this has that as its self," and "All this is indeed Brahman," which refer to three distinct entities—the agent, the object, and the instrument—demonstrate through the phrasing of words joined with terms like "Being" (*sat*), "Brahman," and so forth, that the entity in the causal state and the entity in the effected state are one and the same. [This is done] by means of words that denote the Supreme Self alone.

The meaning is: "by means of words such as 'akṣara' (the Imperishable) and 'sarvajña' (the Omniscient). He demonstrates the semantic power [of these terms] with the words "of consciousness and the unconscious," etc. He demonstrates the etymological power [of the terms] with the words "the words 'sat' and 'vahu'," etc. To point out the cause for the disparity between the example and the thing exemplified would be of little fruit.

Since it might be unsatisfactory that the word *ātman*, though denoting the pervader, does not by the force of its own meaning (*śabdasāmarthya*) bring to mind the pervaded, and because there is a concern regarding a transformation of its own nature (*svarūpapariṇāma*), he introduces the commentary with the words "of Him whose body consists of conscious and unconscious entities" (*cidacidvastuśarīriṇaḥ*) in order to dispel that suspicion. Alternatively, [he introduces it] with the verse: "From the Imperishable, the universe here comes into being. Regarding the phrase "by the logic of the *pṛṣadājya*": the meaning is that just as, for the purpose of consecrating the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter), another vessel is employed even though it was not specifically enjoined, so it is here.

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is prescribed that "one takes eight portions in the upabhṛt ladle"; thus, two sets of four portions for the prayājas and anūyājas are taken simultaneously into a single upabhṛt. This same procedure applies to the animal sacrifice (*paśu*). However, regarding the anūyājas therein, a modification of the substance is heard in the text: "One performs the anūyājas with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*). *Pṛṣadājya* is simply clarified butter mixed with curd.

In this regard, since the non-confusion of the two [substances] is inevitable, the consideration arises: should both be taken in that same vessel at different times, or at one and the same time in separate vessels? Regarding this, the scriptural text "He takes eight portions in the *upabhṛt* vessel" establishes the unity of the vessel. However, the sequence of ritual acts (*padārtha-krama*) is a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) of the acts themselves, and it is to be inferred from the order of recitation (*pāṭha*). Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that one should take the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) in the same vessel, and after the *prayāja* offerings have been made, the speckled butter should be taken again. To this, it is replied: "Because both the unity of the vessel and the sequence are subordinate to the act of taking both."
"And when [the procedure] is obtained through inference in a modification (vikṛti), the relative strength [of the rules] is equal.

Thus, since there is no distinction, there is no reason for not performing the taking of the clarified butter for the after-offerings (anūyāja) which is present by virtue of the taking of the butter for the fore-offerings (prayāja); therefore, one should take it at that very time using another vessel. This was considered [in the following]: "In a modification, however, there should be a difference of vessels for the after-offerings because of the difference in purpose."

However, some maintain that since the meaning of the term *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter)—which is clarified butter mixed with curds—is capable of being denoted by the word *ājya* (butter) alone, the unmodified form *ājyapān* ("those who drink the butter") is used in the ritual invocations (*nigada*) such as "Bring the butter-drinkers," and not the modified form *pṛṣadājyapān* ("those who drink the speckled butter"); this was determined in the tenth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]. Similarly, they argue that here too, the use of a word denoting only the substantive is appropriate when applied to the one who presides over both the conscious and the unconscious.
(The impossibility of cessation.)

By the phrase "because of being capable of causal efficiency" (*arthakriyākāritvāt*), the impossibility of [the world] being a cause is stated; by the phrase "because of having an origin" (*utpattimattvāt*), the impossibility of its being an effect is to be understood. Furthermore, since dependence upon a cause is not observed [in the case of Brahman], the sense is that it is not logical for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) to be false, as it does indeed depend upon that [cause]. Nor is the causal complex of a sprout, etc., the same as the causal complex of an error; this means that it is not the causal complex of that [specific] error. [The phrase] "of the cognition of non-difference whose object is different" refers to...

The meaning is: of the cognition of non-difference that arises with respect to an object that is in fact distinct. As for the question of why the scriptural passage, "He who separates the Self," is cited after the Smṛti passage, "But the Supreme Person is another," he says: "of the two Smṛtis and the word [of Śruti]. The meaning is: for the sake of confirming the two Smṛti passages.

Regarding the term *dāvānala*: the meaning is that just as a forest fire (*dāvānala*) perishes by itself upon the exhaustion of its fuel after having destroyed that fuel, so it is here. As for the question, "What is the knowledge that brings about cessation, and what is its destruction?"; if it is argued: "Since it is the destruction itself that is perceived as the object of refutation, how can you say that the intended alternative is whether that knowledge is distinct from Brahman or not?"—we reply: No, for the falsity of destruction does not consist solely in its being distinct from Brahman.

However, it has been stated that the alternative regarding the sublation-cognition (*nivartakajñāna*)—whether it is distinct from the nature of Brahman and so forth—is intended to highlight the flaw that because the sublation-cognition is false, its counter-correlative destruction (*vināśa*) is also false. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* states, "because their nature, origination, and destruction are conceptual (*kālpanika*)," thereby declaring that the very nature of cognition is conceptual.

If it is asked: "In that case, since it must be stated that only the destruction of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) is conceptual, for what purpose is the statement that the arising of knowledge is conceptual?"—the answer is: no, because its presentation is justified as being by way of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). However, some maintain: "Since [the phrase] 'by the conceptuality of its nature, its arising, and its destruction' serves to establish the conceptuality of destruction, and since in the *Bhāṣya* passage, 'its destruction is indeed the very nature of Brahman,' only destruction is perceived, it is more appropriate to adopt [the conceptuality of] destruction alone."

Therefore, they say that regarding the knowledge that brings about cessation (*nivartakajñāna*), the alternative view of those who maintain [the self] is distinct from Brahman does not lead to the heart's desire. This means "of ignorance (*avidyā*) of such a nature. It should be understood that this is stated thus by way of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*). "A location such as the courtyard of a house delimited by a specific time" means a particular place qualified by a particular time. If it is argued, "The objection is equal for you as well," the intention is that there would be no destruction of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of all karma without remainder.

Regarding the phrase "with the intention of [excluding] conceptual construction" (*vikalpābhiprāyeṇa*): if one were to state, "of the knowledge whose object is the negation of everything other than Brahman," without mentioning "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*), then since it would be possible for some things other than pure consciousness to be included within the referent of the word "Brahman," there would be no negation of the ultimate reality of everything other than pure consciousness when negating the ultimate reality of everything other than the referent of the word "Brahman. Consequently, because that [reality] would not be the object of negation, the objection—that [Brahman] would be the object of the negating knowledge—would fail to apply. Therefore, [the term] "pure consciousness" is used.

The sense is that the word *padam* (the term) is necessary. Regarding the phrase "first, the question of the substratum" (*dharmipraśna*): it should be understood that this was stated because the alternative views concerning the attribute of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) will be presented later on. Considering that if the word *svarūpam* were taken in its literal sense, the commentary’s refutation—"if the nature of Brahman itself were the knower"—would be inconsistent, he says: "the meaning is that 'nature' (*svarūpam*) refers to what is inherent (*svābhāvikam*). In the commentary, the words "if it were superimposed" (*adhyastaṃ cet*), "this superimposition," "another ignorance which is its root," and so forth [are used].

The meaning is that the superimposed knowerhood—which is characterized by being the substratum for the knowledge that effects [the removal of ignorance]—and the ignorance that causes it, do not contradict [the true nature of Brahman], because they are conducive to the knowledge that effects [liberation] and are dependent upon that [liberating] knowledge; therefore, they are not sublated by it. Regarding this, they say that the portion of the text following the introductory commentary (*avatārikā*) to the concluding commentary (*upasaṃhāra-bhāṣya*) beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) has been omitted due to a scribe's error. In the *Bhāṣya*, it says: "Because that too possesses a threefold form."

The meaning is that [the objection] holds because another subverting cognition would depend upon the ignorance (avidyā) and the knower (mātṛ), thereby possessing three forms [of contradiction]. He refutes the first alternative in the Commentary with the words: "if the nature of the Brahman itself were the knower. This means that the state of being a knower would be inherent to the nature of Brahman. He says in the Commentary: "because the destruction of that [ignorance] is admitted to be the very nature of Brahman," implying that this may well be the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha).

"Therefore, [the qualification] 'of one who possesses the fourfold means' (sādhanacatuṣṭaya). The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is the term to be explained. "A form devoid of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of the knowledge of the true nature of the Self" means that it is a "mere form" (*kevalākāra*), characterized by the absence of being preceded by the knowledge of the Lord's supremacy (*śeṣatva*). The meaning is that neither abandonment (*hāna*) nor acquisition (*upādāna*) is possible. The meaning is that for one who has not yet engaged in the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), a superficial understanding—that the meditation on Brahman (*brāhmopāsana*), which consists of the obligatory and occasional rites as its constituent parts, is the means for attaining the infinite and eternal Brahman—cannot possibly arise.

However, it should be understood that by the words "rejection" (*hāna*) and "acceptance" (*upādāna*), non-performance and performance are not intended; for although such non-performance and performance of ritual acts may be useful for the meditation on the *brāhmaṇa* texts, they are not useful at the point when the status of being a prerequisite for the inquiry into the *brahman* (*brahmavicāra*) is being discussed, as they are not useful for that specific inquiry.
(Regarding the body of the *Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa*):

Now, what is the intention of one who says, "The statement is contradictory"? After providing the construction of the words of the Sūtra as "inquiry must be performed," there follows the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "it need not be performed."

Intending to present the following alternatives—namely, whether the demonstration [of the subject matter] is improper, or whether such a presentation is not appropriate because the author of the Sūtras did not indicate that the word *vyutpatti* (derivation/acquisition of meaning) is already established—one first refutes the former with the words: "In the case of 'Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma' (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*)," etc. This is because, according to the Prābhākaras, the purpose of Vedic study is to qualify one for the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*).

The point is this: in both views, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that inquiry need not be undertaken because study does not have the purpose of understanding the meaning; and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it must be undertaken because it does have the purpose of understanding the meaning—thus, these two positions are identical. In the Bhaṭṭa school, having raised the prima facie argument that inquiry into *dharma* need not be undertaken because study has heaven as its purpose (according to the principle of the "wish-granting cow") and thus lacks the purpose of understanding the meaning, [the author] concludes that since an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) is possible, it is improper to postulate another unseen result; therefore, the fruit is indeed the understanding of the meaning itself.

Furthermore, it was established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that one should not suspect the injunction to be redundant on the grounds that the fact that study is a means for knowing the meaning is already established; for it is justified as being for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*). However, according to the *Guru-mata*:
"The Veda (*svādhyāya*) exists for the sake of the mandate (*niyoga*) to become a teacher, because it is prompted by that;
since it is understood first, that indeed is the appropriate purpose."
But the cognition of the sentence-meaning does not arise [at that time], for that is understood only later;
therefore, because the Veda has no intended meaning [for its own sake], there is an investigation into its meaning.
"Therefore, the treatise called Mīmāṃsā should not be composed, as it would be purposeless.

Regarding the injunction "One's own Veda should be studied," when there is an expectation for a purpose for the study of one's own Veda, the very mandate to become a teacher (*ācāryaka-niyoga*) is its purpose, because it is the first thing understood. It is not, however, the knowledge of the meaning, because that occurs later. Even though the status of being a teacher is "external" (*bahiraṅga*) insofar as it pertains to another person, nevertheless, because it is the first thing understood, it is logical that the accomplishment of that [status] alone is its purpose; it is not the knowledge of the meaning, because that occurs later.

Therefore, because the study of the Veda serves another purpose, its literal meaning is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). And that which is not intended to be expressed need not be determined, as there is no purpose in determining it. Since an undetermined meaning does not deserve investigation, the Mīmāṃsā system—which consists of such [investigation]—is not to be commenced due to its lack of utility; such is the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). How is it that the study [of the Veda] is prompted by the injunction to perform the ritual acts (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), and not prompted by the injunction for study itself? It is said in reply: In the injunction regarding one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), there is no person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).

And in that case, since [an eligible person] does not exist, it is not logical for [the injunction] to have the status of an impeller (*prayojaka*), as in the case of the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. For an injunction whose subject lacks an eligibility (*adhikāra*) cannot possibly possess the capacity to cause the performance of its own object, just like the injunctions for the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Furthermore, no eligible person is heard mentioned in the injunction for Vedic study. Therefore, it is impossible for this [injunction] to function as an impeller.
