"Nor can an eligible person be postulated here, as in the case of the *pitṛyajña*; for even when such a person is not postulated, the performance of the rite is well-established."

It might be argued that even though he is not explicitly heard [in the text], the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is to be inferred, as in the case of the *pitṛyajña*. That is not so; for the performance of the rite is established even without such an inference. Once that [performance] is established, it is not possible to infer a person to be enjoined, because there would be no logical inconsistency [otherwise]. For an injunction (*niyoga*), whose establishment depends upon performance, implies a performer for the sake of its own fulfillment. Since one who lacks qualification cannot be a performer, and since there can be no qualification for one who is not a person to be enjoined, it infers a person to be enjoined, just as in the case of the injunctions for the *prayāja* and other such rites.

In this case, the fulfillment of the injunction for study (*adhyayana-niyoga*) occurs precisely through the object (*viṣaya*) brought about by the performance of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*); thus, there is no possibility of postulating a separate person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). But how does the injunction for becoming a teacher impel one to study? It is said: "One becomes a teacher by initiating [a pupil] and teaching him. Since teaching is not possible without studying, it implies that [the student must study]. Furthermore, since initiation (*upanaya*) is understood to have the same agent as teaching, it is indeed a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that [teaching].

And when there is a requirement for a means (dvāra) for that [initiation], it is precisely the act of bringing [the student] near (*upanayana*) that is understood as the means through the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For that which is to be brought near cannot be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) if it performs no function; thus, when its activity is required, the study (*adhyayana*)—which is taught within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the initiation—is determined to be that very activity, because it serves the purpose of teaching (*adhyāpana*).

And thus, since it is understood that the student who performs his study in this very manner (i.e., with the specific restrictions) is an auxiliary to the act of teaching, the act of teaching directed toward him alone is the means for attaining the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*). Consequently, because every subsidiary element of study is an auxiliary to that [act of teaching], the performance of the vows and other such requirements—which constitute the purpose of the study—is established precisely through that [teaching]. Therefore, since study has as its motive the injunction to become a teacher, the meaning of the Veda is not intended to be expressed; hence, an inquiry into the determination of its meaning need not be undertaken.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is this: study is indeed prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*); yet, the attainment of that [teacher-status] alone is not its purpose, because it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Since it is intrinsic (*antaraṅga*), the knowledge of the meaning residing in the student itself is determined to be the purpose. Now, one might object: because it is first encountered, study—which requires a purpose—first adopts the status of a teacher as understood from the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*) as its very purpose.

And once that [status of being a teacher] has been accepted, because there is no further dependence, the knowledge of the meaning—even though it is internal—does not become a purposeful factor by virtue of being understood later. It is not so; for the status of being a teacher cannot be conceived as the purpose at the very outset. If the performance of study could not be established without conceiving that [status], then one might conceive it. But this is not the case, because the performance is achieved even without conceiving it.

When this injunction (*niyoga*) has been performed, if there is an expectation for a purpose, it is the knowledge of the meaning (*arthajñāna*) itself that is accepted as the result, because it is more intimately related (*antaraṅga*). Now, one might object: the injunction alone, understood from the word, should be the purpose, not the knowledge of the meaning. This is not so; for it is improper to discard the knowledge of the meaning as well, since it too is being perceived. Therefore, it is logical that both are purposes, because both the knowledge of the meaning and the injunction are apprehended.

In this regard, it has been explained that since the purpose consisting of the knowledge of the meaning cannot be accomplished through mere study without inquiry, the injunction for study itself implies inquiry for the sake of achieving that purpose; therefore, the treatise whose nature is that inquiry must be commenced.

He refutes the second [position] with the words: "In the application of the syllables, there is the commencement of an investigation into the Veda. The sense is that the possibility of validity is untenable; even if this comprehension were produced, it could not be correct due to the absence of a foundation, and thus the possibility of its validity does not exist. [This refers to the statement: "The meaning characterized by the injunction alone is what is propounded by the Veda. In the aphorism "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma," the word *atha* (now) means "immediately after the study of the Veda."

Furthermore, when the Sūtra ought to have been formulated as "After the study of the Veda, there is the desire to know its meaning," Jaimini’s formulation of it as "The desire to know Dharma" (Dharmajijñāsā) leads to the conclusion that Dharma alone is the entire subject matter of the Veda. Consequently, since he states in the Codanā-sūtra that "Injunction alone is the means of valid knowledge for Dharma, which is the subject matter of the entire Veda," it follows that only those sentences that communicate an action (kārya) are authoritative regarding Dharma as the Vedic subject matter. Thus, it results that the Vedic subject matter is exclusively what is to be accomplished (kārya).

Consequently, it is understood that Jaimini’s intention was that there is no linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) at all regarding established facts (*siddhārtha*), nor is there any purpose in explaining them. Among these, the lack of purpose will be refuted in the *Samanvaya* section; the present point, however, is to establish that linguistic acquisition does indeed occur with respect to established facts. It should also be noted that this is merely an illustration, as the fact that the Veda has action as its purpose is stated explicitly in the Sūtra itself: "Because the Veda has action as its purpose" (*āmnāyasya kriyārthatvāt*).

Nor should it be argued that if Jaimini himself were the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), how could the unity of the school (*ekaśākhya*) between two mutually contradictory positions be maintained; for the unity of the school is possible through the mere refutation of the statement regarding the *anvāruhya* (concession). (The prima facie view of the section: Anticipating the objection—"According to the maxim 'the subject matter and the doubt must indeed [be stated],' when it ought to be demonstrated that 'this is the subject matter' and 'thus is the doubt,' how is it appropriate in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) not to demonstrate them?"—he says, beginning with "In the word-by-word explanation," etc. Therein, the meaning is: "given that the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has been established."

In this regard, some—considering the impossibility of a causal relationship (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*) between the establishment of the reality of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca-satyatva*) and the demonstration of the acquisition of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*)—believe that the word "therein" (*tatra*) in the Bhāṣya means: "when there exists a doubt as to whether the undertaking of the inquiry into Brahman is necessary or not. Regarding the phrase "having grasped the connection" (*saṃbandhaṃ gṛhītvā*): the meaning is "intending that the connection is appropriate" (*yujyate*).

Furthermore, in the case of the word "cow" as it recurs through multiple usages such as "bring the cow," "look at the cow," and "tie up the cow," the referent is the individual cow (*gopiṇḍa*) that persists through all those actions. Since the varying words such as "bring" have varying meanings such as the actions [of bringing], there is no room for the objection that the sequence of the suffix *katṛ* (agentive) and its meaning is untenable; for the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] itself consists in the apprehension of the word's power (*śakti*), which depends upon the process of insertion (*āvāpa*) and exclusion (*uddhāra*).

One might object: "Since the intended meaning is already established by the phrase 'because the causes of joy are infinite,' the addition of the words 'existing in the three times' is redundant. On the contrary, it is even illogical, because past and future things cannot be causes for a joy occurring at the present moment; furthermore, resorting to the interpretation that this refers to the cognition of the causes of joy is unnecessarily strained. Anticipating this objection, [the author] states, "existing in the three times" as found in the *Pañcikā*, intending to show that there is no fault because this is merely a restatement of what was said in the *Pañcikā*.

One might object: "Even if there is no certainty regarding the specific cause of joy, there is certainly a determination that the word refers to the cause of joy in general; so how can it be said that there is an absence of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) consists in... [The text continues: "An example of the determination of the meaning of another word from words whose meanings are already known. Although in the *Bhāṣya* only the linguistic competency regarding the case-meaning of the other words is cited—namely, the phrase "of the case-meaning of the other words whose meanings are known"—and not each individual word separately.

If the intention were for each [factor] to be independently derived, then an example of the derivation of a mere case-ending alone would also have to be shown; nevertheless, since the Bhāṣya has presented both types of derivation—the derivation of another word and the derivation of a case-ending—as being equally instrumental, it should be understood that the author of the present work has cited this as the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya, with the view that even the derivation of another word alone can determine the meaning. There is a variant reading in some places: *vyutpannena kaḥkūjatiśabdena*.

Even so, it must be stated that the capacity for linguistic usage (*vyutpannatva*) belongs only to another word that is co-occurrent (*samabhivyāhṛta*), because, according to the principle stated by the elders—"the meaning of an established word is [determined] through proximity"—it is precisely proximity, characterized by co-occurrence with a well-known word, that is said to be the grasper of word-meaning power (*śakti*).

For this very reason, even the logicians have cited examples such as "here on the mango tree the cuckoo sings sweetly," where the acquisition of linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) occurs through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with well-known words; nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated with the intention that for one who knows the answer "cuckoo" to the question "what?", a certain determination of the word's meaning is possible. The reading "by the word *kūjati* [which is] already proficient" is indeed easy to understand.

This is an illustration of the determination of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) for one who has mastered the meanings of the case-endings (*vibhakti*) of both [types of] words—those whose meanings are already known and others. Although in the Bhāṣya, the natural sense suggests a correspondence according to the respective order—namely, that for one who has mastered the meanings of other words, there is the determination of the meaning of the other word, and for one who has mastered the case-endings, there is the determination of the meaning of the base—[the present example serves as an illustration].

Nor should it be suspected that there is no example for determining the meaning of a base (*prakṛti*) for one who has only mastered the knowledge of case-endings (*vibhakti*). For when a person seeking to acquire linguistic proficiency sees Devadatta looking at Yajñadatta being killed, and someone utters the sentence, "Devadatta is killing Yajñadatta," it is possible for that person—who already knows the meanings of the nominal and verbal suffixes—to determine the meaning of the base by means of identifying which words denote the agent, the object, and the action. It is with this very possibility in mind that the aforementioned point was stated.

This should be observed: in expressions such as "the cuckoo coos" (*pikaḥ kūjati*), even when the meaning of the word *kūjati* ("coos") is determined, if the primary meaning of the word *pika* ("cuckoo") is not understood, there arises a suspicion that it might be another grammatical factor (such as an agent other than the subject). Consequently, because the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the words *pika* and *kūjati* is not perceived, the meaning remains undetermined. This is because the determination of the meaning of the word *pika* occurs only through the combination of the mastery of the word's etymology (*vyutpatti*) and the mastery of its case-ending (*vibhakti*).

Nor should it be argued that for one who is proficient in the sentence of the questioner, "What is cooing?", there can be a determination of the referent of the word *pika* even without knowing the meaning of the case-ending, provided they possess proficiency regarding the word *kūjati*; for the intention of the Bhāṣya is that since the determination of the meaning of the nominative case-ending is necessary precisely in the word "what" (*kaḥ*), the case-ending of the word *pika* is also determined by virtue of the identity of the case-ending, and thus the two [the word *kūjati* and the case-ending] function as causes in combination.

And it should not be said that, this being the case, the mention of "ascertainment of the meaning of another word" in the Bhāṣya would be improper; for they say that, having stated "by ascertainment of the meaning of another word" in accordance with worldly convention, the statement of the second alternative—"or by ascertainment of the meaning of the base"—was made precisely because of such a lingering doubt (*anuśaya*). Thus, the Bhāṣya reads: "by ascertainment of the meaning of another word, or by ascertainment of the meaning of the base."

The meaning is: "by observing the determination of the meanings of other words" or "by observing the determination of the meaning of the base (prakṛti). Consequently, one should not raise the objection that there is an inconsistency regarding the relationship of cause and effect, since that very [determination] consists in the form of the ascertainment of the denotative power (*abhidhākti*). [This occurs] "from seeing a few words situated in a sentence whose meaning is already known. Now, [the word] *kārya*...

If it is argued: "By observing the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with a word denoting [the action] of going, one ascertains that even another word within that same collection denotes that [action]; however, because of the co-occurrence with yet another word denoting going, it would follow that the other word [the first one] also has that [action of going] as its meaning. On the contrary, since such co-occurrence actually gives rise to the suspicion that it is merely a synonym (*paryāya*), it is precisely the certainty of its not having that meaning which serves as the reason"—we say: no.

At the very outset, for a person who has determined that the word *padaja* expresses the general category of action (*kāryasāmānya*), it is impossible to abandon that previously apprehended expression of the general category of action because the cognition of the signifier-signified relationship—being established through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with well-known words—is understood as having that specific form. Regarding the phrase in the *Bhāṣya*, "because it consists in the determination of a specific part of that" (*tadaṃśaviśeṣaniścayarūpatvāt*), after explaining the word *tat* as referring to "action" (*kārya*), he explains it as referring to the collection of proximate words by saying, "or rather, 'a specific part of that'. Furthermore, in the third [alternative], there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of words denoting grammatical factors (*kāraka*).

Nor should it be argued that even if the capacity to denote one’s own meaning as connected with a *kāraka* (case-factor) exists, the rejection of this position is futile because the status of being for the sake of an action (*kāryārthatva*) is not established; for since only an action is connected with *kārakas*, if all words were to denote their own meanings as connected with *kārakas*, the denotation of an action would be unavoidable, and thus that too must be rejected. If it is objected: "Even if the denotation of one’s own meaning as connected with *kārakas* implies—due to the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between *kārakas* and action—that the word denotes action alone, it does not necessarily follow that it denotes an action that is a *kārya* (something to be accomplished), since we observe exactly that [denotation of action] in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*."
True; for since the proponent (siddhāntin) must also refute the view that all words denote action, it is appropriate to raise and then reject this position as well.

Regarding this, some ask: "Is it not observed that Vācaspati has established the validity of established entities (*siddhavastu*) in this manner? For in that regard, the statement of Vācaspati is as follows: 'Moreover, the author of the Śāstra [states] that "since the Veda (*āmnāya*) has action (*kriyā*) as its purpose. If, in that context, the term "purpose" (*artha*) denotes the denotable object (*abhidheya*), then it would follow that words for substances and qualities (*dravyaguṇaśabda*) which refer to already existing things (*bhūtārtha*) are purposeless—that is, they would lack a denotable object—because they do not have action as their purpose.'"

If it should be argued that "having action as its purpose" does not mean having action as its denotation, but rather having action as its motive, and that words denoting substances and qualities denote existing substances and qualities solely by virtue of having action as their purpose—never as being self-sufficient—as those learned in the scriptures have said: "For an injunction [makes known] what has been, what is," and so forth; this is what is meant: an injunction, while making known a task (*kārya*) as its object, also makes known such objects as existing things (*bhūta*) and the like for the sake of that task.

It has already been established that the acquisition of the relationship between words does not occur solely with respect to an object that is a remainder of an action (*kāryaśeṣabhūta*), as we have demonstrated that linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) exists even regarding objects that are already accomplished (*bhūta*). Nor is it the case that words are restricted solely to their own individual meanings (*svārtha*); for if that were so, there would be no cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Indeed, a single syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is never observed among things that are each independent, primary, and devoid of the relation of subordinate and principal. Therefore, while words express their own individual meanings, they constitute a single syntactic unity by virtue of being directed toward the meanings of the words as having a single purpose (*ekaprayojana*).

And thus, the cognition of a single sentence-meaning qualified by those respective distinct meanings becomes logically established. Furthermore, since the cognition of the sentence-meaning is established merely through the fact that words have as their purport the connection between distinct meanings, there is no restrictive rule that words must have as their purport a connection with an action (*kārya*). These alternatives are not seen in this passage from Vācaspati’s work, nor is the refutation [of the opponent's view] presented in this manner.

Indeed, this is the meaning of this composition: What is intended by the statement, "Because the Veda has action as its purpose"? Is it that all words denote an action (*kārya*)? Or is it that they denote what is connected to an action or what is subsidiary to it (*taccheṣa*)? Not the first, because that is absent in the case of words denoting substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*). Nor the second, because it has been established that linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) occurs even with respect to established entities (*siddhārtha*). If it is objected that, in this way, words would not have as their meaning being connected to something else (*itarānvita*), we say no; for through words that directly express their own meanings (*svārthābhidhāyin*), there arises—by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication)—a cognition qualified by connection to something else.

In this context, the threefold alternative presented in the *Śrutaprakāśikā* is not seen; nor is the manner of refutation observed to be of such a kind. Furthermore, even in the instance where the derivation [of the word] is shown to refer to an already established fact (*bhūtārtha*), this alternative is not demonstrated. For it is stated there as follows: "Just as purposeful activity is the inferential mark for the cognition of something to be done (*kārya*), so too are joy and other [emotions] the mark for the cognition of an established fact (*siddha*). Thus, let there be meaningfulness through the cognition of the established; and let the status of being a scripture (*śāstratva*) arise from teaching what is beneficial."

For if the capacity of words to denote either an action (*kārya*) or their own meanings as subservient to that action were definitively established through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), then the Upaniṣads would not have as their purport the nature of Brahman—the Self—which is neither to be rejected nor to be acquired; this is because the capacity of words in that regard would be unknown, and because the comprehension of Vedic meaning is preceded by worldly usage.

Now, even if the comprehension of the relationship between words is possible in the world regarding existent (bhūta) objects, one cannot—by disregarding the fact that the Upaniṣads are understood to have that [existent] as their purport through a thorough examination of their internal consistency—imagine them to have action (kārya) as their purport, for that would entail the fallacy of imagining what is not heard in scripture (śruta-kalpanā-prasaṅga). In this regard, there is no comprehension of the relationship of words with respect to an object that is not an action, provided that no usage directed toward such a purport is observed in the world, or provided that the cognition of such a meaning cannot be inferred in one who is already proficient in language.

It is not the case that such usage is not observed in the world; for we frequently encounter in common usage combinations of words that are not intended for action, being employed for the purpose of dispelling curiosity, fear, and so forth.

For example: "The king of mountains, Sumeru, which is the abode of the circle of world-protectors beginning with Ākhaṇḍala; which is surrounded by hosts of Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases; whose rocky surfaces of refined gold are washed by the falling streams of the Mandākinī descending from the realm of Brahmā; and which is enchanting with the lovely warbling of jewel-like birds sporting in pleasure-gardens such as Nanda"; or, "This is not a serpent, it is a rope," and so forth.

Nor can it be inferred that the cognition of the actual state of affairs resides only in a person who has mastered the language, for causes such as joy and so forth are capable of being inferred. To illustrate: a Draviḍa man, ignorant of the meaning of the language of the Āryas, was preparing to go to the city when he sat down in the middle of Devadatta’s house near the royal highway. He encountered a messenger who had come from Devadatta, who resided in the city, bearing news of the birth of a son—the cause of delight for his father—preceded by the presentation of fine garments and perfumes as a gift. [The messenger said: "Congratulations! You have prospered!"

Upon seeing Devadatta—his body covered in a mantle of horripilation immediately after hearing the report from the messenger, his lotus-like eyes blossoming, and his great lotus-face breaking into a wide smile—one infers that joy has arisen within him; and since this joy, which did not exist previously, occurs immediately upon hearing those words, one concludes that it has that [report] as its cause.

And since this person, not being one who fails to communicate, would not be capable of joy without a cause for joy, it is understood that the cause of his joy has been stated by him. Because no other cause for joy is perceived, and because the birth of a son is known to be such a cause, he concludes that the messenger himself must have announced that very fact. Thus [it is established regarding] fear...

"Sorrow and the like are also not to be removed [by mere knowledge]. Thus, it is established that the teaching of an existent reality (bhūtārtha) is purposeful, and the employment of such by a discerning person is likewise justified. And so, because the knowledge of Brahman is the cause of the supreme human goal, the status of the Vedāntas as a scripture (śāstratva) is established, since they instruct what is beneficial for man—even though they do not enjoin activity or cessation. To this, they raise an objection: "We do not understand how this can be said. To that, the following reply is given: "It is true that you do not understand it."

The non-existence of the object is not established by this much alone, according to the maxim: "It is not the fault of the post that the blind man does not see it. This is because [the existence of the object] can be established in other places and in other texts, and because even these [present] statements can, in their intended meaning (*tātparya*), establish that very same object. Enough with excessive scrutiny.

Intending to show that—since the cognition of a word’s capacity to convey a meaning that prompts action is not produced by the force of an invariable concomitance between the cognition of an effect and the activity [of the listener], and since it is possible to grasp a word’s denotation of a meaning that prompts action merely by grasping the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of the word with activity, even without grasping the causal relation between the cognition of an effect and the activity—he says later on, "of all words."

"By way of intending [the fallacy] of 'unestablished for one of the two parties' (*anyatarāṃśāsiddhi*). However, some maintain that the commentary as it stands is more appropriate; for they argue that since this section also demonstrates the possibility of the qualifying condition—namely, the realization of the impermanence of the fruits of action through the injunction for the repetition of the inquiry into action—it is possible to speak of the unestablished nature of both parts as well.
(The *Adhikaraṇasiddhānta*)

"The authors of the Sūtras state the resolution" (*parihāra*). This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood as meaning "the resolution intended by the author of the Sūtras is stated," because in passages such as "this being the case, we reply" (*evaṃ prāpte pracakṣmahe*), it is described in exactly that way. "Accepting the object through a means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇena arthaṃ svīkurvadbhiḥ*): the sense is that the suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of "playing with," "digging," "conquering," or "won" (*tena dīvyati khanati jayati jitam*).

Now, one might object: "Since the group 'mother, father, maternal uncle, moon, animal, man, deer, bird' should have been indicated as a single compound (*aikapadyena*), what is the purpose of mentioning them separately? Anticipating this doubt, he states the purpose of the separate mention in the verse beginning with *ambātātaprabhṛti*. In the Bhāṣya, the reading is *enam avehi*. In some manuscripts, the reading *avaihi* is observed; however, that is due to a scribe's error, for it should be understood that *ehi* cannot be formed here because of the continued application of the rule *ety-edhaty-ūṭhsu* (Pāṇini 6.1.89), which requires a long vowel when followed by a *ec* vowel.

"Awaken him with this word. [Objection: But how can there be an *enādeśa* (the substitution of *ena*) in the absence of an *anvādeśa* (a subsequent reference)? [Response: No; for in the context of grammatical derivation (*vyutpādana*), since the word *amba* was previously employed, an *anvādeśa* is possible regarding that object. Nor should it be asked how there can be a pointing with a finger toward the word "this" (*enam avehi*) in the phrase "Know him"; for that is justified as referring merely to the object already indicated by the words "And grasp this one."

"By the intention 'let [the child] comprehend,' [it means]: when stating the form of the intention, since it is appropriate to use the first person—thinking, 'Let this child comprehend this meaning'—while pointing with a finger, the purport lies precisely there. "They might think that these words have been assigned by convention," because of the *Bhāṣya*’s statement, "because no other relation is observed and because another person is seen to be the assigner of the convention," the reversal of the two doubts should be understood.

Now, it must be said that for a child, the acquisition of linguistic usage is not based on the prior apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*), because at that time there is no certainty regarding such potency when the cognition of the referent arises through words such as "mother," "grandfather," or "uncle. Rather, the capacity of a word to convey its meaning occurs solely by virtue of a relationship characterized by concomitance (*sāhacarya*), namely the pointing toward the object with a finger.

Thus, knowing that the arising of the cognition of that meaning in oneself is caused by such a relationship [of similarity], how could one postulate another relationship characterized as the signifier-signified relation (*vācyavācakabhāva*)? Furthermore, during a child's practice with syllables made of dust, adults repeatedly instruct them by pointing to specific lines of dust with their fingers, saying, "This is the letter *ka*; this is the letter *kha*. Subsequently, upon seeing a particular script, the child recognizes the syllable; and upon hearing a particular syllable, he remembers the corresponding script.

In that case, one does not postulate any other relationship characterized by the nature of the "object of cognition" and the "cognizer. If it is argued, "Let it be so here as well," we reply: when pointing out a specific object with a finger, people employ words such as "mother"; since there is no other [relationship], the child, searching for some restrictive factor in this matter, determines a specific innate relationship between the two—therefore, there is no fault in this statement. However, in the case of scripts and the like, one might determine an innate relationship during a state of ignorance regarding their being preceded by convention.

What is our loss? For there is no fault, since that [alleged consequence] is refuted by the knowledge that [the relation between word and meaning] is preceded by convention. As for the objection, "it would follow that there is denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*): those established in the systems [of Mīmāṃsā] declare two distinct methods for the determination of sentence-meaning—namely, *anvitābhidhāna* (denotation of the related) and *abhihitānvaya* (relation of the denoted).
"The entire collection of words, having been heard, recalls their respective meanings as unconnected;
subsequently, its manifestation being brought about through logical reasoning, it conveys the meaning of the sentence."

Thus ends the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of related meanings). This is the meaning of the verse here: first, the words are heard. Having been heard, they cause the individual forms of the word-meanings—according to their conventional usage—to be recalled as being mutually unrelated. Once the word-meanings have been recalled, there occurs a consideration of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and other factors. From that follows the operation of logical reasoning (*nyāya*). Through the operation of this reasoning, the manifestation of a specific syntactical form (*vacanavyakti*) is accomplished.

Therefore, words assisted by correct logic express the meaning of a sentence, which consists of a single primary meaning qualified by various word-meanings. However, those who maintain the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what is expressed) have stated as follows: word-meanings are denoted individually by their respective words. And that denotation culminates merely in the recollection of the word-meanings, according to the statement: "A word does not differ from a mere reminder, because it lacks any additional [function]."

And those word-meanings (padārtha), when reflected upon through their mutual compatibility (yogyatva), themselves bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha), which consists of the specific relation between them. In that process, there is no further operation of the words, since the specific meaning is established by the meanings alone. Just as word-meanings, when contemplated by poets, themselves bring about the understanding of the sentence-meaning—which consists of the relation of specific meanings—the composition of words occurs only afterwards in accordance with the meanings already apprehended. Thus, it is the meanings themselves that convey the specific meaning. Consequently, in the linguistic derivation (vyutpatti) that "this is the meaning of this [word]," for each individual word—

The point is this: since linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) consists in the understanding of a word as being directed solely toward its own specific meaning, that alone would be what is denoted; thus, the denotation of a meaning as connected with the meanings of other words would not be established. Regarding the phrase "of individual proficiency" (*prātisvikavyutpatteḥ*), it means "of proficiency regarding each individual word. However, the distinction here is that [this proficiency] occurs prior [to the understanding of the sentence].

The meaning is as follows: in the case of acquisition through chance, one first understands that "the meaning of this sentence is the task of bringing the cow," based on the observation of activity toward the act of bringing the cow; thereafter, through the process of insertion and deletion (*āvāpoddhāra*), one determines the word-meanings, thinking, "this is the meaning of this word. However, in the case of acquisition preceded by deliberate intention, the understanding of the sentence-meaning is preceded by the cognition of the word-meanings, such that one knows, "this is the meaning of this word."

The meaning is that words also denote their own referents by virtue of being mutually compatible with one another; that is to say, words themselves possess the power to instill the capacity for the cognition of the connection (*saṃsarga*) among word-referents. On this point, some teachers maintain that there is no burden of three powers at all, because they accept that words alone have the power to denote word-referents, and because it is possible for those referents themselves to convey the connection. Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the foundational knowledge for a poet's composition could not be accounted for.

Since the status of being verbal (*śābdatva*) is also established by following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with words, and since the absence of mediation (*avyavahitatva*) is not a determining factor, they maintain that the theory of the connection of the expressed (*abhihitānvayapakṣa*) alone is what the author of the Bhāṣya intended. [The statement] "the word 'budhyasva' (understand) is thereby said" has this underlying meaning: for whatever one intends to establish by means of something, that thing is the purpose (*artha*) of the latter; this is seen from the fact that a jar, which is intended to be produced by a staff, is the purpose of the staff.

In the present context, the speaker’s intended goal is to produce in the child a cognition of the actual mother and so forth, which is conveyed by the words "mother" and so on. Therefore, since the cognition of the actual mother and so forth residing in the child—which is the purpose of employing the words "mother" and so on—is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is not yet established; thus, the words must indeed have a causal function (*kāryārthatva*). This doubt should be understood as arising from a failure to distinguish between the "purpose" (*artha*) denoted by the word *artha* in the phrase "denoting a purpose" (*kāryārthābhidhāyitva*) and the "purpose" (*prayojana*) that is the object to be achieved.

"Buy a cow. In some manuscripts, the reading "sell" (*vikrīṇīhi*) is observed; however, in that case, the prefix *vi-* is due to a scribal error, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the ātmanepada by the rule *parivyavebhyaḥ kriyaḥ*. Furthermore, the root *kṛṇāti* itself can indeed have the meaning of selling, as has been established in the *Bhāṣyapradīpa* on the sūtra *krathyastadarthe*.

Regarding the phrase "in the latter [section]": this means in the section concerning the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*). One might raise the objection: since only knowledge (*jñāna*), desire (*icchā*), and volition (*kṛti*) possess objects, how can there be the statement "one who is authorized by the task whose object is meditation" (*upāsanāviṣayakāryādhikṛta*) with respect to the *apūrva* (unseen potency), which is itself objectless? Anticipating this, the author says "delimited by meditation" (*upāsanāvacchinna*), intending to show that because volition—which enters into the body of the task to be accomplished through action—possesses an object, the *apūrva* also possesses an object by way of that [volition]. As for the reading "for that which binds is called an object" (*visinvan hi viṣaya ucyate*), that is correct, because the word *viṣaya* is derived from the root *ni* preceded by the prefix *vi*.

"For the word *vi* has the sense of 'distinction,' while *sinoti* (from the root *si*) is said to mean 'binding. That which binds specifically is therefore the *viṣaya* (object), for it is the regulator."

This is because of the statement by the learned (*abhiyukta*): "But when the reading is *viśiṃṣan*, it should be understood that this is an explanation of the matter (*vastu*), not an explanation of the word (*śabda*). For the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) states: "One should approach these nights; indeed, those who approach these nights become firmly established. What is to be said regarding this has already been stated previously. [The phrase] "beneficial to the thing to be enjoined" (*vidheyopakāraka*) means that it is beneficial to the cessation of threatening (*apagoraṇa-nivṛtti*), which is the thing to be enjoined, because it serves to establish the fact that threatening—once it is to be avoided—is a means to an undesirable end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*).

The point is that if threatening (*apagoraṇa*) were not a means to an undesirable end, its cessation would be impossible. Regarding the phrase "the hundred-fold torments of threatening": threatening is the attempt at killing; "hundred-fold torments" (*śatayātanā*) is a specific hell. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of a fruit opposed to liberation": the point is that this refers to such scriptural passages as, "He makes a distinction [between himself and the Self], and then fear comes upon him. Regarding the statement "because it is established precisely through its utility for the task": the word "utility for the task" (*kāryopayogitva*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: by the phrase "because it is established through its utility for the purpose," the non-concomitant reason (*atulyāyihetu*)—which consists in the form of "utility for the purpose"—is stated as "utility for the purpose. For this very reason, [the text says]: "He lays down four bricks."

Regarding the statement, "The *nīvāra* grains are indeed the food of Bṛhaspati," it was stated in the second book (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 2.1.46), under the section beginning with "But that which is connected with a word denoting a purpose" (*saṃyuktastvarthaśabdena*), that the connection with a deity provided by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) need not be accepted, because it is not required by the injunction for placing the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) upon the altar (*sthaṇḍila*). Therefore, the implication is that only that explanatory passage which provides what is required by the injunction should be respected, and no other. (This concludes the refutation of the view that the apūrva is the primary object of the action.)

Regarding the statement here that "by the word *artha*, prominence (*prādhānya*) [is indicated]," what is the proof for the word *artha* having prominence as its intended meaning? Nor should it be said that the passage from the *Pañcikā*, "The *kārya* (the 'thing to be done') conveys the *artha* as the predominant factor," serves as such proof; for the fact that the word *artha* signifies prominence is not perceived from that statement of Śabara’s. In that context, it is understood only that "the *artha* in the form of the *kārya* is conveyed as the principal element (*śeṣin*) in relation to the sacrifice and other factors mentioned in proximity."

Nor is the statement from the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, “the primary [object] is that which is to be accomplished by effort (*kṛti-sādhya*”), a valid authority; for even there, because of the co-occurrence of the words “the primary [object] is that which is to be accomplished by effort,” one understands that the primary [object] is characterized by effort, and it is precisely that which is fit to be designated by the word ‘purpose’ (*artha*). This is the intended meaning. Regarding the point that “being the object of effort” (*kṛti-karmatva*) means “being the motivator” (*pravartakatva*), he says: the meaning is that being the motivator consists in that specific mode (*prakāra*) of cognition which prompts action.

In the statement, "Nothing is perceived as being the object of an effort (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*) in the commentary," the author's intention is that "being the object of an effort" means "being the motivator" (*pravartakatva*). This is the underlying thought: in his view, *kāryatva* (the state of being a task) is the status of being the object of an effort that is yet to come into existence through volition; it is the state of being the object of volition (*kṛtikarmatva*). And it is established that this [status] is the mode of the motivating cognition. Furthermore, it is proven that the mode of the motivating cognition is "the state of being most desired (*iṣṭatamatva*), while being achievable through volition (*kṛtisādhyatva*)."

And in that context, since the existence of the end of action (*satyanta*) is already established by the very phrase "existing when there is the existence of volitional effort" (*kṛtibhāvabhāvī*), the portion intended to be expressed by the term "inducement" (*pravartakatva*) is simply the state of being most desired (*iṣṭatamatva*). Consequently, "inducement," defined as existing when there is the existence of volitional effort, results in the state of being most desired while being achievable through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*). In this regard, "incitement" (*prerakatva*) means being the object of volitional effort; one acts upon knowing the incitement inherent in what is to be done (*kārya*).

The meaning is that, because it is the mode of the motivating cognition (*pravartaka-jñāna*), the nature of being an instigator (*prerakatva*)—which consists in the form of being the object of the act of doing (*kṛti-karmatva*)—is logically established. (This is the intended sense. For it is not the case that the cessation of suffering itself becomes pleasure. Regarding this, some hold that the literal reading is correct, since even the cessation of suffering, though distinct from pleasure, is observed to be conducive [to human ends].

They say that doubt is removed by the mere hearing [of the teaching] itself; thus, it is "desirable" (*iṣṭa*) because it consists in the cessation of what is undesired (*aniṣṭa*). Now, one might ask: why is the cessation of the undesired not intrinsically desirable (*svata iṣṭatvam*), in the same way that pleasure is, simply because it is the object of a desire that does not depend on the knowledge of it being a means to some other human goal (*puruṣārtha*)? Nor should it be argued that it is not intrinsically desirable because its desire depends on a cognition whose qualifier is "the cessation of suffering," for if that were the case, then even the desire for pleasure would not be intrinsic, since the desire for pleasure also depends on a cognition whose qualifier is "pleasure-ness."

Desirability (*iṣṭatva*) would not exist. Nor should it be argued that desirability is intended here as intrinsic (*svataḥ*), without depending on the knowledge that it is the cause of another desired thing or the cessation of an undesired thing; for if that were so, it would result in [the term] being merely technical (*pāribhāṣikatva*). Furthermore, because the subsequent commentary states, "Because it is other than pleasure and the cessation of pain, which are the direct objects of desire," it implies that even the cessation of pain is a direct object of desire. To this, some reply: the desire for the absence of pain is dependent upon aversion toward pain, and not intrinsic.

Therefore, [pleasure] is not desired for its own sake. Nor should it be argued that, since in our system "aversion" (*dveṣa*) is nothing other than the desire to abandon (*jihāsā*), and that very [desire] is the wish for cessation (*nivṛtti*), one who asserts that aversion toward suffering is natural—and who asserts that aversion takes the form of the desire to abandon—must necessarily admit that cessation, characterized as abandonment, is desired for its own sake. This is because, in common worldly experience, a desire for a non-entity is observed to depend solely upon aversion toward its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); thus, it must necessarily be stated that aversion is a specific type of cognition whose mode (*prakāra*) is the state of being something to be abandoned.

They say that the absence of suffering, which is the object of a desire dependent upon that [absence], does not possess desirability (*iṣṭatva*) in itself. Now, an objection may be raised: "The cognition of favorableness (*anukūlatva*) is indeed the cause of desire. Since favorableness consists in being the most desired (*iṣṭatamatva*), it follows that the cognition of being the most desired is the cause of desire. Furthermore, the cognition of being the most desired depends upon being the most desired in the sense of being the object of desire; thus, there is the fallacy of circularity (*ātmāśraya*). This is not so; for there is no circularity or similar fault, because the specific nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*) that serves as the basis for being the object of desire is itself what constitutes favorableness. Thus, the objection of circularity is avoided.

Now, one might object: "If abiding in one's own nature (*svarūpa*) in the absence of both favorable and unfavorable [states] constitutes the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nivṛtti*), then just as the cessation of the unfavorable is the cessation of suffering, so too would the cessation of the favorable result in the cessation of suffering. Anticipating this objection, he states that the cessation of suffering is co-referential (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the aspect of the cessation of the unfavorable, by saying: "Abiding in one's own nature consists in the cessation of pleasure," and so forth. The mention of action (*kriyā*) and the rest is intended as an illustration.

In this regard, some [hold] that, in accordance with the introductory *bhāṣya* stating, "Even in sentences such as 'Bring the cow,' there is no acquisition of linguistic competency (*vyutpatti*) regarding a task to be accomplished (*kāryārtha*)," one perceives that what is to be defined is precisely a "task-ness" (*kāryatva*) common to both action (*kriyā*) and the *apūrva* (unseen potency) distinct from it. Following that [view], they argue that since the *bhāṣya* statement, "It is not possible for action and so forth to possess suitability (*anukūlatva*)," can also be interpreted as a denial of suitability in a manner common to both action and non-action, we do not see any natural elegance in the claim that [the *bhāṣya*] was stated with the intention of providing an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhiprāyeṇa*).

For this very reason, we see no basis for the statement: "The primacy of the effort (*kṛti*) is described as that which excludes [the status of] being a fruit, a state of being, or a purpose. Consequently, since there is no "primacy of effort" that is distinct from "desirability" (*iṣyatva*) or not constituted by "desirability" (*iṣṭatva*), and since the *apūrva*—being distinct from pleasure and the cessation of pain—is not inherently desirable, and since, according to your own view, that which is understood as having no other purpose is not considered desirable even as a means to pleasure or the cessation of pain, the status of being a "task to be accomplished" (*kāryatva*) does not exist in the *apūrva* you intend. Thus.

They also say: "Since we perceive that the intention of the Bhāṣya is not fully concluded [on this point], we see no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) for the claim that the author is refuting the 'task-ness' (*kāryatva*) favored by opponents—which is distinct from both the meaning of the verbal root and heaven. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of pleasure," this passage—"for the staff, the wheel, and so forth do not become a jar"—should have been read before the passage "because it consists of suffering" (which follows the word *kartum*). Or rather, it should not be read anywhere at all, as it serves no significant purpose.

Therefore, one should not suspect that the citation of the individual words is out of order; rather, the intended meaning is the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). This means that the intended meaning is the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*).

Regarding the phrase "the definition of the remainder (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*) is shown as it is," the ellipsis is "by the author of the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "its meaning is stated," the ellipsis is "by me. As for the statement "the attainment of existence (*sattālābha*) is called excellence (*atiśaya*)," the underlying sense is that it was not said that existence itself is excellence.

Now, one might object: since in the phrase "an excellence residing in another" (*paragatātiśaya*), the meaning of the word *para* is understood as having the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa-kāraka*), and because a causal factor (*kāraka*) must necessarily precede [the effect], how can that which does not yet exist possess the status of a causal factor with respect to an excellence consisting of origination in a case where something is to be produced? Anticipating this doubt, it is replied: even for that which has not yet originated, the status of a causal factor is possible because it exists in a subtle form revolving within the intellect (*buddhi*). In this very same way, the agency of the one being born (*janikartṛtva*) must also be explained.

In this very way, he says "even though its own nature (*svarūpa*) is non-existent," intending to establish that [the sacrifice] serves as the cause for a future, unprecedented result (*apūrva*). He states that "the excellence of another (*parātiśaya*)" is the supreme purpose (*paramaprayojana*). [Objection: But in this case, heaven (*svarga*) would not be a subordinate element of the person (*puruṣaśeṣa*). For that [status] must be understood through the force of desire (*kāma*) and the force of the injunction (*vidhi*), since it is impossible for something intended for another purpose to be desired [as an end in itself]. Indeed, no one desires anything for its own sake alone; even that [desire for another's excellence] is ultimately for one's own sake, and likewise so is the force of the injunction.

For an injunction (*vidhi*) is by nature an impulsion (*pravartanā*). Since it would be impossible for a person to be impelled toward the means of attaining heaven if heaven were not for the sake of the self, the fact that heaven is for the sake of the self must be established through the force of these two arguments. If it were argued that both the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and the activity directed toward it are solely for the sake of another, and thus neither of the two arguments could establish that it is for the sake of the self—this is not so. It should be understood that through the force of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) in the word *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), it is understood that heaven accrues to the agent, thereby establishing its status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

Having explained that—by virtue of the particle *eva* (only) functioning as an exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavacchedaka*) with respect to the phrase "the very nature of which is being worthy of acceptance through the desire to bestow a pre-eminent excellence upon another"—there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to those things that are occasionally accepted and associated with supreme compassion and affection; and having considered that the status of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*) is observed in those [entities] characterized by the roles of being endowed with compassion and affection, or being agents, etc.; and intending the connection of the particle *eva* with the phrase "through the desire to bestow a pre-eminent excellence upon another" as an exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavacchedaka*).

Intending to show the possibility of the meaning in the form of having the production of an excellence in another as its sole purpose, [the author] explains—intending that when something has the production of an excellence in another as its sole purpose at a certain time, then that thing is a *śeṣa* (subordinate) to that other—by saying, "or in some manner. [Objection: But let it simply be that whatever has the nature of being sought for the sake of producing an excellence in another is a *śeṣa* to that other; what is the use of the word *svarūpa*, which denotes the defining property (*nirūpaka-dharma*)? [This is asked] because the definition would otherwise be unestablished. To this, he replies: "Nor is there [any problem] with the word *nirūpaka*..."

The term "nirūpaka" (defining) was used because the word *svarūpa* is conventionally understood to denote a defining attribute (*nirūpakadharma*). The underlying intention is that there is no fault even if one states: "that whose specific attribute is having excellence as its sole supreme purpose is subordinate (*śeṣa*) to that [excellence]. Regarding the phrase "by way of bestowing another excellence upon the thing that has become subordinate": since the subordinate is to be performed by means of the principal (*śeṣin*), the production of the subordinate thing [also serves this purpose].

The sense is that since the substratum (the *śeṣin*) can also be the cause of excellence in the subordinate element (*śeṣa*) by virtue of its being the locus of that excellence, the term "supreme" (*parama*) serves to exclude [any other] supreme purpose. The phrase "of the excellence residing in the subordinate element" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Having established that for those endowed with superior compassion, the supreme excellence is naturally understood to be the supreme purpose, he now establishes it for those endowed with affection as well, beginning with the words "likewise toward friends and so forth. "Those endowed with specific bonds" means those endowed with specific relationships.

It is not restricted to a particular person, nor is it unrestricted across different persons. For this affectionate one, there is no fixed rule that its sole purpose is to reach a state of excellence toward a specific affectionate object. Just as the service of a servant toward someone else is restricted for as long as he lives, so too, even in the absence of a restriction to a specific affectionate individual, there is likewise no rule that it must persist as a benefactor toward some other specific affectionate individual. This is the meaning.

One solution is that for those who, despite performing services for the sake of another out of a sense of independence, still maintain the notion that it is for their own benefit, there is no fault of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) because they are not the intended objects of the definition (*alakṣya*). However, considering it improper to accept such a status as being outside the scope of the definition—since the *Bhāṣya* states that "if such a state is not observed in them, they do not possess the nature of a servant"—he offers another solution: "Or rather, although [there are cases like] born slaves (*garbhadāsa*) and so forth... The point is that the actual state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) alone is the defining characteristic, not merely what is perceived.
And its being known is a certain effect; by the word "and" (ca), the previously mentioned production of the rasa of divine play is conjoined.

He demonstrates another objection with the words beginning "by a single word, the effect [is denoted]," and so forth. Now, one might object: it is incorrect to say that any one of the three [the sacrifice, the apūrva, or the heaven] is perceived as being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhya*). Since the sacrifice is neither pleasure nor pain, and since its status as a means (*sādhana*) is not perceived at the outset, there would be no perception of the sacrifice as being achievable through effort. Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies]: because something distinct from the action, namely the *apūrva*, cannot be the direct object of an effort and thus cannot be the thing to be achieved (*sādhya*), there arises an expectancy as to what the *apūrva* achievable through effort has as its object. In response to this expectancy—

In the cognition "that which is to be accomplished by an effort directed toward sacrifice," only the status of being an object (*viṣayatvamātra*) is perceived through the sacrifice’s role as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatayā*), not its status as the thing to be accomplished (*sādhyatvam*). This is because an effort is never observed to have anything other than an action as its object. Alternatively, this is the meaning of the passage beginning with "pleasure" (*sukha*): in the previous position, desirability (*iṣṭatva*) was not put forward as the motivating factor for being to-be-accomplished-by-effort; rather, it was stated that [the motivator] consists in being one or another of pleasure, the absence of pain, or the means thereto.

In our view, however, the distinction is that it is precisely *iṣṭatva* (desirability), as common to all three [forms], that is stated to be the determinant of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatvaprayojaka*). Demonstrating how the charge of redundancy is avoided by showing that this passage is intended to refute other possible ways of establishing *prayojanatva* (the state of being a motive), he introduces the Bhāṣya beginning with "Moreover" (*api ca*) by means of the words "Previously, in the form of the third aspect," and so forth. He does so because of the possibility of using a plurality of synonymous terms (*paryāyaśabda*); for if one were to say "a synonym for *niyoga*," it would be understood that the word *niyoga* itself is the synonymous term.

The sense is that when another word is employed, among those words expressive of an injunction (*niyoga*), it too is understood as some synonym. As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "but later one will experience [the result]," the meaning is that it is experienced as pleasure at the stage of full maturation. "Fixed" refers to rites such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice; "fixed in the hereafter" refers to rites intended for heaven.

However, rites for the sake of cattle, sons, food, and so forth are "fixed in this world" (*aihika*) if the maturation of the action occurs in this very birth, whereas otherwise they are "fixed in the hereafter" (*āmuṣmika*). Therefore, it is established in the *Pūrvatantra* that these are "not fixed in this world."

Furthermore, since the *Bhāṣya* includes actions whose fruits are not restricted to this world—such as food, drink, health, and so forth—as distinct from those [actions] being experienced [in this life], the term "restricted to this world" (*niyataihika*) in the *Bhāṣya* refers merely to those actions that are distinct from those whose means for attaining heaven and other results are restricted to the next world. Having kept in mind that even actions for the sake of cattle, food, and wealth are included by the term "restricted to this world," [the author notes that] among those actions, when an obstacle exists, it is impossible for the fruit to be experienced here at that very moment.

Considering the inconsistency of the text [if one were to say] "other than the food, drink, health, and so forth being experienced at that time," he explains it with a supplementary addition: "of the karma which is an unmentioned obstacle; 'iti' [is used] in the sense of 'iti śeṣaḥ' (the remainder is thus). [The phrase] "dependent on the desire for the final state" means: [The full sentence is: "Of the karma which is an unmentioned obstacle to the attainment of the final state, other than the food, drink, health, and so forth being experienced at that time. This is the meaning. "Dependent on the desire for the final state" means: [it refers to the karma] which requires the aspiration for the ultimate goal.

In the ritual involving the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), even the disposal (*pratipatti*) of vessels such as the *juhū*—which is enjoined by sentences such as "he places the *juhū* in the right hand"—serves as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the rite for the sake of attaining heaven and so forth. Consequently, because the supreme apūrva (*paramāpūrva*), which is to be accomplished by the apūrvas of all subsidiaries, occurs only after the disposal of the *juhū* and other vessels, it has not yet been produced prior to that disposal; this is the intended meaning.

The phrase "it is abandoned because it is stated in an *arthavāda*" means that since the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of *arthavādas* is accepted even in the final system (*siddhānta*), we do not say that something should be abandoned merely because it is stated in an *arthavāda*. The phrase "the inquiry as to whether there is no etymological derivation" means that the position that there is no etymological derivation is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). For an inquiry (*vicāra*) consists precisely in the shifting of the intellect through various perspectives.

One might object: "If the commencement of the inquiry into Brahman is established by logic (*nyāya*), then the scriptural statement enjoining it—namely, 'Having examined the worlds' (*parīkṣya lokān*)—would be redundant. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The statement beginning with 'Having examined the worlds,' etc. He explains: "Possessing the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*). Although a sentence can exist even without the distinction between subject and predicate—as in the case of the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*)—the point here is that a sentence in the form of a *sūtra* must possess that [specific] character. For that which is to be enjoined is the predicate (*upādeya*).

Although, in an injunction regarding place, time, and so forth, even that which is enjoined—such as place and time—is not something to be adopted (*upādeya*), nevertheless, this statement should be understood as being made with reference to what is generally the case (*prāyikatva*). By the phrase "there is no proficiency [in understanding] by means of the sentence," the meaning is "by means of the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). It is also possible for this Sūtra to function as an instigator of what has not yet been undertaken. For example, regarding the injunction "one should cook a *kṛṣṇala* grain," since there is no purpose for the cooking, one would naturally desist; therefore, it is an injunction in the form of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). Thus he says: "for here, [it applies] to one who is inclined toward action through worldly passion (*rāga*)."

Since the general enumeration (*uddeśa*) was made in the first Sūtra, the following is the analysis: regarding the first and second positions, there is one section (*peṭikā*) consisting of the third and fourth topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), which serves to remove doubts concerning the nature of the definition and the defined, and their status as objects of investigation. Even therein, the first position follows the view that in the passage beginning with "from which indeed these [beings arise]," Brahmanhood is enjoined by restating the cause of the world.

The second position follows the view that in the sentence "from which [these...]," while the status of being the cause is restated (*anuvāda*), the status of being the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Although it is necessary for the *Nyāya* system to consist of enunciation (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and examination (*parīkṣā*), such necessity does not apply to this particular treatise. Therefore, the first and second sections (*adhikaraṇa*) do not function for the purpose of enunciation and definition; rather, they serve to dispel doubts regarding the non-commencement of the work, based on the absence of prior knowledge (*vyutpatti-abhāva*), the difficulty of comprehension (*pratipatti-dausthya*), the existence of other means of knowledge (*mānāntara-sattva*), and the lack of fruitfulness (*aphalatva*).

The third position is that all four sections constitute a single chapter (*peṭikā*). "The mere *kṣetrajña*" means the general category of individual souls (*jīva*). The sense is that, because the reasoning is identical through the medium of the [acquisition of] knowledge (*vidyā*), those positions are equal. Having taken for granted that the subject matter is the Hṛdaya, on account of the uniformity of the path found within other Upaniṣads...

And because it is presented as the cause, he states that the passage concerning the knowledge of Being (*sadvidyā*) alone is the subject matter, saying: "by way of being its support. This means: by way of supporting the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Nor should it be argued that this implies other Vedāntic texts are also included in the category [of the subject], resulting in a contradiction with the preceding text; for it should be understood that this will be resolved later. The phrase "appropriate for being the material cause" implies the sense of being subject to modification (*vikāritva*).

Now, even though the doubt regarding insentience is to be rejected, one might argue that the subject matter [of the inquiry] is the sentence containing words such as "Brahman. To this, he says: "Being, Brahman, Self, and so forth. The intention is that since "being" (sattva) is common to all things in relation to "Brahman-ness," it is appropriate to investigate that very [being].

The sense is this: if a specific [referent] such as space (*ākāśa*) or the sense organs (*indriya*) were accepted [as the object of the term "Being"], then the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on those terms would be refuted right from the outset; consequently, the prima facie argument based on general terms like "Being" (*sat*) and so forth would be struck down by the "stick-and-cake" logic (*daṇḍāpūpanyāya*). Therefore, it is appropriate that this very [argument] should proceed first. Thus, when he says "he states the existence of doubt," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "only in a sentence joined with the word 'Being' (*sat*)."

However, some connect [the text] as a single unit, stating that "since the operation of logic (*nyāya*) occurs when there is doubt, he declares the existence of doubt for the sake of introducing logic," and thus include "disagreement" (*vipratipatti*) as well. By the phrase "stated by others" (*paroktam*), since there is an implication of what has been stated by oneself as well, a disagreement consisting of two statements conveying contradictory meanings is presented. Here, by the phrase "stated by others," the fact that [the world] consists of the three *guṇas* is indicated; thus, the reason in the form of "similarity of characteristics with the effect" (*kāryasālakṣaṇya*) is supported.

The intention is that by the phrase "what was stated by itself" (*svoktam*), the indication of sentience (*cetanatva*) implies the support of the primary status of being a seer (*īkṣitṛtva*). As for the remark, "the inquiry is common to the remainder of the section," one might object: "Since this inquiry is actually common to the entire chapter, how can it be said to be common only to the remainder of the section? This is not so.

Are all Vedānta passages intended to propound the Pradhāna and so forth, or are they intended to show that [the Self] is distinct from them? Regarding this point, it should be understood that since the existence of the sentient and insentient as distinct from [the Self] has already been established in the first pāda, the remaining three pādas serve to exclude other possible connections and thus concern only a limited number of passages. The meaning is: "Is it a proving factor or not, which contradicts the sense of the word *brahman*? Consequently, the word *ātman* contradicts the sense of the words *tejas* (fire) and so forth being synonymous with the word *brahman*.

The doubt as to how this statement could be made—given that even the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) does not accept this [position]—is thereby dispelled. The same should be understood for what follows. The phrase "of the two horns" indicates the expectation: "Between these two, which horn is worthy of being determined as possessing sound reasoning? This is the meaning.

"Because it is observed to be the cause of pleasure, pain, and delusion. For example, a single woman, endowed with beauty, youth, noble birth, and good character, brings pleasure to her husband; for what reason? Because she gives rise to a state of pleasure in him. That same woman brings pain to a co-wife; for what reason? Because she gives rise to a state of pain in her. Likewise, that same woman causes delusion to another man who has not obtained her; for what reason? Because of her [giving rise to a state of delusion] in him.

Because they arise from the form of delusion (*moha*), all objects (*padārtha*)—being causes for the association with pleasure, pain, and delusion—are themselves of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion; thus, the meaning is that they are rooted in *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. For this very reason, the non-difference between cause and effect is stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) by explaining the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) as referring to what has been previously mentioned. Alternatively, he explains [the passage] as referring to the scriptural text (*śruti*) beginning with "In the beginning, this was Being alone" (*sadeva...*).

Immediately after the statement "here this formal argument (*prayoga*) is to be understood," the portion of the text explaining the nature of that formal argument has been omitted due to a scribe's error. It is as follows: "This world is known by a single material cause-consciousness (*ekopādānavijñāna*), because it is an effect, like an object produced from a single lump of clay as commonly agreed upon. In the *Bhāṣya*, [the phrase] "in which the word itself is not the means of valid cognition" [is used].

On this point, some [commentators] hold that the particle *eva* here is displaced; its meaning is that verbal testimony (*śabda*) is not indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). According to the Sāṅkhya view, since the Veda merely restates what is already established by inference, it lacks the status of a means of valid cognition, and thus the quality of being non-verbal (*aśabdatva*) truly exists. As Vācaspati has stated: "The Sāṅkhyas maintain that the Upaniṣads merely restate that the Pradhāna is the material cause of the world, as established by inference.

For this very reason, there is no room for the objection raised in the *Ṭīkā*: "If it is argued that the scripture does not teach what has already been obtained through other means of knowledge," nor for its subsequent refutation.

Even if one accepts that scripture (*śruti*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the term "non-verbal" (*aśabda*) refers to a means of knowledge other than verbal testimony; by adding the suffix *ac* (as in *arśa-ādi*), the meaning obtained is "that which is inferential. This is because it will be stated later in the *Ṭīkā*, during the refutation of the opponent's view, that [the term] is like the word "inferential" (*ānumānika*). To explain it as implying a restrictive determination—that "verbal testimony alone is not a valid means of knowledge"—is overly strained. For if that were the case, the usage of the expression "there is no jar" (*aghaṭam*) would be justified even when a jar is present on the ground along with a cloth, they say.

Others, however, argue that since we observe the usage "the chariot, the city gate, and so forth are not made by a single agent" with respect to things lacking a single maker, the statement that [the Veda] is "not based on scripture" (aśabda) is justified by taking it to mean the absence of being established by scripture alone (*śabdamātra-pramāṇakatva*). Nor is it right to say that, in their view, the objection and its refutation by the author of the *Ṭīkā* are misplaced because they do not accept the authority of scripture—since for them, scripture merely restates what is established by inference; for there is no insistence that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) must proceed solely on the grounds of being a restatement.
They say that this is because a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is possible, namely that scripture (śruti) and inference (anumāna) establish [their objects] by acting as mutual auxiliaries.

The intention is that by demonstrating—through the author of the Sūtras—that the nature of sound (*śabdatva*), as conceived by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), namely its being characterized by having a means of knowledge other than sound, is untenable, the proponent's status as one who speaks contradictory words is revealed. The phrase "because it is intent upon defining the sentence" means that the entire definition of *samanvaya* consists of an investigation into the fact that everything is conveyed by the sentence. The phrase "the fallacy of the unestablished due to a different locus" means the exclusion of the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*).

In the statement of the verbal root as *īkṣ-tip-ā-v-i-t*, the meaning is that it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the root. Because it is marked with *ś* (the *śit* designation), the suffix *śap* is applied. They say that by the force of the *śit* designation, *śap* is applied even when the *sārvadhātuka* suffix denotes the agent. [Objection: Should it not rather have been stated as *īkṣateḥ*? Indeed, because *īkṣati* is heavy (*guru*), the suffix *aṅ* would apply by the rule "after a heavy [root] ending in a consonant" (*gurośca halaḥ*), and thus the form should be *īkṣā*. [Reply: But [the suffix] *ktin* applies in the feminine; and since there is no application of the rule "optionally different forms may be used" (*vāsarūpa*) within the section governing the feminine (*stryadhikāra*), if *ktin* were present, the form would be *īkṣateḥ*.

This would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Since the suffix *iṭ* is prohibited by the rule *titutreṭo niṣedhaḥ*, and since the letters *sk* are elided by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca*, the form would then have to be *īṣṭeḥ*; if this is argued, it is not so. The word *iti* here signifies "in this manner" (*prakārārtha*). According to the rule *gurośca halaḥ*, the form would be *īkṣā* when the suffix *aṅ* is applied. If it is argued that there is usage with the suffix *ktin*—as in the rule *striyāṃ ktinnabādibhyaḥ*—then why would *ki* (the suffix *ki*) be an exception to *aṅ* here, as in the case of *āpti*, *dīpti*, and so on? For the author of the *Vṛtti* has stated: "The roots beginning with *āp* are to be followed according to actual usage."

If it is argued that there is the usage *īkṣateḥ* with the suffix *ktin*, [we reply: since it has been stated that "the augment *iṭ* is not applied to roots beginning with *gṛh* in the case of the suffixes *ktin*, *tu*, and *tre*", the augment *iṭ* would apply here as well, just as in the case of *nigṛhīti* and so on; otherwise, the form would be *īṣṭiḥ*, and it could not by any means be *īkṣateḥ*. Thus, the natural fitness (*svārasya*) regarding the intended meaning is indicated; the point is that by not employing the actual meaning-form (*arthasvarūpa*) "from seeing" (*īkṣaṇāt*), but rather employing the verbal form "of the root *īkṣ*" (*īkṣateḥ*), the natural fitness of the verbal root (*dhātusvārasya*) is signaled.

The meaning is that one should not be deluded into thinking that the intention of the Commentator (the Bhāṣyakāra) is that the word *īkṣati* in the Sūtra is intended to be in the genitive case and that the word *śravaṇāt* must be supplied. The phrase "even from mere consciousness" means even from the general category of the individual soul (*jīva*). The phrase "obstruction of his resolve" implies that having an unobstructed resolve is precisely what constitutes being "one whose resolve is true.
