[The phrase] "the state of being the body of the conscious and the unconscious... [is as follows].

"How so?"—this is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as asking, "How can there be a causal relationship between two dissimilar things? Since the sūtra *na vilakṣaṇatvāt* (*Not so, because of dissimilarity*) is intended to refute that very doubt, the sense is that there is no desire to state [the existence of the Pradhāna] here, as that [dissimilarity] is absent. Nor can it be argued that, because of the presentation of the effect as a logical mark in the passage, "O dear one, seek the root of Being by means of the sprout of fire," an intention to employ inference is indeed perceived, and thus the Pradhāna—which is known solely through inference—is what is to be established here; for Brahman is to be understood through Scripture alone.

It should not be said that the presentation of a logical mark (liṅga) is impossible; for there is no failure to present a reason (hetu) that follows from the stated proposition (pratijñā) and example (dṛṣṭānta), and because even in the case of Brahman, there is no contradiction in the operation of inference supported by scripture. This is evident from the Śvetāśvatara mantra: "Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the source (yoni), and the person (puruṣa)—these are to be considered. Their conjunction [is the cause], but not from the self-nature [of the Self]; for the Self too is not the master over the cause of pleasure and pain. For in this mantra, we see the presentation of an inference based on the mark of the effect (kāryaliṅga) specifically for Brahman, who is distinct from time, inherent nature, karma, the great elements, primordial matter (prakṛti), and the person.

Nor does this entail a loss of the scripture’s independence (*nirapekṣatva*); for although the scripture requires the collection of logical principles (*nyāyakalāpa*) composed in the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra to determine its intended meaning (*tātparya*), and even requires inference that supports it as shown by the scripture itself, once the intended meaning has been determined, there is no dependence on other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) for the sake of verifying the object. This is because the dependence on inference for determining the intended meaning is well-established, since inference—in the form of supporting arguments (*upapatti*)—is included within the methods such as the introduction and conclusion (*upakramopasaṃhāra*). Furthermore, the illustration of the lump of clay and so forth is not merely for the purpose of removing doubts regarding impossibility.

It should not be said that inference is not to be presented [as a means of proof], for even in such passages as, "There is no loss of the vision of the seer, because of the indestructibility of the Self," the occurrence of inference is indeed evident.

Because it is impossible for that [reason] not to be included by direct perception (*darśana*). If it is asked: "In that case, for what purpose is there a rejection of the connection as a reason in the formulation of the *hetuvannigada* (statement resembling a reason), such as 'One offers with a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), for by it food is prepared'? Is it not so? The answer is no. For if the preparation of food were connected as a reason, it would imply a universal pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that "whatever prepares food, with that one must offer. This would lead to the inference that even the ladle (*darvī*), the cooking pot (*piṭhara*), and so forth, are means of offering. Consequently, the winnowing basket mentioned in the directly revealed scripture (*pratyakṣa-śruti*) would be rendered inappropriate (*anyāyya*) by those inferred means, such as the ladle and the cooking pot.

The phrase “because it rests upon conceptual construction” (vikalpassayāt) serves to exclude the connection with a logical reason (*hetu*) for that purpose; it does not, however, aim to exclude it on the grounds that its validity would be dependent [on such a reason] when there is a connection with a reason. For this very reason, in that same section of the *Nyāyasudhā* regarding the *Ātithyeṣṭi*, concerning the statement: “There are four portions of clarified butter (*ājya*), for no after-sacrifices (*anūyāja*) are offered elsewhere,” [it is explained as follows].

It has been stated that because the absence of after-offerings (*anūyāja*) is made the reason for the absence of the intermediate fourfold drawing of ghee (*caturgṛhīta*), it is established that wherever there is an absence of after-offerings, there is everywhere an absence of the intermediate fourfold drawing. The claim that this refutation of the logical connection of the reason is merely for the sake of dispelling invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is nothing more than the insistence of the author of the *Nibandhana*. Therefore, since the reason favored by the Sāṅkhyas—which would imply the Pradhāna—is not presented here as a primary inferential mark, the intended meaning is that [the text] does not have the Pradhāna as its ultimate purport.

The meaning of the statement is that "the identity of all consciousness" would result either from the identity of their attributes (*dharmaikyāt*) or from the absence of any distinct entity. Regarding the phrase "in jars, cloths, and so forth": the connection is that there is an absence of both the identity of attributes and the possession of a common form among jars, cloths, and the like, when considered through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the exclusion of anything else (*vyatirekeṇa*). By the expression "through positive concomitance with the exclusion of anything else," the absence of the distinction from other entities—which is characterized by the non-existence of other entities—is introduced. For its meaning is: "by way of distinction" (*vyatirekeṇa*) means "by way of existence as something distinct" (*vyatiriktatayā sadbhāvena*).

He explains that the phrase "residing in the conscious" (*cetanagata*) means "that which establishes consciousness," because even though "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) is not primary [in the case of primordial matter], it is said to be seeing insofar as it serves as a proof for consciousness; thus he says, "conducive to consciousness" (*cetanatvānuguṇam*). For the sake of uniformity, he likewise explains the phrase "residing in the principal" (*pradhānagata*) as meaning "conducive to unconsciousness" (*acetanatvānuguṇam*). The principle of the "foremost" (*agrayaprāyanyāya*) applies here; for when there is no sublation, the term "foremost" (*agra*) implies "best" (*śreṣṭha*), as in the maxim regarding what is written in the "foremost" part of a document.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the principle of *āgrayaṇa-prāya* (the rule of the majority) applies only in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), whereas here there is indeed such a subverting factor? For the scriptural mention of "beholding" (*īkṣaṇa-śruti*) itself acts as a subverter, since the principle of *āgrayaṇa-prāya*, which relies on proximity (*sannidhi*) and indication (*lakṣaṇā*), is weaker when in conflict with the scriptural mention of "beholding. Furthermore, according to the principle "In a matter of doubt, [the meaning is determined] by the observation of the majority," the rule of majority-recitation (*prāyapāṭha*) only comes into play when there is doubt; however, in the present case, because the scriptural mention of "beholding" exists, there is no doubt. [Reply: This is not so.

The intended meaning is as follows: since it must be stated that that which consists of *sattva* and the other [guṇas] is produced from a cause of a similar nature, the scriptural mention of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) lacks any opposing force due to its contradiction with inference; thus, while doubt indeed arises regarding the subject at hand, a definitive conclusion becomes possible through the principle of "contextual predominance" (*prāyapāṭha*). By the phrase "by this very logic," it is meant "by the logic of the predominant case" (*agrayaprāyanyāya*).

"Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self and differentiate name and form"; "Having entered these three deities with this living self, he differentiated name and form"; "Just as indeed, my dear, these three deities"—in these passages, the word "deity" (*devatā*) is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) for fire, water, and food.

It should be understood that the status of being the object of a plural number is established because there are many sentient beings (*sattva*); therefore, one should consider that the statement made here in the *Tūlikā*—namely, "Even though only a single word for 'deity' (*devatā*) is heard in reference to insentient objects, nevertheless, because the form ending in the plural is used, three words exist through the application of the *ekaśeṣa* rule, and thus the status of being the object of a plural number is established"—is not correct.

"If it is argued that [the term 'Self'] is secondary, we say no, because of the word 'Self'. Regarding the phrase "This whole world has that as its Self; that is the Self," one should understand that both expressions—"the jar has clay as its essence" and "clay is the essence of the jar"—are indicated with the intention of using the word "Self. In the Siddhānta, however, the meaning is that the nature of being the Self (*ātmatva*) is possible in the sense of being the controller of the body.

Having explained the word *api* as signifying conjunction (*samuccaya*), he explains it as signifying contradiction (*virodha*) as well, with the words: "or [it means] 'even those things accepted by you [the Sāṅkhya], because they do not have that [Brahman] as their essence. Regarding the Bhāṣya, [it says]: "The designation of 'seeing' (*īkṣaṇa*) is indeed primary. Now, [one might object]: after fire, water, and earth have been created, there is the resolve preceded by the thought, "Entering with this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me manifest names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2). This refers to the Supreme...

If it be asked: "How can the entry of the Self establish that the preceding [elements]—fire, water, and earth—are characterized by the predominance of seeing and so forth?"—the answer is: No. This is because, according to the maxim that "an example need not be strictly adhered to," there exist means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishing the Supreme Self as the Self; furthermore, the principle that words denoting the body extend to the embodied one is established in the *Akṛtyadhikaraṇa*. Such is the meaning of the Sūtra. As for the phrase "this is the intention of the Sūtra," the sense is that having multiple intentions within a single Sūtra is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).

Regarding the phrase "among those that favor the primary and secondary meanings," although it appears in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) that the term "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) is not to be understood in a secondary sense according to the context of the *prāyapāṭha* (a reading consisting mostly of primary meanings)—because such a context is weaker than the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) whose nature is to favor the primary meaning—nevertheless, the intention here is that it is still possible to establish that very same principle [that even a secondary meaning may be followed].

The phrase "the suspicion regarding its having a subordinate probandum as its object" means the suspicion regarding its having as its object a subordinate probandum consisting in the absence of figurative usage (*gauṇatvābhāva*). Regarding the expression "by defining the attribute of *īkṣaṇa* (seeing) which is conducive to [establishing] causality": one might object that this is not a satisfactory reply to someone who asserts that the Pradhāna alone is the cause of the world, because the opponent does not admit that the attributes of *īkṣaṇa* and being an object of meditation for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) are pervaded by the status of being the cause of the world; therefore, stating that the Pradhāna lacks causality simply because it lacks *īkṣaṇa* and is not an object of meditation for those seeking liberation would be inadequate.

If it is argued that this cannot be maintained—because it is impossible to prove the absence of causality apart from the absence of those [qualities], and therefore the Pradhāna is not what is taught by the *Sadvidyā* since "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) occurring at the beginning is impossible there, and because the qualities heard in the conclusion are also not present there, and thus it cannot be the subject matter of the entire textual context—we say no; for the purport of this very treatise is precisely that.

The sense is this: since liberation is taught for one who is devoted to that [Self], how is it understood that [the teaching] is for the purpose of contemplation (*anusandhāna*)? Therefore, the meaning of the statement "having taught the contemplation of the nature of Being" is as follows: the meaning of the commentary's statement, "the contemplation of the nature of Being is taught by the words 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*)," is this.

It must be stated that the meaning is: having taught that "the person who has a teacher knows" (*ācāryavān puruṣo veda*), one then instructs on the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the nature of being *Sat* (Existence) for one who has already realized "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Otherwise, even if the nature of being *Sat* were taught by the words "That thou art," it would be impossible to teach the contemplation of that nature of *Sat*. And if this meaning were thus explained, these two [alleged] doubts and their refutations would not arise. If you say this:

True; for there is the possibility of success because this serves to establish that the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) understood from the words of the Veda is of the nature of meditation (*upāsanā*). By means of the introduction and conclusion, along with explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) containing results, he demonstrates through the body of the textual collection that the purport of the sentences is meditation, beginning with the words "It is said" (*ucyate*) and so forth, until the word "he knew" (*vijajñau*) is reached; by this, the mark of the purport of meditation in the form of repetition (*abhyāsa*) is established.

Nor should it be argued that because the repetition serves to indicate the completion of the chapter, it lacks the status of being a "repetition" (abhyāsa) as an indicator of the intended meaning (tātparya-liṅga); for even while indicating the end of the chapter, its nature as a repetition is not lost.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that each one becomes threefold? Therefore, let me understand that; O dear one, understand the state of dream-sleep itself! Let the venerable sir explain this to me further. Regarding the occurrences of the word *vijñāna* (understanding) within this section, they refer exclusively to verbal knowledge (*śābdajñāna*) and not to meditative worship (*upāsanā*). For the phrase "He understood that" (*taddhāsya vijajñau*) does not mean "He performed meditation. Because of the lack of natural consistency [in the opponent's view], [the author] states even in the middle: "The man who has a teacher knows."

The meaning is that the phrase "the mark for what is to be investigated" is a praise of meditation insofar as it has the state of having a teacher as its fruit; thus, it serves as a mark (*liṅga*) regarding the purpose of meditation. Now, one might object: although the passage "When speech merges into the mind" actually concerns the departure from the body, since the body is not explicitly mentioned there, [the author] states with this reservation: "And elsewhere, 'rising up from this body. The term "body" is understood here to mean the *prārabdha* karma that initiates the body.
In the commentary on the Sūtra, "But having exhausted the others by means of experience," [it is said]: "For him, the delay is only so long as he is not released from these two through experience."

This is because it will be stated later that there is "liberation from the two karmas. It should also be observed that for Vasiṣṭha, Āvantaratapas, and others, there was no attainment of Brahman even after the fall of their bodies resulting from knowledge and their [past] origins. In the phrase "I shall be liberated, I shall attain," the change of person (from first to third) is a Vedic usage; the meaning is "he shall be liberated, he shall attain. To dispel the doubt that the word "attainment" (*sampatti*) in the phrase "attainment of the insentient" (*acetana-sampatti*) might mean attaining its very nature, he explains it as "the reaching of the insentient" (*acit-prāpti*).

To the question, "What determines that the word *sampatti* has the sense of 'attainment' (*prāpti*)?", he says: "Of the word *sampatti*... The meaning is that because [the text] establishes that [the attainment of the unconscious] is the cause of being struck by the threefold suffering (*tāpatraya*), and because only the attainment of the unconscious is the cause of being struck by the threefold suffering, it is determined that the word *sampatti* signifies attainment. He dispels the doubt—namely, what is the basis for the use of the word "and" (*ca*) in every sūtra, at the very end, as a word signifying conjunction (*samuccaya*), and in the middle of the section—with the passage beginning "Thus it thought" (*evaṃ tadaikṣata*).

The meaning is that the use of the word "ca" (and) at various intervals serves to indicate the conjunction of reasons contained within the preceding statements. Alternatively, since there is little purpose in explaining the conjunction by making such a division, he states the purpose of the word "ca" in another way, beginning with the words "by stating its acceptability," and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "And because knowledge is possible through the non-produced nature of the conscious aspect," he says this: when the primary matter (*pradhāna*) is known, knowledge of the conscious aspect is possible by way of its being a non-product of that [primary matter]; for if the primary matter is not fully understood, knowledge of the conscious aspect as its non-product is impossible, since knowledge of the primary matter serves as the cause for a cognition whose qualificandum is the conscious aspect and whose mode is its being a non-product. Thus, upon knowing that [primary matter], [the conscious aspect is known] as its non-product.

The sense is that even the knowledge of the *cit* (consciousness) is established. Regarding the phrase, "O dear one, understand from me the end of dream": the meaning is that you should understand from my words the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is the "end of dream. "The suspicion of it being something else" means the suspicion that the word *sat* in the passage "O dear one, [merged] with Being" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a different entity from Brahman.

The intention is that it depends on the inherent nature of verbal roots (*dhātu-svabhāva*); the point is that while one can use a form like "merged with Being" (*satā saṃpannaḥ*) using a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), one cannot say "merged into Being" (*satā apītaḥ*), as this is determined by the specific nature of the verbal root.

Now, one might object that if the two words *sva* and *sat* terminate in the same meaning, one of them would be redundant; anticipating this doubt, he says: "by the living self" (*jīvenātmanā*). Just as in the passage "by this living self," the word *jīva* is not redundant because it serves to convey that the Supreme Self—presented by the word *ātman* as the essential nature—is the embodied self of the *jīva*.

Thus, the sense is that the two words [“sva” and “rūpeṇa”] are purposeful because they indicate that the Supreme Self, which is present by its own nature through the word "self" (*sacchabdena*), has the individual soul as its body. "By its own nature" means by the nature of the Supreme Self, according to such passages as "because of the non-difference between cause and effect. Furthermore, the word "self" does not refer to the abstract Brahman; this is the remainder of the sense. This is because maintaining [the world] in its essential form is equal [in both cases], as in the case of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).

The meaning is that if it were asserted that [the body] is maintained by the power of its own nature alone, then there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the body would continue to be maintained even during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). Thus, neither the inseparable establishment (apṛthaksiddhi) of the body with respect to the individual soul (jīva), nor the definition of the body, would be tenable. If it is objected: "What inconsistency is there in the inseparable establishment of the soul with the body, given the soul's existence within the body?"—it is not so.

Non-separability from the nature of the *jīva* is not [mere] non-separability; for if it were so, then since non-separability from the nature of the *jīva* would be impossible in all the bodies of Saubhari, they would fail to attain the status of being bodies. Rather, it is the state of being pervaded by the knowledge that constitutes its attributes (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). For this very reason, the statement, "When the *jīva* leaves one branch, then that branch withers," indicates that the portion of the body where there is an absence of the pervasion of the knowledge constituting its attributes undergoes withering; thus, the meaning is that there is non-separability from the *jīva*’s knowledge that constitutes its attributes.

The meaning is that because of the pervasion of knowledge, there is no abandonment of the body by the *jīva*; the sense is that even in the absence of external exit—since such exit depends upon the senses and other factors—there exists merely the presence of the knowledge necessary for maintaining the body. Furthermore, "because of its fitness for maintenance" means "because it is being maintained. Now, [an objection]:

If it is argued that "merging" (*laya*) consists in being included within that which persists through the causal state, then there is a contradiction: for as much as something possesses the status of being a locus of merging, it does not possess the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*); and for that portion which possesses the status of being the material cause, it cannot be the substratum of merging, because inclusion within that very portion is impossible. Anticipating this objection, he states the lack of contradiction with the words beginning "of the one Supreme Self," etc. This is intended to exclude other interpretations and to indicate the distinctiveness of his own commentary, characterized by its conformity to the explanations composed by the Great Sage (Vyāsa).

The meaning is that [the author] mentions the commentator (Vṛttikāra) from time to time. Since it is unnatural for the word *asampatti* to mean "departure," he explains it otherwise by saying, "or rather, in the Supreme Self. By stating "the state of the commentator" (*vṛttikārasya bhāvaḥ*), he indicates—through agreement with the commentary—that this is also the intended meaning of the sūtra *svāpyayāt*. Thus, the fruit of citing that example is not established by any other means.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [indicates the end of the commentary]. Now, one might object: "In the Bhāṣya, since the unity of meaning with other scriptural passages such as 'In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone' establishes that the cause must be conscious, a specific conclusion—that the Lord of All alone is the cause—should have been made at the point of summary; why then is there a conclusion that merely excludes the non-conscious? Anticipating this doubt, he says in the previous sūtra, "by the Intelligent One," and so forth. Regarding the Bhāṣya statement, "This Rigveda and so forth are His breath," the meaning is that the entire manifold world, beginning with the Rigveda, arose effortlessly, like a mere exhalation.

Regarding the phrase "nanvetatsūtraviṣayavākyatvena" (But surely this [is the case] because it is the subject sentence for this sūtra), some say: In the previous sūtra, what was intended was the "commonality of movement" (*gatisāmānya*) which makes known the conscious nature [of the Self]; here, however, the distinction is that there is the hearing of many attributes that are unique to the Supreme Self.

They say that this very distinction lies between the scriptural passages cited from the previous sūtra and those cited here; otherwise, there would be no reason for not including the passages found within this very Upaniṣad, since they share the same general purport (*gatisāmānya*). Now, one might object: when citing other scriptures, the other passage that first sets forth the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) should have been cited first; why then was the sentence concerning another attribute, "He has no lord" (*na tasya kaścit patiḥ*), taken up earlier? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "There is no intention here to express a sequential order."

The meaning is that it was stated previously that the doctrine of Brahman as the material cause (*upādāna*) is inconsistent [with scripture], and thus it was said in the *Janmādi-sūtra* that the same applies to the subsequent sūtras as well. "Because of the conceit of being authoritative regarding what is not authoritative" means that even for one who is authoritative, a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhāntatā*) is observed due to the conceit of being authoritative; this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). "Deviation from established tenets" (*apasiddhāntatā*) means the state of having no established tenet (*asiddhāntatva*). The sense is that, for example, Brahman’s status as the material cause is not established by other scriptures.
"The mention of both the author of the Sūtras and the Śruti" implies that because of the mention of the Śruti, there is the possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*).

The meaning is that because this has been stated by the author of the Sūtras, there is not even the slightest suspicion that it is not an established tenet (*asiddhānta*). The intention of the word "also" (*api*) is as follows: the word "also" serves to include the quality of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). For this very reason, the meaning of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "pure consciousness devoid of distinctions" (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*) is this: by establishing that the Brahman which is the object of inquiry possesses the attribute of ultimate seeing, the author of the Sūtras has refuted the doctrine of a Brahman devoid of distinctions. Nor should it be argued that although the Brahman which is the object of inquiry possesses attributes, the Supreme Brahman does not likewise possess them.

Having first proposed that Brahman alone, who is to be known through the Vedāntas, is the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*), and having established its status as a seer (*īkṣitṛtva*) characterized by consciousness (*cetana*), the text establishes the exclusion of the *pradhāna* by means of that [seership]. Nor should it be argued that "seership" characterized by consciousness—defined as the nature of being conscious—is stated merely for the sake of excluding the *pradhāna*; for the word "conscious" (*cetana*) does not have that [exclusion] as its primary meaning. Consequently, if seership characterized by consciousness were established, the exclusion of the *pradhāna* would not be established at all; thus, for the sake of establishing the differentiator...

Regarding the phrase "because exclusion is unestablished": he explains that it is natural for the commentary's statement, "to be known through the Vedānta," to be intended as a rebuttal to the objection raised in the preceding sentence; or alternatively, he explains it by stating that "witnesshood is simply its own essential nature. Since it is accepted [by the opponent] that [the Self] is a substance, it cannot be said that the word [denoting it] expresses a quality distinct from a substance; therefore, he says, "the word 'quality' refers to a property (dharma). This is said while accepting its capacity for that [function], even though it does not have the form of a means (*upāya*) for it.

The meaning is: "having accepted the possibility that it may be capable of such [transformation]. Now, one might object: "But regarding the statement, 'O King, that which does not even over time assume another designation, though produced through transformation and so forth—that is a real entity (vastu), and what is that?'—it is not the case that this 'reality' (vastutva), which resides solely in the Supreme Self, is necessitated by being an object of valid cognition (pramāṇa-viṣayatva); for such reality is absent even in non-conscious entities (acid-vastu) which are objects of valid cognition. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Reality is common to both the conscious and the unconscious."

Regarding the passage beginning with "paraistu," [the author] specifies the *jīva* by saying "of that which is denoted by the word 'Sat'. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "in the sentence, 'Having entered with this living self (anena jīvenātmanā...)'". The sense is that the phrase "with this living self" refers to the Deity denoted by the word "Sat," meaning "with this living self, which is my own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Now, one might object: even if it is said that [the term *ātman*] is not figurative because of the word *jīva*, there is still no inherent cogency, because the point—that the *jīva* is designated as the *ātman*—remains unproven. Anticipating this lack of conviction, [the author] states: "The word *ātman* refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and is dependent [on another]."

For this very reason, in the statement "If he sings on the *yoni*, he sings on the two *uttaras*," the word *uttara* refers only to those [specific verses] because it is a conventional term (*rūḍha*) for a particular name of a textual collection; it does not refer to the two [verses] following the *yoni*. This is because, as a relative term (*sambandhi-śabda*), it would otherwise be dependent on a correlative.

It has been stated [in the *Bhāṣya*] that this is because the cognition is delayed. Regarding the phrase, "But the quality of being the subsequent is understood as occasional due to immediate sequence," this was discussed in the ninth chapter (*navama-adhikaraṇa*). Having raised the objection that the word "self" (*ātman*) in the passage "by this living self" (*anena jīvenātmanā*) is used in a secondary sense—just as in the expression "my self is Bhadrasena"—the Sūtra, "Because liberation is taught for one who is established in That," was explained by others as being intended to refute that objection.

He refutes that [position] with the words, "consisting of consciousness and non-consciousness. It is logical that [the third sūtra] expresses the reason for the ultimate probandum; therefore, because of this very lack of natural fit, one should observe that even in Śaṅkara’s commentary, the third sūtra is applied as the reason for the ultimate probandum itself, starting with the words, "Or rather, in the previous sūtra itself," and so forth. As in the passage beginning, "O dear one, just as the honey-makers..."—the "honey-makers" are bees—and "honey... [is produced].

They settle and bring about the collection of the juices of various trees—such as the *nānātyaya*, *āmnāta*, and *adika*—by gathering them together. They reduce them to a single state, a single nature, bringing the juice to the state of honey; that is, they cause it to attain the condition of honey. Once those juices have become unified as honey, they do not attain distinction therein, such that one could say, "This is the juice of the *vakula* tree, and this is not the juice of the mango.
The meaning is that even though the creatures have thus become unified, they do not attain distinction. Thus ends the section on *Īkṣati*.

The phrase "the intellect descending into the inner self" means the notion of [the self] being the cause of the world. Now, one might object: in this section, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) does not posit that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the cause of the world, followed by the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it is the Brahman distinct from that; rather, after deliberating whether the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is the individual soul or the Supreme Self, the prima facie view is established as "the consisting of bliss is the individual soul," and the final conclusion is established as "it is the Brahman. Otherwise, if the prima facie view were that the individual soul is the cause of the world...

Since it is more appropriate to present all the scriptural passages that teach attributes impossible for the individual soul (jīva), it would follow that it is improper to compose a system of reasoning that determines the meaning of the *Ānandavallī* alone; furthermore, because the existence of a Brahman distinct from the jīva is established by the very attributes impossible for the jīva taught in the scriptural citations quoted in the ancillary sūtra (*guṇasūtra*) of the preceding section—"And because [these qualities] are heard [in scripture]" (*śrutatvācca*)—and because the matter has already been settled by such [sūtras] as "But on account of the teaching of what is superior, Bādarāyaṇa [holds this], for he sees thus" (*adhikopadeśāttu bādarāyaṇasyaivaṃ taddarśanāt*) and "But [the Self is] superior, on account of the mention of difference" (*adhikaṃ tu bhedanirdeśāt*).

Therefore, one must investigate whether the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) taught in the *Ānandavallī* is the individual soul (*jīva*) or the supreme Brahman. Nor should it be argued that if this does not concern the causal aspect [of Brahman], it would lack connection with the first chapter (*samanvayādhyāya*); for its inclusion is justified in the same manner as the investigation in the subsequent three chapters (*tripādī*). Nor should it be argued that even there, the inquiry consists solely of the nature of causality; for the *Bhāṣya* states that the possession of various attributes by Brahman is what is being established, and the *Adhikaraṇasārāvalī* states: "By means of the qualities of the respective sections, it proclaims those very qualities [of Brahman]."

If it be argued that one should not, in general, contemplate whether the cause of the world is the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Brahman, we reply: true, it is indeed contemplated in that very manner. However, this is done with the intention that if the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) were the *jīva*, there might arise some deficiency of faith in the doctrine that the cause is the Brahman who is distinct from the *jīva*; thus, the statement serves to exclude what is impossible.

Having raised the objection that this has already been determined in the *Jyotir-adhikaraṇa*, and having refuted it by stating that there is no cause for doubt, [the author] will again raise the challenge: "In that case, there would be no reason to begin the first pāda, which concerns the existence of a cause distinct from consciousness. He will resolve this by stating that there is no pointlessness [to the pāda], because if many Vedānta passages were intended to refer merely to the cause consisting of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*), then doubt would likewise arise regarding the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Others, however, [hold that] in the third quarter (tripādī), which aims at the exclusion of what is fit for other [systems], the author of the Sūtras—by using the word "also" (*api*) in the sūtra "And some [consider it] based on inference" (*ānumānikam apy ekeṣām*)—demonstrates that even *pradhāna* might be the cause of the world; thus, the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the first quarter is inferred to be that the cause of the world is indeed nothing more than *pradhāna*. For this very reason, in the section concerning the inferential [cause] (*ānumānikādhikaraṇa*) in the *Kalpataru* commentary, it is stated: "For in the preceding [quarter], it was argued that *pradhāna* and so forth alone constitute the meaning of all Vedāntas; [this is now refuted] by negation."

In this case, however, having admitted that [the Self is the cause], they argue that even *pradhāna* and so forth are causes; and it is said that the author of the Sūtras, by employing the word "even" (*api*), indicated through his acceptance of the Brāhmaṇical [view] that this inquiry is merely occasional.

In this section, which is devoted to an investigation of statements concerning the cause, one might ask: since it ought to have been stated that [the passage] beginning with "From that very Self, indeed, ether was produced" is what is heard in scripture, why did the author of the Commentary cite the passage beginning with "That indeed is this"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of that which has the cause as its object. This is because it serves as the introduction to the explanation of the word "Self"; therefore, from the word "Self,"...

The sense is that, among the various explanations of the word, because "sa vā eṣa" (that indeed is this) serves as the introductory statement, the claim that [the passage] is "pertinent to the subject at hand" (*prakṛta*) is justified, even though it does not serve as the introduction to the causal statement which constitutes the actual subject matter. Regarding the phrase "acceptance of sentience and so forth": the meaning is that there is acceptance of sentience as established by the word "omniscient" (*sarvajña*), and acceptance of [the Self] as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) as established by the word "Lord of All" (*sarveśvara*).

Furthermore, since [the reasons] such as "being distinct from the individual soul" were not previously stated, one should not object: "How can the word 'true' (*satya*) be applied to that which was not stated? This is merely an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication); it should also be understood that while there is acceptance regarding the portion already stated, there is non-acceptance regarding the aspect of its being real (*vāstavatva*), based on the natural sense of the text: "What was stated is true. The point is that the particle *eva* (only/alone), when connected with the verb, serves to exclude absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*), thereby indicating a lack of natural appropriateness (*asvārasya*).

Now, one might object that in the Sāṅkhya system, since the individual soul (jīva) lacks agency—which is the meaning of the suffix [in the word "seer"]—its being a "seer" (īkṣitatva) is untenable. Anticipating this, the author states "only witnesshood" (sākṣitvam eva), intending to show that even if the meaning of the suffix is untenable, the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is nonetheless possible. But is it not the case that in this section (adhikaraṇa), the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is the position of the opponent (pūrvapakṣin), whereas their non-difference is the position of the proponent (siddhāntin), according to the Commentator?

It is explained [by some] that this is due to the persistence of an aversion to the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman; however, such is not the intention of the author of the Sūtras, because there is no evidence for such an intention. Therefore, he says: "And because of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśācca*). The phrase "because the distinction from the individual soul is not established" means that the distinctness of the [Self] from the individual soul is not proven. The phrase "of a cognition that is not of a single form" refers to that which possesses states consisting of contraction and expansion of cognition.

The sense is: "because it is to be attained. The intention is that since the nature [of the Self] when dissociated from the non-sentient (acid) is what is to be attained, its status as a human goal (puruṣārtha) consists in its being composed of bliss (ānandamaya). Regarding the etymology "that by which something is known," the sense is that according to the Sāṅkhya school, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is considered to be threefold—namely, mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), and ego (ahaṅkāra); and in the Sāṅkhya system, the word *buddhi* refers to the internal organ, so it is possible for the word *vijñāna* to have an abstract (bhāva) derivation in that context.

And [the phrase] "because there is no intent to refer to a modification" (vikāraparatvābhāvāt)—surely, the rejection of the intent to refer to a modification by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) contradicts the sūtra: "If it be said that [it is not so] because of words denoting modifications, we say no, because of abundance" (*vikāraśabdānneti cenna prācuryāt*).

If it is argued that this is because the meaning of "modification" (*vikāra*) alone is presented as the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in that Sūtra, and because the fact that the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies either its own meaning (*svārthika*) or modification is shown to establish the prima facie view in the very section discussing that meaning—thereby contradicting your own statement—then they reply: In this section, the prima facie view is twofold: one relying on the Sāṅkhya position and one relying on the "tail" (puccha) Brāhmaṇa passage. Among these, regarding the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*), and that refers to the nature of the liberated soul attained [in liberation], and not...

The suffix *mayaṭ* does not signify modification (*vikāra*), nor does it signify abundance (*prācurya*), because the essential nature of that which is to be attained is devoid of modification; therefore, there is no room for either the proponent of the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) or the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*). This is the first [position]. Alternatively, the suffix *mayaṭ* signifies modification and is neither pleonastic (*svārthika*) nor signifying abundance; consequently, in accordance with the suffix *mayaṭ* denoting modification, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) must be the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, either by virtue of being reflected in a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of happiness, or by virtue of being conditioned (*upahita*) by it, or by virtue of being a modification of bliss. This is the other [position].

In this regard, the distinction is that in the first [case], the objection "if it be said on account of the word 'modification'" (*vikāraśabdāt*) is made by a neutral observer (*taṭastha*), whereas in the second, it is made by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*). Thus, it should be understood that the phrase "and because of the absence of the sense of modification" (*vikāraparatvābhāvāt ca*) is intended according to the first position. Some, however, hold that the meaning of "and because of the absence of the sense of modification" refers to the word *vijñānamaya*.

The phrase "because there is no sense of being subject to modification" (*vikāraparatvābhāvāt*) is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as "because there is no sense of denoting abundance" (*prācuryārthakatvābhāvāt*). For they say that if the word *vijñānamaya* were to signify either modification or abundance, there would arise the suspicion that it refers to the individual soul (*jīva*).

The phrase "by way of being the substratum and that which possesses it" means that it is impossible for the *brāhmaṇa* (the substrate), which is the form of the substratum, to be identical with the *ānandamaya* (which is the superstratum). Regarding the expression "of human form": in the scriptural passage, "Following its human form, he too is of human form," the meaning is that this *ānandamaya* is of human form by imitating the human form of that *vijñānamaya*; it is a person who conforms to that [other] person.

The sense is that the natural force (*svārasya*) of the negative description (*vyatireka-nirdeśa*) is established; for if one were to accept that the word "self" (*ātman*) refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) rather than the middle portion, there would be a lack of natural force, as in the expression "the essential nature of a jar" (*ghaṭasya svarūpam*). With the intention of asking, "What loss is there for us?", he replies, "Then what? With the intention of saying that if both parties agree that the tail is the "Brahman-hood," then the dispute is settled, he asks, "But what then? [The opponent says: "By you, Brahman-hood is asserted of the tail alone, not of the *ānandamaya*; by us, however, [it is asserted] of both, because of their identity."

The meaning is that "liberation" implies "discrimination. The sense is that by [the phrase] "avoiding the literal meaning," he avoids the objection that the status of the *brāhmaṇa* passage as referring to the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is unestablished. The sense is that even if [the term] exists, it is a statement based on a hypothetical doubt; for it would not be appropriate to state a hypothetical doubt such as, "if one were to know the pot as an object of cognition. The intention is that even the metaphorical representation "what is done here? is for the purpose of understanding the essential nature as distinguished from others. [The objection] "because it is not the primary subject matter" is addressed as follows: surely being common to all the successive sections (*paryāya*) does not contradict its being the primary subject, as seen in the *Antaryāmin-brāhmaṇa*.

If it is argued: "Just as in passages such as 'He who dwells in the earth,' even though this applies to all the successive sections (paryāya), the primacy of that which is indicated by the word *yat* is perceived everywhere; likewise here too, in all five sections, the primacy belongs only to that indicated by the word *ātman* in the phrase 'This is indeed his embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*). Consequently, since it is the tail-Brahman alone that is indicated by the word *ātman*, it is possible for that very entity to be referred to by the masculine pronoun *saḥ* in the passage 'He desired' (*so'kāmayata*'). To this, it is replied:

The intention is that in the passage, "This very one is his embodied self," the term *eṣaḥ* (this one) naturally refers to the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) itself in its masculine gender; therefore, even in that sentence, there is no reference to Brahman.

And because of the natural force of referring to the primary substance (*pradhānaparāmarśitvasvārasyāt*): in the passage, "One pours curd into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas," it is proper that the word *tat* (that) refers only to the milk, which is the primary substance—even though it is being pervaded by the curd being poured in—and not to the curd, which is secondary despite its proximity. Therefore, the meaning is that the milk itself, having become solidified, is the *āmikṣā*, as established in the fourth and eighth chapters of the *Pūrvatantra*.

The sense is that [the text] understands "consciousness is Brahman" in the *Bhṛguvallī*. One might object: "By the criterion of location, the Self is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because it is located there. However, even if the location of bliss is the same as that taught in the *Bhṛguvallī*, since the suffix *-maya* is identical in all five [sheaths] beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*), the similarity of location for the one consisting of bliss is more powerful; therefore, the status of being Brahman for the one consisting of bliss taught in the *Bhṛguvallī* is established from that as well. To this, we say: not so.

The sense is that, since it has not yet been determined that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) mentioned in the *Ānandavallī* is Brahman, the similarity of an undetermined location is irrelevant; rather, it is the similarity of the location of bliss whose Brahman-nature is already established that serves as the determinant of the meaning. This is also because of the force of the word "this" (*etad*) in the phrase "this self consisting of bliss," which refers back to the bliss under discussion. For it has been stated in the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* on the passage beginning with "the knowledge of Bhṛgu" (*yā tu bhārgavī*), [that this is so]. (Note: The word "iti" is understood at the end.)

The phrase "having the form of removal and so forth" intends, by the word "and so forth," the state of being the object to be purified within the context of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Now, one might ask: how can there be a state of being purified in the case of the Supreme Self? For purification can only be imparted to that which was previously impure.

If it is argued that there can be no prior impurity for Brahman, who is eternally pure, we reply: here, by the words "purity" and "impurity," anger and grace are intended. For even if there were impurity in the form of anger in Brahman, it would not contradict His eternal purity characterized by being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*). Otherwise, even the statement "Let the water of the Gaṅgā be purified by *kataka* nuts" would be untenable, since there is no prior impurity in the eternally pure water of the Gaṅgā. And if [it were otherwise], even for the eternally pure water of the Gaṅgā...

If impurity in the form of defilement caused by connection with Kardama and so forth is accepted [as a reason for exclusion], then let the same logic be applied to the present case as well. The point is that, among the sections beginning with "consisting of food" (*annamaya*), it is observed that the primary subjects of each respective section are the objects of the verses contained within those specific sections; therefore, that [subject] which is not the object of the verse belonging to its own section cannot be considered the primary subject.

Regarding the phrase "by means of those not distinct from itself," it should not be argued that the fact that the head, wings, and tail of the "mind-made" (manomaya) being consist of the Ṛg, Sāman, Yajus, Atharvan, and Aṅgiras [Vedas]—which appear to be distinct from the mind-made being—proves that the context does not intend to describe the form of the head, wings, and so forth by means of its own parts which are not distinct from itself; for in that case, the Ṛg, Sāman, etc., [are indeed not distinct].

Because words have as their ultimate purport the mental operations directed toward their respective objects, they too are not distinct from that which consists of mind (*manomaya*); thus, they culminate in the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Now, an objection may be raised: even though for Nārada—who approached with the desire to know the Self, saying, "I have indeed heard from those like your reverence that the knower of the Self overcomes grief"—the instruction proceeded through a succession of questions and answers regarding progressively higher realities than name and so forth, such as "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than name? to which the reply was "Speech is indeed greater than name," and so on, until the process reached its conclusion in the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself; [how can this be reconciled with the claim that the series culminates in the *ānandamaya*?]

Even without such questions and answers, it is accepted that the passage beginning with "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly by means of the Truth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.16.1) aims at teaching something other than the vital breath—both because of the direct hearing of the word "Self" (*ātman*) and because of the indicative mark of the origin of the vital breath—and thus its culminating point is the teaching of the Self, not in the previously mentioned vital breath.

If it is argued that here too, since the *puccha-brāhmaṇa* has been understood as primary through the previously cited means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is proper to accept that the instruction commenced therein reaches its conclusion, we say no. For in the *Bhūmavidyā*, when the instruction on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) was given, the teacher himself introduced another subject—namely, the existence of something else—because he perceived that the instruction regarding the Self had reached its limit at each respective stage (from name up to the vital breath), even though the student had not yet asked a further question despite the mention of "speaking the supreme" (*ativāda*). Thus, it is logical [that the teacher acted in this way].

The point here is that, since the style beginning with "Therefore, from this very [Self]" has been observed in the progressive instruction regarding the Self, there is no reason to abandon it in the case of the Brahman. As for the argument that the subject matter is like a tail, one should not say that the subject matter of the verses situated within the section on the mind-made (manomaya)—such as the verse found in the section on the mind-made, "But when he finds no joy, then he goes to fear... from whom words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—he who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing at any time"—is not the subject matter of the Brahman, and thus the claim that the verses in the context have the tail as their subject matter is unproven. This is because...

Because that verse also—meaning that the wise person does not fear when they reach that bliss of Brahman, which consists of a multitude of auspicious qualities, from which speech turns back unable to grasp it, and which is realized by means of the completely purified mind along with Brahman—it is possible for it to be intended as a praise of the "mind-made" (manomaya) state, just like the "tail. But this is not the case; for the verse, "He becomes non-existent indeed," [means]: if that one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), who is the individual soul (jīva), perceives Brahman as non-existent, he himself becomes non-existent.

It should not be argued that because the text says, "If one knows it as 'He exists,' then he becomes being," this must refer to the *ānandamaya* (the one consisting of bliss), just as in the case of the "tail"; for if "he" (*saḥ*) referred to the *ānandamaya*, it would fail to be a praise of him, resulting in the undesirable consequence that the passage does not have him as its primary subject. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

One might object: "If it is intended here to draw upon the words of the Sūtras—namely, 'Because of seeing, not that which is non-scriptural,' 'Not another, because of impossibility,' and 'And because of the designation of difference, it is other'—then let those very words be employed; what is the purpose of using the term 'Supreme Self' (paramātman)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The succession of inner selves. The point is that by the word *parama*, its unsurpassable nature (*niratiśayatva*) is established.

The meaning is that by the use of the word "kutaḥ" (why) immediately after the term "paramātma-pada," it is demonstrated that the expectation for a reason pertains specifically to the probandum-element consisting of being the Supreme Self, and not to the more remote quality of being composed of bliss (*ānandamayatva*).

Although it could easily be stated that even if it were merely said "the one consisting of bliss is the Supreme Self because of repetition," the phrase "because of repetition" would still connect as a reason for the immediately preceding designation of the Supreme Self in the manner already explained; nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated in that way because one means does not invalidate another, and because what is established must be maintained. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and because it occurs in its own sentence": since "another inner self consisting of bliss" is the subject sentence, and [the term "bliss"] occurs therein, the Sūtra should have been formulated simply as "the one consisting of bliss [is the Supreme Self] because of the designation of difference."

The state [of being]. Because it depends upon supporting arguments, the doubt that "even for one who is liberated, such bliss might exist" must be removed by another argument consisting of the impossibility [of such a thing]; thus, [the term] "modification" (vikāra)...

The meaning is that [the argument] depends on two sūtras beginning with "If it be said, not so, because of the word" (ŚBh 3.3.54). He clarifies that the phrase "being practiced as culminating in the state of unsurpassed bliss" contains a reason by stating "in a sequence increasing hundredfold each time. He demonstrates the contradiction with the sūtra in the view of those who explain the sentence "That one is the bliss of Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8) as referring to the bliss of Prajāpati, by saying "of the sentence 'That one is the bliss of Brahman'."

The meaning is that, because the word "this" (*sa yaścāyam*) refers back—via the pronoun *tat*—to Brahman alone, whose infinite nature, form, qualities, and majesty have been described in the passage beginning with "He who knows Brahman attains the Supreme" and ending with "That is one Brahman-bliss. This is because [the reference] depends upon the context of the bliss of the Blessed Lord.

The sense is that otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of this verse also being restricted solely to the bliss of Prajāpati. He states the reason for setting aside the literal meaning (*śrautārtha*) in favor of explaining the resultant meaning (*phalitārtha*): "And that is for the purpose of removing the suspicion of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the cause and its effect. Regarding the phrase "by way of being a single part of a similar object": although there is a similarity to the bliss of the four-faced Brahmā multiplied a hundredfold—as expressed in the passage, "That is one Brahman-bliss"—[the comparison is made with the bliss of the individual soul].

It is the bliss of Brahman alone that is being described, and not merely a portion thereof; nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated with the intended meaning of the sentence, "from which words turn back. Because it is improper to rely on a figurative application (*aupacārikatva*) of the word "repetition" (*abhyāsa*) to the bliss of Brahman, he says, "Or rather, it is repeated utterance," as an alternative view reflecting his own preference.

If it is argued that the repeated mention [of bliss] refers to the aspect of unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*), whereas the repeated mention of bliss-in-general (*ānandamātra*) is a mark indicating an intention toward bliss-in-general rather than unsurpassed bliss—and that bliss-in-general alone serves to distinguish the Self from the individual soul (*jīva*)—we say no. This is because both of the two successive passages—the section on the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and the section on the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—namely, "That is one Brahman-bliss" and "From which words turn back," have unsurpassed bliss as their subject matter; thus, the repeated mention of unsurpassed bliss is logically established. Furthermore, [the bliss mentioned there] possesses the quality of being the "turner-back" (*nivartakatva*).

"Intended" (*vivakṣita*) means that its cessation is not dependent on anything else; this should be understood in accordance with the subsequent text. Regarding the phrase "due to contradiction with the scriptural hearing of unsurpassability" (*niratiśayatva-śravaṇa-virodhena*): if [cessation] were dependent on a cause, then because the cause itself would be superior to it, the entity dependent on the cause would necessarily be surpassable. This is because only that which has nothing surpassing it is unsurpassable.

Now, one might object: since the bliss of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is not dependent on anything else, and because of the scriptural statement, "That is one Brahman-bliss; and [the bliss] of the learned Śrotriya who is unassailed by desire," it follows that for liberated souls (*mukta*), that very bliss must likewise be independent of anything else. Anticipating this doubt, he states: "And [the phrase] 'of the learned Śrotriya who is unassailed by desire'. Although bliss is uniform in nature, that bliss in Brahman is without cause (*nirhetuka*), whereas in the liberated soul it is with cause (*sahetuka*). This is because, in that context, the phrase "unassailed by desire" specifies a distinct cause. The meaning is that this is another scriptural passage (*śrutyantara*), and thus the term "unassailed by desire" used therein has exactly the same sense.

He establishes that this statement indicates such reasoning in the phrase "for here" (*atra hi*). The sense is that it is shown by the power of its constituent parts, because the suffix *mayaṭ* has the meaning of "abundance" (*prācurya*). Regarding the commentary’s statement "mere cognition" (*buddhimātra*), one might object: since the author of the *Ṭīkā* has explained the word "cognition" as referring specifically to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the refutation of that [view] could have been accomplished simply by the words "not cognition" (*na buddhiḥ*).

The word "mere" (*mātra*) would be redundant if the word "cognition" (*buddhi*) were intended to mean "awareness" (*jñapti*); for only then would the word "mere" be fruitful as a means of indicating that [the cognition] culminates in pure awareness alone. Furthermore, if the word "mere" is indeed intended to be favored [by the author], then the word "cognition" (*buddhi*) occurring in the *pūrvapakṣa* commentary—namely, in the phrase "and the cognition which follows immediately after it"—must be explained precisely as being intended to mean "awareness."

If it is argued that [the term "intellect"] does not refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it is replied: the phrase "not mere intellect" (*na buddhimātram*) is intended to exclude both the internal organ and pure consciousness (*jñapti*) by relying on one of the three types of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member). Therefore, in the case where pure consciousness is excluded, the term "mere" (*mātra*) is meaningful as a demonstration that the result culminates in that which possesses consciousness, and not in consciousness alone. Some, however, maintain that the word "intellect" (*buddhi*) everywhere refers only to pure consciousness, and not to the internal organ through its derivation from the sense of "instrument" (*karaṇa*).

He shows that the intention of the *bhāṣya*—namely, "because there is a cognition of difference through the suffix *mayaṭ*"—extends up to the point that "if one resorts to [interpreting] the suffix *mayaṭ* as having its own inherent meaning (*svārthika*), it would result in the suffix *mayaṭ* being redundant. He clarifies this redundancy of the suffix by stating, "words denoting properties that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*)," in order to include words such as "blue" (*nīla*) and so forth as well. The phrase "by means of the Sūtra and the logical reasoning" means "by means of the Sūtra and the logical reasoning of the *Śārīraka-sūtra*, namely, 'and because [the self] exists as long as the soul exists' (*yāvad-ātmabhāvitvāt*). Regarding the first position, since it would have to be assumed that the word refers to the agent (*kartṛ*), one must resort to the rare grammatical rule (the *bāhulaka*) which allows for the sense of the agent.

Or rather, the suffix *lyuṭ* is understood here as denoting the agent (*kartṛ*). Alternatively, by relying on its inclusion in the *nandy-ādi* group, the suffix *lyu* is applied according to the rule *nandi-grahi-*, etc., to denote the agent. For this very reason, the scripture declares that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the agent of sacrifice and other acts, stating: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice; it also performs ritual actions. Indeed, agency is not possible for mere intellect (*buddhi-mātra*). For among the insentient sheaths—beginning with the one consisting of food (*anna-maya*) and preceding the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñāna-maya*)—which serve as instruments for the conscious self, no agency, which is a property of the conscious self, is heard of in scripture.

For this very reason, the statement "consciousness and non-consciousness," which distinguishes and points out the conscious and the unconscious by means of their respective specific attributes such as having a locus and being without a locus, uses the word "vijñāna" to denote the conscious [Self] characterized by that quality. Likewise, in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa, regarding the passage "He who dwells in consciousness... [it is the same].

The meaning is that it must be accepted [as such]. The meaning of "inclusion within another class" is that this is not recited in the *nandī-ādi* class [of roots]. Regarding "because of conformity with direct perception," and so forth: because the self's nature of being composed of consciousness (*vijñānamayatva*) is established by direct perception in the form "I know," and because it is established by scripture in the passage "This which is composed of consciousness" (*yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ*), and because—relative to the statement "Consciousness performs the sacrifice" (*vijñānaṃ yajñaṃ tanute*)—the word "composed of consciousness" is heard first and thus its meaning is not yet contradicted, [it is understood] through the etymological derivation "that by which one knows" (*jñāyate 'nena*).

The sense is that even if the word *vijñāna* were intended to refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it would involve an unnatural strain on both the root and the suffix; whereas if it refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), the natural sense of both is preserved. Therefore, in accordance with the term *vijñānamaya*, the word *vijñāna* must be interpreted accordingly. The meaning is "precisely because it refers to the conscious [soul]. This is because, in the sūtra *vyapadeśācca kriyāyām* (and because of the designation in action), opponents have cited the passage "Consciousness performs the sacrifice" as proof for the individual soul's status as the agent.

The meaning is that the agency belongs to the knower alone, as established by the direct perception of "I know" and "I act," by such scriptural passages as "For he is the seer, the hearer, the thinker, the knower, the agent—the person whose nature is consciousness," and by such sūtras as "He is the agent, because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless."

Now, is agency not invariably restricted to sentient beings, since agency is possible even for insentient things? Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that—in rites such as the touching of the *śukra* vessel as prescribed in the injunction "the sacrificer touches the *śukra*," and specifically in the case of the bone-sacrifice (*asthi-yāga*)—agency characterized by independence is impossible for insentient bones, and therefore the touching of the *śukra* and so forth should not be performed; [the author replies] that since agency is possible even for pieces of wood in acts such as burning, and since agency does not depend upon sentience, the bones possess agency.

Anticipating that [the term] "is possible" has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the tenth [chapter], he raises an objection with the words, "But for all... He does so because the lack of natural fitness regarding the word *vijñāna* is common to both [interpretations]; thus, regarding the word *vijñāna* in the passage, "Vijñāna performs the sacrifice... [he objects].

This is the meaning. However, it does not refer to the word *vijñāna* within the compound *vijñānamaya*; for it should be understood that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is no lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya*) in the word *vijñāna* occurring therein, as it refers to consciousness (*jñapti*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if it continues through the context," the intention is that the word "in all" (*sarveṣu*) must be supplied from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) passage: "in the cases of the *annamaya* and so forth, which precede the *vijñānamaya*."

"Because of the hearing of entry" means because of the hearing of [the Lord] being the object of entry; that is to say, because of the hearing of His being all-pervading. Regarding the phrase "because of the hearing of His abiding within another self," one should not argue that the distinction is merely figurative—as in the case of the statement "He is established in His own glory"—for in the Sūtra, "Both indeed read this as distinct," the word *vijñāna* refers precisely to the individual soul (*jīva*) and not to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), since one need not resort to the cumbersome effort of figuratively attributing non-difference where there is actually difference.

It should be understood that this is because [the meaning] has been stated by others themselves. Regarding the phrase "of that which is employed everywhere": in every such sentence as "consciousness and non-consciousness" (*vijñānaṃ cāvijñānañca*) or "consciousness performs the sacrifice" (*vijñānaṃ yajñaṃ tanute*), the word *vijñāna* is employed. If it ends in an affix denoting an agent, it would be masculine; however, since it is neuter, it must end in the suffix *lyuṭ* prescribed for the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) by the rules "*ktaḥ*" and "*lyuṭ ca*. Since a *lyuḍ*-ending form other than that [denoting state] depends on a substantive (*viśeṣya-nighnatayā*), [the word *vijñāna* here denotes the state of consciousness].

The point is that, in the absence of a rule restricting it to the neuter gender, the word *vijñāna* when referring to the Self would result in being masculine. Furthermore, even if the verse does not have the knower as its primary referent, a neuter gender designation based on the intention of the word *vastu* (entity) is not appropriate here, since the word *vastu* has not been employed in this context.

Therefore, having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that in the case of the ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī, the instruction "Bring him forward, O Agni" (*prāsmā agne bharata*) is appropriate because of the intended meaning of the word "animal" (*paśu*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the ninth book of the *Pūrvatant*ra is that since the word "animal" has not been previously mentioned and the ewe dedicated to Sarasvatī actually exists as a female entity, the feminine form "her" (*prāsyāḥ*) must be used; thus, an instruction in the neuter gender based on the actual object is untenable. However, [the text continues]: "Another inner self consists of consciousness" (*anyo'ntara ātmā vijñānamayaḥ*).

Since it was previously designated by the word *ātman* (which is masculine), the use of the masculine gender alone is appropriate; therefore, even if one accepts that the neuter word *vijñāna* in the phrase "consciousness performs the sacrifice" (*vijñānaṃ yajñaṃ tanute*) refers back to *jñapti* (cognition), this is the sense. He states the purpose of the two words "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*) and "its modification" (*tadvikāra*) with the words "consisting of that," etc. "By the realization of the superimposition of contradictory attributes" means by the realization of being the substratum of contradictory attributes. "Non-contradictory along with its cause" refers to the absence of defects such as being opposed to what is to be abandoned (*heyapratyanīkatva*).

The meaning is that [the author] first addresses the reconciliation of the non-contradiction between the locus (*āśraya*) and its attributes (*āśrita*), and then, after presenting the reason, raises an objection from the perspective of another. He explains the *bhāṣya* passage, "The appearance of connection with the avoidable (*heya*) is of a false nature," by stating, "The avoidable is suffering; [its] appearance is false. Now, one might object: "It is improper to say that the appearance is of a false nature, because whether it takes the form of the witness (*sākṣin*) or the modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*), it is real in its own essence and thus lacks falsity. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "[It is] erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*)."

The commentary stating that "the state of being the locus for the manifestation of suffering, which is its effect, is indeed the connection with that which is to be abandoned (*heya-sambandha*)" is incorrect; for if that were the case, the state of being the locus of suffering would not constitute the nature of the connection with that which is to be abandoned. Anticipating this objection, [the author] connects the particle *eva* (indeed) here with the qualifying attribute "the state of being the connection with that which is to be abandoned."

Intending to show that this [term] excludes connection with anything other than that, and not that it excludes connection with anything else, he says: "It is not suffering alone. In order to establish that a momentary act such as a sacrifice is a means for attaining heaven—which occurs at a later time as heard in scripture—an operation characterized as *apūrva* (unseen potentiality) is postulated to persist until that point; however, it is neither postulated that a sacrifice which has perished and is non-existent can produce an effect, nor is it postulated that the sacrifice itself persists until the attainment of the fruit.

Intending to convey that the purport of the Bhāṣya is that [the opponent's position] has been determined in the *Apūrvādhikaraṇa* (the section on the unseen potency) because it contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says, "he refutes. The meaning is that "non-existence would follow. This implies that since no one would engage in the study of Mīmāṃsā—which resembles an inquiry into the teeth of a crow—the Veda, even when assisted by its auxiliary limb in the form of Mīmāṃsā, would fail to produce comprehension; thus, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) in the sense of being a generator of true knowledge would not exist. "Included within its object" refers to what is included within the content of the cognition.

The sense is that by what has been stated, its being included within the scope of [a single] object is indicated. The word "all" (*sarvam*) is understood as a remainder; the meaning is that if the entire collection of things that constitute the objects of all cognitions were included within the scope of a single cognition. The phrase "not indeed in the form qualified by being known" implies that there is no "allness" (*sarvatva*) for that which exists only in a state of oneness (*ekatva*). This refers to the passage beginning with "in the form qualified by allness," such as "the lotus is all."

The Brahman denoted by the word *sat* (Being) does not depend on any other cause distinct from itself; at the time of creation, there is its unique and extraordinary resolve, "May I become many," in the form of infinite moving and stationary beings; according to that resolve, there is a creation characterized by an infinite variety of principles and specific, distinct orders; through the entry of its own self as the individual soul (*jīva*) into all insentient things, there occurs the manifestation of infinite names and forms; and everything distinct from itself has its root in itself.

Infinite specific attributes—such as being one's own abode, being self-governed, subsisting by oneself alone, and being self-established—have been set forth as cognizable solely through the scriptures. Furthermore, in connection with that [Self], even in other contexts, there have been extensively expounded, beyond the reach of all other means of knowledge, such qualities as freedom from sin, the state of having all defects eliminated, omniscience, lordship over all, the possession of true desires, the possession of true resolves, and the union with unsurpassed bliss which is the source of all joy.

Thus, if the word *tat*, which refers to the present Brahman characterized by infinite distinctions that are not within the range of any other [means of knowledge], were intended solely to teach a reality devoid of all distinctions, it would be incoherent and would be regarded as the prattle of a madman.

The word *tvaṃ* (thou) denotes the individual soul (*jīva*) as characterized by transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*). If this word were intended to bring about the presentation of its own nature as devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*), its own primary meaning would have to be abandoned. Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that the concealment of a reality whose very nature is the light of non-duality by means of ignorance (*avidyā*) is impossible, as it would entail the destruction of that very nature. This being the case, one must resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for both words—*tat* (that) and *tvaṃ* (thou)—which function in grammatical apposition, by abandoning their primary meanings.

Now, it may be argued that since words functioning in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) are intent upon conveying a single referent, there can be no intentionality regarding the qualifying portion; thus, because the qualifiers are excluded, they merely convey the oneness of the thing-in-itself, and consequently, there is no occasion for the charge of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For example, in the expression "blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), the two words are intent upon conveying the oneness of the qualified object, and therefore the two qualifiers—blueness and lotus-ness—are not intended to be expressed.

For if that were intended, it would follow that the form qualified by blueness (*nīlatva*) and the form qualified by lotus-ness (*utpalatva*) are established as one; but that is not possible. Indeed, that object is not qualified by the term "lotus" through its form as qualified by blueness, because that would entail the mutual inherence (*samavāya*) of the universal (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), only the oneness of the object indicated (*upalakṣita*) by blueness and lotus-ness is expressed.

Likewise, in the case of the expression "This is that Devadatta," since it is impossible to establish—in terms of that very same form—an entity qualified by a past time and a distant location as being simultaneously qualified by a present time and a proximate location, what is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is merely the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as characterized by both those locations and times. Although a qualifier perceived upon hearing a single word such as "blue" is not established at the time of coreferentiality due to contradiction, [the identity of the essence is nonetheless established].

Nevertheless, since the primary aspect of the denoted meaning is being conveyed, there is no *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication); rather, there is merely a lack of intention (*avivakṣā*) regarding the qualifying aspect.
