The sense is that, because this [explanation] consists of a detailed procedure for subsuming the subject within the scope of the alternative [view] in all cases of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), even the suspicion of redundancy is avoided. Indeed, the *Bhāṣya* states: "by way of the form qualified by blueness. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood in accordance with the subsequent *Bhāṣya*, which says: "for that object is not qualified by blueness by way of the form qualified by *utpala*-ness (lotus-ness), lest there be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the mutual inherence (*samavāya*) of the genus and the quality."

The final meaning is as follows: having stated an example where there is an absence of clear intention regarding the connection with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), even though such a connection is evident, he now states another example where that intention is clear. In that context, "because the connection with the qualifier is not clear" means that the connection with the state of being a lotus (*utpalatva*) occurs only at the very moment of its being blue (*nīlatva*). "Because there is no operation toward what is impossible" means that since the definition [of indication, *lakṣaṇā*] consists precisely in an operation directed toward an impossible object, and since such an operation is absent in the present case, it is not a case of indication.

He demonstrates the very absence of an impossible operation with the words "even regarding the portion that is the object of the operation. In the reading "because there is no operation upon what is possible," the meaning is that the definition does not apply even to the possible portion merely because of the absence of an operation in some part of the possible. Now, [consider] "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*).

In the phrase "mānayet" (one should honor), the cognition of the qualification of blueness in the lotus is not dependent on a co-referential sentence, but rather arises from perception itself; intending to dispel this doubt, the author of the Bhāṣya has presented the remote example "in the Vindhya forest. Thus he says: the opponent’s assumption that [the word] is intent upon exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) regarding an object of perception is untenable for the opponent—this is the sense.

The phrase "the postulation of another derivation when that [primary meaning] is impossible" means the postulation of another power (*śakti*). This is because a word's meaning must be something not obtainable by other means; since a meaning obtained through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth is already accessible, a power cannot be postulated for it. For this very reason, the power of the word *gaṅgā* is not postulated for the riverbank. However, in the case of words such as *saindhava*, since there is no relationship with the primary meaning [in the context of salt], one does not admit multiple powers; this is the intended sense. Regarding the term *bāhlīka*: *Bāhlīka* is the name of a specific region. The meaning is that a person residing there is like a cow.

The meaning of "distinct because of being related to another qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇāntarapratisambandhitvāt*) is that it is "residing in a different locus" (*vyadhikaraṇa*) due to its connection with another qualifier. Therefore, it should be understood that this objection—that although there is a distinction in attributes (*dharmavailakṣaṇya*), a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*) is not established, and thus this is not something undesirable for the opponent—is refuted. Some, however, interpret the Bhāṣya's phrase "because of being related to another qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇāntarapratisambandhitvāt*) as follows: that which has a connection (*pratisambandhitva*) with another qualifier is "that which has a connection with another qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇāntarapratisambandhitvaḥ*).

"Of the subject matter that follows upon the [preceding] quarter" means "of the existence of a cause characterized as distinct from both consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit). Now, one might object: "If the sequence of quarters is justified simply by the difference in subject matter, how can it be said to be the intended connection (saṅgati) of the author of the Sūtras? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the division of quarters is due to the difference in subject matter. The underlying sense is that it is not merely a specific means of knowledge (pramāṇa). The phrase "due to a specific connection" implies that only that which serves as the object of inquiry—thereby determining the fixed order of succession—is what constitutes a true connection.

In this context, the question "What is the proof? means: what is the proof for the fact that this particular connection is intended by the author of the Sūtras? Now, one might object: even if the three Sūtras beginning with "janmādi" (the origin, etc. also depend on the first Adhikaraṇa for their commencement, their status as the purpose for establishing the commencement of the Śāstra remains unimpaired, because the Śāstra begins with the Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa. Therefore, it is improper to state that the first Adhikaraṇa alone serves the purpose of establishing the commencement of the Śāstra. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Or rather, [it is said] of the Sūtra beginning with 'janmādi'..."

The meaning is that since there is a thematic connection (*saṅgati*) in the first quarter (*pāda*), it is also included within the scripture (*śāstra*). Now, one might object: "Does the scripture begin only from the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* onwards, such that what precedes it does not possess the status of scripture? Yet, even the first *adhikaraṇa* is included within the scripture by virtue of serving as the introduction to the scripture."

It is the same. Therefore, having raised the objection that the statement "for the sake of establishing the commencement of the treatise" (*śāstrārambhasiddhaye*) in the sequence of the first section is improper, he says: "Or rather, [it refers to] the phrase 'for the sake of establishing the commencement of the treatise'. This is with the intention of [the attainment] culminating in absolute dissolution (*atyantikalaya*); the meaning is that absolute dissolution is liberation (*mokṣa*), because liberation consists of bliss (*ānanda*). Having raised the further objection—how, in reality, the immortality residing in the liberated one, which is a function of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), can be considered its exclusive property—he says: "By way of being the object to be bestowed" (*pradeyatvena*).

The meaning is that it serves as a "sign" (*cihnabhūta*); thus, the intention is that even something which does not possess that property can function as its sign. In the *Bhāṣya*, the word "transcended" (*atipatita*) means being devoid of even a trace of being an object of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). In the *Autpattika-sūtra*—namely, "But the [relation] of a word with its meaning is innate..."—it is stated:

The meaning is: "in the sūtra [dealing with] *sambandha*. The meaning of "in the *pratyakṣa*-sūtra" is: "in the sūtra, 'Perception is the arising of cognition when there is contact of a person's sense organs with what exists. The phrase "the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is effected by the three chapters (*tripādī*)" means that dharma is not [exclusively] characterized by the exclusion of connection with something else, as demonstrated through the refutation of objections. "Residing in the mark (*liṅga*) of the Veda (*brāhma*)" means...

The meaning of "as stated by others" (*parairuktam*) is as follows: it has been stated by others that in the first chapter (*pāda*), those passages containing clear indicators (*liṅga*) of Brahman and so forth have been deliberated upon; in the second and third chapters, those passages containing unclear indicators of Brahman and so forth are investigated. Among these, the second chapter primarily concerns [Brahman] with attributes (*saviśeṣa*), while the third primarily concerns [Brahman] without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*). The fourth chapter, however, is devoted to resolving contradictions regarding the statements about the cause. This is the sense of "as stated by others. The phrase "the presentation of the possessor of the indicators" (*liṅgipratipādana*) means that the primary principle (*pradhāna*) and other such entities are presented through words such as "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*).

The meaning is that it is not merely a presentation of the *liṅga* (inferential mark), as is the case with the second and third quarters [of the verse]; rather, it is not a presentation of the *liṅga* alone. Regarding the passage beginning with "All this, indeed," [it says]: "All this, verily, is Brahman—'tajjalān'; one should meditate upon it with a calm mind. Now, man is indeed composed of resolve (*kratu*); according to his resolve in this world..."

"As a person is here, so does he become after departing from this world; let him form a resolve: 'He consists of mind, his body is breath, he is of the nature of light, whose resolve is true, whose self is space, who performs all actions, who possesses all desires, who has all fragrances, who has all tastes, who pervades all this, who is without speech and without concern. This is my Self within the heart, subtler than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a mustard seed, or a grain of millet, or the kernel of a grain of millet. This is my Self within the heart, greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate region, greater than the sky."

"Greater than the higher worlds, possessing all works, all desires, all odors, all tastes, pervading this entire universe, speechless and indifferent—this is my Self within the heart. 'I shall attain this after departing from here,' he who has this firm conviction has no doubt; thus said Śāṇḍilya, [the son of] Śāṇḍilya. This is the Śruti. Furthermore, the author of the Bhāṣya shows the purification of the subject as intended by other commentators: "He should perform that resolve (kratu)."

The intended meaning is as follows: the phrase "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) is connected [to Brahman] as an object of meditation. One should not argue that, because the words beginning with *manomaya* end in the nominative case, they properly serve only to qualify the agent of the meditation under discussion—as in the passage "He should form a resolve"—and not to qualify the object of meditation; for it is more appropriate to set aside their function of qualifying the agent of meditation (which is not required) and, by changing the case-ending, have them serve as qualifiers of the object of meditation.

The phrase "in the proximity of that which possesses a fruit" refers to the statement, "All this is indeed Brahman; [it is] born from that, dissolved in that, and breathed by that; let one meditate on it with calmness," because that meditation is enjoined for the purpose of attaining tranquility and thus possesses a fruit. The point is that in the statement, "Let him form a resolve," no fruit is heard; therefore, according to the principle that what lacks a fruit is subordinate to what possesses a fruit, it would necessarily follow that it is a subsidiary part of the former. As for the claim that it is only for one already qualified for the enjoined meditation that another meditation is enjoined—what is the proof for this, such that this doubt should even arise?

It should not be argued that this is like the case of the Upakośala-vidyā and others, where there is the possibility of eligibility for one who is not qualified for other vidyās; for the intention is that since tranquility (śānti) is an auxiliary to the meditation on Brahman, only one who is eligible for the meditation for the sake of tranquility is also eligible for the meditation expressed as "he should perform that kratu. Although it is not the view of the opponents (the Mīmāṃsakas) that there is an injunction for meditation for the sake of tranquility—since that is not accepted by the Mṛṣāvādins (the Vedāntins)—[the argument still holds].

For this is their view: in the sentence "He should perform that sacrifice" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*), meditation (*upāsana*) is enjoined; then, by way of restating that [meditation], the quality of tranquility (*śama*) is enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it by the sentence "tranquil, let him meditate" (*śānta upāsīta*). This is the purpose (*arthavāda*) of that injunction: because everything here is indeed Brahman—since everything is born from it, dissolves into it, and breathes in it—and because all things are thus of one essence with Brahman, it is improper to engage in passion or hatred; therefore, tranquility alone is what ought to be practiced. (Just as in the case of the rule: "One offers with a winnowing basket, for with it food is prepared... [the remainder of the *arthavāda* explains the reason].

The phrase "it is done, as it were" is stated in that way because it is the view held by other commentators; for this very reason, it should be understood that even the term "other commentators" used later refers exclusively to those other than the proponents of falsehood (the Mṛṣāvādins). The reason given is "because of the abundance of meditation" (*upāsanapracuratvāt*); the point is that in the passage "man consists of resolve" (*kratumayaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the word *kratu* signifies meditation (*upāsana*), and the suffix *mayaṭ* denotes abundance.

"Because this [text] is devoted to the injunction for ritual action (*kratu*)"—the meaning is that it is devoted to the injunction for sacrifice (*yāga*). Regarding the phrase "being the subject matter of the meditation under discussion," one might object: "Since qualities such as 'consisting of mind' (*manomaya*) are indeed qualifiers of the Brahman under discussion in the passage 'All this, verily, is Brahman,' they will thereby serve to provide the qualifiers for the object of meditation under discussion. Anticipating this, he says: "because there is no certainty that it is devoted to Brahman. [This refers to the fact that] the quality of consisting of mind...

The sense is that the doubt regarding the doubling [of the number] is indicated; the word "intermediate" (*antara*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). Consequently, it should be noted that the apprehension—that there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the instrumental case-ending in the word *upāsanasya*—is dispelled. This is because the specific relationship characterized by the status of being the instrument and the object of the instrument is not explicit; this [statement] is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, the claim of the Mṛṣāvādins—that because the previously cited indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) are more explicit than the marks of Brahman found in the opening of the passage (such as "being born from that" and "dissolving into that," which establish its identity with all), those marks of Brahman that are not explicit are to be discussed in the second pāda—is incorrect. Nor should it be argued that the indicative mark of Brahman is not explicit in the sentence concerning the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*)—the subject passage of the pūrvapakṣa—because it constitutes a separate sentence; for if that were so, then the sentence concerning "light" (*jyotis*) would also have to be discussed in this pāda.

Although the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of Brahman, namely "being the feet of all beings," was clear in the preceding passage, because it is not clear in the passage concerning the light (*jyotiḥ*), there arises the contingency that it too must be considered here; let this matter rest for now. The phrase "mutual expectancy" (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) is the term to be explained. By the statement "it is not proper to say there is a connection with the ablative case," the fulfillment of mutual expectancy is established; such is the meaning of "connection with the ablative. Having completed the construction of the sentence, he demonstrates the purpose of the phrase "possessing qualities such as consisting of mind" (*manomayatvādi*) which occurs within that sentence, by means of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) method, starting with the words "and [the quality of] consisting of mind, etc. (*manomayatvādi ca*).

Regarding the phrase "explained by others" (*parairvyākhyātam*): although it has not been explained by others in this way—namely, that the Supreme Brahman alone is to be meditated upon through attributes such as consisting of mind (*manomayatva*) and so forth—[the opponent argues]: "Why? Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere (*sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt*). That which is well-known in all the Vedāntas as the referent of the word 'Brahman' and the cause of the world—that very same [cause], heard at the beginning of the passage here in the words 'All this, indeed, is Brahman' (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma*), is taught as qualified by the attributes of consisting of mind and so forth. This is how it has been explained.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated by taking the resultant meaning into account. The question "How is this statement justified? means: disregarding the reasoning cited by others, for what purpose is another line of reasoning being presented? By stating that the first half [of the verse] is read as having a single form, the intention is that since the two first halves have a single meaning, it is likewise appropriate for the two second halves to have a single meaning. Furthermore, by the phrase "one whose self is composed perceives the nature of knowledge," it is indicated that [the object] is to be grasped by a purified mind.

The intention is that the word *ātman* here refers to the mind (*manas*). By means of fortitude (*dhṛti*), one whose self is composed beholds the Supreme Person; that is, he perceives Him directly and attains Him. This is in accordance with the statement: "But by unswerving devotion He can be known."

That this is due to the sense of "solidification" (kāṭhrya) has been established here in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha* and should be kept in mind. Now, one might object: "How can a passage such as 'All these indeed... serve as a proof for having the Prāṇa as its body? For it was previously established that, through etymological derivation (*yaugika-vṛtti*), the passage refers to the Supreme Self. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the passage beginning with 'All these... The intention is that this is by way of the secondary function of denoting the whole (*aparyavasāna-vṛtti*), according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.

The meaning is that this is according to the principle of the Vaiśvānara section, as it has been stated [in the sūtra]: "Jaimini [holds] there is no contradiction even directly. Regarding the phrase "pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, etc.": although in passages such as "possessing all odors, possessing all tastes," the term *manomaya* (consisting of mind) may refer to auspicious modifications of the mind such as pleasure, or—as in the passage "All this, indeed, is Brahman"—may have an unrestricted sense, there is no contradiction [in our position].

Furthermore, even if an object in the form of something graspable by the mind were possible, the statement that [Brahman] consists of mind (*manomaya*) would be untenable, because it would merely be a figurative identification of Brahman with the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a modification of the mind due to being reflected therein; this is the intended meaning.

"Because the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*) must be supplied"—the word "of the whole" (*kṛtsnasya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, the intention is that in the second interpretation, unlike in the first interpretation, there is no need to supply the entirety [of the text]. Now, "of the injunction for meditation" (*upāsanavidheḥ*) means "of the meditation being enjoined. "The state of being the self of all, taught in the originative injunction" (*utpattiśiṣṭasarvātmakatva*) means "enjoined by the originative sentence" (*utpattivākyavihita*). The originative sentence is the primary...

A sentence is that which generates the comprehension of a meaning. [Objection: But if the word *brāhma* ends in the accusative case, its syntactic connection (*ekavākyatā*) with the word *iti*—which itself ends in the accusative—would not be possible. [Response: This is not so; for by first understanding through the teaching that "everything has Brahman as its essence" by virtue of being born from it, dissolved into it, and breathing in it, one becomes free from passion, hatred, and the like, and then the meaning is: "one should meditate upon Brahman possessing the qualities about to be described. Thus, according to the method to be explained, syntactic unity is indeed possible as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the injunction regarding tranquility (*śama*), just as in the view of the opponent.

In both systems, the status of being an explanatory *arthavāda* in the form of a statement of reason is common to both the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman; it originates from that, it dissolves into that, it breathes in that" (*sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma tajjalān*), and the passage, "He offers with a winnowing basket; for by means of it food is prepared. However, there is this distinction: according to the other system (the Mīmāṃsā), meditation is enjoined in the passage, "He should perform that sacrifice" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*), while in the sentence "All this, indeed," tranquility (*śama*) is enjoined as a restatement of that [meditation].

[The opponent] maintains that [the qualities] are enjoined [separately]. In our view, however, in the sentence "All this, indeed," meditation qualified by tranquility (*śama*) is enjoined. But in the sentence "He should form a resolve" (*sa kratuṃ kurvīta*), the qualities such as being composed of mind (*manomayatva*) and so forth are enjoined by way of restating the meditation already enjoined in the sentence "All this, indeed. Nor should it be asked how multiple qualities such as being composed of mind can be enjoined in a single sentence by way of restating a meditation already established; [for there is no such rule against it].

Even though there is a multiplicity of attributes such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, because they are perceived here through the word "this" (*itaḥ*) as being qualified by a specific mode consisting of a particular sequence—as in the phrase "departing from here, I shall attain this"—there is no contingency of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*), since the delimitors of the predicated properties (*vidheyatāvacchedaka*) are one and the same despite the multiplicity of the predicates themselves. Consequently, even in this case, the status of being a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) is established for the sentence "All this, indeed, is... If it is asked how there could be a split, it is said in reply:

It is true that there is syntactical unity; nevertheless, when there is a requirement for an object of meditation (*upāsya*), it is the *brāhmaṇa* alone—established through the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the injunction for tranquility (*śama*) according to the principle of the *Rātrisūtra*—that is connected as the object of meditation. It is not the *brāhmaṇa* qualified by being the "self of all," because the requirement for an object of meditation is satisfied by the *brāhmaṇa* in its mere form. Thus, the sense is that there would be no suspicion of conflict with a quality already established by the originative injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).

In reality, however, since there is no contradiction between the quality of being the self of all—which is taught as a primary injunction regarding origination—and the qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomayatva*) that will be mentioned later, one should also observe that the subsequent qualities like consisting of mind do not form a syntactical connection [with the primary injunction]. For this very reason, in the injunction for meditation, "Meditate on me as life, as immortality,"...

In the section [of the Brahmasūtras] titled "Prāṇa, because of the concordance" (*prāṇastathānugamāt*), it was explained that the qualities mentioned in the concluding passage—"Bliss, undecaying, immortal"—are enjoined as objects of meditation. Similarly, in the section "Merely a praise, because of the inclusion" (*stutimātramupādānāt*), it was established that when the meditation on the syllable *praṇava*—characterized by its being a part of the *udgītha*—is enjoined in the text "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*," qualities such as being the "highest essence" (*rasatama*) are also to be meditated upon.

For this very reason, there is frequent usage in several places in the *Bhāṣya* and its *Ṭīkā* stating that "omnipresence (*sārvātmya*) is the object of meditation" in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā. Nor should it be doubted how omnipresence—which is taught for the sake of tranquility—can function as a qualification of the object of meditation; for just like the *brāhmaṇa* [in the preceding section], being the Self of all is logically established as an object of meditation. Otherwise, even the *brāhmaṇa*, though mentioned for the sake of tranquility, would not be an object of meditation, which is not an acceptable conclusion.

It should be understood that the presentation of the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions proceeds precisely by taking for granted that that which is denoted by the word *brāhmaṇ* is the object of meditation (*upāsya*). However, some [maintain] that according to the principle "and because qualities are for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*), since the fire is already occupied by a previously understood, scripturally stated, and independent unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa-kārya*), namely the *āghāra* libation, it is not proper for the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices—which have their own distinct unseen effects—to find a place therein. For this very reason, when the fire is occupied by the *āgneya* sacrifice, the *prayāja* offerings and others are not performed.

They say that although there is no contradiction with the statement in the *Nayaviveka*—namely, "otherwise there would be equal primacy"—it is not appropriate to enter [into that view], because the word *brāhṛ* occurs here and there in the *Bhāṣya*; the sense is that this is seen in passages such as, "This reaches the *brāhṛ*, that knowledge is designated as *brāhṛ*."

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "By the word 'Brahman,' that which is enjoined as being of the nature of that [Brahman]"; the meaning of "being of the nature of that" is "by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). That is to say, it means "enjoined as the inner controller of the entire world. As for what was stated—that the *Bhāṣya* passage "tajjalān" (from which it is born, in which it dissolves, and into which it breathes) refers to the reason—meaning that because the birth, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world], as well as the identity consisting in being produced by that [Brahman], are well-known and thus taught—that is incorrect.

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) explaining that [passage], having raised the objection that it merely establishes the well-known fact of being a cause—since the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of the world are well known—it says: "of the identity based on causality. The intention is that when the well-known status of being the cause of the world's birth, maintenance, and dissolution is established, the establishment of identity as its effect is also stated by implication.

The meaning is that it should be understood as being well-known precisely through its status as the cause of the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the world, as established in the Vedānta; this is to be seen because that very point was set forth in the preceding sentence of the commentary (*bhāṣya*). He says "identity is also established by implication," which means he speaks with the intention that identity is also established by implication. [This is expressed in the *bhāṣya*: "Identity is appropriate because of having that as its essence."

Having raised the objection here that the reason is non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśeṣa*), he states "by way of having that as its nature" (*tadātmakatayā*) and "referring to another scriptural passage" (*śrutyantaraviṣayam*), meaning that the identity established by another scripture is the reason, and the identity apprehended by this [present] scripture is what remains to be proven. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should also be understood that because the statement "identity by way of having that as its nature" is equivalent to the statement "identity by way of the relationship between body and embodied," there is not even the suspicion of the probandum being non-different from the reason.

The sense is that if [the cause] were of both natures (ubhayaliṅga), then at the time of dissolution, when only Brahman remains, the very nature of Brahman would necessarily undergo transformation, which would result in the defect of being subject to change (savikāratva). Furthermore, this is explicitly stated by other scriptural passages (śrutyantara), such as "Darkness existed" and "Whose body is darkness," and so forth. To the question, "What follows from this regarding that which possesses both natures? the opponent asks: what solution has been stated for the contradiction of possessing both natures that was raised by the proponent of the prima facie view? This is the meaning of the doubt.

"Contradiction with prohibitive statements" means for the sake of resolving the contradiction with the statement "He is without breath, without mind. "In accordance with specific statements" means in accordance with the statement "But by the pure mind," and so forth. He says, "The meaning is that it shines for itself," in order to exclude knowledge that has become a property (*dharma*). "Because of its identity with the term *satyakāma*"—the fact that the term *satyakāma* signifies the possession of eternal glory will be clarified in the *Dahara-adhikaraṇa*; here, it is an injunction of a quality consisting of self-appropriation. [Objection: But this is established even without being stated.

If it is argued that the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [Self] is already established simply by the demonstration of its possessing those qualities, we say no; for the purpose of the repeated recitation of "the performer of all actions" and so forth is to show that all previously mentioned qualities are to be meditated upon, thereby refuting the suspicion that the single recitation of qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) might serve to exclude them from meditation. The specific purpose of this repetition will be explained later in the passage beginning with "This is not for one who has just begun his practice."

Regarding the initial objection concerning the rule *gatyarthākarmakaśliṣaśīṅsthāsavasajanaruhajīryatibhyaśca*, which prescribes the *kta* suffix in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), [the author] refutes it with the words "nor does he take up" (*na cābhyādadāti*) and so forth. This is the resolution offered by the proponent of the primacy of the objective (*lakṣyaprādhānyavādin*), who suggests that the *kta* suffix should be understood as having the sense of the agent precisely because of that [very rule].

The meaning is: "Let it be postulated by accepting that [the root *ad*] has the sense of 'going' (*gatyarthatva*). In the *Mahābhāṣya*, having raised the objection—"How can it be said that 'the Brahmins have eaten' (*bhuktā brāhmaṇāḥ*) or 'the cows have drunk' (*pītā gāvaḥ*)?"—a resolution is provided by treating the words as being formed with the suffix *ac* (in the sense of *arśa-ādi*). In accordance with that, he shows the resolution: "Alternatively, the cognition (*pratīti*) is the apprehension (*pratipatti*). The intention is that by the word "participial suffix" (*kta*), the apprehension produced by a suffix ending in *kta* is indicated.

The meaning is that "the absence of the capacity for speech" is what is expressed by the term *avākī*; this is the sense to be supplied. With the intention of explaining the purpose of the word *tu*, it has been said:

"While there exists a cause for doubt regarding one who is bound, its resolution must be established [in a specific way], but in the case of the liberated, even the cause of doubt does not exist"—this is the disparity indicated by the word *tu*. By "attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*)," the meaning is "such as consisting of mind (*manomayatva*) and so forth."

The meaning is this: by stating "he declares the reason for the ultimate impossibility," the author of the Bhāṣya intends that this Sūtra expresses the reason for the soul's distinction [from Brahman] by way of the impossibility of the intended qualities, and not that it is concerned with the impossibility of the qualities themselves.

The phrase "for [it is] only the attained and the attainer" means that in the passage "Having departed from here, I shall attain Him," the word "Him" (*etam*) refers back to the previously introduced object of meditation; this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase "of the very nature [of Brahman]," the point of the objection is that, as in cases such as "You are the tenth," it is possible for the very nature [of Brahman] itself to be both the attained and the attainer. The phrase "a violation of the natural force of the scripture" means a violation of the natural force of the scriptural text "Having departed from here, I shall attain Him. Now, one might argue: since in this sentence "Having departed from here, I shall attain Him," the object to be attained is indicated by a masculine noun, this [object] must be something other than the attainer.

In the Śruti, a specific word is heard regarding the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (para), as in: "Just as rice, or barley, or śyāmāka grain, or the kernel of a śyāmāka grain—so is this understood. Regarding the question of how there can be a neuter designation (*napuṃsaka-nirdeśa*) in the Bhāṣya, he says: "In this context, the designation is 'this' (*idam*)."

The meaning of "not a circular dependency" (*nānyonyāśraya*) is as follows: once it is established that a particular word refers to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*), the distinction between the object of worship (*upāsya*) and the worshiper (*upāsaka*)—which are specific attributes of the words referring to the soul and the Supreme—is established; and once the distinction between the object of worship and the worshiper is established, it is established that the particular word refers to both the soul and the Supreme. This is what constitutes a circular dependency.

The meaning is that the word *sarva* (all) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and not to the aggregate of the body and so forth; for if it were the latter, the distinction between the means (*upāya*) and the worshipper (*upāsaka*), namely between the individual soul and the Supreme (*para*), would not be established. Regarding the phrase "because it is the locus of delusion" (*bhrāntyāśrayatvāt*), the meaning is: because it is the locus of the delusion described in the passage, "causing all beings to wander. Regarding the phrase "the removal of an intermediate doubt," the meaning is: it serves to collect the reasons stated in the two preceding sūtras for the purpose of refuting the doubt that the status of being the goal to be attained (*prāpyatva*) and the status of being the attainer (*prāptṛtva*) could be justified through a difference in states (*avasthābheda*).

Because equality between Śruti and Smṛti is impossible, he says, "or rather, it is a mere corroboration" (anvācaya). Regarding this Sūtra, the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya asks: "Who, then, is this so-called embodied self (śārīra), distinct from the Supreme Self, who is denied [as the creator] in such passages as 'But because of impossibility, it is not the embodied self'? For Śruti, in passages of this kind such as "There is no other seer than He; there is no other hearer than He," excludes any self other than the Supreme Self. Likewise, Smṛti also [says]: "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) in all..."

"...in the fields, O Bhārata," and so forth. To this it is replied: This is indeed true; however, the Supreme Self itself, when delimited by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body, senses, mind, and intellect, is figuratively designated as the "embodied one" (śārīra) by the ignorant. Just as the ether (nabhas), though unlimited, appears to be limited due to the influence of limiting adjuncts such as jars or water-pots, so it is in this case. And with reference to that [limited state], the conventional distinction of action, agent, and so forth, is not contradictory.

It was previously stated that until the instruction "That thou art" is received, and once the oneness of the Self is grasped, all worldly transactions such as bondage and liberation would simply come to an end; having restated that, he refutes it with the words "here some [say]... The underlying sense is that this is the position of others who hold that the Veda itself is deluded, since there is no delusion regarding the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) for them. The phrase "even though others lack the delusion of difference between the jīva and the īśvara" means that, because the Lord is not an object of any other means of knowledge, a delusion concerning His difference [from the soul] is impossible for them.

The phrase "it should be taught as 'Thou art'" refers to Śvetaketu; this is the sense. The meaning is that it is possible for [the passage] to be intent upon recording the births of Manu, Sūrya, and others, because of the natural force of the use of the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense, which denotes non-recent past time. Furthermore, because qualities such as being the goal attained by the liberated cannot be inferred, the sense is that there can be no restatement (*anuvāda*) of those things which are accessible through scripture alone. The expression "based on being the object of meditation" means for the purpose of worship (*upāsanā*).

This is the meaning. He establishes that very point by saying, "for those desiring various specific fruits. If it is argued that "the Śruti postulates [this]," one might ask: "Since the distinction between the ritual action and the agent postulated by the Śruti does not establish the effects of difference, how can such a doubt arise? This is because such a doubt is plausible for one who has no other recourse (*atyantāgati*). Furthermore, it should be understood that since one engaged in meditation requires only the cognition of a distinction between the object of meditation and the meditator—and not an actual, ontological distinction—such a doubt is indeed appropriate.

The meaning is: having proposed the distinction of the individual soul (*jīva*) by stating that [the object] is a reality distinct from the individual soul. This is because, according to the subsequent text, no unreal distinction is being proposed. "Understanding the designation of non-ultimate distinction" means understanding the distinction characterized by the relationship between the object and the agent. "By way of being the cause for the true nature [of the Self]" means by way of being the cause for the distinction consisting in the state of being distinct from the individual soul. [The phrase] "because of the contradiction with the opening statement 'the desire to know Brahman'" implies the following intention: otherwise, the author would have formulated the aphorism as "Now, therefore, the desire to know the unreal distinction."

He refutes the interpretation of others with the words, "It is said that space is to be seen. The sense is that a demand for proof arises: when it is stated that [the smallness of the abode] and so forth must be understood as being due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), like space, one might ask why it could not be intrinsic (*svābhāvika*)? Since there is no evidence for its being due to limiting adjuncts, a demand for proof arises—this is the meaning. The phrase "it is designated by scripture" means that the very proof is thereby shown; thus, the intention is that the proof itself is demonstrated.

One might object: "Since the rule *praśasyasya śraḥ jyaca* prescribes the substitution of *jy-* for the word *praśasya*, the form *jyāyas-* is derived from the word *praśasya* by adding the suffix *īyasun*, and not from the word *vṛddha*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For the rule is *jya ca vṛddhasya ca*. The meaning is that the sequence of rules is indeed *jya ca vṛddhasya ca*.

The meaning is as follows: in the rule *vṛddhasya ca*, the word *jya* is understood from the preceding context; when the suffix *īyasun* is added to the word *vṛddha*, the word *vṛddha* undergoes the substitution *jya* by the rule *vṛddhasya ca*, and then the vowel *ī* of the suffix *īyasun* is replaced by *ā* by the rule *jyādādīyasaḥ*, thereby producing the form *jyāyas*. It is not, however, produced by the rule *praśasyasya śraḥ*.

The meaning is that its formation [occurs] by the rule *jyacaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.61), which is recited under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) *praśasyasya śraḥ*. Here too, the reason—that the word *jyāyas* refers to a form that is not related to the comparative suffix *īyasun*—should be understood exactly as it will be stated later. Furthermore, "because of the hearing of greater greatness than that" means because of the hearing of greater greatness than the earth and so forth, as in the passage beginning with "greater than the earth."

Regarding the phrase "because it stands within another sentence": although it will be stated later that there is syntactic unity (ekavākyatva) with the passage beginning "being free from passion, hatred, and so forth," after one has understood from the scripture that the Brahman-self constitutes everything; nevertheless, the intended meaning here is that the all-pervasiveness of the Brahman-self is subordinate to tranquility (śama). In reality, however, just as in the case of the Brahman-self which is taught for the purpose of tranquility...

Just as in the case of the injunction, "Having stripped the branch from its base, he makes the *upaveṣa*," where the phrase "from the base" (*mūlataḥ*), though connected to the stripping of the branch (*śākhā-parivāsana*) as its ablative source, is also accepted as being connected with the clause "he makes the *upaveṣa*" by virtue of the requirements of the context (*ākāṅkṣā*), so too it should be understood that there is no contradiction in the fact that the "consisting of all selves" (*sarvātmakatva*), although designated for another purpose, serves as the object of meditation (*upāsya*). This has also been established previously.

The phrase "the indication of the subject (*dharmin*) by way of its characteristic" means that the nature of the subject, which is Brahman, is indicated by means of stating the characteristic of being the cause. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "and for the purpose of investigating the certainty of attainment," this means an investigation consisting of the certainty of attainment; this should be understood both in accordance with the subsequent commentary, which speaks of "one endowed with the certainty of attainment," and in accordance with the *Śruti* texts.

Regarding the phrases "as the object of worship" and "as the goal to be attained": although the state of being the goal to be attained is already established by the state of being the object of worship, it should be understood that the repetition is for the purpose of contemplating [the Lord] in that specific sequence. As for the statement "the repetition refers to His abiding in the heart," the meaning is that there is a repetition in the text: "This is my Self within the heart."

The phrase "the apprehension of pleasure in the pursuit of enjoyment" means "in the pursuit of that which is not a human goal. This is because the Śruti cannot serve as a source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the stated point by way of direct confrontation. Thus, he explains the expression "and so the Śruti" with the words "and so the Śruti. The phrase "due to the non-acceptance of the individual soul" (*jīvasyānabhyupagamāt*) means "because of the non-acceptance of the individual soul. The term "being understood" (*avagatatve*) carries the specific sense of "being necessarily accepted."

Ānandagiri presents an alternative view: "Is the understanding derived from the scripture [in general], or from this specific passage? The phrase "the absence of being an enjoyer for the other" means for the other, namely the *jīva*; this is in accordance with Śaṅkara’s commentary, which states that it first precludes the status of being an experiencer for the embodied self (*śārīra*) alone. This is because the possibility of being an enjoyer depends on the non-difference between the enjoyer and the *jīva*, and it must be refuted in exactly that manner.

Regarding the second alternative, however, if it is understood through our statement that the identity of the *jīva* and Brahman is established by delusion (*bhrānti*), then the defect of that position is likewise avoided.

The manner [of its refutation] is also to be understood from what I have already stated; the sense is that even there, it would not be by way of the "half-old woman" (ardha-jaratīya) maxim. The phrase "refuted by non-acceptance" is used because the second position is self-evident. Thus ends the section on "Universal Renown" (Sarvatraprasiddhi).

"Because there is no direct praise of the fire-pit (agnisthali)"—the meaning is that "direct fire" (*sākṣādagni*) refers to the primary fire, the fire in its form as a flame; the word "fire" is applied metaphorically (*upacaryate*) to the fire-pit because it serves as the locus for that [primary fire]. Now, one might object: "The doubt concerns only the fire-pit, and it is precisely that which is well-known to be the 'eater of food' (*annāda*. To this he replies: "Because of the context of fire (*agniprakaraṇasya*).

The sense is that since rice and so forth are well-known in the world as objects of enjoyment, and this is understood through the capacity for the addition of sauce (*upasecana*), the state of being an "eater" (*bhoktṛtva*) first enters the mind.

Now, it may be argued that in the mantra, *odana* (rice) is not mentioned in its primary sense, such that its correlate could be the *attṛ* (eater). Rather, a mere metaphorical representation of the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya as *odana* is being made; for even in the case of something used figuratively as *odana*, it need not necessarily have a correlate who is an eater. Nor is it the case that in the expression "for one who finds diversion in hunting, other kings are non-deer," the actual hunter—the Kṣatriya—is perceived as the correlate of those who are [metaphorically] non-deer, rather than the Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*).

It might be argued that one should say [the word *odana*] refers to a Brahmin; however, there is no such rule. If it is objected that in the verse, "The milk of your sword-serpent is the fame of your enemies," the quality of being a drinker (*pātṛtva*) is not perceived in the sword—which is related to the figurative milk—and even if it were perceived, actual drinking is not observed, we reply: in this case, the word *odana*, which has boiled rice as its primary meaning, must necessarily function by depending on some quality residing in the literal object [of the comparison].

In this case, since the quality of being an object of enjoyment—which belongs to the expressed meaning (vācya) well-known as such—resolves into that very nature of being enjoyable, the cognition of "being the enjoyer" (bhoktṛtva) for its correlative, denoted by the word *yasya* ("of whom"), becomes unavoidable. Even in the example *kṛpāṇabhujaṅgasya* ("of the sword-serpent"), there is indeed the cognition of the sword possessing the status of a drinker [of blood] through superimposition; yet, in that instance, the cognition of being a drinker does not arise merely from the metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) of the sword with a serpent, but rather from the metaphorical identification of fame with milk.

Furthermore, it must be explained how the status of being a consumer (*pātṛtva*) is understood merely by the metaphorical representation of the *brāhmaṇa* and the *kṣatriya* as rice-porridge (*odana*). [For example,] in the verse, “O hero, the milk of your sword is the fame of your enemies,” although there is no metaphorical representation of the sword as a serpent at the beginning, there is still the metaphorical representation of [the fame] as milk.

Since the state of being an agent (*pātṛtva*) is perceived merely through [the presence of] the instrument, so too must the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) be understood as superimposed in that very same way. Consequently, since in reality the absence of being an enjoyer results for that which is not connected to it, how could being an enjoyer serve as a proof for being a living individual (*jīvatva*)? To this it must be said: because there is no sublation (*bādhaka*), the perception of being an enjoyer is appropriate as a valid cognition (*pramātmaka*); thus, the sense is that it is possible to establish the state of being a living individual.

The phrase "because of having the nature of both female and male" means that the state of being an object of enjoyment for women is already established; the underlying intention is that even for males and neuters, there is a state of being objects of enjoyment in the form of servants and so forth. The phrase "with the intention that [it] is to be enjoined" means with the intention that [it] is not a sublater [of other rules].

If it is argued that it is not appropriate for the word *upasecana* (condiment) to indicate merely the state of being non-obstructive—which is common to all—but rather [to indicate] the state of being eaten by oneself while serving as the cause for another's eating, and that such eating is possible only in the case of the Supreme Brahman as the consumer and sustainer, and not otherwise—this is not a fault. For the quality of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) is perceived through the word *odana* (food), which is heard first; and it is proper that the word *upasecana*, heard later, should likewise signify the sense of being non-obstructive in accordance with that [prior perception].

Nor should it be argued that the word "rice" (odana) must be understood as referring to that which is to be destroyed, following the sense of the word "condiment" (upasecana); for it is improper to distort the natural sense of what is heard at the beginning of a passage in order to conform to the natural sense of what is heard at the very end.

"Setting aside the common form"—for this very reason, in the Adhvaryu's direction, "Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forward; let that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin go forward; let that of the Udgātṛs go forward; let that of the Sacrificer go forward," although one would have to state that the word *udgātṛ* applies to many through a conventional indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its established usage as a plural, the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā has determined that it indicates specifically only the group of Udgātṛs, setting aside the common form of the sixteen priests. Regarding the phrase in the Bhāṣya, "of that which is being poured over": the meaning is "of that which is mixed with it."

Regarding the phrase "because Viṣṇu is heard [in the context]," although the passage beginning with "He [is the end] of the paths" is the subject matter of the subsequent sūtra, "And because of the context," and not of this sūtra—since here the reason provided is specifically the status of being the destroyer of all moving and non-moving beings, and that status is obtainable through its association with the mention of death as the condiment (mṛtyūpasecana) without requiring anything else—nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated thus in order to indicate that the context is also a supporting factor for the association with death as the condiment.

If it is argued that—given the force of the opening statement regarding "death as the condiment" (mṛtyūpasecana)—the final mention of death as a condiment must be interpreted as not being contradictory, in accordance with the state of being an object of enjoyment established by the natural sense of the word "rice" (odana) heard at the beginning—it is replied: here, because the three worlds, the two kinds of food, and death are metaphorically represented as rice and its condiment, their relationship is perceived as being like that of curd and rice; and thus...

In accordance with the connection to "Death as the seasoning," the words *brāhmaṇa* and *kṣatriya* must be taken figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote all perishable things, both moving and non-moving. Precisely because of the proximity to the metaphorical description of Death as the "seasoning," the word *odana* (rice) must also be taken figuratively to denote the state of being perishable. Furthermore, it is more appropriate to accept the quality presented by another word within the same syntactical unit—due to the economy of mental effort (*buddhilāghava*) and the power of syntactical unity—rather than accepting the specific forms, qualities, and attributes suggested by one's own immediate cognition.

For this very reason, it has been determined in the Pūrvatantra that in the injunction, "He places the anointed pebbles," when there is a requirement for a means to perform the anointing, one must accept only the ghee mentioned in the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa), "Ghee is indeed luster," and not merely any liquid substance that might be imagined by human intellect.

But even so, how is the inclusion of all moving and non-moving beings established by the words "brahmin" and "kṣatriya"? For while it is necessary that the word *odana* (boiled rice) functions figuratively—such that it indicates a quality (*guṇa*) presented by another word uttered in proximity—it is possible for the phrase "the brahmin and the kṣatriya" to function in its primary sense. Nor is it correct to say that because death is mentioned as the condiment (*upasecana*), everything upon which it is poured must be understood by those two terms.

In the passage, "One offers with a winnowing basket; by that, food is prepared," although the word *śūrpa* (winnowing basket) is praised in its supplementary context (*vākyaśeṣa*) by mentioning its being an instrument for preparing food, if one were to say that the term applies figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) everywhere to whatever is an instrument for preparing food—[the opponent might object]: "But praise as an instrument for preparing food is possible even for the winnowing basket alone, because the property of being an instrument for preparing food does not exist as a collective attribute (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) residing in both the winnowing basket and other implements like the ladle (*darvī*) or the cooking pot (*piṭhara*). [The author replies: This is the same here as well; for it is equally possible to demonstrate that even the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas alone are mixed with death.

Furthermore, it may be argued that the demonstration that the words "Brāhmaṇa" and "Kṣatriya" denote the entire aggregate of moving and non-moving beings is redundant; for even by demonstrating that the word "food" (odana) denotes the state of being withdrawn, it is established that its correlate is the Destroyer. Thus, since the Supreme Self is established as the Destroyer by the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of being the destroyer of all individuals belonging to the classes of Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas—encompassed by the unrestricted application of the words throughout all cosmic cycles—it is unnecessary to establish the broader scope of those two terms. To this, we reply:

Whether one adopts the position that [the two terms] denote agency (*kartṛtva*), enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*), or the power of withdrawal (*upasaṃhartṛtva*), it is inevitable that both the words *brāhmaṇa* and *kṣatriya* function as indicators (*lakṣaka*), just like the word *odana*. For there is no individual soul (*jīva*) who is the enjoyer of these two classes specifically as objects of enjoyment in the form of death and so forth, nor is the Supreme Self the withdrawer of those two alone; furthermore, even if He were the enjoyer of more than those two, there would be no purpose in specifically grasping only those two. Nor is there any [such purpose] in the *Antarāditya-vidyā*, where [it says]: "Those..."

If it is argued that—just as the Supreme Self, who is the Lord of all worlds and desires, possesses lordship over specific worlds and specific desires—the attribution of being the destroyer of the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas is also possible for the Supreme Self as the destroyer of all—this is not so; because in that context, due to the difference in location (the eye and the sun), we observe a distinction in the designation: "He is the lord of those worlds which are beyond this one, and of the desires of men. While such a distinction is established there, here [in the case of the *dahara*], if only that [specific] portion were taken, [there would be no such distinction].

Since there is no restrictive factor [to limit the scope], the mention of "Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication) and does not rest solely on its own literal meaning; thus, when there is a requirement for that which is to be indicated, it is determined from the subsequent mention of "death as the sprinkling" (*mṛtyūpasecana*) that everything being sprinkled by that death is what is to be indicated.

Furthermore, since the word *odana* (rice/food) stands as a metaphorical designation for that which is subject to withdrawal (*saṃhāryatva*) according to the reasoning already stated, it follows that in this mantra—which functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*) due to its connection with the relative pronoun *yat*—the phrase "the priesthood and the nobility" (*brāhmaṁ kṣatraṃ ca*), which serves to present the objects of withdrawal, must necessarily be understood as indicating all perishable things consisting of the moving and the unmoving, in accordance with the preceding statement (*purovāda*) such as: "All these beings, O Somya, have their root in Being (*sat*), they have Being as their abode, and Being as their support. Let this suffice for now.

The term *prākaraṇika* here means that the reason being stated is "pertaining to the context" (*prakaraṇa*), that is to say, accompanied by the context. Furthermore, in the sūtra *prakaraṇācca*, the word *ca* (and) conjoins the mark (*liṅga*); thus, the meaning is that [the Supreme Self is the subject] because of the context of the Supreme Self and because of the recognition of the mark consisting in its difficult-to-know nature from the verse "Who indeed knows thus? It does not mean, however, that the reason consists in greatness, omnipresence, and so forth found in the preceding sentence relative to the subject-sentence (*viṣayavākya*).

Since there is no dispute regarding the fact that Brahman is the subject under discussion, it is unnecessary to establish this through the inferential mark (*liṅga*); furthermore, this is evident from the natural sense of the word *prakaraṇa* (context) as used in the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya. As for the question of how there can be a single context (*ekaprakaraṇatva*), although Brahman is the subject in passages such as "the great, all-pervading [Self]" (*mahāntaṃ vibhum*), and it is not proper to abandon what is already the subject, nevertheless, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is also the subject in passages such as "He is not born, nor does He die" (*na jāyate mriyate*), our view is that we see sufficient grounds for accepting Brahman alone as the referent.
The meaning is that the disciple—who already knows in general that the Supreme resides in the body, as he seeks to know its specific location—asks about a particular part of the body.

"He shows a break in the context" means that he shows a break in the context of the Supreme Self regarding the sentence, "The two who drink the *ṛta*. With respect to the passage beginning with "Of whom the *brahman*... [it is said]: by the force of the mark (*liṅga*) of drinking the *ṛta* in the sentence "The two who drink the *ṛta*," there is no loss of the eater's status as the Supreme Self, even though the context of the Supreme Self is interrupted by the subsequent recitation of "Of whom the *brahman*... and so forth.

The intention of the objection is that the sentence beginning with *yasya brahma ca* does not belong to the same context as the passage beginning with *mahāntaṃ vibhum*, and thus it lacks the status of being part of the same context as the verse *ṛtaṃ pibantau*. [The opponent replies: "An interruption is justified because of the separation. [The author asks: But is there not likewise no separation in the case of *mahāntaṃ vibhum*? For such is the order of the recitation: [The opponent continues: "Indeed, there is a separation here too, for after the words *mahāntaṃ vibhum* there follows the mantra *ṛtaṃ pibantau*; therefore, the two are separated by the intervening mantra. Furthermore, the word *pibantau* is in the dual number, while the word *mahāntam* is in the singular; thus, they cannot be connected. Moreover, the word *ṛtam* is neuter, whereas the word *brahma* is masculine; therefore, they do not agree in gender either. Consequently, the sentence beginning with *yasya brahma ca* does not belong to the same context as the passage beginning with *mahāntaṃ vibhum*, and thus it lacks the status of being part of the same context as the verse *ṛtaṃ pibantau*. [The author replies: This is not so. Even if there is a separation by the intervening mantra, the connection is established through the power of the subject matter (*prastuta-vaśāt*). Just as in the case of the sentence *sa ātmano vapām udakhidat* ("He cut out his own omentum"), even though there is a separation by the intervening mantra *tasmād yajñāt sarvahutaḥ sambhṛtam* ("From that sacrifice, from which everything was offered, it was brought together"), the connection is made by virtue of the subject matter. Similarly, here too, the connection is established by the force of the subject matter. Furthermore, the dual number in *pibantau* is used in reference to the two selves (*ātman*), namely the individual self (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). As for the difference in gender, it is resolved by the fact that the word *brahma* is used in a neuter sense, as in the phrase *brahma ca brāhmaṇaśca* ("the Brahman and the Brāhmaṇa"). Therefore, the sentence beginning with *yasya brahma ca* belongs to the same context as the passage beginning with *mahāntaṃ vibhum*, and thus it possesses the status of being part of the same context as the verse *ṛtaṃ pibantau*. [The opponent objects: "But how can there be a lack of separation in the case of *mahāntaṃ vibhum*? For such is the order of the recitation: *mahāntaṃ vibhum*, *ṛtaṃ pibantau*, *nityam*, *vṛddhaṃ ca*, *anaśnann anyaḥ*, *guhāyāṃ nihitam*, *na dṛśyaḥ*, *sahasraśīrṣā*, *yo vedādau*, *tad etad*, *yasmāj jātam*, *yasmāj jātam*, *yasmāj jātam*, *yasmāj jātam*, *yasmāj jātam*,

"Having realized the Self as great and all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve. This Self is not attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only he whom this Self chooses, by him is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form. Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed, nor even one whose mind is not at peace, can attain this Self through wisdom. For whom both the priesthood (brāhmaṇa) and the nobility (kṣatra) are but food..."

"Death is the condiment for whom; who indeed knows where he is?—the two who drink the reward of good deeds in the world of merit. Consequently, the lack of intervention [between the two passages] is equal for both. And in that case, since one obtains a reference to what is about to be introduced, it is improper to abandon the subject under discussion. Furthermore, there exists the mark of "difficulty of attainment," which serves as a sign of recognition for the subject at hand.

If it is asked: "How can there be an abandonment of the unity of context (*ekavākyatva*) with the present subject matter out of a desire for a single context with the subsequent sentence located in another section, namely 'drinking the nectar'?"—it is replied: In the sūtra *prakaraṇācca*, the word "context" (*prakaraṇa*) intends the state of being situated within a collection of sentences that propound the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This point, which is raised as an objection in the sūtra *guhāṃ praviṣṭāviti*, is here resolved; thus, there is no fault.

Although these two [objections and] resolutions—being part of that same context—are intended by the Bhāṣya to apply to what was previously introduced and should therefore be stated in that very place, they are nonetheless stated here because the word "immediately following" (anantaram) serves to establish their belonging to the same context. This is to be understood as follows: [they are stated here] for the purpose of resolving the doubt regarding equal primacy; for if that were the case, there would also arise the doubt that the Supreme Self is the subject to be propounded.

Regarding the phrase "the internal nature of intellect and vital breath," the word "intellect" (buddhi) refers to the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). This is because, as in the statement "it is not said that [the intellect] is the destroyer," the remainder of the sentence is "of which [it is said] 'and the heart'. The term "in some way or other" (yathākathaṃcit) is to be explained [as follows]. He states another reason for this with the words "there, first of all": the sense is that [the intellect] is mentioned together with many [other things].

Regarding the question of how there is no contradiction: since both [types of indication] are equally established through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that does not abandon their own primary meanings (*ajahatsvārtha*), how can one be primary and the other secondary? For instance, in such cases as "The curd must be protected from crows," the crows are certainly not primary; nor is the primary meaning found to be predominant, while the other is subordinate, in examples such as "He lays down the *sṛṣṭi* bricks," "He lays down the *prāṇabhṛt* bricks," or "He recites the *pṛṣṭha* hymns. To this, it is replied:

For in the world, a word denoting excellence is indeed seen to be applied metaphorically to that which is not excellent; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "A word denoting the agent is used metaphorically for another grammatical factor (*kāraka*), but a word denoting another grammatical factor is not used metaphorically for the agent. Consequently, it is established as a general rule that when a word denoting X is employed metaphorically for Y, X is superior to Y. Therefore, by that principle, the sense is that the primary meaning possesses primacy over the metaphorical meaning.

The objection—namely, that since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is merely an instrument (*upakaraṇa*), it cannot be considered the second [entity], and that by the method stated in the Sūtra, "And thus the presentation and the question concern only three," only the means (*upāya*), the goal (*upeya*), and the attainer (*upetṛ*) are to be presented; and since intellect (*buddhi*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*) are not included within those three, how can a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding them arise?—is refuted. It should be understood that the prima facie argument can indeed arise because intellect and vital breath, being instruments for the accomplishment of meditation (*upāsanā*), can certainly be included within the category of the means (*upāya*).

The word "hi" indicates that the meaning of the Sūtra serves to establish that the Eater is the Supreme Self; this point will become clear later on. The phrase "it is seen" implies *anvaya*, which means syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*). The same should be understood for what follows. The idea is that the meditation on the individual soul (*jīva*) is enjoined as a subsidiary part (*aṅga*), and thus the term "attainment through the yoga of the self" (*adhyātmayogādhigama*) has the meditation on the individual soul as its meaning.

And because [the term] is well-known in the sense of "earth" from the Vedas—meaning that in passages such as "I place you on the lap of Aditi," there is no usage [of the word *bhūmi*] to denote the earth—the intention is as follows: only two members of the same class (*sajātīya*) are fit to be designated by a dual number. If one were to include members of different classes (*vijātīya*), there would be the complexity (*gaurava*) of having to bring to mind both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*).
However, if one includes only those of the same class, there is the simplicity (*lāghava*) of having to bring to mind only the individuals themselves. This is the intended meaning.

The phrase "other attributes mentioned in various passages" means qualities such as being the source of the Veda (*brahmaja*), omniscience (*jña*), and being a bridge (*setu*). Regarding "the state of being the object of meditation and the meditator": the intention is that the statement "two who drink the Truth" (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*) establishes the presence of both [the Self and the Supreme Self] within the cave of the heart, in order to dispel the doubt that the object of meditation—the Supreme Self—is distant from the meditator. As for the commentary's phrase "this bridge of those who sacrifice" (*aseturījānānām*): the meaning is that He is the bridge, the establisher, for those who perform sacrifices.

One might object: "The statement in the Bhāṣya that 'here too, those two alone are specifically designated by means of ignorance and omniscience through the words *chāyā* and *ātapa*' is improper; for it is unestablished for the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) that the words *chāyā* and *ātapa* refer to ignorance and omniscience, and thus it is impossible to employ such a qualification as a logical reason. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states, "by means of [the phrase] 'through ignorance and omniscience,' etc.," explaining that it is indeed possible to employ them as a reason because the words *chāyā* and *ātapa* serve to remind one of the Śruti passage: "The ignorant and the wise" (*ajña-jñau*).

In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated: "At the time of the conclusion of a sacrifice in which all one's possessions (*sarvavedasa*) are given as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). The relevant scriptural passage (*śruti*) is cited here: "Uśan Vājaśravasa indeed gave away all his possessions. The word *uśan* means "desiring" or "wishing. "He had a son named Naciketas. While he was still a boy, faith entered him as the sacrificial fees were being led away [from the house]. 'Those who give such [cows] go to those worlds called Ānanda—cows whose water has been drunk, whose grass has been eaten, whose milk has been milked, and whose vigor is gone. By giving old cows, one goes to the joyless worlds. [The commentary continues: "By giving old cows, one goes to the joyless worlds."

The meaning is that he thought, "He will obtain [me]. He said to his father, "Father, to whom will you give me? A second time and a third time. To him he said, "I shall give you only when you are dead. Thus addressed by his angry father, Naciketas lamented: "Of many I go as the first; of many I go as the middlemost. What indeed must be done for this one? What will he do with me today?"

The meaning is: "I am either the chief or at least the middlemost among my many sons or disciples; I am certainly not the lowest. Why then has he given even someone like me to Yama? Or what purpose does he have for me as a ghost? Nevertheless, thinking that the father's word must not be false, he spoke to his grief-stricken father, saying: "Behold how it was with those of old, and behold how it is with others. Like grain, mortals ripen; like grain, they are born again."

The meaning is: "Having understood the conduct of former ancestors, such as fathers and grandfathers, as well as that of the virtuous living today, and having realized the impermanence of the body, send me to Yama. When he was addressed thus, his father sent him; and seeing him staying at the gate of Yama’s abode for three nights, the noble ones spoke these words to Yama upon his return from his journey: "The guest Vaiśvānara enters the houses of the Brahmins; perform for him this pacification—O Vaivasvata, offer water! The meaning is: "Perform worship beginning with the offering of water."

And they spoke of the transgression incurred by failing to do so: "Hope, expectation, alliance, pleasant speech, the merit of sacrifices and public works, sons, and cattle—all these a man of small intelligence loses if a Brāhmaṇa dwells in his house without eating. The meaning is that the guest, while fasting, destroys the desires, intentions, virtuous associations, truthful words, sacrifices, public works, sons, cattle, and so forth of the host. This was the statement made to Mṛtyu by the ministers: "O Brāhmaṇa, since you have stayed in my house for three nights as a guest worthy of honor, yet without eating..."

"Salutations be unto you, O Brāhmaṇa; may there be prosperity for you. Therefore, choose three boons. Being addressed thus, Naciketas said: "O Death, may Gautama be of peaceful resolve, well-disposed, and free from anger toward me; and may he speak to me with a gracious mind when released by you—this, I choose as the first of the three boons. The phrase "of peaceful resolve" (*śāntasaṅkalpaḥ*) means one whose deliberations have ceased. "Toward me" (*mām prati*) means directed toward me.

"Recognizing me as one sent by you, he would say, 'This is my son,' meaning he would converse with me. This was the reply of Mṛtyu to him who had spoken thus: "As before, Auddālaki Āruṇi will recognize [me] and be satisfied; free from anger, he will sleep happily at night, having seen you released from the mouth of Death. The meaning is that he will recognize [me] as he did previously. "He has seen" (darśitavān) means "he has perceived" (dṛṣṭavān).

Naciketas spoke again: "In the heavenly world there is no fear whatsoever; one does not fear you there because of old age. The meaning is that, abiding there, even while possessed of old age, one does not fear you. Thus [he described] heaven.

Naciketas said: "O Agni, you know that being which is in the midst of heaven, O Death; tell that great one to the seeker who is striving. Those who attain the heavenly world partake in immortality; this I choose with my second boon"—the meaning is: that which pertains to heaven, the means for attaining heaven. Having been addressed thus, Death said: "I shall tell it to you; understand that from me, O Naciketas, knowing that which pertains to heaven, Agni. Know this as the attainment of infinite worlds and as the foundation; it is hidden in the cave of the heart."

The meaning is: know that which has become the means for attaining and being established in the infinite worlds, and which is submerged within the intellect of the wise. In this regard, there is a scriptural passage: "He spoke to him who was submerged at the beginning of the worlds: 'What bricks there are, how many they are, or how [they are placed]'"; the meaning is that he instructed him regarding the nature of the bricks, their number, and so forth. "And he too repeated it to him exactly as it was told; then Death, being pleased, spoke to him again. "Repeated" (pratyavadat) means he recited it after him (anvavadat).

The Great-Souled One, being pleased, said to him: "I grant you yet another boon here today. The fire shall be known by your very name; take also this *sṛṅkā* of manifold forms. A *sṛṅkā* is a garland made of jewels. "One who has kindled the Nāciketa fire thrice, having attained union through the three [paths] and performing the three duties, transcends birth and death. Having known and realized the God praised in the Veda, he attains ultimate peace. Having understood this mystery of the triple Nāciketa, the wise man thus builds the Nāciketa fire."

Having cast off the noose of death before him and transcended sorrow, he rejoices in the heavenly world—whosoever, having understood this altar of consciousness which has become the very self of Brahman, builds the Nāciketa fire-altar. Having himself become that which has become the very self of Brahman, he performs that by which he is not born again. This is your Agni Nāciketa, the one you chose with your second boon; O Agni, people shall proclaim this very one as yours. Choose, Nāciketa, a third boon.

"This doubt regarding a person after death—that some say he exists and others say he does not—may I know this, instructed by you; of all boons, this is the third boon. The meaning of these words will be explained by the author himself in the section on *Anumānika*. Having been addressed thus, Death said: "Even the gods had doubt regarding this in the past, for this principle is not easily understood. Choose another boon, Naciketas; do not press me, let go of this one."

"Do not obstruct me; release him; do not harm me. Release this boon to me—meaning, let him go. Being addressed thus, Naciketas said: "Even the gods have indeed had doubts regarding this, O Death, for you say it is not easily understood. A speaker of this [truth] like you is not to be found elsewhere, nor is there any other boon equal to this. Being addressed thus, Death said: "Choose sons and grandsons with lives of a hundred years; choose many cattle, elephants, gold, and horses."

"Choose a vast domain of land, and live yourself as many autumns as you desire. Here, "domain" (*āyatana*) means a place of residence. "If you consider this equal [to immortality], choose instead wealth and long life. Prosper on a great domain, O Naciketas; I shall make you a partaker of all desires. "Prosper on a great domain" (*tvamedhi mahābhūmau*) means "become a king over a great territory. "Whatever desires are difficult to obtain in the world of mortals—pray for all those desires according to your wish."

"These beautiful women, with their chariots and musical instruments—such as these are not to be obtained by men. With these, given by me, enjoy yourself; Naciketas, do not ask about death. The meaning is: you ought not to ask this question concerning the dead, which concerns death. Though thus tempted, Naciketas said: "O End-maker, that which is the state of tomorrow for a mortal—that [uncertainty] wears away the vigor of all the senses. Even the entirety of life is indeed very short; your dancing and singing are yours alone."

"Those whose existence is tomorrow" (*śvobhāvāḥ*) means that all the enjoyments you have proposed are perishable.
