Regarding the phrase "of all the senses": furthermore, those enjoyments are destroyers of the strength of all the senses. "Let your states alone be your dancing and singing" (*tavaiva bhāvās tava nṛttagīte*): the meaning is that let your women and so forth, as well as your dancing, singing, and the like, belong to you alone. [As it is said: "A man is not to be satisfied by wealth; we shall obtain wealth if we behold you."

"We shall live as long as you rule; this alone is the boon I choose from among those worthy of being chosen. Wealth is not the cause of satisfaction; moreover, in the sight of you, what burden could there be for either wealth or life? Therefore, that alone is to be chosen—this is the meaning. "Having approached those who do not age and are immortal, while one is aging and mortal, standing where? Knowing [the truth], and reflecting upon the pleasures of color, beauty, and delight—who would take pleasure in a life that is not very long? "Standing where? means existing in the lower world, which is of the nature of the earth (bhū).

A discerning person who understands this, even having gone into the presence of the gods, would not be inclined toward sensual enjoyments; the meaning is: who would take delight in such a very brief life? "O Death, tell us that about which they have doubts in the great hereafter"—the meaning is: tell us precisely that regarding the next world about which even the gods have doubts. Following this is the statement of the Śruti: "This boon which has entered into the secret [of the Self], Naciketas chooses none other than that."

Following this is the statement of Mṛtyu: "The beneficial is one thing, and the pleasant is indeed another; these two, having different purposes, bind a person. Of these two, for him who takes up the beneficial, it becomes well-being; he who chooses the pleasant is deprived of his true purpose. *Sinītaḥ* means "they bind. The beneficial (*śreyaḥ*) and the pleasant (*preyaḥ*), which have distinct objectives, both relate to a person. The meaning is that between these two, for one who adopts the beneficial there is excellence (*sādhu*), whereas for the other there is its absence.

"Both the beneficial (*śreyaḥ*) and the pleasant (*preyaḥ*) approach a person; the wise man, having fully circled around them both, discriminates between them. For the wise man chooses the beneficial over the pleasant, while the dull-witted chooses the pleasant for the sake of acquisition and security (*yogakṣema*). The word *etaḥ* means 'they approach. Having fully circled around them—that is, having reflected thoroughly—the wise man chooses the beneficial as being more worthy than the pleasant. But the dull-witted chooses things such as food and drink that nourish the body, which constitute the form of the pleasant."

"O Naciketas, you have not disregarded the desirable and lovely objects of desire by coveting them; you have not attained this wretched snare consisting of wealth, in which many men sink. 'Snare' (sṛṅkā) means a contemptible state. These two are far apart, opposite, and divergent: that which is ignorance and that which is known as knowledge. 'Divergent' (viṣūcī) means having contrary courses. I consider Naciketas to be one who desires knowledge; many desires did not entice you. "Desirous of knowledge" (vidyābhīpsinam) means one who longs for knowledge.

"Existing in the midst of ignorance, yet considering themselves wise and learned, these deluded ones wander about, striking themselves, like blind men led by one who is himself blind. The word *dandramyamāṇāḥ* means going toward a flickering, unstable state.

"The world beyond does not reveal itself to the fool who is heedless, deluded by the infatuation for wealth; thinking 'this world exists, there is no other,' he repeatedly falls under my sway. Regarding the fool—the ignorant one—the meaning is that the *sāmparāya*, the world beyond, does not appear to him. The meaning of the phrase "this world" will be explained later in the verse beginning with "But having experienced [the results] in this world of restraint... Furthermore: "He who is not obtained even for hearing by many, and whom many who hear do not know..."

"Wonderful is the speaker, skillful is its obtainer; wonderful is the knower, well-instructed by the skillful. This means that hearing, knowing, speaking, obtaining, or understanding this [Reality] is difficult to achieve. "Well-instructed by the skillful" means instructed by a skillful teacher. "It is not easily understood when proclaimed by an inferior man, even if one reflects upon it in many ways. There is no way to reach it unless it is proclaimed by one who is non-different [from it]; it is subtler than the atom, yet more massive than the mountain."

This Self, though contemplated in many ways by disputants, can be known when taught by a teacher who is not inferior—that is, one who possesses little knowledge; for there is no comprehension when it is taught or instructed by another ordinary person, since this Self is subtler even than the subtle. He says that very thing: "This understanding is not to be attained through reasoning, O dearest one, but when taught by another, it leads to right knowledge. You have indeed reached [this state] with steadfastness in truth; may you, O Naciketas, be such as we are, having asked [this question]."

The Self as an object cannot be attained through a husband; O dearest one, O most beloved! even that which is taught by another, or taught by one unacquainted with the scriptures, does not lead to right knowledge. That Self concerning which you have attained this understanding is difficult to comprehend. Since you remained unshaken even when being tempted, you are steadfast; therefore, the meaning is that only one such as you would be a true disciple.

"I know that treasure is impermanent; for the eternal is not attained by means of the transient. Therefore, by me, through transient materials, the Nāciketa fire was built, and the eternal has been attained. Having seen the fulfillment of desire, the foundation of the world, the infinite end of sacrifice, and the great, far-reaching hymn of praise as the firm basis, the wise Naciketas, through steadfastness, has transcended all fear. He is difficult to see, hidden, entered into the secret cave of the heart, dwelling in the abyss, the ancient one."

Having known the God through the attainment of inner yoga, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow. Having heard this and fully grasped it, a mortal who practices the dharma that is to be inferred and attains it, rejoices indeed upon obtaining that which is worthy of joy; for I consider the house to have been opened for Naciketas. Tell me that which you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than what is done and what is not done, and other than the past and the future. That goal which all the Vedas proclaim and which all beings strive to reach—[tell me that].

That goal for which they practice the life of a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*), that I shall tell you briefly: it is "Om. For this syllable is indeed supreme; for having known this very syllable, one obtains whatever one desires. This is the best support; this is the supreme support. Having known this support, one is magnified in the world of Brahman. The wise one is neither born nor does he die; he has not come from anywhere, nor has anyone become him.

Unborn, eternal, ever-lasting, and ancient, this [Self] is not slain when the body is slain. If the slayer thinks to slay, or if the slain thinks himself slain, both of them do not understand; this [Self] neither slays nor is slain. Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, the Self of this living being is hidden in the cave of the heart. Free from desire, one beholds that Lord, the Greatness of the Creator, and becomes free from sorrow through His grace. Sitting, He goes far away; lying down, He travels everywhere.

We speak of that God as the Setting; none other than me is worthy to know Him. Bodiless, yet dwelling within bodies that are transient; the Great, the All-pervading Self—having realized this, the wise man does not grieve. This Self is not attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only by him whom He chooses is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form. Neither one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil, nor one who is not composed, nor one whose mind is not at peace, can attain Him even through wisdom.

"For whom both the priesthood (brāhmaṇa) and the nobility (kṣatra) are the rice-mess, and for whom death is the condiment—who truly knows where he is? Drinking the Truth (ṛta) in the world of good deeds, having entered the cave in the highest supreme heaven, those who know the Brahman call them shade and light; so do those who maintain the five fires and those who have thrice performed the Nāciketa rite. That which is the bridge for sacrificers, the imperishable Brahman that is supreme, the fearless further shore for those wishing to cross over—that Nāciketa fire may we master.
Know the Self as the charioteer, and the body as the chariot," and so forth.

The sense is this: if liberation were the attainment of a state devoid of all distinctions, then the determination of specific means would be impossible, as it would not be possible to determine the nature of liberation—which consists in the ascertainment of non-existence [of the world]. Therefore, it is logical that knowledge associated with that [liberation] has the purpose of knowing liberation. This is because the subject matter other than what is already known is [the self]; for the eternal self, distinct from the body, is not already known [to the ordinary person].

The meaning is that [the knowledge] has as its object something other than those [elements]. Regarding the phrase "corroboration by another scriptural passage" (*śrutyantarasaṃvādam*), the intention is that the statement, "There is no consciousness after departing," means that in the state of liberation, because there is no contraction of one's natural, unlimited knowledge, there is no knowledge of forms such as gods within the self by identifying it with the aggregate of elements. The term "knowledge of the reality of the higher and lower selves" (*parāvarātmatattvavijñānam*) is what should be explained.
As for the second [term], which refers to the reason found in the preceding contextual sentence, that which needs to be said regarding it has already been stated previously.

The meaning is that because both the word *hi* and the word ending in the fifth case (the ablative) are heard [in the text], otherwise there would be the contingency of redundancy since the word *hi* already conveys the sense of being a reason (*hetutva*). He establishes the absence of redundancy in his own position with the words "of the two who have entered the cave" (*guhāṃ praviṣṭayoḥ*). This means he demonstrates the meaning of the Sūtra, namely the meaning of the Sūtra consisting in the nature of the Selfhood of those two who have entered the cave. Of the two who have entered the cave...

The meaning is that because its nature is *rā* (pleasure), it is the "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*). Now, this is indeed the interpretation of others: "The two who have entered the cave" are precisely the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self. Why? Because they are both "selves" (*ātmānau*), which means they are both conscious. Since both possess consciousness and are thus of the same class (*sajātīya*), when there is a need for a second [entity] following the mark of drinking the *ṛta*, it is appropriate to understand a second conscious being of the same class. When it is said, "A second for this cow must be sought," one seeks a second cow, not a horse or the like.

As for what was said—that it is not tenable for the Supreme Self (paramātman) to reside in the cave—that is not so; for in the Śruti and Smṛti, the residence of the Supreme Self in the cave is also observed. Thus, the statement "the two have entered the cave" is, in our view, an indicator of the established conclusion (siddhānta) and its supporting reasoning, whereas in your view, it is an indicator of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

Therefore, because the indication of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not necessary, [the author] says "due to having a small abode" (*arbhakaukastvāt*), breaking the compound as *parasyopapanna iti*. The phrase "because its purpose has been fulfilled" (*kṛtakaratvāt*) means by the sūtra "due to having a small abode. In this section, he refutes what was stated in Śaṅkara’s commentary regarding the verse "Two birds, inseparable companions... (*dvā suparṇā sayujau sakhāyau*) with the words beginning "in the sentence 'two birds'... (*dvā suparṇā iti vākye* etc.).

One might object: "Since the *Ṣaṅgirahasyabrāhmaṇa* interprets the mantra 'dvā suparṇā' as referring to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), why is there an attempt to refute that very interpretation—which has already been refuted in its own commentary—by extending this same logic? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states, 'And of that sentence...,' in order to show that even the interpretation favored by that [commentary] as referring to the intellect and the individual soul is not possible. Thus ends the section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Since the mere presence of that which exists in its own nature is useless for establishing [the existence of the Self], and because there is no presence in the eye of that which resides in the heart—the root of all the senses—he explains [the sūtra] as "from the apprehension of presence" (*sannidhānāvagamāt*). This means "from the apprehension in the eye," or rather "from the apprehension by means of the eye," in accordance with the subsequent text. Now, it may be objected that the commentary beginning with "For when [the eye] is opened" has already established that the eye is the means of determining the staying and moving of the living self within the body.

One might suspect that the locative sense in the phrase “the person is seen in the eye” has not been established by this much alone; therefore, he says, “in this action. The intention is that while one ought to say, “his capacity is seen through this action,” the expression “his capacity is seen in this action” is used analogously; and while one ought to say, “he is seen by means of the eye,” it is stated as “he is seen in the eye. The meaning is that it is indicated by the word “seen” (*dṛṣṭam*), in accordance with the later text which uses the term “indicator” (*sūcaka*).

Alternatively, the meaning of the word *sūcaka* (indicative) may be understood as *darśaka* (showing). Now, one might object: since the status of the passage "This person who is seen within the eye" as referring to the Supreme Self—rather than the individual self—has already been established by the section *Antastaddharmopadeśāt*, how can this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arise regarding this sentence which contains an identical description? This is true; however, in that case, the prima facie view was that it refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), because the attributes mentioned therein could not otherwise be explained.

[The opponent might argue: It was refuted by the mark of proof (*siddhaliṅga*); however, here, because there is an absence of a subverting mark (*bādhakaliṅga*) and because [the reflection] is commonly known and perceived, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the reflection and so forth arises. But even so, [the scripture says]: "They call him 'the one to whom all blessings come' (*saṃyadvāma*). For all blessings (*vāmāni*) come together unto him; indeed, all blessings come together unto him who knows this. He is also 'the leader of blessings' (*vāmani*). For he leads all blessings; indeed, he leads all blessings for him who knows this. He is also 'the leader of light' (*bhāmani*)."

For these concluding attributes—namely, being the center of all blessings (*saṃyadvāmatva*), being the leader (*vāmanitva*), and being the illuminator (*bhāmanitva*)—which are characterized by the attainment of all desires, the acquisition of all auspicious things, and the state of shining in all worlds, as demonstrated by the passage beginning with "He indeed shines in all worlds; he shines in all worlds, for one who knows thus," and which are supported by indicative marks (*liṅga*) signifying their purpose as corresponding fruits, are set forth in the concluding portion of the text by the Śruti: "He said: 'This is the Self; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman.'"

One might raise the objection: "Since there exist many unestablished marks of Brahman—such as being the Self (*ātmatva*), immortality (*amṛtatva*), fearlessness (*abhayatva*), and being Brahman (*brāhṛtva*)—how can a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arise based on the two marks of 'being well-known' (*prasiddhi*) and 'being seen' (*dṛśyatva*), even though these are mentioned first? Anticipating this, he says: "The particle *iti* indicates the intended meaning (*arthatātparya*). The sense is that when the word *iti* is used in such passages as "one should meditate [on the mind] as Brahman" (*mano brahmety upāsīta*), it is observed to indicate the intended meaning.

He says "in the established conclusion" (*rāddhānte*) for the sake of facilitating the understanding of the disciples; the word "is being explained" (*vyākhyāyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. To express the intention behind the plural number, he again takes up that same subject with the words "of these" (*eṣām iti*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the phrase "it is observed that [words] have meaning as their primary referent" serves to exclude the desire to express a specific meaning in that very context, whereas the desire to express a connection with knowledge occurs where there is an injunction to meditate, such as in "one should meditate on the mind as Brahman," and so forth. This is the function of the particle *iti*.

However, where there is a connection with a statement that serves to delimit the meaning already expressed, the word *iti* does not preclude the intention to convey that meaning; such is the sense in examples like "Thus indeed the teacher used to say" (*iti ha smopādhyāyaḥ kathayati*). He refutes the reasoning of the opponent's established doctrine with the words beginning "Even though in this... (*tadyadyapyasmin...*) and so forth.

And because the exclusion (vyatireka) will be stated later—meaning that since the exclusion from persistence (sthitivyatireka) is intended to be made the logical reason (hetu), it is appropriate to make its positive concomitance (anvaya) the reason; this is the sense. "But not as referring to location" means not as referring to a substratum (adhikaraṇa), unlike the view of other schools.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is possible in the individual self" (*jīvātmani sambhavatastasya*), others have argued as follows: one might object, "How can the Brahman, who is all-pervading like space, have a small location such as the eye? To this, they reply that just as there are designations of location such as "He who dwells in the earth," and just as there are teachings of names and forms for the Brahman—who is actually devoid of name and form—such as "His name is 'The Risen One' (*uditināma*)" and "He has golden beard and golden hair," so too, even though the Brahman is all-pervading, a specific location is not contradictory for the purpose of its perception; however, this does not imply that the Brahman possesses actual name and form.

If it is argued that another proof for [the Lord] not being the Supreme Self has been presented—namely, that this [Brahman] is subject to the aforementioned defect—it is replied: When the doubt arises as to how the all-pervading Brahman could have such an extremely limited location as the eye, it can be explained according to our stated method by pointing to the designation of the eye as its location in another scriptural passage, "He who dwells in the eye. Thus, since we observe the designation of names and forms—which are inappropriate for the nameless and formless Brahman—as its locations, it is like covering one's head with a turban [to hide a flaw].

The point is that [the opponent's argument] is improper because it involves grasping the tip of the nose; the remainder of the sense is that this [objection] results in a "proving the already established" (*anyathāsiddhi*), as it is possible even in our own position. Regarding the phrase "both by implication and by word," in passages such as "He who dwells in the eye," there is establishment by implication (*arthataḥ*); in passages such as "But it is seen by the subtle intellect," there is establishment by word (*śabdataḥ*). This is an illustration; in the "Eye-Knowledge" (*akṣividyā*) passage, "This person who is seen in the eye," one should observe establishment both by word and by implication.

Is this sūtra intended to demonstrate other means of proof? Surely, the combination of abiding in the eye, controlling it, and so forth, constitutes the proof for being the Supreme Self—or is it abiding alone? It cannot be the first, because although the combination of abiding, controlling, and so forth might prove the status of the Supreme Self, such a combination is not heard in the sentence "He who is here in the eye. Nor can it be the second, because abiding alone exists even in things other than the Supreme Self, and thus lacks the quality of being a unique, defining characteristic (asādhāraṇa) of Him.

If it is argued that, for this reason, one must simply state that the arguments presented in the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) are established otherwise, we reply: there is no need for such insistence, because the Teacher himself will state later, at the occasion of extracting the meaning of the sūtras, that the second sūtra is intended to resolve the doubts contained within its own statement by means of citing another scriptural passage (śruti). Thus, there is no room for misapprehension there.

Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) with Satyakāma Jābāla. For thirty-two years he tended his fires. While he was doing so, he allowed other students to return home after completing their studies, but he did not allow him to return. His wife said to him: "This student has performed his penance and has served the fires well. Let the fires not speak out against you; let them declare for you. Having spoken thus to him, she went away on a journey. Then the fires said to him: "Student, speak the truth! Truth alone makes one a brahmin. He replied: "I do not know the truth. I have lived here for thirty-two years, serving you, O venerable ones, yet you have never told me, 'Speak the truth! They said: "It is indeed truth that makes one a brahmin. You have tended us well. We shall tell you the truth. They said to him: "The earth is the fuel-wood, fire is the smoke, the sun is the flame, the moon is the embers, and the stars are the sparks. "And what is the sacrificial food? he asked. "Water," they said. "One who knows this, even if he eats food at a low-caste's house, is not defiled by sin, for he eats only the sacrificial food. Then they said to him: "The wind is the horse Uccaiḥśravas; its chariot is the sky, the day and night are the two wheels, the four quarters are the horses, and the dawn and twilight are the two side-horses. The sun is the yoke-pole, and the air is the charioteer. The clouds are the leather straps, lightning is the lash, thunder is the clatter of the wheels, and rain is the chariot-rattle. One who knows this becomes a conqueror of chariots. Then they said to him: "Fire is the priest called Hotṛ; the wind is the priest called Adhvaryu; the sun is the priest called Udgātṛ; and the moon is the priest called Brahman. The dawn is the offering of the morning libation; the day is the midday libation; and the evening is the third libation. One who knows this attains the world of heaven. Then they said to him: "The eye is the Garhapatya fire; the breath is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; and the mind is the Āhavanīya fire. "And what is the sacrificial food? he asked. "Food," they said. "One who knows this, even if he eats food at a low-caste's house, is not defiled by sin, for he eats only the sacrificial food. Then they said to him: "The water is the altar; the hairs of the body are the sacrificial grass; the heart is the sacrificial seat; the mind is the vessel for the Soma; the mouth is the ladle; and the truth is the vow. "And what is the world he attains? he asked. "The world of Brahman," they said. "If one knows this, he does not grieve. Then they said to him: "The person seen in the eye is the Self. This is the immortal, the fearless. This is Brahman. Even though the waters of the world flow toward it, they do not wet it. Even though the streams of the world flow toward it, they do not moisten it. It is free from desire, for there is no desire in it. It is free from evil, for there is no evil in it. This is the world of Brahman, O Upakosala. You have attained it. You will not grieve. And he did not grieve.

He resolved to fast due to illness. His teacher’s wife said to him, "O student of the Veda, why do you not eat? He replied, "There are many desires in this person, various obstacles; I am filled with diseases, so I will not eat. Then the fires deliberated among themselves: "The student of the Veda is distressed; he has not attended to his well-being. Come, let us instruct him. They said to him:

"Breath is *brahma*, *ka* is *brahma*, *kha* is *brahma*. He said, "I understand that breath is *brahma*, but I do not understand what *ka* and *kha* are. They said, "That which is *ka* is indeed *kha*; that which is *kha* is indeed *ka*. Thus they told him both breath and space. Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him: "Earth, fire, food, and the sun."

"That person who is seen in the sun, I am he; indeed, I am he. He who, knowing this, worships him thus, shakes off evil-doing, becomes a possessor of the world, reaches a full lifespan, and lives radiantly. His descendants do not perish, and they say, "We enjoy [the fruits of] one who approaches us," both in this world and in that world—he who, knowing this, worships him thus. Then the Anvāhāryapacana fire instructed him further: "The waters, the quarters, the stars, and the moon."

"The person who is seen in the moon—that am I; that indeed am I. As before, [the text continues]: "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon him," and so forth. Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him: "Breath, space, heaven, lightning. "The person who is seen in the lightning—that am I; that indeed am I. As before, [the text continues]: "He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon him," and so forth. They said: "O Upakosala, my dear, this is our knowledge for you."

"And the knowledge of the Self; but the teacher will tell you the path. He arrived, and as he was about to laugh, the teacher addressed him: "Upakośala! "Revered sir," he replied. "My dear, your face shines like that of one who knows the Brahman. Who, pray, has instructed you? "Who indeed would instruct me, sir? he said, as if shrinking away. "Surely these fires of mine must have taught you such things, and not otherwise," he said, and he questioned the fires.

"What, my dear, did they indeed tell you? "They told me this," he replied. "Did they indeed tell you, my dear, about the worlds? But I shall tell you that—how, just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this. "Please, let the venerable sir tell it to me. He said to him: "That person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self (ātman). This is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman."

Therefore, even if one pours clarified butter or water upon this [breath], it passes through as if on a path. They call this "the gathering of all that is lovely" (*saṃyadvāma*), for all lovely things gather toward it; all lovely things gather toward him who knows thus. This, indeed, is the "leader of the lovely" (*vāmani*), for he leads all lovely things; he leads all lovely things who knows thus. This, indeed, is the "shining leader" (*bhāmani*), for he shines in all worlds; he shines in all worlds who knows thus.

Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him or not, they pass into the flame; from the flame into the day; from the day into the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight into those six months during which the sun moves northward; from the months into the year; from the year into the sun; from the sun into the moon; from the moon into lightning. There a person who is not human leads them to the world of Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman. Those who proceed by this path do not return to this human whirlpool—they do not return.

Such is the sequence of the *śruti*. Having applied the *sūtra* in accordance with the *śruti*, he now applies the *śruti* in accordance with the *sūtra* by means of the principle "because its essence consists of those qualities" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*). However, this [reason] is independent of the statement of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); this is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), and it should be understood as being independent of any other reason for establishing its own existence. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that the particle *eva* in a general sense indicates independence (*nairapekṣya*).

Furthermore, although the Brāhmaṇa is the subject under discussion, it is not referred to here because it is separated by the knowledge of Agni; therefore, the doubt that the reason "because of the mention of one distinguished by happiness" is unestablished (*asiddhi*) is also set aside by the author of the Sūtras through the particle *eva*, which indicates independence—this is the intention of the Bhāṣya, such is the sense.

The sense is this: just as the throwing of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is for the sake of the sacrifice itself—since it is an act of disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *prastara* used for the *pātra-dhāraṇa* (supporting the vessels), which is not incompatible with the fruit of the principal rite—it nevertheless functions as a means to a fruit because it is performed by means of the *sūktavāka*, which, as enjoined by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), bestows fruits such as longevity; and since this would otherwise be inexplicable, the knowledge of Fire (*agnividya*), though being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of the *brāhmaṇas*, can likewise be understood to have a fruit. This is the intended meaning. The construction is "in both the beginning and the conclusion," and this is not a word requiring further explanation.

It should be understood that this is because that statement will appear later on. Regarding the phrase "by the fourfold reason": although the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* in both the introduction and the conclusion—just like Agni’s statement, "But the teacher will tell you the way"—is a reason why the knowledge of the *brāhmaṇa* was not yet completed prior to the knowledge of Agni, [the present case is established] because it falls within the introduction and the conclusion of the knowledge of the *brāhmaṇa* under discussion, and because of the reference (*anvādeśa*) in the words, "Then, indeed, him... (*atha hainam*).

It can be said that only these three reasons are presented by means of the phrase "and because of the teaching as a collection. This is understood exactly so even in the Bhāṣya, and not in any other manner; nevertheless, [the reason is stated] in a way common to both direct and indirect proofs.

The fourfold [classification] presented should be understood as follows: "anvādeśa" (subsequent mention) means a re-statement of what has already been introduced through verbal expression, by way of its connection with another action; that is to say, it is the presentation through verbal expression of something previously mentioned as being connected to one action, now being connected again to another action. The sense is that although there is no conjunction (*samuccaya*) because there is no equal primacy between the two regarding the fruit of liberation—which is what is intended to be taught by the qualification "to be instructed"—nevertheless, a conjunction is possible with respect to the act of instruction itself.

Alternatively, the meaning is that [the word] refers merely to a relationship, and not to a relationship where there is equal primacy. The reading of Jaimini’s sūtra is: *dravyasaṃskārakarmasu parārthatvāt phalaśrutir arthavādaḥ syāt*. In some manuscripts, the reading *dravyaguṇasaṃskārakarmasu* occurs, but this is due to a scribal error. The meaning of this sūtra will be clarified by us under the section beginning with *śeṣatvāt puruṣārthavādaḥ*.

The meaning is that [the text] demonstrates that [this practice] has a fruit consistent with the knowledge of Brahman (*brāhmī-vidyā*), because it is the cause for the increase of the lineage of virtuous sons, grandsons, and so forth, which in turn increases the fruits of the meritorious deeds and the pursuit of knowledge acquired by one's fathers, grandfathers, and ancestors. This should be understood from the statement of Āpastamba: "Those who abide in the prescribed duties increase the fame and the heavenly realm (*svarga*) of their ancestors after death. As stated in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "In another Vedic scripture (*śruti*), it is heard as the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman."

Nor should it be argued that, in the context of the *agnividyā* where the production of the fruit in the form of the continuity of the True (*satsantati*)—which is employed in the *brāhmavidyā*—is being proclaimed, it is improper to cite another scriptural passage (*śruti*) that establishes that the continuity of the True is the fruit of the *brāhmavidyā*; for [the cited passage] concerns those fruits specified [in the *agnividyā*] which are [actually] the fruits of the *brāhmavidyā* as maintained by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*).

This is because the intent [of the author] is merely to reject the notion of contradiction. For the Commentator’s emphasis lies precisely in the fact that the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*) is possible even in the absence of producing a result favorable to the principal (*aṅgin*), and even in the absence of producing a result contrary to the principal. Therefore, he will state under the sūtra "But otherwise, on account of the word" (*anyathā tv aṃśabdāt*) that even a result mentioned in an explanatory passage (*ārthavādika*) must indeed be accepted provided it is not contradictory to that [principal].

Regarding the meaning of the prefix *upa*: by means of the prefix *pari*, which expresses a limit (*paryanta*), the proximity that constitutes the meaning of *upa* is indicated; thus, the intended sense is the attainment of the state of being limited by the removal of obstacles. As for the phrase "even though it remains within a single context": this means even though the Brāhmaṇa was previously under discussion and there was no intervening break caused by the knowledge of Agni (*agnividya*). Intending to convey the meaning of the sentence, "He gave [the instruction] to fast together with his illness," the Commentary states: "lack of confidence" (*anāśvāsam*).

"Upeyivān anāśvān": this is the form derived from the root *aś* preceded by the negative particle *nañ*, meaning "one who has not eaten. He explains the word *yāvatā* with the word *pratyuta*. The sense is that it is not by means of the word *brāhma*; for if it were taught by the *Brāhmaṇa*, the concluding statement (*nigamana*) would have been simply "they said the *Brāhma*. The phrase "masculine gender in the concluding sentence" refers to the concluding sentence: "And they told him of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and of space (*ākāśa*). Nor [is there a problem] because the word *ākāśa* possesses both genders.

It should not be argued that even though the masculine gender is possible, because of its co-occurrence with the neuter word *tat*, the word *ākāśa* in the concluding sentence must also be neuter; therefore, how can the masculine usage *saḥ* (he) be used in reference to it? For the compound *tadākāśaḥ* (that Ākāśa) is a single term, and there is no evidence that it is neuter. This is supported by such scriptural passages as: "From the Self, Ākāśa was produced" (*ātmana ākāśassambhūtaḥ*), "He said, 'Ākāśa'" (*ākāśa iti hovāca*), "Ākāśa, indeed, is the bearer of name and form" (*ākāśo ha vai nāmarūpayornirvahitā*), and "That which is this... (*yadeṣa*).

In accordance with such usages as "ākāśa ānando na syāt" (there would be no bliss in space), the masculine gender of the word *ākāśa* is established due to its common prevalence in that form; furthermore, this is merely an illustration. For one who argues that passages such as "kaṃ brahma khaṃ brahma" constitute injunctions for meditative visualization (*dṛṣṭividhi*) because they resemble other passages beginning with "brahma," it must also be accepted that the passage "prāṇo brahma" likewise constitutes an injunction for meditative visualization.

Therefore, even in the passage "The breath is Brahman," what is intended to be established here by this Sūtra is that the breath itself is Brahman, rather than avoiding the interpretation as an injunction for a meditative vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*). Consequently, since there is no fault in stating that the word "He" refers to the breath in accordance with the masculine gender of the word "prāṇa" heard at the beginning of the section, one should not object that the status of Brahman has thus not been stated for those two [bliss and space] indicated by the words *kaṃ* and *kha*. For even when it is said that the one denoted by the word *kha* is space (*ākāśa*), the same principle applies to the other two.

If it is held that by the mention of one, the mention of the other two is also established, then let that remain for now, as it is the same even in our own position. Regarding the phrase "those situated in the two sentences": in the passage "this person who is in the eye," a specific individual instance characterized by bliss—mentioned in the sentence "Kaṃ brahma" for the purpose of enjoining the qualities of its location—is cited in the preceding Sūtra as the means of proof.

In this context, however, the meaning is that there are two specific instances of the word (*vyaktiviśeṣa*): namely, the specific instance of the expression found in the sentence "Or rather, what is *kaṃ*, that is indeed *khaṃ*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1). The establishment of these specific instances of the word follows from the force of the sense (*arthasāmarthyāt*). Regarding the phrase "not because of the scripture concerning the Self" (*nātmāśruteḥ*), the intended scripture is that which establishes the non-origination of the Self, such as "It is not born, it does not die" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18), and so forth; it is not that specific instance of the scripture [concerning the ether] which is being referred to by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) in the immediately following sūtra, "But [the soul is] conscious for this very reason" (*jño'ta eva*). Rather, it is the scripture establishing consciousness, such as "The knower, O friend... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).

The meaning is that there is another Śruti beginning with "By what... and so forth, which is similar to that [previous one]. Now, an objection may be raised: for Upakosala, who had not heard the Vedānta, it would not be appropriate to instruct a meditation on a mere symbol (pratīka) for the sake of one desiring liberation. Likewise, in the passage "Prāṇa is Brahman," how could there arise the knowledge that Prāṇa is the body, and that words denoting a body refer ultimately to the embodied self? Furthermore, how could there be the knowledge that "the body is that which is to be controlled"?

Likewise, in the passage "Kaṃ is Brahman, Khaṃ is Brahman," just as in the case of "Prāṇa is Brahman," it is possible that there is only a determination that [Brahman] has the body of the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) which is the object of sensual pleasure; therefore, how could a doubt arise regarding the possibility of establishing a mutual qualifier-qualified relationship, which has never been seen before? Consequently, he dispels this doubt—namely, "How can such an inquiry be possible?"—with the words beginning "The meditation on a symbol for one desiring liberation" (*mumukṣoḥ pratīkopāsanam*), etc.; the phrase is to be split as "sambhavati tadvat. This refers to the doubt concerning the meditation on a symbol.

Raising the objection that if the distinction between the known and the unknown were not intended to be refuted because it is taught for the sake of those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), then the *sautra-hotṛ* would lack the power of refutation, [the author] establishes that even the *sautra-hotṛ* possesses the power of refutation by means of the passage beginning with "Or rather, that which is *kaṃ*, that is indeed *kha*. The meaning of the phrase "for there is no ignorance of the injunction regarding the vision of another object" is directed toward one who says, "I do not know either of these two modes. The phrase "because of the mention of ignorance" means that, as previously stated, everything is already known through the nature of the injunction regarding the vision [of Brahman].

It cannot be argued that there is no fault in the mutual exclusion between "blue" and "lotus"—just as there is between the meanings of the words *ka* and *kha* regarding their being of the nature of undifferentiated bliss—because they stand in a relationship of mutual qualifier and qualified, since such a relationship lacks any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*). For it is possible to say: "That which is blue is indeed a lotus, and that which is a lotus is blue."

They say that if it were so, then in a compound formed by the rule "the qualifier [is placed] before the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of no fixed rule regarding the prior placement [of the words]; furthermore, even in the phrase *utpalanīlam*, one would have to abandon its natural sense and treat the two as mutual qualifiers, whereby the passage would refer only to the essential nature of Brahman and not to the object of meditation.

The meaning is that he explains [the qualification] as "of one who has realized the true nature of the Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣayāthātmya*) in order to exclude those who, despite having heard the Upaniṣads, meditate upon a mere symbol (*pratīka*); for such people lack the necessity of following the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*). Now, one might object: even so, there remains the same defect, because for those who have realized the true nature of the Supreme Person but—due to some deficiency in their unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—do not meditate on Brahman, they likewise lack the necessity of following the path beginning with light. To this, we say: no.

The phrase "of one who has realized the true nature of the Supreme Person" means "of the worshiper of the *brāhmaṇa*. The word "śruta" (heard) is used to indicate other scriptural passages that establish the status of these [Upanishadic texts] as auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of the *brāhmaṇa*. The "Upanishads" are those that have been recited; thus, "one whose Upanishads are heard" (*śrutopaniṣatkaḥ*) refers to a person for whom there is a "going" (*gati*) that serves to demonstrate their status as an auxiliary. The meaning is that this is because the "going" which is taught by the recited Upanishads that demonstrate auxiliary status is being designated here. Thus, by way of repetition, it means: "because the 'going' of the person whose Upanishads are heard is being designated."

The meaning is that [the addition of the word *upaniṣat*] is for the sake of illustration; the intention of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) is that the inclusion of the extra syllables in the phrase *śrutopaniṣatka* refers to the path beginning with light (*arcis*) as set forth in another scriptural text (*śruti*). Consequently, one might ask: how is this meaning obtained from the expression *śrutopaniṣatka*, and why is it not obtained when one says simply *śrutabrāhmaṇa*? This doubt is refuted by observing that since a sūtra is like the face of a person, repetition is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*); this is said with the intention of avoiding contradiction with that principle. The underlying sense is that the Supreme Person, who is to be attained, must necessarily be the object of meditation (*upāsana*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the preceding sentence states, 'Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him or not,' using the singular demonstrative 'for him' (*asmin*), how can there be the statement, 'They go toward the light itself' (*te 'rciṣam evābhisambhavanti'), which uses the plural 'they' (*te*)? Anticipating this, the author says, "before the words 'toward the light itself,'" intending to show that there is no fault because the word 'for him' in the preceding sentence refers to the class [of persons] in general. Now, in this [Upanishad]...

The exposition of the path beginning with light (*arcis*) in the *Kauṣītaki-vidyā* would be redundant, because that is already established by the statement of the *Pañcāgni-vidyā*: "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity... Nor should it be argued that since the teacher is to speak of the path—as stated in "But the teacher will tell you the way"—the path must have been taught by the fires rather than by the teacher; for the same objection could be raised there as well: why did the fires say so? To this, he says: "By the *Pañcāgni-vidyā*... [referring to the fact that the path is already established therein].

Now, one might object: how does the description of the path for one who has heard the Upaniṣads establish that the person within the eye is the Supreme Self? For, with reference to the meditation on Brahman as characterized by bliss taught by the Fires, the path was mentioned as something to be told by the Teacher in the words, "But the Teacher will tell you the way," and it was merely taught by the Teacher as a subordinate element of that meditation. What follows from this regarding the status of the person in the eye as Brahman? Even if the path described by the Fires were appropriate simply because the knowledge of Brahman characterized by bliss is indeed a form of Brahman-knowledge.

Nor should it be argued that once the Brahman-hood of the one distinguished by bliss taught in the context of fire is established, the Brahman-hood of the person within the eye is also established by the very same reasoning stated in the sūtra "and because of the designation of the one distinguished by bliss"; for if that were the case, the sūtra *Śrutopaniṣatka* would become redundant.

If it is argued that even this Sūtra does not establish the state of being Brahman for one who is merely distinguished by the bliss taught in relation to fire, because the author of the work intends this Sūtra only to establish the status of the person in the eye as Brahman directly—then it is replied: in the passage, "Now, whether they perform funeral rites for him here," it is impossible to abandon the fact that the word "this" (idam) refers to the person in the eye who is established in that knowledge; therefore, this establishes the person in the eye as Brahman directly.

Now, one might object: how can the heart be the root of the sense-faculties located in regions such as the eyeballs? Anticipating this doubt, the author intends to show its status as a root by means of the channels established in such passages as "A hundred and one," and thus says, "A hundred and one," and so forth. And this scriptural passage refers to the scriptural passage, "Then [the soul moves] into these channels. Everything that needs to be said on this point has been made clear under the sūtra *jagadvācitvāt* (1.4.16).

The term "heart" (*hṛdaya*) refers to the Supreme Self residing within the heart; this is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication). Just as one says "the man is in the palace" when he is actually on a couch located within the palace, the designation "being in the heart" applied to the person residing in the Supreme Self within the heart is indeed primary. However, in the system of Yādavaprakāśa, the proof of the status of the Supreme Self [as the referent] is untenable; thus, the exclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*) is untenable—this is the meaning.

The meaning is that, by restating that [the breath], it serves to establish its status as the Supreme Self; having taken for granted the exclusion of a reflected image (*pratibimba*), it serves to establish the exclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*). Alternatively, the meaning is that, having restated the reasons previously set forth, it serves to establish the exclusion of the individual soul by means of those very reasons. Now, one might object: "This will have the same logical status as the Sūtra, 'For this very reason, neither the deity nor the elemental being'"; anticipating this lack of conviction, he says: "of the passage beginning with 'The breath is Brahman'."

Therefore, although it was stated that the status of being Brahman need not be separately asserted—since, in the passage "And from this very [text] he is Brahman," the exclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established by the very same reasons that exclude the reflection, and thus it is the exclusion of the *jīva* alone that is being asserted, not Brahman—nevertheless, the intended sense is that it is more appropriate for [the exclusion of the *jīva*] to serve as a subordinate support (*upapādaka*) for the ultimate probandum (*paramasādhya*), according to the method that will be explained hereafter.

The meaning is this: since it is not based on logical reasoning (*nyāyanibandhana*), one must accept that even the explanations regarding the excellence of the *sukha* (pleasure) [of the self] intended in that very Sūtra are meant for that purpose alone; it does not merely aim at the nature of an explanation of the excellence of *sukha* devoid of reasoning. In another Śruti, regarding the right and left eyes, it says: "He who is this person in the right eye is indeed named 'Indha' (the Kindler); though he is Indha, they call him Indra. Now, the form of the person in the left eye is his wife."

In another region of the *Virāj*, those two were united as a couple; from that, Prāṇa was born. The scriptural passage beginning with "of Indra," cited in the *Jyotir-adhikaraṇa* (the section concerning Light), should be consulted. As for the phrase "in all the sections," the sense is that it is improper to claim that [the present sūtra] "ata eva ca sa brāhmaṇaḥ" serves as a proof for the ultimate conclusion (*paramasādhya*). The meaning of "it is weaker because it is what is to be proven" is that even the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa* is to be established by the logic of the subsequent section.

Regarding the statement that the status of the meditation on the Person in the Eye (*akṣipuruṣavidyā*) as a subsidiary part [of the meditation on the path] is expressed by way of restating the reflection on the path, the intended meaning is posed as a dilemma: is it meant that the meditation on the Person in the Eye is enjoined as a subsidiary to the reflection on the path, or that the reflection on the path is enjoined as a subsidiary to the meditation on the Person in the Eye? Having raised this alternative, he refutes the first with the words, "because of the determination of the Person in the Eye to be the Supreme Self. He refutes the second with the words, "because the reflection on the path is a subsidiary to the Savitrī-vidyā."

"Purifying the object" refers to the purification of the object (*viṣaya-śuddhi*) as follows: When Janaka brought a thousand cows as the bride-price for the most excellent Brāhmaṇas, and after some Brāhmaṇas had been defeated by Yājñavalkya in a debate, Uddālaka Āruṇi posed a question regarding the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the *sūtra*. Then, indeed, Uddālaka Āruṇi approached him [Yājñavalkya] and said, "O Yājñavalkya! We were dwelling among the Madras in the house of Patañjala Kāpya, studying the sacrifice"—that is to say, in the country of the Madras.

He had a wife possessed by a Gandharva. We asked him, "Who are you? He replied, "I am Kabandha Ātharvaṇa. *Kabandha* means one whose name is Kabandha. He said, "O Kāpya Patañjala, do you know that Sūtra, O sacrificers, by which this world and the other world, and all beings, are strung together? The meaning is that they are threaded like flowers upon a string.

Patañjala Kāpya said, "No, venerable sir, I do not know that. He said to Patañjala Kāpya and the ritualists, "Do you, O Kāpya, know that Inner Controller who controls this world and the other world, and all beings from within? Patañjala Kāpya said, "No, venerable sir, I do not know that."

He said to Patañjala Kāpya and the ritualists: "O Kāpya, whoever knows this *sūtra* and that Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), he is a knower of Brahman, a knower of the worlds, a knower of the gods, a knower of the Vedas, a knower of all beings, a knower of the Self, and a knower of everything. Having praised them with these words—"I know that; I am a knower of Brahman," and so forth—he taught both the *sūtra* and the Inner Controller to Kāpya and the ritualists. The meaning is: "I know both of those as well."

"If you, O Yājñavalkya, do not know that thread and that Inner Controller, and yet venture to drive away the cows given by Janaka as the bride-price for Brāhmaṇāvasyū—the *brāhmaṇāvasyu* being the cows bestowed by Janaka because of his status as the foremost among the Brāhmaṇas—then your head shall shatter apart. "I do indeed know that thread and that Inner Controller. "Whoever here might say, 'I know, I know,' tell us how you know it."

"If anyone were to say, 'I know [this],' the meaning is: 'If you know it, then speak. He said: "Vāyu indeed, O Gautama, is that thread. By Vāyu as the thread, O Gautama, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together. Therefore, O Gautama, they say of a dead man: 'His limbs have fallen apart,' meaning they have become scattered. For by Vāyu as the thread, O Gautama, they are held together."

When the answer to the question from the Sūtra had been given in this way, [Yājñavalkya] accepted the portion stated—"It is just so, Yājñavalkya; tell me about the Inner Controller (antaryāmin)"—and then asked about the Inner Controller, beginning with: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal," and continuing in sequence with: "He who dwells in the waters, he who dwells in fire," and so forth.

Having taught the successive series [of objects] beginning with water, fire, the intermediate space, air, the sun, the directions, the moon, the stars, the ether, and darkness, and concluding with "Thus far with respect to the deities" (*ity adhidaivatam*); then, having begun with "Now, with respect to the elements" (*athādhibhūtam*), and having introduced the series beginning with "He who [dwells] in all beings," and concluding with "Thus far with respect to the elements"; then, having begun with "Now, with respect to the self" (*athādhyātmam*), and having introduced the series beginning with breath, speech, eye, ear, mind, skin, understanding, and semen; [the text concludes: "This is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal... unseen... (*eṣa ta ātmā antaryāmy amṛto 'dṛṣṭo*).

"The Seer who is unheard, the Hearer who is unthought, the Thinker who is unknown, the Knower who is unperceived—other than Him there is no hearer, other than Him there is no thinker, other than Him there is no knower. This is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal; everything else is afflicted. Thus concludes the [Kāṇva] recension. However, in the Mādhyandina recension, the sections concerning the worlds, the Vedas, and the sacrifices are additional. Since the position that the Inner Controller is the mere individual self (pratyagātman) is impossible, he states that the word "individual self" refers to a specific living being (jīva) characterized by accumulated merit. The word *pratyagātman*... [text ends]

Thus [it is said]. When the negation is untenable—this refers to the fact that the state of being a "seer" (draṣṭṛtva) consists in being the agent of the direct perception of form and so forth; this is the sense of the ellipsis. He establishes that the act of governing (niyamana) is established by implication through the phrase "consisting of the impelling of another. Now, one might ask: which individual soul (jīva) could be the inner ruler (antaryāmī) here? It cannot be the soul of the worshipper, because for such a soul, abiding in the earth and so forth—as taught in passages such as "He who dwells in the earth"—and the governing thereof would be impossible.

Nor is it a specific deity presiding over earth and so forth; for although such a deity might have the capacity to govern the stability and regulation of earth and the rest, it is impossible to designate it as "That is your Self," since it is distinct from the individual soul who is the object of instruction and the practitioner of meditation.

Nor is it the aggregate of all individual souls (*jīvasamudāya*), because that aggregate does not abide within earth and the rest, and thus it is untenable to designate the aggregate as "That is your Self. Having raised this doubt—that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) it is not intended that any single one among these—the practitioner, the deity presiding over earth and so forth, or the aggregate of souls—is the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*)—but rather [it is something else].

It should not be argued that what is intended is the inner controller-ship (*antaryāmitva*) of things belonging to the class of living beings (*jīvajātīya*), and that such a state would render the designation "That is your Self" (*sa ta ātmā*) untenable because the living being to be instructed (*upadeśya*)—the one who meditates (*upāsaka*)—cannot consist of many living beings as their inner controller; for there is no fault here, since the meaning to be expressed is "You are of that same class," as will be explained later. With this intention, he says: "by the repetition of the word 'yat' in each successive turn."

The meaning is as follows: just as when it is said, "He who stands there is your son; he who cooks is your son," a distinction between sons is understood, so it is here. This is intended to show the absence of any other pervasive or restrictive entity; that is to say, there is nothing whatsoever that is either pervasive or restrictive of the state of being delimited by the class of living beings (*jīvajātīya*).

As for the statement that [the Lord] is the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) with respect to specific individual souls (*jīva-viśeṣa*), the sense is that this status as the inner ruler of specific individual souls is established by such passages as, "He who dwells in the sun," and "He who dwells in the moon. The phrase "like the eightfold form" means, for example, that Rudra is the controller of his eight forms, such as fire and the rest. The phrase "of the respective lords of the hosts" means, specifically, of the lords of the host of Adityas.

In some manuscripts, the word "sūtra" is read immediately after "evam prāpte"; we do not see any purpose for that. Regarding the commentary's phrase "in those characterized by the divisions of *adhidaiva*, *adhiloka*, and so forth": an objection is raised—surely, having begun with "He who dwells in the earth," and having pointed out the earth, water, fire, the intermediate space, wind, the sun, the quarters, the moon, darkness, and light, the term "thus far with respect to the divine (*adhidaivam*)" is heard only at the final section concerning light, and not in the preceding sections?

If it is asked, "How then do these [subsequent sections] bear the mark of the term *adhidaiva*?"—the point is that this is not so, because by the use of the particle *iti* in the phrase "thus with reference to the divine" (*ityadhidaivam*), there is a reference back to the preceding sections as well, and thus it is established that they too bear that mark.

Since it is possible to explain this [sūtra] in all the sūtras as "the inner controller (antaryāmī) is the Supreme Self with respect to the divine, the worlds, and so forth"—that is, regarding the objects consisting of the gods, the worlds, and the elements—by setting aside that [explanation] and accepting that the words *adhidaiva* and so forth refer to the sentences themselves, one may explain it as "the inner controller is that which is propounded by those sentences. Thus, in all the sūtras, [it refers to] that which is propounded by each respective sentence.

The intended meaning is that the author of the *Bhāṣya* intends "otherness" (*paratvam*) alone to be the desired probandum (*sādhya*), because this chapter is devoted to demonstrating the coordination (*samanvaya*) of the sentences. By the phrase "the two words," it is shown that the reading of the sūtra by others, which lacks the word *adhiloka*, is indeed unauthoritative. By the term *adhidaiva*, which serves to demonstrate numerous synonyms, the sense is that there are many synonyms for earth, water, fire, intermediate space, wind, sun, directions, moon, stars, and ether that are included under the category of "pertaining to the divine" (*adhidaiva*).

The sense is that the restriction has borne fruit; however, it should be understood that this was stated after reflecting on the meaning of the Bhāṣya, which holds that the Upaniṣadic passages declare the supreme self alone as the ruler of all—expressing such forms as "the rulership of all" and "being the self of all."

The meaning of the commentary’s statement, "and immortality is inherent," is as follows: between that which is inherent and that which is adventitious (aupādhika), the adventitious is perceived only after the perception of its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and thus its cognition is delayed; therefore, the inherent alone is what must be grasped. As for the phrase "by the force of the nature of things" (*arthasvabhāvāyattam*): by virtue of the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*), even for the Supreme Self, seeing, hearing, and so forth would not be possible without instruments; thus, [the capacity for these acts] depends on the very nature of the thing itself.

Regarding the statement "the status of being a seer and so forth does not depend upon instruments," although the reading of the Bhāṣya is *na ca paramātmanaḥ karaṇāyattaṃ draṣṭṛtvādikam*, it should nevertheless be understood that this is a partial citation (*pratīkagrahaṇa*) for the sake of the meaning. Now, one might object: is it not the case that the Bhāṣya reading *na ca parasyātmanaḥ karaṇāyattaṃ draṣṭṛtvādikam* is more appropriate?

Because the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*), which consists in the agency of seeing, is necessarily dependent upon instruments, and because such a state of being a seer is not admitted in the Supreme Self, he explains [the term] as "by means of form and so forth. Now, one might object: the word *svabhāva* does not refer to a property (*dharma*), but rather is a synonym for the word *svarūpa* (essential nature). Anticipating this doubt, he states that it is not a synonym, because we observe its usage in close syntactic proximity [to words denoting properties].

Regarding the words *svarūpa* and *svabhāva*: by the word "and" (*ca*), he also includes the volition of another conscious being distinct from himself, thereby excluding dependence on the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Having explained the word *svabhāva* as referring to knowledge that constitutes an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), he explains it as referring to existence (*sattā*), or alternatively, as "not dependent on instruments. Anticipating the objection that this would be indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*), he says: "by the Lord's knowledge in its general aspect."

The phrase "of the connection with a universal form" means that, as delimited by the nature of being God (*īśvaratva*) and the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*), there is independence from instruments, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth. And thus, the construction of the commentary's statement "and such is the scripture" (*tathā ca śrutiḥ*) is "and there is a scripture to that effect."

For in the scriptural text that is about to be cited, "He sees without eyes," there are two aspects: the fact that it specifies a particular kind of knowledge (*jñānaviśeṣopādānavattva*), and the fact that it contains an explicit denial of specific causes (*kāraṇaviśeṣaniṣedhakaṇṭhoktimattva*). In the passage, "And His power of knowledge, strength, and action are inherent" (*svābhāvikī jñānabalakriyā ca*), although there is an explicit denial of causes, there is no specification of a particular kind of knowledge. In passages such as "the seer, the hearer," etc., although there is a specification of particular [faculties], there is no explicit mention of specific causes. However, it is established that both [aspects] are present in the phrase "He sees without eyes. And in that context, regarding the word *tathā* in the expression *tathā ca*:

Intending that an explanation is possible—either by reflecting on the explicit statement negating the cause, or by reflecting on the specific mention [of the senses], or by reflecting on both—he explains it in three ways, beginning with "the seer, the hearer," and so forth. One should not object that there is the consequence of tautology in such cases as "the seer of form" (*rūpadraṣṭṛ*), because the meaning of the words *rūpa* and *śabda* here is "one who directly perceives."

Just as in the expression "he cooks the cooking" (*pākaṃ pacati*), the word "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) there refers merely to the state of being a direct perceiver; having raised the objection as to what the status would be for terms such as "knower of the jar" (*ghaṭadraṣṭṛ*) or "thinker" (*mantṛ*) in similar contexts, he states that in such cases the meaning is, through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the possession of a direct perception whose object is identical to that of the mental reflection. Thus he says, "Those who [know] by means of the mind... Now, one might object: let the Supreme Self possess eternal reflection and so forth. To this he replies: "by means of external instruments such as the eyes..."

Regarding the phrase "by grasping the common form": having grasped the common form through the external instruments such as the eyes, the individual soul (jīva) determines it by means of the internal instrument in the form of the mind (*manas*), which is of the nature of deliberative intellect (*buddhi*). This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the phrase "the jīva is its substratum" implies that the application of terms such as "knower of the mantra" to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) would be difficult to refute [if they were taken literally]. Therefore, the expression "on account of the natural force of the word" means that a pronoun necessarily refers back to that which has been previously introduced and qualified by specific attributes.

Therefore, the intention is that in the passage, "Its secret name (upaniṣad) is 'I' with respect to the divine; its secret name is 'I' with respect to the self," the word *tat* does not merely refer back to the Brahman previously introduced, but rather refers to [Brahman] as qualified by specific locations and so forth; this will be explained in the sūtra, "In other cases also, it is thus because of the connection. Furthermore, due to the natural force of the word *ataḥ*, this should be understood as an illustration, and it should also be seen that the same applies to the natural force of the word *anya*.

Because the word *anya* (other) refers to things similar to those previously mentioned; for this very reason, in the ritual named *Iṣu*, following the injunction of specific auxiliary parts (*vaiśeṣikāṅga*) in the text, "The *Iṣu* sacrifice lasts seven days," there occurs the statement, "The rest is the same as the *Śyena*. In that sentence, by the word *itarat* (the rest), only those specific auxiliary parts similar to those previously mentioned are grasped by the word *itara*, due to their similarity to what was previously specified, and not the archetypal (*prākṛta*) parts. Since this has been determined in the *Pūrvatant*ra (Mīmāṃsā), by that same principle, the word *anya* [is to be understood in the same way].

The sense is that by means of the pronoun, there is the apprehension of the very controller who is similar to what was previously indicated. Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to present in the Commentary as a supporting argument the distinction-indicating expressions such as 'This is your Self' and 'That is your Self'—which were not intended [as arguments] in the portion of the Sūtra beginning with 'Because of the designation of His attributes'? Anticipating this doubt, he shows that this is indeed intended by the author of the Sūtras by stating, "In the first section of this Pāda."

Now, one might object: since the sūtra "Because of the specific word" (*śabdaviśeṣāt*) intends to determine the meaning of the Vedic statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman," the mention of the distinction (*vyatireka*) in the form "This is your Self" is not intended;
therefore, its presentation as a logical argument (*yukti*) is improper. To this, he replies: "Because that is for the purpose of illustration. (*tasya pradarśanārthatvāt*).

One might object: "In a case such as 'The person is neither a god nor a man,' there is no contradiction in taking words like 'god' to refer merely to the body. Anticipating this, he says: "And that [is established] by the absence of any exception" (*taccāpavādābhāva*). The meaning is that not only is there an absence of any contradiction to the natural sense (*svārasya*) of the negative formulation (*vyatireka-nirdeśa*), but there is also a positive proof for that natural sense, namely, that the lack of naturalness constitutes an exception. Thus, it is not merely the absence of a subverting factor against the natural sense of the negative statement; rather, there exists a factor that establishes that very natural sense.

The phrase "ruled out by impossibility" (asambhavanirasta) means that there is no possibility whatsoever of anyone existing outside the triad beginning with the *paramātman* who could occupy the position of being an inner controller (*antaryāmin*). Regarding the term "perfected through yoga" (*yogasiddha*), its meaning—whether it refers to a perfected one (*siddha*) endowed with the mastery of powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*) and so forth, or a perfected one endowed with the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*)—is impossible [in this context]. Since both of these two meanings occur only among gods who possess bodies and other attributes due to their preeminent merit, they are already included therein; therefore, the postulation of a separate head [for them] is futile. This is the meaning.

The meaning is as follows: since possessing a body and organs (*kāryakaraṇavattva*) has been stated as the reason for being a living soul (*jīvatva*), and since the status of being a controller is possible only for one who possesses a body and organs, the possession of a body and organs is required for the state of being an inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*). And such possession of a body and organs is possible only for the living soul; therefore, it was stated that the Lord’s status as an inner ruler is not possible. This is in accordance with the commentary of Śaṅkara, the opponent mentioned earlier.

The meaning is this: because each one among earth and the other elements is understood to be a body. For while there is a dependence on a body, sense organs, and so forth for the governance of something distinct from the body, no such dependence on another body is observed even for the governance of one's own body; and thus, since earth and the others are indeed the bodies of the Supreme Self, by those very [elements] the Supreme [Self governs].

Since [the Lord] possesses his own body, there is no requirement for another body in order to exercise control; however, one might suspect that if the Supreme Being were to possess a body in relation to the earth and other elements, the consequence would be that he would become a *jīva* (an individual soul). Anticipating this objection, the author says: "Regarding the suspicion that [he] would thereby become a *jīva*. For the relationship characterized as that between an instrument and its agent is what establishes *jīva*-hood; indeed, the relationship characterized by being a body and an enjoyer is what establishes *jīva*-hood. The point is that such a relationship is not required for the act of governing.

Thus, the meaning is that there is only one sūtra ending with "and the embodied soul" (*śārīraśca*), and not a single sūtra stating "for both [recensions] read this as distinct. Furthermore, the objection that there would be an infinite regress—namely, that there must be another controller for that [controller], since they are not different—is not possible because of the absence of any distinction between the controller and the controlled.

While commenting on the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya* regarding the point that "if there were difference, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result," Ānandagiri explains the meaning of the phrase "due to the absence of difference" as follows: the Supreme Self must indeed possess unimpeded sovereignty over all; and since it is impossible to postulate another controller for such an all-controlling Lord, there is no difference among controllers. Thus, even in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the fault of infinite regress—where one might suppose a controller other than the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*)—does not arise. However, this does not refer to a difference between the controller and the controlled.

If it is argued that [the objection does not apply] because one takes the absence of difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Lord (*para*) as the basis, we say no; for this has been repeatedly declared by Vācaspati Miśra himself—the foremost debater among the assembly of false speakers—who, in elucidating the intent of that very *Bhāṣya*, stated: "There is neither an infinite regress nor another controller, for that which is controlled is not controlled by another controller; rather, that soul who is the controller is the Supreme Self alone, appearing as such through a difference imagined by the delimiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, whence could there be another controller, and whence an infinite regress?

And thus, scriptural passages such as "There is no other seer" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23) also become meaningful, because there is no self other than the Supreme Self who acts as the inner controller; for the distinctions between knower and known found in the scriptures are based on the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) as imagined through ignorance. Likewise, the means of valid cognition such as perception, the experience of transmigratory existence, and the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions merely manifest the distinction between the controller and the controlled. Let this suffice for now. The meaning is that even though difference is perceived, it is entirely false.

For this very reason, there is no infinite regress; the meaning is that this follows precisely from the falsity of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*). "Just as with respect to earth and so forth, [there is no need for another controller] for the soul"—the sense is that just as the soul, who is devoid of a distinction from its own object of control (such as earth and so forth), has no requirement for another controller; likewise, even for the Lord, who is devoid of a distinction from His object of control, such a requirement would necessarily arise. Thus ends the section on the Inner Controller (*antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa*).

The author's intention is that invisibility is presented as a proof for the status of the Supreme Self because it is stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) that "by being invisible, [the Self] possesses the nature of the Supreme Self," meaning that He governs even while remaining unperceived by those things governed by Him, such as the earth and so forth; however, in reality, this intention is not found in the *Bhāṣya*.

Furthermore, upon careful consideration of the commentary beginning with, "Moreover, in this case, no specific attribute of consciousness such as 'being a seer' is heard of in this [text], as is the case in passages like 'the unseen seer,'" it should be understood that the state of not being a seer and so forth serves to establish insentience; whereas the state of being a seer and so forth is perceived only as a negation of that [insentience], and not as a means of establishing insentience through the absence of being a seer.

The meaning is that one should not be deluded into thinking that both possess a dual nature—that is, that the one characterized by qualities such as invisibility possesses the nature of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and likewise that the one who is higher than the Imperishable (*akṣara*) also possesses the nature of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. The word "in both" (*ubhayatra*) is to be explained as follows: it means "by way of reinforcing the capacity to indicate a non-conscious substratum," which refers to the capacity to indicate a non-conscious locus residing in the invisibility and other qualities that are being negated.

Thus, here the purity of the subject matter [is established]; where the meaning is not already explained, it is written in some places as well. In the *Ātharvaṇa* [Upaniṣad]: "The Brāhma was the first among the gods to come into being, the creator of the universe, the protector of the world. He taught the Brāhma-knowledge, which is the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son. Atharvan, who had been told that Brāhma-knowledge by the Brāhma, spoke it truly to Aṅgiras. He spoke it to Bharadvāja Satyavāha."

Bharadvāja [learned] the higher and lower [knowledge] from Aṅgiras. Śaunaka, indeed, having approached Aṅgiras, who was at Mahāśāla, according to the prescribed rule, asked: "Venerable sir, when what is known does all this become known? To him he said: "Two kinds of knowledge are to be known—thus indeed do those who know the Veda declare: the higher and the lower."

In that regard, the lower [knowledge] consists of the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda, phonetics (śikṣā), ritual science (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), prosody (chandas), astronomy (jyotiṣa), history and legend (itihāsa-purāṇa), logic (nyāya), hermeneutics (mīmāṃsā), and the treatises on law (dharmaśāstra).
