Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained—that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without caste, without eyes or ears, and without hands or feet; which is eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, exceedingly subtle, and undecaying; that which the wise behold as the source of all beings.

There is nothing whatsoever beyond Him; like an immovable tree, He stands alone in heaven. By that Puruṣa, all this is filled. As a spider emits and reabsorbs [its web], as plants sprout from the earth, and as hair grows from a living person, so does this universe arise from the Imperishable (Akṣara). Through austerity, the Brahman is built up; from that, food is produced. From food come life-breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and the immortality found in ritual acts.
From Him who is all-knowing, who knows all that is to be known, and whose austerity consists of knowledge—from Him this Brahman, name, form, and food are born. First Section.

This is the truth: those rituals which the seers beheld in the mantras, they were performed in many ways during the Tretā age. Practice them with self-restraint, O you who desire the Truth; this is your well-trodden path to the world of Brahman. Just as the flame flickers when the fire-god has been kindled, so one should offer the oblations between the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*). [The sin of him] whose *agnihotra* is without the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa*, without the *cāturmāsya*, without the *āgrayaṇa*, and devoid of guests—[is great].

An offering that is not made as an oblation (*ahuta*), one that is not accompanied by the *vaiśvadeva* rite, or one offered without faith or contrary to the rules, destroys the worlds of that person up to the seventh generation. "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven your seers, and seven your beloved abodes. The seven priests worship you in seven ways; fill the seven wombs with clarified butter. He names the seven distinct varieties of Agni’s tongues: Kālī, Karālī, Manojavā, Sulohitā, and she who is Sudhūmravarṇā.

"Sphuliṅginī, Viśvarūpī, and the goddess Lelāyamānā"—these are the seven tongues. He who performs his work in these blazing tongues at the proper time, the oblations, bringing delight, lead him by means of the rays of the sun to where the sole Lord of the Gods has his abode. The meaning is this: when he performs his ritual action at the proper time within these seven blazing tongues, the oblations, taking hold of him, become the rays of the sun and lead him to the world of Indra and the other gods.

"Come hither!"—thus do the oblations of great splendor, by the rays of the sun, carry the sacrificer away. Speaking pleasant words and offering praise, they say: "This is your holy world of Brahman, earned by good deeds. But these eighteen forms of sacrifice are but frail rafts; inferior is the work prescribed in them. Those fools who rejoice in that as the highest good return once again to old age and death. Dwelling in the midst of ignorance, yet considering themselves wise and learned, they wander on.

Being tormented, the deluded wander about like blind men led by one who is himself blind; existing in various ways within ignorance, these fools imagine they have achieved their goal. Because they do not understand that which is beyond the reach of thought, they fall away, afflicted by passion and with their worlds exhausted. For this reason...

The meaning is that those who perform ritual actions (*karmiṇaḥ*), being afflicted by passion, do not know reality; therefore, they fall away. "Thinking that sacrifice and charity (*iṣṭāpūrta*) are the highest, these deluded ones perceive no other good. Having experienced the reward of their well-done deeds on the back of the firmament (*nākasya pṛṣṭhe*), they enter this world again, or even one lower than that. The word *anubhūtvā* means "having experienced" (*anubhūya*). "Lower" (*hīnataram*) means either inferior or even very inferior, such as hell. "But those who dwell in the forest with austerity and faith, peaceful and wise, practicing the life of a student (*brāhmacarya*)."

Through the gate of the sun, those free from passion depart for that place where the immortal, immutable Person dwells. Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, the seeker of Brahman attains detachment, realizing: "There is nothing uncreated to be gained by what is created. To understand this, he should approach a Guru with fuel in hand—a learned scholar of the Vedas who is firmly established in Brahman. To him, who has approached properly, whose mind is perfectly tranquil, and who is endowed with self-restraint, that wise teacher imparts in its true essence that knowledge of Brahman by which one knows the Imperishable, True Person.
The second section.

This is the truth: Just as from a well-kindled fire sparks of the same nature fly forth in thousands, even so, O gentle one, various beings are born from the Imperishable and into it they also dissolve. Divine, formless, that Person is both within and without; he is without breath, without mind, pure, and higher than the high Imperishable. From Him is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses; [as well as] space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe.

Agni is his head; the sun and moon are his eyes; the quarters of space are his ears; the Vedas are his opened mouth; the wind is his breath; the universe is his heart; and the earth is established in his feet. He is the inner self within all beings. From him comes Agni, whose fuel is the sun; from him come the moon, the rain-cloud, and the plants upon the earth. The male pours his seed into the female, and thus many kinds of offspring are produced. From him come the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, the Yajus-formulas, the initiations, all the Brāhmaṇas, the sacrifices, and the sacrificial fees.

The year, the sacrificer, the world, Soma where he purifies himself, and where the sun—therefrom the gods have been produced in many ways, as well as the Sādhyas, humans, cattle, and birds; the out-breath and in-breath, rice and barley, austerity, faith, truth, celibacy, and sacred ordinance. From that the seven vital breaths arise; there are seven flames, seven fuel-sticks, and seven oblations. These are the seven worlds in which the vital breaths move, hidden in the cave, placed seven by seven.

From Him all oceans and mountains arise; from Him flow the rivers in their seven forms. From Him come all herbs and juices, by which this inner Self exists within all beings. This entire universe is indeed the Puruṣa; beyond that is Brahman, the Immortal. He who knows this hidden in the secret cave, O gentle one, unravels the knot of ignorance in this very world. Third Section.

"The great state called the cave-dweller is present nearby; therein all this is contained—whatever moves with life-breath and whatever is motionless. Know this as the existent and non-existent, the most excellent, the highest beyond cognition, the best among creatures. "Know this"—the word "O disciples" is to be supplied as the remainder. "That which is luminous, subtler than the subtle, and in which the worlds and the inhabitants of the worlds are established—that is this Imperishable, that is Brahman, that is Prāṇa, that is beyond speech and mind. The meaning is that it is beyond the range of speech and mind.

"O gentle one, know that this is the Truth, this is the Immortal, which is to be pierced. Taking up the bow of the *Ṛgveda*, the arrow of the *Yajurveda*, and the twang of the string of the *Sāmaveda*, let the one of noble vows receive the pure *Atharvaveda*. Having taken up the great bow of the Upaniṣads, he should fix upon it the sharp arrow of the practice of *Hrūpāsana*. Drawing it with a mind absorbed in that state, O gentle one, know that the target is that One Syllable (*ekākṣara*). The *Praṇava* is the bow, the *Ātman* is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be the target."

One who is vigilant must pierce [the target]; becoming one with it, he should be like an arrow. The target is all-pervading, and my arrow faces in every direction. The piercer is all-pervading as well; the target is pierced—of this there is no doubt. Making the self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* (Om) the upper fire-drill, through the practice of churning with meditation, one shall behold the God hidden within.

In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all the vital breaths—know Him alone as the one Self; cast off other words. He is the bridge to immortality. Just as spokes are fixed in the hub of a wheel, so are the channels gathered in Him. He moves within, being born in manifold ways. Meditate upon the Self with the syllable *Om*, for the sake of crossing over to the further shore beyond darkness—"crossing over" meaning reaching the state of liberation (*pārāya*). "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving; whose majesty is on earth..."

In the divine city of Brahman, the Self is established in the sky; consisting of mind, the leader of the body of vital breaths, it is established within the heart-cavity, having entered therein. By the knowledge of that, the wise behold the immortal form of bliss which shines forth. When He is seen—the higher and the lower—the knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and one’s karmas are exhausted. In the supreme golden sheath, there is the stainless, partless Brahman.

That is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know. There, the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. It is only by shining after Him that everything else shines.

Everything shines with its light; all this vibrantly gleams therein. Therein the form of the moon and sun does not shine, nor do the winds blow; how much less other deities? That very God, the creator of beings, himself free from conflict and stainless, shines forth. This which was before is Brahman; Brahman is behind, to the south, and to the north. From there it extends upward; Brahman indeed is all this, the most excellent Brahman.
One should know that the heart is like the calyx of a lotus, hollow and facing downward; it is the great abode of the universe. The Fourth Section.

Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree. Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by his own powerlessness. But when he sees the other, the Lord who is adored, and understands His greatness, he becomes free from sorrow. When the seer beholds the golden-hued Creator, the Lord, the Person whose source is Brahman—

In the same way, the wise man, having shaken off both merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equanimity. This very Prāṇa shines forth through all beings; he who knows this becomes a wise man, not an over-speaker. "Not an over-speaker" means he does not speak many harsh or deceitful words. "He sports in the Self, rejoices in the Self, and is active in spiritual practice; for such a one is the best among those who know Brahman. This Self is to be attained through truth, through austerity, through right knowledge, and through constant celibacy (brahmacarya). For He is indeed the radiant, pure light within the body."

That which ascetics with extinguished defects behold—truth alone conquers, not falsehood. The path of truth is wide and well-trodden, by which the seers, satisfied in their knowledge, attain that supreme treasure of truth. That is the Brahman, divine and of inconceivable form; subtler than the subtle, it shines forth. Farther than the far, yet here near at hand, you see it hidden within the cave of the heart.

It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other senses, nor by austerity or ritual action. But he whose being is purified by the clarity of knowledge beholds Him, the partless, through meditation. This subtle Self is to be known by the mind, in which the vital breath has entered fivefold. By the vital breaths, the entire consciousness of living beings is woven; when that is purified, this Self manifests. "Manifests" means it becomes endowed with omnipresence.

The meaning is that when the Supreme Self is propitiated, one’s knowledge becomes uncontracted. "Whatever world a person of purified being contemplates in his mind and whatever desires he longs for, he conquers that infinite world and those very desires; therefore, one who desires prosperity should worship the Self residing within. — Fifth Section.

"Those wise ones who, free from desire, worship that supreme abode of Dharma—in which the universe is established and shines brilliantly—they transcend this white [state]. 'The white person' is the grammatical connection; 'white' means that which is the material cause of the body, which is white. "He who, thinking upon them, desires objects of desire, is born here and there as a bearer of those desires. But for one whose self is desireless and whose mind is perfected, all desires dissolve away even in this very world."

This Self is not attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. Only he whom this Self chooses is able to attain Him; to him this Self reveals its own form. This Self is not attained by one devoid of strength, nor through negligence, nor even through austerity that lacks the proper mark. The word "austerity" (tapas) here refers to knowledge; the meaning is that it is not attained through knowledge devoid of such marks as the branding of the discus and so forth. "But for the wise man who strives by these means, this Self enters the abode of Brahman."

"By these means"—the meaning is: by the powers of grace (*prasāda*) and the knowledge of the signs (*liṅga*). "Having attained Him, the sages—satisfied with knowledge, perfected in self, free from passion, and tranquil; those wise ones, having reached the omnipresent One everywhere and being disciplined in soul, enter into the All itself. Those who have well-ascertained the meaning through the realization of Vedānta, who are seekers striving in the yoga of renunciation and are pure in being—all of them, at the time of their final end, are liberated into the supreme immortality in the world of Brahman. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6)

The fifteen parts that have their foundation, and all the gods within their respective deities, as well as actions and the self consisting of consciousness—all these become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman]. Just as rivers flowing toward the ocean disappear into it, casting off name and form, even so the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high. Whoever truly knows this Brahman becomes Brahman itself; in his lineage, no one shall be without knowledge of Brahman.

He crosses over sorrow; he crosses over evil; freed from the knots of the heart, he becomes immortal. Regarding this, there is this verse: "Those who perform their duties, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), who are firmly established in Brahman, who themselves offer oblations with faith to the Single Seer—only to them should one impart this knowledge of Brahman, provided they have duly performed the vow of wearing the turban upon the head. This truth was proclaimed by the seer Aṅgiras: one who has not observed the vow does not study this; neither does one who has not purified himself, nor one who is not a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*). Homage to the supreme seers! Homage to the supreme seers! The Sixth Section.

But what is the authority here for the view that the word ending in *tṛc* has the sense of "deserving" (*arha*)? For, by the rule "the suffix *tṛc* [is used] after a root," it is possible only for *tṛc*; furthermore, since that suffix rests upon a permanent direct perception (*nityasākṣātkāra*), it is improper to assign it the sense of "deserving" according to the rule "the *kṛtya* suffixes and *tṛc* are used in the sense of 'deserving'. Even if it were to have the sense of "deserving," there would be no contradiction between its sense of "deserving" and the sense of "having come to be" (*bhūta*) in the word *adṛṣṭa*, because the suffix *ṇini*—prescribed by the rule "suffixes [denote time] in connection with a verbal root"—functions here in the sense of "having come to be."

If it is argued that—since the term *agniṣṭomayājī* means "one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma," and because the future tense (*bhavitṛ*) required by the suffix *lyuṭ* cannot apply to that which has already occurred—the adoption of a future sense for *agniṣṭomayājī* is not contradictory due to the rule *dhātusambandhe pratyayāḥ*; yet here there is no such evidence—then it is replied:

In accordance with such Smṛti passages as, "I know them all, but no one knows me," which mean that while remaining invisible to others, He perceives others; and since the term *adṛṣṭa* signifies invisibility, and since invisibility was established in the previous section concerning Brahman, how [can this objection stand] by relying on the word *adṛśyatva* (invisibility)?

The sense is that this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The meaning is that it does not serve as an exclusion of the non-conscious (*acid-vyāvartakatva*); on the contrary, the meaning is that it actually establishes the non-conscious. As for the example "the conscious one" (*cetana*), the sense is that the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*) is indeed conscious. Regarding the phrase "connected with the negative particle" (*nañ-upaśliṣṭa*), the sense is based on the maxim: "When joined with the negative particle, the understanding proceeds toward something else similar [to what is negated]," because the words *nañ* and *iva* function with a single meaning. Furthermore, this should be understood as referring to the position that accepts a distinction between the material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeya-bheda*).

Since similarity is inherently grounded in difference, he says, “not like the unwise and not lean,” having accepted the distinction between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*). Now, although one might resort to the Pradhāna as the referent—by setting aside the view that the passage beginning with “that which is invisible” refers to the Supreme Self on the grounds of the natural emphasis on denying physical similarity and the need for consistency with the examples of conscious beings—we do not see any authority for abandoning the status of the Supreme Self based on the statement “higher than the high Imperishable. On the contrary, [the opposite is true] in accordance with such scriptural passages as, “He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving.”

Furthermore, anticipating the objection that—following the designation of this as *brāhṛ-vidyā*—it might be intended to refer to the Supreme Self just as in the first prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of others, [the author] replies: Just as it is stated that, by virtue of the natural force of the negation, it is that very substance itself in another state that is being grasped, so too, because the mantra "The divine, formless Person" is seen to negate form and the possession of mind and vital breath (which are well-known of the individual soul), it is appropriate that it is that very soul in another state that is being grasped.

Therefore, intending to show that even omniscience and other such qualities can be attributed to the *jīva* alone with reference to its state of liberation, he says: "having relied upon the establishment of [the *jīva*] as the primary subject. Now, one might object: is it not improper to advance the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the *pradhāna* is the subject of the passage beginning "That which is invisible" (*yattadadreśyam*), by relying on the natural force of the negation?

"Since there is an abundance of negations of well-known attributes such as lineage (*gotra*) regarding the individual soul (*jīva*)—as in the passage, 'It is without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, and it is without hands or feet'—why might that sentence also, like the second position favored by the opponent, have the individual soul as its subject? Otherwise, [consider the following]: 'Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable is attained—that which is unseen, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, extremely subtle, and imperishable; that which the wise behold as the source of all beings.'"

The passage ending thus refers to the Pradhāna (primordial matter). The subsequent passages—"There is nothing higher than which there is another," "There is none smaller or greater than He," and "Like a tree, He stands alone, firm in heaven; by that Puruṣa all this is filled"—refer to the Jīva (the individual soul). The subsequent passages—"As a spider emits and withdraws [its thread]," "As plants grow from the earth," and "As hair grows from a living man, so does the universe arise here from the Imperishable"—refer to the Pradhāna. [And it is said: "By austerity, the Brahman is built up."

"From that, food is produced; from food, life-breath, mind, truth, the worlds, and immortality in the works. Beginning thus, [the text continues]: "Having examined the worlds acquired through action, the knower of Brahman (brāhmaṇa) should attain detachment, realizing that 'there is nothing uncreated by means of the created. For the sake of knowing That, he should approach a Guru alone, with fuel in hand—a learned (śrotriya) knower of Brahman who is established in Brahman. To him, who has approached properly, whose mind is perfectly tranquil, and who is endowed with self-control, that wise teacher [should speak]."

"He who knows that Imperishable Person as the Truth—He truly taught that knowledge of Brahman. The subsequent passage beginning with this refers to the individual soul (*jīva*). Then, "This is the Truth: just as from a well-kindled fire sparks of similar form fly forth in thousands, even so, O gentle one, various beings are born from the Imperishable, and into it they also merge"—this refers to *pradhāna* (primordial matter). [And: "The divine, formless Person, who is both within and without all beings..."

If it is argued that how could this—"Breathless, without mind, pure, beyond the imperishable, higher than the high"—enter the hearts of the wise as referring to the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (paramātman) respectively? We say: no.

The sense is this: according to the principle of the section [in Mīmāṃsā] stating, "He who has a purposeful connection with someone, even if that person is far away, is connected with him," mere proximity is not the determining factor; rather, because a connection is possible even with one who is distant through the force of fitness (*yogyatā*), it must necessarily be accepted—despite the inversion between the primary subject and the living being—that the Pradhāna is what is to be propounded. To the question, "How can there be an analogy with a conscious being? he replies: the phrase "the Pradhāna is what is to be propounded" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Thus, the examples cited in the Bhāṣya are intended for that [point].

The word "iti" here signifies the reason; the meaning is that since the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) brings forth [the world] when presided over by the *puruṣa* (spirit), examples consisting of both conscious and unconscious entities are presented. Now, one might object: "But surely the previous position (*pūrva-pakṣa*), which relies on the Sāṅkhya doctrine, maintains that it is the *pradhāna* and the *jīva* that are being expounded here; and in the Sāṅkhya system, the *puruṣa* assists merely by its proximity, not by acting as a presiding controller. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that because there exist corresponding examples, the *pradhāna* undergoes transformation when presided over by the *puruṣa*.

Intending to show that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) may proceed by relying on some such view as that "it transforms merely through the proximity of the Puruṣa," he says: "even in the absence of superintendence" (*anadhiṣṭhitatvepi*). He concludes the prima facie argument with: "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Immediately after the word *iti*, the reading *adṛśyatve ti* is seen in the manuscripts regarding the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*); although its purpose is slight, it should be understood as being for the sake of the students' proficiency. Now, one might ask: how can there be omniscience for a soul that possesses preeminent merit while in a state of bondage? To this he says: "characterized by that state. This means characterized by merit. [This applies] to the eternally liberated one whose lineage and caste...

It should be understood that because there is no inherent force in the prohibition, it was stated that [the one] liberated is characterized by merit (*puṇya*). The intention is that there is no dispute even on the part of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) regarding the point that [the term] refers to the *akṣara* under discussion. And by the phrase "and because of the recognition of causality," the recognition of the previously introduced ablative form in the passage "so from the *akṣara* the universe arises here" is conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*). The intention is that since there would be prolixity (*gaurava*) in enjoining its causality as well after merely restating it, [it is not so enjoined].

Is it not so that identity [of the two] is accepted on the basis of the recognition of the characteristic mark of being the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), as well as the recognition of the causality of that which is set forth by the passage, "Now, the higher [knowledge], by which that Imperishable is attained," and that which is indicated by, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge; from Him..."? Rather than postulating a difference between the Imperishable that is the source of beings and the one indicated by the word *akṣara* in the ablative case in the phrase "higher than the high Imperishable," [one should accept identity] based on the passage, "Now, the higher [knowledge]... and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: it is more appropriate that the "syllable" (akṣara) understood from the statement "That syllable" (tadakṣaram) is identical with the Pradhāna indicated by the word "akṣara" in the ablative case in the phrase "higher than the high akṣara" (akṣarātparataḥ paraḥ), because the term "akṣara" is recognized as recurring in both instances. Consequently, the attribution of omniscience and other qualities to that Pradhāna is untenable.

The point is this: although the quality of being the source of beings (*bhūtayonitva*) is not explicitly heard in the passage "by whom the Imperishable Person [is reached]," nevertheless, because the unity of meaning between the passage "by whom the Imperishable Person... and the passage "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge; from Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food" is accepted by both sides, the recognition based on the term "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) as being assisted by the mark of being the source of beings is powerful. This is the intended meaning.

"Because that which arises first is more powerful"—by this, it should be understood that the claim that these [scriptural passages], such as "thus from the Imperishable the universe arises here," "thus, O gentle one, various beings arise from the Imperishable," and "higher than the Imperishable is the Supreme," share a single referent due to their common form as words ending in the ablative case, is also refuted. The sense is that because of its nature as *puruṣa* (the Person), being conscious, the capacity for omniscience is possible.

The phrase "the meaning is that it is designated [as such]" is followed by the statement, "In this regard, he states the reason: 'because it has been introduced as having the qualities of invisibility and so forth,'" which has been omitted from the text. Therefore, there is no room for the suspicion that the citations of the *pratīkas* follow a different sequence than the original; rather, it should be understood that, in accordance with the subsequent text, it is precisely that [quality of having invisibility and so forth] which is appropriately made the reason, since the subject has been introduced as possessing those qualities. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and because it is denotable by the word *puruṣa*," this does not apply to the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).

It should be understood that it is incorrect to claim that passages such as "By him this whole [world] is filled with the Puruṣa" refer to the Imperishable (akṣara) which is the source of beings (bhūtayoni); rather, one must say that their intended meaning is that they refer to the individual soul (jīva) denoted by the word *puruṣa*. This is because, in the verse "Than whom there is nothing higher," the word *puruṣa* must be understood as referring to the previously mentioned Imperishable which is the source of beings, based on the force of the relative pronoun (*yat*) and other indicators. Furthermore, in the verse "By whom one knows the true Imperishable Puruṣa," the term *puruṣa* must be interpreted in accordance with the word *akṣara* heard at the beginning of the context; thus, it must be maintained that both passages have the same subject matter.

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), regarding the phrase "the subject under discussion, characterized by qualities such as invisibility," he explains it—intending that the meaning of "subject under discussion" (*prakṛta*) is its being the primary topic of exposition—as "the Imperishable (*akṣara*) itself, characterized by qualities such as invisibility. The thought is that one must accept [the opponent's position] that it is spoken of as being "higher than the high" (*parataḥ paraḥ*), because it would be impossible to speak of that which is not the primary topic of exposition as being higher than that which is the primary topic of exposition. Furthermore, the observation that the two words "Brahman" (*brāhma*) have different referents is made clear later in the *bhāṣya* itself.

The meaning is that this is because of the natural force of the indication by identical case endings; that is, it applies to both members of the two-word phrase, "beyond the syllable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*). It is because [the word *para*] depends upon a word ending in the ablative case; for this very reason, one should observe that in expressions such as "Devadatta’s son" (*devadattaputra*), there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), since the word "son" depends upon a word ending in the genitive case.

The meaning is that *parāvidyā* (higher knowledge) refers to knowledge whose object is Brahman, but its sense is not "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) as it is in the scriptural passage, "Now, the higher [knowledge]... The commentary states that it was obtained by Aṅgiras through the lineage of teachers; here, the scriptural text beginning with "Brahmā was the first among the gods" should be reflected upon. He describes the method of explanation there with the words "by some," stating the view of the proponents of illusion (*mṛṣāvādin*).

The point is that Śaṅkara has explained it thus in the *Muṇḍaka-bhāṣya*: "By some [it is said] that the knowledge of action is the lower [knowledge], and the other [is] regarding the means and fruits of dharma. "The knowledge of the lower self" (*aparamātmajñāna*) means the knowledge of the individual soul (*jīva*). By the statement found here—"Not by intellect, nor by much learning"—the meaning is that even meditation, which is denoted by the word "intellect" (*medhā*), is understood to be fruitless.

Regarding the phrase "supported by the sevenfold means beginning with discrimination" (*vivekādisādhanasaptakānugṛhīta*), since the sevenfold means themselves do not constitute a constituent part of the knowledge produced by scripture, the author—intending that "supported" (*anugṛhīta*) here means "assisted" (*sahakṛta*)—states: "the sevenfold means and the knowledge born of the scriptures. Regarding the word "arisen" (*utthita*), he explains that it is the word "arisen" that is to be supplied as the ellipsis in the verse: "born of scripture and from discrimination" (*āgamotthaṃ vivekācca*).

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "by the sentence beginning with 'tatra'," the word *tatra* found in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) does not belong to the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*), but rather belongs to the scripture (*śruti*). For the scripture says: "It is both higher and lower; there, the lower is the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda... and so forth. As for the statement "it has been made clear," this was indicated in the commentary by the word *veda* in the passage "because the Veda is the cause of the arising of knowledge. One should understand that the doubt as to whether, by that [word], the verbal nature of the cognition derived from scripture (*āgama*) is implied here has already been refuted within the commentary itself.

The phrase "immortality is dependent on karma" implies "the worlds," as is understood from the context; the meaning is that karma is the means for attaining immortality. Here too, the sense is that it is the means for attaining both heaven and immortality, in accordance with the Bhāṣya which mentions "heaven and liberation" (svargāpavarga). Thus, the intended connection of the Śruti is that both the worlds and immortality are dependent on karma. Alternatively, the meaning is that the word *anna* is explained by the term *bhogya* (that which is to be enjoyed); the sense is "for the sake of being desirable" or "for the sake of being an object of longing. Regarding the term *anāgrayaṇa*, [it refers to] the *āgrayaṇa* [sacrifice].

This refers to a specific sacrifice to be performed in autumn. "Not offered" (*ahuta*) means not offered at its proper time. It concerns actions that accomplish the three aims of life (*trivarga*); this should be understood as follows: since the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the *Āgrayaṇa*, the *Vaiśvadeva*, and the honoring of guests are obligatory and must be performed according to one's capacity even within the context of rites for liberation (*apavarga*), there is no fault in being intent upon them [provided they are performed with the right attitude]. "Desiring the fruit of action" (*karmaphalābhisandhimat*) means that the inferiority of an action consists precisely in its being characterized by a desire for its fruit.

And this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood as referring to the fact that [action] is not preceded by knowledge (*jñānāpūrvakatva*). The phrase "those who rejoice" means "those who do not rejoice. Consequently, the meaning is that those who perform actions with an attachment to results (*phalābhisandhi*) and those who rejoice in such [actions] are subject to old age and death. Therefore, regarding the passage ending with "all herbs," [it says]: "From Him are born the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and all the senses; from His feet comes the earth—He is the inner self (*antarātman*) of all beings; from Him come fire, the sacrificial fuel, and the sun."

"Therefore from Him came the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the Yajus-formulas; from Him the *dīkṣā* [initiatory rite]; and from Him the gods were produced in many ways. From Him the seven vital breaths (*prāṇas*) proceed; from Him all oceans and mountains; and from Him all herbs and juices. This is the meaning, by means of the words "that" (*tat*) and "this" (*etad*) occurring in that context. An ellipsis must be supplied: "having established in detail the state of being the source of beings (*bhūtayonitva*), which immediately follows the reference made by the words 'that' and 'this'."

One might object: "Is it not inconsistent that the Bhāṣya describes the nature of devotion (*bhakti*)—which consists of the meditations taught in the sixth section—as being prior to the fruit of the experience of Brahman characterized by identity with Brahman, which is taught in the fifth section? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*). It has been stated that this [devotion] occurs sequentially in the passage beginning, "Those who have well-ascertained the meaning through the knowledge of Vedānta" (*vedāntavijñānasuniścitārthāḥ*). Those who possess certainty regarding the meaning of Vedānta, who are endowed with the yoga of renunciation of ritual action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*), and whose internal organs are purified—they, at the time of the supreme end, that is, at the conclusion of the body, become "supremely immortal" (*parāmṛtāḥ*), meaning they attain the supreme immortality that is Brahman.

The meaning is that those for whom [the Self] exists as their very essence are "supremely immortal" (parāmṛta), being indeed liberated while living (jīvanmukta). They are released within the worlds of Brahman (brāhṛlokeṣu); the meaning is that they attain liberation (nirvṛti) like the space within a broken jar. Thus, the sense is that the sequence of liberation while living and supreme liberation has been described in Śaṅkara’s *Muṇḍaka-bhāṣya*. The phrase "of the all-pervading Brahman" means "of Brahman," and not "of a universal void."

The phrase "it will be stated that [the soul] is taught to attain the state of Brahman" refers to the section [of the *Brahma-sūtras*] beginning with "Bādari [holds that the soul goes] to the effected [Brahman], because that is logically possible for it" (*kāryaṃ bādarirasya gatyupapatteḥ*). One should not say that this need not be stated because [the soul's existence] is established as being like other sentient beings; rather, it should be understood that this is intended to demonstrate that in the state of liberation there is no dissolution [into Brahman], but rather that the sense organs of that [soul] also persist until the final dissolution (*pralaya*).

[The opponent objects: "Because there is no attainment of identity with the Supreme Self. Now, regarding the mantra, "The fifteen parts have returned to their foundations," the meaning is that at the time of liberation, those parts (*kalā*) which constitute the body—consisting of the ten organs and the five elements—return to their respective foundations, that is, they reach their own respective causes. And as for the deities residing in the body and established in the instruments such as the eyes, they go to [the presiding deities] such as Āditya.

In the *Muṇḍaka-bhāṣya*, Śaṅkara explains the meaning as follows: "The actions, the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), and the actions whose fruits have not yet been experienced—the individual soul (*jīva*) characterized by the limiting adjunct of consciousness—attain non-distinction within the Supreme Brahman. This is indeed the case; however, it does not mean that the liberated [soul] has abandoned [its identity] or that there is an actual oneness of the body and so forth with the Supreme Self. This is true.

In the *Taittirīya-Āraṇyaka*, the subsequent passage from the *Aharahar* section—"Just so, these sixteen parts of this seer, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and vanish"—is cited by those who maintain that the Supreme Brahman is the object of knowledge. Having raised the doubt that this concluding statement implies the entire collection of parts merges into Brahman alone, it should be understood that [the text] intends to show that [the soul] is not [merely absorbed]. Rather, it is intended as a conclusion regarding the attainment of similarity with the previously mentioned [state], as indicated by the term "Vaiṣṇavam" (belonging to Viṣṇu).

In the passage, "One who is contending should sacrifice a dwarf; having become Viṣṇu himself, he conquers these worlds," the word *eva* signifies similarity (*sādṛśya*). This is because the *Nighaṇṭu* lexicon records: "The words *sāmi*, *evam*, and *eva* [denote similarity]. This is the intended meaning.

It should not be argued that if the word *brāhman* were taken to refer to the *brāhman*-nature (the Self), there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), because while words denoting the body may extend to the embodied being, words denoting the embodied being do not denote the body. This is incorrect; for by the same logic, it is possible for words denoting the embodied being to denote the inseparably related body, and in the absence of any other recourse, even figurative indication is not a fault.

Regarding the principle "prokṣaṇīṣvarthasaṃyogāt" (in the case of the *prokṣaṇīs*, [the word applies] because of its connection with the purpose): since the application of the word *prokṣaṇī* to water is possible through its very etymological derivation—as that by which one sprinkles (*prokṣyate*) or pours out—it has been stated that a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) need not be postulated there; such is the sense of the phrase "by that principle. On this point, some say:

"Now, how can that which possesses qualities such as invisibility be denoted by the word 'akṣara' (the Imperishable)? For the word 'akṣara' is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*), and conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) overrides etymological derivation (*yoga*). Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: "Or because it pervades (*aśnute*), or because it does not perish (*na kṣarati*)," pointing out that there is no fault here because, according to the principle of the *prokṣaṇī* (sprinkling water), the conventional meaning is absent and the etymological derivation applies commonly to Brahman. This is what they say is the introduction to the commentary (*bhāṣya*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "This too is [an example of] two incorrect meanings," as will be stated later.

The phrase "established as a specific deity" means that this is the intention based on the reading in the *Nighaṇṭu*: "Kṛśānuretās, Sarvajña, Dhūrjaṭi, Nīlalohita. Regarding the two words "akṣara," the repetition [of the word] is not intended here; rather, it should be understood that the three passages—"From the Imperishable (akṣara) the universe arises here," "Thus, O Somya, from the Imperishable arise various beings," and "Higher than the Imperishable is the Highest"—all establish the same single meaning. "Its nature is heard" means that its status as the cause of the phenomenal world of food and so forth is heard in scripture. The same meaning applies to the phrase "its nature" in the subsequent passage as well. "Brāhṛ-vanam" refers to the forest.

The term *adhikaraṇa* (locus) is stated [in the sense of] "That is the Tree" (*tad vṛkṣaḥ*), while the term *upādānatva* (material causality) is expressed by "He stood upon the Brahman, supporting the worlds" (*brahma adhyatiṣṭhad bhuvanāni dhārayan*). Thus is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: since in the Śaiva system the two words ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*) have the same referent, and since the two occurrences of the word *brahman* in the two sentences—"By austerity the Brahman is built up" (*tapasā cīyate brahma*) and "Therefore this is the Brahman" (*tasmād etad brahma*)—also have the same referent, the words *akṣara* and *brahman* cannot possibly refer respectively to cause and effect.

Furthermore, in their view, since the Person denoted by the term "akṣara" is accepted as the material cause of all things but not as an effect, an inquiry into whether [the word] refers to the cause or the effect is not appropriate.

Therefore, even in the passage "From that [Brahman] this [world], name-and-form, and food are born," the origination of that which is denoted by the word *brahman* is not heard; rather, it is stated that this Imperishable (akṣara), the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), undergoes transformation into the form of this *brahman*, food, and so forth. For when it is said, "From the potter the lump of clay becomes a jar," neither the origination of the lump of clay nor its status as the potter's body is understood. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Moreover, by which the Imperishable... and so on.

The meaning is that there is recognition [of the subject] through its qualities of being the source of beings and being imperishable, such as having neither hands nor feet and being formless. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and because of grammatical coreferentiality with the word *tat*," one should not argue: "Why could *sa bāhyābhyantaraḥ* not be a single compound word denoting the combination of 'external' and 'internal'? For if that were the case, since that meaning would already be obtained by the term *bāhyābhyantaraḥ* alone, it would follow that the word *sa* (he/that) is redundant.

The meaning is that the proof of their non-difference [is established] because there is no evidence for a plurality of Puruṣas. The phrase "the word *puruṣa* is not to be interpreted [otherwise]" means that the word *puruṣa* in the passage "The divine, formless Puruṣa" [is not to be so interpreted]. [This refers to] Puruṣa, Nārāyaṇa, and Uttara-nārāyaṇa; thus, [it is] Puruṣa...

Because the *Puruṣasūkta* has the deity [Nārāyaṇa] as its subject and Nārāyaṇa as its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *Puruṣa* is Nārāyaṇa; this should likewise be understood in the case of the "Uttaranārāyaṇa. Regarding the phrase "one who is proficient in the knowledge called Akṣahmadayā," the meaning is "one who is proficient in the knowledge named Akṣahmadayā. Now, it may be objected that the statement in the Commentary—"it is possible only for the Supreme Self, who is the inner self of all beings"—is incorrect, since even the state of being the inner self of all beings belongs to this [individual soul]. Etadvā... [text fragment]

Raising this objection—that since it is more appropriate to state that the possession of all attributes, from being the head of the heaven (*dyu-mūrdhatva*) down to being the inner self of all beings (*sarva-bhūtāntarātmatva*), which are to be propounded by this sentence, can belong only to the Supreme Self—one explains: because in the passage "For He is the earth, the inner self of all beings," the word "for" (*hi*) establishes that being the inner self of all beings is the reason for [His] having the heaven as His head and so forth; thus, the meaning is that the status of being the inner self of all beings—which is to be supported by the attributes such as having the heaven as His head—can belong only to the Supreme Self.
Intending this, he says: "It is spoken of as being connected with the inner self of all beings."

Regarding the phrase "distinguishes from the embodied" (*śārīrāt*), the word "as being of a different nature" (*vilakṣaṇatvena*) must be supplied immediately after "from the embodied. This is because it has been stated by others that the source of beings under discussion is indeed distinguished from the embodied self as being of a different nature; thus, since the embodied self is specified merely as the limit of distinction (*avadhi*), it is not specified as the limit of the act of distinguishing (*viśeṣaṇa-kriyā*). Furthermore, while there might be an expectation [of clarification] when it is said "he distinguishes," such as "by what qualification?"—no such expectation is seen here regarding "from what does he distinguish?"* *Note: The original Sanskrit text likely intends to argue that the term *śārīrāt* functions as an ablative of comparison (indicating difference) rather than an ablative of separation (indicating the object of an action). Thus, one cannot ask "from what [specific quality] does he distinguish? because the context implies a natural ontological distinction.*

Nor should it be asked: "How then is it that the author of the Bhāṣya specifies [the distinction] by stating, 'For he distinguishes the *prakaraṇa* from both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*'?"; for the phrase "from both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*" has the sense of "he excludes [it from]," as it is connected with the subsequent sentence. Nor should it be asked: "How then is the statement in the *Ṭīkā*, 'What [is distinguished] from what'?"; for that too must be understood as having the meaning, "What does it exclude, and from what?"

The point is that the statement "the individual soul (jīva) is indeed higher than the Imperishable" is more appropriate as a construction involving different grammatical subjects (vaiyadhikaraṇya), rather than as a construction involving grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the phrase "higher than the Imperishable," as has been established previously. Now, regarding the phrase "by the word 'dharma,'" the meaning is "by the word 'dharma' [in the sūtra] *adṛśyatvādiguṇako dharmokteḥ*."

Based on the mantra "From this [Brahman] is born Prāṇa," and by connecting it with the action [of the preceding context], others have proposed an alternative interpretation: that the mantra "Agni is his head" intends to convey that Hiraṇyagarbha, whose body is the three worlds, is born from the Imperishable Source of Beings (*bhūtayoni*); and that the Sūtra "Because of the presentation of form" refers to the presentation of the characteristic mark of omniscience in the passage "The Person alone is all this. Having restated that, he refutes it with the words "And because of the presentation of form."

"By virtue of the context" (prakaraṇavaśāt) means by virtue of proximity (sannidhivaśāt). This means that because proximity is weaker than context, it belongs to the intermediate context (avāntaraprakaraṇa). Consequently, this is indeed the context of the Source of the Universe (viśvayoni), while the proximity belongs to those things being born; and since context is stronger than proximity [it pertains to the former]. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that, without the need for supplying the word 'was born' (ajāyata), the description of the form belongs to the Source of the Universe itself, which is the subject of the context? No; [this is not so].

Furthermore, the consistency with Vācaspati’s position is established by the fact that there is a contradiction between the subject of the discussion—the [Self] devoid of body and senses—and its possessing a physical form. Moreover, there is no conflict with the doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas regarding Brahman. In this regard, the following should be noted:

In our view, as in the Bhaṭṭa school, there is no such thing as a twofold division of context (*prakaraṇa*) based on a distinction between primary and intermediate contexts; rather, there is merely the proximity of a matter denoted by the term "intermediate context. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the status of the *abhikramaṇa* (stepping forward) as an auxiliary to the *prayāja* offerings would not be established; for its establishment is possible according to the method of the Guru school (Prabhākara). Thus ends the section concerning the qualities of invisibility and so forth (*adṛśyatvādiguṇakādhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is that this is because of the scriptural statement in the *Agnirahasya*—which belongs to the same section as the *Vājasaneyi*: "The venerable one indeed knows Vaiśvānara thoroughly; tell us that. The opening with the word "Agni" should be seen in the commentaries (*kośa*). He demonstrates the usage in all three [texts] in sequence, beginning with "Higher than the high Imperishable" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*). The term "Hara" means the individual soul (*jīva*).

Regarding the principle that "when a word from an injunction [is used] in a mantra, it denotes the entity [itself]," it is heard in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "The cake on eight potsherds is for Agni. Furthermore, there are many designations for Agni, such as "Agni is the pure one, the purifier," and so forth. In this regard, concerning the *nigadas* (recitations) beginning with *svāhākāra* and *uktham*, there arises the doubt: should the naming be performed by any word whatsoever denoting Agni, or only by the word "Agni" found in the injunction? In this matter, the purpose of the injunction is merely this: that the deity must be addressed by the meaning of the word "Agni."

Since the status of being a deity belongs to that which is indicated by the word, the utterance of the word necessarily follows at the time of performance; yet there is no authoritative means of proof (*pramāṇa*) for restricting that [utterance]. Even if the deityhood of Agni, as enjoined by the scriptural injunction (*codanā*), is accomplished when he is indicated by the word *pāvaka*, it follows that there is no restriction regarding the use of the specific word. Having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the siddhāntin replies]: "In this case, a person must necessarily be enjoined to the utterance of the word itself, because the utterance of the word alone constitutes the human activity (*puruṣavyāpāra*)."

Consequently, it is the form of the word itself that is enjoined as being connected with the act of utterance; and when that is enjoined, the deity-status of the object is merely restated as something already established, since the word by which the oblation is offered is [the deity].

The deity belongs to that [specific] meaning; therefore, since only the utterance of the word itself is enjoined, there is no possibility of synonyms, and thus there is an exclusion (*bādha*) of synonymous terms. This was established in the section on the definition of exclusion (*bādhalakṣaṇa*), under the heading: "If the word of the injunction were a mantra, there would be exclusion because of that injunction. Just as there is no loss of the authority established in the first chapter even when there is a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the lack of restriction to specific words, so too here, even when there is a prima facie argument regarding the lack of restriction to the specific meaning of the word *vaiśvānara*, there is no such loss.

The meaning is that there is a loss of the established authority [of the scripture]. This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood as including the raising of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in cases such as "Or the goat [is the animal], because of the wording of the mantra" (*chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*). On this point, some say: in the prima facie argument of that [other] section, there is neither a failure to determine the meaning of the word nor a failure to determine the meaning of the sentence; however, here, since the word *vaiśvānara* is not determined, the sentence containing it becomes a source of doubt, and thus there is indeed a loss of the established authority.

For this very reason, it was stated that when the meanings of the words *pika*, *yava*, *varāha*, and *vetasa* are not determined, the injunction (*codanā*) composed of them lacks authority. For this same reason, in the section concerning the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha-naya*), when there is a doubt as to whether the object is enjoined as the content by the nominal suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*) or by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was formulated precisely as one characterized by non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*).

Regarding this, one might suspect that if invalidity were the issue, this inquiry should have occurred precisely in the chapter on the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇādhyāya*). Anticipating this, it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa* that it is appropriate to consider it right here as an incidental introduction (*upoddhāta*), because an incidental introduction is more powerful than a direct connection (*sākṣātsaṅgati*). Consequently, they argue that just as in the sections concerning those desiring heaven (*svargakāmādyadhikaraṇa*) there is an objection to well-established validity, so too here the opponent’s objection to validity does not constitute a fault.

"By way of grammatical coreferentiality with the word 'Agni'" means by way of the coreferentiality established in such passages as: "This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the person; he who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara as a person, person-shaped... and so forth. Because the word *vaiśvānara* is common to three possibilities—namely, the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), the third element (fire), and its presiding deity—and because the word *ātman* is common to two possibilities—the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—there arises a fivefold doubt.

Having thus described [the opponent's position], he refutes it with the words "even though the word 'Self' (ātman) exists as common to both the individual soul and the Supreme," and so forth. The explanation of the term "fire" (agni) is "the third of the great elements. Although the entire third element is not the meaning of the word "fire," its meaning is nevertheless the general property of burning; the sense is that it refers neither to a deity nor to a specific digestive fire (jāṭharāgni). Regarding the phrase "the banner, the sun": since the designation "day" occurs upon the rising of the sun, the sense is that it possesses the character of a "banner" (ketu), meaning a sign or indicator.

The meaning is: "May he have a beautiful mind directed toward us, [thinking], 'May we become objects of that [mind]'; for since a connection with the intellect (*mati*) is impossible in the past passive participle (*bhūtatṛtīyā*) when applied to an insentient object—whether it be the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) or anything else—the intention is that one must resort to the deity as the referent. As for *hikam*, it is understood that it exists as a well-known indeclinable (*avyaya*)."

Although it is naturally understood that the *bhāṣya* statement "it is qualified, therefore it is a *viśeṣa*" is an explanation of the meaning of the suffix as having the sense of the object (*karman*), nevertheless—since the word *viśeṣa* in the sūtra "from a common term and a particular term" (*sādhāraṇaśabdaviśeṣāt*) would have to be taken as a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the common term itself is the particular"—and since in a *karmadhāraya* the word *viśeṣa* ought to appear first, its subsequent mention is inappropriate; therefore, for the sake of conforming to the natural sense of the sūtra, [the word *viśeṣa*]...

He explains that the *Bhāṣya* statement, "it is qualified," is intended to explain the objecthood (*karmatva*) which constitutes the meaning of the genitive case in the word "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), by taking it to mean "having the sense of being an action" (*bhāvārthatva*); this he does with the words beginning "this is not [the case] for a specific term."

One might object: "If 'viśeṣyate' (it is qualified) does not take the form of an explanation of the word 'viśeṣa' (particularity), then the separate word 'viśeṣa' would be syntactically unconnected. Anticipating this doubt, he states, "The word 'viśeṣa' is a *kṛdanta* [primary derivative] word," explaining that it should be understood by supplying [the word] as the cause for a genitive case expressing the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*). Intending to show that the location of the ellipsis is flexible and that the relationship between qualifier and qualified is a matter of choice, he offers an alternative explanation in accordance with the natural sense of the *Bhāṣya*, beginning with "Or rather, it is qualified... and so forth.

Because the descriptions of specific fruits and so forth do not constitute attributes of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), he says "indicative mark" (*liṅga*) as the primary referent. The intention is that even for one who does not primarily focus on that [Self], its status as an indicative mark is still established. Now, if the word *viśeṣa* were taken as common to both [the Self] and ritual action (*karman*), how could the meaning "because of being qualified" be obtained without resorting to the view that it emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*)? To this, he says: "the resultant meaning. In the commentary, the phrase "Aupamanyava and others" refers to...

Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, Janaka Śārkarākṣya, and Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi—these five, whose names begin with Prācīnaśāla and so forth, were great householders (*mahāśālā*) and great Vedic scholars (*mahāśrotriya*). Having come together, they deliberated: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? Thus they resolved to investigate. [Note: *Mahāśālā* means those who possess extensive halls; the sense is that they were prosperous and well-endowed. "Who is our Self? What is Brahman?"—thus they set about their inquiry.

The meaning is that they reached a certainty. "O venerable sirs, this Uddālaka Āruṇi is currently studying the Vaiśvānara Self; come, let us go to him. So they went to him. He prepared himself [for them], thinking: "These great householders and great Vedic scholars will question me; I shall not be able to provide a complete answer to them all; I am not capable of explaining everything. Come, let me instruct another instead. He then said to them: (Note: The provided text contains a portion of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, 5.11–12.)

"Venerable sirs, this Aśvapati Kekaya is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self; let us go to him. So they went to him. When they had arrived, he caused separate sacrificial fires to be prepared for each of them. Then, as he was rising in the morning, he said: "In my realm there is no thief, no miser, no drunkard; no one who has not established the sacred fires, no one who is ignorant, and no unchaste man—how then could there be an unchaste woman?"

"Venerable sirs, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice; as much wealth as I shall give to each individual officiating priest, so much will I give to the venerable ones. May the venerable sirs stay. They said, "A person should speak of that very purpose for which he acts; one should state the specific objective toward which a person proceeds. You are currently studying this very Self, Vaiśvānara; tell us about that."

He said to them, "I shall answer you in the morning. With fuel in their hands, they returned in the forenoon. Without even initiating the formal initiation (*upanayana*), he spoke this to them: "Since these great householders (*mahāśāla*) and great Vedic scholars (*mahāśrotriya*), though being Brāhmaṇas, have abandoned the pride of being great householders and approached the king—who is inferior by birth—with humility and with fuel-bundles in hand for the sake of knowledge, so too should others who desire to acquire knowledge act; knowledge must be given only to those who are worthy. This is the meaning conveyed through this narrative."

It is indicated that "the specification of the particular fruit" means the instruction regarding two fruits: the experience [of all worlds] and the burning away of all sins, which arise from being the substratum of all worlds and so forth. Others have stated that the conceptualization of being the support of heaven, earth, and so on is possible only in Brahman, which pervades all modifications; he refutes that with the words "being the support of heaven, earth, and so on."

The term *liṅga* (mark) is understood as it is used in the sūtra beginning with *śrutiliṅgavākyaprakaraṇasthānasamākhyānāṃ samavāye pāradaurbalyam*, and not in the sense of a "mark" consisting of an attribute unique to that [entity], as in the case of the sūtra *ākāśastalliṅgāt*. This is because the nature of the entity as it is remembered lacks attributes unique to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), and thus it would be improper to describe it as a "mark" for establishing the status of the Supreme Person. Therefore, the intention is that the word *liṅga* here refers to a "cognizer" (*jñāpaka*). Although in the sūtra on *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth, *liṅga* is defined as "capacity" (*sāmarthya*), and that is indeed categorized as being either residing in the word or residing in the meaning.

Nevertheless, the sense is that even this [definition] does not exceed what is indicated by the [authoritative] source (*jñāpaka*). Alternatively, it should be understood that the mention of *śruti*, *liṅga*, and *vākya* is for the purpose of describing their essential nature (*svarūpa*). Having raised the objection that there is a redundancy between the commentary beginning with "In this way, 'earth'... and the commentary beginning with "the sky, etc. which sets forth the meaning of the Sūtra, he resolves it through the connection or non-connection with the word *iti*, stating: "It is connected with the meaning of the word *iti*. [He then quotes] the commentary: "For it is so... (*tathā hi*).

"Aupamanyava, upon what self do you meditate? "On heaven alone, O Venerable King," he replied. [The King said: "This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self, the One of Excellent Splendor (sutejas). Since you meditate on this Self, therefore, pressed Soma (suta), further-pressed Soma (prasuta), and extracted Soma (āsuta) are seen in your lineage. By the words *suta*, *prasuta*, and *āsuta*, the performance of the *ekāha*, *ahīna*, and *sattra* sacrifices is indicated."

"He eats food and sees what is dear; he eats food and sees what is dear, and there is Vedic splendor (*brāhmarcasam*) in his family—he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self. 'This, however, is only the head of the Self,' he said. 'Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me.

Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi, 'Prācīnayogya, upon which Self do you meditate? 'The sun alone, O venerable King,' he replied. 'This indeed is the all-formed (*viśvarūpa*) Vaiśvānara Self. You meditate upon this Self; therefore, many all-formed things are seen in your family.'"

"One who sets out on a chariot drawn by mules will see what is desirable, and one who gives food will see what is desirable; he who venerates this very Self as Vaiśvānara finds that what is desirable becomes his, and there is Vedic splendor in his family. 'But this is only the eye of the Self,' he said, 'you would have become blind had you not come to me.'"

Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: "O Vaiyāghrapadya, upon which Self do you meditate? He replied, "Venerable King, I meditate upon Vāyu alone. [The teacher said: "This Vaiśvānara, indeed, is the one whose paths are manifold; this is the Self upon which you meditate. Therefore, offerings come to you from various directions, and rows of chariots follow you in various directions."

"You eat food; you see what is dear. He eats food and sees what is dear; he becomes one who possesses this abundance of *brahmacarya* who meditates upon this very Self as Vaiśvānara. "But this is only the breath (*prāṇa*) of the Self," he said. "Your breath would have departed had you not come to me. Then he said to Jana Śārkarākṣya: "Upon which Self do you meditate? "Space alone, O Venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is the manifold Self, Vaiśvānara. You meditate upon that Self; therefore, you are manifold in offspring and in wealth."

"One who eats food sees what is dear; one who eats food sees what is dear, and there arises in his family spiritual luster (*brāhmarcasam*), he who thus meditates on Vaiśvānara as such. "But this is only the trunk of the Self," he said. "Your trunk would have perished had you not come to me. Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi Vaiyyāghrapadya: "On which Self do you meditate?"

"Water indeed, O venerable King," he said. "This is the Vaiśvānara Self that is wealth; you worship this Self. Therefore, you are wealthy and prosperous; you eat food and see what is pleasing; you eat food and see what is pleasing. This happens for one who, amidst the distractions of his student-life (*brahmacarya*), worships this Vaiśvānara Self in this way. 'But this,' he said, 'is only the bladder of the Self. Your bladder would have burst had you not come to me.'"

Then he said to Uddālaka Āruṇi, "Gautama, as what Self do you meditate upon? "The earth alone, O Venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self that is the foundation; this is the Self you meditate upon. Therefore, you are firmly established with offspring and cattle; you eat food and see what is pleasing; he eats food and sees what is pleasing, and there is Brahman-splendor in his family who thus meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self. But these two are merely the feet of this Self," he said.

"Your feet would have withered away had you not come to me. He said to them: "Indeed, you all eat food knowing this Self, Vaiśvānara, as if it were separate. But he who meditates upon this very Self, Vaiśvānara, as of the measure of a span and as the pervasive measure, eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head is indeed *sutejas* (of excellent luster), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform), the breath is *pṛthagvartman* (having diverse paths), and the trunk is..."

"Abundance is indeed the bladder; the earth is the feet; the chest is the altar; the body hair is the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); the heart is the *gārhapatya* fire; the mind is the *anvāhāryapacana* fire; and the mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire. Whatever food arrives first, that is to be offered as an oblation. The first oblation he should offer, he should offer with the words: 'Svāhā to Prāṇa! Prāṇa is satisfied,'" and so on, having thus shown the fivefold oblation to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and others, the text continues: "Now, if one who does not know this performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice... Such is the sequence of the Śruti.

The phrase "he asked each one individually" (*ekaikam*) is an adverbial modifier of the verb "asked"; this should be understood similarly in subsequent instances, as well as in passages such as "of those mentioned as objects of meditation one by one. As for the statement "but not the navel," the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "even though it is consistent with the corroborative text (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), 'The sky, indeed, is the navel'. The sense is that since the *Smṛti* stating that Vaiśvānara is "the self-existent" must necessarily have a Vedic basis, the very sentence "Sutejas (the Radiant) is the head" will serve as the source for that *Smṛti*.

Is it not the case that the Atharvaṇa statement, "Agni has the earth as his head" (*agnirmūrdhā*), is capable of satisfying the requirement for a source of the Smṛti passage, "Heaven is his head" (*dyāṃ mūrdhānam*)? For even though "having Agni as his head" is heard there, "having heaven as his head" is not heard. Nor [can it be argued] that, in accordance with the Śruti passage, "That world indeed [is heaven]," the word *agni* [should be understood as heaven].

It cannot be said that the heaven-world (*dyuloka*) possesses the status of being the highest [element], because since the figurative application of the word "fire" (*agni*) is found even in the case of rain-clouds, the earth, and so forth, the meaning cannot be determined by following that usage. Therefore, if it is argued that the Vaiśvānara-vidyā passage itself is the source [of this definition], we say no; for there is the possibility that many other passages—such as "From his head the sky arose, from his feet the earth, and from his ears the quarters"—which have been determined to refer to the Supreme Self, may serve as the source. Thus, the sense is that the Smṛti statement relies solely upon the disputed Vaiśvānara-vidyā.

Regarding the phrase "because of being situated at a distance": since this very same subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) applies to the Vājasaneyaka passage just as it does to the Chāndogya passage, there is no disparity such as "being situated at a distance"; nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated because the Vājasaneyaka was cited as if from an external standpoint in the statement, "And they also study him as a person. In the Bhāṣya, it says, "Agni is heard [there] in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatayā*)."

In the *Vājasaneyaka*, within the *Agnirahasya*, after having explained the Vaiśvānara-vidyā in detail, it is heard [in scripture]: "This very Vaiśvānara is the Puruṣa; he who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara as such—namely, as the Puruṣa-form established within the Puruṣa. Regarding the doubt as to how the intention to indicate that being "established within" is established through its association with the designation by the word "Agni," the author shows that it is because they are taken up in a single sentence, stating: "He who knows this Agni as such... etc.

Regarding the portion of the Sūtra beginning with *śabdādibhyontaḥpratiṣṭhānāt*, other [commentators] have explained it as being concerned with the doubt concerning the triad beginning with the digestive fire (the gastric fire). The author states the reason for the Commentator’s disregard of that [interpretation] and his explanation of that Sūtra-portion as being concerned solely with the doubt regarding the gastric fire, by means of the passage beginning with *śabdādibhya* etc.

Similarly, in the case of *dṛṣṭyupadeśāt*, the word *dṛṣṭi* has been explained by others as referring to the meditation on the Supreme Self within the gastric fire. He raises a doubt as to what the reason is for disregarding that [interpretation], stating: *dṛṣṭiśabdo'tasmin tathātvānusandhāna*.

Although it might be argued that there is no contradiction—just as in the case of the ether and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) superimposed upon the *udgītha* and *prastāva*, which do not contradict the intent of the Sūtras such as "Ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic marks" (*ākāśas talliṅgāt*) and "For this very reason, the vital breath [is Brahman]" (*ata eva prāṇaḥ*), which establish their reference to the Supreme Self—and even in those cases, there is no disagreement regarding their being intended for the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) of that which is contrary [to the literal sense].

Since this has been explicitly stated in the Bhāṣya on the passage, "If [it is] by way of a designation (saṃjñā), that has already been said; however, that [designation] also exists," nevertheless, because there is no other alternative there, even though it might be an injunction for a meditative visualization (dṛṣṭividhi), it is improper to rely upon that here. For this very reason, others also have abandoned the position of it being an injunction for a meditative visualization and stated: "Alternatively, it is the Supreme Lord himself, having the internal fire (jāṭharavaiśvānara) as his limiting adjunct (upādhi), who is taught here as the object to be seen. This is how it should be understood.

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the objection is raised that it is improper to deny that the gastric fire (*jāṭhara*) is being presented by the word "fire" (*agni*) and other such terms, as well as by the indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as the arrangement of the three sacrificial fires (*tretākalpanā*), on the grounds that indicative marks lack the capacity to present [an object]. Anticipating this, the author explains the word "is presented" (*pratipādyate*) as being intended to convey a general cognition common to both words and indicative marks, stating: "the meaning is 'it is made known' (*jñāpyate*)."

One might object: "If words such as *vaiśvānara* refer to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), how can marks such as the 'conception of the three sacrificial fires' (*tretākalpanā*) be directly connected to the Supreme Self? Anticipating this doubt, he says "that" (*tad*). In the commentary, the phrase "moreover" (*kiñca*) indicates that the presentation of two cumulative reasons is established as being rooted in the Sūtra itself. The phrase "and also here" (*api cātra*) is intended to show that [the Supreme Self] is also studied as being denoted by the word *puruṣa*; thus, the meaning of the verb "is studied" (*adhīyate*) is that it is the object of the verbal action of the word.

Because it has been so stated. Having kept in mind the ultimate meaning of the portion of the Sūtra, *puruṣam api cainam adhīyate*—"they recite the word 'puruṣa' for this [Being] as well"—namely, that they employ the word *puruṣa* with high pitch (*tāra*) in the middle of this [text], he says: "but also by virtue of being denoted by the word *puruṣa*. Regarding the phrase "by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) such as perishability," the intended sense is: by the force of the limiting adjunct consisting in the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *kṣara*, as in the passage, "There are two unborn beings (*puruṣau*) in the world, the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*) indeed."

The opponent has argued that because the text states, "He who knows the person as person-shaped, dwelling within the person," it is not the gastric fire (jāṭhara), since it is heard that it possesses both the nature of a person (*puruṣatva*) and the state of dwelling within the person; for it is not merely the state of dwelling within the person that is heard. To refute this, [the author] says: "Precisely for this reason, 'the person'... and so on. This refers to the phrase "of other reasons as well" and "and likewise, because of impossibility."

The sense is that the established distinction—that the phrase "of this" (dityasya) serves to exclude other reasons, while the phrase "and also the person" (puruṣam api ca) serves to exclude [the idea of] internal abiding—is without foundation. The term "of the aggregate" (samuditasya) means "of that which has been triplicated," namely, that which consists of the third of the elements.

Regarding the phrase "without the grammatical coreferentiality with the word *agni*": although the word *agni*, like the word *vaiśvānara*, is indeed common to many meanings—as seen in its usage for the third element (*bhūta*) in "O Agni, for the sake of the entire world" (*viśvasmai agne bhuvanāya*); for the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*) in "This is the Vaiśvānara fire by which this food is cooked"; for the deity in "O Agni, you are the invoker of sacrifices" (*tvam agne yajñānāṃ hotā*); and for the Supreme Self in "He threw [it] into the Vaiśvānara fire within the heart"—nevertheless, the point is that while the etymological meaning is manifested in the word *vaiśvānara*, there is no manifestation of the etymological meaning in the word *agni*.

Regarding the phrase "because it would entail tautology": one should not argue that since the term *vaiśvānara* itself, through an elliptical function (*aparyavasāna-vṛtti*), denotes that which is qualified by fire, the word *agni* might as well be taken as referring to its etymological meaning; for, since the word *agni* occurs earlier in the context as "one should cast [the oblation] into the fire, *vaiśvānara*," there is no possibility of suspecting tautology with respect to *agni*, and thus it is established that *agni* refers to the Supreme Self through an elliptical function. Consequently, it is the subsequently occurring word *vaiśvānara* alone that gives rise to the suspicion of tautology.

The meaning is as follows: "In other passages concerning the Supreme Self" means in those passages devoid of the word *agni*, such as "You are indeed now studying this very Vaiśvānara Self," and so forth. "For the sake of establishing a single motivator" means for the purpose of proving that there is only one motivating factor. It may be asked: why was the word *vaiśvānara* mentioned as an illustration? [The answer is: the etymological nature (*yaugikatva*) of the word *vaiśvānara* was resorted to in order to avoid the charge of redundancy.
