If it is asked, "Since there is no such sublation (bādhaka) regarding the word *agni*, how can there be a derivative sense (*yoga*)," the answer is: No; for the intention of Jaimini is that when a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is impossible, the derivative sense alone is superior, as established in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*. The phrase "even though it is more transparent, because of usage" means that we observe usages such as "the directness of knowledge" (*jñānasya sākṣāttvam*). As for the suffix *-añ* in *bhidā* and so on, or the suffix *-aṇ* derived from a sage's name: the meaning is that the suffix *-añ* is applied for a descendant in the fourth generation (*gotra*), while the suffix *-aṇ* is applied for a descendant in the immediate next generation.

Furthermore, since the suffix *aṇ* derived from the root *ṛṣi* (in the sense of "seer") is superseded by the suffix *añ* following [the word] *bhidā* and others, how can the doubt regarding the application of *ṛṣyaṇ* here be dismissed? As for the phrase "even when it denotes the collective totality of persons (*puruṣasamaṣṭi*)," the meaning is that even though it is the name of the collective person, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is prescribed by the rule "in the case of *nara*, when it is a proper name" (*nare ca saṃjñāyām*). Thus, *vaiśvānara* is simply *viśvānara* with the addition of the suffix *aṇ* according to the rule beginning with *prajñādi*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied because it belongs to the class of words formed by the rule *rākṛtigaṇa*. Regarding the distinction between meditations (*vidyābheda*), although the mere difference in the forms of the object of meditation does not constitute a difference in the meditation—since we observe many non-contradictory forms of the object of meditation, such as "consisting of mind" and "having breath for a body," within the very same Śāṇḍilya-vidyā—nevertheless, in all meditations on the Supreme, qualities such as reality, knowledge, and bliss [are included] according to the principles: "Bliss and so forth belong to the Principal" (*Brahmasūtra* 3.3.11) and "But there is inclusion of the attributes of the Imperishable" (*Brahmasūtra* 3.3.34).

Furthermore, because it is observed that many forms follow [the same entity], there is no contingency of a difference in the Vidyās; nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated only by assuming a contradiction between being the body of Agni and being the leader. Regarding the equality of strength due to the similarity of delay and non-delay: the weakness [of the conventional meaning] is rooted in the recollection of the impossibility of the conventional sense, while the strength [of the etymological meaning] is obtained through a function that does not terminate in the conventional sense; thus, these two are equal.

In this regard, for one who has obtained a meaning through uninterrupted function, the fact that it conforms to the meaning established by primary usage is the cause of its predominance, because in that case the established meaning is not abandoned; however, for the etymological meaning, its very status as the primary sense is the cause of its predominance. Since the etymological meaning is also primary—just like the established meaning—the sense is that they possess equal strength.

If it is argued: "Surely, by asserting that the secondary meaning (yaugika-artha) obtained through the non-termination of the conventional meaning (*rūḍha-artha-aparyavasāna*) is equivalent to the secondary meaning based on convention (*rūḍhi-pūrvaka-lakṣaṇā*), you are effectively admitting that there is *lakṣaṇā* in the meaning obtained through non-termination; this is not a desired conclusion, because in the *Carācara-vyapāśraya-adhikaraṇa*, it was established—following the logic of the *Akṛti-adhikaraṇa*—that the primary sense (*mukhyatva*) indeed resides in the Supreme Self," we reply: [This is not so] because [the secondary meaning] is rooted in the recognition of the impossibility of another primary meaning.

Even though the term *brāhmaṇa* involves a delayed cognition because its meaning is derived etymologically (*yaugika*), it nevertheless possesses the status of being within the scope of a collective denotative power (*samudāyaśakti*). This is in accordance with such authoritative texts as: "The Brahman is the supreme object of all words," and "We bow to that wherein the eternal foundation of all words resides."

It should be understood that the primary meaning (*mukhyārthatva*) is not lost merely by a delay [in cognition], because even in cases such as "the rays of the sun illuminate," the rays and so forth—though their apprehension is delayed—are seen to possess primary meaning. Furthermore, regarding the claim that two optional meanings are enjoined by a single sentence: if the two meanings, namely "having Agni as one's body" and "being a leader," were both enjoined by the same sentence, then—just like the *aruṇā* (red) and *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow)—their simultaneous combination (*samuccaya*) would necessarily follow, making an option (*vikalpa*) impossible; thus, for the proponent of the injunction of two optional meanings...

If it is argued: "Since an option (*vikalpa*) must be accepted precisely by resorting to a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), how can the introduction of a split in the sentence be undesirable? Furthermore, in the view of one who objects that one should abandon the option and accept a difference in the meditations (*vidyābheda*) out of fear of a split in the sentence—because when two meanings are enjoined by a single word 'Agni' through recourse to two modes of signification (*vṛtti*), there arises the contingency of a conflict between those two modes of signification, necessitating the acceptance of a split in the sentence characterized by repetition (*āvṛtti*)—then the fault of the split in the sentence has not been avoided."

It is said: [the opponent argues that] there would either be a difference in the meditations (vidyābheda) due to the injunction being characterized by two qualities—having fire as its body and being the leader—or else, if one were to resort to a syntactical split (vākyabheda) within that very same meditation and accept an option (vikalpa), there would be the fault of optionality corrupted by eight defects as well as the fault of syntactical split; such is the intended meaning here.

The intention of the Sūtra is that [the term] is etymological (*yaugika*). Thus, in the absence of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the etymological meaning alone is superior because it is primary; it is not a secondary or figurative application (*aparyavasāna-vṛtti*), since such a usage lacks primacy in the same way that an etymological meaning does. This is the view of Jaimini, and not that both [conventional and etymological meanings] possess equal force, which would result in either a difference between the meditations (*vidyā-bheda*) or an option (*vikalpa*). This is the sense.

"Thinking that there is no second [purpose]," as stated in the section concerning "those [substances] being twofold, as subordinate and primary," a discussion is raised regarding the injunction "one threshes the rice": are the rice grains for the sake of the threshing, or is the threshing for the sake of the rice? Having considered this, and following the logic of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* (the section on the meaning of verbal roots), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is established by arguing that since a visible purpose—the preparation of the substance—is obtained, the rice grains are for the sake of the threshing, while the threshing itself serves an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose. [Then follows: of the threshing...

It has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that since the purpose of threshing is evident—characterized by the removal of the husk for the sake of the ritual action—it is improper to assume an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), as in the case of sacrifices and the like; therefore, threshing serves the purpose of the rice-grains themselves. Furthermore, since the rice-grains serve the purpose of the sacrifice through the intermediate stages of rice-powder and flour, there is no need to postulate an unseen result anywhere.

In this regard, one might object: "Since the second case ending in the scriptural statement 'one threshes the rice' (vrīhīnavahanti) indicates that threshing is for the sake of the rice, how can the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) arise? Anticipating this, the meaning is that the Pūrvamīmāṃsakas have explained that the prima facie view proceeds by taking it as an established fact that the second case ending is not present.
The sense is: why should it not have the purpose of ascending to awakening, just as in the case of [the qualities] such as having "pleasure as the head"?

Now, one might object that since it would have been sufficient to say simply "it shows the attainment," the specification in the Commentary that "it shows the fruit appropriate for the meditation on the Supreme Self" is without authority. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states here—following the argument previously introduced that the offering to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) is of the nature of propitiating the Supreme Self—that this is the justification for the fact that the perfection of the *agnihotra* has the purpose of propitiating the Supreme Self. Para...

The sense is that the propitiation of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the oblation of breath (*prāṇāhuti*); for the purpose of making that [oblation] an *agnihotra* sacrifice, there is the requirement of the household fire, the domestic fire, and so forth. The sense is that the specific fruit mentioned in the passage beginning with "in all worlds" indicates that the oblation of breath is indeed the propitiation of the Supreme Self. Since everything becomes propitiated—because sacrifice has the purpose of worshipping the gods, and worship is a form of propitiation—[the result follows].

The sense is that since sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*) do not differ significantly from the nature of giving (*dāna*), the root *hu* has "propitiation" as its meaning. It shows the fruit of the worship of others which is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to that [sacrifice]; the purpose of demonstrating the burning away of all sins—which is the fruit of worship—in the *prāṇāgnihotra* is to make known that the *prāṇāgnihotra* is an ancillary to that [worship]. And this is intended to be made clear in the subsequent passage beginning with "And this [is the fruit] of the mere *prāṇāhuti*."

[The head and other parts belong] specifically to the *upāsaka* (worshipper), because in the preceding sentence, "But he who thus [knows]," the *upāsaka* is the subject under discussion; therefore, in the phrase "Of this very one," the pronoun *tasya* must refer to that same person. Furthermore, since in the subsequent sentence, "His chest indeed is the altar, his hairs the sacrificial grass," the chest and other limbs of the worshipper are what must be referred to, [the same applies] in the passage beginning with, "Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head is Sutejas."

Furthermore, it is appropriate that the words "head" and so forth refer to the head and other parts of the worshipper. Nor should it be asked how the designation "of the Self, Vaiśvānara" can be consistent in this case; the point is that the use of terms such as "Vaiśvānara" is justified by the intention to express the non-difference between the object of worship and the worshipper. The phrase "the fruit belongs only to the liberated one" connects with the expression "stated for the purpose of making known."

Although in the passage, “He eats food in all selves,” the aspect of the cessation of the undesirable is not explicitly stated—since only the experience of Brahman is mentioned—nevertheless, intending to show that this [cessation] is included therein, he says, “included in the fruit. Regarding the phrase “of that which has the status of a subordinate member as understood from the sentence”: although the relationship of principal and subordinate is not established by this particular sentence, the intention is that its purpose is achieved through the implication (*anukarṣa*) of the words “Of this very one” (*tasya ha vā etasya*) from the sentence effecting the identification with the Agnihotra sacrifice, namely, “The chest itself is the altar, the hairs are the sacrificial grass” (*ura eva vedirlomāni barhiḥ*).

Śaṅkara and others, however, have explained the four sūtras beginning with "abhivyakteḥ" as demonstrating different ways of reconciling the scriptural statement that [the Lord] is "only the size of a span" according to various viewpoints. They state that the meaning of the sūtra "abhivyakteḥ" is as follows: Āśmarathya maintains that although the Supreme Self is beyond measure, its being "only the size of a span" is possible through the power of yoga; thus, the mind, when delimited by the grace of Brahman who is the size of a span, [perceives Him].

They state that the meaning of the second sūtra is as follows: because it is possible for [the Self] to be manifested in a limited measure (prādeśamātratayā) for the sake of favoring its worshippers (upāsakānugrahārtha), that which has a measure (mātrā)—that is, a dimension—connected to a limited space such as heaven, earth, and so forth, is thus described; and thus, through a conventional metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) based on common usage (rūḍhi), there is the state of being "measured by a span" (prādeśamātratva), according to Bādari.

In the Vājasaneyaka, the status of being "the size of a span" (*prādeśamātra*) is established for Vaiśvānara—the self of the three worlds—by identifying the heaven and other elements as his head and other limbs within the space between the top of the head and the chin for the sake of the worshiper. For it is heard thus in the Vājasaneyaka:
"The gods, indeed, attained a well-known state that was as if the size of a span. But I shall explain them to you in such a way that I will make them appear as if they were the size of a span."

He said, pointing to the crown of the head: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the Summit. Pointing to the eyes, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara of Good Brilliance. Pointing to the nostrils, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara of Diverse Paths. Pointing to the space within the mouth, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the Abundant. Pointing to the moisture within the mouth, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as Wealth. Pointing to the chin, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the Foundation."

The meaning is this: when the gods, beginning with Sūrya, have attained—that is, reached—the state of being "span-long" (*prādeśamātra*) through meditation, then they become known. Having made a promise to Aupamanyava and the others, saying, "I am the King of Kekaya; I shall describe these gods to you in such a way that I shall bring them to the state of being span-long," King Aśvapati spoke to them. When asked, "Doing what? he replied while pointing to his head.

Pointing with the tip of his hand, [the teacher says]: "This one indeed stands transcending the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ; thus he is 'Atiṣṭhā' (the Transcendent). Since it is well known that the sky is a limb of Vaiśvānara, the meaning is that one should perform the visualization (*dṛṣṭi*) of the heavenly world as the head of Vaiśvānara in its cosmic aspect (*adhidaiva*).

Showing his own eyes, he said: "This indeed is the one of good splendor (sutejas), for the sun is the deity corresponding to the eye of Vaiśvānara. The meaning is that the vision of the eye of Vaiśvānara—which is well-known as the sun—is to be seen in one's own two eyes. This principle is to be understood everywhere in such contexts; thus they explain the meaning of the Sūtra: "Because of the attainment [of the whole] in this manner. Regarding this Supreme Self within the span of a span—the space between the top of the head and the chin—the Jābālas also study as follows:

"This infinite, unmanifest Self is established in the *avimukta*. Regarding this *avimukta*, it is said that he is established in this; specifically, he is established in the middle of the *varaṇā* and the *nāsī*. As for what the *varaṇā* and the *nāsī* are, they explain there that the nose itself is the *varaṇā* and the *nāsī*. Furthermore, they declare: "What is its location? It is the junction of the eyebrows and the breath (*prāṇa*); this is the junction of the heavenly world and the beyond."

And therefore, they state that the meaning of the fourth sūtra is that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is established as being "the size of a span" (prādeśamātra) because it resides only in the region between the nose and the eyebrows. In their view, since even the group of four sūtras is intended merely to demonstrate the consistency of the "span-sized" nature [of the Self], there is no room for doubt regarding distinct exclusions for each [sūtra] as there is in our own system; thus, [the objection] is not very purposeful. He states this with the words "non-manifestation, the state of being remembered," and so forth. The reading is: "the accomplishment of heaven and so forth, and of being above and so forth."

The phrase "between the head and the chin" is connected to both [contexts] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). That is to say, the accomplishment of [the Lord] as being above heaven and below the earth occurs between the head and the chin, and the abiding of the Supreme (Parameśvara) between the head and the chin is also connected to both; after the statement "established by scripture," the remainder must be supplied as: "it is conducive to the reconciliation of the scriptural passage concerning His being the size of a span (*prādeśamātra*)."

Now, one might object: "In the preceding section, it was precisely the qualities such as having heaven as the head that were presented as marks of the Supreme Self, not merely the connection with heaven and so forth. Anticipating this unease, he says: "Or rather, [it refers to] 'that which has the qualities of invisibility and so on'. The phrase "with the notion of incompleteness" means "with the notion of invisibility."

Although the opponent of this section does not actually challenge the status of the one possessing qualities such as invisibility as being the Supreme Self—rather, having accepted that very point, he proceeds with the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the mantra "In whom the heaven... refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) on the basis of its indicative marks (*liṅga*) due to a break in the context of that [preceding] section—nevertheless, the underlying intention is that if the mantra "In whom the heaven... were to refer to the individual soul, then even in the passage concerning invisibility and so forth, the doubt regarding its being the Supreme Self would fail to sprout.

The entire sequence of the scriptural passages from the relevant sections has been recorded in the *Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa*; it should be consulted therein. The phrase "the subject matter of the verse concerns the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth" means that its purport is directed toward the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.

Now, one might object: since the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "On account of the teaching of his attributes within" states that, by the force of the scripture "The Unborn is born in many ways," the Supreme Lord, out of His supreme compassion, assumes by His own will forms such as gods and humans in accordance with the perceptions of His worshippers—how then can being born in many ways be a characteristic of the individual soul (*jīva*)? To this, he says: "Within the sun."

Regarding the phrase "in the case of knowledge" (*vidyāyām*): the sense is that the meaning of the word *bahudhā* (in many ways) was not examined there by the author of the Sūtras. Regarding the "first resolution": even though the etymological meaning is primary in the view of *yoga* (derivation), the total abandonment of the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) which was first apprehended is a fault. Regarding the second [resolution], however, although the conventional meaning is not abandoned at all by adopting a meaning similar to it, the acceptance of an impossible meaning is a fault; this is the sense. Regarding the phrase "a specific cause": the meaning is that a specific cause in the form of [divine] will, as well as a specific fruit in the form of grace toward the worshiper, are indicated.

Since the explanation of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is preceded by the explanation of the meanings of its constituent words (*padārtha*), he states the reason for explaining them out of their sequential order with the phrase "because of the connection with the Sūtra" (*sūtrasaṅgateḥ*). This means "that which is connected," i.e., that which possesses a logical connection (*saṅgatimant*); the sense is that when that which possesses the connection is stated, the connection itself becomes present to the mind. The phrase "because of the extreme length of the Sūtra" means because the Sūtra beginning with "an indeclinable [is compounded] with a case-ending" (*avyayaṃ vibhaktyādi*) is exceedingly long. The phrase "other than the Supreme Self under discussion" implies that since both *Pradhāna* and the individual soul (*jīva*) are under discussion in this Sūtra, it is possible for the pronoun *tat* to refer to those two. [The opponent asks: "If it were the Supreme Self..."?

Although it is possible that there exists another entity distinct from the Pradhāna and the individual soul (jīva), nevertheless, since only the Pradhāna, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self (paramātman) are under discussion here, the word "tat" (that) refers specifically to them. For this very reason, later on, intending to establish that the phrase "from a word other than one denoting that" means "from the word 'Supreme Self'," he will state that the expression "from its own word" (tatsvaśabdāt) does not add anything further to the meaning.

Therefore, by the principle of elimination (pāriśeṣya), there is an absence of [any other] meaning; and as for the feminine form "ambhāḥ," it is established because the rule "after an indeclinable compound ending in 'at', the fifth case suffix is not used" (Pāṇini 1.1.39) serves as an exclusion (paryudāsa). Thus the formation of the word is accomplished.

Raising the objection that since being distinct from Īśvara is common to the *jīva* as well, how can this refer to *prakṛti*, he says: "On account of the force of the feminine gender. Now, one might ask: how can there be a reference to the present tense (*prīyamāṇam*) for a word prescribed in the sense of a past fact? To this he says: "The sense is that the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the inception of an action (*ādikarman*). Since the word *tadā* is not heard in the mantra, he says: "Of *yat* and *tat*. He states another alternative: "The word *iti*. The meaning is: "The meaning of that" (*tadarthaḥ*) means the meaning intended by the word *tadā*; thus, the meaning of the word *iti* is the meaning of the word *tadā*.

The word "likewise" (*tathā*) found in the commentary means that it is an explanation of the word "thus" (*iti*). Now, one might ask: "How is it that the support of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self merely by the mention of a distinction [between them], and why could it not be the individual soul (*jīva*)? To this he says: "concomitant with the state of being the seer," and so on. This applies both to what precedes and what follows.

The meaning is: [this applies] both in the refutation of the living being (*prāṇabhṛt*) and in the establishment of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). "Stated by virtue of being topical" means that they are not what is to be propounded by this particular mantra. The intention is that omniscience (*sārvajñya*) also refers to the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth under discussion, because it is heard in this very context [of the text] that "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving. "Because of its own suitability" means...

The sense is that, although the individual soul (jīva) possesses attributes such as omniscience and being the bridge to immortality, these can somehow be explained in a non-primary sense through the mediation of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and so forth. Now, one might object: "In this sūtra, it is established by scripture that [the subject] refers only to the Supreme Self; for there is no connection here with the reason stated in the sūtra 'Because of the designation of difference,' since that reason serves to reject the view that [the subject] refers to the inner self (pratyagātman). To this, he replies: "That too is the inner self."

Now, one might object: "How does the introduction of the soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) as the subject matter in this *sūtra* serve—rather than contradicting—the proof that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self, or the refutation of its being the individual soul? Furthermore, if the status of the Supreme Self is established by other contextual reasons intended in the preceding *sūtras*, which are unique to the Supreme Self, what is the purpose of this [present] one? Anticipating this doubt, he states the intended meaning of the *sūtra*: "He shines forth... [referring to] the Supreme."

This mantra is employed for the purpose of demonstrating that the Supreme Self is devoid of the status of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). In that context, in order to strengthen the proof of His lack of enjoyment, it establishes that the status of enjoyer—well-known both from worldly experience and from the Veda—belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, and not even to the Supreme Self when residing within the body. Therefore, the demonstration of the soul's status as an enjoyer serves to demonstrate its absence in the Supreme Self.

Nor can it be argued that the demonstration of the non-enjoyership of the Supreme Self is for the purpose of establishing the enjoyership of the individual soul (jīva), because such a reversal would be untenable; for what is already well-known is intended for the sake of establishing what is not yet known, and the nature of the Supreme Self is not more well-known than that of the individual soul, whereby such a case could arise, nor is there [any need] for the realization of the Supreme Self...

The cognition of the individual soul (*jīva*) is also purposeful even with respect to the body, such that the teaching regarding the Supreme Self might be for the sake of understanding the individual soul. Therefore, the teaching regarding the individual soul as an enjoyer is for the sake of understanding the Supreme Self as the non-enjoyer. Consequently, it is established that the Supreme Self is what is being taught in that mantra. Furthermore, that mantra refers precisely to the substratum consisting of heaven, earth, and so forth, which was introduced previously; for there would be an inconsistency in denoting something not under discussion. Thus, it is concluded that the Supreme Self is the substratum of heaven, earth, and the rest.

The sense is that [the reading] *siddham* is established. And because it would result in the words being inconsistent with their own meaning; the sense is that sorrow and delusion are impossible in the insentient internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). "Behold" (*paśya*) refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the beholder; the sentient is the beholder, while the insentient is the non-beholder; the Supreme Self is the beholder; both the sentient and the insentient are the beholder and the non-beholder; and because of being the beholder and the non-beholder—meaning, because His essential nature consists solely in being seen by the beholder—the Supreme Self does not "behold. Here, the phrase "by some," etc., refers to the connection with being the sustainer (*dhārakatva*). This is also illustrative; one should also understand it as referring to the connection with being the higher and the lower (*parāvaratva*).

The meaning is that others have indeed described the phrase "from its own word" (*sva-śabdāt*) as also meaning "from the word *ātman*"; furthermore, in another context, because of the use of the term *sat*—which is unique to itself—in the passage "the abode of *sat*" (*sad-āyatana*), they have explained that the meaning is that the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is the intended sense.

Regarding the phrase "and of the second Sūtra": although in this Sūtra as well another interpretation has been stated—namely, "because of the designation [of Brahman] as that which is to be attained by those liberated from ignorance"—nevertheless, since that [interpretation] is accepted [by the opponent], it should be understood that only the alternative interpretation, "because of the designation [of Brahman] as that which is to be known by those who are liberated," is refuted here because it is not accepted by [the author] himself. The reading "vākkartṛkamuktapratyabhijñānam" (the recognition of the liberated one made by speech) is correct. It should be understood that "vāgvimukteḥ" refers to what has been stated by others.

And in that context, the meaning of "by the transformation of the suffix" (*pratyayavipariṇāmena*) is "by the transformation of the accusative case ending" (*dvitīyāyāḥ*). In the reading *vākkartṛkā*, the suffix *kta* in *muktā* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule for initial action (*ādikarmaṇi*). Thus, it is the suffix *kta* denoting the agent. The compound *vākkarmaka-pratyayaḥ* is a possessive compound (*svārthika*) meaning "a suffix whose object is speech" (*vāgrūpaṃ karma*). The compound is formed by the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) [Pāṇini 2.1.32] regarding the accusative case. This applies to the phrase "by the transformation of the suffix."

The meaning is that it refers to the modification of the suffix *kta* according to the rule *ādikarmaṇi ktaḥ*. The intention is that, having set aside the exclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*), the very term "the living being" (*prāṇabhṛt*) is what is to be established by the sūtra "and by abiding and eating. The intention is that, regarding the demonstration of the exclusion of the intellect (*buddhi*), it is precisely the exclusion of the individual soul that ought to be presented through the attributes of being an eater and not being an eater.

The meaning of "he becomes the Supreme Self" and consequently "he does not become a living being" is that he does not become consciousness as delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); it does not mean, however, that even the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) freed from its adjuncts does not exist, for if that were so, there would be an inconsistency.

The sense is that [the latter interpretation] is untenable as a reason for the argument, because the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), which is superimposed during the state of conjunction with adjuncts, persists even in the case of the pure consciousness; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between bondage—consisting of agency and so forth—and liberation.

The point is that if the verse "dvā suparṇā" (Two birds... were to have as its object the conditioned and the isolated consciousness respectively, there would be the undesirable consequence of designating "two men" even when only one man has entered inside a house, since duality could exist through the distinction between the conditioned and the isolated. By the phrase "by way of exclusion" (*vyatirekeṇa*), it is meant "by way of exclusion [of the individual soul]," as indicated by the words "because of the word 'not-that'" (*atacchabdāt*).

In the seventh prapāṭhaka of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, it is said: "Nārada approached Sanatkumāra, saying, 'Teach me, venerable sir. He said to him, 'Approach me with what you already know; thereafter I shall tell you what is beyond that. [Nārada] replied, 'I have known only this much,' meaning, 'Perform meditation upon me. Nārada said, 'Venerable sir, I have studied the Ṛgveda and the Yajurveda; thus, venerable sir, I am merely a knower of mantras, not a knower of the Self (ātman). I have heard from those like your venerable self that one who knows the Self overcomes sorrow.'"

"Venerable Sir, I am grieving; may the Blessed One carry me across the ocean of grief. He said to him, "Meditate upon Name. "He who meditates upon Name as Brahman attains freedom of movement as far as Name reaches. [The teacher asks: 'He who meditates upon Name as Brahman—Venerable Sir, is there anything greater than Name? [The teacher replies: 'There is indeed something greater than Name. [The student asks: 'May the Blessed One tell me that. "Speech, indeed, is greater than Name. Meditate upon Speech. "Venerable Sir, is there anything greater than Speech?"

"Is there, indeed, something greater than speech? May the Blessed One tell me that. "Mind, indeed, is greater than speech. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, something greater than mind? "Is there, indeed, something greater than mind? May the Blessed One tell me that. "Volition, indeed, is greater than mind. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, something greater than volition? "Is there, indeed, something greater than volition? May the Blessed One tell me that. "Thought, indeed, is greater than volition. "Is there, O Venerable Sir, something greater than thought? "Is there, indeed, something greater than thought?"

"May the Blessed One tell me that," [he said]. "Meditation (*dhyāna*) is indeed greater than thought (*citta*); consciousness (*vijñāna*) is indeed greater than meditation; food (*anna*) is indeed greater than strength (*bala*); water (*āpaḥ*) is indeed greater than food; fire (*tejaḥ*) is indeed greater than water; space (*ākāśaḥ*) is indeed greater than fire; memory (*smaraḥ*) is indeed greater than space; hope (*āśā*) is indeed greater than memory. After these questions and answers, [it continues]: "Vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed greater than hope. Just as spokes are fixed in the hub, so everything is fixed in this vital breath. By the vital breath [one lives], by the vital breath..."

The vital breath departs; it gives life, it bestows life upon life. Indeed, the vital breath is the father, the vital breath is the mother, the vital breath is the brother, the vital breath is the sister, the vital breath is the teacher, and the vital breath is the Brahmin. If one should do anything harsh here to a father, or a mother, or a brother, or a sister, or a teacher, or a Brahmin—

He replies, "Fie on you! and they say this to him: "You are indeed a slayer of your father; you are indeed a slayer of your mother; you are indeed a slayer of your brother; you are indeed a slayer of your sister; you are indeed a slayer of your teacher; you are indeed a slayer of a Brahmin. But even if one were to burn them all together with a spit while their life-breaths have departed, they would not say of him: "You are a slayer of your father," nor "You are a slayer of your mother," nor "You are a slayer of your brother," nor "You are a slayer of your sister," nor "You are a slayer of your teacher," nor "You are a slayer of a Brahmin."

"Prāṇa alone indeed becomes all these. He who sees thus, knows thus, reflects thus, and understands thus, becomes an 'over-speaker. If they should say to him, 'Are you an over-speaker? he should say, 'I am an over-speaker,' and he should not deny it. But he indeed is an over-speaker who over-speaks by means of truth. 'Venerable sir, may I over-speak by means of truth? [The teacher says: 'Truth, indeed, must be sought to be understood. [The student says: 'Venerable sir, I wish to understand truth.'"

"When one truly knows, then one speaks the truth; one does not speak the truth without knowing. Only when one knows does one speak the truth. Therefore, knowledge itself is what one should seek to understand. "Venerable sir, I wish to understand knowledge. "When, indeed..."

"When one thinks, then one understands; therefore, one should desire to understand thought (mati). 'Venerable sir, I desire to understand thought. 'When one has faith, then one thinks; therefore, one should desire to understand faith (śraddhā). 'Venerable sir, I desire to understand faith. 'When one is steadfast, then one has faith; therefore, one should desire to understand steadfastness (niṣṭhā). 'Venerable sir, I desire to understand steadfastness. 'When one acts, then one is steadfast.'"

"When one attains happiness, then he acts; O Venerable Sir, I desire to understand happiness. "That which is the Infinite (bhūman) is happiness; O Venerable Sir, I desire to understand the Infinite. "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite. But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite. That which is the Infinite is immortal, and that which is finite is mortal. "O Venerable Sir, on what is it established? "On its own greatness."

"Or perhaps it is not 'greatness,'" [the teacher said]. "In this world, they call cattle and horses 'greatness,' as do elephants, gold, slaves, wives, fields, and dwellings. "I do not speak thus," he replied. "For one thing is established in another. But He is below, He is above, He is behind, He is in front, He is to the south, He is to the north—He indeed is all this. Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the 'I': I am indeed below, I am above, I am behind, I am in front, I am to the south, I am to the north—I indeed am all this."

Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the Self: the Self alone is below, the Self is above, the Self is behind, the Self is in front, the Self is to the south, the Self is to the north—the Self indeed is all this. He who sees thus, who thinks thus, who understands thus, rejoices in the Self, sports with the Self, revels with the Self, and finds bliss in the Self; he becomes a self-ruler, and for him there is freedom of movement in all worlds. But those who know it otherwise than this are ruled by others; their worlds are not inexhaustible, and they do not have freedom of movement in all worlds.

It is so. For him who sees thus, who reflects thus, and who understands thus—[realizing] "from the Self come breaths, from the Self comes hope, from the Self come actions, and from the Self indeed all this"—there is this verse: "The seer sees no death, no disease, nor any sorrow; the seer sees all, he attains all in every way."

The connection of this section is established by way of the following reasoning: since the quality of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) is mentioned immediately after the mention of the capacity for violence (*hiṃsā-yogyatva*), the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and final (*uttara-pakṣa*) positions proceed as if that *jīvatva* were already established; thus, the textual sequence is intended. Otherwise, since *jīvatva* related to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) would be accepted by both sides, one could have argued whether the *jīvatva* related to the *prāṇa* constitutes the prima facie view or the final conclusion. Consequently, while the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātmatva*) of that which is related to the *prāṇa* was established previously, here—

The final conclusion is that the "abundance" (*bhūmatva*) belonging to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is refuted after having been presented as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Now, one might object: even in the absence of another word ending in the genitive case denoting a substratum (*dharmin*), let it be admitted that the term refers to the attribute (*dharma*) simply because it is mentioned as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to the word "abundance" which denotes the attribute; anticipating this unease, [the author] says: "And because of the scriptural passage, 'where one sees nothing else'. In some places, the reading *saprāṇaniṣprāṇaviṣayopamardatadabhāvayoḥ* is seen, but the reading *saprāṇaniṣprāṇaviṣayopamardayoḥ* is the correct one.

The meaning of that [passage] is as follows: because it is heard that when there is destruction of objects containing living beings, there is violence caused by the destruction of a body with life, whereas when there is destruction of a body devoid of living beings, there is an absence of violence caused by the destruction of a body without life.

Regarding the phrase "in those without breath" (*aprāṇeṣu*): one might object that since the earth-element within plants—which have a thirst for water poured at their roots—is taken up [by them], breath (*prāṇa*) certainly exists even in insentient things; and it has been stated in the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*: "Its existence is present even in stationary beings (*sthāvara*). If this is asked, the answer is: True, breath certainly exists there. Nevertheless, because of the absence of that specific function of breath—namely, the maintenance of the body—which is established by the sūtra "Because of the difference taught in scripture" (*bhedashruter vailakṣanyāt*) and which is divided into five kinds, they are described as being "without breath."

For this very reason, it will be stated in the commentary on the Sūtra, "But not because of the existence of examples," that although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) exists in stationary beings (*sthāvara*), it does not abide as the sustainer of the body by existing in its fivefold state. The term *āvistarām* means "more clearly" or "more fully" known through the Vedas. Now, an objection might be raised: since the commenced instruction regarding the Self culminates with the vital breath, and the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) does not accept that the vital breath is the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), it would follow that in his system the vital breath is not the inner Self; to this he replies with the words beginning "of the commenced instruction regarding the Self," etc. The intended meaning is "the state of being a sustainer"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

"In the words expressing the cause" means among the three words beginning with "because of the instruction as being superior to the state of serene bliss" (*samprasādādadhyupadeśāt*). As for the phrase "for there is a mention subsequent to what was previously indicated": although in the previous section there was an explicit mention at the beginning of the words "or greater than this" (*asmādbhūyaḥ*), such is not the case here; nevertheless, since the superiority requires a correlative of comparison (*pratiyogi*), [the meaning follows].

The sense is that the intention of the Bhāṣya is that, according to the principle of "the vessel above the measure" (*upariveṣāmitānadhikaraṇanyāya*), only the immediately preceding *prāṇa* is to be understood as the limit. The meaning is that the intention—that the Supreme Self alone is denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*) because it is devoid of any modification in its essential nature or intrinsic being—is thereby clarified. [Objection: But surely, since the particle *tu* has the sense of distinction, it can only be understood as having an exclusive or differentiating function (*vyāvartakatva*).

Anticipating the objection that [the difference] does not constitute a differentiating factor by way of superiority, he says: "It is true that the word 'tu' (but) merely indicates a distinction; nevertheless, superiority is established by the force of the context," namely, "of that which is mentioned later over that which was mentioned before. Now, one might ask: even if the superiority of the worshipper is stated by the word 'tu', since the superiority of the object of worship has not been mentioned, how can the superiority of the object of worship be established? To this he replies: "For the word 'tu'...

Indeed, although no other word such as *juhoti* (he offers) is heard—so that there is no difference between the words *agnihotra* and *juhoti*—nevertheless, because an injunction is possible upon hearing the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), [the meaning follows].

The sense is that, because it is impossible to enjoin what has already been enjoined, there arises the possibility of suspecting that this is a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*). In the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase "the third [case-ending] in the sense of a characteristic" (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇe tṛtīyā*) means "characterized by the meditation on the *Brāhmaṇa*. This should be understood as a mere illustration; since the *Brāhmaṇa* can function as an instrument (*karaṇa*) by being the cause for speaking excessively, it is also appropriate to treat it as a case-ending expressing a grammatical relation (*kāraka-vibhakti*). The phrase "only the alternative of speaking the truth" implies that this is the position favored by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*).

Since the distinctness established by the natural force of the sentence must not be sublated, it would be strained to assume that the word *ataḥ* (therefore) refers to a remote, non-proximate limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); for this reason, he says, "Or rather, [the meaning] of the word *ativādin*... Since there has been no explicit introduction of a dispute regarding whether [the term] is etymological (*yaugika*) or non-etymological (*ayaugika*), he says, "Or rather, 'having transcended' (*atikrānta*). Now, although it was stated that being an *ativādin* means speaking of one's own object of meditation as having transcended other things in terms of being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), [the phrase] "having transcended one's own object of meditation" [remains to be explained].

One might object: "Since *ativāditva* (the state of being an eloquent speaker) has not been previously specified as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *ativādin*, how can the word *ataḥ* (therefore) refer to its being the ground for application? Anticipating this doubt, he states: "The meaning is that this is the result of the previously mentioned matter. This is because it was stated that *ativāditva* is the speaking of a subject of meditation that is exceedingly sublime; thus, the fact that this very thing is the ground for the application of the word *ativādin* follows as a necessary consequence (*phalita*), and it is therefore appropriate for the word *ataḥ* to refer to that consequential meaning. Thus, he says: "This meaning is the result of what was said before."

The masculine reading *phalaḥ* is correct. Its meaning is as follows: the sense that "the state of being one who speaks of a reality transcending what one's own object of meditation is" constitutes the ground for the application of the term *ativādī* (one who speaks beyond); this is the "fruit" (*phala*) of the previously mentioned etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*). Thus, the demonstration that [the Lord] speaks of a reality transcending His own object of meditation results in establishing His etymological nature. Therefore, they say that it is appropriate for the passage beginning with "ata eva" (for this very reason) to be intended as a demonstration of His etymological nature.

The meaning is as follows: because the very state of speaking beyond one's own object of worship (*upāsya-vastu*) is the basis for the application of the term, and since the Brahman alone—which is the referent of the word "Truth" (*satya*)—constitutes the unsurpassed human goal, it is only the knower of that [Brahman] who possesses the quality of speaking beyond his own object of worship. Therefore, in the statement "But Truth indeed must be sought to be known," it is the Brahman alone, denoted by the word "Truth," that is declared as the object of worship (*upāsya*), and not as the object of knowledge (*veditavya*).

One might argue that the literal sense of the word *vijijñāsitavya* (to be desired to be known) would be lost; however, let the meaning here be the same as in passages such as "But knowledge indeed is what one should desire to know" (*vijñānaṃ tveva vijijñāsitavyam*) and "Venerable sir, I desire to know knowledge" (*vijñānaṃ bhagavo vijijñāse*), where it is understood as "it should be accomplished. It is not necessarily the case that in the context of knowledge and so forth, *vijijñāsitavyam* must mean "it must be accomplished," for later [in the text] it says: "When one reflects, then one knows; when one has faith, then one reflects."

It might be argued that because the means [to liberation] are proclaimed and shown therein, the terms "desiring to know" (*jijñāsitavya*) must refer to objects other than the Truth (*satya*) and signify what is to be accomplished; this will be stated later. If that is so, then let the meaning be exactly the same even with respect to the Truth.

If it is argued that this is because of the observation of the mention of a means—namely, "When one truly knows, then one speaks the truth"—we reply: no, because it is improper to employ the word *satya*, which is well-known in the sense of the Supreme Self, figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) for speech that conveys the ultimate reality; furthermore, the instrumental case in "one should excel by means of the truth" (*satyenātivadāni*) would be improper, the prefix *ati-* would be redundant, and the natural force of the word *tu* [in the subsequent passage] indicates that even in the statement "I desire to know the Truth, O Venerable One," the meaning to be adopted is that the speaking of truth is what must be accomplished.

This is because the intent [of the author] is to offer such refutations as "because it is afflicted" (*kliṣṭatvāt*) and so forth. By the word "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), *śruti* and *liṅga* are intended, as another means of knowledge has already been mentioned. It should be understood that this is because the author himself explains the sentence "when one truly knows" (*yadā vai vijānāti*) as being devoted to establishing that the status of being an "exaggerator" (*ativāditva*) is based on direct perception (*sākṣātkāritva*).

The meaning is that one should perform the worship of Truth (*satyopāsana*), which serves as the means for that [realization]; this is the sense of the remainder of the sentence, "But Truth indeed must be sought to be known" (*satyaṃ tveva vijijñāsitavyam*). Now, the passage beginning with "When one truly knows, then one speaks the truth; one who does not know does not speak the truth," etc., is recited in the section immediately following "But Truth indeed must be sought to be known. Furthermore, the context is intended to demonstrate that each subsequent statement serves as a reason for the preceding prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), and not as a reason for the subsequent [conclusion].

This [section] is intended to demonstrate that each preceding stage is to be accomplished by the one following it. If it is asked: "Having prescribed the meditation on Truth (*satya*) in the first section with the words 'Truth indeed is what one should desire to understand,' how does the subsequent section establish the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that is to be accomplished by that [meditation]? It is said in reply: In the first section, the meditation on Brahman was enjoined for the sake of attaining the status of an "exceeding speaker" (*ativāditva*). In the second section, it is demonstrated that this meditation on Truth is the cause for attaining that status of an exceeding speaker by means of direct realization. Thus, by both sections together—

The sense is that the intention of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) is as follows: by means of the "state of being an over-speaker" (*ativāditva*), the meditation (*upāsana*) which is the cause of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is enjoined; then, by the subsequent sections, the reflection (*manana*) and other practices useful for that meditation are enjoined. Regarding the term "accidental" (*yādṛcchika*): it means that in the case of Jānaśruti, it is observed through his conversation with the swan and so forth that he attained the knowledge of the unsurpassed human goal (*niratiśaya-puruṣārtha*) regarding the *bahṛc* [Veda]; and likewise, through his conversation with Mahābhāgavata and so forth, it is seen that he attained the knowledge of the unsurpassed human goal regarding the *brāhmaṇa*.

The sense is that because the root *labh* (to obtain) signifies attainment (*prāpti*), knowledge (*jñāna*) is also of the nature of attainment. He states the undesirable consequence if [the text] were intended in the primary sense of attainment: "For [knowledge] does not result from hearing and so forth. [This is because] they have objects distinct from reality, as in: "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is to be desired to be known; but the intellect (*mati*) alone... and so on.

The sense is that in passages such as "it is to be desired to be known," the possibility of [the term] having the meaning of *upāsanā* (meditative worship) is excluded. Regarding the phrase "there might be a suspicion of the falsity of the visible world" (*dṛśyamithyātvaśaṅkā syāt*): the absence of perception other than Brahman must result either from the exclusion of the visible (*dṛśya-vyatireka*) or from the exclusion of the Seer (*dṛśi-vyatireka*). Since that [Seer], being the very nature of consciousness (*svarūpa*), is eternal, it results in the exclusion of the visible alone; thus, the falsity of the visible world is established—this is the intention of the opponents, which is the sense [of the text]. In the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase "whose nature is of unbounded excellence" (*anavadhikātiśayasvarūpa*) [is used].

Although in the sentence defining the Infinite (*bhūman*), “where one sees nothing else,” it would be more appropriate—just as in the sentence defining the small (*alpa*)—"where one sees nothing else"—to understand this as referring to an unspecified object, rather than as a reference to [the Self] qualified by attributes such as being unlimited; for this very reason, it is also improper to state that the absence of seeing anything else and so forth are obtained through the force of that [infinite].

It is not correct to say that in the statement "whatever possesses a dewlap is a cow," the possession of a dewlap is obtained through the reference to the particular qualified by cowness (*gotva*) via the word *yat*; nevertheless, it should be understood that a solution is possible because all commentators on the *Janmādi-sūtra* employ the expression "from which [proceeds] the omniscient one" (*yataḥ sarvajñāt*). Consequently, the phrase *tato 'nyat* (other than that) must be explained as follows: the meaning is that one does not perceive anything else apart from that which is of the nature of suffering (*duḥkha-rūpa*); thus, *duḥkha-rūpam* means "the state of being suffering" (*duḥkhatva*).

In accordance with the verse that will be cited as a witness—"The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering; the seer sees everything"—the two words *yatra* and *yataḥ* should both be applied to the phrase "he sees nothing else. Thus, the meaning is: that [state] which, while being experienced, is the "Fullness" (*bhūman*), wherein one does not see its opposite—suffering—and from which one sees nothing else.

In this context, "the cause for the absence of the perception of suffering" means that it is the cause for the absence of perceiving the nature of suffering within Brahman, which is distinguished by its qualities of manifestation (*vibhūti*). "He does not perceive suffering" means that he does not perceive the state of being suffering in Brahman, which is distinguished by its qualities of manifestation. "The qualities such as knowledge are included within its own nature" means that knowledge, bliss, and so forth are the determiners of its essential nature (*svarūpa*); this is the intended meaning.

The meaning of "for the purpose of collecting the intended reasons" is as follows: the intention is to collect the intended [reason], namely that the state of being of the nature of unsurpassed and infinite bliss—which is the reason for the absence of the vision of suffering—is [established] by the qualifying term "of the nature of unsurpassed and infinite bliss. Regarding the phrase "in case of the doubt that the manifestation (*vibhūti*) is other than Brahman": when it is stated, "wherein, upon perceiving the manifestation, one sees nothing else," since both instances of the word *yat* (wherein) refer to Brahman itself, the meaning is that the manifestation is also non-different from it.

Regarding the commentary’s phrase *aiśvaryāparaparyāyavibhūtiguṇaviśiṣṭam* ("distinguished by the quality of manifestation, which is another synonym for sovereignty"), there are three intended meanings: (1) "the quality whose object is manifestation" (*vibhūtiviṣayo guṇaḥ*), or "the quality of manifestation" (*vibhūtiguṇaḥ*) where sovereignty is another synonym for that quality; (2) "manifestation and it is also a quality" (*vibhūtiścāsau guṇaśca*); or (3) "sovereignty is another synonym for it, and it is also the quality of manifestation" (*aiśvaryāparaparyāyaścāsau vibhūtiguṇaśca*). With these three meanings in mind, he explains [the passage] with the words beginning "the quality whose object is manifestation," and so forth.

The sense is that the word *yat* itself refers to the qualified Brahman. If we were to assert that "plenitude" (*bhūmatva*) belongs to the mere nature of the substantive alone, then there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) regarding the definition "where one sees nothing else," and a term expressive of its manifestations (*vibhūti*) would have to be sought elsewhere. Rather, the meaning of the word *bhūman* is precisely that which is qualified by the attributes of manifestation, not the substantive alone. Consequently, the word *yat* would also refer to that very same qualified entity intended as the object of definition; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever—this is the underlying point.

Nor should it be argued that if the word *bhūman* refers exclusively to the qualified [Self], then—since the qualified [Self] lacks both the nature of being the referent of the term "I" (*ahaṃ-artha*) and the nature of being the Self (*ātmatva*)—the teaching regarding the meditation on *bhūman* as having the nature of the "I-grasp" (*ahaṅgraha-upāsana*) in passages such as "Now, therefore, the instruction concerning the 'I'" would be untenable. It should be understood that the teaching of its being the "I-grasp" and the Self is possible with reference to the aspect of the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, the phrase "not seeing anything else" does not mean that there is no perception of anything other than the substantive.

The phrase "the non-perception of suffering is untenable" means that the perception of its nature as suffering is untenable. The word "of all" (*sarvasya*) is the term to be explained. Although the second example is mentioned in the commentary (*bhāṣya*), he states that the same applies to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).

Although this has been stated explicitly by way of the throat [of the text], nevertheless, it should be understood that the similarity (*sādharmya*) with the first illustration is also intended. The word *etad* (this) is the term to be explained; *aupādhika*, etc., is the explanation. "Well-done" (*sukṛta*): the state of being an effect is expressed in the passage, "He is indeed flavor" (*raso vai saḥ*). The state of being a cause is expressed in the passage, "From bliss, verily, indeed... (*ānandāddhyeva khalu*). In the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), it says: "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra-ādeśa*)."

Regarding the phrase "because of the introduction of the 'I'-grasping" (*ahaṅgrahopakramāt*): the sense is that if the intent were to teach the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), the text would have said, "Now, therefore, the teaching of the 'I'" (*athāto'hamupadeśaḥ*). Therefore, the word *ahaṅkāra* refers to the intellect (*buddhi*). Intending to show that even in this section the state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmatvam*) is taught, [the author says] "even though," etc. Although the state of being the Self of all was already stated previously by the passage beginning with "He indeed is below" (*sa evādhastāt*), nevertheless, the meaning is that he intends to demonstrate it again later on in order to further consolidate that state of being the Self of all. And this is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇam*).

Now, if the statement "Next, therefore, the instruction regarding the Self" were absent, there would arise the suspicion that the instruction on the Self—which was introduced with the words "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow"—remains incomplete; thus, one might think that something else was begun and something else has arrived. Therefore...

It should be understood that the textual passage beginning with "the instruction regarding the Self" is intended to demonstrate that "Earth alone is the Self. It was stated that "Selfhood is the result"; this means that once the state of being the Self of all has been declared, the intention is to show that the state of being the Self of the worshipper is also implied as a result, and thus the sentence "Now, therefore, the instruction regarding the Self" is cited. Regarding the phrase "of the sentence containing an explicit statement," this refers to the sentence "Of him, indeed, of this... [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8]. In the Commentary, the phrase "because the worshipper exists as the inner controller" [is used].

The meaning is that the phrase "of the knower as the Self" (vijānata ātmataḥ) refers to the worshipper [as] the inner controller (antaryāmin), according to the Śruti. Regarding this, the Vivaraṇakāra has stated: "Since the ego (ahaṅkāra) is established by perception as being one with the Self, the separate instruction—'Now, therefore, the instruction on the ego' (athāto 'haṅkārādeśaḥ); 'Now, therefore, the instruction on the Self' (athāta ātmādeśaḥ)—is for the sake of indicating difference. Conversely, the separate instruction regarding the well-known distinctness of the Infinite (bhūman) and the Self is for the sake of indicating identity, because it is impossible for both to be the universal Self. This is unsound.

It might be argued that there is a reversal of the situation: since a self other than the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is not established by perception as being distinct from the *brāhman* called "the Infinite" (*bhūman*), the instruction regarding those two is for the purpose of [establishing] their difference; whereas, since the referent of "I" is not established by perception as being distinct from the *brāhman*, the instruction regarding those two is for the purpose of [establishing] their identity. Furthermore, one cannot claim that the teaching of the non-difference of the referent of "I"—which is the insentient internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—from the Infinite is sublated, while such is not the case for the [sentient] Self.

Since that [instruction] is intended only for those who have faith in his view and is not meant for everyone, it is logical to see that—after the "Bhūman" has been taught as the Self of all through the passage beginning with "That indeed is below," and after the meditation on the "I" (ahaṅgrahopāsana) has been enjoined by the passage "Now, therefore, the instruction on the I"—the text, in order to dispel any suspicion that this might be a mere injunction for a ritual visualization (dṛṣṭividhi), reaffirms the previously introduced state of being the Self of all and demonstrates that the initial teaching of the Self culminates in that very point, by means of the passage beginning with "Now, therefore, the instruction on the Self. Thus it should be understood.
Thus ends the section concerning the "Abundance" (bhūman).

The Gārgī Brāhmaṇa: "Then Gārgī Vācaknavī questioned him. She said, 'O Yājñavalkya, that which is this entire universe, woven like warp and woof upon the waters—upon what, then, are the waters woven like warp and woof? 'Upon the wind, Gārgī,' he replied. 'Upon what, then, is the wind woven like warp and woof? 'Upon the worlds of the intermediate space, Gārgī. 'Upon what, then, are the worlds of the intermediate space woven like warp and woof? 'Upon the worlds of the Gandharvas, Gārgī. 'Upon what, then, are the worlds of the Gandharvas woven like warp and woof? 'Upon the worlds of the Ādityas.'"

"O Gārgī," he said, "upon what, indeed, are the worlds of the sun woven back and forth? "Upon the worlds of the moon, O Gārgī. "Upon what, indeed, are the worlds of the moon woven back and forth? "Upon the worlds of the stars, O Gārgī. "Upon what, indeed, are the worlds of the stars woven back and forth? "Upon the worlds of the gods, O Gārgī. "Upon what, indeed, are the worlds of the gods woven back and forth? "Upon the worlds of Indra, O Gārgī. "Upon what, indeed, are the worlds of Indra woven back and forth? "Upon the worlds of Prajāpati, O Gārgī. "Upon what, indeed..."

"In the worlds of Prajāpati, Gārgī," [Yājñavalkya replied]. "In what, then, are the worlds of Prajāpati woven to and fro? He said, "Gārgī, do not ask beyond this, lest your head shatter. You are asking about a deity that should not be asked beyond. Gārgī, do not ask beyond! Thereupon Gārgī Vācaknavī ceased questioning. "Vācaknavī" means "the daughter of Vācaknu. "That which should not be asked beyond" means that it is unfit for questioning in a debate intended for victory.

Immediately following that is the question of Uddālaka: "Then Vācaknavī said, 'Venerable Brahmins, come now, I shall ask these two questions; if he answers them for me, then truly none among you will ever defeat him in debate. [Yājñavalkya said,] 'Ask, Gārgī.'"

She said, "Yājñavalkya, just as a warrior-son of the Kāśis or the Videhas might string a drawn bow, take two arrows with feathered shafts capable of piercing the enemy, and stand ready—just so have I approached you with two questions. Answer them for me. "Ask, Gārgī," he replied.

She said: "O Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—in what, indeed, is that woven lengthwise and crosswise? "In space alone," he replied, "is that woven lengthwise and crosswise. "But in what, then, is space woven lengthwise and crosswise?"

He said: "Gārgī, the knowers of Brahman declare this very syllable to be neither coarse nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, neither shadowy nor dark, neither air nor space; it is without attachment, without taste, without smell, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind, without radiance, without breath, without mouth, and without measure. It has no interior and no exterior; it eats nothing whatsoever, and nothing whatsoever eats it. By the command of this very syllable, Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart."

"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, moments, hours, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and years stand held apart. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the rivers flowing from the white mountains flow eastward, while others flow westward toward whatever direction they follow. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, humans praise those who give; the gods are intent upon the sacrificer, and the ancestors are dependent upon the ladle."

"O Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, performs sacrifices, or practices austerities without knowing this Imperishable—one may do so for many thousands of years, yet all that belongs to them becomes finite. Furthermore, O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is pitiable; but he who departs from this world having known this Imperishable is a true Brāhmaṇa."

This very syllable, O Gārgya, is unseen yet the seer, unheard yet the hearer, unthought yet the thinker, unknown yet the knower; other than this there is no seer, other than this there is no hearer, other than this there is no thinker, other than this there is no knower. In this very syllable, O Gārgya, the ether is woven like warp and woof.

She said: "O venerable Brāhmaṇas, you should consider yourselves fortunate if you can escape from him by merely paying him homage; for truly, none among you will ever defeat him in debate regarding the Veda. Thereupon, Vācaknavī ceased speaking. "None among you... and so forth: the meaning is that not even one among you will be a victor over this Yājñavalkya in debate concerning the Veda (*brāhṛodya*, i.e., *brāhṛvāda*). [The king] was the Kāśyan Videha—the King of Kāśī, the King of Videha. "With the bowstring unstrung" means with the string removed.

"Be prepared for the second question, 'Hold it for another,'" means: "Be ready. From the white mountains, such as the Himavat and others. "Why do you hold me in such high regard?"—what is that? It is because of departing after having offered salutations to this Yājñavalkya; the sense is that his victory is not to be doubted even by the mind. And that...

Regarding the phrase "of that which is distinct from the Supreme Self," the opponent's position here is twofold: either, in the passage "That, O Gārgī, which is above the sky, and that which is below," the word *ākāśa* refers to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), and the "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) is designated as the unmanifest ether (*avyākṛtākāśa*) by virtue of being its substratum; or else, the word *ākāśa* refers to the unmanifest ether itself, and [the Imperishable] is pointed out as its substratum.

The meaning is that pride (*māna*) is also that very same thing, just as [it is said] "he is established in his own greatness. Regarding the phrase "not in the intermediate space" (*nāntarikṣe*), this is a supplementary statement to the injunction: "Fire is not to be piled on earth, nor in the intermediate space, nor in heaven; therefore, having placed gold [therein], it is to be piled. In light of a careful consideration of the natural sense of the sentence—"the word 'imperishable' (*akṣara*) is seen to refer to the Supreme"—the passage appears to be merely a statement made out of zeal to refute the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding Pradhāna. Because of this lack of intrinsic force (*asvarasa*), he says: "Or rather, it is a challenge from a bystander. The statement that the word *anta* signifies a limit (*avadhi*) and so forth is illustrative; for *anta* indeed means dissolution (*laya*).

It should also be understood that the word "end" (*anta*), by its mention of reaching the state of being a cause, indicates the *kāraṇa* (the cause). [The text states: "It is fit to be the substratum for the entire collection of modifications. Now, one might object: while it is possible for space (*ākāśa*) to be the locus of all contracted modifications by means of providing room for air and water, the status of being the locus of all uncontracted modifications is not possible even for the *pradhāna*, because it is not the locus of the modifications residing in the individual soul (*jīva*).

If it is argued that, for this reason, the abandonment of the conventional meaning of the word *ākāśa* is useless, we say no; because of the reference to that which has arisen from the body as existing within the space between heaven and earth in the passage, "That which is between heaven and earth," and because in that context the inclusion of the *ākāśa* containing air is inevitable, the sense is that the elemental *ākāśa* cannot possibly be its substratum.

Now, how can the question—"O Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky and that which is below the earth"—and its answer, have the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) as their subject? For this would contradict the preceding context; for it is related in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* that at Janaka’s sacrifice, because [the sages] were from the lands of the Kurus and Pañcālas, the current demonstration of the word *akṣara* as being used in its etymological sense is false.

When it is stated, "That which they call the past, the present, and the future—all that is woven, both lengthwise and crosswise, in space alone," the space (ākāśa) indicated as the substratum for the entire collection of modifications existing in the three periods of time cannot be the elemental space accompanied by air, because even that is included among the modifications; therefore, what is designated here by the word "space" is understood to be the subtle essence of Being (bhūtasūkṣma).

Therefore, it is asked what serves as the support even for that subtle element: "In what, indeed, is space woven like warp and woof? Consequently, the Imperishable (akṣara) which is pointed out as the support cannot be the Pradhāna.

As for the claim that what is established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is perceived prior to what is established by scripture (*śruti*), that is not so; for when the word *akṣara* conveys its own meaning through its etymological power (*avayava-śakti*), it does not depend on another means of knowledge. Whatever means of knowledge apprehends the nature of an object at the time of grasping the relationship between word and meaning, that same means need not be relied upon at the time of conveying that meaning.

Anticipating this objection, the venerable author of the Bhāṣya, following the actual state of things, has proposed that the word *akṣara* possesses a derivative (yaugika) meaning in both instances; he does not do so because it is useful for the present context, as he states by saying "either by conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) or by the power of its constituent parts (*avayava-śakti*)," and so forth.

The phrase "for [this] would be the case when there is a conclusion in a specific [meaning]" means that if the word were to conclude in a specific meaning without depending at all on the means of knowledge that establishes its etymological derivation, only then would it be appropriate for the statement in the Bhāṣya—that the sentence-meaning is free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*)—to hold true during the stage of its communication; therefore, the sense is that even when there is a conclusion in a specific meaning, freedom from expectancy is what is intended by that Bhāṣya.

Now, one might ask: what is the contextual indicative mark (*liṅga*) here that establishes the conclusion regarding the specific [nature of the Self] within this Brāhmaṇa? To this he says: "The indicative mark of the Supreme Self is shown here. By the word *dharma* in the phrase "merit and demerit" (*dharmādharmādi*), in contrast to worldly attributes such as the whiteness or redness of a jar, there is the reference to the non-worldly [attribute] consisting of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

The meaning is as follows: because of the observed swiftness [of cognition] by those who have practiced the term *dharma*, so too, by means of the word *adharma*, there is observed swiftness in the cognition of the non-worldly (*alaukika*), unseen form of *adharma*—in contrast to worldly objects such as the pot itself, which is distinct from properties like "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Similarly, by means of the word *īśvara*, there is observed swiftness in the cognition of a non-worldly object in contrast to worldly earthen objects. The point is that regarding the word "cow" (*gavī*), the first cognition occurs only for a cow-individual with which one has long been familiar through repeated practice.

The phrase "it will be stated that validity is possible" refers to the section [of the *Brahma-sūtra*] beginning with "on account of the impossibility of the composition" (*racanānupapatteḥ*). The word "akṣara" (the Imperishable) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*). Regarding this, the Vedāntācāryas state in the *Nyāyasiddhāñjana*: "And that is the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) consisting of the three qualities in equilibrium. Even in that [state], by resorting to a slight distinction, the word 'akṣara,' which is mentioned alongside the 'unmanifest' (*avyakta*), is frequently employed as referring to the conscious [soul]. Or, following the manner of its explanation elsewhere, although the soul is by nature changeless, [it is so designated] in relation to the individual soul."

Because of the statement regarding being created; and because, even though there is a modification of the nature of consciousness, the application of the word *akṣara* (the Imperishable) occurs [in that sense], it is established that it is appropriate to assume a primary power (*śakti*) of the word *akṣara*—which otherwise refers to something other than the Supreme Brahman—even for a particular non-intelligent state (*acid-avasthā-viśeṣa*). To demonstrate this, since the word *akṣara* cannot have its primary meaning applied to a particular material cause (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*) in various places in the Brāhmaṇa, and since there would be no purpose for a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on a connection with the *akṣara* that is the Supreme Brahman, whereas it is fitting to explain specific types of dissolution (*laya-viśeṣa*) through a non-abandoning metaphorical indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) based on a connection with the individual soul (*jīva*), [it is said]: "Both of these dissolve into the Supreme Self."

Furthermore, because both [the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* and the *Chāndogya*] speak of dissolution (*laya*) and so forth, the intention is that here only *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication) is appropriate; thus, it has been stated that there is no contradiction whatsoever, which should be reflected upon here. Now, one might object: "In this context, the word 'Supreme Self' (*paramātman*) in the phrase 'because of the support of everything up to the ether being dependent on the command of the Supreme Self' does not refer to the *Akṣara* (the Imperishable). For even though such scriptural passages as 'By the command of this very Akṣara, O Gārgī, the sun and moon stand supported' exist, the word 'up to the ether' (*ambarānta*) is not heard there. This is the sense of the objection.

"Due to the excellence of the object" means due to the non-restriction of the object. As for the phrase "in other Śrutis": if it is argued that although in other Śrutis the quality of being the support of all things dependent on His command is heard as a characteristic of the Supreme Self, there is no hearing of such a unique characteristic of the Supreme Self in the Akṣara Brāhmaṇa—then it is replied: in the passage, "O Gārgī, by the command of this very Imperishable," the word *vai* (indeed) indicates what is well-known from other sources of knowledge; therefore, it is necessary to demonstrate another authoritative means of proof [for that claim].

It should be understood that this statement was cited with the intention that the meaning of a corroborative (anuvāda) sentence must be described in accordance with its source (prāpaka) sentence; since the source sentence is heard to enjoin "all" without restriction, the corroborative sentence must also have that same meaning. Now, one might object: "If it follows that heaven, earth, and so forth are not subject to His control, and you accept this as a desired conclusion (iṣṭāpatti), then you must simply rely on other means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
