Why cite this [scriptural] passage which depends upon them? Anticipating this dissatisfaction, he says, "Furthermore, of whom... and so forth.

It is heard that there is the upholding of the indeterminate; therefore, having established the upholding of the indeterminate, in response to the inquiry as to how that indeterminate is upheld, the passage beginning with "In the governance of this very Imperishable" is taught to demonstrate that upholding is dependent upon the Teaching (Śāsana).

The context has begun; its intended meaning is this: for the Imperishable Supreme Brahman, who sustains the entire collection of objects beginning with the sun and the moon by His command, what burden is there in sustaining [the earth] by His governance? And thus, because the passage beginning with "By the governance of this very Imperishable" is intended to establish the manner in which everything up to the sky is supported, the sense is that even the support of everything up to the sky is established as being dependent upon His command.

Now, one might object: "The state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) consists in possessing knowledge produced by the eye, and the state of being a hearer (*śrotṛtva*) consists in possessing knowledge produced by the ear; these cannot possibly exist in the Supreme Self, which is devoid of instruments. To this, he says: "The words 'seer' and so forth... The meaning is as follows: the seer is the direct perceiver of form, the hearer is the direct perceiver of sound, the thinker is the direct perceiver of what is to be thought, and the cognizer is the direct perceiver of what is to be determined.

He demonstrates the utility of the present teaching by means of the words "of the teaching" (*śāsanasya*), which explain that the terms "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) and so forth signify the state of being the direct perceiver of form and other objects. The phrase "because they are unfit" (*teṣām ayogyatvāt*) means because seeing, hearing, reflecting, and so forth—which consist of knowledge produced by the eyes, ears, mind, and other senses—are unfit [for the Self]. Now, one might object that even the Supreme Self is seen by yogis who are eternally liberated, as well as by Himself; therefore, he says "by all yogis."

He states the reason for the term *sarva* (all) referring to the totality of each individual class [of qualities] with the words: "because its function is unrestricted" (*asyāsaṅkucitavṛttitayā*). The meaning is that the capacity to see (*draṣṭṛtva*) and so forth, when qualified by being "unseen" (*adṛṣṭatva*) and so on, serves to distinguish the inner self (*pratyagātman*) [from others]. That is to say, it is qualified by being unseen by those who are not yogis. [Objection: But even the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is seen as being known through one's own notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*); thus, there is no distinction. [Reply: No, because the intended meaning here is "unseen by those who are not yogis."

"Like its own nature" means like the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Now, one might object: since in the passage beginning with "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*), qualities such as being unseen and being the seer are heard of individually as attributes, how can the exclusion of the inner self be achieved by means of "being a seer qualified by being unseen"? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "by the words ending in the locative case," intending to show that the desired conclusion is established because the meaning of the scripture is obtained as "that which is unseen is the seer."

[Objection: But surely, since the property belongs only to that which is qualified, it is improper to state the distinction by saying that "the quality of being a seer" (draṣṭṛtva) excludes the Pradhāna while "being qualified by not being seen" (adṛṣṭatva-viśeṣita) excludes the inner self (pratyagātman), because the property belongs only to the qualified entity. Furthermore, the restriction "by those who are not yogis" is also redundant, since the same would apply to the quality of being a seer as qualified by not being seen by others. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Or rather, [it is seen] by those who know the objects of form, sound, and so forth."

In this second interpretation, the sense is that the subject matter of the statement beginning with "nānyadataḥ" (nothing other than this) alone is intended. [The phrase] "it would be explicitly stated" refers to the fact that in the second interpretation, [the meaning] is established by implication; this will be clear later on. The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the reasons already mentioned.

Thus, the interpretation regarding the interval between [the *iṣu* and *viṣṭuti* sacrifices] is that it aims to include unmentioned reasons, as will be clear later. The phrase "in another similar person under discussion" refers to the fact that in the seventh book (*adhyāya*) it was established that in the passage, "The *iṣu* and *viṣṭuti* last for seven days; the rest is the same as the *śyena*," the word "rest" (*itara*) refers to the specific auxiliary parts of the previously mentioned similar *śyena*. This is the intended meaning.

In the commentary on the phrase *etasyādhārabhūtam*, it is possible that the word *etad* (this) refers to the syllable (*akṣara*), and it is also possible that it refers to the world (*jagat*), since both have been previously introduced. Considering that if it referred to the syllable, then by stating that there is nothing whatsoever that supports the syllable, an excessive negation would have been made; whereas in the alternative case, there would be a symmetrical negation—bearing this in mind, he explains [the passage] with the words *etasyākṣarasya* and so forth: "What is here, that is there; what is there, that is also here."

"One goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity. It should be seen as one alone; 'there is not anything here that is diverse. One goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity. Since the negation of difference is possible in such passages as the *Kaṭhavallī* and the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, the opponent raises a doubt with the words "But [the text] says 'nothing else... etc., asking: what is the reason for resorting to the interpretation that the Brāhmaṇa passage intends to negate only equals and superiors? By the phrase "if in some place," the intention is to refer to passages such as "for where there is, as it were, duality" (*yatra hi dvaitam iva bhavati*).

The sense is that even by going as far as possible with the phrase "if it were possible," [the statement] remains merely a subordinate element to the injunction of identity. Therefore, one should not argue that this sentence is intended to negate other perceivers similar to the subject under discussion, and thus, even on this view, the previously mentioned defect remains unavoidable; for since the fact that the perceiver alone is the hearer—and that there is no other perceiver—is already established by the very statement "there is no other perceiver than this," a separate negation for each would be redundant.

The point is that even though the functions of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*), a hearer (*śrotṛtva*), and so forth do not exceed [the nature of] the Self, there is a purpose [in the statement]. For when it is said, "there is no seer," although one might perceive that there is no equality regarding the aspect of being a seer, there remains the possibility of the doubt that there *is* equality regarding the aspect of being a hearer. Regarding the phrase "giving at the command" (*praśāsane dadataḥ*): the locative case in *praśāsane* is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). Thus, humans praise those who give by his command, and the gods praise one who performs sacrifice by his command.

The meaning is that the ancestors praise the *darvī-homa* (ladle-oblation) performed according to His command. Regarding the phrase "they are obedient" (*anuvaśāḥ*), it means they are dependent upon Him. The meaning is that although gods, ancestors, and others are powerful lords who could subsist otherwise, they have adopted this wretched mode of life because of His decree.

Regarding the phrase "in that [case], desiring to avoid": if the falsity (mithyātva) of the Brahman is what is desired to be avoided, then, since a distinction between the Brahman and the seer must necessarily be admitted, the Brahman could not be the subject of the statement "the unseen Seer" (adṛṣṭaṃ draṣṭṛ). This is the meaning. As for the phrase "of the Pradhāna being the Lord," the sense is that since the quality of being a ruler (praśāsitṛtva) culminates in lordship (īśvaratva), whereas the quality of being a seer (draṣṭṛtva) culminates in the state of being the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Thus ends the section on the Imperishable (akṣarādhikaraṇa).

In the *Praśnopaniṣad*: "Then Śaibya Satyakāma asked him: 'Venerable sir, if one among men should meditate upon the syllable Om until the end of his life, which world indeed does he win by that? To him he said: 'Satyakāma, this syllable Om is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, the wise man, by means of this very support, attains one or the other. (1–2)

If he meditates on it as having only one measure, he is led by that very [meditation] at once to the world of the earth; the Ṛg-verses lead him to the world of men, and there, endowed with austerity, celibacy, and faith, he experiences greatness. But if he attains the mind through two measures, he is led up to the intermediate space by the Yajus-formulas; he goes to the world of Soma, and having experienced splendor in the world of Soma, he returns again.

Furthermore, he who meditates upon the Supreme Person by means of this very syllable "Om" consisting of three measures, having attained the sun, becomes like a snake that is freed from its slough; even so, indeed, he is freed from evil. Led upward by the Sāmans, he reaches the world of Brahman. From this mass of life, he beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high. Regarding this, there are these two verses: The three stages of life, which lead to death, are employed in three ways; they are mutually connected, yet not joined together.

When the intermediate and middle rites are properly performed, the knower does not tremble. (6) With the *ṛg* verses he reaches this world, with the *yajus* formulas the atmosphere, and with the *sāman* chants that which the seers know; the wise one follows that which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme, by means of the *oṃkāra* as its very abode. (7) "Unperceived" means favored. "He merges into the mind" means he meditates with the mind. "Driven by the mortal" means driven by those who are afraid of death.

The meaning is that if they were mutually attached yet not intentionally employed, the Knower would not tremble even when the measures (*mātrā*) are correctly applied. The reading "the unseen Seer" (*adṛṣṭo draṣṭā*)—which asserts that the Supreme Self is the Seer—is due to the error of a scribe; for it should be understood that in the *Akṣara-brahman* [section], the neuter reading "the unseen Seer" (*adṛṣṭaṃ draṣṭṛ*) alone exists.

Since it could be argued that the term *brāhmaloka* found in the subject sentence (*viṣayavākya*) is difficult to interpret otherwise, the statement that the term *antarikṣa* is difficult to interpret would be inappropriate; therefore, with this underlying concern, he says, "Or rather, [the difficulty applies] to the word *ākāśa*. Intending to show that the phrase "he is led up by the Sāmans" refers to a single stage because of the hearing of a different word there, he explains: "The meaning is 'by those accompanied by the singing of the Sāmans. Since it is impossible for liberated beings who are *ativāhika* (conveyors) to say "come to this world," he says: "by those employing conciliatory speech."

Nor should it be argued that because of the frequent mention of the *Ṛk* and *Yajus* in the passage, "The *Ṛks* lead him to the world of men, by the *Yajuses* he is led to the world of Soma," it is proper to take the word "Sāman" as referring to the Veda itself; for even in the case of the *Ṛk* and so on, the Veda cannot possibly be the leader, and since one would have to resort to figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*) and other difficulties there as well, the argument from frequent mention (*prāyapāṭha*) does not hold. Thus, having established the nature of the Supreme Self—although [the objection continues]... "nor indeed... [is stated].

In the *Vācaspatya*, it is observed that "every philosophical system has reality (*tattva*) as its object," because there are also systems whose objects are not reality. Thus, since the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) shows that even the act of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) has the Supreme Self as its object, it should be understood that this statement was made with the intention that the opponent does not accept the restriction that the object of "seeing" must necessarily be the Supreme Self. Nevertheless, even while accepting that the object of "seeing" is the Supreme Self, the prima facie position proceeds by asserting that the object of "meditating" (*dhyāyati*) is different from that; it is with this in mind that the aforementioned [statement] was made.

"It attains that" means it attains the word ending in the fifth case (the ablative). It should be understood that this is in relation to the states of gods and animals; this is the implied sense. Now, an objection: since at the very beginning [of the text] Brahman is divided into two as "the higher and the lower," and because of the qualification by "higher" in the passage, "One should meditate upon the higher Person," and "He sees the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high," it is already established that "Brahman" here refers to the higher one; furthermore, the word "Person" qualified by "higher" is unique to that [highest Brahman], and [qualities such as] being peaceful, undecaying, and so forth [belong to it].

If it is asked, "How can there be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) given that the mere mention [of the word *manuṣya*] in the context of the sequence of worlds beginning with 'human' cannot override the indicative marks (*liṅga*), since those marks conflict with many other indicatory signs?"—it is replied: because the prima facie proponent maintains the conviction that the indicative mark consisting of the act of beholding the Person situated in the world of the Four-faced One (Brahmā)—as understood from the sequence of worlds—is not otherwise established. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "indicated by a word ending in the neuter gender," the term "this" (*etad*) refers to the fact of being indicated by a neuter word.

The sense is that it is being grasped. Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "embodiedness has action as its cause": the word *ghana* is prescribed [as a synonym] for *mūrti* (form/shape) in the rule "mūrtau ghanaḥ. It is explained that *mūrti* means solidity (*kāṭhinya*). The point is that the solidity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is mediated by the body, and precisely because of this embodiedness, its being produced by karma is also established. Regarding the phrase "for indeed, because of having a body": the meaning is that the four faces of the Self are possible [only thus]. According to the *Bhāṣya*, "the world of the four-faced one is perishable."

Objection: If the term *brāhmaloka* refers to the supreme world of Brahman (*parabrahmaloka*), then since the four-faced Brahmā has not been previously mentioned, the word "from this" (*etasmāt*) could not refer to the subject under discussion (the *jīvaghana*). Therefore, one must accept—following the tradition of Śaṅkara and others—that the term *brāhmaloka* refers specifically to the world of the four-faced Brahmā, and that the pronoun "from this" (*etasmāt*) refers to the four-faced Brahmā as indicated by the word *brahma* contained within the compound *brāhmaloka*. Response: This is not so.

Even if the word *brāhmaloka* refers to the world of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), it is impossible to refer back to the Four-faced One because he is subordinated within the compound; nor should it be argued that the reference is to the world of the Four-faced One itself as the primary element [of the compound], for the term *jīvaghana* (the mass of living beings) does not apply there.

Even if it were somehow assumed that [the term] refers to the *vṛtti* (mental modification), it would be improper to establish the superiority of the conscious being over the unconscious world of the four-faced Brahmā; therefore, it should be understood that this word [“this”] correctly refers to the *jīvaghana* (the mass of individual souls) as something about to be introduced, just as in the passage beginning with “Now, light...”. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), etc., although [the word] “etcetera”...

In the sentences presented as the literal meaning of the words, the state of being visible to the wise (*sūri-dṛśyatva*) is not perceived; rather, only the state of being the support for the sun (*sūryādhāratva*) is evident. Even in the verse, "That [state] the inspired ones (*viprāsaḥ*), the praising ones (*vipanyavaḥ*), ever extol and kindle," the term *vipanyavaḥ* means those whose nature is praise, and *jāgṛvāṃsaḥ* means those whose knowledge is unerring. Since this has been explained in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* with the words, "Ever extolling that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, they kindle [it]," nevertheless, it should be understood that the statement was made with the intention that the state of being visible to the wise is also established by implication for that which serves as the station of the wise.

Regarding the phrase "the other world called Brahman" (*yadaparaṃ kāryaṃ brāhmam*), the interpretation in the *Bhāṣya* is that it is appropriate for the word "the world of Brahman" (*kāryabrāhmaloka*) to denote the world of the four-faced one (Caturmukha) as being designated by the term "the other Brahman" (*apara-brāhma*), and not as being the world of the Supreme Brahman (*para-brāhma*). This is the construction [of the argument]. By the phrase "by way of indication" (*upalakṣaṇatayā*), it is meant that if one accepts the primary meaning of the word "intermediate space" (*antarikṣa*), then in both positions [of the opponent], there remains the qualification of an intervening distance. Furthermore, if, in order to avoid this intervention, one resorts to the view that the word "intermediate space" indicates merely the worlds situated below the world of the four-faced one, thereby removing the intervention, then one must likewise resort to the view that the word "intermediate space" indicates merely the world beyond [this one] (*amuṣmika*).

The sense is that the avoidance of intervention is the same [in both cases]. Regarding "the attainment of the subsumer" (*saṅgrāhakalābha*): while it is easy to state that the subsumer consists in being situated between the earth-world (*bhūrloka*) and the brahma-world (*brāhmaloka*), the sense is that because such a subsumer is cumbersome, it is not easily understood. "Contradiction with the statement of the fruit" means contradiction with the word "person" (*puruṣa*) in the sentence concerning the fruit. The section on the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.

Now, regarding this small lotus-like dwelling within this Brahma-city, there is a small space (ākāśa) within it; that which is inside it is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand.

If they should say to him, "In this city of Brahman, there is this small lotus-palace; within it is this small ether. What is there that is to be sought after, or that one should desire to understand? he should reply: "As vast as this external ether is, so vast is this ether within the heart. Both heaven and earth are contained within it; both fire and wind, both the sun and the moon."

"Lightning, the stars, and whatever else belongs to him here, whether it exists or does not exist—all that is contained within this. If they should say to him, "If all this is contained within this city of Brahman—namely, all beings and all desires—then when one suffers old age or perishes, what remains of it? he should reply: "It does not age with his aging; it is not slain by his being slain. This is the true city of Brahman; within it, desires are contained."

This Self is free from evil, without blemish, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst; its desires are true, its resolves are true. Just as subjects follow their king, entering wherever he goes, according to his command—whatever region they desire, whatever country, whatever portion of land—they subsist upon that very thing; even so, in the next world, the world acquired through merit is exhausted. Therefore, for those who depart having discovered this Self and these true desires, there is no lack of freedom of movement in all worlds.

"Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds. In the scriptural passages cited here and there, the meaning is not clearly defined according to the views of others; however, the meaning intended by our own school (*siddhānta*) will be clear later on. "If they should say to him"—that is, to the teacher who has spoken thus.

If they should say, "The disciples might urge: 'How is it that within this limited city of Brahman, there is a small, tiny lotus-palace, and even therein is space? What is there [in that space]?'—the meaning is that there is nothing at all."

"If there were indeed something [within] the size of a jujube fruit, what would be the purpose of searching for it or desiring to know it?"—when addressed thus, the Teacher would say: "As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart. By demonstrating such magnitude, the smallness that served as the seed of the objection is set aside. The answer to the objection—"What is there found therein?"—is stated with the words beginning, "Both [the heaven and earth] are in this," and so forth.

That which is to be sought within that [space] is taught by the passage beginning with "And what he has here," and so forth. This is its meaning: whatever belongs to this embodied being in this world, and whatever does not exist here now—whether it has perished or is yet to come—all that is contained within this small space (daharākāśa).

And this refers here to the collection of objects of enjoyment—such as fathers, mothers, brothers, sons, wives, songs, musical instruments, and so forth—which arise from one's own volition and relate to the infinite previous births one desires to see; this will be described later for one who has reached the world of Brahmā through the meditation on the "small" (dahara), in the passage beginning: "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers rise up for him."

If they should say: "If this city of Brahman were to perish, all this and all beings would be dissolved within it," the meaning of such an objection is as follows: just as when a granary or similar vessel becomes worn out and incapable of supporting its load, the rice and other grains stored within it can no longer remain; so too, when the body—which is designated by the term "city of Brahman"—is affected by old age and the like, the heaven, earth, and so forth existing within it would not remain. This is the intent of the objection. But what is the intent behind the claim that "when the body is destroyed, the heaven, earth, and so forth existing within the space of the *dahara* (the small lotus) would perish"?

Having set forth the dilemma in his mind—namely, whether the destruction of heaven, earth, and so forth necessarily follows from the destruction of the body because the small ether (*daharākāśa*) which supports them would also necessarily perish when its support is gone; or else, whether even though the small ether still exists, it no longer functions as the sustainer of heaven, earth, and so forth (just as the space within a granary does not sustain things once the granary is destroyed), and thus the destruction of heaven, earth, and so forth follows from the body’s destruction acting as the sole sustainer—he first refutes the former alternative with the words: "Not by its decay."

He refutes the second [position]: "This is true: 'In this city of Brahman, all desires are contained'. And thus, since the small ether (daharākāśa) itself—which is of the nature of Brahman and distinct from the space within a granary—is the substratum for the containment of all desires, the body is not the determining factor; therefore, even upon the destruction of the body, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the destruction of heaven, earth, and so forth—such is his intention. "One whose desires are true" (satyakāma) means one whose desires are not false; "one whose resolves are true" (satyasaṅkalpa) means one whose resolves are not false.

And because there is a relationship of cause and effect between desire (*kāma*) and volition (*saṅkalpa*), there is no tautology. For instance, the meaning of the passage beginning with "Just as here on earth creatures enter [into others]" is as follows: just as in this world creatures, regarding another as their master, enter into and follow that master's instructions exactly as they are given, and thereby obtain the objects desired by themselves; in the same way, those who perform meritorious deeds also become partakers of the fruits thereof by following the commands of the Supreme. This is the intended meaning.

With the words beginning with "Just as here," etc., he states the perishability of the fruit obtained through service to a king, and likewise the perishability of the fruit obtained through merit. The rest is clear. Regarding the phrase "of the one reclining in the city" (*puriśayasya*): although in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*—in the passage, "Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace"—only the mere existence within the city of Brahman is heard and not the act of reclining, nevertheless, because reclining is heard in the *Vājasaneyaka*, which belongs to the same context, namely, "He who is in this space within the heart, therein he lies," it is so understood here as well.

It should be understood that the state of dwelling in the city (*puriśayatva*) has thus been established. The meaning is that the status of the one denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) as the lower self (*aparamātman*) is being refuted; that is, the status of the one dwelling in the city who is denoted by the word "ether" as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is being refuted. Regarding the words "the world of Brahman" (*brāhmaloka*) and "the city of Brahman" (*brāhmapura*), the meaning is the words found in the passages "they do not find this world of Brahman" and "this is the true city of Brahman. The intention is that, by establishing that these refer to the world situated above which is the abode of the Supreme Self, rather than to the well-known intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

The meaning is as follows: although the three [terms] are equal in their capacity to postulate an unestablished meaning due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the *dahara-ādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the small space) and the *akṣara-ādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the Imperishable) possess a greater degree of proximity than the *antarikṣa-śabda* (the word "intermediate space") does in its postulation of an unestablished meaning, when compared to the *īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the object of the act of seeing). Thus, it is because of this superior connection (*saṅgatyatiśaya*). [Objection: But surely, the common characteristic of all three is their intent to establish that a word denoting "space" (*ākāśa*) has a meaning beyond its conventional sense.
By way of establishing that the term "space" (*ākāśa*), which denotes both the syllable and the locus of the act of piercing, has a meaning distinct from its conventional sense.

The common characteristic [of the two] is that they both serve to establish the state of being the Supreme Self for one who has fallen into error. If it is asked, "Since the word *antarikṣa* also denotes the ether (*ākāśa*), what is the deciding factor here?"—if the underlying assumption is that there is no difference [between the two cases], then the sequence of the section on the "Object of Vision" (*īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*) immediately following the section on the Imperishable (*akṣarādhikaraṇa*) is indeed appropriate; for in the former, there is the additional connection of an objection: since "the unseen Seer" (*adṛṣṭaṃ draṣṭṛ*) is heard as being "unseen," it would follow that it cannot be the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*). Thus, the sequence is justified.

The venerable one should be satisfied. The phrase "in some cases, [the word] *paramātman* has the sense of the Supreme Self" means that this occurs in passages such as "They arise from space alone," and so forth. The expression "by way of the sentence" (*vākyadvārakam*) implies that the meaning of the term "from the subsequent ones" (*uttarebhyaḥ*) is "from those occurring in the subsequent sentences. This is for the purpose of clarifying the ablative case. Thus, the intention is that the word "from the causes" (*hetubhyaḥ*) serves to clarify the grammatical sense of the ablative in the phrase "from the subsequent ones" (*uttarebhyaḥ*).

The sixth rule concerns the restriction regarding the use of the causal (*hetu*) [in compound]. Regarding the statement "when a causal term is used, the genitive [is employed]" (*ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge*), because the word *uttara* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), there would be either the genitive or the instrumental case according to the rule "and the instrumental for pronouns" (*sarvanāmnas tṛtīyā ca*). The intention of the objection is that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) should not occur here. Furthermore, this should be understood as stated without regard for the Vārttika: "In the senses of 'occasion,' 'cause,' and 'reason,' all cases are generally seen. One might object: "But surely this is not explained in such a way in the *Vṛtti* and other treatises."

If it is argued that this [interpretation] is not correct because, in cases such as *vidyāyā hetoḥ yaśaḥ* ("fame due to learning"), the genitive case would be untenable since learning lacks the status of being a *prayojaka* (instigator) of fame—and thus the rule for the genitive of cause (*ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge*) would find no application—we say no. For in the grammatical treatises (*śābdika-grantha*), examples such as *annasya hetor vasati* ("he dwells for the sake of food") are cited, while constructions like *vidyāyā hetor yaśaḥ* are not accepted. Furthermore, if the genitive in *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* were intended only to denote a *prayojana* (purpose) and not the domain of causality (*hetutva*), the sūtra *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23) would result in being rendered purposeless.

Nor should it be said that the rule *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.26) prescribes the scope for the employment of the word *hetu*; for the Kāśikā states that this [rule] applies when the word *hetu* is employed [to express the sense of cause]. And since this is universally accepted, some maintain that there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

[Objection: Since the exclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*) is what is about to be introduced, it is the exclusion of the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) that is actually under discussion; and since the exclusion of the elemental ether is established by its being merely the Self (*ātman*), the mention of its being "without limiting adjuncts" (*nirupādhika*) is redundant. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says, "Or rather, even of the ether... The word "inherently" (*svataḥ*) connects with the phrase "related to the body. "Inherent usage" (*svataḥ-prayoga*) means "primary usage" (*mukhya-prayoga*). In the commentary, the passage beginning with "Now, he who here [meditates on] the Self," etc., follows.

Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all worlds. If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him; endowed with that world of the fathers, he is magnified. In this very same way, the successive worlds of the mothers, the brothers, the sisters, the friends, the perfumes, garlands, and scents, the worlds of food and drink, the worlds of songs, instrumental music, and so forth, and the world of women are to be understood.

Immediately following this, it is heard in scripture: "Whatever end he desires, whatever wish he wishes for, that arises for him by his mere volition (saṅkalpa); endowed with that, he exults. Thus should the sequence of the scriptural texts be understood.

Regarding the phrase "of one alone": the point is that, for this very reason, in the case of the injunction "One practicing sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," since the simile of the hawk (*śyena*)—namely, "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes"—recorded in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*) would not be consistent if it were a prescription of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*), it is therefore accepted as being a name (*nāmadheya*).

Regarding the phrase *hmadayāvacchede* (delimitation by the substratum): even when there is non-difference between the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), a simile (*upamā*) is indeed possible provided there exists a difference between the delimiting property of the standard of comparison (*upamānatāvacchedaka*) and the delimiting property of the object of comparison (*upameyatāvacchedaka*). For this very reason, [it is said]: "He took from him the umbrella, newly fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, which possessed rays of light along with its handle..."

The meaning is that in the verse, "He shone with his head close to that silk garment, like the Ganges falling upon the head [of Śiva]," the theorists have accepted this as a variety of simile (*upamābheda*), because there exists a distinction between the delimiters of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*)—namely, the state of having the Ganges stream falling on the head versus the state of having the head near the white silk garment—even though they refer to the same single entity, Hara.

Regarding "emptiness of comparison" (*upamānaśūnyatā*): in instances such as "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa," since similarity—which depends on a distinction between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object compared (*upameya*)—is impossible where there is an absence of both real and adventitious distinctions, this constitutes the figure of speech *ananvaya* (non-comparison). In that case, the non-corresponding [subject] being described in relation to itself results solely in the manifestation of its incomparability. The sense is that just as being established in one's own majesty manifests the fact of having no other support, so it is here.

Regarding the phrase "as far as the word 'yāvat'": the figure *ananvaya* (non-correspondence) occurs only where there is identity between the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), as well as between the standard and the object themselves. In the present case, however, because there exists a difference between the two delimiters—namely, the property of being "as far as" (*yāvatva*) and the property of being situated within the heart—and because there exists a distinction between the standard and the object due to the mutual difference among the various internal portions of space (*ākāśa*), it follows that this is not *ananvaya*. This is the intended meaning.

"Situated between the two sentences" means that it is situated between the two sentences, "What is within that is to be sought" and "This is the Self. Now, one might object: since it is mentioned first, the sentence "This is the Self" shares a uniform case-ending with "that is to be sought"; to this he replies, "And because of its proximity."

Although it might be argued that—even in the phrase "the city of Brahman" (*brāhmapuram*)—the word *brāhma* implies proximity to the Brahman contained therein, making it easy to say that proximity applies even to one who maintains that the Brahman is distinct from the small ether (*daharākāśa*)—nevertheless, because the word *brāhma* ends in the genitive case and thus lacks uniformity in case-ending with the other terms, and because the ether indicated by the compound "city of Brahman" is more proximate than that [contained Brahman], it is appropriate that the pronoun "this" (*eṣaḥ*) refers to the ether itself; such is the intended meaning of the objection beginning with "although."
The reflection upon the Self that is to be sought is [the subject]; therefore, the intention is that in the passage "This Self is free from evil," the portion "this Self" is a restatement (anuvāda).

Consequently, the meaning of the phrase "by way of being the locus of the Self" is that since the marks such as freedom from evil reside within that [Self], there is no evidence to establish that the small ether (daharākāśa) understood from the opening statement is Brahman.

If it is asked: "But how is the question 'What is there within that? or the subsequent passage containing its answer justified, given that the Self has already been determined to be within the small ether (daharākāśa) by the very context?"—it is replied as follows: The intention of those who maintain that the Brahman residing within the small ether is the subject here is this: in the statement "That which is within that is to be sought," it is precisely something other than the small ether that is to be sought; and this is understood to be of the nature of the Self upon a thorough consideration of other scriptural passages.

Nevertheless, the question arises: what is it that exists there, and of what nature is it within those who possess the Self? [The answer is: "As vast as this external space is, so vast is this space within the heart. The meaning of this is as follows: just as this space exists as something exceedingly vast, so too is this entire space within the heart. The word *hṛdaya* refers to the Supreme Self, because it is heard in this very context: "That indeed is the Self in the heart; and since this is not fully expressed [by other words], it is called *hṛdayam* (the unexpressed), therefore it is called 'heart' (*hṛdaya*)."

Furthermore, within the heart—that is, inside the city of Brahman (brāhṛ)—all space exists, as well as heaven, earth, and so forth; this is the meaning. In the preceding sentence, "This is the true city of Brahman," the city of Brahman itself is primarily indicated first and is thus proximate [to the subsequent reference]. Therefore, in the phrase "this is the Self" (eṣa ātmā), it is possible for the pronoun "this" (etad) to refer back to that very city of Brahman. Consequently, it should be understood that there is no room for the objection raised regarding the statement, "As large as this space is," and so on.

[The opponent says: "It might be so according to this commentary, provided that the Śruti itself did not distinguish between the small ether (daharākāśa) and that which dwells within it; however, it *did* distinguish them—this is the reading [of the text]. For in the present context, the very act of distinguishing is what is intended to be expressed. [The author replies: "If you argue, 'It might be so,' and claim that the conditional suffix (*liṅ*) here indicates a counterfactual action (*kriyātipatti*), such that one should have said, 'This would have been so if the Śruti itself had not distinguished between the small ether and that which dwells within it'—that is not correct."

The *Vibhāṣā* states that since there is the possibility of other causes for the conditional suffix (*liṅ*) in expressions such as "if" (*yadi*), which denote probability, one should understand that the application of the periphrastic future (*lṛṅ*) does not follow in either case. The meaning of the phrase "designation by means of the specific [cause]" is that even though a sprout arises from the conjunction of earth, water, wind, and so forth, it is observed in common usage to be designated as a "rice sprout" (*śālyaṅkura*) solely by means of its specific cause, the rice seed. The term "the sovereign of the city subject to that" means the individual soul (*jīva*) residing in the city whose master he is.

The meaning is that at the very beginning [of the passage], with the words "Now, as for this city of Brahman," there is the perception of a city whose master is the individual soul (*jīva*); therefore, it is only logical that its residence should be within that city belonging to him. The reading "the individual soul is a resident of the city subject to his command" is indeed easy to understand; and it has been stated in the Śāṅkara-bhāṣya: "In that regard, the residence of the master of the city in a single part of the city is observed, just as in the case of a king."

And in the *Bhāmatī*, it might be argued: "Let the body be the city of the individual soul (*jīva*); however, the state of being within the small lotus-heart will belong to another, just as Ujjayinī is the city of Vatsarāja while Maitreya’s residence is elsewhere. This is not so; for a dwelling is indeed a locus that requires a specific occupant when no occupant has been specified. Since the owner of the city is the subject under discussion, one connects it with that very occupant rather than postulating a connection with some other, unspecified occupant. Thus it has been stated.

Regarding the phrase "of the primary meaning" (*mukhyārthasya*): in the expression *brāhmapura*, since the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) takes precedence over the genitive case, one must respect the natural sense of the meaning of the nominal stem *brāhman* itself, rather than the natural sense of the relationship characterized by the lord-and-owned relation that constitutes the meaning of the genitive. Consequently, it is appropriate to understand the Supreme Self alone by the word *brāhman*; the intention is that the relationship denoted by the genitive may be either common or uncommon—whatever it may be.

[Objection: But since only two qualities—*satyakāma* (having true desires) and *satyasaṅkalpa* (having true resolves)—are mentioned, the statement that there is a "multitude of qualities" (*guṇajāta*) is inconsistent. To this, he replies: "Because of having true desires and true resolves. [The reason is] that meditation on the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is impossible without meditation on the qualities themselves. [Objection: If meditation on the qualities is necessary because meditation on the possessor of qualities is impossible without it, then since that very meditation is already established by the mere mention of the qualities, there is no inconsistency here. [Reply: No; for...

Furthermore, according to the principle that "that which is obtained through implication (ākṣepataḥ) is subordinate to that which is obtained through direct denotation (abhidhānika)," since it is possible for the possessor of qualities (guṇin) to also be directly denoted as the object of meditation, it is improper to discard that [direct denotation]. Moreover, it would be unjustifiable to resort to such a discrepancy (vairūpya)—wherein the portion concerning the qualities in the sentence stating the result, "Those who depart from here after having found the Self and these true desires," is a restatement of what is obtained through direct denotation, while the portion concerning the possessor of qualities is a restatement of what is obtained through implication.

The meaning is that since the qualities (*guṇa*) are included within the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), when meditation on the possessor of qualities is enjoined, meditation on the qualities is thereby enjoined as a matter of course (*arthasiddha*). One should not, however, be deluded into thinking the meaning is that it would be obtained through implication (*ākṣepalabhya*). For if that were the case, even though the meditativeness of the qualities has been stated, it would be possible for meditation on the possessor of qualities to be obtained through implication; consequently, the subsequent sentence—"but [this is] not [the case] when the meditativeness of the qualities has been stated"—would result in being inconsistent.

It should be observed that this is because it was accepted in the earlier treatise (*pūrvagrantha*) that when meditation on the qualities (*guṇadhyāna*) is enjoined, it necessarily implies meditation on the possessor of the qualities (*guṇidhyāna*), since meditation on the qualities is impossible without [meditation on] the possessor of the qualities. The word "to be sought" (*anveṣṭavya*) refers to the possessor of the qualities; the meaning is that it refers to the possessor of the qualities residing within the small ether (*daharākāśa*). And the point is that this [possessor] is merely the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), and not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Regarding the phrase "by the end of the word 'veśma'": one might object that even if the small lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) as a dwelling is established by the statement "the small lotus is the dwelling" as being the support for the body called the city of Brahman (*brāhmapura*), it has not yet been established that the ether (*ākāśa*) is supported within the lotus of the heart. Therefore, how can the refutation of the opponent's view be accomplished by the end of the word "veśma"? Furthermore, it cannot be argued that the entire textual passage ending with "therein is the small ether" is intended there [as the basis for the refutation].

Furthermore, since it has already been established that the sky (ākāśa) is also the support of the lotus, the restatement of what was merely repeated in the phrase "that which is within it" would be purposeless; thus, it must be explained that this serves to indicate the refutation of the opponent's view.

If that were the case, then the commentary on the passage, "That which is this small lotus-palace in this city of Brahman," would have to be understood as being intended to state the entire textual context up to the words, "In this [palace] there is a small ether. Consequently, the subsequent commentary, "In that small lotus-palace," would not be intended to state the meaning of the sentence "In this [palace] there is a small ether," because the meaning of that sentence would have already been presented. And therefore...

If it is argued that this is true because the phrase "that which is within it" does not refer to the lotus as separated by another [entity] according to the opponent's view, and because the author himself will state later on that he is explaining the sentence "In this, there is a small [space]," we reply: True; nevertheless, the intent here is to indicate that the expression "having restated" (*anūdya*) implies that there is no purpose in restating again an object that has already been restated. As for the reading "anūdyetyādinā," it is indeed easy to understand.

Nor should it be argued that the purpose of the restatement "that which is within it" (*yad antaḥ*) is to establish that what is to be sought is not merely the space itself, but rather the lotus-fiber (*kārṣṇya*) located therein—lest there be redundancy (*vaiyarthyam*). For there is no evidence that such a purpose is established by a subsequent restatement. Furthermore, since pronouns can refer to something immediately preceding when possible, they do not refer to something remote (*vyavahita*).

Because such a construction would be improper, for this very reason, in the *Sākaṃmedha* sacrifice, regarding the statement "This is the one-potsherd cake for Brāhmaṇas," the word *etat* (this) refers to the immediately preceding one-potsherd cake for Varuṇa and others, and not to the distant one-potsherd cake belonging to the Vaiśvadeva; this was established in the seventh [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]. However, in the passage "Cows, horses, donkeys, goats, sheep, sesame, and beans—his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of twelve hundred of these," since it is impossible for merely twelve hundred beans alone to constitute a sufficient sacrificial fee, [the word "twelve hundred"] must refer to those items ending in the plural number.

The sense is that, because it would be improper to refer to "his" (tasya) by means of the singular number while referring to *māṣas*, and because there is an inconsistency in referring to the immediately preceding *māṣas*, [the pronoun] must refer to the more distant *go*; yet, in this case, there is no such obstacle.

Regarding the phrase "of the Supreme Self" (*paramātmanaḥ*), the reading *paraivaṇryata iti* is found in many manuscripts; its meaning is as follows: having raised an objection with the statement "Is there anything existing therein?"—on the grounds that no subtle cause whatsoever can exist within the Supreme Self—the [text] provides a resolution by showing that the effects such as heaven and earth exist within it. Furthermore, the intention of the objection in this work is that no cause can exist within all causes.

The meaning is clearly perceived as follows: others describe the intended resolution as being that there is no fault, because even though no other cause is possible within the Supreme Self—which is the cause of all—there is still the possibility of effects such as heaven and earth arising from It. However, others do not describe the context of this objection and its resolution in this manner; rather, they argue that the small lotus is already extremely subtle, the space contained within it is even more subtle than that, and nothing at all can be measured within that most subtle space.

The intention of the objection is: "What could possibly be sought after? The intention of the reply is that, because the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is as vast as the Brahman-ether (*brāhmyākāśa*), there is no logical impossibility based on its extreme subtlety; therefore, the coexistence within it of all kinds of objects of enjoyment, such as heaven and earth, and its being the object to be sought after, is possible. This is what was stated, and not in the manner [suggested by the opponent]. Therefore, since the meaning of a subsequent explanatory statement must be described in accordance with the preceding statement, the meaning of this text is also exactly that.

Because there is no one whatsoever existing within the Supreme Self, this is precisely the meaning of the subsequent restatement as well. Regarding the phrase "by supplying the masculine pronoun *yat*," the ellipsis is "in the sentence *tasmin yad antar*," and not in the sentence *daharo 'smin*; for if *yat* were supplied in that [latter] sentence, it would result in *daharo 'smin* and so forth forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*), since a sentence containing the word *yat* must necessarily form a single syntactical unit with a sentence containing the word *tat*. Nor is such an unintended consequence desirable, for it is precisely the latter position [that we maintain].

It should be understood that this is because the recourse to a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*) will be explained later. Some, however, say: "The insertion of the word *yat* occurs precisely in the passage 'In this, there is a small inner space' (*daharo'sminnantara ākāśaḥ*), and the status as a single sentence for the portion beginning with 'In this, there is a small... remains established in both views; the only difference lies in whether or not the masculine pronoun *yat* is supplied. In this regard, it should be observed that the insertion of the word *ca* is common to both these positions.

In the phrase "and whatever collection of qualities exists within that," the commentary shows that the word *antarvartī* is an explanation of the word *antaḥ* occurring in the scriptural passage. Now, one might ask: how is it possible for two things—the ether and that which resides within it—to be referred to by a single word? To this, he says: "The pronouns *tyad* and so forth [are used with all genders and numbers]. But then, if there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of the pronouns beginning with *tyad*, how can there be a singular number? Nor should it be argued that the singular number is obtained by the rule "and optionally as a singular" (*ekavaccānyatarasyām*).

If it is argued that this [word *yad*] refers specifically to the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) formed by the fragment of the rule “*napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*” (Pāṇini 1.2.69), since it is referred to by the word in the Sūtra itself, whereas the *ekaśeṣa* formed by other rules does not have that status; [we reply: no, because the form *yad* is possible either through the rule “*vyatyayo bahulam*” (Pāṇini 3.1.85) or “*supāṃ suluk...*” (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Alternatively, just as in the rule “*karmaṇo romanthatapobhyām*” (Pāṇini 3.1.15), the singular form may be justified by intending singularity for each individual member; and likewise, the neuter gender is appropriate here because of the desire to express the commonality of gender (*salliṅgasāmānyavivakṣayā*), just as in the rule “*dvigurekavacanam*” (Pāṇini 2.4.1).

In this very context, it is because the phrase *dṛṣṭam* (seen)—which is neuter singular—can be justified by the very same method explained for the masculine dual adjective *gatiśabdābhyām* in the sūtra: “*gatiśabdābhyāṃ tathā hi dṛṣṭam*. Having established such numerous intrinsic consistencies and the non-application of the rule that serves as an exception (*nivartaka-sūtra*) beginning with “*yacchabdaviṣaye...*” regarding the word *brahma* and so forth, he states another alternative: “*napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*. And here, the word *vā* (or) is required and must be supplied.

The meaning is that there is an inconsistency [in the objection] regarding what could exist within the subtle space residing in the subtle lotus of the heart, concerning the "innermost Self" (*sarvāntara*), which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Here, the phrase "of the Supreme Self" is stated with the intention that its status as the Supreme Self is established by the logic of the final conclusion (*siddhāntanyāya*); however, being the Supreme Self is not the seed for the objection.

It should be understood that for disciples who have heard only this much—"In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small ether"—while the word *ākāśa* (ether), which is incompatible with being the Supreme Self, is still active, and while contradictory marks such as "smallness," "being something to be sought after," and "being the locus of other things" are present, and the marks specific to Brahman have not yet been introduced, neither the ascertainment of [the ether] as the Supreme Self nor the engagement in challenging that [ascertainment] based upon it is possible.

In the phrase "of space and that which exists within it," the genitive case is used in a restrictive sense (*nirdhāraṇe*), meaning "because space is already known. The phrase "and for the purpose of indicating its predominance" is understood to refer to the author of the *Bhāṣya*, and not to the *Śruti*.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the objection—that the entire section concerning these demonstrative pronouns (*idam* and *etad*) referring to the ether (*ākāśa*), including the insertion of the single term "ether" in the passage, "Both heaven and earth are contained within this very ether," would render the textual sequence from "As large as this external ether is, so large is this ether within the heart" superfluous—finds no ground for application. This is because all such references can be established simply by the inclusion of that one term "ether."

"Because it is separated by the word 'space' (ākāśa)" means that the word "space" is separated [from the term for Brahman] in the passage, "As far as this space extends. "Because existence and non-existence are understood to have counter-correlates" means... [that they require a correlate].

The meaning is: "In response to the inquiry, 'Of what is there existence, and of what is there non-existence? The point is this: when the questioner asks, "What exists and what does not exist?", the respondent repeats the words, "All desires. From this repetition, it is determined that the word *yat* (whatever) refers to the entire class of objects of enjoyment (*bhogyajāt*). Although the plural number is understood for the questioners from the phrase "if they should say to him" (*taṃ ced brūyuḥ*), nevertheless, it should be understood that the singular number is used without intending to convey that plurality.

The phrase "anubhāṣaṇavākya" means the restatement of the passage: "If all this—that is, this city of Brahman (brāhmapura)—is contained herein, as well as all beings and all desires. It is appropriate that its purport is unsurpassed enjoyability, for it says: "Whatever living beings belong to him here, and those who are deceased, and whatever else he desires but does not obtain—all that he finds upon going there; for here indeed are his true desires, should he become desirous of the world of the fathers (pitṛloka)."

Since the subsequent textual context—beginning with the words "ityādi"—establishes that the abundance of desired fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, priests, perfumes, garlands, food, drink, dance, song, and so forth, associated with infinite previous births, arises solely from His own volition (*svasaṅkalpa*), and since the reality of these things is accepted in the passage "By His will alone that [creation] comes into being" (*saṅkalpādeva tacchuteḥ*) by accepting their reality while demonstrating that they arise from mere volition, one must set aside the literal meaning and understand that the intended purport lies solely in the state of being unsurpassed objects of enjoyment.

If it is asked, "Why should this be accepted?"—it is true that the status of being a substratum for objects of enjoyment is indeed being established; nevertheless, since the Brahman is what is intended to be sought, the demonstration of the enjoyability of the father and others who reside within it is utterly irrelevant.

Furthermore, even the statement beginning with "And whatever belongs to him here" is intended to demonstrate the unsurpassed enjoyability (*niratiśaya-bhogyatva*) of Brahman by way of establishing that He is the substratum of all objects of enjoyment belonging to the father and others. Thus, although there is an intention regarding [Brahman] being the substratum of the enjoyments of the father and so forth, the *bhāṣya*’s underlying purport is that its ultimate intention (*paramatātparya*) lies in Brahman’s unsurpassed enjoyability; it is precisely on this point that the Teachers (*ācārya*) focus their efforts, and therefore there is no inconsistency. It is not necessary to state separately that [Brahman] possesses unsurpassed enjoyability.

Nor should it be argued that although the state of being bliss (*ānandatva*) alone defines the essential nature (*svarūpa*), the state of being unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānandatva*) does not define the essential nature; for the intended meaning here is that the state of being an unsurpassed object of enjoyment is established precisely because [bliss] is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). Furthermore, regarding the words of the objection and its resolution beginning with "Now, if they should say to him" (*atha taṃ ced brūyuḥ*), it should be understood that the word *atha* is not part of the Vedic text, but rather the author's own introductory remark.

One might object: "Since the answer to the question 'What is found there? has not yet been completed, how can there be room for this objection? To this he replies with the words, "The answer to the question 'What is found there? and so forth. The phrase "because of the abiding of heaven, earth, and so on" connects with what precedes. Thus, the intended meaning is that even if the small ether (*daharākāśa*) were to perish, it would be impossible for heaven, earth, and the rest—which continue to abide—to have that small ether as their substratum.

If it is argued: "But surely this [body] is called the city of Brahman (*brāhmapura*); for there is a scriptural passage stating, 'If all this is contained within this city of Brahman—namely, all beings and all desires—and if one reaches old age or perishes, what remains of it? In this sentence, there is no mention of the *dahara-ākāśa* (the small ether). Therefore, how can you proceed with the objection and its resolution by assuming that the body, denoted by the term 'city of Brahman,' is separated from the *dahara-ākāśa*? [The answer is: "In this [passage], *asmiñ ced idam*..."

The term "concentrated" (*samāhitam*) includes the small ether (*daharākāśa*) as well, because it is possible for it to be encompassed by the word "all" (*sarva*). Nor does the inclusion of the small ether by the word "all" contradict the subsequent text—which explains that the word "all" refers to objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and so forth—since that [subsequent passage] serves as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the small ether; thus, the author’s intention is that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is not separated from the city of Brahman (*brahmapura*).

Alternatively, it should be understood that this was stated with the intention that the word *brāhmapura* (the city of Brahman), which is mentioned in close proximity in the phrase "if this [city] in us," functions as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) for the ether of the day located therein. Nor should it be argued that, under this view, there is a contradiction with the subsequent text—which states that the body is not the subject under discussion because the immediately preceding word *brāhmapura* does not refer to the body—since the underlying point is that even the primary meaning (the body) is indeed the subject under discussion by virtue of being the means through which the indicated object is presented.

"Because its truth will be stated later. Although the fact that its truth will be stated later does not actually prevent the previous objection, it should nevertheless be understood as being presented as a supplementary argument (*abhyuccaya*).

Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that there is a restriction of the word 'all' (sarva)? For instance, in the passages 'The Jyotiṣṭoma is for all desires' and 'The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are for all desires,' according to the principle stated in the *Arthavāda* section of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtras*, the term 'all' refers only to those things within the context of the qualification (*adhikāra*)—namely, the cattle, sons, rain, food, drink, and so forth, which are presented in the Vedas. It does not refer even to unmentioned things such as traveling through the sky or obtaining celestial maidens, because it is natural for a pronoun to refer back to what is under discussion."

The intention of the objection is this: likewise here too, it is more appropriate for the word *sarvakāma* (all desires) to refer to the fathers, mothers, perfumes, garlands, dancing, singing, women, and so forth, which will be described in the passage beginning with "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," and not to mean all kinds of objects of enjoyment; for if the word *kāma* were taken to mean objects of enjoyment, there would be a lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya*). [This refers to the phrase] "because it is heard first."

Nor should it be argued that, because of the risk of restricting the first-mentioned term, one must accept a non-primary sense for the word "kāma" heard last—just as in the case of the sentence "All Brāhmaṇas have assembled," where to avoid restricting the first-mentioned word "all," the word "Brāhmaṇa" would likewise have to refer to Śūdras. This is not to be said.

Just as with the word *brāhmaṇa*, the word *kāma* lacks conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for the mere objects of enjoyment by the individual soul, such as perfumes and garlands; however, there is this distinction: while the word *kāma* is extremely well-known (*atyantaprasiddhi*) in reference to the perfumes, garlands, and so forth enjoyed by the soul, its status as an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatā*) is merely a general convention (*prasiddhimātra*) and not an extreme one. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. Furthermore, it is because it is consistent with what will be stated later.
This means that it is consistent with the unsurpassed nature of the fruit of meditation which [the text] will state: "He becomes one who moves at will in all worlds."

"He states the form [of Brahman] as established by implication. Now, one might object: since this is heard even prior to hearing the sentence, "This is the true Brahman-city; it does not age with his aging, nor is it slain by his slaying," how can its extreme subtlety—as the supreme cause—be established by implication? To this, some say that the explanation is provided by the commentary (bhāṣya) ending with, "By the scriptural passage ending in 'This is the true Brahman,' [Brahman's] changelessness is stated," whereas the subsequent section beginning with "From that very [source]"...

This is merely an explanation of the word *pura* occurring in the Vedic passage; and thus, since it is possible for the word *brāhma* to indicate—by way of secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*)—the state of being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world which is its defining characteristic, and since the word *satya* explicitly states the quality of being changeless (*nirvikāratva*), there is no inconsistency. Otherwise, since the quality of being changeless would already be established by the [scriptural] statement, "It does not age with his aging, nor is it slain when he is slain," the subsequent presentation of the quality of being changeless through the word *satya* in the phrase "this is the Truth" would be entirely redundant.

Furthermore, for this very reason, the fault of "non-distinction from the probandum" (sādhyāviśeṣa) is unavoidable in the Bhāṣya, because the state of being changeless (nirvikāratva)—which is the meaning of the word *satya*—is referred to as the reason for [the world] being changeless. Nor should one raise the objection that the meaning of the word *satya* is "constant uniformity" (satataikarūpatva) obtained by implication through its power of denoting changelessness; thus, neither the word *satya* nor the probandum would be redundant. This is because such an objection contradicts the subsequent passage, which states: "The intention is that the meaning of the word *satya* occurring in the Vedic sentence is 'changelessness'."

Therefore, they say that one must follow the very path already described, on the grounds of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Truth" (*satya*). Consequently, the intention is that even this discrepancy in the meaning of the term "city of Brahman" (*brāhmapura*), as seen in the passage beginning "this city of Brahman," must be tolerated. As for the statement "in this [city] are the desires," it is the response to the first objection.

In this regard, some maintain that the phrase, "Whatever he has here and whatever he does not have," is itself the answer to the question, "What is found there? This very thing is then restated in the explanatory passage, "All beings and all desires are contained within this city of Brahman," where they are referred to by the word *kāma*. Furthermore, it is also referred to by the word *kāma* in the passage: "This is the true city of Brahman; in it are contained the desires. Those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires—they [attain them]; these are the true desires."

It is argued that [the qualities] are referred to because the words "desires" (*kāma*) are recognized as the same, and because it would be strained to refer by the word "these" (*etān*) to those "true desires" (*satyān kāmān*) while simultaneously implying that "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth are qualifiers of something else; however, this is incorrect.

If identity were accepted merely on the basis of the recognition of the word "kāma," then by the force of the recognition of the word "brāhmapura" in the passage, "Now, that which is here in this city of Brahman, this is the true city of Brahman," the identity of these two would also follow; thus, mere similarity of form is not a sufficient ground [for identity]. Furthermore, it is incorrect to say that there can be no reference by the word "etān" (these) to qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), because they are perceived as qualifiers of another [the Self], for [the text] says, "and these true desires. This is because those very [desires] are indicated as primary in the statement, "In this [Self], all desires are contained."

Nor should one suspect that because the reference "these true desires" (*etāṃśca satyān kāmān*) is possible, and because in the phrase "desires are contained herein" (*asmin kāmāḥ samāhitāḥ*) there is the recognition of the restating sentence "all desires" (*sarve ca kāmāḥ*), it is therefore only heaven, earth, and so forth that are being spoken of, and not qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*); for if that were the case, the entire context beginning with "free from evil" would be rendered purposeless, since it was stated there by way of a specific formulation that the capacity to be the substratum for the containment of desires is possible precisely because of possessing qualities such as being free from evil.

There is no fault whatsoever in this, because [the passage] regarding "freedom from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth has its purpose solely in providing the meaning of the word "desire" (*kāma*); otherwise, a mere indication of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) would serve no significant purpose. Regarding the phrase "this truth" (*avyavahita-etatsatyam*), here even the expression "this truth, the city of Brahman" (*etatsatyaṃ brāhmapuram*) lacks elision of the case-ending (*sublopābhāva*) because it is an imitative word (*anukaraṇaśabda*). The intention of the *Bhāṣya*—which states "by means of the power of the parts" (*avayavaśaktyā*)—is that the sentence must be completed by supplying the words "having been indicated by the power of the parts" (*nirdiśya*).

This is because [the term] is already established even by the word "satya-saṅkalpa" (one whose resolve is true). Nor should it be argued that there is a purpose for the separate mention of desire (*kāma*) and resolve (*saṅkalpa*), as in passages such as "desire, resolve, doubt," and so forth; for even then, they are effectively one, and thus the separate mention serves no further purpose. This is because certain other qualities have been mentioned separately. Although truthfulness (*satyatva*) is indeed propounded within those very groups of qualities mentioned separately, in order to refute the claim that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*).

Thus, there is indeed redundancy; however, the intended meaning here is that one path does not invalidate another path. The meaning of the term *satyakāma* is "being distinguished by eternal glory" (*nityavibhūtiviśiṣṭatva*); the sense is that the word *satya* means "eternity," while the word *kāma* refers to objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and so forth, which have become the objects of desire.

If it is argued that the term *satyakāma* occurring in the Prajāpati-vākya also implies the possession of eternal, non-material glory (*nityavibhūti*) by way of logical necessity (*arthasiddhi*), we reply: this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). For even the liberated soul (*mukta*) possesses a non-material body and so forth, and thus the status of being its master is possible; this is the sequence of syntactical connection (*anvaya-krama*) here, according to the first instance of the word *yathā*. Here, whatever village or portion of land the subjects (*prajā*) may desire, they enter and obtain (*anvāviśanti*) it exactly in accordance with the king’s command (*rājaśāsana*), just as it is. So too [does the Lord].

"They subsist upon that very thing" means they enjoy it; thus, it is stated that just as following the king's command is the fruit of serving the king, so too is the enjoyment of its fruit. Regarding the phrase "just as the king's command," although in the expression *yathānuśāsanam* (according to the instruction), the word *yathā* has the sense of "not exceeding the meaning of the term" (*padārthānativṛtti*), and since this forms a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*), there is no analytical expansion (*svapadavigraha*) for it.

Likewise, there is no requirement for the word *tathā* (thus) as a correlative; for in expressions such as "he acts according to rule" (*yathāvidhi karoti*), there is no expectancy for the word *tathā*. Nevertheless, it should be understood that by taking the word *yathā* in the sense of similarity, this serves to state the meaning of the compound as a result, and for this very reason the employment of the word *tathā* is justified. The Bhāṣya dispels the delusion that [the term] pertains to what is heard in the scripture (*śruti*); it does not, however, refer to the desires expressed by the word *satyakāma*. The meaning is that it does not pertain to the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*).

"By way of having the mentioned qualities as their object" means by way of having all the mentioned qualities as their object, as in the phrase "desires are contained herein. He raises an objection: "the qualification by the word 'truth'"; this means "prior to that," i.e., prior to the word "truth."

And because it is qualified by the word "truth" (*satya*), one should not say that this [objection] does not apply, for even in the case of [the qualities] such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*), it is necessary to establish that they are covered by untruth (*anṛta-apidhāna*); thus, there is no authority for restricting [the application] to those alone—this is the sense. [The phrase] "because it must necessarily be accepted as having a uniform nature" means that, consequently, a strained interpretation would have to be adopted—this is the sense.

What is the intention of one who refuses to accept a strained interpretation (*kliṣṭanirvāha*) regarding the sentence "In Him, what is within"? Does the concluding sentence, "He who here [meditates on] the Self," (1) merely restate both the meditation on the quality and the qualified object; or (2), relying on a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), enjoin both; or (3) enjoin a meditation on the qualified object as connected with the fruit, while enjoining only the connection with the fruit for the quality? Having thus set forth these three alternatives in his mind, he refutes them in succession, beginning with: "Not indeed that which is not already established... (*na hy aprāptam*).

By the words "the worship of the possessor of qualities" (*guṇyupāsanam*) and so forth; considering that the intention of the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*) is that the word "going" (*gati*) in the Sūtra also intends "departure," since the Śruti passage beginning with "He, having approached him" (*sa ta āgamya*) is cited in the Commentary, he states the meaning of the word "departure": "departure is the attainment of the state of being fit for separate existence. Having established the otherwell-known usage of the word "going" in the phrase "by the two words 'going' and 'word'," he [establishes] the otherwell-known usage of the word "word" (*śabda*).

The meaning is that it establishes renown; the intention is that this is supported by the analogy of a treasure. Consequently, one should not suspect that going there day after day proves [the space] to be the Supreme Self, because the quality of being a destination—characterized by the attainment of the supreme human goal through the analogy of a treasure—is absent from the elemental ether delimited by the lotus of the heart. This is the intended sense.

The reading of the sūtra is: "The carpenter [is] from among the Niṣādas, on account of the force of the word. This means that the denotable object is qualified by its relationship [to the word]. The meaning is that it is what one intends to communicate. Regarding the phrase "because there is no hearing of the genitive [case-ending] there," the meaning is that this refers to the position that it is a genitive compound (ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa). Having disregarded that [position], it has been explained in this manner.

Nor should it be argued that since the word *brāhmaloka* is well-known as referring to the world of the four-faced [Brahmā], one must resort to the method of the opponent (the *pararīti*) to exclude other meanings—just as in the case of words such as *narapati*, *rāja*, or *kumāra* where the maxim of the "chief of the Niṣādas" (*niṣādasthapati-nyāya*) does not apply—in order to establish its exclusion from other senses. For the word *brāhmaloka* is also well-known in the sense of "belonging to Brahman," as seen in the passage, "This is the world of Brahman, O Emperor"; thus, no suspicion arises regarding the non-application of that maxim. As for the illustrative example...

Thus, there is no connection with the word "above" (*upari*). For the state of deep sleep consists in an abiding that is characterized by the abandonment of distinctions, as it exists in a manner not conducive to separate cognition or worldly transaction; therefore, in that case—the subject of the illustration—there is no connection with the word "above" in the phrase "going upwards day after day. Now, one might object: "The abiding is actually in Brahman in the form of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), and not in Brahman in the form of the small ether (*daharākāśa*); so how can the Commentary say 'of the small ether, above'? To this he replies: "This was stated with the intention of [identifying] the substratum (*dharmin*) as one and the same."

The meaning is that this is understood from the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word "Truth" (*satya*): "The name of this very Brāhmaṇa is 'Truth' (*satyam*). These, indeed, are its three syllables: *sa-ti-ya*. Now, that which is *sat* (being) is immortal; that which is *ti* is mortal; and by *ya*, he holds both together. The sense is that the intention is to show that [the Self] is distinct from the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) has not yet been refuted.

The phrase "of the previously mentioned reasons" means of those such as the relationship between the simile and the object of comparison regarding the space within the heart (*daharākāśa*), which were set forth in the four preceding sūtras. By the expression "begins [the discussion]," the intention is to indicate that this is not a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*), because the perception of continuity with the *dahara* is maintained; for it begins [the discussion] by raising the doubt that the *daharākāśa* might be the reality of the inner self (*pratyagātmatattva*) and then proceeds to refute it.
