However, it should be understood that the indication of this is not achieved by the mere fact that he "begins," since such a conclusion does not follow from that alone.

Although Virocana also [taught this], for it is thus recorded in the tradition: "That Self which is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand; he obtains all worlds and all desires."

"He who, having discovered that Self, understands it"—thus spoke Prajāpati. Both [the gods and the asuras] understood this; that is to say, they heard it from ear to ear. They said, "Come, let us seek that Self, by discovering which one obtains all worlds and all desires. Indra, indeed, set out among the gods, and Virocana among the asuras.

"Without mutual understanding"—that is to say, not revealing their own intentions due to mutual envy—they approached Prajāpati with sacrificial fuel in their hands. They lived the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*) for two hundred and forty years. Prajāpati said to them, "Desiring what have you dwelt here?"—the meaning of "dwelt" (*avāstam*) being that they have resided there.

"Those two, having approached with humility, said: 'That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, hungerless, thirstless, whose desire is the True, whose resolve is the True—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand; he who, having found that Self and understood it, obtains all worlds and all desires. Thus do they proclaim the words of the Blessed One. Desiring that [Self], we have come here. Prajāpati said to them:

"That person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self," he said; "that is the immortal, that is the fearless, that is Brahman. When Prajāpati had thus taught the inner Self, [Naciketas], mistaking the reflected person for the Self as taught, and in order to confirm his own understanding of the reflected person as the Self, asked with the intention of determining whether the reflection in water, mirrors, and so forth is also the very same Self as the reflection in the eye—being non-different from it—or whether it is different from it and not the Self: "Now, O Venerable One, that which is perceived in the water, and that which is in a mirror..."

"What is this? they asked. Thus questioned by them, without yet dispelling their confusion, he replied: "It is indeed He who is perceived within all ends. The meaning is that he gave this answer: "He whom I have described as being seen within the eye is the same one who exists within all things, such as water and so forth, and does not differ therein."

The intention of the Teacher, who provides this answer without first dispelling the student's delusion—thereby actually reinforcing that delusion—is as follows: Virocana, the lord of the Asuras, and Indra, the lord of the Suras, are both renowned in the world for having superimposed upon themselves an excellence of wisdom and greatness. If he were to tell them now, "You two are mistaken," they would become discouraged in mind, and their enthusiasm for further questioning, grasping, and retaining [the teaching] would be broken. Therefore, at this time, only an answer to the question exactly as it was heard must be given.

If, by this subsequent [instruction], the previously arisen delusion regarding the self as a reflection should become more firmly established, let it be so; even when firmly established, it will be removed by some means. This concludes the first section. For this very reason, in order to remove that delusion, [the text] says: "The two of them looked at themselves in a bowl of water. Prajāpati said to them: 'What do you see? They both replied: 'Venerable Sir, we see our entire self here, down to the hair and nails, as a reflected image.'"

Thus, after they had seen the shadow-person (chāyā-puruṣa) endowed with long nails, hair, and so forth—having grown such through thirty-two years of student-life (brahmacarya)—Prajāpati said to them: "Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, look into a water-jar. They looked into it. Prajāpati said to them: "What do you see? They both replied: "Just as we are here, O Venerable One, well-adorned and well-dressed..."

"You two are adorned; even so, O Blessed One, these two are well-adorned, well-clothed, and adorned. Herein, the intention of Prajāpati in thus instructing them was this: "Know that the reflection is also non-self, because it possesses qualities and defects corresponding to the body—qualities and defects such as coming and going, hunger, thirst, and ornamentation—which belong to the unstable body."

Even though this was so, when Prajāpati asked, "Do you see [the man] now that the illusion has ceased?", they remained silent after reporting exactly what they had seen. Then Prajāpati thought: "Because their impurities have not been destroyed, these two do not understand the intention behind my showing the two kinds of reflections for the purpose of removing their delusion; furthermore, you two are not in a position to say that your perception was an illusion. Therefore, out of compassion for them, I shall show the reflection itself once more."

Having pointed out the Supreme Self as the innermost of all and having placed it in their minds, [the Teacher] thought: "I shall satisfy the curiosity of these two by the instruction, 'This is the Self. When their impurities have been worn away by time, they will themselves understand the intended meaning of my entire discourse; or, being filled with doubt, they will come into my presence. Thinking thus, he said: "This is the Self; this is the Immortal; this is the Fearless; this is Brahman. The phrase "they were tranquil" means that their curiosity had ceased.

Having observed them thus returning, Prajāpati said: "Let these two not perish through their faith in an object grasped by delusion because they have turned back in this manner. Let them hear even this word of mine from ear to ear, just like my previous statement 'That which is the Self'. This is the intended meaning. He spoke with the thought that they were departing without having examined or understood the Self; "those who shall have this as their secret doctrine" (upaniṣadaḥ) means those who hold this [view].
"Whether they be gods or asuras, they will perish. Thus, Virocana, with a peaceful heart, went to the asuras and proclaimed this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) to them.

Virocana, considering that the instruction of Prajāpati—given upon the demonstration of two types of bodily reflections and intended to suggest that the self is the body because a reflection conforms to the body—was directed toward the decorated body when he pointed to it saying "this is the self"; and thinking that just as one says of two garments seen in a mirror, one blue and one not blue, "that which is blue is the more precious," the intent lay in the decorated body as the object of the reflection, he concluded that the self must indeed be served with ornaments and the like for the sake of the body alone.

The meaning is that, having obtained the kingdom from the Asuras, he likewise began to instruct them. "The Self alone is great here" means it is worthy of worship. "The Self is to be served"—by magnifying the Self and serving the Self here, one attains both worlds, this one and the other. Therefore, even today, those who do not give, who lack faith, and who do not sacrifice are called "Asuras. The meaning is that even now, the learned call those who are devoid of rites such as sacrifice and giving "Asuras."

The secret doctrine of the Asuras is this: they adorn the body of the deceased with alms-food, clothing, and ornaments—even by begging for them. By this means, they think they will conquer the world of *hram*. That is to say, by this adornment of the corpse. Then Indra, even before reaching the gods, perceived this danger.

Just as indeed this [self] becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-dressed when it is well-dressed, and embellished when it is embellished; even so, it becomes blind when [the body] is blind, leprous when it is leprous, and maimed when it is maimed. One whose eye or nose is always diseased is "leprous" (ruāma); one whose limb is severed is "maimed" (parivṛkṇa).

"Thinking, 'When this very body perishes, others perish; I see nothing here to be enjoyed,' he returned with fuel in his hand. Prajāpati said to him: 'O Maghavan, you went away with Virocana in a peaceful state, free from anger; desiring what have you come back? The meaning is: 'Why have you returned?'"

"Just as indeed, O Venerable Sir, this [reflection] of mine becomes well-adorned when my body is well-adorned, well-dressed when it is well-dressed, and well-groomed when it is well-groomed; even so, this [reflection] becomes blind when this [body] is blind, lame when it is lame, and maimed when it is maimed. It perishes upon the destruction of this very [body]; I see no object of enjoyment here. "It is exactly so, O Venerable Sir," he said.

"I shall explain this very matter further to you. Dwell for another two hundred and forty years. He dwelt for another two hundred and forty years, and then he said to him: "He who moves about as a great being within the dream state—that is the Self," he said; "that is the immortal, that is the fearless, that is Brahman. He went forth, tranquil and free from fear. But even before reaching the gods, he saw this fear: namely, that although this body may become blind, it remains sighted for him; or if...

"He is neither wounded by its being wounded, nor is he killed by its being killed; he is not wounded when it is wounded. They merely strike him, or disperse him, or he feels as if he has experienced something unpleasant, or even weeps as it were. 'I see nothing enjoyable in this,' he said, and returned with fuel in his hand. Prajāpati said to him: 'O venerable one, you went away with a tranquil heart; desiring what have you come back? He replied: 'Venerable sir, although this body is blind...'"

"It happens," he said; "even though he does not see, he is as if seeing; even though he does not hear, he is as if hearing; even though he does not think, he is as if thinking; even though he does not know, he is as if knowing. That it is so, O Mādhava, is indeed the case. "But I shall explain this further to you," he said. He lived there for another two hundred and forty years, and then he spoke to him: "Now, when one is thus asleep—gathered together and serene—and does not perceive any dream..."

"This is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. He went forth, calm and serene. But even before reaching the gods, he saw this fear: "Verily, O Venerable One, this one does not now know himself as 'This I am,' nor indeed these beings; he has gone to utter destruction. I see no enjoyment here. With fuel in his hand, he returned. Prajāpati said to him: "Maghavan, since you went away so calm and serene, desiring what?"

"Return," he said. He replied, "Indeed, O Venerable One, I do not yet know myself, nor do I see anything here worth enjoying. "It is even so, Maghavan," he said, "but I shall explain this very thing to you further; however, there is nothing other than this. Dwell here for another five years. He dwelt there for another five years, so that they amounted to one hundred and one. This is what is meant when it is said: "For one hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) with Prajāpati. To him—

Prajāpati spoke again; to Maghavan, who had dwelt there for another two hundred and forty years, he taught the individual soul (*jīvātman*) in its state of sleep, which does not conform to the defects of the gross body. Therein, Indra perceived a defect through the appearance of being killed, being devoured, witnessing the death of kinsmen and other unpleasant things, and weeping; seeing this fault, and reflecting upon the inconsistency of the previously stated meaning, he approached Prajāpati once more.

Prajāpati, as previously stated, likewise instructed him—who had dwelt there for thirty-two years—in the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptāvasthā*), which is the individual self (*jīvātman*) free from fear, grief, and the like caused by the appearances of dreams and so forth. Indra, however, perceiving that this state—devoid of specific cognition—is almost equivalent to destruction and thus lacks the goal of human life (*apuruṣārthatā*), returned once more to Prajāpati, reflecting upon the aforementioned logical inconsistencies.

"Prajāpati said, 'I shall indeed explain this further to you, but not otherwise than this; dwell [with me] for another five years. The meaning is that, after Indra had dwelt for that duration of time and his impurities were completely destroyed through the service of a hundred and one years, Prajāpati began to instruct him."

"O Maghavan, this body is mortal; it is seized by death. It is the substrate for this immortal, bodiless Self. Indeed, one who possesses a body is seized by pleasure and pain. For as long as one has a body, there is no escape from pleasure and pain. But when one is bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch him. Wind is bodiless, as are the cloud, lightning, and thunder—these are bodies. Just as these, having risen up from yonder sky and attained the highest light, appear in their own [forms]..."

"He is manifested in form; he is that supreme person who moves about there, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, whether with women, or vehicles, or kinsmen, not remembering this body of birth. Just as a draft-animal is yoked to a wagon, even so is this vital breath (*prāṇa*) yoked to this body. Now, where this space is extended, there is the eye and the person of the eye for the purpose of seeing. And he who knows, 'Let me smell this,' he is the Self (*ātman*); the nose is for the purpose of smelling."

Now, he who knows "I shall speak this" is the Self; speech is for the purpose of speaking. Now, he who knows "I shall hear this" is the Self; the ear is for the purpose of hearing. Now, he who knows "I shall think this" is the Self; the mind is his divine eye. With that divine eye, the mind, he sees these desires and rejoices in them which are in the world of Brahman.

"The gods indeed worship this very Self; therefore, all worlds and all desires have been attained by them. He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires"—thus spoke Prajāpati. Thinking that the "shadow-person" had been taught, the two asked again, beginning with the words, "O Venerable Sir, as for this one... [and so forth].

This should be understood as being due to the nature of the question: "O Venerable One, which one is this that is perceived in water, and which is this that is perceived in a mirror? For the response, "It is perceived in all ends (objects), such as the eyes and other locations," takes the form of an answer to these two questions. However, some read the text as: "O Venerable One, this which is perceived in water—this indeed is that very same one. This is the meaning.

"This very one indeed is perceived in all limits—both he who is here in the mirror and [he who is in the eyes]"—"Which one is this?"—"This very one indeed is perceived in all limits"—this much is the question; "Thus he spoke"—this constitutes the remainder of the subsequent *udaśarāva* (bowl-of-water) section. And therein, the question is: "O Venerable One, which is that who is perceived in the waters, and who is perceived in the mirror—that very one who is perceived in all limits, such as the locations of the eyes and so forth? Which one is this?"

They say that the word *iti* occurring in the middle of a question should be placed at the end of the question, and so forth. "Of the visual body" means of the shadow-person (*chāyāpuruṣa*) perceived in the eye. It should be understood that because that very sequence is firmly established, it is precisely that which must be removed. "Non-selfhood" (*anātmatva*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood that there is an absence of such enjoyments as the sound of the word "immortality" and fearlessness; for this very reason, it should be seen that later on [in the text] the statement "I see no enjoyment here" is made. And by the phrase "through positive and negative concomitance," the meaning is: because [the self] follows the presence and absence of the qualities and defects of the body.

The meaning is as follows: just as clothing, ornaments, and so forth—which follow the qualities and defects of their constituent material—are not the self (*ātman*), so too the "shadow-person" (*chāyāpuruṣa*), whose qualities and defects correspond to the presence and absence of the qualities and defects of the body, is not the self. In the phrase "the body is not the self," the word "body" refers to the shadow-person; likewise, in subsequent passages such as "the immortality and fearlessness of the body," the word "body" should also be understood as referring to the shadow-person. [The statement] "the distinction is difficult to perceive" refers to this...

The meaning is that the absence of conformity to the presence and absence of the qualities and defects of the body is difficult to perceive. However, in the state of dream, that absence is easily perceived; therefore, one should understand that the statement of Indra—“Even though this body is blind, [the self] belongs to one who is not blind”—refers specifically to the state of dream. “One who is ignorant of its intended meaning” means one who is ignorant of the ultimate purport concerning the nature of the pure Self.

The phrase "of one who adopts [the reading] beginning with 'evam'" means: of one who adopts the sentence beginning with the word *evam*—which expresses similarity—as "In this very way is this serene being (*samprasāda*"), rather than adopting merely the words "This is the serene being. Regarding the term "illustrative example" (*dārṣṭāntika*), the illustrative sentence is: "Wind is bodiless; clouds, lightning, and thunder are bodiless. Just as these, having risen from yonder sky and reached the highest light, appear in their own form... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.2–3).

"Even so is this serene being"—this is the statement regarding the point of application (*dārṣṭāntika*). It is like the expression, "He sleeps with his mouth open. Just as the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open" is used even though the opening of the mouth occurs prior to the sleep, so too, although the manifestation in one's own form occurs after the attainment of the supreme light—which consists of the realization in the form of a mental state that dissolves the phenomenal world—the expression "having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own form" is logically justified; such is the meaning.

Having raised the dilemma—whether discrimination (*viveka*) has the body as its object or the self as its object—he refutes it with the words "having the body as its object" and so forth. An indifferent bystander, being mistaken about the proponent's position, objects with the words "if what is intended is the rising of the self from the body" and so forth. One must not, however, be deluded into thinking that this is an objection from the opponents' side. And when the direct realization of discrimination is the "rising from the body";

It should be understood that Vācaspati has established that while movement having the body as its point of departure (*apādāna*) is not possible for one who possesses a body, "rising" (*samutthāna*), which consists in the separation from the body, is indeed possible even for one dwelling within the body. Thus, the phrase "because it is possible for one possessing a body" means that it is possible precisely for one endowed with the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*). [Otherwise] it would not have liberation as its subject matter.

It should be understood that this doubt belongs to one who is deluded, thinking that even the phrase "having risen from the body" refers to the time of liberation; for the gerund suffix (*lyap*) in such cases—as in "he sleeps having opened his mouth"—is intended to denote an action occurring immediately after the preceding one.

The expression "he sleeps having opened [his mouth]" is logically consistent; however, in the present case, since there is no opportunity for a direct realization in the form of mental activity (*vṛtti*) immediately after the state of Brahman, the suffix *tvā* is in every way untenable—this is the intended meaning. Its grammatical correctness should be understood as being like the usage in the expression “*parajyotirbhāve karaṃ kāryatvāt*” (the hand is used when there is the presence of the supreme light). It should be noted, however, that there is no such fault in the case of "*parajyotirbhāve*. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and the uselessness of the statement," the sense is that the dissolution of difference is already established by implication through the very word "attains" (*abhiniṣpadyate*).

This is the refutation of the position that the dissolution of differentiation (*bhedapravilāpa*) is also accomplished [by the Self] and is therefore included within the meaning of the word [“Self”]. Regarding the phrase “the exclusion of having a second” (*sadvitīyatvavyudāsa*), the meaning is as follows: if only the expression “is accomplished” (*abhiniṣpadyate*) were stated, there might arise the suspicion that there exists a second [entity] consisting of the knowledge that effects this cessation; so that such a suspicion may not arise, even the state of having a second caused by that knowledge-cessation is negated by the words “having reached the highest light” (*parañjyotirupasampadya*). This refers to the natural force of the perception of the verb as being transitive (*sakarmakatva*).

The meaning is that it is improper to interpret the word *upasampatti* (attaining) in the phrase "having attained the highest light" as having the sense of the intransitive verb *bhavati* (becoming). The intention behind the phrase "by the performance of action" is that insentient things such as the wind lack agency in performing action. The phrase "for the sake of performing their own functions" means that they swell during the rainy season. Furthermore, in the sūtra "And the reference is for another purpose," the passage beginning with "this serene being" (*eṣa saṃprasādaḥ*) has been explained by others as referring to the self in the state of deep sleep.

He refutes even that [objection] with the words "of this statement. The construction is: "The author of the Sūtras uses the designation of difference with the intention of indicating the distinction between the nature of the individual soul (jīva) [and Brahman]. Ānandagiri has stated that the author of the Sūtras does not mention a difference that would result in the following undesirable consequence: if the non-transmigratory nature of the Lord were not stated by declaring the difference of the transmigrating soul from the Lord, then even though non-difference is taught, the non-transmigratory nature of the soul would not be established. To this he replies with the words "as long as by the designation of difference," etc. [The phrase] "upon the cessation of ignorance" refers to the soul...

The sense is that through the realization of the distinctness [of Brahman] as the primary human goal, the notion of its being a non-goal—which is caused by ignorance—is removed upon the cessation of that ignorance; therefore, the designation of difference is purposeful. The sense is that the mention of the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) occurs as a contextual digression within the section concerning the individual soul (*jīva*), since He is introduced as the object to be attained. "First mentioned" refers to...

Because there is uniformity in the case-ending when referring back to what was previously designated in the nominative, the meaning is that in the passage, “Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa; he [sa] approached his own deity,” the word *sa* (he), which ends in the nominative case, refers back to Prajāpati due to this uniformity of case-ending. The phrase “it would be intended to mean the nature of Brahman” means that the word *sa* should be taken as referring to the Supreme Self whose body is that [of Prajāpati].

"Because of the non-abandonment of the original [subject]" means because of the non-abandonment of the *samprasāda* (the serene state) first mentioned. "By way of grammatical disagreement" (*vaiyadhikaraṇyena*) means that there is a reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, without extending up to the supreme person (*uttamapuruṣa*). "If it be argued that they should be in grammatical agreement" (*samānādhikaraṇam astu iti cet*): the meaning is that even in the passage "he moves about there" (*sa tatra paryeti*), the word "he" (*saḥ*), being in the nominative case, must likewise extend up to the supreme person; and thus, there would be no difference in syntactical style (*rīti*).

The point is that the meaning of the word *upajana* (arising) is precisely the state of not being the goal of human life (*apuruṣārthatva*), because [the body] is born from the mutual union of a man and a woman, as expressed by the phrase "not remembering the arising. Now, one might ask: what is the fault in remembering? To this he says: "For that which has been experienced... Having explained the word *ākāśa* as referring to light and so forth which illuminate, [he continues with] "shining forth" (*prakāśamāna*).

He explains [the term] by way of its dependence on form (*rūpa*), stating "either the manifesting form. In both cases, he supplies and connects the word "manifests" (*prakāśayati*). Consequently, where the eye, acting as an instrument, manifests either the light of space or form, that person—the Self—is "visual," meaning it has the eye as its instrument. Here, "Self-ness" is the predicate with respect to that which has the eye as its instrument; this is because it conforms to the structure of subsequent sentences such as "that Self [uses] the nose for smelling. And this is the method [of interpretation].

The very fact that [the eye] serves as an instrument for the light that illuminates all things—which has already been attained—is intended to manifest a specific excellence of the Self (*ātman*). This is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The knowers of Brahman know [it]" (*jñānino jānanti*). In this context, it is said with reference to the meaning of the word "gods" (*deva*) in the passage: "The gods indeed worship this Self."

The sense is this: since the meditation on the Supreme Self alone is the object of the practice for the sake of the dharma of liberation (*mokṣadharma*), what utility could there be for the meditation on the individual soul (*jīva*)? Thus, in the subsequent passages as well, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) should be understood as referring to "meditation" (*upāsana*). Now, one might ask: since the individual soul must be stated to be the object of meditation precisely because its meditation is enjoined as a subordinate element (*viśeṣaṇatayā*), what is the purpose of stating its status as an object of meditation by means of the logical argument consisting of its inclusion within that which is to be attained (*prāpya*)? This is the meaning of the objection.

The meaning is that because the author of the Sūtras has established it in that manner by saying "it is said," the same method has been followed by the author of the Bhāṣya. The meaning of the Sūtra, "But they approach [the Self] as the Self, and they cause [others] to grasp it as such" (Brahmasūtra 4.1.3), is this: former practitioners have approached the Supreme Self as their own Self for the purpose of worship, and the scriptures likewise cause [others] to grasp it in that very way.

Regarding the statement "the distinction [is established] because [the Self] exists when that [body] exists," some hold the following view: having accepted—as established by the context—that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the object of meditation, there arises a doubt as to whether the form qualified by agency and so forth, which belongs to the transmigratory state, is to be meditated upon, or rather its distinction from that [body]. On this point, they believe that only the form qualified by agency and so forth is to be contemplated, because for the meditator who exists within the body, the Self is of such a nature.

The meaning is as follows: having raised an objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of the sūtra, "Because [the qualities] exist in the body of the self alone" (*eka ātmanaśśarīre bhāvāt*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established by the sūtra, "The distinction [is real], because [the qualities] arise when that [body] exists" (*vyatirekastadbhāvabhāvitvāt*). This is because, only if the distinction from the nature of transmigratory form is indeed what is to be meditated upon, will the attainment of the fruit consisting of the nature of such a Self follow according to the principle of "as one intends, so one attains" (*tatkratu-nyāya*). Now, if the Dahara-Brāhmaṇa meditation were merely an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the Prajāpati-vidyā, it would have to be taught only to one who is already qualified for the Prajāpati-vidyā; likewise, if it were an ancillary to the Upakośala-vidyā...

If this is argued, the answer to that has already been stated previously by the phrase, "Because He is to be perceived thus. Therefore, the small ether (daharākāśa) is none other than the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is untouched by even the slightest scent of defects such as ignorance and the like, and who is an ocean of infinite, noble qualities—natural, unsurpassed knowledge, power, sovereignty, vigor, capacity, and splendor—by His very nature.

But the one indicated by Prajāpati’s statement—whose assumption of a body caused by karma is understood from such passages as "they indeed strike him down" and "they cause him to disappear"—is subsequently one whose own nature manifests upon reaching the supreme light, characterized by qualities such as being freed from sin; therefore, he is not the small ether (daharākāśa).

Furthermore, for this reason it must be so: just as in the case of the knowledge of the fire within the elements (*bhūtāgni-vidyā*), this knowledge being taught to Indra—who was already possessed of the knowledge of the small ether (*dahara-brāhmaṇa*)—cannot possibly be a subsidiary part of that knowledge of the small ether. If this is argued, we say no; because the speech of Prajāpati proceeds for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the word *samprasāda* occurring at the end of the passage on the small ether in the words "This is the serene one" (*eṣa samprasādaḥ*), it is established that they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) directed toward that same purpose. Consequently, it is understood that the knowledge of the small ether was indeed taught to Indra subsequently. Thus, [the objection does not stand].

There is no fault. Intending to explain the meaning of the sūtra *dahara uttarebhyaḥ* (The small [ether] is [Brahman], because of the subsequent [reasons]), he says, beginning with "because of being compared to ether" and ending with "the eight qualities. Intending to explain the meaning of the sūtra *gatiśabdābhyām* (Because of the movement and the word), he says "movement and word. Intending to explain the meaning of the sūtra *dhṛteśca* (And because of support), he says "because of supporting. Intending to explain the meaning of the sūtra *anyārthaśca parāmarśaḥ* (And the reference is for another purpose), he says "for the sake of a specific fruit."

The meaning is that this is because we observe the natural force (*svārasya*) of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), which begins with "likeness to space" (*ākāśopamāna*) and ends with "the specific fruits" (*phalaviśeṣa*). Now, one might object: "Let it be granted that there is no redundancy [with the previous section] on the grounds of 'having a small abode' (*arbhakaukastva*); nevertheless, the fact that the mere opening statement is overridden by the natural force of the great sentence was already established in the sūtra *'prāṇastathānugamāt'* (I.1.28), so there would indeed be redundancy with that. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the conclusion."

If it be objected: "If, even when there is a reference to the individual soul (jīva) in the conclusion, that [reference] is set aside by the natural force of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya) situated in the introduction, then the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) of the section 'The Vital Breath (prāṇa), because of the concordance' would be struck down by the 'stick-and-cake' logic (daṇḍāpūpanyāya)," we say no; for the meaning is that the marks (liṅga) of the individual soul and the primary vital breath heard in the introductory passage—like the quality of being minute (daharatva) and so on—are not established otherwise [than as referring to Brahman], and thus this [present case] does not have its purpose already exhausted by that [previous discussion].

By means of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokita), he demonstrates the resolution of a further doubt through a different perspective regarding the phrase "because of having a small abode," or rather, as it occurs here in the supplementary portion of the text. He shows precisely this surplus [of meaning] by stating: "For it is not so in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā."

The phrase "of one who is not such" means that it is not so, just as an actor does not [become the character] despite imitating Rāma and others. Now, an objection may be raised: for one who asserts that the small ether (daharākāśa) is the individual soul (jīva), the statement "the small ether is not the soul because the soul is an imitator of the small ether" is untenable, since there is no evidence for the soul being an imitator of the small ether. Nor can the imitation be established from the passage "When he sees," for even if that establishes the soul's imitation of the Supreme Self, it does not establish its imitation of the small ether.

If you argue that the status of the small one (*dahara*) as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is not yet established, because if that were so, the dispute would come to an end—you are mistaken. For in another Sūtra, the individual soul’s (*jīva*) imitation of the small one is not made the reason [for its identity], such that its non-establishment might be suspected.

Rather, since the scripture states, "When the seer sees the golden-colored one," it is heard that the soul's imitation depends upon the meditation on the Supreme Self; thus, the soul does not possess eternally manifest qualities, whereas the Supreme possesses eternally manifest qualities. Therefore, the Supreme alone is worthy of being referred to in the passage concerning the small one.

The meaning of the sūtra, "If [it be said] from the latter [section], [we reply]: 'But [the soul's] true nature has been manifested,'" is precisely what is being stabilized here. For this very reason, the *Śrutaprakāśikā* introduces this sūtra with the following commentary: "In this way, the consistency between the opening and the conclusion is established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), once it has been proven whether qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) are natural or non-natural to the Supreme Self and the individual self (*jīva*). Otherwise, based on the maxim that 'what is not stated [here] should be understood from elsewhere,' there might arise the suspicion that even in the context of the 'small [space]' (*dahara-vākya*), the connection with the eightfold set of qualities is intended for the state of liberation; it is in response to this doubt that he [the author] states this sūtra."

Regarding the objection raised by others that the *adhikaraṇabheda* (difference in subject matter) has been committed: the Supreme Self is not the entity taught in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad passage—"The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Everything shines after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined"—because it is seen to be a subduer of the sun and other luminaries, and because the light of the sun and so forth is heard to follow after it. Therefore, it must be a particular kind of light, for it is observed that light indeed overcomes another light.

Furthermore, such reflection (anubhāna) is possible only for that which is of the same genus; for this very reason, it was stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the passage "the cows run after the boar" that it is logical for cows to run after a boar similar to themselves, but not to run after crows. Having thus established that [prima facie] position, the question arises: in the verse "after Him shining," should one postulate some extraordinary light and then postulate the reflection of the sun and other luminaries upon that, or rather, should the reflection of the sun and others be understood as resulting from the shining of the well-known Brahman, who is of the nature of light (*bhārūpa*) and possesses true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*)?

Regarding the doubt as to what is to be understood [by the word *tat*], since it is possible to adopt what is well-known from the Śruti, it is improper to postulate an unknown other light; therefore, Brahman alone is what is being expounded. "Anukṛti" means imitation or following after; furthermore, the genitive *tac-chabda* (the word *tasya*) in the Sūtra indicates the fourth quarter of the verse: "By its light all this shines. Consequently, the fourth quarter of the verse indicated by the *tac-chabda* in the Sūtra—

The capacity to illuminate all manifold phenomena (*prapañca*), which is the subject to be established by the verse, is possible only in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who illuminates the entire manifold superimposed upon Himself by the light of consciousness; therefore, He alone is the subject to be established. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement "the sun does not shine there" is explained by the supreme [commentator] as "it does not illuminate that," in accordance with the following Smṛti: "Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor even fire illumines That; having gone to which they do not return, that is My supreme abode. This is the intended sense.

The purpose of the prefix *anu* is because of its utterance in the Śruti passage, "it shines following that very one which shines. Everything else should be understood as being exactly like the view of the opponent. This is the meaning of the rule: "In this treatise, the own form of a word is to be understood, except when it is a technical grammatical term (*saṃjñā*). That is to say, in this system, the actual form of a word itself is to be taken, provided it is not a technical grammatical designation.

Consequently, the suffix *ḍhak* prescribed by the rule "agner ḍhak" (Pāṇini 4.2.33) occurs only from the word *agni*, and not from the word *pāvaka*. Regarding technical designations (*saṃjñā*), however, there is the inclusion of the designated object (*saṃjñin*)—that is, the meaning—and not of the word-form itself; as in the case of [the rules] "siddhi," "vṛddhi," and so forth, there is no inclusion of the word *vṛddhi* itself, but rather of the designated object alone. The phrase "both defects are common to all" means that they are common to the three false views (*kudṛṣṭi*) that assert a difference between the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and its properties.

Although in the view of the proponents of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādin*), it may be possible to say that the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a conjunction of another reason indicated by the genitive-ending pronoun *tat*, nevertheless, in their view, the syntactic connection of the word *tat* in the Sūtra is difficult to establish. Furthermore, in the passage "there the sun does not shine," the interpretation that it means "it does not illuminate that" would be forced.

Furthermore, according to that view, in the case of "Yajñadatta follows Devadatta as he walks," there are two acts of walking; however, here, since the phenomenal world does not appear apart from the manifestation of consciousness, the meaning of the Śruti text "it shines [along with] Him" is also untenable. Likewise, the distinction expressed by the genitive case in "tasya bhāsā" (by His light) is difficult to establish, because there is no manifestation apart from Him.

Furthermore, since there is no other manifestation to be accomplished by its own manifestation, the designation "it shines by its own shining" is untenable; such criticisms are clear. The phrase "it has been established as such" implies that this was established by the followers of Yādavaprakāśa—this is the objection. He refutes this with the words "only the supreme ether," and then with "this being so. However, the sense is that [the term] refers to an object present in the intellect, just as in the cases of "colored by passion" (*rakta*), "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), or "the state of having that as its qualifier" (*tatprakāratvam*). Thus ends the Daharādhikaraṇa.

The phrase "it was said by the Blessed One" means that this [measurement] is possible even for the Blessed One; however, it should be understood that the passage is intended merely to show the possibility of smallness in the Blessed One. The expression "is seen as distinct from the Supreme Self" means that it is seen as the individual soul (*jīva*) alone. Therefore, the connection [of the discussion] arises from the doubt: "Since a specific dimension such as being the size of a thumb—like the quality of being minute—is impossible in the Supreme Self, let the one measured by a thumb be the individual soul. This is the underlying intention.

"Then one should feel aversion through [understanding] the commentary. The meaning is that because he is the Lord of both what has been and what is to be, there is no aversion even toward the objects of his rule, even if they are to be abandoned. "He alone is today, he alone is tomorrow"—the meaning is that he is eternal at all times. "One should draw out" means one should separate; the meaning is that one should know him as distinct from one's own self which has become the body. "The pure" means having the nature of light.

The meaning is that it is not [the Supreme Self], but rather the individual soul (*jīva*), because it has been stated that if one hears of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of a specific location, then even in the case of the Great Supreme Self, the description of a small dimension is appropriate; however, since there is no hearing of a limiting adjunct consisting of a specific location here, it is impossible to say that the statement of limitation is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Thus, it is argued that it must be the individual soul. It is logical that the Supreme Self possesses the abode of the heart-lotus as stated in the previous section, because of the mention of various distinct locations for the Supreme Self.

For that [heart] is indeed the locus of its perception, just as Śālagrāma is for the Blessed One whose navel is a lotus. And here, in the scriptural mention of "the size of a thumb," no difference in location is specified, because only the measurement is indicated. Now, an objection might be raised: "A Śūdra requires knowledge in its entirety for the performance of ritual acts and meditative worship (*upāsana*), whereas for members of the three higher castes, that [knowledge] consists only of a portion [of the Veda], namely those qualities not prescribed in their own specific recension. However, this objection is weak.

If it is argued that the injunctions for the knowledge of sacrifice (*kratuyajña-vidyā*) should enjoin only those belonging to the three higher castes and not the *śūdra*, then, by the principle that "the principal [action] is also enjoined where its constituent parts are most extensively prescribed" (*bhūyastvenobhayaśruti-nyāya*), the injunction for the principal [sacrifice] would likewise apply to whichever branch (*śākhā*) contains the most extensive prescription of its constituent parts (*aṅga*). In other branches, [these parts may be fewer].

However, regarding certain subsidiary prescriptions (*aṅga-vidhāna*), only those who study that specific recension (*śākhā*) have the authority (*adhikāra*) for that ritual action, because of the brevity resulting from the implication of knowledge [of those subsidiaries] within that very recension, and not those who study other recensions. Furthermore, there may be a certain ritual action or one of its subsidiaries for which no prescription exists in this recension, but rather the prescription for it, along with all its subsidiaries, exists only in another recension.

In that case, those who study only a specific recension (*śākhā*) would have no entitlement to perform that ritual, just like a *śūdra*, because they would need to possess the complete knowledge required for its performance. For indeed, minor rituals consisting of injunctions regarding qualities and results (*guṇaphalavidhi*), which are entirely unestablished within a particular recension, may exist in other specific recensions.

Therefore, since it is accepted that even those belonging to the three higher castes require the induction of knowledge, it is possible for a Śūdra as well to induce the knowledge necessary for its practice; thus, the practice of knowledge after learning from those learned in the Vedas is logical. Otherwise, if there were no acquisition of knowledge due to the absence of Vedic study, what would be the recourse for women such as Maitreyī in their attainment of the Brāhma-vidyā? For even according to the Siddhāntin, it is not established that the word "Śūdra" occurring in the Saṃvarga-vidyā refers to a Kṣatriya, nor is it established that the word "Maitreyī" refers to men.

It cannot be so imagined, because it would contradict other scriptural passages such as: "Now Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī. Therefore, the Śūdra’s lack of qualification [for Vedic study] follows precisely from the prohibition itself. However, in reality, even gods and others possess the capacity characterized by knowledge rooted in Vedic study—of which initiation (*upanayana*) is a constituent part—acquired in previous births; thus he says: "because of the non-loss of prior knowledge."

Regarding the statement "only for the *ādhāna* performed by a human": although there is indeed no selection of three *ṛṣis* (*tryārṣeyavaraṇa*) in the *ādhāna* itself, nor can it be argued that—even in the absence of the direct selection of three *ṛṣis* in the *ādhāna*—there exists an extended application (*atideśika*) of the selection of three *ṛṣis* in the *pavamāna-havis* offerings which are its constituent parts (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, since it has been established in the passage "and because qualities are for the sake of another" (*guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*) that the *pavamāna* oblations do not have the purpose of establishing the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), one might object. Nevertheless, here the word *ādhāna* refers to the ritual acts intended for the accomplishment of the fires; thus, the *pavamāna* oblations are also included, and since the selection of three ancestors (*trayārṣeya-varaṇa*) exists in those [oblations], it should be understood that there is no fault. The phrase "given to the gods" (*devānāṃ dattam*) is quite clear.

But surely, it is not reasonable to admit a collapse of the boundaries of Dharma by asserting that a religious practice which previously proceeded in one way—based on such explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) found in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas—now proceeds in another way.

Otherwise, even the boundaries of unrighteousness (*adharma-maryādā*) would have to be accepted as having been violated. For in the *Bhārata* itself, there is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the violation of unrighteousness, stating that from the time of Śvetaketu’s curse onwards, the practice of monogamy (*ekapatnītva*) began among women who were previously unrestrained: "O dear one, on this earth, the women of all castes were indeed unrestrained, just as cattle are; so too were the offspring. From this day forward, it shall be a sin for a woman to deviate from her husband; [such an act] is equivalent to the killing of an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*)."

"Evil will come, bringing unhappiness. But surely, in the narrative of Śvetaketu, if women were previously unconcealed, then just as there would be no anger on the part of a son toward his father when he, being penniless, requests ornaments for the sake of a festival, so too there would have been no anger from Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, when his father requested the wife of Uddālaka for the sake of offspring; yet anger is described in that very account: "Then, seeing his mother as if being forcibly led away..."

Indeed, Śvetaketu, whose splendor was kindled by asceticism, could not endure it; grasping his mother by the hand, Śvetaketu spoke: "O evil-minded one, release my mother, who is devoted to her husband!"

If it is argued that—since the vow and observance of women’s status as having only one husband (*ekapatnī*) is understood to have been violated [by the gods], the statement regarding women being previously unconfined (*anāvṛta*), and the statement establishing the rule of having only one husband from that time onward, are merely intended as inducements for Pāṇḍu—who desired to engage Kuntī with another man for the sake of offspring—and thus refer only to a matter he himself devised—then let it be determined that the entire collection of statements concerning the narrative of the sacrifice and the seizing of the city (*yajñāgrahāropākhyāna*) is likewise so; otherwise, many inconsistencies would arise therein. Thus it stands.

For in that sacrificial session (*satra*), regarding the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering, if the cake for Agni-Viṣṇu were performed by Agni alone, it would not be a portion for Agni; yet if it were performed [by him], the continuity of Viṣṇu’s portion would now be absent. Furthermore, if the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice during the *upasads* were performed by some other deity, it would then belong to that deity alone and would no longer be Vaiṣṇava.

If the sacrifice were not performed in its entirety, it would be deficient. If all the constituent elements, ending with the *udavasānīya* rite, had been performed by all the gods and sages, then all of them would have been entitled to shares in all the oblations. However, if some parts were performed by some and others by others, that sacrifice would be deficient for everyone; consequently, there would be no gratification for Viṣṇu, nor would the gods receive their boons.

Furthermore, if one accepts that the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice was originally a single deity and later became one with various deities at a specific stage, then a previously unseen twofold meaningfulness would result: namely, that the words designating the deities heard in the injunctions—which operate through direct instruction (*upadeśa*) and extended application (*atideśa*)—would have denoted Viṣṇu previously, but now denote various other deities. By this same reasoning, the claim that "the gods such as Indra worship Viṣṇu" does not entail a contradiction regarding the relationship between the sacrificer and the object of sacrifice.

The objection that "human beings worship Indra and others, so there is no contradiction with the well-known status of Indra and others as objects of worship" is refuted. For, in that case, the words denoting deities in the injunctions would invariably result in being purposeless. Furthermore, just like the narrative of the installation of the sacrificial cups (*yajñāgrahāropa*), the accounts of the gods performing Vedic sacrifices are likewise not intended to convey a literal meaning; otherwise, inconsistency would arise even in those cases. To illustrate:

It is stated that "The gods, desiring glory, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*), with Agni, Indra, and Vāyu as the leaders"—thus the performance of a *sattra* by four gods is mentioned. Here, how could only these four perform a *sattra* without being Brāhmaṇas? For the performance of a *sattra* belongs only to Brāhmaṇas numbering at least seventeen, according to such scriptural texts as "Brāhmaṇya is Bṛhaspati among the gods" and "Kṣatra is Indra. If it is argued that there is likewise a division into Brāhmaṇas and so forth even among the gods, let it be so; nevertheless, [only] Bṛhaspati among the gods...

Since the qualification for the *satra* sacrifice is determined by being a Brāhmaṇa, Agni, Indra, and the other gods have no qualification for the *satra* at all. Likewise, in the *Sarpāṇām Ayana*, it is heard: "The two, Carkapiśaṅga and others, are the *unnetṛ*s"; thus, the duty of the *unnetṛ* is assigned to two individuals, Carkapiśaṅga and the rest. How could two perform the duty of the *unnetṛ*, which has a single agent? Therefore, if it is argued that the explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) regarding the performance of sacrifices by gods and others have no intended meaning, we reply: [The text continues with the refutation of this argument.]

For in the Vaiṣṇava sacrificial session (*sattra*), Viṣṇu alone is the deity throughout all the subsidiary and principal sacrifices; and that [desire] was accomplished for those gods who, desiring such a share in the sacrificial offerings—consisting of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), curd, clarified butter (*ājya*), and so forth—undertook that very Vaiṣṇava sacrificial session.

Now, since it has been stated that this sacrifice has fallen into desuetude due to the absence of anyone to perform it, there is no contradiction [in our position]. If one were to object by seizing upon some perceived inconsistency within the narratives found in the Mahābhārata, then, because such inconsistencies would apply everywhere, all the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth would become utterly meaningless; therefore, enough of this excessive scrutiny.

[The objection states: "Because presence [of the deity] is impossible," according to the Bhāṣya. Now, one might argue: "Even under the view that [the deity] lacks a physical body (avigraha), since a deity is not present everywhere, the contradiction regarding its being a subordinate element (aṅga) remains exactly as it was; therefore, this objection is without substance. This is true; however, there is no fault in the Sūtra because it is merely a restatement of what was said by the Pūrva-mīmāṃsakas who hate the idea of a deity having a physical body. Furthermore, the reading "yogyānupalabdhis tu" (but there is non-perception of something perceptible) is observed.

In this context, the word *yogya* appears as if it were adventitious (*sampātāyāta*), since what actually needs to be demonstrated is precisely the unfitness for perception (*upalambhāyogyatva*). The meaning is: "You have carried the oblations (*havya*) that were to be carried upward. The word *akṣan* means "they have eaten" (*bhakṣitavantaḥ*). The word *prāmīyanta* means "they have died" (*mṛtāḥ*). In the form *pariṇāmyamānasya*, the shortening occurs according to the rule *ṇici mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*.

In the mantra *indra āgaccha hariva āgaccha meghātithe meṣa*, the portion ending with *indra* is the vocative address to Indra. Regarding *hariva*: because the two fortnights—the bright half (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the dark half (*aparapakṣa*)—are Indra’s bay horses (*harit*), he is called *harivan*. Then, in the vocative case, by the rule *matuvasorussambuddhau chandasi*, the *v* is replaced by *ru*; by the rule *bho bhago agho apūrvasya*, the *ru* is replaced by *y*; and by the rule *lopaśśākalyasya*, the *y* is elided, thus establishing the form *hariva āgaccha*.

It is heard in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) of the *Subrahmaṇyā* liturgy that Indra, having become a ram, carried off Medhātithi, the son of Kaṇva; for it is stated there that [Indra] was satisfied by the mere touch [of the girl].

The meaning is that [the satisfaction] is heard to result from merely touching [the ladle] with the hand used for the *agnihotra* oblation. Regarding the phrase "but by others," this refers to Śākalya’s question to Yājñavalkya, "How many gods are there? After Yājñavalkya has explained, "Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three," and has demonstrated their inclusion within the number thirty-three by stating, "These are merely their manifestations; there are only thirty-three deities," Śākalya asks about the specific entities to be numbered: "Which are they? [To which he replies: "Eight Vasus, eleven Rudras..."

Having stated, "The twelve Ādityas, Prajāpati, and Indra—these are the thirty-three," he showed their inclusion therein; then again, showing the inclusion of even those thirty-three gods within six gods—Agni, Earth, Vāyu, Antarikṣa, Āditya, and Div—as being the majesty (*mahiman*) of these six, he showed their inclusion within three worlds as being the majesty of the three worlds; and having stated that even those are the majesty of the two, food and breath (*anna* and *prāṇa*), he [showed] those two as belonging to the One.

The meaning is that because of the residual statement, "This is the greatness of the vital breath (prāṇa)," the connection of a single [entity] with multiple forms has been established by others. Now, one might ask: why did the author of the Bhāṣya disregard the second interpretation provided by Śaṅkara and others for the portion of the sūtra beginning with "aneka-pratipatteḥ"? To this he replies with the words "by other commentators," etc., up to "the perception of multiple objects."

Although in the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya*, *Vācaspatya*, and *Ānandagiriya* commentaries it is explained simply as "because one and the same entity is seen to attain the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) in multiple rituals," nevertheless, in the *Vācaspatya*, [the phrase] "in multiple rituals" refers to its being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*).

The practice consists in understanding the state of being a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) simultaneously; this is seen from the following: just as a single salutation is performed toward one Brāhmaṇa by many people, so too, while aiming at a single deity situated in her own place, oblations are offered simultaneously by many sacrificers residing in various locations. And although she is present [only there], she becomes a subordinate factor [for all]; for it has been stated that she possesses the capacity to perceive multiple objects even when they are distant. In that regard:

It should be understood that this description was given with the intention that "the capacity to perceive many distant objects" may also serve as another interpretation for the statement "because multiple cognitions are observed. Alternatively, there is no inconsistency in taking the term "other commentators" (*vyākhyātrantara*) to refer to Yādava and others. The phrase "possessing a *vigraha*" means "endowed with a formal analysis (*vigraha*). Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of a rule for the production of similar forms," it should be understood here that because of the impossibility of a rule for the production of similar forms, a dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is possible.

In the second [verse], however, the reading "yā vyaktiḥ" (whatever individual) is correct; the intervening passage beginning with "tataśca" appears as if it were an interpolation, since it pertains to the second position, and the manuscript collections should be examined. "Yā vyaktiḥ" means "as many individuals as there are. "Of that which is the object of the linguistic convention" means "of everything intended as its object. He states another refutation: "like the words 'Devadatta' and so forth. He leaves [the matter] open for the sake of providing a refutation: "if [it is argued] that the primary [meaning]," and so on.

Now, one might object that being "grasped by perception" (*pratyakṣagrāhyatva*) is over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), as it applies even to jars and the like; therefore, he says, "the Veda is grasped by perception. The intention is that, consequently, the meaning of the word "perception" here is "being a Veda grasped by perception," and thus there is no over-extension. Regarding the phrase "the apprehension of the relation [of denotation] through the universal residing therein": the connection of the phonemes *ga* and so forth with their meanings occurs only through their nature as the universals *gatva* and so on, not in their individual (*vyakti*) forms. Just as jars and the like are not denotable in their individual forms, but rather through their universal nature, such is the sense here.

Now, in the *Vācaspatya*, it is argued that since it must be admitted that gods originate from expressive words (*vācaka-śabda*), and since expressiveness cannot belong to phonemes (*varṇa*)—for if each phoneme were individually expressive, other phonemes would be redundant; and because there can be no "collection" (*samudāya*) among momentary and sequential entities—expressiveness cannot belong to the *sphoṭa*. Thus, by establishing the relevance of the investigation into the *sphoṭa* through this alternative approach, the statement is not incoherent, given that the eternity of the cause of all past and future things is necessarily established.

Since that [objection] regarding their being eternal is also inconsistent, he says, "Furthermore, even for those that are eternal," and so on. [He states the reason: "Because of their momentary perishability. The meaning is that, consequently, it is impossible to establish the eternity of that which is qualified by such [perishability]. Now, one might object: "It is not the eternity of the qualified entity that is being established, but rather the eternity of the phonemes alone. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The purpose is the comprehension of meaning. This is because [the word] functions as a signifier (*vācaka*) in a form qualified by a specific sequence (*ānupūrvī*), and because that sequence is eternal.

He states an illustration: "by means of the earth in the form of a jar. And because of contradiction—that is, because it contradicts the doctrine that Brahman is the cause in every respect. The phrase from the Sūtra has been explained otherwise; this means it has been explained in this manner as well. It should also be observed that in the Śāṅkara-bhāṣya it has been established that scripture (*śruti*) is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is independent with regard to its authority, whereas inference (*anumāna*) and tradition (*smṛti*) are dependent with regard to their authority.

But if it is argued that this [rule] applies even in some cases—as in the passage beginning "But there is a restriction of the notions based on the syllables, because of the commonality and the presence of that"—then the sense is as follows: Now, one might ask, "Since the purpose is to avoid a contradiction with scripture by establishing that words such as 'Indra' denote the genus (jāti) of Indra-ness and so forth, why did the author of the Sūtras describe how the gods originate from the Word? To this it is replied: The status of denoting a genus depends upon the establishment of the genus residing in the various Indras and others mentioned earlier and later; therefore, for the sake of establishing those very genera, [the origin of] the gods and so forth was described.

In the Sūtra, Prajāpati’s act of fashioning is described as being preceded by a contemplation of the various names and forms (nāmarūpa) as depicted in the Vedas; for it is through this that the identity of names and forms across former and later Indras and others is established, just as it is with jars and other objects. Thus, the universals (jāti) residing in Indra and others—which serve as the direct grounds for the application of those names and are manifested by a common genus—are established. However, if one were to take the direct denotation of the universals themselves, such as "Indra-ness," as the reason...

Although the fact that these classes possess identical names and forms could have been directly stated as the proof [for their identity]—since that will be established by the scriptural citations to be quoted later—nevertheless, for the sake of strengthening that reason, the fact that the gods originate from sound, which further establishes that very point, was also set forth in the Sūtra. Furthermore, this reference is intended so that the reason "because they possess identical names and forms" may be demonstrated therein, and also so that the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) in the subsequent Sūtra, "And for this very reason, there is eternality," may refer back to the fact of originating from sound.

For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states that words such as *Indra* and *Vasiṣṭha*, which denote gods and sages, denote their respective forms (*ākṛti*). Although the fact that words like *Indra* and *Vasiṣṭha* denote form is useful only for dispelling the doubt regarding the non-eternality of the object (*artha*), and not for dispelling the doubt regarding the non-eternality of the word (*śabda*) itself—such that the denotation of form by these words need not have been introduced in this Sūtra—nevertheless, because words like *Indra* do denote form, there is no room for the doubt that the object is non-eternal; likewise, [there is no room for the doubt] regarding the authorship of the mantras.

The intent here is that even for those such as Vasiṣṭha and Indra whom you favor, their status as "makers of mantras" (*mantrakṛt*)—since it is established by valid means of knowledge that they originate from the words of the Veda—is in fact merely being "seers of mantras" (*mantradraṣṭṛ*); therefore, there is no suspicion of impermanence. Thus, the purpose of stating that Indra, Vasiṣṭha, and others denote *ākṛti* (class-essence) is precisely to serve as an illustrative example. Furthermore, the Śruti [implies] that [the mantra] is preceded by the knowledge of the seer; the sense is that if the seer were indeed the author, then he would have shown that the rite to be performed was preceded by the knowledge of the author himself.

"He who, indeed, performs a sacrifice or teaches with a mantra whose *ṛṣi*, *chandas*, deity, and *brāhmaṇa* are unknown"—this is the reading [of the text]. "The *dāśatayya*" means the *ṛc*s contained within the *Ṛgveda*. "Ancient occurrences" (*purāvṛttāni*) means narratives (*ākhyāyikā*). "At the end of the night" (*śarvaryante*) means at the end of the dissolution (*pralaya*). "From those very ones" (*tānyevaibhyaḥ*) means from these Vedas themselves as the cause. Regarding the phrase "because there is no contradiction with their being composed by the Lord" (*īśvarapraṇītatvāvirodhāt*): although even in the case of works composed by the Lord, there was initially the status of being the first proclaimer (*pravaktṛtva*) by Kaṭha and others...

Nevertheless, this should be understood as stated with the intention that the word *proktam* (proclaimed) has the meaning of *uktam* (spoken). Although there is evidence for its being a portion of the Veda, even so—given that the word *Kāṭhaka* means "the Vedic hymn (*chandas*) proclaimed by Kaṭha"—the suffix *ṇini* is applied according to the rule "after Vaiśampāyana and his pupils" (*kalāpi vaiśampāyanāntevāsibhyaśca*). Since the word ending in that suffix is restricted to refer to those who study or know [the text] by the rule "Vedic hymns and Brāhmaṇas pertaining to them," one studies that [text].

When the suffix *vyatīya* prescribed for the sense of "studied by" is elided by the rule *proktālluk*, and the suffix *ṇini* is also elided by the rule *kaṭhacarakālluk*, we have *kaṭhāḥ*. Then, when the sense intended is "their tradition" (*teṣām āmnāyaḥ*), the suffix *vyañ* is applied by the rule *gotracaraṇādvyañ*. This suffix would generally apply to all secondary meanings (*śaiṣikārtha*) under the rule *tasyedam*; however, by the Vārttika *caraṇāddharmāmnāyayoḥ*, its application is restricted to these two specific meanings. Thus, by applying *vyañ* in these two senses, we derive *kāṭhakam*.

The etymological derivation provided by the grammarians (*śābdika*) as "it exists" (*bhavati*) has indeed been shown; nevertheless, the meaning is that this grammatical explanation should be disregarded because, according to the principle stated in the sūtra "the *lu*-suffix is not applied when the connection [of the parts] is not perceived" (*lubyogāprakhyānāt*), such a derivative meaning is not cognized and cannot withstand logical scrutiny.

By the phrase "preceded by the recollection of those respective meanings," the eternality of meaning (*arthanityatva*) stated in the sūtra "If it be argued that [the Veda is non-eternal] because of the word, no, because of its origin from that" is challenged; and by the phrase "and because of the absence of the word," the eternality of the word (*śabdanityatva*) stated in the sūtra "And for this very reason, [the Veda] is eternal" is challenged. Thus, the sense is that this sūtra is intended to resolve the challenge regarding the non-eternality of both word and meaning. The sense is further that one must accept the beginninglessness of the flow of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-pravāha*), and not admit a dissolution of the primary elements (*prākṛta-pralaya*) in the interim.
Now, as for the point regarding "having the same names" (*samāna-nāma*)...

Raising the objection as to how the commentary can say "as stated previously" when the nature of *rūpa* (form) was not explicitly mentioned in the preceding sūtra, he replies: "by that which was stated in the two previous sūtras. He means that the *Śvetāśvatara* passage has been recalled; therefore, one should not be deluded into thinking that the *Śvetāśvatara* verse which will be cited—"He who ordains the Brāhmaṇa in the beginning"—refers to some other deity.

The meaning is that both [theories] are established: first, because the Veda possesses names and forms identical to those of the Ṛgveda and other Vedas belonging to other kalpas, and because it possesses a form characterized by a sequence identical to the sequence of other kalpas, its eternity as a word—defined by its fixed order—is logically consistent; second, since the referents such as Indra also possess identical names and forms, and [the words] denote universals manifested by those identical names and forms, their eternity is likewise established. Thus, both [theories] are tenable.

The meaning is that according to the Mīmāṃsakas—who do not accept a primordial dissolution (*prakṛtapralaya*)—there is simultaneous creation and dissolution, and thus the world has never been otherwise than it is now. "A sequence unlike the previous" means a sequence dissimilar to the prior succession (*pūrvānupūrvī*). Regarding the phrase "this much, however," the sense is that in the commentary passage "and therefore that [is] in us," the word "that" (*tat*) refers specifically to the aspect of being uttered in that very same sequence. Regarding the expression "independent of impressions" (*saṃskārānapekṣam*), one might object that restricting it to mean only the impressions produced by one's own utterance is without proof; anticipating this, he says, "Alternatively, 'independent of impressions'... [and so on].

One might object: "Since all objects are at all times situated within the intellect of the Supreme Self (paramātman), it could be argued that the very distinction between eternal and non-eternal objects would not exist; what then is the point of this doubt? Anticipating this by noting that mere presence in the intellect does not constitute existence, [the author] says: "At all times, by each preceding... [and so on]. The sense is that there is a difference between what is of human origin and what is not, and for this very reason, there is a difference between the Veda and what is not the Veda.

The phrase "the mere existence of one who initiates the tradition" means the existence of the Supreme Self as the initiator. He states that the collection of cited statements is for the sake of illustration because they lack the status of being a formal proof regarding the identity of name and form. Regarding the expression *hiṃruāhiṃruo*, he explains that previously, being *hiṃruā*—that is, being permeated by those latent impressions—one becomes *hiṃruā*.

He attains that; the meaning is that the same applies to Ahiṃsā and the others as well. "In the form desired to be accomplished" means the state of Indra and so forth sought in another *kalpa*. The meaning is that a person, having propitiated Indra existing in that *kalpa*, attains the status of Indra in another *kalpa*. "By way of the nature of the successive preceding Agnis, Indras, and so forth" implies that it follows the same logic as those [preceding cases]. "Simultaneously and by way of a continuous flow."

The meaning is as follows: although many eggs may arise simultaneously, while some eggs are currently arising, eggs produced at a previous time also exist; consequently, at the moment one four-faced Brahmā appears at the beginning of a kalpa, because another four-faced Brahmā residing within a contemporary egg also appears, there is no state of being perceived by a single kṣetrajña (individual soul); and because the great sages created by the four-faced Brahmā residing in previously arisen eggs also appear, there is no state of being perceived by that single kṣetrajña alone.

The phrase "that very scripture" (*saiva śrutiḥ*) means that [the opponent's view] is of the same class as that [scripture], namely, the scriptural passage beginning with "By speech, O Virūpa, which is eternal" (*vācā virūpanityayā*). Regarding the first alternative, he raises the second horn of the argument: "the status of being a sentence manifested by one [person]. The sense is that the doubt arises because all four-faced Brahmās possess the certainty that the Lord is authoritative (*āpta*); thus, due to the eternity of the Veda taught by the Lord, the doubt emerges. This is an illustration; it should be understood that the doubt likewise emerges for other followers of the Veda as well.

The phrase "arising from external causes" (bāhyahetūttha) means that since the syntactic connection (anvaya) must be stated precisely as the provision of a reason for the explanatory passages (arthavādas), their authority is dependent upon that [reason]; such is the sense.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is argued that there is a lack of authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*) due to indecision (*anadhyavasāya*). This indecision arises as follows: should the word *akta* (anointed), occurring within the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) in the context of the opening section, follow its literal denotation of "any substance" in general, and thus the word *ghṛta* (clarified butter) appearing in the concluding explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) be taken as indirectly indicating (*lakṣaka*) any liquid substance? Or, should the word *akta* be restricted to "clarified butter alone," in accordance with the primacy of *ghṛta*, which is required by the injunction to provide the specific detail not contradicted by the injunction? [The siddhāntin replies: Even for that which occurs in the injunctive statement of the opening section...

The meaning is that, according to the view of the Guru (Prabhākara), the authority [of the Veda] is established because there is no sublation even by concluding explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) regarding the word "anointed" (*akta*), since it is determined—by virtue of the remainder of the sentence—that [the oblations] are anointed with ghee. "Denotative power" (*abhidhāna-śakti*) means the power of the word. "That is the same for our position" means that even though the authority of the Veda and its eternity are established, there might still be a suspicion of the non-eternality of words and their meanings due to the absence of anyone to transmit the tradition during the dissolution of the primordial elements (*prākṛta-pralaya*).

Regarding the term "mahāmātra": therefore, it is established that even gods and others possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, because they are endowed with both the desire for liberation and the requisite capacity.

The sense is that this is the same [point]: even when the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) has occurred, the existence of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as the initiator of the tradition is understood from another scriptural passage; thus, the meaning is that this very "counter-argument" (*pratibandī*) will be stated hereafter. The phrase "the removal of the lack of authority characterized by doubt" implies a circularity (*cakraka*); the meaning is that the refutation is equal [in both cases]. Thus ends the section on the Deity (*devatādhikaraṇa*).

Yonder sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods. Of it, the sky itself is the cross-beam, the intermediate space is the sacrificial post, and the rays are the sons. Those rays of his which extend toward the east are its eastern honey-cells; the *Ṛgvedic* verses are the honey-makers, the *Ṛgveda* itself is the flower, and those are the immortal waters. These, indeed, are the *Ṛgvedic* verses.

They brooded over this Ṛgveda; from it, thus brooded upon, glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, food, and essence were produced. That flowed forth and took refuge all around the sun; that indeed is this very red form of the sun. Now, those rays of his that are to the south are its southern honey-cells; the Yajus formulas are the honey-makers, the Yajurveda is the flower, and these are the immortal waters.

These very *yajus* formulas heated this *Yajurveda*. From it, thus heated, glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, food, and essence were produced. That flowed forth and took refuge around the sun; that indeed is the white form of the sun. Now, those rays of his which are directed westward are his western honey-cells; the *Sāmans* are the bees, the *Sāmaveda* is the flower, and those are the immortal waters.

These very Sāmans heated this Sāmaveda. From it, thus heated, glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, food, and essence were produced. That flowed out and took refuge all around the sun; that indeed is this black form of the sun. Now, those rays of his which point upward are its northern honey-cells; the Atharvans and Aṅgirases are the honey-makers; the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are the flower; and those are the immortal waters.
These very Atharva-Aṅgirasas brooded over this Itihāsa-Purāṇa; from it, when it had been brooded upon, fame and splendor issued forth—that, indeed, is the form of the sun which is exceedingly black.

Now, those which are its downward rays are its downward honey-cells; the secret places (*guhā*) are the honey-makers (*madhukṛt*); the *Brahman* is the flower; those are the immortal waters. These very secret places, these honey-makers, and this *Brahman* heated that [flower]. From it, thus heated, glory and splendor issued forth—that which is this shimmering, as it were, in the midst of the sun. These are the essences of essences, for the Vedas are essences, and these are their essences. Or rather, these are the immortals of immortals, for the Vedas are immortals, and these are their immortals.
