Now, that which is the first nectar, the Vasus live upon it with Agni as their mouth. Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar. They enter into this very form and emerge from this very form. He who knows this nectar thus becomes one of the Vasus themselves and, with Agni as his mouth, is satisfied merely by beholding this nectar. He enters into this very form and emerges from this very form.

As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so long does he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Vasus. Now, the Rudras subsist upon that which is the second nectar; with Indra as their mouth—since the gods do not exist apart from the Rudras—they, having become one with Indra, behold this very nectar and are satisfied. They rise from this form, and as long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice as long does it rise in the south and set in the north.

Twice as long as that, he shall rise in the west and set in the east; he shall attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Ādityas. Now, as for the fourth nectar, the Maruts subsist upon it with Soma as their mouth. Indeed, having become one of the Maruts, he shall subsist with Soma as his mouth. As long as the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, twice as long as that he shall rise in the north and set in the south; he shall attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Maruts.

Now, as for that fifth nectar, the Sādhyas subsist upon it through the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa. Indeed, having become one with the Sādhyas, he does not [subsist] through the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa; rather, having seen this very nectar, as long as the sun rises in the north and sets in the south, twice as long as that he shall rise above and set below, and for that long he shall attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Sādhyas.

Then, rising from there, he rises no more; he neither rises nor sets, but remains alone in the center. Regarding this, there is this verse: "There, indeed, he never sets nor does he rise. By that truth, may I not be separated from the Brahman. For him, the sun neither rises nor sets; for him, it is always day. This is the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the Brāhmaṇa. He who knows this Brāhmaṇa *upaniṣad* in this way—for him, the sun neither rises nor sets; for him, it is always day. This very [doctrine] the Brāhmaṇa told to Prajāpati; Prajāpati told it to Manu; and Manu told it to his offspring.

Now, this very same Brāhmaṇa was told by his father to Uddālaka Āruṇi, his eldest son. This indeed is what a father should tell his eldest son, or to a worthy pupil, but to no one else whatsoever—even if one were to give him this entire earth, surrounded by water, filled with wealth. "This is more than that; this is more than that. The meaning of this is: *devamadhū*—it is honey because it gladdens the gods (*devānām modanāt*), like honey.

Now, as to how the sun can have the nature of honey, he says: "The sky itself. Of that honey, the sky—the celestial world—is the horizontal beam; the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is the middle cake. For a cake, which is the support for the honey, hangs suspended while attached to a horizontal beam; likewise, the intermediate space also appears as if hanging, being attached to the celestial world, and thus it has the nature of a middle cake.

The "rays" (*marīcayaḥ*) are the sons; by the word "rays," the waters drawn by the Sun from the Marīcis—which are of the nature of *mauma* (moisture)—are meant. They are called "sons" because they are like sons, being the seeds of bees, namely the minute insects residing within the cells of the honeycomb. Regarding the phrase "those of his which are directed eastward": those rays of that Sun are themselves the honey-cells (*madhunāḍyaḥ*), the apertures of the honey. The *Ṛks* are the honey-makers; the *Ṛk* mantras are the bees. The *Ṛgveda* itself is the flower; the action prescribed by the *Ṛks* occupies the place of the flower.

Those waters are immortal; when employed in the ritual action, taking the form of Soma and clarified butter, they are cast into the fire and, upon completion of the cooking, become immortal waters of extreme sweetness.

These very *ṛks* are like bees gathering nectar from flowers; they "heated," as it were, the ritual action prescribed by the *Ṛgveda*, which stands in the place of a flower. When these *ṛks* are employed in the ritual—having attained the status of constituent parts such as the *śastra* hymns—the action being performed releases a nectar that produces honey. Just as a flower is sucked by bees, fruits such as fame, splendor, sensory power, and vigor are produced.

The meaning is that it went specifically toward those syllables, and having gone there, it took refuge in the eastern part of the Sun, Savitṛ. This is the distilled sense here: the five nectars—red, white, supreme black, and those described as "as if agitated in the middle"—namely red and so forth, have been brought from the solar orb by the honey-bees of Vedic mantras from the flowers of ritual acts prescribed in the various Vedas, via the channels of rays situated in the regions from the east to the zenith; these nectars are produced from substances such as Soma, clarified butter, and austerity.

It is said that for those who meditate on [the rays] as consisting of fame, splendor, vigor, and sensory power—being connected to the honey of the sun and serving as the sustenance for the Vasus and others—the fruit is the attainment of the status of the Vasus and so forth. Now, the passage beginning with "And those which are its southern rays" is clear. "Exceedingly black" (*paraḥ kṛṣṇam*) means extremely black. The "secret instructions" (*guhyā ādeśāḥ*) are the esoteric teachings and the meditations concerning the constituent parts of ritual action. The "flower" is indeed the *brāhmī*, meaning the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) itself is the flower.

In the center, to one with concentrated vision, it appears as if agitated or as if moving. The Vasus subsist by means of Agni alone as their mouth; the meaning is that, being presided over by Agni, they subsist. He attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) and experiences the lordship over the Vasus for that duration. For twice that time—meaning double the period—he rises from the south; the same applies to the subsequent directions. "Single" (*ekala*) means having a singular nature. "He does not set" (*na nimrocati*) means he does not go down into disappearance.

[Objection: "But surely, once the specific subject to be explained has been determined, Indra’s entitlement (*adhikāra*) is also established; therefore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) need not be commenced for the purpose of determining that entitlement. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "Furthermore, there is only the initial statement (*upakrama*," etc.). Thinking that there is a total contradiction between the opening and the conclusion, he raises an objection: "How then," etc.

Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of [the soul] being a seeker [of liberation] and so forth," the sense is this: even if there is a contradiction between the opening and the conclusion when examined with precision, nevertheless, at the stage of reflecting upon the conclusion, one relies on the superficial understanding (*āpātapratīti*) produced by words such as "Vasus" occurring in the opening; thus, the initial flash of doubt arises. In the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*), the phrase "of the portions of the Sun being enjoyed by the Vasus and others" [is used].

Now, if the rays of the sun—which are subsisted upon by the five classes of gods beginning with the Vasus—are objects of meditation in the Madhu-vidyā, what inconsistency is there in the Vasus and others having the qualification for that [meditation]? For it is not contradictory for one to meditate upon another who is one's own source of sustenance; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all forms of meditation, since in every meditation, qualities such as being superior to oneself and being one's source of sustenance must necessarily be contemplated. Furthermore, regarding the Vasus and others who are included among the five classes of gods that subsist [upon the sun]:

If it is argued: "Since there would be no one among all living beings who has the qualification for the meditation on the Lord of All—given that there is no qualification for the worship of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) which are subsisted upon by the five classes of gods, because He Himself is included within everything—how then can this be a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), or how, by accepting this very prima facie argument, can the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) be that Brahman is to be meditated upon as existing in the states of the Vasus, Ādityas, and so forth? To this it is replied: By the force of the scriptural text, "The gods worship Him, the light of lights, as life, as immortality," [Brahman is indeed the object of meditation] through the five nectars, such as Rohita and the rest.

The intended meaning here is that even the status of being a thrower (pāsakatva) is not possible. The phrase "in the case of the higher knowledges concerning both" means in those knowledges of the Supreme which have as their object the Supreme as qualified by the individual soul (jīva). Now, one might object that since the resolution of the contradiction through the distinction of states was already established previously even for the Prāṇa-vidyā, it would be appropriate for that [Prāṇa-vidyā] as well to be the subject matter of this section. Anticipating this, and demonstrating another contradiction between the object and the agent by way of capacity and incapacity, being pleased and being the pleaser, bestowing the fruit and desiring it, and so forth:

He states another alternative with the words, "Or rather, because [the individual soul] itself is incapable of accomplishing the desired end," and so forth. Now, one might ask: how can there be a resolution for the *prāṇavidyā* by relying on the principle that will be stated later? For the principle to be stated later—that in the *madhuvidyā* meditation is intended as being of the nature of the Brāhma-vidyā—is not required for the *prāṇavidyā*; for in that case, it is possible that when the individual soul (*jīva*), who has become the body, is meditated upon, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) bestows grace and grants the fruit.

One might raise the objection that there is a contradiction between being the object of delight (*prīṇanīyatva*) and being the delighter (*prīṇayitṛtva*), since the quality of being the object of delight resides in another self; for a resolution of this is possible there. Anticipating this, [the author] says, "In the Prāṇavidyā, by way of being of the nature of Brahman," and so on. Although a resolution of other contradictions may be possible in that manner, he intends to show that the contradiction consisting of excellence (*prakarṣa*) and non-excellence (*aprakarṣa*) must be resolved specifically through the distinction of states (*avasthābheda*). Thus he says: "Excellence and non-excellence... and so forth.

The meaning is that there is a contradiction in that the exalted [Brahman] is the object of meditation (*upāsana*), while the non-exalted [individual soul] is the agent of meditation. As for the resolution "by way of having Brahman as its essence" (*brāhmātmakatayā*): this means the resolution is by way of the distinction between states (*avasthābheda*). In the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*), since it is impossible for the state of having Brahman as one's essence to be included within the category of the object of meditation, the resolution is made by the distinction between the bound and liberated states. However, in the knowledge of the honey (*madhuvidyā*) and others, the distinction between the object of meditation and the meditator is based on the presence or absence of the state of having Brahman as one's essence; this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "meditation on the Brahman in its own state," the meaning is that meditation on the Brahman as delimited by immortality is possible through words such as "Rohita" which serve as its own basis of support (*upajīvya*); however, one should not think that in the phrase "the Vasus subsist [on it]," the word *vasu* itself refers to the Brahman in the state of the Vasus. This is because there is no evidence for such an interpretation, and furthermore, because subsistence—in the form of relying on something to obtain what has not yet been obtained—is impossible for the Brahman in the state of the Vasus.

In the passage, "Having become one of the Vasus," it must be understood that there is an impossibility either of selecting [one] from among many within a single Brahman, or of the worshiper attaining the state of being that Brahman.

For this very reason, the subsequent commentary states: "The meditation being enjoined pertains to the portion of the sun that has become an object of enjoyment for the Vasus and others. This is because [the passage] is devoted to the meditation on what is not the Brahman.

Regarding the phrase "it has been explained": the statement from the Brāhmaṇa, "Indeed, neither does the sun rise for him, nor does it set," which describes the attainment of the state of Brahman, is intended to refer to gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) by way of becoming the Vasus and so forth. Furthermore, the interpretation that the word "Brāhma-upaniṣad" refers to the Vedic Upaniṣads is to be disregarded because it involves a strained meaning. And as for the status of being an object of meditation (*upāsyatva*), it belongs only to the portion of the sun that is the object of enjoyment for the Vasus and others. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the preceding text, which speaks of the Vasu-group as the object of meditation.

There is no contradiction in the fact that the aggregate of the Vasus and others is to be meditated upon as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), while the solar portion (*ādityāṃśa*) is to be meditated upon as the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Thus, such a mental synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) itself is the purpose. Now, one might object: "In a particular section concerning a specific meditation (*vidyā*), if the status of being an object of worship for the gods or the granting of divine fruits and so forth is not mentioned in the scripture (*śruti*), then that [aggregate] need not be mentally synthesized therein."

If it is asked: "In cases where [the deity] is mentioned in scripture (*śruta*), even in the absence of establishing a physical form for the deity and so forth, the status of the deity as an object of worship is certainly possible; therefore, how can these two sections (*adhikaraṇa*) be useful for the contemplation of the deity as an object of worship?"—this is true. However, it should be understood that this investigation is intended for the purpose of contemplating the deity as an object of worship in a non-superimposed sense (*anāropita*). This also serves as an illustration regarding the names of deities.

If [the goal] were merely success (*siddhi*), then the attainment of the state of those respective deities would not be the fruit of the *madhu-vidyā* and other such meditations; for even though something obstructed (such as release from Varuṇa’s grasp) is heard in scripture, it cannot logically be the fruit of the enjoined action. Why?

Otherwise, a different result would have to be postulated. In the *Antarāditya-vidyā* and similar meditations, the meditation on Brahman as existing within the deities such as the sun would not be established; rather, that meditation would be established only as existing within the spheres of light and so forth. Furthermore, in the *Upakośala-vidyā* and the *Pañcāgni-vidyā*, the specific deities presiding over the path—such as those presiding over the *arcis* (flame) and so on—would not be objects of contemplation as the path itself; instead, only the non-sentient *arcis* and so forth would have to be contemplated in that manner.

Likewise: "Just as the gods there consume King Soma, saying, 'Swell up! Wane away!', even so do they consume them there. Just as many animals serve a single man, so does each individual person serve the gods. When even a single animal is taken away, it causes distress; how much more so when many are?"

Therefore, because of such scriptural passages as, "Therefore, that is not dear to them, lest men should know this," which state that for both those who have attained the status of gods through ritual action (*karmadeva*) and those who have not yet attained it, there exists a state of being born as servants to the *ājānadevas* throughout their lives, dispassion (*vairāgya*) would not be established. The accomplishment of such a desired state is the purpose of proving the actual existence of the deities.

"Just as here on earth the world acquired through action perishes, even so there in the other world the world acquired through merit perishes"; "Be born and die—this is the third station; by that means this world is not filled; therefore one should feel aversion"—from such scriptural passages consisting of mantras and arthavādas, it should also be understood that the attainment of dispassion (vairāgya) is the fruit. Thus ends the section concerning honey (madhu-adhikaraṇa).

"For it is indicated by the hearing of that disrespect toward Śuka and by his rushing toward him," he says. This means: "intending to say 'conjunction' (saṅgati), he says [this]. Regarding "its conclusion" (tadupasaṃhāra): "conclusion" (upasaṃhāra) refers to the performance [of the rite]. Regarding "by way of strengthening independence": one might object—since we do not see a Śūdra listening to Itihāsas and Purāṇas preceded by an invitation, how can this serve to strengthen his independence?

If it is argued that it is easy to say that the address "O Śūdra" constitutes direct evidence (*liṅga*) for the Śūdra’s qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brāhmavidyā*), because of the instruction on the knowledge of Brahman after addressing him as "Śūdra"—this is true. However, it should be understood that such was stated because one path does not invalidate another. "From the Veda alone there is the comprehension of Brahman" means the comprehension of Brahman necessary for the practice of the knowledge of Brahman; the same applies to what follows.

It should be understood that even the proponent [of the Siddhānta] cannot deny the mere comprehension of the Veda (*brāhma*) through means such as *itihāsa* and *purāṇa*. He explains the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) as "the knowledge of the Veda. In this context, the reading "study" (*adhyayana*) is seen in some manuscripts; however, that is due to a scribe's error.

It should be understood that since the word "knowledge" is fit to denote either the knowledge of the collection of auxiliary sciences (*aṅga-kalāpa*) and so forth—which is useful for the performance of rituals and is produced by study—or the Veda itself, "study" is not fit to be denoted by the word "knowledge. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "due to the absence of knowledge" (*vidyābhāvāt*):

The word "study" (*adhyayana*) is employed to indicate the absence of knowledge refined by study (or, alternatively, to emphasize its priority). He explains the word "fire" (*agni*) as "the fire that has been established" (*āhita*); the meaning is: the Āhavanīya and other fires consecrated by the rite of establishment (*ādhāna*). It should be observed here that since the sequence [of words] is not intended to be significant, there is no fault in explaining the words "fire" and "knowledge" in reverse order. Now, [the text says]: "Therefore, a Śūdra. But how does this doubt arise?

If it is argued that this is because the fact that the meditation on the *brāhmaṇa*—whether directly or through a lineage—is to be accomplished by means of the knowledge of the fires (*agnividyā*) has already been refuted even earlier, some reply as follows: "If the statement 'Therefore, a Śūdra is not entitled to the sacrifice' were intended merely to indicate that a Śūdra lacks entitlement to those sacrifices specifically accomplished by the knowledge of the fires, then, since that [lack of entitlement] would already be established by the logic of the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning non-Śūdras), the statement would result in redundancy. Therefore, the statement 'not entitled to the sacrifice' applies to all Vedic ritual action in general, encompassing both ritual acts and knowledge."

One might raise the objection: "Could this [statement] not be intended to prohibit the eligibility (*adhikāra*) of a Śūdra? Anticipating this, [the author replies: since it would follow that a sentence expressing an already established fact would be purposeless, if one were to admit that such a sentence expresses an unestablished fact through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then there would be the consequence of the total abolition of all restatements (*anuvāda*). For example, just as the sentence "the darbha grasses which are turned eastward" is a restatement of what is already obtained from the Smṛti rule "they have tips facing upward," so too is the sentence "a Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice."

Intending to state that this is merely a restatement of a meaning already established by the logic of the *apaśūdra-adhikaraṇa*, they provide the following introduction to the commentary (*bhāṣya*): "Therefore, even [the statement] 'the Śūdra is not entitled to the sacrifice'... and so forth. They explain: "It should be according to the explicit statement. For a matter that is to be understood solely through direct revelation (*śruti*) must be accepted exactly as it is revealed; however, this particular matter is one established by logical reasoning (*nyāya*).

The sense is that the extent of the scope of the fundamental principle (*mūlabhūtanyāya*) must be stated as being the same as the extent of the scope of the sentence which is based upon it (*mūlin*). Or, it is a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyā*); [the meaning is] that the sacrifice alone is enjoined, and thus it is a restriction.

The meaning is that there is either no number [limit] or none at all; thus, the qualification for meditation (*upāsanā*) is permitted. The intention is based on the maxim: "What is not prohibited is permitted. Now, one might object: "Even though there is permission for a Brāhmaṇa to cause [the text] to be heard, as seen in the injunction 'let him cause [it] to be heard,' since no such permission for a Śūdra to hear it is observed, how can this be so? To this, he says: "Because of the absence of a person to be employed. This means that the employment of a person to perform the action is established by implication. The intention is that, through the injunction to cause [it] to be heard, the injunction to hear it is implied, such that members of all castes (*varṇa*) may indeed listen.

Regarding the statement "it is an injunction for the activity of the person to be employed": just as in the case of "one desiring food and drink should cause [another] to sacrifice," it is not the act of officiating at the sacrifice (*yājana*) that is enjoined—because that is already prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*)—but rather the act of sacrificing (*yajana*) itself; so too, in the case of "one should cause [him] to hear," since the act of causing to hear is already prompted by natural inclination, the injunction applies to the hearing (*śravaṇa*) itself. Therefore, the meaning of the objection is that hearing is not something already established by the purpose of the injunction.

Regarding the phrase "because no specific qualification of the eligible person (*adhikāri-viśeṣaṇa*) is heard": although there is indeed the hearing of a specific qualification of the eligible person in the form of caste (*varṇa*) in the words "the four castes," nevertheless, since it is impossible to enjoin the act of officiating at a sacrifice (*yājana*)—as that is already prompted by worldly desire (*rāga-prāpta*) in the injunction "one should cause him who desires food and other things to be sacrificed"—the statement "one should cause the four castes to hear [it]" must be understood as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the prohibition "and one should not teach him the Dharma" and so forth. Therefore, rather than abandoning that [prohibition], [the text] adopts this [statement].

The sense is that it is improper for [the text] to be devoted solely to the injunction of hearing (*śravaṇa*). "With this intention" means with the intention that [the text] has as its object the injunction of hearing implied by the injunction of hearing. Now, let it be granted that there is hearing; however—

Furthermore, raising the objection that since knowledge in the form of certainty—which is required for meditation—is not established for a Śūdra through the mere hearing of Itihāsas and Purāṇas without inquiry (vicāra), and because he lacks the impetus for such inquiry, how can he possess the requisite capacity?—the author, intending to show that because the hearing of Itihāsas and Purāṇas has a visible purpose and is for the sake of knowledge useful for practice, and since that [knowledge] cannot be established without inquiry into them, a Śūdra’s inquiry into the Itihāsas is as valid as the inquiry of the three higher castes into Vedānta, says: "And when this is so... (yadā caivam).

"He fears that one might say..."—if one asks what the answer would be [to such a fear], the construction should be understood by supplying the word "yadi" (if). The phrase "because of the mention of the fruit of hearing" means that since it is impossible for there to be a mention of a fruit for hearing that is not enjoined, the intention is that an injunction regarding hearing must be accepted. He then dispels the doubt that "in that case, there would also be recitation for a Śūdra" with the words "for hearing and recitation... Now, while the status of hearing as something to be enjoined may be granted on the grounds that the mention of its fruit would otherwise be inexplicable, this does not, however, establish that its fruit is the knowledge of the meaning.

If it is argued that this is established by the fact that the fruit of merely hearing the *Nāmasahasra* is taught, we say no. Since the status of hearing as something to be enjoined is proven by the impossibility of explaining the teaching of its fruit otherwise, and since it is improper to assume an unseen result in the form of the destruction of sins when a seen purpose in the form of knowledge is possible for hearing, the sense is that hearing culminates in the knowledge of the meaning. As for the phrase "if non-qualification has been determined": it is only the knowledge produced from the Veda acquired through study that is useful for the performance of Vedic rituals.

The meaning is that [the qualification] does not apply to the other [caste], because this has already been determined in the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* of the earlier system (*pūrvatantra*). Regarding the phrase "if the logic of the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* does not apply," the construction is "he states the reasoning. In that context, the phrase "not having been refuted" means "not having been refuted in the *apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* of the earlier system."

Immediately after the phrase "the fulfillment [of the injunction] itself is scriptural," the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) must be supplied as a supplement. "Due to the absence of extraordinary power" (*alaukikasāmarthyābhāvāt*) means due to the absence of the scriptural cause consisting of knowledge produced by the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) as acquired through formal study. As stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "For just as [one obtains knowledge] by acquiring the knowledge produced by the *svādhyāya* established by the injunction to study the subject matter of the three social classes (*varṇika*)."

If it is objected that in the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*), the three castes are not heard to be the qualified persons (*adhikārī*), we reply: it is true that the three castes are not explicitly specified in the injunction for study; nevertheless, since the injunction for initiation (*upanayana-vidhi*) states, "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn," it is established that initiation belongs to the three castes alone. Thus, the fact that the three castes are the qualified persons is confirmed by the hearing of this in the injunction for initiation.

Consequently, the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), having no agent explicitly specified and thus requiring an agent, accepts as its agents precisely those Brāhmaṇas and others who have been connected to the previously mentioned initiation (*upanayana*) and who require a purpose—thinking, "For what purpose have we been led into the presence of the teacher? It prescribes study for them alone and not for the Śūdra; thus, it should be understood that the injunction for study is appropriately restricted to the three higher castes. In this context, "being established by injunction" (*vidhisiddhatvam*) is a qualification of the Veda (*svādhyāya*).

But this does not apply to the knowledge produced by that [study]; for according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) rests solely on the acquisition of the mass of syllables (*akṣararāśi*), and thus lacks the fruit of producing knowledge of the meaning. Now, if the injunction for study were to extend as far as the knowledge of the meaning, then even the Vedic injunctions for ritual acts—which operate without distinction prior to the grasping of specific phonemes and so forth—would necessarily imply the knowledge of the matters to be performed for the sake of executing those rituals.

Just as the injunctions for sacrifices, depending upon officiating priests, do not fulfill themselves by enjoining Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas to act as priests—since they find fulfillment by reaching Brāhmaṇas who are already spontaneously engaged in officiating as a means of acquiring wealth appropriate to their own class—even though these other two castes possess the capacity for Vedic study, they do not imply that they must become priests.

Furthermore, it can be argued that by the force of the restrictive injunction regarding the means of acquiring wealth—namely, "A Brāhmaṇa shall acquire wealth through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts"—there is a restriction that only Brāhmaṇas are entitled to officiate as priests (*ṛtvij*). Likewise, by the force of the injunction for Vedic study, there is obtained the restriction that the performance of Vedic rituals belongs only to those who possess knowledge of the matters to be practiced, which is acquired through such study.

If it is argued that, since the injunction for study rests solely on the acquisition of a mass of syllables, there would be no knowledge obtained through an injunction for anyone at all—and since the implication of knowledge is possible everywhere—how could there be an eligibility for those who are not Śūdras? This is true; in our view, knowledge is not established by an injunction. Nevertheless, knowledge required for the performance of ritual action, which stands in need of a cause and is not connected to any other purpose, and which itself stands in need of a purpose, accepts the Veda (svādhyāya) as its cause, once that Veda has been refined by the act of study.

There is no other means of knowledge distinct from that [study]. Consequently, it follows that the knowledge produced by study alone is a subsidiary element (*kratvaṅga*) of the sacrifice. Just as in the *Vihārādhikaraṇa*, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was advanced that the fires such as the *Āhavanīya*—which arise independently [of specific rites], are produced by the *Ādhāna* rite, and stand in need of a purpose—must be accepted as being employed even for worldly acts such as cooking and lighting; by that same logic, the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text), which has been refined by study and stands in need of a purpose, [is employed] in relation to that which stands in need of a cause.

Thus, it is established that there is an application [of knowledge] to the knowledge conducive to action (*karmopayika-jñāna*). Consequently, since it is established that only those of the three higher castes who have studied the Vedas possess the qualification for ritual action (*karma*), there is no inconsistency with the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

It is said that the "vow of study" (*adhyayanavrata*), the initiation (*upanayana*), and so forth are mentioned. It should be understood that the "vow of study" is a vow that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to study, since "study" is already included by the word "means" (*upāya*). Alternatively, it should be understood that this was stated with the intention that the word "means" refers to the Veda, while the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the act of study itself. Furthermore, the term *upanayana* here has entered [the text] through the error of a scribe.

Since the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), which is prescribed as pertaining exclusively to the *brāhmaṇa* and other [upper] castes, cannot possibly apply to a *śūdra*, the section concerning those other than *śūdras* (*apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*) describes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in two ways: First, even though the injunction to study the Veda is not mentioned in a specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), it is nonetheless an auxiliary part of the sacrifice because it serves the purpose of providing the knowledge necessary for the performance of the sacrifice. And since the sacrifices, without distinction, authorize all four castes, they necessitate the study of the Veda for all four. In that regard, the preparatory rite of initiation (*upanayana-saṃskāra*) is enjoined for the three [upper castes] as an auxiliary to that study.

As for the fourth [position], since there is no injunction for the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), let the Śūdra, even while remaining uninitiated, personally approach [a teacher], study, and thereby acquire knowledge. Therefore, the study of the Veda, being taught as an independent rule (*anārabhyādhīta*), serves only the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*) and is not an auxiliary to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*). Consequently, since there is no deficiency in the sacrifice even in the absence of that [study], let the Śūdra, though having not studied the Veda, be entitled [to perform sacrifices] after acquiring knowledge through means such as looking at manuscripts. Thus, it should be understood that in both these positions, there is no possibility of implying initiation (*upanayana*) connected with the Brāhmaṇas and other [castes] for the Śūdra.

The meaning is that they do not depend [on them]. This means that in the case of a Śūdra, knowledge and its means (such as Vedic study) are not implied; this is the sense. "Also because study is a motivator" means that there would be excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in assuming that the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*) alone are the motivators for the study undertaken by a Śūdra. "Being a descendant of Sudhanvan is a favorable indicative mark (*anukūlaliṅga*)."

The sense is that, because the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantra beginning with "The Ṛbhus bend the felly" (*ṛbhavo nemiṃ namanti*) reveals that the word *ṛbhu* denotes one who is skilled in the construction of a felly, and because the word *saudhanva* is heard in the mantra "The Saudhanvanas, the Ṛbhus" as being in grammatical apposition with them, it follows that the specific caste denoted by the term *saudhanva*—which is a synonym for the teacher’s term *ṛbhu*—is intended; namely, those born of a Vaiśya woman from the teacher Sudhanvan himself.

One might object: "If this meaning were intended by the sūtra *śugasyeti*, it should have been stated at the very time of its explanation. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "here, for the sake of comprehension... [and] "...for those who are not qualified to explain [the Veda]. An objection may be raised: "Histories (*itihāsa*), Purāṇas, and the like do not constitute an explanation in the form 'having first cited a portion of a Vedic sentence, such-and-such is the meaning of this word,' whereby they would be dependent upon the Veda."

Therefore, there is no inconsistency even for one who has not studied the Vedas, provided that the meaning is clearly understood through the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth. For this very reason, the subsequent argument—that [the study] is either prescribed as an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) or independently (*svatantra*), and so on—is also untenable; for, in accordance with the injunction regarding the recitation to Śūdras, its adoption as an independent practice must also be admitted.

If it is argued that since the purpose of reciting [the Vedas] to a Śūdra can be seen as having a visible purpose, it is improper to assume an invisible (transcendental) purpose, and therefore it is more reasonable to conclude that its purpose lies solely in the performance of ritual worship and the like—this is true; however, because texts such as "That man shall encounter no evil here or in the hereafter" clearly declare that the fruit is indeed the destruction of sin, that alone must be accepted as the result. Therefore, it should be understood that it is for the sake of the fruit of destroying sin by means of understanding the sacred narratives.

"Because it does not conflict with that" means: because it serves as the cause for clarifying the meaning of the Veda, it does not conflict with the scriptures that enjoin the acquisition of that [knowledge]. "And because the injunction to hear would otherwise be purposeless" means: if hearing the Itihāsas and Purāṇas by Śūdras were fruitless, it would follow that the injunction to hear them is useless. "Because of the contradiction with the words of Śaunaka."

Now, one might object: "Granted that there is no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman in the case of Vidura and others due to a contradiction with scriptural statements; however, why should there be no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman in the case of those whose minds were purified by actions performed in previous births, who developed the desire to know Brahman (*brahmavividiṣā*), and who—by the force of their *prārabdha* karma—attained birth as Śūdras while having learned from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas the true nature of Brahman and the methods of its worship? Furthermore, it should not be suspected that, according to the reasoning stated, they would likewise possess qualification for rituals such as sacrifices, since [the scripture states]: 'Therefore, a Śūdra is unqualified for sacrifice. [To this we reply: In the case of sacrifices and the like...

Because specific prohibitions are observed [in the case of Śūdras regarding Vedic study], whereas such prohibitions are not observed regarding meditative worship (*upāsana*), Nārada’s eligibility for the worship of Acyuta as taught by ascetics in his previous birth, and for the worship of Viṣṇu and Śiva performed with the eight-syllabled and five-syllabled mantras (devoid of the *praṇava*) as taught in the Śaiva, Pāśupata, and Pāñcarātra traditions—provided these are preceded by the sacraments appropriate for a Śūdra—is not to be barred. Nor does this contradict the [relevant] *adhikaraṇa* (section of the Brahma Sūtras).

If it is argued that although there exists an entitlement for a Śūdra based on sources such as the *itihāsas*, this particular section [of the *Brahmasūtra*] is intended to preclude his entitlement to meditations like the *saṃvarga-vidyā* which are rooted in the Veda—and for this very reason, the prohibition against hearing the Veda and so forth was also set forth by the author of the Sūtras—it is replied: we do not deny the entitlement of Śūdras and others to those meditations specifically enjoined and mentioned in the *Āgamas* of the Śaivas and others; rather, we establish only that they have no entitlement to those meditations generally heard in the Veda, just as they have none to sacrifices and the like.

Nor should it be suspected that, despite the lack of qualification for sacrifice based on the statement, "Therefore, the Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice," he might nonetheless have a qualification for meditative worship (*upāsana*). This is because that statement merely restates a matter already established by the reasoning of the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning those other than Śūdras); and since that reasoning applies equally to ritual action (*karman*), Vedic recitation (*brāhmaṇa*), and meditative worship. Furthermore, it should be understood from the traditional law of Manu: "He has no qualification for dharma, nor is there a prohibition against adharma," which indicates that the Śūdra lacks qualification specifically regarding all dharmas other than those expressly prescribed for him.
Therefore, the Śūdra has no qualification for Vedic knowledge (*brahmavidyā*).

He states both the cause of grief (*śoka-kāraṇa*) and the effect of grief (*śoka-kārya*) as the reason (*hetu*). Since both the effect and the cause can function as indicators (*jñāpaka*) by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), they are possible as reasons; thus, the ablative case in the Sūtra is used for an indicative reason (*jñāpaka-hetu*). Consequently, the meaning is that [the word *śūdra*] is made known through two forms—cause and effect—namely, the hearing of disregard (*anādara-śravaṇa*) and the act of running toward (*ādravaṇa-rūpa-liṅga*). The sense is that the Sūtra’s meaning is that the grief produced by the hearing of disregard, which is the cause of the running toward, is indicated by the address "O Śūdra" (*śūdrety-āmantraṇena*). Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "by [Pāṇini's rule] *śucer daś ca*" (A 7.1.60).

It should be understood that those who claim this Sūtra is an interpolation have been refuted, because it was cited by [Kṣīrasvāmin] in his *Dhātuvṛtti* during the etymological derivation of the word *śūdra*. The phrase "including even non-flowing" implies that the etymology of *śūdra* as "one who flows (*dravati*) with grief (*śucā*)" is accepted by others. Now, one might ask: how can Jānaśruti’s hearing of the swan’s words of disregard be a cause for grief? For the censure directed at great souls by anyone whatsoever does not lead to sorrow; on the contrary, it serves only to increase their glory.

Furthermore, Manu and others record: "From insult comes the increase of austerity; from honor comes the destruction of austerity. One should desire insult from all sides as if it were nectar," and so forth. If you argue that for one who knows the Haṃsa to be a promoter of his welfare, joy alone is appropriate, this is true; nevertheless, for so long a time I have not attained such knowledge. Therefore, grief certainly arises because I have been censured by the Haṃsa, who stands in the place of a father. Consequently, my fleeing from him is also entirely justified.
Otherwise, if the censure uttered by one's father and others were not a cause for grief, it would follow that such censure would be ineffective; this point should also be observed.

He introduces [the following] for the sake of clarity. For thus says the Śruti: "Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a man of faith, a giver of much, a provider of many cooked meals. He had dwellings built on every side, thinking, 'People shall eat my food from all directions. Then, at night, some swans flew over. One swan addressed another swan: 'Ho there, O Bhallākṣa! Bhallākṣa! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is spread out as far as heaven. Do not touch it!'"

"Lest it consume you," he said. The other replied to him: "Who indeed are you that speak thus of Raikva with the cart, as if he were a mere acquaintance? How, pray, is Raikva with the cart? "Just as all the lower throws of dice go to one who has won the *kṛtāya* throw, even so everything that people do that is good goes to him. Whoever knows what he knows—that is what I have told you. Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa heard this in a low voice.

As he was rising, he said to the charioteer, "My dear man, have you spoken to Raikva, who possesses the cart? "How indeed is this Raikva with the cart? the charioteer asked. Having searched for him, he returned and said, "I did not find him. He (the king) said to him, "Where, my friend, one searches for a Brāhmaṇa, there you shall find him. So he sat down near a man who was scratching his itch beneath a cart. He addressed him, saying, "Are you, venerable sir, Raikva with the cart? "Indeed, I am," he replied.

The steward returned, saying, "I have found him. Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules, approached him. He addressed him, saying, "O Raikva! Here are six hundred cows, this gold necklace, and this chariot drawn by mules. O venerable sir, [teach] this to me."

"Instruct me regarding that deity whom you worship. To him the other replied: "Go away, O Śūdra! Let this [deity] remain with your cattle alone! Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa once again brought a thousand cows, this gold necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, this wife, and this village in which you dwell, and said: "Venerable sir, instruct me further! Grasping his face, the other said: "I have already taken these [gifts], O Śūdra! You shall speak through this very mouth [of mine]."
They are the Raikvaparṇas by name, among the Mahāvṛṣas, where he dwelt; to him he spoke.

Jānaśruti is the offspring of Janaśruta. A grandson (pautra) is the son of a son. His offspring is Pautrāyaṇa. "Śraddhādeya" means one to whom gifts are to be given preceded by faith. "Bahupākya" means one for whom much food is to be cooked in his house. "Sarvataḥ" means he has constructed dwellings for guests and visitors filled with food, drink, and other necessities in all directions—in other words, with the intention that guests coming from every side would eat his food.

The address "Bhallākṣa, Bhallākṣa" is a vocative used twice out of agitation through the figure of *viparītalakṣaṇā* (ironic indication), meaning "O dull-eyed one. This is similar to the expression "for the one who has won against the *kṛta*. In the terminology of the treatises on gambling (*dyūtaśāstra*), *kṛta* is a well-known name for the throw consisting of four dots.

In that context, for one who has conquered (*vijitāya jitavate*), the lower throws (*adhare ayāḥ*)—consisting of three, two, or one point—are named *tretā*, *dvāpara*, and *kali*. The meaning is that these [lower throws] merge—that is, are included—within the four-point throw called *kṛta*, because the existence of the three, two, and one points is contained therein. "He who knows that which he knows"—the construction is to be supplied as follows: "Whoever else also knows that which Raikva knows, to him too he goes. "As he was rising up" means while actually leaving his bed.

"Where, O friend, the seeking of a Brāhmaṇa takes place"—O friend! where in a secluded forest, on a riverbank, or elsewhere, the seeking and searching for a Brāhmaṇa—one who knows the Veda—occurs; there you must go and search for this Raikva. "Scratching his itch"—the meaning is, scratching his scabies. "Wearing a gold necklace. "A chariot yoked with mules"—a chariot drawn by two mules. Therefore, at that time...

Immediately thereafter, having recognized his exertion in the desire to know Brahman and having discerned his fitness for the knowledge of Brahman, [the teacher] thought: "Since he is serving me with the offering of wealth even without long-term service, the knowledge of Brahman shall become firmly established in him through my bestowing it to the full extent of my capacity. Thus, favoring him and indicating his state of being overwhelmed by grief—which signaled his fitness for instruction—by addressing him with the word "Śūdra," he said this: "Ah! O Hāretva Śūdra, let it be yours alone, together with the cows."

"Let this chariot be yours along with the cows"; the meaning is that by giving merely this much, the knowledge of Brahman does not become firmly established in you who are overcome by grief despite your desire for Brahman-knowledge. Then Jānaśruti again approached him, offering wealth such as cattle and a maiden according to his own capacity. Raikva, however, once more declaring his [Jānaśruti's] fitness, addressed him with the word "Śūdra," saying: "Bring these, O Śūdra; through this very mouth you shall cause me to speak."

"You have brought these riches according to your capacity; through this very means, even without long-term service, you shall speak to me—that is, address me with the words of Vedic instruction which you desire. Having said this, he instructed him. Therefore, by the word "Śūdra," it was intended to indicate his fitness for the instruction of knowledge; it does not signify that he belonged to the fourth caste. || 33 ||

The meaning is that he took [the wealth] at the proper time and went into the presence of Raikva. "Aha hāretvā śūdra!"—"Aha" is an interjection; "hāretvā" refers to a chariot (*itvā*) accompanied by a necklace (*hāra*). [Raikva says: "Let this [wealth], along with the cows, remain yours alone; what satisfaction do I have from this? For me, who am without a wife, what capacity do I have for protecting such wealth? Or how could your learning be established by the gift of such small wealth? This is the sense. Then, leaning toward her face, he spoke.

The meaning is that, knowing the face of the king’s daughter—who had been brought there for the sake of becoming his wife—to be the gateway and the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) for the imparting of knowledge, he spoke thus. This is because of the statement of Knowledge (*Vidyā*): "One who follows the Vedic conduct, one who gives wealth, one who is intelligent, a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), one who is dear, or one who speaks for the sake of knowledge—these six are my sacred fords. [He said: "Bring these gifts; you shall cause me to speak through this very mouth. The meaning is: "You have brought these sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); by this very mouth—that is, by this means of receiving knowledge—you shall cause me to recite."
These places, known as the Raikvaparṇas, are among the Mahāvṛṣa regions; he gave those villages where Raikva had lived to him—that is to say, after that, he instructed him in the knowledge.

And because of the attainment of the status of a Kṣatriya: for indeed, in the Mahābhārata, we hear of Karṇa—who considered himself the son of a Sūta—possessing the qualities of being a lord of gifts and a sovereign of a kingdom; and in the *Vārttika* on the *Aveṣṭi-nyāya*, it is stated: "The four castes are seen performing kingship without distinction. Thus, the status of being a lord of gifts is possible even for a Śūdra. Nor [is it impossible] for a Śūdra who is capable...

"One should accumulate wealth; for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses even Brāhmaṇas"—since it is heard [in this text] that he must be without wealth, how can his status as a lord of gifts (*dānapati*) be maintained? To this it must be said: in the *Vyāsa-smṛti*, in the section on Śūdras, it says: "Or, permitted by the king, a righteous man may perform [the rites] at will."

If it is argued that this is not so because a righteous Śūdra is permitted to acquire wealth for the sake of dharma—on the grounds that "a wicked man, having acquired wealth, might bring his superiors under his control"—we say no; for although qualities such as being a great benefactor might occasionally be possible in a Śūdra, the sending of a messenger by Kṣattṛ and the gift to him of the villages inhabited by Raikva are impossible in a Śūdra, since they can only be accomplished through the sovereignty over a kingdom, which is the duty of a Kṣatriya.

For the governance of the kingdom is the specific duty (*vṛtti*) of a Kṣatriya, since even as a means of subsistence in times of distress (*āpad-vṛtti*), it is possible only for a Brāhmaṇa. This is because of such traditional legal texts (*smṛti*) as: "But a Brāhmaṇa who cannot subsist by his own prescribed work should live by the duty of a Kṣatriya, for he is the one immediately following him [in rank]. But he who, out of delusion, being of lower status, should live by the work of a superior, the king shall deprive him of his wealth and swiftly banish him," and so forth; for sovereignty over a kingdom is not sanctioned by the scriptures.

Since the protection of a kingdom by non-Kṣatriyas, as shown in the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other texts, can be justified even as being contrary to the Śāstras, and since it is improper to accept what is prohibited when the assumption of sovereignty over a kingdom is possible without being forbidden by the Śāstras; furthermore, because Raikva’s residence in the kingdom ruled by Jānaśruti is established, his status as a Kṣatriya must be accepted.
It should also be observed that a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra is prohibited, according to the rule: "One should not dwell in a Śūdra-kingdom, nor in one overrun by heretics."

And because of the indicative mark [found] later regarding Caitraratha; the meaning is that the indicative mark of belonging to the three castes (*traivarṇikatva*) is established. It should be understood that there is no inconsistency, because the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Gautama—"The practice of begging for alms is common to all castes, except for those who are accused or outcasted"—is explained as having as its scope cases where the status of belonging to the three castes is not otherwise obtained. Regarding the phrase "in her who is known to be connected with two castes": the word "in knowledge" (*vidyāyām*) is to be supplied as the remainder; the meaning is "because of being recited together with Kāpeya. The meaning is "because of the mutual association understood from their being recited together."

Thus, it is established that the son of the family priest was Citraratha. Now, [it is said]: "By this [sacrifice], the Kāpeyas indeed caused Citraratha to sacrifice; they made him the sole overseer of food."

If it is argued that because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) within the context of the *Dvirātra* sacrifice states, "From him was born one named Caitrarathi, a lord of the Kṣatriyas," and since Citraratha is understood to have been the patron of the Kāpeyas, Abhipratārin must also be Citraratha himself and not Caitrarathi—this is not so; for it is impossible for a person already designated by the distinct name 'Abhipratārin' to be simultaneously designated by the distinct name 'Citraratha'. Furthermore, since it is customary for those of the same lineage to have patrons from the same lineage, if the patron of the Kāpeyas belongs to the lineage of Citraratha, [then Abhipratārin must likewise belong to that lineage].

This is not untenable. [Objection: But surely, if it were established that Abhipratārin was a sacrificer for the Kāpeyas, then his descent from the lineage of Citraratha would be established; and if his descent from Citraratha’s lineage were established, his status as a Kṣatriya would be determined; and once his status as a Kṣatriya is determined, by association (sāhacarya), Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya could also be ascertained—thus the indirect sequence is possible. [Reply: This is not so, because the fact that Abhipratārin was a sacrificer for the Kāpeyas is itself unestablished merely by his association with the Kāpeyas.

For the fact that Kāpeya and Abhipratārin shared a single meal does not depend upon a priest-patron relationship (*yājyayājakabhāva*); for we observe people who have come from various regions and are unrelated to one another eating together in one place. Furthermore, other types of relationships, such as those based on marriage or blood ties, may exist. Or, let it be granted that Abhipratārin was a patron of the Kāpeyas; even so, his status as a descendant of Citraratha is not thereby established, because while the Kāpeyas may have been priests to Citraratha, they could equally well have been priests to some other person. Or, let it be granted that Abhipratārin was a Kṣatriya; [the conclusion still does not follow].

If it is argued that even so, there is no evidence for Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya merely by virtue of being addressed as "Śūdra" in that context—[we reply: when a man is seen near an elephant previously unknown to someone, and it is recognized that "this is the king's mahout," the natural (autsargikī) understanding arises that "this elephant of his mahout is to be trained, and it belongs to the king."

Likewise here, when Kāpeya is heard in proximity to Abhipratārin, and since he is recognized as the priest of Citraratha by virtue of another scriptural passage, the cognition arises that "this Abhipratārin, who has Kāpeya as his priest, belongs to the lineage of Citraratha," and this cannot be set aside. And because there is no subverting factor, this cognition remains valid; thus it is stated by relying on the general principle (*autsargika-nyāya*).

And thus, since it is determined that Abhipratārin, who is accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa, is a Kṣatriya by virtue of being a Caitraratha, it is indeed proper to conclude—on the basis of his association with him—that Jānaśruti, the companion of the Brāhmaṇa Raikva, is also a Kṣatriya; this should be understood as being due to the concomitance of signs such as the instigation of the charioteer (kṣattṛ), which cannot be otherwise accounted for.

Because of the adherence to [worldly] impressions (*saṃskāra*) and because of the desire for the absence of those [impressions]. In the *Bhāṣya*, it says: "And one does not deserve [the title of] 'refined' (*saṃskāra*). Now, in that very same *Mānava Dharmaśāstra*, it is said:
"But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who follow the conduct of the virtuous, do not incur fault by omitting the sacred mantras (*mantra*); rather, they obtain praise."

In the subsequent verse, the performance of sacraments excluding the mantras is permitted for *dhārmika-śūdras*. If it is argued that sacraments devoid of mantras are not conducive to knowledge (*vidyā*), and that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even women such as Maitreyī and others would lack them—this is not so. For even though other sacraments exist, the initiation (*upanayana*) sacrament is prohibited for them by the rule: "The Śūdra is the fourth caste, born once. If initiation were present, there would be the consequence of a "twice-born" status (*dvijatva*) due to the occurrence of two births.

If it is argued that initiation (*upanayana*) is stated to be a "second birth" only in reference to its being an auxiliary to Vedic study (*adhyayana*), and not in reference to its being an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), we say no; for by the Vedic indicative mark, "Thou art indeed our father, who carries us across to the further shore of ignorance," even the initiation that is an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman constitutes another birth. If it is then argued that, in this way, the occurrence of another birth through the initiation that is an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman would result in the three twice-born castes having three births, we say no, because we accept this consequence as desirable.

"Birth occurs first from the mother, the second at the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, and the third at the initiation for sacrifice; these are the births of the twice-born ordained by the sacred law. Thus [it is said].

For Manu has also declared that even the initiation for sacrifice (*yajñadīkṣā*) constitutes a different birth; and because of the indicative marks found in the meaning of the mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such as: "From untruth I go to truth," "From the human I go to the divine," and "He anoints the right hand first, for humans anointed the left first," it is indicated that during the initiation for sacrifice preceded by the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), one transcends the human state and attains a divine birth. [Objection: But is it not observed that even in the absence of the initiatory rite (*upanayana*), kings such as Ajātaśatru of Kekaya served as instructors of knowledge?

As it is said: "With fuel in their hands, they approached him in the forenoon. Without having initiated them, he said this to them: 'Bālāki approached with fuel in his hand, saying, "I come to you as a pupil. Ajātaśatru said to him: "It would indeed be contrary to the natural order if a Kṣatriya were to initiate a Brāhmaṇa. However, I shall make it known to you. "

If it is argued that, since instruction is observed even in the absence of the *upanayana* ceremony, the same should apply to the Śūdra as well, [the response is]: no; for in that case, because the *upanayana* of non-Brāhmaṇas by a Brāhmaṇa is improper, such a state exists only due to the force of an overriding factor (*bādhaka*). However, elsewhere, the *upanayana* is mandatory; this is the intended meaning.

And because activity proceeds from the determination of the absence of that [status]. In the Bhāṣya, it says, "the determination of the absence of Śūdra-status. Now, one might object: since we see only the determination of the absence of non-Brāhmaṇa-status in the passage, "One who is not a Brāhmaṇa is not fit to utter this; my dear, bring the fuel; I shall initiate you," there is no determination of the absence of Śūdra-status, and thus this [argument] is incorrect. Furthermore, on account of this indicative mark (liṅga), even Kṣatriyas and others who are not Brāhmaṇas would have no entitlement. Moreover, this initiation is not a subsidiary part of Vedic knowledge.

Moreover, it is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of Vedic study. This is because Satyakāma had not previously performed his studies. Thus the story is told: Satyakāma Jābāla addressed his mother Jabālā, saying, "O Mother! I wish to live as a religious student (*brahmacarya*). Of what lineage (*gotra*) am I? She said to him, "I do not know this, my son—of what lineage you are. In my youth, while I was wandering about as a servant, I obtained you. Therefore, I do not know of what lineage you are. [She was] indeed Jabālā.

"My name is Satyakāma, and your name is Satyakāma. You should say you are Satyakāma Jābāla. He went to Hāridrumata Gautama and said, "I wish to live as a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacarya) under you; may I approach you as a pupil? He said to him, "Of what lineage (*gotra*) are you, my dear? He replied, "I do not know this, sir, of what lineage I am. I asked my mother."

She replied to me: "While I was wandering about as a servant in my youth, I obtained you; therefore, I do not know of what lineage you are. I am Jabālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. "I am Satyakāma Jābāla, sir," I said. He said to him: "One who is not a Brāhmaṇa does not deserve to speak thus. Fetch a fuel-stick, my dear; I shall initiate you. You have not departed from the truth. Having initiated him, and so forth...

Furthermore, in this narrative it is stated that ignorance of one's lineage (*gotra*) is possible for a child who has not yet undergone the initiatory rite (*upanayana*), which is a limb of Vedic study; however, it is not possible for one who has been initiated, who has studied the *svādhyāya* along with its auxiliary limbs, and who approaches a teacher with the desire to learn the knowledge of Brahman (*brāhṛvidyā*). If it is asked how this can be so, it is replied: in the phrase "this one does not deserve to speak as a Brāhmaṇa," the word "non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*) must be understood as referring specifically to a Śūdra, for speaking the truth is indeed impossible for a Śūdra.

"Untruth, excessive speech, backbiting, excessive greed, depravity, and arrogance—these entered the Śūdra from birth. On account of this Smṛti passage, Gautama’s intention that such truthful speech is impossible for a Śūdra is indeed appropriate; it cannot be otherwise. Furthermore, since the initiation (*upanayana*) of the three higher castes is established by the Śruti, the determination of the absence of Kṣatriya-hood and so forth does not serve as a prerequisite for initiation; therefore, in this context, even the common term "non-Brāhmaṇa" is properly understood to refer exclusively to the Śūdra.

As for the claim that this initiation (*upanayana*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) solely to Vedic study, that is not correct. Since we observe the instruction of the "Sixteen-fold Brāhma-vidyā" later on as well, this initiation serves both purposes. Furthermore, from the observation that Gautama proceeded with such an initiation only after ascertaining the absence of Śūdra-status, it is concluded that the absence of Śūdra-status is required for both types of initiation. If the absence of Śūdra-status were not required for the initiation that is an auxiliary to Brāhma-vidyā; [then Gautama would not have acted in that manner].

If, however, it were said that initiation (*upanayana*) is required only as a subsidiary element of Vedic study, then the initiation—which is a subsidiary element of the knowledge of the *brāhma*—would have been performed for Satyakāma even without examining his caste; therefore, it is concluded that two types of initiation are required, and the absence of Śūdra status is a necessary condition for them.

"And because of the Smṛti. This means it is intended as what is signified by the word "Smṛti"; that is to say, it is intended as a Smṛti text prohibiting hearing and study. Consequently, the sense is that one should not raise the objection: "How can a Smṛti statement regarding penance for hearing and study be considered a Smṛti statement of prohibition? [The author says: "When contrary impressions have ceased, knowledge will arise," as stated in the Bhāṣya. Now, one might object: "For human beings, there are many sins that act as obstacles to the arising of Brahma-knowledge."

In this regard, those obstacles which impede the arising of the desire to know [Brahman] are to be removed by the unseen merit (*apūrva*) resulting from the study of the Vedas, sacrifices, charity, and so forth; and those obstacles which, even for one who has already developed the desire to know, disrupt the attainment of the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), are to be removed by the unseen merit resulting from renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

Furthermore, those obstacles which—by way of producing an abundance of disbelief and contrary mental cultivation even in one who has successfully heard the scriptures—prevent the arising of the direct realization of Brahman that removes ignorance, are to be removed by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced through the observance of rules such as hearing the Vedānta. If it be asked how, then, Śūdras and others—who lack the unseen merit produced by the rule of hearing—can have the qualification [for this], we reply: because nowhere is it observed that the failure to produce a visible result occurs merely due to a deficiency in the unseen merit resulting from the non-observance of a rule.

For even when there is a deficiency in the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rules (*niyama*) governing study as an ancillary to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), one does not observe the non-occurrence of the visible result, namely the acquisition of a mass of syllables or the knowledge of their meaning. However, this much is the distinction: if the restriction subserves the sacrifice (*kratu*), then upon a deficiency in the unseen merit of the restriction, the deficiency of the sacrifice falls upon the person, just as in the case of a deficiency in the restriction regarding the means of acquiring wealth.

Furthermore, since it is not possible for the rule of listening (*śravaṇa-niyama*) to be for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), one must simply state that "if there is a deficiency in that [rule], the person incurs sin. Consequently, even for one who has already developed the desire to know Brahman (*brāhma-vividiṣā*)—whether he be a Śūdra or anyone else—who, having accepted the possibility of sin and with the thought "I shall burn away even the sin already incurred by means of the knowledge of Brahman," engages in worldly speech, literary compositions, and so forth; for such a person, the arising of knowledge is unavoidable even without the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*), once that knowledge has indeed arisen.

We observe that the view of others is untenable because the cessation of ignorance cannot be avoided [for them]. Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "functioning through perception and inference": the word *vṛtta* means "cognition. As for the phrase "by the Sāṅkhya, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others": the sense is that when the Sāṅkhyas and others have presented a nature of the self that contradicts natural worldly experience—such as a nature opposed to agency and so forth—there certainly arises a desire to know the modes of perception and inference out of a wish to investigate the nature of the evidence for and against [that view]; thus, there is no need for the Vedānta merely to introduce [the topic]. [The phrase] "useful for [establishing] the status of being the supreme cause" [is explained as follows].

The meaning is that, in the sūtra, "And there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence because names and forms are the same," the status of the Supreme Self as the ultimate cause is revealed by virtue of its being the substratum for [the manifestation of] the four-faced Brahmā and others. Regarding the statement, "It is said in the Madhuvidyā": this refers to the causal basis for the passage beginning with, "Then, rising up from there, he neither rises nor sets."

The sense is that it is because the state of being intent on the supreme Self (paramātma-paratva) of living beings residing in the body is established therein. Thus, the fact that the subject matter is the Supreme Self has been made known. Although the Saṃvarga-vidyā is taken for granted as having the Supreme Self as its purport—on the grounds that the quality of being the substratum of the dissolution of fire and other elements, as stated in passages such as "Vāyu indeed is the absorber; when fire goes out, it merges into Vāyu alone"—the engagement in the prima facie and final positions is observed [to proceed] precisely by taking this for granted.

However, it is not observed that the demonstration of that particular Vidyā’s focus on the Supreme Self occurs within that specific Adhikaraṇa; nevertheless, the intention is that there is an even greater degree of thematic connection because, in some way or another, that Adhikaraṇa also possesses the nature of an inquiry concerning the concomitant attribute of causality. The phrase "here too" means "even in the Adhyāya on Concordance (Samanvaya)."

"Because of trembling. It has been established that [the passage] refers to the Supreme Self. Now, an objection may be raised: if the status of referring to the Supreme Self in the sentence "Whatever this is" is to be established by virtue of its being situated between two sentences concerning the thumb—which themselves establish the Supreme Self with certainty—then, according to the Siddhāntin’s own position, the "trembling" would not serve as a support for the Supreme Self-referential nature of the two sentences concerning the thumb; for that which is itself to be established cannot logically be the means of establishing another. To this we reply: there is no fault in offering this criticism from the perspective of one who maintains that these are separate *adhikaraṇas* (sections).

Alternatively, due to a lack of satisfaction with that [previous] view, he says, "in this very mantra. The intention is that there would be no arising of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). This too should be considered here: if [the sūtra] "on account of trembling" were merely an introduction of a supporting reason as a supplement to the section "known from the word alone," then it would serve as a support for the meaning of those scriptural passages accepted as referring to the Supreme Self—such as "He is the eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious," and "That indeed is the pure, that is Brahman, that indeed is called the immortal"—precisely by way of being a support for that very sense.

It should not be argued: "Since the sutra could have been composed [otherwise], what is the purpose of introducing this mention of 'trembling' (*kampana*), which constitutes the meaning of a sentence formed by the word *prāṇavajra*—a source of doubt regarding conflicting interpretations? For, since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) would never arise [if that were the case], there is no possibility of suspecting it to be a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*). Rather, it must be stated that it is a supplement to the section beginning with "From the word itself, it is known" (*śabdādeva pramitaḥ*). This is because, in the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*), the term 'trembling' can possibly indicate other contextual attributes besides the observation of light (*jyotirdarśana*).

In the sūtra *kampanāt*, [the phrase] "because there is no impossibility" [is understood]. As for the objection that "it is not heard that 'breath [is Brahman] because of trembling'," it should be observed that by this, even the talkative person has no room to argue: "If, by the principle of *kampanāt*, [the section on] the separated *pramitādhikaraṇa* is a supplement to the preceding, then why, by the same logic, could the section on *ākāśo'rthāntaratvādivyapadeśāt* not also be a supplement to the *daharādhikaraṇa*? [The answer is: "It is caused by air alone."

The meaning is that it is precisely *vāyu* (air/wind) which, through its transformation into the form of a thunderbolt (*aśani*), can assume the nature of a raised vajra that is the cause of great terror. By the word "vajra," there is no suspicion that the fivefold-functioning vital breath (*prāṇa*) is intended. Although, by the force of the scriptural mention of *prāṇa*, the internal air with its five functions might be designated; yet, by the force of the scriptural mention of "vajra," the external air transformed into the shape of a thunderbolt is designated. For it is not merely the vital breath that raises the vajra...

Because the possibility of [the two] being the cause is impossible; therefore, their contemplation is performed as in the Saṃvarga-vidyā—this is their prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), as it is clearly stated thus in the Kalpataru.

Even though Vācaspati, by the force of the scriptural mention of "breath-vajra," set aside both the sentence and the context to assert that what is taught here is the internal vital breath (ādhyātmika-prāṇa) and the external air (bāhya-vāyu), nevertheless—since his commentary on that [text] shows a conclusion in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) stating that "only air is to be understood"—it is perceived that the subject matter is indeed such [air]. One should understand that he spoke thus with the intention that such an interpretation was possible; the sense is that [otherwise] there would be the contingency of resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

One should not say that this is not a definition because the etymological derivation "that from which one does not fear" is possible; for the word *bhaya* (fear) conveys the cause of fear, and since it would not arise in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), its cognition must rely solely on the definition. This is the intended meaning. "Also because of an ellipsis" means: also because of the ellipsis of the word *iva*.

The point is this: for this very reason, in the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra), under the section on application (*prayukti-lakṣaṇa*), regarding the passage "he brings the eastern [branch]," although the word "eastern" (*prācī*) primarily denotes a direction, its status as the primary meaning is set aside because it is impossible for that direction to be brought. Consequently, by the force of supplying the word "with" (*prati*), it is accepted that the word "eastern" indicates a branch whose tip points eastward. As for the question, "How is the understanding of causality obtained?"—the meaning is: when the word "from fear" (*bhayāt*) is not actually heard in the text, how is the sense of "from fear" understood?

He states that this [second] pair of introductory commentaries (*ādi-bhāṣya*) also intends to remove another objection to the commentary (*bhāṣya*) previously introduced, by saying "If that were so" (*evaṃ tarhi*). Alternatively, there is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "or" (*vā*) here. This means that there would be a violation of the natural consistency (*svārasya-bhaṅga*) of coreferentiality with words ending in the nominative case; specifically, a violation of the nominative status of the words and a violation of the natural consistency of coreferentiality with the word *vajra* for the word *bhaya*. Furthermore, there would be the necessity of supplying the word "as it were" (*iva*), which means that there would also be a metaphorical usage (*lakṣaṇā*).

Because *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis) has already been refuted. Although the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "vajra" is common to all positions, nevertheless, the intent is to refute the previous [position]. As for the statement "because the nominative case is prescribed": although by the rule *supāṃ suluk...* only the substitution of *su* is prescribed, nevertheless, the statement that "the nominative is prescribed" is made with the intention of prescribing that very [substitution] because it is recognized as being a part of the nominative case. Alternatively, according to the *vārttika* on that rule, *supāṃ supo bhavanti*, all [case endings] may take the place of all [other case endings].

It should be understood that this was stated with the intention that, because case endings are prescribed [for all], the nominative (*prathamā*) is also prescribed in place of all case endings. The meaning is that there is either a substitution of one case ending for another as in the rules *supāṃ supo bhavanti* and so forth, or a transposition of case endings (*vyatyaya*) as prescribed by the rule *vyatyayo bahulam*. The point is that since the transposition of case endings is observed in instances such as *saktūn juhoti*, its observation is not a fault.

"Because of the mention of light. This means that since this very [mention of light] is the reason for the context of this [passage], it shows that it is not proper to suspect that this mantra—which stands between two statements concerning the measure of the thumb—deviates from that context and refers instead to the ordinary element of fire (*tejo-dhātu*). "Luminous," "blazing," and "majestic" [are the qualities of that light].

Nor should it be argued that even here, since the word *jyotis* can possibly refer to fire (*tejas*), its meaning as "light" (*dīpti*) is not accepted; for the implication is that this would result in a tautology with the term *mahasvat*. Furthermore, "nourishment is observed" means that "favor is observed."
