One might object: "Since there is no causality (*nimittatva*) apart from being a supporter (*anugrāhakatva*) of the primary fire (*prākṛtatejas*), how can it be said that 'causality and supporting' are what are taught in the third and fourth chapters? To this we reply: It is true that causality culminates in supporting. Nevertheless, in the production of fire, the meaning of the third chapter is causality characterized by being a supporter of its causes; whereas the meaning of the fourth chapter is supporting characterized by bestowing upon the produced fire the capacity to initiate its own effects.

Intending to explain the meaning of the fourth quarter (of the verse), he says, "And [the status of] being an efficient cause," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "while that [Brahman] is manifest": the meaning is that since superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) occurs only while the Supreme Person, distinguished by infinite attributes, is manifest, it is untenable to claim that the manifestation of the superimposed phenomenal world conforms to the manifestation of that [Brahman]. This is because such a claim would lack any basis.

For even in that [Advaita] view, it is not accepted that the manifestation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) follows the manifestation of the qualified [Brahman]; rather, the intended sense is that only the pure [Brahman], as the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), is accepted as following its own manifestation. "Because there is no possibility of another light to be excluded" means that there is no possibility of another light capable of being experienced as shining in such a way that [the sun] does not shine after it. "The context concerns the scriptural passage on the golden color" refers to the *Śruti* describing the golden hue.

That [Brahman] which is established by the scriptural statement of its golden color (*rukmavarṇa*) in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*—"When the seer sees the one of golden hue" (*yadā paśyaḥ paśyate rukmavarṇam*)—occurring within the context of the passage beginning with "The sun does not shine there" (*na tatra sūryo bhāti*); and by the scriptural statement of its solar color (*ādityavarṇa*) in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*—"I know this great Puruṣa, of solar hue, beyond darkness" (*vedāhametam puruṣam mahāntamādityavarṇam tamasaḥ parastāt*)—which is recognized through the word "Puruṣa" (*puruṣaśabda*) occurring in the same context as "The Puruṣa is the size of a thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣaḥ*).

The meaning is that he possesses unsurpassed radiance by means of a divine body; that is, he is distinguished by that [body]. Regarding the scriptural mention of "rising": since, due to the all-pervasiveness of Brahman, no departure from the body is required for its attainment, the suffix *-tavat* in the word *upasaṃpadya* indicates that [the rising] occurs prior to the attainment of Brahman, which follows immediately after the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman.

Furthermore, because the [opposing] explanation is untenable; for it has been described that for those who meditate, there is an emergence from the body through the cranial nerve (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*)—as in the passage, "There are a hundred and one nerves of the heart; one of them extends to the crown of the head. Going upwards by that, one attains immortality; the others lead in various directions for departing"—and immediately thereafter the attainment of the sun is described, as in, "As far as the mind can be cast, so far does he go to the sun. Therefore, here too, [the text says], "having emerged from the body" and "having attained the supreme light."

Because that very object is recognized through the two words [“supreme light” and “light”], and because the status of being “supreme” can somehow be established for the solar light in relation to the light of the first stage on the path (the *arciḥ*); and because, for one who has reached the sun, the statement “he manifests in his own form” is also appropriate with reference to the liberation-by-stages (*kramamukti*) occurring immediately after reaching the world of Brahmā; therefore, the meaning of the sentence “having attained the supreme light” is simply the attainment of the sun, which is a stage on the path consisting of the *arciḥ* and so forth.

The meaning is: "If it is argued that the reason for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been set forth. Regarding the phrase "because it will be stated later," the remainder of the sentence is "in the fourth chapter. Regarding the phrase "immediately after the application of the reason": in the sūtra, "But if [it be said] from the word *uttara*, [the answer is] no, because the Self whose true nature has become manifest... it is stated that the Self whose true nature has become manifest is taught in the Prajāpati discourse as possessing qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), and not the individual soul (*jīva*) which is the substratum of evils such as agency.

The meaning is this: in the passage concerning Prajāpati, that which has manifested its true nature (*āvirbhūtasvarūpa*) is not the subject of instruction; rather, it is the bound soul (*baddha*) who has attained the Sun, as in the phrase "having reached the highest light" (*paraṃjyotir upasaṃpadya*). Thus, when the reason [for the soul's identity with Brahman] is suspected of being unestablished (*asiddhi*), it is appropriate to place the sūtra *jyotirdarśanāt* right there, as it serves to resolve that doubt. "But others say..."—the word *tu* (but) has the sense of *api* (also). This means that others also say exactly the same thing.

Consequently, the doubt as to what difference there is between this position and the previously stated position is dispelled. Thus ends the supplement to the section on the "Established" (*pramitādhikaraṇa*).

"Space [is Brahman] because of designations such as being a different entity," as in "Space, indeed, by name... and so forth. Some read it as "Space, indeed, [is other] than name and form," while another reading seen is "Space, indeed, [is other] than name and form. Therefore, both readings should be regarded as authoritative. Regarding the phrase "a mark of the Supreme Self in its own sentence": an objection is raised that in Śaṅkara’s commentary, it is stated precisely that no mark of Brahman, such as being the seer and so on, is heard there.

If it is argued that [the term *brahman*] does not occur in its own sentence, and therefore how can it be said that it occurs in its own sentence—[we reply]: No, for in the sentence, "That which is within them is the *brahman*; that is the immortal; that is the Self," it is the Supreme *brahman* alone that is being taught.

Regarding the section, "Space, indeed, is the bringer-out of names and forms," one should understand that Vācaspati’s intended prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows: by virtue of the conventional usage of the word "space" (*ākāśa*), the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*)—acting as the bringer-out of names and forms through the provision of room—is presented as a means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman. Furthermore, it should be observed that he uses the phrase "in its own sentence" (*svavākye*) to state that his own scriptural passage merely says, "Space, indeed, is the bringer-out of names and forms," and that no mark of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-liṅga*) is found therein.

Regarding the phrase "of name-and-form which are mutually sustained": [the opponent objects] that even for one who is liberated, the state of having name-and-form sustained by another is the same. That too cannot be established by referring to the present condition; rather, it must be understood through the perspective of what previously occurred. Furthermore, there is no natural fitness (*svārasya*) in the words "Brahman" and "Self."

If it is asked: "Since the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) favored by the opponent—which is rooted in the scriptural mention of 'ether'—does not arise due to the force of the indicative mark (liṅga) consisting in being the bearer of name and form, how can the prima facie view that relies solely on the context (prakaraṇa) arise? We reply: we do not raise the prima facie view based merely on the fact of being the subject matter at hand.

Because of the recognition [of the same subject] in the statement, "Having risen from this body, having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own form," which describes the two states—possessing name and form and being devoid of them—at different times; and because in the phrase, "The one who leads you out from within [name and form]," the reference is to that very same entity previously described as possessing name and form.

It should be understood that there is no fault in raising the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the liberated soul, because liberation is perceived only for one who has been previously liberated; and because in the immediately preceding statement of Prajāpati, "This person who is seen in the eye, he is the Self," "He said: 'This is the Immortal, the Fearless, this is Brahman'," the attributes of being the Self, being Brahman, and immortality are heard in reference to the liberated one, and these very same terms are recognized here [in the present context]; furthermore, since the status of being *ākāśa* (ether/space) is also appropriate due to the justification of the word *ākāśa* as having an etymological sense (*yaugika*) in the *Ākāśādhikaraṇa* and *Daharādhikaraṇa*.

The meaning is that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was stated by those very [commentators] who maintain that the liberated self (*muktātman*) is the supreme [Brahman]: namely, that the portion of the text, "That which is between them is the heart," refers to the liberated self, whereas the portion, "Space, indeed, is the revealer of name and form," refers to the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*). By this, a distinction from the position of Vācaspati is indicated. The phrase "restatement of the Śruti" is used because otherwise there would be the contingency of the form being "the revealer" (*nirvoḍhā*); this is the underlying intention. This should be understood in the same way throughout the subsequent sections as well.

For the sake of ease of understanding, he says: "The established conclusion" (*rāddhānta*). Regarding "is shown": since it is possible for something to be shown even without a formal proposition (*pratijñā*), and since a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is possible according to the method to be explained, it would be improper to abandon that [unity]; thus he states another alternative: "Or rather, the one who brings forth name and form. This is a designation (*vyapadeśa*).

Regarding the phrase "thus the syntactical connection (*anvaya*)": although even in this view the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of one of the verbs *asti*, *bhavati*, or *vidyate* is required, the sense is that this does not constitute a fault. Now, as to how the designation of being the "sustainer" (*nirvoḍhṛ*) of name and form can be called a designation of "being a different entity" (*arthāntaratva*), he says: "it indicates the property that establishes that. The sense is that the expression "from the designation of being a different entity" means "from the designation of a differentiator. [The opponent asks: "How is the liberated one mentioned immediately after?"

It should be understood that such a statement was made because of the opponent's (pūrvapakṣin) misconception that it is a designation of one who is already liberated. Regarding the Bhāṣya, the meaning is that [the Lord] is the sustainer also because of His "truthfulness of resolve" (satyasaṅkalpatva). Now, an objection may be raised: since the phrase "that within which they [name and form] are" mentions the state of being untouched by name and form, it is possible to imply the absence of sin (apāpmatva), which is the cause of that state; thus, while it is possible to speak of "freedom from sin," how can "truthfulness of resolve" be established by the phrase "that within which they are"? If this is asked, the answer is: it is not so, because [freedom from sin] has already been established.

If it is argued that although the state of being free from evil (*apāpmatva*) can be mentioned, since the state of having true resolves (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) has not been demonstrated, how can the latter be established by the phrase "that which is between them" (*te yadantara*), we reply: no. Since the state of having true resolves necessarily follows from the state of being free from evil, its demonstration is also possible; therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "that which is between them" serves to establish the meaning of "the creator of names and forms. This refers to greatness by way of knowledge (*jñāna*).

The sense is that the greatness of the individual soul (*jīva*) consists in its being conditioned by the grace of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and knowledge. Now, one might object: "How can the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* as something to be reached indicate that the primary subject matter is not [the Supreme Self]? Anticipating this doubt, he explains the intention of the portion of the *Bhāṣya* containing the objection "even though" (*yadyapi*), with the passage beginning "of that which is mentioned in the nominative as the one to be reached" and ending with "even though there is natural consistency. Regarding the phrase "by means of the intermediate context" (*avāntaraprakaraṇena*): it is beyond dispute that in the sentence "having shaken off the body," the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*) are both set forth.

In that case, if—by virtue of the intermediate context consisting of Prajāpati’s statements—that [reference] were intended to refer to the individual soul (jīva), then, according to the principle that "the reference is for another purpose," the reference to Brahman within those statements of Prajāpati would have the individual soul as its purport, because it would serve to establish the attainment of the individual soul, just as in the statement from within Prajāpati’s discourse: "This serene being, having emerged from this body... and so forth.

The sense is that, by the force of the *mahāprakaraṇa* (the great context), just as the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the sentence "This serene being" (*eṣa saṃprasādaḥ*) within the Dahara-vidyā is subordinate to the exposition of the majesty of the Supreme Brahman, so too the reference to the individual soul in the sentence "Having shaken off the body" (*dhūtvā śarīram*) must be for the purpose of expounding the majesty of the Supreme Brahman. Thus it is said in the Commentary: "it is concluded as that which is to be attained."

If it is objected: "Since the conclusion of the section was already indicated by the double repetition 'Thus indeed Prajāpati said,' how can there be a concluding summary with the words 'I am attaining the world of Brahman'?"—the sense [of our position] is that although the intermediate section concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) has been concluded, the great section concerning the small ether (*daharākāśa*) has not yet been concluded; therefore, this mantra remains a supplement (*śeṣa*) to that [great section]. This is because the author of the Sūtras has not yet dealt with this matter prior to this point. Furthermore, in the two Sūtras "On account of his imitation" (*anukṛteḥ tasya ca*) and "And it is also mentioned in Smṛti" (*api smaryate*), [the author] merely provided grounds for the existence of a distinction between liberated souls.

The sense is that the resolution of the objection regarding the teaching of identity based on the aspect of being the object of vision (*darśanārthatvena*) was not addressed there. Although here too only supporting evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) is presented, the intention is that these two sūtras, by means of strengthening this supporting evidence, extend as far as overturning the scriptural passages concerning the teaching of identity and the prohibition of difference.

In reality, however, just as in the first chapter (*pāda*) of the *Pūrvatantra*, the authority of the injunction (*codanā*)—though already established—is stated again in the words "the sequence is characterized by the Veda" (*śrutilakṣaṇam ānupūrvyam*) for the purpose of further establishing what was previously proven, so too is this restatement justified here for the sake of strengthening the distinction between the liberated and the bound. The phrase "of that which has been described as attained by the liberated" refers to the preceding statement, "like a horse shedding its hair," which is the required ellipsis (*śeṣa*). Thinking that the instruction on unity and the prohibition of difference are mutually dependent and stand in the relation of the means and the end to be achieved, he says, "or in a reciprocal conjunction" (*itaretarayoge vā*).

"It is indicated in his own work. Therefore, the sense is that wherever the word *nirvahitṛ* (conductor) is heard, since all such instances are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of what is already established by scripture (*śruti*), they do not constitute his own original composition; thus, there is no lack of correctness (*asādhutva*). [This applies] to words such as *pati* (lord), etc. Now, one might object: "The sequence of the Śruti is indeed: 'He is the controller of all, the ruler of all, the lord of all; he does not become greater by good action, nor smaller by evil action; he is the Lord of all, he is the sovereign of beings, he is the protector of beings, he is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded.'"

Furthermore, [the opponent asks: "Whence is this introduction of the *śruti* in reverse order in the *bhāṣya*, by abandoning that [sequence]? To this he replies: "From the words 'sūtrapati' etc. Regarding the word "pūrva" [in the compound *pūrvādiśabdebhyaḥ*], it should be understood that the genitive case is grammatically correct because the rule "tasya paramāmraḍitam" (Pāṇini 8.1.2) indicates that when used in connection with words such as *pūrva* which denote parts (*avayava*), the genitive case occurs. Nor is the sentence "He is the lord of all" (*sa sarvasyādhipatiḥ*) not a part of the sentence "May he be great through what is auspicious" (*sa na sādhunā bhūyāt*).

It should be understood that the doubt as to whether the word *pūrva* (prior) signifies a constituent part does not apply to the phrase "He does not become greater by good action" and so forth; this is because the word found in the *Ṭīkā* refers exclusively to the sentence within the specific context [of the *Śruti*]. The phrase "afterwards, 'This is the lord of beings'" refers to what is recited in the *Śruti*—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. "For the sake of inclusion through *tantra*" means for the sake of including with care those sentences such as "He does not become greater," which stand between the two occurrences of the word *pati* (lord) in the *Bahuvrīhi* and *Tatpuruṣa* compounds.

One might object: even if it were stated "from words such as *vaśya* and so forth," this would merely establish the inclusion of the preceding and following sentences; therefore, with this underlying intention (*asvarasa*), he says "in the form of repetition. The sense is that by setting aside the word *vaśya* heard first and adopting the word *pati* heard in the middle, the sūtra's formulation as "from words such as *pati* and so forth" indicates that the repetition resides in the word *pāta*. Regarding the phrase "together with the words *pati* and so forth": it should be understood that this was said with the view that it is appropriate to include under the term "words such as *pati*" those nominative forms such as *vaśī*, *īśānaḥ*, and *bhūtapālaḥ*.

In accordance with the natural sense of the Bhāṣya beginning with the words "eta cet" (and this), and in conformity with the intention of the Sūtra "suṣuptyutkrāntyorbhedena" (by the difference in deep sleep and departure) which asserts the distinctness of the Lord from the bound soul, the author of the Bhāṣya intends that these two Sūtras respectively aim at establishing the distinctness of the bound soul and the liberated soul. With this in mind, he says: "Is there a disagreement regarding whether [the Lord] is something other than the mere individual soul? and so forth.

With the intention that the exclusion of the liberated (mukta) is established by both sūtras—since even the embracing and ascending mentioned in the preceding sūtra are capable of excluding the liberated—he says: "Or rather, by those stated in the two sūtras... they are to be described."

The phrase "the seed of doubt" means that by establishing that [Brahman] is the two things to be described, the seed of doubt—consisting of scriptural passages characterized by the negation of identity and difference—is removed. The phrase "only this much" implies that there is no tautology with the *Ārambhaṇa* and subsequent *adhikaraṇas*. The phrase "by the logic that establishes [Brahman's] status as the cause of the world" means that since Brahman, as the mere substantive (*viśeṣya*), lacks the capacity to be the material cause (*upādānatva*) of the phenomenal world, it must be stated that Brahman as qualified by subtle consciousness and matter (*cid-acit*) is the cause of [Brahman] as qualified by gross consciousness and matter. This is the intended meaning.

He shows that the establishment of primacy will be explained later by the words "In that regard, in the section on *ārambhaṇa*," and so forth. The phrase "from the waking state (*buddhānta*) etc. means "from the waking state (*jāgrat*) etc. [The objection] that "the non-hearing of a word denoting the subject (*dharmin*) is not a defect" refers to [sūtras such as] "Because of denoting the world" (*jagadvācitvāt*) and "Because of the connection with the sentence" (*vākyānvayāt*), etc.; this is the sense. The word "of that" (*tasya*) means "of the fourth pāda. Now, one might object: "In [sūtras] such as 'Because of denoting the world,' even a formal proposition of exclusion (*vyudasana-pratijñā*) is not heard. Anticipating this, he says: "Not so, because of the word *na*."

"Even in the case of *anuṣaṅga* (supplying a word from a previous context), there is no fault," he says, because *anuṣaṅga* is superior to *adhyāhāra* (the supplying of a word not found in the text at all). The sense is that for you, however, even *anuṣaṅga* is impossible here. Furthermore, he states another argument—that there is no fault in *anuṣaṅga* when it pertains to a supplementary proposition (*pratijñā*)—by saying, "of the exclusion of [the view] that [Brahman] has *pradhāna* and so forth as its primary object. Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to supply the word 'not' (*na*) to the phrase 'as the cause in the case of ether and so forth'?"

Anticipating the objection that the proposition stated in the Commentary—that it is possible to determine that the Supreme Brahman is the source of the world—is not certain, he says: "Even though an ellipsis is observed in some places. This means that even if [the passage] refers to the Supreme Self, there is no doubt. For although words such as "the controller of all" could, in some way or another, be applied to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone.

Vācaspati has presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in this context as follows: "In this passage, there is not even a single sentence that establishes the Supreme Self. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the claim that passages such as "the controller of all," "the lord of all," and so forth, establish the individual soul (*jīva*), is undoubtedly an act of extreme audacity. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*): indeed, it is for the purpose of removing the delusion of the individual soul superimposed upon the Lord that the identity of the soul with the Lord—who is its substrate—is taught.

In that regard, as for the delusion regarding the Lord (*īśvara*), does it belong to the Lord or to the individual soul (*jīva*)? It cannot be the first, because delusion is impossible for anyone [who is the Lord]. Nor can it be the second, because [the soul] would be devoid of knowledge of the Lord who serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) therein.

The meaning is that no delusion arises for the individual soul (*jīva*). "And because we observe the marks of *tātparya*" means that we observe the marks of *tātparya* consisting of repetition (*abhyāsa*) and novelty (*apūrvatva*). "In another branch" means in the *Kaupītakī*, *Śvetāśvatara*, and other Upaniṣads. "And because it is heard in the *Sadvicā* [Saddhida]" means because it is heard in the *Sadvicā* [Saddhida] thus: "O dear one, then he becomes united with Being. "Because the scriptural reason is contradictory" means that the distinction between deep sleep and departure does not prove the position that [the self] is the individual soul (*jīva*). This is the sense.

As for the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated previously, he says that it is not based on scripture (*na śābda*), because the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) is the subject under discussion. Now, one might object: "The prima facie view is indeed independent of the Sūtras; let the first Sūtra itself be a proof for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In order to dispel that doubt. Furthermore, [he mentions] "the possession of sovereignty free from limiting adjuncts" (*nirupādhikaiśvaryavattva*). The underlying intention is this: since it is possible to employ as a reason in the proof of the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious (*cid-acid-vailakṣaṇya*) such qualities as "being the Supreme Lord" (*prājñatva*) independently of corroboration by other scriptural branches, it is impossible to employ corroboration from other branches as a reason in that specific context.
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of being a different entity.

Thus ends [the section] from the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads and the one who adorned the creation of sixty-four literary works.
The third quarter of the first chapter.

In response to the doubt—namely, "What is the purpose of mentioning again here the exclusion of other connections (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*) for the three-quarter [definition] stated at the beginning of the second quarter, which was already established as being connected to that quarter?"—the author says: "In the first quarter... The phrase "of the nature of the substratum" (*dharmisvarūpa*) means that the qualities such as omniscience and so forth are ultimately auspicious (*kalyāṇatva*). [The quality of] being the inner self of all beings refers to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*).

How is it established that [the Self] is the subject matter of the Vaiśvānara section? Anticipating the objection that in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa and in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, one does not hear a statement of such a form as "the inner Self of all beings," he says: "He is the inner Self of all beings," and so forth.

The meaning is that because the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad statement—"From his feet came the earth; he is the inner Self of all beings"—which belongs to the same context as the subject-vacana of the *dyubhv-ādy-adhikaraṇa*, is cited as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) in the *vaiśvānara-adhikaraṇa* quality-sūtra, "That which is being remembered may be an inference" (*smaryamāṇam anumānaṃ syāt*).

Regarding the phrase "now thus" (*idānīm iti*), it means that immediately following the [previous] text, there is an exposition by way of demonstrating the primary matter (*pradhāna*), the spirit (*puruṣa*), and so forth. Thus, these are not merely indicators of the *liṅga* (the mark); rather, they follow the method of demonstrating the causality of the primary matter and other principles by way of demonstrating those very principles which possess the *liṅga* (the marked). This reading is correct, though the lexicon should be consulted.

"Because of the negation of anything other than the inner self (pratyagātman) and the Supreme" means that, as in the Sāṃkhya system, there is a negation of anything distinct from the inner self, according to the statement: "There is nothing whatsoever higher than the Puruṣa. The phrase "distinct from both the bound and the liberated states" is explained as indicating the meaning of the first quarter of the verse; however, it should be understood that this was stated with the intention that it also serves to remind one of the subject matter of the immediately preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).
The word *rūpyate* means "it is made to possess form"; the sense is that it is rendered so by means of this [instrument].

From the word *rūpa*, by adding the suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "he makes that" (*tat karoti*), and because of the application of the rule "like the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*" (*iṣṭhavadbhāva*) to the *ṇi*-affix, there is the elision of the *matup* suffix according to the rule "elision of *mat* after *vimat*" (*vimato rluk*), as well as the elision of the *ṭi* portion; thus, from the causative form *rūpī*, the usage *rūpyate* ("it is made into form") occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*).

The derivation of the word *rūpaka* is as follows: from the root *kṛ* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*), followed by the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of the agent, and with the elision of the *ṇi*, one who makes something "possessed of form" (*rūpin*) is called a *rūpaka*. This is precisely the statement of the Alamkārikas. Consequently, charioteers, chariots, and so forth are *rūpakas* because they make the body and other such objects of comparison (*upameya*) possessed of form by means of their own form. Therefore, the meaning is: "because of the grasping of the body arranged in the form of a chariot that is a *rūpaka*. The phrase "intended as primary" implies that there is freedom of choice regarding the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*).

The intention is that [the term *avyakta*] should be placed first [in the compound]. If it is asked, "What is the purpose of such an instruction? it is replied as follows: since the senses and so forth are "placed in the metaphorical body" (*śarīrarūpakavinyasta*)—meaning they are deposited within the body by way of being its substratum—and because they have already been grasped by their respective designating words, they are grasped by the word *avyakta* through the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*). Since the principle of elimination must be presented here as the restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*), there is also a purpose in resorting to a different compound to demonstrate that [principle].

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated up to the verse beginning with "That highest step of Viṣṇu": "The senses, they say, are the horses; the objects are their paths. The wise say that the Self, joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. But he who is devoid of wisdom, being as if unyoked from his mind, his senses remain unsubdued, like the horses of a driverless chariot. However, he who possesses wisdom, being joined with a disciplined mind, his senses remain subdued, like the well-trained horses of a skilled charioteer."

But he who lacks discernment, who is without a disciplined mind, and is always impure, does not attain that state; he enters into the cycle of rebirth. But he who possesses discernment, who has a disciplined mind, and is always pure, attains that state from which one is not born again. The man for whom discernment is the charioteer and the mind is the rein reaches the end of the journey—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. Higher than the senses are the objects; and higher than the objects is the mind.

Higher than the mind is the intellect (*buddhi*); higher than the intellect is the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*). Higher than the Great is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); higher than the Unmanifest is the Person (*puruṣa*). There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal. This Self, hidden within all beings, does not shine forth; it is seen [only by the subtle].

With the subtlest intellect, those who perceive the subtle should restrain speech within the mind; the wise man should restrain that [mind] within the knowing self (*jñāna-ātman*); he should restrain that knowing self within the Great Self (*mahat-ātman*); and he should restrain that [Great Self] within the Peaceful Self (*śānta-ātman*). Arise! Be awake! Having attained the supreme, understand! The edge of a razor is sharpened and difficult to traverse; the poets say that path is hard to pass. "Soundless, touchless, formless, and imperishable"—such is the sequence of the Śruti. The meaning is that the excellence characterized by being the goal (*sādhya*) implies the excellence characterized by being the sovereign (*śeṣin*). [The functions are] determination (*adhyavasāya*), egoity (*abhimāna*), and thought (*cintā*).

Due to its differentiation, the mind itself is designated by the terms *buddhi*, *ahaṅkāra*, and *citta*. Intending to show that there is no inconsistency even if the word *buddhi* refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—as established in the Sūtra-bhāṣya stating that "the fivefold function is designated as the mind"—he says: "Alternatively, it has been stated by some that the word *buddhi* refers to the internal organ. For indeed, by the term *mahat*, the proponents of falsehood [cite]: "Mind, the Great One (*mahān*), intellect (*mati*), the heart (*hr̥d*), the world (*bhūḥ*), intellect (*buddhi*), renown (*khyāti*), and the Lord (*īśvara*)."

On the basis of the traditional authority (smṛti) stating, "Wisdom, consciousness, thought, and memory are indeed grasped," this refers to the intellect (buddhi) of Hiraṇyagarbha that arose first; and since that [intellect] originates from the Unmanifest (avyakta), the statement, "The Unmanifest is higher than the Great One (mahat)," is logically consistent.

Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) itself is denoted by the word "the Great" (*mahat*), because of its qualification by the word "Self" (*ātman*). Even in that case, since the state of being an individual soul is dependent upon the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), the transcendence of the Great is logically established. The sense is that, in both views, the fact of being grounded in ignorance—which is denoted by the term "Unmanifest"—and the transcendence of the Great are figuratively attributed to the body, which is its effect. Now, one might ask: how can it be said that [this] extends as far as the individual soul?

Anticipating the objection that—since in the preceding statement, "The Unmanifest is greater than the Great," the body denoted by the word "Unmanifest" is presented as being superior even to the individual soul (jīva), it would therefore be appropriate to include the entire series of principles ending with the Unmanifest—he says:

"In this statement" means in the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "as previously described, ending with the Self. "And because the *pada* is not mentioned here" means that the "supreme *pada* of Viṣṇu"—which is metaphorically represented as the "far shore" (*pāra*) in the verse "he reaches the far shore of the path, that supreme *pada* of Viṣṇu"—is not mentioned in the passage "the objects are superior to the senses," etc. "In some places it exists" refers to passages such as "the unborn, desireless [nature]," since such an investigation will be shown later.
"From the intellect (*buddhi*) by way of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)"—here, *buddhi* is the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*). In that system...

The sense is that there is a contradiction with the systematic process (*prakriyā*) because, according to the *Tantra*, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is produced from the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*), and thus is not produced from the mind (*manas*). The phrase "of the portions of the Sūtras" means that the passage beginning with "and [the scripture] shows" (*darśayati ca*) is in the nature of a commentary on those specific portions of the Sūtras. Consequently, the objection—that if "and [it] shows" refers to the portions of the Sūtras, then the portion of the Bhāṣya beginning with "that very same... (*tadeva hi*) would result in being unconnected anywhere—is to be understood as irrelevant.

One might object: "Since the *sūtra* *supāṃ suluk...* mentions the *su*-affix first, and there is no reason to bypass it, why would the status of being in the accusative case not be established—given that the *su* is replaced by its own substitute (*svādeśa*) and the elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*halṅyādi-lopa*) occurs? Anticipating this doubt, he states, beginning with "nanu vākchabdāt... etc., that this path is not taken due to the excessive complexity of the grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-gaurava*). Furthermore, one might ask: "How is the form *manasī* used in the *Bhāṣya*, since a long vowel (*sarvaṇa-dīrgha*) ought to have occurred here? To this he replies: "Because [the rule] *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe* applies."

The meaning is that the designation "in the mind" (*manasi*) is based on the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*), which is caused by the *pragṛhya* designation prescribed by the rule *īdūtau ca saptamyarthe*; this [preservation] is, in turn, based on the recollection of the rule for the preservation of the original form. Although the reading *prakṛtivadbhāvasmaraṇa* is seen in some places, it is merely due to a scribal error or a slip of the pen; for it cannot be justified even by means of an *upasaṅkhyāna* (supplementary rule).

We say: the meaning is that even the rule *iyāḍiyājīkārāṇām upasaṅkhyānam* cannot be applied as a solution, because it pertains specifically to the Vedic domain (*chāndasa*) and thus cannot be relied upon here. He rejects the suspicion that *vāṅmanasī* might be a dual form ending in the accusative case, and clarifies both its consistency with the context and the justification for its being in the singular.

Regarding the phrase "of those who say *yacchet*," some explain it as referring to the followers of Yādavaprakāśa; this is the meaning. He demonstrates his own text by stating, "In their commentary on the final sūtra, they have said: 'Now, they might mean by the word *buddhi* the *ahaṅkāra*'"—the meaning is that this was stated by the followers of Yādavaprakāśa themselves in their commentary on the sūtra "And like the *mahat*."

He states another argument with the words, "This avoidance of the proximity of sense-objects is for that purpose," and so forth; the phrase "at the time of emergence from yoga" means during the state of being devoid of yoga. As for the absolute prohibition [of sense-objects], the intention is that the non-mention in this mantra of the avoidance of the proximity of sense-objects and so forth—which are to be practiced at the time of emergence from yoga—is not a defect. He concludes the subject at hand with the words, "Therefore, only at the time of yoga"; although this doubt—namely, "why should the word 'body,' which denotes an effect, not be used metaphorically?"—has already been refuted previously by the reasoning of the *Upakrama-adhikaraṇa* (the section on the initial statement) and other arguments, [it is raised here again].

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this is a restatement intended to present another argument implied by the fragment of the Sūtra beginning with "tathāpyarhatvāt" (nevertheless, because of its fitness for that). Now, one might object: "In the phrase 'tadarhatvāt' (because of its fitness for that), how can the word 'that' refer to the unevolved (*avyākṛta*) non-sentient entity that has undergone modification? For, since the word 'subtle' (*sūkṣma*) in the Sūtra refers only to the subtle state, the modified and evolved (*vyākṛta*) state is not the subject under discussion. Anticipating this doubt:

Since "body" was mentioned in the preceding sūtra and since it is specified here as "subtle," the subtle [state] that has attained the condition of a body is present in the intellect (*buddhi*), being distinguished from what preceded it.

He states that its reference by the word "that" (tat) is possible because it has been introduced [in the previous sūtra]; the meaning is that "subtlety" (sūkṣmatvam) is presented by its own word, namely by the word "subtle" (sūkṣmam) in the sūtra. "Presented in the intellect" (buddhistham) means that it is present in the intellect as the "likeness of the body" (śarīrarūpaka) in the preceding sūtra. "He states the form which is the cause for defining the entity as persisting through the two states" means that he states the impossibility of the primary sense [of the word] being the seed for defining the entity as qualified by the other state.

The sense is that it must be stated that the conscious entity (*cidvastu*), being subject to modifications in the form of contraction and expansion of knowledge, lacks the capacity for activity toward human goals—just like a chariot—whereas only the unconscious entity (*acidvastu*), when undergoing modification, possesses such capacity. By means of demonstrating the specific activity directed toward the accomplishment of human goals, [it is shown that] speech and so forth are the instruments for achieving those goals, while "specific activity" refers to their regulation; consequently, it is only the instruments for achieving human goals that are intended in the metaphorical statement (*rūpakavākya*) and even in the statement defining the ultimate limit (*paratvāvadhivākya*).

The sense is that, because the subtle [body] is what is grasped and the physical body is not so, it is logical to understand the term as referring to the body alone. "The absence of a form not delimited by another time" means the absence of a form excluded from another time; that is to say, the absence of exclusion from another time, which amounts to its persistence through another time.

The meaning is as follows: since even the dependence on that which has its purpose served (tadupayuktārthatādadhīnya) [is to be considered], that by which something is unmanifested is "that which has its purpose served" (tadupayuktārtha); this refers to the Great One (mahat) and the rest, which constitute the objects to be accomplished. The sense is that because the nature and activity of those things whose purposes have been served are dependent on [the Unmanifest], it is observed that the objects to be accomplished by them are likewise dependent on it.

One might object: "Granted that their identity [with Brahman] is established through the teaching of their being the body in the doctrines concerning the expansion [of the universe], how is it established in the doctrines concerning dissolution (*pralaya*), since those only teach the dissolution of earth and the other elements into the [unmanifest] *avyākṛta*? Anticipating this doubt, the author of the *Bhāṣya* says, "also because of the scriptural texts whose purport is dissolution. He states the reason for not citing the passages on origination: "because [dissolution] is preceded by [origination]. The word "by others" (*itaraiḥ*) means by Yādava and others. The reading is *nirūhyate*.
[This is justified] because when the suffix *yak* is added to the root *vah*, there is no possibility of lengthening [the vowel] due to the absence of a consonant following the *aṅga* [stem].

It should be understood that even by relying on the verbal root *ūha* in the sense of "reflection" (*vitarke*), the shortening [of the vowel] occurs due to the rule "after a prefix, [the final vowel of a root ending in] *ṛ* becomes short," as seen in the form *ūhate*. The phrase "by what power of expression? implies the remainder: "by the quality of being directed toward the unmanifest."

The objection is raised: "On account of the context and the remainder" (*prakaraṇapāriśeṣyābhyām*), meaning that because the word *avyakta* is determined to refer to the body—based on the intended meaning of the first sūtra beginning with "because of the apprehension of what is set forth as a metaphor" (*rūpakavinyastagṛhīteḥ*)—and because a "supreme" entity other than the Self is impossible in the case of the body, it is understood that the intention of the Śruti is that the quality of being "supreme" (*paratva*) is to be explained in some way or another throughout this entire section. Consequently, it is established that the "supremacy" of objects such as wealth (*arthādi*) is also somehow possible. This is the sense. The phrase "by that very [reason]" (*tenaiva*) implies "by the force of reasoning" (*yuktibalena*).

"In the *Hetusamuccaya*" means that it combines the reason stated in the preceding sūtra with the reason stated in this sūtra. Regarding the phrase "having begun with 'He spoke to him who was submerged in the world, etc.'": the sequence of the relevant scriptural passage (*śruti*) has been set down and explained under the sūtra "The Eater [is Brahman], because of the inclusion of the moving and the unmoving"; it should be understood from that very source. The phrase "he taught that he leaves behind" is to be construed with what precedes it—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Regarding the reading "he asked again": the sense is that a reading of "he asked again and again" is not appropriate. This refers to that which is pointed out in the *Bhāṣya*: "Having reflected, the wise man leaves behind joy and sorrow."

The reading is *brāhṛopāsanasya*. It should be understood that the reading *dhīro na śocati* is due to a scribal error, as it has been corrupted. Now, an objection is raised: if the threefold—past, present, and future—is a qualifier of the means (*upāya*), the end (*upeya*), and the agent (*upetṛ*) as indicated by the phrase "from this dharma and adharma," then the word *anyatra* (elsewhere) in the expression "elsewhere than from the past and the future" would be redundant; anticipating this unease, he says: "Or rather, [the meaning is] elsewhere than from dharma and adharma."

Others, however, have explained it as follows: by the words *dharma* and *adharma*, their resulting fruits are intended; by *kṛta* and *akṛta*, the entire manifold of effects and causes is intended; by *bhūta*, that which is delimited solely by the past time is referred to; by *bhavya*, that which is delimited solely by the future time; and thus the meaning is that [the Self] is excluded from all of these. To this, he raises an objection with the words "But [if it were] accomplished by dharma and adharma," etc., [suggesting] that the presentation of Brahman is being expressed by means of the syllable *praṇava*.

And therefore, the sense is that this portion—"I shall declare that state to you in brief"—is intended as a praise of the *praṇava*, because it establishes the *brahman* denoted by the word "state. In the commentary, [the phrase] "making known in a general way" means by means of the *praṇava* itself in its general form, namely "Om."

The meaning is "making known. As for the phrase "for it is denoted by a portion of the *praṇava*": the intention is that there is a rule that what is denoted by a portion of something must itself be a portion of what is denoted by that thing. Regarding the word "this" (*etat*) in the passage "this very syllable is Brahman," one might object that its reference to the object denoted by the *praṇava* is strained; therefore, with this reservation, he says: "when [it is] that which is to be attained," etc. "This very syllable is supreme," and so forth. Having known this very syllable, whatever anyone desires, that is obtained; this support is the best, this support is the supreme.

The meaning is that he intends the statement, "Having known this object, one is glorified in the world of Brahman," by means of these two mantras. The phrase "these two mantras" refers to the following: "This person is neither born nor does he die; this wise one has not come from anywhere, nor has anyone become him. He is unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient; he is not slain when the body is slain. And: "If the slayer thinks to slay, or if the slain thinks himself slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. This is the meaning of the two mantras.

The phrase "and of having another meaning as its primary purport" means "of having the Pradhāna as its primary purport. Now, although this sentence—"Hanta, I shall declare this to you"—occurs immediately after the series of replies concerning the Supreme Self, beginning with "The wise one is neither born nor dies," nevertheless, by virtue of contextual fitness (*yogyatā*), this reply refers to the question concerning the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, it should be understood that in the Śruti, the sequence of the replies does not necessarily follow the sequence of the questions.

Now, is the question "Is it not [the case] that it is due to unrighteousness (*adharma*) and so forth? on the same subject as the question "What is this person who has departed? or does it have a wider scope than that? It cannot be the first, because if that were so, since questions regarding only fire and the individual soul (*jīva*) would be observed, there would be no question regarding all three; this would contradict the Sūtra which states: "The mention and the question concern three—fire, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self."

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because that which exists immediately after the triad of "others" is unfit to be the subject of the question; otherwise, since the Pradhāna could also be introduced, it would result in a contradiction with the *adhikaraṇa*. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says, "And not of the question concerning the individual soul," intending to convey that—since in reality the Supreme Self is non-different from the individual soul, its inclusion within the triad of "others" is also untenable—and that by taking into account the difference between the individual soul and the Supreme Self as being merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), the reference in the Sūtra to "the three, namely fire, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self" is also justified.

The phrase "the inconsistency regarding the Supreme Self as the subject" (paramātmaviṣayatāvaighaṭyam) means, however, that in the reading "the inconsistency regarding the reply concerning the Supreme Self" (paramātmaviṣayaprativacanavaighaṭyam), it refers to the inconsistency between the question about the individual soul—namely, "This one who is dead"—and the reply concerning the Supreme Self—namely, "Him, difficult to see. The sense is that even if there were no great contradiction, our position would still be favorable because the Sūtra establishes the very difference between the individual soul and the Supreme Self by introducing the triad of fire, individual soul, and Supreme Self.

The phrase "of the absence of being the object to be explained" means that the primary subject—the substance consisting of the three *guṇas*—is not the object to be explained. He establishes the absence of a reason for the inclusion of the presentation of the question by stating: "the means... [is the reason].

The word *hi* [means] "because. [It refers to] that which exists as the object of meditation in the abode of the heart. If it is asked, "But since the abode of the heart and the one residing in the sun were not previously introduced, how can this be said?"—it is replied: by means of the mantra, "Jātavedas is deposited in the two fire-sticks, like a well-nourished embryo in pregnant women; day after day he is praised by watchful men who offer oblations with fires"—this indeed is that [abode of the heart]. And of him [who resides there]: "From whence the sun rises and where it sets..."

"All the gods are centered in Him, and no one transcends Him. Immediately following this, with the mantra "This indeed is That," it is shown that even the one residing in the solar orb is the subject previously under discussion. For it is thus:

Like fire placed within two kindling sticks, or like an embryo well-nourished by a pregnant woman with food, drink, and other necessities—day after day (dive dive), every single day—he is to be praised (īḍaḥ) and meditated upon by men who are ever-watchful (jāgṛvadbhiḥ), vigilant, possessing the materials for oblation, and equipped with the means of worship; he is Agni because of his connection with leading the way and other such functions. "This indeed is that"—the meaning is that he who thus abides in the heart as the locus is precisely what was asked about by you in the passage beginning with "That which is beyond dharma" and so forth.

Therefore, in this mantra, that which is to be meditated upon is introduced as residing in the abode of the heart; for it is from there that the sun rises, being the substratum for the origin and dissolution of the sun. "All the gods are centered in him" means that all the gods are its worshippers. Thus, having introduced that which is identical with the solar orb and other such forms as the object of meditation for the gods dwelling within it, and having demonstrated the non-difference of the Brāhmaṇa passage by stating "this indeed is that," [the identity is established].

Immediately following that, the doubt as to how this [Brahman] can be non-different from that [Brahman], given that they appear distinct due to the difference in their abodes—the former being worshipped by men through the heart-space and the latter being worshipped by the gods within the solar orb—is set aside by the passage beginning with "That which is there, that very same is here," and "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity. By such statements, the non-difference is made known through a single Brāhmaṇa.

Therefore, it should be understood that there is no room for the suspicion that this is a negation of something not previously established. The phrase "weaker than this" means that it is weaker than the scriptural text concerning their distinction, namely, "the two who drink the *ṛta*. And that has been shown by such passages as "by attaining the Lord through the yoga of the self," and "the wise one is neither born nor dies. The term "uninterrupted by the answers" means not separated or intervened by the answers; the same applies to the phrase "uninterrupted by the questions.
Now, in this context, is there not also mention of Agni, who is distinct from the means (*upāya*), the goal (*upeya*), and the seeker (*upetṛ*)?

In your own view as well, the restriction to only these three [entities] as being the objects of inquiry is untenable; nor should it be argued that fire is also included within the category of means, because liberation is to be accomplished by knowledge alone—anticipating this objection, he says: "And of the three objects... The meaning is that the cause is *pradhāna* alone, which refers specifically to independent *pradhāna*.

It has been explained as referring to fire, water, and food. Now, one might ask: does this Vedic verse refer to the independent *pradhāna*, or is the Supreme Lord’s power of *māyā*—the cause of the transformation of fire, water, and food—being spoken of? Thus, in the Siddhānta, it is shown that the reference is indeed to the root-primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) itself, and not to the intermediate natures consisting of fire, water, and food. This is true, as Vācaspati has stated; nevertheless, because of the phrase "starting from light" (*jyotir-upakramāt*), [the text continues].
Since the production of fire, water, and food is heard of in both the Sūtra and its Bhāṣya, how can they be "unborn"? [The answer is: because it is taught as a figurative description (kalpanopadeśa).

Furthermore, it must be understood that this [interpretation] is disregarded because it contradicts the introductory commentary (*sūtrāvatārikā-bhāṣya*) to the verse. For if the *mūlaprakṛti* were intended as the subject propounded by the words of the mantra, then—since it is birthless—it would be impossible to either raise the objection, "How can it be called 'unborn' (*ajā*)? or to offer the resolution, "It is so called because of its conceptual designation," by way of imagining it to be a she-goat. According to a figurative sense (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*), the word *rajas* is denoted by the term *rakta*, meaning "that which dyes," just as safflower and the like are called *rakta*. Thus, *mūlaprakṛti* consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

The meaning is as follows: since the obscuring darkness (*mandhakāra*) is blue and the quality of darkness (*tamas-guṇa*) is also an obscurer, *tamas* is also expressed by words such as "blue" due to the common property of being an obscurer. The reading is *pariṇamyamānam*. For the shortening [of the vowel] is prescribed by the rule "ṇici mitāṃ hrasvaḥ," or alternatively, the correctness of the form *pariṇamyamānam* should be understood from the fact that the word "optionally" (*vā*) is carried over into the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ. The compound *prakṛtyādīnām* is the term to be explained.

One might object: "Since the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of *prakṛti* and the other categories has been stated here, how can it be said [that they are not the subject]? For just as in passages such as 'They say it consists of twenty-six parts,' here too—in the verse 'But the one God drinks alone, here following his own will'—the Lord (*īśvara*) is also presented. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In these sentences, there is the presentation of the Lord. Consequently, the intention of the commentary's statement "the essential nature of *prakṛti* and the others has been stated" is that the essential nature consisting of the *brahman* has been stated. This is the underlying meaning.

That is a statement establishing the Lord as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), because in the Uttara-khaṇḍa, after praising the All-pervading Controller with the word "Vibhu" in the verse, "He is praised by the powers of the mantras and consecrations ordained in the Atharva," He is established as the sixfold [Lord] through the passage beginning with "the sixfold one. Thus, of the sixfold one—

The meaning is that there is the conceptualization of [the cup] as a seer (*ṛṣi*); this is the intended sense of "comprehension of the meaning. In the *Bhāṣya*, the statement that "only the state of being a means (*sādhanatvamātra*) is understood by the word *camasa*" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), the sense being that its having a downward opening and an upward nature is thereby established. [This is supported by] the *Gītā*, chapter thirteen, beginning with "both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*," and chapter four, beginning with "sattva, rajas, and tamas," and [the passage on] "all beings..."

In the *Kaunteya* section and elsewhere, in both the commentary (*bhāṣya*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), after the citation of the sūtra "Like the cup, because there is no distinction," the sentence "The *prakṛti* established in the *Tantra* is not what is being denoted here" is seen in some manuscripts; however, it should be understood that this was interpolated by those who consider themselves scholars but have not seen or heard the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, as it is stated in the *Ṭīkā* that this is intended to connect with the statement of the initial proposition (*pratijñāvākya*) located at the beginning.

In reality, however, the appropriate thesis here is simply that the *prakṛti* established in the Tantras is not being denoted; for since the thesis that "the *prakṛti* is being refuted" is improper, the objection regarding the [unwanted] implication (*anupaṅga*) has been disregarded. Therefore, we follow the Bhāṣya exactly as it stands. In the Bhāṣya, regarding the passage in the fourth chapter of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, in the *Śiśubrāhmaṇa*: "As there is a ladle with its mouth downward and its bottom upward," and "On this point there is a verse: 'A ladle with its mouth downward and its bottom upward—in it glory is deposited, the form of glory;
on its bank are the seven seers of the non-existent.'"* *Note: The verse cited is Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.3.*

"Speech is the eighth, in harmony with the Brahman," [he says]. "A cup turned downward, with its mouth above and its bottom below"—this is indeed this very head; for the cup turned downward, with its mouth above and its bottom below, is the head. "In it glory, multiform, is placed"—glory that is multiform is indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); he thus refers to the vital breaths. "Of it, the seven seers sit upon the rim"—the seers are indeed the vital breaths; he thus refers to the vital breaths. "Speech is the eighth, in harmony with the Brahman"—for speech is the eighth, in harmony with the Brahman; so it is heard there.

Upon a close examination of the mantra regarding the *camasa*, no specific [physical] understanding is obtained; however, in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), one conceives of the nature of a *camasa* (soma-vessel) in the region above the throat, namely the head. One conceives of the nature of the *vila* (the cavity) in the opening of the mouth located therein. One conceives of the nature of the *budhna* (the base) in the form of the lower part of the vessel's base, situated in the upper portion of that, namely the crown of the head. One conceives of the nature of *yaśas* (glory) in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*, etc. which reside there in a state of rest. And [one conceives of it] in the sense organs, such as hearing, which are situated all around that.

It should also be observed that by means of the two words *budhna*, the state of having its opening facing downward and its base facing upward is likewise understood. Nor is there a specific cognition [of Brahman] arising solely from the power of these qualifiers—namely, having an opening facing downward and a base facing upward—because those two qualities are common to caves and other such things; thus, they have been explained as examples based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). In this regard, the sense is that the intention of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) is that the passage beginning with "Just as this [is], so is that head" constitutes an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

The meaning is that in the *Bhāṣya*, under the section beginning with "because of the designation [of the term] in the case of the *camasas*" (*camaseṣu samākhyānāt*), it is stated that the word is etymological (*yaugika*). This is an illustration; for although in the present context the word *camasa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as a specific type of vessel due to its fixed usage, there exists a desire to know the specific nature of this particular *camasa*—namely, "What kind of *camasa* is this?"—since it differs from the well-known *camasa* (which has an upward opening and a horizontal base) by having a downward opening and an upward base. Thus, when these characteristics are mentioned, the inquiry into its specific identity remains.

Because there is no specific determination [of the meaning], for this very reason, it should be observed that even though words such as *yaśas* (fame) are conventional (*rūḍha*) in passages like "In that [unmanifest] the multiform was deposited; on its shore are the seven seers of the non-existent" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 3.12.6), we still observe a desire to know the referent of the word *yaśas* and so forth as being of such a nature. The phrase "Balabhid, etc. implies that the state of being the agent of the splitting of Bala is unique to Indra. Regarding the word "yathā," the reading is *naḥ śrutipadam*, and that is...

This is for the purpose of removing a misconception regarding the Vedic text (*śruti*). Consequently, in the phrase "just as here also" (*yathātrāpi*), the word *yathā* is the counterpart to the word *tathā*. It should not be argued that this word *yathā* cannot be construed with the commentary's phrase "so also here" (*tathātrāpi*) because the construction has already been shown elsewhere; for there is no fault in the fact that what is referred to by two instances of *yathā* can be referred to by a single *tathā*, and furthermore, because the word *yathā* is not actually seen in the Vedic text itself. Thus it should be understood.

The meaning is that independence (*svātantrya*) alone is what is expressed by the suffix; thus, by the *śānac* suffix [denoting] the agent (*kartṛ*), it is independence—the very state of being an agent characterized by autonomy—that is expressed. The word "only" (*mātra*) indicates the absence of any certainty regarding other unintended meanings, as in the phrase "if it were of the nature of Brahman. The phrase "by being contained therein" means by being contained within Brahman, whose body is the primordial matter (*prakṛti*). || 6 ||

Regarding the phrase "because it is a context of creation" (*sṛṣṭiprakaraṇatvāt*): although in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, the context characterized by the expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatākāṅkṣā*) is the authority for their status as subsidiaries, whereas here the context characterized by the placement of items belonging to the same class of things being created (*sṛjyamānaprāyapāṭha*) is the authority; nevertheless, since both are conventionally designated by the term "context" (*prakaraṇa*), it was stated in that manner.

It should be understood that [the context] was not interrupted previously; the sense is that there was no interruption in the passage, "The path of the gods, the track of the seers" (*brāhmī devānām padavīḥ kavīnām*). Although it might be argued that even if the statement "creating" (*sṛjamānām*) establishes a creation whose agent is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), this scriptural authority still does not interrupt the context of creation whose agent is the Lord (*īśvara*), nevertheless, this should be seen as stated merely to demonstrate the continuity of the context of creation in some general sense.

The meaning is that since it was stated "while being processed" (*prakriyamāṇa*), the present tense of the process is understood through the suffix *śānac*. "As a qualifier of this" means as a qualifier of the base (*prakṛti*).

The sense is that, in that context, because the subject to be explained is presented without any other qualification, its origin must be accepted on the basis of its position in the sequence of the text (*prāyapāṭha*); this has been shown in another Vedic branch (*śākhā*). Now, one might object: even in the Taittirīyaka, how can the Supreme Self be established as the cause merely by its being mentioned within the section concerning created things? For it would follow that the liberated soul (*mukta*) could likewise be the cause. Nor can it be argued that the liberated soul is mentioned for some other purpose, because there is no evidence that an entity first mentioned is intended for something else.

Furthermore, since the opposite view is equally easy to maintain; and moreover, if it is asked how her status as an effect can be established while the word *ajā*—which occurs in the context of the majority of the reading (*prāyapāṭha*) and prohibits birth—is present, some here reply: the word *upakrama* is primarily expressive of "commencement," but by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to "being the controller. Thus, the meaning is that she consists of the *Brahman* whose commencement is light (*jyotis*). And the reason for this is precisely the context of the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*, for therein it says: "Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the power of the Divine Self... [and so forth].

[The Lord] is concealed by His own qualities (*svaguṇaiḥ nigūḍhām*); yet [the opponent claims] Maheśvara is possessed of *māyā*, because He is presented as having that [power] as His own capacity (*ātma-śakti*) and as a qualification of Himself in the passage: "The possessor of *māyā* creates this entire universe from himself" (*asmān māyī sṛjate viśvam etad*). And this reason [of the opponent] is not supported by the Sūtra itself. Anticipating the objection—"Since the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad contains the scriptural statement 'ātma-śakti,' even though it teaches a primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of Brahman, how can it be said that the Taittirīyaka Upaniṣad teaches a primordial nature consisting of Brahman?"—he says: "Because it is taught thus in one place. The meaning is that even there [in the Taittirīyaka], the primordial nature taught is indeed that which consists of Brahman.

For instance, after it has been stated that the entire world originates from Brahman in passages such as, "The seven vital breaths come forth," this verse concerning the *ajā* (the Unborn) proceeds to dispel the doubt: "How can Brahman, which is changeless, produce modifications? If this verse did not establish the *ajā* as being of the nature of Brahman, it would fail to fulfill the purpose of establishing Brahman as the material cause previously proposed; for that would lead to the logical fallacy of "one thing being introduced and another resulting. Therefore, this mantra also refers exclusively to Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*) whose essence is Brahman.

If it is argued that, since the word *jyotirupakrama* (having light as its beginning) establishes merely that [the source] is of the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there would be no contradiction between its being unborn (*ajā*) and its having light as its beginning—and thus the subsequent Sūtra would coherently serve to resolve that objection—this is not so. For in the present context, its being of the nature of Brahman must be established precisely by way of being its effect; however, since the eternal *prakṛti* cannot be an effect of that [Brahman], how can it be of the nature of Brahman? To this objection, [the Sūtra cites: "From Him, the Illusionist (*māyī*) creates this entire universe," referring to the changeless Supreme Self.

Since *prakṛti*—which is presented as that which effects the causal state and is employed for creation—is necessarily an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddha-viśe�ṣaṇa*) [of the Supreme Self] at all times, there is no inconsistency in its being identical with Him. Consequently, the intention of the Sūtra, "Because of the teaching of a metaphorical designation" (*kalpanopadeśāt*), is that *prakṛti*, whether its name and form are undifferentiated or differentiated, is always the body of the Supreme Self, just as the sun, whether its name and form are undifferentiated or differentiated, is the body of the Supreme Self.

Thus they say; in the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase "hidden by its own qualities" (*svaguṇairnigūḍhā*) is to be understood as following immediately after "the power of the divine Self" (*devātmaśaktim*). It should be observed that the suffix *-kratv-* (forming *vīpsā*) is justified starting from that point. The meaning is "Prakṛti, which is the source (*yoni*) of the world. Nor should it be asked how there can be repetition (*vīpsā*) if the word *yoni* refers to Prakṛti, since Prakṛti is one; for the intention is that the word *yoni* is used elsewhere as a common term for both Prakṛti and the principles such as Mahat, or that the repetition is justified by resorting to distinctions based on the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of different cosmic cycles (*kalpa*). [The phrase] "by those who follow the usage of Vedic terminology" [is explained as follows].

Furthermore, since the employment of words is within one's own control, the objection—"Why was it not formulated as a sūtra according to the maxim: 'Why should a word that conveys no meaning be employed?'—namely, 'But [the passage] beginning with 'Br̥hatī' is taught in that way,' and 'And because of the instruction regarding creation, there is no contradiction, as in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and others'?"—is refuted by the fact that the word *sedī* serves to bring the original subject matter (*prakṛti*) to mind.

He cites the Bhāṣya as authority for the fact that [the honey] exists up to the level of Brahman, stating: "The causal state is Brahman alone. The word "of one" (*ekasya*) is to be explained as follows: in the Bhāṣya, it says "the honey is imagined for the sake of being enjoyed by the Vasus and others"; the meaning is that the designation "honey" applies to the enjoyer because he is the substratum of the essence produced by karma for the purpose of enjoyment by the deities such as the Vasus.

The concluded meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is as follows: just as the sun, in its state of activity, is the substratum of the essence produced by the rites propounded in the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures, and possesses rising and setting, so it is here. The phrase "for the sake of establishing the oneness of the genus" (*ekājātvasiddhyartham*) means for the sake of establishing the oneness of the single genus (*ekājātvasiddhyartham*). This is because it will be stated later, "for the sake of establishing the oneness of the genus (*ekacchāgatvasiddhyartham*)," [and] "by means of the word denoting fire, water, and food."

The meaning is that by means of the words "red" and "black," one indicates fire, water, and food (tejas, ap, anna) as possessing those respective forms, and through them, their causal source—the root-primal nature (mūlaprakṛti)—is indicated. The sense is that there are only three groups; the idea is that there are three groups: earth made of the triad, water made of the triad, and fire made of the triad. [Objection: If there were no intermediate door (advārakatve), there would be a contradiction regarding the red, white, and black colors. This is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa); it should also be understood that there would be a contradiction with scriptural texts concerning the absence of modification (nirvikāratva).
In the commentary (bhāṣya), the phrase "of the alternative and the refutation" (vikalpaparihārayoḥ) means "of the alternative and the criticism" (vikalpadūṣaṇayoḥ).

The meaning of the passage beginning with "In the third alternative also" (*tṛtīyavikalpe’pi*) is as follows: [the opponent argues that] the *ajā* (the unborn) is designated by the word *ajā* because it is indicated (*lakṣita*) by the words "red," "black," and so on, which stand for the causes—fire, water, and earth. In this third position, having indicated fire, water, and earth by means of the words "red" and so forth, the causal state indicated through them must be presented by the word *ajā* through a figurative application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). This is because it is possible to denote the cause of fire, water, and earth—which are themselves indicated by the words "red," "white," and "black"—by means of the primary etymological application (*mukhyavṛtti*) itself, namely, "that which is not born" (*na jāyate*), thus being *ajā*.

This is because it is improper to accept that the term refers to that [Supreme Cause] through figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*) by means of the metaphor of "goat-skin. This same meaning is found in the *Ṭīkā* regarding the phrase "not denoting fire, water, and food": rather than assuming that the word *ajā*, which does not denote fire, water, and food, indicates such causes through figurative usage, it is better that the word *ajā* refers to the Root Cause (*mūlakāraṇa*) through its etymological sense (*yogavṛtti*). Thus, in this sentence, the word *ajā* does not have as its secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) the causes [of the world] by way of indicating fire, water, and food.

It should be understood that [this view] is rejected. It should be understood that others, not having stated it in that way, have merely said that the word *ajā* has a secondary (*gauṇī*) application based on the definition of words such as *lohita* (red), [meaning] "one who does not give birth. This occurs either by convention (*rūḍhi*) or through the power of its etymological parts (*avayava-śakti*). Now, one might object: in this case, regarding the mantra "Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forward, let that of the Udgātṛs go forward," since the plurality of the conventional meaning of the word *udgātṛ* is untenable, one takes recourse to the etymological meaning; yet, the four *subrahmaṇyās* are not thereby included.

If it is argued that, rather than this, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—namely, that by means of a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the three priests, the Udgātṛ, Prastotṛ, and Pratihartṛ, who possess an internal proximity due to their entry into the sacrificial assembly (*sadas*), are to be understood—this is not so. For even when the etymological meaning of the word *prodgātṛ* is accepted, in the case of the text "Let the cup of the Hotṛ go forward" (*praitu hotuś camasaḥ*), those who are to consume [the Soma] standing in the assembly are addressed regarding the bringing of the cup there for the purpose of consumption.

And since Subrahmaṇya is not present there, the eating of those [cups] alone is established even in the context of the *yoga* (figurative application); thus, we see no purpose in denying the *yoga* by attempting to justify a *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) based on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

Since it is agreed that in the view where *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) is preceded by *rūḍhi* (conventional usage), only those [entities] other than the *subrahmaṇyā* priests are included, whereas in the view of *yoga* (etymological derivation), all four are included; therefore, when the multiplicity of the conventional meaning in that context is impossible, the etymological meaning must be accepted. However, this does not imply a state of total helplessness as in the case of the word *pāśa*, because no etymological meaning is perceived in the word *pāśa*. This is the intended sense. Consequently, since the etymological meaning of the word *ajā* in the present context is clearly perceived, there is no occasion for the application of *lakṣaṇā* preceded by *rūḍhi*. Therefore...

The point is that when it is said, "the *kumuda* [is] the *paṅkaja*," only the meaning of being the agent of production from mud (*kaṅkaja-nikartṛtva*) is understood, and not that it is something invisible. In the *Bhāṣya*, the neuter gender (*napuṃsaka-liṅga*) in the expression "of those connected with one's own [nature] since beginningless time" is used in reference to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Alternatively, there is the intention to express the feminine gender—as in the rule "*dvigurekavacanam*"—in the sense that "one who possesses firm devotion is capable of warding off hunger by this [means]. Similarly, in the subsequent *Bhāṣya*, the mention of gender in the phrase "capable of conjunction, whether by this or by another" should also be understood in this way.
In the *Bhāṣyas*, the phrase "being the cause for non-abandonment" refers to the means of liberation (*apavarga-sādhana*).

Even if one does not accept figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*), there is no pointlessness in [interpreting] the *bhūtāditya* (the elemental sun) as its counterpart. Now, an objection is raised: in the *ajā* mantra, this much meaning is understood according to the natural sense: "A certain three-colored she-goat, possessing many offspring and many young, has a single ram following her with affection, while another abandons her once she has been used.
