Although such a meaning is possible in the world, it ought not to be insisted upon here in the Veda, specifically within a section concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*). Therefore, it must refer only to an internal, spiritual entity.

Once it is determined that "a yojana" is the measure to be employed, by virtue of its suitability, there certainly arises the understanding that this term applies figuratively (gauṇyā vṛttyā) to the primordial matter (prakṛti), which is the root of fire, water, and earth.

Just as in the mantra, "Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree," there is a metaphorical attribution of the body to the tree, the individual soul and the Supreme Lord to the two birds, and the fruit of karma to the fruit of the tree—for otherwise, that [mantra] would remain unintelligible—so too in the passage, "The Cow is without beginning or end," this very same mode of figurative application (vṛtti) must be resorted to if the word "cow" is taken in a secondary sense; for otherwise, this mantra would refer to some particular individual cow existing at the present time.

If it is argued that the understanding [of the word] arises from the statement "let him cause [it] to be understood," that is true; however, the point is that when it is possible to adopt a derivative meaning suitable for the context of the inner self (*adhyātma*), it is improper to accept a secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning. Regarding the phrase "because no word denoting a chariot is heard": this means that even though no word denoting a chariot is heard—as in passages such as "Know the Self as the rider of the chariot"—the term "ajā" serves to exclude [other meanings], which is to say, it determines the conventional (*rūḍhi*) sense.

Therefore, regarding the alleged redundancy of the term used [in the *ajā* mantra], there is an avoidance of redundancy for the term expressing "silver" (*rūpya*) employed in the passage, "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot. However, in the case of "The Cow (*gauḥ*) is without beginning or end," the natural force (*svārasya*) of the words "without beginning or end" and so forth exists only when a secondary sense (*gauṇārtha*) is accepted; this is understood from the propriety of the meaning due to the hearing of appropriate qualifiers such as "the milker of all desires. But in the *ajā* mantra, it is not so, because no term expressive of "silver" is heard; furthermore, even if a secondary sense were adopted, the masculine gender of the word "Cow" (*gauḥ*) and the word "unborn" (*aja*) would both remain [applicable].

The meaning is as follows: because it would follow that [the word] functions according to its own inherent sense (*svarasa*); because even when accepting the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense, it is possible for the word *ajā* to convey the intended meaning through its etymological derivation (*yoga*); and because there is also the consideration that, since qualifiers such as "begetting many offspring" do not serve to exclude the primary sense of a goat (*mukhyājā*), the suitability of the meaning lies precisely in the secondary sense; and finally, because there is no intention to refer to something similar to the conventional (*rūḍha*) meaning.

Although the word *camasa* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as a specific type of vessel, and others maintain that its application to the head is figurative (*gauṇa*) based on a conceptualization of similarity to that vessel, nevertheless—according to the principle of the *prokṣaṇī*s (sprinkling-water vessels)—since its function is possible through [the sense of] sacrifice (*yāga*), there is no evidence for assuming a conventional meaning for the word *camasa*. Furthermore, just as the word *udgātṛ* is accepted as being conventional (*rūḍhi*) with respect to the *prastotṛ* and others because it is not used of them, or as the word *dhāyyā* is [conventional] in the sense of "those which are placed" (*adhīyante*), so too, if the word *dhāyyā* were merely etymological (*yaugika*), it would follow that it could be applied elsewhere as well.

It might be argued: "Since the two verses beginning with *pṛthuvājivatī* are used as *dhāyyās*, and although the word *dhāyyā* is recorded in the Smṛti—according to the rule *pāyyasānnāyyanikāyyadhāyyāmānahavirnivāsasāmidhenīṣu*—as a term denoting *sāmidhenī* verses in general, it nevertheless possesses a conventional (rūḍhi) meaning; likewise, let the same apply to the word *camasa*, for the *Nighaṇṭu* reads: *camasaḥ sāmapātram syāt*. This argument must be rejected, because there is no evidence that the word *camasa* is ever employed to denote anything other than a specific type of vessel.

And even if [the term] were established in its conventional sense, nevertheless, due to the previously mentioned defect, the interpretation proposed by the opponent is not tenable; this is the intended meaning. The section concerning the *camasa* cups is concluded. 6.

"The gods meditate upon Him as the light of lights, as life, as immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16); "In whom the five groups of five and space are established" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.5); "Knowing that very Self thus, I, being immortal, shall protect myself as the immortal" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1); "They who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of mind—they have perceived the ancient, primordial Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1)—such is the Śruti.

The meaning is that those [passages] are also the subject matter, as is the statement beginning with, "That very person is fivefold, having five natures" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.5), because [the Self] is not one of the five [elements or faculties].

Although it might be argued that, according to Kaiyaṭa’s statement—"The chariot-maker (rathakāra), the fifth; the four castes are the five peoples (pañcajanāḥ)"—the word *pañcajana*, as a name for human beings, shares the same status as the word *saptarṣi* (the seven seers), nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated thus with the intention of deriving the word *pañcajana* from humans and so forth as "those born from the five elements" (*pañcabhir bhūtaiḥ jananam asya*).

Nor should it be argued that even by resorting to such an etymological derivation, the status of being preceded by a numeral (saṅkhyāpūrvakatva) is not established; for how could there be an implication that it is a compound preceded by a numeral? The point is that this is because a compound with a coreferential (samānādhikaraṇa) numeral as its prior member is impossible. [The opponent] says this with the intention that being a compound preceded by a numeral is indeed logical.

The meaning is that one should understand this as intending that the compound is appropriately a *saṃkhyā-pūrva* (numeral-initial) compound as prescribed by the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*; however, it should not be considered a *saṃkhyā-pūrva* compound as prescribed by the rule *dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām*. For if that were the case, just as there is no cognition of the number fifty-seven in the expression "the seven Saptarṣis," there would follow the undesirable consequence that there is no cognition of the number twenty-five when "the five Pañcajanas" is stated.

"It should be seen that [the word] 'then' (tadā) [indicates this]" means that when the word "five" (pañca) is used in a collective sense, it attains the state of "ten" (daśatva). The intended meaning is that this is like the cognition of the absence of rain for twelve years in such passages as, "The performer of a hundred sacrifices [Indra] rained for five and seven years, [making] nine hundred years. [This refers to] that which is presented by the word *viśeṣaparyanta* (the limit of particulars).

The point is that there is no expectancy [for further qualification] because of the absence of an independent presentation [of the number]. Nor is it the case that, as in the examples "two hundred" (*dve śate*) or "two hundred Brāhmaṇas, three hundred Brāhmaṇas," where—in order to establish grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *brāhmaṇa*—the word *śata* extends to include the substantive possessing the number one hundred, and we observe the number "one hundred" (which is the qualifier) being construed with the subsequent number even though it is presented by a word that extends to the substantive; likewise here too, [the number] five...

The meaning is that there exists a connection with the number five (*pañcatvasaṅkhyā*). Regarding the phrase "intermediate number" (*avāntarasaṅkhyā*): just as in the case of the great number "thirty-three gods," where there is the inclusion of intermediate numbers—such as the eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, and Prajāpati and Indra—as established by the scriptural statement, and which are caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as being a Vasu; so too here, because one is observed to be the limiting adjunct that serves as the cause for the inclusion of the intermediate number in the form of the number five. This is illustrated by the phrase "by means of the limiting adjunct of residing in a single village," and so forth.

Even though, among men living in the same village who possess the number five, no mutually exclusive limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are observed to serve as the basis for the application of the number "hundred"—which consists of the intermediate numbers contained within the total number five—nevertheless, in cases such as "five and seven syllables" or "fifty-five threefold years," we observe the application of certain intermediate numbers merely as a means to arrive at the intended large number, even in the absence of any single defining delimiter. For indeed...

During the twelve-year drought, over five or seven years, and within the *ayana* (course) of the Creator (*Viśvasṛj*), amidst two hundred and fifty-three threefold years, there exists a single characteristic for every fifty years; nevertheless, this should be understood with reference to the possibility of occurrence. "The unity of a group of persons numbering one hundred" means that the unity of the group is due to the unity of the characteristic defined by the number one hundred.

It should be understood that when there is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the cause for the application of a number, there is the application of that number; and when there is the application of a number, there is the unity of the aggregate. The point is that there is no certainty regarding the meaning stated in the *Tantra* [of the *Mahābhārata*], because twenty-five types of beings are possible in such forms as: "The gods, ancestors, Gandharvas, Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, the four castes, the six *anuloma* [castes], and the six *pratiloma* [castes]. The phrase "because of the observation of a single word" (*aikapadyadarśanāt*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), referring to the word *pañcajana*.

It should be understood that the compound is also prescribed by the final-acute (antodātta) accent as ordained in the *Bhāṣika*—the treatise on accents within the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*—by virtue of its co-occurrence with the word "five" (*pañca*), as in examples such as *pañca saptarṣayaḥ* ("five seven-sages") and *sapta saptarṣayaḥ* ("seven seven-sages"). Even when there is co-occurrence with a numeral-denoting word, there is neither a predominance of the number nor the acceptance of a collective (*samāhāra*) sense; nevertheless, rather than relying on the technical designation (*sañjñā*) of a compound where the individual meanings of the members have been set aside, [one should follow the rule].

The recourse to a collective compound (*samāhāra-samāsa*) alone is superior; furthermore, even if one were to accept it as a technical-name compound (*saṃjñā-samāsa*), it would not be possible for the word "pañcajana" to denote human beings, because it is inappropriate to speak of five types of humans within this context of the internal self (*adhyātma-prakaraṇa*). Moreover, since other things denoted by the term "pañcajana" are unknown, the recourse to a collective compound is indeed appropriate—this is the sense of the phrase "of the word 'pañca' within the word 'pañcajana'," which refers to the feminine gender used in the traditional recollection (*smṛti*).

The sense is that, according to the rule "a *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in *a* is stated to be feminine," an exception (*pratiṣedha*) must be stated for words such as *pātra*, because in cases like *tribhuvana* and others, there is no such exception; therefore, the feminine gender here is due to its being *chāndasa* (Vedic/irregular). This is merely an illustration: just as in the rule "the duration of *u* is short, long, or protracted" (*ukālo’j jhrasvadīrghaplutaḥ*), the absence of the neuter gender is accepted as *chāndasa* by the rule "it [the *samāhāra-dvandva*] is neuter" (*sa napuṃsakam*), so too here, by virtue of being *chāndasa*, the absence of the neuter gender—according to the rule "it is not neuter" (*sanapuṃsakam*)—is also to be understood.

Now, one might object: "In the mantra 'In whom the five groups of five people [dwell],' twenty-five principles are perceived even apart from the Self (ātman) and space (ākāśa); since the number twenty-seven is thus completed by adding those two, this [Sāṅkhya doctrine] is not consistent with the Sāṅkhya system. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by showing that there is no contradiction even for the number twenty-seven in their own view, because the substance of primordial nature (prakṛti) consists of three substances. He does so by stating, "by the Self indicated by the word 'in whom,' etc."

The sense is that because the Self is established within itself—just as it is said, "He is established in His own glory"—the *Bhāṣya* states: "Root-nature is unevolved. Root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not the modification (*vikṛti*) of anything. The seven principles—the intellect (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—are modifications with respect to something else, yet they are also natures (*prakṛti*) with respect to something else. The sixteen principles—the five gross elements, the five organs of perception, the five organs of action, and the mind—are exclusively modifications; they are not natures.

The meaning of the verse is that the Puruṣa is neither primordial nature (*prakṛti*) nor a transformation (*vikṛti*). Regarding the reference by the word "him" (*tam*) in the commentary, the intention is that the mantra-text reveals his status as Brahman, since it says: "Knowing that Self, which is Brahman and immortal, another becomes immortal. [Objection: But in the *Viśvasṛjām Ayana*, it is said: "Fifty-five years consisting of the *trivṛt* [stoma], fifty-five [years] consisting of the *pañcadaśa*..."

Just as in expressions such as "five times fifty-seven," where there is a designation in that manner even though no recurring qualifier (*anugata-upādhi*) exists across each set of fifty days, so too here, even though no recurring qualifier exists across each set of five, the cognition of the number twenty-five is possible through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Having kept this lack of intrinsic cogency (*asvārasya*) in mind, he says, "because the aggregate of elements is not established," and so forth, using the phrase "and so on" (*ityādi*) as an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

The phrase "he states their meaningfulness" means that he states it in order to dispel the doubt that the qualification by the word "five" would be redundant, since the number five is already understood through the compound *pañcajana* itself. Regarding the expression "due to the absence of the capacity of the compound": the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of a compound consists in its dependence upon semantically capable words; the semantic capability of words consists in their having mutually related meanings. Consequently, if the word "five" were devoid of meaning, the capacity characterized as dependence upon words with mutually related meanings [would be absent].

The meaning of the passage beginning with "In this regard, the intention is as follows" is this: Grammarians, engaged in the formal derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of words, provide etymological explanations by postulating some meaning—whether real or unreal—and yet, by that much alone, there is no actual cognition of that specific meaning from the word. For instance, when the word "cow" (*go*) is uttered, there is no cognition that it "goes" (*gacchati*). Consequently, since the word *pañcajana* has its constituent parts' meanings obliterated (*pratyastamitāvayavārthaka*), it is untenable for it to be qualified by the number five (*pañcatva-saṅkhyā*).

Furthermore, in cases such as "the one who possesses a garment is Devadatta" or "that which is in the cage is a lion," although at the time of learning the linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) the garments and so forth function as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), they are not perceived at the time of actual denotation (*abhidhāna*). Thus, in expressions like "Devadatta who possesses a garment," there is no tautology or similar fault; the same applies here, and therefore the qualification by the word "five" is logically consistent.

Furthermore, even when the meaning of the individual parts is understood at the time of naming, it is only sometimes that their mere existence is perceived, and not necessarily their existence at the time of actual usage; thus, the usage of the term *gaur* (cow) is successful because it conveys its meaning. Similarly here as well, the qualification *pañca* (five) is indeed purposeful for the sake of establishing the cognition of the connection with the number five in that specific context. For this very reason, the author of the *Vārttika* raises the objection: "Regarding the rule *pañcajanādupasaṅkhyānam* (an addition must be made after *pañcajana*), how is there the singular number here? and then proceeds to resolve it.

Just as in the case of *Pūrvaiṣukāmaśamī* and similar compounds, the singular number is used because a term functioning as a collective whole is applied to its individual parts—as in the word *saptarṣi*. Consequently, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with numbers such as "two *pañcajanas*," "three *pañcajanas*," or "five *pañcajanas*" would be contradictory [if *pañcajana* were a singular collective].

It should be understood that because [the forms] "dvau saptarṣī" and "trayaḥ saptarṣayaḥ" are recorded in works such as Kaiyaṭa’s *Padamañjarī*, there is no fault of redundant explanation or the like; for it is said that the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) possesses the power to express the meaning. Consequently, when the analytical sentence expresses the meaning, it possesses its own inherent form (*svarūpa-yogyatva*), and from that, the capacity of the compound (*samāsa-sāmarthya*) also exists.

The state [of being]. The phrase "with reference to the non-comprehension of the twenty-five principles" means that when the fivefold aggregate—which is the cause for the non-comprehension of the twenty-five principles—is impossible, it is precisely that which is being turned over [as an alternative]. Regarding the rule "but in case of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence": if it is argued that no doubt can arise because the word *pañcajana* is conventionally established as referring only to human beings, we say no; for this occurs within a context concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*).

In the doubt as to whether the meaning of the sentence "five types of men are established" is to be understood as referring to the number five—thereby resulting in the sentence being devoid of purport by abandoning the word "five" in its sense of numerical category and instead adopting subordinate attributes such as Brahminhood and so forth, resulting in the sentence-meaning "fivefold men"—or whether it refers to the vital breaths (prāṇas) and others mentioned in the supplementary portion of the text: [The answer follows: It is not so; for the word "five" is used in its primary sense of number, and since the word "men" is used in its primary sense, the sentence-meaning must be accepted as "five types of men are established. Furthermore, if the word "five" were taken in its secondary sense of a numerical category, it would result in the undesirable consequence that the word "men" would have to be taken in a secondary sense as well, because the number five does not exist in the individual men themselves. Therefore, the sentence-meaning "five types of men are established" is to be accepted. The sense is that a definitive conclusion is possible on the basis of the remainder of the passage, which establishes that the functions of breathing and so forth for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the rest depend upon Brahman, as stated in: "Those who know the breath of the breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of the mind—they have discerned the ancient, primordial Brahman. Furthermore, there is no single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that would justify the inclusion of the number five.

Although it might be argued that even though the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the others lack a single common limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of being sense organs (*indriyatva*), they nonetheless possess a single common limiting adjunct insofar as their respective functions depend upon Brahman—this being established by the supplementary portion of the scriptural passage, "the breath of the breath"—nevertheless, the underlying intention is that when another alternative is available, one ought to accept only a well-known limiting adjunct.

Regarding the phrase "the maker of the inner sun": the sense is that since a refutation of the doubt concerning the body being composed of the three *guṇas* and being a transformation of *prakṛti* is seen here, it is understood that even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), that same doubt was intended. Now, one might object: why could the word *jyotis* (light) not refer back to the meaning of the accusative case, as in the view of others? Anticipating this, he says, "on account of the natural force of the scriptural statement. That this would involve an unnatural strain is something that will become clear immediately below in the words, "for by others... etc.

But surely, others have stated that the number five is completed by the light indicated by the word *jyotis* in the genitive case, just as by the light of the sun and so forth; even if there is no mention of light among the Kāṇvas, their number five would still be fulfilled by that light. For they too read the light in the mantra preceding "in whom the five groups of five" (*yasmin pañca pañcajanāḥ*) for the very purpose of defining the nature of Brahman, as in "the gods [meditate] on him, the light of lights" (*taṃ devā jyotiṣāṃ jyotiḥ*). Thus says Ānandagiri, while explaining the commentary, regarding this mantra and the light in the genitive case.

If it is argued that [the objection] is not valid because it has already been explained that for that single [Self], there can be no relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyatva*) due to its being the self-luminous light consisting of the five fullnesses (*pañcapūrṇānna*), we say no; for the refutation was stated with the intention of raising an alternative view (*vikalpa*), namely, that if the referent of the word "light" (*jyotis*) in the accusative case were [that very Self], then the relationship of container and contained and so forth would be untenable.

It must be seen that [the meaning] is obtained through mutual expectancy by means of the mantra "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*), nor even by the preceding mantra "them the gods" (*taṃ devāḥ*); therefore, the meaning is that for the sake of determining its sense, it is through mutual expectancy. By the word "svara," they are explained as such; the meaning is that they are explained by the very words "eye" and so forth, such as "of the eye" (*cakṣuṣaḥ*) meaning the sense-organ of sight.

He explains the word "anna" (food) with the phrase "of food" (*annasya*); he repeats it twice, though we do not see the purpose [of this repetition]. It is intended to show that it conveys the meaning through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). If one accepts the etymological meaning [of *anna*], then—

The meaning is that there would be the consequence of a contradiction regarding the two functions of the word. By the phrase "by a single operation," the sense is "by a single operation consisting of the nature of being connected with food. The meaning of the word "indicated" (*pradarśita*) in the expression "the indicated meaning" (*pradarśitārtha*) is "that which has been pointed out"; thus, the intention is that the phrase "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*) is an indication of all the sense organs. This is stated while explaining the purpose.

The meaning is that he speaks thus while expressing the purpose, which consists in the total absence of any hope for the Sāṅkhya doctrine. "Of the fivefold aggregates of the five elements and their principles" means that there would be a self (ātman) belonging to these: namely, the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements, and the remaining five [categories]. This is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase "without an intermediary," it means that in the case of the *ānandamaya* sheath, it is direct, whereas elsewhere it is mediated by an intermediary.

"In the case of the impossibility of calculation" means that it should be described in that way because its nature is Brahman; "and in the case of impossibility" means in the case of the impossibility of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the cause for determining the number of incarnations (*avatāra*). Regarding the phrase "the unavoidable cognition of the non-conscious," there is confusion precisely because the apprehension of the non-conscious is unavoidable; such are the causal statements.

"Subject matter" (viṣayaḥ) means that all causal statements are the subject matter. Regarding the phrase "from one," we do not see the appropriateness of the interpretation "from a single-natured cause. The phrase "creation is recorded as preceded by 'Being' in the Chāndogya" is the ellipsis; "and as preceded by 'Non-being' in the Taittirīyaka" is the ellipsis; "elsewhere" means in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. The term "the doctrine of Brahman as the cause" (brāhmakāraṇavāda) is used in the locative sense of occasion (nimitta-saptamī); it refers to the determination of the cause of creation as being applicable to the doctrine of Brahman as the cause.

The meaning is that in the Vedāntas there is no such thing as "non-existence," because the cause of creation is established; this is the sense. Consequently, the intention is that since the word "creation" (sṛṣṭi) is not restricted solely to [efficient] causes, it also includes the material cause (upādāna); this is the result of an effort to consider the preceding and following context.

The consideration of what precedes and follows [the statement] "He performed austerity" (*tapo'tapyata*) is as follows: for the verbal root *tap* means "to contemplate" (*ālocane*), and the sense is that it denotes an effort (*prayatna*). This refers to the intention of being oriented toward the production of the eyes and so forth; the meaning is that it refers to the intention of being oriented toward seeing, which constitutes the ground for the application of the terms "eye" and so on. Consequently, the meaning of the sentence "He sees without eyes" (*paśyatyacakṣuḥ*) is that, because of its orientation toward the production of seeing, it partakes of the name of the object of action (*karman*). By this, [it is shown that] "while breathing, he becomes what is called breath" (*sa prāṇanneva prāṇo nāma bhavati*).

"Speaking is speech, seeing is the eye, hearing is the ear, and thinking is the mind"—these, according to the Śruti, are merely names for its functions (*karmanāmadheya*). Thus, the terms *prāṇa*, *vāk*, *cakṣus*, *śrotra*, and *manas* are [names for the functions], just like the words *lāvaka*, *pāvaka*, and so forth.

It is understood that because of their association with the activities of breathing, speaking, seeing, hearing, and thinking, these are merely names for the Self based on its functions; however, the doubt—that in the phrase "the eye sees," seeing is perceived as an action belonging to the eye, characterized by the eye's orientation toward its object, and that this has been explained similarly by others—is refuted. Now, it was previously stated that by the word *avyākṛta* (the Undifferentiated), there is first of all the apprehension of something insentient; yet, since the state of being undifferentiated does not necessarily imply a lack of sentience, [the following] depends upon that very point.

The entire subsequent passage is not tenable; therefore, out of this sense of dissatisfaction (*asvarasa*), he says: "Or rather, [the word 'seeing'] refers to those residing in the cause. Now, one might object: rather than abandoning the primary sense of "seeing" in its entirety, it would be more appropriate to accept the abandonment of its primary sense only in part—thus the opposite position would be more logical. Anticipating this doubt, he states: "In an entity other than that," meaning that since the causality of the conscious aspect (*cidaṃśa*) is established by means of evidence that cannot be otherwise accounted for (*ananyathāsiddha*), it is only logical that the term "seeing" and so forth be used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*) everywhere.

The phrase "resulting from the attachment of the word *na*" means that it results from the attachment of the negative particle (*nañ*) found in the sūtra "Not even because of the inclusion by number" (*na saṃkhyopasaṃgrahād api*). Now, one might object: "Just as [the Lord] who is designated in the sūtra beginning with 'Because of the difference of cause' (*kāraṇatvādivailakṣaṇyāt*)—possessing qualities such as omniscience—is also spoken of as the cause of the world in the passage 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent' (*asad vā idam agra āsīt*)."

It must be stated that [this objection] is directed against that very [position], because it stands in opposition to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and not because it is improper to establish that in such passages as "From the Self, space was produced," the Omniscient One alone is taught as the cause of space and so forth; furthermore, the citation of the passage from the *Sadvidyā* ("He created fire from that") is also improper, since the causality of space and so forth is not heard there—anticipating this doubt, he says: "By its own nature, it is exclusively sentient."

The meaning of this sūtra is that since the principle of "the stronger force of the majority" applies, one must interpret terms such as *kva*, *itaḥ*, *asat*, and *avyākṛta*—which appear in numerous passages establishing Brahman as the cause, such as those beginning with the word *ākāśa*—in some way so as not to contradict the doctrine of Brahman as the cause. The intention is that by examining the preceding and following sentences, terms like *asat* are likewise to be reconciled in that very manner; this is the meaning of the subsequent sūtra. Furthermore, the phrase "because of the teaching of omniscience" (*vipaścitva-pratipādanāt*) is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa), referring to [passages] such as "Truth, Knowledge... (*satyaṃ jñānam*).

It should also be understood that this is because [the text] establishes [Brahman] as being of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*). Now, one might ask: "If the word *sat* refers to the conscious [Self], how can it be in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *idam*, which denotes the insentient? To this, he says: "Of the word *sat*... The intended meaning is that it has been established; thus, the phrase "by way of the purport" (*tātparyataḥ*) is to be supplied. Starting from the passage "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) should be seen by supplying appropriate words that denote an action having the same agent as the initial action. This is because there would otherwise be a contradiction with the many Śrutis located at the commencement [of the text]. Even though this very sentence is the opening statement of the *Avyākṛta-Brāhmaṇa*,...

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated because of such scriptural declarations as "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" found in earlier Brāhmaṇas. Regarding the phrase "by the masculine word *sa*," the meaning is that the pronoun *tat* occurring in each subsequent sentence draws back (*samākarṣaka*) that which is qualified by the attributes established in its own respective preceding sentence; thus, it draws back that which is qualified by the attributes established in the sentence "He desired. This is because the superiority of many scriptural passages, such as those concerning knowledge and the wise (*vipaścit*), is thereby established.

Now, one might object: even though Brahman is the subject under discussion through words such as "the Knower" (*jñānin*) and "the Wise One" (*vipaścit*), in the passage "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*), by the force of the scriptural mention of "non-existence" (*asat*), that which is other than the Brahman under discussion must be intended, because direct statement (*śruti*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, since the Vedānta texts are incapable of reaching a definitive conclusion due to mutual contradictions, their meaning must be determined in accordance with the Sāṅkhya Smṛti—so argues the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*). To such an opponent, the mention of the superiority of numerous scriptural passages such as "the Knower" and "the Wise One" would be useless; for it is by the opponent himself that...

If it is argued that, having accepted the superior strength of scriptural passages such as "He who knows" (*jñāna*) and "the wise one" (*vipaścit*), the sublation of the mere *prakaraṇa* (context) was proposed precisely so as not to contradict them—this is true. If the *prakaraṇa* were to be sublated by a stronger scripture, that would be appropriate to accept; however, it is not so here.

For if the scriptural words "He who knows" and so forth were stronger, then the scriptural passages establishing the causality of the world through the meanings of the words "He who knows" and "the wise one," as well as the scriptural uses of pronouns referring to the subject at hand in passages such as "He desired" and "Regarding this there is also this verse," would also [be contradicted].

The sense is that there would be the consequence of contradiction (*bādhaprasaṅga*). Now, one might object: even in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* Śruti passage, "In the beginning this was non-existent alone," since the subsequent sentence—"That became existent"—is an injunction establishing its nature as existent (*sad-rūpa*), and because it is impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent to attain the state of being existent, it is possible—just as in the view of the opponent—to demonstrate a "drawing back" (*samākarṣa*) by means of the word "that" (*tat*) in that very same way. Why, then, is that not accepted in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "There, of that which is denoted by the word 'non-existent'... etc.

The meaning is this: since, unlike the position of the opponent, the suspicion that the void (tuccha) might be the cause has not even been raised in our own prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa), it is appropriate to draw in the word "existent" (sat) as that which excludes the void. Now, one might object: "Why not raise the suspicion that the void is the cause even in this prima facie argument? To this he replies: "In the state of being a cause... and so forth.

Since the distinctions of being differentiated by name and form (*nāmarūpavyākṛtatva*) and its absence do not exist in the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātmasvarūpa*), [the author] explains—intending that differentiation and non-differentiation apply only through a medium—in the Commentary: "the undifferentiated" means "the body of the undifferentiated. The sense is that this is for the sake of consistency with the statement, "It made itself its own self" (*tad ātmānaṃ svayam akuruta*). Thus, the intention is that the verbal suffix in *vyākiyata* is used in the sense of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartari*).

Now, one might object: since in the passage "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifested" (*taddhedam tarhy avyākṛtam āsīt*), the suffix *tiṣṭha* occurs in the sense of the object (*karman*), so for the sake of consistency here as well in "it was manifested" (*vyākriyata*), the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) must be stated to denote the object alone, not the agent; and furthermore, in "it was unmanifested," let the *kta* suffix be treated as the object by virtue of the *karmavadbhāva* (the status of being like the object). This should not be said, because in the rule "The *liṅ* [is used] in the sense of benediction" (*liṅyāśiṣyaṅ*), the dual mention of the *lakāra* indicates that the *karmavadbhāva* is prescribed only with respect to the operations of those suffixes ending in *la*. Therefore, by virtue of the *karmavadbhāva*, [the desired result follows].

If it is argued that since the suffixes *kṛt* and *ktā* and so forth are impossible [in this context], and therefore the suffix *la* (the verbal ending) must also be used in the sense of the object (*karman*) to match the form of the suffix *kta*, then—according to the rule "not in the case of the agent who is also the object" (*na karma-kartari*)—how could the self-agency of the differentiation of name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa*) be established? The answer is: No. In the expression "un-differentiated" (*avyākṛtam*), because the agent is intended to be expressed as the object, the root is intransitive; thus, by the rule "after roots meaning motion or being intransitive" (*gaty-arthā-karmaka-*), the suffix *kta* is possible in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency; this is the intended meaning.
In this regard, there is the purification of the object [of knowledge]; in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, [the king] named Ajātaśatru...

The King of Kāśī, having approached Bālāki—who had said, "I sacrifice to the *brāhmaṇa* who is in the fire"—praised him, saying, "Together with his chariot, Janaka [of Videha] indeed runs toward this speech, for people cry out, 'Janaka! Janaka! Then, after Bālāki had taught him about the persons residing in the sun, the moon, lightning, thunder, space, wind, fire, and so forth, as being the *brāhmaṇa*, the King rejected each of those persons immediately after they were mentioned by Bālāki, declaring them not to be the *brāhmaṇa*.

When Bālāki had become silent, [Ajātaśatru] asked him, "Is your knowledge only this much? When he replied, "It is only this much," [Ajātaśatru] said, "Do not deceive me with falsehood; you have merely repeated the words of a Brāhmaṇa. Then he recited the passage beginning, "O Bālāki, he indeed who is the maker of these persons, whose work this is, he is the one to be known. For such is the sequence of the Śruti: "He said: 'O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these persons, or whose work this is—he indeed is to be known. Thereupon Bālāki, with fuel in his hand, approached [him]."

"Let us employ means," Ajātaśatru said to him. "It would be contrary to the natural order for a Kṣatriya to initiate a Brāhmaṇa; come, I shall indeed instruct you today. Having taken him by the hand, he led him away.

The two of them went to a sleeping man. Ajātaśatru called out to him, "O Great One, clad in white raiment, O King Soma! But he lay there quite silent. Then he prodded him with a stick, and he rose up immediately. Ajātaśatru said to him, "Bālāki, where was this man lying here? Where did he go while he was thus? Whence has he come back? Bālāki did not know this. Ajātaśatru said to him, "Where this man here, Bālāki, was lying..."

Where this was, from whence it came—those channels called *hitā* extend from the heart to the pericardium; they are as fine as a hair split a thousandfold, and they exist with the subtle essence of the tawny, the white, the black, the yellow, and the red. When one has fallen asleep and does not see any dream at all, then he becomes one with this vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone. Then speech enters him together with all names, sight with all forms, hearing with all sounds, and the mind with all thoughts. When he awakes, it is as if from a blazing fire sparks were to fly forth in all directions; even so, from this self, all the senses go forth toward their respective objects, and from the senses, the deities proceed toward their respective domains. It is from that very source that this [world] comes. Thus it is said: "From whence indeed did he come? From that very source. Now, when one is about to depart, one sees this very same sight that one saw when falling asleep. Then the upper part of his body becomes hot, and he departs either through the eye, or through the head, or through other parts of the body. As he departs, the vital breath follows him; as the vital breath departs, all the vital functions (*prāṇāḥ*) follow. He becomes one with this great being, and having become one with it, he no longer knows anything external. His form is the same as that of the Great Being: vast, bright, and free from limitations. Just as a razor placed in its case or firewood placed in its container is contained within, so too is this consciousness contained within these elements. When the fire is extinguished, its heat remains; when the sun sets, its heat remains; when lightning flashes and vanishes, its heat remains. Even so, though this [consciousness] is imperceptible, its heat remains. That which is the heat of this [consciousness] is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). That which is the vital breath is fire. This triad—fire, earth, and food—is this very triad. Whatever there is here, whether moving or stationary, is composed of these three. These three become one: the mind (*manas*) is fire, speech is earth, and the vital breath is food. For one who knows this, his offspring do not perish, and he attains the full measure of life. One who knows this becomes immortal. Thus it is said: "He who knows the connection between these three becomes immortal. This is the secret doctrine (*rahasya*). "The ear goes together with all forms; the mind goes together with all sounds; the intellect goes together with all thoughts. When he awakens, just as sparks fly out in different directions from a fire, even so from this [Self] these persons emerge.

He who is the maker of these persons, whose work this is—he indeed is to be known. At the beginning of the passage, that which was introduced by Bālāki as the object to be explained—the knowledge of Brahman—is taught by Ajātaśatru as "he indeed is to be known."

From the connection with action in the phrase "of whom this is the work," it is determined that the *brāhmaṇa* refers to the Person (*puruṣa*), the enjoyer and supervisor of the primary elements (*prakṛti*), who is taught as the object to be known; it does not refer to anything else, for no other entity is admitted to have a connection with action. Furthermore, action characterized as merit and demerit is possible only for the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). Nor should it be argued:

By the etymological derivation that "it is acted upon" (*kriyate*) it is "action" (*karman*), this entire world presented by means of perception and other valid cognitions is designated as "action"; thus, when it is said, "He whose action is this entire world is to be known," it is understood that [the object to be known] is indeed distinct from the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

Because the separate designation, "O Bālāka, he who is the maker of these persons, or whose work this is," would otherwise be purposeless; because the word *karma* (work) is well-known in both common usage and the Veda as referring only to action consisting of merit and demerit; and because the origination of the world is caused by the karma of the respective enjoyers, it is logical that "the maker of these persons" refers to the enjoyer alone. Thus, the meaning is: [He is the maker] of these persons who have the spheres of the sun and so forth as their substrata, and who constitute the objects of enjoyment and the instruments of enjoyment for the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*).

From the self, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) establish themselves according to their respective abodes; from the vital breaths, the gods; from the gods, the worlds. Just as a razor might be placed in a razor-case, or as the world-sustainer (*viśvambhara*) in the nest of the world-sustainer, even so this wise self has entered this body as its self, down to the very hair and nails. These selves depend upon that self, just as subjects depend on a lord. As a lord enjoys his own subjects, or as Indra [enjoys his], so did he not recognize this self.

The Asuras overcame him; when he became aware of this, he then slew the Asuras, conquered them, and attained preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all the gods. Indeed, he who, knowing this, slays all evils and attains preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings—he who knows thus, he who knows thus—verily, he is to be known; such is the scriptural passage concerning the Infinite.

The sense is that the phrase "it is indeed to be known, so it is studied" connects with what precedes it. The doubt regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) being the subject of the connection with karma has been refuted; for although the sentence beginning with "O Bālāki, he who... teaches the soul's connection with karma, there is no denial of a Brahman distinct from that [soul]. Thus, the doubt that nothing undesirable has befallen the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) is refuted, because by demonstrating the connection with karma specifically for the Brahman, there is a denial of a Brahman other than the individual soul—this is the sense.

Regarding the phrase "of those specified here": the meaning is "of the persons, beginning with Āditya, specified in this context. This is the intention of the opponent (the *pūrvapakṣin*) that the channels (*nāḍī*) are the locus of deep sleep; for the question, "O Bālāki, where was this person when he lay thus unconscious? has been raised.

The question, "Where was this [person] when he was thus asleep? concerns the state of that living being while in the locus of deep sleep; it refers to the group of organs indicated by the word "this" (*etad*), which had ceased its activity prior to his awakening and is subsequently experienced as becoming active again. The question, "Whence did this come? concerns the point of departure for the emergence of that very same group of organs. And thus, it is said: "He is then in those [elements] when, being asleep, he does not see any dream whatsoever."

The response to the first question is [the statement] that "then he becomes one with this very breath"; the response to the second question is "then speech [merges with him]," and so forth; and the passage beginning with "when he awakens" and ending with "the worlds for the gods" is the response to the third question, serving as its detailed explanation.

According to the Siddhāntin, however, the first question concerns the locus of the soul during dreaming; the second concerns the locus of the soul during deep sleep; and the third concerns the source from which the soul emerges at the time of awakening. The intention is that the answer to the first question begins with "Then he becomes that," the answer to the second question begins with "When he is asleep," and the answer to the third question begins with "When he awakens. Thus, the word "then" (*tadā*) refers to those respective occasions.

The meaning is: the position that accepts the channels (*nāḍīs*) as the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Regarding the phrase "he said," the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since the state of deep sleep consists precisely in the unification of the collection of organs, the meaning of the connection is that [the text] stated by means of the passage "Prāṇa alone becomes unified" that [Prāṇa] is the substratum of deep sleep. In the *Bhāṣya*, [there is a discussion of] dream and deep sleep...

Regarding the phrase "in the waking state": although, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the persistence [of the Self] during the dream state is not perceived—since the question and answer lack any connection to dreaming—nevertheless, the intention is that the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of dreaming, waking, and deep sleep is established by implication. Alternatively, it is because of the statement: "When one is asleep and does not see any dream whatsoever."

This should be observed. Regarding the phrase "if it is argued that predominance [is meant] by the word *eka*": although the suffix *dhā*, prescribed after a numeral in the sense of distribution (*vidhārtha*) according to the rule "after a numeral, *dhā* is used in the sense of distribution" (*saṅkhyāyā vidhārthe dhā*), cannot possibly follow the word *eka* when it denotes predominance, nevertheless, such a doubt was raised because of the similarity of sound; this is how it should be understood. In the Bhāṣya, it is stated: "While this Self exists, the vital breath alone becomes singlefold (*ekadhā*); the collection of instruments, beginning with speech, [becomes manifold]."

If it is objected that there is a contradiction with the preceding commentary—on the grounds that if the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) were the substratum for the collection of unified organs, it would follow that it is the substratum for deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and consequently, both deep sleep and awakening would be impossible for the primary vital breath as well as for the Lord (*īśvara*)—we reply: no, because deep sleep consists precisely in being supported by the vital breath which is itself the substratum for the collection of unified organs.

It should be understood that this position arises due to the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). The phrase "by means of being addressed by the names of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), hearing [the call], and so forth" will be clarified later. Regarding the phrase "in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the words 'agent' and so forth," the meaning is that in the Sāṅkhya school—the view of the proponent of the prima facie position—there is necessarily a lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya*), because agency and the rest are merely superimposed (*adhyasta*).

Although it was stated during the commentary on the *sūtra* "Like the cup, because there is no distinction" (*camasavad aviśeṣāt*)—in the context of explaining that [the meaning] is intended as the fitness for connection with other words situated within its own sentence—that "meaning" (*artha*) refers to the inherent capacity of the thing (*vastusāmarthya*), and although rhetoricians define "meaning" (*artha*) as "purpose" (*prayojana*), as in the example "Worship the pillar (*sthāṇu*) for the destruction of worldly existence," where the word *sthāṇu*—which commonly denotes both a pillar and Śiva—is restricted to Śiva by virtue of the purpose consisting of "destruction"; [The intended meaning is as follows:]... (The remainder of the passage would follow here).

*Prakaraṇa* (context) is the subject matter; for example, when someone has been addressed with "I shall know everything, O Lord," the word "Lord"—which is common to many referents such as Indra and others—is determined through context to have its final meaning restricted to the sense of "you" (the king). *Liṅga* (indicative power) is the capacity of the thing itself.

Just as it was stated in the phrase "the enraged Makaradhvaja" that the word *makaradhvaja*—which is common to both the ocean and the god of love—is restricted to the god of love by virtue of the mark (*liṅga*) of anger, so too should it be understood here that this was said despite the lack of significant contradiction. Now, one might ask: why could this pronoun (*etacchabda*), being used in conjunction with the word *karman*, not refer back to what was previously specified, namely, "the agent of these persons"? To this, he replies: "because of the contradiction in gender and number."

[Objection: "Let there be a reference by this word (*etac-chabdena*) to the creation of human action (*puruṣa-karmanirmāṇa*), which is presented by the phrase 'the agent of these persons' (*kartā eṣām puruṣāṇām*). To this he replies: "the operation consisting of the creation of persons" (*puruṣa-nirmāṇa-rūpa-vyāpāram*). The meaning is: [whether] by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇataḥ*), or by virtue of being connected to another relevant subject matter (*prakṛtārthāntara-sambandhitvena*), that is, by being presented by the word either directly (*sākṣāt*) or indirectly (*paramparayā*). Or, "well-known" (*prasiddhaḥ*) means [known] through other means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. [The phrase] "because restriction by context and so forth is untenable" refers to the fact that the subject under discussion—which ought to be indicated in the singular neuter form—is...

The meaning is that there is no reason to assume a restricted application (*saṅkucitavṛttitva*) for this word based on its actual usage (*bhāvena*). He shows that even as something connected to a different subject matter under discussion, it remains present in the minds of some by saying, "consisting of the conscious and the unconscious" (*cidacinmiśra*).

If one objects: "But since no stronger reason (*balīyastvahetu*) was previously mentioned, how can you state another reason (*hetvantara*)?"—the answer is: No; here the word *antara* signifies a distinction (*viśeṣavacana*). This is because Kaiyaṭa, while explaining the Bhāṣya passage, "This is indeed another technical rule (*paribhāṣāntara*)," has commented that the word *antara* denotes a distinction.

However, some argue that because the word *karman* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) not only for the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) but also for motion, and because these two conventional meanings are in conflict with one another, the reason consisting of the absence of the conventional meaning "ram" is valid; furthermore, since it was intended in the previous commentary that "karma is characterized by merit and demerit," the status of the subsequent passage beginning with "brāhme vāci brāuvāṇi" as a separate reason is justified. To provide yet another logical argument, he states: "of the sentence 'the agent of the persons whose substratum is the solar orb, etc.'"

The meaning is that [he is] the creator of the persons who preside over the sun and so forth, according to the statement [of the scripture]. Furthermore, the word "Self" (ātman) is also employed; for if there were an instruction such as "That which is the Self is to be known," in the same manner as "Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen," then...

The meaning is that the common term *ātman* would have to terminate in a specific intended sense, yet there is no such indication here. Some, however, considering the commentary "of this word" (*etacchabdasya*) to be syntactically one with the subsequent commentary "or [the word] 'whose action is this' (*yasya vaitatkarma*"), argue that if the word *etad* did not refer to the aforementioned meaning, an undesirable consequence would follow; thus they prefer the reading: "only of the connection with action" (*karmasambandhitvamātrasyaiva*).

One might object: "Since the status of being the cause of the entire universe, endowed with specific deities such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others, is already established by the phrase 'of whom this is the work' (yasya vaitat karma), the phrase 'the agent of these' (eteṣāṃ kartā) is redundant. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Regarding the agency over the world. The intended meaning is that through their mutual conjunction, the absence of limitation is established. The expression "one who possesses the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of application" means one who possesses the unseen merit resulting from eating. The phrase "indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a word denoting an action" means indication of a word denoting something related to an action.

Now, one might object: "When it is said, 'the son of Devadatta and Yajñadatta,' the relationship is not perceived as being toward Devadatta by way of sonship, nor toward Yajñadatta by way of son-in-lawhood. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says, "Alternatively, a *liṅga* is an indicator. In the Sūtra, there is an indicator (*liṅga*) of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*).

Regarding the term "appropriated" (*mupātta*): if it were intended that the characteristic of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is also characterized by the living self (*jīva*), then the Sūtra should have been formulated simply as "because of the characteristic of the living self" (*jīvaliṅgāt*), and not as "because of the characteristics of the living self and the chief vital breath" (*jīvamukhyaprāṇaliṅgāt*). To this we reply: no; for according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), although there is no difference in their being characteristics of the living self, it is appropriate to mention them separately in order to show that the mention of the vital breath holds a position of prominence relative to the other characteristics of the living self.

The point is this: when it is said, "This [mountain] possesses fire because of the indicator of smoke," although the indicator of the property (*dharma*) is also an indicator of fire by way of smoke, we observe a separate mention due to the intention to express a distinction. Now, one might object: the mere mention of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is not the mark of a living being (*jīvaliṅga*); rather, it is the relationship characterized by having the vital breaths as instruments. And that [relationship] is not heard in this context.

If it be argued that this is not so, because from the statement, "Then he becomes one with this very breath," there is only the perception that the breath is the locus for the unification of the collection of organs, and thus the breath's status as an instrument of the individual soul (jīva) is not perceived—[we reply: no, for in the alternative view where the two locative cases in "athāsmin prāṇe" are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*), the locative case in "asmin" establishes that the entity indicated by the word "this" (*idaṃśabda*) is the locus of the breath. Since it is well known that the individual soul alone is the sustainer of the breath, the mention of being the substratum of the breath serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*); therefore, there is no inconsistency.

For this very reason, in the *Dyubhv-ādy-adhikaraṇa*, the state of being the support of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) was described as a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). Now, one might object: "In light of the characteristics of the individual soul—such as its nature as an enjoyer—as set forth in the passage 'Just as a lord eats with his own [servants],' what is the primary significance of the mention of the state of being the support of the vital breaths, which is propounded in the passage 'Now, in this breath'? On the contrary, it is established otherwise according to the method stated in the *Dyubhv-ādy-adhikaraṇa*. This is true.

The sense is that, because movement must be predicated of that which is stationary, some specific distinction must be established; furthermore, since the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is already well-known, it is not necessary to extend [the teaching] for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*).

Thus [it is said]. The sense is that it is only when those marks (*liṅga*) are not established otherwise (i.e., are not shown to have another purpose) that it is possible for them to serve the purpose of meditation qualified by them. Now, one might object: "The statement in the Commentary—that the mention of *prāṇa* as a mark is appropriate for the sake of meditation on the *prāṇa-śarīra-brāhmaṇa*—is incorrect; for such a reply would be appropriate only if the mark of *prāṇa* were presented as something not established otherwise. Since the non-existence of such a mark of *prāṇa* has already been demonstrated," he says in response: "The meaning is that it was stated that the mark of *prāṇa* is subordinate to the *brāhmaṇa*."

The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* is that, in accordance with the marks (*liṅga*) of Brahman which cannot be established otherwise, the word "prāṇa" must be explained as referring to Brahman; the intention is that [the word] does not intend anything else. Regarding the phrase "the desire to resolve the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*)," since the mark consisting of the word "prāṇa" itself has already been resolved by the preceding sūtra, the meaning is "the desire to resolve marks of the individual soul other than that. The meaning of the *Bhāṣya* passage, "How then can the marks of the individual soul refer to Brahman? is likewise the same.

One might object: "Since it is possible to account for other indicative marks (*liṅga*) through the very same portion of the Sūtra, 'nanu taduktam' (But that has been stated), which already accounts for the indicative mark consisting of the mention of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), what is the purpose of another Sūtra for the sake of accounting for those other marks? Nor should it be said that the subsequent Sūtra is for the purpose of accounting [them] in a different manner or for a different purpose, and therefore the commentary (*ṭīkā*) stating that it teaches an accounting by way of a different method is appropriate; for this would contradict the subsequent text which says, 'having stated the accounting for both the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the vital breath,' and so forth. If you say this, it is not so.

There is no fault here, because it will be stated later that this [sūtra], by means of the passage beginning with "by demonstrating the inequality of the conclusion," serves to remove the suspicion of an over-extension (*atideśa*) of the rule "for another purpose" (*anyārtham*). He says, "possessing a prāṇa whose activity has not ceased," because [the prāṇa] is impossible during both sleep and waking.

It should be understood that the mention of the non-cessation of the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is intended to dispel the doubt that the failure of the vital breaths to hear the address was caused by the absence of the vital breath as an enjoyer, rather than by the cessation of its own functions. Furthermore, while it is easy to recognize the distinction from the body and the senses during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), it is difficult to recognize the distinction from the vital breath whose functions have not ceased; therefore, the non-cessation of the vital breath’s functions is mentioned in order to demonstrate the necessity of making that distinction known.

[The word] *moktiḥ* [is used]. Thus, indeed, is the Śruti. Furthermore, the reading "the two went to the sleeping person" (*tau ha suptaṃ puruṣam ājagmatuḥ*) is seen in some copies of the Bhāṣya, but the sense is that this is due to the scribe’s lack of attention. Nor should it be asked: "How can the individual soul (*jīva*), which is referred to in the singular in the phrase 'when he awakens' (*sa yadā pratibudhyate*), be designated by the plural term *prāṇāḥ* (the vital breaths) in the same sentence, namely, 'from this Self the vital breaths proceed each to its own abode' (*etasmād ātmanaḥ prāṇā yathāyatanaṃ vipratiṣṭhante*)? [This is not a fault.]

The meaning is that such a discrepancy in grammatical number must be tolerated, just as in the passage, "Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him here or not, they all proceed toward the light" (*arciṣam evābhisambhavanti*), where that which was indicated by the singular ending in "for him here" (*asmin*) is indicated by the plural ending in "they proceed toward the light," and just as in the case of that which was indicated by the plural ending in "they proceed toward the smoke" (*te dhūmam abhisambhavanti*) is indicated by the singular ending in "this King Soma" (*eṣa somarājā*).
Although another scriptural passage has not been cited as the basis for the status of the departure as the locus of action, nevertheless, that too was intended [by the author].

[The author] states: [This is] the state of being. Regarding the phrase "in the beginning, middle, and end," although it is established that the opening statement, "He said to them, 'The Brāhmaṇas,'" refers to the Brāhmaṇas, and the reference to the one whose "work is this" is established as referring to the Brāhmaṇas in the very sūtra "Because it denotes the world" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.27), and the concluding statement, "He drives away all evils," is likewise established as referring to the Brāhmaṇas; therefore, the uniformity of the beginning and the conclusion points toward the Brāhmaṇas alone, and not toward the individual soul (jīva).

Nevertheless, because the opening—"Come, I will make you understand that very thing; having taken him by the hand, he departed"—the middle section describing the raising [of the king] by a blow with a staff, and the conclusion—"This self has entered this body as far as the hair and the nails... just as a chief enjoys his own [possessions]"—are understood to concern the individual soul (jīva), and because, unlike in the Pratardana-vidyā, no numerous indicative marks (liṅga) concerning Brahman are heard in the conclusion, [the text refers to] all [the selves].

The sense is that the individual soul (*jīva*) is what is being propounded by its own nature, because there is no possibility for a further objection [to arise] based on the consistency of the concluding passage—"striking away evil"—with the preceding statement, "When he had understood, then, having struck down and conquered the Asuras, he attained preeminence and sovereignty (*svārājya*) over all the gods. This is because the striking away of all evil and the attainment of sovereignty can be understood as being merely relative (*āpekṣika*), just like the conquest of the Asuras and the sovereignty mentioned in the earlier text.

In reality, however, the intention of the doubt is that the principle [of the Pratardana-vidyā] does not apply because of the mention of different substrata (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Although there is room for this objection—since if the awakening of the individual soul (*jīva*) were for another purpose, the principle of the Pratardana-vidyā would indeed be unnecessary, as the marks of the individual soul (such as the slaying of Vṛtra) could be interpreted as residing in the Supreme Self who has the individual soul as His body—nevertheless, it should be understood that the statement was made with the view that the principle of the Pratardana-vidyā consists precisely in the alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*) of the marks of the individual soul by any means whatsoever.

"Because of the understanding of a different state"—this is the connection [of the text]: "Now, when one has fallen asleep and does not see any dream whatsoever. The meaning is that the sentence beginning with the word *atha* (now), and the word *atha* itself, expresses a different matter from what was previously discussed; thus, the word *tadā* (then) must be supplied as an ellipsis. "From the time delimited by the absence of dreams" means "from the time delimited by deep sleep (*suṣupti*). "Unquestioned."

"How is the dissolution of the collection of organs described?"—the answer is supplied by the passage beginning with, "Then speech, together with all names, dissolves into it," and so forth. The meaning of the question "Where does he sleep? is as follows: the intention is that when this living being (jīva) is asleep, where is he then sleeping? The phrase "the mind whose activity has ceased" means that the "taking" (ādāna) of the mind consists in bringing about the cessation of the mind's activity, because no other [meaning] is possible. By this [statement], since "taking" consists in the production of the cessation of activity, the "taking" of the cognitions produced by the senses is likewise the cessation of their activity.

The meaning is that its form consists of the cessation of activity. Because these [other senses] depend upon the mind (*manas*), when the taking up (*ādāna*) of the mind—which culminates in the cessation of mental activity—is established, then for the cognitions produced by the organs of speech and so forth, which are designated as being associated with that [mind], the "taking up" must likewise be of such a nature (i.e., the cessation of activity). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of breaking the association within a single action. Therefore, the intended sense is that whatever is the meaning of the word "taking up" regarding the mind, that same meaning applies to the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as well.

Alternatively, the meaning of the scriptural passage "by means of the consciousness of the vital breaths" (*prāṇānāṃ vijñānena*) is as follows: the consciousness of the vital breaths and so forth, by means of speech and the other organs, is the capacity for grasping their respective objects; this is a capacity consisting of the activity of the mind. Thus, the meaning is "having taken up the mind along with that [capacity]," that is, having rendered the mind devoid of its own operations. With this intent, the text beginning with "denoted by the word *prāṇa*" should also be construed.

It should be understood that although one ought to say "taking the mind along with knowledge" (*jñānena saha mana ādāya*), the expression "with the mind" (*manasā saha*) is used here for the purpose of implying [the cessation of all other faculties]. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the statement that the cessation of the activity of the senses is explicitly taught by the Śruti as the result. Regarding the phrase "the words *prāṇa* and *ātman* occurring in the same context," this means the words *prāṇa* and *ātman* found in the Kauṣītaki passage: "Then he becomes one in this very *prāṇa*; from this *ātman*... The phrase "and because of the mention in a non-co-referential construction" means that there is an absence of a co-referential (grammatical) construction, unlike [the example] "Worship me as life, as immortality" (*taṃ mām āyur amṛtam upāsva*).

Now, an objection might be raised: since in the sūtra "The absence [of that dream-consciousness] is in the channels (nāḍīs), because of the scriptural statement regarding them," the channels are described as the locus of deep sleep based on the passage, "When he is thus completely unified and serene and does not perceive any dreams, then he is asleep in these channels"; and since the passage, "Now, those channels of the heart are situated within the subtle essence of the reddish-brown, the white, the blue, the yellow, and the red," is recognized here as well; therefore, the channels alone must be the substratum of deep sleep.

Furthermore, the question regarding the place of deep sleep—"Where was this person sleeping, O Bālāki?"—is answered in the Vājasaneyaka by the statement, "He sleeps in that space which is within the heart," because the word "sleeping" (śayana) is used for the state of deep sleep. The question regarding the state of being unified—"Where did he become one?"—is answered by the fact that the second question [concerning the state of being one] refers to the vital breath (prāṇa) alone, since it is logical to connect the words "when" and "then" in the first question with the passage: "It is then that he becomes one when, being asleep, he sees no dream whatsoever. Thus, the second question [regarding the state of being one] refers to the vital breath alone.

If it is argued that the answer might simply be "it becomes [one with the Self]," that is true; however, although the state of deep sleep as being located within the channels (*nāḍī*) has been established, there is nonetheless no evidence for the claim that the channels mentioned here—those heard of in the text as "the channels called *hitā*"—are those same ones. On the contrary, in this very context it is stated: "Now, when one is fast asleep, when one knows nothing whatsoever, the channels called *hitā*—seventy-two thousand in number—extend from the heart to the pericardium."

Because it is clearly established by the statement, "Having descended through these [channels], he lies in the pericardium," that lying in the pericardium at the time of deep sleep (suṣupti) is preceded by moving through the channels named *hita*, it is proven that the phrase "in the channels" (*nāḍīṣu*) is indeed the answer to the question regarding dreaming, since reaching the channels named *hita* is impossible at the time of deep sleep.

One might object: "Since in this section the Puruṣa is presented as that which is to be known, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) based on the Pradhāna does not even arise; so how can the Commentary (Bhāṣya) conclude with 'the Puruṣa established in the Sāṅkhya system (tantra), or the Pradhāna presided over by him'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The mention of the Pradhāna... Thus ends the section [on] "Because it denotes the world" (Jagadvācitvādhikaraṇa).

In the sixth [chapter] of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Now, Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī. Of these two, Maitreyī was a knower of Brahman, while at that time Kātyāyanī possessed only the wisdom of women. Then Yājñavalkya, intending to enter upon another stage of life, said to Maitreyī: 'Truly, I am about to depart from this state; come, let me make a final settlement between you and Kātyāyanī. She said, 'Yājñavalkya, what indeed..."

"Suppose this entire earth were filled with wealth; how could I become immortal by means of that? "How indeed could one become immortal by that? It would simply be a life possessed of the means of subsistence; there is no hope for immortality through wealth," said Yājñavalkya. Maitreyī replied, "What should I do with that by which I cannot become immortal?"

"O Blessed One, tell me exactly what you know. Yājñavalkya said: "You have indeed been dear to us, and now that you are even dearer, I shall explain it to you; however, as I explain it, you must concentrate your mind upon it."

He said: "Verily, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the husband is dear. Verily, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the wife is dear. Verily, it is not out of love for the sons that the sons are dear; nor, indeed, out of love for wealth, nor out of love for cattle, nor out of love for the elements, nor out of love for everything. The Self, verily, my dear, is to be seen, is to be heard, is to be reflected upon."

"One must meditate upon it, Maitreyī. Verily, my dear, when the Self has been seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known. Brahminhood deserts him who knows Brahminhood as other than the Self; the Kshatriya deserts him who knows the Kshatriya as other than the Self; the worlds desert him, the gods desert him, the beings desert him—everything deserts him who knows everything as other than the Self. This Brahminhood, this Kshatriyahood, these worlds, these gods, these Vedas, these beings, this entire universe—all that is what this Self is."

Just as when a drum is being beaten, one would not be able to grasp the individual sounds; rather, by grasping the drum or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped. Or, just as the sound of a conch being blown is grasped. Or, just as when a lute is being played, one would not be able to grasp the individual sounds; rather, by grasping the lute or the playing of the lute, the sound is grasped.

Just as from a fire kindled with damp fuel various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, Atharvāṅgirasa, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, the sciences, the Upaniṣads, the verses, the aphorisms, and all beings are the breath of this Great Being; all these are indeed His breaths. Just as the ocean is the one goal of all waters, so the tongue is the one goal of all tastes, and so [the nose] is the one goal of all odors.

The nose is the sole point of convergence for all odors; likewise, the hands are the sole point of convergence for all actions; the organ of generation is the sole point of convergence for all pleasures; the feet are the sole point of convergence for all paths; and speech is the sole point of convergence for all Vedas. Just as a mass of salt has no interior or exterior but is entirely a single mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior but is entirely a single mass of consciousness. Arising from these elements, it vanishes again into them. After death, there is no consciousness.
"I am telling you," he said. Maitreyī said to Yājñavalkya, "Right here, sir, you have plunged me into further confusion; indeed, I do not understand. He said, "Indeed, I am not confusing you."

I declare: "Verily, this Self is indestructible, O Maitreyī, for its nature is not subject to perishing. For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; there one smells another; there one tastes another; there one speaks to another; there one hears another; there one thinks of another; there one touches another; there one perceives another. But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he perceive? This [is that] by which this...

"It knows everything; by what means could one know that? This very Self is 'not this, not this' (neti neti). It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached, for it does not attach itself; untroubled, for it is not troubled; it does not suffer harm. O Maitreyī, by what means could one know the Knower? Thus has been given the instruction. "This much alone, indeed, is immortality," having said this, Yājñavalkya departed. So it is heard in the scripture. And in the fourth chapter (*pāṭhaka*), this same passage is recited with some slight variation.

"Her offspring is like that of other women"—the meaning is that her wisdom is such as that of other women; she does not speak of Brahman and so forth. "I shall make an end"—the meaning is that I shall effect a division of property between you two. The remainder is clear in the original source (*ākara*). [The phrase] "because of the scriptural hearing of being an enjoyer resulting from the fruits of action" means that the sense is that one is perceived as an enjoyer through relations such as husband, wife, and son. In the *Bhāṣya*, even in the middle [of the passage], it says "a mass of consciousness alone."
