Nor should it be argued that this statement regarding origination and destruction does not concern the subject matter under discussion—the object to be seen—but rather concerns the Self as the object of creation; for in the sixth chapter, the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, it says: "Just as a mass of salt has no interior or exterior, being entirely a single mass of consciousness..."

The sense is this: because the passage beginning with "arising from these elements" describes the origin and destruction of that very Self which is the subject under discussion—the Self to be seen and referred to as "this Self"—and because in the fourth [chapter], the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, the passage "Thus indeed, my dear, this great being, infinite and boundless, consisting of nothing but consciousness, [arises] from these elements," contains the word "this" (idaṃ) referring back to the subject at hand, the presentation of origin and destruction must likewise concern the Self to be seen.

Now, one might ask: how can the phrase "the knower, O Maitreyi" (*vijñātāram are*), occurring in the concluding portion [of the text], indicate the individual soul (*jīva*), given that it is common to both the individual soul and the Supreme Self? To this, he says: "supported by the reasons for [identifying] the individual soul."

However, some say that since in passages such as “Consciousness performs the sacrifice” and “consisting of consciousness,” the state of being *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness) is well-known to belong specifically to the individual soul (*jīva*)—as it is a particular modification of the mind—it follows that the term *vijñānaghana* (mass of consciousness) refers to the individual soul. They argue that there is no fault in this, because it is likewise possible for the word *vijñātṛ* (the knower) to refer to the individual soul. The intention [of the author] is that the difference between the two is stated [in the text] for the purpose of supporting the meaning of the subsequent passage.

Regarding the phrase "the so-called perception of otherness," it should be understood that this was stated by taking for granted the established meaning of the commentary—that it is a negation of otherness—in accordance with the scriptural text: "Whatever else one sees apart from the Self. The meaning is that the perception of otherness is negated; that is, within the isolated essential nature of the Self, the perception of it as being something else, such as a deity or the like, is prohibited. Consequently, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the meaning of the scripture is this: the suffix *tral* (in the word *anyatra*) has the sense of the second case (*dvitīyārthe*).

He who perceives everything other than the Self—such as the Brahminhood, the Kṣatriyahood, and so forth—as being the Self, would cast away even all that is characterized by Brahminhood, Kṣatriyahood, and the rest.

"Of the awakened one" means of one in whom the knowledge of reality has arisen. "Is stated by others" means it is stated by the Sāṅkhyas, who act as the proponents of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*). The sense is that by the word *mātra* (only), "limited power" is intended; thus, the purpose of the word *mātra*—which serves to exclude other [possibilities]—is to exclude "great power. Having explained "of the inactive one" as a qualifier of the liberated one (*mukta*), he now explains it with reference to the person-in-general (*puruṣamātra*) by means of the passage beginning with "or, of one who is subject to karma," and so forth.
"In order to indicate that it is his own statement" means that it is employed because it belongs to his own discourse.

The sense is that one who is independent cannot be subjected to questioning. Consequently, one should not raise the objection as to what the purpose of making known [the Lord's] status as one's own word (svavākya) might be. However, the phrase "the negation of the vision of gods and so forth" has "in the nature of the Self" as its ellipsis. Because it is based on the reasons previously stated—since the fact of being of the nature of Brahman was stated earlier—the negation of difference means the negation of difference from that which is not of the nature of Brahman.

The point is that where, having introduced the discrimination between the body and the self (*dehātma-viveka*), the oneness of selves is established by virtue of their having the single form of knowledge (*jñānaikākāratvena*), the negation of difference heard there must be understood as the negation of differences such as those of gods and so forth. The phrase "because of the multiplicity of the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇas" means that the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa is seen in both the fourth and sixth [adhyāyas]. The plurality in the expression "of the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇas" is not intended to be significant; or it should be viewed as referring to the different recensions (*pāṭha-bheda*) of the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina schools. In the Bhāṣya, the phrase "having a restricted place, time, nature, and dimension" refers to the fact that in the world, some object...

The meaning is that [affection] experiences a state of being most dear in varying degrees toward a particular person, at a particular time, and in a particular place. The sense is this: a dependent enjoyer attains independence by performing an act of affection for the sake of achieving his own desired end; however, for one who performs affection for the sake of achieving the desired end of another, dependence is inevitable.

The sense is that because the word *priya* (dear) has the meaning of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*), the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is also established; for when it is said, "the husband is the object of enjoyment for the sake of the husband's desire," the implication is obtained that "the husband enjoys [her] for the sake of the husband's desire. The phrase "due to the absence of any contradiction with the word *ātman*" means "due to the absence of any discrepancy in the word *ātman*."

Therefore, in accordance with the three sūtras beginning with "Because of the fulfillment of the promise" (*pratijñāsiddheḥ*), rather than resorting to the view that either one of the two words *ātman* or both words *ātman* denote the individual soul (*jīva*)—which would require breaking the natural force (*svārasya*) of many passages capable of leading even the word denoting the individual soul up to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—it is more consistent to maintain that the natural inclination of the two words *ātman* to support the Supreme Self indeed has that [Supreme Self] as its referent.

The sense is that resorting [to this interpretation] alone is logical. Now, it might be argued that describing the uniformity of the object (arthaikarūpya) is appropriate; however, it would not be fitting for the statement "for the sake of his own desires" (*ātmanaḥ kāmāya*) to have as its purpose establishing the nature of the Self as bliss by way of producing dearness in the husband, wife, and so forth, for the sake of fulfilling the will of the Supreme Self. This is because, just as there is the production of dearness in the husband, wife, etc., at certain times, there would also follow the possibility of the production of non-dearness at other times, which would imply a non-blissful nature.

Furthermore, if the statements such as "It is not for the sake of the husband's desire" were intended to refer to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the word *vai*—which indicates what is well-known—would not be appropriate. For it is not a matter of worldly common knowledge that the dearness of a husband, wife, and so forth is dependent upon the will of the Supreme Self; nor can it be argued that this is established by scripture, because Maitreyī, who had not studied the Vedas and was unaware of their meaning, must be informed of what is already established in the world. Therefore, in the phrase "for the sake of the self's desire," it is most fitting that the word *ātman* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*).

For it is attested by experience that, while one's own self is dear to everyone, even a husband, wife, and so forth are dear; in this regard, the dearness of all those things other than one's own self—such as a husband, wife, and the like—is not caused by their status as a husband, wife, or the like.

Rather, [the Self] is dear only to itself; for while its dearness is not observed to cease even when it brings about what is undesirable—as it does when it accomplishes what is desired—its own dearness is observed without distinction both when it accomplishes what is desired and when it accomplishes what is undesirable for those such as husband and wife. Since the Self possesses a superior status as a human goal (puruṣārtha) compared to husband, wife, and so forth, it is only logical that the individual self (jīvātman) alone is the one to be seen. This is the correct meaning.

On this point, some maintain that although the word "self" (*ātman*) in the passage "Let one desire the self" may refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), because the context—due to factors such as the means for attaining immortality—is clearly understood to concern the Supreme Self, it is the Supreme Self alone that is intended to be "seen. However, we have not sought to prove here that this much is the case; for what loss is there to us if the textual sequence beginning with "desiring the self" refers to the individual soul? Nor should it be suspected that the preceding sentence would lack coherence if the individual soul were its referent.

Since one is oneself the object of one's own supreme love, it follows that for the sake of achieving one's own supreme human goal (mahāpuruṣārtha), the Supreme Self must be perceived; thus, there is no fault in this interpretation. Nor is the inconsistency of the word *ātman* a defect, for according to the maxim, "And [the same word] may apply to one thing as the word *brāhmaṇa* does," such inconsistency is to be tolerated. The essential meaning is that because the Sūtra pertains to a single context, and because that context takes the form of a Great Sentence (mahāvākya), the Sūtra has as its subject matter the Great Sentence under discussion.

If it is argued that [the passage] might be unintended by the Sūtra, one might ask: "In that case, how could the connection of the intermediate statement beginning with 'a mass of consciousness alone' (vijñānaghana eva) also be unintended, given that the same logic applies? This is true; however, because the opening (upakrama) is primary, its intended meaning is necessary. Therefore, it has been said: "And the opening is the most important among the constituent parts of a great sentence."

If it is argued that this [passage] is intended solely to establish the designation of the Supreme Self by the word "jīva"—and that one must indeed say it is intended to establish that the mark of being a "jīva," characterized by birth and destruction, refers to the Supreme Self because there is no word denoting "jīva" therein, and because there is no evidence that the term "mass of consciousness" (vijñānaghana) denotes the individual soul—[we reply: even if the term "mass of consciousness" does not denote the individual soul, the state of being a "mass of consciousness" consisting of a particular modification of the mind serves as a mark of the jīva; thus, for those [terms] expressing the marks of the jīva...

The sense is that words such as "arising" and "destruction" applied to the mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*) can appropriately be grasped by a word denoting the individual soul (*jīva*). The meaning of the three sūtras beginning with "Because of the establishment of the proposition" (*pratijñāsiddheḥ*) is also intended by the author of the sūtras; thus, the phrase "the exclusion of Yādavaprakāśa’s interpretation" means that the interpretation offered by Yādavaprakāśa is set aside. [This is because] the designation of the Supreme Self by a word denoting the individual soul implies the identity of the individual soul and the Supreme Self.

Although it possesses that characteristic by virtue of being indicative, he says "that which establishes the proposition of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one," because [the former] lacks the capacity to establish the proposition of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one. Now, one might object: "Since the designation of the Supreme Self by the term 'individual self' (jīvātman) was not previously introduced, how is it obtained? Anticipating this doubt, he says "by the force of the reason" (*hetuvaśāt*). This means "by the force of fitness" (*yogyatāvaśāt*).

Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is that the Supreme Self is denoted by a word referring to the individual soul (jīva) in order to strengthen the identity of the causal and functional relationship that establishes the proposition "by the knowledge of one, all is known. This is the position of Yādavaprakāśa; the implication is that since the view of Āśmarathya is not favored by the author of the Sūtras, this position [of Yādavaprakāśa] is likewise not favored.

The meaning is that for the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman existing as effect and cause, there is difference by way of their natures as effect and cause, while there is non-difference by way of [their common nature of] *sattva* and so forth. Thus, the doctrine of the Pāñcarātra school—"Until liberation there is indeed a difference between the individual soul and the Supreme; but for one who is liberated, there is no difference, due to the absence of any cause for difference"—is presented in this sūtra. Or else:

We do not see that what was stated by Vācaspati is based on the *tantra*. Now, since the position of inherent [difference] favored by Yādava has already been discussed, and since only the views of Śaṅkara and Bhāskara are intended to be refuted—given that his own view does not admit inherent difference—the doubt arises as to why the alternative between inherent and adventitious [difference] is presented in this sūtra; anticipating this, he says: "of the two possible positions, that which is favored by the opponent. Therefore, the meaning is that both the positions of Bhāskara and Śaṅkara involve the two alternatives regarding whether the adjunct (*upādhi*) is ultimately real or not ultimately real. [The phrase] "incapable of being cut by the *brahma*" refers to the *brahma*.

The meaning is that because there is no relation with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) other than its own nature (*svarūpa*), and because it is related solely through its own nature, the identification of the locus of the rejected and accepted adjuncts would be indistinguishable for both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*); thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of any distinction between the individual soul and the Lord. If one asks, "In that case, what is the meaning of the scriptural text concerning 'manifestation' (*abhiniṣpatti*)?"—the intention is that the word "manifestation" is well-known to mean the appearance of a form not previously existing. The phrase "it does not exist anywhere" means that it does not exist in an intense or absolute sense.

The meaning is that because the entry into non-intelligent things is explicit—since in the passage, "Come, let me enter these deities with this living self," the entry into non-intelligent things is clearly perceived—it is for the purpose of making that known with clarity. The phrase "in another Śruti of even clearer meaning" refers to passages such as, "He who dwells in the self," and so forth.

The phrase "the hearing of a meaning that is even more explicit" means that it is with the intention of [teaching] non-difference; the sense is that even those scriptural passages describing the creation and dissolution of the world do not have as their primary purpose the teaching of non-difference by way of establishing the relationship between material cause and its effect. The phrase "the reason for accepting this interpretation" means the reason for accepting the interpretation of Kāśakṛtsna. The phrase "the dialogue between Yājñavalkya and Janaka" [is used].

Furthermore, since the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa is also composed by Yājñavalkya, the intention is that its meaning must be stated as being identical to the verses composed by Yājñavalkya beginning with, "And another, O King, is that Supreme One. As for the verse, "And another, O King, is that Supreme One," one might object: was not the same expressed previously in, "And another is the eternal Unmanifest, and likewise another is the twenty-fifth"?

Since it has been stated in the world that "the virtuous perceive him who resides therein as if he were one," meaning that those whose intellects are inclined toward worldly experience perceive the Self residing in the body—which is designated by the term "unmanifest"—as non-different from the body; and since this verse is recognized as having the same purport, why could the verse "And another, O King, is the Supreme" not also be intended solely for the discrimination between the body and the Self? Nor should it be argued that the word "Supreme" (para) is fit only for application to the Supreme Self and not to the body, for [the word is used in such contexts as] "The Unmanifest is beyond the Great."

If it is argued that [the term *para*] refers to the body because the word *para* is used for it, we say no; for if two verses occurring within the same section were to have the same meaning, it would result in the internal inconsistency of one being redundant. The verse, "And another, which is eternally unmanifest," is intended to distinguish the Self from the body. However, the verse, "And another, O King, who is the Supreme,"—in accordance with such scriptural passages as "When he sees the other, the Lord, who is gratified" and "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct"—refers to the Supreme Self, who is different from the individual soul (*jīva*) and free from transmigratory existence (*asaṃsārin*).

The sense is that it is only logical [to understand the text] as being intent on demonstrating this very point. Now, one might object: if its being of that nature were due merely to its abiding therein, then it would follow that even space (*ākāśa*) is of that nature. To this he replies: "And its abiding is by way of connection with a body. But surely, abiding as a body is indeed abiding as the self (*ātman*). Consequently, if the state of being everything is caused by abiding as the self, does this mean being the body of all, or being the essential nature of all? It cannot be the first, because there is no difference between the cause and the effect.

If it is argued that the second [alternative] is not tenable because nothing possesses that very nature [of Brahman], we say no; for "being the self of all" means the fitness for being designated in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with everything, and since that is based on the state of being the self of all, there is no fault. Regarding the phrase "all the senses," he establishes coreferentiality by stating, "For that which is called the Person (*puruṣa*), consisting of all the senses and the internal organ, is indeed the world," and provides the reason for this: "Because He is the self of all beings, the universal-formed, and the imperishable."

The point is that in the expression "that beautiful statue" (*cārurūpā sālabhañjikā*), the word *rūpa* is seen to refer to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Consequently, [the author] refutes the misconception that "you" (*tvam*) arises from that [nature] by stating "and therefore you. Now, one might object: "By the phrase 'because of being all-pervading' (*sarvagatatvāt*), only pervasion would be established; how then is corporeality (*śarīratva*) established? To this he says: "For the body... Here, it should be understood that "king" is the antonym of "servant," and "sky" is the antonym of "jar. (i.e., *nṛpa-nabha-bhṛtya* means: servant as the opposite of king, and jar as the opposite of sky).

He states that the two scriptural passages—“Having entered into that, he became the manifest and the unmanifest” and “All this indeed is Brahman”—are the authority for the fact that being denoted by the word ‘That’ (tat) is based on the relationship between the body and the embodied; thus he says, “Therefore, having entered into that. Now, one might object: in this sentence, it is not perceived that being denoted by the word ‘That’ is based on the relationship between the body and the embodied, but rather it is perceived as being based on the act of entering; anticipating this doubt, he says, “by means of internal entry.”

An objection is raised: "In the sentence 'All this, indeed, is Brahman,' it is understood that Brahman is the denotation of the word 'all' simply because [the world] originates, persists, and dissolves within Brahman; it is not based on the relationship of body and embodied being. Anticipating this, he says: "Persistence is denoted by the word 'Being' (sat)," because the word "having Being as its abode" (sad-āyatana) expresses the state of being the cause of persistence, as shown by the two phrases, "Having Being as their root" and "Having Being as their support."

Having stated through two sentences that origination and dissolution are dependent upon *Sat*, the sentence "having *Sat* as their abode" (*sadāyatanāḥ*), which proceeds to state that maintenance is also dependent upon *Sat*, demonstrates its quality as a sustainer; therefore, the sense is that the sustaining power indicated by the term "having *Sat* as their abode" serves the purpose of maintenance. Regarding the phrase "because of the presentation of the reason," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "in the sentence 'All this, indeed, is this [Sat]'"; the meaning is that the relationship of body and embodied being (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*) alone is what is implied by the reason.

The connection with what follows is that the reason—namely, that it is established as being consistent with all scriptural texts and as being the primary [meaning]—is proven. Regarding the phrase "by the seeing of the Self, O dear one," it should be understood that the reading "ātmano vā are darśanena" is cited in the *Bhāṣya* as from the sixth chapter, whereas the reading "ātmano vā are darśanena" is cited in the commentary on the fourth chapter. The expression "the statement of the definition" means the statement of the definition consisting in being the cause of the world.

Regarding the phrase "except for the self" (*anyatrātmanaḥ*), because the meaning "excluding the self" is somewhat obscure, he says "or else, 'elsewhere' (*anyatra*). Others have explained the meaning in this way: by the expression "of the drum being beaten," the general category of sound produced by the drum being struck is indicated; likewise, by the expression "but of the drum," that same category is indicated; whereas "the striking of the drum" refers to a specific resonance of the drum that accords with the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) predominant in the battlefield.

Therefore, this is the meaning: just as one cannot grasp any of the specific sounds that constitute the generality of the sound of a drum by extracting them from that general sound of the drum as something separate from it, but rather, by the very grasping of the general sound of the drum, its specific sounds are also grasped.

For by the term "sound of a drum," specific instances of drum-sound are indeed grasped; consequently, just as those specific instances do not differ from the generality of "drum-sound" and the generality of "sound produced by striking a drum," so too, without the manifestation of the conscious Self, the world—which is devoid of manifestation—does not exist apart from the conscious Self. This is the intended meaning. The point is that the examples of the conch, the lute, and so forth should also be applied in this very same manner, as has been stated.

The reading "superimposed upon the sound of the drum" (*dundubhiśabde'dhyastāḥ*) is observed; its meaning is that they are non-different from the sound of the drum. It should be understood that this is because there is no superimposition of a particular upon a universal. Regarding the phrase "of the two subsequent [sounds]": one might object that it is not the mere sound of the drum (*dundubhiśabda*) that is indicated by the term "sound produced by the striking of the drum" (*dundubhyāghātaśabda*), but rather the latter; therefore, it was stated as "of the two subsequent sounds of the drum. It should have been said precisely as "of the sound of the drum and the sound produced by the striking of the drum," and not otherwise.

If it is argued that this is so, we say no; for since this sentence also has its purport directed toward that very same point, the preceding sentence would be rendered redundant. Although the sentence "of the drum being beaten" possesses utility insofar as it conveys the meaning that one is able to grasp the specific sounds by extracting them from the general sound of the drum, nevertheless, it does not serve an ultimate purpose.

By the phrase "by the apprehension of the drum," etc., the meaning is established that the particular sound is apprehended precisely through the apprehension of the general sound of the drum; for by this very [statement], the fact that the particular sound is not apprehended without that [apprehension of the general] is also proven. Since the intended meaning is obtained, and since it would be redundant to employ further words once the point is established, he provides an illustration with the words: "For indeed, in the case of 'in the Ganges'... [and so forth].

Regarding the term *āghāta-śabda*, the meaning is "the sound produced by striking a drum" (*dundubhyāghāta-śabda*). It should not be argued that there exists a specific sub-variety of the drum-sound designated as the "sound of striking"; for there is no evidence for such a thing. The point is that even if such a distinction existed, the purpose would already be served by the statement: "by the grasping of the drum itself, its specific qualities are grasped. Regarding the phrase "being taken up by another," and so forth, the meaning is "by the removal of either the drum or the person striking it. This should be understood in all three sentences; the word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied as having the same sense in each. [This applies] to the two words ending in the instrumental case.

The meaning is that the connection [of the words] is as follows: by the phrase "from fire, etc. (*teja-ādi-śabdaiḥ*), [the text] declares [Brahman's] being the sole cause of the universe; and by the phrase "the single resort" (*ekāyanam*), it declares the governance of the collection of organs. Thus, many specific modes of functioning (*vṛtti-viśeṣāḥ*) are shown. Since the diversity of cold and heat is already established by the plural number in the word "touches" (*sparśānām*), one ought to have simply stated that the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the further internal diversity of cold, heat, and so forth; yet instead, it is said that "many specific modes of functioning are shown."

How is this stated? [The opponent objects: "It is not the case that words such as 'touch' (*sparśa*) refer to specific functions (*vṛtti*); for if that were so, there would be no need to resort to the laborious interpretation that 'being the substratum' (*anuvṛttamayanatva*) means 'being the appropriator' (*tadupādātṛtva*). [The author replies: True; however, there is no fault, because this is merely a statement of the resultant meaning, showing that many specific functions have been demonstrated. The phrase "of even the sentence *saṅghātatvāt* (due to being a composite)" means "even of that which occurs in the fourth [chapter]. The phrase "of that very" (*tasyaiva*) means "of that which is the object of such love."

"Of one whose [knowledge] has been awakened" means of one whose knowledge is uncontracted. "Because of the recognition of the meaning of another scriptural passage" means that the intention is that the two phrases "there is no consciousness" (*na saṃjñāsti*) and "he does not remember" (*na smarati*) have the same meaning. "The state of being natural is established" means that no limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is mentioned. "Sam- signifies unification" refers to the sense in which "consciousness exists" (*saṃjñāsti*) is used here. "And because of the statement regarding the eternity of knowledge" means: that which has no cutting off (*ucchitti*), i.e., destruction, is *anucchitti*; he whose knowledge has the property of being *anucchitti* is *anucchittidharmā*. This is the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*.

"The restatement of an error residing in oneself" means that one who considers the self to reside in itself perceives the object as the locus of the conceit of residing in itself by means of the instrument [of perception] which is conceived as residing in itself; the meaning is that the error of regarding [the agent, instrument, and object] as residing in the self persists. "There would be the perception of another object residing in the self" means that if the true nature of Brahman does not manifest, it is impossible to perceive [anything] as being of the nature of Brahman, and thus there would be the perception of another object that is not of the nature of Brahman.

Regarding this, the supreme [commentator] has explained the meaning of the sentence "He by whom one understands this" according to the manner stated in Sureśvara’s *Vārttika*: "Tell me, by what could that be known, by which immutable witness the entire world—including the grasper and all else—understands? The meaning is that since the whole world understands by means of that which is of the nature of the witness (*sākṣin*), by what could that witness itself be known? It cannot be an object of perception for anyone. He states the inconsistency in the opposite case with the words: "Otherwise, 'The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen,' and so forth."

Otherwise, the meaning is that it is described as being solely difficult to comprehend. The word "mode" (*prakāra*) is to be supplied with the term "is excluded" (*vyudasyate*), which refers to the Brahman. [The phrase] "unfit for apprehension" means that, consequently, it is not apprehended.

The sense is that there is no tautology by means of this [statement]. Now, one might ask: "If association with the non-intelligent (acit) exists, how can there be a negation of association with the non-intelligent? To this, he says: "For he has no association with the non-intelligent. The sense is that there is no tautology between these two [passages]: "By what should one know Him by whom one knows this? and "O, by what should one know the Knower? This [latter passage] is intended to negate other means [of knowing], and by the word "vijānīyāt" (should one know), the experience of Brahman at the time of liberation is not being expressed.

The meaning is: "Then, by what means other than worship might one know [Brahman] and experience liberation? He explains the meaning of the phrase "this much" (*etāvat*) with the word "one should know" (*vijānīyāt*). The intention is that since the attainment characterized by the experience of Brahman has been stated by the phrase "one should know," it is appropriate to refer back to that very point with the phrase "this much. Furthermore, because it is useless and contradictory, the contemplation of the birth and dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*) is irrelevant to the subject at hand; for a single person, even if deluded, would never accept a matter that contradicts his own intended goal, as will be made clear later.

The phrase "it has been explained in two ways" refers to one interpretation of the three sūtras as being intended to refute the seed of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which consists in the opening statement concerning the Self as enjoyer, indicated by the mention of the husband, wife, son, wealth, and so forth—and another interpretation as being intended to establish the alternative possibility (*anyathāsiddhi*) of the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) found in the intermediate passage, namely its arising and perishing in the form of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), with reference to that which was introduced as the object to be seen in the statement: "Having arisen from these elements alone, it perishes after them."

The meaning is that this has already been explained under the second application [of the argument]. Regarding the phrase "of the designation of non-difference, namely 'all this is what this Self is,'" the meaning is: of the designation of non-difference—which culminates in the designation of non-difference—found in the opening statement, "Everything becomes dear for the sake of the Self; indeed, the Self, my dear, is to be seen," which begins with the experiencing subject (bhoktrātman). "[When the Self is known..."

The meaning is that it has been described as follows: the meaning of the first sūtra is the indication of unity based on the absence of the relationship between cause and effect, which establishes difference, [as expressed by] the knower [of Brahman]: "All this is known," and "All this is what this Self is. If this very reading is correct, otherwise one should apply it by supplying words so that this meaning is established. Regarding the phrase "the attainment of the state of being a brāhmaṇa for one about to depart," here too the ellipsis must be completed with "of the commencement [of the discussion] regarding the enjoying self."

The same should be understood regarding the statement that Brahman alone remains unmodified. Although the intention of one who speaks thus must be refined—since, according to Śaṅkara’s commentary, the teacher Kāśakṛtsna held the view that the individual soul (jīva) is indeed the unmodified Supreme Lord; whereas Āśmarathya, although he intended the soul to be non-different from the Supreme, nevertheless seems to have intended some degree of distinction characterized by the relationship of cause and effect; and in the case of Auḍulomi’s position, difference and non-difference are clearly dependent upon different states—nevertheless, [the meaning remains as stated].

It is understood [that two views are presented]. Among them, it is understood that the view of Kāśakṛtsna follows the sacred scripture (*śruti*), for the intention of the author is clearly perceived in the text: "Because it conforms to the meaning intended to be taught by such scriptural passages as 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*). Likewise, in the *Bhāmatī*, the view of Āśmarathya is stated: "Just as between fire and a spark, there is both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) caused by the relationship of material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*)."

It has been established that Auḍulomi’s view is that, by taking up a future non-difference, there is a designation as non-different even at the time of difference; nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated merely as a possibility. Furthermore, it has been applied in this way, for the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya states: "As for what was also said—that by showing the emergence of the very subject under discussion, the Great Being who is to be seen, from the elements in the form of the cognitional self (vijñānātman), [the text] shows that this state of being 'to be seen' belongs to the cognitional self alone."

In this regard as well, this very same triad of sūtras is to be applied. "Āśmarathya [holds that] it is a sign for the establishment of the proposition. Here, the following has been proposed: "When the Self is known, everything becomes known; all this is what this Self is. And this has been demonstrated by showing that the entire manifold of names, forms, and actions possesses a single essence and a single place of dissolution, and by establishing the non-difference between cause and effect through the analogies of the drum and so forth. It is precisely for the sake of establishing that proposition that this [sūtra] indicates a sign.

The teacher Āśmarathya maintains that the emergence of the Great Being from the elements is described as having the nature of consciousness (*vijñānātman*). For if there were non-difference [between them], then the declaration that "by knowing one, all is known" would be possible. The teacher Auḍulomi maintains that this assumption of non-difference is because of the state of being [achieved] by the self as it is about to depart; for when the conscious self, having become serene through the power of knowledge, meditation, and so forth, is about to depart, its identity with the Supreme Self becomes possible. Thus thinks the teacher Auḍulomi.

"Because of the continued existence [of the Self], so says Kāśakṛtsna. Since this very Supreme Self exists even in the form of the individual cognitional self (*vijñānātman*), Teacher Kāśakṛtsna considers this declaration of non-difference to be logical. [Objection: But surely this is a statement regarding the annihilation of the Self, since it says, "Arising from these elements, one perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death. How then can this be a statement of mutual non-difference? [Reply: This is not a fault.
This mention of "perishing" is intended to mean the destruction of specific cognition (*viśeṣavijñāna*), not the annihilation of the Self.

Therefore, the meaning of Śaṅkara’s commentary, which was previously stated, should be construed by resorting to ellipses, transpositions, and so forth, in such a way that it is established through our own statement; for this does not preclude the fact that the context concerns the Supreme Self. Indeed, in this way, [the passage] beginning with "Now, this Self is without interior or exterior, a mass of pure consciousness alone; having arisen from these... refers precisely to the Self under discussion, the Self that is to be seen.

If it is argued: "Since the description of origination and destruction is made through the absence of consciousness (*vijñāna*), how could the non-mention of origination and destruction not preclude the fact that this section concerns the Supreme Self? Furthermore, because the doubt that the Self to be seen is not the Supreme Self—arising from its designation by terms denoting the individual soul (*jīva*)—is groundless, as will be stated by [the author] himself," then that is true; however, [our position] intends to present other objections, such as the impossibility of the unmodified Brahman existing in the state of the individual soul.

However, the justification for the designation of non-difference (*abhedavyapadeśa*) is absolutely required; thus, by this very point, the objection that "the defects of not performing what is beneficial and so forth would follow from the designation of [Brahman] as other" is addressed. Since such distinctness has been established, the sūtra "Because of the persistence [of the world], [it is Brahman]; so says Kāśakṛtsna" is appropriately connected right here for the purpose of justifying the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is because it will be stated later that these three sūtras constitute the remainder of this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*). How, then, is there a connection here?

The suspicion regarding the *rīti* (style) is thus dispelled. However, Yādavaprakāśa and others explain even these three sūtras—beginning with "Because of the fulfillment of the proposition"—as being solely intended to establish the view favored by the author of the Sūtras; they do not maintain that the meaning of the first two sūtras is subject to refutation, nor that the meaning of the third sūtra is merely intended to establish the view favored by the author of the Sūtras. The phrase "because it is unfit for an alternative" means that it is improper to refute it by means of an alternative (*vikalpa*). The thought is that [the view of Auḍulomi] would also be presented here, due to the recognition of the opinion of Auḍulomi.

"Like fullness" means "like that which depends on other parts. "Because of the absence of being denotable by those respective words" means "because of the absence of being denotable by words such as 'grass' (tṛṇa)," etc.; this is the sense. Thus ends the section on the "Connection of Sentences" (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa).

"Connection with the two baskets" (peṭikāsaṅgati) means the connection of this section with the two baskets. Regarding "by way of an alternative" (vikalpena): in the three sections beginning with "Also that which is inferential" (ānumānikam api), having accepted the causality of Brahman precisely by not rejecting the [prior] non-establishment of Brahman's causality, the alternative view arising from the thought "let even Pradhāna be the cause in some cases" was refuted by the exclusion of any other possibility (anyayogavyavaccheda). However, in the three sections beginning with "And as the cause" (kāraṇatvena ca), the restrictive rule arising from the idea that "Pradhāna alone is the cause of the world" [is refuted].

The sense is that the status of being a cause has been refuted in order to exclude any non-connection [with the subject matter]. But how is the second section (*adhikaraṇa*) and the triad of subsequent sections incidental (*prāsaṅgika*)? One might object that because the passage concerning "that which follows the shadow" serves as its subject matter, they are directly connected to the three chapters (*tripādī*). Anticipating this, he states, "In that regard, that which follows the shadow," etc., to show that there is a direct connection in both ways. Now, even in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since the causality of both Pradhāna and Īśvara is accepted, the refutation of their conjunction [would seem unnecessary].

Anticipating the objection that [the two paths] are not logically consistent, he states "of two entities established in themselves" (*svaniṣṭhavastudvayasya*), intending to show that their conjunction (*samuccaya*) is to be rejected because they are distinct paths. [This is so] because there is no mutual relationship of body and embodied (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*) between them.

The meaning is: "not [the cause] of two unestablished entities. Regarding the phrase "because of being all-powerful" (*sarvaśaktitvāt*): that which possesses all power is "all-powerful"; the meaning is "because of being that. The sense is that since it is stated, "O twice-born one, whatever class of beings is created by whomsoever, in the production of those created things, all that is indeed the body of Hari," everything stands as a locus of power; thus, *prakṛti* (primordial nature) functions as a qualifying attribute. The word "by the Vedāntas alone" (*vedāntaireva*) is to be explained [in this way].

Regarding the phrase "as its qualifier": it should be understood that this does not contradict the statement "the world is presided over by Him alone," which—by virtue of the meaning—establishes through the instrumental case that the Lord, though the primary subject, functions as a qualifier for the nominative term. As for "the state of being the impeller with respect to Māyā": since "ruling" (*īśanam*) means "governing" (*niyamanam*), and that consists of "impelling" (*preraṇam*), the sense is that when there is a requirement for an object to be impelled, Māyā alone is obtained as that object due to its proximity. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇam*).

In the passage, “One should know Māyā as Prakṛti,” the word *prakṛti* refers to the material cause (*upādāna*), as in the grammatical rule “the *prakṛti* of that which performs the action of originating” (Pāṇini 1.4.30) and in such scriptural statements as “Prakṛti [is Brahman], because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples. Consequently, since this establishes that Māyā is the material cause and the wielder of Māyā is the Lord (*īśvara*), the distinction between the efficient cause and the material cause is what is taught by the Śruti; this should also be understood as the anxiety of the opponent (the Pūrvapakṣin).

In some manuscripts, the reading "samarthayati" (he establishes) is observed; in that case, it expresses the sense of "parivṛḍhaṃ karoti" (he makes powerful), and the active voice (parasmaipada) must be justified by applying the *ṇic* suffix according to the rule "tat karoti" (he does that) to the word "samartha. However, the reading "samarthayate" (he establishes for himself) is indeed straightforward.

He explains the commentary beginning with "evameva hi" as being intended to support the interrupted scriptural passage (even though it is separated by sentences establishing the position that does not accept scripture), in accordance with the natural force of the word *hi*, stating: "because of the scriptural statement regarding causality. [Objection: But has not the purpose of the sūtra "na tu pariṇāmāt" been stated [in the commentary] as: "But [it is not so] because of the absence of examples; if [it be argued that there would be] non-distinction due to the consequence of the enjoyer [becoming the enjoyed], it would be as in the world"?

Having raised the objection regarding futility because [the Lord’s activity] is accomplished effortlessly—as in the passage beginning with “But as in the world, His sport alone” (2.1.33)—he states [the answer] in many sections of the second chapter. Here, the phrase “as from the word, etc. refers to the remainder of the sūtra “He is known from the Word alone” (1.3.24). Regarding the phrase “of those [scriptural passages] which maintain the Pradhāna as the cause”: although it is not explicitly stated here in the Bhāṣya that passages such as “The Cow is without beginning or end,” which maintain the Pradhāna as the cause, ultimately refer to the Supreme Self;
nevertheless, since darkness and the rest are declared to be the Lord, words denoting the body [must] refer to the embodied one.

The sense is that even for those words, the state of extending up to the Supreme Self (paramātman) has already been stated. In that context, since mere association is intended, the meaning is that "the ether (ākāśa) is conjoined with the senses. He says that the intention lies in the use of the plural number because, in the state of dissolution into the ether, the subtle elements (tanmātras) of touch, form, taste, and smell have perished. By the word "dissolution" (laya), he refers to the identity of nature between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, and so forth. Here, in the first and third explanations, one should rely on the reading: "even in the state of having reached [the stage of] differentiation, the conscious reality (cidvastu) remains extremely subtle, accompanied by karma and its latent impressions (saṃskāra)."

It should be understood that this is the second explanation, based on the reading *cidacidvastvatisūkṣmam*. The phrase "due to consistency with another Śruti" means due to consistency with other Śrutis such as, "The wise one is neither born nor does he die."

In the *Bhāṣya*, after stating that the phrase "from the one, non-dual [Self] whose body consists of extremely subtle sentient and insentient entities" (*atyantasūkṣmacidacidvastuśarīrāt*) serves as an explanation for the phrase "from the one, non-dual [Self]" (*ekasmādevādvitīyāt*), he explains the latter as an illustration for the acceptance of having a subtle sentient and insentient body, saying: "Or else, in the *Ānandavallī*," meaning "in the cited passages such as 'He performed austerity' (*sa tapo'tapyata*)."

"From the verbal root *tapa* in the sense of 'perception' (*ālocana*). Although the root *tapa* in the sense of 'perception' is not listed in the [Dhātupāṭha] lists, where *tapa* is listed under the *śab*-class in the sense of 'heat' (*santāpa*), or *tapa* in the sense of 'sovereignty' (*aiśvarya*) under the *div*-class, or *tapa* in the sense of 'burning' (*dāha*) under the *cur*-class; nevertheless, the point is that since roots have multiple meanings, "perception" is also one of its senses. "Of the constituent specific sentence" means of the constituent sentences of the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference, such as "He entered into that very [Being]" (*tadevānuprāviśat*), and so forth.

An objection is raised: "Since it is heard that 'having created, he entered after,' the entry occurs immediately following creation; therefore, even for a substance undergoing modification, how can it be said that it exists as the Self precisely in the state of being modified? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: "Having created that, he entered that very thing," and so forth. Intending to avoid the undesirable consequence of the suffix *tvā* (in *sṛṣṭvā*) being rendered ungrammatical, he says: "Or rather, prior to creation. Regarding this alternative view, he provides the resolution for the statement "even for a substance undergoing modification" by saying: "In that case, what was stated here [is applicable]."

And then, in the statement "having created that," the entry into the purpose of its maintenance is stated; by the phrase "having entered that," the entry is shown to be the cause of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The meaning is that in the foundational sentence (*pādakavākya*), only the entry into the time of creation is stated, and not the manifestation of the entry mentioned in the preceding sentence. Regarding the phrase "of that which was stated by others as being merely instrumental," the sense is: "as a means of proof for the state of being a mere instrumental cause, according to what was stated by others. The phrase "because of the unity of purpose with such [passages] as 'He made Himself His own Self'" means: "because of the unity of purpose with all the Śruti texts. The phrase "by others" means: "by Śaṅkara, Yādava, and so forth."

The meaning of the mantra, "A womb has been prepared for you, O Indra, in the seat" (*yoniṣṭa indra sadane akāri*), is as follows: "O Indra! A *yoni*—that is, a place—has been made for your seat, for your sitting. As for the objection raised here—that since the word *yoni* does not denote material cause (*upādāna*), the Brahman must be stated to be the material cause in order to avoid contradicting the promise of knowing all through the knowledge of one, and the illustrative example [of clay and pots]—that is not so; for that [the status of being a material cause] is established either by way of predominance or by way of similarity.

For in the world, when Caitra, who is the principal person in this village, is seen, the designation "all have been seen" is observed; because the seeing of the principal carries out the function of seeing the others, so too here, since the seeing of the *brāhmaṇa* is capable of accomplishing the function of seeing the others, such a designation is appropriate. Likewise, a designation based on similarity is also seen, as for example: "By this [explanation of the Jyotiṣṭoma], the sacrifices beginning with the Gava are also explained," where the others are designated by means of the explanation of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

The explanation for cows and other such things is based on their similarity to that [original]; likewise here as well, when the Brahman is known, it is possible for everything else to be known through its similarity to it by way of being composed of the *sattva* quality and so forth. For this very reason, the objection regarding the inconsistency of the illustration is also untenable; for when a single lump of clay is known, not everything made of clay becomes known, because not every product of clay is originated from that one specific lump of clay, and because a single piece of iron used for cutting wood or a single piece of gold does not constitute the material cause for all iron or all gold objects.

Nor should it be argued that in the phrase "and everything is made of clay," the word "everything" (sarva) refers only to those effects produced from a single lump of clay; for there is no evidence to support such an interpretation. For this very reason, even the resolve to become manifold mentioned in the Sūtra—"And because of the teaching of meditation" (Abhidhyopadeśāt)—is not a valid proof. This is because, while it is possible for the resolve to have as its object becoming manifold in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), there is no evidence that the resolve to become manifold specifically in the form of fire, water, and food was its intended object. As the learned have said: "May I be many."

"The creation of fire and so forth is from the resolve [of the Lord]; just as there is the production of a disciple from the resolve of a teacher, thinking 'let him be my pupil. For this very reason, the passage "He made himself his own self" is also explained; for it is logically consistent that [the Lord] is His own effect in the form of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) and so forth. By this, another argument—"because both are directly declared" and "for He is celebrated as the source"—is also explained.

To this it is replied: if, in the proposition that through the knowledge of one everything is known, the knowledge of all were stated only in a secondary sense (gauṇa) based on either similarity or predominance, then the question, "How indeed, O Venerable One, is the instruction? and the reply, "As, my dear, by one," would result in being irrelevant; for only if the knowledge of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) through the knowledge of Brahman is taken as primary does the entire context of the scripture become consistent.

Thus it is narrated: Uddālaka Āruṇi, having sent his son Śvetaketu away at his own command to stay in the teacher’s house for twelve years, questioned him upon his return after he had studied all the Vedas: "Did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? When asked again by the son, who was intent on understanding how such an instruction could possibly exist—asking, "How, O Venerable One, can there be an instruction? How is it possible for there to be knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one thing?"—the father explained it by means of examples such as a lump of clay.

Regarding the phrase "He taught [it]": if, in this context, the knowledge of all were intended as primary while the knowledge of the One were secondary, then—since it is a worldly fact that through the knowledge of the primary everything else, though not primary and even if unknown, becomes for all intents and purposes known—one who perceives the impossibility of knowing all through the knowledge of one would not have asked the question, "How indeed, O Venerable One, is there instruction? Even if the question were asked by someone unaware of that intention, [the answer] would still be [given] because of the primacy or similarity of all.

One would have to reply simply, "It might be so," yet neither of these two positions is tenable. Furthermore, the illustration that "speech is a modification and not something to be added" would become entirely groundless as a supporting argument. Likewise, the instruction regarding the volition, "May I be many, may I procreate," serves precisely to establish [Brahman] as the material cause (*upādāna*), because what must be stated as the object of that volition is the becoming manifold through the forms of fire and the other elements that are to be described immediately thereafter, such as in the passage, "That created fire. This is in accordance with the statement, "One only, without a second," and so forth.

Furthermore, since that which was determined to be one and without a second prior to creation must necessarily be both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*), we consider it logical to conclude that the rejection of its status as the material cause is motivated by a hatred for the Vedānta. The sense is that [the passage] is concerned with the fruit of meditation, because it occurs within a statement regarding such a fruit: "When the seer perceives the golden-hued one, the maker, the Lord, the Person born of Brahman, then the knower, having shaken off merit and sin, becomes stainless and attains the supreme equality."

"Because of the lack of connection with the definition [of superimposition]" means because of the lack of connection with the definition of material cause (*upādāna*). In the phrase "of a yellow conch by another conch," the word "conch" refers to another conch. Thus, the sense is that a yellow conch is superimposed upon a white conch. "Because it is superimposed upon the body as its substrate"—the sense is that the definition lacks connection, since that which is perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as being superimposed is the material cause. "If it is argued that there is superimposition of the body upon the Self..."

And thus, the meaning is that the self alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the body, but the body is not the material cause with respect to the self. Regarding the statement, "It is proper that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) should be false," the reading *anyonyasminnanyonyātmakatāmanyonyadharmāṃścādhyasyeti ca viṣaye yuṣmadarthaḥ* is observed; therein, having raised an objection against the word *bhavituṃ yuktaṃ*, the ellipsis must be completed by adding *tathāpi*. The meaning of the entire passage ending with "it is proper that superimposition should be false" is that there is no such thing as superimposition.

It should be understood that this is because the *Śāṅkarabhāṣya* ending with those words consists of a critique of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), whereas the passage beginning with "the mutual attribution of the nature of one in the other" is intended precisely to establish superimposition. He states Bhāskara’s view with the words "And he who... Regarding the phrase "In Yādavaprakāśa’s [work]," the meaning is as follows: "by the immediately proximate probandum" refers to the fact that the Brahman's status as material cause (*upādānatva*) is the immediately proximate probandum which is to be established; the identity with Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), however, is the mediate probandum. The phrase "it must be stated" means that it must be stated as a probandum by the word "and Primordial Matter" (*prakṛtiśca*).

For the state of being the appropriator (*upādātṛtva*) is primarily to be accomplished; thus, the distinction is that it is "immediately preceding" (*adhyavahitam*). The phrase "showing transformation" (*vikriyām iti*) connects with what precedes it, namely "shows. The sense is that there is no attainment of unity prior to dissolution, because according to the scriptures—namely, "One only, without a second" (*ekamevādvitīyam*) and "It thought: May I be many, may I grow forth" (*tadaikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeyeti*)—the state of unity must necessarily exist prior to the volition of becoming manifold.

The phrase “because the case-ending is not elided” means that although the elision of *am* by the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt* certainly occurs even when there is no compound, nevertheless, since it is possible for the remembered case-ending itself to convey the meaning—as in examples such as *dadhi paśya*—it is improper to resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in a compound; this is the intended sense. Furthermore, the phrase “and because a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified is not admitted” implies that if such a relationship were admitted, our desired conclusion would be established.

The meaning is that *prakṛti* alone would be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest; consequently, the doctrine of Brahman as the non-different efficient and material cause (*abhinnanimittopādāna*) would not hold, because the portion consisting of the Controller (*niyantr-aṃśa*) would be merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*). This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that there would be a multiplicity of Brahmans. [Objection: In that case, what is this "collection of trees" (*vṛkṣasamudāya*)? Are the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the Controller...?

The phrase "each one [is] Brahman" does not differ from the previous alternative (*vikalpa*). Consequently, it appears that the section of the text ending with the words "even though the three are mutually distinct" serves no significant purpose. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this alternative is presented again in order to state another objection. He raises the doubt: "even though the three are mutually distinct."

If it is argued that the identity of the three with the single Brahman-Ātman must be described—given that, just as the non-difference from a single tree is established for leaves, branches, and so forth by not abandoning their distinction as such, so too the non-difference from the single Brahman-Ātman would appear to be intended even by the proponent of the Siddhānta (the final conclusion) because they do not abandon the distinction of the bricks as being "bricks"—this is not accepted by the Siddhāntin, because the three do not possess the nature of having a single Brahman-Ātman as their essence. To this, we reply: no.

It should be understood that it is stated that "oneness must be described in terms of Brahman" with the intention that Brahman is indeed the Lord qualified by consciousness and matter (*cid-acit*), and not the substantive alone; therefore, being included within the qualified entity is common to all three, and thus oneness is to be described through the nature of Brahman. In the phrase "when a finger is cut off," the meaning is that it has been separated from one's own body by the act of cutting. "The nature of something" means the nature of the qualified entity. The phrase "those that exist as long as the substantive exists" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be observed that there is no fault even if the staff is included within the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the "staff-qualified" [person]. As for the claim that "the heat of fire is the production of a blister," one might ask: how can hot touch be the very nature of fire? This is because of the distinction between a quality (*guṇa*) and its possessor (*guṇin*); for indeed, "own-nature" (*svarūpa*) is said to be one's own form, but not everything inseparable from oneself is called "own-nature. If, however, everything that enters into the scope of the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of causality is called "own-nature," then [it would follow] that in visual perception, the manifested color residing in light...

If light were the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the causality residing in manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*), it would follow that light itself must be of the nature of manifested color. Similarly, since the state of being fire produced from wet fuel (*ārdrendhana*) is the delimiting factor for the production of smoke, it would follow that wet fuel and so forth must also enter into the very nature of fire. Therefore, the doctrine regarding their "nature" (*svarūpatva*) refers to their own specific form (*svīyarūpatva*), and not to the sense of being non-different in nature (*svābhinnarūpatva*). And thus, since primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest are also inseparable attributes (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) of the Supreme Self, [the same logic applies].

Granted that [the Self] may indeed be denoted by words such as "power" (śakti), "form" (rūpa), or "part" (aṃśa) with respect to the body; yet, by this much alone, it does not follow that the state residing in that [body] has its locus in this [Self]. For if that were the case, then [the Self] would possess the properties of being a power, having a body, being a part, and being insentient (jaḍatva) as they reside in that [body].

[Otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence that even insentient matter (*dīna*) would reside in the Supreme Self; consequently, since primordial nature (*prakṛti*) transforms into the form of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth, primordial nature alone would be the material cause (*upādāna*), and not Brahman. He dispels this doubt under the guise of a conclusion by stating: "They [the states] reside in the very essence of Brahman as qualified by the insentient [matter] in its states of the Great Principle and so forth. The meaning is this: Brahman is indeed qualified by both the sentient and the insentient, not merely the substantive itself; and in that which is qualified by the sentient and the insentient, there certainly exists the capacity for connection with the states of the Great Principle and so forth. Thus, there is no lack of proof for the reason (*hetvasiddhi*).

The meaning is as follows: just as the hub, spokes, and rim of a chariot wheel—which have entered into a mutual relationship of support and supported—are included within the essential nature denoted by the word "chariot wheel"; or just as the essential nature of an arrow, characterized by its feathers and shaft, is denoted by the word "muñja" (arrow); or just as the essential nature of a stalk, consisting of its sheath, leaves, and so forth, is denoted by the word "kali" (stalk); in the same way, the essential nature of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller, which stand in a relationship of support and supported, is what is denoted by the word "Brahman."

[Objection: But surely, if the flame residing in the wood were to establish the wood’s status as the instrument (*karaṇa*), then the state residing in primordial nature (*prakṛti*) would merely establish primordial nature’s status as the material cause (*upādāna*), and not establish Brahman’s status as the material cause. To this, he says: "But because the instrumental factor (*karaṇakāraka*) resides in itself. The sense is that primordial nature, however, lacks such self-residence, and therefore it does not [itself] constitute the material cause.

One might object: "Why should the wheel, which rests upon the lump of clay, not itself be the locus for the pot-ness and other properties residing in that lump? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "residing in the substratum" (*āśrayiniṣṭhām*). The meaning is that an independent entity, such as the lump of clay, cannot bring about its own state of being connected to a condition within its own substrate, namely the wheel. "Piercing through an intervening leaf" (*vyavahitapatravedha*) means piercing a leaf that is separated by another act of piercing a leaf. The point is that, in the case of the potter, [the action] is mediated by a homogeneous operation acting as a cause.

The meaning of "of that which is obstructed by an arrow" is that both the bow and the arrow are pervaded by the nature of being weapons, which is a subordinate form of the cause [of the action]. The phrase "because of the existence of some causal operation in the form of producing the producer" means because of the existence of some causal operation in the form of producing the activity that produces that [effect]. By this, all [potential] over-extensions (*atiprasaṅga*)—both those already explained and those not yet explained—are refuted. || 29 ||

The phrase "because it is excluded" means that over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is to be prevented by means of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Regarding the expression "of fire and so forth," the words "even though it is immediately adjacent" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. The idea is that being a mere conjunction constitutes an intervention; for instance, a bedspread merely obstructs the contact between a reclining person and the couch, but it does not obstruct their relationship as substratum and resident (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*).

"Because it is a mediator residing in a substance capable of supporting itself. [Objection: If this were so, then in the states of being *darbha* grass and so forth, *darbha* grasses would not be mediators of their dependence on the ground; likewise, in the states of being lice and so forth, lice and the like would not be mediators of their dependence on humans. [Response: This is not so, because the phrase "capable of supporting itself" means "capable of supporting that which is supported by itself."

Earth, humans, and the like lack the capacity to possess the state of being *darbha* grass or *yūkā* lice, because there is no evidence for their being dependent upon those [entities]. Now, it might be argued that wherever there is evidence establishing dependence upon something, then intervening entities do not constitute an obstruction; for this very reason, in cases such as "he sleeps on the palace," "he sleeps on the couch," "he places the oblations on the altar," or "he places the oblations on the sacrificial grass," intervening entities such as the couch or the sacrificial grass do not act as obstructions.

If it is argued that [the argument] is exhausted [by this], we accept that as our conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). For even in the case of something separated [in time or space], if there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) grasping its status as a substratum (*āśrayatva*), then it possesses the nature of a substratum. And in the present case, there exists a means of valid cognition—such as the scriptural passage "That became both the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*)"—which grasps that Brahman, though separated by the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, is the substratum for those respective states. Therefore, the sense is that primary material causality (*upādānatva*) is established because [Brahman] is the substratum of these states.

Now, if it is argued that since the status of being the primary locus for states such as the "Great Principle" (mahat) and so forth resides primarily in the Supreme Self, then by the same logic, the status of being the primary locus for states such as "godhood" and so forth must reside primarily in the individual self (ātman); why, then, is there no denial [of these states] in the statement, "He is neither god nor man"? Nor should it be said that the denial is justified because [the self] lacks the status of being a direct locus; for if a jar resting on the ground were a locus of the ground through conjunction, yet lacked the status of being a locus of the jar through some other relation, it would be improper to say, "The ground is not a locus of the jar."

Furthermore, if it is argued that the scripture establishing such a prohibition would itself be unacceptable because it generates delusion, we say no; for the intended meaning of a statement must be determined in accordance with its preceding and succeeding sentences. Thus, since the scriptures prohibiting divinity and so forth would otherwise contradict scriptures such as "Four [sacrifices] lasting fifteen nights attain divinity," one must necessarily accept that they intend an unqualified (direct) prohibition. Therefore, there is no inconsistency; this is the sense.

Regarding the phrase "only three [are] performers of sacrifice" (*traya eva yajvānaḥ*), the particle *eva* (only) is seen in the manuscripts; however, we do not perceive much purpose for it. The words "by means of the terms *sat*, *brahma*, and *akṣara*" require the completion of the remainder of the sentence, such as "connected with," and so forth. As for the statement "because it has been determined by the logic of the thirty-two topics," this refers to the fact that in the previous thirty-four topics, the general necessity of investigating the *brahma* was established in the first topic.

The mention of "thirty-two" [adhikaraṇas] is intended to show that the *Raṇa* and *Apaśūdra* adhikaraṇas are not useful for determining specific deities; for this very reason, he will later treat them separately by stating, "of the adhikaraṇas beginning with 'janmādyasya yataḥ'," and he will not cite the *Apaśūdra* adhikaraṇa. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the upcoming text which states that the equality of the word "Bhagavat" was established in the first sūtra; [for that statement refers to the primary group of thirty-two].

In that case as well, it should be understood that it was stated thus with the intention of establishing the supremacy of the Blessed Lord. Alternatively, since it will be stated later that "the third [category], however, is employed in a general sense," the number thirty-two should be understood by excluding the third section. Regarding the phrase "other than Nārāyaṇa," the meaning is that this refutes the Pāśupata doctrine, because in their system it is taught that "the Blessed Lord is the material cause, while Maheśvara is the efficient cause," thereby positing an efficient cause other than Nārāyaṇa.

The sense is that by the qualifying attribute of being "made of gold," there is a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the phrase "having the color of the sun. The intent is that this [sūtra] is devoted to establishing [the subject] as having the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) as its object. This is because, in the *Ākāśādhikaraṇa*, by the mention of the superiority of ether (*ākāśa*) over the elements in the statement "Ether is greater than the elements," the meaning stated in the *Puruṣasūkta*—"Greater than that"—is established; and in the *Prāṇādhikaraṇa*, by the extension of that same reasoning, the meaning denoted by the word "ether" is shown to refer to the Supreme Self; and in the *Jyotiradhikaraṇa*, regarding the word "light" (*jyotis*), [it refers to the verse] "A foot of Him... [and so forth].

The meaning is that the demonstration of the text's intent to convey the subject matter of the *Puruṣasūkta* is clear; for, by the phrase "all beings," its focus on the *Puruṣasūkta* is established, and in the *Prāṇādhikaraṇa*, Indra and Prāṇa are perceived as the objects of the most beneficial meditation through the words "Know me alone, worship me. Furthermore, the intent to convey the subject matter of the *Puruṣasūkta* is naturally evident from the statement, "Knowing Him thus, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path. In this context, the word "Indra" should be understood as referring to the word "me" (*mām*).

And this has already been demonstrated by the statement, "He was fashioned by the mind, by thought, and by meditation," because the purport of this sentence from the Taittirīya is that it concerns the Puruṣa. He establishes that immortality proves [the subject] to be the Supreme Person by noting the recognition of the phrase "in him" (tasmin ayam).

The meaning is that because of the repetition of the word *puruṣa*—as seen in the passage from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "He who knows the imperishable Puruṣa, the Truth... he truly taught that Brāhma-vidyā," and further, "The divine, formless Puruṣa... the Puruṣa who is the agent and Lord"—it follows that [the subject] is indeed the one heard there. This is because of the connection with the specific form (attributes) heard therein; this is the sense of the phrase "from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad. And this [point] is clear in the discussion regarding how what is being remembered may serve as an inference (*smaryamāṇamanumāna*).

And because it is taught in the subsequent passage by one who knows the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). Although the *Uddālaka-brāhmaṇa* is the answer to the question regarding the Inner Controller posed by Uddālaka, while the *Gārgī-brāhmaṇa* is the answer to Gārgī’s question regarding the substratum of space, there is no rule that these two have the same subject matter. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this has been presented as a supporting argument (*abhyuccaya-yukti*) on the grounds that whatever slight determining factor may exist should not be disregarded.

The intention is that the phrase "Ākāśo ha vai nāma" (Indeed, space is called by name) is a restatement [of the same teaching], because it is recognized as such through its correspondence with the *Puruṣasūkta*, which states: "Having fashioned all forms and made their names" (*sarvāṇi rūpāṇi vicitya dhīro nāmāni kṛtvā*). Furthermore, the phrase "That than which there is nothing higher" (*yasmāt param*) refers to the fact that the word "Puruṣa" is heard therein in the passage: "By that Puruṣa, all this is filled. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, it says: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; being one, it did not flourish. It emitted from itself the Kṣatra as a form superior to itself."

These are the divine powers (*devakṣatra*): Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna. There is nothing higher than that *kṣatra*. Therefore, at the Rājasūya sacrifice, the Brāhmaṇa sits below the Kṣatriya; he thereby bestows that glory upon the *kṣatra*. The Brāhmaṇa is the womb of the *kṣatra*; therefore, even when a king attains the highest state, he finally resorts to the Brāhmaṇa alone.

He who destroys his own source reaches that very source and becomes worse; as one who, having abandoned a superior, does not prosper. He did not yet flourish; he created all these classes of divine beings that are enumerated in groups: the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts. He did not yet flourish; he created the Śūdra caste, namely Pūṣan. Pūṣan is indeed this earth, for she nourishes (puṣyati) everything here that exists. He did not yet flourish; he created a form even more excellent than that.

This Dharma is the ruler of the ruling power (kṣatra); therefore, there is nothing higher than Dharma. Consequently, a stronger man seeks refuge with one who is even stronger, just as [one seeks refuge] with a king through Dharma. That which is indeed Dharma is truth; therefore, when someone speaks the truth, they say he is speaking Dharma.

When one speaks of Dharma, one speaks of Truth; thus indeed both become that same thing. This [universe] consists of the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatra, the Viś, and the Śūdra. Among the gods, it became the Brāhmaṇa through Agni; among humans, it became the Brāhmaṇa through the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya through the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya through the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra through the Śūdra. Therefore, among the gods, those desiring the world seek it in Agni alone; among humans, they seek it in the Brāhmaṇa. For by these two forms it became the Brāhmaṇa. "It did not expand" (na vyabhavat) means it was not sufficient for the performance of ritual action.

He created that which is of the form of excellence—that is, of a praiseworthy form—exceedingly; namely, the *devatākṣatrāṇi*, the ruling powers among the gods. Regarding the king who has been consecrated and is seated [in the Rājasūya], the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) standing below him should say: "O King, you are a Brāhmaṇa! Thus is the meditation (*upāsana*) prescribed. By this, he bestows his own glory upon himself; he attains supremacy—that is, excellence through the consecration of the Rājasūya—and finally, at the conclusion of the ritual, he takes refuge in the domestic priest (*purohita*) alone. This is the meaning.

But that Kṣatriya who destroys his own Brāhmaṇa-womb, which is the cause of his existence, destroys his very source; the meaning is that this earth is the *kṣatra*—the restrainer—of the *kṣatra*, even of the Kṣatriya.
