One who is weaker, being powerless, hopes to conquer by means of *dharma* even one stronger than himself, more powerful than he; just as in the world some poor man seeks to triumph over a king who is far more powerful through *dharma*. Therefore, the power of *dharma* is established.

The phrase "referring to the Brāhmaṇa caste presided over by that [deity]" means referring to the Brāhmaṇa caste presided over by the deity Agni. It should be understood that even though the first position involves reference to the Brāhmaṇa caste, this present position is distinguished from it because it lacks reference to the Brāhmaṇa caste as presided over by the deity Agni. Regarding the statement "because of the hearing of the creation of the Kṣatriya": the sense is that if only the Brāhmaṇa had been introduced, then the creation of all the social orders (varṇas) would have been mentioned, rather than a creation beginning with the Kṣatriya.

By the phrase "the word *brāhma* refers to the *brāhmaṇa*," he establishes that the term refers to the *brāhmaṇa* caste; then, with the words "it refers to the fire presided over by that [caste]," etc., he introduces the other two positions. The intention is that since the word *brāhma* occurring at the conclusion of the section on the four castes is accepted as referring to the *brāhmaṇa* varṇa, the same applies to the word *brāhma* situated at the beginning. Furthermore, the phrase "the impossibility of being created from Agni" is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood to include "the impossibility of being created as the *brāhmaṇa* caste."

Regarding the objection that Indra and others might attain the state of Agni due to differences in kalpas, the author says: "Of this Śruti. It is indeed perceived that there is a difference between the Brāhmaṇa and Agni. Now, one might argue: "Granted that the Brāhmaṇa referred to by the word 'that' (tat) is perceived as different from Agni—indicated here with a different grammatical case (vyadhikaraṇa)—but how can his non-difference from the Brāhmaṇa be perceived? If this is asked, the answer is no; for just as in the statement "the lump of clay becomes a jar," when it is said "he becomes that Brāhmaṇa," the identity of that which is denoted by the word 'that' [is established].

The meaning is that the fact that [the state of] being a Brāhmaṇa is perceived as having existed prior [to other distinctions] is established by experience. "By way of the division into gods and humans" means that there exists a Brāhmaṇa in the form of a god and one in the form of a human. "As previously stated to have been created by the Supreme Self" refers to the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here. "Possessing the conceit of those [classes], like the division into Kṣatriyas and so forth" means the creation of Indra and others who possess the conceit of their respective castes (jāti) as divided by the distinctions of Kṣatriya and so on.

The meaning is that from the creation of Agni, who possesses the conceit (*abhimānin*) of being a Brāhmaṇa, his energy (*tejas*)—belonging to the previous Brāhmaṇa—departed when he was weary and heated. This is because the division [of castes] such as Brāhmaṇahood has already been stated. Consequently, the meaning is that one need not resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word *brāhṛ*, which denotes a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding the phrase "that subsequent *brāhṛ* among humans," the sense is that after the passage "among the gods, it became a *brāhṛ* by means of Agni itself," the word *tad* (that) is drawn over (*anukṛṣyate*) from the word *brāhṛ*. Furthermore, the phrase "it became a *brāhṛ*" (*brāhṛābhavat*) is also drawn over from the passage "among the gods, it became a *brāhṛ* by means of Agni itself. Thus, the meaning is that the word *brāhṛ* refers to the same entity in both contexts.

Now, regarding the statement, "Among the gods, he became Brāhmaṇa through Agni alone; among humans, [he became Brāhmaṇa through the Brāhmaṇa]," it means that among the gods—within the class of gods—he came to be as Brāhmaṇa through Agni alone; without undergoing any further modification, he remained possessed of the very nature of Agni. Among humans...

And the meaning is that the Brahmin-status remains as the very nature of the Brahmin without undergoing any modification, both in the case of the fire and in the caste of the Brahmin, being unmodified by the state of being a Brahmin. However, in the case of Kṣatriyas and others, the status of being a Kṣatriya arises for the Brahmin due to the cause of modification into a Kṣatriya and so forth. Therefore, one might raise the objection: "Since the fire and the Brahmin possess the nature of a Brahmin without modification, why not accept the position stated by the opponent—that those desiring the world perform [the rites] in the fire and in the Brahmin? Anticipating this, he says: "by means of the connection with the words heard in the scripture."

[The opponent asks: "Since it is intended to praise those [two], one might ask: given that the context (prakaraṇa) is common to the four castes and the creation desired by them, what is the basis for praising Agni and Brāhmaṇa specifically? For in this context, Agni and Brāhmaṇa do not enter the category of the subject or the predicate as unique [entities] excluded from Indra, Kṣatra, and so forth, such that their specific praise would be intended; rather, the intention is to praise the four castes and those who identify with them by means of praising Agni and Brāhmaṇa."

The meaning is that while the primary sense is possible in the case of "By fire alone [he became] a Brāhmaṇa among the gods," where one may accept the primary sense consisting of the Brāhmaṇa caste, it is nevertheless improper to accept the secondary sense consisting of the Brāhmaṇa caste even in a context where the primary sense is possible, such as in the passage "A Brāhmaṇa was here in the beginning. Thus, the point is that the primary sense must be adopted wherever it is not impossible.

"It was the Self alone. "The Self alone existed in the form of a person. Having looked around, he saw nothing other than himself. He first said, 'I am. From that, the name 'I' arose. Therefore, even today, when addressed, one first says, 'It is I,' and only then utters another name, whatever it may be. Because he burnt (auṣat) all evils prior to all this, he is called a *puruṣa*. Indeed, he who knows this burns up anyone who wishes to be before him. He was afraid; therefore, one who is alone is afraid. He looked for a companion."

"Since there is nothing else besides me, why should I fear?"—from that very [realization] his fear departed; for from what could he have feared? Fear arises from a second entity. "He indeed did not find delight in being alone; he desired a second," and so forth. *Etad dhrāmantritaḥ* means "even at this time, summoned. *Sa yat pūrvaḥ*: because he was prior to all this, having driven away (*aṭahat*) all evils (*pāpman*), he is therefore called *puruṣa*.

"He surely burns him," and so forth; the meaning is that he who knows thus burns one who previously desired the state of Prajāpati for himself. For in the world, one possessed of superior means is seen as if burning one who lacks such means.

"There was nothing whatsoever here," and so forth: "In the beginning, this was indeed death; it was not immortal. Hunger is death, for hunger is the desire to eat. He created the mind, thinking, 'May I have a self. He moved about performing *arcana* (worship/striving). From his *arcana*, the waters were born. [He thought], 'Verily, through my *arcana*, this has become one (*eka*). That is the reason for the name of the *arka*; for he who knows thus the nature of the *arka* becomes happy (*ka*). The waters, indeed, are the *arka*. Whatever essence of the waters there was, that condensed; it became the earth. Upon it, he exerted himself. From him, having exerted himself, *tejas* (heat/luster) was the essence."

For the Śruti says, "The fire came into being. The meaning is that, having formed the resolve, "May I possess a self" (ātmanvī) and "May I possess a mind" (manasvī), he created the mind. As for the phrase "because of my being distinguished by hunger" (arcate vai me aśanāyā): although it appears to be a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with death, as in "death made me hungry," and not a qualification by hunger, nevertheless—since it is impossible for death itself to be hunger here—the intention is that the word "hunger" (*aśanāyā*) indicates (*lakṣya*) one who possesses hunger (*aśanāyāvān*).

The phrase "the agency of performing rites such as worship" means the agency of performing actions such as worship. Regarding the *Subāla Upaniṣad*, at the beginning of that Upaniṣad it says: "They ask: 'What was there then? He said to him: 'Neither being, nor non-being, nor being-and-non-being. From that, darkness (*tamas*) is born; from darkness, the origin of the elements (*bhūtādi*); from the origin of the elements, space (*ākāśa*); from space, air (*vāyu*); from air, fire (*agni*); from fire, water (*āpaḥ*); from water, earth (*pṛthivī*). That became an egg. Having remained thus for the duration of a year, it split into two."

"Below is the earth, above is the sky, and in the middle is the divine Person—He who has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. "In fear of Him, O Agni, Death created all beings—the three-eyed, three-headed, three-footed one with the broken axe; even Brahmā trembles before Him. Such is the Śruti. Regarding the phrase "in death" (*mṛtyoḥ*), the ablative case indicates that the merging into the Supreme Deity beyond death is heard [in scripture]; thus, the meaning is that the liberated soul attains oneness with the Supreme Deity beyond death.

The point is that because the section beginning with "He breaks the sheath" concerns the subject of one who is being liberated, it is heard here that "being beyond death" means being the cause of death, and that this [cause] is designated by the word "Deity. He states another argument: "of the source of non-distinction itself.

Since in this very Upaniṣad it is established that the Supreme is the locus of the non-distinction of darkness—by the statement "the Imperishable dissolves into darkness; darkness becomes one in the Supreme"—it is logical that darkness arises from the source of non-distinction itself; such is the meaning.

The phrase "because it is to be attained by the liberated" refers to the fact that the section concerning the destination of the liberated begins with "He pierces the Imperishable," and because it is established in passages such as "He reaches the end of this path, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu" that this [attainment] belongs to Nārāyaṇa alone—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "from pure consciousness alone," etc.: by the two terms "neither being nor non-being," the distinction from both pure consciousness and pure non-consciousness is intended; by the term "neither being-nor-non-being," the distinction from a mixture of the two is not intended.

It should be understood that the phrase "from the individuals" (*vyaṣṭibhyaḥ*) is an explanation of the word "from the mixed" (*miśrāt*). The expression "as stated by the seer" (*taduktam ṛṣiṇā*) means "by the Veda," which is the seer. "Of the moving and the stationary" (*jagatastasthuṣaḥ*) means "of the mobile and the immobile. The phrase "because of being pervaded by the supreme cause" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should be understood as meaning "because [the Lord] is also pervaded by the causality of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of both the mobile and the immobile."

The meaning is that by the statement "he is born from the sun," the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-gati*) is recognized through this demonstration of the attainment of the solar world. "The inner self (*pratyagātman*) is purified" means that the true nature of the inner self is set forth for the purpose of reflecting upon the inner reality—which serves as an auxiliary to the meditation on the Supreme Self that is the means to liberation—and for the purpose of distinguishing it from other things.

One might object: "In this very same verse, 'He supported the earth and this heaven,' the quality of supporting the earth and so forth may serve as a differentiator. Anticipating this, he says: "But the support of the earth and so forth... In the Śruti, *dadhāra* means "he supported" (*dadha-re*). In roots such as *dhṛ*, the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is a Vedic usage according to the rule "the reduplicated syllable is long" (*dīrgho'bhyāsasya*).

Now, one might object: since in this very eight-verse hymn it is heard that "of whom immortality and death are the shadow," there is a mention of bondage and liberation—designated by the words *amṛta* (immortality) and *mṛtyu* (death)—as being subject to His control, and therefore [the hymn] must refer to the Supreme Self; anticipating this doubt, he says: "And the words *amṛta* and *mṛtyu*... Regarding the phrase "whom within the ocean": "within the ocean the seers weave" means they understand [Him]. Regarding the word *tapas*: the meaning is "by the word *tapas*" as in the passage, "From the kindled *tapas*, Ṛta and Satya are born. And the word *tapas* is used in such passages as, "And those who in the forest worship with faith and *tapas*..."

The sense is that [the term *dhātu*] refers to the Supreme Self, just as in the passage beginning with "He who exists" (*sate*). Regarding the phrase "on account of the uniformity of the word *dhātṛ* occurring in the opening," the meaning is that since the word *dhātṛ* heard in the preceding sentence—"The Creator (*dhātṛ*) fashioned the sun and moon as before"—must be adopted even for the word *dhātu* in the expression "by the grace of the Creator" (*dhātuḥ prasādāt*), there is uniformity. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and in the subsequent section," the sense is that it is established in the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka by the statement, "He is Brahman, He is Śiva."
In the section explaining the group of duties pertaining to the Brahmin: "From that, the seven vital breaths arise; seven are the flames, and seven the fuel-sticks."

"Seven tongues; seven worlds in which the vital breaths move, seven by seven deposited in the secret cave. From Him all oceans and mountains arise; from Him flow the rivers of every form. And from Him come all herbs and juices, by whom this inner self exists as a being. He is the Brahman of the gods, the path of the seers, the Rishi of the wise, the buffalo of wild beasts, the hawk of vultures, the axe of the forests; Soma, lowing, passes through the filter"—such is the context.

Therefore, are not the two scriptural texts (*śruti*) concerning Rudra and Maheśvara of equal strength? For in the *Pūrvatantra*, in the section dealing with "the case of a conflict between elements of equal force" (*vipratiṣiddhadharmāṇāṃ samavāye*), it is stated that "when there is a conjunction of conflicting properties, those of the majority shall possess the common property. This was established in the context of a certain optional sacrifice (*kāmyeṣṭi*) where there are five oblations: a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra and Agni, and curd, honey, ghee, and water for Prajāpati; since the first two are modifications of the *aindrāgna-sānnāyya*, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the New Moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*) applies to them.

It has been determined that, although the modifications of the *upāṃśuyāja*—consisting of honey, water, and clarified butter—are heard last in the text, the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Full Moon sacrifice applies to them because of their greater number, so as to favor them. Therefore, if it is argued that a single element at the beginning is weaker than the multiple means of proof located in the conclusion—as established in the section [of the *Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra*] beginning with "Because of the intermediate [text], on account of the logical possibility" (*antara upapatteḥ*)—we say no.

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "when there is a conflict between contradictory properties, the property of the majority should prevail," the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached with the statement: "Or rather, the primary [property prevails], because of the prior injunction, as in the world. Therefore, one should understand that these two *sūtras* belong to a single topical section (*aikādhikaraṇya*), according to the opinion of a certain school (*ekadeśin*). Furthermore, in this context as well, it should be understood that there is no disparity in terms of "more" or "less," because of the repetition of the word "Creator" (*dhātṛ*) in the passage: "The Creator fashioned [the world] as before; by the grace of the Creator... and so forth.

"Because restatement (anuvāda) is dependent upon something else. Now, one might ask: how can there even be a suspicion that the statement "He who [created] the Vedas" is a restatement? For the meaning perceived here—the fact that Rudra, the great seer who transcends the universe, is the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha—is not something already established by another means of knowledge (*māna*), such that this sentence would be a restatement. And in the absence of establishment by another means of knowledge, it is impossible to conceive of this as a restatement, even when accompanied by the particle *yat* (which typically introduces a corroboration).

Nor should it be argued that, by the force of the particle *yat*, the word *nārāyaṇa* is taken as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), whereby the status of being the original injunction (*purovāditva*) is assigned to the sentence "The Brāhmaṇa is born from Nārāyaṇa," while the status of being a restatement (*anuvāditva*) is attributed to this [present] sentence; for if that were the case, then even in sentences such as "That which is dedicated to Agni" (*yad āgneyaḥ*), one would have to resort to the force of the particle *yat* to take them as referring to the *saurya-caru* offering, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of their being mere restatements. If this is raised, we say no.

The sense is this: since it is impossible for both [Rudra and Nārāyaṇa] to be the cause of Hiraṇyagarbha, and since one of the two terms, Rudra or Nārāyaṇa, as heard in the specific scriptural passage must necessarily be taken in a secondary sense (lakṣaṇā), the secondary sense is adopted for the word "Rudra" alone; for it is improper to abandon that which is possible and serves as the restrictive factor by following the connection with the word "yat" (which).

Now, one might object: "Viṣṇu is denoted by the letter *a*" is one statement establishing that Viṣṇu is the referent of the letter *a*, while "He who is the Great Lord of the Supreme" is another statement establishing that Rudra is the referent of the letter *a*. What distinction is there between these two? One sentence is "Caitra is the husband of Mitrā," and another is "He who is the husband of Mitrā is Maitra. In these cases, neither the relationship of the dependent and the basis (*upajīvya-upajīvaka-bhāva*) nor the relationship of the restated and the restater (*anuvādya-anuvādaka-bhāva*) is observed to be the determinant of relative strength (*balābala*), even when sought after.

Because of this lack of internal consistency, he says: "And because the fact that Nārāyaṇa is denoted by the syllable *a* is established. Regarding Nārāyaṇa’s being denoted by the syllable *a*, [it is said]: "By the syllable *a*, the Supreme Self, the support of all, is designated, because *a* is by its very nature the root of all words, and because Brahman is by its very nature the root of all that is denotable; thus, the relationship between the signified and the signifier is understood from their very meaning."

The meaning of this sentence must be described in accordance with many established authorities, such as: "The letter *a* denotes Viṣṇu; the letter *a* is said to be Viṣṇu; 'A' is the first name of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa," and so forth. Therefore, the intention is that by the phrase "who is supreme" (*yaḥ paraḥ*), Nārāyaṇa himself is referred to, and having set aside the conventional (*rūḍhi*) sense of the word *maheśvara*, its etymological (*yoga*) meaning—lordship qualified by greatness—is predicated of him.

The phrase "by way of being a restatement" (*anuvādarūpatayā*) means that because it is heard as containing the word "who" (*yaḥ*)—as in the verse: "May that God, who is the source and origin of the gods, the supreme Rudra, the great seer, who in the beginning generated Hiraṇyagarbha, endow us with auspiciousness"—it has the character of a restatement; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, "non-contradiction through the identity of the substance" means that since a jar produced from clay in the form of a lump is seen to be the cause of the clay existing in the state of potsherds, the identity of the substance brings about non-contradiction; this is the intended meaning.

The meaning is as follows: although one observes that clay in its prior state produces a jar produced from it, one does not observe that the jar’s being produced from clay in that [specific] state entails the clay’s being the producer [of the jar] in that same state.

The point is this: since there is no contradiction even in such statements as, "All these beings indeed arise from space alone," and "All these beings indeed enter into prāṇa," because they may refer to events occurring during specific cosmic cycles (kalpa), one should not assume that those passages have the Supreme Self as their subject matter. [Objection: But surely, "These three causal selves were born directly from Maheśvara..."?

In the creation [of the world], Brahmā was the agent; in its protection, Hari; and in its dissolution, Rudra. Nevertheless, out of mutual rivalry and desiring to surpass one another, they propitiated their father, the Supreme Lord, through austerity. First, in a previous kalpa, Rudra created Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa; then, in another kalpa, the World-Soul (Jaganmaya) created Brahmā and Rudra-Viṣṇu; and likewise, the Blessed Viṣṇu again created Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa; and again, Bhava created Brahmā and Nārāyaṇa. Thus it continues through the kalpas.

In various kalpas, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara arise from one another, each desiring victory over the other. It is with reference to the specific events of those respective kalpas that the great sages describe their power arising from their mutual birth. In some instances Brahmā is praised, in some Rudra, and in some the seed of Viṣṇu; yet by this, there is no superiority or inferiority among them in any way. It is only with reference to the specific events of those respective kalpas that the great sages [speak].

The wise man does not become deluded by those various excellent things there. But for one who is possessed by agitation and dogmatic attachment, thinking "this is it" or "this is not it," he undoubtedly becomes a *yātudhāna* or a *piśāca*. That man who establishes a distinction between Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra out of ignorance becomes afflicted with a disease of the stomach. It is declared that Maheśa, the Blue-and-Red One (*nīlalohita*), the Supreme Lord, having become a son and the younger brother of Brahmā, bestows grace upon Brahmā.

"And at the end of the kalpa, from your mouth, I shall become the wielder of the trident, assuming a terrible form born of your wrath, O dear son. Mahādeva, the portion [of the Supreme], who is saluted by all the gods, having become Ardhanārīśvara, appeared as a treasure-house of compassion. By the command of that Lord, who was seated upon my lotus, he was born as a portion."

Because the *Kūrma*, *Sūta-saṃhitā*, and *Laiṅga* Purāṇas establish through their scriptural statements that [the Lord] appeared by piercing the forehead of that [Brahmā], and because they demonstrate both the distinction between Kalpas and the nature of the incarnations, and because the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*—stating "He has no progenitor and no superior"—establishes Rudra’s status as a progenitor, one must accept it in that way; however, due to a sense of unease [regarding this], he says:

Regarding the phrase "the descent of the distinction between the oneness of the object and its conceptualization": it should be observed that one must not argue that, in accordance with the cited statement, there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the emergence of the identity of the three forms (trimūrti-sāmyaikya). This is because, although such [statements] are heard in the Tāmasa Purāṇas—which, being in a state of deviation, are themselves subjects of suspicion regarding interpolation—such [statements] are not heard in those [texts] that are not of that nature; furthermore, the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is not accepted as having Śiva as its primary purport.

It should be stated that because the word *rudra* alone is well-known [in common usage], there is no disregard for it; and since between the two words *rudra* and *hiraṇyagarbha*, the word *rudra* is primary and its meaning has not yet encountered any contradiction, it is not proper to abandon its primary sense therein. Rather, it must be said that the secondary word *hiraṇyagarbha* itself refers to Skanda.

The meaning is as follows: since the word *rudra* is used with reference to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān) in passages such as "Rudra is the many-headed, the tawny one" (*rudro bahuśirā babhruḥ*), whereas the word *hiraṇyagarbha* is never seen to be applied to Skanda, and furthermore, because there exist many primary terms such as "the Supreme of the Universe" (*viśvādhika*) and so forth [which apply to the Lord], it is logical that the word *rudra* itself refers to the Blessed Lord for the sake of His grace. This is stated "in accordance with the *Udagād* Brāhmaṇa," meaning the *Śailāli-Brāhmaṇa*; the *Śailāli-Brāhmaṇa* is cited in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*.

"Of this god, the bounteous one..."—that is, of this Viṣṇu, the radiant god, the impeller (*eṣa*), who is to be sought after by all as their master, the bounteous one (*mīduṣ*). Regarding the word *mīduṣ*, the Nirukta commentary states it means either "one who bestows" or "one who possesses power. Just as there is a branch on a tree, so too Rudra stands in the place of a branch to Viṣṇu, who stands in the place of a tree. In the powerful sacrifice performed by Rudra, [the sacrificer] has obtained the greatness of Rudra through the oblations; such is the meaning.

Regarding the statement "one should worship the Mahāpuruṣa," although the term *mahāpuruṣa* is not explicitly used in the passage "I know this great Puruṣa" (*vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam*), the intention is that the word *puruṣa* in grammatical apposition with the word *mahat* (great) is unique [to Him].

Now, one might object: "Just as by the scriptural statement, 'From Nārāyaṇa was born Brahmā,' it is determined that the quality of being the progenitor of Brahmā belongs to Nārāyaṇa, so too here, by the scriptural statement, 'The great seer Rudra begot Hiraṇyagarbha,' let it be determined that the quality of being the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha belongs to Rudra. Anticipating this objection, he states the difference [between the two cases] based on the presence or absence of an obstructing factor: "And not by this very scripture... [and so forth].

One might object: "In the statement 'From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā was born,' there too such a mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya) is evident; nor can it be said that there is a distinction based on the presence or absence of an obstacle. If this is said, we reply: then that is indeed a fault, but it is not a case of mutual dependence. For the determination of this sentence's intent toward Rudra is not dependent upon the determination that the status of being the progenitor of Hiraṇyagarbha is a characteristic mark (liṅga) of Rudra; rather, its intent toward him can be determined by the very scriptural mention (śruti) of the name "Rudra. Otherwise, there would be no way out even in the case of the statement "From Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā was born. It is with this underlying unease that he says: "And because it is in the form of a restatement (anuvāda)."

Regarding the phrase "by the words *deva*, *ātman*, *preritr̥*, *īśa*, and *brāhma*": although no scriptural passage (*śruti*) is seen later on that explicitly identifies the word *preritr̥* (the impeller), one should nevertheless look to such passages as the *Saubāla* Upaniṣad, which state, "He who dwells within the heart" (*antah-omayayata*), and so forth. The phrase "in the third" implies "in the section. As for the word *īśāna*, the meaning is that it refers to the word *īśāna* found in the scriptural text: "The Lord of all, the Ruler (*īśāna*), the refuge of all, the benevolent one. The phrase "intended to mean the impelling of Māyā" means that it is intended in its etymological sense (*yaugika-artha*).

The meaning is that the word *maheśvara* when applied to the impeller of *māyā* is purely etymological (*yaugika*), because it is heard [in scripture] that Nārāyaṇa alone is the presiding deity of *tamas* as propounded in the Subāla Upaniṣad. Thus, he is denoted by the word *īśāna*.

"For that by which all this is perceived, Him, the Lord, the boon-bestowing God, we praise"—so says the Śruti. Regarding the phrase "that Lord," the sense is that when there is an expectancy for a correlate to the word "Lord," one must take as the correlate everything previously specified in the preceding sentence by the words "in which this [world exists]. In that context, although it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, "The Lord of the past and the future," and also, "The Person of the size of a thumb is the inner self, always seated in the heart of men."

The reading is indeed: "Those who know this through the mind fashioned by the intellect (manīṣā) become immortal"; there is no word "Īśāna" therein. Likewise, in the Kaṭhavallī, having recognized this same statement in the passage concerning the "thumb-sized" one, the sense is that the word "Īśāna" refers to its etymological meaning (yogārtha) by virtue of taking up the correlative term. The phrase "here by the word 'all'" means the sentence: "by whom all this is pervaded and known."

He is also the delimitator of time; therefore, the sense is that he is called the "Slayer of Antaka" (the Destroyer of Death) because he is the "Time of Time. Regarding the phrase "in every womb," the meaning is "in each and every womb. By changing the case endings, the connection is made as follows: the Creator, the Ordainer, the Meditator, the Originator of the primordial creation, who is the cause of causes.

The intended meaning is that the construction [of the sentence] is: "the creator of volitions (saṅkalpa) is not produced. This means that there is no origination [of him] as there is of Brahmā and the others. [Objection: But surely, since the statement "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—all these are produced; he is the sustainer (dhātṛ), the meditative object (dhyātṛ), the cause of causes" establishes the fact of the origination of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra, it must be stated that this is the purport of the passage insofar as it teaches their status as objects of meditation (dhyeyatva).

If it is argued that this is not tenable for the proponent of the Siddhānta, because the rejection of Viṣṇu—as situated between Brahmā and Rudra—as the object of meditation is not accepted by the Siddhāntin, we say no; for [this refers to] an incarnation of Viṣṇu situated in the midst of the three forms (trimūrti).

It should be understood that this scripture is intended as an injunction for meditation, because it prescribes as the object of meditation precisely that form which is established by such authoritative texts as: "O King, having set aside the state of being meditated upon by those seeking liberation, there is another great form of Hari, different from the universal form (viśvarūpa), wherein all these powers are established; O Lord of Men, He creates through His own play the forms of all powers known as gods, animals, and humans, endowed with activity. Thus, the passage refers to the Supreme Vāsudeva-form, in which all these powers reside, rather than rejecting it as an object of meditation.

The point is this: it is not because of the impossibility of attributes unique to the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa). For in the Pratardana-vidyā, it was stated that the passage refers to the Supreme Self as having Him for His body (*taccharīraka*) due to the non-connection with attributes that exclude both the conscious and the unconscious; whereas here, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established by demonstrating that omnipresence (*sārvātmya*) is an attribute unique to the Supreme Person, through the non-connection with those [other] attributes. The sense is that this specific reasoning was not set forth there, such that the present discussion would be redundant.

But [it is argued] that this is not the word of Rudra; therefore, in the Vedic passage, "He entered from within to what is more internal," the pronoun *tat* refers specifically to Rudra, and thus the sense is that his very status as the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) is being declared. Furthermore, by the statement "I alone existed," his causality is expressed. Now, [an objection is raised]: "Who are you? was addressed to one who was facing him...

When the gods asked Rudra about his true nature, his reply—beginning with "I alone existed first"—identifies him as the Supreme Self who dwells within me. How could this not follow the maxim: "Asking for a mango, one is given a *kovidāra* tree"? Nor should it be argued that because the statement "I am the inner controller of all" concludes with the sense "I am the body of the Blessed Lord who is the Self of all," it cannot serve as an answer to the question "Who is the Blessed Lord? [since it does not explicitly name Him].

If that were so, the intended meaning of the question would culminate in: "Are you the remainder (the subordinate) of all causes and the inner controller of all, or are you independent? Consequently, since a response such as "I am not independent, but rather the remainder of all causes and the inner controller of all"—which is appropriate for such a question—is impossible because it would produce a contradictory notion, [one might object]. To this we say: no, for the Śrutis, being fond of the indirect (parokṣa-priya), possess hidden intentions.

It should be understood that there is no fault in [the text] having as its intended meaning that which is to be determined through the *Mīmāṃsā* of the *Samīcīna*. "He entered with his intellect" means he took it to heart. "For by this and that he entered that man" means he knew him as being endowed with those respective states. "By restating the words of Rudra" means that because it is intent on praise, it restates the fact of Nārāyaṇa’s being the inner controller of all, which constitutes the meaning of Rudra’s statement beginning with "I alone existed first."

"The meaning is that [the word] *pāśupata* is the name of the scripture taught by Paśupati because there is no basis for deriving two secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and it is the *pāśupata* that is its subject matter because there is no basis for deriving two secondary suffixes. This is an elliptical indication; one should also observe that since the word *pāśupata* contains a *vṛddhi* vowel, the suffix *cha* would be required, which would result in the form *pāśupatya*, thus making the form *pāśupata* unestablished. Regarding the phrase "but the touching with ashes accompanied by mantras," the meaning is: having taken ashes with the mantra beginning with "Agni" and having rubbed them, one should touch the limbs; this is the *pāśupata* vow, as heard in the scripture: "for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the bound soul (*paśu*)."

Now, since the *Śātātapa-smṛti* records that [the rite] is a cause for the destruction of all sins—stating, "Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of a guru, having committed theft, and having perpetrated a grave assault, one who is covered in ashes, lying on a bed of ashes, meditating on Rudra, is released from all bonds"—and since the destruction of sin is required by all Vidyās consisting of Brāhmaṇas, one must admit that [this rite] pertains to all Vidyās, overriding the context of the Pāśupata [Vidyā] by means of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the capacity of the object characterized by such requirement.

If it is argued that for this very reason—in the passage "Him [Brahman] by the study of the Vedas" (*tametam vedānuvacanena*), although the *dahara-vidyā* (the small-space meditation) is the subject under discussion—the rites such as sacrifices are common to all meditations because the means consisting in the destruction of sin produced by karma, which is established by the scriptural statement "By dharma he wipes away evil," is required by all meditations;

and likewise, in the scriptural passage "Therefore, one who knows thus, being calm and self-controlled" (*tasmādevaṃvicchānto dānta*), although the word "thus-knowing" (*evaṃvit*) refers only to the meditation currently under discussion, mental one-pointedness and so forth, which are to be accomplished through calmness, self-control, and other virtues, are common to all meditations because they are required by all of them—[we reply: no.

If even those [elements] recited within a specific context were common to all [actions] merely by virtue of being required, then there would follow the undesirable consequence that the *sannipatyāṅgas* (directly contributing subsidiaries) such as the sprinkling and threshing of rice (*vrīhi*) recited in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), as well as the *prayāja* subsidiaries which generate the assistance required by the sacrifice as understood from explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "this armor of the sacrifice is made," would also be common to all sacrifices simply by virtue of their direct instruction (*upadeśa*). However, in cases such as "by sacrifice, by gift," [the meaning is different]: "When the impurity has been cooked away by rituals, then..."

Although the common applicability [of *śama*, *dama*, etc. to all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) is established by virtue of other scriptures stating, "Knowledge proceeds," and so forth—which demonstrate their universal applicability—nevertheless, since there is no evidence for such a rule in other cases, even in the context of *śama*, *dama*, and the like, these are common to all *vidyās* only because they are accomplished solely through tranquility and the like, which are themselves accomplished solely through one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*). As for the smearing with ashes (*bhasmoddhūlana*), since there is no evidence that the destruction of sins required for the *Brahma-vidyā* is accomplished solely by it, the smearing with ashes is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to all *Brahma-vidyās*. Enough of this excessive deliberation.

Since this indicates the completion of the subject matter to be known—as seen in passages such as, "Therefore, one should make a Brāhmaṇa of exactly this kind, not one who is otherwise; for when a man knowing this thus meditates upon the Āditya as the Brāhmaṇa, even if harsh sounds should come toward him, they will reverberate [for him], they will reverberate," and so forth—and because repetition is observed even in the Upaniṣadic portions that do not teach the Brāhmaṇas, as well as because repetition is observed in every section of Gautama’s Dharmaśāstra, it should be understood that this [definition] is merely general.

The sense is that since the state of having six legs is observed in bees and others—just as the state of having eight legs is observed in *śarabhas* and others—it would follow that there should be a composition based on the chapter of bees (*bhramarādhyāya*) just as there is one for the chapter of *śarabhas* (*śarabhādhyāya*), because the work consists of six quarters (*pāda*). Anticipating the objection that the logical principles supporting the *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and so forth should be collected and indicated through repetition, he says: "of the *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and so forth."

The meaning is this: since the completion of the subject matter (*arthasamāpti*) has already been understood by the mere statement "all [the topics] have been explained," the conclusion of the chapter will also be understood; therefore, what is the purpose of repetition (*abhyāsa*) as an indicator of completion? However, the phrase "at the end of the treatise" (*śāstrāvasāne*) is merely illustrative; it should be understood to apply to the ends of other chapters as well.

One might object: "Since the statement 'the Unmanifest is beyond the Great' (mahataḥ paramavyaktam) establishes that the Great Principle (mahattattva) is distinct from the Unmanifest, the Brahman-hood of the Great Principle and those following it is not proven merely by establishing the Brahman-hood of the [Unmanifest] Prakṛti; therefore, this section is fruitful. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And of the passages such as 'the Unmanifest is beyond the Great'. The meaning is: it is not contradicted by the fourth chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras], because it has been established that the word "Great" (mahat) is an epithet of the Self (Ātman) and does not refer to the Great Principle.

The phrase "and because it was not previously established" means that since the refutation of the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause was not established previously, it is impossible for that [refutation] to be referred to by the word "this" (etac-chabdena). The phrase "the non-ultimate purport of the unquoted passages" means that those unquoted passages do not have atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth as their primary subject matter. The phrase "the fact that the senses also have that as their body has been stated" refers to the Sūtra: "And because of the designation of place and so forth. Thus ends the section on the explanation of all [scriptural passages].

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the Bhāvaprakāśikā, a commentary on the Śrutaprakāśikā, composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads.

Regarding the phrase "from the domain of means of valid cognition such as perception," one should not suspect how that which is accepted by the Sāṅkhyas can be within the domain of perception; for it is possible to perceive [the cause] in its state as an effect. For this very reason, he will later say, "like the object of self-awareness. He states the intended meaning of the word *pada* (term) as "for the purpose of excluding what has already been refuted. He states the intended meaning of the word *eka* (one) as "in the form of both efficient cause and material cause."

Intending to show that the *bhāṣya* intends to convey that the "uncontactability" (*asparśatva*) of the embodied one (*śarīrin*)—which exists as the innermost of all—is the intended meaning regarding the defects residing in the body, he provides the introduction with the words "regarding its being the cause of the world" (*jagatkāraṇatve*). The phrase "will be stated" (*vakṣyate*) means that the objections raised by opponents have been refuted; now, for the sake of protecting his own position, the positions of others are being rejected, according to the opening of the second quarter (*pāda*) of the *bhāṣya*. [In the word *cālayitum*,] the suffix *iṭ* is applied because the root *cal* (to move) belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group, which takes *mit* status.

Intending this, he says: "But in case of contradiction, it should be independent," provided that this reading is correct. It should be understood that the phrase "for it has been said" refers to what was already introduced earlier in the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Therefore, the intention behind the statement "because the Vedānta passages are confused" is as follows: there is no fixed rule of strength or weakness between Śruti and Smṛti based merely on their being Śruti or Smṛti; rather, it is a general principle (*utsarga*) that in the case of a contradiction between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti is stronger. However, that principle is sometimes set aside by a cause for the reversal of the relative strength of the two.

For this very reason, regarding the conflict between the Vedic text concerning the sequence—which is a property of the constituent elements (*padārtha*), namely, "having made this, one should make the altar"—and the Smṛti rule concerning the person—the subject (*dharmin*)—which states, "one should sip water upon sneezing," the latter is accepted as stronger because its subject matter is the primary entity itself; thus, a reversal of the usual relative strength is resorted to. As stated by the authors of the *Vārttika*: "When a weak means of knowledge has a powerful support, then indeed the opposite occurs, as declared in the case of the non-contradiction of the learned (*śiṣṭa-akopa*). Even people who are extremely powerful among the citizens and country-folk [are overruled by the king]."

"Even by weak men who have taken refuge with a king, [the powerful] are overcome. Similarly, here too, there exists another cause for the reversal of strength and weakness, consisting of the lack of fixed meaning and the presence of fixed meaning.

Therefore, in the passage, "When they praised with the *ṛc*, the Asuras followed after that; when they praised with the *sāman*, the Asuras did not follow after that; he who, knowing thus, praises with the *sāman*..."—where the opening and conclusion consist of injunctions for praise, just as in the case of the *apratigraha-iṣṭi*—is the *ṛc* being censured by the phrase "when they praised with the *ṛc*" etc. on account of its being a cause for the arrival of the Asuras (thereby implying its weakness), or rather on account of its being a cause for subjugating even those things that cannot otherwise be subjugated (thereby implying its strength)?

Because its meaning is not fixed; whereas the Smṛti of Kapila has a fixed meaning because its sole subject matter is that the Pradhāna is the cause [of the world]. Therefore, the Smṛti of Kapila alone possesses greater authority. The phrase "contradiction of the statement" (vacanavirodha) means contradiction with the statement of the Smṛti of Kapila. Consequently, one might raise the objection: "How can this be said? For since the statement itself is rooted in a fallacy of reasoning, when there is a contradiction of the statement, the reasoning is weak."

[This objection] is refuted. The meaning of "having this point in mind, he says" is that these two statements are cited with reference to this very disparity. The proof for his authority (*āptatva*) has been stated; the sense is that, just as in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha, it is established here that Kapila likewise possesses an excellence of knowledge beyond compare, obtained through the glance of the Blessed Lord directed at him at the moment of his birth, according to the passage: "He who, in the beginning, sustains with his knowledges the seer Kapila, whom [the Lord] brought forth, and who does not see [him] being born."

Since it has been stated that [the Sāṅkhya texts] have another purpose (*anyaparatva*), one should not even introduce the objection in the introduction to the work—asking, "In accordance with this text, why might the Sāṅkhya Smṛtis not also have another purpose?"—by claiming that they lack scope in their entirety. This is just as [in the case of the rule]: "Whatever is prior to the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, they perform in a low voice," which is set aside by the specific injunction of low voice for the *Prāyaṇīyā* sacrifice, namely, "One should recite softly at the *Prāyaṇīyā*, and more softly at the *Ātithyā*. Thus, there is no lack of scope.

The sense is that, just as the injunction regarding the low (*mandra*) and other tones prescribed for the *prāyaṇīya* and other rites possesses greater authority due to its lack of any other scope (*anavakāśatva*), so too here the Smṛti of Kapila possesses greater authority because it is likewise without any other scope. In that regard, since it will be demonstrated that rituals consisting of the propitiation of Agni, Indra, and others are in fact of the nature of the propitiation of the Lord, and since this cannot be established without the Lord’s identity with all deities, [the text speaks of] His causality through such identity.

The meaning is as follows: since the Vedāntas establish that creation is preceded by dissolution, [the author] first describes the state of dissolution in order to demonstrate, by way of that [dissolution], that the Lord alone possesses the causality that effects identity [with all things]—thereby establishing His status as Brahman characterized by such definitions as "from which indeed these [beings arise]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1)—and because He is the bearer [of all]. This connects with the phrase "for the purpose of establishing identity with all deities," which means "to declare His status as the supreme cause."

"In every respect, for the purpose of excluding similarity" means that it is for the purpose of excluding similarity by virtue of having only a few things as its object. For it was stated in the *Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa* that there is a partial dissolution during deep sleep, whereas here the meaning is that there is a total dissolution. Regarding the phrase "when the time for creation had arrived," this refers to the verse from the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*: "When the time for creation had arrived, he agitated the perishable and the imperishable. The sense is that the suffix *śatṛ* (present participle) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*, just as in the example "he dwells [there] while acquiring wealth" (*ārjayan vasati*).

He explains the meaning of "this was once enveloped in darkness" (*āsīd idaṃ tamobhūtam*) by saying "the body of undivided darkness" (*avibhaktatamaśśarīraka*). He explains the meaning of "manifesting" (*vyañjayan*) by saying "the creation of individual manifestations" (*vyaṣṭisṛṣṭi*). He explains the meaning of "whose power functions as the great elements and so forth" (*mahābhūtādivṛttaujas*) by saying "by his own volition" (*svasaṅkalpāt*). He explains the meaning of the word "dispeller of darkness" (*tamonuda*) by saying "the body of divided darkness" (*vibhaktatamaśśarīraka*). Here, the word *bhūtvā* ("having become") is to be supplied. Regarding the form *tamonudaḥ*, one might raise the objection that since the suffix *aṇ* (as in *tamonuda*) is prescribed for a root ending in a vowel when no upapada is present—contrary to the rule for roots with an *ik* vowel which would require *ac*—the formation would be incorrect due to this conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). However, this is resolved because the term belongs to the class of words beginning with *mūlavibhuja*.

One might object: "Is it not the case that *tamonudaḥ* is a word ending in the *kvip* suffix and in the ablative case? And since the previous verse established that 'this was then enveloped in darkness,' could it not mean that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) emerged from Śiva—who is taught in the mantra 'when there was darkness'—as the presiding deity of that darkness? If this is argued, we say no; for even so, by examining such passages from the *Subālopaniṣad* as "He whose body is darkness," it is understood that the Lord alone possesses darkness as His body, and no other deity is perceived. Thus, the opponent's desired conclusion is not established.

He states the meaning of the term *avyakta* as "the unmanifest state. Now, one might ask: even though the neuter word *avyakta* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the "three qualities" (*triguṇa*), what is the proof that the masculine word *avyakta* refers to that same thing? For when it is said, "The *paṅkaja* exists," there is no cognition of one who possesses lotuses (an *arśa-ādyac* derivative), because the word *avyakta*—due to its juxtaposition with the word *vyakti*, which denotes manifestation—reveals only the meaning of the absence of manifestation.

Furthermore, since the word "prādurāsīt" (appeared) can be construed with the proximate term "tamonudaḥ" (dispeller of darkness), its construction with the remote term "avyaktaḥ" (unmanifest) would be strained; therefore, one might ask: why not take the meaning to be that at the time of dissolution, the Supreme Self—being unmanifest due to being devoid of form and other qualities—appeared with His body clearly differentiated? If this is asked, we say no, because even that meaning is acceptable and thus not a fault.

Regarding the term *atīndriyagrāhaka*, since the prefix *ati-* can form a compound with either *indriya* or *indriyagrāha*, he explains it in both ways by saying "that which exists beyond the senses," and so forth. The fact that the scripture is "beyond the senses" means that its power of apprehension transcends the senses.

The sense is that [the opponent] holds this to be the case. And regarding the primacy of the literal meaning: the sense is that in the passage, "In him was born the self-existent Brāhma," they do not accept that the word *brāhma* refers to the Lord whose body is the four-faced [Brahmā]. Regarding the phrase "the one unborn is eternal": the meaning is that this refers to such statements as, "The one unborn is eternal, whose body is the earth," and so forth.

The meaning is that by the word *aja* (unborn), His changelessness is stated; and by the words "whose body is the Imperishable" and "whose body is Death," His causality and His nature as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmitva*) are also expressed. He shows the specific distinction of the meaning of the prefix *vi-* by the phrase "without the intervention of the individual soul (*jīva*) or the intellect (*buddhi*). However, regarding the creation of objects within the cosmic egg, the sense is that [the Lord] creates by first producing in Hiraṇyagarbha and other individual souls a creative intellect in the form of a desire to create, and then acting through that medium.

The word *bhūta* refers to that which is established (*siddha*). Thus, the word *bhūmi* has the sense of "state" (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning. Consequently, the compound means: he by whom the ground (*bhūmi*) of the possibility of all other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—such as perception and the rest—has been transcended;

that is to say, he for whom perception and the other means of valid cognition are not objects. The intended sense is that this is a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*) consisting of "he" (*sa*) and "the established reality" (*bhūtārtha*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the acceptance of a Lord (īśvara) is indeed no different for the Sāṅkhyas as well, since the refutation of even those Sāṅkhyas who accept a Lord must have been performed in the previous section on the basis of scriptural statements? Anticipating this objection, the author says: "And because Yoga is also mentioned [in the Bhāṣya]. The intention is that the Yoga system is not equal to the Sāṅkhya Smṛti, because the Pradhāna—which is the primary subject of the Yoga Śāstra—is prescribed in direct Vedic texts such as the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad as a means to liberation.

One might object: "How can the scriptural statement regarding [Brahmā's] being created serve as proof for his status as a *kṣetrajña* (individual soul)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By means of names and forms produced by karma. The intention is that this is established by the words of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*). The meaning is that Śaunaka demonstrates Brahmā's nature as a portion (*aṃśa*) of the Blessed One. [The objection continues: "Because it would follow that even a blade of grass (*stamba*) is not subject to karma. Now, in the verse beginning, "From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, all living beings situated within the world are subject to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) produced by karma," the phrase "from Brahmā down to a blade of grass" (*ābrāhṛstambaparyantāḥ*) is not a single compound word; rather, the prefix *āṅ* [is connected] with "Brahmā" (*brāhṛ*).

To avoid a lack of uniformity (vairūpya) in the grammatical derivation (*anvaya*) with the two preceding [words], one would have to assume that both [terms] have the same meaning; however, *stambaparyantāḥ* is a separate word. Otherwise, [the fault would remain].

Because it would result in the redundancy of the word *paryanta* (limit), and because of the natural sense (*svārasya*) of the word *paryanta*, even though the pillar (*stambha*) is included within the *māṇikya*, it is not proper to include the *brāhmaṇa* therein, since in that case the prefix *āṅ* could be taken in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*). If this is argued, we say no; for, due to its association with the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), it is more appropriate to understand it as inclusive, and it is improper to resort to such a diversity of meaning (*vairūpya*). This is the intended sense. Furthermore, the phrase "having entered thus into the unprecedented" (*praviśya ca tathāpūrvām*) is to be analyzed as *apūrvābhimukham*. The phrase "in the state of yoga" (*yuktāvasthāyām*) means "in the stage of meditative union" (*yogadaśāyām*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is that because the recollection of effects is untenable—just as the recollection concerning effects such as the Mahat and Ahaṅkāra lacks authority due to the non-perception of its source in Śruti—likewise, the recollection concerning the cause, Pradhāna, also lacks authority. However, others [hold] that the Yoga-smṛti is authoritative because it is dependent upon the Upanishads and because of the abundance of corroboration from Śruti.

The additional doubt has been described by means of two arguments. Since it was stated in the Bhāṣya that "because the first argument mentions Yoga, which is enjoined in the Vedānta as a means for liberation," [the author] restates and refutes the second argument—the argument based on the abundance of corroborative evidence—starting with the words: "The additional doubt and its resolution have been stated by others as follows... One should not say that the Śāṅkara Bhāṣya explains the words *sāṅkhya* and *yoga* as referring to knowledge (*jñāna*), because there is no reason to abandon their well-known meanings; this is the intended sense.

Anticipating the objection that the treatise (*śāstra*) cannot be independent because it depends on other tasks such as the acquisition of proficiency (*vyutpatti*), he explains [the term] with the words "of that which is independent of other means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāntarānapekṣasya*). "Independence from other cognitions" (*pramityantaranairapekṣyam*) means independence from other cognitions regarding the same object. "The establishment of the means of valid cognition" refers to [the fact that] visual cognition, such as "the sky is blue," does not have the formless ether (*nīrūpākāśa*) as its object.

Or, it is the knowledge whose other synonym is *ūha* (presumption), which takes the form of a procedural requirement (*itikartavyatā*) that establishes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a specific object through an investigation of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Furthermore, the dependence upon this [reasoning] is common to all means of valid cognition; however, it is especially required for the scripture (*śāstra*), whose status as a means of valid cognition depends upon the knowledge of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*). And it has been stated by Manu: "He who investigates by means of reasoning knows Dharma, and no other."

For that very establishment of the meaning of the scriptures supported by reasoning is what is stated by the Śruti as "it must be reflected upon" (*mantavya*). Now, it might be argued: since the Śruti has determined that Brahman alone is the single cause of the world, it is accepted that the world, which is its effect, also possesses the persistence of consciousness. Just as there is a non-perception of consciousness in a conscious being during deep sleep, fainting, and so forth, so too in jars and other objects, consciousness exists but is merely unmanifest; it is for this reason that the distinction between the sentient and the insentient exists. This is not tenable.

Since the perpetual non-perception of something establishes its very non-existence, for this very reason, even the possession of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*) has been refuted in their case. For one who asserts that a certain causal capacity exists in something when its effect is never perceived at any time or place, is like one who asserts the procreative capacity of barren women in the assemblies of the sons of barren women.

Furthermore, if the determination that the Vedāntas establish Brahman as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world were to depend upon the determination of the existence of consciousness—whether as the causal power of jars and the like, or as the experienced consciousness itself—and if that determination [of consciousness] were to depend upon the determination that the Vedāntas establish Brahman as the material cause of the world, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Indeed, a causal relationship between two dissimilar things cannot even be established.

What, then, do you intend by "similarity" (*sālakṣaṇya*) between the material cause and its modification, the absence of which you claim makes it impossible for the Vedāntas to establish Brahman as the material cause of the world?

The meaning is that [the object] does not exist, but rather it is established as having clouds and the like as its objects; for, by virtue of being a specific form that generates the cognition of being conducive to the highest good (*śreyaskaratva*), it functions swiftly.

The meaning is that this is an analysis of the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*): namely, that in the case of ritual killing (*vaidhahiṃsā*), which is already occupied by the causal complex for the cognition of its being a means to a desired end, the causal complexes for the cognition of its being a means to a powerful undesired end cannot coexist. Having stated that the determination of the nature of the object and the nature of the causal complex have distinct domains, he says, "the determination of the nature of the object and the domain [of the causal complex]," indicating that both can function alternately with respect to each single object.

Anticipating the objection—“How can a counter-argument (pratibandī) be made on the grounds that the existence of consciousness is not perceived during states such as sleep and fainting, since this is not accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others?”—he says: “by the Vedāntins, [it is] established. This means: because the Sāṅkhya accepts the authority of the Vedānta, the world has Brahman, as known from the Vedānta, as its material cause.

The meaning is that he speaks with the intention of raising the objection: "In order to establish [the identity of cause and effect], the connection with consciousness must be admitted. Regarding the phrase "sālakṣaṇyamiti" (similarity), the meaning is that by the genus directly pervaded by *dravyatva* (substantiality), the similarity between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*) is intended. Consequently, it should be understood that there is no fault even if there is an absence of similarity in terms of being a lump, a potsherd, a gold nugget, a svastika ornament, and so forth. And in this context, that [similarity] is "consciousness," which is [the property of] *ātmatva* (selfhood).

The intended meaning is: "because it is a genus directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*). However, some [object] that consciousness (*cetanatva*) also persists [in the effect]. In this regard, in order to establish that Brahman—which serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) in the category of the cause—is also the material cause (*upādāna*) for those insentient things which serve as the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the category of the effect, otherwise its status as the material cause of everything would not be proven; for this very reason, in the method of the Śruti, the word *jagataḥ* (of the world) is used as a term of extraction (*niṣkarṣaka-śabda*).

By stating that the word *brahman* refers solely to the substantive (*viśeṣya*), the Teacher himself has demonstrated that the world—which serves as the qualifier within the category of the effect—possesses both the status of being "to be taken up" (*upādeyatva*) and the status of being the "body" (*śarīratva*) in relation to the Brahman which is the substantive within the category of the cause. Consequently, there is an absence of identity of form (*sālakṣaṇya*) in that case.

They say that since the objection—that "the state of having a material cause is not possible"—cannot be resolved by the reply that "there is also a persistence of the nature of consciousness in the conscious portion," one must instead resolve it according to the principle stated in this sūtra: that there exists a relationship of material cause and effect even between two things that are dissimilar. Thus, "of the honeybee" means "of the honey"; the meaning is that such [a relationship] does not exist in the case of worms and the like.

If it is objected: "But since homogeneity (*sālakṣaṇya*) with respect to the genus directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) was intended previously, how can an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) be shown there?"—the answer is no; for since honey (*mākṣika*) is earth (*pṛthivī*), and worms and the like are sentient and thus of the nature of self (*ātman*), there is indeed a deviation even in that case. Furthermore, it should be observed that the deviation remains as it is, because fire is seen to arise from earthly sources such as aranis (fire-drills), and a pearl, which is earthly, arises from seawater.

If it be argued that [the world] does not exist [in the cause], we say no, because that would be a mere negation. In the Commentary, it is stated that the effect—the world—exists in the supreme Brahman, which is the cause.

The ellipsis is "by way of identity" (*tādātmyena*). The meaning is that if the effect—the world—did not exist in the state of the cause by way of being the nature of the cause, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the arising of what is non-existent (*asat*). The ellipsis is that it has been refuted that the cause and effect must necessarily belong to the same genus (*sajātīyatva*). The explanation of that [refutation] is as follows: the rule of similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) based on a specific intermediate genus (*avāntarajāti*) suitable for recognition as "this is that" has been refuted, but not their being a single substance (*ekadravyatva*). [The Sūtra states: "Because of the consequence of that [effect] remaining [in the cause] at the time of dissolution, [the doctrine is] inconsistent."

In the Bhāṣya as well, it is stated that [the passage] is for the purpose of demonstrating creation and so forth preceded by dissolution. On this point, some maintain that although the world is defiled by those defects during the period of its existence, at its dissolution it remains as Brahman, free from defects and distinguished by auspicious qualities; thus, the applicability of the Vedānta texts to that [Brahman] is established.

They say that the specific inclusion of the word "in absorption" (*apītau*) in the Sūtra is for the purpose of refuting the doubt that—just as sentences such as "he lives happily"—refer only to a period free from disease and the like; for even during dissolution (*pralaya*), since the evils (*pāpman*) which are the causes of the fruits to be experienced by future *kalpas* must necessarily exist within the individual souls (*jīvas*) in their subtle form, it would follow that Brahman is tainted by them during the time of dissolution just as during the time of its manifestation, and thus there would be an inconsistency with the scriptural texts concerning His being "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*) and so forth. This is the sense they express.

The intention is that the suffix denotes a possessive sense (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*), and the expression is intended to emphasize the state of being (*bhāva-pradhāna*). "As stated by others" means the three definitions of the Logicians (*tārkika*) consisting of being the locus of effort, experience, and the sense organs. He demonstrates how these are indeed included [within his own definition] with the words "pleasure, pain," and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "being the locus of experience" implies "being the locus of the sense organs": although the single defining characteristic is "being the locus of the sense organs which are the means for pleasure and pain"—since the quality of being a means for the enjoyment of pleasure and pain serves as a qualification of the sense organs—nevertheless, the intended meaning is that this [other characteristic] is also indicated by implication. The phrase "of the body of the liberated soul and the Lord" is for the purpose of indicating the impossibility of a body existing for either the liberated soul or the Lord. Regarding the statement "being the locus of activity," [this refers to] the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

The intention is that only action which has conjunction with the body as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) constitutes "volitional movement" (*ceṣṭā*). He refutes separately the status of being a "locus of experience" (*bhogāyatana*); thus, the previously mentioned definitions were not refuted earlier, but rather, taking those definitions for granted, he refuted the very nature of being a body on the grounds that such definitions do not apply to either the conscious (*cit*) or the unconscious (*acit*), and therefore the status of being the Lord’s body is impossible.

The sense is that one should observe the "disparity" (vairūpya), meaning that even the definition itself is flawed due to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the characteristics of the locus of enjoyment (*bhogāyatana*). If it is asked, "What does he state regarding impossibility?"—the meaning is that he states the non-existence of the definition in those conscious beings who are considered to be bodies. However, it should not be thought that the definition is refuted by an "impossibility" (*asambhava*) form of defect mentioned alongside under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). The point is that [the definition fails] by way of negating the limbs that serve as the substrata for the senses, because only that which possesses hands and so forth is a body.

"But not so, because of the existence of examples. Intending that the word *tu* (but) in the Bhāṣya is intended to indicate the possibility of the relationship between the body and the embodied, since the impossibility of even a trace of connection with what is to be abandoned (*heya*) is already established by the very word *na* (not) which negates the lack of consistency (*asāmañjasya*), he says: "by the word *na* alone," and so forth. Some, however, hold that the word *na* refers to the lack of consistency (*asāmañjasya*) as it was suspected in the Sūtra, "That being so, there would be the contingency of [the Lord] being connected with what is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*)," by means of the Sūtra, "But not so, because of the existence of examples."

They justify the commentary exactly as it is heard, stating that while [the former] is prohibited, by the word "but" (tu) the absence of even a trace of connection with the defects to be abandoned—which were said to follow by analogy—is demonstrated;
and that is its defining characteristic.

The meaning is that the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which constitutes the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) [of a word]. This is the intended sense: for a cow, there are three defining characteristics. One is the etymological definition (*vyutpattilakṣaṇa*), consisting in being the agent of the act of going (*gamikartṛtva*). Another is the possession of a dewlap and so forth (*sāsnādimattva*), which manifests the "cowness" (*gotva*) that is the ground for the application of the word "cow. And the third is cowness (*gotva*) itself, which is the actual ground for the application of the word "cow. In this context, however, the defining characteristic that constitutes the ground for the application of the word "body" (*śarīra*) is the experience of the fruits of karma (*viśaraṇa-karmaphalabhoga*), and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: [the definition] cannot be a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) in the form of a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), like a dewlap and so forth, because there is no universal (*jāti*) called "body-ness" (*śarīratva*) manifested by being the locus of experience, sense organs, and so on—just as there is no universal "cowness" (*gotva*) manifested by a dewlap and so forth. Therefore, it concludes that this very [definition], namely "being the cause of the fruit of karma" and so on, is the defining characteristic that serves as the basis for linguistic application (*pravṛttinimitta*). With this intention, the *Bhāṣya* restates "being the cause of the fruit of karma" etc. as the defining characteristic that serves as the basis for linguistic application. The phrase "first mentioned" refers to [the fact that] being the locus of the sense organs and so forth is excluded in the case of a liberated [person].

The sense is that [the senses] arise within bodies. Now, one might object: since the senses persist until the end of the kalpa, and because the section beginning with "Upon entering another body, it departs" (Brahma-sūtra 3.1.1) describes the continued persistence of the subtle elements and the senses, how can it be said that the bodies of Ahalyā and others lack the status of being supports for the senses? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The status of being a support for the senses consists in generating the activity of cognition. [This is stated in the definition: "The body is the support of effort, the senses, and their objects."

The word *artha* refers to objects of enjoyment (*bhoga*). It is not the sense that "knowledge [is the body] because it is qualified by knowledge"; rather, the intended meaning is that whatever is supported (*dhārya*) and governed (*niyamya*) by one's essential attribute of knowledge (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*) is that person's body. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to lice and the like, which are supported by a living being, nor to a creature that has perished while in the womb. As for the exclusion of light (*prabhā*), it is because light is eternally supported by its possessor (*prabhāvat*).

[The author] states the [opponent’s] position. He refutes the position of the proponents of falsity with the passage beginning "on account of the non-establishment of reasoning" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*). Regarding the statement "and because of the designation in action" (*vyapadeśācca kriyāyām*), this is its meaning: because of the designation of agency in worldly and Vedic actions in the passage, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs ritual acts," the agent is the individual soul (*jīva*). If it is argued that the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) does not designate the Self, but rather the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);

This being the case, there would be a reversal of the grammatical designation, because the intellect (*buddhi*) is the instrument; thus, there should have been a designation using the instrumental case-ending, as in "by means of consciousness" (*vijñānena*). However, these three sūtras have been explained by others in this manner, and since the other sūtras lack any extreme dissimilarity [to that style], they have not been criticized. Even though in the sūtra, "If it be said that it is non-existent, no, because it is a mere negation," the objection is raised: "If the world, which is of a different nature, arises from Brahman, which is of a different nature, then prior to its production the effect would be non-existent, leading to the consequence of the doctrine of *asatkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect does not pre-exist); if this is so, it is not a fault. Prior to production—

The meaning is that since the doctrine of *rasādi* (the six tastes, etc. is a mere negation, and since a negation is devoid of the object to be negated, it is without a referent (*nirviṣaya*). Regarding the objection that "prior to its production, the effect would be non-existent"—is it being argued that the effect's existence in the form of the cause would not exist, or that its existence independently, apart from the nature of the cause, would not exist? It is not the first, because the effect exists even prior to its production by virtue of its existence as the cause. Nor is it the second, because independent existence does not occur even now.

Thus, the meaning has been explained that the statement "it is non-existent prior to its arising" is merely a verbal assertion and lacks real significance. Nevertheless, because that meaning is not entirely contradictory, it was set aside. Just as a dreamer is not touched by the illusion of seeing a single dream—since his true nature remains unchanged during both waking and deep sleep—so too the one Witness of the three states, being unchanging, is not touched by the three states which are subject to change; for this [change] is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*).

This restates, in substance, the illustration given in the *Parabhāṣya*—that the manifestation of the three states of the Supreme Self is like that of a rope appearing as a snake and so forth—by stating: "And the person who perceives the dream is not touched by his own *māyā*."

And this is its meaning: just as the single dreamer, who persists through both the waking and deep-sleep states, is not touched by the illusion (*māyā*) that constitutes the dream—which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the dream-vision—because he is not seen to persist in other states; so too the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which perceives the states consisting of origination, maintenance, and dissolution, is not joined with the three states, because even those three states are illusory (*mithyātva*). "This is its material cause" means that this—the mind, the senses, and so forth—is the instrument of its experience.

"Because there would be no abandonment of insentience and unreality"—although this objection stated in the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya* is quite slight, it applies equally even if one holds that the effect, upon dissolution, merges with the cause by means of its own attribute; for this undesirable consequence remains the same, since the non-difference of cause and effect is admitted.

The Śruti text, "All this is what this Self is," teaches the non-difference of cause and effect without distinction across all three periods of time. In that regard, the rebuttal—that the cause is not affected by the effect or its attributes because they are superimposed through ignorance—is equally applicable to the state of dissolution (*apyaya*).
