Since this establishes the equality between the states of dissolution and persistence, the defect resulting from the non-difference of cause and effect must be raised [as an objection] regarding [the cause's] grossness.

Since defects such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and unreality (*anṛtatva*) can likewise be attributed [to the individual soul], just as grossness and the like are, what is the basis for this disparity—that even when the forms of grossness and so forth are discarded, there is no abandonment of insentience and unreality? For it is not accepted by them that there is identity during the state of grossness, while there is identity with the Insentient (*jaḍa-aikya*) at the time of dissolution (*apyaya*), such that this effort would be fruitful. Nevertheless, because "dissolution" (*apyaya*) is specifically mentioned in the sūtra *tathāpyapītāv* (BrSū 3.2.7), there is some distinction in that regard.

It should be understood that this was stated with the intention that it must be explained; the meaning is that because objects such as elephants and weapons are not distant [from the body], they do not occupy a location greater than the body, since even elephants, weapons, and so forth are derived from the same material cause (*upādāna*) that constitutes the cognition of the body. Furthermore, there would be a beginning for present ignorance, because the preceding ignorance would have been destroyed at the time of prior liberation—this is the intended sense.

The statement regarding the "establishment of bondage and liberation" means that because the ignorances (*avidyā*) which serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for individual souls (*jīva*) are manifold, liberation belongs only to that soul whose ignorance has been destroyed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), and not to any other; this is the meaning of the "establishment. Regarding the phrase "the previously mentioned fault," it means that there would be a recurrence of ignorance in those whose ignorance has already ceased. As for the phrase "if it is argued that difference consists solely in the absence of adjuncts": although the objection that "difference is simply the state of having the adjuncts removed" was already raised previously, it is brought up again here in order to provide a further refutation.

It should be understood as "the path" (*panyāsa*). Regarding "the non-sublatability of the distinction of parts": the meaning is that the distinction of parts, which consists in the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is not subject to sublation. Regarding "even a momentary withdrawal": the meaning is that the doctrine of the proponents of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādin*) endures one stage because it resorts to a cloak that is not ultimate reality, whereas the doctrine of Bhāskara does not endure even that much. Regarding "only in the state of being an effect": the meaning is "in a state distinct from the condition of the root cause."

Regarding the verse *ānīdavātam*: the meaning is that by saying *ānīt* (it breathed), which is derived from the root *ana* meaning "to breathe," there is a statement of its connection with the breath (*anana*) characterized by sentience (*sattva*). "Because it would follow that the cause of destruction is purposeless" means that it would follow that the desire to withdraw (*sañjihīrṣā*), which is the cause of dissolution, would be rendered useless. "Because it would follow that it is like that, there is a lack of consistency" means that because it would follow that it is like that, it would follow that [the cause] is non-existent (*śūnyatva*). "Even that which is denoted by the word 'non-existent' (*asat*)"—this is to be connected with the phrase "in the state of being an effect. "It has been determined by two sections" refers to the section beginning with "If [it be said] 'it was non-existent'" and the section beginning with "even when merged."

The meaning is "by means of the two preceding sections. "Of that absence" means "of the absence of existence. By this, those [theories] not accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) are also explained. For if it is interpreted as "those which are both learned and unaccepted," then the previously mentioned doctrine of the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause would also be established as being "not accepted by the learned."

The point is that if one were to explain [the phrase] as "not accepted by the learned," it would follow that only the Vaiśeṣika and other doctrines to be discussed later are not accepted by the learned, whereas the previously mentioned doctrine of the Primal Cause (pradhāna) would be understood as being accepted by the learned. He resolves this objection through a counter-argument (pratibandī), asking: "How can that which is accepted by the Dharmaśāstras... and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Even though the system of Nyāya is accepted in the phrase 'the expansion of the Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya,' the Vaiśeṣika system is not accepted. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "The Naiyāyika and the Vaiśeṣika. He raises a further objection regarding causality: "Of causality... [and so on]. This refers to the mention of the doctrine of atoms (*paramāṇu*) in the commentary of the opponent, beginning with the words "the theory of atoms as the cause," and so forth.

No other ground for doubt has been indicated; for in the case of threads, cloth, and the like, where the dimensions of the material cause (*upādāna*) and the effect (*upādeya*) differ slightly, it is observed that the former is the cause and the latter the effect, but never the reverse. Therefore, it is logical that atoms alone are the causes of all effects, from the *trisareṇu* up to the earth and the world, and not something like *pradhāna*, which possesses a dimension greater than its effects. This is what Ānandagiri restates by saying, "because of the renown of his skill in logic. Thus ends the section on the non-acceptance by the learned (*śiṣṭāparigrahādhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is that "the final deliberation" refers to the fact that [bondage] does not indeed belong to one who possesses a body; it does not, however, mean by way of being a unique property. Is the state of being an enjoyer caused by the possession of a body, or is it caused by dependence on karma?

The meaning is that reflection itself constitutes the function (*kṛtya*) regarding that locus. "But there would be a division of the Sūtras" means that there would be a split between the Sūtra "attainment of enjoyment" (*sambhogaprāpti*) and the Sūtra "because of the consequence of [the self] becoming an enjoyer" (*bhoktrāpatteḥ*). "In the section on liberation" refers to the Sūtra "Jaimini [thinks so] because of the intention. Regarding the phrase "abounding in *dandaśūkas*" in the Commentary: one should understand that the word *dandaśūka*—derived etymologically from the root *daṃś* (to bite)—refers to gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, and does not refer to snakes by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). "The consequence of the object of enjoyment becoming the enjoyer" means that, since they are both subsumed under a single Brahman, the enjoyer and the enjoyed share a common material cause (*upādāna*).

The meaning is as follows: having raised the objection that because the Brahman is non-different [from them], there would follow the mutual non-distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, this is resolved by the fact that even though foam and dye are non-different from the ocean—since they have the single ocean as their material cause—their respective distinction as enjoyer and enjoyed remains, just as there is mutual difference between them. Furthermore, the phrase "the designator of all three" refers to the fact that it denotes all three, including those struck by the three false views, by reflecting upon the one who is conditioned by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of *avidyā* and power (*śakti*) inherent within the Cause. Thus ends the section on the "Enjoyer and what is to be enjoyed" (*Bhoktrāpattyadhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is that the aphorism "tadasattvam" (its non-existence) must be studied; for since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is equally the subject under discussion in passages such as "because of having different characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇatvāt*), it is possible for the pronoun "tat" (that) to refer to the phenomenal world as well. Thus, the non-difference of pure Being (*sanmātra*) from the cause would mean that the non-difference of the effect from the cause refers to pure Being, which is indicated by the word "effect."

The intended meaning is that because it is characterized by the word "cause," its ultimate conclusion is non-difference from pure Being (*sanmātra*). The phrase "being the material cause of leaves, flowers, and so forth" means being the material cause of the leaves, flowers, and other parts belonging to the branch.

[Objection: But surely, since there is no evidence that the leaves and flowers on a branch have reached the moon, they lack the moon as their material cause (*upādāna*). Likewise, although there is no evidence that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) resides in ignorance (*avidyā*) rather than in Brahman, on the contrary, because there exist scriptural texts (*śruti*) establishing Brahman alone as the material cause, it is quite possible to say that Brahman—characterized by those [attributes]—is the material cause. [Reply: This is not so, because such a thing is impossible due to the strength of scriptural texts stating that Brahman is changeless (*nirvikāra*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction because the transformation is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*); for the point is that since its ultimate unreality has not yet been established, such an explanation is untenable. As for the phrase "if [it were] apart from," in the sūtra *bhāve copalabdheḥ*, the term *bhāva* is an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for *upalabdhi* (perception), and the term *upalabdhi* is an elliptical indicator for *bhāva*.

And thus, the meaning is: "from the existence [of the cause] and from the perception [of the cause]"—that is, *bhāvād upalabdheśca*. Consequently, because the effect exists when the cause exists, and because the effect is perceived when the cause is perceived, it has been explained that the effect is non-different from the cause; this is the meaning. Regarding "smoke and fire": only when fire exists does smoke exist.

The point is that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because the perception of form occurs only when light is perceived—just as even if each individual instance of smoke exists, it lacks the status of being an object of perception that follows upon the perception of fire—and because the existence of the perception of form does indeed follow upon the presence of light. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and because of the non-exclusive nature [of the relationship] between the universal and the individual": although there is no strict rule that the perception of the universal is necessarily the perception of the individual—for it is possible to perceive an individual due to defects such as distance, even when the universal such as "cowness" or "brāhmaṇahood" is not apprehended—[the relationship remains valid].

Nevertheless, the sense is that, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), there exists the property of being perceived in accordance with its own perception. This is because the possibility of an error without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna-bhrama*) has been refuted. Thus says the verse: "There are indeed four possible courses: [the beginninglessness] of the essential nature (*svarūpa-anāditva*), the difficulty of establishing [it] through itself or another, and furthermore, the beginninglessness of the stream (*pravāha-anāditva*)."

The meaning is that this has already been answered by the statement: "If knowledge (*vidyā*) were non-existent, these [categories] would clearly be equal in the path of having a non-existent substratum, for they would be equally incapable of being expressed and avoiding infinite regress. "Having the nature of a universal" (*sāmānyarūpa*) means having the nature of a genus (*jāti*). "Having the nature of an adjunct" (*upādhirūpa*) means having the nature of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), being an object of valid cognition (*pramāviṣayatva*), fitness for such [cognition], and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "because the effect such as covering is seen only when the threads and so forth are in that state": since the effect characterized as covering and the like is seen only from the threads and so forth when they are in the state of a cloth, it is the threads and so forth themselves that constitute the covering and the like.

The meaning is that the cause [is the reality]; there is no cloth or the like existing apart from the threads and so forth. He establishes the consequence of the object’s non-existence with the words "for [it would be] a real substance," etc.; the refutation of that has already been stated.

The meaning is: by the commentary beginning with "Even though... and ending with "...one must not cease from the operation of the causal factors at all times. [The objection is: "Is it not the case that [the object] is superimposed for the sake of the jar? [To this we reply: But surely, even on the view that phonemes are eternal, just as there is a rule that specific articulations manifest specific phonemes, it is possible to establish a rule regarding what is manifested among the operations of the causal factors; for even on the view that phonemes are eternal, when blue color and the state of being a blue lotus are manifested simultaneously by the rays of the sun, it is only the state of being a blue lotus that is manifested by the light of a lamp, and not the blue color.

If it is argued that the manifestation of states by specific manifestors is established because we observe such regularities—for instance, although both the whiteness and the water-ness of the water scattered in a well in the sky are perceived simultaneously with the sun's rays, at the time of being situated inside the well, it is only the water-ness that is manifested by those very rays—then it must be asked: what is this "manifestation"? If it is cognition, then since the conjunction of the staff, the wheel, and so forth would become the cause of the cognition of a jar, the cognitions of the jar and so on would [not occur] after those [causes] have been removed.

They would not [arise], if it were merely the removal of an obstruction. For what obstruction is removed by the causal complex of a jar? Is it not the case that the state of a lump previously existing in the clay is the obstruction to the state of the jar? Even though that [lump-state] remains eternally present, it is not perceived at that time because it is obstructed by the jar-state. When the lump-state is suppressed by the causal complex of the jar, it is perceived—just as oil is from pressing sesame seeds, rice from threshing, milk from milking, water from digging a well, or the whiteness of cloth from washing.

Nor should it be argued that, such being the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the state of the jar even after the falling of the mallet, because the state of the lump—which serves as its veil—would also have been concealed; for the state of being shards, manifested by the falling of the mallet, acts as the veil for that [jar-state]. This is because it is accepted that a certain effect-state, when manifested in its cause, serves as the veil for all other effect-states residing therein.

And this being the case, there is no contingency of the manifestation of the state of a jar occurring at some time within the potsherds even when the causes of the jar have met, for that is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). For it is observed that by grinding the potsherds into powder, mixing them with water and clay, and through the operations of kneading to achieve plasticity, and then joining them with a staff, a wheel, and so forth, the manifestation of the state of a jar is seen to occur.

Nor should it be said that the state of being cloth is not seen again in burnt cloths; for when their ashes fall upon the surface of the earth and, through the ripening of the fruits of the cotton trees grown from that soil, the state of being cloth eventually arises for them in due course. Nor should it be argued that because the state of the threads must be described as the concealer of the state of the cloth, the manifestation of the state of the cloth would not occur in a cloth woven from sparse threads, since there is no room for the suspicion of such concealment.

Because, by the force of the result, one might imagine that the state of the threads—devoid of the specific conjunction produced by the weaver—is what conceals [the cloth]; therefore, whether undifferentiated or differentiated, it is simply the prior causal state that constitutes the concealment of the states such as the jar or the cloth. This is not tenable; [The reason being: because if that were so, there would be no difference between the state of the jar and the state of the cloth, since both would be merely the prior causal state. Furthermore, if the prior state were the concealment, then even when the jar has been destroyed, its concealment would persist, and thus the jar would never be perceived. Moreover, since the prior state is common to all effects, it would follow that the concealment of one effect would be the same as the concealment of another. Therefore, this position is incorrect.

Likewise, does the state of being a cloth, which possesses expansion, exist already in a gross form as it is subsequently perceived—even prior to the operation of the weaver—yet remain concealed by its nature as threads? Or does it exist in a contracted form, like the limbs of a tortoise? Not the first; for it is impossible for the state of being a cloth, as it is seen, to exist pervasively in the threads whether they are separate or combined, scattered or gathered together, prior to the weaver’s operation.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because, as in the case of the observed state of the cloth, the quality of being adventitious (*āgantuka*) cannot be avoided. Nor should it be argued that this state of the cloth is indeed beginningless, but does not reside in the threads of today; rather, it resides in the primal cause (*mūlakāraṇa*). For if that were so, then in a place where there are currently no threads—such as a location where a cloth is about to manifest in the future—the manifestation of that [state] would follow by virtue of the absence of any obstruction. And yet, it is not the case that [the state exists] there.

It must be stated that whatever state of being an effect exists, that itself would constitute an obstruction; for since such a state would be unavoidable everywhere even after the operation of the weaver, it would follow that the cloth would never be manifested. Therefore, the sense is that all effects are indeed beginningless [in their causal status]. "Another reason for falsity" means that falsity is distinct from being neither existent nor non-existent, and consists of such qualities as being sublatable by knowledge. He states a negative (vyatirekin) reason. Upa...

The meaning is that he states a *vyatireka* (negative) reason characterized by the connection with the destruction of what has been obtained. The sense is that "even in the subject (*pakṣa*)" means there is a sublation (*bādha*) consisting in being contradicted within the accepted locus; this is because the probans would pervade the subject due to the presence of the *upādhi* within the subject. Since the indicative mark of the intended meaning—such as the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*)—has not been stated previously, a reference by the phrase "as stated" (*yathokta*) is not possible; therefore, out of this dissatisfaction, he says: "Or rather... (*yadvā*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of the word 'what'": although it is impossible for the position that "there is no cognition [of contradiction] by means of the word 'what'" to arise—since one cannot even suspect a contradiction with perception regarding an object known through scripture—it should nevertheless be understood that this was stated merely as a possibility.

Regarding the position that ignorance resides in the individual soul (*jīva*), Vācaspati, while commenting on the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* on the sūtra "Because it is dependent on that [the Lord], it is purposeful" (*tadadhīnatvādarthavat*), explains that "deep sleep is that seed-potency consisting of ignorance (*avidyātmikā*), denoted by the term 'unmanifest' (*avyakta*), which has the Supreme Lord as its substratum and is composed of *māyā*; thus, ignorance has the individual soul as its locus."

It is called "having Īśvara as its support" because it takes Īśvara as its cause or its object, and not because He is its substratum (*ādhāra*), since it has been established that such [a relationship] is untenable in the case of the Vedic knowledge (*vidyā*) which is Brahman in its essential nature. In that very context, we do not declare ignorance (*avidyā*) to be one for all individual souls (*jīva*) like the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), whereby we might perceive it as such; rather, this [ignorance] differs with each individual soul. Therefore, it belongs only to that specific soul whose ignorance...

When knowledge arises for a particular [individual], it is that very person’s ignorance which is removed, not the ignorance of another individual; for there is no contradiction between knowledge and ignorance when they reside in different substrates. Therefore, how could there be the undesirable consequence of the total eradication of the entire cycle of transmigration? Nor is it tenable to argue that the distinction between individuals depends on the distinction of the limiting adjuncts of ignorance (*avidyopādhi*), while the distinction of ignorance depends on the distinction between individuals—an argument based on mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*)—which would result in the non-establishment of both.

The meaning is that he presents the position of individual ignorance (*jīvājñāna*) as favored by Vācaspati; for it has been established—on the basis of its beginninglessness, like the seed-and-sprout relationship, and because both [the self and ignorance] are equally established—that the designation of "oneness" occurs merely by virtue of being ignorance (*avidyātva*). Furthermore, this is supported by the statement of Vācaspati in the commentary on the Sūtra "Beginning with Light" (*jyotirupakramā*), where he says that due to the distributive force of the phrase "each womb" (*yoniṃ-yoniṃ*), the ignorance denoted by the word "womb" differs for every individual soul (*jīva*). The intention is that the entire portion of the Bhāṣya ending with "because the status of being the locus of ignorance is possible" conveys precisely this much meaning.

It should be understood that the phrase "the establishment of its being conceptual" will be explained later as referring to the conceptual nature of birth, old age, death, and so forth. Regarding the expression "by means of the error concerning impurity," the meaning is that since it is impossible for the pure [Self] to be the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*), even though ignorance is dependent on impurity, impurity is likewise dependent on ignorance. The intended sense is that there is a lack of skill even in the doctrine of duality (*bhedavāda*); thus, the phrase "those who look upon [him] with great respect" refers to those who belong to other schools of thought, yet have fallen away from both [truths].

The meaning is that because one necessarily falls from both sides by desiring to gain respect while remaining within another school of thought. In the Bhāṣya, the phrase "you have come to my path" means the doctrine of the Vedic injunction regarding knowledge (*brahmajñānavāda*).

The meaning is as follows: having restated the position that those very forms of ignorance (*avidyā*) which are accepted as the basis for the distinction between bound and liberated souls—and as the substratum of the soul—are themselves the cause of the conceptualization of the difference between souls, [the author] refutes it with the same previously mentioned objection, namely, that "that which causes such a conceptualization cannot be its own substratum. Consequently, since the previous refutation remains valid, one might ask: "How can another alternative position be proposed? [The answer is: it is not so.

This is to be noted: although the reading "kalpikā avidyā" (conceptualizing ignorance) is found here with frequent repetition and its justification is possible, nevertheless, the reading "kalpikāvidyā" (without the *iti*) alone is correct; it should be understood that the other reading arose from a scribal error. In the phrase "pūrvapūrvajīvabhāvāśrayāvidyā," "pūrvapūrvajīvabhāva" refers to that which is the basis (*āśraya*), meaning the cause (*nimitta*), of the ignorance.

Thus, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; the meaning is "the locus of error. The sense is that "being the producer of silver" means being the locus of the error of silver, and likewise, "being the producer of the individual soul (*jīva*)" means being the locus of the error regarding the individual soul. The phrase "because of its own dependence on itself" means that if it were dependent upon itself, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). The phrase "this is the cause for the distinction" means that since the Lord is described as "the master of illusion" (*māyin*), this demonstrates the existence of a distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā*. And the phrase "because that [illusion] is not ultimately real" means that *māyā* is not ultimately real because its manifestation cannot be established as being subject to [the Lord’s] will.

The meaning is that, because of this, that perception is indeed produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). "Containing the inference to be stated" means that he speaks while keeping in mind the establishment of the falsity [of duality] through the inferences to be stated later—such as the establishment of the distinction between bondage and liberation, and the distinction between self and other, as being imagined by one's own ignorance. "And that [is the case] for both the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*) and [the proponent of non-difference]"—the point is that in the view of those who maintain that the ignorance belongs to the individual soul (*jīva-ajñānavāda*), bodies do not possess selves through distinct individual souls; rather, it is not accepted that Māyā alone possesses the selves. And it might be asked: why could the first and third inferences not also serve to refute the proponent of difference?

This must be stated: in that [Advaita] view, it should be understood that the reason—namely, "because it is unreal" or "because it is imagined"—is unestablished (*asampratipanna*). Furthermore, the reason "the property of being excluded from that which is negated in a locus where the adjunct (*upādhi*) is present," which is intended to prove falsity (*mithyātva*), is itself subject to the fallacies of being "vitiated by an adjunct" (*sopādhika*) and "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). There is an adjunct because falsity is negated in the locus where the adjunct is present. Moreover, there is a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding falsity. If the thesis to be proven is that everything other than Brahman is false, then there is a self-defeating consequence (*vyāghāta*) in proving the falsity of falsity itself.

Furthermore, one should observe such refutations as the "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntya*) resulting from the fact that [the reason] is excluded from Brahman while not being excluded from [the class of things under consideration].

If "only sublation" (*bādhāmātra*) is the reason—if the meaning is that "only sublation" is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—as in the example, "on a cloudy day, accompanied by the delusion of evening": [Objection: But surely, in the case of a cloudy day where there is a delusion of evening, since the time itself in the form of the cloudy day is the locus denoted by the word "limiting adjunct," this is not an example of the deviation [of the rule] that space and time are limiting adjuncts. [Reply: True; the intended meaning is that only that which is distinct from the time being superimposed is the limiting adjunct. In the case of a delusion regarding space, time is the limiting adjunct; for instance, when one has reached the city of Kāñcī at the time of evening, time serves as the limiting adjunct.

It should be understood that "the evening has arrived in Kāñcī" is a case where "place" (*deśa*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). By the commentary stating "the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been stated," the meaning is that perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition has been stated, namely, that which is seen and uncontradicted (*abādhita*). "If that cognition were false" means "if that cognition were an error" (*bhrānti*). Even in the position that it produces an error, the causal relationship between the body and the sun is already established; thus, while this criticism remains, he states another criticism: "only sublation" (*bādha eva*).

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that there is no contradiction because gold also persists by virtue of being the substratum of the *svastika*. Now, one might ask: how can there be non-difference between the gold, which is the substratum, and the *svastika*, which is the superstratum? If so, how can the cognition of the identity of the *svastika* and the gold be possible? If this is raised, the answer is no; for although the "cowness" (*gotva*) is of the nature of the parts of the cow, it is nevertheless not separate from the cow due to its state of being inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), just like [the universal] "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth. Thus, the intended meaning here is that there is no contradiction in the cognition "it is gold," just as there is none in the cognition "the *svastika* is a substance."
For it is not the case that the self residing in another's body is directly perceived; rather, its existence is inferred through such signs as purposeful movement.

The sense is that [the world] would not exist. Now, one might object: since it has been stated previously that all sentient beings are non-different from one another because anything other than consciousness is observed to be insentient (*jaḍa*), the commentary’s statement "as for what was said" is untenable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "I alone am the entire collection of sentient beings," and so forth. The point is that when he states an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*), it must be understood as having the nature of *tarka* (logical reasoning), because—given that the presence of ignorance within the body is admitted by both disputants—it cannot function as an inference (*anumāna*) in the form of a formal reason (*hetu*). This is the intended meaning.

If it is argued that "she [liberation] will simply not exist later"—meaning that if no one's liberation exists prior to this [present moment], then even the scripture (śruti) which proclaims the liberation of certain individuals must be regarded as equivalent to a dream—then, by that logic, there could be no liberation for anyone even after this point, nor would there be any scripture to proclaim it.

The meaning is that it is like the words of a dream. Alternatively, in the former position—that of *nirviśeṣa-jñāna* (non-dual knowledge)—it was stated that because non-dual knowledge lacks both the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and the state of being contained within knowledge (*jñānagatatva*), there is no causality for either appearance or linguistic usage (*pratītibhāsavyavahāra*). In the second [position], however, the distinction is that causality is not asserted either by way of being perceived or by any other means. The point regarding the terms "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*) and "non-ultimate" (*apāramārthika*) is that the ultimate or non-ultimate status of appearance, linguistic usage, and so forth, is dependent upon their object. Such being the case, they are infinite.

The meaning is that there is an infinity [of forms] due to the relationship of deficiency and excess. On this point, some say that the explanation of the intent of the *Bhāṣya*—which raises the objection against infinity by pointing out that "ten jars" or "a thousand māṣas" are seen to possess numerical quantity—is incorrect. They argue that when it is said "ten jars" or "a thousand māṣas," these are not ten jars or [a thousand māṣas] in a uniform manner (*ekarūpyeṇa*).

The meaning is that "māṣas" refers to a jar together with its contents, or "māṣas" refers to the contents together with the jar; this is what is stated. Regarding the intention of one who asserts the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): because meditation (*dhyāna*) is intended to be expressed, the reflexive middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not used, according to the rule "sam-prati-bhyām-anādhyāne. Now, one might object: how is the meaning of *vācā* explained as "by means of verbal discourse preceded by speech"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "This is a non-abandoning indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*). [He adds: "Because both are causes," for although the act of naming denoted by the word *vāk* serves as the purpose for the name itself, it does not serve as the purpose for the modification (*vikāra*); thus, [the suffix] *aja*...

The meaning is that [the opponent] is intent on conventional usage through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Regarding the statement "this is a [fallacious] argument based on a genus" (*jātyukti*): its definition is given in the verse: "Since the conceptualization of the nature of a property as being either that [nature] or not that [nature] is untenable, the destruction of the substratum's being qualified by it would constitute the *nityasama* fallacy. This is because it is accepted that arising is merely a state (*avasthā*). Now, if arising were indeed the very state of the jar-ness, then as long as the state of being a jar arises...

If it is argued that there would be the conventional usage "it has arisen," but not "it has been produced" because the arising has not yet passed away; and that there would be "the lump of clay is perishing," but not "it has perished" because the perishing has not yet passed away—this is not so.

There is no fault, because we accept that the connection with the first moment belonging to the state of being a jar is the "origination" (*utpatti*) of the entity in its state as a jar, while the destruction of the previous state is its cessation. If it is objected: "Is this not some kind of technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) that contradicts common worldly experience? For it would mean that origination belongs neither to that which is adventitious nor to that which is connected with the first moment, yet it is claimed that origination belongs to a substance that is neither adventitious nor connected with the first moment"—we reply: No; for such a convention is indeed excellent when it conforms to scripture and reason.

"Independent of separate origination. But [one might object]: would this not lead to a contradiction with those scriptural passages that establish the origination of qualities and actions—such as, "The Vedas, sacrifices, rituals, vows, the past, the future, and whatever the Vedas declare were born from Him"—as well as with those scriptures that establish the differentiation of names and forms, and with all means of valid cognition such as the perception of the entire world which apprehends the origination of qualities, actions, and so forth? For, in the final analysis, everything is non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*) from Brahman.

Because it would follow that even something distinct from Brahman could not have an origin—since it would be incapable of having a separate existence, location, or function—there would result a collapse of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor should it be argued that while the origination of a substance non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*) from Brahman is possible, there is no origination for anything different from a substance; for there is no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) [to favor one view over the other], and the contradiction with all scriptural contexts remains the same. True, it cannot be denied that adventitious attributes (*āgantuka-dharma*) distinct from the substance originate.

Since arising in the form of coming into being after not having existed is established by both worldly experience and the Vedas, it cannot be denied; however, such an arising cannot be admitted in the case of a substance (*dravya*). If, according to the system of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, another distinct substance produced from clay and so forth were admitted, then, because that substance would serve as the locus for an additional gravity through the sequence of the qualities of its causes, a doubling of gravity would be perceived.

Moreover, when a large golden chain or an iron fetter is being woven by smiths, one must admit that intermediate links and segments of the chain are produced therein; otherwise, if after some weaving has been done, the weaving of the upper part of the chain or the link were abandoned, [the result would be incomplete].

In the case of a knotted portion, there would be no application of the term "chain of threads" (*sūtrṛṅkhalavyavahāra*); nor would there be the application of the term "chain of threads" once that [chain] has been cut after the knitting of the great chain of threads (*mahāsūtrṛṅkhalagrathana*). And thus, where the knitting of a great chain of threads is completed through a process of knitting smaller fragmentary chains of threads one above the other, there the great chain of threads should be accepted as being composed of a multitude of fragmentary chains of threads. In that regard:

If, for the purpose of constructing a chain of thread-rings, as much colored iron as the black metal were placed in the hands of a smith, then the weight of that material, the weights of the individual small rings of the chain begun from it, the weights of each of the large chains begun from those, and finally the weight of the great chain begun from them, would result in an exceedingly greater weight; therefore, the jar, the bowl, and the great chain of thread-rings are not, in reality, distinct from the lump of clay and the small rings of the chain.

It must be accepted that [the effect] does not exist [prior to its manifestation]; furthermore, since the explanation is established by the very state admitted by both parties, it is more cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate the production of a distinct substance possessing different states. Moreover, because it is established by uncontradicted recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that the clay, which existed in the form of a lump in the forenoon, assumes the nature of a jar and so forth in the afternoon, there is no production of a non-existent substance. As for the doctrines concerning production, our concern lies solely with the fact that they are based merely on changes of state; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

"The lack of contradiction is due to the mediation of states" means that the sense is that within a single Brahman, the existence of multiplicity is mediated by [different] states. He states a solution that is common to threads and so forth, and which is ultimately real: "And there is no contradiction because of the difference in time."

[Objection: But how can there be a simultaneous perception of both unity and plurality in a single cloth produced from discrete threads? This cannot be, because two contradictory properties cannot coexist in a single substratum (*dharmin*). [Reply: No, for it is logically consistent—just as in a single tree there exists both conjunction and its absence due to the difference in delimiting factors (*avacchedaka*) such as the roots and so forth—so too in the case of threads, there is "cloth-ness" and unity delimited by the specific conjunctions produced by the weaver, while there is plurality delimited by "thread-ness."

If it is objected: "But surely the conjunctions produced by the weaver are already mixed with the nature of the threads (*tantutva*); how then can there be a delimitation by contradictory properties?"—we say no. For, in the case of a single fire, while there is pervasion (*vyāpti*) delimited by the property of being a fire produced from wet fuel (*ārdrandhanaprabhavavahnitva*), and while that which is pervaded is delimited by the property of being a fire unmixed with [other types of] existence (*sadasaṅkīrṇavahnitva*), there is an absence of being a delimitum of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedakatvābhāva*) in the state of being fire (*vahnitva*)—delimited by the general property of being fire (*aviśeṣitavahnitvatva*)—with respect to being delimited by the property of being a fire produced from wet fuel.

Because [the properties] are admitted as modes (*vṛtti*). Thus, even in the doctrine of the non-difference of cause and effect, there is no fault whatsoever; for it is possible for both cloth-ness and thread-ness, as well as unity and plurality, to coexist within a single substance. Specifically, thread-ness and unity reside in that substance delimited by a particular conjunction that brings about the state of being a thread; and cloth-ness and unity reside in that same substance delimited by a particular conjunction of threads that brings about the state of being a cloth. Therefore, their coexistence is logically consistent.

Even though there is non-difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), as in the case of grass and a roof, or bricks and a wall, one should observe that there is no contradiction in the coexistence of the nature of "grass" and "roof-ness," or "brick" and "wall-ness. However, this is the distinction: in the case of a roof, the specific forms of the grass—such as its thinness and so forth—and in the case of a wall, the specific forms of the bricks—such as their squareness and so forth—are not perceived; whereas such forms are indeed perceived in a cloth woven from loosely spun threads.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "this very [thing] is this now," it must be said that this was already stated in the first sūtra itself. He states the inconsistency in the view that the sentence "Being alone, one only, without a second" effects a negation of difference consisting of the similar (sajātīya), the dissimilar (vijātīya), and the internal (svagata) by saying, "for not [negating] the similar... Furthermore, he states that the non-difference between cause and effect is thereby established by saying, "having willed the manifold becoming of the Self. If the reading were "saṅkalpyeta" (it would be willed), it would be correct, as it serves to eliminate a specific doubt.

If it is asked: "How can the passage beginning with 'Is this that deity? (nanu seyaṃ devatā), which functions to fulfill the promise that by knowing one thing everything is known—by means of demonstrating the entire world's status as its material cause through the presentation of individual instances—serve to dispel specific doubts regarding the meaning established in the preceding passage?"—the answer is: True; however, the sense is that even such a [subsequent] passage cannot be abandoned when it is possible [to be consistent].

Intending to show the impossibility of the identity of the aspect of volition (*cetanā*), he says: "oneness due to the absence of division between name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Intending to show that if the word *sat* refers to the world, there would be a contradiction with such passages as "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), he says: "the act of seeing in the form of the resolve to become many. This reading is correct; however, [the opponent objects] because of oneness in the causal state. The sense is that the relationship of body and embodied (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*) inherently contains difference. [The author replies: In the case of the power [of the mantra] and the elephant-gate, etc.—[this refers to] the elephant-gate.

When the sense of capability (*śakti*) is understood regarding the two feet [of the agent], the suffix *iṣṭhak* is applied after the root *han*: *hastighna* "an elephant-killer" (a soldier), meaning "capable of killing an elephant. In the same way, *kavāṭaghna* "a door-breaker" (a thief) should also be understood. Regarding the rule *śaki liṅ ca*: after a verbal root whose meaning is conditioned by the sense of capability, the suffix *liṅ* is used; and because of the word *ca* ("and"), the *kṛtya* suffixes are also used. Examples: *bhavān khalu bhāraṃ vahet* ("You surely ought to carry the burden") and *bhavatā khalu bhāro voḍhavyaḥ* ("The burden must indeed be carried by you"), meaning "it is possible to carry. In the phrase "other than those ending in *kṛt* suffixes," the word *antara* expresses a distinction.

The meaning is "of the specific *kṛt* suffixes," that is, of the *kṛtya* suffixes; this is because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule "and the *kṛtya*s. Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "in cases such as *pācaka* etc., [it is] non-attainment": the meaning is that where the word *pācaka* is employed based on mere capacity even when one is not performing cooking at any time, there is the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *pācaka*; however, it should not be thought that the indication of the word *pācaka* occurs merely due to the absence of cooking at that particular moment.

One should understand that the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument—namely, that the mention of "present time" (*vartamānakāla*) in rules such as *tṛn* [Pāṇini 3.2.135] is for the purpose of teaching the Vedas, as stated in the Vārttika—is refuted by the Vārttika: "Or rather, it is not so, because we see [the suffixes] used for other times as well. This is because the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of suffixes such as *ṇvul* is established even in the absence of the present tense of the verbal root's meaning.

Nor would it follow that knowledge is eternal on the grounds that, just as terms such as "knower of the scriptures" are primary when applied to a sleeping person, so too the term "omniscient" could be validly applied to the Brahman consisting of pure Being during the state of dissolution—which corresponds to deep sleep—even in the absence of constant knowledge. For when one says, "Bring the knower of the scriptures," there is no eternality to the knowledge of the scriptures, nor is there knowledge present at that very moment.

Or rather, it must be stated that [the term "knowledge" here] refers to the capacity [to know]; for the point is that in the passage "Intrinsic are knowledge, power, and action," since words such as "knowledge" (jñāna), which end in the suffix *lyuṭ* denoting an action (*bhāvārtha*), do not have the capacity (*śakti*) as their primary meaning, they necessarily possess a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*).

Alternatively, because there is no usage of the term *śāstrajña* (knower of the scripture) in reference to one who is about to study a treatise or one who has forgotten a studied treatise, the word *śāstrajña* and similar terms refer only to those who possess the object [of knowledge] in reality. Furthermore, its application in states such as deep sleep is based on a metaphorical attribution of "presentness" (*vartamānatvopacāra*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For this very reason, since the word *sṛj* (creator) is not used in common parlance for a person who has ceased creating, the word *kāraṇa* (cause)—which is based on the production of an effect—is not primary when applied to a lump of clay that is not currently producing; rather, its use in that instance is merely figurative.

The meaning is that, according to the Mīmāṃsaka’s statement, the word "cook" (*pācaka*) is purely figurative when applied to one who is in a state of not currently cooking; however, such a resort to figurative usage is not appropriate here, because it is improper to employ a secondary sense when the primary sense is possible. Although "clinging to *kāśa* and *kuśa* grass" (*kāśakuśāvalambana*) literally means clinging to *kāśa* in place of *kuśa*, it should be understood that this expression is used here because its underlying sense is particularly fitting for the present context.

"Non-difference established by the perception of recognition" means non-difference established by the perception in the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). He states the reasoning for why recognition is intended through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "the persistence of the inherent cause. [The phrase] "because it does not prove one's own position" means because it proves the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

This is the meaning. For although the statement "the water is in the jar" [is not used] because one admits that the nature of gold (*hiraṇyatva*) exists both in the ear-ring (*kuṇḍala*) and in the parts of the bowl—as it does in earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so on—the fact that "the ear-ring is gold" does not prove the non-difference between material cause and effect; nevertheless, the intention here is that this very same gold in the state of a lump became the ear-ring, and thus recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is intended in this Sūtra as the proof of non-difference. This is the sense.

The cognition "this is that" is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). For recognition is of two kinds: that which has the object "that" as its qualificandum and the object "this" as its qualifier, and that which has the object "this" as its qualificandum and the object "that" as its qualifier. When the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is predominant and the sense organ is subordinate, it has the object "that" as its qualificandum; when the sense organ is predominant, it has the object "this" as its qualificandum and the object "that" as its qualifier. Consequently, since in the previous sūtra the recognition "that very same gold became a bracelet" was cited as an instance of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it has the object "that" as its qualificandum.

[The word] *ekatvam* [is used]. However, in this Sūtra, since the intended meaning of the Śruti passage "Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning" is what is being expounded, it should be understood that this statement is made by relying on the view that the object denoted by *idam* (this) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), while its nature as Being (*sad-rūpatā*) constitutes its qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*). If the reading were "That which is the recognition as 'This is that' was mentioned previously; that which is the recognition as 'This is he' is stated here," then it would be correct.

Regarding the reading "the knowledge that 'this is that' is supernormal cognition (*abhijñā*)," it is not correct; for this very reason, it is stated in the *Sarvārthasiddhi* that "this is that" is a case of erroneous recognition (*viparītapratyabhijñā*). As for the phrase "established by scripture," the meaning is that it is established by the scriptural passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*).

Although the distinction between the preceding and following sūtras based on the difference between "knowledge" (jñāna) and "designation" (vyapadeśa) has already been described, it should be understood that the phrase "tathāpi" is used here to demonstrate that there is yet another distinction between knowledge and designation, namely that they are established by scripture (śruti) and established by worldly convention (loka), respectively. Regarding the resolution [of the apparent contradiction] in various passages, one observes the citation of the pratīka "yukteśca" immediately after the text beginning with "tadaikārthyāt"; however, we do not perceive any purpose for that.

The meaning is as follows: "the state of being a particular place qualified by a particular time" refers to the fact that when the absence of a jar is admitted in a certain place at a certain time, the absolute absence of the jar is precisely that particular place qualified by that time. "Conjunction with another location qualified by a smallness [of space]" means...

The meaning is this: for a delimited jar, which is incapable of existing simultaneously in two places, its connection with another location constitutes the absolute absence of that jar in the former location. Regarding the phrase "when [the probandum] has been established," the meaning is "when it is almost established. Consequently, the objection—that if it were already established, there would be no portion remaining to be proven, and thus the citation of an example would be futile—is refuted.

The phrase "as in the case of a qualified entity" means as follows: just as in Brahman, which is qualified by the sentient and insentient (cid-acid-viśiṣṭa) and constitutes their constituent parts (aṃśabhūta), there is oneness because the state of being qualified (viśiṣṭatva) pervades the whole manifestation; yet there is a mutual distinction among the sentient and insentient entities that constitute the parts by virtue of their being qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa). Similarly, the intention is that "cloth-ness" (paṭatva) occupies the place of the state of being qualified, while "thread-ness" (tantutva) occupies the place of the state of being a qualifier. By the phrase "by cloth-ness residing in the entirety of the threads," the meaning is that within the threads themselves, there is oneness delimited by thread-ness, and oneness delimited by cloth-ness.

One might object: "If a cloth distinct [from its parts] is not admitted, how can there be the conventional usage of 'cloth-ness' with respect to the threads? For one thread lacks the status of being a part (*aṃśatva*) in relation to another thread. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the state of separate existence. The meaning is that the "whole" (*aṃśin*) is both the aggregate and the qualified entity; the threads are the qualifiers and the constituent parts (*aṃśa*).

The meaning is as follows: although there is no difference between the threads and the cloth, even though the threads lack the status of being partial qualifiers (*prādeśika-viśeṣaṇa*) with respect to themselves, they do become partial qualifiers with respect to the cloth because of the existence of a difference in their form (*ākāra-bheda*). Since these partial qualifiers are occasional, they are termed "occasional" (*kādācitka*).

The meaning is "thus. The doctrine of intrinsic parts (*svābhāvikāṃśavāda*) is also refuted; the implication is that if intrinsic parts existed, certain localized particularities would necessarily be eternal. The phrase "of pervasive entities such as space" means "of pervasive entities whose nature is space and so forth. He establishes the very momentariness of space and the like by the passage beginning with "due to a specific transformation," and so on.

The meaning is that if the word *arhat* were intended merely to exclude the liberated (mukta), then by stating [the soul] is "superior to the inner self (pratyagātman) associated with pleasure and pain," one would not have established its superiority over the liberated state. Now, one might object: how can the sūtra "ubhayathāpi" (in both ways) be understood as including the word "ādi" (and so forth)? For, since that sūtra is solely engaged in establishing difference (*bheda*), it does not establish the relationship between the mode (*prakāra*) and the possessor of the mode (*prakārin*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The sūtra beginning with 'ubhayathāpi'..."

The meaning is that [the text] has as its subject matter the sentences concerning the "pot" (the body), because the relationship between the body and the embodied is established by such passages as "He who dwells in the intellect" (*yo vijñāne tiṣṭhan*). In the Bhāṣya, the phrase "with reference to the state free from ignorance" means that they describe the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated. For this is how the commentary of the opponents stands there:

We declare that the creator of the world is that which is omniscient, omnipotent, the Brahman, whose nature is eternally free and pure, and which is distinct from the embodied soul (*śārīra*). Therefore, regarding one who says, "This refers to the state [of Brahman] when it is separated from ignorance (*avidyā*)," how can the subsequent commentary—which proceeds by means of the following dilemma—be applicable? Namely: "Is [the creator] that which is separated from ignorance, or that which is joined with it? And likewise, how [is it applicable] regarding the difference of the Brahman from the individual soul (*jīva*)?

The two-fold doubt that there might be a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is rendered groundless; for it should be understood that there is no fault, as that statement is intended to establish the difference of Brahman—which is by nature eternally pure—from the individual soul as its counter-correlative.

In this regard, having kept in mind the possibility of two positions—since the qualification "eternally pure, bound, and liberated by nature" in the opponent's commentary gives rise to the position that [the inquiry concerns] one who is already separated from ignorance, and the qualification "all-knowing and all-powerful" gives rise to the position that [it concerns] one who is imagined through ignorance—he refutes [the view] after proposing these alternatives, stating: "of one who is separated from ignorance from the individual soul," and so forth.

The meaning is that, according to the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*, the inquiry must be undertaken for the sake of the knowledge of the unimagined nature of the individual soul—that is, for the sake of the knowledge of the nature of Brahman, which is ultimately non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

When the conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) is not contradicted, the superiority of Brahman understood through such scriptural indications of difference as "He is to be sought, He is to be known" precludes defects such as the failure to act for the benefit [of others]; thus he restates the meaning of the *Parabhāṣya*. Furthermore, prior to the awakening to the meaning of statements such as "That thou art," there is no possibility of the Lord being accused of failing to act for the benefit [of others] and so forth, since He is presented as distinct [from the individual soul].

The meaning is: "of that which is being presented as distinct, yet indicated as non-distinct. Now, one might raise the objection: "Even if difference exists, why would the fault of not performing what is beneficial and so forth not apply to Him who experiences those individual souls as non-different from Himself? This is true; however, because this Supreme Self is omniscient, He perceives the individual souls as being in reality distinct from Himself. At the same time, He perceives that in truth these souls possess a connection with the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and that they harbor an identification [with those states] due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). And thus, for them...

"Even in the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, I am indifferent; nor is there any injury to my vital core even upon being confined in a prison. Thus he restates what Vācaspati Miśra has said: "By means of the false defects residing in the individual soul (*jīva*). The meaning of this is as follows: just as the Lord, by virtue of His omniscience, perceives the individual souls as non-different from Himself, so too, precisely because of His omniscience, He perceives the defects residing in them as being false. Therefore, even though the cycle of transmigration proceeds, since suffering does not attach to Him who is non-different from Himself, there is no contingency of the defect of failing to act for their benefit and so forth.

When non-difference is realized through such an instruction of difference as "That thou art," then the transmigratory state of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the creatorship of Brahman vanish; for all conventional usage based on difference, which is a manifestation of false knowledge, is sublated by the arising of right knowledge. Thus, how could there be creation, or how could defects such as the failure to accomplish the welfare [of beings] exist? This is what the *Bhāṣya* restates with the words "after the arising of the knowledge of unity. As for the phrase "of the speakers" and so forth, the intended meaning is this:
prior to the knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art," there exists the conventional usage of difference.

Therefore, it is not correct to say that subsequently there is no discourse regarding differentiation, because of such scriptural passages as: "Among the gods, he who first awakened became this [Brahman]," and so forth. "But Śuka, having attained a speed swifter than the wind, traveled through the intermediate space."

Based on such scriptural evidence as, "Having displayed his own power, he became one with all beings," which establishes the attainment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) by Śuka and others, it follows that Śuka and the rest necessarily possessed the knowledge of reality. Furthermore, since the conventional usage of difference (*bhedavyavahāra*) among others continued as before even after the knowledge of reality had arisen in Śuka and others, one must simply state that for whom there is the knowledge of reality, for him there is no appearance of difference.

Consequently, even if the Lord possessed knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there would be no occurrence of the appearance of difference, the mechanism of saṃsāra, and so forth. The ablative case in the phrase "due to the apprehension of difference" (*bhedena pratipatteḥ*) is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*; the meaning is "with reference to the apprehension of difference. The sense is that it is untenable for the Lord to avoid the fault based on being a creator, which depends upon the apprehension of difference resulting from His lack of comprehension of the meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). Since He is a creator, the faults such as failing to act for the benefit [of others] must be accounted for.

The point is this: since the agency [of the Self] is dependent upon the perception of difference, which in turn depends on the failure to understand the meaning of statements such as "That thou art," there would be no possibility of the charge that [the Lord] fails to accomplish the welfare [of beings] based on creation; therefore, the refutation of that charge would not need to be established.

If it is argued that the avoidance of defects is untenable, [we reply: indeed, in the commentary of the opponent on the sūtra "And like stones and so forth, that is untenable" (2.1.23), it was stated that just as there is a variety among diamonds, lapis lazuli, sun-crystals, and so forth despite no difference in their being stone, and just as there is a variety of leaves, flowers, and so forth in a tree, and just as there is a variety of objects seen in dreams, so too the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Consciousness (*prājña*) is untenable. Furthermore, that very sūtra has been explained by the opponent as a refutation of the contingency of defects such as the failure to act for the welfare [of beings].

If the individual soul (*jīva*) were to evolve from Brahman, then—alas!—the consequence would be that everything would possess consciousness just like the soul. To this, [the Sūtra] says: "And as in the case of stones and so forth, that is untenable" (*aśmādivacca tadanupapattiḥ*). If it is argued that since Vācaspati introduced the Sūtra "And as in the case of stones and so forth, that is untenable" merely to demonstrate the diversity between the conscious and the unconscious, and not for the purpose of avoiding defects such as the Lord's failure to act for the benefit [of all], then the aforementioned defects would still apply—this is true; Vācaspati has indeed explained it in that manner.
But that [position] is not tenable, because since the fault of failing to act for the benefit [of others] and so forth would follow, no suspicion of its lack of variety could even arise; therefore...

Because [the opponent's position] is inexpressible (*avaktavyatva*), and because [it is refuted] by the statement "not on account of having different characteristics" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*) and so forth, as well as by the fact that [the opponent's view] has already been dealt with (*kṛtakaratva*); therefore, with the intention of showing the untenability of what was stated by Vācaspati, the refutation of the literal reading of the Bhāṣya has been set forth. The words "by the body initiated by karma" (*karmārabdhena*) have "by the body" (*śarīreṇa*) as the ellipsis; the words "by the one under the power of karma" (*karmavaśyena*) have "by the individual soul" (*jīvena*) as the ellipsis. In that regard, the phrase "because the refutation of the theory of non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*) is seen there" means that the refutation of the theory of non-existent effect is also observed in that [section]. [End of the Section: On the Designation of the Other (*itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇa*)]

"Because of the arising of the fear that its functioning is restricted" means that although the resolve (*saṅkalpa*) is true during a state when other instruments exist, there is no truth to the resolve during a state devoid of them; this is what is meant by "restriction. Is it [the case] that there is dependence on external instruments?

Is it [the case that Brahman] is independent, or is there a dependence upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the instance of milk and the like. In the second case, since there exist infinite causes such as time and unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), there is no contradiction with Brahman being the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Intending this, he says in the Commentary: "Just as in the case of milk, water, and so forth. The meaning is that he cites a Vedic example because one might raise the objection that while non-conscious milk is independent in producing its effect, consciousness does require other external instruments; thus, he provides a Vedic illustration.

It should be understood from the commentary that [the word "easy"] is used for the sake of easy comprehension. The meaning is: if such power is admitted even for gods and others who possess limited capacities on the basis of scripture, what need is there to mention the Supreme Brahman, who possesses all powers? Thus it is "for the sake of comprehension."

Fearing the charge of redundancy regarding the sūtra, "But because scripture is rooted in the Word," he says: "By scripture, [it is established] that it is partless. Now, [one might object]: "But [attributes such as] 'free from evil' and so forth also [distinguish it] from the substrate..."

One might raise the objection: "Since it is possible for [the qualities] to bring about a distinction from other attributes characterized by the possession of all powers through another means, how can the Bhāṣya state that the phrase 'whose desires are true and whose resolves are true' serves to establish the possession of all powers as a quality of the subject? Anticipating this, he says: "Thus, due to the distinction of the substratum (dharmivailakṣaṇyāt). By the proximity [of the terms], only a general distinction of the attribute from others would be established, but not the specific attribute consisting in the possession of all powers. Its establishment through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) and so forth, however, would be delayed.

The sense is that the cognition of all-pervasive power, characterized by the effect of having true volition (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), occurs swiftly. Although there is no actual duality of the moon, the reading "the moon is divided in many ways" is observed; however, in reality, the meaning is that although there is no multiplicity of moons, the moon is perceived as manifold. The final sense is that this is like the multiplicity of the moon imagined through ophthalmia (*timira*), even though the moon is in fact devoid of multiplicity. Regarding the sūtras beginning with "Not the Self, on account of scripture" (*nātmā śruteḥ*): the meaning is that in these sūtras, the absence of a false object for the words "scripture" (*śruti*) and so forth is established.

The sense is that because [the Self] is eternally accomplished, it is therefore untenable to say "at the time of deep sleep. The sense is that because it is already present through the senses, the injunction "it should be seen" would be rendered purposeless. He anticipates the rebuttal regarding the second alternative with the words: "That which is Brahman... and so forth.

One might object: "Even though a non-ultimate association with ignorance exists everywhere, since there is an absence of an association with ultimate ignorance, there is no consequence of the entire [Brahman] undergoing transformation. To this, he replies: "By that much alone, the establishment of a Brahman liberated from ignorance is not achieved. The meaning is: the establishment of a Brahman disjoined from that ignorance which is conducive to transformation is not achieved. The meaning is: the entire Brahman would undergo transformation into the form of the world. "Of whatever kind it is intended" means: of whatever kind it is intended to be conducive to transformation into the form of the world.

He provides an illustration for the fact that when the form that acts as the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the body exists, the cessation of the form that does not act as its motivator (*aprayojaka*) results in its non-motivating status: "as in the case of what is seen in a dream. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "imagined by ignorance" (*avidyā-kalpita*): indeed, in the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya*, it is established that all worldly transactions—such as the transformation of Brahman—are based upon a differentiation of forms characterized by name and form (*nāmarūpa*), which consists of the manifest (*vyākṛta*) and the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), is indefinable as either identical to or different from reality (*tattvānyatvābhyāmanirvacanīya*), and is imagined by ignorance; [not] by means of the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*).

And since it remains unevolved, transcending all worldly transactions (*sarvavyavahāra*), by way of a "seizing the tip of the horn" (*ṛṅgagrāhikā*) demonstration, it is shown that the differentiation characterized by name and form (*nāmarūpalakṣaṇabheda*)—which is itself indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*)—is merely a form imagined through ignorance (*avidyākalpita*). Likewise, in the *Vācaspatya* as well: "Brahman, which is the locus of the conventional usage of transformation (*pariṇāmavyavahārāspada*), attains a differentiated form (*rūpabheda*) consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest (*vyākṛtāvyākṛtātman*), characterized by name and form, which is indeterminable in terms of being either identical to or different from the [ultimate] reality (*tattvānyatvābhyām*); yet an imagined form does not touch the real entity."

For the conceptualization of duality by those suffering from ophthalmia does not bring about a duality in the moon; nor does the impossibility of duality entail the impossibility of the moon. Therefore, since it has been clearly demonstrated that even though the postulation of a real transformation is untenable, it does not entail the impossibility of Brahman which exists in the ultimate sense, how can there be any room for this objection? Or, let us grant some room for it for the sake of argument; [the response follows].

Even so, if the referent of the word "differentiation" (*bheda*) were either the primary cause (*pradhāna*) as qualified by ignorance (*avidyā*), or that [cause] as characterized (*upalakṣita*) by it, then for those [parts] only the status of being a limb (*avayavatva*) would be established, and not the state of having limbs (*sāvayavatva*). Just as when it is said, "Devadatta has Yajñadatta as his father," only Yajñadatta’s status as a father is established, and not Devadatta’s state of having a father; likewise, if it is said that [the cause] "has limbs" (*sāvayava*) by means of a differentiation of form imagined through ignorance, only the status of being a limb of that differentiation imagined through ignorance would be established, and not the state of having limbs [for the cause]. If this is argued, we say no.

Since it is possible for the meaning of "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*)—in the sense of "having a division of forms imagined through ignorance" (*avidyākalpitarūpabheda*)—to apply here, there is no inconsistency; for in that context, regarding the Brahman endowed with names and forms imagined through ignorance which one intends to demonstrate as having parts, the following alternatives are possible: is it qualified by ignorance (*avidyāviśiṣṭa*), or indicated by it (*upalakṣita*), or is it the primary [cause] (*pradhāna*)? Furthermore, in the text asking "is it imagined through ignorance (*avidyākalpita*) or qualified by ignorance (*avidyāviśiṣṭa*)?", the term "form imagined through ignorance" (*avidyākalpitaṃ rūpam*) refers to this very point.

The term *yasya* (of which) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound; therefore, the meaning is "that which is endowed with name and form imagined through ignorance. Thus, one should understand that there is no logical inconsistency. "The resolution of the contradiction between those two" means the resolution of the [objections] regarding the consequence of the whole [Brahman] being affected and its being partless. "Of the meaning of the latter two sūtras" refers to the meaning of the two sūtras beginning with *sarvopetā ca* and *vikaraṇatvānneti cet*.

The phrase "that which establishes [the fact] through logical proof" means that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) are endowed with it because they are established by its being the cause of all things. Now, an objection is raised: if the partless [Brahman] is the cause of all, then since the scriptural statement itself is the direct proof, let that alone be intended here; what is the use of introducing the possession of all powers? [The reply is: It is appropriate for the undertaking of a ball-game and the like to be considered a mere sport, and so forth. Now, merely...

It is observed that undertakings such as playing with a ball (*kantuka*) have play (*līlā*) as their sole purpose. Since there exists a commentary stating that for [the Lord] the very purpose of birth, maintenance, and destruction is play—thereby establishing that undertakings such as the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world have play as their purpose—it is logical that the undertaking of a ball and the like is play. If it is argued: "The status of the world-activity as play is untenable because it lacks the weightiness of effort (*yatna*); how then can it be said that the activity itself is play?"—to this, some reply: "Some say the creation is for the sake of sport (*krīḍā*), others say it is for the sake of enjoyment (*bhoga*; *Brahma-sūtra* 2.1.32), while others say it is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the Divine."... [text continues] ...[Brahma-sūtra] 2.1.33. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established by the scriptural statement that it is the Divine's nature. Furthermore, since the Lord is omnipotent, His power is not dependent on any other means; therefore, the fact that He does not create the world at all times is due to His own will, and thus the status of the world-activity as play is proven. Moreover, in the case of a ball and the like, the undertaking of play is seen to be preceded by a desire for play, and the cessation of that undertaking occurs when that desire ceases. Similarly, the undertaking of the world-activity is preceded by a desire for play, and its cessation occurs when that desire ceases. Therefore, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions engages in activities such as walking about out of a natural inclination, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity out of a natural inclination. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of sport, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of sport. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of amusement, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of amusement. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of diversion, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of diversion. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of pastime, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of pastime. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of pastime, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of pastime. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of recreation, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of recreation. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of relaxation, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of relaxation. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established.
