Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of diversion, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of diversion. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of sport, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of sport. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is established. Furthermore, just as a person who has attained all desires and is free from all afflictions may engage in activities such as walking about for the sake of amusement, so too the Lord, having attained all desires and being free from all afflictions, engages in the world-activity for the sake of amusement. Thus, the status of the world-activity as play is

In the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti*, with the statement "What desire can there be for one whose desires are fulfilled?", the view that creation is for the sake of sport (*līlā*) is presented as the position of others; here, the word *līlā* refers to effortless action, as seen in the expression: "The carrying of the three worlds is merely his sport. This is because such usage is observed even in that context, just as actions such as moving a finger, which are accomplished without effort, do not depend upon any external purpose.

For this very reason, there is no question regarding a motive (*prayojana*) in that case; even if such a question were raised, the answer would simply be silence. Likewise, the activities of creation and so forth of the Supreme Self are accomplished without effort and do not depend upon a motive. In this regard, the verse beginning with "The sport (*līlā*) consisting of the birth, maintenance, and destruction of all worlds" serves as direct evidence. Furthermore, the *Bhāṣya*—which states that the sole motive is mere sport, citing the example of the commencement of games like ball-play where the destruction [of the opponent] is itself the sport—intends to convey the sense that for the Lord Himself, He is His own motive, just as one might say, "I am my own servant. This is how the teachers describe the intention of the Master.

The connection with the subsequent portion is as follows: "And because of the knowledge of [the world] as being other than Himself, there is no possibility of [His acting out of mere] sport. Now, regarding the phrase "it deserves a connection with unequal creation": according to the view of others (*pararītyā*), this means that the creation was performed by the Lord. The meaning is: "It is not the case that there is a rule stating that the Lord is dependent upon karma"; that is to say, such a restriction does not exist. This should also be understood in the subsequent sentence, "If creation were thus... Regarding the phrase "in the creation of the collective reality (*samaṣṭitattva*)," one might object: "Since the karma perceived by individual souls (*jīva*) is the cause for every effect, one could argue that even in that [collective] case, dependence on karma is possible. If this is raised, the answer is: No.

The meaning is that because there is a deviation in the creation of objects of enjoyment such as paintings—which do not depend on a mother—there is no necessity for dependence upon such [a cause] in every effect. "With the intention that this is the purport of the Sūtra" means he spoke with the intention that this is what is intended by the Sūtra.

Regarding the statement "they say the Sūtra is also a separate topic (*adhikaraṇa*)," although it is clearly stated in the *Kalpataru* that this Sūtra is a separate topic even according to the view of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), it should be understood that it was stated thus because it is not perceived as such in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Bhāmatī*. The phrase "because it is produced by the knowledge that the dissolution has passed" means "because it is generated by the knowledge that the dissolution is over. The phrase "because no other capacity is possible" implies that the power of awakening (*prabodha-śakti*) is also of the nature of a capacity (*yogyatā*). The phrase "from the knowledge of the passing of the time of dissolution" refers to the passing of the period of dissolution (*pralayakālātyaya*).

In the Bhāṣya, it says: "The so-called *mūlaprakṛti* consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion," and so forth. As the Sāṃkhyas have said: "The *guṇas* consist of joy, sorrow, and despondency; their purposes are illumination, activity, and restraint. They function through mutual suppression, support, and companionship. *Sattva* is held to be light and illuminating; *rajas* is stimulating and mobile; *tamas* is heavy and enveloping. Their operation is for a single purpose, like a lamp."

The meaning is this: the qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are, respectively, of the nature of pleasure, displeasure, and despondency; they are, respectively, of the nature of happiness, suffering, and delusion; and they are, respectively, illumination, activity, and restraint.

The *prayojana*s (purposes) cause the pure *sattva* to manifest and impel *sattva* toward its illuminating function. Since it would follow that the light *sattva*-quality would impel [the mind] everywhere due to the impelling power of the *rajas* quality—which is mobile—the heavy *tamas* quality restrains it according to the specific task at hand. Consequently, *rajas*, being restrained by *tamas*, impels only in certain instances; and thus, *sattva*, being impelled only in certain instances, manifests only something specific. Therefore, there is a fixed order such that everything is not manifested for everyone at all times.

Thus, the purpose and the essential nature of the *guṇas* have been stated; now their function (*vyāpāra*) is being described: "They function through mutual suppression, support, production, and companionship. Function means activity; each [term], beginning with suppression, is connected individually. The *guṇas* function by mutually suppressing one another: depending on the requirements of a particular purpose, when one of them becomes predominant, the others are suppressed. Thus, *sattva*, sometimes suppressing *rajas* and *tamas*, attains a peaceful state; likewise, *rajas* [suppresses] *sattva* and *tamas*.

Having overcome its own fierce activity, as well as having overcome darkness and the sevenfold qualities of passion (rajas) and their own deluded activity—since the *guṇas* have activities that are mutually dependent, that upon which the activity of another depends is intended here as its "support" (*āśraya*). Furthermore, the *guṇas* have activities that give rise to one another; one is produced by another, and "production" here refers to a specific transformation (*pariṇāma-viśeṣa*). Moreover, they have activities that are mutual companions; that is to say, they are co-existent and inseparable (*avinābhūta*).

"For they are all mutually paired, always moving everywhere; neither their beginning conjunction nor their separation is perceived"—such is the scriptural authority (āgama). According to the Sāṃkhya teachers, *sattva* is held to be light and illuminating. In that context, the property (*dharma*) of fire, wind, and so forth, which causes upward flaming and horizontal movement, is *lāghava* (lightness). That *sattva* and *tamas* are impelled toward their own effects by *rajas*, which is itself oriented toward its own effects—this is what constitutes the "assistance" (*upaṣṭambha*) provided by *rajas*.

The qualifying attribute "mobile" (cala) serves to establish that [nature]. By the qualification "mobile," it is shown that rajas is that which brings about the state of sattva and tamas being oriented toward their respective effects, despite their being inactive.

Tamas is heavy; for this very reason, it obstructs the activity of even the light *sattva*, which by its own nature is mobile. Because of the heavy *tamas*—which acts as an impediment to activity—the *rajas* only occasionally becomes active, resulting in action. Thus, *tamas* is the veiling factor and the regulator. It is said that these qualities, though mutually contradictory, perform a single function together; their operation is purposeful, like a lamp. Just as the wick and the oil, though opposed to fire, act together with the fire to produce the manifestation of form, so too [do the *guṇas*].

The term *upaṣṭambhaka* (supportive) refers to the fact that *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, though mutually opposed, perform their functions together for the sake of a specific purpose. The meaning of "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*) is that *rajas* acts as a sustainer precisely by inducing *sattva* and *tamas* toward the manifestation of their respective effects. Regarding the commentary’s phrase "the root of the knowledge of the Omniscient," this means it is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). The commentary states that "unity of source must necessarily be accepted"; this implies that if one postulates the phenomenal world to have its root cause in *pradhāna*, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) due to the oneness of that cause.

In the hypothesis that atoms are the cause, since it is impossible for a single atom to be the cause of everything, one must necessarily assume a plurality of causes; thus, there is "complexity" (gaurava), which is what is intended by the phrase "having a single root. As for the statement in the Bhāṣya, "by means of six sides":

Just as fingers and other objects occupying ten spatial points in the ten directions, when pressed together, connect with one another through three points each—being delimited by one great direction and two intermediate directions—in the same way, even threads being pressed together produce an effect such as a cloth that possesses a dimension greater than themselves, provided they are not joined on their own sides; likewise, since it is impossible for partless atoms to have unjoined points when they are conjoining, [the production of a larger whole is impossible].
The meaning is that there would be no production of an effect possessing a dimension greater than its own. In the Bhāṣya, it says: "Because of the transformation of the differences. For this...

This verse has been explained by Vācaspati as follows: "It might be argued that the manifest arises from the manifest; thus say the followers of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣikas) and Akṣacaraṇa (the Naiyāyikas). For atoms are manifest, and through them, by way of dyads and so forth, the manifest effect characterized as earth and the rest is produced. Furthermore, in earth and the other elements, the production of color and other qualities occurs through the sequence of the qualities of the cause. Therefore, since the manifest and its qualities arise from the manifest, what is the use of an unmanifest [cause], which is never observed? To this he replies with the words 'of the particulars' (bhedānām)."

How is it that there exists the Unmanifest (avyakta) as the root cause of the specific evolutes beginning with Mahat and ending with Earth? [It is so] because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe; thus it is established that the effect pre-exists in the cause. And so, just as the limbs already exist within the body of a tortoise and emerge and become distinguished—such that one thinks, "This is the tortoise's body" and "these are its limbs"—in the same way, they enter back [into the cause].

In that [unmanifest], they become unmanifest. Thus, from the cause—the lump of clay or the lump of gold—the effects such as jars and crowns already exist and are merely differentiated; the earth and other elements already exist and are differentiated from their cause, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); the subtle elements already exist from their cause, the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); the ego already exists from its cause, the Great One (*mahat*); and the Great One already exists from the supreme unmanifest (*paramāvyakta*). This is the differentiation of the entire universe of effects, both directly and through a succession of causes, from the supreme unmanifest.

At the time of re-absorption (*pratisarga*), however, [the elements] such as the Earth enter the mass of the supporting substance (*bhṛtpiṇḍa*) and become unmanifest; they do not manifest their own causal nature, but rather become unmanifest in relation to their effects. In this way, the Earth and other elements, entering the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), render those subtle elements unmanifest in relation to themselves. Likewise, the subtle elements enter the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and render the ego-sense unmanifest. Similarly, the ego-sense, entering the Great Principle (*mahat*), renders the Great Principle unmanifest. And the Great Principle, entering its own cause, Nature (*prakṛti*), [renders it unmanifest].

It makes the *prakṛti* unmanifest; since there is no location for the *prakṛti* anywhere [apart from itself], it remains unmanifest (*avyakta*) for all its effects. This is the non-differentiation (*avibhāga*) of the effect, which possesses manifold forms (*vaiśvarūpya*), within the *prakṛti*. Therefore, because the effect exists even while in the state of cause, the cause is unmanifest through both differentiation and non-differentiation. For this reason as well, he says that the cause is unmanifest: "Because of activity proceeding from power" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛtteśca*). It is established that the effect proceeds from the power of the cause; for from an incapable cause, the effect cannot arise.

Furthermore, the power residing in the cause is not distinct from the effect itself because the effect is merely unmanifest; for in the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*), there is no evidence for a power other than the unmanifest state of the effect.

For this indeed is the difference between sand and sesame seeds: that oil exists in these very sesame seeds even in its unmanifest state, but not in the sand. It might be argued: "Activity proceeds from potentiality (*śakti*), and both the distinction and non-distinction between cause and effect will establish the supreme unmanifested nature (*paramāvyaktatva*) of the Great One (*mahat*) alone; what is the use of a further unmanifested principle beyond that? To this he says: "Because of transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*). This means because it is completely transformed, which is to say, because it is non-pervasive (*avyāpitva*).

The various objects under dispute possess an unmanifest cause, because they are finite, like jars and other such things; for jars and the like are observed to have finite, unmanifest causes such as clay.

It has been stated that the unmanifest state (*avyaktāvasthā*) is indeed the cause of the effect characterized by suffering and so forth. That which is the cause of the Great One (*mahat*) is the supreme unmanifest (*paramāvyakta*), because there is no evidence for postulating an unmanifest beyond that. Furthermore, the categories under dispute possess an unmanifest cause, because of their homogeneity (*samanvaya*). Homogeneity is the similarity among distinct things. Intellect (*buddhi*) and the other principles, characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth, are perceived as being permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion (*sukha-duḥkha-moha*). And those things which are permeated by a certain nature [must have that as their cause].

These [effects] have the unmanifest as their cause, because they possess the nature of that [cause], just as jars, crowns, and so forth—which are endowed with the form of clay or gold—have the unmanifest lumps of clay or gold as their causes. Thus, it is established that there exists an unmanifest cause of the differentiated effects; and since this [unmanifest] is not contradicted [by perception], it should be understood that it too is indeed an object of apprehension. "It teaches the pervasion useful for the counter-inference"—here he demonstrates the counter-inference. Some say that the reading "na bhavaduktam" (not as stated by you) is the correct one.

It should be understood that [the qualities] are the causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth, but they do not themselves possess the nature of pleasure and so on; for if that were the case, it would result in the absurdity of applying such expressions as "pleased" or "pained" to a cloth or similar object which is the substratum of the three *guṇas*. Thus, according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, since the cloth itself consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, the cloth would be pleasure, pain, and so forth.

Furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence of such cognitions and linguistic usages as "this is pleasure" and so forth. Nor should it be argued that if the object does not possess the nature of pain and so on, then internal pleasure and the like could not arise from the cognition of that object; for even though the object lacks the nature of desire and so forth, both desire and effort arise from the cognition of it, and thus both are logically accounted for. Moreover, if one were to assume that [the self] consists of pleasure by virtue of pleasure, pain, and ignorance, or that it consists of something else by virtue of effects such as lightness, it would follow that one must postulate other natures as well, which would result in the collapse of the state of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).

Furthermore, there is no evidence for the assumption that pleasure (*sukha*), lightness (*laghava*), and illumination (*prakāśa*)—which are associated with the support of pain (*duḥkha*) and activity (*pravartana*), as well as heaviness (*gaura*) and obstruction (*āvaraṇa*)—are each bound to only one of the qualities (*guṇa*). For if that were the case, the established system of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) would not be undermined; indeed, it would then be possible to assume that pleasure, pain, and delusion (*moha*) are also each connected to only one quality. Moreover, any contradiction can be easily resolved by means of a difference in their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), since even the opponent must resort to such a distinction when explaining the emergence of the forms of pleasure and so forth. This is the intended meaning.

Considering the untenability of the doctrine that a state both exists and does not exist, as well as the doctrine that a state arises and does not arise—since these two are equivalent—he explains [the passage] as intending to negate the existence of a substance characterized by states. Although one might think that the phrase "characterized by the state of dissolution" (pratisargāvasthopalakṣitā) contains an emphasis (avadhāraṇa), such an emphasis need not be assumed here; for the purpose of emphasis is already achieved by the word "entirety" (samasta) itself. Nevertheless, since one means of expression does not invalidate another, [this interpretation is acceptable].

It should be observed: "by that, there is a loss of independence" means that by such an occurrence of a specific transformation (*pariṇāma-viśeṣa*), there is a loss of independence. Therefore, the reason [given for] mercilessness is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

The meaning is that if compassion (*dayā*) is a quality (*guṇa*), then in the case of mercilessness, there would be an absence of qualities; thus, the reason is inconclusive. And as for the living beings' lack of connection with results: [this refers to] the living being's dependence on another.

The meaning is that there would be the objection that, [if Brahman were] insentient, the connection with the fruits of karma would not belong to the individual soul (*jīva*). Regarding the phrase "the inability of the dependent to endure the suffering of the supported": the inability of those who depend [on another] to endure the suffering of the one upon whom they depend follows precisely from the principle that their own purpose would be frustrated. In that case as well, if there is no regard for one's own interest, it is precisely what is intended by the term "compassion" (*dayā*); this is the sense. As for the phrase "of those who are constantly devoted" (*satatayuktānām*), everything that needs to be said regarding this has already been stated in the first sūtra.

The phrase "for the sake of excluding mere wood and the like" means that since grass situated near a piece of wood is not observed to lack milk, one must conclude that it is merely the proximity to consciousness (*cit*) that is required. Furthermore, it should not be argued that even that [grass] is included within the subject of the proposition; for by the inference that "the insentient functions only when presided over by a sentient being," grass and such would also have to be made the subject. The word "merely" (*tāvatā*) means "by the mere proximity to consciousness."

"He knows it to be abandoned" connects with the preceding phrase "it is corrupted by that. It should be understood that the same applies to what follows. The phrase "for the purpose of demonstrating deviation in the commentary" means for the purpose of demonstrating the avoidance of deviation in the example of milk, just as in the expression "smoke from mosquitoes."

In the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the verse "for the sake of the experience of the *pradhāna*," the intention is that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of "action" (*karman*) with respect to the *pradhāna*'s requirement for perception. The phrase "inference itself is present in the intellect by implication" means that even if one accepts the establishment of the *pradhāna* through inference—this is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* passage "even if inference is accepted. Regarding the *Bhāṣya* statement beginning with "because of being for the sake of another in the case of a composite," it is established that the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth, are composites because they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion; and therefore, just as...

The meaning is that because beds, seats, and so forth are composite entities (*saṃghāta*), they exist for the sake of another; thus, their being for the sake of another must likewise be asserted [for the body]. Now, one might object: "Let there be existence for the sake of another; nevertheless, let that existence for another be directed toward yet another composite entity, and not toward a non-composite self. To this, he says: "Because of the reversal of the three attributes (*triguṇa*) and so forth. The intention is as follows: if a composite were for the sake of another composite, then since that too would be composite, its existence for the sake of another would have to be asserted, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore...

Even after traveling very far, the Self must be accepted as remaining non-composite (*asaṃhata*). Consequently, in such a Self, the property of being composite, upon its own exclusion, also excludes its pervaded properties, such as the three *guṇas* and so forth. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the meaning of the verse is intended: "The Manifest is composed of the three *guṇas*, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, productive; likewise is Pradhāna; and the Person (*puruṣa*) is the reverse of that."

This is its meaning: that which possesses the three qualities (*guṇas*)—pleasure, pain, and delusion—is "three-qualitative" (*triguṇa*). By this, the view that pleasure and the others are qualities of the Self (*ātman*) is refuted. "Non-discriminative" (*aviveki*): just as the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) is not distinguished from itself, so too the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest are not distinguished from the Primal Nature, because they are of its very essence; or alternatively, "non-discriminative" refers to acting in combination, meaning that nothing single is sufficient for an effect, but rather they act together. To those who hold that consciousness itself takes the form of the object, he says: "the object."

The object (*viṣaya*) is that which is graspable, meaning it is distinct from consciousness. For this very reason, it is a universal (*sāmānya*), that is, common; for if it were of the nature of consciousness, then since cognitions are unique to each individual, the objects would also become unique. And in that case, there could be no unification (*pratisandhāna*) by many people regarding a single movement of a dancer’s brow. [The term] *acetana* has a clear meaning.

The meaning is that [the manifest] has the nature of production and transformation; such is the manifest, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat). He extends this property to the Pradhāna as well by saying, "so too is the Pradhāna. The rest is clear. The meaning is that because of the reversal of such a form [the Puruṣa exists]. For this reason also the Puruṣa exists: because of being a presiding controller (adhiṣṭhānāt); for it must be stated that that which consists of the three guṇas, like a chariot and so forth, requires a presider, meaning it depends on another as its controller. Because of the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛbhāvāt), meaning because of the state of being an enjoyer of pleasure and pain.

Pleasure and pain are to be experienced as agreeable and disagreeable; therefore, there must exist something that is to be made agreeable and something that is to be made disagreeable through pleasure and pain. Furthermore, because of the activity directed toward the goal of isolation (*kaivalya*), and since isolation is the absolute cessation of suffering, this cannot belong to an entity composed of the three *guṇas*, for that would entail the impossibility of its separation from its own inherent nature. This is the meaning. And "from that reversal" means from the reversal of the three *guṇas* and so forth, as stated in the preceding verse.

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: because the Puruṣa is devoid of the three guṇas, because it is discriminative, because it is an object, because it is non-common, because it is conscious, and because it is non-procreative. Here, by means of consciousness and being an object, the states of being a witness (sākṣitva) and being a seer (draṣṭṛtva) are established; for one who is conscious is a seer, not one who is unconscious. And one who is a witness of suffering is one whose object has been shown [to him], but this does not mean that the Puruṣa is a witness of the objects themselves, precisely because it is devoid of the three guṇas. Absolute liberation (kaivalya), which consists in the absolute absence of the threefold suffering, results from this very state of being devoid of the three guṇas.

The establishment of neutrality (*mādhyasthya*). Since the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) exist as pleasure and pain, neutrality in the form of indifference would not be established due to the presence of attachment and aversion; however, because of its discriminative nature (*vivekitva*), its state of non-agency (*akarmakatva*) is established for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa. As it is said: "Just as the activity of insentient milk is for the sake of the growth of the calf, so too is the activity of Pradhāna for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa. [Regarding the term] *nānāśrayaprakṛti*, the meaning is that Prakṛti has various supports (*nānāśrayā*).

However, one might object: "If the conscious self is not the agent, how can there be the experience of the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between agency and consciousness, such as 'I know' and 'I act'? Anticipating this doubt, he states, "Therefore, from that conjunction," because it is established by reasoning that consciousness and agency have different substrates, the perception of their co-referentiality is an error. "Therefore" means because it is established by reasoning that agency and consciousness have different substrates.
"From that conjunction" means from the conjunction with the conscious [self]; [the result arises] in the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body).

The meaning is that just as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth appear as if they possess consciousness, so too the indifferent Self (*ātman*), through proximity to the active *guṇas* which have become the agent, appears as if it were the agent itself. This verse, beginning with "For the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception," has already been explained previously. In the commentary, it was stated to be for the purpose of establishing the systematic order of the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments: "Because of the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments, and because of their non-simultaneous activity."

"The plurality of souls is established by the Sāṃkhya verse beginning with *traiguṇye*. This is the meaning: birth is the connection with the body, senses, and so forth; death is the abandonment of that. The "instruments" are the senses. If there were only one Person (*puruṣa*) existing in all beings, then when one is born, all would be born; when one dies, all would die; and if one were blind or deaf, others would likewise become so. Furthermore, [souls must be many] because their activities do not occur simultaneously.

If the Puruṣa were one in all bodies, then when one body exerts effort, that same [Puruṣa] would exert effort in all bodies; consequently, all bodies would move simultaneously. Furthermore, regarding the "reversal of the three qualities" (*traiguṇyaviparyaya*): *traiguṇya* is formed by adding the suffix *ṣyañ* in its own sense (meaning "the state of the three qualities"), and its "reversal" (*viparyaya*) is its being otherwise. For instance, some are abundant in *sattva*, such as those whose vital seed flows upward (*ūrdhvaretas*); some are abundant in *rajas*, such as human beings; and some are abundant in *tamas*, such as animals. The meaning is that this established order of diversity is not possible if the Puruṣa is one.

Is it not the case that the sūtra "payombuvacca" (like milk and water) is intended to dispel the doubt that the causal state—the state of the *pradhāna*—might transform into the form of the body and organs independently of the superintendence of a conscious being? Rather, the refutation of that doubt will be carried out in the very sūtra "anyatrābhāvācca na tṛṇādivat" (and because of its absence elsewhere, it is not like grass, etc.). And this present sūtra [is for the purpose of] the impossibility of activity conducive to the purpose of the Puruṣa on the part of an insentient entity unsuperintended by the Puruṣa, as stated in the preceding sūtra "apravṛtteśca" (and because of the lack of activity).

Anticipating the objection, "Why should it not be intended as a justification for what has been stated?", he says: "Because the refutation is conducive to the accomplishment of the human goal. The meaning is that while some describe three internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—namely, intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*)—others have described the internal organ as being of the nature of intellect alone. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because of its denoting that [state] and its independence," the sense is that mutual contradiction is well-known from the rule *īdavadhye paraṃ kāryam*. The terms "caused" (*hetumat*) and "non-eternal" (*anitya*), and so forth, mean "dependent," that is, dependent upon a cause. "Dissolution" (*laya*)...

"Because it moves, the *liṅga* (the subtle body) must have a root; that is to say, its root must be *prakṛti*. Thus ends the section on the "Inexplicability of the Arrangement" (*racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa*).

The intended meaning is that the "collection of the objects of refutation" (dūṣyasamuccaya) refers to the collection of the objects of refutation such as the eternality of space and so forth. The words "large" (mahat) and "long" (dīrgha) are used here with the abstract state (bhāva) as their primary sense.

[Objection: One might argue that even if the primacy of the individual entities (*bhāva*) is not accepted, a copulative compound (*dvandva*) could still occur simply because of the difference between the delimiters of the referential capacities (*padārthatāvacchedaka*). [Reply: This is not so, because the author of the *Bhāṣya* has rejected the occurrence of a *dvandva* based merely on a difference in the delimiters of referential capacity in the absence of a difference in the referents themselves. Under the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ*, the author of the *Bhāṣya* raises the objection that a *dvandva* might apply in cases such as "this is both a ritualist (*yājñīyaka*) and a grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*)" due to the difference in the delimiters of referential capacity; he then refutes this by noting the recurrence of the word "remainder" (*śeṣa*) from the rule *śeṣo bahuvrīhiḥ*. This is because...

Since it has been established that [the rule] does not apply because there is no status as a "remainder" (śeṣa) due to being the domain of a *samānādhikaraṇa* compound, and since even in a *dvandva* compound where there is a difference in the delimiters of the word-meanings (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), the application of this rule is unavoidable because the words *mahat* and *dīrgha* are not *samānādhikaraṇa*, the point is that this reference is indeed primarily concerned with the abstract state (*bhāva*).

One might object: "If by the words *mahat* (large) and *dīrgha* (long) the qualities of largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*) are intended, then the words *hrasva* (short) and *parimaṇḍala* (spherical) would likewise have to be understood as emphasizing the state [of the quality]. Consequently, the meaning would be 'just as largeness and minuteness are established from the short and the spherical,' which is not accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas. This is because, in the sūtra on the causes of largeness—'Largeness arises from plurality of causes, from largeness of the cause, and from a particular kind of aggregation'—the causes of largeness are specifically enumerated. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In this way, by means of those two words that emphasize the state..."

Regarding the mention of two causes here: one might object that since there is an inconsistency in the doctrine of the production of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) from partless atoms (*paramāṇu*), everything else accepted by them—just like the production of a dyad from an atom—is improper; and that this alone should have been stated. Why, then, is the production of a large, long triad (*tryaṇuka*) from a dyad cited as an example? Is it not because there is no inconsistency in that case? No, for when there is mutual conjunction between two dyads, there must necessarily be a conjunction of their constituent parts.

Because of the refutation that all six atoms would result in being atoms of the same size as a single atom, [it is argued] that the production of a large and long *tryaṇuka* from a small *dvyaṇuka* exists.

It should be understood that this [example] must also be treated as an illustration. Regarding the phrase "even if God is established," the underlying intention is as follows: In his [the opponent's] view, the absence of creation during the dissolution (*pralaya*) must be accounted for by some singular cause. It cannot be due to *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), because that exists even during dissolution. Nor can it be due to the "ripening" (*vipāka*) of *adṛṣṭa*, because in his view the meaning of the term "ripening" consists either in the arrival of the time for the fruit or in its being accompanied by the absence of obstructive karma; and since that [absence of obstruction] exists at the time of dissolution just as much as at the time of creation.

Furthermore, because among the infinite karmas residing in infinite living beings, some karmas are simply unavoidable; nor can it be the Lord’s will, for His eternal will, which has all things as its object, never loses its nature as "will-to-create" (sisṛkṣā); and even the technical designation of "will-to-create"—defined as the conditioning factor that brings about the ripening of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) suitable for creation—is common to the state of cosmic dissolution (pralaya) as well.

Nor should it be said that the period of dissolution (*pralayakāla*) alone is the obstructer [of creation], for it would be incoherent to speak of the time serving as the substratum of dissolution being an obstructer of creation to one who maintains that dissolution itself is impossible. Nor should it be said that the period of two half-cycles (*dviparārdha*), beginning from the end of a *kalpa*, which possesses a duration equal to the time of the previous creation, is the obstructer; for, unlike in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), you do not accept the specific natural transformations of time characterized by moments (*kṣaṇa*), lava, and *nimeṣa*.

Furthermore, because of the absence of a temporal adjunct (*upādhi*) characterized by the movement of the sun, it is impossible to state that "this much time" constitutes the period of two *parārdhas*. In the Siddhānta, however, according to the scriptures, [the Lord] intends to create the world for the duration of two *parārdhas* through the natural specific transformations of time, such as the divisions of moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), and so forth; likewise, He intends to cause the world—which has been continuously active for two *parārdhas*—to rest. Thus, there is a specific transformation of the Lord’s will, characterized by the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) and the desire to withdraw (*sañjihīrṣā*).

"And because it is accepted [as such], there is no inconsistency. Now, one might object: "If *samavāya* (inherence) is rejected, why should *saṃyoga* (conjunction) not also be rejected? Anticipating this, he says: "But conjunction...

[The phrase] "it is better than postulating a substratum" means that rather than postulating *samavāya* and then postulating its status as a relation, it is simpler (*laghu*) to merely postulate the status of being a relation for those things already established as having the nature of being inseparably connected (*ayutasiddha*). This is the meaning.

Now, an objection may be raised: in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), only two things need to be postulated—the nature of that inherence itself and its status as a relation; whereas in the case of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*), since a single relation-ness (*sambandhatva*) must be admitted as pervading parts and wholes, qualities and so forth, an infinite number of instances of relation-ness would have to be postulated. Thus, there is simplicity (*lāghava*) in postulating inherence. Nor should it be argued that the status of being a relation for the essential natures of parts and so forth is already established with respect to their respective absences (*tattadabhāva*) and the like.

If it is argued that although the property of being a non-relation as defined by absences and the like is postulated in parts and so forth, the property of being a relation as defined by parts and so forth is not postulated [in the whole], then it would follow that even in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), since the property of being a relation would also be distinct due to the difference between its respective relata, one would have to postulate something other than [the single inherence]. Now, when a thread is destroyed, the qualities, motions, and so forth residing in that thread [would likewise be destroyed].

If it is argued that [the destruction] perishes, but does not destroy even that which resides in the threads, and that since there is a need for a determining factor here, the property of "being a destruction inherent in the threads" must be the operative cause, and therefore inherence (samavāya) must be accepted—[we reply] no, because it is logically consistent that upon the destruction of the thread, there is the destruction of the substratum that is inseparably established with the thread.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the destruction of even the destruction of a cloth produced from ten thousand threads; for then, on your own view as well, there would be the consequence of the destruction of universals (jāti) and so forth inhering in the threads. If, however, you claim that "being the destruction of something impermanent which inheres [in a substance]" is the necessary condition (prayojya), then it is the same for me as well, because destruction (dhvaṃsa) is eternal (nitya); so enough of this excessive discussion. As for the claim that "impermanence follows from the absence of an intrinsic nature" (svarūpābhāva) in the doctrine that inherence (samavāya) is eternal: when the color residing in a jar is lost, since the inherence residing in the jar remains eternal...

Even in the case of its destruction, one must state that the relation characterized by color does not exist; and if the relation characterized by color were indeed the very nature (*svarūpa*) of inherence (*samavāya*), then the loss of the inherence characterized by color would simply mean the loss of inherence itself, and thus it would follow that inherence is non-eternal—this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "possessing the qualities of smell, taste, color, and touch": she is one whose qualities (*guṇāḥ*) are smell, taste, color, and touch; thus, she is "one possessing the qualities of smell, taste, color, and touch."

Regarding the specific effect that is the aggregate, the logicians maintain that the body is so called because it consists of the constituent parts of food, medicinal juices, and substances that are being digested by the digestive fire and have been consumed; due to the disparity caused by the moment-by-moment increase and decrease of these parts, the composite whole—the body—also undergoes increase and decrease at every moment and thus becomes something else. Although there is no visible perception of the body’s increase and decrease at every single moment, nevertheless, it is like the water in a pond due to the falling of rain showers, or like the water in a well due to the lifting of buckets from a water-wheel at the end.

The meaning is as follows: they maintain that upon seeing this, there is indeed a certain extraordinary knowledge of increase and decrease occurring at every moment, just as one perceives the attainment of different locations by the moon, stars, and so forth at every moment—given that they are seen to traverse vast distances over intervals of time such as a *muhūrta*.

Likewise, they accept the momentariness of the terrestrial globe due to the inevitable digging and filling that occurs every instant, and the momentariness of ocean water due to its increase and decrease caused by contact with river waters and the rising of spray.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the term "fourfold" refers to the four types of Buddhists known as Mādhyamikas, Yogācāras, Sautrāntikas, and Vaibhāṣikas; all of them are disciples of Ādibuddha. They are, respectively, proponents of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*), the inferability of external objects (*bāhyārthānumeyatva*), and the perceptibility of external objects (*bāhyārthapratyakṣatva*). Among these, when things are analyzed by the intellect (*buddhi*), no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) can be determined; therefore, they are shown to be inexpressible (*nirabhilāpya*) and devoid of intrinsic nature (*nirasvabhāva*).

By such principles as, "In whatever manner things are investigated, they fall apart in that very same manner," when the disciples have been taught the universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*) by the Guru, those who accept the Guru’s words exactly as they were spoken and do not engage in further questioning are the "superior" because they accept what the Guru said out of faith; yet, because they fail to engage in questioning, they are also the "inferior. Thus, due to this combination of being superior and inferior, they are said to be "established in a middling state."

The Mādhyamikas, however, having accepted the emptiness of external objects, raised the objection: "How can consciousness itself also be empty? [If so], it would follow that the world is blind. Because they accepted the position stated by the Teacher (Guru) under the designation *ācāra* (practice), and because they engaged in that very objection under the designation *yoga* as defined in the Buddhist system, they are called *Yogācāras*. To them, the Teacher replied: "There is only internal consciousness (*vijñānamātra*); that alone possesses the forms of blue and so forth, but not..."

Apart from that [consciousness], there is no external blue or other object, because the non-difference between blue and its corresponding cognition is established by the rule of their simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of this rule being absent, as it is not the case with a cow and a horse. Thus, when it is explained that blue and so forth—which are essentially consciousness—appear as if external due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), how can the external object be entirely non-existent? For there is the appearance of external blue and the like; and while consciousness is internal through the manifestation of "I," the object is [external] through the manifestation of "this."

Furthermore, since blue and other objects appear as distinct from one another by virtue of being external, the mere necessity of simultaneous perception—which is itself non-conclusive—is incapable of proving their non-difference; for by the very mention of "simultaneity," difference is already admitted. To those who have thus questioned this, [the response is]: It is true that blue and so forth exist externally, but they are not perceived [by themselves], because what has not yet arisen or what no longer exists cannot be perceived, and what has already arisen is momentary and lacks duration; rather, blue and the rest perish while imparting themselves to consciousness at the very moment of their arising.

When it was thus explained that past objects such as blue and so forth are inferred through the aspect (ākāra) present in consciousness, they asked at the conclusion of the discourse, "To what extent will this instructional sūtra proceed according to the students' inquiries? When they had thus questioned the end of the sūtra, the teacher said, "Since you have asked for the end of the sūtra, may you be Sautrāntikas! Therefore, they are called Sautrāntikas.

Regarding those Vaibhāṣikas who have been questioned as follows—"Therefore, the claim that 'this external [object] is to be inferred from consciousness' is a contradictory statement, because that very consciousness is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of its own object, and because inference cannot function in the absence of any object whatsoever, since there would be no basis for perceiving the pervasion (*vyāpti*)"—[the author replies: "The fourfold [classification of pramāṇas] is taught precisely in order to show that even external direct perception exists. This is the intended meaning.

"Mental factors" (caitta) refers to those beginning with attachment; the meaning is that the four aggregates distinct from the aggregate of consciousness are mental factors. That which is designated by the terms "mind" (citta) and "mental factors" (caitta) constitutes the five aggregates, namely: form, consciousness, feeling, [perception, and formations].

Vācaspati has stated that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) consists of this kind of knowledge—namely, the *ālayavijñāna* characterized by the form "I am," produced by the sense organs and so forth, and having objects such as form (*rūpa*) as its domain—which exists as a continuous stream like a staff; thus, they say that even the cognition of form and other objects is the aggregate of consciousness. The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*) means conceptual cognition (*savikalpakapratyaya*). Its form is, for example, "the coiled one is a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, in the Śāṅkara-bhāṣya, although earth and the other elements are external as they are being perceived, nevertheless, because they reside within the body, or [because of] the sense organs...

The meaning is that because it has been stated by Vācaspati Miśra that "the internal [elements] arise from a connection with *yas*," this is also largely established in the Śāṅkara Bhāṣya. The phrase "Who said this? implies the sense that one of the two positions is the primary one. The meaning of "because another entity is not admitted" is that, if it were admitted, the Self itself would have been admitted under a different name.

Regarding the phrase "the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*)," although one might argue that even if atoms (*aṇu*) were to arise, just as the conjunction of atoms and the primary elements (*bhūta*) would be untenable, so too—even if the aggregates were to arise—the fivefold aggregate (*pañcaskandhī*) consisting of their collection would be untenable; nevertheless, the intention is that since this sūtra seeks to refute the view that the form-aggregate (*rūpaskandha*)—characterized by the primary elements, the sense faculties (*indriya*), and their objects—is a composite caused by atoms, the emergence of such a collection must likewise be rejected here as faulty.
If it is argued that the recitation is established by usage, and therefore [the sequence] is justified because of mutual dependence;

The reading "because it is merely the cause of arising" (*notpattimātranimittatvāt*) is not traditional; rather, the [correct] reading is as follows. The word *pratyaya* signifies a cause; the point is that, according to that school's terminology, the word *pralaya* is used in its conventional sense. Now, one might object: how can a momentary mental continuum (*cittasantāna*) undergo such things as traveling to another place or entering a womb? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "like the continuum of a lamp. In this context, the reading "thirst is the activity of speech and body" is seen in some places; there, a portion of the text has been omitted due to a scribe’s error in the middle.

For thus is the text of Vācaspati: "When feeling exists, there is this duty: the determination that 'this is happiness' is the state of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the activities of speech and body are grasping (*upādāna*); from that, existence arises, and since birth proceeds from this, 'existence' (*bhava*) refers to merit and demerit; and the manifestation of the aggregates conditioned by those [karmas] is birth (*jāti*)."

The non-maturation of the aggregates that have been born is aging; the destruction of the aggregates is death; the internal burning of one who is dying and is attached to children, wife, and so forth, is sorrow (*śoka*); the lamentation arising from that is wailing (*paridevana*); the experience of unpleasantness associated with the five sensory consciousnesses is physical pain (*duḥkha*), and mental pain is dejection (*daurmanasya*). Now, according to the *Vācaspatya*, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest have birth and the rest as their cause, and birth and the rest have ignorance as their cause.

It has been stated that [these factors] revolve incessantly like a water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*); however, in the *Bhāṣya*, a mutual dependence between sensation (*vedanā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is observed. Raising the doubt as to what the determining factor (*vinigamaka*) here might be, he says, "Sensation and so forth [arise] through ignorance and so forth," implying that there is no difference in meaning even in either case. In the Buddhist system, which refers to momentary entities, since time does not exist in reality, the designation "moment" is conceptually attributed to things like jars, which are inherently fragile.

The point is that even a jar, which is conventionally designated as "momentary" by virtue of its lack of permanence (*animittatā*), is also conventionally designated as a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) from the root *kṣi* (to perish). Regarding the Bhāṣya’s statement that "no object whatsoever possesses the status of being an object of cognition," the meaning is that this would not be the case because [the object] is the object of a perception that grasps its present existence.

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that "simultaneity of cognitions arising from sense-organ contact would result," because if the subsequent moment of the jar—which is the object of perception grasping its presentness—and the preceding moment of the jar with which the sense-organ was already in contact were to exist at the same single moment, then [the sense-organ]...

The meaning is that by the consequence of the simultaneity of associated cognitions (*samprayoga-jñāna*), there would follow the consequence of the simultaneity of cause and effect. In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that [cessation] is designated by the two terms "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). "Deliberation" (*saṃkhyā*) is the cognition [of an object]; "deliberation against" (*prati-saṃkhyā*) is that which is opposed to such cognition. Cessation resulting from that is "cessation through deliberation. Cessation distinct from that is the one characterized by the absence of the cognition in the form: "I am making this existing thing non-existent."

Alternatively, *pratisaṃkhyā* is the worldly cognition that is contrary to [the notion of] number—that is, a cognition apprehending non-existence (*asattva*). Cessation (*nirodha*) which is made the object of such a cognition is *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*. The sense is that cessation which is the opposite of that is *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*. [In the] Bhāṣya, it says "na ca" (and not).

The meaning is that you accept the world to be of the nature of the void even at the stage of its origination; however, it should be understood that in the subsequent moment, it is accepted that it reaches a state of utter non-existence (*tucchatā*) through a destruction that leaves no trace (*niranvayavināśa*). Now, one might object: "The origination of the world from the void is not admitted, so how could it be of the nature of the void? To this, he says: "The destruction of the existent [is] without a trace."

In the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase "along with those two as being insubstantial" means that it is included in the enumeration together with them—as in the statement: "Space and the two types of cessation are eternal and unconditioned. Regarding the *Bhāṣya*’s phrase "as the location for the flight of a hawk," one should not argue that "let there simply be the absence of light perceived here as the substratum for the hawk’s flight"; for the point is that what is perceived as the substratum for light and darkness—such that one says "light is here" and "darkness is here"—cannot possibly be of the nature of the mere absence of light.

In the Bhāṣya, the phrase "nor merely the absence of earth and so forth" means that it cannot be maintained that the meaning of the word *ākāśa* is simply an empty space consisting of the absence of dense substances. The point is that while absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of earth and the rest is not possible [in general], this is because absolute non-existence is possible for all things, since there exists prior non-existence (*prāgbhāva*) of some things yet to be produced, and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of others already produced.

This is merely an illustration; one should also observe that since it is impossible for the eastern direction and so forth—which are perceived as the substrata of both a dense substance and its absence—to be of the nature of an "interstice" (avakāśa) consisting of the absence of that dense substance, it must necessarily be admitted that space (ākāśa) is what is cognized by the cognition of the eastern direction and so forth.

One might object: "How can space, being formless, be an object of visual perception (cākṣuṣapratyakṣa) such as 'here is a hawk'? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says in the Bhāṣya: "In the instruction on triplication (trivṛtkaraṇopadeśa). The meaning established in the Bhāṣya is as follows: "Because the final moment of the jar exists, the previous moments of the jar exist" [is the thesis]; "The previous moments of the jar are perishable because they are moments of the jar, like the final moment of the jar. It should be understood that since there is no difference between the moment of the jar and its existence (satva), the term "existence" (satva) is used as a conventional designation.

For this very reason, he will state later: "Because the destruction of the final moment of a jar is seen to occur without a cause," and so forth. It was previously stated that [the reason] is "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*), meaning it proves even the opposite of what is to be proven; now, however, it is stated that it proves only the opposite of what is to be proven.

The sense is that the term "distinction" (bheda) refers to what is called [the difference between the two]. The phrase "due to the impossibility of activity" (*vyāpārāsambhavāt*) is to be explained as follows: the meaning is that if either the status of being a locus of activity or the status of being a cause of activity is absent, the state of being an agent (*vyāpāritva*) itself is impossible. Regarding the phrase "proving the opposite of what is intended," the meaning is "proving a mere opposite. Consequently, the distinction is that by the words beginning with "and therefore something... (*tataśca kiñca*), the contradiction (*viruddhatva*) is stated, whereas by the preceding commentary (*bhāṣya*), the equality of the reason with the context (*prakaraṇasamatva*) is stated. This is the intended distinction.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase "due to the occurrence of causes such as a mallet" has "prior to" (*prāk*) as its ellipsis; the reading "until the occurrence of causes such as a mallet" (*āmudgarādihetūpanipātāt*), however, is quite easy to understand. The construction in the *Bhāṣya* is to be joined as follows: "even if the destruction is admitted to be distinct from the production of the potsherds. Now, one might object: what is the cause of recognition—is it the sense organ (*indriya*) or the mental impression (*saṃskāra*)? It cannot be the sense organ, because there is no sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) regarding the aspect of "that-ness" (*tattā*). Nor can it be the mental impression, because a mental impression is impossible for an aspect of "that-ness" that has not been previously experienced. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And yet... (*na ca*).

Regarding the phrase "of recognition" (*pratyabhijñāyāḥ*): because it appears through a single act of cognition—namely, by the force of the experience "I am directly perceiving this very thing"—there is indeed direct perception (*sākṣātkāratva*) in every respect. Nor should it be suspected that there is a lack of perceptuality in the aspect of "that-ness" (*tattā*) due to the absence of sense-contact; for it is established that either "qualified by what is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatā*) or the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) serves as the means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). And if those two were not means of proximity, then one should observe that just as the cognition "this is silver" possesses validity regarding its objective aspect (*dharma-aṃśa*), there is no sublation even if the aspect of "that-ness" is indirect (*parokṣatva*). Thus it should be understood.

In the Bhāṣya it is stated that cognition assumes its own form; for such is the established position of that school: when there is contact between an object and a sense faculty, the cognition produced arises with that object as its content.

The immediate form does not have external objects as its domain; rather, that very cognition itself becomes endowed with the form of blue and so forth. And that cognition, by virtue of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatā*), while making itself its own object through self-luminosity, also makes the form of blue and so forth residing within itself its object. Therefore, there is no contradiction regarding the immediacy of the cognition of blue and so forth, nor is there any contradiction with the conformity to the operation of the sense faculties; for subsequently, when the external object is inferred by means of the form of blue and so forth residing in the cognition, [the external object is established] on account of that [form].

Activity directed toward an external object does not arise from immediate (non-conceptual) cognition; for example, one who desires to find wind, having seen the movement of branches, proceeds to the foot of the tree—not because of the visual cognition of the moving branches, but rather through the inference of the movement of wind based upon them. Consequently, in that immediate cognition wherein the object bestows its own form [upon the cognition], the external object is not the object of that cognition; and in that inferential cognition wherein there is the status of being an object, there is no bestowal of its own form.

If it is argued that at the moment preceding the inferential cognition (*anumiti*), the momentary jar (*ghaṭakṣaṇa*) which was in contact with the sense organ has already perished, [we reply] no; for its status as an object (*viṣayatva*) is due to its being a cause through a succession of processes such as the imparting of its own form (*svākāra*). This point will become clear in the subsequent sūtra when the Yogācāra view is raised. In the Bhāṣya, regarding the phrase "in the stream of blue-cognition" (*nīlajñānasantatau*), the words "while it is persisting" (*anuvartamānāyām*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The phrase "not merely of the property alone" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); for if there were a transfer of blue and other qualities belonging to something external, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a transfer of properties such as grossness and insentience (*jaḍatva*) inherent in that [external object]. This is not an acceptable conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because if that were the case, when redness is transferred to a crystal, its contradictory property, whiteness (*śauklya*), would no longer be perceived.

It should also be observed that [if the cognition were merely a reflection], there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of not perceiving the specific qualities of the object—such as its particular hardness, its internal nature, and so forth—just as one does not perceive the qualities of the mirror when it reflects an object. Thus ends the section on the aggregate (samudāyadhikaraṇa). The meaning of the statement "the final cognition has the power to produce a dissimilar [effect]" is that the capacity (śakti) of the cause is to be inferred from the effect; this is the intended sense. Furthermore, it is not the case that the cognition of the form of the potsherds [is the same as] the cognition of the form of the jar...

It should not be argued that because the stream of cognition is not itself a latent impression (*vāsanā*), its being produced by a latent impression cannot be established; for it is impossible for a stream of cognitions regarding a pot-sherd at a different time, which is temporally remote, to constitute a latent impression. This is because we observe that a latent impression acquired in an animal birth—which was interrupted by a human birth—can still produce its effect immediately after a human body [is discarded] and one enters an animal womb. This is the intended meaning.

The phrase "dwelling outside as if" means that it is produced by delusion, just as those situated above perceive the stars as being on the ground; such is the intended meaning. Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "And because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension," the intended inference here is: "Blue and so forth are non-different from cognition, because they are necessarily apprehended simultaneously with cognition, just like cognition itself, or like a second moon. He explains the *Bhāṣya*—which states that this is not contradicted by one's own words because "simultaneity" implies a difference in objects—by the passage beginning with "Simultaneity belongs only to two things" and ending with "the fallacy of the inconclusive due to lack of commonality. The meaning of that [passage] in the *Bhāṣya* is as follows: ... [text continues] ... the meaning of that [passage] in the *Bhāṣya*.

Since cognition has as its sole nature the fitness for being conveyed [by words], the necessity of its simultaneous apprehension with that [object] serves as the proof of their non-difference; thus, in accordance with the word *tat* (that), one must supply the word *yat* (which) and state the syntactical connection as a single sentence. Thus ends the section on Apprehension (*upalabdhyadhikaraṇa*).

Fearing that there might be no refutation of the position "or otherwise" (*anyathā vā*) in the *Bhāṣya*, he says: "In the case of its being of both natures" (*ubhayātmakatve ca*). "By the manner of the opponent's admission" means by the manner admitted by the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*). Now, [it may be argued]: "Even that cognition is not accepted by the wise as ultimate reality, because it is devoid of the nature of being one or many, like a sky-lotus. The Mādhyamikas know the reality to be free from the four alternatives: neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither."

Since it has been stated that [the entity] is indeed free from the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), one might raise the objection: "How can there be such a thing as existence and non-existence? Anticipating this, he says, "For the proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*)," with the intention that even the state of being free from the four alternatives results in non-existence itself—whether by way of having the nature of existence, the nature of non-existence, or a nature distinct from both existence and non-existence—and thus ultimately culminates in the category of non-existence. Furthermore, the state of possessing both natures would merely be a transition to another state; he establishes this point by means of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*) method.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "the jar, in relation to itself" and so forth is as follows: others have stated that the external aggregate consisting of a collection of primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika) is caused by atoms; the internal [aggregate], consisting of mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta), is the commencement of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha); and the aggregate in the form of the five aggregates is both external and caused by both [atoms and consciousness]. This is because it would follow that either the cognition is false or the object is real: if the cognition of identity between the two were true, the object would also have to be real; if the object were false, the cognition would also have to be false.

The meaning is that there would be falsity (*mithyātva*). Alternatively, regarding the phrase "by means of the non-attainment of the object" (*arthānupalabdhyā*), although this explanation is not explicitly evident in the *Śāṅkarabhāṣya*—since it is explained solely with the intent of referring to the non-perception of the object (*arthānupalabdhi*) and no explanation is seen with the intent of referring to the non-perception of latent impressions (*vāsanānupalabdhi*)—nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated [here] because such an intention is possible.

The passage beginning with "others, however" (*anye tu*) and so forth has been explained as being intended for the refutation of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*). It should be understood that the two sūtras—"Because [the object] is perceived, it is not non-existent" (*nābhāva upalabdheḥ*) and "And because of the difference in nature, it is not like dreams and so forth" (*vaidharmyācca na svapnādivat*)—are not explicitly raised in his system, even though they constitute the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because they are likewise devoted to the refutation of the Yogācāra position.

The meaning is that the existence of cognition is common to all three—the Vaibhāṣikas, Sautrāntikas, and Yogācāras—by way of the negation of the actual existence of an object; and among them, the intention is that for the first two, the refutation of the proponent of the negation of the manifestation of an object is desired. Furthermore, the meaning is that the two propositions intended in the Sūtra are: "nor is it non-existent by itself," and "there is no arising from a non-existent entity," which is to say, there is no arising of a non-existent entity.
Thus ends the section concerning the impossibility in every respect.

In the *Bhāṣya*, it says "the five *astikāyas*"; the intention is that the etymology of *astikāya* is "that which is called (*kāyante*) 'it exists' (*asti*). In the *Bhāṣya*, it says "the *ākāśāstikāya*"; they describe the *ākāśāstikāya* as being twofold: *lokākāśa* (world-space) and *alokākāśa* (non-world-space). *Lokākāśa* is the space situated within the successive worlds; *alokākāśa* is the space above those, the place of liberation (*mokṣa*), where no worlds exist. And it has been said: "The planets, such as the sun and moon, having gone [there], return."

"Even today they do not turn back, traveling along the path of the space of the visible universe. Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya* that "the means to liberation is also grasped," although the means to liberation is indeed already expressed by the word *saṃvara* itself—given that "influx (*āsrava*) is the cause of existence, while restraint (*saṃvara*) is the cause of liberation"—nevertheless, this should be understood as stated for the purpose of including other means besides those specific causes of liberation intended by the term *saṃvara*.

In the Bhāṣya, the statement that the sense organs and so forth are the instruments of enjoyment should be understood as being according to the intention of another school, based on the words of Jinadatta: "Influx (āsrava) is bondage through karma; shedding (nirjarā) is liberation from it."

In the Bhāṣya, there are the four *ghāti* (destructive) karmas and the four *aghāti* (non-destructive) karmas. The four *ghāti* karmas are: *jñānāvaraṇīya* (knowledge-obscuring), *darśanāvaraṇīya* (perception-obscuring), *mohanīya* (deluding), and *āntarāyika* (obstructive). The four *aghāti* karmas are: *vedanīya* (feeling-producing), *nāmika* (name-determining), *gotrika* (lineage-determining), and *āyuṣka* (life-span-determining). Regarding this, [the opponent claims]: "Right knowledge is not the means to liberation, for the realization of an object does not follow from knowledge alone, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This misconception is called the *jñānāvaraṇīya* karma. Furthermore, the notion that "liberation does not result from the practice of cultivated perception" is [also a form of] ignorance.

The *darśanāvaraṇīya* [karma] is that which obscures right vision; the *mohanīya* karma is that which causes a failure to discern the specific distinctions among the many mutually contradictory paths to liberation shown by various *tīrthaṅkaras*; the *antarāyika* karma is the knowledge that creates obstacles for those engaged in the path to liberation. These are called the *ghāti-karmas* because they destroy what is beneficial (*śreya*). When the union of semen and blood has occurred, that which is formed from the nature of both is designated as *āyuḥ* (life-span) and *kāya* (body); thus it is produced.

By means of the "door of giving" (*danadvāra*), there is *āyuṣka* (life-span); its capacity for transformation into the form of a body is *gotrika* (genus); once that capacity is established, the specific activity within that seed which initiates the state of the embryo, the bubble, and so forth, is *nāmika* (name); and the cause of the transformation into the shape of a body through a slight thickening—like the ripening of a seed by the heat of a nurse—is *vedanīya* (feeling). These four are called *aghāti* (non-obscuring) because they do not destroy what is auspicious; such is their process. In the commentary, the term "austerity" (*tapa*) means practices such as the ascetic discipline of the heated stone-bed (*taptasīlārohaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "what is called restraint (*saṃvara*) in the commentary": by the etymological derivation that "it restrains (*saṃvṛṇoti*) the activity of the senses," the means to liberation consisting of *gupti*, *samiti*, and so forth, is called *saṃvara*. The technical definition of the Jains is that *gupti* is the restraint of body, speech, and mind. *Samiti* is defined as: walking after having carefully observed the path trodden on the ground—well-illuminated by the rays of the sun—in order to avoid injury to living beings; speaking measuredly; and partaking of restricted food, and so forth.

In the Bhāṣya, regarding the manifestation of the nature of the self, some say that liberation is the abiding in the space of the world (lokākāśa) for one whose afflictions have entirely ceased; others declare that liberation is the constant upward motion of one who, like the five-fold liberated Śuka, is freed from the bondage of the astikāyas of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma), just as the mud-smeared coating on a gourd fruit is washed away by immersion in water and it then dries.

In the commentary, the word "syāt" occurs; this term is a particle resembling a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) that indicates non-absolutism. There are four positions consisting of existence, non-existence, being distinct from both existence and non-existence, and the nature of being distinct from both existence and non-existence. Furthermore, by combining these with the states of being existent, non-existent, and both existent and non-existent, seven positions can be conceived by those who advocate the doctrine of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīvāda*). All of these positions are accepted in a limited sense (*iṣad-iṣad*) by the Jains regarding all categories of reality they themselves acknowledge.

The sense is that, according to his view, the word *paryāya* is defined as "state" (*avasthā*), because the term *paryāya* is conventionally designated for states. The meaning is that the existence (*sattva*) and so forth of a substance is thus logically established. The underlying intention is that, unlike in the systems of Bhāskara and others, there is no need to rely on another mode of being—such as unity through the nature of a universal (*jāti*) and plurality through the nature of individuals (*vyakti*)—to resolve contradictions; [in this view], such a mechanism is unnecessary. [Objection: But since the opponent has introduced the coexistence of existence and non-existence specifically by means of a difference in modes (*ākāra-bheda*), and you have not stated that this applies to every instance of the coexistence of existence and non-existence, how [can this be justified]?

Anticipating the objection that this [existence] is negated, he says: "There is no contradiction between existence and non-existence due to a difference in form. In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated at that very moment: "This is not the opposite. Now, one might object: just as there is a coexistence of contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence even in a single thing through the distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as place and time, so too—

If it is argued that even without a distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there exist means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) established by worldly consensus, then here too such means of valid cognition certainly exist—those very arguments set forth by various disputants to establish the existence or non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Syādvādamañjarī*: "Just as others are renowned for being envious due to the mutual distinction between their own positions and the opposing positions of others..."

"Neither remaining in a vehicle, nor desiring distinction, nor partiality—such is your doctrine. In reality, even the differentiation of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as space and time does not apply everywhere; for in the cognition "that place does not exist here" or "that time does not exist now," there is an absence of further limiting conditions of space, time, and so forth. If one were to search for yet further limiting conditions in those cases as well, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, while other [conditions] are not admitted, the differentiation of space, time, and so forth is nevertheless included by way of the maxim of the "sugarcane on the tongue" (*guḍajihvikā-nyāya*).

The cognition of existence and non-existence is being presented; in reality, while tolerating existence, that [cognition] is indeed a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the commingling of existence, non-existence, and so forth, precisely when it is devoid of qualifications. For this very reason, the proponents of *syādvāda* accept the very perceptual cognition—such as "the jar exists," "the jar does not exist," "the cloth exists," or "the cloth does not exist"—as the means of valid knowledge for the non-absolute nature (*anaikāntika*) of existence, non-existence, and the like. They also employ the following inference as a means of valid knowledge: "Everything is non-absolute because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like a variegated cloth."

If it is argued that "the secret of the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda) is this: in a variegated cloth, one need not resort to distinct spatial locations to avoid the confusion of blue, yellow, and other colors; for if one were to seek further limiting conditions (upādhi) to avoid the confusion of those distinct locations, there would be an infinite regress. By this same reasoning, the non-confusion of conjunction and its absence is also refuted. Therefore, every entity is indeed non-absolute (anaikāntika)," we reply: as long as one follows the boundaries of worldly experience, the distinction between limiting conditions—which is established by the universal consensus of all people regarding the mutual interpenetration of properties—cannot be denied.

Even when the existence of space, time, and so forth is negated, the delimitation by conditions such as space and time is indeed experienced. In this case, neither self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), nor infinite regress (*anavasthā*) constitutes a fault, just as in the case of the application of properties such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*). Furthermore, just as in the causal relationship between the seed and the sprout, even when contradictory properties coexist, one must reject all objections regarding distinctions. Otherwise, how could the established social order—such as "this is her son," "this is her husband," "this is her father," or "this is her father-in-law"—even be possible?
