How [could it not be established]?

In each respective case, one should carry out the appropriate worldly conventions—such as those regarding motherhood and so forth—with due regulation; for the doctrine of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) cannot be entirely rejected. This has been explained at length. The meaning is that the suspicion of its non-existence finds no room. Therefore, the underlying point is: why should time not be denoted by the term *astikāya*? He explains the word "thus" (*evam*) means he explains it by supplying [the missing word] from the context.

In the Bhāṣya, regarding the phrase "of one residing in the body of an elephant and so forth," it means that for the individual soul (jīva), there would be entry into the body of an ant and so forth from the body of an elephant and so forth by abandoning a portion [of its size] within that [new body].

The meaning is that, compared to its previous state, there would follow the consequence of a lack of completeness (*akārtsnya*) due to its nature as being limited by conceptual distinctions (*vikalpatva*). This is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an illustrative indication); for instance, when one enters the body of an elephant from the body of a mosquito, one would not possess a dimension capable of pervading [the whole body], and thus one would not experience pleasure and so forth extending to all parts of that body. Furthermore, it should also be observed that if the individual soul (*jīva*) were of the same size as the body, then when a yogi accomplished in yoga assumes a multitude of bodies (*kāyavyūha*), it would be impossible for it to pervade the entirety of those bodies, and consequently, he would be unable to preside over multiple bodies simultaneously.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: when it comes to describing non-contradiction by means of accepting a difference in states (*avasthābheda*), they establish [the soul's] subject to modification (*vikāritva*). Indeed, such is the introductory commentary (*bhāṣya*) of the opponents to the Sūtra: "Now, if it is argued that there is no contradiction even through succession (*paryāya*), because upon obtaining a large body some parts of the soul arrive, and upon obtaining a small body some depart—[we reply: 'And there is no non-contradiction even through succession, because of [the resulting] modifications and so forth.'"

The phrase "exclusion of growth, decay, and so forth residing in trees and the like" means that in this sūtra, growth and decay are not intended by the word *paryāya*, such that there would necessarily be an accession and departure of parts; rather, it refers only to contraction and expansion, because even Jaimini accepts only contraction and expansion—this is the sense. [It is] without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).

The phrase "because it is the nature of consciousness" refers to the fact that eternity is established by scripture in the statement, "For the knower, there is no loss of the act of knowing. This is because, according to the maxim "But [the Veda] is authoritative because its source is the Word," one must accept things in accordance with the means of valid cognition. The implication is that this fault indeed accrues to the Jainas who attempt to construct their views based on mere reasoning.

In this regard, others [argue] that the initial, middle, and final dimensions are eternal because they are the dimensions of the self, like the final dimension; and consequently, since all three—the initial, middle, and final dimensions—would be eternal, there would be equality [of size] across all bodies.

However, there is no difference in modification characterized by the increase or decrease of parts due to a difference in the body; in this view, one interpretation is that the word "both" (*ubhaya*) in the Sūtra refers to the initial and intermediate dimensions, because three dimensions are admitted. A second [interpretation], however, holds that since the dimension of the self at the time of liberation is eternal, and because it is impossible for that [eternal thing] to have previously existed and then not exist, that dimension must also exist prior [to liberation]; thus, a dimension contrary to it is untenable, and therefore the initial and intermediate dimensions are that very same [dimension] during the initial and intermediate times as well.

The soul would have to be of only one single dimension, and there would be no difference in dimension due to the difference in bodies; and in this view, the word "both" (*ubhaya*) in the Sūtra refers to the initial and intermediate states, and not—as in the prima facie argument—to the initial, intermediate, and final dimensions, because there is no difference in dimension [in that case]. Thus, two explanations were provided. He restates this very point.

Regarding the statement, "And because the final state [is eternal], the final dimension is eternal," and so forth: here, if the final dimension were eternal, then since there would be no distinction in its being the dimension of the self, the initial and intermediate dimensions would also be eternal, resulting in a lack of distinction between them. Furthermore, there would be a single body-dimension; that is, one who possesses all dimensions eternally would possess only a single body. Consequently, there would be no attainment of bodies that are either increased or decreased in size. Others argue that if the final dimension were eternal, it could not be established as something that did not previously exist and then came into being; therefore, it must have existed even prior to that.

Because it is impossible for a dimension contrary to that [initial one] not to contradict it, the initial and middle dimensions must be that very same [dimension]; thus, in both the initial and middle states, [the substance remains identical].

"Because the ultimate dimension (*antyaparimāṇa*) is eternal, there would be no distinction; [the dimension] would always be of a single form, namely minuteness (*aṇutva*), or it would be magnitude (*mahattva*). Regarding this, they say that the reading "te cāpare ca yojanāntaram āhuḥ" (and others have stated another interpretation) is correct, because it has been explained by the *Kalpataru* after such an analysis, and because it is appropriate to the sense. As for the phrase "it would be merely a matter of names, such as 'difference-and-non-difference' (*bhedābheda*)," the sequence is intended here; the meaning is that it would be merely a matter of names, such as "non-difference-and-difference."

The phrase "having many counter-correlates" (*bahupratiyogika*) means that "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is common to many; the point is that since "many-ness" (*bahutva*) inherently contains difference (*bheda*), being common necessarily involves difference. He explains how a common form can tolerate difference: "because it does not serve as the locus of contradictory properties," for non-difference (*abheda*) is of the nature of its own absence. The meaning is that when [the pot] does not differentiate [itself from others], then because non-difference—which consists in the absence of difference—is present, the pot and so forth would themselves cease to exist as distinct entities. The term "from the Vivasanins" refers to the Jainas and others.

The meaning is as follows: if it is argued that "for one who does not depend upon the modes (*paryāya*)" means he asserts [the identity] independently of any other factor that would reconcile the lack of contradiction, whereas we assert it precisely with dependence upon such [a factor]; [the author replies: "Because of the acceptance of both difference and non-difference"—this is the ellipsis referring to Yādava and Bhāskara. Now, one might object: since there is no reason to postulate another state for a state and its possessor, their difference and non-difference are accepted independently of such [a factor]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as of a single substance," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: because a substance (*dravya*) depends upon other states (*avasthā*), even though the difference and non-difference between the possessor of a state and its states—when these two are defined by the states themselves—are independent of any further establishing factor due to the states' capacity to establish both themselves and others, nevertheless, the difference and non-difference between the possessor of a state and its states—as defined by those very states—do require another state to establish them. The phrase "by whichever state" means "together with whichever state.

The phrase "the dispute is over the name" means that one would merely be making a technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) that the state of being a cloth (*paṭatva-avasthā*) itself is both different and non-different [from the cloth]. [This is like] the case of the mother-in-law and the beggar's husband...

The meaning is this: by saying, "The doctrine of the non-exclusivity (anaikāntya) of all things is appropriate for us Vedāntins, but not for the Jains," the author of the Sūtras fails to follow the principle of "rejecting the alms of one's mother-in-law" (*śvaśrūbhikṣā-pratikṣepa*). He states that the fault lies in your own position by means of the word "without distinction" (*aviśeṣa-śabdena*). Thus ends the section on "The Impossibility in One" (*ekasminn-asambhavādhikaraṇam*).

He states the contradiction in the Siddhānta with the words "mudriketara" (other than the [prescribed] mudrās). It is stated in many Tantras that the wearing of the six mudrās, sitting upon the vulva-seat (*bhagāsana*), meditating on the Self, and so forth, are means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). In another Tantra, however, practices contrary to those—such as the installation of a jar of wine and the invocation of deities residing therein—are described as means for attaining the supreme good. Thus...

The meaning is that the various means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) taught in different places—such as wearing the eight seals (*mudrā*), sitting upon the vulva (*bhaga-āsana*), and meditation on the Self (*ātma-dhyāna*)—are enumerated in the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya* at the point "because of being the source of the scripture" (*śāstra-yoni-tvāt*), the fault has already been stated: [the body of God] cannot be eternal, because that would not contradict [the fact that] God is unestablished; nor can it be non-eternal, because it has been stated that something other than Him cannot exist at that time as its cause, and so forth. This is the meaning.

One might object: "Surely, for the author of the Sūtras who accepts that the Supreme Self has the world as its body, it cannot be argued that there would be the consequence of [experiencing] pleasure, pain, and so forth, simply because He possesses a body. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The resolution is by virtue of accepting His bodilessness (*aśarīratva*). The sense is this: even if He were to possess a body, there would be no consequence of experiencing pleasure, pain, and so forth, due to the authority of the scriptures which establish that He is devoid of both types of attributes (*ubhayaliṅgatva*). [Regarding the phrase: "the consequence of being rendered superfluous" (*kṛtakaratvaprasaṅga*).

Therefore, the sense is this: this section (*adhikaraṇa*) does not aim at demonstrating that [the Śaiva Āgamas] have meanings contrary to the Veda; rather, its purpose is solely to establish the non-contradiction between the Śruti and the Śaiva Āgamas, preceded by a demonstration of the fragility of the perceived contradiction despite the established absence of such conflict. The phrase "even though one desires to lead [them] to non-contradiction" implies "in this section. The expression "one who breaks its natural consistency" means "one who breaks the natural consistency of the Śruti."

The phrase "by sublation, option, combination, and restriction" means by forms of sublation consisting of option, combination, and restriction. For an "option" (vikalpa) is partial sublation; "combination" (samuccaya) is sublation of the independence [of the texts] as heard; and "restriction" (saṅkoca), however, is sublation in one respect. This is because it should be understood that if sublation of the scripture were intended in its entirety, it would be impossible to bring about non-contradiction.

"By the rule for the slaughter of animals in the Śrāddha-kalpa" means by the rule for the immolation of cattle established in the Śrāddha-kalpa. This is because the mere rule for meat does not conflict with the prohibition "one shall not kill," and thus lacks the restrictive power [to override it]. Just as in the case of the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, where the rule "they perform the Patnīsaṃyājas with a Jyādhinī cow" prescribes the use of a naturally occurring Jyādhinī (a cow suffering from chronic lameness) rather than one produced through ritual action—since this is established in the third section of the *Tarkapāda* (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.25) under the principle "and the Jyādhinī, because it is a part"—so too is it here.

It should be understood that the statement "by means of the flesh of fish, deer, ruru-deer, hare, tortoise, boar, ram, and [the meat of] the vārdhrīṇasa, kālaśāka, goat, iron-colored [beast], and rhinoceros, mixed with honey, there is infinity for years" is possible even otherwise than through prescribed meat; this is because there is practice in other Yugas. Alternatively, he says "or else, there is a contradiction of many meanings," because it has been established in the *Śiṣṭākopādhikaraṇa* that Smṛtis such as "one should perform [rites] having sipped water" and "one should perform [rites] with the right hand" restrict Vedic Śruti passages that prescribe the order of actions, such as "having made the pedestal, one should sacrifice. This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, the contradiction regarding the fundamental principles (*tattva*) is difficult to avoid. One might argue: "In the *Śrī-Pāñcarātra* as well, although there are passages in the descriptions of specific yantras and the like that establish Lakṣmī, Sudarśana, and others as limbs (*aṅga*) of Vāsudeva, its authority is maintained by somehow reconciling these without contradiction; its lack of authority is not accepted by asserting a perversion of the fundamental principles. If it is the same in the *Pāśupata-āgama*, then [we reply]: No, for in the midst of the *Śrī-Pāñcarātra* scripture—which from beginning to end propounds Nārāyaṇa—"

The point is this: while it might be appropriate to interpret one particular passage differently within two or three sentences that appear to establish a misconception, it does not ascend even slightly into the hearts of the wise to claim a different meaning for the *Pāśupata-Āgama*—which is established in the Purāṇas as being intended to delude by establishing misconceptions from head to toe. [This applies] to those who are "mere bards" (vaiḍālika), that is, those among the great offenders other than Vābhravya and Śāṇḍilya.

The meaning is that because there is no entry into the Vedic *Niḥśvāsa-saṃhitā*, one has attained the state of a "cat-like hypocrite" (*vaiḍālika*). For it is recorded in the Smṛti: "He whose banner of dharma is always raised high like the banner of the gods, yet whose conduct is sinful—that is the vow called 'cat-like'. The genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental according to the rule "kṛtyānāṃ kartari ca," meaning the genitive denotes the agent. Anticipating the objection—"How can that which is directed toward the Arhats and Buddhas, being non-scriptural, have the nature of a sacrifice?"—he says: "the statement regarding its nature as a sacrifice. This is with reference to them, namely, the Buddhas, Arhats, Bhīṣma, and so forth.

The meaning is "generally. Now, one might object: in the Lord's statement, "I am to be worshipped by those other than the Tamasic," how can the Lord be said to be the object of worship? For those established in Tamas do not worship the Lord in any way, since they worship Rudra alone. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "the statement that 'I am to be worshipped' [is made] with reference to them. This means it is with reference to the intention of those Tamasic people. "What was stated in the middle verse" means what was stated in the verse beginning, "that action which is outside the Vedas... (Gītā 17.5).

Thus addressed, [the response is: "Having been thus addressed, I have made myself manifest and concealed my own self"—this is the construction. Since the status of being the source of the Trayī (the three Vedas) and so forth is established [in this way], one should not think that the practice of the Brāhmī-vidyā—which has Paśupati as its embodied deity—as previously described in the *Atharvaśiras*, is non-Vedic.

It must be stated how pride (*māna*) arises for the Trayī-bāhyas (those outside the three Vedas) and the Pāśupatas; for even they, being both Vedic and Tantric, lack pure Vedic status. Thus, one should understand that their eligibility [for this practice] is established therein. "Direct connection with Vedic ritual" means a connection with the pure Vedic dharma.

"Worthy even of the worship of the Lord established by the Śruti without mediation" means that practices such as the *dahara-upāsanā* (the meditation on the small space within the heart) are worthy of the worship of the Lord established by the Śruti without mediation, because there is no intervention by another individual soul (*jīva*) in those cases. Therefore, the meaning is that they are worthy even of that.

He demonstrates the consequence that the scripture would lack authority due to its having either a redundant object (*prāptārthatva*) or a sublated subject matter (*bādhitaviṣayatva*), by means of the passage beginning with "by inference" (*anumānena*), stating that [the scripture] would be either contradicted or sublated. The underlying sense is that, in order to avoid the consequence of the scripture's lack of authority arising from these two factors—having a redundant object and a sublated subject matter—it is necessary to refute inference at the very commencement of the scripture. It should be understood that this point was not demonstrated here because it is clear that the purpose of this section is to demolish the authority of those scriptures that contradict the *Śruti*.

The sense is that because the *Saṅkarṣaṇakāṇḍa* also belongs to the earlier portion [of the scripture], it is stated [in the *Brahmasūtra*] as "that has been explained like the [chapter on] giving" (*pradānavadeva taduktam*), and so forth. Furthermore, the consequence would be the doctrine of nihilism (*śūnyavāda*), because what is non-existent at one time would have to be non-existent at all times. "Real number" (*vāstava-saṅkhyā*) means ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). "Even in the reversal of the proponent" means that even when there is a reversal of the possession of number—which was the reason for proving impermanence—the undesirable property to be proven, namely impermanence, does not necessarily follow in the absence of that possession of number.

Regarding the phrase "consciousness and that which begins with *ghu*," one might object: "How can this be so, since the word *ghu* and others are invariably masculine? To this we reply: this is not the word *ghu*; rather, from the root *ad* (in the sense of "eating"), by adding the suffix *ini* in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*), the form *ādi* is established. It should be understood that through this very term, the status of being the cause is demonstrated by way of [Brahman's] being the destroyer of the entire universe. Having restated the alternative interpretation, he refutes it.

Regarding the phrase "sovereignty over consciousness" (*vijñānaiśvaryādīti*), one might raise the objection: "Since it should be stated that [the Lord] is distinguished by the divisions of *paravyūha* and *vibhava*, why is it said instead that He is distinguished by the subtle *vyūha* and *vibhava*? Anticipating this, he states: "The two words 'subtle' (*sūkṣma*) and 'supreme' (*parama*) have the same meaning. Then, considering the designation "*vyūha* as the fourfold *vyūha*" to be improper, he says: "*caturvyūha* means the fourfold division."

The meaning is that he states the authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the stated point: namely, that the supreme Brahman called Vāsudeva, worshipped through action preceded by knowledge, is the goal to be attained; this is the sense in which he states the authoritative evidence. [Objection: "Is it not contradictory that these very [entities] are designated by the terms *jīva* and so forth? For, in the Pañcarātra, it is appropriate to designate the individual soul (*jīva*), mind (*manas*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*) by the terms Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, since those terms are conventionally defined (*paribhāṣita*) as referring to the soul and so on within that scripture. In whatever scripture a term is used, it must refer to that specific meaning."

When a word is thus defined, its own specific meaning alone is to be understood there, just like the technical designations such as *nadī* and *vṛddhi* found in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*). For this very reason, the statement that "the mind is designated as Pradyumna" is also consistent; otherwise, [it would not be so].

If it is argued that this is not so because there is an absence of natural consistency regarding the neuter gender when Pradyumna is manifested as the presiding deity of the mind (*manas*), we say no; for there is no evidence for such a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) in this scripture. This is because the fact that Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the presiding deities of the individual soul (*jīva*), the mind (*manas*), and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) respectively, and the manifestation of Saṅkarṣaṇa from Vāsudeva, Pradyumna from Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Aniruddha from Pradyumna, have been extensively established many times in that scripture. Therefore, [the neuter gender refers] specifically to Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others who are the presiding deities of the soul and so forth.
The meaning is that this is because [the word] is appropriate to be grasped [in that sense]. Alternatively, the meaning of the verse is:

"Even regarding objects already understood, without doubt as to whether 'this is better' or 'that is better,' I do not know which is the supreme good (*śreyas*). He cites a statement from the *Mokṣadharma*, which is the root of the *Ekāyana-śāstra*—the root of the venerable *Pāñcarātra*: "In the *Mokṣadharma*... Here, it should be understood that by the word *niṣat*, the *Ekāyana-mantras* are meant. "This is the root" means that by the word "this," the *Ekāyana Veda* is being referred to.

"By resorting to division" means by relying on Vedic ritual action, [referring to] the Asuras who are intent upon the oppression of virtuous people (*sāttvika-jana*). "And that is not useful for protection" means it is useful for protection in the form of the expulsion of the Asuras. "For the sake of protecting the devotees" means for the sake of directly protecting the devotees without [first] destroying their evil deeds. Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the two sūtras," the words "as in this established doctrine (*siddhānta*)" are to be supplied. The phrase "the meaning is inconsistent with the words of the sūtra" will be clarified later.

"By difference of qualified persons (*adhikāribhedena*)" means that there is an option between the *uditahoma* (offering after sunrise) and *anuditahoma* (offering before sunrise) based on the difference in the qualified persons. "By difference of time (*kālabhedena*)" means that sometimes the performance of *ghrī* is undertaken and sometimes the performance of *vidyā*. Regarding the taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup and so forth, there is an option based on the difference in results; for the sense there is that the taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* must be performed by one who desires an abundance of results. "Those included by the word 'beginning with' (*ārabhya*)": this means that these statements are intended [by the author] as being contained within the commentary (*bhāṣya*).
"Unity was stated for the sake of the meaning (*ārtham*)" refers to the passage: "But the Pāñcarātra is now being described."

The meaning is that the singular sense of the term *pañcarātra* has been stated. "The commonality of the author has been shown" means that it has been demonstrated. "Of those matters intended [by others] as being contradictory."

The meaning is: "due to the abandonment of the three dharmas" refers to the abandonment of the *trayī-dharma* (the Vedic dharma) and so forth, which are set forth in the *Pañcarātra*. Regarding the phrase "direct perception is the cause," the sense is that for those following the Yoga system, liberation results from direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), whereas for the Sāṅkhyas, they maintain that the cause of liberation is knowledge produced by scripture; such is the meaning of the verse. As for the question "how does the statement regarding the absence of delusion (*bhrāmarāhitya*) hold?": the meaning is, "how is the demonstration of the absence of delusion logically consistent?"
He shows the very statement that establishes this error, beginning with "by Kapila and others," and so forth.

"By the word 'fear' and so forth. "In this way, of that feeling"—this means "such being the case. [The opponent objects: "Is it not the case that the extraction of the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) is more appropriate? For it is said: 'Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—know these, O royal sage, to be various systems of knowledge (*jñāna*). Kapila is called the supreme seer who taught Sāṅkhya; Hiraṇyagarbha is the ancient teacher of Yoga, and no other. He named Avāntaratapas is called the teacher of the Vedas.'"* *Note: This passage is a citation from the *Mahābhārata*, Śāntiparvan, Mokṣadharma section (12.306.58–59).*

Some indeed declare that Ṛṣi to be Pracīnagarbha. Śiva—the Lord of Umā, the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), Śrīkaṇṭha, and the son of Brahmā—having become composed, spoke this knowledge that bestows the state of Paśupati. Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra; and in all these systems of knowledge, O best of kings, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is seen as the ultimate goal, according to scripture and according to reason. Yet those who are shrouded in darkness do not recognize him thus, O lord of the people.

"The wise declare that very author to be the creator of the scripture"—thus it is established that the Sāṅkhya and other systems are indeed internal to the Vedic tradition and are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa. Likewise: "Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—these are authoritative regarding the Self; they must not be refuted by means of [mere] reasoning. And similarly: "For all are authoritative, just as this scripture [is]."

This is the supreme truth of the Sāṅkhyas who have realized the Self, as it was declared by the foremost ascetics, Kapila and others, who are lords themselves; in which no delusions whatsoever are seen, O bull among men, and in which many virtues and the absolute elimination of defects reside. Likewise, the scriptures proclaimed by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, and others are to be interpreted according to this direction, and not otherwise, O wise ones.

Otherwise, if they were to be interpreted differently, they would undoubtedly be contradictory. Thus, there are passages such as: "In that very way, others worship the Lord in the form of Śiva, according to the path spoken by Śiva, through various distinctions of Vedic conduct," which establish the authority of all the Āgamas in common with the *Mahābhārata*, the *Mānava-dharma-śāstra*, the *Bhāgavata*, and other texts. Furthermore: "Therefore, O Bull-bannered One (Śiva), we two shall compose scriptures for the purpose of defining those who drink outside the Vedas (*veda-bāhya-pāyin*), and for their delusion."

Thus urged by Mādhava Murāri, Rudra likewise incited Keśava to compose treatises of delusion. Along with Hara, he produced the Kāpāla, Lāguḍa, Śākta, Bhairava, Pūrva-paścima, Pañcarātra, Pāśupata, and other such systems. Furthermore, there arose the Buddhists, Śrāvakas, Nirgranthas, those who know the Pañcarātra, the Kāpālikas, the Pāśupatas, and other heretics of that kind—those evil-minded and tamasic beings upon whom the sacrificial offerings of such a person fall.
For him, that [faith] would not be true faith, and it would yield no fruit either in this world or after death. Those who follow the Vāma and Pāśupata practices, as well as the Pāñcarātrikas—

In that Kali age, there will be Brahmins as well as Kṣatriyas who have lost faith in the expiations prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti-śiṣṭas; such men, in due course, shall resort to the Tantras established by the Śruti. Thus are the common criticisms regarding the Vaiṣṇava and Śiva Āgamas. Furthermore, it is indeed stated in the Dharmaśāstra and the Purāṇas that for the most wicked of men, there is a most terrible expiation ending in death. For those whose minds are weakened by fear, death occurs most intensely.

"Indeed, for the sake of protecting them alone, I have proclaimed this Tantra. Likewise, there was a powerful and high-souled devotee of Viṣṇu named Aṃśa Sātvata, who was devoted to charity and the best among those skilled in the science of archery (dhanurveda). Following the words of Nārada, he became intent on the worship of Vāsudeva and set forth the scripture that had been heard from the Kuṇḍas, Golakas, and others. Renowned by his name, this excellent and great scripture called the Sātvata, which brings benefit to the Kuṇḍas and others, has come into being. Thus [it is said].

Thus he spoke concerning the Sātvata Tantra, by knowing which one becomes a partaker of liberation; wherein the Vaiṣṇava sacrament for women, Śūdras, and servants is prescribed. The Lord of Kamalā spoke the Pañcarātra, Bhāgavata, and the Tantra known as Vaikhānasa, intended for those who have fallen away from the Vedas. "O Śāṇḍilya, my dear one, by resorting to that very Tantra, you have performed my worship; I am highly pleased with your austerity. O Śāṇḍilya, even though it was through a wrong path, you have performed my worship."

"Therefore, after a long time, you shall go upon the path of the gods"—such are the passages from the *Kaumāra*, *Bhāgavata*, *Vāsiṣṭha*, *Laiṅga*, and other scriptures that disparage the Pañcarātra. Conversely, there are passages from the *Mahābhārata* cited in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) that praise the Pañcarātra, such as: "This [work] has been extracted like butter from curds by churning the intellect with the churning-stick from the vast narrative called the *Bhārata*, which consists of a hundred thousand verses. Furthermore: "O best of the twice-born, having been thus entreated by them in the past, I..."

I composed the *Saṃhitā* known as the *Niśvāsa*, joined with the Vedic ritual (*vedakriyā*) and the Sāmas. Within it, the lineages of Vābhravya and Śāṇḍila became absorbed; they were considered to have committed only minor offenses and thus became the *vailālikas*. O twice-born ones, those [others] were deluded by me alone, who knew the future, for in the *Niśvāsasaṃhitā* the measure is merely one hundred thousand [verses]. That indeed is the Pāśupata initiation, and that is the Pāśupata Yoga. For whatever else arises here outside of this Vedic path [is not true].
This fierce [text], which is purified by ritual purity, is to be understood through the sequence of faith; those men who, in the Kali age, subsist upon Rudra as professional bards.

They should be known as the Ucchiṣṭa-Rudras; I do not abide within them. For due to the curse of Gautama, there will arise secondary twice-born ones among them. Among them, those who follow right conduct and are devoted to my teaching shall indeed go to heaven and liberation; this is certainly a settled truth. But those bards who shall go about defiling my lineage—twice-born ones already scorched by the fire of Gautama’s wrath—shall, by my word, fall again into hell; no deliberation is required on this point.

Indeed, I previously established this auspicious Pāśupata vow—more secret than the secret, subtle, the essence of the Vedas—for the sake of liberation. This Pāśupata Yoga is to be practiced by those seeking release; it must be constantly observed by those free from desire while covered in ashes. Such is the Vedic revelation. [The path of] Vāma, Pāśupata, and Soma...

"The plough and the Bhairava [cult]—these are not to be practiced; they are declared to be outside the Vedas, as is anything else. In such statements, having first established the distinction between what is Vedic and what is non-Vedic, the status of certain specific Pāśupata Āgamas as being outside the Vedas is demonstrated. This being the case, regarding the Pāśupata and Pañcarātra [traditions]...

If it is asked, "What is the discrepancy? it is said: regarding those portions that do not contradict the Vedas, all [systems] possess authority; however, since even in Sāṅkhya and Yoga the view that *prakṛti* is non-Brāhmaṇic—which contradicts the Vedas—is held, they lack authority in that respect. As for Pāśupata, the Śaiva Āgama is also twofold: *śrauta* (Vedic) and *smārta* (traditional). The latter is remembered as being independent, tenfold, and furthermore eighteenfold; it is established in many ways through divisions such as the *Kāmika* and others.

"Another [tantra], however, consisting of the essence of the Śruti, has an extent of one hundred crores; therein the supreme Pāśupata vow and knowledge are expounded. Thus, because the independence of the Siddhānta Tantras—comprising twenty-eight divisions beginning with the Kāmika—is established, their non-Vedic character is proven. However, in the case of the Pañcarātra, such a claim is not seen in the Purāṇas, which are free from the suspicion of interpolated passages intended to disparage it; therefore, its authority is established everywhere. For this very reason, regarding Vāsudeva, the author of the Pañcarātra, [he is recognized] right at the beginning of the Vedas...

The author of the *Kalpataru*, remaining impartial, has demonstrated that [the validity of the Pāñcarātra] is not already established by the section concerning Yoga and other systems—because [Patañjali and others] are accepted as omniscient while still being living beings, and because the Pāñcarātra, like the Buddha’s teachings in the Purāṇas, was composed by the Lord for the purpose of deluding [those of inferior intellect]. Enough of this excessive discussion. As for the phrase "by others, however," etc., it means the existence of a specific excellence in the form of particular effects, namely, the collection, maintenance, and creation [of the world] belonging to Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of origination.

Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the Bhāvaprakāśikā, a commentary on the Śrutiprakāśikā, composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads.
The total number of topics (adhikaraṇas) is 53; the total number of sūtras is 206.

The phrase "this is the meaning" connects with the subsequent section as "this is the meaning" [of the word] *saṃgati*. Regarding the subject of the effect (*kārya*), although the doubt concerning the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Vedāntas—due to mutual contradictions—is raised as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the sections on ether (*viyat*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*) just as by the opponents, this is because [the sūtras] are solely intent upon resolving the contradiction regarding the modes of being effects; nevertheless, following the raising of prima facie arguments such as the non-origination of ether, the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the scriptural texts on the origination of ether and so forth with their own literal meanings is established according to the maxim of "driving in a pillar" (*sthūṇānikhanana*).

The sense is this: once [the Sāṃkhya position] has been refuted by means of contradiction, the counter-objection regarding contradiction raised against the Vedāntins—which was merely revolving in the minds of the Sāṃkhyas—is also cast far away; for this very reason, the connection with the chapter on "Contradiction" (Virodhādhikaraṇa) is also established. The intent of the Sūtra is to provide an exposition of its own purport, and not to demonstrate that the word *śruti* has the meaning of "hearing"; such is the sense. This is the natural force of the mention of *śruti*.

The sense is that [the reason] might be considered secondary (*gauṇatva*), because being a property of a word does not constitute being a property of a cognized object. To avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding partlessness—which is common to both eternal and non-eternal qualities—it is stated that [the subject] must be a substance (*dravyatvāt*). Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it is impossible for its absence to ever enter the intellect; for a negation such as "there is no ether here" would be contradictory. This is because, in the *Vaibhāṣika* section of the *Sūtras*—"And because there is no distinction in space"—it is stated that space is the locus known through the cognition "here."

Because it has been established; nor is the reason (hetu) ineffective, for the sense is that an impartite and all-pervading entity cannot have an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) or the like determined. "Contrary to the reasoning found in the Taittirīyaka" means contrary to the reasoning contained within the Taittirīyaka [Upaniṣad]. "The Śruti serves as the proof for the fact that 'it exists'" means that the Śruti serves as the proof for this meaning, namely, that "it exists. "It is precisely the cause for generating the cognition of its origination" means that being beyond the scope of other means of knowledge is consistent with its being known through Śruti.

"By the mere fact of being established through perception" means by the mere fact of being established through another means of knowledge (*māna*). "Either perception or inference" means either the word [itself] or the inference that "sound is dependent on a substance distinct from non-substances. "And another inference" means another inference such as "space is eternal because it is a partless substance."

Now, one might object: if the ether (ākāśa), which has been uninterrupted since the beginning of creation, is made the subject of the inference, then—since that ether is knowable solely through scripture (śruti)—there would be a contradiction with the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇavirodha*) when proving its non-origination. However, if only the ether within the stomach is made the subject, what possibility is there for a sublation of the means of knowledge apprehending the subject? Anticipating this unease, [the author] says: "In the case of the great elements and so forth, because of the reason of being partless. The phrase "because of the reason of being partless" means "because of the reason of being a substance devoid of parts. And the phrase "and because of the mention of a particular kind of conjunction" implies that there is no conjunction for that which is partless.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the reason "because it is a substance that is omnipresent," when it is stated "because of omnipresence," since in the Nyāya system knowledge produced by proximity such as "knowability" (prameyatva) has omnipresence due to its having everything as its object, one must state "because it is a substance" in order to avoid a lack of pervasion (vyabhicāra) in that case. Regarding the statement "One becomes a Brāhmaṇa through austerity; one should desire to know the Brāhmaṇa through austerity," the word *brāhmaṇa* is used in its primary sense [in the first sentence], whereas in the supplementary passage "Austerity is the Brāhmaṇa," it is used in a secondary (gauṇa) sense because austerity is a means to the knowledge of the Brāhmaṇa.

"Because there is an absence of being either primary or secondary [objects]," as stated in the passage, "If it be argued that it is due to the connection (anvaya), it would be so because of the restriction,"—in the cases of *annamaya* and the others, the word "Self" (*ātman*) was not used figuratively through the notion of the lower self, but rather precisely through the notion of the Supreme Self. By the entry into each respective layer, as expressed in "He has entered within as the ruler of people," He possesses the nature of the Self by virtue of being the controller. There, in the case of the *prāṇamaya*, the notion of the Supreme Self arose merely through its being the inner self of the *annamaya*; then, upon seeing what was even more internal than that, the notion of the Supreme Self arose there as well, while in the previous instance it had ceased.

Since no other interval, such as a moment (*kṣaṇa*) or the like, is heard of that which is [described], the cognition of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the cognition of the Self (*ātman*) are firmly established therein; and since, as previously stated, the word *ātman* was used there with reference exclusively to the Supreme Self, and because it will be explained that in all the subsequent sections (*paryāya*) the word *ātman* refers only to the Supreme Self and is not figurative (*aupacārika*), by that same principle, in the passage "Food is the Brahman" (*annaṃ brahma*), the word *brahman* also does not possess a figurative sense, because it is employed through the cognition of Brahman, just as [in the previous cases].

The meaning is that the word "silver" used with the cognition of silver in the case of mother-of-pearl is not figurative; likewise, the sense is that in both cases there is a "sublation of the convention" (*samayabhaṅga*), which means that a breach of the rule consisting of the contradiction between the two functions—namely, the hearing of the suffix and the repetition [of the stem]—must be effected. The intention is that non-difference is intended precisely as something to be accomplished.

Now, it might be argued: "Even though eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*) and so forth are not effects, just as there is no contradiction with the *pratijñā* [regarding the creation of all], there does not follow a similar lack of contradiction with the *pratijñā* regarding the fact that space (*ākāśa*) is not an effect; nor can it be said that in passages such as 'That by which the unheard becomes heard,' the words 'unheard' and so on refer to something other than eternal glory, because in the subsequent passage, 'In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone,' the state of being prior to that is presented as being merely the 'Being' (*sanmātra*) of that very thing which is the object of the word 'this' (*idam*). [Response: This is not so. For even if eternal glory and the like are not effects, the *pratijñā* is not contradicted because they are included within the category of "all" (*sarvam*). However, in the case of space, its non-origination would indeed contradict the *pratijñā*. Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that the words "unheard" and so on do not refer to eternal glory, because in the subsequent passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," the fact that the object of the word "this" was previously nothing but "Being" is established. Thus, the word "this" refers to the entire universe, including eternal glory, and since space is also included therein, its non-origination would contradict the *pratijñā*. Moreover, the word "this" (*idam*) denotes proximity, and since eternal glory is not proximate to the time of the initial creation, it cannot be the referent of "this. Therefore, the claim that the word "this" excludes eternal glory is untenable. Consequently, the objection that the non-origination of space does not contradict the *pratijñā* is refuted. Furthermore, the word "this" (*idam*) is used here to denote the totality of the universe, and since the word "all" (*sarvam*) is subsequently used in reference to that same totality, it follows that space is also included within "all. Thus, the non-origination of space contradicts the *pratijñā*. Therefore, the conclusion remains that space is an effect. Finally, the word "this" (*idam*) is employed here to indicate the totality of the universe, and since the word "all" (*sarvam*) is subsequently used in reference to that same totality, it follows that space is also included within "all. Thus, the non-origination of space contradicts the *pratijñā*. Therefore, the conclusion remains that space is an effect. Finally, the word "this" (*idam*) is employed here to indicate the totality of the universe, and since the word "all" (*sarvam*) is subsequently used in reference to that same totality, it follows that space is also included within "all. Thus, the non-origination of space contradicts the *pratijñā*. Therefore, the conclusion remains that space is an effect.
