Since the word "this" (idam) refers to all things presented by means of valid cognition such as perception, there is no basis for its not including eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*); otherwise, supersensible objects would not fall within the scope of the claim that [the Lord] possesses all knowledge. Consequently, one must either abandon the eternity of eternal glory or accept the eternity of space (*ākāśa*) as well.

No, for this objection must be resolved by everyone; otherwise, since space (*ākāśa*)—like ignorance (*avidyā*)—is beginninglessly superimposed, let it also be unproduced (*ajanya*), as it is possible even while being non-different from Brahman, just like that [ignorance]. Since such a resolution must be sought, and because it is stated in the *Kalpataru* under the section "Likewise the Vital Breaths" (*tathā prāṇa*) that if the vital breaths were beginninglessly superimposed like ignorance, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of their being perceived even in deep sleep due to the lack of mediation in the Witness (*sākṣin*), the same logic applies here as well regarding deep sleep.

It should not be said that this leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of being perceived [as an object]. For it is logically possible, like the Lord (*īśvara*) who exists from beginningless time; and since the non-perception [of the Lord] is possible due to the ignorance (*avidyā*) residing in other individual souls (*jīva*), one must accept that [the Lord's manifestation] is produced by ignorance on the strength of evidence that cannot be established otherwise. This is not the case with space (*ākāśa*), for in its case there exists only the scriptural statement regarding its production. If, then, this is the same even in the present case—that is, in the eternal realm (*nityavibhūti*)—[then the objection fails].

The phrase "of the distinctions between reasons regarding intermediate objects of proof" means that in passages such as "If it be said 'no, because of the designation of the non-existent,' we say no, because of another attribute, from the remainder of the sentence, from logic, and from another word," the reasons contained in uncompound words are seen to be presented within a single sūtra despite having intermediate objects of proof. Furthermore, the fact that reasons contained in compound words are presented within a single sūtra is also observed in relation to the ultimate object of proof, as in "Upon the exhaustion of [the fruit of] what was done, one possessing residual karma [returns], according to scripture and tradition, in the same manner and not so," and so forth; this is the intended meaning.

And this should be understood as a case where the word *ca* (and) is absent; therefore, one should not raise an objection on the grounds that in such passages as "Because of perception [of speech] in the mind, and because of the word [of scripture]" (*vāṅmanasi darśanācchabdācca*) and "Because of the teaching of its taking up [the elements], and because of the teaching of its departure" (*upādānādvihāropadeśācca*), even though the reasons are expressed by non-compounded words, they are nevertheless seen to be presented within a single sūtra as part of the ultimate probandum. Now, an objection may be raised: having taken for granted that [ether] is an effect (*kāryatva*), how can origination—denoted by the term "division" (*vibhāga*)—be established?

If it is argued that there is dispute only regarding the state of being an effect denoted by the term *vikāra* (modification), whereas otherwise there is no dispute even regarding origination (*utpatti*), we say no; for in the *Chāndogya*, the absence of any statement regarding origination in certain cases of modification is not a fault, as its purpose is to demonstrate the underlying principle (*gati*). The phrase "others, however" (*pare tu*) and so forth means that since [the mere contradiction] lacks the status of being the ultimate thesis (*paramasādhya*), and because a mere contradiction is not in itself undesirable, it cannot serve as the basis for the conclusion of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It is not merely a contradiction that was proposed as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), nor is there a reading suggesting that the position of a certain partial proponent of origination (*utpatti-siddhānty-ekadeśin*) was adopted; for although it is stated in the *Kalpataru*—up until the conclusion of the chapter—that first the prima facie view is presented as invalidity due to contradiction, then an explanation according to the partial proponent's view follows, and finally the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is shown, nevertheless, because that text is a modern work, it should be understood that this point has not been raised therein.

Is it not the case that Vācaspati [stated] that the introduction [of the ether] as a cause is untenable? For even though there is a scriptural text regarding the origination of the ether in the *Taittirīyaka*, nevertheless, because it contradicts other means of valid cognition and because it contradicts many other scriptural texts, it must be taken in a figurative sense; and therefore—

The meaning of the phrase "because of the absence of scriptural statement" (*aśruteḥ*) is precisely the absence of a scriptural statement regarding the primary sense [of ether]. Consequently, if one were to argue that the four sūtras—"Because of the absence of scriptural statement regarding ether" (*viyadaśruteḥ*), "Because of the impossibility of a secondary sense" (*gauṇyasambhavāt*), "And because of the word" (*śabdāt*), and "And there may be [a difference], as in the case of the word 'Brāhmaṇa' applied to a single person" (*syāccaikasya brāhmaṇaśabdavat*)—constitute the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie view) representing the opinion of a certain portion of the Siddhāntin (the proponent), and that this has been explained as follows: "In the Taittirīyaka there is a text teaching the priority of the creation of ether, while in the Chāndogya there is a text teaching the priority of the creation of fire; therefore, there is a mutual contradiction between the two scriptural statements"—then it is true that it has been so explained, but that [explanation]...

It should be understood that [this objection] has already been refuted by the very interpretation favored by Śaṅkara’s commentary (Bhāṣya), as it is not something that needs to be separately addressed. Now, one might argue: since immortality is stated generally for both [Vāyu and Ākāśa] in the passage, "Vāyu and the intermediate space—this is immortal," and then Vāyu is specifically mentioned again, "This deity, namely Vāyu, is never-setting," it is known from this repetition that Vāyu’s immortality is intended; for according to the maxim, "In the case of repetition, there is an abundance of meaning."

It is more appropriate to maintain that this is simply an *atideśādhikaraṇa* (an extended application) for the purpose of removing further doubts, rather than treating it as a separate section for the sake of subsequent topics; for since there is no partiality toward any specific alternative therein, one should have stated either, "From this [fire], light [is produced], for so he says," or "The ego-sense [is produced] in the same way, for so he says."

If it is argued that this is not very appropriate because the *Bhāṣya* itself will later state that even the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth, are objects within that same locus, and therefore the formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of what follows, [we reply: True; however, the previous [rule] applies only to those things common to the Great Principle, ego-consciousness, ether, air, and so forth.

Even though [the objection] has been refuted, nevertheless, considering that it is easy to introduce the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by clearly demonstrating that creation is preceded by the volition to become manifold—as in the text, "It thought; It created fire"—he intends to formulate the aphorism, "Fire [originates] from this, for thus the Scripture says. To that end, he extends the same [refutation] to the first [element, ether] as well, stating, "By this, the opinion regarding air is explained. Therefore, we perceive that there is no fault whatsoever. Thus ends the section on ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*).

The statement that [the Lord] is "embodied" is figurative, based on His entry immediately after creation. The designation "body" is made merely because of the rule of occasional entry, and not with the intention of [His] supporting [the body] for as long as it exists and so forth, by which [the status of being a body] would be primary. This is the sense.

If it is objected: "Since the logical principle is the same for fire as it is for water—namely, 'From that [water], likewise, [fire] was born' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3)—for what purpose was a separate aphorism composed for water? We reply: No. Even though the portion "was born likewise" is common to both, one must provide a resolution by showing that regarding the subject of fire, the statements "It thought" and "It created fire" can be established even through a traditional succession of interpretations.

The opponent maintains that the act of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) must be understood as figurative, either by following the word *tejas* (fire/heat) heard first in the passage, "In [the waters] it saw... it created the waters," or by the principle stated in the Sūtra, "But there is designation of the presiding deities because of distinction and subsequent connection," since the complementary portion of the text states, "Therefore, wherever one feels heat or perspires, it is from fire alone that those waters were produced."

Because there exist distinct modes of dissolution (*nirvāha*), the composition of a separate *sūtra* is purposeful; nor should it be argued that a separate *sūtra* for earth is redundant. It should be understood that even in that case, a separate *sūtra* was formulated for the sake of resolving the contradiction between the two uses of the word "earth" (*pārthiva*).

The meaning is that he states this because the fact of having that [Brahman] as its body is based on scripture; the intention is that the causality of that which has that as its body is scriptural. This should be understood because, in the passage "He who rules the earth from within," it is heard that the capacity to produce effects belongs only to the entity presided over by Him.

Regarding the statement, "For them too, the establishment of creation preceded by [divine] reflection [is proven]," some hold that the introduction to this section is as follows: they consider it improper to state that the fact of having the Supreme Self as one's body (*taccharīrakatva*)—which was previously established in the earlier text as being necessary for the justification of creation preceded by reflection—is itself intended for the purpose of establishing that very creation preceded by reflection; and therefore, they believe the introduction should simply be: "And he shows a scriptural passage demonstrating that even the *mahat* and other principles have the Supreme Self as their body, in the Subāla Upaniṣad."

Regarding the phrase "because of the cognition of a sequence in the form of immediate succession" (*ānantaryarūpakramapratīteḥ*): although sequence (*krama*) consists precisely in priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*), it does not consist in immediate succession (*ānantarya*) characterized by non-intervention (*avyavadhāna*).

Nevertheless, since there is no contradiction in the sense that a sequence characterized by a specific anterior-posterior order—distinguished by the absence of any interval in the form of an *ānantarya* (immediate succession)—is perceived, one need not claim that such sequence must necessarily be mediated by action (*kriyā*). For if that were the case, the phrase "therefore [it] is born" would be understood to mean "from [the Self] intent upon creation"; and consequently, since the intentness toward creation and the emergence of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are sequential, this applies by extension to the body (*kārya*) and the instruments (*karaṇa*) which are their substrata. Thus, there is no fault.

The phrase "with the intention of [showing] positive concomitance" means that the intended sequence is not the one found in the passage, "From this the vital breath is born, from that the mind and all the sense organs. This is the underlying thought.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "it is designated by breaking [the connection]," in this view, from the root *bhañj* (meaning 'to crush' or 'to break') with the suffix *ktin*, we have *bhaktiḥ*, which means 'breaking'; thus the sense is that it is employed by way of breaking. As for the phrase "from the preceding thesis, starting from the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)," since in the sūtra "The earth" (*pṛthivī*), only the origination of the earth is the point to be established (*sādhya*), and because there [in that context] the subject matter, form, and other words [are present], here...

The sense is that although [the earth] is the cause of the word's denotation of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), it is not the cause for the production of the earth itself. Furthermore, because it has already been stated that [the activity of elements] is based on the entry of a presiding conscious being (*abhimānicetana*), the implication is that there is no inherent consciousness (*svataścaitanya*) [in the elements]. If it is argued: "But did not Vācaspati initiate an inquiry as to whether the deities who preside over fire and the other elements proceed toward the creation of the gross elements only when presided over by the Supreme Lord, or even without being so presided over?"—this is not so, because such a view contradicts his own commentary, and because [the question] is rendered superfluous by [the Sūtra] *parāttu tacchruteḥ* (BrSū 2.3.41) and other passages. Therefore, [the elements do not act] independently.

It should be understood that the refutation has been stated exactly as it appears in the commentary (bhāṣya) according to what was heard. [The objection] that "because there is no reason for the word 'one' (eka) to be intended" is not valid; nor is the intellect (buddhi) denoted by the word "vital breath" (prāṇa). For the intellect is a state of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) that serves as the cause of certainty, whereas the mind (manas) is a state of the internal organ that serves as the cause of doubt; thus, there is a distinction between the two. In this context, based on the etymological derivation "that by which one knows" (jñāyate anena), the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) used in the Sūtra includes both the intellect—denoted by the term "vital breath"—and the sense organs, while the word "mind" (manas) refers to the mind itself.

And it must be stated that such a perception is possible; the sense is that there is no evidence for such a hypothesis. Regarding whether the soul's origination from the Supreme Self exists or not—as with ether and the rest—the author will state this in a subsequent sūtra. However, he has stated here [in this sūtra] that the soul’s origination and dissolution, which depend upon the body, do not exist in a gross form; thus he refers to what was stated in the commentary of the other [school]: "here, those depending on the body."

Since there is no possibility of suspecting that birth and destruction belong to the living being (jīva) rather than the body—given that names such as "Devadatta" pertain to the living being and not to the body, for it would be illogical to perform a *śrāddha* rite for a body by its [the living being's] name;...

Therefore, for one who considers the designation "Devadatta has died" or "has been born" to be primary, this constitutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is clearly stated in the *Vācaspatya*, which—taking the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) as established—presents as the prima facie view that the soul, distinct from the body, possesses an arising and perishing that conforms to the arising and perishing of the body, and then establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Likewise, in the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya*, it says: "If the soul were perishable and followed the body," and "only by taking the distinction between them as established does the soul arise when the body arises."

If it is asked, "How can this be so, given that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) understands [the text] to mean 'when that [body] perishes, he himself also perishes,' and since the very same point—that the gross birth and dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*) do not exist—is what is being restated in the Bhāṣya by the words 'dependent on the body' (*dehāśrayau*), which also conveys the meaning 'birth and destruction dependent on the body'? [The answer is: True. However, if one were to assume that the nature of the *jīva* itself undergoes birth and destruction following the body, there would be a redundancy with the sūtra "The self [is eternal], because of scripture" (*nātmā śruter*). Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "dependent on the body" (*dehāśrayau*) must be accepted exactly as it is heard [in the text]: namely, that birth and destruction are dependent upon the body.

This should be understood as having been stated with the intention that there is no other possible state [for the soul]. As for the passage beginning with "Others, however," and so forth, the phrase "and of the person in the state of dissolution" means "and of the aspect of the enjoyer in the state of dissolution. Regarding the phrase "of this sequence of recitation," the meaning is that your preferred sequence of the Sūtra's recitation is not established anywhere.

"Having made the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣīkṛtya) that there is either the origination of all [elements] or the non-origination of all"—this is the meaning of "having made the prima facie argument. And because of the usage "and space itself in the mind": the sense is that if, in the scriptural passage "from this it is born," the word *manas* refers to the mind, then the dissolution of space into the senses, of the senses into the mind, and of the mind into the principle called *mahat* (the Great One), which is denoted by the term *prāṇa*, is being described.

The meaning is: "Because a sequential intention is observed regarding ether and the others," that is, because a sequential intention is observed in the subsequent sentence, "Space, wind, fire, water... The meaning is that here there is merely a mention of the categories [of elements], since there is no perception of an intention regarding the sequence of speech and so forth. The meaning of "born from the ego-sense" (ahaṅkāra) is that from the ego-sense [the elements] such as space arise.

The sense is that while [the elements] are born directly, the senses are born through their own respective doors (svādi-dvārā). Therefore, there is no contradiction; for, in accordance with the Śruti passage, "Higher than the senses are the objects," the contradiction in the statement, "All the senses, as well as its own [self], air, fire, water... has already been resolved. Furthermore, between the *ahaṅkāra* denoted by the word "mind" (*manas*) and the Great Principle (*mahat*), [the text speaks of] that which is denoted by the words "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "discriminative knowledge" (*vijñāna*), namely: "But higher than the mind is the intellect; know the intellect to be the charioteer; but he who has discriminative knowledge as his charioteer... and so forth.

The meaning is that there is a contradiction because [the mind] would be perceived as a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*). The intention is that the relationship of superior and inferior heard in the scripture, "But the intellect (*buddhi*) is higher than the mind (*manas*)," must be explained in some way or another [if the mind were not a separate entity]. If it is argued that "space (*nabhas*) and the others would be the primal causes (*prakṛti*)," then the intention is that this contradicts the scriptural statement, "There are eight primal causes and sixteen transformations. The phrase "the mind is indeed the sense organ" means that the mind is precisely the internal sense organ (*antarindriya*), and not the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

Nor should it be doubted how the mind (*manas*), as a specific sense organ, can be superior to the objects that were established as superior to the senses in the statement, "The objects are superior to the senses," since superiority can be established in a different manner; this is the intended meaning. As for the phrase "lest there be a violation of propriety" (*aucityabhaṅgaprasaṅgāt*), the meaning is that it is more appropriate to qualify the word *ātman* itself with the attribute "greatness."

The meaning is: if it is argued that because this composition establishes objects consisting of primordial matter (prakṛti), mahat, and ahaṅkāra—which are contradictory to the [intended] meaning—it is logical that the section concerning "mastery" (vaśīkārya-prakaraṇa) is sublated; [the response is: "by the previous section," which means by the section on inference (ānumānika-adhikaraṇa).
Thus ends the section concerning the superiority of splendor.

One must consider whether a fixed relationship between property (*dharma*) and its substrate (*dharmin*) is possible, and whether, in relation to the substrate, it is possible for a larger locus to possess the status of a property; this is because this point must necessarily be addressed as it is established in the Sūtras:

"There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood," or "Or [it is so] because of the quality, as in the world. The meaning is that since it is impossible to perceive or fail to perceive objects at a distance—and thus since the all-pervading nature (*vibhutva*) of the Self must be asserted through the possibility of experiencing [sensations] in all limbs—there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the Self, being the substratum of eternal cognition, would have to be perceived as eternal.

In the commentary, although it has been established that [the Self] is the knower—neither being mere consciousness nor having an insentient nature—the exclusion of insentiency is not yet fully achieved, because the Naiyāyikas accept that [the Self] is insentient; nevertheless...

It should be understood that the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and because [the soul] is not manifested to the full extent" (*yāvadātmābhāvitvācca*) is stated with the intention of establishing a proof. Regarding what was stated in the Commentary—that if the status of being a knower were inherent (*svābhāvika*)—one might ask: how does the refutation of omnipresence (*vibhutva*) serve [the argument] if the status of being a knower is inherent? For omnipresence is not an obstacle to the mere fact of having an inherent capacity for knowing, according to the logic set forth in the Sūtra: "If [the soul were all-pervading], there would be constant perception and non-perception. [This is so] because of the omnipresence...

Because it contradicts all positions—including those of the Siddhāntins—by asserting that [the Self] is the substratum of adventitious knowledge, has the nature of knowledge, and possesses innate knowership, for that very reason, even the status of being in the same *adhikaraṇa* (section) as the sūtras beginning with "utkrāntigatyāgatīnām" is not tenable; for the demonstration of atomicity (*aṇutva*) is useless for establishing innate knowership, and if one were to resort to a single *adhikaraṇa* by assuming some incidental utility, then [the sūtra] "kartā śāstrārthavattvāt" [would be rendered irrelevant].

Why should there not be a single locus for the arguments establishing both the nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and the nature of being an agent (*kartṛtva*)? If the refutation of agency is useful for establishing the nature of being a knower, then those arguments intended for that refutation ought to be placed in one and the same section. Thus, having concluded the discussion on the nature of being a knower with the following [sūtras]: "He is a knower for this very reason; there is a distinction [from the body] as in the case of smell; because of the separate teaching; the designation [of Him as 'agent'] is due to His having that as His essence; and because it persists as long as the self exists, there is no fault; because we see [it so]; and because, like manhood and the like, there is a manifestation of what already exists."

Regarding the passages concerning the soul's departure, its movement [to other worlds], and its return; and regarding the two subsequent [sections] where it is said that the soul is not atomic because of the scriptural teaching to that effect—[the reply is]: this is not so, because of the context of the other [passages], and because of the direct statement [of its small size] and the measurement [given]. There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood paste; if it is argued that there is a difference in its location [due to the pervasiveness of its qualities], we say no, because of our own admission [that the soul resides in the heart], or because of its quality [of being minute], as in the world. If it is argued that the arrangement of the Sūtras should have been "nityopalabdhiḥ" (there would be eternal perception), it is replied: what was stated—that omnipresence does not contradict the soul's essential nature as a knower—is true; nevertheless, for the sake of the opponent...

Since such a misconception could arise, it is necessary to refute it; as for the claim that the sūtra "The [Self] is the agent because of its being the subject of the scriptures" (JS 3.2.40) shares the same locus [as the preceding sūtras], therein "knowership" (*jñātṛtva*) indeed means being the substratum of knowledge, but not agency (*kartṛtva*), because the suffix [-tṛ] has the sense of merely being a substratum. Or, even if there were some utility [in this interpretation], one cannot conclude a common locus on this basis alone, since that is not intended by the author of the Sūtras. In the present context, however, the sūtras establishing knowership and atomicity are interspersed among one another.

From this very fact of their being instruments (*karaṇa*), it is determined that the author of the Sūtras intended them to have a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇya*). Otherwise, according to the method you have described, the Sūtras refuting "largeness" (*mahattva*) would have been arranged in a confused manner for the sake of ease of understanding; therefore, everything is consistent. "When he [the soul] fully absorbs those subtle elements of light..."

He states the reason for not citing the scriptural passage regarding the manner of departure as taught by others—namely, "Taking the essence of the body, it departs from here and returns again to its place"—with the words: "immediately after the word 'departure'. The meaning is as follows: in the commentary, [the phrase] "by way of being of the nature of moving out of the body" is used because "departure" (utkrāmaṇa) is conventionally established, like a crawling away, specifically in the context of death. And that is possible even for one who is not actually moving, through the cessation of identification with the body upon the exhaustion of karma. This is because "going" and "coming," which are firmly established as movements, are essentially the nature of an agent.

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that after extracting a substance similar to an atom (*aṇu*), the soul (*jīva*) is heard to possess that measure; and "extraction" (*uddharaṇa*) means separation. In the phrase "of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair," the extraction of the part from the whole is heard—that is, it is declared and demonstrated—and for this reason, since both the extraction and the hearing (the scriptural statement) have the same agent (the Śruti), the identity of their agents is established; this is how it should be understood. "The tip of an awl" (*ārāgra*) refers to the point of a needle that pierces leather. [Objection: But was it not said that "knowledge alone is the Self"? [As in: "The person is the knowing self" (*vijñānātmā puruṣa*).
The meaning is: "in such scriptural passages as these."
"By a word denoting that which is qualified" means by a word denoting cognition as its qualifier.

Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else the restriction of one or the other. How could there be the consequence of constant perception? How could there be the consequence of constant non-perception? Or how could there be the consequence of both?

Regarding the claim that the self is perceived somewhere—namely, that the self is perceived within the body and likewise not perceived outside—it is established by the universal experience of all people that "I am right here in this house, not knowing. This [experience] is not tenable under either of the two positions. For, if the self were omniscient and all-pervading, would it have the nature of being both perceivable and imperceptible, or the nature of being exclusively perceivable, or the nature of being exclusively imperceptible?

In the first case, there would be perception within the locus of the burner and non-perception outside it; in the second case, there would be perception everywhere; in the third case, there would be non-perception [everywhere]. It is not tenable to establish a distinction such that the nature of the burner is perceptible within its own locus but imperceptible elsewhere, for it is impossible to say that the very same thing has its own form in one place and lacks it in another. This same refutation should be understood to apply to the position that [the self] is insentient (*jaḍa*).

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "by being always connected with all instruments," one might object: "Is this not the same even in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*)? For the infinite, eternal, and liberated qualities of consciousness (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) exist everywhere, and since these qualities of consciousness are related to all selves, it is impossible to determine from among them, 'this is his,' and 'that is his. How then is this so? If you ask this, the answer is: No, for according to the principle, "But because of scripture, [it is so], for [the Veda] has sound as its source," one must accept a matter established by scripture exactly as it is presented in that scripture.

This is logical, for the intent here is that otherwise it would not be logical. The point is that even the word *jña* (knower) does not denote an individual substance (*vyakti*), because the suffix *ka* in the rule "*igupadhajñā-prī-kiraḥ kaḥ*" is taught to have the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) by the rule "*kartari kṛt*". The phrase "only as the unmodified Brahman" should be construed as follows: because [Brahman] exists in the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) through an adjunct (*upādhi*) while remaining unevolved (*anutpanna*), it is only the unmodified Brahman [that is meant].

The meaning is that because Brahman has consciousness as its essential nature (*caitanyasvarūpa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), which is non-different from it, also has consciousness as its essential nature. The phrase "introduced as the subject to be established" means that it was introduced as the subject to be established in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).

"Because it directly possesses the state of being the means of proof for the nature of knowledge as such"—this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa); for even mediately, there is no status as a means of proof. For otherwise, regarding the non-difference from Brahman—which establishes non-origination—there would follow either the [absurd] consequence of both eternal perception and non-perception of the nature of consciousness, or the restriction of one or the other. [Objection: Let eternal perception follow; how could there be the consequence of eternal non-perception, or how could there be the consequence of both?

By the statement "there is the status of being a means" (*sādhakatvamasti*), it should also be understood that there is an indirect utility (*upayoga*) for non-origination (*anutpatti*). "Its nature as knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpatva*) means the nature of the Brahman as knowledge. "The ultimate probandum" (*paramasādhya*) means the nature of the consciousness of the living being (*jīvacaitanya*). "And of the identity of the meaning of the base" (*prakṛtyarthasāmyasya*) means because the identity of meaning between the verbal root and the word, or between the word *śruti* and the pronoun *etat*, is made known by the scripture (*śruti*).

One might object: "Is it not improper for the word *śruteḥ* from the preceding sūtra and this word *ataḥ* in the present sūtra to have the same meaning, since the scriptural authority (*śruti*) proving non-origination and the scriptural authority proving omniscience have different meanings? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By virtue of fitness" (*yogyatāvaśāt*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and because of the absence of the three delays," the sense is that in the opponent's view, the three delays have already been established previously by such arguments as "the non-difference from Brahman which proves that [delay]."

The intended meaning is that the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-dharmatva*) is devoid of annihilation; thus, in the term *anucchitti-dharma*, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*. Although the syntactical connection with "from them" (*tābhyaḥ*) is established, since the word "hence" (*ataḥ*) refers back—by means of the pronoun "hence"—to those very Śrutis mentioned in the preceding Sūtra by the word "from them," those same Śrutis continue to apply even in the Sūtra concerning departure (*utkrānti*). Consequently, [the question arises] regarding the departure, the going, and the returning.

Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other. How could there be the consequence of perpetual perception? How could there be the consequence of perpetual non-perception? Or how could there be the consequence of both?

There is no fault because the meaning of "from the scriptures" (*śrutibhyaḥ*) is possible; nevertheless, since "from them" (*tābhyaḥ*) requires a substantive, the supply of the word "from the scriptures" (*śrutibhyaḥ*) is also necessarily required. Therefore, the sense here is that there too, two words—*tābhyaḥ* and *śrutibhyaḥ*—must be supplied. The phrase "futility of the operation of the causal factors" means the futility of the operations of the eyes and so forth, given that [consciousness] is of the nature of the living self's consciousness itself.

The meaning of "because of the scriptural statement regarding the identity of the meanings of the bases" (*prakṛtyarthasāmyasya śruteḥ*) is that the identity of meaning between the word-base and the word "this" (*ataḥ*), as well as between the two words "this" (*etacchabda*), is being made known by the scripture. Now, one might object: it is not logical for the word "because of the scripture" (*śruteḥ*) found in the previous sūtra and this word "because of" (*ataḥ*) found in the present sūtra to have the same meaning, since the scripture cited as proving non-origination has a different meaning from the scripture cited as proving sentience. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by virtue of fitness" (*yogyatāvaśāt*).

The sense is that, according to the opponent's view, the three delays have already been established previously by such arguments as "because there is no difference from the Brāhmaṇa who provides that [instruction]. Regarding the phrase *anucchittidharmā*, the intended meaning is that it possesses the quality of knowledge which is not subject to annihilation; thus, the sense is that this is a *bahuvrīhi* within a *bahuvrīhi*.

The connection [of the word] "to them" (*tābhyaḥ*) is established; however, the intention of the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) is that the words "to them" in the preceding sūtra refer to the Vedas (*śruti*) present in the mind, and thus there would be no purpose for the word "from this" (*ataḥ*). The phrase "in those dependent on that" means that the primary vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the support, while the other vital breaths are dependent upon it. The phrase "of the nature of an aggregate" means that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is of the nature of an aggregate.

Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception, or else the restriction of one or the other. How could there be the consequence of perpetual perception? How could there be the consequence of perpetual non-perception? Or how could there be the consequence of both?

"By reason of non-awakening during deep sleep and dissolution" means that during deep sleep and dissolution, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth have dissolved. [Objection: "If there were perception whenever the self, the senses, and objects are in proximity," then it would follow that perception would occur constantly when the self, the senses, and objects—the instruments of perception—are present. Consequently, even when the collection of causes is absent, the absence of the effect [perception] would result in constant non-perception. Therefore, since the occasional absence of perception despite the presence of the self, senses, and objects must be necessitated by the absence of some other cause, [the internal organ is established].

The sense is that, since there must be a counter-positive for the absence that necessitates the absence of the cause when other causes are present, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) must be admitted [as the locus of cognition]. He explains the portion of the Sūtra, "Or else, there is a restriction to one or the other," as "either in the self or even in the sense-organ. Thus ends the section on the Knower (*jñādhikaraṇa*).

The phrase "setuṃ jantum iva" (like one calling a bridge a living being) refers to a word ending in the *tumun* suffix according to the *Uṇādi* rules. The intended meaning is based on the statement from the *Gītā*: "He who thinks that this slayer kills, and he who thinks that this [self] is slain—both of them do not understand; this [self] neither kills nor is killed. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* cites the *Jaimini-sūtra*: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer, because that is its characteristic; therefore, there should be personal performance. The meaning of this is: since the fruit of the scripture, such as heaven and so forth, accrues to the performer, as established by the authority of the scripture which says, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," therefore...

"In the case of his own activity, he would be the agent. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "As it is said, 'Just as a great king, having taken hold of the provincial subjects, moves about as he pleases in his own kingdom, even so this [Self], having taken hold of these vital breaths (*prāṇas*), moves about as he pleases in his own body. This scriptural passage concerning the state of dream means that, having taken hold of the vital breaths and withdrawn them from the locations of the waking state, he wanders at will within his own body.
Regarding "and in the impelling of the body": the sense is that the impelling of the body is also established by the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) within the body.

In your view, the fact that the redness of a crystal is dependent on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of proximity to a hibiscus flower is established because, prior to that proximity, the absence of redness is observed in the crystal even though it exists there. Similarly, if agency were not perceived in the individual soul (*jīva*) prior to the proximity of the limiting condition of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then one could claim that the internal organ is the limiting condition for the agency residing in the soul; however, such is not the case—this is the meaning.

The meaning is that the insistence on the term *vijñāna* referring exclusively to the intellect (*buddhi*)—as shown by the designation, "Consciousness performs the sacrifice"—is untenable, for it indicates that the agency belongs to the intellect alone, since the word *vijñāna* is well-known in that sense. This is the point regarding the interpretation of the Sūtra, "And as the carpenter [acts] in both ways," which is thus rendered inconsistent. He proceeds to demonstrate precisely why there is nothing left to be refuted.

It has been stated that there is no dispute regarding the name, for it is simply said that a conscious being performs everything with the intention of its own welfare. The meaning is this: that which you designate as the "internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa) because it is distinct from the instruments [of action] and functions as the agent, is precisely what I designate as the "individual soul" (jīva).

"Like that of *citta* and *manas*" means: just as there is no teaching of a relationship of material cause (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikṛti*) between the mind (*manas*) and that specific function of the mind called *citta*—which consists of the nature of intending (*cetayitṛtva*) and has the form of cognition corresponding to the appropriate time—so too, if the intellect (*buddhi*) were merely a function of the mind, there would be no teaching of a relationship of material cause and modification between the intellect and the mind; yet such a relationship is indeed observed between the intellect and the mind.

The instruction regarding the relationship between the primary cause (*prakṛti*) and its modifications (*vikṛti*) would not be possible; yet, it is observed that the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and indeed the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) are taught as being in a relationship of cause and effect. This is the intended meaning. Therefore, although the injunction for meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is intended precisely because [the Self] is distinct from *prakṛti*, [one might object]: just as one engages in sacrifices and other rites by contemplating the agency of experiencing the fruits of actions upon *prakṛti*—even though *prakṛti* itself is devoid of the status of an enjoyer—so too [might one engage in meditation].

Even in the case of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) on distinctness, there is no fault; however, the point is that the meditative absorption of one whose agent is *prakṛti*—namely, the thought "I am other than *prakṛti"*—cannot be a cause for liberation because it is of the nature of an error (*bhrānti*). "The use of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth" means the wearing of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth. Thus ends the section on the Agent (*kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*).

He establishes, in sequence, how the specific proximity of objects—characterized by the particularity of the emergence and suppression of the three *guṇas* and the particularity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is the cause of specific inclinations (*ruciviśeṣa*). This is done through the passage beginning with "tathā hi" and ending with "vastusvabhāvaviśeṣarūpā," which means "having the nature of a specific proximity of objects. Thus ends the section on dependence on another (*parayattādhikaraṇa*).

In this context, the sense is that the status of being embodied (*śarīritva*) itself is raised as an objection due to the apparent contradiction in the scriptural statement "of the word for the body," and is then resolved by the Commentary. The intention is that the lack of contradiction between the two mutually opposed qualities of non-difference and superiority can only be resolved through the relationship of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*); for being a part consists precisely in having a mode of existence that is not established separately (*apṛthaksiddha*).

The meaning is as follows: there, non-difference is established by means of non-separate existence (*apṛthaksiddhatva*); difference is established by means of being a mode (*prakāratva*); and the primacy of both designations is established by the combination of both non-separate existence and being a mode. Although it might be argued that—just as in the case of light and its source—the determination of the relationship between part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*) through non-separate existence is what is to be established in the sūtra *tadananyatvam* (II.1.14), which establishes non-difference as the identity between the causal state and the effected state, rather than the relationship between the world and Brahman as part and whole; [the answer is as follows: [This is because] the relationship between part and whole is indeed intended here, since the sūtra *prakṛtiśca pratijñādṛṣṭāntānuparodhāt* (I.4.23) establishes that the material cause (*prakṛti*) is Brahman, and the sūtra *tadananyatvam* establishes that the effect is non-different from that [cause]. Furthermore, the relationship of part and whole is clearly indicated by the word "body" (*śarīra*) in the sūtra *śārīrakam* (II.2.26). Moreover, the relationship of part and whole is well-known in the world in cases such as the body and the soul, or fire and sparks. Therefore, it is not contradictory for the relationship of part and whole to be established here by means of non-separate existence and being a mode. Thus, the relationship of part and whole is established by the two means of proof [mentioned above]. Consequently, the relationship of part and whole is established by the two means of proof, namely non-separate existence and being a mode. This is the meaning. It is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Just as the light of a lamp is not different from the lamp, so too this world is not different from Him. And in the *Vivaraṇa*: "The relationship of part and whole is established by the two means of proof, namely non-separate existence and being a mode. This is the meaning. Nevertheless, since the non-difference of the gross body composed of *cit* (consciousness) and *acit* (non-consciousness) from the subtle body composed of *cit* and *acit* must be established, the nature of the world as a body—specifically as a part (*aṃśa*)—must be established. In this regard, it should be understood that the status of the conscious portion (*cidaṃśa*) as a part is being proved here, whereas the status of the unconscious portion (*acidaṃśa*) as a part is proved in the *Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa*. Regarding the *Bhāṣya* passage: "The slaves of the Brahmin, the fishermen of the Brahmin, these gamblers of the Brahmin," the term *dāsāḥ* refers to fishermen (*dhīvarāḥ*), and *kitavāḥ* refers to gamblers (*dyūtakṛtaḥ*).

The meaning is as follows: regarding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with superior [entities], when it is said that one who is perfected in Vedic study is "Viṣṇu himself," the interpretation as being for the sake of praise (*stuti*) is untenable; however, coreferentiality with inferior [entities] does not serve to praise a Brāhmaṇa, because it is contradictory. Nor does it serve to praise slaves and the like, because they are unworthy of praise. Nor is it for the purpose of censuring the Brāhmaṇa, because a Brāhmaṇa is not something to be censured. Nor is it for the purpose of censuring slaves and the like, because that is impossible. Therefore, the coreferentiality of the Brāhmaṇa with slaves and so forth indicates precisely the reality of non-difference (*abheda*).

"One who is speaking must wander"—that is, by virtue of being a speaker, one must wander; the Veda wanders as it were while speaking, and thus it is not taught—this is the final meaning. He raises an objection regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

The meaning is that even when there is a single portion (*aṃśa*) in a commentary (*bhāṣya*), a mantra, or a sūtra, the singular number is used; likewise, even when there is a partial portion (*pārdośa*) in a mantra or a sūtra, the singular number is used. Furthermore, the statement "and difference is apprehended through the state of being remote (*parākatva*)" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication) for the purpose of establishing the apprehension of difference among the supreme self (*parātman*). This is because it has been stated: "The powers of all entities are within the scope of inconceivable knowledge. Thus, it should be understood that there exists a mutual difference characterized by power (*śakti*) and so forth, which is distinct from [the difference consisting in] proximity (*pratyaktva*) and remoteness (*parākatva*).

In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that "being a part" (*ekadeśatva*) means being a portion (*aṃśatva*). If this were so, it would follow that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), is also a portion; for there is no difference in the fact that both are parts of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavastu*). Consequently, it would follow that there is no distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*). Furthermore, in the verse, "A portion of My very self becomes the individual soul in the world of living beings," the individual soul is understood to be a part in relation to the Supreme Self as the substantive, and not in relation to the qualified entity as a whole; for there is no evidence that the word "My" (*mama*) refers to the qualified entity. Indeed, being a portion of the Lord (*īśvara*)...

Furthermore, since it will be stated later that [the meaning] is understood by its own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*), and because it is well-known in common worldly usage that a qualifier is a part of the qualified, the instruction that "this alone is the part" would be redundant; consequently, even the state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) for that purpose would be useless. Moreover, the declaration that the eternal one is a "part" within the qualified individual soul—as in the phrase "being the eternal individual soul"—would likewise be redundant.

If it is argued that since such "being a part" (*aṃśatva*) is common to both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), the *Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa*—which aims to establish the status of being a part for the unconscious separately—is therefore redundant; we say no. For in this present *adhikaraṇa*, what is to be established is that "being a part" consists in having the nature of a body (*śarīra*), defined as being subordinate to and governed by [the whole]. And as will be stated in the *Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa*, even when establishing the "part-ness" of the unconscious, there is no contradiction, because the qualificand (the conscious) is established as the primary whole (*aṃśin*).

Therefore, its purpose is not already established; for this section (*adhikaraṇa*) provides a method for resolving the contradiction with those scriptural passages that establish difference, non-difference, and the nature of being a part (*aṃśatva*). Thus, because the subject matter is distinct, its purpose is not redundant. For this very reason, its purpose is also not covered by the sūtra "Because of the subsistence [of the world], [the Lord is] the part, according to Kāśakṛtsna" (*avasthiter iti kāśakṛtsnaḥ*). Indeed, the intended meaning of "being a part" here is simply "being a portion of a single entity. Even if one were to argue that "part-ness" is established here as characterized by non-separability (*apṛthaksiddhatva*), then—

If it is argued that since defects residing in the conscious and unconscious entities—which serve as inseparable qualifiers (*apṛthaksiddhaviśe�ṣaṇa*)—cannot possibly attach to Brahman or to one another, the sūtras intended to resolve such issues (such as "But like light, etc., the Supreme is not so" [2.3.46] and "Permission and prohibition are due to connection with the body, as in the case of light, etc. [2.3.48]) would be rendered meaningless, we say: no. For, by merely hearing the word "part" (*aṃśa*), one might fall into the error of thinking that what is intended here is a "part" in the sense of being a portion of the substantive (*viśeṣyaikadeśatva*). It is said that [the author of the commentary] dispels this objection, which has arisen from such a misconception, by demonstrating the "part-ness" that is actually intended.

Because there is no fault. Regarding the statement "the sun (bhānu) is that which measures (mānu-mān)," some maintain that just as the two words "pot" and "pot-possessor" (*ghaṭa-ghaṭavat*) used with respect to a pot that serves as the substratum for a pot are not synonymous, so too are the two [words] applied to the sun, which is the internal substratum for the sun in the form of light.

The words *bhānu* and *bhānumat* do not have identical meanings; for if the word *bhānu*, while primarily denoting light (*prabhā*), were to denote "one possessing light" through a secondary function (*paryavasānavṛtti*)—like words denoting genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth—then there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) independent of a possessive suffix (*matvarthapratyaya*). Therefore, they say that words expressing genus and the like are what should be cited as examples. The passage beginning with "Others, however" (*pare tu*) concerns the determination of the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

The meaning is that this is an investigation as to whether the relationship is like that between a master and a servant, or like that between fire and its sparks. "Because being a part with respect to one's own self is untenable" means that it is untenable for a qualified entity to be a part of another qualified entity. "Because in reality there is no distinction of parts by itself" refers to space (*ākāśa*), which [lacks such parts] by its very nature.

The sense is that the distinction between the conditioned (*upahita*) and the unconditioned (*anupahita*) is logically established because they are both its own parts (*svāṃśatvāt*). "In the state of non-yoga" means in the condition of being devoid of yoga. "And because it is impossible to speak of a lack of connection" means that it is impossible to speak of a lack of connection with the status of being an object of injunction (*niyojyatva*). The point is that "atomicity" (*aṇutva*) consists in not being perceived while being delimited; it does not mean having a minute dimension (*aṇuparimāṇatva*).

"Because it is untenable [for the individual soul] to have the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that in the section [of the *Brahma-sūtra*] beginning with "The penetration is like that of a lamp, for so [the scripture] shows" (*pradīpavad āveśas tathā hi darśayati*), even in the case of a plurality of bodies (*kāyavyūha*), a distinction of internal organs is admitted, and yet a unifying recognition (*pratisandhāna*) is accepted despite that distinction of internal organs. "[Because there is an absence of being divided into parts such as cows, buffaloes, gold, etc. (referring to the nature of the Supreme Self).

Now, even when the predominance characterized by the ground's status as a substratum (*ādhāra*) and so forth is intended to be expressed, the conventional usage "the cow, buffalo, and so on are parts of the ground" is not observed. Likewise, even when the predominance characterized by the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—as in the case of Devadatta and his staff or earring—is intended to be expressed, the conventional usage "the staff, earring, and so on are parts of Devadatta" is not observed. However, the usage regarding the "part-ness" (*aṃśitva*) of the owner of a substance is based on the whole; for this ownership belongs to the substance as a whole through its parts.

If it is argued that [the term "part"] does not apply to Devadatta and others merely on the basis of their being a primary authority characterized by ownership and so forth—for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using the term "having parts" (*aṃśitva*) for one who owns cows, buffaloes, and the like acquired through purchase or gift—[we reply: no, because it has already been stated that here the word "part" (*aṃśa*) means "body" (*śarīra*), and thus there is no fault. Some, however, maintain that the underlying ground (*pravṛttinimitta*) common to the usage of the word "part" in all instances—such as the threads that originate a cloth, the space delimited by a jar, or a fragment of stone delimited by a hammer—is simply "being a single portion" (*tadekadeśatva*). Therefore...

They argue that since the referent of the word *brahman* is precisely that which is qualified by both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), it is logical for the conscious and unconscious to be its parts (*aṃśa*) insofar as they constitute a single portion of it; however, the pure substrate (*viśeṣya*), namely the Lord (*īśvara*), is not a part.

Even in passages such as "a part of My very self," the status of being a part is intended with reference to the qualified [Brahman] alone. Furthermore, this does not entail the undesirable consequence that the Lord would likewise be a part like the individual soul (*jīva*), because the designation "part" is observed to apply to small portions, whereas Brahman, being infinite, cannot logically be designated as a "part. Thus they say.
Thus ends the section concerning parts (Aṃśādhikaraṇa). || 7 ||

The sense is that [the sūtra] "separately, 'so too the vital breaths'" (*pṛthak tathā prāṇāḥ*) is a sūtra presenting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding the phrase "because the effect consisting in the persistence of the impressions of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa-saṃskāra*) is observed": the meaning is that even when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have perished, the effect in the form of the persistence of the impressions of the unseen is observed. As for the passage beginning with "by others, however" (*paraistu*), it refers to the scriptural passage that was the subject of the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*). This is read in certain manuscript copies; therein—

The word "pūrva" (previous) has entered [the text] due to a scribe's error; for this is seen in the Śāṅkara-bhāṣya, where it states that the collection of passages concerning the origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is the illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*). The phrase "extension of its attributes" (*taddharmātideśaḥ*) means the extension of the attributes of the worlds and so forth, namely their origin; the sense is that it would be inappropriate to refer back to the word "birth" (*janma*) from the immediately preceding sūtra when such a reference is already possible. The phrase "of the word 'birth'" (*janmaśabdasya*) means "of the word denoting birth."

"Considering it as already established even prior to the emergence of the aggregate of the sense faculties" means that [the existence of the Self] is determined independently of the emergence of the aggregate of the sense faculties.
Thus ends the section concerning the origin of the vital breaths.

The meaning is that those vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are specified as possessing movement by their very nature; they are specifically pointed out by way of enumeration as "the five cognitions (*jñāna*), intellect (*buddhi*), and mind (*manas*). This is because, in the *Bhāṣya*, movement is heard of only in respect to these seven, and because in the state of dissolution, the cessation of exactly these seven—the five cognitions, mind, and intellect—is heard of; thus, the intention is that only these possess the status of *prāṇa*. Regarding the phrase "because they are specified as 'cognitions'" in the *Bhāṣya*, this is a citation of the representative term; the meaning is that they are specified as "cognitions, mind, and intellect" in such passages as "the cognitions together with the mind."

"But others are to be spoken of. In some places, eight vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are mentioned as having the quality of being "seizers" (*grahas*): "There are eight seizers and eight over-seizers" (*atigrahas*). The objects of the senses (*viṣayas*) are the over-seizers, because they are called "over-seizers" since they attract the sense organs by generating passion. In other places, nine are mentioned: "There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head and two directed downwards."

The term *viti* means the anus and the generative organ (*upastha*). In some places there are ten, as in: "Indeed, there are not ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person; the navel is the tenth. In other places there are eleven, as in: "These ten are the vital breaths in a person; the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh. Here, by the word *ātman*, the mind (*manas*) is meant. In some places there are twelve, as in: "The skin is the single resort for all tactile sensations (*sparśa*)," referring to the forms consisting of skin, nose, tongue, eye, ear, mind, intellect, hands, feet, generative organ, anus, and speech. In some places there are thirteen, as in the passage: "The eye and the object to be seen," and so forth.

The thirteen previously mentioned [organs] are explained as being predominant in *ahaṃkāra*; however, in certain instances, fourteen are mentioned, such as in the passage beginning with "seven and seven. In the Bhāṣya, it is stated that even for the hands and so forth, there is a distinction of function, namely grasping and the rest. Although the Śrutis are not required as self-evident authorities (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), nevertheless, due to their mutual contradictions, they are not sufficient for determining the true nature of reality. Furthermore, regarding an established entity (*siddha-vastu*), an option consisting of ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is not possible; therefore, they are established according to the force of the objects presented by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).

Just as in the case of the injunctions, "he cuts with the hand," "he cuts with the ladle," and "he cuts with the knife," where—although there is a scriptural statement that the hand, the ladle, and the knife are general instruments for the act of cutting—on the basis of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), a specific restriction is adopted: the ladle for cutting liquid substances, the knife for cutting meat, and the hand for cutting the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).

In the same way, here too, on the basis of the effects—the fivefold perception of smell and so forth, the fivefold actions such as grasping, internal cognition, and the known object—it is proper to maintain that there are exactly eleven [senses]. This is the intended meaning.

It should not be argued that this is explained in the Bhāṣya as meaning "in all legal disputes (*adhikaraṇa*), it is stated that one should not hold the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)," and that "this same fault applies equally to our own position (*svapakṣa*)," and thus the meaning is "one should not think that hands and so forth do not exist. This is because the statement regarding the presence of faults is intended to show the scriptural authority (*śruti*) that supports the reasoning already stated. Thus ends the section on the sevenfold course (*saptagatyadhikaraṇa*).

"Being delimited and yet being fit for perception while lacking the state of being like cotton or a star. Now, one might object: "If the body is emaciated by the summer heat and the navel is submerged in the cold of winter, since a sensation of cold is perceived pervading all limbs, how can the sense-organ of touch (*tvag-indriya*) be atomic? Furthermore, if it is atomic due to its power of departing [the body], why would the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) not also be atomic? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the internal difference of dimensions..."

"Even though [it is so]" means that the statement of infinity is for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*), being qualified by the distinction of the multiplicity of effects; nor should it be argued that the infinity of the essential nature itself should serve as the object of meditation, because when a non-superimposed meditation is possible, a superimposed meditation is inappropriate. In the form *alaṅ*, the augment *iṭ* is applied according to the rule "after *rud* and others, the fifth [tenses take *iṭ*]"; although this same form exists in the *luṅ* tense as well, it is stated to be in the *laṅ* because of the absence of the "immediate past" (*anadyatana*) time-reference. Thus ends the section concerning the minuteness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

One might object that since the term "saha-śiṣṭy-ādi" refers to that very designation of the qualified object (viśeṣyābhidhāna) which has "being taught together" (saha-śiṣṭi) as its first member, it would be more appropriate to say "by this [designation] beginning with being taught together" (*saha-śiṣṭy-ādinā*), rather than "from those beginning with being taught together" (*saha-śiṣṭy-ādibhyaḥ*). Even if one resorts to a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities are included (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi*), there would still be a dual ending because the designations of the qualified objects to be taught together are two. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By this, in the case of multiple Vedic recensions (*bahuśrutiṣu*). By this...

The meaning is: by means of the plural number. He shows that this point is intended by the author of the Bhāṣya with the words: "because it is taught along with the distinction of the Vedic texts" (*śrutibhedena saha śiṣṭya*). Now, an objection may be raised: just as the doubt regarding [the prāṇa] being independent is removed by establishing it as an instrument (*upakaraṇa*)—like the eyes and other senses—the doubt regarding its being a distinct element (*bhūtāntara*) is not thereby removed; for even if it were a distinct element, it could still function as an instrument. Furthermore, if that doubt is warded off by the scriptural text, "That which is prāṇa is air" (*yaḥ prāṇaḥ sa vāyuḥ*), then its status as an instrument is irrelevant. To this we say: No, for we do not [establish the prāṇa] as an instrument...

We reject the notion that [prāṇa] is a distinct element (bhūtāntara), for by that [notion], this fault would arise; rather, it is by the word *tu* ("but") that its status as a distinct element is rejected. And in that regard, the very scripture stating "that which is prāṇa is air" (*yaḥ prāṇaḥ sa vāyuḥ*) is the reason. Consequently, when its status as a distinct element has been rejected by the word *tu*, and there arises the inquiry "What then is it?"—

It is said to be "beneficial" (upakāraka) like the eyes and other organs; thus, the intended meaning is that both [the individual soul and the supreme self] are established by this very same Sūtra. In the Bhāṣya, it says: "But surely, because of the difference in name and the difference in form... One might ask: how does this doubt arise? For one who asserts that [the self], having divided itself fivefold, remains in five ways according to the Śruti passage, "Supporting this body (bāṇa)," and performs such functions as sustaining the body and the senses—against such a person, this doubt ought not to be raised.

This is stated because of the intention of the doubt that even when there is the attainment of different states due to the existence of a distinction in the functions of designation, there would be a contradiction with the statement "divided fivefold. It should be understood from the Bhāṣya that desire and so forth are not distinct principles from the mind; by the phrase "desire and so forth," the various modifications of desire and the rest are meant. Some, however, say that by the word "mind" (manas), knowledge as a quality is expressed. Regarding the Bhāṣya's statement that "the downward breath (apāna) and others are also specific functions of the vital breath (prāṇa)," the sense is that the vital breath itself, when delimited by its function in specific locations, receives the designations of apāna and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Are not the fivefold functions of the mind—having sound and the other objects as their respective causes through the ear and so forth—well-known? Therefore, since the mind possesses these five functions, it is precisely this aspect of its fivefold nature that should be stated as the illustrative example. If one insists on this, then with that intention, he states another alternative: "the five functions beginning with valid cognition (pramāṇa) and error (viparyaya)," which are well-known in the Yoga scriptures. He refutes the second position by stating: "because volition (saṅkalpa) is something additional."

Therefore, since it is established that there is no regard for a specific number on account of "propriety" (*aucitya*), it is appropriate to grasp [the breath] by way of its functions (*vṛtti*) as "fivefold," just as the various functions such as desire (*kāma*) and resolve (*saṃkalpa*) well-known from scripture are grasped; but not by way of the various functions of the ear and so forth. This is the sense. Thus ends the section concerning the activity of air (*vāyukriyādhikaraṇa*).

Although it might be argued that the consistency of this statement is not thus maintained—since meditation (*upāsana*) is understood from the phrase "he who knows this Sāma-veda"—nevertheless, because there is no mention of equality (*sāmya*) in the injunction for meditation, such as "He who meditates on these [worlds] as infinite," whereas in the cited scripture the equality of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with everything is stated and supported by the explanatory passage "all this is enveloped by the vital breath," the apprehension of its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is stronger due to being accompanied by a supporting reason; this constitutes the further objection.

Even though this is possible, nevertheless, because of the hearing of contradictory measurements— such as "equal to a flea, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, equal to all"— and because the departure [of the soul] and so forth cannot be explained otherwise,

the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the statement "all this is pervaded by Prāṇa" is justified in relation to Prāṇa either as referring to its general nature or, in some way, as referring to its omnipresence (*vaibhava*), [the latter being] in its aspect as the divine (*ādhidaivika*).

He restates what is stated in that commentary: "This omnipresence is traditionally taught in its collective form as the Hiraṇyagarbha, whose nature is *prāṇa*, and not in its individual (*adhyātmika*) form. [The objection] "because of the final hearing" refers to others; "collective form" means the universal totality. Thus ends the section on the smallness of the *śreṣṭha* (the chief vital breath) and so forth.

The sense is this: since the individual soul (*jīva*) also possesses lordship (*ādhipatya*), let there also be independence for the sun and others—who are the presiding deities of the eyes and other senses and have been granted sovereignty by the Supreme Self—given that they possess both the quality of being objects of worship and the power to bestow boons, just like the Lord. For while the scriptural texts concerning [the soul's] dependence on another may be restricted to human beings and the like, it is impossible to deny the independence taught by scripture [regarding the gods]. Thus, the soul also [possesses such qualities].

It should be understood that [the examples] are intended as illustrations of the *pādānas* (the things to be established). Now, one might object: since even fire and the like possess the nature of a living soul (*jīva*), they are already established as subjects for the aphorism "But [it is] from the Supreme, because of the scriptural statement" (*parāttu tacchruteḥ*); therefore, how can the distinction be maintained that fire and the rest are the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) while the possessor of vital breath (*prāṇavat*) is the subject of illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)? To this we reply: True. However, the intention is that there might arise a doubt that even for fire and the like—which possess great majesty—their agency is not dependent upon the Supreme Self; thus, the purpose is to show that such a doubt is possible regarding the case of fire and the others.

However, some say that in reality, this is for the purpose of reminding [the reader] of that very point; for this reason, it was recalled in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Saṃjñāmūrtiklṛpti* section for the sake of stabilization. As for the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "because this has the Supreme Self as its substrate and is eternal," the sense is that since the Supreme Self was mentioned in the preceding sūtra, the word "this" (*tasya*) refers back to that very "becoming" (*bhavana*) which was perceived in the phrase "it comes to be" (*bhavati*), and that is its state of having the Supreme Self as its substrate. Thus ends the section concerning the presiding over light and so forth (*Jyotirādyadhiṣṭhānādhikaraṇa*).

The phrase "of the gods also" implies "by the example of the living soul" (jīva). The meaning is that, considering that even by determining the dependence of the gods' activity upon another through the example of the living soul, the state of the living souls' agency being dependent on another becomes firmly established, that very [example] was recalled as an illustration; for indicating something as an illustration serves the purpose of indicating a point of agreement. "Connection with the *peṭikā*" means connection with the *peṭikā* (the chest/case), and not a connection between two *peṭikās*, because since the subject matter (*saṃjñā-mūrtty-adhikaraṇa*) is a single unit, it is impossible for it to constitute two *peṭikās*. "Three reasons" is the reading according to the manuscript.

The meaning is that the scriptural passages concerning *trivṛtkaraṇa* (the tripartition of elements) demonstrate the process of tripartition occurring within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the phrase "it would be figurative" means that there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), such that [the root] would mean "causing to enter. In the commentary, the phrase "by the Self characterized by the aggregate of individual souls (*jīvasamaṣṭi*)" means "by the essential nature (*svarūpa*) characterized by the aggregate of individual souls."

In expressions such as "the pot has clay as its essence" (*mṛdātmako ghaṭaḥ*), the word *ātman* is seen to refer to the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Consequently, by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the essential nature is treated as distinct; thus, because the essential nature is not denoted [as the agent] by the phrase "I shall manifest" (*vyākaravāṇi*), the use of the instrumental case is justified. If it is objected: "In this way, why could the word *ātman* not instead refer to the body, while the word *jīva* is taken to refer only to the individual soul?"—we reply: No, because in that case the suffix *-tvā* would be rendered unconvincing (or grammatically inconsistent). If it is further objected: "Even so, [in the phrase] 'by me, whose body is the living soul' (*jīvaśarīrakeṇa mayā'), [the word *ātman*... [the argument remains incomplete].

If it is asked, "Why should it not have the sense of being directed toward the inner self (*pratyag-artha*)?", we say no; for in that case, when the agent of grammar is expressed, the third case ending prescribed under the heading *anabhihita* (when not already expressed) would be untenable. [Objection: Even if the agent of grammar is expressed, the third case ending is still tenable because the agent of entering (*praveśaka*) is not expressed, since we adopt the view of *paryudāsa* (exclusion) for the term *anabhihita*. [Response: Precisely for this reason, the *Vārttika* on the *anabhihita-sūtra* states that there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of case endings when two actions are involved and the *kāraka* is expressed by one of them.

The term *prāsādākhyaka* (that which is called a palace) is expressed by the suffix *ghañ* through one of the two [alternative] suffixes (*anyatareṇa*), according to the rule [Pāṇini 3.3.18]. It is a "palace" (*prāsāda*) because people find pleasure (*prasīdanti*) in it. An objection is raised by resorting to the position of prohibition, arguing that if it were stated that [the locative case] does not occur when the *kāraka* is already expressed, then the seventh case (*saptamī*) would not be possible. To this, the reply is: "No, because it is not expressed by the other. Since the expression of the locus of the action of sitting (*āsikriyādhikaraṇa*) occurs by means of the subsequent suffix, the seventh case will indeed occur based on that; thus, this fault does not apply.

If it is argued that the resolution is described by resorting to *paryudāsa* (exclusion), then in that case, in the instance of the usage "I, having eaten, am going" (*ahaṃ bhuktvā vrajāmi*), there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "by me, having eaten, I am going" (*mayā bhuktvā vrajāmi*). Likewise, in the instance "the rice is being eaten after being cooked" (*pakvā bhujyate odanaḥ*), since the rice is already expressed by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*, there would be the consequence of a second case ending (*dvitīyā*) based on the assumption that it is not expressed by the suffix *ktvā*. Therefore, this is the definitive conclusion of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) in this matter.

In the sentence "I, having eaten, am going," the referent of the word "I" (*ahamartha*) does not have a direct verbal connection (*śābda-anvaya*) with both the actions of eating and going simultaneously. Rather, it has a verbal connection with the action of going alone due to its predominance; however, its connection with the action of eating is merely contextual (*ārtha*). Therefore, with respect to the operation of the word, there is only denotation (*abhidhāna*) and no non-denotation; consequently, the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) does not apply after the word "I. Likewise, in the sentence "Cooked rice is being eaten," the rice also has a verbal connection only with the verb "to eat" (*bhuj*), due to its proximity (*sannidhāna*).

There is no connection to the speaker's intention; however, when merely defining the operation of the word, why would the accusative case not occur in the question, "Is rice cooked with bricks eaten, or is it rice alone? [The same applies to] "the palace."

In the case of the word *āste* (he sits), however, the palace (*prāsāda*) has a direct verbal connection (*śābda anvaya*) with both the act of pleasing (*prasādana*) and the act of sitting (*āsana*). For at the stage of the word-meaning (*padārtha*), the substance "palace"—which is already connected as the locus of the act of pleasing by means of the nominal stem ending in the suffix *ghañ*—is also connected at the stage of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) as the locus of the act of sitting.
