Therefore, there, even though the capacity of being the locus of the act of sitting is not explicitly expressed (*anabhihita*), it exists in the palace by virtue of the operation of the word itself; thus, the use of the locative case (*saptamī*) is justified there. Kaiyaṭa, however, [states as follows]:

Relying on one's own proficiency [in grammar], since the suffix *ktvā* has the sense of "being" (*bhāva*), in the cases of "Devadatta eats cooked rice" (*pakatvaudanaṃ bhuṅkte devadattaḥ*) and "Devadatta is eaten by the cooked rice" (*pakatvaudanaṃ bhujyate devadattena*), there arises the doubt: "Why are the second and third case endings not used here, given that the *ktvā*-suffix denotes the agent and the instrument? The answer is as follows: The action expressed by the verbal root (the finite verb) is the primary element because it is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). The other [the rice] is secondary because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Consequently, even though the two capacities (*śakti*)—the agent and the instrument—are the means (*sādhana*) for accomplishing that action, they possess a relationship of primary and secondary status mediated by that [action]. In this regard:

He resolved that when the power of the principal [element] is expressed, the power of the subordinate action appears as if already expressed, because subordinates follow the principal and look toward the face of the principal, and thus there is no separate commencement of their own contradictory effects; this being so, there is no fault even if both are construed simultaneously in the verbal expression. Enough with this elaboration: therefore, the meaning of "by this living soul" (*jīvena*) is not "by me," but rather "in its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*); and thus, by the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvena*).

Furthermore, because that [intellect] is distinct [from the Self] and serves as an instrument (*karaṇa*), the use of the instrumental case is justified; for this very reason, the Vedāntācāryas stated its status as an instrument in the *Adhikaraṇasārāvalī*: "Therefore, even though the Lord enters [the body] by way of having that [intellect] as His specific instrument, He remains the agent."

In the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the passage beginning with "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts," and so forth, it is heard thus in the *Chāndogya*: "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts. Of that, the grossest part becomes feces; the middle part becomes flesh; the subtlest part becomes mind. Water, when drunk, is divided into three parts. Of those, the grossest constituent becomes urine; the [middle part becomes blood; the subtlest part becomes breath]."

The middle [portion] becomes blood; that which is the subtlest is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The fire consumed is divided into three parts: its grossest constituent becomes bone; the middle one becomes marrow; and the subtlest one becomes speech. For, my dear, the mind consists of food (*annamaya*), the vital breath consists of water (*āpomaya*), and speech consists of fire (*tejomayī*).

Regarding the phrase "by conforming to their causes" and so forth: through the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), earth, water, and fire enter into a relationship of cause and effect, becoming gross and subtle; therefore, even within these triplicated elements, the respective portions of each element would possess grossness, subtlety, and extreme subtlety in accordance with their own causes. Consequently, if the passage beginning with "Food when eaten" were intended merely to demonstrate triplication, it would refer only to the grossest aspect of the person, which is the earthly part.

The subtle flesh would attain the nature of water and the even subtler mind would attain the nature of fire; likewise, in the second stage, the thread [of the body] would be earthen, the blood watery, and the vital breath fiery; and in the third stage, the bone would be earthen, the marrow watery, and speech fiery. Consequently, this would contradict the statement, "The food that is eaten becomes threefold," which declares that feces, flesh, and mind are earthen, and the statement, "The waters that are drunk become threefold," which declares that the thread, blood, and vital breath are watery.

Furthermore, that which is said to "melt away" refers to the fiery nature of bone and marrow; yet again, it has been stated that the mind consists of food and the vital breath consists of water, thereby attributing an earthy nature to the mind and a watery nature to the breath.

All of that would be contradicted; therefore, the process of tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is not being taught here. As for the demonstration of tripartition regarding fire, the sun, and so forth existing within the cosmic egg, that is for the purpose of harmonizing the understanding of Śvetaketu, the one to be instructed, and not for the purpose of teaching that this tripartition first originated there. [Objection: But according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) are identical, how can something contradictory to that be stated? Anticipating this objection, he says: "by means of a shadow" (*chāyayā*).

Regarding the term *ādarśa* (mirror): the meaning is that, in order to avoid a specific inconsistency with the third sūtra, the author will state in the subsequent sūtra the reason for the specific designation [of the elements] as "this is food," "these are waters," and "this is fire"; and since that [subsequent sūtra] is required for that purpose, he states in the sūtra "flesh, etc., are earthly" the very matter already established by the scriptural text, "Food, when eaten, becomes divided into three parts. He mentions Vācaspati’s statement regarding the mind's being derived from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkārika*) and its eternity.

This should also be understood as an illustration for speech (*vāk*). Since both speech and mind are known to be products of the *ahaṅkāra* according to the Sāṅkhyas, and according to the view of Vācaspati, this is the meaning of the Sūtra: the statement "flesh and so forth are earthly" is for the sake of an illustration; just as flesh and so forth are earthly, so too are speech and mind fiery and earthly. The section concerning the fashioning of names and forms (*saṃjñāmūrtikalpti*) is completed.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Śrutiprakāśikā* composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads.
The total number of topics (adhikaraṇas) is 68; the total number of sūtras is 287.

In the commentary, the phrase "by the reasons for its being difficult to assail" means by the reasons for the difficulty of assailing the subject matter of the first chapter; by this, it is indicated that the subject matter of the second chapter is supplementary to the first chapter. For this very reason, the subject matter of the second chapter is pointed out by the two words ending in the third case (instrumental); for there is a traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating, "When joined with [another], the subordinate [element takes the instrumental]. Now, the word to be explained is "idānīm" (now).

The meaning is that "reflection on the subject" (viṣayicintā) is being performed. The intention is that since both attainment (*prāpti*) and meditation (*upāsanā*)—which are taught in the third and fourth chapters respectively—are of the nature of experience and have Brahman as their object, it is appropriate to include them under the category of "reflection on the subject. In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the meaning of the term "dispassion" (*vairāgya*) is stated as "the defects of one who is waking while wandering through other worlds," meaning one who is conscious while moving among different worlds.

For this very reason, the Commentator himself will state in the Sandhyādhikaraṇa that the suffering of the waking individual soul (jīva) is made known through its connection with going, coming, birth, and so forth, in accordance with its past actions. Furthermore, it has been stated in that very same section that the distinction between the states of that very same jīva—whose movement between this world and the next during the waking state was described in the preceding pāda—is being elaborated for the purpose of establishing its nature as self-luminous light.

Regarding the expression *svapataḥ* in the Bhāṣya, this refers to one in the state of dreaming; however, because of its co-occurrence with the term *suṣupta*, according to the maxim of the "ox and the bull" (*gaubalīvardanyāya*), it actually denotes the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), and thus the past tense is not intended here. Although for the sake of consistency one should have used the present participle form *susvapataḥ*, the use of the past participle form is intended to reflect the usage of such scriptural passages as: "There, when one is asleep, withdrawn, and serene, one does not perceive dreams," and "When one is in deep sleep, one does not see any dream whatsoever."

It should be observed that after the word *bhāṣya* (in the phrase *kalyāṇaguṇakaratvañceti bhāṣyānantaram*), the word *iti* must be supplied as an ellipsis; and since that word expresses a manner (*prakāra*), the meaning established is that the nature of possessing both genders, being superior to everything, and being the bestower of fruit—such is the sense conveyed. Furthermore, in this way, there is no logical inconsistency even if the singular verb *pratipādyate* is not syntactically connected with the plural noun *doṣaśabda*.

However, some, justifying the singular number by asserting that each term is connected individually—similar to rules such as *ādiñiṭuḍavaḥ*, *karmaṇoromanthataṣobhyāṃ vartticaroḥ*, and *divādibhyo bhuvyacveḥ*—and considering that the qualities of being the supreme of all and bestowing the fruit are included within the quality of being a mine of auspicious virtues (*kalyāṇaguṇākaratva*), did not tolerate the insertion of the word *iti*.

If it is argued that the *Bhāṣya* is inconsistent—since it was already stated in the summary of the meaning of the first two sections (*pādas*) that the Supreme Brahman is free from even a scent of all defects and is an ocean of immeasurable qualities, and thus its freedom from defects and its being a mine of auspicious qualities have already been established; and since the second section (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*) would then be redundant—it is not a fault, because that section serves to further strengthen what has already been established.

As for the statement that the defects of the individual soul (*jīva*) wandering through other worlds are set forth [in this section], that is indeed accepted, as such was established in the first section (*pāda*).

To explain: first, in the initial section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is established that there is a continuity of the subtle body—consisting of the aggregate of elements and sense organs and serving as the locus of the miseries of *saṃsāra*—in its coming and going between this world and the next. In that very same context, by the sūtra "Or [the enjoyment] is figurative, because of the lack of knowledge of the Self" (*bhāktaṃ vā'nātmavittvāt*), it is revealed that the experience of heavenly enjoyments—which brings about affliction due to assuming the status of a servant to the gods—is subject to exhaustion and is characterized by degrees of excellence. Furthermore, in the second section, even regarding the subtle body...

It will be demonstrated that, as the cause of the entire mass of afflictions of saṃsāra, the bondage of karma persists until liberation; furthermore, the perishable nature of the enjoyment of heaven in that very context will be shown by the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "Upon the exhaustion of what has been performed" (kṛtātyaye). Thus, even sacrificial rites and the like, which produce the enjoyment of heaven, are likewise tainted by numerous defects.

Because it depends upon the conduct of a *smārta* (one who follows the traditional law), which is accomplished through manifold hardships consisting of the performance of prescribed duties—such as lifelong bathing and twilight prayers (*sandhyā-vandana*)—and the avoidance of prohibited acts, [the path] will be shown to be difficult by means of the sūtras beginning with "caraṇād" (JS 1.3.8).

For those who perform undesirable acts and the like, there is no attainment of heaven even by the maxim that "one going to a village passes by the roots of trees"; rather, there is an extensive experience of torment in the abode of Yama and in places such as Raurava, as well as the attainment of birth as insects and so forth, which will be described in the third [chapter]. In the fourth [chapter], in order to dispel the doubt that those descending from heaven might experience some degree of dualistic enjoyment—since scripture mentions their becoming ether and so forth, just as the presiding deities of ether and the rest possess bodies made of ether and so forth—it is stated that their connection with ether and the other elements is merely one of contact (*saṃśleṣamātra*).

It will be described [in the fifth chapter]. Under the guise of refuting the lack of restriction regarding whether one remains for a long or short time, it will be established that there is an extremely long stay among rice and other grains, devoid of the enjoyment of pleasure. Furthermore, if the stay among them were as the individual soul (jīvātman) identifying with each respective thing, it would last only until their cutting; thus, the extreme wretchedness [of that state] would not be proven. Therefore, to establish that extreme wretchedness, it will be described that there is merely a "clinging" (saṃśleṣa) to them—that is, their clinging to those [grains].

In the *Retassig* Sūtra, it is explained that the connection of those possessing residual karma (*anuśayin*) with rice and other grains—which have reached the state of being consumed by men—occurs through a sequence of successive transformations of those grains, beginning from their state as red paddy, their storage in a granary, threshing, husking, cooking, and eating, continuing until they are transformed into the nature of semen; and this transformation into the nature of semen occurs only after they have somehow reached the state of being consumed by men. This process continues until the final transformation into the nature of semen.

It will be indicated [later]: likewise, even upon the entry of the male semen (*puruṣavīrya*), there is no acquisition of a body for those [souls] if they do not reach a woman; if that semen were to be discharged into barren women or the like, then, through a subsequent sequence of transformations of that semen, having again become the object of consumption by a man and being conjoined with his semen, immediately after entering the womb of a menstruating woman, [the soul attains] in some birth a physical basis for experience that is conducive to both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Regarding the acquisition of a body: thus, that embryo, having lain within the womb for ten months or more, is born; it lies in the mother's belly which is filled with urine, feces, wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth. For that embryo, smeared by those [substances] and enveloped by the impurity of the placenta and membranes, whose seed is the impurity of blood and semen, which grows through the entry of the essence of what the mother has eaten and drunk, and whose strength, capacity, vigor, splendor, wisdom, and movement are all obstructed—its lying there, and then its emergence through the birth canal under great pain as it is being squeezed, is birth. This will be indicated by the aphorism: "The body is from the womb."

For this very reason, immediately after the answers to the five questions, it is heard in the scripture: "Therefore, one should feel aversion [to them]. Consequently, it is appropriate that the defects of one wandering here and there are being set forth; however, it is not tenable to say that the defects of the states such as waking are being set forth, because no defects are set forth regarding those states anywhere in the context of "here and there."

Since movement belongs only to one in the waking state, although the demonstration of defects pertaining to the waking state results in the attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*) in the *Vairāgyapāda*, there is no section (*adhikaraṇa*) dedicated to demonstrating the defects of the states of dream and so forth; for the sections such as "In the intermediate state there is creation, for so [the scripture] says" (*sandhye sṛṣṭir āha hi*), which belong to the *Ubhayaliṅgapāda*, are devoted to demonstrating the great majesty of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), such as His being the creator of the most wonderful objects of dreams and His being the substratum for repose in deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

He dispels the doubt that [the text] is not intent on demonstrating the defects of states such as dreaming by means of the passage beginning with "In other worlds" and ending with "is the result. The underlying meaning is this: in the sections concerning the twilight [states] and so forth, the description of states such as dreaming is based on such [scriptural] passages as, "I see nothing here to enjoy," "Indeed, I do not at present know myself as 'this is I,' nor these beings; he has gone to utter annihilation; I see nothing here to enjoy."

Because it indicates the defects proclaimed in the Prajāpati-vidyā, and because of the description of the concealment of qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) in the state of dream—due to the connection with a body for action—as stated in the sūtras, "But [the Self] is concealed by the meditation on another" and "Or that [concealment] is due to the union with a body," the defects of one in the states of dream and so forth follow even from those topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) devoted to establishing the majesty of the Supreme Self. He states the doubt regarding the first topical section; here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the relationship between part and whole.

"What is the purpose of the words 'faith' and so forth? By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), soma, rain, and the like are included. Regarding the phrase "this is King Soma," the term "returning" (*nivartana*) refers to the journey; for it will be demonstrated later in the passage beginning with "then they return again by this very same path" that returning is indeed what is being taught. Alternatively, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*); thus, "returning" means from which heavenly world they return by way of the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāna*). In that context, [the statement] "this is King Soma" [is made].

The construction is with the word *somaśabdasya* (of the word "Soma"). This is the meaning: the fact that the word "Soma" occurring in the passage concerning the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*)—namely, "From ether [he goes] to the moon; this is King Soma, the food of the gods; the gods eat it"—refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) characterized by a body of Soma, makes it understood that the word "Soma" occurring in the previously mentioned Pañcāgni-vidyā passage—"In this very fire the gods offer faith (*śraddhā*); from that oblation King Soma comes into being"—also refers to [the soul] characterized by a body of Soma.

"Without" (utaneti) refers to the word *soma* occurring in the sentence immediately following the statement on the oblation of faith (*śraddhā-huti*). That is to say, it refers to the word in the sentence: "From that oblation, King Soma arises," which follows the sentence "They offer faith as an oblation. In the Commentary, it is said that subtle elements (*bhūta-sūkṣma*) are easily available; for, just like objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment, the bodies that serve as the substrata for experience are also produced from those very same elements drawn there by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

The sense is that since [the soul] arises from its own undertaking (*rārambha*), there is no need to bring in subtle elements for that purpose. The meaning in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) "it goes" (*raṃhati*) is "it moves" (*gacchati*), because it is derived from the root *rahi* meaning "to go"—this is the sense. Now, one might object: since only the answer to the opponent's question regarding the embrace by subtle elements should have been presented, the introduction of more than that is inconsistent. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "by means of the question and the answer," and so forth.

In this regard, it is stated by way of a question and its answer; for, following the further question concerning the envelopment by the subtle elements—"Do you know how, at the fifth libation, the waters come to be called 'man'?"—no answer concerning the envelopment by [the gross] *sampariṣvaṅga* is seen, because of the intervention of another question posed by Gautama: "Tell me those very words which you spoke to the boy at the end. This refers to the statement, "At the fifth libation, the waters come to be called 'man'."

This is because the reply given by the King of Pañcāla—“Do you know how, at the fifth oblation...”—cannot possibly be an answer to a question posed by Gautama that was separated from it by the King of Pañcāla’s own question; for it is heard there: “The King of Pañcāla, Pravāhaṇa, questioned Śvetaketu Āruṇeya: ‘Do you know where people go from here? [regarding] the destination to which those performing ritual acts go; “Do you know how they return again? [regarding] the manner of their return; and “Do you know the two paths, the path of the gods... [and so forth].

Regarding the passage, "And [he asked about] the turning away from the path of the fathers," he questioned him concerning the two paths by way of their distinguishing characteristics: "Do you know how that world is not filled?"—asking about those who do not reach that world—and "Do you know how, at the fifth libation, the waters come to be called 'man'?"—asking about the state of being called "man" for these waters at the fifth libation. For the answer to that question—"Thus, at the fifth libation, the waters come to be called 'man'"—is the reply given by the King of Pañcāla.

The phrase "imāṃ mandāśaṅka" (regarding this, [the King] was free from doubt) indicates that the five responses beginning with "In the fifth oblation, the waters... were given by King Pañcāla in a sequence uninterrupted by the five questions posed by King Pañcāla; such is the meaning.

Because the question posed by Gautama—"the very word which you spoke in the presence of the prince"—cannot logically be distinct from the five questions asked by the King of Pañcāla (since it would otherwise be impossible for it to be different from them), if this question were indeed distinct, there would have been only a single reply; therefore, since five replies are observed, it is determined that these are the answers to the very five questions posed by the King of Pañcāla. For this very reason, "yāmeva... [and so forth].

Since Gautama’s question, "You spoke these words in the presence of the prince," is identical to the question of the Pañcāla king, the sequence consisting of the uninterrupted order of question and answer is established.

One should not be misled here into thinking that the answers to the five questions follow their respective order—namely, the first answer for the first question, the second for the second, and so on—for the answers have not been presented here according to the sequence of the questions. Rather, he (Asvalāyana), being unable to answer these questions himself, reported them to his father; and the father, likewise being ignorant, questioned the King of Pañcāla.

It should not be objected that an answer is seen at the very beginning [of the section] and yet no sequential order consisting of the succession of questions and answers is shown in the Bhāṣya; for, by the Bhāṣya passage stating "he asked this matter" and "he replied," the fact that those [initial statements] are answers is made known, thereby making their immediate sequence evident.

Regarding the phrase "when there is a requirement for the substance to be offered": although the verbal expression [of the text] consists merely of a connection with the act of becoming (*bhavana*) as qualified by the human form of water, nevertheless, when there is a requirement for a substance for the oblations (*āhuti*), water alone is connected as that substance by virtue of its proximity. Consequently, the meaning of the question regarding the fifth oblation—the fifth question—is resolved as follows: "Do you know the transformation of those very waters into the form of a person? And it is not the case that, despite the proximity of water, the proximity of the person [is intended].

However, because the word [‘āhutiḥ’] has as its meaning the connection with the act of becoming (i.e., pouring) without further qualification, it is not possible for the oblations (*āhutis*) to be qualified by the water which is present for another purpose. It should not be argued that when one says, “He goes by horse, covered with a white cloth,” the horse is also qualified by the white [color] which is present for the sake of the cloth; for when there is an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), even that which is present for another purpose can qualify another. This is seen in the case: “Having stripped a branch from its root, he makes a seat.”

The sense is that this has been demonstrated in the section on "application" (*prayukti-lakṣaṇa*), where the term *mūlataḥ* (from the root), which is connected by way of being the basis for the *parivāsa*, is construed with the expectant phrase *upaveṣaṃ karoti* (he makes a fire-stick). This is what is meant by the expression "of another sentence."

If it is asked: "How can it be that, even though *śraddhā* (faith) is mentioned in relation to the first fire in another sentence, one abandons that *śraddhā* and instead postulates *ap* (water) as the object of oblation (*homya*), relying merely on proximity (*sannidhi*)—the fact of being situated in its own sentence?"—[the answer is: because the status of water as the object of oblation is determined precisely in the opening question, which has not yet encountered any contradiction; and because this is understood in exactly the same way in the conclusion: "But thus, at the fifth oblation, water comes to be called 'man'" (*iti tu pañcamyām āhutāv āpaḥ puruṣavacaso bhavanti*). Thus, the *śraddhā* mentioned in the other sentence [is set aside].

The word *antara* signifies "middle," being situated within the sentence consisting of the question and the answer. This is because it will be stated by the author himself later on that even in the middle [of the passage], that very same mode [of inquiry] is established, as in the phrase "because it is mentioned first. Consequently, by the principle of the "tongs" (*sandaṃśanyāya*) and the principle of the "opening section" (*upakramādhikaraṇanyāya*), it acquires its own status precisely in accordance with those [surrounding elements], and not in contradiction to them; thus there is no fault. The phrase "incompatible with transformation" (*pariṇāmasyāyogyā*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be observed that it is impossible to extract faith—which has become the very nature of the Self—from the Self and offer it as a libation; all of this is intended by the Sūtra, "If it be said that [the fires] are not mentioned in the first [chapter], no, for they are indeed [mentioned] because of the logical possibility," which should be introduced right there for the sake of ease of comprehension.

It should be understood that this has been included here according to the principle of "looking back at what precedes" (*nāgatavekṣaṇanyāya*), by means of the question and the answer—that is, it should be explained as being "by those two," namely, by the investigation of the questions (*praśnanirūpaṇa*). The sense is that the analysis (*vigraha*) is intended. "But because [the self] consists of three parts, and because of their predominance. This refers to the word "embracing" (*pariṣvaṅga*) found in the passage containing the doubt. Its connection is with what precedes; in response to the doubt, "How is there embracing?", he says, "Because it consists of three parts."

The sense is that by means of the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the connection [of the words] as "an embrace consisting of three" (*tryātmatvam*) has been demonstrated. Regarding the sūtra-portion *prāṇagateśca*: the meaning is that it is for the purpose of excluding the connection with the intermediate probandum (*avāntarasādhya*); that is, for the purpose of excluding the connection with the intended object of the reason-part *bhūyastvāt* (on account of abundance), namely, that the hearing of these [deities] alone is logically consistent. Regarding the objection *agnyādigatiśruteriticenna bhāktatvāt*: [the answer is] no, because [the scriptural statement] is figurative.

Regarding the phrase "and [the dissolution] of herbs and trees through non-injury": the sense is that, upon the death of a person, because the hairs of the head and body are seen to repeatedly spring up and dissolve into the herbs and trees, there is no visible dissolution [of the person's constituent parts] into them.

Regarding the deities presiding over the body hair (*lomābhimāninī devatā*): by reflecting upon such scriptural passages as, "Agni, becoming speech, entered the mouth; Vāyu, becoming breath, entered the nostrils; Āditya, becoming the eye, entered the eyes; the quarters, becoming the ear, entered the ears; the herbs and trees, becoming the body hair, entered the skin," [one understands] the deities presiding over the herbs and the deities presiding over the body hair.

Unity is established; consequently, even regarding the statement from the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, "The herbs [become] the body hairs, the trees the hair of the head," one must accept that "dissolution" (*apya-ya*) among the deities presiding over the body hairs means the relinquishing of their status as controllers—that is, their state of being the presiding subjects—over them. The sense is that this same principle applies to speech and the other organs as well.

[Objection: But surely, if at the time of death the deities such as Fire (Agni) were to relinquish their presiding over speech and the other organs, then the effects such as the departure and movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), as well as the dialogue with the Moon, would not be established. Consequently, by attempting to avoid the inconsistency of the Sūtra "And because of the departure of the breaths" (*prāṇagateś ca*), one would instead only reinforce that very inconsistency through another means. Therefore, since the sense organs such as speech do not assist the dying person and are thus as good as non-existent, it is better to resort to a figurative expression (*upacāra*) and say that "speech and the rest are absorbed" (*apīta*) simply because they resemble what has been drunk. If this is argued:

This is because, with respect to the living being at the point of death, what is intended to be expressed is precisely the relinquishment of those specific forms of conceit (abhimāna) that are conducive to providing particular services to speech and the other organs; nor should it be argued: "Since the recourse to a figurative sense (bhāktatva) is equally applicable [to both views], why not accept the opponent's claim that the figurative sense arises from a similarity to 'being drunk' (apīta) due to its being virtually non-existent? For it is established that words denoting the body extend to the embodied self, and thus it is possible for words such as "speech" (vāk) and so forth to refer to their presiding deities.

The intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is that even there [in the path of the fathers], since the scriptural statement can somehow be explained by the mere abandonment of a specific form of conceit (*abhimāna-viśeṣa*), it is superior in comparison to that [other path]. Regarding the objection: "If it be said that [the performers of sacrifices] are not mentioned [there], we say no, because those who perform sacrifices and so forth are understood [from the context],"—one might argue that the Bhāṣya's statement "in this very passage" is incorrect, because the status of being the King Soma for those who perform sacrifices and so forth is heard only in the passage concerning the Path of the Fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*), and not in this passage concerning the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*). To this he says: "The meaning is 'in the great sentence' (*mahāvākya*). This means that although the specific details are stated in one part, they are understood within the entire great context.

In the Bhāṣya, the designation *somarājānaḥ* is due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the rule for compound suffixes; and this is indicated by the inclusion of the word *rāja-* in rules such as "after *prati*, [words] beginning with *aṃśu* etc., in a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Therefore, the reading should correctly be either *somārājānaḥ* or *asomarājāḥ*. This is according to the method explained above.

In the phrase "they perform" (*anuṣṭhanti*) found in the Śruti, the word *iti* expresses a manner or mode. Consequently, the meaning is: those who perform actions of this kind—namely, sacrifice (*iṣṭa*), works of public utility (*pūrta*), giving (*datta*), fasting (*anaśana*), and so forth—which are denoted by the term "well-performed deeds" (*sukṛta*). The same meaning applies to the expression "in the aforementioned manner," since no specific mode of performance was previously stated in the Śruti. Thus, the sense is that one becomes associated with that [mode]. This point, however, will be clarified by the author himself in the *Retassig-sūtra*.

The phrase "by means of the word *somarāja* in both cases" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood as being by way of their connection with the location of the heavenly world (*dyuloka*). Regarding the phrase "because of being its servants," the meaning is: because they serve it through dance, song, and so forth.

The phrase "others, however," and so forth, connects with the preceding statement "because of the abundance of liquid substances. The sense is that since the Agnihotra and other rites have liquid substances as their means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), and because one perceives a great abundance of such sacrificial offerings (*havir*)—such as curd and milk—among those things connected to those rites, it is these very substances that are designated here by the word "waters" (*ap*). "Those two offerings"—namely, the two Agnihotra offerings—"this," meaning this earth; "in the form of *apūrva*" refers to the offerings inherent in the ritual action.

The meaning is that, according to the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya, the waters—which possess a unique form and are real—envelop those individual souls (jīvas) who perform sacrifices and the like, and lead them to this world to bestow their fruits. The reading "pariṣvajate" (embraces) is a part of a whole; just as when one part of a cloth is burnt, the conventional usage "the cloth is burnt" is secondary (amukhya), so too the use of the word "āhuti" (oblation) in the passage "te vā ete āhutī" would be secondary, referring only to a portion of the oblation.

The phrase "the [sections] devoted to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) have been explained" means they have been explained as being formulated as prima facie views. Now, one might object: since there are many indicators of identity (*pratyabhijñāpaka*) in the *pañcāgnividyā*—namely, the forms of heaven, earth, man, woman, and so forth—there is indeed recognition based on the authority of the six questions. Furthermore, if recognition were to fail due to some slight deficiency or excess, it would lead to a contradiction with the established sūtras, such as "Because of its renown through the path beginning with light" (*arcirādinā tatprathiteḥ*) and "Because of the non-difference of all, the same [path] elsewhere" (*sarvābhedādanyatremo*). This is because [the path] serves as the cause for the satisfaction of the deities.

There is no inconsistency even in the specific final state of the human voice having become that which is heard; for the Siddhāntin also accepts—as established by the principle "having seen this very nectar, they are satisfied"—that the quality of being the object of sight, which serves as the cause of satisfaction, belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the same way that the gods consume Soma (according to the scripture, "the gods consume him"), namely, in the form of the body transformed into the shape of Soma. Since the quality of being the cause of the gods' satisfaction is not in conflict with its transformation into rain, food, and so forth, [the opponent], expressing dissatisfaction, says: "Or let there be a division."

Regarding the phrase "of the oblations": the point is that just as in the case of the word *apsu*, even though one might resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to establish the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *apsu* with the word *puruṣa* by taking it to refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), once that meaning is established through either figurative or primary denotation (*mukhyā vṛttiḥ*) by one [of these means], who would abandon it? Regarding the phrase "at the time of reaching the moon": the pronoun "this" (*eṣa*) refers back to what was previously specified in the passage, "They reach the moon from space."

The point is that because [the passage] refers to the individual soul as distinguished by its attainment of the moon, once its status as the King Soma is established immediately after reaching the moon, its identity with the Soma [in the *pañcāgni-vidyā*] is recognized; thus, it is proven that the state of being Soma in the *pañcāgni-vidyā* also occurs immediately after reaching the moon.

The phrase "by the word 'this' (eṣa)," which is a pronoun, means by a pronoun ending in the nominative case; for it is logical that the reference (*parāmarśa*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) who is the attainer, as indicated by the nominative case. Just as in the passage, "Prajāpati led a horse to Varuṇa; he [sa] lost his own deity," the pronoun "he" (*sa*) in the nominative case does not denote Varuṇa, who is designated by the dative case as the recipient, but rather denotes Prajāpati, who is designated by the same case-ending.

The sense is that, according to the established position in the *Pūrvatantra*, this is an *iṣṭi* (sacrificial rite) enjoined by the rule, "One should offer cakes on four potsherds to him alone, who is Aruṇa. Furthermore, if one were to accept the referent of the nominative case-ending based solely on the uniformity of the case-terminations, then in the passage "That is the Supreme Person," the pronoun "that" (*sa*) would likewise have to refer only to the individual soul (*jīva*), which was designated by the word "serenity" (*samprasāda*) in the nominative case in the preceding sentence: "This serenity, having risen from this body and having reached the highest light, manifests in its own form."

If it be argued that [the word "supreme"] refers not to the Supreme Brahman indicated by the accusative case in the phrase "having attained the supreme light," but rather to the individual soul (jīva) indicated by the nominative case in the word "he" (saḥ)—we say no. For if the individual soul were grasped by the word "he," then its status as the Supreme Person, which is being established by the term "Supreme Person" (puruṣottama), would be contradicted in the soul. Therefore, even setting aside the individual soul—which is denoted by the word *samprasāda* understood through the uniformity of the case endings—there is no obstacle to the principle that uniformity of case endings can serve as a determining factor when there is no contradiction.

The phrase "of the mere case-ending" (*vibhaktimātrasya*) means "of the mere word" (*vacanamātrasya*); likewise, in what follows, the word "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) should be understood as referring to the "word" (*vacana*), since there is no possibility of a difficulty regarding the meaning of the case-ending. Consequently, even in a ritual application involving many wives, just as in the expression "he girds the wife" (*patnīṃ saṃnahya*), the number—which is subordinate to both the sentence and the nominal stem—should be construed either with reference to the singularity of each individual or with reference to the genus (*jāti*). This is similar to the case in the *Abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice: "For whom the oblation has been set out before the moon [has risen]... (*yasya havirniruktaṃ purastāccandramāḥ*).

Regarding the statement, "If [the moon] should rise [while the sacrifice is being prepared], he should divide the rice-grains into three parts," the division of the rice-grains into three parts is not what is being enjoined. This is because the division into middle and other portions is already established by the very sentences beginning with "those which are the middle ones," and thus there would be the contingency of the sentence being redundant. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding the redundancy of the sentence—and since it is established by logic that one may resort to the non-literal sense of multiple words within a sentence to avoid such redundancy—the word "rice-grains" (taṇḍula) is used as an indicator (lakṣaṇā) for the sacrificial oblation (havis) of the New Moon sacrifice, and the removal of its previous deity is what is being enjoined. Thus, the sentence is rendered meaningful.

The sense is that resorting to the natural meaning of the mere words is established by *kaimutya* (a fortiori). Regarding the phrase "because we observe an absence of insistence on the meaning of case-endings," this means there is no fixed rule that what is indicated by a singular ending must be indicated by a singular ending, or that what is indicated by a plural-ending word must be indicated by a plural ending.

As for the phrase "even in the Pañcāgni-vidyā," the intention is as follows: since it is established that in the Pañcāgni-vidyā the term *somarāja* refers to something other than the moon, the statement "this is King Soma" is purposeful because it serves to identify that [other object].

In the passage concerning the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*), the word *etad* (this) would have to refer to what has already been attained; for even if the word *somarāja* in the passage on the five-fire knowledge (*pañcāgnividyā*) refers to the moon, there is no difference in its being purposeless if the phrase "this King Soma" were also intended to refer to those who attain [the path]. Thus, by the natural force of the singular number, it would be so. The phrase "of this word *somarāja*" means "of the word *somarāja* occurring in the passage on the five-fire knowledge."

If it is argued that [the cognition in question] is merely a cognition whose object is distinct from the moon, then even if there were a certainty regarding its having the moon as its object, it would be impossible for the statement "This is Soma" in the *pitṛyāṇa* passage—having first pointed out the performer of sacrifices—to convey the identity with the moon as understood in the *pañcāgni-vidyā* passage. Now, if it is objected: "Granted that the absence of a certainty regarding the moon being the object is required as the absence of an obstacle, yet a certainty that the object is something other than the moon is not required," we reply: True.

It should be understood that this was stated here because the impossibility of the fitness for being offered (*sambhavahomyatva*)—which constitutes the causal complex for determining that the object is distinct from the moon—is present. By the phrase "due to the impossibility of the fitness for being offered," the meaning is: due to the impossibility of those two [properties] of fitness for being offered having been established by the statements "the King Soma exists" and "they offer the King Soma."

Is it not the case that the purpose of the statement "This is King Soma" is to inform [the sacrificer] of the state of becoming King Soma produced from the oblation of faith at the time of reaching the moon? Since this can also be understood by the word "this" (*eṣa*), the living self (*jīva*) is described as reaching the moon while characterized by the present attainment, indicated by the suffix *laṭ*; however, by the phrase "King Soma," King Soma is identified as that which is being produced from the oblation of faith, as established by the passage on the five fires: "From that oblation, King Soma comes into being."

[The identity] is enjoined; and consequently, since the cognition of non-difference between those two leads to the realization that the attainment of the moon and the state of being Soma-rāja are simultaneous, why resort to the laborious justification that the state of being Soma-rāja at the time of attaining the moon is the purpose [of the injunction], when it is established simply by the cognition of the non-difference of the one indicated as "this" (the attainer) from Soma-rāja, as found in the passage concerning the knowledge of the five fires?

If it is argued that this is because, just as the term *somarāja* occurring in the passage concerning the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*) has as its purpose [denoting] those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*, then that is true; however, since another possible purpose exists, it was not abandoned, and thus it too has been presented. But is it not the case that it is improper for the word *somarāja*, when used in reference to one who performs sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*—as in "This is King Soma"—to convey the identity with the body of nectar produced from the oblation of faith (*śraddhā-huti*), which serves as the secondary (metaphorical) meaning of the word *somarāja* found in the passage on the five fires? Therefore...

In that context, when the word *tat* (that) is employed, it merely conveys similarity to that [original object], and not the non-difference (*abheda*) between that and a secondary sense (*gauṇārtha*) similar to it; because of this underlying unease, the author introduces the section on *kṛtātyaya* (the passing away of what was done) with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*). The phrase "the knowledge of similarity to the moon" is used because we see an explanation of precisely that in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), "That is the food of the gods," which means "it is the food of the gods," i.e., the object of enjoyment for the gods.

Nor should it be said that the purpose [of the statement] is to establish similarity with that [moon], because its meaningfulness is established by the fact that it conveys the state of being food for the gods, as in the passage, "The gods eat him. Furthermore, under this view, since there is no cognition of identity between the Soma-king mentioned in the *pañcāgnividyā* passage and [the one in the other context], it would not be established that the word "Soma-king" occurring therein refers to those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*. Consequently, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra: "If it is argued that this is not so because it is not heard [therein], we say no, because those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi* are understood [to be meant]. This is because in the *pañcāgnividyā*, it is stated: "The waters, having become human speech... [and so on].

The sense is that since the attainment of success (*siddhi*) is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "person" (*puruṣa*), which denotes volition, it is impossible to deny the resulting recognition of identity (*pratyabhijñāna*)—which is produced as a byproduct—based on the connection with the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) and the metaphorical application of the word "moon. This applies to them...

Is it intended that the status of being denotable by the term "Soma-king" is denied for those who perform sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*, thereby negating the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense of the word "Soma-king," or is it negating its primary (*mukhya*) sense? Having thus raised the dilemma, he refutes the first alternative. The phrase "of the word 'Soma-king' occurring in the Chāndogya" implies the following: just as in the case of the injunction "One desiring to practice sorcery should sacrifice with the Śyena," the statement "Just as a hawk [pounces]" is introduced so that the word "Śyena" may indeed apply to the sacrifice, so too is it here. This is the underlying intention.
He refutes the second alternative by admitting it as a desired consequence: "For there is no other mode of functioning," etc. Thus ends the section on the attainment of another body.

In this commentary (*bhāṣya*), immediately after the mention of "the returning is also recorded," one should understand the syntactical connection as follows: beginning with "Now, those who here in the village worship [sacrifices] as 'the performed and the offered' and 'the given,' they enter upon the path of smoke... and so on, and having supplied the words "until the point of exhaustion" (*yāvatsampātam uṣitvā*), it continues with "then they return again by this very same road. Consequently, even in the scriptural passage cited in the *bhāṣya*—namely, "until the point of exhaustion"—there is no fault in the fact that the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa-patha*) is not explicitly mentioned; or rather, [this refers to] those who perform only sacrifices and the like.

The journey by the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) via smoke and so forth, characterized by the embrace of the elements (*bhūta-pariṣvaṅga*) and other modes, has been concluded by supplying the word "contemplated" (*cintitam*). The phrase "at the conclusion of the fruit of karma" and so forth, however, constitutes a separate sentence. In this view, because the intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) is explicitly set forth in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) is well-integrated for the sake of clarifying the subject matter and establishing the intermediate connection. By the words beginning with "as long as saṃsāra," he shows another connection between these two sections that indicates their relation to the chapter (*pāda*); the meaning is that "the sense" (*artha*) is the "connection" (*saṅgati*).

Here, the word *ati* expresses a manner; the meaning is that a connection of this kind is the purpose, which is to say that the result has been fully realized. Anticipating the objection that there is a contradiction in the statement "the remaining karma does not remain," he says "tacchabde" [referring to the word *tat*]. The sense is that the phrase "it does not remain" means "it is not possible [for it to exist]"—that is, the meaning of "it does not remain" is "it is no longer possible. The sense is that this would otherwise render the sentence redundant, like the sentence "life lasts until death."

The intention [of the author] is that the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*), as in the rule "that by which something falls together is called *bhāṣya*. Regarding the prefix *abhi-āṅ-pūrva*, although the sense of "one who comes near" is not possible in such passages as, "Meditating with vigilance according to his desire, indeed, that desire of his will quickly (*abhyāśas*) be fulfilled," yet the sense of "quickly" mentioned by others is possible; nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated thus because this meaning is applicable here. This is seen in the *Bhāṣya*: "in those who have descended" (*pratyavarūḍheṣu*).

It refers to that very same subject. Furthermore, the destruction of those actions whose fruits have not been experienced and for which no expiation has been performed—merely through the experience of the fruits of other actions—is untenable. Therefore, having gone to this world, they return with their *saṃśaya* (residual karma) intact, "by the same way and by a different way"; the meaning is that they return by the manner of ascent and by another manner. For the ascent proceeds by way of smoke, night, the waning fortnight, the six months of the sun's southern course, the world of the ancestors, space, and the moon.

The descent, however, is from the station of the moon by way of space, air, smoke, mist, and clouds. In that regard, because of the descent through space, it is "as they went" (yathetam); but because of reaching the air and so forth, and because of not reaching the world of the ancestors and so forth, it is "not thus" (an evam). || 8 ||

The locative case here is used in the sense of restriction (*nidrdhāraṇe*). In the *Bhāṣya*, the word "shows" (*darśayati*) is supplied, as is the word "scripture" (*śruti*). The phrase "the statement of Gautama and Āpastamba" refers to Gautama’s statement beginning with "the castes" (*varṇāḥ*), and Āpastamba’s statement beginning with "from that" (*tataḥ*). Regarding the *Bhāṣya* passage "as long as the momentum lasts" (*yāvat-sampātam*), this refers to specific actions that have begun to yield their fruit; for even when one has ascended to the moon, it may not be possible to exhaust all of one's actions, since among the actions belonging to one who has been caught in the beginningless stream of birth and death, some remain from which [the momentum] proceeds.

Since [the fruits of action] have already been experienced—because it is impossible to experience with a single body the various karmas that are declared in scripture to be the objects of enjoyment for the bodies of various gods, humans, animals, birds, reptiles, and so forth—the point is this: although the word *sampāta* occurs in the opening section, since it requires a restriction of its own accord, it is proper to apply such a restriction in accordance with the scriptural passages on "pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇa*) and so forth found in the concluding section, which are supported by Smṛti. Thus [it is said]: "He desires that [world]."

The meaning is the exclusion of that portion of karma intended for heaven which has not yet begun to yield its fruit. This would contradict the natural sense of the Vedic injunction, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice"; for if the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice intended for heaven were to have results such as a pleasant birth, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts establishing that heaven is the independent goal to be achieved. For this very reason, [the rule does not apply] to the Saurya and other rites whose fruits—such as Brahmanic splendor—are established by sentences like, "One desiring Brahmanic splendor should offer the Saurya oblation."

The point is that it was stated in the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā) that [the sacrifice] does not have heaven and so forth as its purpose; for if, in order to establish a multiplicity of objects, heaven were also postulated as a fruit according to the principle of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, there would follow the consequence of subverting the independent status of the goal as established by the scriptural injunctions regarding specific desires (*kāma-śruti*). For this very reason, it was also described in the *Pūrvatantra* that even for sacrifices such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, which are understood to be the means for accomplishing all desires, there cannot be the accomplishment of two fruits within a single performance. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya that "destruction occurs through the experience of the fruit," the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of cause; by the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.25) with its subsequent separation (*yogavibhāga*), the meaning is that destruction occurs by means of the experience of the fruit. This dispels the doubt that—based on the passage "one should generally know sin [to be] the mind's suppression"—only sin is destroyed by expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and not merit, by specifying that this refers to meritorious action from the perspective of one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).

[Objection: Is not the portion of the Sūtra, "as they came, so [they go], and not otherwise" (yathetamanevaṃ ca), redundant? For there is no doubt to be dispelled, as this matter has already been clearly established by the scriptural statement itself; therefore, since the Sūtra consists of logical reasoning (*nyāya*), for what purpose is this reasoning provided here? To this we reply: Although from the words, "Now they return again by that same path, as they came to the ether" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15), a sequence is understood even for the descent in the reverse order of the stages of ascent, [the Sūtra provides this reasoning].

Just as the descent is accepted as being both "in that same way" (*yathā*) and "not so" (*anevam*) in accordance with the many concluding statements such as "from space to air," so too, although the introductory scriptural passages—by the phrase "as far as" (*yāvat*)—imply the enjoyment of all karma without remainder, the enjoyment of karma is understood to have a remainder in cases such as "those of pleasant conduct" (*ramaṇīyacaraṇāḥ*) and "those of foul conduct" (*kapūyacaraṇāḥ*), due to the force of those many concluding statements; this is for the purpose of indicating the illustrative example.

The meaning is that a separate mention is made because it is based on a difference in meaning; for this very reason, the Sūtra "Not [the breath] and the function, because of their being taught separately" (BS 2.4.9) indicates that a separate teaching is grounded in a distinction of meaning—this is the intention. Regarding the word *ācāra*: the meaning is that of the word *caraṇa* as presented by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) as denoting conduct (*ācāra*). In the Bhāṣya, the statement "he performs (*ācarati*) meritorious action" involves the use of the prefix *āṅ*, which is not intended to be significant; for this very reason, the subsequent Bhāṣya states, "because of the use of the root *car* in the sense of an object," employing the root *car* alone for the sake of consistency with the term *caraṇa*.

It should be understood that this is because it is expressible [as an object]. Regarding the phrase "because of its application in the performance of ritual action" (*karmānuṣṭhāne prayogāt*): the point is that since one performs (*caryate*) or carries out (*anuṣṭhīyate*) it, the word *caraṇa* denotes the object (*karman*) when the suffix *lyuṭ* is applied according to the rule *karmaṇi kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Thus, its status as denoting an object is established.

In the Bhāṣya, the phrase "of the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) and so forth, which are enjoined by Vedic texts inferred from traditional practice" means that, according to Smṛti usages such as "The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of traditional practice," it is logical that those acts denoted by the term 'traditional practice'—namely the twilight worship and so forth—which are enjoined by Vedic texts inferred from traditional practice, serve to confer eligibility for performing Vedic rites such as the Agnihotra. This is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: how can the entirety of conduct (*ācāra*) be denoted by the word *ācāra* on the grounds that it is prescribed by Vedic texts inferred from conduct, given that among certain conducts—such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and others—it is observed that they are prescribed by Vedic texts inferred from Smṛti, and because the twilight worship itself is established by direct Vedic revelation in the injunction, "One should perform the twilight worship day after day"? What more need be said? For according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since it is accepted that the scattered Vedic branches (*viprakīrṇa-śākhā*) alone are the source of Smṛti and conduct, [the same applies] to all forms of conduct.

If it is asked how the status of *saṃdhyāvandana* and other practices denoted by the term "custom" (*ācāra*) as auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is established—given that they are not established by direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*)—we reply: It is true that all ritual action is established by direct Vedic revelation; nevertheless, there is indeed a means of determining what is Vedic and what is non-Vedic. For the three Vedas (*trayī*) function primarily with reference to sacrificial rites (*vaitānika-karma*); within them, however, certain non-sacrificial matters are mentioned only incidentally (*prasaṅgāt*). Therefore, that which the three Vedas have as their primary subject matter...

That which proceeds from the Veda is Vedic, while that which is other than that is non-Vedic; consequently, everything else—whether worldly (laukika), based on tradition (smārta), or customary conduct (ācāra)—is indeed the conventional usage within the assembly of those learned in the Veda. This point is clear in the seventh section, concerning "other injunctions" (vidhyantara-adhikaraṇa), of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā-sūtra; and thus, the meaning is that in a rite pertaining to the three fires (vaitānika-karma), that which does not pertain to the three fires (avaitānika) is merely an auxiliary (aṅga).
Thus ends the section concerning those whose transgressions have been expiated.

Regarding the statement, "It is said that there is no restrictive rule for the connection with the results of good deeds," it should be understood that here the term "good deeds" (*sādhukarma*) indicates by implication (*lakṣaṇā*) the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), which is the fruit of those deeds; this is because the present section is intent on demonstrating the absence of a connection with the heavenly world for those who are devoid of good deeds. Alternatively, in the phrase "it is said" (*ity ucyate*), the word *iti* denotes a manner or mode; consequently, for the purpose of inducing dispassion (*vairāgya*), it is stated that even among certain souls who perform undesirable acts and so forth, some remain in the third place, while others undergo the torments of Yama.

The sense is that it is established in this section that all [those who perform sacrifices] experience [the results] and go to the moon; such is the nature of what is being propounded here. In the Bhāṣya, regarding the phrase "mere iṣṭāpūrta," the word "mere" (kevala) serves to exclude those sacrifices and works (iṣṭādi) that are constituent parts of the Brāhma-vidyā.

Or [it may mean] the turning away from evil; that is, they do not perform what is forbidden by the scriptures. Now, one might ask: how can both groups be included by the term *aniṣṭādikārin* (those who perform undesirable acts and so forth)? It is not the case that, by connecting the negative particle (*nañ*) with the word *iṣṭādikārin*, those who do not perform good deeds are obtained; nor is it the case that, by connecting it with the word *iṣṭādi*, those who perform the opposite—evil deeds—are obtained. Rather, because there is no restriction [on the scope of the compound], there is an inclusion of the two meanings obtained from the two possible compounds. Consequently, this also includes those who, while pursuing good deeds, do not even practice evil deeds.

It need not be said that the exclusion of reaching the world of the moon is established [by this alone], because the objection—that resorting to two compounds by means of any one of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa* would be cumbersome—is thereby dispelled.

In the commentary, regarding the phrase "both are performers of evil deeds," the intended meaning is as follows: there is a compound of the negative particle *nañ* with words such as *iṣṭa*, which denote good deeds (*sukṛta*). Consequently, the meaning of the term *aniṣṭādikārī* is simply the performance of evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*). Since that evil deed is of two kinds, and because in reality it is possible for all performers of merit (*puṇyakārin*) to have committed some prohibited act—thereby making it possible for all of them to reach the moon—the term *iṣṭādikārī* refers specifically to those who perform sacrifices and other rites directed toward the fruit of heaven.

Because [the term] ends in the suffix *ṇini* denoting habitual practice (*tācchīlya*), those other than such persons are here called "those who do not perform sacrifices and so forth" (*aniṣṭādikārin*); thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. The sense is that since "Datta" and "Pūta" are mentioned, the word "iṣṭādi" (sacrifices and so forth) is indicative of all meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*).

The phrase "presumption based on scripture" (*śrutyarthāpatti*) means a presumption based on scripture consisting of the requirement for a fifth libation; this is because of the scriptural statement without qualification: "At the fifth libation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (*pañcamyām āhutāv āpaḥ puruṣavacaso bhavanti*). Nor should it be said that this refers only to human beings, because there is a scriptural statement without qualification: "Those of pleasant conduct and those of foul conduct [are born] in the womb of a dog or the womb of a pig," and because in the Bhāṣya it is stated that the departure [of the soul] is heard of for all without distinction. By this, [the author] addresses the specific mention in the preceding passage, "as far as the point of convergence" (*yāvatsampātam*).

It should be understood that the connection characterized by an objection is indicated here: although a restriction might be adopted in accordance with the concluding statement, "Those of pleasant conduct," for one who naturally desires such a restriction, nevertheless, no restriction is possible here because of the scriptural text, "They all go to the moon alone. This means that there would be fruitlessness for sin.

Although it would have been more appropriate to say that if the two [sin and merit] yielded equal results, then the well-performed action (sukṛta), which is accomplished through great expenditure of wealth and effort, would be rendered useless; nevertheless, [the author says], "But having experienced [it] in Saṃyamana... [and so on].

It should be understood that it was stated thus because it is a commentary introducing the sūtra which demonstrates the experience of the fruits of evil. [Regarding the phrase] "by his command," the meaning is as follows: but surely, the word *saṃyamana* refers to restraint (*nirodhana*)?

This is well-known, but not within the [Buddhist] teaching; even there, the meaning "in the instruction of Yama" is difficult to establish, because Yama is not relevant [to the context]. Furthermore, the locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta-saptamī*) is extremely strained; for while it is taught that the locative is used with a cause when there is a connection with an object—meaning it is used precisely as a cause by way of being a purpose—and this is prescribed in cases of such connection, as in: "One kills a leopard for its skin; one kills an elephant for its tusks."

In Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on such examples as "one kills the yak for its hair" (*keśeṣu camarīṃ hanti*) and "the musk deer is killed for its scent-gland" (*sīmni puṣkalako hataḥ*), it is explained that here the fruit of the action is intended as the cause (*nimitta*). Since the third case ending would otherwise apply by the rule *tato hetāv* (Pāṇini 2.3.23)—which prescribes the third case when the cause is that which prompts the action or for whose sake the action is undertaken—the seventh case is specifically enjoined. It is further described that if there is a connection with the object (*karman*) by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with that cause, the seventh case does not occur; for instance, in the example "he reaps grain for wages" (*vetanena dhānyaṃ lunāti*), the seventh case is not used because there is no conjunction between the wages and the grain.

For here, the command of Yama does not possess the status of a cause (*nimitta*) by way of being the purpose; if the word *saṃyamana* were intended to mean the command of Yama, there would be no consistency with the [Brahmasūtra] statement: "And even there, because of his activity, there is no contradiction. Indeed, the Sūtra would be consistent only if *saṃyamana* were intended to mean the abode of Yama, for in that case the Sūtra would serve to resolve the doubt regarding the contradiction between going to the abode of Yama and going to hell. Likewise, if the term *saṃyamana* were intended to mean the command of Yama, the introductory commentary (*bhāṣya*) to that Sūtra would also lack consistency; and this is not the case.

It should not be said that the suspicion of contradiction arises by taking the "going to the abode of Yama" established in another Purāṇa as the basis for the objection; for that [interpretation] is overly strained (*atikliṣṭa*). Furthermore, the commentary (*bhāṣya*)—which states, "In *saṃyamana*, in the domain of Yama, one experiences the torments of Yama (*yamayātanā*)"—is also capable of being explained as follows: the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), meaning "in *saṃyamana*, which is the domain (*śāsana*) of Yama"; thus, it means "one experiences the torments employed by Yama in the city of *saṃyamana*, which is the object of Yama’s command. Even in that case, there is no contradiction, because [the soul's movement] occurs within the scope of his activity.

If it is argued that there is no fault in adopting this meaning in accordance with the *Sūtrāvatārikā-bhāṣya*, that is true; however, since the meaning must be described in conformity with the commentary (*vṛtti*) of Bodhāyana, who perceives the intention of the author of the Sūtras, such an explanation is justified. This is because the word *saṃyamana* is seen to be used in the sense of "governance" (or "instruction") in passages such as "Viṣṇu is capable even of restraining me," and because although the word *saṃyamanīya* denotes the city of Yama, the word *saṃyamana* lacks any established usage as a name for the city of Yama.

Because it is possible for [the object] to be the cause (*nimitta*) as the fruit of the command being observed, there is no inconsistency in using the locative case (*saptamī*) even in the absence of a connection with an action (*karmasaṃyoga*). For the commentators (*vṛttikāra*) have explained that in the rule *antarddhiḥ yenādarśanam* (Pāṇini 1.4.28), "disappearance" (*antarddhi*) means "obstruction," and thus the locative is a "locative of cause" (*nimittasaptamī*), since here there is no connection between disappearance and the object of desire (*icchākarma*). Consequently, in the phrase *antarddhiḥ*, even though there is an absence of connection with an object, [it functions] by way of being the purpose (*prayojana*).

Even in the absence of being a cause (*nimittatva*), there is no fault here because we observe the locative case used in the sense of a mere cause (*nimittamātra-saptamī*). Now, one might object: if "cause" (*nimitta*) is understood in the *Padamañjarī* as a "reason" (*kāraṇa*)—according to the rule "the seventh case [is used] after a cause when there is connection with an action"—then it would also apply in cases such as "he is bound because of his birth" (*jātyā baddhaḥ*). Therefore, "cause" must be understood as the "purpose" (*prayojana*), as in "one kills a leopard for its skin" (*carmaṇi dvīpinam hanti*). In this instance, disappearance is the cause of non-perception; he is indeed hidden, and thus he is not seen. Therefore, it is due to that cause.

If it is argued that the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) intended to express the remainder (*śeṣa*) of the meaning of the fifth case, and that consequently either the seventh case is used according to the rule "the seventh case is used when there is a characterization of an action by another action" (*yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam*), or it is a locative of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*) according to the rule "the seventh case is used for the locus" (*saptamy adhikaraṇe ca*), then let it be so here as well; or else, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the phrase "in *saṃyamana*" does not explain the meaning of *saṃyamana* as "Yama’s command," but rather [refers to] Yama’s city (*yamapura*) within *saṃyamana*, because the torments are experienced there as being employed by that [command].

The meaning is that while Yama’s command exists—that is, while Yama’s decree is in force—one experiences the torments prescribed by him. This very meaning is intended by the commentary (*ṭīkā*) which states that "in *saṃyamana*" is a locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), meaning "by Yama’s command. This is the sense of the sentence: in the word *yamaśāsana* within the phrase beginning with *saṃyamane*, there is a locative of cause, and this has already been established above. Nor is there any possibility of a doubt regarding a contradiction between such a state of being restrained (*saṃyamana*) and the act of going to hell.

It should not be said that the lack of elegance in the *Ṭīkā* text lies in the objection that these statements in the *Purāṇas* and other works regarding the attainment of Yama’s abode (*yamasadana*) are the cause of this doubt; for the contradiction between being bound and going to hell is not what is suspected and resolved by the statement, "And there too, because of his activity, there is no contradiction. Rather, in the sūtra "In the binding," only entry into Yama’s city is mentioned, not entry into his abode (*sadana*). Therefore, since no contradiction exists with what is actually propounded by the sūtra, [the objection is invalid].

The statement in the *Śaṅkā-bhāṣya*—"The declarations regarding the attainment of Yama's abode are recited in the Purāṇas and other texts; this doubt arises based on that; for thus, even there, there is no contradiction because of its operation"—addresses the objection: "But how can those who are wandering through, or going to, the seven worlds attain Yama's abode? This is how the text is consistent.

"This world exists, but there is no other"—this is the statement of Death to Naciketas in the *Kaṭhavallīs*: "The hereafter does not appear to the fool, who is deluded by the infatuation for wealth and is heedless; thinking 'there is no this world, nor any other,' he falls again and again under my power. Here, "the hereafter" (*sāmparāya*) refers to that which is gone to or reached after death, following this world's dissolution; specifically, it denotes the particular means for attaining that state. "To the fool" (*bālam*) means to one who lacks discernment.

For this very reason, it does not appear to one who is negligent and inattentive; for this same reason, the conceited person—one whose nature is to think—thinking "this world alone consisting of food, drink, and so forth exists, and there is no other world," and acting accordingly, falls under my power through the repeated attainment of birth and death. Thus, regarding the phrase "this world" (*ayaṃ lokaḥ*), others have explained it by supplying the word *eva* (alone), while the Teachers, however, explain it by supplying the word *ca* (and).

The meaning is that there is no happiness either here or in the next world; the phrase "to be experienced in another body" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding the statement in the Commentary, "the meeting place of people with Vaivasvata," the word *saṃgamana* means "that which is to be met. Since the sūtra beginning with "they remember" (*smaranti ca*) has not been introduced [previously], he introduces it himself with the words "because their destination is seen," and so forth, after the proposition has been established in the sūtra: "But in the case of the Restrainer (Yama), the others experience [the results] and then ascend and descend."

The demonstration of authoritative evidence is intended for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of evil deeds, but not regarding their cessation; therefore, the author of the Sūtras, desiring to demonstrate their destination, showed the very statement of Smṛti—"All these come under its control"—as the authoritative proof in the Sūtra "And they remember" (3.1.24). [Objection: But even now that same defect remains as it was: "Not even an eighth part of a finger's breadth exists, O best of the twice-born."

If it is argued that this cannot be used as proof for the sinful experiencing the results of Yama’s tortures—since the text begins with "There are no living beings there who are bound by the fetters of karma," and then states, "And all these, O Blessed One, indeed fall under the power of Yama"—because this statement merely records subjection to Yama in a general sense applicable to everyone and does not specifically refer only to the sinful; we reply: No, for it says, "At the end of their lifespan, they go there and are impelled toward those tortures."

This is because one observes the experience of torments as the fruit of evil deeds; yet this cannot be taken as authoritative on the grounds that it applies universally to all sinners through their experience of the fruits of evil, for later on, by demonstrating that devotees of the Lord do not go to the domain of Yama, it can be determined that the statement "all these come under his control" refers exclusively to those who perform undesirable acts and the like.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*—since this statement extends as far as demonstrating the experience of torments resulting from sinful fruits, whereas Parāśara and others remember [the state of] being subject to Yama, and thus the *Bhāṣya* says "they remember the experience of the fruits"—this is not so, because [the phrase] "being subject to Yama" refers to that very [experience].

Because there is a contradiction [in the opponent's view] due to the possibility that the necessity [of the path] extends up to the experience of the fruit. "But on account of knowledge and action, because they are the subjects under discussion. Here, the genitive case denotes a general relationship. This is the sequence of syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here: the word "devayāna-pitṛyāne" (the path of the gods and the path of the fathers) must be supplied as a dual neuter nominative. And thus, since the path of the gods and the path of the fathers belong to knowledge and action—that is, they are related to knowledge and action, or rather, are for the sake of knowledge and action—and this [genitive] expresses that sense of purpose (*tādarthya*).

It is precisely for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of those [actions]; the word "iti" here denotes a reason. And therefore, since the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna paths have as their purpose the fruits of knowledge and action, the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna do not exist for those devoid of knowledge and action, because they are intended for the fruits of knowledge and action; this is the meaning. Now, one might ask: from what source is it known that the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna have knowledge and action as their purpose? To this he says: "because they are the subject under discussion" (*prakṛtatvāt*).
