The meaning is that [the text] refers to the learned man and the performer of sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*, because they are mentioned in the context of the primary subject matter (*prakṛta*). Although the genitive case in the phrase "of knowledge and action" (*vidyākarmaṇoḥ*) denotes a relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), it is more convenient for comprehension to rely on the sense that the paths of the gods (*devayāna*) and the fathers (*pitṛyāna*) are accomplished through knowledge and action respectively. For this very reason, the author will later state: "The path of the gods has knowledge as its object, and the path of the fathers has merit as its object. Consequently, the intended meaning can be easily understood without resorting to the aforementioned strained interpretation; nevertheless, [the other explanation is also possible].

It should be understood that the statement was made in that way to indicate that the two paths—the path of the gods (*devayāna*) and the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*)—which are themselves results, also serve as subordinate elements for other results. The reading *viśiṃṣan hi viṣayaḥ* is the correct one; for as the learned have said: "The word *vi-* has the sense of 'distinction' (*viśeṣa*), and the root *si-* denotes 'binding' (*bandha*); since it binds specifically (*viśeṣeṇa sinoti*), it is therefore a regulator (*niyāmaka*), and thus an object (*viṣaya*). [In this derivation] the root *si-* means 'to bind'; the suffix *ac* is added in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule *kṛt-sarvadhātubhyaḥ*. (Pāṇini 3.1.135).

[The suffix] *śatṛ* [is used in the sense of] "distinguishing" (*viśiṣan*)—or rather, this is a statement of the resultant meaning (*phalitārtha*). Now, one might object: since the Devayāna and Pitṛyāna paths have as their purpose the fruits of knowledge and karma respectively, then just as there is an absence of the Devayāna due to the absence of knowledge, there must likewise be an absence of the Pitṛyāna due to the absence of karma; thus, relying on the meaning of the Sūtra [in that way] is an instance of misplaced reasoning. For the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) did not suspect that the attainment of the moon occurs via either the Devayāna or the Pitṛyāna, given the scriptural statement: "Whoever departs from this world, they all go to the moon."

According to the statement of Kauṣītaki, only the mere attainment of the moon is suspected; there is no restrictive factor here that would lead to the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāna*), by which the position favored by the opponent (the *pūrvapakṣin*) might be established. For this very reason, the Teacher himself will state at the occasion of refuting the view of Yādavamiśra: "Even when the destination is one and the same, the restriction of the path occurs due to the difference between the travelers," and likewise, "the attainment of the world of the fathers is possible independently of the smoke and other [signs]. Therefore, regarding the path of the gods (*devayāna*):

If it is argued that making this an illustration is also improper because there is no evidence for its non-existence, we say no; for, in accordance with the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* Śruti—"There are two paths, one of the ancestors and one of the gods, and by these two this entire universe moves"—there is no other path apart from these two courses. Furthermore, because the path of the gods (*devayāna*) is the cause of non-return, as stated in: "Those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool," whereas [those on] the path of the ancestors go to the moon.

Since the statement "they go" is to be treated as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) according to the method stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, there is no room for expanding upon the interpretation of the sūtra "vidyākarmaṇoḥ" [1.3.27] in that manner. Furthermore, in the *Rahatyadhikaraṇa* (1.3.10–14), the phrase "na tṛtīye tayopalabdheḥ" means that [the path] is not completed or reached in the third [state], in the sense of being one who has not attained that world, as expressed in the passage "of that world, he is a non-attainer."

It should be understood that this was stated [in the commentary] based on the observation of the *Bhāṣya*. Now, one might object: why does the *Bhāṣya* interpret the passage "yathāsau loko na saṃpūryate" by abandoning the natural sense of the words *yathā* and *sampūrṇa*, and instead adopting the meaning "by which person is that world not filled"? For the meaning "by what cause the lunar world is not filled—that is, not exhausted"—is indeed what is perceived naturally. To this we say: no, [it is not so]. "Be born... [The full context is: "O Jābāla, you must be born and die again and again; only then will you attain that world. Thus, the *Bhāṣya* interprets it as "by whom [the world] is not filled," meaning "by whom [the world] is not reached through repeated births. This is because the word *yathā* here signifies "in such a manner" (i.e., by means of repeated births), and the root *pṛ* (in *saṃpūryate*) signifies "to reach" or "to attain," rather than the sense of "filling" or "exhausting. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

"In the reply, 'Fill yourself up—this is the third place; by that [place], this world is not filled,' since it is established that [the third place] characterized by worms and so forth, which are the result of sinful karma, is unattainable, it is appropriate that the question also concerns what is unattainable; such is the intention of the Commentary. Now, one might object: "This is like giving a staff to a blind man by someone who is also blind," for in the reply, the following meaning is perceived, as this reply to that question is heard: "Now, of these two..."

"By neither of these paths do those small creatures go, which repeatedly return; they become such beings, [with the thought] 'Be born! Perish! This is the third station; by that [station], this world is not filled. Thus, by neither of these two paths—the path of the gods nor the path of the fathers—do they go; rather, those small creatures such as lice, bugs, mosquitoes, and so forth, which repeatedly return, come into being with the thought, "Be born! Perish!"

They are characterized by repeated recurrence in the form of birth and death; this third station (*sthāna*), consisting of the repeated turning back in the form of birth and death, is the third path. Therefore, because these small creatures follow a different path, they do not reach the path of the gods (*devayāna*) nor the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*), and thus, due to the absence of reaching the moon, that world is not filled, just as this world is overrun by small creatures—this meaning is understood from the context. Furthermore, there is no [contradiction] regarding the word "station" (*sthāna*).

It should not be said that the word "you" (*tvam*) lacks its own inherent meaning; rather, with respect to the two paths under discussion in the phrase "of these two paths," the state of being "third" connects only to a different path, because it is appropriate for a number to refer to members of the same class, as in the expression "a cow is to be sought as the second. Furthermore, the word "place" (*sthāna*) does not refer to the locus of the experience of the fruit; thus, one [path] has as its locus the attainment of Brahman, which is the fruit of knowledge, while the other has as its locus the attainment of the moon, which consists of the experience of the fruits of sacrifices, works of public utility, and charity.

It should not be argued that the third [place] is the locus for the repeated returning in the form of birth and death resulting from evil fruits, because it would then follow that those who experience the results consisting of birth in the womb of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth—which are the fruits of specific meritorious deeds—would also be included in the third group in relation to the two other places consisting of the attainment of the world of Brahman and the world of the Moon. Therefore, in the phrase "this is the third place," the word *sthāna* (place) [must be understood differently].

One must indeed accept that [the word] denotes a different path characterized by repeated and manifold cycles of birth and death; therefore, in the passage "by that, this world is not filled," the word *tena* means "from that" (*tasmāt*), the third case (*tṛtīyā*) being used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), meaning "because there exists another path, for that reason. If it is argued: "But surely, in the phrase 'by that living being (jīva) denoted as the third place, through evil karma,' the third case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*); therefore, even in the concluding summary, one should not resort to an unintended meaning [of 'by that']"; [we reply:]...

To this we reply: for it is established by logic that pronouns refer to what has been previously mentioned as the primary subject; therefore, in the passage, "When one pours curds into heated milk, that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas," the word *tat* (that) refers only to the milk, which is the primary substance because it is the substratum permeated by the act of pouring as well as by the curds, and not to the curds, which are secondary. Consequently, it is established in the fourth and eighth [books of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra] that *āmikṣā* is a modification of milk, just as...

Regarding the passage, "There are twenty-six ribs of this [animal]; pull them out one by one," it is established that the referent of the pronoun *tat* (this) is the primary object itself. This is because we observe that the feminine dual-bahuvacana ending of the pronoun *tāḥ* (them) in the phrase *anuṣṭhayocyāvayatāt* (pull them out one by one) refers specifically to the ribs (*vaṃkrīṇām*). Therefore, those [ribs] alone possess primacy; neither the number twenty-six nor the animal denoted by the word *asya* (of this) possesses primacy. Consequently, the sentence has the ribs as its primary subject matter.

It is established in the ninth [book] that a modification (*ūha*) must be made to demonstrate the crookedness [of the sacrifice]; consequently, in the passage "Be born, die; thus do beings exist; this is the third station," it is appropriate to understand by the word "this" (*etad*) the very *bhūtas* (beings) mentioned in the preceding sentence as the substrata of the activity of "existing" (*bhavanti*), and not the act of becoming (*bhavana*) in the form of birth, death, and so forth, which is presented merely as a qualifier of the agent and is not being enjoined as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by the verb "they exist."

Furthermore, the reference by means of the pronoun *etad* (this) as a reflective term for the perfected ones (*siddhas*) is not its natural sense; consequently, since those characterized by birth and death who perform evil deeds are referred to by the term "third place," the word *tena* (by that) in the passage "therefore that world is not filled" must also refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) denoted by the previously mentioned "third place. Moreover, the third [case ending] here denotes the agent, and not the causal particle *tasmāt* (from that); nor does it refer to those previously mentioned in the phrase "this is the third place," namely, "beings undergo repeated returns."

It should not be argued that since the evil deeds previously specified are plural, a singular designation by means of this word "this" (etac-chabdena) is untenable; for just as in the passage "That indeed is the curdled milk (āmikṣā) belonging to the Viśvedevas," the pronoun *tat*—though referring with a neuter gender—is used in conformity with the feminine gender of the word *āmikṣā* due to its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it, so too here, the neuter singular form "this third place" (*etat tṛtīyaṃ sthānam*) is used in conformity with the gender and number of the word "place" (*sthāna*), which is likewise neuter singular.

[They] are reborn; thus, in subsequent cases as well, the grammatical justification for the reference by the word *tena* (by that) in the phrase "therefore that world is not filled" is established. However, some maintain that according to the maxim that "the verb is primarily denotative of action," since the action of *bhavana* (coming into being) alone is primary in the word *bhavanti* (they come into being), it is this [action] alone that is referred to by the pronoun *etat* (this), and not the agent (*bhavituḥ*). For this very reason, even by the rhetoricians, in the verse: "The ocean, as if with the tips of its waves, grinds the sandalwood-foam; taking that, the moon, as if with its rays, anoints the women who are the quarters," [it is understood that] the ocean [is the agent] of the sandalwood-foam.

In the verse, "Taking that [foam], the moon, as if with his hands, anoints the women of the quarters," there is merely a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) of the identity between the pounding and the smearing: the ocean, possessing the quality of sandalwood paste, has its foam propelled by waves from its shore—which stands in the place of a stone slab—and the moon's rays spread to whiten the women of the quarters. However, there is no identity between the two acts in terms of their being the agents of the pounding and the smearing; for although the verbal suffixes in *pinaṣṭi* (he pounds) and *limpati* (he anoints) denote the agent, according to the principle "the verb expresses the action" (*bhāvapradānam ākhyātam*), the primary denotation is the action itself.

It has been stated that there can be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for that which is subordinate to the primary action; for this very reason, Daṇḍin, who cited the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) "Darkness, as it were, smears the limbs; the sky, as it were, rains collyrium," raised the doubt that the simile (*upamā*) between darkness and the sky might be with the agents of smearing and raining because of the hearing of the word *iva* in the examples, [and then refuted it by stating]: "If the agent were the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), it would be subordinated to the verbal element."

It has been argued that [an action] is incapable of depending on anything else because it is preoccupied with accomplishing its own function; for this very reason, there is the usage of the learned (abhiyukta) stating that in such expressions as "look, the deer runs," the act of running is the object (*karman*) of the act of seeing. Therefore, in the phrase "be born and die, being," what is capable of being referred to by the word *etat* is precisely the repeated occurrence of birth, death, and becoming. Consequently, even in the passage "therefore that world is not fulfilled," the meaning is simply that it is incomplete for that reason.

It is understood that because the non-fulfillment of the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) is mentioned due to the absence of ascending to the heavenly world, the *Bhāṣya* declares that the non-attainment of the heavenly world is caused by the non-fulfillment of the heavenly world. To support the natural sense of this, it is maintained that the word "evil-doers" (*pāpakarman*) found in the *Bhāṣya* refers to those in the third place by way of indicating the path; thus, they explain that even the text of the Teacher (Śaṅkara) should be interpreted accordingly.

"Following the command of the Lord" refers to the imitation of the Lord's command, [expressed as] "be born" and "be nourished. The phrase "due to the independence of the Veda" means because of the grammatical rule: "In the *chandas* (Vedic), transposition is frequent. This [rule] is connected with what follows—"he was born" (*jajñe*) and "he killed me" (*mamārayat*)—according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). Some read the text as *jajñe mamre*, but in that case, since the rule "after the root *bhṛ*, the *parasmaipada* occurs in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* tenses" would apply, some say it is used in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve prayoga*). [The text continues: "having attacked the city... (*purīmavaskandha*).

"Like *lunīhi nandanam* and so forth. Here, from the rule *bhūtārthatā vā*, the word *vā* (or) is carried over; thus the meaning is "like *purīm avaskanda lunīhi nandanam* and so forth. This is the underlying intention: according to the rule *samuccaye 'nyatarasyām*, a conjunction (*samuccaya*) consists of the utterance of multiple actions. Because it denotes actions being conjoined, there is optionally (*vibhāṣā*) the imperative (*loṭ*), and for that [imperative], the suffixes *hi* and *sva* occur; however, they occur optionally when [the action] is not characterized by that [conjunction]. This is the meaning of the sūtra. In that context, [there is the rule]: "In a conjunction, [the imperative occurs] after a word expressing a general [action]."

The employment of a verb expressing a general action (*sāmānyavācin*) after [the preceding verbs] is prescribed, as in: "Eat the rice, chew the parched grains, drink the flour; thus one consumes," where the optional second-person imperative (*loṇmadhyamapuruṣa*) is used by the rule *samuccaye 'nyatarasyām* to indicate a collection (*samuccaya*), and the employment of the verb *bhavati*, which expresses a general action, occurs because these actions are repeated multiple times. Consequently, [one may say]: "Ravage the city, pluck the Nandana grove, steal the jewels, carry off the celestial damsels!"

In the case of *vigṛhya cakre*, there is the use of the second person singular imperative (*loṭ*) in the middle voice (*madhyamapuruṣa*) according to the rule *anyatarasyām* for the conjunction (*samuccaya*) of actions such as attacking, cutting down, and plundering; and there is the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the general verb *kṛ*, according to the rule *samuccaye sāmānyavacanasya*. Just as this occurs there, so too here, in the conjunction of the actions of being born and dying in the phrase *jāyasva mriyasva*, there is the second person singular imperative, and the subsequent employment of the general verb *bhavanti*. This alone is the ultimate interpretation.

The *Hāra* (the "Stringing Together") is the opinion of the teachers, since no other refutation is presented beyond this point. Regarding the statement, "Indeed, for these beings there are only three seeds," once the threefold nature of the seeds has been asserted, one might object that it would have been more appropriate to say "egg-born, living-born, and sprout-born" rather than "egg-born, living-born, and sprout-born. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states, "the threefold nature of the seeds," explaining that because an independent scripture cannot be subject to questioning, it teaches the method which results in the threefold classification of seeds.

"Born from an egg" (*aṇḍaja*) means that which is born from an egg (*āṇḍaja*); the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*). "Born from a womb" (*jarāyuja*) refers to humans, cattle, and so forth, where *jarāyu* is the membrane enveloping the embryo. The meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) here is that this is also seen in the Śruti; for even in the Śruti, the fourfold origin of beings is observed, and among those, it is seen in the world that certain beings—namely, those born from sprouts (*udbhijja*) and those born from sweat (*svedaja*)—do not require the fifth oblation. The subsequent portion of the commentary beginning with "Of these beings indeed... (*teṣāṃ khalveṣāṃ bhūtānām...*) is of the nature of an explanation of this point.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and from seeing" (*darśanācca*), the term "from seeing" conveys two meanings by resorting to one of the three grammatical devices: *tantra* (repetition), *āvṛtti* (iteration), or *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one). However, the literal meaning as heard in the text is not to be accepted here; for in the scriptural passage, "born from an egg, born from a living being, and born from a sprout," no independence from the fifth oblation is heard. If this were so, then according to the view of others, one might explain that among the four classes of beings, the birth of some is seen to occur without dependence on the fifth oblation—so what need is there even for the scriptural mention of "seeing"?

If it is argued that this is due to the effort of synthesis (*saṅgraha*), the intention is that the presentation of these two meanings occurs by resorting to one or another of the methods such as *tantra* (repetition) or *āvṛtti* (iteration), for the purpose of raising a doubt regarding the meaning of the subsequent sūtra. Others, however, [hold] that by the scriptural statement (*śruti*) "the moon of all... [Candra...].

Regarding the phrase "the suspicion of reaching": the meaning is that a suspicion arises in everyone from the Kauṣītaki Śruti passage, "They all go to the moon alone. In the second sūtra, however, it refers to the "suspicion to be set aside"; the meaning is that the doubt to be refuted by the word "but" (*tu*) in the sūtra *saṃyamane tu*—namely, that the journey might be the same for both those who perform good deeds and those who perform evil deeds—is presented here. Regarding the phrase "the torments of Yama and the Āryas": [this refers to the specific experiences of the two classes of beings].

The suffix *ṇya* is to be understood as being used in the sense of "from which [they go]," as in the reading *yāmīryātanāḥ* (the torments of Yama); however, if that reading were not present, another interpretation should be considered. Furthermore, because a descent from there [the moon] would otherwise be impossible, this indicates that by the words "but having experienced [the results] in the world of Saṃyamana" (*saṃyamane tvanubhūya*), it is immediately understood that it is *Saṃyamana* itself that causes the descent, and not the lunar orb; for the latter would require the supply of the word "from the lunar orb" (*candramaṇḍalād*) to complete the sense. Therefore, this is indeed a sūtra establishing the final conclusion (*siddhāntasūtra*), and not according to the view of Bhāskara.

The claim made in the *Bhāmatī*, the *Kalpataru*, and other works that this is a *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra has been refuted; for if *saṃyamana* (the place of restraint) alone were the point of departure for the descent, then since it must also be stated that *saṃyamana* is the locus of the ascent—as indicated by the phrase "having experienced [there], he ascends"—it would be impossible for that [soul] to exist there [in *saṃyamana*].

It should be understood that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the phrase "immediately after the experience of the hells" (*narakānubhavādanantaram*) is employed with the intention that the word *anantara* functions as a directional term (*dikśabda*), similar to words such as *paścāt*. Alternatively, by supplying the word "upwards" (*ūrdhvam*), the ablative is used to denote spatial relation (*digyoga-lakṣaṇā*), just as the grammarians state regarding the rule "the *anusvāra* follows from a nasalized [consonant]" (*anunāsikātparo'nusvāraḥ*), where the ablative *anunāsikāt* is used by supplying the word "other than" (*anya*).

The word "immediately after" (*anantaram*) is an adjective for "the abode of Yama" (*yamālayam*); the meaning is that the abode of Yama is situated directly above the experience of the hells. He states the validity of the Sūtra according to his own view in the phrase "in the statement regarding the attainment of Yama"; this means in the statement, "This world does not exist, nor the next. Regarding the passage beginning with "Others, however," he first refutes the first alternative, intending the following dilemma: do those who perform undesirable acts go by way of smoke and so forth for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their sins, or for the sake of experiencing the fruits of their good deeds?

"In that case, because there is no experiencing of the fruits of evil" means that on that path, the experience of the fruits of evil is impossible; he refutes the second [position] with the words "without action," meaning without meritorious action such as sacrifices and the like.

"And because the scripture would otherwise be purposeless": if the fruit [of the sacrifice] were obtained even without performing the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, then no one at all would engage in them. Thus, the scripture such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," which is intended for the sake of attaining heaven and serves as an incentive for engaging in the Jyotiṣṭoma and so forth, would be purposeless; that is to say, it would not function as an incentive. Alternatively, the word *śāstra* refers to the ritual action (*karman*) taught therein. "Two paths" means two ways of going. "I have heard" means I have heard from the tradition. "Leading to the ancestors and the gods" means leading to their respective attainments. Regarding the phrase "of mortals" (*martyānām*): [The rest of the passage continues: ...the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāna*) is attained through the performance of sacrifices and rites, while the path of the gods (*devayāna*) is attained through knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, the statement "I have heard of two paths" is made in order to distinguish between these two. Furthermore, the mention of "two paths" is intended to exclude a third possibility, namely, that there is no liberation (*mokṣa*) at all. This is because the term "paths" implies movement toward a destination, and since liberation is the cessation of all movement, it is not included here. Moreover, the mention of "two paths" is intended to indicate that the attainment of the results of rituals depends upon the performance of those very rituals, whereas the attainment of the result of knowledge does not depend on anything else. This is because the scripture teaches that the result of knowledge is attained immediately upon its realization, without requiring any further action. Thus, the mention of "two paths" is intended to show that the attainment of the results of rituals is contingent upon their performance, while the attainment of the result of knowledge is not. Furthermore, the mention of "two paths" is intended to show that the path of the fathers leads to rebirth in this world, while the path of the gods leads to the world of Brahman. This is because the scripture describes the path of the fathers as returning again to this mortal world, whereas the path of the gods is described as leading to the world of Brahman from which there is no return. Therefore, the mention of "two paths" is intended to distinguish between these two distinct outcomes. Finally, the mention of "two paths" is intended to show that the path of the fathers is characterized by darkness (*tamas*), while the path of the gods is characterized by light (*jyotis*). This is because the scripture describes the path of the fathers as being enveloped in smoke and darkness, while the path of the gods is described as being luminous and radiant. Therefore, the mention of "two paths" is intended to illustrate the difference in the nature of these two paths. Thus, the entire passage is intended to clarify the distinction between the paths of the fathers and the gods, and to demonstrate that the attainment of the results of rituals is dependent upon their performance, while the attainment of the result of knowledge is independent of any external action. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the passage regarding the two paths.

The connection is with the one who attains [the goal], expressed as "father and mother"; for father and mother are indeed heaven and earth. Since the journey is not dependent on human effort—because the path, which is accomplished of its own accord once the means consisting of knowledge and action have been performed, cannot be something to be enjoined.

The meaning is as follows: for this very reason, satisfaction (*tṛpti*), which arises as a byproduct of eating, does not depend on any other operation; thus, because it is not dependent on a person, it is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), and consequently, being non-performable (*ananuṣṭheya*), it cannot be illuminated by a mantra. Therefore, it has been established in the section on the definition of the "subordinate" (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*) that the portion of the mantra revealing satisfaction is not to be applied separately with respect to that satisfaction. Regarding the phrase "in the third place for those who have died," the meaning is "for lice, flies, and so forth"; [it refers to] the state of sinners being experiencers of suffering.

Since there is no doubt that the seven suns, beginning with Āroga and Bhrāja, must experience suffering as sinners, or else must cause others to experience suffering through their nature as *yātudhānas* (tormentors), the second interpretation beginning with "or else" (*yadvā*) and so forth is also irrelevant. For this very reason, regarding the third point—that those who have died in the third place [do not reach the moon]—the sense is: if it is established that even those persons who perform undesirable acts do not attain the moon, what need is there to mention insects, flies, and the like who have died in the third place? Thus ends the section concerning those who perform undesirable acts (*aniṣṭādikāryadhikaraṇam*).

"By means of a different box" (*peṭikābhedena*) means by means of a specific box; the meaning is that, starting from the section "one whose transgression has been completed" (*kṛtātyaya*) up to the end of the chapter, this section is connected as a "descending box" (*avarohaṇapeṭikā*). For in the preceding section, since the paths of the gods (*devayāna*) and the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) serve as the fruits of knowledge and ritual action respectively, and since those who perform undesirable acts lack the fruits of knowledge and ritual action, they lack the path of the gods; likewise, they would also lack the path of the fathers.

It has been stated that [it] does not exist; likewise here too, because there is an absence of the experience of pleasure and pain—which are the fruits of having space and so forth as one's body—for those who possess latent impressions (*anuśayin*), it is established that having space and so forth as one's body does not exist. This should be seen as the connection with the subject matter of the current section (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "as they went, and not so," the meaning is that this was stated in the sūtra "kṛtātyaye" (BS 3.1.8) in the form "yathetamanevañca bhavati. However, some take the phrase "yathetamanevañca" itself to be what is being referred to by the word "stated."

They explain that even the neuter designation [of the word *anuśaya*] is appropriate, as in the case of rules such as "the *dvigu* compound takes the singular ending. By this statement in the Bhāṣya, the connection with the distant section (*vyavahitādhikaraṇa*)—namely, "one who possesses *anuśaya* after the completion [of the sacrifice]"—is indicated; meanwhile, the immediately preceding section is shown to be merely incidental (*prāsaṅgika*).

Regarding the word *abhra*: [it is derived] from the root *bhṛ* (to carry) with the suffix *kap*, according to the rule for words such as *mūlavibhuja*. From the root *miha* (to sprinkle), by virtue of belonging to the *pacādi* class, the suffix *ac* is applied—this overriding the suffix *ka* which would otherwise be prescribed by the rule for words with *di* or *gupadha* [roots]. Then, by the rule "*nyaṃkkādīnāṃ ca*," the *k* is changed to *g*, resulting in the form *abhra*. In this context, the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* passage "in the case of the cognition of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth" is as follows: although in passages such as "having gone thus, from space to air" (*yathetam ākāśād vāyum*), the attainment of space and air is not clearly understood due to the mention of the object (*karmanirdeśena*), [nevertheless, in the sequence] "having become air, he becomes smoke; having become smoke... [the transition is established].

Since it is established that what is taught here is precisely the attainment of the state of ether and so forth—following the subsequent, clearer, and more frequent statements such as "having become [ether], it becomes [air]"—the question arises: does this state of being ether and so forth consist in having a body made of ether and so forth, like the states of being a god or a human, or is it merely the attainment of similarity to them?

Regarding the phrase *tatsvābhāvyāpattiḥ*: *svābhāvyam* is simply *svabhāva* (inherent nature), with the suffix *-ṣyañ* added in the sense of the base word itself, as in *vartamānasāmīpya* and other such cases. Those things whose state (*bhāva*) is like their own state (*svasya bhāva*) are "those having inherent nature" (*svabhāvāḥ*), meaning similar things; the state of being that is *svābhāvyam*, which means similarity. Thus, *tatsvābhāvyāpattiḥ* means the attainment of similarity to that. They say that because of the Mahābhāṣya’s indication that "this is indeed inherent" (*svābhāvikam evaitat*), the augment *aij* does not apply to the word *svabhāva* by the rule *dvārādīnāṃ ca*. Following this traditional reading, [the text continues].

If the justification [of the text] is possible, one should not assume a reading such as "the attainment of its own nature" (*svābhāvyāpatti*) according to the *Bhāmatī* school. The meaning of the passage beginning with "as they came, [they reach] the ether" (*yathetamākāśam*) is as follows: those waters which have begun the formation of a body in the lunar orb, upon the exhaustion of their karma, become liquefied and, reaching the ether, lose their distinct forms; through this loss of form and their similarity to the ether, the latent dispositions (*anuśayin*) clinging to them also become like the ether. Those waters, being led hither and thither, become like the wind, and the latent disposition likewise becomes like that. This same principle is to be understood to apply to the stages of becoming clouds and so forth.

In the commentary here, the phrase beginning with "in the case of ether, etc. raises an objection: surely the abandonment of what is explicitly stated in scripture (*śruta*) cannot occur on the grounds of a lack of purpose. For if that were so, since the elements (*bhūta*) are easily available everywhere, one would not even have to postulate the departure of the soul enveloped by the elements due to a lack of purpose. Furthermore, having raised the objection that in the passage "they [merge] in the highest, so he said," the merging into the Supreme Self (*paramātma-sampatti*) mentioned in the scripture "the fire [merges] into the highest deity" is impossible because there would be no purpose in attaining the Supreme Self for those who have departed, [the author proceeds].

It has been stated that since a purpose must be postulated in accordance with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no abandonment of an object already established by such a means; therefore, in accordance with the evidence for ether and the other elements having the body as their form, one must admit that even for those with residual karma (*anuśayin*), ether and the rest serve as the substrata for their enjoyment, which is the satisfaction of the deities presiding over them. If this is argued, we say no. For if two experiencers were to occupy the same body simultaneously, and both desired the enjoyment of the other, it would follow that the body would be torn asunder. [Objection: But surely [the elements serve as substrata] precisely because they are the deities presiding over them?

If it is argued that [the souls] may possess space and so forth as their bodies, the sense [of the author] is this: since from the time of the beginning of creation until the dissolution there exist other well-established deities presiding over space and so forth—distinct from those who are subject to residual karma (anuśayin)—it is impossible for the descending souls to become the presiding deities of space and so forth at every moment. Others, however, take the opponent's position to be that the souls actually attain the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of space and the rest.

Now, it may be argued that it is not impossible for one thing to become another, since the *Bhāmatī* states that this is established by the fact that Nandikeśvara transformed his human body into the form of a divine body by worshipping Śiva, and likewise that the divine body of Nahuṣa was remembered as having become an animal; and the *Kalpataru* further states that Nandikeśvara, having propitiated Rudra, was transformed into a deity while still in a human body, and similarly that Nahuṣa, having attained the status of Indra, became a python due to the curse of Agastya.

If it is argued that since the opponents have proposed as their prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) precisely that [the self] has space and so forth as its body, how can there be a refutation of their view? We say no, because in the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya*, the prima facie position is stated as "they perceive the very nature of space and so forth," and because in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is stated that "the becoming of one thing into another thing is not possible. Thus, having determined that such was the intended meaning, a refutation is appropriate; and by those commentators who consider such a prima facie position to be untenable, our own intended meaning alone [is upheld].

If it is concluded that [the soul's state] has reached its end, then one should see that there is no fault whatsoever. (22) Now, one might argue: "Since the phrase 'from this, indeed, it is very difficult to emerge' specifically describes a long emergence from rice and so forth, it can be said that in the preceding passage, a short emergence is understood upon reaching space and the other stages. Therefore, by the sentence "from this, indeed, it is very... and so on, what is intended to be taught is merely the existence of a long stay in rice and so forth; for by the very mention of staying in rice and so forth, whether it be for a long or a short time, an indefinite long stay is already implied.

Because that [long duration] is already established, it is not something to be enjoined; rather, by virtue of the capacity of the injunction to establish a rule for long-duration storage in the case of rice and other grains, the rule of long-duration storage is excluded from space and so forth, but not even the non-optional long-duration storage itself. For this very reason, in the case of the *Aṅgirasa-dvirātra* sacrifice, where it is specifically stated, "The *Vaiśvānara* *sāman* occurs on the previous day, and the *Ṣoḍaśin* on the subsequent day," the rule enjoining the *Ṣoḍaśin* cup on the subsequent day establishes that the *Ṣoḍaśin* is drawn on the subsequent day of the *dvirātra*.

It has been stated in the tenth [book] that the *ṣoḍaśī* cup is also obtained through a general statement; for this very reason, regarding the scope of the genitive case prescribed by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti," the prohibition "akākārayoḥ pratiṣedhaḥ" applies to the restrictive rule "ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi. Consequently, there is no prohibition of the non-restrictive genitive obtained by "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti," as is accepted by grammarians in the example "bhedikā kāṣṭhānāṃ devadattasya" (Devadatta’s wood-cutter). And thus, in the case of rice and other [grains]...

Since the rule regarding long-term persistence was established [in the previous section], let the restriction on long-term persistence be excluded from the preceding case; however, the very nature of long-term persistence itself is not to be excluded. Anticipating this objection, the Bhāṣya states, "The word *tad* is elided according to Vedic usage," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: here, the word *durniṣprapataram* does not establish a rule regarding difficult departure by assuming it to be formed with the suffix *lyuṭ*; rather, from the root *sval* (to go forth), the comparative suffix *tarap* is applied according to the rule "in the sense of excellence" (*atiśāyane*), and in accordance with Vedic usage, the syllable *ta* is elided, resulting in the form *durniṣprapataram*. Consequently, when there is a requirement for a correlate (*pratiyogi*) for this excellence, since the ether (*ākāśa*) and others mentioned previously are present in the mind, they are construed as its correlates.

And thus, because it is stated that [the soul] remains for a long time in rice and other grains in comparison to space, it follows that its duration in space and so forth is relatively brief; therefore, the desired conclusion is established.

If it is asked: "Is this not a modification of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*), but rather simply the elision of the words *tara* and *pit*, and what is the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) here?"—[the answer is: because the suffix *lyuṭ* is set aside by the rule *īṣadduḥsuṣu kṛcchrākṛcchrārtheṣu khal* (Pāṇini 3.3.126), one might attempt to support it by grasping at the straw of *kāśa* and *kuśa*; however, it is improper to resort to such a modification of phonemes as changing the *n* into *r* and *e*. Some, however, maintain that when the suffix *ḍa* occurs after the root *pad* with *dur* as a prefix in the sense of *khala*, the form *durniṣprapam* is established, and from that, the suffix *tarap* [is added].

Regarding the derivation of the word *durniṣprapataram*: the formation of the term *durniṣprapatara* is as follows. In the rule prescribing the suffix *ḍa* when the root *jan* is used in conjunction with other upapadas—specifically the rule stating "it is also seen in other cases"—it is stated that it should be added that "it is also seen after other roots as well. Since the suffix *ḍa* is taught to apply even to other verbal roots, the inclusion of the word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) in the commentary indicates that this applies regardless of all specific conditions (*sarvopādhi*). Furthermore, because of the mention of "variously" (*bahulam*) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, it is understood that other *kṛt* suffixes also deviate from their prescribed meanings.

"Because it has already been stated in the *Vṛtti*, and because it is logical for that *ḍa* to have the sense of the suffix *khal*, the form is established even without the addition or elision of phonemes (*varṇāgama-varṇalopa*)," he says; this is extremely weak, because resorting to such a strained interpretation is inferior to simply resorting to Vedic phonetic elision (*chāndasa-varṇalopa*).

However, some [hold] that because the word *vai* in the phrase "from here, indeed, it is more difficult to escape" (*durniṣprapataram*) has the same meaning as the restrictive particle *eva*, it functions like the restriction by *eva* in the passage: "There are three bellies of the sacrifice—the Gāyatrī, the Bṛhatī, and the Anuṣṭubh; in these alone they insert [the verses], and from these alone they take them out. Just as in that case, this restricts the insertion [of verses] to the Gāyatrī and others occurring in the Pavamāna [laud], and excludes other places; so too, since the Śruti prohibits a long departure from this state for anyone other than those such as rice and the like, there is no long duration in the case of ether and the rest.

This is the accomplishment of departure (*niṣkramaṇasiddhi*). Therefore, by the rule "in the Veda, the suffix *yuc* is added after roots meaning 'to go'," this word ends in *yuc*, which is specifically prescribed for the Vedic language; the modification of the phoneme into the letter *r* is a Vedic peculiarity. Otherwise, since the suffixes with the sense of *khal* are prescribed only for the meanings of "state" (*bhāva*) and "object" (*karman*) by the rule "only those two [roots] take the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal*-meanings," and since this [root] is intransitive, it would have to signify a state.

Or rather, because it is a remainder, and since its meaning lacks excellence, the suffix *tarap* is difficult to obtain from it; nor should it be argued that this contradicts the Bhāṣya’s statement that the elision of the word *tara* is Vedic (*chāndasa*), for they say that since excellence is possible in the case of a word ending in the *ac* affix added after a root in the sense of an agent (*kartṛ*), the suffix *tarap* is indeed possible.
Thus concludes the section concerning "not too long."

Since even obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) and the like are associated with impurity due to the immolation of animals for a year and so forth, the mention of "a year" is intended to indicate that they become equivalent to mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) through the habitual performance of censurable acts. Here, by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the consumption of the remnants of oblations (*havir-śeṣa*) in the Agnihotra and other rites at forbidden times—such as evening and morning—is included; thus, it should be understood that even rites like the Agnihotra, though free from violence, are associated with impurity. Or, according to the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), the phrase "or rather this... and so on means: "this [you] do not die now, nor are you harmed; that is to say, you will not be injured."

The verbal root *ruṣ* (or *riṣ*), meaning "to injure," is indeed the most appropriate and unassailable resolution [to the objection]. Now, although there is no sublation of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating that "one with a golden body goes upward" regarding the attainment of heaven through the ritual of animal sacrifice (*paśusaṃjñapana*), one must nonetheless necessarily admit that it constitutes violence (*hiṃsā*), since it is an activity conducive to death intended for the purpose of death.

Nor can it be argued that this [act] is non-violence because it takes the form of protection; for just as burning and cutting may take the form of protection when they serve to heal a wound, so too, even though they are forms of violence, their nature as protection of the animal is logically established. Furthermore, this defense would apply universally to all cases.

Indeed, it cannot be said that in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice there is no drinking of liquor made from flour (*paiṣṭī surā*), which is prohibited for all three castes; nor can it be said that in the Aśvamedha, the seizing of cows by those guarding the horse—which is performed by order of the king and consists of the taking of Brahmins ignorant of the Aśvamedha mantras and Brāhmaṇas—is not the seizing of a Brahmin; nor can it be said that the seizing of all women requested by one who worships Vāmadeva is not the seizing of another's wife. Therefore, a different justification must be stated for those cases; let that same justification apply to the case of violence (*hiṃsā*) as well.

What is the use of this denial of the nature of injury (*hiṃsātva*) which contradicts worldly consensus? What, then, is the universal solution? In the prohibitive statement "one should not injure," it is only the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) that is restated by means of the verbal root for injury, and not its being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatā*). This is because, on the view that the agent is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), injury is understood through the force of the co-occurring word (*samānapada-śruti*) to be subordinate to that [human purpose]; and even on the view that the agent is merely implied by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) denoted by the suffix, it is understood to be subordinate to that agent who is so implied. In this regard, there is nothing whatsoever that denotes the sacrifice.

In the sentence taught independently (anārabhyādhīta), "With this, they subsequently sacrifice by means of the Agniṣṭoma," one might understand that this [prohibition] is subsidiary to the sacrifice, just as the earth-fire is subsidiary to the sacrifice denoted by the word *yajati*; nor is there anything that implies a specific sacrifice (*kratu*), by which its subsidiarity to a sacrifice could be understood—just as the *parṇa*-woodness is understood to be subsidiary to the sacrifice through its connection with the *juhū* ladle; furthermore, there is no presentation of a sacrifice by means of context (*prakaraṇa*), such that [the rule] "one should not speak untruth" [would apply].

In the sentence recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there would be an understanding that the prohibited act—just like the speaking of untruth—is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*). Therefore, here, by means of the verbal root *hiṃs* (to injure), there is a reference (*anuvāda*) to injury for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*); thus, only that [injury] is prohibited, not that which is for the sake of the ritual. If it is argued: "Nevertheless, since the verbal root *hiṃs* brings to mind both types of injury—those for the sake of the ritual and those for the sake of the person—by the power of its own denotative capacity (*śabdaśakti*), let both types of injury be referred to and prohibited," this is not tenable.

For since the person—who is presented as the primary agent through being denoted by the verbal suffix and through being implied by the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) which is the meaning of that suffix—is subordinate to the act of injury, and because that injury is quickly presented [to consciousness], the sentence prohibiting injury has already fulfilled its purpose; thus, it is impossible to assume that it also prohibits the injury that is subordinate to a sacrifice, which is only presented after a delay.

Now, even if the verbal power (*śabda-śakti*) is equal, if one accepts a distinction such that only that which is denoted (*śakya*) and has immediate presentation (*śīghropasthiti*) enters into the syntactic relation of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), while that which has delayed presentation does not, then in the case of the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the terms *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* would immediately convey their respective times as heard in the originative injunctions (*utpatti-vākya*) for the Āgneya and Agnīṣomīya sacrifices; thus, these two, having immediate presentation, would be connected to the fruit, whereas the Upāṃśuyāja—[would not].

It might be argued that because the two sacrifices to Agni and to Agni-Soma are prescribed as being performed on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), the time for the full moon—which is established by implication—is understood immediately as the occasion for performance; whereas the connection with the result would not occur for the *upāṃśuyāja*, since its presence is delayed. This is true; however, just like the sacrifices to Agni and Agni-Soma, the *upāṃśuyāja* also possesses Vedic authority regarding the full moon day. Therefore, since there is no difference in the speed with which the occasion for performance is understood, it is precisely for the sake of establishing its connection with the result that [the text] says: "Those two said, 'Of ghee alone... [and so forth].

The injunction for the time of the full moon sacrifice is explicitly adopted in the statement, "One should not sacrifice with the *upāṃśu* [offering] on the full moon day. This very purpose of this injunction has been clarified by the sūtra "And because of the purpose" (*prayojanācca*) and its corresponding Vārttika in the section concerning the *upāṃśuyāja*. Consequently, since it is established that only a word-meaning which is quickly apprehended enters into the syntactic connection of the sentence-meaning, and since injury to persons is more quickly presented than other meanings, it is that [injury to persons] alone which is to be prohibited; moreover, as for that purpose for which...

It is the established limit of logical principle that the negation of something applies to that which is relevant; otherwise, there would be inconsistency due to the negation of what is not relevant. For this very reason, the prohibition "one should not speak untruth," though recorded in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) by virtue of that context; thus, it is a prohibition specifically against speaking untruth for the sake of the sacrifice. Consequently, if one speaks untruth for the purpose of procuring materials or other requisites necessary for the sacrifice, there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*) in the sacrifice due to the transgression of the prohibition intended for the sacrifice—even in the midst of the sacrificial performance.

When there is a false statement regarding a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), there is no deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratu*). This is according to the principle: "If one who is in the midst of a sacrifice should eat *kalañja* and such things, there is no deficiency for that sacrifice, because it is accomplished as prescribed. However, there is merely a transgression for the person. Furthermore, even a prohibition recorded in the context (*prakaraṇa*) cannot be a prohibition for the sake of the sacrifice; it is not for the sake of the sacrifice. For example, the prohibition recorded in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: "One should not converse with a woman in her menses, nor [should she converse] with him... [and so on].

There is a prohibition stating, "He should sit with her; he should not eat her food. Although both conversing with the wife and sitting with her would naturally follow as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), nevertheless, this does not apply to a woman in her courses (*malavadvāsas*). This is because, regarding the sacrifice, the seclusion (*avarodha*) of the woman in her courses is enjoined by the rule: "If on the day of the vow (*vratyehana*) the wife should be in her courses, one should perform the sacrifice after having excluded her," which constitutes a total withdrawal from the ritual. However, as for eating her food... [the text continues: "Furthermore..."

Indeed, they say that "either anointing or the food of a woman is not to be accepted as anointment"; this is explained as being of the nature of skin and limbs denoted by the word "anointment," and thus it cannot in any way be obtained as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). And so, regarding the prohibition "one should not kill," if it were of the nature of both killing for the sake of the sacrifice and killing for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), then the [prohibitory] statement itself—being likewise of the nature of both serving the sacrifice and the person—would split the sentence in order to indicate its connection with both the sacrifice and the person. It is exactly like this.

It must be stated that even those scriptural injunctions prohibiting the taking and drinking of *surā* do not touch upon its consumption for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*); there is no other way to explain them. Furthermore, it should not be argued that these acts possess inherent sinfulness (*pāpatva*) and are merely remedied by expiation (*prāyaścitta*), for if that were so, violence (*hiṃsā*) too would be remedied in the same manner. What is the use of this obsession with refuting the world-renowned status of violence as such? As for what was said regarding the drinking of *soma*, there is indeed a prohibition against the fault of being "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*), based on the rule: "They do not become impure by *soma*. But this does not apply to violence.

It might be argued that this [statement] is the subject matter of the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*); however, that is not so. In the passage, "They become impure by means of the Soma," since it is the state of being impure itself that is prohibited, the fault [of drinking] is not prohibited. Nor can it be claimed that the purpose is to prohibit the fault because the state of being impure cannot be prohibited; for in that case, in the passage, "Indeed, you do not die here, nor are you harmed," since the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*) cannot be prohibited, it is possible that the purpose is simply to indicate the absence of fault regarding that [act], and thus there is no fault in the act of violence.

Because we find in some instances the teaching that there is an absence of fault even in specific forms of violence—as in the mantra, "In battle, they slew the sinless ones"—and because the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* scripture, by acknowledging that sacrificial violence is indeed violence, reveals its status as something prohibited in the statement, "Not harming any living beings, except at the sacred sites (*tīrtha*)"; and because even in the *Śrutis*, the designation of sacrificial slaughter as "violence" is frequently encountered—it must be accepted that the resolution [of the contradiction] is to be sought in the manner described, precisely by admitting its nature as violence.

If this is argued, we reply: as for the claim that it is the rule of logical propriety (*nyāyamaryādā*) that "the purpose of the negation is the same as the purpose of its counter-positive," that is not so; for in the case of the statement, "The initiated one does not give, does not offer oblations, and does not cook," it has been established that the prohibition concerns only those oblations intended for human ends (*puruṣārtha*), while [the other] is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Furthermore, as for the claim that because injury for human ends is more immediately present, it alone is what connects with the meaning of the prohibitive sentence, that too is not correct, as seen in the case of the statement, "When one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire..."

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the killing of animals for immediate human purposes would have the *āhavanīya* fire as its constituent part (*aṅga*). Therefore, since the injunction and prohibition—consisting respectively of impulsion and dissuasion regarding the two types of killing—are mutually contradictory like the terms *pada* and *āhavanīya*, it is more appropriate to assume, by way of the maxim of the general rule and the exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), that they refer to subjects distinct from killing for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha-hiṃsā*). For this very reason, according to the *Bhāmatī* and the *Kalpataru*, that which is enjoined by a specific rule...

When a general rule (*sāmānyavidhi*) takes something as its object, the principle of the general rule versus the exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) applies; for instance, by the injunction "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire," which prescribes the connection of the *āhavanīya* with all oblations (*homa*), even the *padahoma* (oblation on the footprint) becomes an object of that rule. However, because a specific rule (*viśeṣavidhi*) ordains the connection of the *āhavanīya* specifically with the *padahoma*, the general scripture is understood to refer to what is other than that. In the present case, however, according to the logic already described, since at the very time of its origin the prohibition has as its object violence for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha-hiṃsā*), there is no inclusion of violence for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha-hiṃsā*). As for the mention of the principle of the general rule versus the exception in Śaṅkara’s commentary: [The text continues: ...the mention of the principle of the general rule versus the exception in Śaṅkara’s commentary [is merely illustrative].

The attempt to justify the *gauṇī* (secondary) sense of the scripture—on the grounds that it appears to apply without distinction but possesses the common quality (*guṇa*) of excluding specific cases—is indeed improper. As for the statement regarding the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), the claim that the scripture’s appearance as applying without distinction is secondary due to its similarity to the quality of excluding specific cases is likewise incorrect; for the principle of general rule and exception is the universal resolution, whereas in the case of [the injunction] regarding violence (*hiṃsā*)...

Since an alternative avoidance is possible through the understanding that there is an absence of the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*) based on the *mantras*, *arthavādas*, and so forth—and because one who has avoided [violence] in this way is not fit for neglect—the venerable author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) stated another alternative avoidance regarding the subject of violence. As for what was said—that the nature of violence, which is the basis for the application of the word "violence" (*hiṃsā*), consists in being an action conducive to death intended for the purpose of death—that is not correct; for it would lead to the undesirable consequence that no conventional usage of "being a perpetrator of violence" could apply to one who causes great pain by means of a blow with a mallet or a sword and the like.

Since the property of being an activity conducive to the production of sensation is the only factor that persists in all cases, it must be stated that this is the basis for the application of the term *hiṃsā* (harming). For, in the case of a physician treating a wound who produces intense pain at that moment, there is no designation of him as a "harmer" (*hiṃsaka*). Therefore, the basis for the application of the term *hiṃsā* is simply the property of being an activity that brings about suffering while not producing a powerful desired [result]. This is because the conventional usage of the term "harmer" applies only to the agent of such an act; and even in the case of an activity conducive to death intended for the purpose of death, by this very [definition], provided it does not produce a powerful desired [result]...

For it is possible to designate [the act] as "himsā" (violence) by means of the common ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely, being an operation that achieves an undesirable result; it is therefore inappropriate to postulate "being an operation conducive to death with death as its intended object" as a separate ground for its application. With this in mind—namely, that the ritual slaughter of an animal (*paśusaṃjñapana*), although it produces immediate suffering, does not constitute *hiṃsā* because it generates heaven, which is a powerful desired end—the venerable author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) has offered this resolution, and not by way of accepting that it is indeed *hiṃsā*.

The resolution is by way of the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*). For instance, when one ignorant of the distinction between the scope of injunctions and prohibitions regarding violence raises the objection in a formal debate that the sentence "One should sacrifice with the Śyena" has an improper meaning—on the grounds that if the bird Śyena were a sacrificial substance like the *puroḍāśa* cake, it would contradict the scripture prohibiting violence—that objection cannot be properly settled merely by invoking the principle of the distinction between scopes, even though such a distinction is necessary regarding the animals used as parts of the Śyena sacrifice. Rather, one who follows the actual state of things should cite the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*)...

This is resolved by the very presentation of [the term] as a name for an action; likewise here too, although this objection must be refuted according to the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), the venerable author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*), following the actual state of things, has established that there is indeed an absence of the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*); thus, there is nothing faulty. [Sūtra: "The body [arises] from the womb."

The transmigrating soul possesses a body; where there are actions consisting of merit and demerit, there alone are pleasure and pain, and where there are pleasure and pain, there alone is the body that serves as their cause. Therefore, since there is an absence of the performance of action in space and so forth, there is an absence of the experience of pleasure, pain, and the like—which are the fruits of such action—and thus there is no body serving as their cause. This is the intended meaning.
Thus ends the section "Controlled by Another" (Anyādhiṣṭhitādhikaraṇa).

This concludes the first quarter of the third chapter in the Bhāvaprakāśikā, a commentary on the Śrutaprakāśikā, composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads.
The total number of topics (adhikaraṇas) is 74; the total number of sūtras is 304.

The sense is that even regarding the experience of happiness, the author of the Sūtras has declared the perishability of heaven through the portion of the Sūtra beginning with *kṛtātyaye* (BrSū 3.1.8). The entire manner in which the state of being subject to suffering is made known has been elaborated by us in the section on the *raṃhati* (going) adhikaraṇa; it should be investigated therein. As for the phrase "with reference to dream" in the Bhāṣya:

The word "pravṛttā" (occurred) is to be supplied as the remainder; the construction is that the Śruti is heard as having occurred with reference to a dream. Therefore, because there is a common agent [for both verbs], there is no inconsistency regarding the use of the suffix -ktavatu. "With reference to" means "having introduced. In the Bhāṣya, the term "rathayogāḥ" means those who are yoked to chariots, i.e., chariot-horses; it is a compound formed by the rule *kartṛ-karaṇe kṛtā bahulam* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). "Veśāntāḥ" means ponds. In the expression "puṣkariṇyaḥ," the nominative plural ending *jas* is used in the sense of the accusative according to the rule *supāṃ supo bhavanti*, or else it is a Vedic usage.

The absence of the *pūrvasavarṇadīrgha* (the lengthening of the preceding vowel) occurs because the subject under discussion is "he sees the dream" (*svapnaṃ paśyati*). For although the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad begins with, "When he sleeps, taking up the measure of this all-encompassing world, having himself struck it down and himself fashioned it, he sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light; here this person becomes self-luminous," and continues, "There are no chariots there," it is for this very reason that Śaṅkara’s commentary states, "having begun with 'when he sleeps' (*sa yatra prasvapiti*)."

Nevertheless, because the expression "he sleeps" (prasvapiti) is not clear in its meaning, another worldly sentence has been cited for the sake of clarity; it should be understood that this is not a scriptural statement (*śrutivākya*) that was cited. The same should be understood regarding the subsequent passage, where the individual soul (*jīva*) under discussion is described as "seeing a dream."

In the *Bhāṣya* it is said: "The intermediate state (*sandhya*) is called the place of sleep. For this person, there are indeed only two places: this world and the place of the other world; the third is the intermediate place of sleep. While staying in that intermediate place, he perceives both these places—this world and the place of the other world—so says the Śruti. Just as a village boundary belongs to two villages, so too does dream belong to both worlds by way of its characteristics:
namely, the characteristic of the other world consisting in the direct perception of forms and so forth produced by the eyes and other senses while existing in this world.

Some explain this scriptural passage as follows: [the soul] "partakes" (bhajate) means that it also partakes of the characteristic of this world, namely, the state of being one who has direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which is produced by the eyes and other organs functioning in the next world. Regarding the *Bhāṣya* statement, "For he creates; indeed, he is the agent," the word "indeed" (*hi*) signifies a reason. Consequently, since the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) has the same meaning as "creates" (*sṛjate*), there is no relationship of cause and effect between them; rather, its meaning is that [the soul] possesses the quality of having true volition (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) suitable for agency. And thus, because of this true volition, [it belongs to] the individual soul (*jīva*).

The sense is that the status of being an agent is logical; such is the position of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*). Nor should it be argued that if the possession of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) and other qualities exists, then the individual soul (*jīva*) would also exercise control over chariots and so forth during the waking state. For it is possible for what was concealed during the waking state to manifest during the dream state, just as it manifests in the case of a liberated soul (*mukta*); and just as dream-objects, which did not exist before or after, come into being at the time of the dream, so too the manifestation of true resolve is logically possible in that very state alone. And this being so—

It should not be argued that, just as one who has awakened has the recollection, "I saw chariots and so forth," there would likewise be the recollection, "I created chariots and so forth" [in the dream]; for there is no fault in the fact that, just as one does not connect with the events of the death of one's father or grandfather experienced during waking, one does not connect with the agency of creating chariots and so forth experienced in the dream upon waking. Nor should it be argued that if the individual soul (*jīva*) were the creator of dream-objects, he would create and see only things indicative of auspiciousness and never those indicative of inauspiciousness; for at that time...

Since it is possible for the dreamer to be the creator of the dream-objects because they do not realize that those objects are indicators of inauspiciousness, and since even in the Siddhānta (the final conclusion) this same reasoning must be applied to cases where the dreamer is the agent—such as drinking oil, immersing oneself in a jar of oil, consuming poison, eating a meal on a journey, or splitting a single lotus—it is the view of the Pūrvapakṣin (the opponent) that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the agent. || 1 ||

The sense is that because it "shows the characteristic marks of the individual soul" (*jīvaliṅga*), even though the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the subject under discussion there, the individual soul alone is presented as the agent in the sentence "while these are sleeping," due to the greater force of the characteristic marks of the individual soul consisting of its relationship with sons, grandsons, and so forth. (2) The meaning established by the word *tu* has been stated; by the force of the word *tu*, which excludes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the dream is the work of the individual soul, the fact that the Supreme Self is the agent is obtained, [as in the statement]: "In a dream, the lotus-pool and so forth are mere illusion" (*māyāmātram*).

The construction in the Bhāṣya is that "this entire multitude of objects was created by the Supreme Person. The term *māyāmātram* (merely illusion) is a qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) containing a reason (*hetugarbha*), because even every single part possesses a nature that is wonderful; thus, the sense is that it was created by the Supreme Self. Consequently, the intention is that one should not think that "created by the Supreme Person" is merely an explanation (*vyākhyāna*) of the term *māyāmātram*.

It should also be understood that there is an inherent inconsistency [in the opponent's position]: the statement "they do not exist" would be redundant, as it would imply a prior non-existence (i.e., "they did not exist"), which would necessitate using the imperfect tense (*abhūvan*) rather than the present tense (*na bhavanti*). Now, even if the non-existence of well-known chariots and such things is established by worldly experience, their non-experience is not so established; for one who has woken from sleep reflects thus: "I experienced in a dream that very same chariot which was previously seen in Māhiṣmatī. And therefore...

If it is asked, "How is it that the absence of experience is established by worldly consensus?"—the answer is: True. Since the statement "for he is the creator" (*sṛjate sa hi kartā*) speaks of the state of being created, the non-experience of those things already well-known [in the world] can be established from that very fact; therefore, the intention is that the passage beginning with "There are no chariots there" (*na tatra rathāḥ*) is not intended to establish that [absence], but rather to convey the creation of diverse objects of a different class (*vijātīya*). But surely, such diversity is already established in the world; thus, the conclusion remains that only the status of being a creator is what is intended to be taught.

If it is argued that, consequently, only the portion consisting of the words "sṛjate" (He creates) has significance, and not the preceding portion beginning with "na tatra rathāḥ" (There are no chariots there), [we reply: True; however, in passages such as "janmādy asya yataḥ" (From which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed) and "yato vā imāni" (From whence indeed these [beings]), the word "idam" (this)—

Just as [the passage] is purposeful by indicating the variety of the objects of experience (*kāryavarga*), so too the statement "There are no chariots there" (*na tatra rathāḥ*) has its purport in establishing the majesty of the Supreme Brahman—consisting in being the creator of the most diverse objects of the dream state—by means of indicating the variety of dream-objects. [The phrase] "it will be explained immediately after" (*ity anantaram paryavasyati*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense], or rather, it should be understood as occurring at the end of the verse beginning with "atha vā. [The suffix] *ṇamul* is used here in the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇye ṇamul*).

And [the suffix] *ṇamul* [is used]; when there is repetition (*ābhīkṣṇa*), there is a doubling [of the word]. (3) Now, if it has been asserted that concealment is dependent upon His will, then one should have specified it simply as "concealment and its opposite" from Him; to this he says: "bondage is dependent upon His will. (4) (5)

If it is argued that there is no obstacle to taking "one who knows the words of the Veda regarding dreams" as referring to the *svapnādhyāya* (the chapter on dreams) found within the Purāṇas, we say no; for in the passage "The Śruti declares and those who know it [say]... (*śruter ācakṣate ca tadvidaḥ*), it is more appropriate that the word "it" (*tat*) refers back to the immediately preceding *Śruti*. Furthermore, since the term "chapter" (*adhyāya*) is used even in the context of the *Śruti*, there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya. The intention is that by the expression "the chapter on dreams" in the Bhāṣya, the *Śruti* itself is being referred to. In the Bhāṣya, [it is stated that the dream] is merely an indicator of what is auspicious.

Nor should it be argued that its creation is due to a lack of knowledge regarding its indication of inauspiciousness; for we observe the creation of thieves, tigers, and the like—who are known at that time to be agents of misfortune—by those who cause such misfortune, and thus the dream-creation cannot possibly have the individual soul as its creator. This is the intended meaning.

Others, however, maintain that dream-objects are real, like the ether and other elements, because the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* Upaniṣad, concerning dreams, records their creation in the passage: "Then he creates chariots, horses for the chariots, and roads for the chariots"; and because at the conclusion it states, "For he is the agent," thus attributing agency to the sleeping individual soul; and because an unreal creator of such a creation is impossible. Likewise, in the Kaṭha branch [of the Veda], it says: "While these sleep, the Person remains awake, fashioning each object according to his desire," referring to the dream-objects by the word "desire" (*kāma*).

Since the creation of sons, grandsons, and so forth is heard [in scripture], and since that creation has the Wise One (prājña) as its agent, it is appropriate that even dream-objects possess reality, just like ether and the other elements which have the Wise One as their agent; nor is the reason—that they have the Wise One as their agent—unestablished, because immediately prior to the passage "while these are sleeping," the Supreme Self alone is the subject under discussion, and because of the supplementary statement, "That indeed is the bright, that is Brahman. Furthermore, even if the individual soul (jīva) were the agent, the soul is non-different from the Wise One.

Because the fact that they are produced by an intelligent agent remains unrefuted; furthermore, because dream-cognition is valid due to its being a cognition—just like a corroborative cognition—and because the reality of dream-objects is established through this inference; nor is there unreality due to the observation of sublation at a later time, since there is no relationship of sublated and sublater when the two cognitions have different objects, given that it is possible for those very things appearing as chariots and so forth in the dream state to undergo transformation into a different form during the waking state, just as milk transforms into the state of curd at a later time.

Because there is no contradiction between two objects perceived as distinct in time when they are regarded as being in a relationship of sublated and sublator; or rather, everything is indeed of every nature, and when in conjunction with the manifesting condition of sleep, it is apprehended in the form of chariots and so forth, whereas the waking state is that which manifests its non-identity with those forms. Furthermore, since some dreams are seen to correspond with waking cognitions, one must assert that other dreams are likewise [valid] by virtue of their similarity to them. Such being the case, it is possible to establish their validity.

Because resorting to invalidity [of scripture] is improper, the scriptural passages such as "there are no chariots there" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10) regarding the absence of chariots and so forth must be explained figuratively as meaning that such things do not exist in a manner perceivable by the waking state. Having thus established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with these two initial sūtras, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established by the sūtras beginning with "But it is mere illusion" (*māyāmātraṃ tu*). The meaning is that it is mere illusion; there is not even a trace of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because the attributes of an ultimately real entity—namely, non-sublation with respect to place, time, and cause—are entirely absent.

Because of its absence there: first of all, a suitable location for chariots, mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth is not possible in a dream, since there is no space for chariots and the like within the extremely small space occupied by the body of the dreamer. Nor does the dreamer [move] from that very place, because of the scriptural hearing of movement outside the body: "Having moved out from the nest (kulāya), he, being immortal, goes wherever he desires.
