For it is heard that he moves outside the body—having gone out from what is called the "nest," namely the body—to whatever object his desire is directed; thus, the dreamer does not [remain within].

It should not be said that one perceives dream-objects in a location within one's own body, which would imply that the location is inconsistent [with the objects]; for if one were to move outside the body, it would follow that one could not respond to being struck with a staff or similar actions, which contradicts the logical consistency of that scriptural statement. Furthermore, based on the scripture stating, "He moves about as he pleases within his own body," the literal sense of the scripture regarding going "outside" must be understood figuratively; thus, the location of the dream-objects is indeed the location within the body of the dreamer, and of that...

Because of the absence of the perfection of a suitable location, it is established that the location [of the dream] is difficult to determine; likewise, within the duration of a mere moment of sleep, events such as marriage and the birth of a son—which require a long period to accomplish—occur, yet neither the wood and other materials that serve as the causes for the production of chariots and the like, nor the hands and organs that serve as the causes for their perception, are possible [therein]. As for the claim that there can be no relationship of sublation between two cognitions because they have different objects due to a difference in time, that is not so; for never, in the house of the Lord...

It is observed that silver vessels which have remained for a long time undergo the state of being mother-of-pearl; nor is it the case that objects experienced as silver by one person are experienced as mother-of-pearl by another person with unimpaired senses; nor is the position tenable that a single thing possesses all forms at all times, for if that were so, it would follow that every object would perform the causal function of every other object. Therefore, [the opponent's] argument is contradictory.

The scriptural statement regarding creation (*sarga-śruti*) must be explained as figurative (*bhākta*), in accordance with the scriptural statements concerning the absence of chariots and other such things that occur in the context of the introductory section accompanied by logical reasoning; its meaning is "he creates" [in the sense of] "he perceives. Furthermore, regarding the statement "for he is the agent," it is not possible to claim that the soul (*jīva*), while asleep, is the creator of chariots and so forth; rather, its agency is metaphorically attributed to it because it is the agent of the good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) which cause those perceptions. By this, the scriptural passage from the Kaṭha school stating "while these are asleep, he remains awake" [is also explained].

It should be explained as being figurative. Furthermore, as for what was said—that they declare this one to be the wise creator—that is incorrect; because in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, there is the hearing of the activity of the individual soul (jīva) in the passage, "Having himself struck down [the senses], having himself created [the world], he lies down in his own luster, in his own light"; and here too, the statement "while these are asleep, he keeps watch" is a restatement of what is already well-known.

In the passage beginning with "dāt," this very *jīva* is declared to be the creator of desires; however, the context of Brahman is not contradicted because it serves to demonstrate the non-difference between them. Consequently, the reason that the *prājña* (the Supreme Self) is the agent is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Alternatively, even if the *prājña* were the agent, we do not deny the activity of the *prājña* even in dreams, since as the Lord of all, it is logical for Him to be the presiding controller in all states. For truthfulness does not follow merely from the fact that the *prājña* is the agent.

It is possible to establish [this], because it would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Likewise, the indicative power of a dream-vision—which is delimited by non-ultimate substance—must also be accepted on the strength of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might raise the objection: "Should not the scriptural statement that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the agent be accepted as figurative, since creation is possible for one whose resolve is true? To dispel this doubt, they explain the two sūtras beginning with "But from the meditation on the Supreme" (*parābhidhyānāt tu*). Therein, he restates and refutes the portion to be criticized, starting with the words "But others... (*pare tu*), and so forth. And of these...

The phrase "immediately after [the statement] 'it is said that [the Lord] creates [the dream world] by means of the individual soul as its agent'"—the remainder of the sentence being "as stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin)"—is explained as follows: "And that is metaphorical" means that this aforementioned agency of the individual soul is metaphorical, i.e., figurative. Now, it may be argued that the location [of the dream world] is difficult to determine; for if we were to accept that the creation of dream-objects occurs within the enclosed space of the body itself, then indeed its location would be difficult to determine. However, it is not accepted in this way, for [the scripture says]: "Having gone out from the nest, moving about outside... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12).

Having raised the objection based on the Śruti text, "The immortal one goes where the golden person, the single swan, dwells," [the author] states that because a sleeping being lacks the capacity to travel to a place separated by hundreds of *yojanas* in a mere moment, and because it is recorded in the text, "He moves about as he pleases within his own body," that the soul in the state of dream revolves only within its own body; thus, the Śruti passage regarding "going outside the nest" is said to have a figurative meaning. He restates this point with the words, "having moved out from the nest," and [concludes with], "while these are asleep, he remains awake."

In the Kaṭha Upaniṣad, the passage "A man creates desire after desire" does not state that the wise one (the *prājña*) is the agent; rather, because it is a restatement of what is well known—"He who wakes while these [others] sleep"—it is the individual soul (*jīva*) alone who is celebrated here as the creator of desires. The commentary restates the point that in that context, the mention of "That indeed is the Bright, That is Brahman" is for the purpose of teaching the non-difference of the individual soul from Brahman.

Regarding the phrase "in that context" (*tasmin prakaraṇe*) and so forth: "in that context" means in the context of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad concerning the dream state; one must not mistakenly think it refers to the context of the passage beginning with "having moved about below his dwelling-place" (*bahiṣkulāyād avaraś caritvā*), because that belongs to the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* and there is no context of dreams there, and because others have not stated it so. Furthermore, the meaning is that this [sūtra] is the second one, being read immediately after the sūtra "mere illusion" (*māyāmātram*) and before the sūtra "due to the meditation on the Supreme" (*parābhidhyānāt*).

The phrase "for his bondage and liberation" means that these two depend upon ignorance and knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Regarding the statement "by way of the dream-objects having the individual soul (*jīva*) as their agent": although opponents have not cited "having the individual soul as the agent" as a reason for proving falsity, they nevertheless describe "having the individual soul as the agent" as serving to establish the absence of the reason consisting in "having the Intelligent One (*prājña*) as the agent. Nevertheless, according to the maxim that "the absence of a prover functions as a refuter," the absence of a prover for [the property of] reality—

This was stated with the intention that there exists a sublation characterized by the establishment of the non-existence of that [prior cognition]; the same should be understood for what follows as well. "The suspicion of truthfulness produced by the scriptural statement..."

The meaning is that there is a suspicion of truthfulness based on scriptural passages concerning creation, manifestation, and so forth. The intention is that there is no contradiction in negating conventional (vyāvahārika) truth; for it is appropriate to abandon [a position] if it contradicts the intended meaning. Although they themselves—and not we—have stated: "It is not the activity of the Prājña that is denied in the dream state, because he is the Lord of all, and it is logical that he is the presiding controller in all states; rather, what is denied is [the dream's] having the Prājña as its agent... [the present argument follows from this].

It has been stated that [the scripture] establishes truth; nevertheless, the sense is this: how can the statement of one who, having first refuted the agency of the Supreme Self in the preceding text and established the agency of the individual soul (jīva), subsequently re-establishes the agency of the Supreme Self, avoid the principle that "it is inconsistent because of contradiction"? The sense is that there is also this further contradiction regarding the individual soul's status as a creator.

The construction is as follows: "In this way, for living beings," because it has been directly stated in the Sūtra [Brahma Sūtra 3.2.1] as "due to the meditation on another" (*parābhidhyānāt*). Alternatively, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is to be construed with "the absence of being the agent of the objects of a dream"; the meaning is "the absence of being the direct agent," that is, the absence of being the primary agent.

"But not those that are useless or contradictory"—even though the contradictory ones are indeed also useless, nevertheless, following the "logic of the ox" (*balīvardanyāya*), they are mentioned in order to demonstrate that a thesis which contradicts the meaning of the Sūtras must be utterly abandoned. The meaning is: only that thesis which would be neither useless nor contradictory to the Sūtras is worthy of being established. The word *arthakriyāyāḥ* is a compound split [for grammatical analysis]; since the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) in the form of mere indication does not prove truth, [it is not a valid definition].

The meaning is "because it is the opposite of falsity" (*mithyātvavirodhitvāt*). Regarding the phrase "the supply of a word (*adhyāhāra*) and the transposed connection (*vyutkramānvaya*)," etc., the sense is as follows: in the construction "from the meditation on the Supreme, that which was hidden becomes manifest" (*parābhidhyānāttirohitamāvirbhavati*), there is a supply of the word "becomes manifest" (*āvirbhavati*). Furthermore, there is a "transposed connection" because the word ending in the ablative case, "from the meditation on the Supreme" (*parābhidhyānāt*), is connected with "becomes manifest" (*āvirbhavati*), thereby abandoning its immediate connection with the word "hidden" (*tirohitam*).

The meaning is that because the word *tirobhāva* (concealment) is the subject under discussion, and because in your own view it is precisely *āvirbhāva* (manifestation)—in the sense that "what was concealed becomes manifest"—that is the primary subject at hand. Furthermore, it is because [the object] is unfit for such a reference (*sa*). Nor should it be argued that this same defect applies equally to our own established position (*siddhānta*), for our intent concerns precisely the aforementioned primacy and non-primacy. Having thus analyzed...

The meaning is that this must be investigated. "By those who know the Nyāya" means by those who know the principles of the section concerning the Ukthya and Agniṣṭoma sacrifices. This refers to the injunction: "One may take the Ṣoḍaśī cup even at the Agniṣṭoma for a Kṣatriya, and it is to be taken even at the Ukthya. If the Ṣoḍaśī cup were to have the Stotra and Śastra as its constituent parts (aṅga), then because that sacrifice would not be completed by the Agniṣṭoma and Ukthya Stotras, there would arise the contingency of violating the qualifying attributes of the intended objects—namely, the status of being an Ukthya and an Agniṣṭoma—with respect to the enjoined Ṣoḍaśī cup.

When the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is reached that one must resort to the absence of the *śastra* and other constituent parts, it is established as follows: since the injunction prescribes the primary rite along with its subsidiaries, its inherent force (*svārasya*) must not be subverted; therefore, the displacement of the intended objects characterized by the *agniṣṭoma* and *ukthya* forms must be tolerated. Consequently, it is determined that whatever was obtained as having the *ukthya* structure must be performed as having the *ṣoḍaśin* structure. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "na ca svāpnārthānām" [from the *Tantravārttika*], the term "prākkālīna" (belonging to the preceding time) is used because of the abundance of usage in the rule *taddhitāḥ*.

Furthermore, because it has been established by the use of the plural number that "taddhita suffixes occur in other instances as well," it should be understood as correct, like the word *saumyadhurīṇa* and others. By the phrase "presided over by knowledge," the sense is that even for the atomic individual soul (*jīva*), presiding over multiple locations is possible through its attribute-like knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*).

The phrase "because of the occurrence of external activity" means because of the occurrence of external operation; by this, the meaning of the scriptural passage, "Protecting the lower nest with the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," is demonstrated. Its meaning is that he protects the nest, together with the *prāṇa*, by means of knowledge as a property (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). By this, those who claim that the scriptural mention of being "outside the nest" is figurative are refuted; for if there were no actual movement outside the nest, the teaching regarding protection would be purposeless, as it would entail the destruction of the previous nest.

It might be argued that, because of the scriptural mention of being "outside the nest" (*bahiṣkulāya*), the intention is understood to be movement [out of the body]. However, this cannot be so, because it would contradict the scriptural statement: "He moves about as he pleases within his own body" (*sve śarīre yathākāmaṃ parivartate*). Therefore, the scriptural mention of being "outside the nest"—as in "having wandered outside the nest" (*bahiṣkulāyād avacāritvā*)—must be explained figuratively. For one who, though dwelling in the body, has no further need for it, is said to be "as if outside the body. And even if there is movement outside the body, since that very body remains his own, it is still referred to as "his own body."

Thus, it must be said that [the soul] is born; for if that were the case, the word "own" (*sva*) would be rendered meaningless, and one would necessarily have to admit that the scriptural passage regarding "being outside the nest" is figurative, otherwise [it would refer to] the Pradhāna.

Because it would result in a contradiction with the meaning of the context (*prakaraṇa*): for in this context, which is undertaken to establish the self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) of the Self, the state of dream is introduced in order to distinguish [the Self] from the sun and other [lights], since [the Self] is difficult to distinguish while in the waking state due to the intermingling of the sun and so forth. If creation were being propounded there [in the dream state], then it too would be difficult to distinguish from that [Self], because the appearance of the sun, moon, fire, and speech still exists at that time. Therefore, it would contradict the primary subject matter being propounded.

In the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice performed for the sake of heaven, the sentence from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding its subsidiary injunctions—"Who indeed knows whether he exists or not in that world?"—does not have its primary purport in its literal sense. Here too, by the very opening statement, "There are no chariots there, no yoke-animals for chariots, nor roads for chariots," it is indicated that the mention of creation refers to something non-literal. Nor is the statement redundant merely because it describes that non-literality as being established in common worldly experience.

If it is argued that this need not be stated because the falsity of dream-chariots and the like, as established by common experience, can be restated for the purpose of discerning self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*), we say: not so. For, according to the reasoning already stated, the scriptural text regarding being "outside the nest" (*bahiṣkulāya*) possesses a specific purport (*tātparya*). Furthermore, the scriptural text "in his own body" (*sve śarīre*) intends to show that the atomic individual soul (*jīva*), presiding over its own dream-bodies through the mere pervasion of its attribute-like knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), moves at will; this is just as a great king, the ruler of many provinces, travels within his own domains without any distinction in their being his own territory.

Because it teaches the ability to move at will through various bodies—following the preceding statement, "Just as a great king, having taken his subjects, moves about in his own kingdom according to his desire," and because this passage is intent on demonstrating movement at will in bodies according to the *saubhari*-maxim—and because its own words are meaningful insofar as they demonstrate the commonality of the reason consisting in "being one's own" (*svīyatva*), while the context [aims] at establishing the unreality of the chariot and so forth by means of that demonstration...

The claim that [the passage] aims to establish the self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) [of the Self] is also untenable. For even in the absence of illuminators such as the sun, the mind—which is distinct from the Self—exists; thus, the self-luminosity [of the Self] remains unproven. Nor should it be argued that although the mind exists during dream, it is not the illuminator of the Self because it is itself an object of perception; for if that were so, the sun and other luminaries would likewise fail to be illuminators due to their shared quality of being objects of perception, rendering the demonstration of their distinction [from the Self] purposeless. As it is said: "O Yājñavalkya, when the sun has set, and the moon has set..."

Furthermore, when it is asked, "When the eye is stilled and speech is stilled, what light does this person have? and the non-existence of the sun and other [lights] has been acknowledged, the statement beginning with "There are no chariots there" would be inappropriate as a means of conveying that [non-existence]. If the intended meaning were the absence of any other illuminator of the sun, the Vedic text would simply have stated, "There is no sun there. Therefore, this scripture is intended to demonstrate the supreme majesty of the Supreme Self, characterized by His being the creator of chariots and all else that is distinct from everything other than Himself. For this very reason, following the description of the creation of the chariots and so forth...

The statement of the reason, "For he is the agent," is thus consistent. When the dreamer sees a chariot in a certain place at a certain time, another person standing there at that moment does not see it; and even the dreamer, upon waking, having gone to that place, does not see it, nor does he find any signs of its being carried away from there or any tracks of its passage. In response to the inquiry as to how such a marvelous creation occurs in a dream, the reason is stated therein: "For he is the agent."

The meaning of the word "indeed" (*khalu*) is that the Lord of All, who is truly the stage-manager of the drama of the entire phenomenal world, is certainly the author therein; what, then, would He be unable to create? Nor is there any contradiction with this fact.

There is no inconsistency with the context: in the passage, "He sees both evils and joys," the dreamer is described as being self-luminous by virtue of his manifestation of favorable and unfavorable objects; in order to dispel the doubt—based on worldly experience—that there might be no other object to be seen at that time, it is established that these [objects] exist with the Supreme Self as their agent. However, this does not entail the consequence of their falsity (*mithyātva*). Nor is it the case that the self's status as the illuminator of objects is not accepted in the Siddhānta, for [this function belongs to] *dharmabhūtajñāna* (knowledge as an attribute).

It should be stated that this is because of its being such (tathātva); for what is intended to be established by means of that [knowledge] is precisely the illuminating nature residing in the Self through its presence in the attribute of consciousness (dharmabhūtajñāna). Since the context is devoted to establishing the self-luminosity of that [Self] after having demonstrated its possession of the quality of consciousness in the passage, "Which is the Self? It is this which consists of intelligence," there is no possibility here of [the Self] being false; thus, enough with this elaboration regarding the justification for the absence of a reply to the question concerning the specific details contained within the region.

The meaning is that there is no perception of any other object distinct from the dream-object located in that place. Now, since even the location of the gold and so forth seen in a dream is distinct [from the waking state], and since the presence of other objects perceivable in the waking state does not apply there, questions and answers regarding them are likewise inapplicable; for the eyes and other senses are capable of perceiving only dream-objects. Thus, the absence of an answer to a question concerning a specific difference in that location is merely an error of misplaced agitation. For this very reason:

If it is argued that the subsequent textual passage, which consists of an investigation into whether there is resistance (*pratighātakatva*) or non-resistance (*apratighātakatva*), is likewise [inconclusive] because an investigation into resistance and so forth is irrelevant due to the difference in location, [the reply is: true; this was stated with the intention that a resolution is possible regarding the nature of cognition (*jñatva*).

This must be observed. The sense is that directions are relative; for example, that which is the eastern direction for the inhabitants of Bhāratavarṣa at the time of sunrise is not necessarily the eastern direction or the time of sunrise for the inhabitants of Ketumāla. Regarding the statement that "an object situated in water cannot be seen," the meaning is that since the conjunction with light (*āloka*) is the cause [of perception], and because there must be a conjunction of light with objects such as sand located within deep, clear water, it follows that water must be admitted to be non-obstructive (*apratighātaka*).

"By way of being subject to falling" means that among liquid substances—which, due to their heaviness, have the nature of falling when joined in an upper-lower relationship—no gap can occur. "By way of being obstructed" means that in the absence of an obstructer such as a dam, no gap can occur even among liquid substances that possess motion conducive to mutual contact and are situated in a south-north orientation; this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the passage beginning with "But because of meditation on the other," the application here is as follows: in the application of these two sūtras beginning with "But because of meditation on the other," although—as in the previous case and like the view of the opponent—there is no lack of utility or contradiction, one should reflect upon the lack of intrinsic consistency (*asvārasya*) in other sūtras and in the Śruti, just as before. Thus, he demonstrates the lack of intrinsic consistency in the sūtras and the Śruti in sequence, starting with the words "of the word *māyā*," etc. Thus ends the section on the Twilight (Sandhyā).

Regarding that which is heard in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad beginning with "tadyatraitat..."—since that [state] exists right there, at the time when one performing this dream is as if cooking a meal while in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), the qualification "completely withdrawn" (*samasta*) is provided for the purpose of establishing deep sleep, because sleep is of two kinds.

The meaning is that all instruments [of perception] have been withdrawn; because there is an absence of the turbidity produced by contact with sense objects, he becomes "serene" (*samprasanna*), which means he has entered into sleep. This refers to the passage from the *Chāndogya* concerning the *Dahara-vidyā*: "Now, as when one is asleep," and so forth; and the passage from the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "When this person sleeps," and so forth, which belongs to the *Sat-vidyā* in the *Chāndogya*. Now, one might object: "In the phrase 'not with Being' (*na satā sāmye*), the locative case is not heard."

If it is asked, "How is there the cognition of being a substratum?"—the answer is true. For in the supplementary portion of that passage, one hears the locative case in the words, "Having attained the Real, they do not know: 'We shall attain the Real,'" and likewise, because of its agreement with another scriptural text, "He lies in that space which is within the heart," the cognition of being a substratum arises. As for the phrase "like a bedstead (khaṭvāparyaṅka)," this word *paryaṅka* denotes something spread out, as seen in usages such as "having abandoned the serpent-bedstead" (*nāgaparyaṅkam utsṛtya*). Therefore, one should not be deluded into thinking that the word *paryaṅka* extends only to a bedstead.

Regarding the phrase "but as for its making known a difference in function": although the Brāhmaṇa's hearing of the awakening is a proof only of the primary probandum—the fact that the Brāhmaṇa is invariably the locus of deep sleep—it is not, by means of making known a difference in function, a proof that the Brāhmaṇa is invariably the locus of deep sleep; nevertheless, since the meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇa*), which consists of a cumulative conjunction (*samuccaya*), cannot be established without the knowledge of a difference in function, it should be understood that this [difference in function] also enters into the category of the proofs. Now, [consider the passage]: "O dear one, these [beings] have Being as their root..."

Since it is heard in scripture that "all creatures always have the Brahman as their support (āyata) and the Brahman as their foundation (pratiṣṭhā)," how can deep sleep be suspected—contrary to this rule—to reside in the channels (nāḍīs) or the pericardium (purītat), independent of that [Brahman]? It is replied: here, the mere Brahman is not the subject of the alternative; rather, it is the one in the form of the space within the heart (daharākāśa). For in the Chāndogya itself, in the Dahara-vidyā, after introducing the space within the heart as the primary subject, it says: "In this very same way, all these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman (brahmaloka), yet they do not find it."

Because it is heard that [the Self] is the locus of deep sleep (suṣupti), and furthermore, because the supplementary portion of the *sad-vidyā* passage also states, "Having come from Being, they do not know; we are coming back to Being," it is established that the locus of deep sleep is indeed limited to a specific region.

For in that case, the arrival of Brahman from an undifferentiated location such as a village would not be possible; moreover, it is determined through an examination of other passages in the Chāndogya itself that this delimiting factor is the lotus of the heart (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*). Furthermore, in another scriptural passage—"He lies in that space which is within the heart"—it is clearly taught that Brahman has as its substratum the one delimited by the lotus of the heart. Therefore, the suspicion regarding the optional nature of the substratum of Brahman is justified, as stated in the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the phrase "because of the perception of independence," it has been stated in the *Pūrvatantra*: "But things serving a single purpose should be treated as options; if they were combined, there would be a repetition of the principal act. For in cases such as "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley," since one must avoid the eight defects of an option (*vikalpa*) in order to favor the injunction for performance that incorporates all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), there should indeed be a combination (*samuccaya*). Consequently, just as in the case of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, a combination must be accepted by resorting to the repeated performance of the offerings of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*. Or else—

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the sacrifice should be performed by mixing rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), [the author] argues: "In the case of items serving a single purpose, which are enjoined for a single benefit independently of one another, an option (*vikalpa*) must indeed be accepted. For in the Jyotiṣṭoma, since the context (*prakaraṇa*) simultaneously grasps the various combinations of substances and deities—which serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*)—it is appropriate to employ all of them for the sake of accomplishing the whole. However, as for rice and barley, they are each enjoined by two separate sentences independently of the other."

The injunction for performance, by enjoining the two [grains] as the material source for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), takes them up alternately through that medium, not simultaneously—by which means there would otherwise be a repetition of the primary sacrifice as in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma; moreover, a mixture is also improper because they are enjoined independently, for if there were a mixture, [the injunctions would be dependent].

Both statements would be contradicted; therefore, since both statements enjoin two [states] as independent primary causes (*prakṛti*), by the force of that, the exclusion of other substances is understood. Thus, it was said that there is an option (*vikalpa*); the sense is that by that same logic, there is an option here as well. "In accordance with scripture" means that the connection between the absence of dreams and deep sleep is well-known from the scriptures.

The sense is that, because [the state] is [of the nature of] sleep, it is appropriate to employ a term denoting the absence of dreams as a *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) for deep sleep (*suṣupti*). The phrase "for the purpose of refuting the reasoning of the prima facie view" (*pūrvapakṣayuktivyudāsārtham*) means for the purpose of refuting its status as a reason belonging to the prima facie view. The meaning is that he says this in order to refute the doubt that—since the scriptural statement regarding the three states establishes only an option (*vikalpa*)—it lacks the status of being a reason that establishes a synthesis (*samuccaya*), and thus remains a reason for the prima facie view. The underlying intention (*bhāva*) is as follows: in a case where a difference in effects is impossible, the mention of things with a single grammatical ending (*ekavibhaktinirdeśa*) [establishes their identity].

Even though an alternative (vikalpa) might be established, in a case where a difference in the resulting effect is possible, one must establish a conjunction (samuccaya) alone—out of fear of the eight defects inherent in an alternative—since otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of violating the scriptural recitation of the word "eternal" (nitya).

The phrase "but rather, sublation according to possibility" means that sublation of the origination of the unprecedented (*apūrvotpatti-bādha*) and sublation of the result (*phala-bādha*) are absolutely impossible. This is an elliptical indication; for instance, just as in the case of the *vrīhi* and *yava* injunctions, there are four defects in a single scripture—namely, the abandonment of authority (*prāmāṇya-parityāga*), the acceptance of lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya-svīkāra*), the abandonment of accepted lack of authority (*svīkṛtāprāmāṇya-parityāga*), and the acceptance of abandoned authority (*parityaktaprāmāṇya-svīkāra*). Thus, one should see that there are twelve defects across the three scriptures concerning the channels (*nāḍī*), the pericardium (*purītat*), and Brahman, with four defects in each. To explain:

In one instance of sleeping in the channels (nāḍī), there are two faults each—namely, the abandonment of authority and the acceptance of lack of authority—in both the statement regarding the pericardium (purītat) and the statement regarding Brahman. Furthermore, in another instance of sleeping in the pericardium, there are two faults each—namely, the abandonment of authority and the acceptance of lack of authority—in the statement regarding the channels. However, in the case of the statement regarding the pericardium, there are two faults: the acceptance of the authority that was previously abandoned and the abandonment of the lack of authority that was previously accepted. Thus, there are four faults. Again, in another instance of sleeping in Brahman, the same applies to the statement regarding Brahman.

There are two pairs of defects each consisting of the abandonment of accepted invalidity and the non-abandonment of it, and the acceptance of abandoned invalidity and the non-acceptance of it; thus, in another instance of sleep—specifically regarding the lying down in the channels (nāḍīs)—there are likewise two defects in the statement concerning the channels as before. Consequently, twelve defects would arise in the fourfold cycle of sleep. As for the statement that "an alternative (vikalpa) is vitiated by eight defects," that is intended with reference to the well-known example of rice and barley; for in the Bhāṣya, it says "in the channels and the pericardium" (nāḍī-purītatau), even though in lexicons the word *purītat* is indicated as neuter when referring to the internal [organ].

Although there is an explanation provided by its commentators, nevertheless, because one observes the Vedic usage "they settle in the pericardium" (*purītatam abhipratiṣṭhante*), it should be understood that the author of the Bhāṣya made the reference in the masculine gender, intending that it possesses both genders (*ubhayaliṅgatva*).

The sense is that there is a single purpose through a traditional sequence (*paramparayā*), because we observe a combination (*samuccaya*) of auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) which, although they culminate in a single purpose—namely, the act of communication—possess the capacity for action by means of their distinct intermediate functions. Nor should it be argued that direct unity of purpose is the cause of optionality (*vikalpa*); for, since redness (*āruṇya*) and a one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*) fulfill a single purchase (*kraya*) and are mutually expectant as being expressed within a single sentence, there is no optionality between them, which implies that independence (*nairapekṣya*) is also required. This is the underlying intention.

The meaning is that the conjunction of the channels (*nāḍī*) and so forth is demonstrated by scripture; thus, by the scriptural statement, "At that time he becomes united with them," the conjunction of the channels and of Brahman—designated by the word *prāṇa*—is demonstrated. As for the question of how there is no contradiction: the sense is that because the pericardium (*purītat*) is outside the heart, the analogy of a palace, a bedstead, and a couch does not apply. Regarding the mention of "in the heart": although the Supreme Self is all-pervading, the Supreme Self as delimited by the heart is not so [all-pervading]; therefore, lying within that [heart] while lying in the pericardium is indeed a contradiction.

[The opponent's] position is that there is no contradiction; however, it must be stated that this is incorrect—this is the remainder [of the argument]. This is because there is a contradiction between [the soul] sleeping in the heart and [the scriptural teaching] that it sleeps in the ether within the heart. For it has been established that its abode is the ether within the heart by the statement, "He lies in that ether within the heart," and there is also a contradiction with its sleeping in the pericardium (*purītat*) by the statements, "The channels called *hitā* extend from the heart to the pericardium in seventy-two thousand [channels]," and "Having descended through them, he sleeps in the pericardium. Indeed, one who has emerged from a palace [cannot simultaneously be inside it].

The point is that one who is lying on the roof, covering, or wall of a palace can be said to be "lying in the palace. What, then, is the solution? If there is one, listen with an attentive mind: the flesh called *purītat* (the pericardium) is situated within the heart and serves as the support for the small lotus (*daharapuṇḍarīka*).

The space delimited by this small lotus is the "small space" (*daharākāśa*); therein occurs the deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). This is according to the *Saubala-śruti*: "In the middle of the heart is a red lump of flesh, from which the small lotus is spread out like a white water-lily."

The statement regarding the *purītat* (pericardium) encircling the heart is intended to mean that it encircles the small white lotus (*dahara-puṇḍarīka*) situated within the heart; therefore, there is not even a scent of contradiction anywhere. Furthermore, that heart has ten openings which serve as the gates of the fortress for the individual soul (*jīva*) during its states such as waking; having experienced the states of waking and dreaming, [the soul] enters within through the channels called *hitā* during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), [reaching] that which is situated in the middle of the heart, which stands in the place of a fortress.

Having reached that lump of flesh called the heart, which is red, there is no contradiction in [the soul] being in deep sleep within the Supreme Brahman—designated by the term "the space within the small lotus" (daharākāśa)—situated inside that [heart]; for just as when it is said, "Having entered through the gate of the enclosure by way of the royal road from the gate of the enclosure, having proceeded toward the king's palace, he sleeps in the palace," while the great king is lying in the palace, there is no contradiction in saying that [he] has emerged from the enclosure and, proceeding by the royal road, sleeps in the king's palace.
Thus concludes the section concerning the non-existence of that.

In this context, the intended scriptural passage is: "No evil touches him there," for it is heard in scripture: "When he is asleep in these channels, no evil touches him, for then he is endowed with light. The sense is that here the word *pāpmā* (evil) refers generally to both good and bad deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*), and thus the intention is to express liberation from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Consequently, since there is no cause for the one who has fallen into deep sleep to return [to the same body], it is another person who arises; and therefore, [the rules regarding] karma, memory, and words [would apply].

They must be explained somehow or other: how can there be a restriction regarding the experience of the fruits of karma in the absence of deep sleep? Therefore, one who desires the enjoyment of the fruits of merit must protect them even from deep sleep. As for the recollection [of dreams], it is merely of the nature of an illusion. The scriptural passage beginning with "those [who perform sacrifices] here [become] tigers or [other animals]" means that another person rises up in that very same body which was the prior embodied self. Even the injunctions for the sake of liberation concern those who seek the experience of the bliss of Brahman; however, for one in deep sleep, there is only the experience of the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*), not even the experience of the bliss of Brahman. Thus, the point is that there is no logical inconsistency.

Regarding the phrase *yadyadbhavanti*: it is heard in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, "Whatever they become here—whether a tiger, or a lion, or a boar, or a worm, or a gadfly, or a mosquito—whatever they become... This means that those who have been [in previous lives] become exactly that very thing; the meaning is that having returned from deep sleep (*suṣupta*), they become [what they were]. To say, "In whatever manner they previously existed, in that same manner they exist," is merely a statement of the resultant meaning (*phalitārtha*), since the words *yathā* and *tathā* do not appear in the scripture; for the scriptural sentence is indeed: "Whatever they become, in that way they become."

If it is argued that "inability to perform [rituals]" is what is intended—[the opponent might say]: "Indeed, in the state of union with the Supreme Self (*paramātmasampatti*), it is taught that by its majesty there is no contact with evil (*pāpmāna*); however, 'inability to perform' is not stated, because it is not the literal meaning [of the word]. Furthermore, this would contradict the subsequent statement which establishes that union with the Supreme Self is the cause for non-contact with evil: 'For at that time he becomes endowed with splendor (*tejas*').”

If it is argued that this cannot be so, because it contradicts the subsequent statement—"for then he becomes endowed with light"—which establishes that union with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the cause for the non-contact of evil, we reply: it is not so. In the phrase "for then he becomes endowed with light" (*tejasā hi tadā sampanno bhavati*), the suffix *-tya* denotes a wish (*āśaṃsā*). The meaning established is that, having attained union with Brahman, he then desires that [state]; and subsequently, being unable to perform [further] practice, he then desires the Supreme Self as his place of rest.

The sense is that there is a difference [between the two cases]: the phrase "the state of being the substratum for the recognition of another object" refers to the recognition of another object expressed by the word *karman* (action), such as "this was begun by me" or "this was seen by me"; whereas the recognition of one's own subject matter, such as "I who was asleep am now awake," is expressed by the word *anusmṛti* (recollection). The intention is that [the former] would otherwise result in the fallacy of being causeless; the meaning is that [the latter] serves as a reminder based on such scriptural statements as "Action is not lost. Thus ends the section concerning the words *karman*, *anusmṛti*, and *vidhi*.

The meaning is that, according to the Bhāṣya, the cause of fainting (mūrchā) is injury and the like, whereas the cause of deep sleep (suṣupti) is exhaustion and the like; furthermore, this is also an illustration of the difference in outward form (ākāra-vairūpya), which was not explicitly cited in the Bhāṣya because it is clear [from the context]. For in deep sleep, a serene facial expression, full respiration, and so forth are observed, whereas in fainting, there is a deformity of form consisting of a distorted face, shallow breathing, and so on. The same distinction regarding the difference in causes and the difference in forms is clearly evident between fainting and death as well. Therefore...

Some explain that both of these—due to the dissimilarity of the cause (*nimitta-vairūpya*) and the dissimilarity of the form (*ākāra-vairūpya*)—apply to both deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and death. Nor should it be said that this contradicts the *Ṭīkā*, which states that "by the dissimilarity of the cause there is exclusion of deep sleep, and by the dissimilarity of the form there is exclusion of death," because one path does not invalidate another. Furthermore, according to this interpretation, since the distinction between deep sleep and death is established for fainting (*mūrchā*) through the dissimilarities of cause and form, [it follows that] death indeed...

It should not be said that the subsequent portion of the commentary beginning with "the cessation of the connection between all vital breaths and the body" is redundant; for this section proceeds because, when it is stated that "fainting is an incomplete attainment [of death] following death," there arises an inquiry as to what that death is and what this incomplete attainment is. Thus, there is no lack of coherence. The meaning of the statement "fainting is an incomplete attainment following death" is as follows: death is...

It should not be argued that fainting (*mūrcchā*)—which consists of the attainment of the separation of some vital breaths (*prāṇa*) for the sake of the separation of all vital breaths—is not truly "fainting" because it lacks the purpose of death characterized by the cessation of all vital breaths, as death does not occur there due to the power of medicine and the like. For in the phrase "the attainment of an act for the sake of death," what is intended is the actual presence of the result [death]; it is not the case that [the definition fails] merely because of the presence of an obstacle.

The state of fainting, which consists in the cessation of the gross vital force (*prāṇavīrya*), loses its character as being for the purpose of death merely by the non-arising of the effects of death; therefore, it is well said that "the attainment [of this state] is for the sake of death. Now, one might object: how is it appropriate to state the remainder as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and death before even describing the dissimilar forms that exclude death? For it would indeed be appropriate to state the remainder as deep sleep only after describing that which excludes deep sleep. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "because of the statement 'neither deep sleep nor death'."
Thus ends the section concerning the deluded. || 4 ||

The phrase "in the states" (avasthāsu) refers to the states of deep sleep, swoon, and departure [from the body], because these cannot serve as locations [for the soul's experience]. The meaning of the Bhāṣya, "And that occurs because the connection with the body is not a human goal," is that actions, by means of their connection with the body, function as instruments for achieving what is not a human goal.

In the previous sūtra, the phrase *nigavyākhyāneti* is to be divided as *nigadavyākhyāneti*. The sense is that *anigadavyākhyā* means "one whose meaning is not clear" or "one whose meaning requires interpretation. *Nigada* refers to recitation; thus, it is so called because its explanation does not exist through mere recitation alone. This is because the word *amṛta*, which is common to meanings such as "eternal" and signifies "faultlessness," has an unclear meaning [in that context].

Regarding the phrase "having a non-material body" (*aprākṛtavigraha*), what is intended here is the *capacity* for such a body; therefore, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency even with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*), which at present lacks a non-material body. In the commentary, regarding the phrase "name and form" (*nāmarūpa*) cited from the scriptural passage, it was stated that the one who brings forth name and form has no connection with them. However, that [statement] is sublated, because a relationship in the form of the relation between the bringer-forth and that which is brought forth certainly exists. Therefore, its effect—the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*)—possesses both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*), namely, the state of being free from all defects and the state of being a mine of auspicious qualities. || 14 ||

The meaning is that the Vedic revelation is concerned with the absence of connection to physical suffering, envy, and so forth. "By the impossibility of the sense" means by the impossibility of the purpose—namely, for an omniscient Lord who governs all things, to possess knowledge dependent on the intellect [of others], or to be impelled by injunctions. "Subordinate dependence on karma" means that even for one who is omniscient and the governor of all, being an object of cognition or being impelled is possible only through an intermediary.

"Adhikāra" means the communication of purpose (*tādarthyabodhana*); for the learned say that "adhikāra" is "viniyoga" (application). The intended meaning is that [the texts] "authorize" (*adhikurvanti*), which is to say they "apply" (*viniyuñjate*). For "viniyoga" is indeed "vyāpāraṇa" (causing to act); the meaning is that they cause the Brāhmaṇas and others—who are already subject to their respective duties—to act by making them understand that purpose. And it has been said: "It is intent upon the exclusion of the negation of the other. This means it is intent upon the exclusion of the view that the sentence beginning with "satya-jñāna" (truth-consciousness) is intent upon the negation of other qualities such as omniscience.

Regarding the statement, "the word *atha* refers to the sense of totality (*kārtsnya*)," the word *artha* here refers to intention (*abhiprāya*). Furthermore, in the rule *atho pīti*, since the technical designation *pragṛhya* applies by the rule *ot*, there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *plutapragṛhyā aci*.

The phrase "negation of specific qualities" means that when there is a negation of specific qualities in the form of parts and actions—as in the statement "partless and actionless"—the general negation "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇam) results in that [specific] conclusion; this is the intended sense. Nor should it be argued: "In that case, why would the prohibition 'a Brāhmaṇa is not to be killed' not result in a specific prohibition such as 'one should not kill an Ātreya'? For in that case, since there exists a scriptural injunction prescribing a specific quality, the prohibition does not apply without restriction.

Because for one who expects a specific conclusion from the scripture, it is necessary that the conclusion rests upon the negation of specific qualities; for this very reason it has been stated: "The meaning is that [the Self] is of a single nature. Just as in the Smṛti passage, "For space is one," space existing separately in conjunction within various objects such as jars remains untouched by the defects residing therein and is of a single nature; likewise, [it is so] in various receptacles of water.

The meaning is that, just as the sun is reflected [in many places], so too the Self, although residing in many locations, remains of a single nature because it is untouched by the defects inherent in those [locations]; this constitutes the relationship between the subject and the predicate. || 17 || || 18 ||

In the commentary [on the phrase] "because of being included within locations such as earth," the word "pratīyamānāt" (from what is perceived) must be supplied as an ellipsis. Consequently, the meaning is that the susceptibility to increase and decrease which follows from being included within locations such as earth is thereby precluded. Furthermore, perception is common to both valid cognition (*pramā*) and error (*bhrama*); thus, even though the sun (*aṃśumat*), which is perceived as situated within jars and the like, does not actually exist there, it remains untouched by the defects residing in them. Likewise, the supreme [Self], which is perceived as situated in locations such as earth...

The meaning is that it is logically established that the Self is untouched by the defects residing therein. By this, the doubt as to how the suspicion of being touched by those defects—based on the [Self's] inclusion [within the body]—can be removed by the example of the sun which is devoid of such inclusion, is also refuted; for it is precisely the doubt occasioned by the perception of inclusion that must be removed here. Furthermore, the presentation of the example is possible because, just as in that case, the sun, though perceived as being inside [the water], does not partake of its defects. As stated in the Bhāṣya: "Or rather, two... regarding the Brāhmaṇa.

Regarding the word "rūpa" (form): here, by the term "mūrta" (the formed), earth, water, and fire are meant; and by the term "amūrta" (the formless), air and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) are denoted, because it is heard later [in the scripture]: "That which is other than air and the intermediate space is the formed; therefore, air and the intermediate space are the formless. Furthermore, [the nature of the Self] is described through such examples as: "like a saffron-colored garment, like a white woolen cloth, like a sapphire, like the flame of a fire, like a lotus," and so forth.

Having presented dream-forms as objects of consciousness produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) born from the experience of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), and having negated both forms with the words, "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'," [the text] concludes by stating that while the phenomenal world—indicated by the term "prāṇa"—possesses empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasatyatva*), it is Brahman alone that possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasatyatva*), according to the passage: "The truth of truth; the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed truth, and He is their truth."
Regarding the term *vṭhadāraṇyaka*, the meaning of the commentary's phrase "atha syāt" is as follows: here, however, both compound forms are intended, namely *tair guṇaiḥ* and *yadetāvatvam*.

Regarding the passage in the Bhāṣya: "Those specific qualities of the *tanmātras* which are primary (*prakṛta*), by virtue of being distinguished from those [other qualities], are perceived as belonging to the *tanmātras*; and that measure (*iyattā*) of the *tanmātras* which is primary is also [perceived]," it might be argued: "Even if the qualities are primary, how can it be established that they possess only those specific qualities [and no others]? For there is no explicit verbal statement (*aśabda*) negating other qualities, and it would also contradict the principle stated as 'only those [specific] *tanmātras*'. This is true.

This is because such a statement is justified by intending that the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) is this specific quality—namely, the possession of those qualities characterized by the exclusion of other qualities—in accordance with the maxim: "Every sentence is restrictive" (*sarvaṃ vākyaṃ sāvadhāraṇam*). While it might seem that one should simply say "only this much" (*etāvat*), in reality even that need not be said; for it should be understood that the purpose is fulfilled simply by stating that [the Self] "denies what is under discussion."

The phrase "abundance is stated" means that an abundance of qualities is stated; thus, the intended sense is that there is no syntactical connection with the verb "he speaks again and again. Regarding the term "sārthasaṃgraham," he takes up the word from the Sūtra once more in order to include the subject-sentence endowed with a summary of the meaning; therefore, one should not entertain any suspicion of tautology. Furthermore, he states another reason for excluding the insentient and the individual soul (jīva).

The meaning is that insentience constitutes a deficiency in its own nature, whereas for the individual soul (*jīva*), there is a deficiency in terms of qualities. Thus ends the section on the two-fold characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "In the passage 'Two indeed are the forms of Brahman,' since it is precisely the composite nature of consciousness and unconsciousness that is designated by the terms 'the formed' (*mūrta*) and 'the formless' (*amūrta*), how can the Bhāṣya state 'of the insentient phenomenal world consisting of the formed and the formless'? Anticipating this, he says, beginning with "consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness," and so forth.

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated "by the analogy of the serpent and its coils": just as there is no difference [between the serpent and its coils] because the serpent is not devoid of its own nature, yet a difference arises through the assumption of specific configurations in the form of coiling or straightness, so too, although there is no difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman, a difference arises through the assumption of the form of the phenomenal world (*kāryaprapañca*). Nor is it correct to say that the serpent assumes the state of being coiled or straight for the sake of obtaining specific experiences resulting from resting or moving; however, for Brahman—which is omniscient and omnipotent—the assumption of the insentient phenomenal world (*acid-prapañca*), which is devoid of knowledge and bliss, would be illogical.

It should not be said that this is inconsistent with the *pūrva-pakṣa*, for the Brahman does not act for its own sake like a human being; rather, it acts for the sake of favoring living beings. And that favor toward them occurs through the Brahman’s attainment of the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is necessary for their experience, performance of duties, and so forth; thus, the Brahman attains that nature. Regarding the "negation of the attributes of the non-intelligent," by the words "unborn" (*aja*) and so on, there is a negation of the non-intelligent attributes such as birth and the like.

This is the meaning. As for the reason why [the previous section] constitutes a separate topical heading (*adhikaraṇa*), one should listen to [the following]: although the conclusion of the topical heading is revealed by demonstrating that the sūtra "Therefore, with the Infinite; for thus is the mark" serves as the summary of the ultimate probandum, and because it will be stated later that [the sūtras] beginning with "The finitude of what is under discussion" do not constitute a separate topical heading due to their being for that purpose (*tādārthya*) and their immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) in that very sūtra is explained by the word "immediately after" (*anantara*), and the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*)...

Since the words "bhūyiṣṭha" and "ataḥ" have already been explained as meaning "the state of being most abundant," no further thing remains to be heard; nevertheless, it should be understood that it was stated thus with the intention of indicating the profundity of its meaning.

In the second [case], regarding the status of being the cause of the world, the meaning is that it is impossible for a universal (jāti) to possess such qualities as being the cause of the world or omniscience.
Just as there is a state of being a part by way of being a qualifier, so too here the individual soul and the insentient entity are parts of Brahman. 28.

"But others," and so forth, [means] that those [texts] which have that [oneness] as their primary purport are more powerful. Since unity and multiplicity, as presented by scripture, cannot coexist in a single reality, when one or the other must be adopted, it is appropriate that unity—being unestablished by any other means of knowledge (*māna*)—be what is enjoined. Therefore, it is fitting that multiplicity, already established by other means of knowledge, be restated (*anūdita*) as subordinate to that [unity] for the purpose of enjoining unity; this is because we hear censure regarding the perception of difference directly from many scriptural passages.

Because non-difference is being established, some Vedic passages concerning Brahman that possess forms are of the nature of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), while certain other passages expressing duality—such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*) and so forth—are useful for the realization of the attributeless [Brahman] by way of negating agency superimposed upon the intellect (*buddhi*) as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Thus, the meaning is that the non-difference texts, which have that [non-difference] as their primary purport, possess greater authority than the difference texts, whose primary purport is not that. Regarding the reading found in some places, "Then, what kind of Brahman is it that negates the manifold world? To that he says," that should be considered with care.

Furthermore, since even by the sūtra "āha ca tanmātram," it is intended to establish precisely the state of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatva*) according to that school's view, the aforementioned sūtra is not introduced at this point—once the state of being free from conceptual proliferation has been taken for granted—in response to the inquiry as to what that [state] is like.

"He made bodies before"—that is, he made bodies characterized by two feet before; "before" means prior to the manifestation of the eyes and other senses, that Lord, the Bird—since the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is described as having wings, a tail, and so forth in the *Taittirīya* and other texts, it is called "the Bird"—the Person who identifies with that [subtle body] entered; this is the meaning. And thus, this scriptural passage, as well as the passage beginning with "having entered by means of this living self," refers to the Supreme Self alone.

The meaning of the sūtra is that it demonstrates the inclusion of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) as stated in the preceding sūtra; this is the intended sense. Regarding the phrase "the non-existence of anything else," the word "of Brahman" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The statement, "For there is nothing higher than this 'not this, not this' (*neti neti*)," is the explanation of the expression "not this, not this. The meaning of that passage is: "Indeed, because there is nothing other than this Brahman, it is called 'not'; it is not, however, called 'not' on the grounds that it does not exist in itself."

And therefore, since that which is other than this is negated by the words "not this, not this," the existence of that Brahman is already established; thus, the sense is that it is not subject to negation. The phrase "this sentence" means the sentence "not from this, not this, there is nothing else beyond."

Furthermore, the phrase "Now, as for its name" cannot be intended to exclude the Brāhmaṇa, because it is devoted to negating other instructions of the form "not this, not this"—as in the passage "For there is nothing higher than this 'Not this'"—and thus lacks the capacity to leave the Brāhmaṇa as the remainder. Therefore, the phrase "Now, as for its name" is the subject matter of the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "And he says again. For in that passage, the Brāhmaṇa statement "The Truth of truth" reveals the ultimate reality of the Truth.

The phrase *sūryaprakāśādyavaiśeṣyam* means the non-distinctness (*avaiśeṣyam*) of the solar light and so forth; "non-distinctness" (*avaiśeṣyam*) signifies being devoid of particularity (*viśeṣarahitatvam*), that is to say, being devoid of particularities such as straightness or curvature produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) like a finger. The word "is admitted" (*sampratipannam*) is to be supplied [as the verb]. The syntactical connection is: "the non-distinctness of Brahman also is equal to that. Just like the solar light and so forth, Brahman also possesses non-distinctness; that is, it is without distinction, meaning it is devoid of particularities created by limiting adjuncts.

It should be understood that one must not mistakenly assume this is an explanation of the Sautrāntika term *avaiśeṣya* (non-distinctness) as being equivalent to that [non-difference], because others have not explained it in such a way, and because since the equivalence is already established by the suffix *-vat* in the expression *prakāśādivat*, the phrase "and the equivalence like light, etc. would be redundant.

The meaning is as follows: in the sūtra "Because of the designation of both" (*ubhayavyapadeśāt*), the absence of contradiction regarding the relationship between the one to be propitiated and the propitiator was presented on the grounds that the individual soul (*jīva*) is a distinct state (*avasthābheda*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); however, in the sūtra "Or like light and its substratum" (*prakāśāśrayavad vā*), the relationship between the one to be propitiated and the propitiator was established because the individual soul is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman by virtue of being a single portion (*ekadeśa*) of It.

The meaning is that one must accept a difference in scope between the scriptural injunction regarding the presence of fragrance and the scriptural prohibition of it, because they refer respectively to natural and non-natural fragrances. This is because omniscience and other such qualities are established by texts concerning the essential nature [of Brahman], as in: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving."

The meaning is that this is established by such scriptural statements as these. This is merely an illustration; one should also observe that, according to the maxim "the [attributes] are for the sake of meditation, like the feet," qualities such as having four feet or sixteen parts—which are intended for meditation—lack empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*). Likewise, if omniscience and other such qualities were intended solely for meditation, the consequence would be that they too lack empirical reality. Thus, it would result in the admission that one or the other [of the two sets of attributes] is not authoritative. For it has been said:

For what investigator would say that when two scriptures contradict each other, one is authoritative while the other is unauthoritative? However, since there is no circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) in establishing a reason consistent with the thesis, once it is determined that the probandum (*sādhya*) is the negation of both characteristics—namely, having form (*sākāratva*) and being formless (*nirākāratva*)—then, because it is appropriate to employ as the reason only that which consistently demonstrates the absence of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*) everywhere, the sense is that its very [negation] is rightly supplied (*adhyāhāra*) by the force of the context (*yogārthatā*).

The meaning is that the designation as a unity is like [the designation of] existence and non-existence. Although it might be argued that the quality of not expressing that [difference] does not exist in the scripture cited there—since in the passage, "That which is this light-filled, immortal, ancient one in this earth, and that which is this light-filled, immortal, ancient one within the body (adhyātma), this indeed is that Self," there is indeed a state of not expressing that [unity] in the form of expressing non-difference through the mention of distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—nevertheless, the establishment of featurelessness (*nirviśeṣatva*) does not follow from that alone; for...

The sense is that because Brahman is omnipresent, its being composed of light (*tejomayatva*) and other qualities taught in the scriptures are established as false by its mere oneness. The sense is that both these qualities—being changeless (*nirvikāratva*) and being of the nature of bliss (*ānandarūpatva*)—are already implied by the word "consisting of nectar" (*amṛtamaya*). Regarding the term *arūpavat*, the sense is that the suffix *matup* is redundant; for the sense of possession is already expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* compound itself (meaning "that which has no form"), according to the maxim that words whose meaning has already been stated should not be used again. Thus, the suffix *matup* is superfluous.

Although the form *anaravanticakrāṇi* is employed in the Mahābhāṣya under the rule *ugavādibhyo yat*, nevertheless, where a *bahuvrīhi* and a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) have the same meaning, the *bahuvrīhi* alone occurs due to parsimony (*lāghava*), as in *aguḥ* (goless) or *anaśvaḥ* (horseless), rather than *agomān* or *anaśvavān*. However, where they do not have the same meaning, a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) is formed with that which ends in a possessive suffix, as in *ahastī* (not having hands); for when one says *nahastaḥ*, there is no cognition of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on genus (*jāti*).

Even where there is the cognition of a specific meaning through a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), and even where there is a negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) ending in such a suffix—as in *adaṇḍī*, *akṣatrī*, and *avāgmī*—there is no understanding from the *bahuvrīhi* that the connection with a staff or an umbrella is being negated, nor that the state of speaking properly is being negated. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa, in the commentary on the rule *ugavādibhyaḥ*, states: "In the case of *anarāṇi*, although one could simply say 'without spokes' (*anarāṇi*), the mention of the possessive suffix (*matup*) is for the purpose of conveying a specific type of genus; for if it were said 'without spokes,' wheels whose spokes were merely broken might also be understood. Therefore..."

The sense is that, by means of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of "possessing spokes" (*sāra*), the cognition of a wheel that has not yet arisen occurs through the term "without spokes" (*anaraka*); thus, because there is a specific meaning [distinguished from the absence], the use of the possessive suffix *matup* is justified. However, in this case, since there is no difference in meaning, the suffix *matup* is difficult to establish. Furthermore, the phrase "and because of the understanding of the marks of purport" means that in the *Sadvidyā*, it was established in the very first sūtra that the sixfold marks of purport apply only to that which possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣa*). The phrase "because of being an example in the case of connection with a conditioned form" follows from that.

The intention is that the sūtra should simply read: "And like light, there is a connection with forms conditioned by limiting adjuncts" (prakāśavaccaupādhikākārayogaḥ). Although this objection—that [the nature of Brahman] is well-known even to women and children—is equally applicable to one's own position, nevertheless, since in our own view the objection extends up to the instability of the substratum such as earth and so forth, and since that must necessarily be refuted, the point is that there is no fault in [the sūtra] being directed toward that.

Nor can it be argued that there is no fault here because the word *liṅga* refers to an "indicative mark consisting in the observation of another meaning" (*anyārthadarśana-rūpa-liṅga*), whereas *śruti* (direct scriptural statement) can possess such a character; for the sense is that the passage "By the Brāhmaṇa [portion] one becomes a Brāhmaṇa," which directly establishes the stated meaning, lacks the nature of an indicative mark consisting in the observation of another meaning. Furthermore, the reason is that the sūtra "Like light, etc. (*prakāśādivat*) does not exclude the distinction of the individual soul (*jīva*) caused by that [limitation]. For if it did, these two sūtras would be intended merely as the presentation of alternative views (*matāntara*), since that very [distinction] has already been refuted. This is the underlying intention.

"But others," and so forth, [is said] because states such as dreaming are the subject under discussion. Now, one might object: in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "If it be argued that [the Brahman in the heart is different] because of difference" (*bhedāt*), it was stated that this refers to the difference in states consisting of the connection with bodies such as those of gods, and not to the difference in states such as dreaming. To this we reply: no, for there is no fault, since what is intended there is precisely the difference in states consisting of the connection with bodies during states such as dreaming; this is the meaning. "But others," and so forth, refers to the passage concerning the Madhu-vidyā. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* Upaniṣad, in the passage on the Madhu-vidyā, [it says]: "And this person who consists of light and is immortal in this earth, and..."

The meaning is that because unity is stated in each successive turn by such sentences as "He who is within the self" (*yam adhyātmaṃ*), starting from "Not even on account of place" (*na sthānato 'pi*) up to "For [Brahman] is indeed without form" (*arūpavadeva hi*).

One section, beginning with "And like light, it is not purposeless" (*prakāśavaccāvaiyarthyam*) and ending before "The limitedness of what has been described" (*prakṛtaitāvatvam*), is devoted to demonstrating that there is no difference from the essential nature of Brahman. Another section, beginning with "The limitedness of what has been described" and ending before "Because of the designation of both" (*ubhayavyapadeśāt*), establishes the conclusion that Brahman possesses two forms. A further section, beginning with "Because of the designation of both" and ending before "On account of the highest [Brahman], because of the bridge and the measure" (*paramatassetūnmānāt*), [establishes that Brahman is distinct from those two forms].

They describe the relationship of material cause and effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) between Brahman and the world as being one of absolute non-difference, according to the analogy of the serpent and its coils; however, because the Lord is changeless, the relationship of material cause and effect between Him and the world is, like that between a gem and its radiance, a relationship consisting in the diffusion of power (*śakti*) from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*). And he states this again, providing further justification.

The meaning is as follows: since he [the opponent] accepts that the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "And it declares further" (*bravīti ca bhūyaḥ*) serves to support the previously stated sense, he must state that this very portion supports the fact that the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "For it denies the extent of the manifested world" (*prakṛtaitāvatvaṃ hi pratiṣedhati*) is what is to be established. However, because the meaning of the sentence "It is real" (*satyam*), which is indicated by "And it declares further," consists in the denial of two forms, it is impossible for it to serve as the support for the existence of a cause distinct from the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Thus ends the section on the "Serpent and its Coil" (*ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the statement "because of the twofold characteristic, [it is] the Brāhmaṇa," although the twofold characteristic of the Brāhmaṇa is not firmly established during the stage of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) of this section—since the purpose of this section is to establish the stability of that twofold characteristic—nevertheless, because the prima facie argument is extremely weak, it was stated thus by taking the twofold characteristic for granted. For this very reason, it should be understood that the *Bhāṣya* says, "having raised a doubt through certain fallacious reasons. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the four-footed Brāhmaṇa" in the *Bhāṣya*, [this refers to] the Brāhmaṇa-knowledges consisting of sixteen parts.

Four quarters of Brahman have been described: "The eastern direction is a quarter, the western direction is a quarter, the southern direction is a quarter, and the northern direction is a quarter. This indeed, my dear, is the four-quartered foot of Brahman named 'The Radiant'."

"The earth is one part, the intermediate space is one part, the sky is one part, and the ocean is one part; this, my dear, is the four-part foot of Brahman called 'The Endless' (Anantavat). Fire is one part, the sun is one part, the moon is one part, and lightning is one part; this, my dear, is the four-part foot of Brahman called 'The Luminous' (Jyotiṣmat). Breath is one part, the eye is one part, the ear is one part, and the mind is one part; this, my dear, is the four-part foot of Brahman called 'The Abode' (Āyatanavat). [Śvetaketu asked: "Why, sir, do cows have two hooves in front on their feet?"

Afterwards, regarding the phrase "two heels," there are four hoof-parts on each foot; these are called "kalās. The four directions—east, west, south, and north—are like limbs or parts (*kalās*). This is the first foot, characterized by luminosity (*prakāśavān*); through its meditation, the worshipper becomes luminous, thus it is called the "luminous foot. The four [elements]—earth, intermediate space, heaven, and ocean—are the four *kalās* of this second foot, which is named "the infinite" (*anantavān*).

Thus, when this [Brahman] is meditated upon through the quality of being infinite (*anantavat*), it brings infinity to the meditator; therefore, it is the "Infinite Foot. Fire, sun, moon, and lightning are its four parts; this is the third foot, named "Luminous" (*jyotiṣmat*). Meditating on it, one becomes luminous; therefore, it is the "Luminous Foot. Vital breath (*prāṇa*), eye, ear, and mind are its four parts; this is the fourth foot, named "Having an Abode" (*āyatanavat*). By meditating on that, one comes to have an abode; therefore, it is the foot named "Having an Abode. Thus, Brahman has four feet and is eightfold.

The hoof consists of sixteen parts; the Bhāṣya indicates the existence of that which is "unmeasured" (anunmita). Now, if this [hoof] is merely measured, how can that which is to be attained by it be unmeasured? For it is not [attained] by means of what is measured.

If it is argued that there exists a limited extent of another region to be reached by means of a bridge composed of an accumulation of earth, wood, and so forth, it is not so. For that which is to be reached is well-known in the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) as being "immeasurable" (*aparimita*); this [text] indicates the existence of that [reached state] through its specific characteristic of being reachable by means of this bridge. Since qualities such as having four feet are "measured," the sense is that the conclusion is that a distinction is established between [this] and the "immeasurable" Brahman well-known in the Vedānta. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, “by way of a commonality with a bridge” (*setusāmānyena*), the word “commonality” (*sāmānya*) here has the abstract state as its primary sense. Since the quality of “not causing confusion among all the worlds”—as heard in the Śruti text, “for the non-confounding of these worlds”—is a shared attribute, the meaning is that the word “bridge” (*setu*) is used there figuratively by virtue of possessing that quality. Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, “a foot of him are all beings” (*pādo’sya viśvābhūtāni*), since this refers to a part (*aṃśa*) and not to an instruction regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*), it should be understood that the mention of it being for the sake of comprehension (*budhyarthatva*) is a *prauḍhivāda* (an assertion made for the sake of argument).
