In the Bhāṣya, the statement that "the designation of speech and so forth as the feet of Brahman is for the purpose of meditation" means that the designation of speech and so forth as the feet of the mind—which is a representative form (*pratīka*) of Brahman—or of space, is for the purpose of meditation. For it is heard in scripture: "One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman; this is with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). Now, with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*): 'Space is Brahman'—thus both are taught, namely, with respect to the self and with respect to the divine."

"This four-footed Brahman has speech as one foot, breath as a foot, the eye as a foot, and the ear as a foot—thus with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). Now, with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*): fire is a foot, wind is a foot, the sun is a foot, and the quarters are a foot. Thus both have been taught: that which pertains to the self and that which pertains to the divine. This is the four-footed Brahman; this is the Brahman measured by the mind (*manas*), for it has four feet. How is there a four-footed nature for the Brahman whose form is the mind? To this he says, "speech as a foot," and so forth.
For the mind [takes] objects of speech, smell, sight, and hearing as its spheres.

Because it moves by means of speech and the other [organs], the mind has "feet" in the sense of being the instrument of movement; the ether, which is the representative image (*pratīka*) of Brahman, has four feet—namely fire, wind, the sun, and the quarters—for these are all-pervading.

The sense is that the feet of the earth appear as if attached to the belly of the sky; therefore, just as the designation of speech and the other organs as the "feet" of the mind—which is the representative symbol (pratīka) of the *adhyātma* Brahman—and of space (*ākāśa*), which is the representative symbol of the *adhidaivata* Brahman, is for the purpose of meditation since it is impossible for the mind or space to actually have speech and the others as their feet, so too the instruction regarding the four-footedness and sixteen-part nature of Brahman is for the purpose of meditation. This is the intended meaning.

The meaning is: "of the Lord who is the cause of the entire universe" refers to either the mind or the ether, which serve as the symbols (*pratīka*) for the Lord who is the cause of the entire universe. Regarding the phrase "in that very [place]," it should be explained thus: the negation of anything superior is established. The meaning is that by stating, "This alone is higher than all; there is nothing else higher than this," the negation of any superior entity is proven. As for the phrase "intended as being supreme," it means that there is nothing other than Rudra—who has become the Supreme—that is higher.

For if the word "other" (*apara*) were absent, it would follow that even Rudra’s status as the "Supreme" (*para*) would be negated; therefore, the intention is that the word "other" must indeed have a referent. Because there is no other possible justification for restricting its meaning—since the word "other" can serve a purpose by negating equals and superiors through its connection with the word ending in the ablative case ("from whom") heard in the scripture—it is not the case that the word "other" acts as a restrictor [of the Supreme] on any other grounds.

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). To the question, "How is its [the relation's] establishment otherwise? he says [the following]; the sense is that he introduces the inquiry in order to state the "establishment otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhi*). Therefore, it should be understood that by using the word "having stated" (*uktvā*), the grammatical requirement of a common agent for the acts of stating and establishing is fulfilled. Regarding the phrase "and because of the logical possibility" (*upapatteśca*), he states the meaning of the Sūtra as follows: "of such a kind. Indeed, a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) does not exist with an essential nature (*svarūpa*) that is non-departing.

It ought not to be so; rather, the meaning is that it consists precisely in the cessation of difference (*bhedopaśama*). For it is not the case that [the bridge] is merely the cause. If the bridge were indeed the cause, and the object to be reached were exclusively the effect, there would be a fixed rule; in that case, just as with a bridge, that which establishes the difference of the object to be reached would also establish the difference between cause and effect. However, this is not the case—this is the point. "Because it lacks the nature of difference" means that the very unfitness for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all things constitutes the nature of the limitation of an entity (*vastupariccheda*).

"Otherwise, there would be the consequence of two lords"—this means that otherwise, one would have to admit a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*). Thus ends the section on the Supreme (*parādhikaraṇa*).

The faultlessness of the Puruṣa, His being a mine of auspicious qualities, and His supremacy over all; beyond this, desiring to explain the meditation [upon Him], [the text speaks] of those who meditate upon the Supreme.

Now he declares that the fruit known as *apavarga* (liberation), which consists in attaining Him, results from this Supreme Person. By the same logic, scriptural fruits pertaining to both this world and the next likewise arise from the Supreme Person; for this very reason, it is stated in general terms that "the fruit is from Him. Why is this so? Because of logical consistency (*upapatti*). For He alone is omniscient, omnipotent, and supremely generous; when propitiated through sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and meditation, He bestows the entire range of enjoyments pertaining to this world and the next, as well as liberation, which consists in the attainment of His own essential nature.
It is capable of giving [the fruit]; for an insentient action, which perishes in a moment, cannot possibly be the means for accomplishing a result that occurs at a later time. || 37 ||

The reading "sarvasmāt paratvaṃ prāpyatvam" (supremacy over all is the state of being attainable) is observed; its meaning is as follows: supremacy over all, which is necessary for being attainable, is included within His auspicious qualities. Thus, there is a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), as in the expression "clarified butter is life. And that [supremacy] is included within the collection of auspicious qualities—this is the ellipsis. Alternatively, the grammatical coordination is due to the metaphorical identification of the whole with its parts, as in the case of a collection and its members. However, if the reading is "kalyāṇaguṇa" (auspicious quality), there is no inconsistency.

However, since the specific means (dvāra) is being determined here, there is a distinction; thus, there is no contradiction between what was stated previously and what follows. The sense is that in the former case, the status of dharma as the means was not explicitly mentioned. Alternatively, in the phrase "attained through ritual action and worship" (*karmopāsanārādhita*), the connection should be understood according to suitability: the state of being attained through ritual action applies to the deities such as Vāyu and others, while the state of being attained through worship applies to Brahman alone. This should be seen as analogous to the designation "water and fire, which possess the qualities of cold and hot touch."

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "action is insentient," the underlying intention is as follows: one must consider these four alternatives: (1) is it the *apūrva* produced by action that serves as the means to the fruit; (2) does the action itself persist until that point; (3) is the fruit produced immediately after the action; or (4) does the action, even though it has perished, produce the effect? Intending this fourfold dilemma, he first refutes the first alternative with the words, "action is insentient."

The meaning is that since it has been established by both perception and scripture that whatever is insentient proceeds only when presided over by a sentient being, the *apūrva* (unseen merit) cannot be the cause of the fruit. He refutes the second [position] with the words "action perishes in a moment. He refutes the third with the words "occurring at a later time," the sense being that [the action] would be sublated by the fact that heaven arises [only] now. He refutes the fourth with the words "it ought to come into being"; the sense is that if even what has perished could produce an effect, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.

[The commentary states: "Agriculture and so forth, as well as the massaging of the body and so forth. Massaging the body and such acts are direct causes of pleasure, whereas agriculture and the like are indirect causes. He shows the scriptural authority [for this], saying, "It is the same in the Veda. Although it is read in some places as *sa tu*, that is not correct; he shows the scripture, which reads *tathā yajeta* (one should sacrifice). This reading, however, is the correct one.

The phrase "the relationship of the end and the means between threatening and the Śatayātana [hell]" means as follows: "threatening" (*apagoraṇa*) refers to the act of raising a weapon; "Śatayātana" is a specific hell. This is because the statement, "He who would threaten a Brāhmaṇa, him he shall torment with a hundred [torments]," is an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) for the prohibitive injunction, "One should not threaten a Brāhmaṇa. In that context, by the force of the grammatical rule "the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used to express cause and effect" (*hetuhetumator liṅ*), one accepts the relationship of end and means between threatening and the Śatayātana hell, which is established by the *arthavāda*. This is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "sugar, ointment-substance, specific animal, and so forth," here the word *viśeṣa* (specific) is connected with the "sugar-ointment substance" as well. This is because, in the injunction "He places down the smeared pebbles," when there is an expectancy for the substance that serves as the means of ointment, one accepts clarified butter (*ghṛta*)—which has been praised by the statement "Clarified butter is indeed luster"—as that very means of ointment. Similarly, when there is an expectancy for a specific [animal] regarding the general scriptural injunction "One should sacrifice with an animal," one accepts the specific form of the goat, which is established by the wording of the mantra, "Of the goat's omentum."

The meaning is "because of its acceptance. Even if one were to argue that the deities themselves bestow the fruit, this cannot be maintained under the view that a deity—propitiated through ritual action (*karma*) and meditation (*upāsanā*)—bestows the fruit; for it is impossible to say that the deity’s grace occurs only immediately after the performance of the ritual. This is because if the grace of the Supreme Independent One (the Lord) were to occur, there would be no reason for delay in the fruit. Furthermore, if grace were granted by the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), such as the *prayāja* offerings, immediately upon their performance, it would follow that the fruit would be produced even if the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*) were not performed or if other auxiliaries were deficient. Therefore, when another action has been completed and the *apūrva* (unseen potency) has been produced, [the fruit arises] due to its maturation.

The sense is that the grace (*prasāda*) of the Lord must be stated as occurring at the stage when He is oriented toward the production of the fruit; [this is because] those who rely on authoritative scripture do not accept [any other cause]. Nor should it be argued that even in the view where the grace of the deity is the cause, the *apūrva* must be accepted as an intermediate medium even against one’s will; for just as among persons propitiating a king with food and so forth, a specific degree of pleasure is produced in the king by means of services such as offering a particular seat which is an ancillary part of the meal, so too a specific degree of pleasure in the Lord is produced by the *prayāja* and other rites as the cause for the granting of the fruit.

The sense is that there is no evidence for postulating an unseen potency (*apūrva*) inherent in the individual soul (*jīva*) as a limb [of the ritual], because it is possible for the production of a specific kind of joy for the deity to occur [directly]. Regarding the phrase "absence of a body and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), satisfaction, serenity, and the like are intended. Regarding the phrase "because it is established by supplementary texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*)," the sense is that [the meditation on the deity] is not a means to liberation (*mokṣa*) in the same way that meditation (*dhyāna*) is.
Thus ends the section concerning the fruit (*phalādhikaraṇa*). 8.

Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter in the Bhāvaprakāśikā, a commentary on the Śrutaprakāśikā, composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads.
The total number of topics is 82; the total number of sūtras is 354.

The connection is as follows: "this is the meaning" and "this is the meaning" are to be construed with what follows later. Regarding the subject of the effect (*kārya*), although the doubt concerning the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Vedāntas—due to mutual contradictions—is raised as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the sections on ether (*viyat*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*) just as by the opponents, this is because [those sections] are solely intent upon resolving contradictions regarding the modes of being an effect; nevertheless, following the raising of prima facie arguments such as the non-origination of ether, there is a firm establishment of the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the scriptural texts on the origination of ether and so forth with their own literal meanings, according to the maxim of "driving in a pillar."

The sense is that once [the objection] is established, the counter-objection regarding contradiction—which was previously set aside for the Sāṃkhyas who were revolving within their own minds—is also utterly refuted with respect to the Vedāntas; therefore, the connection with the Chapter on Contradiction (*Virodhādhyāya*) is likewise established. The intention of the Sūtra is to provide an exposition of its own purport, and not merely to demonstrate that the word *śruti* means "hearing"; such is the sense. This is the natural force of the reference to *śruti*.

The sense is that [the reason] might be considered secondary (*gauṇatva*), because being a property of a word (*śabdadharmatva*) lacks the status of being a property of a cognized object (*pramitadharmatva*). To avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding partlessness (*niravayavatva*), which is common to both eternal and non-eternal qualities, the term "because it is a substance" (*dravyatvāt*) is stated. Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*), since it is impossible for its absence to ever occur to the mind; for the negation "there is no ether here" (*atra viyat nāsti*) is a contradiction, as stated in the *Vaibhāṣika* section of the *Sūtra*: "And because there is no distinction in space," where space is defined as the locus known through the cognition "here."

Because [the Self] has been established as such, and the reason is not irrelevant; the sense is that for that which is partless and all-pervading, no inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or other such causes can be determined. "Contrary to the reasoning found in the *Taittirīyaka*" means contrary to the reasoning contained within the *Taittirīyaka*. "The scripture [serves] as the proof for the fact that 'It exists'" means that the scripture serves as the proof for this very point, namely, that "It exists. "It is precisely the cause for generating the cognition of its origination" means that being beyond the scope of other means of knowledge is consistent with its being known through scripture.

"Merely by being established through perception" means merely by being established through another means of knowledge (*māna*). "Either perception or inference" means either the word [itself as perceived] or the inference that "sound is dependent on a substance distinct from non-substances. "And another inference" means another inference such as "space is eternal because it is a partless substance."

Now, one might object: if the ether—which has been uninterrupted since the beginning of creation—is made the subject of the inference, then, because that ether is knowable solely through scripture (*śruti*), there would be a contradiction with the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇavirodha*) when attempting to prove its non-origination. On the other hand, if only the ether as a mere portion is made the subject, what possibility is there for a sublation of the means of knowledge apprehending the subject? Anticipating this unease, the author says: "In the case of the mahat and so forth, on account of the reason of partlessness. The phrase "on account of the reason of partlessness" means "on account of the reason of being a substance devoid of parts. And the phrase "and because of the mention of a specific kind of conjunction" implies that there is no conjunction for that which is partless.

The meaning is that when the reason "because it is an all-pervading substance" (*sarvagatadravyatva*) is stated as "because of being all-pervading" (*sarvagatatvāt*), one must add the word "substance" (*dravyatvāt*) in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the Naiyāyika position, since knowledge produced by the proximity of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth is all-pervasive in its scope and thus all-pervading. Regarding the phrase "One becomes a Brāhmaṇa through austerity" (*tapasā brāhma bhavati*) or "One should desire to know the Brāhmaṇa through austerity" (*tapasā brāhma vijijñāsasva*), the sense is that in the former sentence the word *brāhma* is used in its primary sense, whereas in the supplementary passage "Austerity is the Brāhmaṇa," it is used in a secondary sense because austerity is a means to the knowledge of the Brāhmaṇa.

Because there is an absence of being either primary or secondary objects [of the term "Self"], regarding the statement, "If it be argued that [the word 'Self'] applies by way of association, no; for there is a restriction," the words "Self" used in reference to the *annamaya* (consisting of food) and the others are not employed figuratively through the notion of the lower self (*aparamātman*), but rather precisely through the notion of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Through the entry into each respective layer—expressed in the text, "He has entered within as the ruler of people"—there is the status of Self due to being the internal controller. In that context, the notion of the Supreme Self arose toward the *prāṇamaya* merely because it was the inner self of the *annamaya*;
then, upon seeing what was even more internal than that, the notion of the Supreme Self arose toward that as well, while the previous notion ceased.

Since no other interval—such as a moment or the like—is heard of [between the individual self and that which is described], the notion of the Supreme Self and the notion of the Self are both established in that [Supreme Self]. Furthermore, because the word "Self" (ātman) was used in the preceding section with reference to the Supreme Self alone, and because it will be stated later that in all the subsequent sections the word "Self" refers exclusively to the Supreme Self and is not figurative, by that same principle, in the passage "Food is the Brahman," the word "Brahman" also does not possess a figurative sense, since it is applied through the cognition of Brahman, just as [in the previous cases].

The meaning is that the word "silver" applied to mother-of-pearl through the cognition of silver is not figurative; the sense is that it is exactly so [in the case at hand]. The phrase "the breach of the convention in both cases" means that there must be a breach of the convention—consisting in the contradiction between two functions (vṛtti)—due to the hearing of the suffix and the repetition [of the word]. The intention is that non-difference is intended precisely as being something to be accomplished (kāryatayā).

Now, it might be argued: even though the eternal glory (*nityavibhūti*) and so forth are not effects, just as there is no contradiction with the *pratijñā* (the initial proposition), there need not be a contradiction with the *pratijñā* regarding space (*ākāśa*), despite its being a non-effect; nor can it be said that in passages such as "by which the unheard becomes heard," the words "unheard" and so on refer to something other than the eternal glory, because in the subsequent passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," the state of being prior to that [creation] is presented as being merely the "Being" (*sanmātra*) of that very thing which is within the scope of the word "this" (*idam*). [Response: This should not be said.

Since the word "this" (idam) refers to all things presented by means of valid cognition such as direct perception, there is no basis for its not including the eternal manifestation (*nityavibhūti*); otherwise, supersensuous objects would not fall within the scope of the claim that [the Lord] possesses all knowledge. Consequently, one must either abandon the eternity of the eternal manifestations or accept the eternity of space (*ākāśa*) as well.

No, for this objection must be resolved by everyone; otherwise, since space (*ākāśa*)—like ignorance (*avidyā*)—is also beginninglessly superimposed, let it too be unproduced, as it is logically consistent even if it is not distinct from Brahman. Since such a resolution must be sought, and because the *Kalpataru* states under the section "Likewise the Prāṇas" that if the prāṇas were beginninglessly superimposed like ignorance, they would be perceived even in deep sleep due to their lack of mediation from the Witness (*sākṣin*), the same logic applies here to the state of deep sleep as well.

It should not be argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the Lord] being perceived; for [His non-perception] is intelligible, as in the case of the Lord postulated by theists (*Ādya-īśvara*), and because His non-perception is intelligible even when other individual souls (*jīva*) possess ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, based on the force of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that cannot be established otherwise, one must accept that [the Lord's non-perception] is caused by ignorance. This is not the case with space (*ākāśa*), for in its case there exists a scriptural statement regarding its production at every moment. If it is argued that "this is the same even in the present case, namely, the eternal realm (*nityavibhūti*)," [we reply:]...

The phrase "of the distinctions between reasons concerning intermediate objectives" refers to instances such as *B.S.* 3.1.6: "If it be said that [the soul does not return] because of the designation of non-existence, we say no, on account of another attribute, from the remainder of the passage, from reason, and from another word," for here the reasons are directed toward intermediate objectives; thus, it is observed that even reasons expressed by separate words may be propounded in a single sūtra regarding a supreme objective, as seen in cases such as *B.S.* 3.1.8: "Upon the exhaustion of [the results of works], one who possesses residual karma [returns], according to what is seen and recorded in tradition, in the same manner and not so. This is the intended meaning.

And this should be understood as a case where the word *ca* (and) is absent; therefore, one should not raise an objection on the grounds that in passages such as "Because of perception [of speech] in the mind, and because of the word [of scripture]" (*vāṅmanasi darśanācchabdācca*) and "Because of the teaching of its taking up [the elements], and because of the teaching of its departure" (*upādānādvihāropadeśācca*), even though the reasons are expressed by non-compounded words, they are nevertheless seen to be presented within a single sūtra as part of the ultimate probandum. Now, an objection may be raised: "How can origination, denoted by the term 'division' (*vibhāga*), be established while taking for granted that it is an effect?"

If it is argued that there is dispute only regarding the state of being an effect denoted by the term "modification" (*vikāra*), whereas there is no dispute regarding its origination (*utpatti*) otherwise, we say no; for in the *Chāndogya*, the absence of any statement regarding origination in certain cases of modification is not a fault, as it is intended to show the underlying principle (*gati*). The phrase "others, however," and so forth, means that since [the mere contradiction] lacks the status of being the ultimate thesis (*paramasādhya*), and because a mere contradiction is not in itself undesirable, it cannot serve as the final ground for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

It is not merely a contradiction that was proposed as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), nor is the reading "having adopted the position of a partial proponent of the theory of origination" (*utpatti-siddhānty-ekadeśin*) [the correct one]. Although it is stated in the *Kalpataru* up until the end of the chapter that "first the prima facie view is presented through invalidity due to contradiction, then there is an explanation according to the opinion of a partial proponent, and thereafter the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is shown," nevertheless, because that work is a modern composition, it should be understood that this [point] has not been raised therein.

Is it not the case that Vācaspati [has argued] that although there is a scriptural statement regarding the origination of ether (*viyat*) in the *Taittirīyaka*, nevertheless, because that [statement] contradicts other means of valid cognition and contradicts many other scriptural passages, it must be taken in a figurative sense? And therefore...

The meaning of the phrase "because of non-mention" (*aśruteḥ*) is precisely the absence of a scriptural statement regarding the primary sense [of ether as a created entity]. Consequently, let it be that the four sūtras—"Because of the non-mention of ether," "On account of the impossibility of a figurative sense," "And on account of the word," and "And there may be [creation] for one, as in the case of the word *brāhmaṇ*"—constitute the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). If it is argued that this has been explained as follows: "In the Taittirīyaka, there is a teaching regarding the priority of the creation of ether, while in the Chāndogya, there is a teaching regarding the priority of the creation of fire; therefore, there is a mutual contradiction between the two scriptural texts," then it is true that it has been so explained, but that...

It should be understood that [the opponent's view] is refuted by the very interpretation favored by Śaṅkara’s commentary, as it is contrary to it; furthermore, because there is no need for a separate refutation. Now, one might object: after stating immortality in a manner common to both with the words, "The wind and the intermediate space—this is immortal," the text then speaks of the wind specifically: "This deity, namely the wind, is never-setting. Therefore, due to this repetition (abhyāsa), it is known that the immortality of the wind is intended, according to the maxim that "through repetition, the significance of the matter increases."

It is more appropriate to maintain that this is simply an *atideśādhikaraṇa* (an extension of a previous section) for the purpose of removing further doubts, rather than treating it as a separate application (*prayoga*) for the sake of what follows; for since there is no partiality toward any specific alternative therein, one should have stated either, "Light [proceeds] from that, for so he says," or, "The ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) likewise, for so he says."

If it is argued that this is not very appropriate because the *Bhāṣya* itself will later state that even the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth have their objectivity (*viṣayatva*) in that same substratum, and therefore the formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of what follows—this is true; however, the previous [rule] applies only to those things common to the Great Principle, ego, ether, air, and so forth.

Even though [the doubt] has been resolved, nevertheless, considering the ease with which the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) may be introduced by the clear exposition of creation preceded by the volition of becoming manifold—expressed in the text, "It thought: 'Let me be many,' it created fire"—and intending to formulate the aphorism, "Fire [originates] from that, for thus it says," he extends the same reasoning to the first [topic] as well regarding the doubt concerning the additional point: "By this, the intellect and the self are explained. Therefore, we perceive no fault whatsoever. Thus ends the section on ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*).

The phrase "the designation 'body' is figurative, based on entering immediately after creation" means that the term "body" is used merely because of the occasional restriction of entering [into the body], and not with the intention of [possessing] qualities such as being supported for as long as existence lasts, by which [criterion] it would be primary. This is the sense.

If it is objected: "Since the logical principle is the same in the case of fire as in the statement 'Thus [it] spoke,' for what purpose was a separate Sūtra composed regarding water?"—the answer is no. For even though the portion "Thus [it] spoke" is common to both, one must provide a resolution by showing that in the case of fire, the statements "It thought" and "It created that fire" can be justified even through a mediated (paramparayā) process.

The opponent maintains that the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) must be understood as figurative, either by following the sequence of the word *tejaḥ* (fire/heat) heard first in the passage, "In [the waters] it saw: 'May I become many, may I procreate,' and it emitted the waters," or by the principle stated in the Sūtra, "But there is designation of the presiding deities because of distinction and subsequent connection," supported by the supplementary statement, "Therefore, whenever one grieves or perspires, those waters are born from heat alone."

Because there exist distinct modes of dissolution (*nirvāha*), the composition of a separate *sūtra* is purposeful; nor should it be argued that a separate *sūtra* for earth is redundant, for it must be understood that even in that case, a separate *sūtra* is formulated for the sake of resolving the contradiction between the two uses of the word "earth" (*pārthiva*).

The meaning is that he says this because the fact of having that [Brahman] as its body is based on scripture; the intention is that the causality of that which has that [Brahman] as its body is scriptural. This should be understood because, in the passage, "He who from within rules the earth," it is heard that the capacity to produce effects belongs only to the entity presided over by Him.

Regarding the statement, "For them too, the proof of creation preceded by reflection [is established]," some consider that the following introduction is appropriate: "It is improper to say that the fact of having that [Brahman] as one's body—which was stated in the preceding text as being established by the proof of creation preceded by reflection—serves the purpose of proving creation preceded by reflection; therefore, he shows a scriptural passage establishing that even the *mahat* and other principles have the Supreme Self as their body, and [he does so] in the Subāla Upaniṣad. Thus they think.

Regarding the phrase "because of the cognition of a sequence in the form of immediate succession" (*ānantaryarūpakramapratīteḥ*): although sequence (*krama*) is indeed nothing other than priority and posteriority (*paurvāparya*), it is not characterized by mere lack of interval (*avyavadhāna*).

Nevertheless, there is no contradiction in the sense that a sequence characterized by a specific anterior-posterior order, distinguished by the absence of any intervening interval of the nature of an *ānantarya* (immediate succession), is indeed perceived; nor should it be argued that such anterior-posteriority must necessarily be mediated by action (*kriyā*). For if that were the case, the phrase "therefore [it] is born" would be understood to mean "from [the Self] intent upon creation"; and consequently, since the intentness toward creation and the emergence of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are sequential, there is no fault in applying this [sequence] to the body (*kārya*) and the instruments (*karaṇa*), which are the substrata of those two states.

The phrase "with the intention of [showing] positive concomitance" (anvaya) means that it does not refer to the positive sequence found in the passage, "From this [Self] is born the vital breath (prāṇa), from that the mind (manas), and all the sense organs. This is the intended meaning.

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), it is designated by breaking [the argument]; according to this view, from the root *bhañj* (meaning "to crush" or "to destroy") with the suffix *ktin*, we have *bhaktiḥ* = *bhaṅgaḥ* (breaking), and thus the sense is "employed by way of breaking. Regarding the previous thesis [starting] from the *ānandamaya*, since in the sūtra "pṛthivī" (Earth) the origination of the earth alone is the point to be proven (*sādhya*), and therein [are found] the context, form, and other words... [of which there is] absence here.

The sense is that although [the earth] is the cause for the word "earth" being denotative, it is not the cause for the production of the earth itself. Furthermore, because it has been stated that [the material elements] are dependent upon the entry of conscious presiding deities (*abhimānicetana*), the implication is that they do not possess inherent consciousness (*svataścetanya*). If it is argued: "But did not Vācaspati initiate an inquiry as to whether the deities who preside over fire and the other elements engage in the creation of the elements only when presided over by the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), or even without being so presided over?"—this is not so, because such a view contradicts his own commentary and because it would render the Sūtra "But [it proceeds] from the Supreme, on account of that being seen" (*parāttu tacchruteḥ*) superfluous. Therefore, [the elements do not act independently].

It should be understood that this refutation has been stated exactly as it appears in the commentary (bhāṣya) according to what was heard. There is no reason for [the term] "one" (eka) to be intended [in the singular], nor is the intellect (buddhi) denoted by the word "vital breath" (prāṇa). For the intellect is a state of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) characterized as the cause of certainty, whereas the mind (manas) is a state of the internal organ characterized as the cause of doubt; thus, there is a distinction between the two. In that context, by the etymological derivation "that by which one knows," the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) used in the Sūtra includes both the intellect—denoted here by the word "vital breath"—and the sense organs, while the word "mind" refers to the mind itself.

And it must be stated that such grasping is possible; the sense is that there is no evidence for such a hypothesis. Regarding the soul's origination from the Supreme Self, [the author] will state in a subsequent sūtra whether this applies to ether and the other elements or not; however, he states here—following the words of the commentary of Para—that for the soul, there is no origination or dissolution based on the body, as expressed by this sūtra. Thus he says: "here, based on the body."

Because there is no possibility of suspecting that birth and destruction belong to the living being (jīva) rather than the body—[an objection might be raised: "But surely names such as Devadatta belong to the living being and not to the body, since it would be illogical to perform a funeral rite (śrāddha) for a body by means of its name;"

Therefore, for one who considers the designation "Devadatta has died" or "Devadatta has been born" to be primary, this constitutes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is clear from the *Vācaspatya*, which states that having taken the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) as established, the prima facie position—that the soul, distinct from the body, possesses birth and destruction corresponding to the birth and destruction of the body—is refuted by the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Likewise, in the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya* it says, "in the soul which perishes following the body"; and by taking that difference as established, [it continues]: "when the body is produced, the soul is also produced."

If it is asked, "How can this be so?"—given that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) understands [the opponent's position] as "when that [body] perishes, the soul itself also perishes," and given that the very same point is restated in the *Bhāṣya* as "first of all, there are no gross birth and dissolution of the soul based on the body" (*dehāśrayau tāvajjīvasya sthūlotpattipralayau na staḥ*), and since the phrase "based on the body" (*dehāśrayau*) is also understood to mean simply "birth and destruction based on the body"—we reply: True. However, if one were to assume that the nature of the soul (*jīvasvarūpa*) is subject to birth and destruction following the body, there would be a redundancy with the sūtra "The soul is not [produced], because it is not heard [so]" (*nātmā śruter*). Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "birth and destruction based on the body" must be accepted exactly as it is literally stated.

This statement should be understood as having been made with the intention that there is no other possible state [for the soul]. As for the passage beginning with "Others, however," the phrase "and of the person in the state of dissolution" means "and of the aspect of the enjoyer in the state of dissolution. Regarding the phrase "of this sequence of recitation," it means that the sequence of the Sūtra-recitation favored by you is not established anywhere.

The phrase "having made the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣīkṛtya*) that there is either the origination of all or the non-origination of all" means having proposed the alternative that either everything originates or nothing originates. Regarding the statement "and because of the usage 'in the mind, space alone,'" the sense is this: if, in the scriptural passage "from this [space] it is born," the word *manas* (mind) refers to the internal organ, then the dissolution of space into the senses, the dissolution of the senses into the mind, and the dissolution of the mind into the principle of Mahat denoted by the term *prāṇa*, is being described.

The meaning is: "Because a sequential intention is observed regarding ether and the others," which refers to the observation of a sequential intention in the subsequent passage, "Space, wind, fire, water... The meaning is that here there is merely a mention of the categories (padārtha), because there is no perception of an intention to follow the sequence of speech and so forth. The phrase "born from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra)" means [the elements] such as space and the rest are born from the ego-sense.

The sense is that while [the elements] are born directly, the senses are born through their respective doors (such as taste) and so forth; therefore, there is no contradiction. This is because, in accordance with the Śruti passage, "Higher than the senses are the objects," the contradiction has been resolved in the statement, "All the senses, as well as its own self, air, fire, water... Furthermore, between the *ahaṅkāra* denoted by the word "mind" (*manas*) and the Great Principle (*mahat*), there is the mention of what is designated as "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "discriminative knowledge" (*vijñāna*) in the sequence: "But higher than the mind is the intellect; know the intellect to be the charioteer; but he who has discriminative knowledge as his charioteer... and so on.

The meaning is that there is a contradiction because [the mind] would be perceived as a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*). The intention is that the relationship of superior and inferior heard in the scripture—"But the intellect (*buddhi*) is higher than the mind (*manas*)"—must be explained in some way or another regarding the word "mind" (*manaḥ-śabdaḥ*) as denoting [the intellect]. If it is argued that "space (*nabhas*) and the [other] primordial elements (*prakṛti*) would be [the eightfold set]," then the intention is that this contradicts the scriptural statement: "There are eight primordial elements and sixteen modifications (*vikāra*). [The phrase] "the mind is indeed the sense organ" means that the mind is simply the internal sense organ (*antarindriya*), not the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

Nor should one suspect how the mind (*manas*), as a specific sense organ, can be superior to the objects that were established as superior to the senses in the statement, "The objects are superior to the senses," for the intention is that superiority can be established through a different aspect. The phrase "lest there be a violation of propriety" means that it is more appropriate to qualify the word "Self" (*ātman*) itself with the attribute of "greatness."

The meaning is: if it is argued that because this textual passage (*sandarbha*) sets forth objects consisting of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the Great Principle (*mahat*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), it is logical that it should be sublated by the section concerning mastery (*vaśīkāryaprakaraṇa*) due to a contradiction in its subject matter; [the response is: "by the previous section" means by the section concerning inference (*ānumānika-adhikaraṇa*).
Thus ends the section concerning the superiority of splendor.

One must consider whether the state of being a fixed relationship between property (*dharma*) and its locus (*dharmin*) is possible, or whether—given the dependence on the locus—the possibility of a property residing in a greater extent [than its locus] can exist. This point must necessarily be addressed because it is established in the Sūtras:

"There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood; or rather, due to its quality, as in the world" (VS 4.1.12–13). The meaning is this: since it is impossible for the Self to perceive distant objects if it were not all-pervading—and since the Self's omnipresence must be asserted because it is impossible for it to experience [pain] in every limb—it follows that, as the substratum of eternal cognition, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving that [omnipresence] as eternal.

In the commentary, it is established that [the Self] is indeed of the nature of knowledge, neither merely knowledge nor of an insentient nature; yet, even though its status as a knower has been proven, the exclusion of its being insentient is not fully achieved, because the Naiyāyikas accept its insentience. Nevertheless...

It should be understood that the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and because of the non-cultivation of the self" (*yāvadātmābhāvitvācca*) is intended to indicate that [the argument] is already established. Regarding what was stated in the Commentary—that if the status of being a knower were inherent—[an objection is raised]: "But if the status of being a knower is inherent, how does the refutation of omnipresence (*vibhutva*) serve [the argument]? For omnipresence is not an obstacle to the mere fact of having an inherent capacity for knowing, according to the logic set forth in the Sūtra: 'Eternal perception and non-perception... [The response follows: Regarding omnipresence...

Because it contradicts all positions—including those of the Siddhāntins—by asserting that [the Self] is the substratum of adventitious knowledge, has the nature of knowledge, and possesses innate knowership, for that very reason, even the status of being in the same section (*ekādhikaraṇatva*) is not tenable for [the sūtras] beginning with "The departure, the staying, and the going" (*utkrānti-gaty-āgatīnām*), since the proof of atomicity (*aṇutva*) is not useful for establishing innate knowership; and if one were to resort to a single section by assuming some incidental utility, then [it would conflict with] the sūtra "The agent [is the Self], because of the meaningfulness of the scriptures" (*kartā śāstrārthavattvāt*).

Why should there not be a single locus for the arguments intended to establish both the nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and the nature of being an agent (*kartṛtva*)? If the refutation of agency is useful for establishing the nature of being a knower, then those [sūtras] intended for that refutation ought to be placed in one and the same section. Thus, having concluded the discussion on the nature of being a knower with: "He is a knower for this very reason; [there is] distinction as in the case of smell; because of separate instruction; the designation [of Him] is due to His having that as the essence of His qualities; and because it persists as long as the self exists, there is no fault; and because we see it, like manhood and so forth, though existing, it is manifested by means of yoga. [The following would have been included there.]

[The Sūtras: "Because of [the mention of] departure, going, and returning; and because of the two subsequent [Sūtras] by its own nature; if it be argued that it is not atomic because of the denial of that, we say no, because of the context of the other; and because of its own word and measurement; there is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood; if it be argued that this is due to a difference in state, we say no, because of the admission [of its presence] in the heart, or because of its quality, as in the world; if it be argued that the arrangement of the Sūtras would have been 'eternal perception,' we reply: what was said—that omnipresence does not contradict the mere fact of being a natural knower—is true; nevertheless, for the opponent..."

Because such a misconception can arise, it is necessary to refute it; as for what was stated—that there is a single locus (ekādhikaraṇya) for the sūtra "The agent [is the Self], because of its being the subject of the scriptures"—in that context, "knowership" (jñātṛtva) indeed means being the substratum of knowledge, and not agency (kartṛtva), since the suffix [-tṛ] has the sense of merely being a substratum. Or, even if there were some utility [in linking them], this does not constitute a single locus, for that is not intended by the author of the Sūtras. In the present case, however, the sūtras establishing knowership and atomicity are interspersed with one another.

From this very fact of their being treated as instruments (*karaṇa*), it is determined that the author of the Sūtras intended them to have a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇya*). Otherwise, according to the method you have described, the Sūtras refuting "largeness" (*mahattva*) would have been arranged in a confused manner merely for the sake of ease of understanding; therefore, everything is consistent. "When he [the soul] absorbs the subtle elements of light... (*sa yadā tejomātrāḥ samabhyādadāti...*)... [text continues].

He states the reason for not citing the scriptural passage regarding the mode of departure as taught by others—"Taking the essence, it departs from this body and returns again to its place"—in the words: "Immediately after the word 'departure'. The meaning is that [the departure] is of the nature of the soul's separation from the body; for "departing" (utkrāmaṇa) is conventionally established, like a physical withdrawal, at the time of death. And this is possible even for one who is not moving elsewhere, through the cessation of identification with the body upon the exhaustion of karma; for going and returning are established as movements, and thus their agent must be of a mobile nature.
In the *Bhāṣya*, having extracted a substance similar to an atom (*aṇu*), it is heard that the soul (*jīva*) possesses that measure;

and "extraction" (*uddharaṇa*) means separation. In the passage, "of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair," the separation of the part from the whole is heard—that is, it is proclaimed and demonstrated—and for this reason, since both the separation and the hearing (the scriptural statement) have the same agent (the Śruti), one should understand that the identity of agent is logically established. "The tip of an awl" (*ārāgra*) refers to the point of a needle that pierces leather. "Now, was it not stated that 'knowledge alone is the Self'? [as in] "the person whose self is consciousness" (*vijñānātmā puruṣa*).
The meaning is: "in such scriptural passages as these."
"By a word denoting that which is qualified" means by a word denoting cognition as the qualifier.

Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other. How could there be the consequence of constant perception? How could there be the consequence of constant non-perception? Or how could there be the consequence of both?

Regarding the claim that the self is perceived somewhere—that the self is perceived within the body and likewise not perceived outside—it is established by the universal experience of all people that "I am right here in this house, not knowing. This fact is not tenable under either of the two positions. Under the position that the self is of the nature of knowledge and is omnipresent, is it of a nature that is both perceivable and imperceptible, or is it of a nature exclusively perceivable, or is it of a nature exclusively imperceptible?

In the first case, there would be perception within the interior of the burning house and non-perception outside; in the second case, there would be perception everywhere. In the third case, there would be non-perception; yet it is not tenable to establish a distinction such that the nature of the object is perceptible within the burning house while its nature is imperceptible elsewhere, for it cannot be said that the very same thing has its own form in one place and lacks it in another. This same refutation should be understood to apply to the position that [the self] is insentient (*jaḍa*).

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "by being always connected with all the instruments," one might object: "Is this not the same even in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*)? For the infinite, eternal, and liberated qualities of consciousness (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) exist everywhere, and since these qualities of consciousness are connected to all selves, it is impossible to determine from among them, 'this is his [consciousness]' and 'that is his. How then is this so? If you ask this, the answer is no; for according to the maxim, "But on account of scripture, because its nature is based on the Word," one must accept a matter as it is presented by scripture.

This is logical, for the intended meaning is that otherwise it would not be logical; the point is that the word *jña* (knower) also lacks the sense of denoting a specific individual (*vyakti*), because the suffix *ka* in the rule *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ* is prescribed in the sense of the agent according to *kartari kṛt*. The phrase "only as the unmodified Brahman" is to be construed as follows: it exists as the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) precisely while remaining as the unmodified Brahman, and thus it is unproduced.

The meaning is that because Brahman has consciousness as its essential nature (*caitanyasvarūpa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), which is non-different from it, also has consciousness as its essential nature. "Prakṛta" (the subject under discussion) refers to what was established as the probandum (*sādhya*) in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).

This is because [the identity of Brahman with the individual soul] is not a direct means of proving that [the soul] has the nature of knowledge; this is an elliptical expression meaning that it is not a means of proof even indirectly. For if the non-difference from Brahman were established as the reason for the absence of origination, there would otherwise follow either the consequence of the eternal perception of the nature of consciousness, or the consequence of its non-perception, or the restriction of one or the other. [Objection: Let the eternal perception follow; how can there be the consequence of eternal non-perception, or how can there be the consequence of both?

By the phrase "there is the state of being a means" (*sādhakatvamasti*), it should also be understood that there is an indirect utility (*paramparayā upayoga*) due to the non-origination [of the effect]. And by the phrase "its nature as consciousness" (*jñānasvarūpatva*), the meaning is "the nature of Brahman as consciousness. By the phrase "the ultimate goal" (*paramasādhyā*), the meaning is "the nature of the consciousness of the living being" (*jīvacaitanyasvarūpatva*). And by the phrase "of the identity of the base-meaning" (*prakṛtyarthasāmyasya*), the meaning is that the identity of meaning between the verbal root and the word, or between the word *śruti* and the word *etat*, is made known by the Vedic scripture (*śruti*).

One might object: "Is it not improper for the word *śruteḥ* from the preceding sūtra and this word *ataḥ* in the present sūtra to have the same meaning, since the scriptural passage establishing non-origination and the scriptural passage establishing omniscience have different meanings? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by virtue of fitness" (*yogyatāvaśāt*). Furthermore, he adds "and because of the absence of the three delays" (*vilambatrayābhāvāt*). The sense is that, according to the opponent's view, the three delays were already established previously by such arguments as "the non-difference from Brahman which establishes that [non-origination]" and so forth.

The intended meaning is that the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-dharmatva*) is devoid of annihilation; thus, in the term *anucchitti-dharma*, there is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*. The sense is that the grammatical connection with "from them" (*tābhyaḥ*) is thereby established. Although this is so, since the word "from these" (*ataḥ*) refers back—by means of the pronoun *ataḥ*—to those very Śrutis mentioned by "from them" (*tābhyaḥ*) in the preceding Sūtra and present in the mind, those same Śrutis continue to apply even in the Sūtra concerning departure (*utkrānti*). Consequently, [the question arises] regarding the departure, the going, and the returning.

Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception, or else the restriction of one or the other. How could there be the consequence of perpetual perception? How could there be the consequence of perpetual non-perception? Or how could there be the consequence of both?

There is no fault because the meaning of "from the Śrutis" is possible; nevertheless, since "from them" (*tābhyaḥ*) requires a substantive, the supply (*adhyāhāra*) of the word "Śrutis" (*śrutibhyaḥ*) is also necessarily required. Therefore, the sense here is that there is likewise a supply of two words: "from those Śrutis" (*tābhyaḥ śrutibhyaḥ*). The phrase "uselessness of the operation of the instruments" means the uselessness of the operation of the eyes and so forth for the nature of the living self's consciousness.

The meaning is that by the scriptural statement "and of the identity of the meaning of the base," it is indicated that the word "ataḥ" (therefore) and the verbal root of the word "etat" (this) have a single meaning. Now, one might object: it is not proper for the word "ataḥ" occurring in this sūtra and the word "śruteḥ" (from scripture) occurring in the previous sūtra to have a single meaning, because the scripture cited as proving non-origination and the scripture cited as proving sentience have different meanings. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by virtue of fitness."

The sense is that, according to the opponent's view, the absence of the three delays is established by the fact that Brahman is not distinct from that [knowledge], and so forth; for the three delays have already been explained previously. Regarding the phrase "possessing the quality of non-cessation" (*anucchittidharma*), the intended meaning is that it possesses the nature of knowledge which is free from annihilation; thus, the sense is that this is a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*.

Although the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) "to them" (*tābhyaḥ*) is possible, the sense of the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) is that the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) serves no purpose if it were merely to refer back to those Śrutis mentioned in the previous Sūtra by the word "to them," which remain present in the mind. Regarding the phrase "in those dependent on him": the sense is that the primary Prāṇa is their support (*āśraya*), while the other vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are dependent upon him. Regarding the phrase "of that which has the nature of an aggregate": the meaning is that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) has the nature of an aggregate.

Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other. How could there be the consequence of perpetual perception? How could there be the consequence of perpetual non-perception? Or how could there be the consequence of both?

"Because of the lack of awakening during deep sleep and dissolution" means that during deep sleep and dissolution, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth have merged into latency. [Objection: "If perception were constant due to the proximity of the self, the senses, and the objects," this would mean that when the self, the senses, and the objects—which are the instruments of perception—are in proximity, perception would necessarily occur at all times. Consequently, even when the collection of causes is absent, there would be no result; thus, non-perception would necessarily be constant. Therefore, since the absence of occasional perception despite the proximity of the self, senses, and objects must be caused by the absence of some other factor, [the internal organ is required].

The sense is that, since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) must be admitted as the counter-positive of the absence that necessitates the absence of [other] causes when other causes are present, the internal organ is required. He explains the portion of the Sūtra, *anyataraniyamo vānyathā*, as "either in the self (*ātman*) or even in the sense-organ (*indriya*). Thus ends the section on the knower (*jña-adhikaraṇa*).

The phrase "setuṃ jantum iva" (like one calling [the soul] a bridge or a creature) refers to the suffix *tumun* derived from the *uṇādi* class. The meaning is based on the statement from the *Gītā*: "He who thinks 'this is the slayer' and he who thinks 'this is slain'—both of them do not understand; this [self] neither slays nor is slain. Regarding the commentary, it cites the *Jaimini-sūtra*: "The fruit of the scripture accrues to the performer, because that is its characteristic; therefore, there should be personal performance. The meaning of this is: since the fruit of the scripture, such as heaven and so forth, accrues to the performer according to the authority of the scripture—"One desiring heaven should sacrifice"—therefore...

"In the case of his own activity, he would be the agent"—thus [it is said] in the Bhāṣya. Regarding the phrase "as if by himself" (*sahārājaiva*), there is the scriptural passage concerning the state of dream: "Just as a great king, having taken hold of the subjects, moves about at will in his own kingdom, even so this [Self], having taken hold of these vital breaths (*prāṇān*), moves about at will in its own body. The meaning is that, having taken hold of the vital breaths—that is, having withdrawn them from the locations of the waking state—it wanders according to its desire within its own body.
Regarding the phrase "and in the impelling of the body," the meaning is that the impelling of the body is also established by the movement of the eight knots within the body.

In your view, it is established that the redness of a crystal is dependent on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of proximity to a *japā* flower, because even though the crystal exists prior to the proximity of the *japā* flower, its redness is not observed; however, if agency were not perceived in the individual soul (*jīva*) prior to the proximity of the limiting condition of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then one could claim that the internal organ serves as the limiting condition for the agency residing in the soul. But such is not the case—this is the meaning.

The meaning is that the interpretation shown in the statement, "He shows that the designation 'consciousness performs the sacrifice' (*vijñānaṃ yajñaṃ tanute*) indicates that the intellect alone (*buddhi*) is the agent, because the word 'consciousness' is well-known in that sense"—this is untenable. He demonstrates precisely why there is nothing left to be refuted.

It has been stated that there is no dispute regarding the name, for it is simply said that a conscious being performs everything with the intention of [its own] welfare. The meaning is this: that which you designate as the "internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa) because it is distinct from the instruments of action, yet functions as the agent—that very thing is designated by me as the "individual soul" (jīva).

"Like that of *citta* and *manas*" means: just as there is no teaching of a relationship of material cause (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikṛti*) between *manas*—which is a specific function of the mind (*manovṛtti-viśeṣa*) called *citta*, characterized by volition (*cetayitṛtva*) and consisting of cognition appropriate to the time at hand—and the [subtle] *manas* itself; so too, if *buddhi* were merely a form of mental function (*manovṛtti-rūpa*), there would be no teaching of a relationship of material cause and modification between *buddhi* and *manas*. Yet, such a relationship is indeed observed between *buddhi* and *manas*.

The instruction regarding the relationship between the primal nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikṛti*) would not be possible; yet, it is observed that the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) are taught to exist in a relationship of cause and effect. This is the intended meaning. Therefore, although the injunction for meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is intended precisely because [the Self] is distinct from the primal nature—just as one engages in sacrifices and other rites by contemplating the enjoyment of the fruits of action on the part of the primal nature, even though that nature is devoid of the status of an enjoyer—[the Self is nevertheless distinct].

Even in the case of the meditation on difference (*bhinnatva-samādhi*), there is no fault; however, the intention is that for one whose nature is that of the agent (*prakṛti-kartṛka*)—namely, for one who meditates on "I am other than Prakṛti"—liberation cannot result because such a meditation is of the nature of an error (*bhrānti*). "The enjoyment of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth" means the wearing of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth. Thus ends the section on the Agent (*kartṛ-adhikaraṇa*).

He establishes, in sequence, how the specific proximity of objects—which are characterized by the particularities of the emergence and suppression of the three *guṇas* and the particularities of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is the cause of specific inclinations (*ruci*). This is done through the passage beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*) up to "having the nature of a specific property of the object" (*vastu-svabhāva-viśeṣa-rūpā*), which means "having the nature of a specific proximity of the object" (*vastu-sannidhi-viśeṣa-rūpatva*). Thus ends the section on dependence on another (*parayattādhikaraṇa*).

The point here is that, regarding the word "body" (*śarīra*), the very state of having a body (*śarīritva*) is raised as an objection due to a conflict in scriptural statements (*śruti-vipratipatti*) and then resolved. The intention of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) in saying "it abides" (*pratitiṣṭhati*) is that the non-contradiction between the two mutually opposed qualities of being non-different (*ananya*) and being superior (*adhika*) can only be resolved through the relationship of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*); for being a part (*aṃśatva*) consists precisely in being a mode (*prakāra*) that is established as non-separate (*apṛthaksiddha*).

The meaning is as follows: there, non-difference is established by means of non-separateness (*apṛthaksiddhatva*); difference is established by means of being a mode (*prakāratva*); and the primacy of both designations is established by the combination of both non-separateness and being a mode.

Although, in the sūtra *tadananyatvam*, what is to be established is non-difference—the identity between the causal state and the effected state, and not the relationship of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*) between the world and Brahman—[the present passage establishes this through the determination of the relationship of part and whole in the manner of light and its source].

Nevertheless, since the non-difference of the gross body composed of *cit* (consciousness) and *acit* (non-consciousness) from the subtle body composed of *cit* and *acit* must be established, the nature of the world as a body—specifically as a part (*aṃśa*)—must be demonstrated. In this regard, it should be understood that the status of the conscious portion (*cidaṃśa*) as a part is established here, whereas the status of the non-conscious portion (*acidaṃśa*) as a part is established in the *Ahikuṇḍalādhikaraṇa*. Regarding the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which states, "The fishermen are Brahmins, the fishermen are Brahmins, these gamblers are Brahmins," the term *dāsāḥ* refers to fishermen, and *kitavāḥ* refers to gamblers.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with superior [beings], when it is said that one who is perfected in Vedic study is "Viṣṇu himself," it is impossible for this to be intended as praise. However, coreferentiality with inferior beings does not serve as praise for a Brāhmaṇa, because it is contradictory; nor does it serve as praise for slaves and the like, because they are unworthy of praise; nor is it for the purpose of censuring the Brāhmaṇa, because a Brāhmaṇa is not subject to censure; nor is it for the purpose of censuring slaves and the like, because that is impossible. Therefore, the coreferentiality of a Brāhmaṇa with slaves and others indicates precisely the reality of their non-difference.

"One who is speaking must wander"—that is, by virtue of being a speaker, one must wander; the heart wanders as if it were speaking. The ultimate meaning is that [the Self] is not taught [in this way]. He raises an objection regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

The meaning is that even when there is a single portion (*aṃśa*) in a commentary (*bhāṣya*), a mantra, or a sūtra, the singular number (*ekavacana*) is used; likewise, even when there is a partial portion (*pārdośa*) in a mantra or a sūtra, the singular number is used. Furthermore, the statement "and difference is apprehended by way of being distant (*parākatvena*)" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication) for the purpose of establishing the apprehension of difference among the supreme self (*parātman*). One should understand that, according to the teaching "the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) of all entities are within the scope of inconceivable knowledge," there exists a mutual difference characterized by power (*śakti*) and so forth, which is distinct from [the difference consisting in] being near (*pratyak*) or being distant (*parākatva*).

In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that "being a part" (*ekadeśatva*) means being a portion (*aṃśatva*). If this were so, it would follow that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the substantive (*viśeṣya*), is also a portion; for there is no difference in its being a part of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavastu*). Consequently, it would follow that there is no distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*). Furthermore, in the verse, "An aṃśa of Me alone, become a living soul (*jīvabhūta*), exists in the world of living beings," the individual soul is perceived as a part in relation to the Supreme Self who is the substantive, and not in relation to the qualified [entity]; for there is no evidence that the word "of Me" (*mama*) refers to the qualified [entity]. Indeed, being a portion of the Lord...

Furthermore, since it will be stated later that [the meaning] is understood by its own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*), and because it is well-known in common worldly usage that a qualifier is a part of the qualified, the instruction "this very thing is the part" would be redundant; likewise, for that same reason, the use of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*) would also be useless. Moreover, the statement "being the eternal living soul" (*jīvabhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ*) would be pointless if it were intended to designate the qualified individual soul as a part.

If it is argued that since such "being a part" (*aṃśatva*) is common to both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), the *Ahikuṇḍala* section—which aims to establish the status of being a part for the unconscious as distinct [from the conscious]—is therefore redundant; we say no. This is because in this particular section, what must be established is that "being a part" consists in having the nature of a body (*śarīra*), characterized by being controlled and subordinate. Furthermore, the *Ahikuṇḍala* section will later state that the status of being the whole (*aṃśitva*) is logically possible for the primary object of qualification (*viśeṣya*). Thus, even though the status of being a part is established for the unconscious in that section, there is no redundancy here.

Therefore, its purpose is not already established [by previous sections], because this section serves as a method for resolving contradictions with scriptural texts that establish difference, non-difference, and the nature of being a part (*aṃśatva*). Consequently, there is no redundancy due to the difference in subject matter; for this very reason, there is also no redundancy with the sūtra "Because of subsistence, according to Kāśakṛtsna" (*avasthiter iti kāśakṛtsnaḥ*). For even the definition of being a part as "being a portion of a single entity" has its primary purport in this very context. Even if the nature of being a part characterized by non-separability (*apṛthaksiddhatva*) were to be established here, then—

If it is argued that—since defects residing in the sentient and insentient entities, which are inseparable attributes [of Brahman], do not apply to Brahman itself nor to each other, the sūtras intended to resolve such issues, such as "But like light, etc., the Supreme is not so" (2.3.46) and "Permission and prohibition are due to connection with the body, as in the case of light, etc. (2.3.48), would be rendered purposeless—the answer is no; for it is said that, by demonstrating the intended nature of "part" (*aṃśa*), he refutes the doubt raised through the mere hearing of the word "part," which arises from the misconception that "part-ness" here means being a constituent portion of the substantive.

Because there is no fault [in this]. Regarding the expression "the sun (bhānuḥ) measures (mānumān)," some hold that just as the two words "pot" and "pot-possessor" used with respect to a pot that is the locus of a pot are not synonymous, so too the two words used with respect to the sun, which is the internal locus of the light-form (prabhārūpa) sun.

The words *bhānu* and *bhānumat* do not have identical meanings. If the word *bhānu*, while primarily denoting light (*prabhā*), were to denote the possessor of light (*prabhāvadvat*) through a secondary function (*paryavasānavṛtti*)—just as words for genus (*jāti*) or quality (*guṇa*) denote their possessors—then there would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) without the need for a possessive suffix (*matvarthapratyaya*). Therefore, they say that words denoting genus and so forth are what should be cited as examples. The passage beginning with "Others, however" (*pare tu*) concerns the determination of the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

The meaning is that this is an investigation into whether the relationship is like that between a master and a servant, or like that between fire and its sparks. "Because it is impossible for [the whole] to be a part in relation to itself" means that it is impossible for a qualified entity to be a part in relation to that same qualified entity. "Due to the absence of any intrinsic distinction of parts in the reality itself" refers to space (*ākāśa*), which [lacks such parts] by its very nature.

The sense is that the distinction between the conditioned (*upahita*) and the unconditioned (*anupahita*) is logically established because [the latter] is its own part (*svāṃśatvāt*). "In the state of non-yoga" means in the condition of being devoid of yoga. "And because it is impossible to state a lack of connection" means because it is impossible to state a lack of connection with the status of being one who is to be enjoined (*niyojyatva*). The sense is that minuteness (*aṇutva*) consists in not being perceived while being delimited; it does not consist in having the dimension of an atom (*aṇuparimāṇatva*).

"Because it is untenable for [the self] to have the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that in the section [of the *Brahma-sūtra*] beginning with "The penetration [of the Lord] is like that of a lamp; for so it is shown," regarding the case of the multiplication of bodies (*kāyavyūha*), even though a plurality of internal organs is admitted, the fact of recognition (*pratisandhāna*) across them is accepted. "Because there is an absence of being divided into parts such as cows, buffaloes, gold, and so forth."

Now, even when the predominance characterized by the ground's status as a substratum (*ādhāra*) and so forth is intended to be expressed, one does not observe the conventional usage "the cow, buffalo, and so on are parts of the ground. Likewise, even when the predominance characterized by the relationship between the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—as in the case of Devadatta and his staff or earrings—is intended to be expressed, one does not observe the conventional usage "the staff, earrings, and so on are parts of Devadatta. However, usages regarding the state of being a part (*aṃśitva*) in relation to the owner of a substance occur with respect to a collection, because this ownership belongs to the substance as a whole through its parts.

If it is argued that [the term "part"] does not apply to Devadatta and others merely on the basis of their status as owners or their primary authority, because if that were so, it would follow that one who owns cows, buffaloes, and so forth acquired through purchase or gift would be conventionally designated as a "part" (aṃśin) of them—[we reply: no, for it has already been stated here that the word "part" (aṃśa) means "body" (śarīra), and thus there is no fault. Some, however, maintain that the common ground (pravṛttinimitta) underlying the conventional usage of the word "part" in all cases—such as the threads that originate a cloth, the space delimited by a jar, or a fragment of stone delimited by a stick—is simply the state of being a "portion" (ekadeśatva). Therefore...

They argue that since the meaning of the word *brahman* is precisely that which is qualified by the sentient and the insentient (*cidacid-viśiṣṭa*), it is logical for the sentient and the insentient to be its parts (*aṃśa*) by virtue of being its constituent portions (*ekadeśa*). However, the pure substratum (*kevala-viśeṣya*), namely the Lord (*īśvara*), is not a part.

Even in passages such as "A part of Me alone" (*mamaivāṃśaḥ*), the status of being a part is intended with reference to the qualified [Brahman] itself. Furthermore, this does not entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the Lord would likewise be a part like the individual soul (*jīva*), because the designation "part" is observed to apply to small portions, whereas Brahman, being the whole, cannot logically be designated as a "part. This is what they say.
Thus ends the section concerning parts (Aṃśādhikaraṇa). || 7 ||

The word *liṅga* (mark/indicator) in the phrase "supported by marks such as the observation of conduct" refers to *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition) in general; the meaning is that it is supported by the means of valid cognition that apprehend the status of being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) in the form of the observation of conduct and so forth. In the same way, the word *liṅga* in subsequent instances should also be understood as referring to *pramāṇa* in general; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the third-case *śruti* mentioned in the sūtra "that [is indicated] by the word" (*tacchabde*) not being included.

However, some explain that even the passage beginning with "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*vidyayā*) is merely an indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the observation of another meaning due to its being stated in the present tense; and they argue that one should not say there is a contradiction with the introductory commentary and its sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), which state: "In this case, let the attainment [of results] be declared as the indicative mark for the phrase 'that [is] his power' (*tacchakteḥ*"), because that [previous position] was stated as a concession (*abhyupetyavāda*).

The phrase "the absence of non-conclusiveness" (anaikāntikatvābhāva) means that [the reasons] such as the observation of conduct (ācāradarśana) and so forth establish that knowledge (*vidyā*) is not otherwise established as being a mere subsidiary (*karmaśeṣa*) to ritual action.
