[Objection: But if the absence of non-conclusiveness in the observation of conduct and so forth establishes that knowledge is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvarthā*), then the relationship between the fruit and the means (*phala-phalibhāva*) is already complete by that much alone; therefore, the subsequent textual passage beginning with "by the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) supported by that" would be redundant. [Response: This is because it depends upon the establishment of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*).

How can the understanding of the existence [of the fruit] serve as a proof for its being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*)? For that would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). To explain: once it is established—by means of the reasoning set forth in the five preceding *pūrvapakṣa* sūtras beginning with "Because of the observation of conduct" (*ācāradarśanāt*)—that knowledge (*vidyā*) is a subordinate element of ritual action (*karma*), then the two *pārvaṇa-homas* would necessarily be merely indirect auxiliaries (*ārādupakāraka*) because they would constitute sacrifices performed at specific times. Consequently, just as one accepts that they are sacrifices within a composite ritual (*karmasamudāya-iṣṭi*) out of a desire to achieve direct integration (*sāmavāyikatva*), so too, by the principle that when direct integration as a subordinate element is possible, it is improper to accept them as merely indirect auxiliaries, [the existence of the fruit cannot be proven].

Since it is appropriate that [meditation] be subsidiary (*śeṣatva*) by way of being a refinement of the agent (*kartṛsaṃskāra*), because the status of the self as a refinement is understood through the accusative case and the suffixes *-tavya* and *aniya* in such injunctions as "The Self is to be seen" (*ātmā draṣṭavyaḥ*) and "One should meditate upon the Self" (*ātmānam upāsīta*); and since, while it is possible for the self to be employed in rituals by way of being the agent, its application [to the ritual] according to the *saktu-nyāya* would be improper; therefore, it is logical that meditation is subsidiary to the sacrifice by way of being a refinement of the agent. Consequently, the agent of the ritual action is not distinct from Brahman, who is the object of the meditation enjoined in the Vedāntas; and thus, "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

If it is asked: "In this way, even the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) becomes supported; however, since the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman depends upon the establishment of [Brahman's] being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*), how can that [non-difference] be included within the category of what establishes its status as the principal element (*śeṣitva*)? To this they reply: It is not by the mere existence of the indicative marks (*liṅga*)—such as the observation of conduct—that the subservience of knowledge (*vidyā*) to the ritual action is established, because indicative marks depend upon supporting means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And since there is no other sentence serving as a support than such passages as "One should meditate upon the Self" (*ātmānam upāsīta*), and therein, regarding the term "the Self" (*ātmānam*):

Since it is impossible for that sentence to convey subservience to the ritual (*kratvarthatva*) by way of being a syntactical injunction (*vākya-vidhi*) whose object is something other than the agent or the individual soul (*jīva*), it is established that the sentence conveys subservience to the ritual as a syntactical injunction supported by indicative mark (*liṅga*). This is because [the statement] would otherwise be impossible without the non-difference of the individual soul from Brahman, thereby ensuring the utility of the subsequent portion of the text.

Some, however, maintain that while the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is indeed established as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*), nevertheless, that very distinction between the *jīva* and Brahman—once established—is not used to re-establish that same [subordinate status] such that there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*). Rather, the subordinate status is established by means of the purification of the agent (*kartṛ-saṃskāra*), based on the distinction between the *jīva* and Brahman already proven to be subordinate. For the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) extends only that far; it does not terminate merely in the subordinate status itself. Even in the sūtra, "Because of being subordinate, it serves the purpose of the person," the subordinate status is understood through the mediation of the purification of the agent.

They say that this is because the intention of the Bhāṣya is that "this is what is intended to be said," and since this section culminates in the demonstration of the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, the intention of the Sūtra must likewise be stated in that very way. The phrase "by means of the removal of obstacles" means that it is so stated because of the scriptural declaration of faultlessness in the passage, "He becomes immortal here. The phrase "both have been stated" means both the removal of obstacles and the attainment [of the goal] have been declared.

The phrase "having studied, one desires to protect" indicates that knowledge is also understood as being subordinate to action; this is an illustration of what was stated in the five sutras beginning with "This is because of the observation of conduct. Here too, the word order is different, meaning that it is also understood as being subordinate to action. The phrase "intended for the exposition of its nature" means intended for the exposition of the meditation upon its nature.

Although this doubt does not arise—since [the meditation] cannot be a subsidiary part of the ritual because it achieves a distinct result, and because its status as a subsidiary to the ritual is already understood through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth—it should nevertheless be understood that this doubt is introduced in order to cite such passages as "one should meditate upon the Self" (*ātmānam upāsīta*) as proof for the view that knowledge (*vidyā*) serves the purpose of the ritual. Or else:

It should be understood that the intended meaning here is that [the Self] cannot serve as a means of proof [for the ritual] because it exists merely as a mark (*liṅga*). Regarding the commentary, the objection beginning with "But [it might be argued] by way of purifying the agent" and its subsequent resolution would not be tenable if the sentence "One should meditate upon the Self" were to convey subservience to the ritual (*kratvarthatva*), just like the sentence "For whomsoever the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood... In that case, since the Self—like the *juhū* ladle—is invariably concomitant with the ritual, it would be capable of bringing the ritual to mind; thus, the word *juhū* [would refer to the Self].

Just as the *juhū* ladle serves to indicate the *kratvapūrva* (the transcendental result of the sacrifice), since the word "Self" (*ātman*) indicates the *kratvapūrva*, its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) would be established by this sentence; and only then would these two [objections and] resolutions be appropriate. However, the sentence was not previously established as the authoritative means of proof in that manner. Rather, the status of being a subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratuśeṣatva*) is understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the observation of practice and so forth, as well as by the scriptural text (*śruti*), "Whatever one does with knowledge. Furthermore, the status of being a subsidiary to the Self (*ātmaśeṣatā*) is understood from the text, "The Self is to be seen.
Therefore, for the sake of consistency between both, [the case of] sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)...

The doubt of certain slow-witted individuals has been refuted on the grounds that while it was proposed that—just as rice, whose status as a subsidiary of the sacrifice is understood from the context, must serve the purpose of the sacrifice by way of purifying the rice in order to fulfill its status as a subordinate element (śeṣabhāva) understood through the direct statement of the accusative case (*dvitīyāśruti*)—so too must meditation (*upāsana*) serve the purpose of ritual action (*karmārthatva*) by way of purifying the agent; it was not proposed that the sentence "one should meditate upon the Self" establishes the meditation's subservience to ritual action by way of syntactical connection (*vākyavidhayā*).

In this context, even the sentence [of the scripture] is validated by the *Bhāṣya*, which states: "Therefore, through the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the agent, knowledge (*vidyā*) is subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratuśeṣatva*). In the *Bhāṣya*, regarding substances, purifications, and ritual acts, it is said: "Because they are for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit (*phalaśruti*) must be an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*)," as in: "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report," and "When he anoints [his eyes], he anoints the very eye of his enemy; when the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are performed, a shield is thereby made for the sacrifice, a shield for the sacrificer."

In the *Pūrvatantra*, it has been determined that in the case of injunctions such as "for the sake of overcoming rivals," where substances like the *parṇa*-wood, purificatory rites like anointing (*añcana*), and rituals like the *prayāja* offerings have their status as auxiliaries to the sacrifice understood through syntactical connection (*vākya*) and context (*prakaraṇa*), any mention of a fruit is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise). The meaning is this: since one thing cannot be an auxiliary to one thing while simultaneously being an auxiliary to another, it is impossible for the Self—which is common to both worldly and Vedic actions—to be invariably connected (*avyabhicaritatva*) with Vedic action alone. For only that which is unique to a thing can be its specific auxiliary; thus, it is that which serves as the means of recognition (*pratyabhijñāpaka*).

Regarding the conflict between the subordinate and the principal (*guṇamukhyavirodha*): since the *Pūrvatantra* has determined that when both the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and the primary (*pradhāna*)—namely the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* and the *Soma* sacrifices—are applicable to a single festival time (*parvakāla*) according to the injunction, "He who shall sacrifice with an *iṣṭi*, an animal, or Soma, shall sacrifice on the new moon or full moon day," the performance must belong to the primary alone and not to the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*. Consequently, because the *sutyā* rite in Soma sacrifices extends over a full day and night, and because the practice of knowledge (*vidyā*) must be cultivated daily, a conflict exists; therefore, [the time for] knowledge [takes precedence].

The meaning is that if [knowledge] were the primary factor, the performance of rituals by abandoning it would not be tenable. Now, one might object: "The instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) in the word 'vidyayā' (by knowledge) cannot be a proof for its being a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*); for although the instrumental case merely indicates instrumentality, it does not indicate subordination in the form of being a means that has already been accomplished. Anticipating this objection, [the author states that] even if the mere *śruti* (Vedic text) is not a proof in that regard, the *codanā* (injunction) together with *śruti*, *liṅga* (indicative mark), and so forth, is indeed a proof.

Intending to show that this is consistent with the statement of the learned authorities: "That by which the agent’s desired goal is accomplished is called an auxiliary (*aṅga*); and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for that is injunction (*vidhi*), joined with direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth," he says: "Direct statement, indicative mark, and the rest are the supporting factors of the means of knowledge that is scripture. The meaning is that an injunction supported by direct statement, indicative mark, and so forth possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge. One should not be deluded into thinking that this is the third *śruti* under discussion; rather, the phrase "this is not the *śruti*" refers to the *śruti* concerning the term "knowledge" (*vidyā*).

For this scriptural statement has as its object knowledge alone; for pervasion (*vyāpti*) is understood through the restrictive force of the pronoun "whatever" (*yat-eva*) and the particle "indeed" (*hi*), just as in the case of "that very place which possesses fire is that which possesses smoke. The meaning of "whatever action one performs" is "whichever action one performs. Consequently, knowledge is enjoined as a means for every action whatsoever. Thus, the fact that knowledge is an auxiliary to all actions is made possible by the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) having as its scope only the Udgītha-knowledge; such is the sense of the word "knowledge."

It must be stated that [the word *vidyā*] has all knowledge as its object; therefore, for this reason as well, it should be understood that the word *vidyā* has everything as its scope. This is because of the Śruti in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the rules, and having returned home at the conclusion of his service to the teacher, performing righteous deeds while reciting his own portion of the Veda in a pure place within the household... Here, the meaning is: "having lived in the house of a teacher, having studied the Veda according to the rules, and being endowed with the observances prescribed in the Smṛtis."

Even among the rules prescribed in the *Smṛtis*, the preeminence of service to the teacher is stated in the passage beginning with "by means of the remainder of the teacher's work. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having studied the Veda during the time not occupied by [the teacher's] work; that is to say, having returned from the teacher’s house (*gurukula*), meaning having withdrawn from it; then, remaining in the household stage of life (*gārhasthya-āśrama*) within the family, while performing the practice of the Veda even in the state of a householder so as not to forget it, and while making his sons and grandsons righteous—meaning making them devoted to dharma—or else, while acquiring wealth suitable for dharma.

Thus, because the injunction for one who has completed his study up to the comprehension of the meaning (*arthajñāna*) prescribes engagement in ritual acts (*karmasu niratiḥ*), those of the opposing view maintain that the comprehension of the meaning is an auxiliary element (*aṅga*) of the ritual act. However, the Teachers (*ācāryās*) observe that in such instances as "having eaten, he sits with joy" (*bhuktvā sānandam āste*), although the term *sānandam* is capable of being construed with the preceding word ending in the absolutive suffix (*vatvā*), its construction is not with that, but rather only with the subsequent verb *āste*. Similarly, in the rule "by the remainder of the teacher's work according to the injunction" (*yathāvidhānaṃ guroḥ karmātiśeṣeṇa*), the phrase is not construed with the preceding word *adītya*.

Furthermore, there would be the fault of a remote syntactical connection (*vyavahitānvaya*). Therefore, in accordance with such Smṛti texts as, "Having studied the Veda while practicing the student's conduct (*brahmacarya*), having approached and served the teacher, being permitted by him, one should take a wife; or, at the end of his studies, having invited the teacher to a gift of wealth, having performed [the rites], or being permitted, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*)," and in accordance with such Śruti texts as, "Having brought a pleasing gift for the teacher, do not cut off the thread of progeny," the duty toward the teacher must be performed without transgressing the teacher’s injunctions as prescribed by rule.

Intending that the meaning must be stated as "having returned completely by means of the remainder of the ritual action (*karmātiśeṣeṇa*), he brings [the sacrifice] to completion," they explained [the term] as *niḥśeṣam* (completely). They held that in the word *atiśeṣeṇa*, the prefix *ati-* functions in the sense of negation (*arthābhāve*), as seen in the usage of *atimaryāda* meaning "beyond limits" or "unbounded. Nor should it be argued that, for the sake of consistency with the Smṛti passage, "He should mutter [the mantra] until there is a remainder of the teacher's work," the word *karmātiśeṣa* here must likewise be understood as referring to the time remaining after the ritual action; for there is no recognition of identity between those two instances, since the words *śeṣa* and *atiśeṣa* have different meanings.

Since the meaning stated by us pertains to the lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), it is proper to say that it is precisely the meaning taught by the Teacher (the Guru) which accords with the Smṛti. The phrase "because the meaning is not intended" (*avivakṣitārthatvāt*) means for the purpose of avoiding defects such as the failure to establish the intended purport (*tātparya*). For in common worldly usage, when words are uttered with the aim of conveying a meaning, one understands the purport of the sentences and, in order to fulfill it, resorts to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and so forth when the primary meaning is impossible; this does not occur through mere utterance alone. Therefore, [in the case of] "cow, horse, man, elephant... [the primary meaning is not abandoned].

Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not postulated merely by the utterance of words; rather, when it is understood that their utterance is intended for the sake of conveying a specific meaning, then, for the purpose of accomplishing that very intention, one postulates indication, ellipsis, and so forth—just as in the cases: "This ox is strong," "The horse is swift," "The man is of disciplined conduct," or "The elephant is of great strength. Likewise, since the intention (*tātparya*) is not established in the case of Vedic sentences if they are uttered without aiming at the comprehension of their meaning, for the sake of accomplishing that intention, [indication must be postulated].

Since the faults of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*), textual insertion (*adhyāhāra*), restriction (*vyavasthāraṇa*), and the assumption of what is absent (*kalpanoccheda*) would otherwise result, it must necessarily be admitted that even in the Veda, the utterance of words is intended for the purpose of understanding the meaning. Furthermore, as in common worldly usage, such an utterance directed toward the understanding of meaning does not occur in the Veda through mere inclination (*rāga-prāpta*); therefore, it must be based solely on an injunction (*vidhi*). And since no injunction other than the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) is observed, it is by that very injunction that study—in the form of repeating after the teacher’s mouth with the aim of understanding the meaning—is enjoined.

This must be accepted even against one's will; the sense is that because the meaning is the same, it was stated likewise in the passage, "Having studied the Veda in the teacher’s house... The point is that, as in the expression "having bathed, he should offer oblations," the suffix *-tvā* indicates—where possible—the identity of the agent (*kartṛkāraka*), and since such identity exists only when there is a single performance (*prayogaikya*), and since a single performance is untenable without a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), and furthermore, because a connection based on time (*kālārtha-saṃyoga*) is inappropriate when another view is held. This is the underlying intention.

Now, one might object: even if there exists a relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*), why could the knowledge of Brahman from the Upaniṣads not itself be the principal? To this he says: "For [the knowledge] of the ritual" (*na hi kratujñānasya*). The meaning is that the knowledge of the subject matter of the Upaniṣads is equal to the knowledge of the subject matter of the earlier portion (the *karmakāṇḍa*). Now, since among the Vedānta passages cited there are those such as "He who is omniscient" (*yaḥ sarvajñaḥ*) which are intent upon teaching the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of Brahman], how can the Bhāṣya state that they are "intent upon teaching knowledge"? To this he says: "Because of their utility for the sentences concerning meditative worship," and so forth.

If it is argued that "non-performance is not possible when [the action] is a subordinate member (aṅga)," then indeed, non-performance is likewise not possible even when it is a subordinate member. If you say, "If only an action whose fruit is not intended has the status of a subordinate member, then its performance does not follow," then let it have the status of a principal member (aṅgin) as well; such is the sense, because that is not what the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) intends.

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "because it is restricted to the specific *udgītha* under discussion": the term "specific" (*viśeṣa*) means that which is qualified; the word *udgītha* refers here to the *udgītha-vidyā*. Therefore, the meaning is that the relative pronoun *yat* (in the phrase *yad... etat*) is restricted to the Soma sacrifice being performed within the context of the *udgītha-vidyā*. Some, however, maintain that there is no fault even if it refers to the ritual act named *udgītha*; for the quality of being "more powerful" (*vīryavattara*), which consists in producing a fruit unobstructed by other more potent rituals, is possible through the *udgītha*, since as a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of a rite, the *udgītha* does not independently produce a fruit.

It must be said that since the function of the auxiliary (*aṅga*) consists precisely in assisting the instrument (*karaṇa*), such a result—being characterized by superior potency (*vīryavattara*) and being unobstructed by other powerful karmas—is possible; so they say.

For "direct denotation" (*śruti*) is defined as the power of a single word; here, "single word" means that which is independent, as the learned have stated: "Direct denotation is a sound (*rava*) that is independent with respect to another word when it expresses [its meaning]. This amounts to saying that it possesses the capacity for certainty by itself. However, there is this distinction: the followers of the *Adhvaramīmāṃsā* hold that direct denotation consists in dependence on other words uttered in proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*). The intention of the Teachers (*Ācāryas*), however, is that because there is no restrictive factor, independence from other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that would provide the [meaning] also enters into the category of direct denotation. Therefore...

The linguistic formulation that "an explanatory restatement (anuvāda) refers to what is proximate" is indeed logical; for even when an explanatory restatement takes the form of a direct scriptural statement (śruti), its restriction [to a specific object] must be established with difficulty by conforming to proximity. However, some explain the phrase "the scriptural statement is not possible" to mean: since an explanatory restatement refers to what is proximate when such is possible, a scriptural statement that would grasp both the relevant and the irrelevant is not possible.

Because the natural force of the word *agni* (fire) applies to that much alone—just as in the case of words such as *juhū*—the property of being for the sake of the *apūrva* of the sacrifice (*kratvapūrvīyatva*) is not to be taken into account. This is the underlying point: the property of being for the sake of the *apūrva* of the sacrifice is not presented by primary denotation (*śakti*), but rather by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and this [indication] is possible only when the primary meaning is untenable. However, in the case of the statement, "He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa-wood," the word *juhū* terminates in the mere form (*ākṛti*) of the *juhū*, and since that [form] can exist even without being made of *parṇa-wood*, [the primary meaning is not precluded].

The meaning is as follows: although the word *juhū* (ladle) must resort to an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of that which pertains to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the sacrifice—due to the contingency of its being purposeless if its state of being made of *parṇa*-wood were restricted merely to the nature of the ladle itself—the word *agni* does not necessarily resort to an indication of that which pertains to the transcendental result of the sacrifice. This is because, upon considering such sentences as "He establishes the *gārhapatya* fire at night," the word *agni* denotes the specific fire qualified by its location and so forth; thus, even if it were restricted to that much, there would be no contingency of purposelessness. Consequently, since it does not extend as far as the sacrifice itself, [the analogy fails]. The phrase "the natural force of the word" (*śabdasvārasya*) means the natural force of the suffix *-tavya*.

The sense is that, by means of the suffix *tavya*, it is understood that the aggregate of syllables known as the Veda—which is denoted by the word "svādhyāya"—is something to be destroyed (or consumed). Although the verbal expression "having studied the Veda, one shall bathe" (*vedam adhītya snāsyann*) signifies that the sequence following study belongs specifically to the entire set of subsidiary elements of the *samāvartana* rite, and not to the *samāvartana* itself—if the suffix *ktvā* were intended to establish that bathing follows immediately after study, then [the meaning] would be like "one bathes prior to cooking" in such expressions as "having cooked, one who is about to eat bathes" (*paktvā bhokṣyamāṇaḥ snāti*).

Since it would follow that [the rites] such as entering the cow-pen (*goṣṭhapraveśa*) and others must also precede the study [of the Veda], the point is this: nevertheless, because the [rites] auxiliary to the *samāvartana* (return home) are immediate, the *samāvartana* itself is also immediate.

The phrase "of the knowledge of objects useful for oneself" means "of that which is currently useful for bathing. It should not be argued that [the ritual] would provide an opportunity for only that much and not for anything else; for by the same logic, since the taking of a wife must be performed immediately after bathing, and since the Agnihotra and other rites are to be performed continuously starting from the time one takes a wife, it is possible that this [knowledge] also provides an opportunity for those [rites]. Now, [one might object]: since even the return home (samāvartana), the taking of a wife, and so forth, are accomplished through the knowledge of objects, [it follows that... of that...

And because [the goal] cannot be accomplished without inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*), and because if the word "study" did not have the knowledge of the meaning as its purpose, it would follow that even such things as the ritual of returning home (*samāvartana*) and taking a wife could not be achieved; therefore, he says: "to the extent of the measure of the meaning. "Not... [he continues].

Even under the view that the study of the Veda extends up to the knowledge of its meaning—based on the rule "one should give instruction to a Śūdra"—it is accepted by the members of the three higher castes that the restrictive injunction for study, "One's own Veda is to be studied," applies only to one's own specific recension (śākhā). Consequently, regarding the collection of auxiliary sciences (aṅga) not prescribed in one's own recension, it is proper to perform their practice after receiving them from respective teachers even without a formal injunction to study them. This is because, with respect to a Śūdra, all recensions are "other than one's own," and thus there is an absence of such study.

If one were to say: "Who could prevent the performance of rituals by those who have acquired [knowledge] from their respective students? Indeed, while the knowledge required for the performance of sacrifices must be imparted in its entirety to a Śūdra, for the members of the three higher castes (traivarṇika), it need only concern the subsidiaries prescribed in their own specific Vedic recension (sva-śākhā) and others; thus, due to this parsimony of implication (ākṣepa-lāghava), only they—not the Śūdra—are entitled to perform sacrifices," then, in that case, whatever ritual is prescribed in whichever recension, the primary rite itself is also prescribed therein according to the maxim: "By the greater number, both [the primary and the subsidiary] are heard."

In another recension (*śākhā*), however, there is an injunction for certain subsidiary elements (*aṅga*). In that case, the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for that ritual action would belong only to those who study that specific recension, because it is simpler to assume that [the required] knowledge is already implied; it would not belong to those who study a different recension. For instance, if a certain ritual action or one of its subsidiaries is not enjoined in a particular recension, but is enjoined along with all its subsidiaries in another recension, then those who study that [first] recension would lack eligibility for that ritual action, just like Śūdras, due to their lack of the knowledge necessary for its performance.

Because [the knowledge] must be acquired in its entirety, and since it is universally accepted that even members of the three higher castes (traivarṇika) acquire the knowledge necessary for the performance of rituals, it follows that for a Śūdra as well, the acquisition of such knowledge is possible; thus, performing rituals after learning them from those who know the respective Vedas is indeed justifiable. Therefore, if study were to extend up to the comprehension of meaning, the eligibility of a Śūdra would be unavoidable. Consequently, the sense is that the prohibitive injunctions, such as "Therefore, a Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice," must be taken as the ultimate refuge.
"Because knowledge is distinct from that which is denoted by the word 'study'" means that knowledge is distinct from the fruit of study.

The meaning is that it has been stated that there is a possibility for the sentence "kurvann eva" (while performing [action]) to refer to action as a constituent part [of knowledge], because it is distinct from the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—which is not fit to be a constituent part of action—due to its being a different object and its possessing the nature of being a constituent part of action, as well as its having the status of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the action. Regarding the *Bhāṣya* passage, "For us, this world is the Self," the word "world" (*loka*) means "as if perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*), and it refers to certain followers of the *Vājasaneyi* school.
If it is argued that "the whole is not [established] by means of its parts," then, in that case, even the status of ritual action as an auxiliary to knowledge would not exist.

If it is argued that this is not so because there can be no suppression of the subsidiary by the principal, we say no; for those actions which are to be suppressed are not admitted to be subsidiaries of knowledge (*vidyā*). Nor should it be said that this cannot be stated even by one who accepts a distinction between types of action, because Jaimini—having set aside the view that the Upaniṣads refer to a Brahman distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), and having instead accepted that they refer to a self distinct from the body—acknowledged that the knowledge of such a self is a subsidiary to all actions pertaining to the next world; and according to his view, even those actions that are to be suppressed by knowledge [are included].

The sense is that since there is no difference in their being accomplished through the realization of the Self—which transcends the world—the subordination (*aṅgatva*) of knowledge must be asserted; for it is impossible for the subordinate (*aṅga*) to destroy the principal (*aṅgin*). In the Commentary, it is said that "the meditation on Brahman by means of the *praṇava* which is under discussion is being praised"; the meaning is "that which is about to be introduced," because the meditation on the *praṇava* is intended to be enjoined later in the passage: "All speech is woven together with the syllable *Oṃ*; this whole world is indeed the syllable *Oṃ*."

The analysis of the phrase is: "of these stages of life (āśramas) it is said. Now, [one might object]: "Even in the case of a mere reference (parāmarśa), the stages of life are indeed understood. True, they are understood; however, their establishment is through Smṛti and established custom (ācāra), not by direct Vedic revelation (pratyakṣa-śruti). And when there is a contradiction with direct revelation, it is established by the principle: "But in case of contradiction, [the Smṛti] should be disregarded. Alternatively, it may have as its subject those who are ineligible for ritual action, such as the blind, the lame, and so forth.

If it is argued that the householder's life is also merely mentioned—as in the passage, "sacrifice, study, and giving"—and therefore that too would not be established, [we reply: this is true; however, since all these duties are prescribed in the Śrutis specifically for the householder, their existence is indeed well-established by the Śruti itself.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the statement "because [the passage] 'And those who in the forest... is intent upon enjoining the path of the gods (*devayāna*)" means that its purpose is to enjoin the path of the gods, as seen in the text: "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity, they pass into the light. The intention is that the phrase "Desiring this world, mendicants go forth into the wandering life" is merely a praise of that world, not an injunction for the state of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*).

Regarding the phrase in the Bhāṣya, "‘He who extinguishes the sacred fire,’ etc.," the word "etc. includes such passages as, "Having brought what is dear to the teacher, do not cut off the line of progeny; there is no world for one who has no son," and so forth. Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "Now follows the restatement of those established in the householder stage of life" (gṛhasthāśramasthānuvāda), the sense is this: since there is an absence of prior acquisition [of the injunction] from any other source, a mere restatement is impossible; therefore, if it is accepted that this very passage possesses the nature of an injunction, that same status applies equally to the others as well.

One should not argue that there is a contradiction with the *Ṭīkā*, which states that both the similarity in being a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of praise and the similarity in being established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) are intended by the Sūtra; for its meaning is that the "similarity" consists in the absence of establishment by another means of knowledge—just as in the expression "the famine caused by the rains"—and thus the final conclusion here is that one must resort to the position of it being an injunction (*vidhi*).

However, some [interpret] the Bhāṣya’s mention of "the view of restatement" (*parāmarśapakṣa*) and "the view of injunction" (*vidhānapakṣa*) as meaning "the view of restating what is not obtained through other means of knowledge" and "the view of restating what is enjoined by other means of knowledge," rather than meaning "only the view of injunctionality" (*vidhitva*) in this very context; for that latter position is not to be propounded by the subsequent sūtra.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that because neither of the two positions is introduced in this sūtra, the Bhāṣya’s explanation—that in the phrase "either a positive injunction or a restriction"—the word *vā* signifies restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) would be inconsistent; for the natural force of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraka*) presupposes the introduction of two positions in the preceding [sūtra]. They say this is so because such an argument lacks logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary, “*tapo brahmacaryam iti sarvaiḥ śabdaiḥ*,” although in the Śruti only the word *brahmacārī* is heard in the passage “*brahmacāry ācāryakulavāsī*,” nevertheless, it should be understood that the word *brahmacarya* is used here to denote the very duty (*dharma*) of the *brahmacārī*. This is because the word *brahmacārī* refers to *brahmacarya*, as required by the subsequent commentary when it says, “*brahmacaryam ity uktam*.”

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "Because celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and austerity (*tapas*) are possible only for the householder," the meaning is that these are possible for the householder who is specifically designated by the injunction, "Sacrifice, study... Thus, the objection—that the restrictive particle (*eva*) is inappropriate because [celibacy and austerity] are also possible for one who is departing from the stage of life (*upakurvāṇa*), and therefore they belong to the householder alone—is refuted; for the particle *eva* serves to exclude others.

[The opponent] has cited [the passage] from the Bhāṣya: "By means of the threefold nature, it is included. Here, if the word *skandha* were not intended to refer to the stages of life (*āśrama*), then with reference to what would the number three be established for the specific originations of the sacrifices and so forth? However, if each stage of life is embraced [by these rites], then because the duties of the stages of life are threefold, it is possible to establish the number three; such is the sense that the promise regarding the stages of life is justified.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the term *diṣṭāgnihotra* means the *agnihotra* performed for one who has died; it is heard in the context of the *diṣṭāgnihotra*: "For he holds [the fuel-stick] above, for the gods. This is a restatement (*anuvāda*), because the holding above is already established by the present-tense instruction, by the particle *hi*, and by the traditional practice (*ācāra*). Since the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is a substance worthy of honor, it follows that some kind of covering would be required. Consequently, when another sentence—"He runs after [the cow], grasping the fuel-stick (*samit*) by its handle"—is understood as providing a specific application, the fuel-stick (*samit*) is restricted [to that purpose]. Thus, since the fuel-stick serves to cover the oblation, [the original statement is not a mandatory injunction but] a restatement.

In the third [book of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*], it was established that although the eastern part of the sacrificial offering is already obtained by the rule "the handle of the *sruk* [ladle] is for the purpose of the *marjana* [cleansing]," the rule is nonetheless an injunction (*vidhi*) because its application over the sacrificial offering itself was not previously established. Regarding the statement, "He who extinguishes the fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods," the word "eṣa" (this one) is to be separated [as the subject]. In the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that these [passages] refer only to those who are not dispassionate (*avirakta*). Since even for a householder, there is the perception of fault in an abandonment that is not preceded by renunciation (*apūrva-tyāga*), the scriptural mention of fault refers only to an abandonment that is not prescribed [by scripture]. Consequently, for one who desires to enter the wandering life (*pravivrajiṣu*) and is dispassionate, there exists the injunction for abandonment.

The renunciation that has been prescribed does not entail any fault; nor can it be argued that the scriptural injunction regarding wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) refers only to those who are blind, lame, deaf, or otherwise incapable of performing ritual duties, because the texts state this without qualification. This is evident from the Jābāla Śruti, which distinguishes various types of persons: "Whether he be one who observes vows or one who does not, whether he be a snātaka or one who is not a snātaka, whether his sacred fires have been extinguished or he is without fires."

Therefore, the sense is that the scriptural statement—"toward one who has entered the householder stage, or toward one who has begun to abandon [the world] through negligence or ignorance, or toward one who is not yet dispassionate"—is appropriate. Regarding the phrase "But others," etc., and "a single topic," etc.: although a distinction between topics (*adhikaraṇa*) is indicated in the *Kalpataru*, it should be understood that this was stated in such a way because it was not mentioned by the author of the *Bhāṣya* or by Ānandagiri (Āmnāyārtha). In the expression "in the subject matter" (*viṣaye*) at the beginning of such passages, the meaning is "in the scriptural passage that constitutes the subject matter" (*viṣayavākye*).

In the passage beginning "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are of dull intellect," the word *anyataraḥ* means "one of them. Now, one might object: in the Śaṅkara-bhāṣya it is stated, "It is not the case that Devadatta and Yajñadatta are of dull intellect, while the other among them is of great wisdom"; rather, it is understood that such a statement is impossible, as in the example, "Devadatta and Yajñadatta are of dull intellect, but Viṣṇumitra is of great wisdom"—yet this is not an acceptance of such an expression [as being logically untenable].

If it is argued that [the statement] is intended to negate that Yajñadatta is being spoken of, we say no; for it does not work that way. This is because when one says, "The pouring of water on fire," the resulting sense—that the state of being spoken of as the pouring of water on fire is impossible—is clearly seen to be the conclusion; thus, it is appropriate to treat it as a restatement (anuvāda) by taking that concluded meaning.

Furthermore, regarding the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), since it is stated in the scripture: "These three become possessors of the worlds of merit; one established in Brahman attains immortality," such a statement is made by taking for granted what has already been established, and does not refer to those previously mentioned. Rather, it refers to someone other than them, namely the wandering mendicant (*parivrāja*).

It should be understood that this was restated in such a manner with the intention that the *Śaṅkara-bhāṣya* also intends the same purport, because it is appropriate to introduce the example precisely in this sense—that is, since the example must be introduced for this very purpose, it is observed that what was previously indicated is stated in the example as if already established, rather than being something else entirely. The meaning is that [the term] "pertaining to the present context" (*prakṛtāśramanayā*) refers to those words which are purely etymological (*kevalayaugika*), because—according to the principle of the *Āgneyī* mantra—they apply to what is proximate.

"By way of a difference in time" means that previously he was indeed of dull intellect, but now, by virtue of proficiency in the study of the treatise (*śāstra*), the possibility of great wisdom has arisen; this is the intended sense. Regarding "that which brings about the presence of another property-bearer": *anyatara-śabda* means "the word *anyatara*" (one or the other), and one should not be mistaken for thinking it means "the word *anyatara*. Consequently, the meaning is: because of the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the word *mahat*, which is one of the two words specified in the statement, and which possesses the quality of bringing about the presence of another property-bearer in relation to the previously mentioned dull intellect.

The phrase "of the etymological" (yaugikasya) means "even of the etymological. Here, however, the meaning is that there is no contradiction even if the statement—apart from the word *brāhmaṇasaṃstha*—signifies that one who is established in Brahman (*brāhmaṇasaṃstha*) partakes in immortality only within the three [lower] stages of life (*āśrama*).

Furthermore, if the term *brāhma-saṃstha* were intended to refer to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśrama*), there would be no higher-celibate stages of life; consequently, the statement "There are three pillars of dharma" would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of praising the enjoined state of being established in Brahman. This would result in a contradiction with the meaning of the Sūtra: "Jaimini [holds] it to be a reference, because there is no injunction," for if that were the case, the very injunction regarding being established in Brahman would, by its nature as an injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), imply the establishment of the higher-celibate stages of life.

It should be understood that this is because neither the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) nor the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) can be applied here. Regarding this, the necessity of the topknot (*śikhā*), the sacred thread (*upavīta*), and so forth for the Paramahaṃsa has already been elaborated upon by the Teacher himself in the *Śatadūṣaṇī*; therefore, no further effort is made here. Thus ends the section on the human goal (*puruṣārthādhikaraṇa*).

The phrase "the two immediately preceding topics" refers, as is understood from the context, to the topic concerning the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Regarding the commentary's statement, "supreme (*parama*) and worthy of the highest (*parārthya*)," it is "supreme" because it is a symbol (*pratīka*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); it is "worthy of the highest" because it is fit for the purpose or station of the highest, namely Brahman.

"Of the seven preceding essences" means that because the essences of the seven [elements] beginning with earth were previously mentioned in the passage: "Of these beings, earth is the essence; of earth, water is the essence; of water, plants are the essence; of plants, man is the essence; of man, speech is the essence; of speech, the *Ṛk* is the essence; of the *Ṛk*, the *Sāman* is the essence; of the *Sāman*, the *Udgītha* is the essence."

It has been established here in the Bhāṣya that [the passage] is devoted to meditation (*upāsana*), and so forth. Now, one might object: in this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*), the inquiry is conducted only as to whether sentences such as "He is the essence of essences" (*sa eva rasānāṃ rasatamaḥ*) serve to provide the specific details of the object of meditation, or whether they are intended as mere praise (*stuti*); however, no investigation is undertaken as to whether sentences such as "One should meditate on the syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha" (*omityetadakṣaramudgīthamupāsīta*) are also intended as injunctions for meditation, or not, because those sentences have not been cited as examples. To this we say: it is not so.

The opponent's position is twofold: first, that even sentences such as "the most savory" (*rasatama*) function as glorifications (*stāvaka*); and second, that here in the phrase "one should meditate upon the *udgītha*" (*udgītham upāsīta*), meditation (*upāsana*) is not being enjoined. Rather, the word *upāsana* denotes a general knowledge conducive to the performance established by the injunction regarding the *udgītha*; therefore, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Consequently, since there is no injunction co-occurring within the sentence "the most savory," etc., those sentences cannot function as glorifications through syntactic unity with that [injunction]. Instead, the sentences "the most savory," etc., function as glorifications solely through syntactic unity with the injunction regarding the *udgītha*—which pertains to the *udgītha* as an auxiliary (*upakaraṇa*) of the sacrifice—as presented by the term *udgītha*.

Furthermore, there is no rule that the words of praise must be construed in syntactic proximity with an injunction for praise; for this is contradicted by the case of extended applications (*atideśa*) such as, "These Brāhmaṇas themselves are the five oblations, namely the other Brāhmaṇas," where the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) do not function as praise. This is one position. Another holds that, having accepted the injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) in "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*," the [explanatory passage] serves as its praise through syntactic unity with that injunction, rather than serving to provide the object of the meditation.

The second position is that [the passage] "Om, this syllable" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.8) serves solely to present the object of meditation. In that case, although meditations do exist according to the second position, it should be understood that the intention here is to establish that the passage is devoted to injunctions for meditation, because such injunctions were absent in the first position. For praise is based on what is already established by other means of knowledge; as it is said: "In case of contradiction, there is figurative description (guṇavāda); where there is no contradiction, there is restatement (anuvāda)."

Since those learned in the science of sentences have stated: "Exegetical statements (arthavāda) are considered to be of three kinds: [those that are] expressive of reality (bhūtārthavāda), [those that are] figurative (guṇavāda) due to contradiction with other means of knowledge, and [those that are] restatements (anuvāda) when [the fact] is already determined by another means of knowledge," for example, "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" and "The pressing-stones sing" are figurative statements because they contradict other means of knowledge; whereas "Fire is the remedy for cold" is a restatement because it is already established by another means of knowledge. [This applies to] the means of proof and the means of sublation...

In the case of an existing fact (*bhūta*), there is a statement of fact (*bhūtārthavāda*), as in "Vajrahastaḥ Purandaraḥ" (the thunderbolt-handed destroyer of cities) and so forth. Or, by the injunction of an unestablished quality (*aprāptaguṇavidhāna*)—that is to say, by a statement of fact that teaches a dharma not previously established. Therefore, one should not raise the objection: "How can that which enjoins a quality be included within an *arthavāda*? For in this case, such [an inclusion] is not possible due to the lack of immediate proximity (*sannihitatva*). The intention is that, by the force of statements such as "These very *brāhmaṇa* verses are the five *havirdhānas*," there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the injunction regarding the five *sañcaras*.

In the commentary, it is argued that it is more reasonable for [the text] to have the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*), because an explicit injunctive suffix is heard and because the term "meditation" (*upāsana*), which is a synonym for "contemplation" (*dhyāna*), has not been previously established. Therefore, it is more reasonable for it to have the nature of an injunction for meditation. And thus:

The meaning is that, since there is syntactic unity with the injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*) which is mentioned in close proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*), it is not proper to assume syntactic unity with the injunction regarding the *udgītha* which is not so mentioned. Now, one might raise the objection: "Granted that there is syntactic unity with the injunction for meditation mentioned in close proximity, why could the connection [of these passages] not still be for the purpose of praise (*stuti*)? He dispels this doubt by means of a concluding summary: "Therefore, these scriptural texts are for the purpose of enjoining meditation. Meditation (*upāsana*) is that which is meditated upon (*upāsyate*); the suffix *-ana* (in *upāsana*) is the *lyuṭ* suffix used in the sense of the object (*karman*), according to Pāṇini 3.3.117. Thus, they are for the purpose of enjoining the object of meditation.

This is the meaning; or rather, the meaning is that they are intended for the prescription of objects for meditation (*upāsana*). The sense is that since it is possible for them to be directed toward specific modes of practice by way of presenting the objects of meditation, it is improper to assume they are merely for the purpose of praising fruitless exertion. Thus ends the section on "Mere Praise" (*stutimātrādhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is that "connection" (*saṅgati*) arises from the consideration that [the connection] occurs through doubt (*śaṅkā*). Now, one might object: since the word *pāriplava* is seen to denote narrative accounts (*ākhyāna*) in the passage, "To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, seated upon a golden cushion, he shall recite the *pāriplava* to the consecrated king who is surrounded by his sons and ministers on the first day, beginning with 'Manu Vaivasvata was the king,'" how can there be a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the narrative accounts serve as the purpose for the ritual recitation (*śastra*) named *pāriplava*? To this, he says: "The *pāriplavas* are the narrative accounts; here, by the word *pāriplava*..."

The intended meaning is that "praising" (śaṃsana) refers to the recitation of narratives; thus, "śastra" means a praise accomplished by means of a narrative. The point is that since the word *pāriplava*—meaning "repeatedly revolving"—is applicable to the *śastra* as well, it denotes the act of praising by repeatedly reciting narratives. In the Bhāṣya, the phrase "for the purpose of demonstrating specific branches of knowledge" is justified because, through the narrative beginning with "Those great Śrotriyas of the Māhaśāla clan, having come together, deliberated," one understands the specific nature of that knowledge as having the Supreme Self as its object. This is further illustrated by the passage concerning "the threshing by hailstones."

The meaning is that they are for the sake of that [knowledge], because through the narrative "Perform [the sacrifice] with Āṭakī as your wife," one observes the comprehension of specific details such as the restriction on food regarding knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, the meaning is that they are for the sake of facilitating comprehension by securing attention even from those who were previously inattentive when hearing the narratives. Now, he dispels the doubt that—even though these are enjoined by a statement for the *pāriplava* (the recitation at the horse sacrifice)—they might also serve the purpose of knowledge due to their proximity; he does so by means of the commentary, stating that it is logical for knowledge to be the primary purpose. The sense is that [to claim otherwise] would contradict the principle: "Because of the difference in purpose, such as piercing, and so forth."

Now, an objection might be raised: in the passage, "The Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed the first of sacrifices; therefore, having sacrificed with this, one should then sacrifice with another," the word "another" (anya) refers to all sacrifices other than the Jyotiṣṭoma. However, because its scope would have to be restricted to that alone—following the mention of sacrifices characterized by the *trivṛt* and other *stomas* in the supplementary portion of the text, such as "He who enters upon another sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) which is *trivṛt* kindles it, he who [enters upon one] which is *pañcadaśa* [kindles it]"—it follows that [the Jyotiṣṭoma] is distinct from those sacrifices consisting of multiple *stomas*.

[Otherwise] there would have to be performance [of these stories] even before [the meditation], and consequently there would be a contradiction with the fifth-book section (pāñcamika-adhikaraṇa) initiated by the two sūtras of the prima facie and final positions: "Or [they belong] to a single stoma, because of the connection with the sacrifice," and "Or [they belong] to all [stomas], because of the specific injunction; [this is] a praise of the stomas. Therefore, since the stories occurring within the context of knowledge (vidyā-prakaraṇa) would—by virtue of the word *sarva* ("all") found in the opening [sūtra]—be applied to ritual acts (karma), they would serve only for the purpose of the *pāriplava* recitation and not for the purpose of knowledge. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Included in the context... (*prakaraṇopāttā*).

Although it is a general rule that the conclusion should be interpreted in accordance with the opening statement (*upakrama*), in this case, because it is impossible to praise [the sacrifice] as described in infinite Vedic branches, there is a requirement for a restriction of the term "all" found in the opening itself. Since the required specification is provided by the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*), the restriction applies to those narratives understood from the context of the sentence. This is just as in the passage, "Now, all indeed desire a share of this *Hāriyojana* cup," where, since it is impossible for the word "all" (*sarva*) to refer to every person without restriction, there is a need for a limiting factor; thus, in the context of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* [sacrifice], [it is restricted to those entitled to the cup].

The restriction applies only to those priests who are present at the ritual, not to all [priests]. Furthermore, if all the narratives were to be included by virtue of the word "all" occurring in the opening statement, then the specific qualification in the supplementary passage, "Manu Vaivasvata was the king," and so forth, would be entirely purposeless; and since it is not appropriate for a meaningful term to be rendered meaningless, there must be a restriction.

The supplementary passage beginning with "He who [performs] the *trivṛt* as another," etc., is consistent through mere connection (*saṃyoga*) alone; furthermore, by the word "another" (*anya*), no specific distinction is perceived. It should be understood that there is a difference [between this case and others], because even in the case of various *stoma*-possessing sacrifices, the illuminating quality (*dīpakatva*) of the *trivṛt* and so forth is possible through mere connection, even without pervasion (*vyāpti*). [Regarding the statement] "by the sentence concerning the gold sacrificial fee," the meaning is "of silver and gold"; the intention is that this is based on the scriptural text, "Therefore, [one should give] gold. Thus ends the section concerning the *pāriplava*.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the statement "because those whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas) lack sacrifices and the like" implies that one must resort to an alternative interpretation (*anyaparyāya*) for those scriptural passages indicating a connection with knowledge, such as "And those who in the forest worship through faith and austerity. Furthermore, if the connection of those whose vital energy is drawn upward with knowledge must necessarily be asserted, then—since the fruit of knowledge is not attained without the performance of its constituent parts (*aṅga*)—the performance of the constituent sacrifices and so forth becomes mandatory; for that purpose, they would have to take another wife and perform the consecration of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).

Nor does the taking of a wife entail a contradiction with the state of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*), because even when one takes a wife for the sake of performing rites that are auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyāṅga-karma*), the state of perpetual celibacy remains possible—as in the case of Bhīṣma. This constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) according to the method of the prima facie argument in the relevant section of the *Pūrvatantra* (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra), which states: "This [initiation] is the time for kindling the fires, because of the connection with the oblation. For in that context, the oblation auxiliary to initiation must be performed in the *āhavanīya* fire; and this taking of a wife occurs after the acquisition of knowledge following the injunction for initiation. Thus, even when there is the taking of a wife, it is not contradictory.

The prima facie argument was set forth on the grounds that "it will be for the sake of progeny"; likewise here as well, it should not be said that because knowledge is established as a limb of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma), there is no resulting implication for the performance of restraints (yama) and so forth, nor does the taking of a wife and the gathering [of provisions] follow as a necessary consequence.

Because the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) in the passage beginning with "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*) specifically prescribes that sacrifices and the like are auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of knowledge (*vidyā*), the scriptural texts regarding the renunciation of action (*karma-tyāga*) refer instead to actions that are auxiliary to knowledge. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is as follows: since it is impossible to take a wife solely for the sake of [obtaining] a son or solely for the sake of [performing] religious duty (*dharma*), according to the Smṛti text, "In matters of dharma and artha, one must not transgress," Bhīṣma’s taking of a wife was indeed for the sake of both dharma and progeny. Once that was accomplished, he desisted from procreating sons by means of his vow of lifelong celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas-tva*) for the sake of pleasing his father.

The meaning is that for him, the purpose of having a wife remains merely for the sake of dharma; thus, he performs sacrifices and other rites, but after his vow of lifelong celibacy (*ūrdhvaretastva*), he does not take a wife solely for the sake of dharma. This is because, upon considering the duties of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)—such as the requirement of living in a fixed abode as established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*—it is not appropriate for a renunciant to take a wife or engage in similar activities.

The meaning is that when the fruit arises through knowledge (*vidyā*), there is no dependence on ritual action (*karman*); because [knowledge] does not subsist for the sake of the ritual, it has no dependence on the ritual action which is its own subordinate element. He states the purpose of this conclusion: "And this is the conclusion. Thus ends the section concerning the kindling of the fires and so forth (*agnīndhanādyadhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the statement in the commentary, "Because of the scriptural injunctions concerning sacrifices and so forth, as in the case of the horse," which asserts that sacrifices and the like are means [to liberation] only when they serve as means to knowledge, it is argued that this is incorrect; for between a base (prakṛti) and a suffix (pratyaya), the meaning of the suffix predominates, and thus by the instrumental case, one perceives them as means only with respect to the desire itself. To this, he replies with the words beginning, "Without the desire for the ultimate goal," and so on.

Now, it may be argued that even when one has reached a state of emaciation due to a hatred for food, and although there exists a desire characterized by an orientation toward other objects as a means to avoid that [aversion], an appetite culminating in actual engagement toward that food does not arise because of the defect of an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) caused by severe indigestion and the like. Just as in the case of medicine for such loss of appetite, so too, regarding the fact that Brahman—which is unsurpassed bliss—is the means for attaining that [state] through knowledge (*vidyā*), [this occurs] by the power of the clarity of mind produced by the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*) throughout many previous births, performed without any [worldly] intention.

If it is argued that, even when a person has attained full confidence and possesses a desire characterized by an orientation toward the acquisition of the heart [of Brahman] and the knowledge that is its means, the inclination extending to active engagement in the means of knowledge—such as hearing (śravaṇa)—does not arise due to obstacles created by the fault of numerous beginningless accumulated sins; and that these obstacles, like prohibited actions for a seeker of liberation (āstika-kāmuka), produce a necessity for the enjoyment of sense objects which obstructs the practice of knowledge, therefore the prescription of sacrifices and other rites to fulfill that desire by first removing such obstacles is most appropriate—[we reply: no.

True; if by this sentence the connection of actions with desire and so forth were being propounded, then one might resort to such an indirect method (*praṇāḍī*) to justify the literal sense of the scripture. But this is not the case. This is not the case because, according to the general principle observed in examples such as *aupagava* (the son of Upagu), between the meaning of the base and the suffix, the meaning of the suffix is predominant. Consequently, in accordance with the specific principle established for sentences such as *svargakāmaḥ* (one desiring heaven), the connection of the verbal means (*śabdasādhana*) occurs precisely with that which is understood from the word as the object of the desire, due to its greater force. [As in: "With a horse..."

In common usage such as "he wishes to go" (*jigamiṣati*) or "he wishes to kill with a sword" (*asina jighāṃsati*), the suffix *san* expresses the desire for the attainment of the object, such as a horse; and in Vedic usage such as "it is to be desired to be known" (*taj-jijñāsitavyam*) or "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyam*), the suffix *san* expresses the injunction (*vidhi*) which is the meaning of the suffix *tavya*.

The sense is that since it is established that the connection with "going" (gamanānvaya) occurs only with respect to the object of the desire expressed by the verbal root, and since it is established that the connection occurs only with respect to the knowledge (vidyā) expressed by the verbal base (prakṛti), [the former is not required]. Although others have stated in the previous sūtra that there is no requirement regarding the production of the fruit, while in this sūtra they have stated that there is a requirement for karma regarding the production of knowledge, nevertheless, in the case of the phrase "like a horse," just as a horse is not employed for pulling a plough but is employed for driving a chariot, [so too is the relationship between karma and knowledge].

It should be understood that the objection was stated with the intention that, because it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that "thus the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarmāṇi*) are not required for the production of the fruit through knowledge, but they are required for its origination," the lack of requirement for the production of the fruit is what is established in this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*). The phrase "the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the immediately preceding section" means "in the section immediately following" in relation to the first sūtra.
Thus concludes the section concerning the requirement of all [auxiliaries].

The doubt [of an opponent] is thus refuted as being improper: "Even so" (*tathāpi*) is redundant. Since the possibility of contradiction arises only in relation to *yama* and so forth (as opposed to *śama*, *dama*, etc.), there is no contradiction with those [latter] when they are not considered; therefore, the word "even" (*api*), which indicates such a contradiction, is superfluous. Consequently, the meaning of "even so" (*tathāpi*) is "even though [there is a need for] sacrifice and so forth," and not "even if there is a need for sacrifice and so forth."

The meaning is as follows: "of that which was intended by the preceding sūtra" refers to the refutation of its being for the purpose of praise (*stuty-artha*). The intention is that it is better [to place this refutation] even there, because since the refutation of its being for the purpose of praise is required in the preceding sūtra—which is intent upon establishing the connection with those who desire to know—it is more appropriate to effect that refutation right there. Thus ends the section on *śama*, *dama*, and so forth.

The phrase "it is deliberated whether [he] exists or not" has "of those who know the vital breaths (prāṇa)" as its ellipsis; that is, it refers even to one established in the knowledge of the vital breaths. Now, one might object: since we see in the case of one established in the meditation on the Vāmadevya-sāman the injunction, "He should not avoid any woman—that is his vow," which permits the non-avoidance of all women, how much more so by logical extension would there be the contingency of non-avoidance of all women for those who know the Brāhmaṇas? And if it is argued that because there is no evidence for connecting what is heard in the context of one meditation with another meditation, the non-avoidance of all women—which is an ancillary of the Vāmadevya meditation—does not apply to one who knows the Brāhmaṇas; [we reply:]...

If it is argued that, in that case, there is no possibility of the practice of eating all kinds of food—which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of *prāṇa*—applying to one who knows the *bṛhat*, we say no. In the meditation on the *vāmadevya*, although the status of being an injunction is understood from the hearing of a clearly expressed injunctive suffix in the statement, "One should not avoid any woman; that is his vow" (*na kāñcana pariharet tad-vratam*), here there is an absence of such an injunctive particle. Consequently, since there is no injunction of the practice of eating all kinds of food as an auxiliary, [the passage]—"sinful action does not cling to one who knows thus" (*evaṃvidi pāpaṃ karma na śliṣyate*)—is like [the following]: "Indeed, sinful action does not cling to one who knows thus" (*na ha vā evaṃvidi*).

In the passage, "Food becomes non-food," once it is established that the intent is merely to demonstrate the absence of fault incurred from eating what is normally forbidden, there arises the consideration: does this teach the absence of fault even when forbidden food is eaten intentionally, or does it refer only to cases of accidental consumption? Since this very inquiry is the subject of our current section (*adhikaraṇa*), and since the opponent has proposed that the power of the fruit of the knowledge of *prāṇa* consists in its being untouched by the defect of food even in cases of intentional action—if such [a power] belongs to the knowledge of *prāṇa* as well...

If someone were to object: "In that case, why should even the Brāhma-vidyā, which is the most excellent of all sciences, not possess the power to cause one to be untouched by the fault incurred from eating forbidden food through the influence of desire?"—one should understand that there is not even a scent of error in this text, because it is intended for the purpose of showing that even this [objection] is not undesirable to the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin).

Regarding the phrase "intended by the prima facie view" (*pūrvapakṣābhipretā*): although there is no connection with the knowledge of Brahman (*brāhmī vidyā*) in this investigation concerning the subject matter of the knowledge of Prāṇa—since this investigation concludes solely with that [knowledge of Prāṇa]—it cannot be said that the existence or non-existence of the omnivorous nature of the knower of Brahman constitutes the result of the prima facie and final positions. This is because, in the final position (*siddhānta*), the absence of omnivorousness in the knower of Brahman is presented merely as a corroborative argument for the absence of omnivorousness in the knower of Prāṇa, and thus it cannot function as a result.

If it is argued that even for those who know the *Brāhmaṇa*, there is no fault in eating forbidden food—since, despite the presence of faults in such cases, it is proclaimed regarding those who know the *Prāṇa* that "for one who knows thus, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food"—we say no. This is because the absence of fault is seen to be equal in both cases, as the statement "evil action does not cling to one who knows thus" refers specifically to the knower of the *Brāhmaṇa*. Furthermore, if you claim that the prohibition against misconduct in the passage "not for one who has not desisted from evil conduct" applies only to negligence (*prāmādika*), then [the rule] "he who eats food from whatever source when his life is in danger... [would likewise apply].

"He is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. Therefore, since the scripture stating "for one who knows thus" (*na ha vā evaṃvid*)—which has the nature of an injunction to be inferred—is sustained only through non-contradiction with established general rules such as "A Brāhmaṇa shall not drink liquor," [the former cannot override the latter]. Alternatively, this is not an injunction regarding a result; for an established specific rule overrides a general rule. In this case, there is no contradiction with the established general rule in the passage: "For one who knows thus, nothing whatsoever becomes unfit food."

Because it is more appropriate to regard [the passage] as a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) than to assume the prescription of a result, there is no such consequence that passages like "evil action does not cling to one who knows thus" would also be mere eulogies; for since the non-clinging of evil would otherwise lead to the impossibility of liberation, the non-clinging of all sins must be accepted as a result prescribed by the scriptures on liberation, and thus it must be stated as a prescription of a result. Furthermore, because the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) has results such as being the most excellent and the best, it has no further desire for a result [and thus cannot be a mere eulogy]. [As it is said: "He said: 'What shall be my food?'"

Thinking, "Something will happen," they said, "This is [the result of] eating hastily and eating inauspiciously. This is indeed a praise of the meditation on the food of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is a limb of the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*) prescribed for the entire class of living beings down to the dog, as expressed in the passage: "For one who knows thus, nothing at all becomes non-food. Therefore, since this is not an injunction regarding a fruit, permission to eat all kinds of food is granted to the knower of the vital breath only in cases of life-threatening danger. As for the rule "one should not proclaim it," this is merely a restriction based on the specific context of the verse "one who has not desisted from evil conduct... and so forth.

The distinction is this: while a specific rule has a restricted scope, here, however, in accordance with the established general rule, there is no sublation of the injunction implied by the phrase "Indeed, for one who knows thus" (*na ha vā evaṃvidi*). Some, however, having formulated a prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) similar to the opinion of others—namely, that just as for a worshiper of the *vāmadevya* there is a prohibition against all women, so for one established in the knowledge of Prāṇa, permission for all food is enjoined as an ancillary part of that practice—they describe the final conclusion (siddhānta) in exactly the same way; and [this is also the view] of the commentary (*ṭīkā*) which is intent on refuting both the higher and lower opinions.

They demonstrate that there is no contingency of contradiction because [the text] is intent solely upon refuting the mere application of the words of the sūtras as stated by others and ourselves. The phrase "because knowledge is the fruit" means that since knowledge—which is a subordinate factor—is mentioned as the fruit, it is an *arthavāda* (eulogistic statement), just like the hearing of the verse concerning the removal of sin.
Thus concludes the section concerning the permission to eat all kinds of food.

The inquiry is whether the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) constitute limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*). The phrase "the duties of the stages of life" is explained as "even by one who is merely a member of a stage of life"; it should not be understood as a presentation of the opposing view that "the duties of the stages of life do not constitute limbs of knowledge," for it must be seen that it is precisely the status of the duties of the stages of life as being limbs of knowledge that is intended to be established in this section.

Regarding the phrase "being a constituent part of the stages of life (*āśrama*) alone": by the word *āśrama*, the person who possesses that stage is denoted; thus, the meaning is "having the goals of the person residing in the stages of life as their purpose. Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one for whom the stage of life alone [is the goal]," where the person is the referent of the other member of the compound.

Regarding the phrase "if they were separate actions" (*karmāntaratve sati*) and so forth, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: Since it would entail the contradiction of the conjunction of the permanent and the impermanent, and because there is an absence of even a separate application (*viniyoga-pṛthaktva*) for a single action, those [acts] arising from the divisions of knowledge cannot possibly constitute mere stages of life (*āśrama-bhāga*) for one desiring liberation; therefore, they are not to be performed by such a seeker. This is because, through a separate application, the contradiction of the conjunction of the permanent and the impermanent does not arise.

If there is no distinctness of action (*karmāntaratva*), then because those [rites] are merely auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*) and cannot be auxiliary to the stage of life (*āśrama*) alone, they must be performed even by one who belongs solely to that stage of life. And since such performance is contradictory, the meaning is that a real contradiction cannot be removed even by the reconciliation of scriptural statements. By this, the *adhikaraṇa* of the *Pūrvatantra* stating, "But when one thing has both [functions], there is separate connection" (*ekasya tūbhayatve saṃyogapṛthaktvam*), should also be regarded as refuted.

The resolution of the contradiction regarding the conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal is the fruit of the two sūtras; this is the underlying sense: in the case of an established entity (*siddharūpa*), there is no real contradiction between eternality and non-eternality, nor between eternality and being produced, just as there is no such contradiction in the case of the performance or non-performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. Rather, a contradiction must be asserted only when it is impossible for a single sentence to convey both [meanings], and when another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) cannot operate upon that which is determined solely by an injunction (*vidhi*).
