In the present case, however, both means of knowledge that determine application (*viniyojaka-pramāṇa*) are present.

In this regard, there is no contradiction because both purposes are served by virtue of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: Since knowledge (*vidyā*) does not have a result that is eternally desired, the obligatory (*nitya*) nature of the rite performed as its subsidiary would not exist; consequently, for one performing the rite for the sake of knowledge, even the obligatory application must be performed separately for the sake of avoiding transgression (*pratyavāya*), and thus the obligatory application itself would become non-obligatory (*anitya*). [Reply: This is not so, because the performance of the *Agnihotra* for the sake of heaven is either occasional (*kāmya*) or conditional (*naimittika*), whereas it is obligatory (*nitya*) with respect to the primary injunction.

According to the maxim "one enters [the ritual] by means of the constant [form]," since there is no distinction between the two types of performance regarding the modified application (*vikṛti*), the constant injunction (*nityavidhi*) enters [the modification] merely by subverting its status as the motivator (*prayojakatva*).

Just as in the case of the text: "If one should officiate at a sacrifice for a Rājanya or a Vaiśya, and he should desire to consume Soma, having fetched Nyagrodha-stibhinīs (shoots of the banyan tree), having ground them and mixed them with curd, one should offer that to him as food, not Soma"—this [substitute] enters [the ritual] by displacing the obligatory Soma; yet, by that much, the obligatory performance does not incur the state of being non-obligatory. So too here, there is no contradiction; this is the sense. But it is not the case that the result belongs to only one [of the two]; such is the opinion of Śeṣa.

Furthermore, because there is no evidence for a difference in the essential nature of the action (*karma*) in the *bhāṣya*, and since it cannot be a restatement (*anuvāda*)—given the impossibility of performing the *agnihotra* oblation in close proximity to the [new] monthly *agnihotra*—its status as an injunction (*vidhi*) is established. Once its status as an injunction is established, this oblation must be distinct from the well-known *agnihotra* oblation already enjoined, because one cannot enjoin what has already been enjoined. Thus, since the name "Agnihotra"—which is dependent on the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) occurring therein—is capable of evoking the recognition of the well-known *agnihotra*, let there be a separate ritual action (*karmāntaratva*) due to the difference in context (*prakaraṇabheda*).

However, in this context, since there is no hearing of an injunction (*vidhi*) regarding sacrifices and the like, whereas an injunction is heard regarding knowledge (*vidyā*) itself, this [sacrifice] is distinct from the well-known sacrifice. Now, one might argue that here too it is the sacrifice and so forth—intended as a means for the desired knowledge—that is enjoined, and not the knowledge itself; for knowledge, being the fruit, cannot be the object of an injunction. Thus, it would be equivalent to the *agnihotra*. Nor should it be said that the well-known sacrifice itself is enjoined merely as being connected to the fruit; for in that case, it would be equivalent to the well-known *agnihotra* being enjoined merely as being connected to the month.

Because of the context of the injunction (*vidhāna*). Therefore, just as in the case of the *māsāgnihotra*, since the sacrifices and so forth denoted by the words "sacrifice" (*yajña*) and the like here are not identical to the well-known sacrifices, it is difficult to determine which form among those well-known sacrifices is being extended (*atideśa*) here. Furthermore, if the name "sacrifice" and the like were to extend the material (*dravya*), deity (*devatā*), and so forth, then the very grounds for the application of the term "sacrifice"—namely, the nature of relinquishing a material substance intended for a deity—would be unavoidably present; consequently, it would be impossible for the action to be enjoined as something distinct from the well-known sacrifices. Thus, [the text says]: "Sacrifice, study, and giving... (*yajño 'dhyayanam dānam iti*).

The first [interpretation] holds that it is appropriate for the term to refer to well-known sacrifices and so forth, as in passages such as "Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of sacrifice" (*yajñānāṃ yajñiyajño'smi*) and "The enjoyer of sacrifice and austerity" (*bhoktāraṃ yajñatapasām*). The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to statements concerning sacrifice and so forth; thus, "statements concerning sacrifice and so forth" (*yajñādivākya*) includes passages such as "When the impurity has been washed away by actions" (*kaṣāye karmabhiḥ pakve*). The syntactical connection here is as follows: by one who asserts subsidiarity (*aṅgatva*)—namely, the statement beginning with "by sacrifice, by gift," etc.—even a statement that describes those very things (sacrifice, etc. as being subsidiaries and performing some function is itself [included under] sacrifice and so forth.

The meaning is that [the author] indicates [the sacrifice] by means of words such as "synonym" (paryāya), "property" (dharma), and "action" (karman). Consequently, the intention is that even in that sentence, a misconception regarding a property distinct from what is well-known must be avoided. The term "as if established" (siddhavat) means "by way of an indication as if [the object] were already established. For in cases such as "one performs the Agnihotra," a form of unprecedented dharma (apūrva-dharma) is produced by the verb (ākhyāta), which by its very nature expresses an object in a state of being accomplished; however, this is not the case with words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, such as "sacrifice" (yajña) and so forth. Thus ends the section concerning the enjoined nature (vihitatvādhikaraṇa).
"Having returned home as one who has not taken a wife" means that he has not yet performed the marriage ceremony.

He says "capable" (*śakta*) because devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*) do not invariably lead to the greater or lesser degrees of dharma respectively. The phrase "for the purpose of excluding the life of a wandering mendicant" (*pārivrājyavyāvṛttyartham*) means that it is stated "provided there is no dispassion" (*avairāgye sati*) in order to dispel the following doubt: "But surely, even for one whose wife has died or who has not yet taken a wife—since the stages of life (*āśrama*) requiring a wife are impossible due to the lack of a spouse—is it necessary to exclude such a person from being without an *āśrama* (an *anāśramin*), given that the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-āśrama*) is still possible? The phrase "and others" (*pare ca*) and so forth refers to the traditional injunctions (*smṛti*) regarding the conduct of those who stand outside the *āśramas*.

The meaning is that [the text] is solely intent upon the recollection of naked wandering (*nagnacaryā*), which lies outside the common duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*). Although in the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya* it is stated that even those such as Savartaka, because of their engagement in naked wandering and so forth, are remembered as "great yogins" (*mahāyogin*) despite not depending on the duties of the stages of life—and thus it was said that what is being recollected is "great yogic power" itself, not naked wandering—nevertheless, when it is said that "great yogic power is recollected just like naked wandering," it follows that the naked wandering of the great yogin is what is recollected.

Since this has already been stated, it should be understood as having been said accordingly. Now, one might ask: what is intended by the statement that the status of a great yogin (*mahāyogitva*) is recorded in the Smṛti for those who disregard the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*) due to their engagement in naked wandering (*nagnacaryā*)? The intended grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "The status of a great yogin is recorded in the Smṛti because of the engagement in naked wandering. Consequently, do the two sūtras—"Also [the fact] is recorded in the Smṛti" (*api smaryate*) and "And there is the favoring of a particular [rule]" (*viśeṣānugrahaśca*)—have as their purport the favoring of uncommon attributes (*asādhāraṇadharma*), or...?

The intended connection is that [liberation] results from the yoga of one's own conduct (*svacaryāyoga*) for those who do not depend on the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarma*). Consequently, with the intention of presenting an alternative view—that the two sūtras, "And also because it is seen even in the interval" (*antarā cāpi tu taddṛṣṭeḥ*) and "It is also recorded in Smṛti" (*api smaryate*), have as their purport the independence from the duties of the stages of life—he first refutes that [view]. He does so by stating, "Since knowledge is assisted by the common duties," and thus [refuting] both sūtras.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "the intent is to favor those who share common duties. He refutes the second [position] with the words "by the recollection of the conduct of the insane. The sense is that since a visible purpose is possible—because there is no production of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) through the performance of duties belonging to a specific stage of life (*āśrama*)—the concealment of one's greatness has a purely visible purpose. This is because no other injunction is observed; the sense is: "One should seek the Self through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge. Thus ends the section on the *vidhura*.

"And likewise the animal sacrifice for the *avakīrṇin*"; this refers to Jaimini’s sūtra: "And likewise the animal sacrifice for the *avakīrṇin*, because the time for the *ādhāna* has not yet arrived. Taking as established the expiation in the form of the *Nairṛta* animal sacrifice prescribed by Smṛti for those who are *avakīrṇins*—that is, those who have fallen from their status as a *brahmacārin*—according to the rule "a *brahmacārin* who has broken his vow (*avakīrṇin*) should sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti," fire is introduced therein. The discussion regarding that [fire] is as follows: since the injunction "he offers in the *āhavanīya*" prescribes the *āhavanīya* as the locus for all oblations, [the question arises] regarding the *avakīrṇin*.

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that one should establish the sacred fires (*agnīn*)—either together with the woman with whom he has committed the transgression (*avakīrṇa*), or having taken another wife—and then perform the animal sacrifice for the transgressor (*avakīrṇipaśu*) in the *āhavanīya* fire; [the author] refutes this by noting that since the Smṛti states, "The husband and wife should together establish the fire," the establishment of the fires must be performed by both spouses, and thus its performance together with a paramour is impossible. Furthermore, because marriage is prescribed for one whose Vedic studentship (*brahmacarya*) has not lapsed in the rule, "One who has not broken his studentship should marry a woman of auspicious marks," and because marriage is not permitted for one who has not yet performed the required expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Because the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is impossible [prior to marriage], the animal sacrifice for one who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇipaśu*) must be performed in the ordinary fire (*laukikāgni*), just like the *upanayana* oblation; this was established in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*). Since the *upanayana* oblation is performed in the ordinary fire—given that marriage, which occurs after the *samāvartana*, is impossible before the *upanayana*, and thus a student lacks the *āhavanīya* fire due to the absence of *agnyādhāna*—it was determined that the *upanayana* oblation takes place in the ordinary fire. That meaning is referred to in the sūtra by the term "that rule" (*tadvid*).

This [sūtra] is called a *codya-sūtra* (an objection-sūtra) because it is stated thus on account of its purpose being to establish the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) by first demonstrating that this [act] constitutes a minor sin (*upapātaka*) and then establishing the existence of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). However, if its purpose were merely to establish the existence of an expiation, it would simply be a *siddhānta-sūtra* (a conclusion-sūtra). For a general rule does not deserve to be restricted even by a specific Smṛti text such as "one who has ascended to the duty of a perpetual student" (*ārūḍho naiṣṭhikaṃ dharmaṃ*), even though that Smṛti refers specifically to a Brāhmaṇa practitioner of the perpetual vow; for [the general rule] states, "I see no expiation."

Even though the Smṛti has a specific subject matter, it ought not to be restricted [by the Śruti]. For, although the Smṛti concerns a specific type of Brāhmaṇical student (naiṣṭhika), there is a double delay: first, the inference of the absence of expiation based on the non-perception of expiation in the statement "I see no expiation"; and second, the inference of the Śruti based on that [absence]. However, since the Śruti regarding expiation—"He who should strike a Brāhmaṇical student"—functions through a general form, its application to the specific case occurs only through the medium of that generality; thus, there is only a single delay.

The scriptural injunction regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is indeed more authoritative; therefore, the Smṛti statement, "I see no expiation," must be understood as referring to the absence of an expiation that would restore one to social intercourse (*saṃvyavahāryatā*). Consequently, since the Sūtra merely culminates in the existence of expiation, it is designated as a "Sūtra of Objection" (*codyasūtra*). One should understand that the designation "Sūtra of Objection" is stated with the intention that this Sūtra ultimately establishes the qualification for knowledge (*vidyādhikāra*) by means of that [expiation], due to its utility in the present context.

Now, one might object: "Since a prohibition against eating honey is not seen for lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) and others, as it is for those who are still studying (upakurvāṇa), how can there be equality? Anticipating this doubt, the Commentary states: "This has been said by the authors of the Smṛtis."

[Objection: But does he not refer to expiation (*prāyaścitta*)? Indeed, expiation was not previously mentioned; for it was previously stated that one must avoid celibacy, kindling the fire, begging for alms, speaking the truth, [eating] honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, ointments, anointing, riding in vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, idle talk, singing, dancing, and the like, as well as bathing and cleaning the teeth, and avoiding joy. Furthermore, its commentators have stated that "this conduct (*vṛtta*) is to be observed by those in the subsequent stages of life (*āśrama*) as well. [Response: Is this without distinction? No, he says:

Regarding the term "non-contradictory" (*avirodhi*): it refers precisely to that which is not in conflict with one's own stage of life (*āśrama*), such as the avoidance of gambling and similar acts; it does not refer to what is contradictory. Therefore, it has been explained that the tending of the sacred fire (*agnīndhana*) does not apply to the wandering mendicant (*pravrajita*), living in the teacher’s house (*gurukulavāsa*) does not apply to the householder devoted to the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, and the practice of celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*) does not apply to the householder. Consequently, since the topic of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has not been introduced here, it is impossible for the word "this" (*etat*) to refer back to expiation. For this very reason, the phrase "non-contradictory to one's own stage of life" excludes expiations and the like caused by contact with women and other such [forbidden] acts.

If it is argued that the textual passage stating "for householders, provided there is no transgression" is inconsistent because penances and the like for causes such as sexual contact with women have not been mentioned previously, they reply: this is one exception to the penance that will be stated in the section on penances under the extended application (*atideśa*) of celibacy (*brahmacarya*): "One who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇin*) should sacrifice to Nirṛti with a donkey at a crossroads; having put on its skin with the hair turned upward and carrying a red vessel, he should beg for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his deed; after a year, he becomes pure. This is the single exception to that rule.

The Śāstra, by the maxim that "technical definitions and rules of interpretation apply at the time of the performance [of the rite]," attains syntactic unity with that [injunction]; thus, with the intention that the expiation is also extended to the instruction regarding celibacy (*brahmacarya*), it is logical that it refers to the expiation. Now, one might object: since celibacy has been specified, the expiation found in the section on penances—namely, "one who has spilled his seed with a donkey"—can be obtained through the very instruction itself, as it applies equally to both the directly taught and the extended (*atidiṣṭa*) celibacy; therefore, [the rule] "and this is not in conflict with the subsequent ones" [would suffice].

If you argue that, by this [principle], the extended application (*atideśa*) is useless, then surely you have never previously considered the maxim: "Those things taught without reference to a specific context (*anārabhya-vidhāna*) belong to the archetype (*prakṛti*), because of the fault of double-statement (*dviruktatva*). For if that were so, then by the general rule of both the directly taught and the extended application, the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood (*parṇatā*) would also necessarily apply; and since the *juhū* ladle is obtained through the very same extended application by which [the sacrifice] is performed, it is possible for *parṇatā* to be obtained by that same means. Consequently, due to the fault of double-statement, the direct teaching of *parṇatā* in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) would be redundant. If this is the case, then even for the student (*upakurvāṇa*)...

If it is argued that brahmacarya has not been taught [for the student], since it was taught specifically for one who is uninitiated (anupanīta) in the rule, "Before initiation, there is freedom of action, speech, and eating; he is a brahmacārī only in respect of the oblations," whereas for the *upakurvāṇa* (the student living with his teacher), brahmacarya is extended by analogy through the rule, "The aforementioned brahmacarya [applies], as well as tending the sacred fires and begging for alms," and thus, on the grounds that brahmacarya is extended even to the *upakurvāṇa*, only the brahmacarya of the uninitiated would apply to the *prāśitra* by direct instruction and not the brahmacarya of the *upakurvāṇa*—we reply: no, for brahmacarya has indeed been taught [for the former].

And let there not be even a penance [for this]; nevertheless, because the penance taught for one who has not been initiated is extended by the rule, "The student's life of chastity (*brahmacarya*), the kindling of the fire, and the begging of alms have been explained," to the *upakurvāṇa* (the student who returns home), and because there is no fault in its reference by the rule, "And this applies to the subsequent [stages] provided it is not inconsistent," [one might argue]. Now, it may be objected that the common applicability of the fire-sacrifice to the *agniṣṭoma*, *ukthya*, and so forth is taught by direct injunction itself: "From that [fire], they sacrifice with the *agniṣṭoma*; that [fire] with the *ukthya*; that [fire] with the *atirātra*; that [fire] with the *dvirātra*."

Furthermore, just as those desiring qualities such as the form of a hawk (*śyenākṛti*) based on that [sacrifice] become common to all, so too, because the rule "and this is not contradictory for the subsequent ones" (*uttareṣāṃ caitadavirodhi*) is equivalent in its specific reference to passages such as "him with the *ukthya*, him with the *atirātra*," celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is a penance common to all by virtue of its direct injunction (*upadeśataḥ*) alone; thus, there is no acquisition of it through extension (*atideśataḥ*). If you say this is not so, we reply: no, for that is our desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). If an acquisition through direct injunction is obtained for those who require even an acquisition through extension, how could that lead to an undesirable result?

It is argued that an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) capable of causing purification in accordance with the scope of the act as described in the *Bhāṣya* is not possible; thus, the statement of Manu—"One should not dwell with fools, ungrateful persons, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed a woman, even if they are purified according to the Dharma"—means that one should not dwell with them, i.e., one should not engage in mutual dealings such as living together or sharing meals. In this world, there is no restoration [to social standing], though their sin is destroyed: "Whatever sin has been committed through ignorance is removed by expiations."

Because of the traditional legal texts (*smṛti*) stating, "In this world, one becomes excluded from social intercourse (*avyavahārya*) through speech [of censure] arising from intentional desire," and because that which is committed through ignorance is remedied by expiations (*prāyaścitta*), the meaning is that if it is done intentionally, one becomes excluded from social intercourse according to the scriptural statement. Therefore, even the *smṛti* passage, "I see no expiation," has a meaning consistent with that very point. As for the phrase "But others... and so forth: "obstruction" (*pratyavarodhaḥ*) refers to the attainment of a previous stage of life (*āśrama*). The phrase "established as being qualified or unqualified for knowledge" (*vidyādhikārānadhikāra-siddham*) is to be construed with what precedes it.

"By the desire to perform the duties of the previous stage of life" means by the desire prompted by the ease with which the duties of the previous stage—such as sacrifices, oblations, and so forth—are performed. "By passion and the like" means with the intention, "May I be a householder surrounded by a wife, children, and so on."

The meaning is that the reading of the sūtra is: *niyamaśrutyā* (by the scriptural injunction of restriction), *na eṣām tadbhūtasya tu nātadbhāvo jaiminer api niyamāt tadrūpābhāvebhyaḥ*. This means: for one who has become that (*tadbhūtasya*)—that is, one who has entered the higher stages of life (*ūrdhvaretas-āśramān*)—there is no "non-becoming-that" (*nātadbhāvaḥ*), which is to say, no falling away from that state, or no descending back from it. This is because of the restrictive rule (*niyamāt*) such as: "Having exhausted himself completely in the teacher's family, he should go to the forest and not return again."

The sense is that, just as there is a scriptural statement regarding the ascent—namely, "Having completed the student life (brahmacarya), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller"—there is no such scriptural statement regarding descent. Furthermore, the meaning is that there is an absence of the practice of the learned (śiṣṭācāra). Thus, by means of the restrictive scripture (*niyata-śruti*) and by the non-existence of anything other than that state, they establish the lack of authoritative basis for descending [from the higher stages]. Immediately after the phrase "they establish its lack of authoritative basis," [the text continues with] "nor... [and so on].

In some editions, the reading "adhikārikam api" is seen, where a subsequent section (*adhikaraṇāntara*) is interpreted as concerning the possibility or impossibility of expiation for those who have fallen from their stages of life (*āśrama*), such as the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*); they conclude that expiation is impossible. This is the correct text, because no refutation of this point is stated anywhere later on; furthermore, in the opinion of others, the impossibility of expiation is established as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by the sūtra: "And even that which pertains to office [is not applicable], because of the inference regarding the fallen and because of the impossibility thereof," and then the final conclusion is reached with: "Some say it applies even to those preceded by a transgression."

In the sūtra, "But some [say there is] penance, as in the case of eating forbidden food; that has been explained," the impossibility of penance is raised as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Then, by the sūtra, "Some say it applies even to those preceded by *upa*; as in the case of eating forbidden food; that has been explained," the existence of penance is established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Furthermore, the sūtra, "But outside [the community], in either case," constitutes a separate section (*adhikaraṇa*) intended to establish that even those who have performed penance are unfit for social intercourse. Therefore, this is not a restatement of another's opinion.

The phrase "it ought to be so" is due to a scribal error; however, some say that this passage intends to show the impossibility of a penance that would restore one to social intercourse, because in the section beginning with "But outside [the village], in both ways," it is established that even one who has performed penance remains unfit for social intercourse (*asaṃvyavahāryatā*).

The phrase "in the case of existence and contradiction with the means of valid knowledge" (sadbhāve pramāṇaviruddhatve ca) means "in the case of being authoritative and not being authoritative. The sense is that the doubt regarding the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) is untenable, because there is no reason to raise a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) against the first section, which consists of its being authoritative. "In the investigation of the root" (*mūlavicāre*) means that the single section [of the *Tantravārttika*] contains the logic set forth in the subsequent sūtras that provide the final determination, specifically concerning the investigation of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) that constitutes the root. "The investigation as to whether there is a lapse or not" (*pracyutir asti na veti vicāraḥ*) means the investigation as to whether the lapse is authoritative or not authoritative.
Thus concludes the section concerning that which has become such (tadbhūtādhikaraṇa).

It has been stated that [meditations] have ritual action as their constituent part and depend upon it; therefore, the meaning is that since the meditation based on the *godohana* vessel—which depends on the act of fetching water—lacks the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *udgītha*, the *udgītha* is merely its substratum (*āśraya*) and does not possess the status of being the principal element (*aṅgin*).

The meaning is that, according to the Bhāṣya, the fruit of the meditation on the *udgītha* is heard to reside in the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This is an illustration [of the principle]: in the section concerning the rule "Because of the connection with the purpose of the action" (*tayā kārmorthasaṃyogāt*), it is established that the fruit of the qualities dependent on the measuring of the *sadas*—which are enjoined by the text, "If he should desire, 'May the sacrificers be showerers of rain,' let him measure the *sadas* low"—belongs solely to the sacrificer. Just as the austerity consisting of "not eating for three days," even though it bears the technical designation (*samākhyā*) of the *adhvaryu*, belongs to the sacrificer, because the austerity [is performed for his sake].

Because they are for the sake of accomplishing the primary fruit, and because the primary fruit belongs to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*), likewise the fruit of the auxiliary parts of the rite also accrues to the sacrificer alone. Why? Because of the connection with the purpose: from the use of the middle-voice ending (*ātmanepada*) in the word "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), it is heard that the fruit of both the auxiliaries and the primary rite belongs to the sacrificer; and since it has been established that even the fruits resting on the auxiliaries are accomplished by him through a mediated succession, the fruit of the meditations (*upāsana*) resting on the auxiliaries also accrues to the sacrificer. Therefore, it should be understood that the fruits such as rain mentioned in passages like "it rains, it rains indeed" also accrue to the sacrificer.

"Of the *godohana* which is its substrate (*tadāśrayasya*). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which this is the substrate. For the Mīmāṃsakas, the term "substrate" (*āśraya*) is used only in reference to that which is being produced (*nirvartya*), because they maintain that a quality attains the status of a causal factor (*kārakatva*) only when it is something yet to be brought into existence. Therefore, the meaning is that it is impossible to treat [the substrate] as something already accomplished by way of being the producer.

In the commentary, the phrase "of that which has become a means to the fruit" (*bhāṣye phala-sādhanabhūtasya*) means "that which has come into being" (*bhūtasya prāptasya*), i.e., that which is joined with qualities such as the *godohana* vessel or meditations (*upāsanā*) that serve as means to the fruit. Alternatively, the term "subsidiary" (*aṅga*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those things dependent upon the subsidiary; thus, the intention of the authors of the commentary is that the meaning of the sūtra "For he is hired for that" (*tasmai hi parikriyate*) is that the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth is a priestly function (*ārtvijya*), and therefore the meaning of the sūtra is: "He is hired from that [function] as a priest."

It is understood from the Bhāṣya that the ritual action, along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga-karma*), is to be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); however, one should not argue that this would imply the primary act—the sacrifice (*yāga*), which consists essentially of the renunciation of a substance (*dravya-tyāga*)—must also have the priests as its performers. For, since the priests lack the capacity to renounce the sacrificer’s own substance, it is determined by the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and by functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) that the agency of the priests pertains only to acts other than the renunciation of the oblation and the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

If the restriction on the agent were based solely on the capacity or incapacity of the person—as in the rule that the *ṛtvij* must not be anyone else—then since the duties of the *adhvaryu* and others could also be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it would follow that those acts belong to the sacrificer. Consequently, according to the logic of the second prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section concerning the principle that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer," it would result in the conclusion that even an incapable sacrificer acts through the mediation of the *ṛtvij*. Therefore, it is precisely by the force of the injunction regarding the hiring (*parikraya*) of priests that the subsidiary acts (*aṅga*) have agents distinct from the sacrificer.

It must be stated that such a statement is no different even in the case of *upāsanā* (meditative worship); this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "based on a scriptural injunction": the sense is that it is by the force of the injunction—"One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with a *godohana* vessel"—which prescribes the *godohana* as an instrumental factor (*kāraka*) in the act of fetching performed by the *adhvaryu* priest; for if the *godohana* were not the object of an activity performed by the *adhvaryu*, its status as an instrumental factor would be impossible. This is the intended meaning.

In the present case, however, it should be understood that the status of the priests as the performers [of the rite] is established by the force of the statement regarding their hiring (*parikraya*); for it is only when [the rite] is subordinate (*aṅga*) that the priesthood serves as the agent. The meaning is that since the priests who have received the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are subordinate to the performance of the primary rite along with its subsidiaries—which is denoted by the term *bhāvanā*—they cannot possibly be the agents in the case of desires for specific qualities (*guṇakāma*).

The sense is as follows: since even meditation—which is an auxiliary (*aṅga*)—cannot be performed outside the ritual application because it is useful for the action performed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), there is no difference in its being included within that ritual application; furthermore, since it is understood that the hiring of priests (*parikraya*) serves all intended purposes, it is established that the meditation on the *udgītha* is also to be performed by the officiating priest. The phrase "like sprinkling and so forth" refers to qualities such as the measuring of the *sadas* shed, which is established by the injunction, "One should measure the *sadas* with reed-measures," where the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes these.

"By the principle of the first and the majority" means by the principle that "what applies to one [member] of a class applies likewise to the others. The principle of the first and the majority is also concluded right here: "Therefore, the Udgātṛ who knows thus should say [to the sacrificer]. The form of the Supreme Self, taught as being in the sun and in the eye, along with the two fruits—the attainment of the world of the gods and freedom from all evil—is what the learned Udgātṛ should say to the sacrificer, asking: "For what desire of yours—whether pertaining to this world or the next—what fruit having in view? should he perform it?
"I shall sing" means "I shall perform the singing accompanied by meditation conducive to that fruit";

for it is this very Udgātṛ who is the master of the "singing according to desire"—that is, of the singing accompanied by meditation which is the means for attaining the desired fruit—the meaning being that he who knows thus, knowing the nature of the Supreme Self as taught in its cosmic (adhidaivata) and personal (adhyātma) aspects, sings the Sāman.

The point here is that since it is clearly understood that the meditation performed by the *udgātṛ* priest alone produces a fruit for the patron (*yajamāna*), and since the patron can be considered the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛ*) because the priests are hired laborers, the maxim "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer" is not contradicted.
Thus concludes the section on the Master.

Even though reflection (*manana*) is of the nature of an activity, [it is like the *yamas* and so forth]; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Furthermore, immediately after the statement that it has a different meaning in the form of reflection, the fact that the word "muni" is seen used for Vyāsa and others who are habitually engaged in intense reflection supports its having a different meaning. If the reading "na iti" exists, it provides a clear explanation.

The question is whether reflection (*manana*) is fit to be enjoined or not; the implied sense is that it is like all the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*), which constitute auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā*) by being subordinate members of the knowledge-constituent, because this very point is the subject matter of this section (*adhikaraṇa*), and because the concluding commentary—“therefore, for one remaining in all the stages of life”—serves as direct evidence. In the phrase “whether reflection,” the word *manana* refers to meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*); it should be understood that the same applies to what follows as well.

The phrase "contradiction with scriptural injunctions such as sacrifice" means contradiction with scriptural injunctions such as sacrifice that establish unrighteousness (*adharma*) as the locus [of action]; nor should a lack of relevance to the present context be suspected regarding this doubt, for [the discussion concerns] that which has all the stages of life (*āśrama*) as its constituent parts.

Since *mauna* (the practice of silence) is enjoined as another auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*), just like the duties of all the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*), there is no lack of consistency with the subject matter at hand. Furthermore, could the mention of only a few [duties] not be based on a disregard for those not mentioned? Thus, in the Vājasaneyaka, the instruction regarding the duty of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*)—namely, "one should live as a seeker" (*yakṣaṃ caret*)—is intended to exclude the duties of the householder stage (*gārhasthya*) prescribed in the Chāndogya, such as "studying one's own Veda while in a pure household in a clean place," and so forth. In this way...

The scriptural passage concerning the duties of the householder found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is intended for the purpose of excluding the duties and other characteristics of the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) prescribed in the Vājasaneyaka; that is to say, it is for the purpose of rejecting those duties not mentioned in its own specific context.

The meaning of this is as follows: since *manana* (reflection) is contrary to such scriptural injunctions as those concerning sacrifice (*yajña*) and so forth, it is unfit to be enjoined; therefore, because *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is independent of the duties of all stages of life (*āśrama*), reflection (*manana*) cannot be enjoined by using the duties of the stages of life as an analogy within the knowledge that has those duties as its constituent parts. Consequently, the word "muni" in the phrase "then [he becomes] a muni" cannot be an injunction for reflection, but rather is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the asceticism (*tapas*) and scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) already established; thus, the result would be that the stage of life (*mauna*) is being restated. Such indeed is the sequence: what then is *mauna* in this sentence?

Is it enjoined or restated? Is "munitude" (mauna) merely scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), or is it something else in the form of reflection (*manana*)? Does the observation of the word "muni" being used for Vyāsa and others—who were habituated to superior reflection—strengthen the view that it is something distinct [from scholarship], or not? Likewise, is reflection capable of being enjoined as a constituent part of knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of being an auxiliary to knowledge, like all the duties of the various stages of life (*āśrama*) which are themselves constituents of knowledge? And for that purpose, is knowledge possessed of all the duties of the various stages of life as its constituent parts, or not?

And for that purpose, there arises the question: Is there a contradiction between knowledge (*vidyā*) and the duties (*dharma*) of all the stages of life (*āśrama*), or not? Does knowledge exclude all ritual actions (*karman*), or not? Furthermore, is the instruction on the duty of wandering mendicancy in the Vājasaneyaka—"one should lead the life of a mendicant"—and the instruction on the duty of the householder in the Chāndogya—"studying the sacred texts while in a pure household at a clean place"—intended to exclude the duties of the other stages of life not mentioned in their respective contexts, or is it intended to indicate those unmentioned duties of the stages of life? When [this doubt arises]...

If it were intended as a mutual exclusion, then, since knowledge depends upon the duties of all stages of life (*āśrama*) and thus can have the duties of all stages as its constituent parts, [the injunction] would apply to knowledge that has the duties of all stages as its constituents; therefore, in all stages of life...

The reflection on the Dharma (*dharma-bhāvanā*) is not something that requires an injunction; and if the observation of the use of the word "sage" (*muni*) in the case of Vyāsa and others—who possess the nature of superior reflection—strengthens the view that it has a different meaning [from the mere absence of worldly activity], then, because such scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) has not yet been attained, it must be enjoined. In the Bhāṣya, it is understood as being a concomitant of knowledge (*vidyā-sahakāritvena*). Therefore, the employment of the example "like the beginning of knowledge" (*vidyā-ādi-vat*) pertains only to the aspect of it being another concomitant factor (*sahakāry-antara*), and not to the aspect of it being an injunction (*vidhitva*); the point is that the status of knowledge and so forth as an example applies only to the aspect of it being another concomitant factor for the sake of enjoining further concomitants.

If there is a desire to state [the meaning], then the phrase "like the injunctions and so forth" (vidhyādivat) should be explained as meaning "like childhood and old age" (bālyapāṇḍityavat); this is because those two possess the nature of being like injunctions and so forth—this is how it should be understood. Regarding the word *pākṣipa* in the commentary, its meaning is "one whose nature is to reflect intensely" (*prakṛṣṭamananashila*), and the term *pākṣipaprayoga* means "employment by way of a partial view" (*pakṣeṇa prayogaḥ*).

Alternatively, *pakṣa* means embracing (*parigraha*). The verbal root *√pakṣ* signifies acceptance with reverence; for by that, movement is intensified. This intensification of reflection consists in its continuous persistence, characterized by affection, as in the case of a heroine or hero who have been long separated. Furthermore, this refers to the repeated contemplation of the auspicious support—the form of the Lord and so forth—which serves as the objective basis for meditation. And that too is solely for the sake of the perfection of knowledge (*vidyā*), because even during the time of meditation, [this intensification is necessary].

Through one-pointed concentration of the mind upon that object, knowledge becomes firm. The sense is that for one who, during intervals between periods of meditation, is possessed by other thoughts, knowledge will not become firm because other objects previously contemplated enter into the mind even at the time of meditation. Regarding the phrase "having understood [the truth] as pure and complete" in the Commentary: *paṇḍā* means the intellect capable of reasoning through inquiry and refutation (*ūhāpoha*); one in whom this has arisen is a *paṇḍita*; his activity is *pāṇḍitya*. This occurs after hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*).

By virtue of proficiency gained through that practice, [he possesses] an intellect capable of reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*), shining with ever-new flashes of insight, which—through its conformity to the meaning of what has been heard and what is yet to be heard—is supremely intent upon establishing the purport of the *Upaniṣads* at all times. [He does this] "by means of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) throughout his life according to the duties of a householder. The word *āvadāyuḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose life is as long as it lasts" (*āvadāyur yasya*).

"Dependent on time": the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used according to the rule *kālādhvanor atyanta-saṃyoge* ("time and distance [take the accusative when there is continuous connection]"); the meaning is that "mauna" (silence/monasticism) consists of an excellence of knowledge. However, regarding the statement "mauna is the forest-dweller's stage" (*vānaprastha*), although that term refers to the subsequent stage of life (*uttarāśrama*) due to its association with other words denoting stages of life and by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the intention here is that the word *mauna* signifies only an excellence of knowledge. "Even though childhood and so forth are predominant" means even though childhood and so forth are the primary factors.

"Because there is no distinction in the instruction" means that [the status of the forest-dweller] is established by such passages as, "Austerity is the second [type of student], and one who dwells in the teacher's family is the third. "The plural number" refers to the plural number used in the Sūtra. "The contingency of having to supply a word ending in the genitive case" means [the contingency of supplying a word like] "of the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other sacrifices," just as in the case of the term *vidhyādi* (beginning of the injunction). If it is argued: "There is no room for the aforementioned defect, because of the statement of Ācārya Vācaspati Miśra that the word *vidhyādi* denotes the primary [act], while the word *vidhyanta* denotes the subsidiary [acts]; therefore, 'like the beginning of the injunction' means 'as in the beginning of the injunction,' i.e., as in the primary act," we say: No, because of the [text] regarding the injunction (*vidhi*)...

The intended meaning is that, just as the word *anta* (end) is not well-known in the sense of a primary limb (*aṅga*), so too the word *vidyādi* (beginning of knowledge) is not well-known in the sense of the primary [object]. The phrase "because of its usage in reference to those who perform it" refers to the word *muni*—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. He raises an objection: "And that is established for one possessing knowledge"; the meaning is that for one in whom knowledge has been perfected, the meditation on the auspicious substratum (*śubhāśraya*) is indeed established, because in the absence of that [meditation], there can be no perfection of knowledge. The phrase "because it concerns knowledge already commenced" means that it does not concern knowledge already perfected.

Regarding the objection that the word *brāhmaṇa* does not denote a caste (*jāti*), [the response is as follows]: since the word *brāhmaṇa* does indeed denote a caste, just as there is no status of being a thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) in the phrase "a Brāhmaṇa," so too there is none in the phrase "then a sage" (*atha muniḥ*). One should understand that this criticism was stated with the view that the denotation of the word *brāhmaṇa* as a caste is accepted by the opponents even in their own final position (*siddhānta*), because the denotation of the word *brāhmaṇa* as a caste mentioned in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not rejected in the final position.

Nor should it be said that the meaning stated regarding the *kalpataru* is that a Brāhmaṇa possesses the realization "I am Brahman," for that [interpretation] is a modern invention. The phrase "the explanation of the third sūtra is also incorrect" refers to the system of Bhāskara (this is the ellipsis). "On account of the introduction of wandering mendicancy" means because wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) is the subject under discussion. "After [the mention of] silence, [comes the mention] of the householder's state" refers to the *daharavidyā*.

The meaning is that in the *Chāndogya*, following the instruction on silence with the words, "They call it 'silence,' but it is simply *brahmacarya*," there is a concluding summary at the very end regarding the householder's life with the words, "He, indeed, living thus... The resolution of the second sūtra has already been answered; this is the remainder [of the argument] during the occasion for refuting the opposing view. Thus ends the section concerning the injunction of another auxiliary practice (*sahakāryantaravidhi*).

The statement that "childlikeness" (*bālya*) consists in an action characterized by the non-manifestation of one's own nature should not be questioned as to how a non-manifestation, being of the nature of an absence, can constitute the meaning of the word "childlikeness. This is because the term "non-manifestation" refers specifically to a particular action that is the opposite of manifestation. The meaning is that such a rule is observed specifically for one established in this stage of life; that is to say, for one established in the knowledge of Brahman. Thus ends the section on Non-Manifestation (*anāviṣkārādhikaraṇa*).

In the Bhāṣya, it is stated: "Meditation (*upāsana*) which has prosperity as its fruit occurs in this life (*aihika*), provided there is no obstruction of what is not yet begun. This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here: meditation having prosperity as its fruit becomes *aihika* when there is no obstruction of what is not yet begun. The meaning is that "having prosperity as its fruit" refers to results other than liberation (*mukti*). Thus, because the discussion of meditation whose fruit is liberation will be introduced later under the heading "the non-fixity of the fruit of liberation," all forms of meditation other than that are intended here. "*Aihika*" means occurring in this birth; it is precisely this term "*aihika*" [that is being explained].

The phrase "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*) means in this very life; however, one should not object that if the word *aihika* from the Sūtra is intended merely to indicate the probandum (the result), then there is a contradiction with the *Ṭīkā*, which states: "Does the meditation with results in this life (*aihika-phala-upāsana*) arise immediately after its own preparatory rites? This is because the word *aihika* in the *Ṭīkā* is distinct from the word *aihika* in the Sūtra, insofar as the former is a *lakṣaka* (indicative) term referring to any result in general, whether pertaining to this life or the next (*aihikāmuṣmika*). For the word *aihika* in common usage [refers to] "here" (*iha*)...

They employ the term *aihika* both for the present birth (*janman*) and for existence (*bhava*). However, the word *aihika* in the Sūtra refers here to the present birth, because that is its primary established usage. For this very reason, in the section on the accomplishment of yoga (*yogasiddhi-adhikaraṇa*), they establish that rites such as the *kārīrī* sacrifice and those intended for immediate results are indeed *aihika*; whereas the attainment of heaven is exclusively *āmuṣmika*. Regarding fruits in the form of cattle, sons, and so forth, they are *aihika* when there is no obstacle, but *āmuṣmika* when there is an obstacle. In this context, *aihikatva* means fitness for this very birth, while *āmuṣmikatva*...

The term "nāma" [in this context] signifies being experienced in another birth; it does not mean "extraordinary" (alaukikatva) or "pertaining to the next world" (pāralaukikatva), because it is not established that cattle, sons, and so forth are things pertaining to the next world. Consequently, the word "aihika" (pertaining to this world) in the Sūtra refers to the probandum (sādhya).

It is more appropriate that [the word *aihika*] is intended as a specification; for if it were accepted as a qualification of the subject (*pakṣa*), one would have to say that the word *aihika* indicates the means of attaining results in this life. Even in that case, in order to include meditations whose fruits are in the next world, one would have to resort to its being intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*). Furthermore, a word expressing the thing to be accomplished (*sādhya*) would have to be supplied (*adhyāhartavya*). If that word were intended to specify the thing to be accomplished, there would be no need to supply it, because the subject consisting of meditation is already under discussion—thus there is consistency. Some, however, [hold that it refers to] in this birth...

The mere fact that [something] "comes into being" (*sambhavati*) is not the probandum (*sādhya*), such that this [word] would serve as its indicator; rather, it is the state of arising immediately after the performance of the ritual act (*sādana-anuṣṭhāna-kālāvyavahita-utpattikatva*). For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states: "It arises immediately after the merit (*puṇya*). Consequently, a word expressing the probandum must necessarily be supplied for all purposes. Therefore, [the result] has enjoyment as its fruit within the sphere of the *prakṛti*. Indeed, the word "here" (*iha*) denotes proximity, in relation to the world of the gods (*magavat-loka*) which is to be reached by the liberated.

The enjoyment of ordinary objects is justified as being denoted by the term "of this world" (*aihika*) because of the proximity of those objects of enjoyment and their instruments; nor does this entail the improper application of the word "of this world" to the heavens (*svarga*), for there is no fault in its usage when intended to convey such a meaning. Thus ends the section on "that which belongs to this world" (*aihikādhikaraṇa*).

The contradiction lies in the mere fact that [the meditation] is not a subject of meditation for this life (*aihika-upāsanā*) according to our own view; for, since it is a subject of meditation whose fruit is distinct from liberation (*mukti*), the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*) concerns only meditation for this life, whereas according to the opponent's view, it concerns all [meditations]. This is the meaning of the contradiction. "At the fall of that body" means at the fall of the body [attained through] knowledge (*vidyā*). The phrase "because gradation is possible in the case of direct realization" implies that even though there is no gradation in the result (*sādhya*), because there is gradation in the means (*sādhana*), the lack of restriction in the form of delay or non-delay is logically established. This is the intended sense.
Thus concludes the section concerning the fruit of liberation.

Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the Bhāvaprakāśikā, a commentary on the Śrutiprakāśikā, composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads.
And the chapter is completed.
The total number of topics is 123; the total number of sūtras is 468.

The meaning is that for the purpose of making known the relationship of the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), it is only when both related members are presented within a single locus (*ekādhyāsa*) that their subsumption under a single cognition is possible. The word "iti" functions as a causal particle (*hetu*), and the word "ca" (and) is displaced in its position; thus, the sense is that because there is a state of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*) in relation to *karmayoga*, reflection (*cintā*) is appropriate here.

The reading is "the purpose of the scripture is accomplished once" (*sakṛtkṛtaṃ śāstrārthaḥ*), because there is no evidence for repeated performance (*asakṛdāvṛtti*) in the Bhāṣya. For this very reason, in the *Pūrvatant*ra, regarding the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, after setting forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that they should be performed again and again by one desiring an abundance of results—based on the inference, "or like a sacrifice, there would be an abundance of results through repetition"—it was concluded with the siddhānta, "or [they are performed] once, because the cause is one," that the task is fulfilled by performing them only once.

The sense is that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that there is no repetition, because there is no evidence for an increase in the fruit when the mere constituent parts of the means to perfection (*siddhi*) are repeated. For this very reason, the doubt that—on the analogy of agriculture where fruits accrue with each new undertaking because the action is not yet completed—there should be a repetition of knowledge (*vedana*) for the sake of a greater abundance of fruit, like the repetition of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*), is refuted; for there is no gradation (*tāratamya*) in the fruit that is liberation (*mokṣa*).

The sense is that it is like the case of threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*. According to the principle that when a visible result is possible for what is heard in scripture—as in the injunction "one threshes the rice"—it is improper to postulate an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*), threshing is for the sake of producing the rice-grains required by the sacrifice; and since the production of rice-grains is impossible without the repetition of threshing, the repetition of threshing must be performed even though it is not explicitly stated. This was established [in the *Bhāṣya*] with the words: "Since actions are subordinate to a purpose, there would be completion upon the direct accomplishment of that [purpose]. It is just like that, according to the *Bhāṣya*. Upāsana... [is like that].

Regarding the phrase "it is to be combined": one might argue that, according to the logic of the goat-sacrifice (*chāgapaśunyāya*), since the word "knowing" (*veda*) in the Saṃvarga-vidyā passage—"He who knows what he knows"—is concluded by the context of the concluding statement "the deity which you meditate upon," it may indeed result in being reduced to the nature of meditation (*upāsanā*). However, this alone does not establish the repetition of the knowledges of Brahman taught in the *Ānandavallī* and other sections, because the vidyās are distinct; for the injunction of repetition for the Jyotiṣṭoma during each spring does not imply the repetition of the Dvādaśāha and other such sacrifices. If this is the objection:

You have fallen into error. If it were being established that because repetition is heard in the case of one particular knowledge, there must likewise be repetition in other forms of knowledge as well, then this objection would be valid; however, it is not established here in that manner. Rather, based on an indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of a statement made for another purpose—which takes the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*) assuming as established that what was introduced by the verb *vid* (to know) is accomplished through *upāsana* (meditative worship)—the word "knowing" (*vedana*) in the Vedāntas refers to repeated knowing. As it is said: "Neither good action nor evil action [remains]; all evils turn back from here."

Furthermore, because the word *pāpmā* (evil) in the Vedāntas refers to merit (*sukṛta*) as well—based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the reference to the word *pāpmā*—the word *pāpmā* is common to both merit and demerit (*duṣkṛta*). Consequently, when it is stated that [the Self] has "risen above all evils" (*sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhya uditaḥ*) or is "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmā*) and so forth, the objection that the word *pāpmā* is common to both merit and demerit does not apply to such observations.

Regarding the phrase "he who knows that," everything that ought to be said has been set forth in the *Laghusiddhānta*; it should be consulted therein, as it bears the same meaning as the *Bhāṣya*. The meaning is: "in the injunctions for the means to liberation. It may be asked: "Is not the maxim 'the goat [is the animal] because of the wording of the mantra' intended here? Indeed, since the mantra "of the goat, the omentum... is perceived as a permanent (nitya) auxiliary (*aṅga*), one should not disregard its status as such; thus, the general [rule applies].

It is appropriate that the word "animal" (*paśu*) in the mantra concludes with the specific form of a goat based on the wording of the mantra; however, in this case, since it is not required that the injunctions for the means to liberation—such as knowing, blowing [the breath], and meditating—which are taught in various contexts, should all conclude with a single purpose, how can the logic of the "goat animal" (*chāgapaśu*) apply here? Nor should it be argued that if certain meditations were means to liberation without requiring repetition, it would follow that the injunctions for meditation and other such means to liberation would lack authority due to being non-informative (*ananuṣṭhānalakṣaṇāprāmāṇya*).

If it is argued that—since knowledge (*vidyā*) which is independent of repetition, like *prapatti*, can be established as having a specific qualification characterized by great confidence, and since there is no necessity for injunctions such as "knowing" (*vedana*) to culminate in meditation (*dhyāna*)—we say no; for even if one were to postulate a specific qualification for *prapatti* on the strength of evidence that cannot be otherwise explained, there is no such postulation of a specific qualification in the case of the injunctions regarding "knowing. Consequently, since it must necessarily be stated that the injunctions of "knowing" culminate in a single purpose, the *chāgapaśu-nyāya* (the logic of the goat and the animal) applies.

"Because there is no defect. Regarding the phrase "of the act of instruction," the intended meaning is that the repetition of the mere act of instruction is what is meant, and not the repetition of an act of instruction qualified by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth; thus, the point is that there is a repetition of the act of instruction in the injunction, "He is to be heard, he is to be reflected upon, he is to be meditated upon. "By merely two or three repetitions" means that one has achieved the goal even with only two or three [repetitions] of the Veda.

The statement "accompanied by knowledge, feeling, and words" refers to those who deliberate on whether repetition (*āvṛtti*) is required for hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). That [position] is incorrect; this appears well-connected if read immediately after the word "that is improper," though the reading should be examined. Now, one might object: "We maintain that the immediate nature of the object arises from the repetition of a cognition whose content is an object of direct perception; therefore, there is no deviation in the case of the repetition of the cognition of the meaning of the *jyotiṣṭoma* sentence. To this, he says: "one..."

Regarding "the moon": the sense is that it is impossible to express any difference [between the two moons], provided there is a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference. Regarding "by the removal of conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpohena*): the meaning is for the sake of ascertaining the falsity of difference, preceded by the exclusion of the conceptualization of difference as real. The sense is that in the cognition of falsity—defined as being the counter-positive of a negation residing in a locus already apprehended—the cognition of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is inseparable. He now refutes *samādhi*, which consists in the dissolution of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because it would entail the refutation of the injunctions for hearing and so forth, which are intended for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence.

The meaning is that the method of *samādhi* is untenable because the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—which brings about the cessation of bondage—is contrary to the *samādhi* you favor, which consists in the destruction of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Furthermore, one should not entertain the doubt that the objections regarding the omniscience of the liberated one and the objection regarding the "excess of blindness" for the liberated one are merely incidental; however, some believe that certain sentences have been misplaced here.

"One should revolve the manifoldness of the rays"—this is a statement by Kauṣītaki addressed to his son: "O son, you should revolve the rays and the sun as non-different," meaning "you should meditate upon them as one. This is what is meant by "meditation through identification" (*ahaṅgrahopāsanā*), which means meditation on the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
Thus ends the section concerning repetition (āvṛttyadhikaraṇa).

The meaning is that, for the purpose of making known the interchange (*vyatikara*) of the terms *vidyā* (knowledge) and *upāsti* (meditation), the definition of the word *ātman* occurring in the sentence taken up in the previous section—"One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self'" (*ātmety evopāsīta*)—is now being performed. In reality, however, the meaning is that this is done to make known the absence of these interchanges being injunctions for a mental vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*), by way of showing them to be merely forms of instruction regarding such interchanges, as in: "O venerable deity, I indeed am you; O venerable deity, you indeed are I," and "One should meditate [on the Self] as 'I am the Self.'"

The meaning is that the nature of the reality previously introduced—which was established in the first three chapters as the cause of the world and as the object of meditation—as being the referent of the word *ātman* found in Vedāntic passages, is now being defined and substantiated. Consequently, any doubt as to how this section could be concerned with defining the meaning of a word is also dispelled. The phrase "by way of grammatical coreferentiality with the sense of 'I'" (*ahamarthasāmānādhikaraṇyena*) means "by way of the quality of being the 'I'"; or, with the intention of presenting the alternative view beginning with "or else," he asks: "What is the object of meditation, the Brahman?"

"To be meditated upon as distinct" means to be meditated upon as being devoid of the relationship characterized by the status of body and embodied one (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*). Regarding the phrase "contradiction with the contemplation of separateness": the sense is that the contemplation of separateness—as in the statement, "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct"—is contradictory to the contemplation of the status of being a body, which consists in being a non-separately established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

When the phrase "thinking separately" (*pṛthaṅmanveta*) is construed with the action of thinking—as in "thinking separately"—the resulting meaning is that the thinking of the self and the thinking of the impeller are two distinct effects. Consequently, the entry of the self and the impeller into a single act of thinking is excluded; therefore, there is no room for the contemplation of the relationship between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) as body and self. For if there were such a contemplation of the body-self relationship, it would follow that both enter into one and the same act of thinking, which would contradict the notion of "thinking separately."

This is the sense. Since meditations on Brahman have been enjoined—as seen in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā where there is the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman," and the grammatical distinction (vyadhikaraṇya) in "This is my Self"—there is no room for the suspicion that these are merely injunctions for mental visualization (dṛṣṭi-vidhi), because that would contradict the intended meaning. Therefore, the point is that this particular inquiry is not applicable there.

The opponent’s position is as follows: since the contemplation of non-selfhood—in the form of being established separately—is prescribed as a means to liberation, non-selfhood alone is what is supported by valid authority; therefore, the injunction "one should meditate [on the self] as the Self" must be a rule for a visionary meditation (*dṛṣṭividhi*) whose fruit is worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Regarding the phrase "with the intention of expressing the referent of the word 'I'," the meaning is that when there is an intention to express the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) as the referent of the word "I," then because primordial matter alone is the agent of the action of existence, the first person singular suffix is used.

Therefore, it should be understood that this is established by the rule: "When *yuṣmad* is present as a coreferential term, even when [the verb] is in its original form (*sthānin*), the second person ending is used," as in the passage, "O Agni, whatever power you are, may I be that. It is shown to be logical because, prior to the connection with the verb, there is an admission of mutual non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) in cases of coreferentiality, such as "to Viṣṇu, the most excellent" (*viṣṇave śiṣiviṣṭāya*). Thus, here too, there is a connection of non-difference.

The meaning is that within that non-difference, there is the existence of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*). [An objection is raised: "Since it is based on authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikatvāt*), a refutation is impossible. Even if one establishes that the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*) has the nature of God (*īśvara*) by negating its state as a transmigrator, there is no consequence of the non-existence of God, because [the opponent] does not admit the establishment of God having the nature of the transmigrating soul. This is another refutation that has been presented. Nevertheless, this refutation—namely, "because it is based on authoritative means of knowledge"—is merely an object of ridicule.

It should be understood that the intended meaning of the phrase "because sublation is consistent with the logical argument" (*tarka*) is as follows. Furthermore, it should be understood that by stating "that is you alone" and "you alone are that," the identity of the Lord (*Īśvara*) with the transmigrating self (*saṃsāryātman*) is being established. The remainder of the sentence is: "Because the world fears the scripture, there would be no inclination toward hearing [it]. [The author] raises an objection regarding the disparity between a rabbit and a buffalo in a dream. [He says: "If, even upon waking... [the result is that] for the individual soul (*jīva*), only the state of being subject to what is to be abandoned (*heyārhatva*) ceases; however, in the case of a dream, both the two substrates (*dharmī*) and the two attributes (*dharma*) cease.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "of the mother-of-pearl-silver and the Lord," one should not object: "How can there be no disparity, given that the nature of the silver is destroyed? For it is accepted that the substrate itself is the nature of the superimposed; and since the nature of the mother-of-pearl is not destroyed, there is no disparity—this is the intended meaning. Thus ends the section on the meditation on the nature of the Self (*ātmatvopāsanādhikaraṇam*).
"The face of Brahman is a qualification of the vision" means that Brahman, which is being meditated upon as independent, is the "face," serving as a qualification for the vision.

But in the case of a servant, the view that he is the King is for the sake of prosperity; "it would be so" is the ellipsis. This is an illustration: in passages such as "one meditates upon the mind as Brahman," because words like "mind" occur first, it is improper to abandon their primary meaning; furthermore, since the word "Brahman" is followed by the particle *iti*, its displacement from its own primary sense is required. Thus, it should be understood that in cases such as "one meditates upon the sun as Brahman," the viewing of the sun and so forth as Brahman is appropriate due to the use of the accusative case.

The phrase "because there would be no contingency of its absence" means "because there would be no contingency of the absence of the symbol (*pratīka*). Although possessing the nature of a *brāhma* body does not by itself destroy the essential nature [of the self], since—according to the reasoning already stated—it is possible for something to be a body without such destruction; nevertheless, that alone is not the cause for being an object of meditation (*upāsya*) as the Self. This is because the very fact of having the nature of *brahman* is what makes it an object of meditation. For if the symbols and so forth were to attain the nature of *brahman*, the contingency of the absence of those symbols would be unavoidable.

If it is argued that this follows as an unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*), we say no; for the intention here is that since insentient things such as the mind (*manas*) would result in having the nature of Brahman, they would be absolutely non-existent, and thus there is no possibility of their being the cause of the absence of a remedy (*pratīkābhāva*).

Regarding the doubt as to whether one should give "clothing" (*vāsaḥ*) and "a cart" (*anaḥ*) by first performing the acts of weaving and carpentry to produce clothing and a cart before giving them, or whether they should be given exactly as they already exist: since the words "clothing" and "cart" are observed to be used when the acts of weaving and carpentry have been performed, these two words—being based on those actions—enjoin the very acts of weaving and carpentry as auxiliary parts of the gift. Therefore, one who performs the act of giving must take threads and wood and perform the weaving and the carpentry.

Since these two words follow the presence and absence of the genus (*jāti*), they are genus-words; however, because the genus is manifested by action, the word is employed after the action has occurred. But in the case of words such as *vāsaḥ* (garment) and *anaḥ* (cart), there is no denotation of an action; therefore, it is established in the seventh book that since the actions of weaving and carpentry are not enjoined, they are not to be performed.

The meaning is that because there is no injunction regarding the *brāhman*, in passages such as "the mind in the *brāhman*," only the meditation (*upāsana*) upon the *brāhman* is enjoined, and not the Self. Nevertheless, one should realize [the object] only in the form in which its meditation is enjoined; for according to the maxim that "whatever is stated is exactly what is to be understood," nothing more should be superadded, lest it lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

"And there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Brahman" means that because Brahman is heard of as the object of meditation, and because in the previous section it was established that in the meditation on Brahman, the nature of being the Self persists everywhere just like truthfulness and so forth. The reason for the redundancy of the particle *iti* is that [the cognition] has the same form as the sentence "one perceives mother-of-pearl as silver"—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the accusative case-ending in the word *pratīpaka* [is used] in the passage: "He who, knowing this thus, [meditates on] the sun..."

The meaning is that in passages such as "He who meditates on will (*saṅkalpa*) as Brahman" and "He who meditates on resolve (*adhyavasāya*) as Brahman," the accusative case-ending is beyond doubt in masculine words such as *āditya* (the sun) and *saṅkalpa*.

The meaning of the section (*adhikaraṇārtha*)—the implied sense—is that the word *hetu* (cause) refers to the fact that the *brahman* alone is to be meditated upon as an independent object, while [terms like] *āditya* serve as qualifiers of the vision (*dṛṣṭiviśeṣaṇatva*). The point is this: if *āditya* and so forth were qualifiers of the vision, then one would expect the passage to first indicate the object of meditation, *brahman*, in the accusative case—as in "One meditates on *brahman* as *āditya*" or "One meditates on *brahman* as *saṅkalpa*"—and only afterwards to mention the qualifiers, *āditya* and so forth, in the nominative case. However, such is not the case here.

Therefore, the meaning is that the accusative case ending in the word *pratīka* and the initial mention [of the *manaḥ* etc. serve as the reason for the conclusion established in this section (*adhikaraṇa*), namely, that the *manaḥ* and so forth are independent objects of meditation, whereas the Brahman is a qualifying attribute of the object of meditation. Thus ends the section on the symbols (*pratīkādhikaraṇa*).

If it is objected that [the connection] is due to the superiority of the deity—given that in the sūtra *brāhmadṛṣṭirutkarṣāt* it was stated that the vision is a qualification of the Brahman alone because of its superiority, and not of deities such as Āditya, which would constitute a connecting link based on an objection—we reply: no. This is because the Brahman is superior to the mind and other organs by virtue of its omniscience, its bestowal of fruits, and so forth; thus, when it is said that the vision of the Brahman should be applied to the mind and other organs, since deities such as Āditya are also superior to the *udgītha* and other elements by virtue of their divinity and so forth, the vision of Āditya and others should likewise be applied to the *udgītha* and other elements.

The sense is that [the result] is indeed established. Because the primary action is enjoined as a means to the fruit, the word "of the primary action" implies "together with its subsidiaries"; therefore, the sense is that even the *udgītha* and other parts which constitute limbs of the *udgītha*-action possess fruitfulness.

The attainment of the deity is merely an intermediate operation, just as the satisfaction of a guest occurs through the guest’s enjoyment [of food]. This is because, according to the maxim "The fruit [comes] from Him (the Supreme Self), for that is logical," the Supreme Self alone is the bestower of the fruit; since it is impossible for other deities—who are merely gratified by the rituals like guests—to be the bestowers of the fruit through their own enjoyment.

The sense is that [the latter] is not primary; and the meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that it is also like the case of the *brāhmaṇa* [meditations], such as the meditation on the Sun. If this passage in the explanation of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is superior, it appears as if well-connected. Nor should one suspect a contradiction with the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "In that case too, the word 'ca' is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*)," because that word, being a particle (*nipāta*), possesses multiple meanings, and because even so, the explanation is logical given that the Sūtra indicates multiple meanings. Now, just as the *udgītha* and other meditations are means to a fruit by virtue of being auxiliary parts of ritual action (*karmāṅga*),...
Since even the Sun and other deities are equally means for attaining results by virtue of their nature as deities, how can there be a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa)? To this he says:

"One should meditate [on the mind] as Brahman," and so forth. The point is that the word *aphala* (fruitless) denotes "that which does not bring about a result," according to a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those for whom no fruit exists. Thus, it refers to those things which are not means for attaining a result.
