If it were argued that—just as in the case of the injunction "one desiring heaven should offer a pap to Aryaman," where although the capacity to bestow results exists for rites enjoined by other injunctions such as those concerning Āditya and others, yet in this context of meditative practice (*upāsanā-prakaraṇa*), because there is no status as a deity (*devatātva*), there is no capacity to bestow results, and therefore the excellence belongs to the *udgītha* and so forth alone since they are the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the fruitful rite—even then, the meditation on Āditya and so forth must be prescribed upon the *udgītha* itself; for meditations involving the co-mention of both constituent and non-constituent parts are [to be applied] to the constituent parts.

Since they have the form of the vision of the Bodiless (anaṅgadṛṣṭi), and because they depend on the subsidiaries (aṅga) impelled by the primary rite (pradhānakarma), it should be understood that even though these [meditations] have independent fruits, their separate application need not be postulated, as they constitute an entitlement for those already entitled (adhikṛtādhikāra); otherwise, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (gaurava) in postulating a separate application. The reading "of the udgītha and so forth, which are of the nature of action" (kriyārūpāṇām) is the correct one; the variant reading "by way of inherence in the ritual act" (karmasamavāyitayā) is due to a scribe's oversight, since the udgītha and so forth are by their very nature of the form of the act of singing.

It should be understood that this is because it is not stated otherwise by others. He states another argument with the words, "This very [verse]," etc. Having stated, "This very *ṛc* is fire, the *sāman*," the subsequent sentence—"That *sāman* is superimposed upon this *ṛc*"—which provides the reason for that, employs the terms *ṛc* and *sāman* for earth and fire; this indicates that in the preceding sentence, earth and fire are to be viewed as the *ṛc* and *sāman*. The underlying idea is that in common worldly usage, one observes the designation of the substratum by means of a word expressing the object superimposed upon it.

The meaning is that there is no use of the word *kṣattṛ* (charioteer) for the superimposed king; that is, when the king is superimposed [upon the charioteer], there is no employment of the word *kṣattṛ*, which denotes the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). In this regard, a reading is occasionally seen stating, "because of the absence of superimposition of the *kṣatriya* [upon the charioteer]," but we do not find it to be consistent. As for the statement that "the action is heard to be more potent," the meaning is that since the scripture declares that only what is performed with knowledge is more potent—based on the text, "Whatever one performs with knowledge"—and since the sun and other such things are not being performed [as actions].

The meaning is that the pre-eminence of the *udgītha* and so forth is established because an object that serves a past or future purpose is intended to be refined (*saṃskārya*); and since the *udgītha* and so forth are ritual actions, and since they will perform assistance for the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other sacrifices, it is those very *udgītha* and so forth that are to be refined by the meditations on the sun and other deities.

"Of the action there is proximity to the *apūrva*"—this means of the action such as the *udgītha* and so forth; and thus, because it serves a purpose, it is logical that it is to be refined (*saṃskārya*) by the meditations on the Sun and so forth—this is the sense. Now, one might object: "The action such as the *udgītha* does not have proximity to the *apūrva*, because only the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*) is proximate to the *apūrva*"; anticipating this, he says: "because that which has not been accomplished cannot function as an instrument."

The sense is that since a principal [action] not assisted by its subsidiaries cannot produce the *apūrva*, the subsidiaries possess proximity to the *apūrva*. Regarding the phrase "because it brings about excellence in the ritual acts," the sense is that because meditation brings about excellence in the ritual acts such as the *udgītha*, the ritual act itself—such as the *udgītha*—is the independent object of meditation. He states another reason: "The Sun and so forth are the principal. Since the word *pradhāna* is eternally neuter in gender, it is referred to in that way; he then provides the justification for this.

By the words "of the fruit of action" (*karmaphalasya*) and so forth, it is understood that the nature of being the *ṛc* (verse) is the predicate to be enjoined. The intention is that if the earth were determined to be the *ṛc*, the arrangement of syllables would be as follows: "This very *ṛc* is the earth. Thus, the word *ṛc* is used for the earth in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*).

The phrase "this very [is] this" is the remainder of the sentence. The meaning of "mere relationship" is that there exists between earth and fire a relationship characterized by the superimposition of what is denoted by the words *ṛc* and *sāman*. "But not excellence" means that it does not depend upon what is superimposed; thus, even in the absence of a word directly denoting the superimposed, the usage of a word denoting the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposed is justified through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is the intended sense.

The phrase "by way of imparting excellence to the ritual acts" means that when the ritual acts are performed, the propitiation of deities such as Āditya serves as the medium for imparting the excellence consisting of the Supreme Lord’s satisfaction; although this passage is not seen in the preceding explanatory texts (*purovāda*), it should nevertheless be understood as stated here in accordance with what is appropriate.

The sense is that there is no contradiction in the statement, "One should meditate on the fivefold Sāman as the worlds," because the meaning of the accusative case is not unconnected [to the action]; thus, by the mere transformation of "in the worlds" (*lokeṣu*) into the accusative, it is like the cases of "One should meditate on speech as a cow" (*vācaṃ dhenum upāsīta*) or "One should meditate on a woman as fire" (*yoṣitam agniṃ dhyāyīta*). The phrase "by one qualified for the sacrifice" (*kratvadhikṛtena*) implies that, like the *godohana* vessel and so forth, this meditation is dependent upon the constituent parts of the sacrifice.

As for the meaning "the earth itself is the *ṛc*, there is nothing else": when it is said "the earth itself is the *ṛc*," the explanatory supplement (*vākyaśeṣa*) "there is no other *ṛc*" is thereby established.
Thus concludes the section concerning the meditation on the Ādityas and others.

The meaning is this: although the two preceding sections are not directly relevant to the purpose of establishing one-pointedness (*aikāgyra*) for the sake of supporting the rules of posture (*āsana*), since one-pointedness of mind is being established here for the sake of supporting the rules of posture, there is no connection with the immediately preceding section—which dealt with meditations connected to the limbs of ritual (*aṅgāvabaddhopāsana*) within the framework of sacrificial action (*karmatantra*) where the support of posture rules is impossible. Therefore, the connection is indeed with the primary subject matter at hand.

It should be understood that a connection with the immediately preceding section is also established in some way, because one considers the restriction of posture in other meditations (*upāsana*) by way of excluding those meditations bound to specific limbs (*aṅgāvabaddha*). Since this was already established in the first section, the intended meaning should be seen as the establishment of one-pointedness (*aikāgraya*) in the words: "And a continuous flow of cognition of that form, free from desire for anything else. He now refutes the interpretation of the sūtra proposed by others [the Pūrva-pakṣin]. The phrase "also because meditation is possible" means "because that [one-pointedness] is necessarily present."

The meaning is that a seat is necessarily required. Now, if it is asked: "But since it is heard in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad that 'one should be situated on a comfortable seat in a secluded place,' how can this prima facie objection arise? [The answer is: because the author of the Sūtras, Śaṅkara and others, as well as others, have not cited that specific passage anywhere, and because our own teachers [have dealt with it] in the section concerning the interpretation of all [Upaniṣadic] explanations.

Some maintain that the *Kaivalya Upaniṣad* is not universally accepted because it has not been cited [in other texts]. Others, however, hold that it is not presented [here] because its subject matter is a specific *dahara-vidyā*, and thus it lacks the status of being common to all meditations (*sarvavidyā*). "Cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass on top"—the meaning is: cloth is the uppermost; the deerskin is superior to the kusha grass; and the kusha grass is superior to the ground. "In a level, pure place, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, which is agreeable to the mind and not distressing to the eyes, and in a cave sheltered from the wind..."

The statement "one should employ [the posture] for the sake of support" refers to this. "Sūkṣmapāṣāṇāḥ" means small pebbles. "Recited in the same context as the seat" (āsanasahapaṭhita) means that it is a constituent part of the seat; the sense is that since no specific place or time other than one-pointedness is heard of, when it is stated that a specific place and so forth conducive to the seat—which is itself conducive to one-pointedness—is required by meditation, what need is there to mention that the restriction of the seat, which has specific places and so forth as its constituents and is required by one-pointedness, is also required? The phrase "in the manner described" implies this by way of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the principle of "how much more so").
Thus concludes the section concerning one who is seated.

The statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "because the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished on that very day," is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). Its meaning is that since the purpose of the scripture has been accomplished through meditation—in the form of devotion whose aspect is identical to direct vision—no further worship needs to be performed thereafter. The opponent's intention is that the scriptural passage, "He, indeed, living thus for as long as he lives," teaches that only ritual actions (*karmāṇi*) are to be performed throughout one's life, and not knowledge (*vidyā*). To this, [the author] replies: "For even there, it is seen [that knowledge is required]. That is, throughout one's life...

The statement that the performance of ritual action results in the fruit of non-return must be explained as being an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of contributing to its very nature. From the force of that statement, it is inferred that the intention there is that knowledge itself is to be practiced throughout one's life. Furthermore, because another scriptural passage—“one should meditate until the end of life” (*prāyaṇāntamabhidhyāyīta*)—is observed, the sense is that meditation (*upāsana*) must be performed according to the literal injunction for as long as one lives, even after the stage of [meditation] identical in form to direct perception (*darśana*).

By this, the following objection is refuted: that because the word *prāyaṇa* is well-known to mean death in accordance with the scriptural text, "One should meditate until the end of life" (*prāyaṇāntamabhidhyāyīta*), the reading of the Sūtra as *āprayāṇāt* (until departure) is incorrect. This is because the word *prayāṇa* is equally well-established in Smṛti texts such as, "At the time of departure, with an unshaken mind," and so forth. The phrase "because the limiting adjunct persists" (*upādheranuvṛttatvāt*) means that the very state of being delimited by the body of a Brāhmaṇa constitutes the limiting adjunct, and that [adjunct] continues to persist. The expression "for one who is liberated there is no desire for liberation" (*muktasya na mumukṣā*) means [it refers to] one who is already liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).

And because joy arises from practice performed according to the scriptures—surely, since it has been stated that "knowledge culminates in meditation," and following the maxim of the goat and the animal, it is the very knowledge that has attained the form of devotion identical in character to direct perception (*darśana*) that is prescribed by the scripture; therefore, repetition must be admitted even by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) until the production of that knowledge identical in character to direct perception—if this is argued, [the reply is: while it is true that repetition up to the point of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) must be admitted, nevertheless, meditation (*upāsana*) does not have direct intuition as its result.

The sense is that the opponent's position—that the meditation should not be performed beyond that point—is logical; for it is taught that [the meditation] has the same form as the vision because it is a means to please the Supreme Person, and since the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by that alone, there is nothing further to be practiced.
Thus concludes the section concerning [the persistence of meditation] until the departure from the body.

"Connection with the Peṭikā" means the connection between the Sādhana-peṭikā and the Kalapa-peṭikā; this removes the objection regarding the lack of connection between the purification of the nature of the Vidyā and the Chapter on the Fruit (Phalādhyāya). [The next term is] Upāya.

The phrase "because there is no doubt regarding non-attachment and destruction" means that it is impossible to state a doubt as to whether non-attachment and destruction are perceived or not. Regarding the commentary's statement "because of contradiction with the scripture," the meaning is that the assumption of those two being the fruits of knowledge is untenable, as it contradicts the scripture which states, "Not until one is liberated does karma perish," thereby establishing that actions are destroyed through experience. Regarding the commentary's statement "because they have different objects," this is an elliptical expression; the traditional teaching that "not until one is liberated does karma perish" is a general rule (*autsargika*).

Because it is accepted that [karma] is to be destroyed by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth, the statement "evil karma does not cling to one who knows thus" must be understood as having a restricted scope when it contradicts specific scriptural injunctions. Its meaning is that [karma] is not destroyed unless there is *brahmavidyā* or an expiation; nor should it be thought that the statement regarding non-clinging is a mere eulogy because knowledge has liberation as its fruit, for if this were a mere eulogy, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation due to the infinity of [past] actions. This is how it should be viewed.

The phrase "previously" refers to the statement that the exhaustion of karma occurs immediately after the fall of the body; the ellipsis to be supplied is "because there is nothing further to be crossed in the next world. The meaning is that the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) has stated that even if the experience of the fruits of karma is not inevitable, once all karma is exhausted through such experience, the knowledge of Brahman produces liberation. The phrase "if it were so" means that [liberation] would depend upon factors such as place and time.

"Because it would follow that the cessation of ignorance (avidyānivṛtti) is non-eternal. [Objection: "But surely there is no consequence of non-eternality because it depends on factors such as time distinct from knowledge. [Reply: No, for since the cessation of ignorance depends on the absence of obstacles in the form of the impossibility of [knowledge arising] apart from knowledge and contrary mental impressions (viparītabhāvanā), the aforementioned consequence of its non-eternality remains the same. "Others, however," and so forth.

For this very reason, the passage beginning with "good and evil deeds" [is stated], meaning that since shaking (vidhūnana) and so forth are impossible regarding the destruction of future demerit (*agha*). The phrase "of future demerit" means the karma consisting of actions such as eating what is forbidden to eat; however, one should not consider it to mean the karma in the form of unseen potential (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by action, because there is no power apart from that [action]. The term "cause of maturation" (*vipākahetu*) refers to maturation as hell and the like.

The sense is that it would be improper to state that "there is a destruction of the portion consisting of *lepa* (adherence)," because the destruction of the ripening (*vipāka*) has already been accepted, which would render the specific mention [of *lepa*] redundant. Thus he raises an objection: "But the adherence of the power of ripening is desired; therefore, there must be a restriction of the statement regarding non-adherence (*aśleṣa*).

[The author replies: "How can there be a restriction of the statement regarding non-adherence here? For in that context, 'adherence to the knowledge of Brahman' (*brāhmī-vidyā-aśleṣa*) means the failure to produce an effect. Consequently, even for that which has arisen, because it does not produce an effect through the knowledge of Brahman, the statement of non-adherence is perfectly consistent. Indeed, the statement of non-adherence does not refer to non-origination."

If it is argued that this statement contradicts the analogy of water on a lotus leaf, it is replied: the Śruti does not say that there is a non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) of sin produced by prohibited actions such that this [objection] would be valid; rather, it says that "evil action does not cling to one who knows thus," thereby declaring the non-clinging specifically of prohibited acts such as eating forbidden food. Furthermore, the non-clinging of that action upon the Brāhmaṇa means precisely that no sin is accumulated by the knower of Brahman, and not that sin is admitted to arise in the knower of Brahman.

The intention is that one must resort to a restriction [of the rule], namely that [the knowledge of Brahman] does not effect the destruction of mere impurities (*lepamātra*). Now, if it is argued that—according to such scriptural passages as "And his actions are exhausted"—there would result only the destruction of prohibited acts such as eating forbidden food upon the destruction of prior *adharma*, we say no; because those actions are momentary and thus perish at that very time, the scriptural statement regarding the destruction of *adharma* refers to the destruction of the sin produced by those prohibited acts. This is evident from passages such as "sinful action does not cling [to him]," where the focus is precisely on the performance of the prohibited.

This is because it must be stated that there is no connection (*aśleṣa*) consisting in the non-earning of effects residing in that [state]. Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the *Upavarṣa* commentary, which states that the four stages are the domain of *śakti* (power); for even that [commentary] has its intended meaning (*tātparya*) precisely in this very point. Thus ends the section on "The Attainment of That" (*tadadhigamādhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is this: by the principle of "thus" (*evam*), there is an extension of the logical rule (*nyāyātideśa*), but not an extension of non-connection (*asaṃśleṣātideśa*), because that has already been indicated by the initial proposition itself. In the passage "all evils" (*sarve pāpmānaḥ*), the author introduces the seed for the category of the word *pāpman* being common to both good and evil deeds. Having first specified "neither good nor evil" (*na sukṛtaṃ na duṣkṛtam*) regarding good and evil deeds, the subsequent specification "all evils" makes it understood that the word *pāpman* is not common to good deeds; such is the final conclusion.

"The stated principle" means the principle intended in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*). It means that it demonstrates the designation (*vyapadeśa*), which is the meaning of the word drawn forward from the previous sūtra. In that context, by the word "thus" (*evam*), the designation of that [result]—which was explicitly stated in the previous sūtra according to the principle of the contradiction with the intended fruit—is also extended by implication. For that designation is the designation of it as a fruit; for in that case, the doubt regarding its non-existence here arises [in the form]: "In one who knows thus, evil action..."

Since it is heard that "it clings [to him], and just as the tuft of *śīka* grass thrown into fire is utterly consumed, even so all his evils (*pāpmānaḥ*) are utterly consumed," and because only evils are mentioned there, the designation [of the *akṣiti*] as being "like that" (*evaṃśabda-anukṛṣṭaḥ*) is not possible.

Therefore, in order to dispel that doubt and for the sake of establishing the designation implied by the word "thus" (*evam*), [the text] first points out both good and evil deeds, and then states generally, "all evils (*pāpmānaḥ*) turn back from here," because it does not reveal even good deeds [as objects of removal] for those seeking liberation; and since the statement "he shakes off good and evil deeds" reveals them as undesirable, they possess the quality of being causes for engagement through having undesirable fruits. Thus, there is also the destruction and non-clinging of good deeds, as expressed in the phrase "all evils are consumed."

The intention is that [the author] demonstrates that there is indeed a designation for the existence of fruits [of action]. As for the statement in the Bhāṣya, "because even well-performed deeds (*sukṛta*) are scriptural," the intention is that since sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Darśapūrṇamāsa are scriptural, they do not mutually cancel one another out. Nor should it be asked, "How can there be this further doubt, given that the destruction of even well-performed deeds is heard specifically in the text, 'He shakes off both his good and evil deeds'?"—for the intention is that that [text] refers to the destruction of well-performed deeds occurring after the fall of the body.
Thus ends the section concerning the other [deities].

The phrase in the Bhāṣya, “only those whose effects have not yet begun,” means those whose bodies born of knowledge (vidyā) or of birth (yoni) have not commenced. This is because the Bhāṣya states that there is no difference heard regarding the fruit [of knowledge]. The meaning is that the scriptural text, “For him, so long...,” is intended solely to demonstrate the brevity of the delay for one who is experiencing [the results], and does not intend to establish a duration; otherwise, if both the absence of delay and the length of time were being established, it would result in a syntactical split (vākyabheda). This is the sense.

The phrase "until I am liberated, then I shall attain [perfection]" means that as long as one is not liberated from *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma), then one will attain perfection; the transposition of the person (*puruṣavyatyaya*) is a Vedic usage. Nor should it be argued that if the word refers to a limit, there would be the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to conveying two meanings—the duration of time and the nature of the limit—because it has already been stated that this is not the case, since this sentence aims merely to establish the limit by restating the duration of time already established in another passage. As for the argument "because of sublation through falsity," it is not so, because knowledge [sublates] only ignorance.

The meaning is as follows: since knowledge is "eliminative" (nivartaka) only insofar as it eliminates ignorance (*ajñāna*) alone, it does not eliminate the *prārabdha-karma* which is an effect of knowledge; therefore, it must be said that such karma possesses the capacity to obstruct the cessation of the ignorance that produced it. For, like ignorance itself, its effects must also be stated to be eliminable; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that it lacks the nature of falsity (*mithyātva*), which consists in being eliminable by knowledge.
Thus ends the section concerning the effects of that which is without rain.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the phrase "since non-performance would result for one who does not desire it" means that there is no desire to perform fruitless action; the sense is that if the *agnihotra* and other rites possessed fruits, then their non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) would not be possible, given such scriptural texts as "by sacrifice" (*yajñena*). Furthermore, since they can be understood as being enjoined for the purpose [of knowledge] prior to the arising of that knowledge which has a form identical to direct perception, there is no evidence that the *agnihotra* and other rites must be performed throughout one's life after the arising of knowledge.

The meaning is that there is no room for Yādava’s position, which holds that the doctrine of combination (*samuccaya*) is untenable; thus, the sūtra "depending on all" (*sarvāpekṣā*) refers primarily to knowledge as a limb [of action], while the sūtra "and by way of being a cooperative cause" (*sahakāritvena ca*) refers to the combination [of knowledge and action] through the removal of obstacles to the fruit.

The objection’s intention is that the scriptural statement regarding "taking over" (*upāyana*) would be rendered objectless, since the subsequent sins and the prior merits and demerits other than those already commenced would be destroyed and not attached [to the self], leaving no scope for such a process. The resolution’s intention is that there is no contradiction between destruction and attachment because "taking over" consists in the production of something of the same nature as the prior merits and demerits that were destroyed or unattached; this meaning has been correctly explained under the sūtra "Upon attaining Him, there is the cessation of both the subsequent and the prior" (*tadadhigama uttarapūrvādyayoḥ*), and should be investigated therein. As for the phrase "But others... and so forth, it is even more so than that.

It is better [to say] "for the sake of the effect called knowledge"; and it should not be argued that, if this were so, the word "effect" (kārya) would be redundant, because it is purposeful as an indicator specifically for that knowledge which produces the attachment of merit (*sukṛta*). Others, however, [say] "of those that have the Vidyā as their auxiliary," and so forth.

The meaning is that the boundary [of the distinction] pertains to the possibility of abandonment regarding those rites—namely, the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) ones performed prior to the arising of knowledge—which serve the purpose of producing knowledge and liberation, as well as those performed immediately thereafter, which are equally principal with knowledge and act as its auxiliaries; this refers to the possibility of "shaking off" (*dhūnute*) expressed in the passage, "He shakes off his good and evil deeds. The point is that the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) does not arise because it is impossible for those acts that are auxiliaries to knowledge to be shaken off by knowledge itself.

The phrase "excluding those performed for specific desires" means that since it is impossible for rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya-karma*) to have liberation as their purpose, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) would not arise [in that context]. The phrase "of those intended for one's own qualification" means "of the injunctions" (*niyoga*). The phrase "because it is not possible for them to have liberation as their purpose" implies that, consequently, the scriptural statement, "Indeed, his work does not perish," must be understood as referring only to those works that act as auxiliaries to knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, both the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion are appropriately concerned with that very subject. The phrase "the subject matter of the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) pertaining to the knower" refers to the lifelong performance of the *agnihotra* and other such rites by the knower.

The sense is that the reflection as to whether these [rites] ought to be performed or not is indeed appropriate. "The statement regarding application" (viniyoga-vacana) means the statement regarding their transition to the *suhṛt* [friend]. "For the sake of the perfection of the rites auxiliary to knowledge" means that we shall establish knowledge in the place of liberation. Thus ends the section on the Agnihotra and other rites.

[The opponent argues: "Because it is heard in the Bhāṣya that [liberation] culminates in the release from this body, and because another Śruti passage is seen stating, 'Having shaken off the body, the self-made one [becomes unmade],' the limit for [the knowledge of Brahman] is the liberation from the body—even though the word 'body' is not explicitly mentioned in the phrase 'for him so long' (tasya tāvad eva) [Chāndogya Up. 6.14.2]. Nor does the phrase 'having shaken off the body' refer only to the body as long as its prārabdha-karma lasts; for the singular number is heard, and there is no intention to express plurality."

It is accomplished at the end [of life], provided that the fruit is to be experienced through multiple bodies; for those two types of karma whose fruits have already begun (*ārabdhaphala*), they must be exhausted by experience alone. Furthermore, the statement, "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released," declares the liberation from those two types of karma through experience, since there is no scriptural injunction regarding a fixed limit other than the body.

Thus, in this manner, the infinite karma—consisting of merit and demerit—that has been accumulated since beginningless time, which was performed prior to the knowledge of Brahman, whose fruits have not yet begun to ripen (*anārabdhaphala*), perishes through the majesty of that knowledge. Furthermore, karma performed after the commencement of knowledge does not adhere to the knower. In this regard, it is faultless that "all his merits are seized by those who love him, and his sins by those who hate him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1). The section concerning the exhaustion of other [karma] is concluded.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

The sense is that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such an assumption; furthermore, because in another scriptural passage—"rising up from this body"—the qualification "from this" indicates that the body which is the source of knowledge is intended, otherwise that qualification would be rendered purposeless. As for the phrase "the body and its limit are not mentioned in the scripture," the word "limit" refers to the state of having that as a limit; the meaning is that the body is not heard of in the scripture as being the limit.

[Objection: Is it not the case that, because of the observation in another Śruti text—"having shaken off the body"—the determination of that [body] as the limit is established? To this, he says: "having shaken off the body. The meaning is that even in the passage "having departed from this body," the word *śarīra* (body) refers generally to the body whose purpose has been initiated (*prārabdhakārya*), and the qualification "from this" (*asmāt*) is intended to demonstrate the state of being subject to abandonment, which is established by inference based on the reasons for renunciation well-known in Śruti and Smṛti. Others [hold a different view].

Regarding the passage beginning with *tasya tāvad iti*, it is by virtue of the Śruti. The meaning is as follows: since the Śruti, in the words *tasya tāvat*, declares that the attainment of Brahman occurs precisely upon the fall of the body which is the source of knowledge (*vidyā-yoni-śarīra*), it is impossible for there to be the experience of the fruits of various actions that project multiple bodies within another body; therefore, the exhaustion of even the *prārabdha* (commenced) karma must be said to occur through knowledge alone. The remainder is clear.
Thus concludes the section on other moments.
Thus ends the first quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, composed by Śrī Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the commentator on the ten Upaniṣads.

If it is argued that [the mention of the other senses] is justified because it occurs in a context primarily concerned with dissolution (*laya*), and since no distinction is perceived between the statement regarding the perfection of speech (*vāk-sampatti*) and the statement regarding the perfection of the other senses, and for this very reason the logic of the statement on the perfection of speech is extended to the perfection of the senses in the Sūtra "all [follow]" (*sarvāṇyanu*) and its commentary—then how can the mention of the other senses be included within the category of what is being established? [Response: This is not so, because of the following passage: "Therefore, one whose heat has subsided, through the senses merging into the mind, enters into a new birth... (*tasmādupaśāntatejāḥ punarbhavaṃ indriyairmanasi sampadyamānaiḥ*).

The meaning of *hram* is that one whose radiance has subsided and whose heat has become calm enters the breath (*prāṇa*) together with the senses as they merge into the mind with a view toward rebirth—that is, toward future birth. For in this context, the merging of the senses into the mind takes the form of dissolution; indeed, if there were a dissolution of the senses into the mind, it would follow that rebirth itself could not occur.

Therefore, the sense that the word "attainment" (*sampatti*) there refers to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) must be stated; and since this applies without inconsistency to the statements regarding the attainment of speech (*vāk-sampatti*), the same must be maintained for the statement regarding the attainment of the senses (*indriya-sampatti*). Thus, the meaning is that the mention of the attainment of the senses is also included within the category of the supporting factors.

In reality, however, there is no difference between the sentence "by the senses merging into the mind" (*indriyair manasi saṃpadyamānaiḥ*) and the sentence concerning the merging of speech (*vāk-sampatti-vākya*); nevertheless, it should be understood that the teachers have included it among the supporting arguments out of their insistence that all the auxiliary sūtras (*guṇasūtra*) must be shown to establish the meaning of the current topical section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Is this inquiry not like an examination of a crow’s teeth, since there is no difference in meaning between the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions? For it is already agreed upon by both that when the nature of speech dissolves into the mind, it does not exist; nor can it be said that the opponent fails to accept the conjunction of speech with the mind as maintained by the proponent, because if there were no conjunction of speech with the mind, even the report of speech dissolving into the mind would be impossible. There is only this much distinction:

This being the case, it is replied: "Speech [merges] into the mind" (*vāk manasi*). It is speech itself that merges into the mind. Why? Because of observation (*darśanāt*). For it is observed that even when the organ of speech has ceased, the activity of the mind continues. If it is argued that this is possible through the merging of the mere function (*vṛtti*), the Sūtra says: "And because of the word" (*śabdācca*). Indeed, the word "speech merges into the mind" refers to the merging of the very nature of speech, not merely the merging of its function.

For at that time, when its function has ceased, the organ of speech is not perceived by any other means of knowledge, such that one could say it merely becomes merged [into the mind]. As for the objection that the merging of speech into the mind is not tenable because the mind is not the material cause of speech—that must be refuted by the statement, "Speech merges into the mind," which implies that speech is joined with the mind rather than being dissolved therein. || 1 ||

If the word *vāk* (speech) refers to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then the word *sampatti* (attainment/merging) must refer to the dissolution of the mental activity characterized by the production of vocal power; however, if the word *vāk* refers to the act of speaking, then the word *sampatti* would refer to the dissolution of the activity that causes that [speaking]. In either case, this [interpretation] is of no use, because it fails to result in a specific determination of the nature of the departure (*utkrānti*). This is just as when, with the intention of referring to Devadatta’s son, one says "Devadatta has perished in Kāñcī"—even though the word "Devadatta" here functions as a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for his son.

It can be justified; even by resorting to the meaning of a lost word characterized by the loss of a son, its sense can be established. However, by this much, no specific distinction is stated regarding the meaning. This consideration is similar to that case. Nor should it be said that this section (adhikaraṇa) is intended to establish the logical principle of resorting to the non-primary meaning of the secondary one—rather than either the primary or the secondary—when one of the two must be adopted as non-primary, for that [principle] has already been established in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā itself.

If it is argued that [this point] has already been discussed, some here maintain that in this section the primary prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is simply that the nature of speech merges into the mind, and thus the scriptural statement regarding "attainment" (*sampatti*) is somehow justified. In this view, since the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*), while demonstrating the latent objection (*anuśaya*), hints at another prima facie position, those familiar with the commentary passage in the subsequent section on the "transference" (*atideśa*)—"That mind [merges] into breath"—which establishes the basis for further doubt, will ask: "Is it stated here that the mind undergoes dissolution (*laya*), or is it a mere conjunction (*saṃyoga*)?"

Furthermore, since this meaning is easily understood by those who have seen the *Ṭīkā* text, if the dissolution of speech (*vāklaya*) were not intended here as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), then the statement in the *Bhāṣya* within the section on "Extended Application" (*atideśādhikaraṇa*) regarding the presentation of further doubts to prove the dissolution of the mind (*manolaya*) would be contradictory. Therefore, even there, the primary prima facie view is precisely the statement of the dissolution of the nature of speech; for the term "attainment" (*sampatti*) is also justified in the sense of a conjunction preceded by the cessation of function. Thus, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that dissolution is not tenable in that which is not the primary subject (*aprakṛti*).

This alone is the truth. Others, however, argue as follows: "It is indeed true that if there were no conjunction between speech and the mind, the statement regarding the dissolution of the function of speech (*vāgvṛtti*) into the mind would be impossible; nevertheless, since the opponent does not accept the specific kind of conjunction favored by the proponent, there is no difference in meaning between the two positions. [They explain] that even when the organ of speech has ceased its activity, the mind continues to function; here, the mention of the mind's continued activity is for the purpose of establishing the cause of the integration of speech (*vāksampatti*), for otherwise—

The meaning is that the state of having its functions dissolved therein does not serve as a cause for attainment. This is precisely the intended sense of the commentary beginning with "pravṛttavyāpāram" (whose activity has proceeded).
It takes on form; therefore, "one whose vital heat has been stilled [takes on form] through the senses merging into the mind for the sake of rebirth. || 2 ||
The section concerning speech is completed.

Regarding the phrase "bhāṣye vācam anu sarveṣām indriyāṇām," the word *anu* is a *karmapravacanīya* used in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*), meaning "together with speech" (*vācā saha*), and not in the sense of "after" (*paścāt*) or "according to" (*anurūpam*). Thus it is.

Some say that because the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* would otherwise entail the formation of an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "subsequent to" (*paścād-arthe*), and because such a compound is a mandatory compound (*nityasamāsa*)—thereby precluding the existence of a sentence—and because even the accusative case would be difficult to justify in that sense, this *karmapravacanīya* must mean "conjunction" (*saha-artha*); thus, the accusative is applied by the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte dvitīyā*, and consequently, the passage in the *Ṭīkā* must be interpreted in some other way. Others, however, maintain that the meaning is "it becomes [accomplished] in accordance with each utterance" (*vācam-anuvācam-anurudhya saṃpadyate*).

The prefix *anu* denotes an action accompanied by its instrument, as in "it rained after Śākalya’s Saṃhitā" (*śākalyasya saṃhitāmanuprāvaṣat*), where the understanding of the meaning arises that "having perceived Śākalya’s Saṃhitā, it rained," thereby establishing the sense of occurring subsequent to the perception. Just as in the case of "he was born after a man" (*pumāṃsamanujāyate*), which gives rise to the understanding of the meaning "he was born following [in dependence upon] a man," whereby birth after that is established; so too here, from the comprehension of the meaning "having followed speech" (*vācamanurudhya*).
Intending that the meaning "afterwards" is established, the Teachers have stated it in this manner; thus they demonstrate. This concludes the section on Speech (*vāg-adhikaraṇa*).

In the *Bhāṣya* on the passage "therefore the mind merges into breath" (*manaḥ prāṇe saṃpadyate*), some explain as follows: In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), one must admit a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word "breath" (*prāṇa*). Furthermore, the statement regarding merging would likewise lack intrinsic propriety, because [breath] is not the material cause (*prakṛti*); indeed, dissolution into a mere material cause is not tenable. Moreover, if the word "breath" were figuratively indicating water, then in the subsequent sentence, "breath [merges] into heat" (*prāṇastejasi*), the word "breath" would also have to refer to water in its figurative sense, resulting in the meaning that "water merges into heat. But this is incorrect, because at the time of death, the dissolution of the gross elements (*bhūta*) is impossible.

Furthermore, since the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) could also be maintained on the grounds that even in the statement "speech merges into the mind" (*vāk manasi saṃpadyate*), the term "mind" (*manaḥ*) could refer to the primary merging within the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which is the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the mind—and thus its resolution could not be established by the reasoning of this very section's final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—therefore, the prima facie position must be stated as the logical consistency of the literal meaning of the scripture (*śruti*), and not by resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In that regard, it is as follows:

Some reconcile [the text] by arguing that because there is no difference between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*), there is no difference between food and the mind, nor between water and the vital breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, the statement that "water dissolves into food" possesses logical consistency, and thus the statement that "the mind dissolves into the vital breath" is justified—this is the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Consequently, regarding the phrase "having pointed out water as the material cause of the vital breath" in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), the word "material cause" (*prakṛti*) refers to "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*); the meaning is "having pointed out water as constituting the very essence of the vital breath," and thus the meaning stated is "because of the non-difference between those two."

The intention is that, because [the earth] exists [in water], the primary dissolution of the form of the earth into the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the form of water, is logically established; the phrase "by way of succession" (*paramparayā*) in the Commentary means "by a succession of arguments. The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) should also be interpreted accordingly; for instance, the meaning of the question "Is it intended to show the relationship of material cause and effect? is "Is it intended to show non-difference by means of demonstrating the relationship of material cause and effect? And the meaning of "into its own cause through the medium of the earth," and so forth, is as follows:

The meaning is that, by way of the earth, the one consisting of food (annamaya) enters into its own cause—the powers designated by the word "prāṇa," which are expressed as the act of breathing—precisely because the earth is the form of the one consisting of food. However, some [commentators] argue that since the verb "sampadyate" (he attains/merges) has the nature of an injunction, it is impossible to resort to an unnatural sense of the word "attainment" according to the maxim "in an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not to be set aside. Furthermore, since the word "attainment" primarily denotes dissolution (laya), and since it is improper to abandon that primary sense when it can somehow be reconciled, they maintain that there is also a metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) of water by the word "prāṇa."

If it is argued that there is a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*) in the statement "the vital breaths [merge] into heat" (*prāṇās tejasī*), then that must simply be accepted; likewise, if another fault arises elsewhere, that too must be accepted. The intention of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) is expressed by saying, "What is wrong with a meaning arrived at through logic? The phrase "But others," etc., refers to the view that the two terms have the sense of "functioning" (*vṛtti*). This means that in the sūtra "Because of the observation of speech and mind, and because of the word" (*vāṅmanasidarśanācchabdācca*), one adopts the interpretation that the word *vāk* (speech) refers to its function (*vṛttiparatva*), while the word *śabda* (word) refers to the logical consistency of the term (*śabdopapattiparatva*).
Regarding the words "of speech and mind" (*manaśśabdayoḥ*), [it is said]: "Speech merges into the mind; the mind... [and so on].

The meaning is: "when the word *prāṇa* occurs" refers to the two words *prāṇa* appearing with the seventh (locative) and first (nominative) case endings, as in the phrases *manaḥ prāṇe* and *prāṇas tejasī*. The phrase "of the two words *prāṇa*" likewise refers to the two occurrences of the word *prāṇa* with the seventh and first case endings.

The sense is this: by one who maintains that in the phrase *vāṅmanasī*, the word *manas* ending in the locative case refers to the *ahaṅkāra* (ego), it must be admitted that in the phrase *manaḥ prāṇe*, the word *manas* ending in the nominative case refers to the mind (*manas*). Likewise, even in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the section beginning with *tanmanaḥ prāṇa uttarā't*, a discrepancy between the word ending in the locative and the word ending in the nominative would have to be accepted; and that is improper.

He demonstrates precisely the contradiction with the accepted prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding the statement "the mind is dissolved into the ego" (*ahaṅkāra*): just as it is contradictory for the mind to depart separately from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) when it is dissolved into the vital breath, so too is it contradictory when it is dissolved into the ego. For at that time, it is not even conceivable that the ego—which is the cause of the elements and the senses and constitutes the covering of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—could depart. This is the sense. Thus ends the section on the mind (*manodhikaraṇa*).

The variant reading "vāṅ-manasoḥ" found in some manuscripts of the Bhāṣya is based on the fact that the rule governing compound endings (*samāsānta-vidhi*) is not universally obligatory. Following the statement that the word *tejas* (fire/heat) refers here to the subtle elements (*bhūta-sūkṣma-aṃśa*), the reading "upagamaḥ sambandhaḥ" (approach is connection) is correct; [the phrase] "anyataravāciśabdanirdeśaḥ" means the mention of a term denoting only one of the two.

The statement that "this commentary goes to the ocean of the Upanishads" is not contradictory; it is just like that. [Objection: But by this very same analogy, why could the scriptural teaching regarding the departure [of the senses] into the *prāṇa* not also be mediated by something else? Furthermore, just as the scripture states "speech merges into the mind" because mental activity is observed even after the cessation of the activity of the external organs, and just as the scripture states "the mind [merges] into the *prāṇa*" because the activity of the *prāṇa*, characterized by breathing and so forth, is observed even after the cessation of the knowledge of other objects, so too—

If it is argued that—even after the cessation of the vital functions such as breathing—the observation of the activity of fire characterized by heat in the body, along with the scriptural statement "the breath [merges] into fire" (*prāṇas tejasī*), suggests that, by parity of reasoning, it is more appropriate to understand this as referring directly to the merging into fire itself; we say no. Just as the scriptural hearing "from air comes fire, from fire comes water" must be understood as referring to the Supreme Self in the states of fire and so on—in order to avoid contradiction with the text "from Him is born the breath, mind, and all the senses"—so too, in accordance with the scriptural teaching regarding the soul's approach to the Self, [the term "fire" refers to the Self].

There is no contradiction because the word *tejas* (fire/heat), when its literal meaning as the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*) is set aside, can be understood as referring to the individual soul (*jīva*) whose body it is. Furthermore, since the scripture states, "The vital breath [merges] into heat" (*prāṇas tejasīti*), the heat must merge first before the soul's departure; however, because the scripture subsequently declares, "Heat [merges] into the highest deity" (*tejaḥ parasyāṃ devatāyām*), the merging of the soul would otherwise find no place once the heat has already merged into the supreme deity. Since a location for the soul's merging must necessarily exist, it follows—in accordance with the scriptural statement of the soul's departure supported by the indicative mark of simultaneous departure—that the merging occurs immediately after the soul's own merging.

The sense is that [the soul's merging] occurs because of the attainment of the state of *tejas*. Although the opponents have described the scriptural passage itself as the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—since the statement "breath [merges] into heat" (*prāṇastejasīti*) is beyond doubt and thus the merging must occur in *tejas* exactly as heard, and it is improper to assume a merging with the individual soul (*jīva*) not mentioned in the text—they have nevertheless also presented the reason "because it is improper to assume what is not heard" (*aśrutakalpanāyā anyāyyatvāt*) as a supporting argument for the scripture. This is done on the grounds that such a reason serves to corroborate the scriptural statement.

It should be understood that this is what was stated. The meaning is that since mere non-hearing cannot function as a logical reason (*hetu*), it is impossible for the absence of the general condition of hearing—despite the fact that the statement "in this very way, at the time of death, all vital breaths (*prāṇas*) gather around this self" exists in another scriptural passage—to serve as a reason. Regarding the phrase "the scriptural authority for co-existence," "co-existence" (*sahāvasthāna*) means existing together with that [the self], which is to say, existing as its substratum; it should not be understood as co-existence in the sense of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

It should be understood that others establish that very [consciousness] as being situated precisely within the locus of the living soul (*jīva*). Thus ends the section on direct perception (*adhyakṣādhikaraṇa*).

This being the position reached, it is said: "In the elements. He becomes merged in the elements. Why? Because of that statement; for there is a scriptural text stating that the individual soul, as it migrates, consists of all the elements: "Consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4). || 5 ||

[Objection: But even if the merging occurs sequentially into fire and the other elements one by one, the scriptural statement beginning with "consisting of earth" (*pṛthivīmayaḥ*) would still be justified; therefore, [the author] says: "It has been explained that [the self consists of the three elements] because of its being composed of the three. One should note that the reading is *tryātmakatvāt* and *bhūyastvāt*, as this is seen in Śaṅkara’s commentary. "Subtle particles" (*aṇvyo mātrāḥ*) means the subtle portions of the five elements. Regarding the phrase "together with the life-breath and the individual soul" (*jīvasahitaprāṇa*), the interpretation of others—that "therefore he is the presiding deity conjoined with the life-breath"—is untenable.

The meaning [of the word *bhāva*] is as follows: the intention is that, in this context, it is appropriate for the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie view) to consist precisely in the doubt regarding the meaning of the *sphuṭa-sūtra* (the clear aphorism) which is to be refuted. Furthermore, the phrase "by way of being the object of re-origination" should be understood as referring to the presence or absence of words establishing re-origination—such as "subtle particles (*aṇvyo mātrā*) perishable" from the *Smṛti*, and "beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*)" from the *Smṛti* cited by [the author] himself—and thus indicating a disparity in sequence. Thus ends the section on the elements (*bhūtādhikaraṇa*).

The nature of destruction is attained; the intention is that this refers to the experience of Brahman which occurs at the time of meditation, as expressed in the passage, "When all [desires] are liberated. || 7 ||

The phrase "due to the power of the substrate" (*vastusāmarthyāt*) connects with what precedes. Immediately after the statement that "the heat of the gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*) is universal," the remainder—"because the subtle body (*sūkṣmadeha*) is universal"—must be supplied. Thus, the meaning is as follows: in the passage "it heats the void and the body from the soles of the feet to the head," the heat denoted by the word "heat" (*ūṣman*), which is experienced in the gross body from the soles of the feet upward due to the application of the flame of fire, is based on the universality of the subtle body, and not on the nature of the gross body itself.

The intention is that it cannot be argued that because the flame of fire is withdrawn gradually, the localized nature of heat arises solely from the localized nature of that flame—and thus the localization of heat is not caused by the localization of the subtle body—since even the localization of the flame of fire is itself caused by the localization of the subtle body; or rather, the point is that there is no flame of fire distinct from the fiery element (tejas) contained within the subtle elements of matter.

The phrase "he departs from the heart" means he is intent upon departing; this too is a statement of the resultant meaning, because it has been stated: "Then these vital breaths (prāṇas) gather around him; taking up these particles of light, he descends into the heart itself. Furthermore, the text reads: "The tip of his heart shines forth; by that radiance, this Self departs. Therefore, in accordance with this context:

It should be understood that due to ignorance of the path of exit, [the soul] wanders within the heart alone; subsequently, when the tip of the heart is illuminated, it is in this sense that "this self departs," for this is precisely what is perceived by its own inherent nature (*svarasataḥ*). However, some maintain that the illumination of the tip of the heart belongs to one who has already departed from a portion of the heart.

They say that [the text] is employed for the purpose of showing the path; therefore, there is no inconsistency even with the meaning as it was heard. Thus, the meaning of the objection beginning with "by that light" (*tena pradyotena*) and so forth is this: if the departure (*utkrānti*) were restricted solely to the ignorant, then the journey via the path of light (*arcirādi-gati*) would not apply to the knower either. Consequently, it cannot be maintained that the statement regarding departure refers exclusively to the ignorant; therefore, the word "of the ignorant" (*aviduṣaḥ*) is stated [in the commentary], which is the required supplement (*śeṣa*).

In the Siddhānta, however, this [statement] refers exclusively to one who possesses knowledge; the word "eva" (exclusively) is to be construed out of its normal position. The meaning is that this very statement applies both to one who possesses knowledge and to one who does not. This is because the phrase "with his head upwards" was previously explained as referring specifically to one who possesses knowledge. If it is objected: "But since the illumination of the heart is common to all, there is a contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the passage 'the tip of his heart flares up,' where it is demonstrated that the non-flaring depends upon the grace of the Heart obtained through the power of knowledge. To this we reply: [no contradiction].

The sense is that there is no contradiction, because the purpose [of the passage] is to demonstrate that the specific fire which discerns more than a hundred channels is dependent upon and subordinate to that [Supreme Self]. In this context, what is intended is the absence of the threefold seeking (*aiṣaṇā*) regarding wealth, progeny, and the worlds; here, the word *artha* refers to the worlds such as heaven, according to the Śruti: "They, having risen above the seeking of progeny, the seeking of wealth, and the seeking of worlds... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22), and as stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) in reference to the wise man: "He destroys death again" (*apunar-mṛtyu*).

The term "the wise one" (*vidvāṃsam*) is used because the glorification of the raft in the form of crossing over *saṃsāra* is intended for those who possess knowledge; furthermore, since the genitive case can denote the point of departure (*apādāna*), the sense is that there is the possibility of intending the relationship of the ablative as a residual relation (*śeṣatvena*). Regarding the phrase "the contemplation of fire as the devourer of these [waters]," the fruit of the meditation prescribed in the passage, "Fire is indeed the consumer; he is the food of the waters" (*agnirvai bhṛtyuḥ so'pāmannam*), is stated as: "He conquers death no more" (*apapunarmṛtyuṃ jayati*). As for the phrase beginning with "But others," it refers to the knower of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇavidvas*).

The meaning is: "of one who meditates upon Brahman with attributes" (*saguṇabrahmopāsakasya*). The compound is formed by a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the second [member]. This is because we observe the usage of the word *vidvas* in the *Ārṣa-kāvya* (the *Rāmāyaṇa*), such as in the phrases "the scripture for one who knows the specific [details]" (*viśeṣaviduṣaḥ śāstram*) and so forth. Therefore, since the word *vidvas* ends in the present participle suffix *-śatṛ*, the genitive case governed by a *kṛt*-suffix is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalārthāḥ*. Furthermore, since the remaining genitive (*śeṣalakṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply here, and because the genitive is used in connection with the word *sat* in the sense of "one who knows the qualities" (*saguṇaṃ vidvān*), the prohibition against forming a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) applies. Thus, the alternative of using the accusative—namely, *saguṇaṃ vidvān*—is the correct formation.

The objection that such an explanation is not tenable because attainment (*prāpti*) is impossible has already been refuted; alternatively, it may be considered correct as a compound formed with *su-suṣu*. Some, observing its inclusion in the list beginning with "gati" (Pāṇini 2.1.40), state in their commentary on Mādhava’s work that it is a "compound with a second-case noun" (*dvitīyā-samāsa*); this too is certainly acceptable. This is their application of the rule: the meaning is that it is an application of the rule "sūkṣmaṃ pramāṇataḥ" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.15). As for the application of the preceding rule "tadāpiteḥ" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 7.1.16), since there is no element in the application itself that is absolutely indefensible, the omission of stating it is not a fault.

Regarding the phrase "due to the authoritative evidence of the scriptural statement concerning the exit through the channels" (*nāḍīniṣkramaṇa-śruti-rūpa-pramāṇāt*): although in the commentary of the other [school] the term *pramāṇataḥ* is understood to mean "by measure" (*parimāṇataḥ*), such is its explanation: that subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) is subtle both by its own nature and by its measure. Its subtlety by nature is like that of a great light [such as the sun] which is invisible to the eye; its subtlety by measure is like that of a mote of dust in a sunbeam. Thus, because of its subtlety by measure, its movement through the channels is possible, and because of its subtlety by nature...

"Non-perception of a side-position that does not fall away"—nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated because [the path] is perceived as subtle due to its being dependent on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth; the reading "in order to pacify the doubt regarding the absence of death" is the correct one; the division [of the compound] is "for the sake of establishing the journey via the path beginning with light" (*arcir-ādi-gati*); and it is "not to be cited as an example" because it does not have that as its object.

Nor should it be objected: "The word *apada* means 'one for whom no place (*pada*) exists'; since this explains that the one who is thus disciplined is devoid of a destination (*gantavya*), how can it not be cited [as an example]? This doubt should not be raised, because the word *pada* here signifies a dwelling place such as that of Indra and other deities. Thus ends the section concerning the commencement of the course of transmigration (*āsṛtyupakramādhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase *yathākarma yathāvidyam*, the form *yathākarma* is derived from the rule *naśca napuṃsakādanyatarasyām*, which allows for the absence of the suffix *ṭac*. Now, an objection is raised: since the meanings of the first three statements—"Speech merges into the mind; the mind into breath; the breath into heat"—have been examined in sequence by the sūtras ending with "Not into one, for [the texts] show" (*naikasmindarśayato hi*), what then is the meaning of the fourth statement, "Heat [merges] into the Highest" (*tejaḥ parasyām*)?

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "They merge into the Highest. They become one with the Supreme Self. Why? Because the Śruti declares: "The fire [merges] into the highest deity. The meaning is that the process must be conceived in accordance with what the Śruti states. Just as in deep sleep and at the time of cosmic dissolution there is a cessation of the exertion involved in the experience of pleasure and pain through merging into the Supreme Self, so it is here as well. The section on merging into the Highest (parasampattyadhikaraṇa) is concluded.

Anticipating the objection that it is appropriate to begin the determination of the commonality of the fourfold path for both the learned and the ignorant—not in the middle—it is held that the author of the Sūtras, in the sūtra *samānā cāsṛtyupakramād* (Brahmasūtra 3.1.8), has established the determination of the commonality between the learned and the ignorant only at a point where there is a basis for doubt regarding a common subject; since the meaning of the passage *tejaḥ parasyāṃ devatāyām* (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.6) is not a locus for such doubt regarding commonality, it was deemed inappropriate to establish it as being common to both.

He provides the resolution with the words "It was established before" and so forth, explaining that the section beginning with "And it was already established" (*samānā ca*) was inserted prior to the two sections that determine the meaning of the fourth statement. Thus ends the section on the attainment of another's perfection (*parasampattyadhikaraṇa*).

He elucidates the very point already stated by showing another illustration, beginning with the words "as one possessing a tunic and a turban," and so forth. "And the rest for one devoid of that" means that there is rest in the state of being devoid of that [tunic and turban]. The phrase "of the mere individual soul (jīva) in deep sleep" implies that this is not like the state of the individual soul characterized by gross and subtle bodies during dissolution (pralaya) or departure from the body (utkrānti). He raises an objection regarding the "qualified portion" (viśeṣyāṃśa), meaning that it is like the case of deep sleep.

[The scriptural authority is cited: "The fifteen parts have returned to their foundations"; here, the ten senses denoted by the word *prāṇa*, the mind (*manas*) as one, and the subtle elements [are meant].

"The five elements" refers to the sixteen digits (*kalās*). In that context, since the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) is a modification of earth, and the mind (*manas*) is also a modification of earth—as evidenced by the statement, "The mind, my dear, consists of food"—it is appropriate to speak of fifteen [digits] by treating these two as one. This statement is not inconsistent, just as there are statements regarding dissolution into the respective material causes (*upādāna*) or into the parts, or into ignorance (*ajñāna*). Furthermore, they object that this reading is not mentioned by others and therefore it is not the correct text; to them we reply: [it is so] because of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth.

In the view that [the world] is an effect of the individual soul's (jīva) ignorance alone, it is impossible for it to dissolve into its own causes because the soul's ignorance has been uprooted by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). However, in the view that it is an effect of the individual soul's ignorance as assisted by the gross elements—which are transformations of Māyā resting upon the Lord—although the individual portion is destroyed by the knowledge of reality, the supporting gross element portion remains; thus, the dissolution of a portion of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth within that [remaining portion] is possible. This is seen in the case of a cloth woven from two threads, where when one thread is destroyed, it dissolves into the other thread.

Furthermore, because this has been established in other treatises (*paragrantha*), it is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the subsequent section (*uttarādhikaraṇa*), which establishes the complete dissolution (*niravaśe�sheṣatva*) of the *kalās*; for there is no contradiction, as that section is intended to demonstrate that the dissolution is "complete" only insofar as it concerns the portion consisting of the effects of the individual soul’s (*jīva*) ignorance (*avidyā*). The phrase "in the first [section]" is an ellipsis for "in the first *adhikaraṇa*. Regarding the statement, "their names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) are divided," the meaning is that the names and forms of these *kalās*, though consisting of their respective powers (*śakti*), are divided—that is, they are dissolved.

The meaning is that because it is not understood even from the perspective of the ignorant, it is invisible to them; thus, its reality—which is to be known solely through the Śruti—cannot be conceived even by a learned person.

Regarding the phrase "because it has purpose by virtue of referring to the dissolution of primordial matter" (*prākṛtapralayaviṣayatayā vārthavattvāt*): although it is taught that the dissolution of the *kalās* occurs through the knowledge of the Self, as stated in the passage, "Their names and forms are dissolved in the Person," and "He becomes partless and immortal," it cannot be maintained that this refers to a universal dissolution of primordial matter common to all. Nevertheless, it should be understood that the intent of the previous objection lies precisely in the fact that [the text] has purpose by virtue of referring to the names and forms of gods, humans, and so forth. The phrase "because the portion of the Lord is the efficient cause" (*īśvarāṃśasya nimittakāraṇatvāt*) is to be supplemented with the words "in his [the opponent's] view."
Thus ends the section on non-differentiation.

Regarding the phrase "in the place from which the fire has been drawn out" (*uddhṛtāgnau pradeśe*), it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that place from which the fire has been taken away. In the Bhāṣya, the expression "from that sun" (*amuṣyādādityāt*) is used. [The rays] "extend" means they continue and protect; the meaning of the sentence is that those [rays], having issued forth from the sun and being connected within the channels (*nāḍī*), and having issued forth from the channels, exist as a continuous stream connected back to the sun.
Thus concludes the section concerning the following of the rays.

If it be argued that because these two [times] are respectively praiseworthy and its opposite, they would serve as causes for high and low rebirths—such that death at night, being a cause for a downward rebirth, cannot be a cause for attaining Brahman—that is not so, because for the knower (*vidvan*), the connection with *karman* persists only as long as the body exists. This is what is meant: by virtue of the connection with knowledge (*vidyā*), those *karmans* which have not yet begun their effects and which would otherwise cause a downward rebirth [are neutralized].

Because there is no attachment to future bodies due to their destruction, because the work already commenced ends with the final body, and because the cause of bondage is absent, the attainment of Brahman for the knower—even if death occurs at night—is established as a certainty. The Śruti also demonstrates this: "For him, there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body; then he shall be united [with Brahman]. As for the statement regarding "day" and "the bright fortnight," which mentions truth and so forth, that refers to those who are not yet liberated. (18)
The section concerning night is concluded.

In that case, regarding the phrase "of one who has died at night," the ellipsis is "by following the rays"; having raised the objection that this would lead to an undesirable consequence, he says, "his independence from the sun's rays. This means that for one who dies at night, there is no dependence on the sun's rays for the journey to Brahman.

The meaning of the phrase "by resorting to the basis of the non-occurrence of the completion of knowledge" is as follows: it is not the intention of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) that knowledge never produces its fruit in the case of one who dies at night, such that knowledge would lack occasional fruitfulness; for the opponent’s position is that [the fruit is delayed] either by uncommenced works (*aprārabdhakarman*) or by commenced works (*prārabdhakarman*) themselves through the intervention of another body. Therefore, there is no contingency of occasional fruitfulness. [Objection: But in this way, the status of being the "last" [moment] would simply not be attained, according to the opponent's view.

If it is argued that in the *Siddhānta-bhā�ṣya*—where it is stated that "because the karma whose fruit has begun is limited by the final body"—the refutation is made by taking the existence of the body as a given so that the rule might not be restricted, then the meaning of the *bhāṣya* passage "because it is limited by the final body" is this: because this karma is limited by the body that constitutes its fruit; since there is a fixed rule that "there are this many bodies which constitute the fruit," the karma lacks the capacity to produce more bodies than those. This is precisely the intended meaning of the portion of the Sūtra: "because it persists as long as the body exists."
Thus it should be understood. Regarding the phrase "in the case of his proposition," the meaning is: "in the case of the proposition that [the soul] follows the rays.

Otherwise, regarding the phrase "of the proposition concerning another required matter," the meaning is: "because of the proposition concerning another matter—that liberation is possible for one who dies at night—[the reason] 'because it persists as long as the body lasts' would be irrelevant here. Thus ends the section on Night (Niśādhikaraṇa).

"Because of the absence of the marks of the path beginning with smoke" means that for those who have died during the southern course [of the sun], there is an absence of any authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*)—such as the mention of smoke—that establishes [their journey] otherwise. This is what is intended by the statement in the Commentary, "When that [merit] comes to an end.

When it says "when," it refers to the time at which that merit which leads to the world of Soma "comes to an end," meaning it is exhausted; this is how it has been explained by others. Now, [one might object]: "These two paths, O Pārtha... [and so on].

One might object that, since the conclusion follows the word "knowing" (*jānan*), the opening statement "At what time [one attains] non-return" (*yatra kāle tvanāvṛttim*) should be set aside; and while this much would suffice to say, one might suspect that the mention of "fire as light" (*agnir jyotir*) and so forth in the middle of the passage is inappropriate in the commentary. Anticipating this, [the author] says "At what time... (*yatra kāle tvatīti*), showing that even the intermediate statement contradicts the opening, in order to demonstrate that the opening must be set aside by the natural force of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), for it is impossible to alter the meaning of the opening merely by means of the conclusion.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the statement] is made with the intention that "whatever effort is undertaken is obstructed," but one should not think that this refers to the literal citation of those specific words. Regarding the phrase "of four kinds" (*caturvidha*), it should be understood as referring to the four types mentioned in the verse: "O bull among the Bharatas, there are four kinds of yogis: the distressed (*ārta*), the seeker of wealth (*arthārthin*), the seeker of knowledge (*jijñāsu*), and the wise (*jñānī*). Consequently, the sense is that the statement teaching return—namely, "At what time yogis [attain] non-return and return"—becomes logically consistent; for the meaning of "at what time non-return" is effectively established as "the return of one who is being led by the *ātivāhika* [guiding deities]. [End of Section on the Southern Solstice (*dakṣiṇāyanādhikaraṇa*)]

Thus ends the second quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Śrutaprakāśikā* composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads.

The chapter is completed. The total number of topics (*adhikaraṇa*) is 142; the total number of sūtras is 507. Regarding the word *śavya*, it means "suitable for a corpse" (*śava-yogya*), derived with the suffix *yat* in the sense of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*). The meaning is that he removes his own limbs (*tvāvayavān vigamayya*) and creates an opening there, just as there is an opening in a chariot wheel. Thus, the wind, which was standing obstructing the path without any gaps, provides a path in the form of an opening the size of a chariot wheel by relinquishing its own parts. As for the phrase "elsewhere":

Or rather, are there other paths different from that one? Is there no fixed rule as to whether [liberation] is attained by those [paths] or by this one? What is the correct view? That there is no fixed rule. Why? Because of their manifold forms and because of their independence.

This being the case, it is replied: "By the path beginning with light" (*arcirādi*). A single path beginning with light is taught everywhere; therefore, one goes by the path beginning with light alone. Why? Because of its renown (*tatprathiteḥ*). That is to say, because that very same path is renowned everywhere; "renown" means well-knownness, meaning that it is recognized as such everywhere.

Because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), that very same path is taught everywhere, though with variations of deficiency or excess; thus, just as there is a combination of the qualities of knowledge (*vidyāguṇopasaṃhāra*), so too should what is stated in one place be combined elsewhere. In the *Chāndogya*, for instance, it is handed down in an identical form both in the Upakośala-knowledge and in the Pañcāgni-vidyā; and in the *Vājasaneyaka*, in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) is handed down in exactly the same way, with only slight differences. Therefore, it is understood that it is the same path even there. Furthermore, in all other instances as well, fire, the sun, and so forth, are recognized. 1.
The section concerning the path beginning with light is completed.

The word *vyākhyāya* means "having explained. The phrase "and because of the difference in the [paths] of those who perform [the rites]" (*kamibhedaśca*) implies that the objects of the sequence—such as the world of the gods (*devaloka*), the world of the wind (*vāyuloka*), and so forth—are taught differently in each Vedic branch (*śākhā*).
