The statement "because of the non-transference of qualities, their combination (*upasaṃhāra*) is not possible" is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood that this is shown in other passages such as "because of the connection with the form of distinction, and so on elsewhere. The term *dārvehomika* is the name of a specific ritual action (*karma-viśeṣa*), meaning "pertaining to the wood-offering" (*dārvehāya*).
Thus ends the section concerning the rays and so forth.

Having established the Veda according to the principles of sequence—namely, the sequence of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), purpose (*artha*), textual order (*pāṭha*), procedure (*pravṛtti*), and the primary [context] (*mukhya*)—one performs the altar-construction (*vedi-karaṇa*) after having performed the Vedic study; this is the sequence based on direct scriptural statement (*śrauta-krama*). In cases such as "He offers the Agnihotra" and "He cooks that barley," the sequence is determined by the purpose characterized by the objective (*artha-lakṣaṇa-prayojana-vaśāt*). In cases such as "He sacrifices to the *samidhs*, he sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*," the sequence is determined by the order of the text (*pāṭha-krama*). Regarding the qualities of the animals dedicated to Prajāpati, such as the tethering and the sacrificial implements, the sequence of engagement proceeds from each preceding act to each subsequent one; as in the case of the statement, "There are two [deities] belonging to Sarasvatī."

When two principal offerings dedicated to Sarasvatī and Sarasvant have been prescribed, the sequence of their constituent acts—such as the pouring out of the oblation (*nirvāpa*) and so forth—is determined by the sequence of those principals. For the *kāṇḍakrama* (textual sequence) is indeed the *sthānakrama* (position-based sequence). This should be understood, for example, in the case of the *Sādyaska* sacrifice, where it is enjoined: "One sacrifices the animals together. Among the Agniṣomīya, Savanīya, and Anūbandhya animals which are thus enjoined to be performed simultaneously, the Savanīya takes precedence because it does not deviate from its proper position.

It should be understood that the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the expressions "the year [comes] after the months" and "the world of the gods [comes] after the worlds of light" indicates that the year and the world of the gods are situated above the months and the worlds of light; for the ablative is used here because it is occasioned by its connection with a word denoting direction (*dikśabda*), such as "above" (*ūrdhva*), which is supplied as an ellipsis. Thus, the term "ablative" (*pañcamīśabda*) is applied metaphorically to the word expressing the direction itself. Now, one might object: this is not an ablative used in the sense of being occasioned by connection with a directional word like "above."

The phrase "api te'rciṣam abhisambhavanti" is governed by the action of "attaining" (abhisambhavana) which is supplied from the preceding context; therefore, one cannot establish that "going upwards" (ūrdhvatva) is directly stated in the scripture by supplying the word "upwards" (ūrdhva).

Furthermore, since the word *kiñcit* (something) and the like denote a sequence characterized by the priority and posteriority of actions, there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) for the ablative case (*pañcamī*) to signify a vertical sequence or a sequence of priority and posteriority, such that the verticality (*ūrdhvatva*) would be directly expressed by the scripture (*śrauta*). If this is argued, it is not so; because the action of "attaining" (*abhisambhavana*) is independent of an ablative point of departure, and in accordance with another scriptural passage stating "by that he ascends upwards" (*tenordhvam ākramate*), the word "upwards" (*ūrdhva*) itself must be supplied [as an ellipsis]. Thus, the intended meaning is that the verticality can indeed be considered scripturally expressed (*śrauta*). And although...

In passages such as "from the months [he goes] to the world of the gods," the ablative case (pañcamī) is used in relation to the action of reaching (*abhisambhavana*). Nevertheless, when the ablative case-ending expresses the status of the *apādāna*—defined as a specific type of factor (*kāraka*) that exists invariably prior to the action of reaching the world of the gods—the sequence characterized by the temporal priority and posteriority of the action and its factors is thereby expressed. Consequently, when the year and the world of the gods are described as the objects of the action of reaching which has the months as its *apādāna*, their existence subsequent to the months is established.

It should be understood that the scriptural status (*śrautatva*) of the upward direction is stated with the intention that [the sequence] of the year and the world of the gods is established by implication; this should be understood likewise in subsequent cases as well. Alternatively, regarding the view that the ablative case (*hetupañcamī*) expresses the state of being a conductor (*ātivāhikatva*), it should be understood that their causality in the form of prior existence is what is stated in the scripture.

If it is asked: "How does the ablative case apply to the light (*arciḥ*) and so forth in the sense of a cause? The ablative is prescribed for a non-feminine cause that is a quality (*guṇa*) by the rule *vibhāṣā guṇe 'striyām*; for example, 'bound because of dullness' (*jāḍyāt* or *jāḍyāt*)," then [the answer is as follows]: In this regard:

Some maintain that here the term "quality" (*guṇa*) does not refer to the technical definition characterized by the statement "it enters into a substance and departs from it," but rather refers merely to that which is dependent on another; therefore, they argue that the ablative case in "from the rays" (*arciṣaḥ*) and so forth is established as denoting cause (*hetu*). This is extremely weak: for even if the quality is taken as being dependent on another, the ablative case still does not apply here. This is because the rays and so forth, being the subjects (*viśeṣya*), are independent and thus lack the state of being dependent on another, and consequently lack the status of a "quality" (*guṇa*). For a quality is that which...

In the phrase *bhāvāt*, by the word *guṇa* (quality), whatever object exists—such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—that is distinct from substance (*dravya*) and serves as a qualifier dependent on another, all of that is included. Even if one adopts the aforementioned method [of interpretation], light (*arcis*) does not incur the status of a quality (*guṇatva*) because it is currently perceived as something distinct [from the substrate]. Furthermore, even if it were a quality, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the word *arciṣaḥ* would not be obtained by this rule [Pāṇini 5.4.153] because of the prohibition "not when feminine" (*astriyām*), since the word *arcis* ends in the suffix *is*.

Since the rule *arciḥ striyāṃ ca* prescribes [the form] for both feminine and neuter genders, the masculine gender does not exist at all. Here, the word *arcis* is exclusively feminine, because of the prior reference in the text: *te 'rciṣam abhisambhavanti*. If it were neuter, the form in the second case singular would simply be *arcir*; therefore, since the word *arcis* is indeed feminine, the prohibition *astriyām* would certainly apply. For there is no grasping of a quality merely as something dependent; rather, [it is grasped as an independent entity].

Because it has been shown in the *Vṛtti* and other works that only the technical sense [of the term] is appropriate, as evidenced by the examples and counter-examples; and although it is established in the rule *yasya guṇasya hi bhāvāt* that the word *guṇa* refers to qualities such as the differentiating genus (*jāti*) which reside in another, and since in common usage the word *guṇa* denotes an attribute (*upasarjana*), and the word *guṇa* is most well-known in reference to qualities like white (*śukla*) and so forth, and the Vaiśeṣikas accept twenty-four qualities such as form (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*), nevertheless, in this treatise [it is said]: "That which enters into a substance... (*sattve niviśate*).

This refers to the inclusion of the quality (*guṇa*) as defined by such rules; or alternatively, just as in the rule *voto guṇavacanāt*, by the maxim that when there is a choice between a technical (*kṛtrima*) and a non-technical (*akṛtrima*) term, the application of the grammatical operation is understood to apply to the technical one, the resolution here is as follows: because of the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) in *vibhāṣā guṇe'striyām*, the ablative case sometimes occurs even from a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) when used in the feminine. Thus, such usages as "there is no jar here, because of its non-perception" (*anupalabdheḥ*) and "this possesses fire, because of smoke" (*dhūmāt*) are also justified.

Enough with this excessive scrutiny; "elsewhere" means in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* itself, at another location. The fact that the priority of the wind over the sun is expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is merely an illustration; for, in the passage, "He ascends upwards; he reaches the sun," since the noble one has not yet reached [the sun] from the wind, the wind is heard as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by means of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*).

It should be understood that it is not merely the act of ascending to an upper region that is heard in scripture as having the wind as its instrument, but rather the ascent to the solar orb; for when there is a desire for a specific location, it must be concluded that this refers specifically to the solar orb.

The sense is as follows: regarding the statement "immediately after [the sun] is air," the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that because of the sequence of the text—"having entered the path of the gods, he comes to the world of the gods, and that is the world of air"—he enters the realm of air immediately after the light (*arciḥ*). However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that because of the scriptural hearing that he goes to the sun by way of the path designated as "air"—in the passage, "He reaches the air; there the air pushes him aside"—the sequence of the *Kauṣītaki* recension is set aside, and air is placed before the sun. The intention is that the Sūtra also aims at placing air before the sun, and not at placing it immediately after the year (*abda*).
Thus ends the section concerning the air.

In the Bhāṣya, regarding the statement that the word *agni* is a synonym for *arcis*, the intended meaning is that the word *arcis* denotes a flame (*jvālā*), and by means of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) and so forth, fire (*agni*) is said to be identical with it. Now, one might object: "In this context, since the rule 'isusossāmathrye nityaṃ samāse'nuttarapadasthasya' (Pāṇini 8.3.44) mandates the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] when there is semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) in a compound where the suffix does not stand at the end of a subsequent member, the form should be *arciṣparyāyatvena*—just as in examples such as *sapiṣkuṇḍikā* and *śociṣkeśaḥ*. Furthermore, the word *arcis* is derived from the root *arc* with the suffix *isi*, according to the rule 'arciśucivisṛpicchardibhya isiḥ' (Uṇādi Sūtra), just like the words *śocis* and others. [The response to this objection follows: This is not so; the form *arciṣparyāyatvena* would indeed be required if the suffix were *isi*. However, here the suffix is *is*, which is distinct from *isi*. Since the suffix *is* is applied to the root *arc* by the rule 'arceryus' (Uṇādi Sūtra 2.109), the resulting form is *arcis*. Therefore, because the suffixes differ, the rule for *ṣatva* does not apply, and the form remains *arcitvena*. Thus, there is no contradiction.

If this is argued, it is replied here: either (1) by the inclusion of the word *kaṃsa* in the subsequent sūtra (*ataḥ kṛkami-ka-se*), which indicates that in some cases within the *uṇādi* derivatives the rule for the originative derivation (*vyutpatti*) does not apply; or (2) because [the word *arciḥ*] lacks the suffix *is*; or (3) because the application of the *ṣatva* [substitution] is non-obligatory (*anitya*), as indicated by the inclusion of forms such as *sapiṣkuṇḍikā* in the list of *kaska*-type words; or (4) because the word *arcis* here refers to the phonetic form itself and is thus secondary, and since the principle holds that "between the primary and the secondary, the grammatical operation applies to the primary"; or (5) [it refers to] a *śūdra* preceded by the word *mahat*.

In such cases, as with the substitution of *āt* and so forth, the change to *ṣ* does not occur; this should likewise be understood in subsequent instances, such as in the passage beginning with "in *arciḥ*" and so on. However, the third resolution is not possible in the latter case, because there the primary sense prevails due to its being directed toward the meaning (*arthaparatvena*). In many manuscripts, the reading is seen as "*arciḥ-prabhṛtiṣu*" rather than "*arciṣ-prabhṛtiṣu*"; in that case, nothing remains to be established, since the word "*arciḥ*" is secondary (*gauṇatva*) and lacks the suffix *-iṣ*.

And there is this summary verse: "Because it is impermanent, the *mūrdhan* [stage] was not placed by him in the position of the *arciḥ*. And in the Commentary, the phrase "of the Sun also here," etc., has this meaning: the order obtained from the text is the "order of recitation" (*pāṭhakrama*). According to the sequence of the text—"He goes to the world of Agni, he to the world of Vāyu, he to the world of Varuṇa, he to the world of Indra, he to the world of Prajāpati"—an order of Vāyu followed by Varuṇa is obtained; by setting aside that [order], the placement of those [deities] above the lightning is justified.

The meaning is that, in accordance with the *Vājasaneyi-śruti*, the placement of Āditya above Vāyu is what is intended to be established in this section (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding the reading in some places, "the placement above the wind denoted by the word 'world of the gods' (*devaloka*) is established"—here, although the rule "ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena" (Pāṇini 2.3.30) would require the genitive case when used with the word "upari," it should be understood that it does not necessarily apply, as the usage in the *Mahābhāṣya*—"tataḥ paścād vrajati"—indicates its non-universality (*anityatva*).
[This is] with respect to Vāyu.

Or rather, it should be understood that the ablative case is used here according to the rule "the ablative is used when there is an intention to express the object of an action, even if that object is not explicitly mentioned" (*atyarthavivakṣāyām kyaṅvyablope pañcamī*); likewise, in the subsequent portion of the Bhāṣya, "now, among Varuṇa, Indra, and so forth," the words "for that purpose" (*tadartham*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The meaning is that there would be a disruption of two sequences: first, if [the soul] were placed either between the sun and the moon or between the moon and lightning, it would result in the sequence from the sun to the moon, or from the moon to lightning; and second, it would result in a disruption of the sequence established by the order of the text—namely, the immediate succession of Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati—as expressed in the scriptural passage: "He [goes] to the world of Varuṇa, he [goes] to the world of Indra, he [goes] to the world of Prajāpati."

Regarding the phrase "below Taḍitatoṣya," the ablative case (*pañcamī*) should be understood as before. [Objection: How can there be a compound here? For the ablative case characterized by connection with a direction (*digyoga-lakṣaṇa-pañcamī*) is sublated by the rule "the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [is used] with words having the sense of *ataḥ* and suffixes" (*ṣaṣṭhy-atasarthapratyayena*). Since a compound cannot occur for an ablative ending when it is not sublated, and because in the case of the sixth case, the rule "with words denoting a full number (*pūraṇa*), a quality (*guṇa*), etc. prohibits a compound of a word ending in the sixth case with an indeclinable (*avyaya*), [how is this possible? [Response: It is said: this is indeed a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). Regarding the prohibition in the rule "with words denoting a full number, a quality, etc."...

However, the prohibition [of compounding] applies only to an indeclinable ending in a *kṛt* suffix that is used in conjunction with the two words *sat* and *asat*, and not with any other [indeclinable]. This is because examples such as *kaṭasya kartuṃ* (to do a mat) and *kaṭasya kṛtvā* (having done a mat) have been cited in the *Vṛtti* and other works. Yet, when joined with an indeclinable that does not end in a *kṛt* suffix, compounding certainly occurs; for this very reason, the venerable Pāṇini taught: *anuryatsamayā* (P. 2.1.15), and the authors of the *Vṛtti* and others explained it as *yasya samayā yatsamayā*. Furthermore, there is another method [for explaining the rule], which has been stated differently by those same commentators.

Furthermore, it has been established more than once previously that this prohibition of compound formation is non-permanent (*anitya*): "Because of the abundance of usage by the learned, because of the inclusion of indeclinables ending in *kṛt*-suffixes, and because of its non-permanence, the specific indications of that [non-permanence] alone are considered authoritative. As for the phrase "the sequence of meaning," this refers to the sequence of meaning characterized by the capacity (*sāmarthya*) consisting in the internal arrangement of the parts of the text. This means that the sequence of meaning is the sequence of the text's constituent elements as they exist within the belly of the book.

The meaning is that, because the lightning is the immediate [conductor] leading [the soul] onward, the sequence "from the moon to the lightning" (*tataś candramaso vidyutam*) must be disregarded; for if that were the case, one would have to accept a reversal of the textual order of Indra, Prajāpati, and Varuṇa. This is because, in order to establish the lack of interruption between these three according to the reading "he [goes] to the world of Varuṇa, he to the world of Indra, he to the world of Prajāpati," if one were to place the mention of the three before the lightning, it would result in a violation of the sequential order based on their actual physical location within the interior of the clouds.

The meaning is that if one were to accept the sequence "lightning immediately after Varuṇa" and then "Indra and Prajāpati after that," it would entail the violation of the order established by the Kauṣītaki recension, which places Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati in a specific succession.

Therefore, although in some manuscripts the reading "he [attains] the world of Varuṇa, he [attains] the world of Āditya, he [attains] the world of Indra, he [attains] the world of Prajāpati" is seen—with the world of Āditya placed between the worlds of Varuṇa and Indra—that is not authoritative. This is because it is not cited as such in certain manuscripts, because this very *Śrutaprakāśikā* serves as its witness, and because if such were the reading, it would result in an inconsistency between the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of this section. For instance, if Āditya were recited immediately after the world of Varuṇa, then...

How does the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) arise that all three—Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati—precede Āditya? For here, the proponent of the prima facie view, by relying on the order of the textual recitation which mentions "the world of Vāyu" and "the world of Varuṇa," asserts that the world of Varuṇa follows immediately after the world of Vāyu; how then could he, like one who has mounted a horse and forgotten the horse itself, disregard the sequence established by the text between the worlds of Vāyu and Āditya and instead propose that all three be placed before Āditya? Nor is this the case.

It must be said that because the immediate succession between Vāyu and Āditya is sublated, [the insertion] should occur precisely where those things are to be inserted; for it could equally well be argued: "Since the sequence 'from Āditya to Candramas' is sublated by Indra and Prajāpati, why should Varuṇa not also be inserted in that very same place? Furthermore, immediate succession is not something grasped through its own inherent force; if it is set aside by some authoritative means of knowledge, it can be set aside even by that which lacks such [inherent] status, since that too is authoritative.

If that is so, then for the sake of following the order of the text, let the mention of those two (the lightning and Varuṇa) occur immediately after the sun; let even the immediate succession established by the natural force of the words—namely, "from the sun to the moon"—be set aside, just as the sequence of wind and sun established by [the text] "from the world of wind to the sun" is set aside by the order of the text. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the mention of the world of the sun before the world of Indra and after the world of Varuṇa would be without basis. For this very reason, in the *Pūrvatantre* (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra), regarding fire...

The performance of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice must occur immediately after the specific performances such as the *Sāvitra-homa*, because we observe a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to enjoin the qualities of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā* following the recitation of the *Sāvitra-homa* and other rites; otherwise, the recitation there would result in absolute meaninglessness, as stated in the fifth book (*Pañcamādhyāya*). Therefore, the mention of the world of Āditya between the worlds of Varuṇa and Indra in the Kauṣītaki text is appropriate. Nor does this contradict the refutation of the opinion of Yādavaprakāśa in the subsequent section (*Uttarādhikaraṇa*).

It should be stated that we consider this [the opponent's position] to be correct, because Yādavaprakāśa has fabricated such a reading, and according to the maxim that an opponent must be refuted by accepting their own admissions, this interpretation is logically tenable. However, others argue that the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is indeed correct: rather than contradicting the sequence found in the Śruti text (*ādityāc candramasam*), it is more appropriate to contradict the sequence of the written text (*sa ādityalokaṃ sa indralokaṃ*); furthermore, since the immediate succession between the world of Vāyu and the world of Āditya can tolerate an intervention, all three [Vāyu, Varuṇa, and Indra] should be placed before Āditya. Thus, the prima facie view is perfectly logical.

For this very reason, in the case of the *jāteṣṭi* (the sacrifice on birth), since the immediate sequence following the occasion of the son’s birth—though established by the scriptural statement of the occasion (*nimitta-śruti*)—would result in the destruction of the son through the postponement of the first feeding with breast milk, it is sublated due to the resulting contradiction of its purpose. Consequently, even after the *jātakarma*, the *jāteṣṭi* is not to be performed. Since the natural immediate sequence of the occasion is thus sublated, the rite must be performed upon the cessation of ritual impurity (*āśauca*) when an auspicious time (*parva-kāla*) has arrived; for this is established in the fourth [book of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra]. By that same principle, the immediate sequence between the world of Vāyu and the world of Āditya is also sublated.

Since it is logical that those [terms] which require a specific location for insertion should be inserted precisely where they are obstructed, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is indeed sound. Nor should it be asked: "Why could the prima facie view not be that all three are inserted only after the world of Āditya? For that too is acceptable due to the symmetry of the reasoning; otherwise, one would have to abandon the order of the first-mentioned sequence—"the world of Vāyu, the world of Varuṇa, the world of Āditya"—in favor of the last-mentioned sequence, "he [goes] to the world of Āditya, he [goes] to the world of Indra, he [goes] to the world of Prajāpati."

Furthermore, because it is improper to override the order of the text, it is indeed correct that the prima facie position (pūrva-pakṣa) is that the three [worlds] should be placed before the world of Āditya. Moreover, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga) if one were to reject the reading of the world of Āditya between the worlds of Varuṇa and Indra—which is observed in all manuscripts and respected by Yādavaprakāśa and others. Nor should it be said that the placement of Āditya between Varuṇa and Indra lacks any basis; for they argue that such a displacement is logically established, just as in the case of the statements, "He offers the Agnihotra" and "He cooks the groats. Thus ends the section concerning Varuṇa (Varuṇādhikaraṇa).

Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "and such-and-such a mountain-side" (*bhāṣye amukaṃ ca parvatapārśvam*), this was stated with the intention of the masculine gender because the word *pārśva* possesses both genders; however, in the neuter, it would be *adakam*. Nor should it be argued that the form *amukam* also exists because of the reference in the Kalpataru on the Sūtra "That very [Brahman] is indeed [denoted by] Satya, etc. (*saiva hi satyādayaḥ*)—where it says "by the bestowing of unliberated fruit" (*amukta-phala-pradāna-sanayā*) due to the non-specification of the object—since that form is unauthoritative as it contradicts the grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇa-smṛti*).

The meaning is that it would follow [from your position] that the term "world" (loka) would have to be applied [to this state], and consequently, since it results in a mere figurative praise, the primary sense of "time" cannot possibly be a locus for experience. The reason for establishing its status as a "world" is already established by implication; thus, the intention is to demonstrate the desire to move about (*vijihīrṣā*), as expressed by the phrase "desiring to sport. This statement regarding the reading *vijihīrṣate* is made with reference to a certain variant manuscript; however, the alternative reading has already been explained above.

In the Bhāṣya, regarding the phrase "appointed by the Supreme Person for the purpose of conducting [the souls]," the intention is that the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "one appointed therein" (*tatra niyuktaḥ*). Regarding the word "of the former ones" (*pūrveṣām*) heard at the conclusion of the Bhāṣya: one might object that it is observed in common worldly usage that a specific injunction implies the exclusion of the remainder—for example, the statement "Devadatta sees with his left eye" is intended to exclude his seeing with the other [eye]. If this is so, how can this [statement] establish that others also possess sentience and the capacity to lead? To this we say: no, because in the sentence "He leads these [souls] to the world of Brahman,"...

It should be understood that by taking for granted both their status as persons (*puruṣatva*) and their nature as lead-ers (*gamayitṛtva*), and by establishing only the specific qualification of being non-human (*amānavatva*), the status of those [deities] such as the *arciṣ* etc. as leaders and persons is also understood. Furthermore, even under the view that Brahman’s role as the leader is what is enjoined, according to the method you have stated, when the leadership of others is negated, Brahman’s leadership as such is established by the maxim: "When a specific instance is negated, the general rule is permitted."

The meaning is that the sentence is intended solely to exclude the state of being human (*mānavatva*) by taking for granted the fact that the one belonging to lightning (*vaidyuta*) is a conductor (*gamayitṛ*). The sense is this: when it is specifically stated regarding the one belonging to lightning that "this Brahmin is not a human conductor," it follows as a matter of course that the preceding ones possess both the state of being human and the capacity to conduct. The phrase "would imply the state of being human" refers to those starting with the one belonging to light (*arcis*). The expression "in another [text]" and so forth is due to the sequence of the meanings.

The meaning is that [Varuṇa] is to be placed [there] by virtue of the sequence of purpose characterized by performing the single function of producing rain. It should be understood, however, that the point that Indra and Prajāpati are to be placed after the lightning is common to both the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta). [Regarding the placement of Varuṇa...]

The phrase "the one preceded by *śa* has been explained" implies that it was explained as a *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra. "They carry him forward" means they lead him toward him. The expression "asaciva," which signifies the characteristic of being the cause of rain, is used because Indra also is a cause of rain by virtue of his being the rider of the horse Bheḍha. Thus ends the section on the "Conductors" (*ātivāhikādhikaraṇa*).

The teacher Bādari maintains that [the scripture] leads only those who meditate upon the effected Brahman (kārya). Why? Because for one who meditates upon Hiraṇyagarbha—the effected Brahman—progression [to a higher state] is logically possible. For one who meditates upon the supreme Brahman—which is perfect, omniscient, omnipresent, and the self of all—progression to another location is not possible for the sake of attaining it, precisely because it is already attained. Indeed, the sole effect of the higher knowledge (paravidyā) is simply the cessation of ignorance regarding the supreme Brahman, which is eternally attained.

However, for one who meditates on the Brahman in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, travel is appropriate for the purpose of attaining that which is to be reached within a limited space; therefore, the group of conducting deities beginning with Light leads him to that very [Brahman]. || 6 ||

The meaning is that in the Bhāṣya, the phrase "he causes [them] to go" is qualified; for it is appropriate that the word *loka*, which ends in the plural number, serves as a qualification of the act of going by way of qualifying the worlds themselves. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "residing in specific worlds. Although the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) was not introduced previously in the Bhāṣya's statement, "having gone by way of light, etc., he intends," nevertheless, since the Brāhmaṇa-knowledge (the *Brahmavidyā*)—specifically the passage "Space, indeed, is the dissolver of name and form"—was introduced, it should be understood that this was said on the basis of taking the path of light, etc., as already established for the knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*).

Regarding the word "prapadya" (having resorted), the intention of resorting (*prapatty-abhisandhi*) is what is intended by the term "counter-intention" (*pratyabhisaṃdhi*). The phrase "from the opinion of Jaimini" is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as "from the opinion of Bādari," because both specific opinions will be set forth later. Now, an objection: the elders have stated that a "symbolic meditation" (*pratīka*) is the application of a cognition belonging to one substrate to another substrate; so how can this be said?

Fearing that the term "not having a symbol as its support" (*apratīkālambana*) might exclude those who meditate on effects (*kāryopāsaka*), he says: "And [the scripture] does not lead those who have a symbol as their support," as used here. Having stated the distinction from the view of Bādari, he states the distinction from the view of Jaimini by means of the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). The ultimate intent of Jaimini’s view is also that he leads those of both kinds; however, due to his great regard [for them], Jaimini has stated that those who meditate on the Supreme Brahman proceed via the path of the rays (*arcirādi*). The reading of others is *pratipattyabhisandhiḥ*, and in their system, the reading of the Sūtra is *na ca kārye pratipattyabhisandhiḥ*.

Since the statement made in the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie view) was not refuted in the *siddhānta* (the established conclusion), the author himself states its meaning: "by the Brāhmaṇa, 'All these [deities]... and so forth. The phrase "of others" and so on refers to the section concerning higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). The meaning is that in the *Kaṭhavallī* Upaniṣad, there is a mention of the path of departure in the words "going upwards from there. The scriptural statement (*śrutivākya*) is more authoritative. This means that both the *Prajāpati-śruti* and the passage associated with it are intended for the purpose of praise.

The meaning is that it is a description of that which consists of all things; however, anticipating the objection that "a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda) is precisely what we desire," he says: "provided that unity of the sentence is possible. The phrase "like going to another place while remaining on the ground" means that just as the earth itself, while remaining on the very ground, goes by way of another location on the earth—it cannot be said that the earth has not already been reached there—just as when a monkey reaches a *nyagrodha* tree, it is the *nyagrodha* tree itself, characterized by its specific upper region, that is reached.

The meaning is "in that same way. And "like the attainment of states such as curd by milk" means that milk, which already exists, is attained in the form of curd and so forth through the application of churning and other means; or alternatively, [it refers to] curd and so forth.

The meaning is: "like the attainment of the very nature of the thing itself. The sense is that there would be no liberation from bondage because it is impossible to effect a change in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Regarding the phrase "because of the fault in both ways," since the reading is *ubhayathā ca doṣāt*, the intention is that this alone is the traditional reading; therefore, the reading *ubhayathā adoṣāt tatkratuśca* is non-traditional. As for the passage beginning with "But others... and so forth:

The phrase "because of the consequence of a split in the sentence" means that it would entail the cognition of both a connection with non-return and a connection with this specific kalpa. Regarding the objection that there is a contradiction with the sūtra "But Jaimini [thinks otherwise]," the meaning is that there is a contradiction between the sūtra "But Jaimini [thinks otherwise]"—which is a siddhānta-sūtra—and the sūtra "Those who do not take the pratīka as their support. This is because the former conveys both the connection with non-return and the connection with this specific kalpa.

The phrase "the movement consists in the transcendence of the sphere of activity" (kāryamaṇḍalātikramarūpā gatiḥ) implies that [such a movement] is logically established; and as for the question of how there can be movement for the individual soul (jīva)—who is like the space enclosed within a jar, being a portion of Brahman delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—[the text] replies: "Because the state of being an individual soul is due to limiting adjuncts. The expression "entering the body of Brahmā" means that he will enter it.

If it is argued that the *paryaṅka-vidyā* and others constitute the authoritative proof [for this], the intention is that it is not possible for the Supreme Brahman to possess a physical form mounted upon a couch (*paryaṅka*). This is because [the scripture] speaks of the possession of a distinct form, as in: "All moments of time were born from the Puruṣa who is beyond the lightning."

The meaning is that it establishes [the body] as the cause for possessing a form with the color of lightning. Regarding the phrase "others say," etc., it is because we observe the usage "the world of Brahmā" (*brāhmaloka*). Since one must state the identity of meaning between the words "world of Brahmā" occurring in the introduction and the conclusion, and since the word "world of Brahmā"—given its placement alongside the worlds of earth and the intermediate space—is to be understood as referring to the world of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), it is established that the world of the Four-faced One is the proper object for the application of the term "Brahmā. This is the intended meaning. As for the passage beginning "hyadanadī," "of that... [and so on].

The sense is that this is based on such scriptural authority as: "The mountain Aha is its axle, the Muhūrta its yoke-pin, the Virajā river its stream, and the Tilya tree its trunk," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of the *ahīna* rule," [it refers to] the *dvādaśāhīna* mentioned in the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma.

The sense is that, just as there is an upward displacement of the twelve-fold *upasads* prescribed for the *nāciketa* fire-altar to the day of the *aśvamedha*, it is possible for this [passage] to have the purpose of demonstrating the excellence [of the path] distinct from the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*). Thus, the statement, "Those who sacrifice with sacrifice, with charity, and with austerity reach the world of smoke," refers to all forms of excellence other than the higher knowledge as having the path beginning with smoke as their means of attainment, and not...

The sense is: "of one who possesses only [the knowledge of] the *jña* [and so forth]. The connection with what follows is that all this is untenable for one who considers Hiraṇyagarbha alone to be the supreme Brahman. He demonstrates this very point in the passage beginning with "for those who do not know Brahman," and so on. The section concerning the effected [Brahman] (*kāryādhikaraṇa*) is concluded.

Thus ends the third quarter of the fourth chapter in the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, composed by the venerable Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, the author of the commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the statement in the Bhāṣya—that the goal has the characteristic of non-return—is incorrect, since that point will be established in the section [sūtra] *'anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt'*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "in the subject-sentence" (*viṣayavākye*). This means: in the subject-sentence of the section beginning with *'āprayāṇāt tatrāpi hi dṛṣṭam'*; for, since it must be stated that this refers to the subject-sentences of the various sections within the chapter on the Path of Light (*arcirādi-pāda*), the intended sentence should be understood as: "This is the path of the gods, the path of Brahman; those who proceed by this do not return to this human whirlpool."

Now, in this section, is the inquiry into adventitiousness (*āgantukatva*) and non-adventitiousness concerned with the states (*avasthā*), or with the substance (*dravya*) that possesses those states? It cannot be the first, because according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is accepted that the state consisting of modification (*vikāra*) occurs immediately after the production [of the effect]. Nor can it be the second, because since the theory of the non-existence of the effect in the cause (*asatkāryavāda*) is not accepted, there is no possibility of suspecting that the substance of knowledge (*jñāna-dravya*), which possesses the states, is adventitious.

This is because the infinity of the bliss of the liberated one is heard in such scriptural passages as, "Having obtained [it], he becomes blissful. Nor can it be maintained that his very nature is consciousness in the form of unlimited bliss, which remains concealed by ignorance during the state of transmigratory existence and manifests upon reaching the Supreme Light; for it has already been stated previously that concealment is impossible for that whose nature is knowledge, since the concealment of knowledge—which is synonymous with light—is nothing other than its destruction.

Furthermore, mere luminosity cannot constitute bliss; for bliss is the very nature of happiness, and the nature of happiness is being favorable to the self (*ātman*). For one who maintains that the self is merely luminosity, whose luminosity could possibly be experienced as favorable? Thus, for a proponent of the doctrine of mere luminosity, it is impossible to establish the nature of bliss in any way whatsoever. Moreover, if the goal to be accomplished were merely the attainment of one's own nature, then since that nature is eternally established, the statement "he manifests in his own nature" would refer to something already fully realized.

Otherwise, the statement would be meaningless; therefore, it is connected with the previously unestablished form as that which is to be accomplished. In this way, the expression "he manifests" (abhiniṣpadyate) retains its primary sense, and it coheres with the phrase "in his own form" (svena rūpeṇa), meaning he manifests in a form that consists exclusively of bliss and is unique to himself.

This being the case, we reply: "The manifestation [of the self] upon reaching [the Supreme]. This inner self, having reached the supreme light by way of the path beginning with light (*arcis*), attains a particular state which consists in the manifestation of its own true nature (*svarūpa*), and not in the production of a previously non-existent form. Why? Because of the word "by itself" (*svena*); for there is the qualification, "in its own form" (*svena rūpeṇa*).

Because [liberation] is not non-existent; because even in the case of jars and the like, there is permanence in terms of their state (*avasthā*), since the very nature of arising consists in the connection with a state; for we do not perceive any difference in the bliss of liberation (*mokṣasukha*) from the bliss of heaven (*svargasukha*) on the grounds that arising is adventitious (*āgantuka*). Furthermore, since bliss in the form of the experience of Brahman exists as the supreme human goal (*mahāpuruṣārtha*), the two sūtras—"On account of the promise, the released [Self]" and "The Self, because of the context"—which establish that the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is the thing to be attained and the human goal, would also be untenable; if this is argued, we say no, because by its own...

Regarding the statement, "He manifests with form (*rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*)," it will be clarified in the sūtra *"brāhmena jaiminiḥ"* that the word "form" (*rūpa*) is intended to mean the Brahman-form characterized by freedom from impurity (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth. Accepting this as established, one may investigate whether that Brahman-form is adventitious (*āgantuka*) or pre-existent (*prāksiddha*); since there is no fault in such an assumption, and because adventitious states of knowledge are not denied, the objection raised beginning with "something [else]" (*kiñcit*) and so forth is invalid, for even the self-nature qualified by freedom from impurity and the rest [is not excluded].

There is no fault [in our position], because it is solely intended to establish that [Brahman] is unsurpassed bliss. Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "favourability to the Self" (ātmānukūlatvam): the meaning is that whatever is experienced as favourable toward a particular Self is the happiness of that [Self]. Furthermore, "Self-hood" (ātmatva) consists in being the substratum of consciousness; therefore, the point is that nothing at all would be logically consistent under a doctrine where the Self is mere cognition (jñānamātra). Thus, the word "own" (sva) refers to what is unique [to each individual].

The meaning is that since it is stated that the word *sva* denotes "self," "one's own," "kinsman," and "wealth," this word *sva* here expresses merely the state of being one's own (*ātmīyatvamātra*), and not the state of being unaccomplishable (*asādhyatva*). Nor should it be asked how the word *sva*, which denotes only self, one's own, kinsman, and wealth, can be suspected of conveying the sense of being unaccomplishable; for the point is that since the word *sva* denoting "one's own" can—by virtue of belonging to the class of words beginning with *sarva*—refer to what is "one's own" in the sense of being dependent on another, it is possible for it to convey the sense of being unaccomplishable as a result.

Alternatively, the word "own" (*sva*) here refers to the self (*ātman*); thus, the sense is that it results in [the self] being unachievable (*asādhyatva*). The meaning is that "form" (*rūpa*) is what is to be achieved (*sādhya*). Immediately after this passage, the phrase "and so" (*evaṃ ca*) is seen as a citation; that should be understood as occurring right before the passage beginning with "how," namely, "how is the word 'own' [used]," or else another manuscript should be consulted. This state reaches a particular stage in the commentary, denoting "manifestation" (*abhiniṣpatti*).

The meaning is that [the self] is brought to a particular state; and thus, "it manifests in its own form" means it manifests in its own form characterized by freedom from taint (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth, and is made an object of the attribute-bearer knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). Consequently, although the origination—which consists in a relation between the state of expansion and [the self]—resides in the attribute-bearer knowledge, there is no origination of the self’s own nature as characterized by qualities such as freedom from taint, which is of the nature of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) due to its being unlimited bliss.

In this state of liberation, qualities such as being free from darkness (*apahatapāpmatva*) and the essential nature characterized by them are not adventitious; rather, they exist [inherently], whereas during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), the attribute-aspect of consciousness (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) was obstructed by karma.

It is taught that while there is no capacity to take as its object the nature of the Self as qualified by the eight qualities such as freedom from impurity (*apahatapāpmatva*) when concealment (*tirodhāna*) persists, once that concealment has ceased, knowledge directed toward that [Self] arises; and subsequently, a supreme knowledge having that as its object is produced. However, this does not deny the production of the attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) even in liberation. This, however, is the distinction: in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), knowledge has objects such as jars and the like.

This conventional discourse regarding the existence of adventitious forms and generalities is intended precisely with the following meaning: that while cognition dependent on the operation of the sense organs such as the eye requires external conditions, once liberation occurs and concealment has ceased, the resulting knowledge of all objects does not depend upon any adventitious cause whatsoever.

It should not be argued that there is a contradiction between the concluding portion of the *bhāṣya*—which states that "the cessation of concealment (*tirodhāna*) is here called 'manifestation' (*abhiniṣpatti*)," and the fact that the manifestation in the form of expansion upon the destruction of the bondage of *karma* and *mala* is not illogical—and the *bhāṣya* on the *adhikaraṇa* "Jaimini [thinks] by means of the *brāhmaṇa*" (*Brāhmaṇena Jaiminiḥ*), which states that the cessation of concealment is indeed the manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), because the two are presented as distinct: the cessation of concealment and the manifestation. This is because [the latter statement] is made by adopting the position that non-existence is a positive entity (*bhāvāntarābhāvapakṣa*).

Some maintain that the statement regarding the non-difference between the cessation [of concealment] and the manifestation [of the Self] is a declaration of difference based on the position that [the manifestation] is something additional. Others, however, resolve this by asserting that the commentary’s statement—that the manifestation is the cessation of concealment—is based on a figurative identification (upacāra). They argue that the claim in the commentary that [the Self] is "devoid of the three states beginning with waking" is incorrect, citing such passages as: "This person who is seen in the eye," "He moves about, becoming great in sleep," and "Then, when he is asleep here, unified and serene."
Anticipating the objection that [the text] teaches only one who is joined with the waking state, he says: "While the states beginning with the waking state are being indicated," and so forth.

If [it is argued that] bliss (*ānanda*) is dependent solely on contact with objects—since such a positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is observed in states such as waking and deep sleep—the [author] refutes this pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words beginning "If bliss... The meaning is that the manifestation in the form of an expansion of the attribute-bearing knowledge (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*) is not untenable; that is to say, the manifestation of the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahata-pāpmatva*) in the form of an expansion of the attribute-bearing knowledge is not untenable. The point is that the manifestation of the eightfold qualities consists precisely in their being made the object of the attribute-bearing knowledge.
[Objection: But if freedom from sin and the other qualities are eternally established, then bondage would be impossible.

It has been well stated that manifestation is not impossible, in the words: "Having become [one with Brahman], there is manifestation" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.2). Thus ends the section concerning manifestation after attaining union.

The ultimate reality [of bondage] is unavoidable. For "the state of having the eternal removal of impurity" (*nityasiddhāpahatapāpmatvam*) means being forever free from sin; and in one who is in fact always free from sin, neither a connection with impurity nor a connection with agency, enjoyment, and so forth rooted therein can possibly exist as ultimate reality. Furthermore, the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the Lord (*īśvara*) is likewise unavoidable, because it is impossible for the bondage that contradicts the non-difference taught by the scriptures to be real; otherwise, it would be illogical for the concealment of the eternally established true volition (*satyasaṅkalpa*) to occur in a transmigrating being. Indeed, not...

It is appropriate to say that the volition (*saṅkalpa*), which persists even during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) for the individual soul (*jīva*) and pertains to some limited range of action, is "veiled" (*tirohita*). Therefore, it must be established that the very same unimpeded and eternally perfected true volition belonging to the Lord—which, during the state of transmigratory existence, does not manifest as His own due to the non-manifestation of the soul’s non-difference from the Lord—is what is veiled with respect to that soul.

The state of having one's eyesight struck away (*apahatapāṣmatva*) does not mean the mere absence of defects (*pāṣma*), for if it were that, then since such a state would be eternally established, it would follow that bondage is illusory. Rather, it is the possession of a power that prevents the arising of sin even when one performs actions caused by sin. Likewise, the state of having true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) is also explained as being of the nature of a power; thus, there is no consequence of identity with God. If this is argued, we say no, because there is no evidence for such an interpretation of the meaning of the words.

If it is argued that a power obstructing the production of sin need not be postulated for the sake of preventing the arising of sin during the state of wandering in *saṃsāra*—since its arising at that time is accepted [as a fact]—and that rather, from the dawning of knowledge (*vidyā*) onwards, non-attachment (*aśleṣa*) occurs solely through the majesty of knowledge, as shown by the Sūtra: "Upon the attainment of That, there is the non-attachment and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, because of the scriptural teaching thereof," and thus the aforementioned non-attachment is established even without such a power, making the postulation of a power redundant; to this it is replied: "The state of having evil destroyed (*apahatapāpmatva*) is not... [the end of the sentence is missing in the source].

It cannot be said that there is an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of sin (*pāpa*), because if sins were the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence by way of their own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), they would result in being devoid of any nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*). Even if it is accepted that they are the counter-correlates of an absence in the form of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), upon investigating what that "ultimate reality" consists of, it ultimately resolves into "non-sublatability" (*abādhyatva*); and it cannot be maintained that what is subject to sublation (*bādhyatva*) can be the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence, whether that be by way of its own nature or by way of the form of ultimate reality.

Because they are swallowed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), however, they are sublatable by knowledge (*jñānanivartyatva*). Consequently, through the characteristic of being unsublatable—which is the absence of sublation by knowledge—the status of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of absolute non-existence is established for the impurities (*pāṣma*). And thus, the resulting meaning is that the impurities are sublatable by knowledge; this is precisely what we accept.

Furthermore, in your view, the manifestation of qualities such as the destruction of ignorance (*apahatapāpmatva*) is not even possible for one who is liberated. First, according to the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), since the entire manifold of distinctions—including the division between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—is merely imagined by that one ignorance, it dissolves upon the arising of that knowledge; thus, the soul remains only as non-dual pure consciousness, and the distinction between the bound and the liberated cannot exist. Even if one accepts the doctrine of multiple souls (*anekajīvavāda*) and admits the distinction between the bound and the liberated, although [it may seem possible] when knowledge arises for someone...

Even though it may be argued that although the expansion of duality created by ignorance has dissolved for him, the expansion of duality created by the ignorance of other bound persons still persists; nevertheless, according to the view that both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are reflections, it is appropriate that the liberated one should abide solely as the pure consciousness that constitutes the original prototype (*bimba*). Consequently, it is impossible for him to become another reflection. For if that were possible, then at some point—

Furthermore, because it is difficult to avoid the consequence that the individual soul (jīva) would become an internal reflection [of Brahman], there would result the recurrence of bondage, just as in the theory of limitation (avacchedapakṣa). For this very reason, in the doctrine of the plurality of souls (anekajīvavāda), the theory of limitation is not accepted; for liberation achieved through one such limitation would lead to bondage once again upon contact with another internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) through that same limitation. Therefore, in the position where the Lord (Īśvara) is the reflection and pure consciousness is that which permeates both, [this applies] to the liberated soul.

It must be stated that liberation consists in attaining the state of the Supreme Lord, who possesses qualities such as omniscience, lordship over all, and the fulfillment of all desires; just as when the reflection of a single face appears in many mirrors, upon the removal of one mirror, that particular reflection persists in the form of the original object (the *bimba*) and not merely as a face, because even then the status of being the original object in the face has not departed due to the presence of other mirrors, so too it is with the reflection of the single consciousness (*caitanya*) in multiple limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

It must be stated that when a single reflection exists, upon the arising of *vidyā* and the destruction of its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), that reflection necessarily persists in the form of the original object (*bimba*); however, this position is not tenable, because a reflection of that which is not endowed with form is not logical—let alone in the case of that which is formless and invisible—since the theory of the reflection of the invisible has already been refuted. Thus it is enough.

[This is] by way of a digression regarding the intellect. As for the passage beginning with "But others," etc., it refers to the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of sin (*pāpa*). The meaning is that since the prior non-existence and the non-existence through destruction of a jar are themselves admitted to be its absolute non-existence, it would be impossible for one who is liberated—possessing the non-existence through destruction of sin—to have the state of being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) in the form of the absolute non-existence of sin.
Thus concludes the section concerning the manifestation [of the soul] upon reaching [the Supreme].

Now, one might object that the statement in the Bhāṣya, "due to the similarity consisting of association" (*sāhityasāmyasādhamryāt*), is improper; for since similarity itself is the nature of having common properties (*sādhamrya*), the meaning is already established by the mention of "similarity" alone. To this he replies: "The words 'similarity' (*sāmya*) and 'having common properties' (*sādhamrya*)," because they refer here to association with objects of enjoyment (*bhogyasāhitya*). "Desires" (*kāmāḥ*) are so called because they are desired; they are the auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇāḥ*). [Thus, it means] the auspicious qualities together with the Brahman.

The meaning is that [the Brahman] experiences all [objects]; however, if the intent were merely to express coexistence with the enjoyer, it would follow that the Brahman is subordinate to the individual soul (jīva) as the enjoyer, and consequently, the status of the Brahman as the subject of manifestation (prakāritva) would be destroyed—this is the intended sense. If it is objected: "Even if there is coexistence with the enjoyer, would it not follow that the Brahman is subordinate to the objects of desire? We say no, because this is an accepted position; for by the mere power of differentiation (vibhāga-śakti), [the Brahman possesses] knowledge of itself and others, and so forth.

The meaning is that a distinction must also be stated because [otherwise] the explanation would be untenable. Regarding the phrase "given that knowledge is dependent on instruments": given that knowledge is dependent on instruments, the state of having ceased functioning as an instrument is the cause for the absence of cognition of oneself and others; for in the case of a liberated being, since there is no dependence on instruments for measurement, there is no absence of knowledge. If it is argued that "there is no mutual identity," the word "in deep sleep" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

One might object: "Is it not the case that difference is not accepted on account of the mind being subtle, but rather that even there, only the power (*śakti*) itself is the differentiator? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because the non-conscious [nature] lacks the state of having only power remaining. The meaning is: if it is argued that although a difference exists in relation to the non-conscious, there is no difference between consciousness and the Lord because of the existence of the forms of differentiators—namely, the states of manifoldness and its absence—[the answer follows].

If it is argued that there is no consequence of [the Lord] being engaged in the activity of the world because He knows [things] as being unconfused—this means that since difference is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) as being the object of the Lord’s knowledge characterized by non-confusion, there is no consequence of His being engaged in the activity of the world; such is the sense. Thus ends the section [of the commentary] on "being seen without division" (*avibhāgena dṛṣṭatvādhikaraṇam*).

The meaning is that, between the two views depending on the two wings of the *ṛṣṭi* (spear), one or the other is to be accepted. As for the claim that "the essential nature [of the self] is insentient (*jaḍa*)," one might object: "In the system of Jaimini, let it be granted that the self does not have the nature of pure consciousness; however, since qualities such as freedom from impurity (*apahatapāpmatva*) exist, the self's insentiency is not thereby admitted. To this we say: there is no evidence for this. The point is that if one were to admit both freedom from impurity and the nature of being consciousness itself, it would result in no distinction from our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Regarding the phrase "the ultimate state of being devoid of occasional pleasure," they raise this objection: if it were heard as *akādācitkasukha* (non-occasional pleasure), then, through the compounding of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the word *kādācitkasukha*, the meaning would be "devoid of occasional pleasure"; for [otherwise], it would not be so.

If it is argued that by resorting to a *bahuvrīhi* compound—taking "anīla" as "one for whom there is no jar"—it can be said that "anīlaghaṭa" refers to a place devoid of jars; and that for this very reason, the subsequent passage stating "satyasaṅkalpaḥ" (one whose resolve is true) means "devoid of a false resolve," is also untenable; then, on this point, some maintain that "sati" is a separate word ending in the locative case, meaning "when [the elements] such as earth exist."

Regarding the object, "akāmaḥ" means "niṣkāmaḥ" (free from desire). This should be understood in the same way for passages such as "satyasaṅkalpaḥ" (one whose resolve is true). They maintain that the purport of this text lies in such an interpretation. [Thus ends] the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The word *kṛtya* means that there is no re-emergence of what has been destroyed; this is the sense. The phrase *anyaparam* is to be explained as meaning the exclusion of insentient matter (*jaḍa*). In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the division is made at *svalpaḥ... asti*. Regarding the passage beginning with *pare tu*, the words *muktaḥ* (the liberated one) are to be supplied, [referring to] "one who remains in the state of being the Self of all. The term *dhruvasya* means "of that which serves as the limit of division."
Thus concludes the section concerning the Brāhmaṇa.

One should not argue that there is a contradiction with the previous sūtra because the statement "consisting of consciousness alone" (*vijñānaghana eva*) is intended to exclude other associations (*anyayoga-vyavaccheda*), whereas the previous sūtra established that the exclusion of non-association (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) was intended—namely, that the entire self is non-inert and self-luminous. This is because the particle *eva* in that context is attached to the qualifier; just as in the expression "the conch is white indeed" (*śaṅkhaḥ pāṇḍura eva*), the particle *eva* excludes the possibility of its being anything other than white, so too this [present] *eva* excludes the impossibility of its being consciousness (*vijñānatva-ayoga-vyavaccheda*).

The meaning is as follows: since the status of being knowledge (*jñānatva*) is excluded in all [other cases], that treatise—by virtue of establishing the exclusion of insentience (*jaḍatva*), which is distinct from that [knowledge]—has no intention (*tātparya*) regarding the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). Furthermore, because the *Bhāṣya* states that [liberated cognition] depends on another effort (*prayatnāntara*), the inference that a liberated volition (*muktasaṅkalpa*) is dependent [on something else] by virtue of its being a volition—just like an ordinary worldly volition—is not a counter-argument (*pratirodhin*), because it is sublated (*bādhita*) by scripture (*āgama*), similar to the inference that a human skull is pure. Otherwise...

The sense is that accounts such as Agastya’s drinking of the ocean would otherwise be rendered untrue. [Objection: But this concern is futile; for just as even a woman brought forth merely by the imagination of lustful men becomes the cause for the emission of their seminal fluid, so too fathers and others, though projected by his own volition (*saṅkalpa*), will suffice for the production of their respective effects. Why, then, is the creation of external objects accepted? [Reply: Not so; for there are certain effects to be accomplished through the actual nature of things, such as tooth-marks or strings of jewels, while others [are not].

Regarding those things to be accomplished through knowledge (*jñāna-sādhya*), such as the emission of the final *dhātu*, horripilation, and so forth, as previously described—if these effects are provided merely by the mental intention (*manoratha*) of the father and others, then they will be effects accomplished solely through knowledge; they will not be effects accomplished by the actual nature of the object (*vastu-svarūpa*). For instance, horripilation and the like do not belong to a lustful man in the same way that tooth-marks, garlands of skulls, and so forth belong to a woman, which are accomplished by the actual object of a woman. Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing all the enjoyments resulting from those effects, the creation (*sṛṣṭi*) must be undertaken.

The phrase "in the case of those who have attained heaven" refers to [the activities] such as eating (*jakṣaṇa*), which constitute the fruits of their past actions; the intended meaning is that neither the inhabitants of heaven nor animals acquire merit or demerit through such acts. Furthermore, it means that by this very fact, the Śruti has made known that they are beyond the scope of injunctions and prohibitions.

The point is this: just as eating at night—which is inferred from the fact of being corpulent—is the means of establishing that corpulence, so too, there is no logical inconsistency in the fact of having no other superior (ananyādhipatitva)—which is inferred from the power of true resolve (satyasaṅkalpatva)—being the means of establishing that [resolve]. For this very reason, in the case of the injunction "He offers the prastara-bundle with the Sūktavāka," since the offering of the prastara-bundle is not of the nature of a sacrifice (*yāga*), a connection with a deity is impossible; therefore, the Sūktavāka, which reveals the deities, cannot be established as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to that [offering] by virtue of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*).

The sense is that, having raised the doubt as to how [the nature of sacrifice] could arise, it has been demonstrated that the character of the *prastara-preraṇa* (the throwing of the grass-bundle) as a sacrifice is postulated solely through the necessity of otherwise explaining the instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the *sūktavāka*, which is understood from the direct mention of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), by way of its connection with the deities propounded in that *sūktavāka*. Now, one might object: since the quality of being "free from evil" (*apahatapāpmatva*) was already established previously, the doubt to be excluded by this sūtra would not arise; anticipating this, he says: "As for what is called 'being free from evil'... The remainder of the sentence is: "...for it has been clearly shown right here in this very sūtra."

"But others," and so forth; for this very reason—namely, because of his power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*)—he does not create the Lord by means of his own resolve, since that would entail the contradiction of his own power of true resolve being dependent upon the Lord. Therefore...

The meaning is that they do not exercise sovereignty (*adhipati*). "By the absence of the cause of suffering" means that whoever has the power to bring about or to remove pleasure and pain in relation to someone is the sovereign (*adhipati*) over that person; this is the intended sense. Regarding the definition of the "subordinate" (*śeṣa*): the point is that even though rice and the like are incapable of bringing about or removing pleasure and pain during acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), they still possess the status of being subordinate (*śeṣitva*). As for the statement "I am the support of the Brāhmaṇa," the meaning is that he is the sustainer of one who is liberated. Thus ends the section on *saṅkalpa*.

One should not object that the statement in the *Bhāṣya*—that a *satra* and an *ahīna* are distinguished by a difference in resolve (*saṅkalpa*)—is incorrect, on the grounds that being a *satra* or an *ahīna* is based respectively on the injunctions to "sit" (*āsīran*) and "sacrifice" (*yajati*), and thus lacks a basis in a difference of resolve. For the connection is not that "by a difference of resolve, it becomes a *satra* and an *ahīna*," which would entail this fault; rather, the meaning is that once the two forms are established through the injunctions of "entering upon" (*upaiti*) and "sacrificing" (*yajati*), whichever form one desires to perform, one carries out that performance. Thus he says, regarding the nature of the *satra*: [the text continues with *satratve*].

Regarding the phrase beginning with "ahīnatve ca" (and in the case of being an *ahīna*), the *Bhāṣya* text states "by means of a difference in intention (*saṅkalpa*)": the *dvādaśāha* (twelve-day rite) is an *ahargaṇa* (series of days) consisting of the following form: "The *prāyaṇīya-utirātra* is the first day; the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*; three *chandomas*; the *avivākya* is one day; and the *udayanīya-utirātra* is the final day. By virtue of the injunctions for the *avivākya* and the *udayanīya*, it takes the form of a *satra* (sacrificial session) as well as an *ahīna*. For in the case of an *ahīna*, there is no restriction on the number of performers, as indicated by the rule: "One, two, or many may sacrifice by means of the *ahīna*"; thus it is not so [in the case of a *satra*].

Since there is a prohibition against the officiating priests being consecrated—based on the rule that "those who have been consecrated should perform the sacrifice"—certain duties such as these are established [for them]. In the case of the *sattra*, however, duties are established such as the restriction that the number seventeen must not be exceeded (as stated in: "The householders, seventeen in number and with four as the limit, being themselves the officiating priests, being Brāhmaṇas, should enter upon the *sattra*"), and the fact that those who are consecrated alone act as sacrificers for one another.

And so, just as the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) possesses a twofold nature, even for one who has been liberated, both embodiedness and disembodiedness are established by valid authority; thus, when these two forms are authoritative, one adopts either the performance of an *ahīna* or a *sattra* according to one's will, and in the same way, one adopts either embodiedness or disembodiedness according to one's resolve (*saṅkalpa*).

The meaning is "appropriation. By the phrase "through the conceptualization of modes conforming to that," the sense is that even in the absence of the will (*saṅkalpa*) of the liberated soul, the creation of the body and so forth occurs through the will of the Supreme Self; thus, the intention is that the will referred to by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) in the preceding Sūtra is necessarily dependent upon the liberated soul. He states [the opponent's view] along with its purpose: however, because the interpretation of the Sūtra as "in the absence of a body" contradicts the section [of the *Brahma-sūtra*] stating "merely by his will, when he desires" (4.4.8), that [interpretation] is not accepted; this is the sense.

The meaning is that [the object] is characterized by the power of being an instigator (*pravartakatva*). The point is this: since self-identification (*ātmābhimāna*) is the cause of activity, there is a conformity to activity through its conformity to self-identification; thus, by the phrase "conformable to self-identification," the possession of the power of instigation is indicated. He establishes that self-identification is the cause of activity with the words beginning "For self-identification... By this, the power of illumination (*prakāśakatvaśakti*) is stated. The meaning is that the pervasion of cognition (*jñānavyāpti*) is endowed with the power to illuminate external objects such as jars and cloths.

Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "And merging (*sampatti*) is death," the entire passage beginning with "Speech merges into the mind" and ending with "Fire [merges] into the highest deity" can also be construed as forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that proposition, because it begins with "Speech merges into the mind" and concludes with "Fire into the highest deity. With the intention of showing its syntactical unity with the subsequent portion of the text—namely, that in those two states there exist both the attainment of the *prājña* (the conscious self) and a state of unconsciousness—he says:

[The author] says, "by means of [passages] such as 'then, my dear, one becomes united with Being,'" intending to show that these form a single syntactical unit with the preceding statement. He then states, "of the union with Brahman and the state of being free from affliction," and so forth. It should be understood that this indicates both modes of interpretation are intended by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakṛt*), because both the "union with Brahman" and the "state of being free from affliction" are heard in the passage, "embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña ātmā*)," and considering that both should be shown even by the portion of the Sūtra, "for it is made manifest."

The scriptural passage concerning the perfection of the *brāhma* state is also to be considered. Regarding the sūtra "Non-existence [of body and senses], according to Bādari" (*abhāvaṃ bādarir*), it is explained that because of the qualification "with the mind" (*manasā*) in the śruti—"He rejoices, seeing these desires with the mind, which are in the world of Brahman"—it is determined that the liberated one lacks a body and sense organs; for if he were to sport with both mind and body and senses, the qualification "with the mind" would be purposeless. This is the remainder of the argument in the sūtra "Existence [of body and senses], according to Jaimini, because of the mention of option" (*bhāvaṃ jaiminirvikalpāmananāt*).

In the sūtra, *dvādaśāhavat ubhayavidhaṃ bādarāyaṇo'taḥ*, the word *ataḥ* has been explained as referring to the scriptural passage, "by the mind these desires," and to the scriptural passage, "he becomes singlefold," and so forth; since that [explanation] is not contradictory, [the author], setting aside that part, states the portion to be refuted with the words beginning "by mere volition" (*saṅkalpād eva*). The phrase "there is no impossibility of enjoyment" means that even if abundant enjoyment were impossible, there certainly occurs a subtle form of enjoyment—just like dream-enjoyment—which is accomplished by mere mental desire.

The meaning is that they have described [the state] as having abundant enjoyment when the body and senses are present, like the waking state, and subtle enjoyment when they are absent; and because the persistence of the body is established otherwise—that is, because enjoyment is established by the mere existence of the mind even without the persistence of the body.

Although, according to the doctrine that [the world] is created by the effort of the Lord alone, there is no distinction between the two states of waking and dreaming—since both are established as having their own created instruments of experience, whether real or unreal—the question arises: what is the basis for the specific instruction that "in the absence of the body, it is like the twilight state (sandhyā)," whereas "in its presence, it is like the waking state"? Furthermore, the opponents rightly remark that it is an artificial interpretation to construe "in the absence of the body" (*tanvabhāve*) as meaning "in the absence of the body created by oneself. Nevertheless, the intent of those [scriptural statements] is to point out the aforementioned defect.

Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of making known that there is no contradiction in intention": one might object that even if the liberated soul has no dependence on others during the experience of Brahman, it is still provided with various instruments for the experience of Brahman created by the Lord; since this was established in the Sūtra "In the absence of a body" (*tanvabhāve*), which reveals precisely the existence of contradictory intentions, how can there be non-contradiction?

If this is argued, we say no; for the intention [of the scripture] would not be contradicted by the statement that even in the state of indifference (audāsīnya), the Lord causes the liberated ones to attain enjoyment. The point is that, by the force of their specific qualification (*adhikāra*), it is manifested at that time. This refers to all instances where the absence of a second object is taught, such as: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? and "When one is asleep, one desires no desire and sees no dream," and so forth; in all such cases, it refers to deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

The sense is that since [the scripture] proceeds precisely with reference to *kaivalya* (isolation), the absence of a second vision has that alone as its object. Now, one might object: "But this [state of] dwelling in the three abodes (*tridhāmavāsa*) and so forth does not have *kaivalya* as its object. To this he says: "It is the ripening of *saguṇa*-vidyā" (qualified knowledge). As for the passage beginning with "Others, however," etc., it means that the functioning of a body such as that of a servant and so forth is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). However, in the state of liberation (*muktidaśā*), the meaning is that there is the functioning of a body such as that of a servant created for the purpose of being an instrument for enjoyment; [this is] "for the sake of following the will of the Lord" (*īśvarānu-mañcaraṇāya*).
