The phrase "moving through the realms of desire, form, and formlessness" means for the sake of following the Lord as ordained by the Śruti; since the state of being a servant and so forth is undesirable, [the Lord] himself stated that there is an absence of the exercise of ego-sense—this constitutes a single sentence.
Thus ends the section concerning non-existence.

In the commentary, it is asked: "What is the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of the liberated one? Sovereignty is the activity (*karman*) of the Lord; the suffix *śyan* is applied in the sense of an action according to the rule "after words denoting qualities and *brāhmaṇa*, etc., [the suffix *kyap* is added] and also in the sense of action. It is just as the activity of a king is "kingship" (*rājya*), which is the protection of subjects. Therefore, this is the meaning.

What is attained by the liberated one through such terms as "equality with the Lord" (*īśvara-sāmya*) or "similarity" (*sādharmya*)? Does that state of being a Lord consist of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe—which is unique to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) and includes universal sovereignty—or does it concern the creation of bodies and so forth within the scope of experiencing the Supreme Person? Regarding the question of whether this universal sovereignty over the creation of the universe and so forth belongs to the scope of experiencing the Supreme Person, all three [interpretations] are to be explained, because they correspond to the nature of one's own self-conception (*ātmābhimāna*). For he who considers his own essential nature (*svarūpa*) to be capable of independence (*svātantrya*) [attains this].

"His independence is the goal of human endeavor; thus the prima facie view has been stated. This is the intended meaning: one should not argue that the statement "No one equal to Him or superior to Him is seen" must be restricted to mean that there is no equality in every respect due to its contradiction with other scriptural texts on equality. For, since that would contradict the scriptural texts on equality, it is more appropriate to restrict the prohibition itself by interpreting it as referring to the denial of equality with Brahman among transmigrating beings—just as the passage "Who indeed knows whether He exists in that world? is restricted because it contradicts the results understood from the injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra-vākya*).

Furthermore, it is appropriate to conceive [the deity] as having its own limbs; moreover, the attainment of the qualities of the object of meditation is understood to be the direct fruit, as in the scriptural passage beginning with "As one acts," and the mere sovereignty of the supreme Brahman is not the object of meditation.

However, it should not be said that unrestricted sovereignty over the entire world [is denied], because even though the liberated one attains sovereignty over a few objects created by his own volition, the principle of *tatkratu* (the attainment of what one intends) remains valid. This is because scriptures such as "The controller of all, the lord of all" and "The cause, however, is the object of meditation, endowed with all sovereignties" demonstrate that unrestricted universal sovereignty is to be meditated upon. Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that the liberated one moves at will through all worlds; it is not [that he does not].

It is logical to conceive of his movement through various worlds as being for the purpose of experiencing the fruits associated with those respective realms; for if one were to admit that even while experiencing the bliss of Brahman he wanders about out of a longing for other objects, it would result in the destruction of its unsurpassed nature. Therefore, the movement of the liberated soul through the worlds is solely for the sake of divine play (*līlā*), such as the act of governing. Consequently, since we observe scriptural teachings regarding supreme equality, the principle of "whatever one's desire" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), and the wandering through all worlds, it must be accepted that the liberated soul, like the Supreme Lord, possesses powers such as the creation of the entire universe. And yet—

There is a rule that the attainment of a certain quality depends on another, and thus the quality of the former is inferior to that of the latter; for we see that disciples who have acquired knowledge from a teacher likewise engage in exposition and the composition of treatises. Furthermore, we observe feudal lords (sāmanta) who possess power dependent on the sovereignty of a king, yet they rival the king and even triumph over him. Therefore, in this case, while it may be that none surpass the Supreme Self due to its unsurpassed sovereignty, there will certainly be those equal to it.

Therefore, being independent, they would proceed even toward the creation of the world. Nor should it be argued that in the contexts dealing with creation and so forth, the activity of creation and the like belongs only to the Supreme Self and not to the liberated ones; for just as in the context of the Śyena sacrifice, although the sacrifice named *iṣu* is not present there, the statement "the rest is equal to the Śyena" establishes its similarity, so too, because of the statement of equality with the Lord of All, the specific subsidiary parts belonging to that [Śyena] are applicable to the *iṣu*, and thus the establishment of their activities such as creation is logically consistent in those [liberated ones].

Furthermore, just as the *sāptadaśya* (the quality of being seventeen) and other such marks forcibly bring about the acquisition of the specific subsidiary details (*dharmāntara*) belonging to the *svarasāman*, *vaiśvadevī-āmikṣā*, and *ādyāvāpa-ātharvaṇa-ekakapāla* mentioned in their own context, so too—by the force of marks such as the movement through all worlds—it is possible for liberated souls to acquire sovereignty and activity over the world, even though these are mentioned in a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) alongside the *svarasāman*, *vāruṇa-ekakapāla*, and *maitrāvaruṇī-āmikṣā*. Therefore, the claim that "activity over the world is excluded" based on the rule *dvitīyāyāṃ ca* (Jaiminisūtra 3.4.14) is without foundation.

It has been stated by the commentators on the *Vṛtti* regarding the rule "anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam" that this [restriction] concerning the search (*parīṣsā*) is merely general (*prāyika*). Alternatively, [the compound] *jagadvyāpāravarja* means "that which excludes the activity of the world"; the word *aiśvarya* (sovereignty) is the substantive to which the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). For this very reason, the subsequent reference—"on account of the contingency of excluding the activity of the world," etc.—is justified. If, however, the form were derived from the suffix *ṇamul*, there would be no abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), and the grammatical form would be different; for in the *Bhāṣya* it says, "the sovereignty of the liberated one."

The word "it ought to be" (*bhavitum arhati*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Therefore, it should be observed that there is no inconsistency in the suffix *ṇamul* being prescribed in connection with a verbal root (*dhātu-sambandha*) under the view that [the term] ends in *ṇamul*. Regarding the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "Therefore, this is the nature of being the Lord of the Universe (*jagad-īśvara-tva-rūpa*)," one might object: "Is it not the case that the definition of Brahman is 'being the cause of the origin and so forth of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) that persists through beginningless and endless cycles of kalpas'? Since liberated souls (*muktas*), however, lack the agency of creating the phenomenal world existing prior to their own liberation, there is no contradiction in [their] not possessing this definition. If this is argued, we say: No, because [the definition applies] to those who are currently engaged in the creation and so forth of the world.

Since there is no rule governing the uniformity of intention among liberated beings, it might happen that while one has the desire to create, another simultaneously has the desire to dissolve; thus, no effect whatsoever would be accomplished. Furthermore, it cannot be the case that all [liberated beings] proceed toward the creation of the world and so forth solely under the control of the Supreme Self.

If it must be said that they attain a single mind, then, because [the liberated soul] is dependent on that [Lord], the scriptural statement regarding equality—which would otherwise be impossible—must necessarily be restricted. This is because, according to the logic of the sūtra to be cited later, "And because there is a mark of equality only in respect to enjoyment" (BS 4.4.21), even by taking equality only in respect to enjoyment, the usage of the term "equality" is possible even without [the liberated soul] being the cause of the world; just as, between two pieces of gold and stone held on a scale, there is a conventional usage of "equality" due to an equality in weight, though there is no absolute identity. Thus, it does not belong to the liberated one.

The meaning is that there was the engagement in the activity of the world; nor should a contradiction with the *tatkratu* principle (the principle that one attains what one intends) be suspected, because there is no contradiction in accepting the attainment of Brahman as qualified by its causality. Regarding the statement in the Bhāṣya, "Being one, it became manifold": from that [Brahman], which was "one"—meaning devoid of the qualities of being a ruler (*kṣatra*) and so forth, such as being a protector—and "being," meaning it did not exist as if manifest, or rather, it was not sufficient for its own purpose—it "emitted" (*atyasṛjata*), meaning it emitted in an excellent manner, that is, in a pre-eminent way, the "form of excellence," the most praiseworthy form.

"Devatrā" means "among the gods"; "kṣatrāṇi" means "the Kṣatriyas. To the question, "What then are those Kṣatriyas? he replies, "Indra, Varuṇa," and so forth. Regarding the root *kan*, [it is used] in the sense of "shining. From the root *kan* belonging to the Bhūvādigaṇa, which signifies "shining, beauty, and motion"—as in the rule "kana dīptikāntigatiṣu"—the suffix *ṇyat* would have been expected; however, due to the specific grammatical instruction "kanyāyāḥ kanīna ca," it does not occur there, but rather that which is actually prescribed occurs instead.

Because of the overflow of joy at the thought that one may act according to one's desire everywhere, [the liberated soul] moves about as he pleases, just like the singing of the *Sāmaveda* authorized by the Śruti, which says: "He remains singing this Sāman: 'Hāu hāu hāu,'" and so forth. Thus, in the sūtra "On account of the statement regarding that being present" (*Upasthite'tastadvacanāt*), the attainment of Brahman is made the reason for acting according to one's desire; for it is precisely for the liberated soul, whose concealment has ceased and who resides in the supreme ether, that the experience of Brahman endowed with all its glories is possible.

The doubt that movement [in another body] would be in vain has also been refuted; for activity prompted solely by joy does not proceed from a specific purposeful aim. Even for one who has attained the experience of the bliss of Brahman, it is possible to assume another body and move about at will out of a desire for direct perception through the senses, such as the eyes, and so forth. Here, the intention of the author of the Sūtras, who points to Brahman as "not revolving within the realm of modifications," is this: there can be no increase or decrease in that bliss which consists in the experience of Brahman, which is devoid of decay and destruction.

Because it is of a constant and uniform nature, for such a liberated one who experiences Brahman, there is no other bliss to be attained by which the experience of Brahman might be conceived as inferior to the enjoyment found within the spheres of those holding office (ādhikārika).

Now, since the phrase "together with the wise Brahman" cannot serve as a proof for equality of enjoyment by virtue of its referring to coexistence with objects of enjoyment, [the author], while acknowledging this objection, cites scriptural passages that establish *sāyujya* (union) in the form of equality of enjoyment, beginning with "He who knows thus... and so on, up to "...the divine Speech enters him from the earth and from fire; that indeed is the divine Speech by which whatever—"

"He speaks, as it were, and the divine mind (*daivaṃ manaḥ*) enters him from the sky and from the sun; that indeed is the divine mind by which one becomes truly blissful and does not grieve. Then the divine vital breath (*daivaḥ prāṇaḥ*) enters him from the waters and from the moon; that indeed is the divine vital breath which, whether moving or not moving, neither suffers nor is injured. Thus, the fruit of the knowledge of the divine speech and vital breath, previously introduced, is stated.

"He who knows thus becomes the Self of all, just as this divinity [is]; just as these deities become all beings, even so do all beings protect him who knows thus. Here, "becomes the Self" means he becomes worthy of worship like the Self; "protect" means they guard and honor him. "By that, he wins union with and the same world as this divinity"—the meaning is that by that aforementioned knowledge, he attains union (*sāyujya*) and co-residence (*salokatā*) with this divinity.

The point is that although the cited passages do not explicitly concern those who hate Brahmins, nevertheless, by virtue of the same underlying principle, they ultimately serve as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the equality of experience even in the case of those who hate Brahmins.

The intention is that there should be this unity of meaning; thus, the sense is that in the Brāhmaṇa passage "rebirth does not exist," the negation culminates in the prohibition of birth characterized by being an abode of suffering and so forth—this is what is meant by "non-return" (*anāvṛtti*). According to the principle of accepting that even if birth exists, there is a negation of birth as a locus for what is to be abandoned (*heya*), so too, even if return exists, there is no return as a locus for what is to be abandoned; rather, it is [the absence of] desire.

The sense is that movement occurs only by means of a sign (nimitta); or, the meaning of the phrase "either by his own will or by karma" is this: even for liberated beings, although their prior merit and demerit have been destroyed through the greatness of knowledge, it is possible for them to fall from their station—just as Nahuṣa and others fell from their positions due to the power of sins such as hostility toward the Lord committed at the time of liberation. Thus, a fall from station is conceivable for him as well.

"Because enjoyment is stated to occur in locations such as the orb of the sun" means that since sovereignty belongs to those [others] depending upon the worship of the Supreme Self residing in the orb of the sun and other places, the sovereignty of the liberated is not unrestrained; this is the meaning. If one asks, "For what purpose are there two sūtras?", the meaning is: "What is the intention behind the two sūtras? [The answer is: "The attainment of the changeless state is thus established."

This is the meaning: just as for those who meditate upon Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahmopāsaka*), the state of being beyond transformation—which, though existing in reality within the qualified Brahman—is not attained because they do not have that as their specific purpose (*atat-kratutva*); likewise, although unbounded sovereignty (*niravagrahaiśvarya*) resides within the qualified Brahman, it is not attained by those who meditate on the qualified [Brahman], because they do not have that as their specific purpose. Even though sovereignty characterized by "having true desires" and so forth is the object of meditation, there is no scriptural injunction stating that one should meditate on [Brahman] as qualified by unbounded sovereignty; therefore, [unbounded sovereignty is not attained].

Because those situated in the portion consisting of the planets cannot be worshipped [as the Supreme], there is no attainment of them; thus, for one who worships the Saguna (the qualified), there is no sovereignty free from limitation. This is because, upon the attainment of the Nirguna (the unqualified), there can be no suspicion of return. Therefore, the meaning is that this [statement regarding non-return] refers exclusively to the attainment of the Saguna. As for the phrase "others, however," and so forth: one should not suspect that the word "iti" (thus) is redundant on the grounds that there is no such rule as "return occurs in another body."

This is because it is fruitful as a sūtra that serves as the locus for multiple meanings. Although, in the view of Yādava, the statement "he attains self-sovereignty" (*āpnoti svārājyam*) does not have liberation (*mukta*) as its subject—since [the liberated soul] cannot be something to be attained—it should nevertheless be understood that this objection was stated with the intention that it refers to the liberated soul, based on the natural sense of the term *svārājya*. The phrase "reflecting upon all the meanings stated in the Bhāṣya" means reflecting upon [it] as the cause of all those meanings.

Having explained that "everything is consistent" by supplying the word "said"—meaning it has been stated that everything is consistent—and intending for the word "all" to refer to the unquoted scriptural passages and so forth, he explains it by supplying the word "to be seen."

One might object: "Since not everything has been cited by the word 'all' (*sarva*), and since the manner of refuting the proofs and arguments (*pramāṇatarka*) put forward by others—which were not actually presented in the Bhāṣya—is not demonstrated, how can the complete consistency (*sāmañjasya*) of the system be seen? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As that which subverts the stated meaning. The sense is that the refutation of the fallacious proofs and arguments—both those imagined by others and those yet to be imagined—is easily accomplished by means of the very same principles (*nyāya*) set forth in the Bhāṣya.
Thus concludes the section concerning the exclusion of the world’s activities [from the Lord].

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, composed by the venerable Śrīraṅga Rāmānuja Muni—the author of commentaries on the ten Upaniṣads; who, like bees at the lotus feet of his preceptor, attained mastery over the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya* through service to Vātsya Anantārya; and who received the state of a Paramahaṃsa from the sage Parakāla.
And he whose fourth quarter [is thus].
The chapter is concluded. The total number of topics (*adhikaraṇa*) is 156; the total number of sūtras is 544.
